items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: REST API Design
items.text:
Q1. Which HTTP method is idempotent but not safe?

  • A. GET — safe and idempotent
  • B. POST — neither safe nor idempotent
  • C. PUT — calling it multiple times with the same body produces the same result, but it modifies server state
  • D. DELETE — safe because it only removes data
Answer

C — PUT.

Safe means the request does not modify server state. Idempotent means calling it multiple times has the same effect as calling it once. PUT /orders/42 with the same body can be retried freely — the result is the same order state regardless of how many times it is called, but the first call did change state, so it is not safe. POST /orders would create a new order on each call (not idempotent).

Q2. A client receives 401 Unauthorized. What does this specifically indicate?

  • A. The user is authenticated but lacks the required role or permission
  • B. No valid authentication token was provided, or the token is invalid or expired
  • C. The requested resource does not exist on the server
  • D. The server encountered an unexpected error processing the request
Answer

B — No valid authentication token.

401 means "you are not authenticated" — the server does not know who you are. 403 Forbidden means "I know who you are, but you are not allowed to do this." Confusing the two is a common mistake: a missing JWT should return 401, not 403.

Q3. Which URI designs follow REST conventions?

  • A. POST /createOrder and GET /getOrderById?id=42
  • B. GET /orders and GET /orders/42
  • C. GET /order-list and DELETE /removeOrder/42
  • D. POST /orders/create and PUT /orders/update/42
Answer

B — GET /orders and GET /orders/42.

REST URIs identify resources (nouns), not operations (verbs). Use plural nouns for collections (/orders), nest for hierarchy (/orders/42), and express the operation through the HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) — never in the path.

Q4. What is the correct HTTP status code when a POST successfully creates a new resource?

  • A. 200 OK — success is always 200
  • B. 201 Created, accompanied by a Location header pointing to the new resource's URI
  • C. 202 Accepted — creation is queued for asynchronous processing
  • D. 204 No Content — used when the server has nothing to return
Answer

B — 201 Created with Location header.

200 is for successful reads and updates. 201 signals that a new resource was created and tells the client where to find it via Location: /orders/42. This allows the client to immediately navigate to or cache the new resource without a separate GET.

Q5. Why is cursor-based pagination preferred over offset pagination for large datasets?

  • A. Cursors are smaller in size than page numbers, reducing request payload
  • B. Offset pagination is not supported by the HTTP specification
  • C. Offset pagination requires the database to skip rows, which is expensive at scale and causes drift when items are inserted or deleted; cursor pagination reads forward from a stable pointer
  • D. Cursor pagination allows the client to jump to any page directly
Answer

C — Offset is expensive and drift-prone; cursor reads from a stable pointer.

OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20 forces the database to count and skip 10,000 rows — slow on large tables. If a new item is inserted on page 3 while the client reads page 4, rows shift and the client sees duplicates or skips items. A cursor (e.g., after=eyJpZCI6NDJ9) encodes the last-seen record and reads forward from exactly that point (WHERE id > :last), using the index and immune to insertions. Option D is wrong: jumping to an arbitrary page is what cursors cannot do.

Q6. Which level of the Richardson Maturity Model describes correct use of HTTP verbs and status codes?

  • A. Level 0 — Swamp of POX (single endpoint for all operations)
  • B. Level 1 — Resources (separate URIs per resource)
  • C. Level 2 — HTTP Verbs (correct methods + status codes)
  • D. Level 3 — HATEOAS (responses include links to next actions)
Answer

C — Level 2.

Level 2 adds semantic use of HTTP methods (GET to read, POST to create, DELETE to remove) and proper status codes (201 Created, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict). Most production REST APIs operate at Level 2. Level 3 (HATEOAS) adds hypermedia links and is rare in practice.

Q7. A client calls DELETE /products/42 and gets 204. The response to a retry of the same request is 404 Not Found. Is DELETE still idempotent?

  • A. No — idempotent requests must always return the same response
  • B. Yes — idempotency is about the effect on server state: after one call or many, product 42 does not exist
  • C. No — the server should have returned 204 again to be idempotent
  • D. Only if the client sends an Idempotency-Key header
Answer

B — Idempotency is about the state, not the response.

RFC 9110 defines idempotent methods by their intended effect on the server. The second DELETE finds nothing to delete, so 404 is a correct answer and the state is unchanged. A client that retries a DELETE should treat 404 as success.

Q8. A mobile app sends POST /orders, the connection drops, and the app does not know whether the order was created. Which design lets it retry without creating a duplicate order?

  • A. Switch the endpoint to GET /orders/create, since GET is idempotent
  • B. Retry immediately, as many times as needed, until a response arrives
  • C. Send a client-generated Idempotency-Key header; the server stores processed keys and returns the stored result when a key repeats
  • D. Return 202 Accepted instead of 201 Created
Answer

C — Idempotency key.

The key identifies the logical operation. The first request creates the order and records the key; the retry finds the key and returns the same order instead of creating another. Option A breaks HTTP semantics (GET must not change state), B creates duplicates, and D changes the status code but not the duplication problem.

Q9. The product service is consumed by the web front-end and the order service. Which change is breaking and therefore needs a new API version?

  • A. Adding a new optional field description to ProductIn
  • B. Adding a new field category to ProductOut
  • C. Adding a new endpoint GET /products/search
  • D. Renaming the response field price to unitPrice
Answer

D — Renaming a response field.

Existing clients still read price and now get nothing. Adding endpoints, optional request fields or response fields is backward compatible as long as clients are tolerant readers that ignore unknown fields. A breaking change goes to a new version (/v2/products) with a deprecation period for /v1.

items.title: OpenAPI & Swagger
items.text:
Q10. What does the springdoc-openapi library generate automatically at startup?

  • A. A PDF export of all controller method signatures
  • B. A Postman collection for manual API testing
  • C. An OpenAPI document by introspecting controllers and model classes, and a Swagger UI served at /swagger-ui.html
  • D. Unit test stubs for every endpoint declared in the codebase
Answer

C — OpenAPI document + Swagger UI at /swagger-ui.html.

springdoc-openapi reads @RestController, @GetMapping, @RequestBody, @Schema and similar annotations at application startup, generates a standards-compliant OpenAPI 3 document at /v3/api-docs, and serves an interactive Swagger UI — all without any manual YAML authoring.

Q11. Where should Swagger UI be disabled, and why?

  • A. In development — developers should use curl instead
  • B. In staging — the staging environment must mirror production exactly
  • C. In production — it exposes the full attack surface of the API to anyone who accesses it
  • D. Only in microservices — monoliths can safely expose Swagger UI in production
Answer

C — In production.

Swagger UI provides an interactive map of every endpoint, parameter, and security scheme. An attacker can use it to enumerate attack vectors without reading the source code. Disable it with springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled: false and springdoc.api-docs.enabled: false in application-prod.yml.

Q12. What is the purpose of @Schema on a Java record field in a springdoc-openapi project?

  • A. It marks the field as required for JSON deserialization
  • B. It maps the field name to a different JSON key in the serialised output
  • C. It adds a human-readable description and example value that appears in the generated OpenAPI document and Swagger UI
  • D. It instructs the validator to reject null values for that field
Answer

C — Adds description and example to the OpenAPI document.

Without @Schema, springdoc only knows the field name and type. @Schema(description = "Unit price", example = "10.12") makes the generated documentation self-explanatory — consumers know what the field means and what a valid value looks like, without reading the source code.

Q13. To allow Swagger UI to send authenticated requests with a JWT Bearer token, what must be configured?

  • A. Add @Secured to every controller method and include the token in the request body
  • B. Enable Spring Security's basic auth fallback in application.yaml
  • C. Add a SecurityScheme of type HTTP/bearer to the OpenAPI bean, then use the Authorize button in Swagger UI to supply the token
  • D. Configure springdoc.swagger-ui.oauth.client-id with the JWT issuer URL
Answer

C — SecurityScheme of type HTTP/bearer + Authorize button.

Adding the security scheme to the OpenAPI bean tells springdoc to render an Authorize button in Swagger UI. The user pastes a JWT there, and all subsequent requests include Authorization: Bearer <token>. Without this configuration, Swagger UI sends unauthenticated requests to all secured endpoints.

Q14. In an OpenAPI 3 document, where are the reusable data models (such as ProductOut) defined, so that several responses can reference them with $ref?

  • A. info
  • B. servers
  • C. paths./products/{id}.get.parameters
  • D. components.schemas
Answer

D — components.schemas.

paths describes the endpoints; each response points to a model with $ref: "#/components/schemas/ProductOut", so the model is defined once. info holds title and version, servers the base URLs, and parameters the path, query, header and cookie inputs of one operation. springdoc builds components.schemas from your DTO records.

items.title: REST API Design
items.text:
Your team must publish the store's Product API: create, list, fetch and delete products. Two other teams (the web front-end and the order service) will call it without ever reading your code. Which URLs should exist? Which HTTP method creates a product? What does the client receive when the product does not exist, or when the request times out and it tries again? REST gives a shared set of answers, so that every API in the platform behaves the same way.

REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style — not a protocol — defined by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation1. A web API that follows REST constraints is called a RESTful API. REST uses HTTP as its transfer protocol and leverages the existing semantics of HTTP methods, status codes, and headers2.

items.title: Resources and representations
items.text:
Two words carry the whole idea:

  • A resource is anything the API exposes that has a name: a product, the collection of all products, the orders of one user. Each resource is identified by a URI (Uniform Resource Identifier), e.g. /products/0195abfb-7074-73a9-9d26-b4b9fbaab0a8.
  • A representation is a snapshot of the resource's state in some format — usually a JSON document. The client never touches the resource itself (a row in Postgres); it reads and sends representations of it. That is the "Representational State Transfer" of the name.
A representation of one product (from the Product API exercise)
{
  "id": "0195abfb-7074-73a9-9d26-b4b9fbaab0a8",
  "name": "Tomato",
  "price": 10.12,
  "unit": "kg"
}

The Content-Type header says which format the body is in (application/json); the Accept header says which formats the client wants back.

items.title: REST constraints
items.text:
Fielding defined REST as a set of constraints. An API that respects them gets the properties the Web is known for: scalability, independent evolution of client and server, and intermediaries (caches, gateways) that work without knowing the application.

Constraint Meaning Client-Server The client and server are separate concerns. The server does not know about the UI; the client does not know about storage. Stateless Each request contains all information needed to process it. The server stores no session state between requests. Authentication tokens (JWT) travel with every request. Cacheable Responses must declare whether they can be cached. Caching reduces load and improves latency. Uniform Interface Resources are identified by URIs. Representations are manipulated through standard HTTP methods. Messages are self-descriptive (Content-Type, status code). Responses include links to related resources (HATEOAS). Layered System Clients cannot tell whether they are talking to the end server or an intermediary (gateway, cache, load balancer). Code on Demand (optional) The server may send executable code to the client (e.g. JavaScript). The only optional constraint.

In the course's platform, Stateless and Layered System are what make horizontal scaling possible: because no replica keeps a session, the load balancer of Hands-on 7 can send each request to any gateway instance, and the client cannot tell Nginx, the gateway and the service apart.

items.title: Resources and URIs
items.text:
A resource is a noun — a thing the API exposes. URIs identify resources, not actions.

✅ Good (noun) ❌ Bad (verb) GET /orders GET /getOrders POST /orders POST /createOrder GET /orders/42 GET /order?id=42 DELETE /orders/42 POST /deleteOrder/42

items.title: URI conventions
items.text:
• Use plural nouns for collections: /orders, /products, /users
  • Use lowercase with hyphens: /order-items not /orderItems
  • Nest to express ownership: /users/7/orders — orders belonging to user 7
  • Limit nesting depth to 2–3 levels; avoid /users/7/orders/42/items/3/reviews
  • Use query parameters for things that are not identity: filtering, sorting, pagination (/orders?status=PENDING)

Actions that are not CRUD

Some operations do not map neatly to create/read/update/delete — cancelling an order, for example. Two common options: model the action as a state change (PATCH /orders/42 with {"status": "CANCELLED"}) or as a sub-resource (POST /orders/42/cancellation). Both keep the verb out of the path.

items.title: HTTP methods
items.text:
Method Idempotent Safe Use GET ✅ ✅ Retrieve a resource or collection. Must not modify state. POST ❌ ❌ Create a new resource. The server assigns the ID. PUT ✅ ❌ Replace a resource completely. The client provides the full representation. PATCH ❌ ❌ Partial update — only the provided fields are changed. DELETE ✅ ❌ Remove a resource.

Safe — the request does not change server state. GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe; POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE are not. Because they are safe, caches and crawlers may call them freely.

Idempotent — calling the same request multiple times has the same effect on the server as calling it once. PUT /orders/42 with the same body can be retried freely; POST /orders would create duplicates. PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent: {"op": "increment", "field": "quantity"} changes the result on every call.

Idempotent is about the state, not the response

DELETE /products/42 returns 204 No Content the first time and 404 Not Found the second. It is still idempotent: after one call or after ten, product 42 does not exist. Clients must therefore treat a 404 on a retried DELETE as success.

items.title: Making POST safe to retry: idempotency keys
items.text:
Networks lose messages. If the client sends POST /orders and the response never arrives, it cannot tell whether the order was created (see Distributed Systems). Retrying may create a duplicate order; not retrying may lose it.

The standard solution is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique id (a UUID) per logical operation and sends it in a header; the server remembers which keys it has already processed and, on a repeat, returns the stored result instead of executing again45.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant O as Order Service
    C->>O: POST /orders, Idempotency-Key k1
    O->>O: create order 42, remember k1 → 42
    O--xC: 201 Created (response lost)
    Note over C: timeout, retry with the SAME key
    C->>O: POST /orders, Idempotency-Key k1
    O->>O: k1 already processed
    O-->>C: 201 Created, order 42 (no duplicate)

The server stores the key with the result (for example, in a table with a unique constraint on the key, or in Redis with an expiry). Payment providers such as Stripe use exactly this mechanism. Retries, timeouts and backoff are covered in Resilience Patterns.

items.title: HTTP status codes
items.text: Use the right code — clients and intermediaries rely on them3. The first digit gives the class: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx the client did something wrong (do not retry unchanged), 5xx the server failed (a retry may succeed).

items.title: 2xx — Success
items.text: Code Name When to use 200 OK Success GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE completed successfully 201 Created Created POST created a new resource; include Location: /orders/42 header 202 Accepted Accepted The request was queued for asynchronous processing; the result is not ready yet 204 No Content No content Success with no response body (e.g., DELETE)

items.title: 4xx — Client error
items.text: Code Name When to use 400 Bad Request Bad request Malformed JSON, missing required fields, invalid values 401 Unauthorized Unauthenticated No token provided, or token is invalid/expired 403 Forbidden Forbidden Token is valid but the user lacks permission 404 Not Found Not found The resource does not exist (or the caller must not know it exists) 409 Conflict Conflict Duplicate resource, optimistic lock failure 422 Unprocessable Content Validation error Well-formed request, but business validation failed (named "Unprocessable Entity" before RFC 9110) 429 Too Many Requests Rate limited The client exceeded its rate limit; send Retry-After

items.title: 5xx — Server error
items.text:
Code Name When to use 500 Internal Server Error Unexpected error Unhandled exception — never expose stack traces 502 Bad Gateway Bad gateway A gateway or proxy got an invalid response from the service behind it 503 Service Unavailable Unavailable The service is down for maintenance or overloaded 504 Gateway Timeout Gateway timeout A gateway or proxy did not get a response from the service behind it in time

In a microservice platform the gateway codes matter: a 502 or 504 returned to the browser usually means "the gateway is fine, the service behind it is not" — the first clue when debugging.

Status codes in the Order API exercise

The Order API asks for 201 when an order is created, 400 when an item references a product that does not exist, and 404 when a user asks for an order that belongs to someone else. Returning 404 instead of 403 there is deliberate: it does not reveal that the order exists.

items.title: Request
items.text:
POST /orders HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9...

{
  "customerId": 7,
  "items": [
    { "productId": 101, "quantity": 2 }
  ]
}

items.title: Response
items.text:
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /orders/42

{
  "id": 42,
  "customerId": 7,
  "status": "PENDING",
  "total": { "amount": 59.90, "currency": "BRL" },
  "createdAt": "2026-04-28T14:30:00Z"
}

Conventions worth keeping across all services: camelCase field names, dates in ISO 8601 with time zone (2026-04-28T14:30:00Z), money with an explicit currency, and ids as opaque strings (the course uses UUIDs).

items.title: Error response
items.text:
Standardise error responses so clients can handle them generically. The IETF standard for this is Problem Details for HTTP APIs (RFC 94576), served with the media type application/problem+json:

{
  "type": "https://store.example.com/problems/out-of-stock",
  "title": "Product out of stock",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Product 101 is out of stock",
  "instance": "/orders"
}
Field Meaning type A URI that identifies the kind of problem (default about:blank) title A short, human-readable summary of the kind of problem status The HTTP status code, repeated for convenience detail An explanation specific to this occurrence instance A URI identifying this occurrence (often the request path)

Spring Boot's @ControllerAdvice / @RestControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler is the standard way to produce consistent error responses, and Spring's ProblemDetail class produces the RFC 9457 shape:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(ProductNotFoundException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleNotFound(ProductNotFoundException e) {
        ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
            HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.getMessage());
        problem.setTitle("Product not found");
        return problem; // serialised as application/problem+json
    }
}

Setting spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled: true makes Spring MVC's own errors (for example, a failed @Valid) use the same format.

Never leak internals in errors

A stack trace or an SQL message in a 500 response tells an attacker your framework, versions and table names. Log the details on the server (with a trace id, see Observability) and return a generic message.

items.title: Pagination and filtering
items.text:
Collections should never return unbounded results. Use query parameters for pagination and filtering:

GET /orders?page=2&size=20&sort=createdAt,desc
GET /orders?status=PENDING&customerId=7
Pattern Parameters Notes Offset pagination ?page=2&size=20 Simple; expensive on large datasets (DB must skip rows) Cursor pagination ?after=eyJpZCI6NDJ9 Efficient for large tables; opaque cursor prevents page drift Filtering ?status=PENDING Always filter on the server — never return all records and filter in the client Sorting ?sort=field,direction Multiple sort fields: ?sort=name,asc&sort=createdAt,desc

Offset pagination asks the database for OFFSET 40 LIMIT 20: the database still reads and discards the first 40 rows, and if a row is inserted meanwhile, the client sees an item twice. A cursor encodes "the last item I saw" (e.g. its id) and the query becomes WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id LIMIT 20, which uses the index and is not affected by inserts.

The response should include pagination metadata. Spring Data's Pageable reads page, size and sort automatically (pages are 0-based, so page=2 is the third page), and its PagedModel serialises as:

{
  "content": [...],
  "page": { "size": 20, "number": 2, "totalElements": 150, "totalPages": 8 }
}

items.title: Versioning
items.text:
APIs evolve. The first question is whether a change is breaking — whether an existing client, unchanged, would stop working:

Backward compatible (no new version) Breaking (needs a new version) Add a new endpoint Remove or rename an endpoint Add an optional field to a request Add a required field to a request Add a field to a response Remove or rename a response field Accept a new value in an input Change a field's type or meaning (price in cents instead of reais) Change a status code clients depend on

Compatible changes rely on clients being tolerant readers: they ignore fields they do not know. (Jackson in Spring Boot ignores unknown properties by default; do not turn that off in clients.)

When a breaking change is unavoidable, version the API so existing clients are not broken:

Strategy Example Notes URI path /v1/orders, /v2/orders Most visible; easiest to test in a browser Header Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json Cleaner URIs; harder to test manually Query param /orders?version=2 Avoid — version is not a filter

URI path versioning is the most common choice for microservices. Major version increments (v1 → v2) signal breaking changes; minor improvements are added without a version bump. Run both versions side by side, announce a deprecation date, and remove v1 only when its traffic has gone — the Sunset header (RFC 8594) tells clients when an endpoint will disappear.

Versioning pitfalls

  • Bumping the version for every change: clients cannot keep up. Prefer compatible changes.
  • Breaking a contract "just for one internal client": in a microservice platform you rarely know every client.
  • Sharing the account interface module between services (as in the hands-on) means a change to AccountOut forces every dependent service to rebuild — treat that module as a published contract.

items.title: Spring Boot quick reference
items.text:
The Product API of the exercise, with the status codes chosen above:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/products")
public class ProductResource {

    @Autowired
    private ProductService productService;

    @GetMapping
    public ResponseEntity<List<ProductOut>> findAll() {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(productService.findAll());               // 200
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<ProductOut> findById(@PathVariable String id) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(productService.findById(id));            // 200, or 404 via the advice
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<ProductOut> create(@RequestBody @Valid ProductIn in) {
        ProductOut created = productService.create(in);
        return ResponseEntity
            .created(URI.create("/products/" + created.id()))             // 201 + Location
            .body(created);
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> delete(@PathVariable String id) {
        productService.delete(id);
        return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();                        // 204
    }
}

@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) on a method also returns 201, but it cannot set the Location header; ResponseEntity.created(uri) sets both. @Valid triggers Bean Validation on the DTO (@NotBlank, @Positive…) and turns a violation into 400 Bad Request.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• URIs name resources (plural nouns); the HTTP method says what to do; clients exchange representations (JSON).
  • GET is safe; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is neither — make it retry-safe with an idempotency key.
  • Return the precise status code (201 + Location, 204, 401 vs 403, 422, 502/504) and errors as Problem Details.
  • Paginate every collection; prefer cursors for large or fast-changing tables.
  • Add, do not remove: compatible changes need no version; breaking ones need /v2/ and a deprecation period.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• Implement these conventions: Hands-on 1 — CRUD, Product API, Order API.
  • 401 and 403 in practice: Hands-on 3 — Security and Security.
  • Retries and 429/503: Resilience Patterns.
  • Document the contract: OpenAPI & Swagger.

  1. FIELDING, R. T. Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures. Doctoral dissertation, UC Irvine, 2000. Read online ↩

  2. RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics ↩

  3. HTTP Status Codes — MDN Web Docs ↩

  4. The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field — IETF HTTPAPI working group draft. ↩

  5. Idempotent requests — Stripe API reference. ↩

  6. RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs ↩

items.title: OpenAPI & Swagger
items.text:
A teammate is building the order service and needs to call your product service. What do they read? Your source code is in another repository, a wiki page goes stale after the first refactoring, and a Postman collection only shows the requests someone remembered to save. What they need is the contract itself, written in a format both people and tools understand, and generated from the code so that it cannot drift. That is what OpenAPI and Swagger UI provide.

OpenAPI is a language-agnostic specification for describing REST APIs2. An OpenAPI document is a YAML or JSON file that describes every endpoint: the URL, HTTP method, parameters, request body, and all possible responses. Swagger UI is the most widely used tool to render that document as an interactive web interface where users can read and execute API calls directly in the browser3.

Together, OpenAPI + Swagger UI give you living documentation that is always in sync with the code.

OpenAPI or Swagger?

Swagger was the original name of the specification. In 2016 it was donated to the OpenAPI Initiative (Linux Foundation) and renamed the OpenAPI Specification. Today "OpenAPI" names the format (versions 3.0, 3.1 and, since 2025, 3.2), and "Swagger" names a family of tools around it: Swagger UI, Swagger Editor, Swagger Codegen.

items.title: Why document APIs?
items.text:
Without documentation With OpenAPI Consumers must read the source code Consumers browse the Swagger UI Integration errors discovered at runtime Contract is explicit and testable upfront Documentation drifts out of sync Documentation is generated from the code Manual Postman collections maintained separately Swagger UI replaces Postman for exploration

Because the document is machine-readable, it also feeds tools: client code generators, contract tests, mock servers, and API gateways that import routes from it.

items.title: Anatomy of an OpenAPI document
items.text:
Before generating a document, it helps to read one. This is the GET /products/{id} endpoint of the Product API exercise, described in OpenAPI 3.1:

openapi.yaml (excerpt)
openapi: 3.1.0
info:                              # (1) metadata
  title: Product Service API
  version: 1.0.0
servers:                           # (2) where the API runs
  - url: http://localhost:8080
paths:                             # (3) one entry per path, one key per method
  /products/{id}:
    get:
      tags: [Products]
      summary: Find a product by ID
      parameters:
        - name: id
          in: path
          required: true
          schema: { type: string, format: uuid }
      responses:
        "200":
          description: Product found
          content:
            application/json:
              schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/ProductOut" }
        "404":
          description: Product not found
components:                        # (4) reusable pieces
  schemas:
    ProductOut:
      type: object
      properties:
        id:    { type: string, format: uuid }
        name:  { type: string, example: Tomato }
        price: { type: number, example: 10.12 }
        unit:  { type: string, example: kg }
  securitySchemes:
    bearerAuth: { type: http, scheme: bearer, bearerFormat: JWT }
Section What it holds info Title, version and description of the API (the version of the API, not of OpenAPI) servers Base URLs where the API can be reached paths Every endpoint: method, parameters (in: path, query, header, cookie), request body and responses per status code components.schemas Data models (the DTOs), referenced with $ref so they are defined once components.securitySchemes How clients authenticate (bearer token, API key, OAuth 2.0)

You will rarely write this file by hand in this course: springdoc generates it from the Java code. Knowing its structure is what lets you read and review the generated document.

items.title: Code-first or contract-first?
items.text:
There are two ways to keep the code and the document together:

Code-first (this course) Contract-first Source of truth The Java controllers and DTOs The openapi.yaml file Document is… Generated from the code at startup (springdoc) Written first, reviewed by consumers Code is… Written by hand Interfaces and DTOs generated (e.g. openapi-generator-maven-plugin) Good for Small teams, fast iteration, one main consumer Public APIs, many consumers, parallel front-end and back-end work Risk The API "just happens" — design is not reviewed before coding Extra build step; generated code can feel rigid

Code-first matches the hands-on: the account module is the contract, written in Java. Whatever you choose, review the generated document as a consumer would, before merging.

items.title: Adding Swagger UI to a Spring Boot project
items.text:
The springdoc-openapi library1 generates an OpenAPI document by reading your controllers and model classes at startup, then serves Swagger UI automatically.

MavenGradle 
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
    <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
    <version>3.0.0</version>
</dependency>

implementation 'org.springdoc:springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui:3.0.0'

Match the springdoc version to Spring Boot

springdoc 2.8.x targets Spring Boot 3.x; springdoc 3.0.x targets Spring Boot 4.x, which the hands-on uses (4.0.3). A mismatched version fails at startup with class-not-found errors. Check the compatibility table on the springdoc site before upgrading either one. For a reactive service (Spring WebFlux, like the gateway) the artifact is springdoc-openapi-starter-webflux-ui.

After adding the dependency, start the application and navigate to:

  • Swagger UI: http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.html (redirects to /swagger-ui/index.html)
  • OpenAPI JSON: http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs
  • OpenAPI YAML: http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs.yaml

No extra configuration is required for basic use.

Where to open it in our platform

In the platform's compose.yaml the business services publish no port to the host — the gateway does (8080:8080) — and the gateway routes paths such as /accounts/** — not /swagger-ui/** or /v3/api-docs. So a service's Swagger UI is reachable while you run the service on its own (from the IDE, on localhost), or if you publish its port in compose.yaml during development. That is a feature: the documentation stays inside the trusted network.

items.title: Annotating your API
items.text: springdoc infers most information from the code — paths, methods, parameter types, DTO fields — but annotations let you add descriptions, examples, and the responses that are not obvious from the method signature4.

items.title: Controller and operation
items.text:
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/products")
@Tag(name = "Products", description = "Manage the product catalogue")
public class ProductController {

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    @Operation(
        summary = "Find a product by ID",
        description = "Returns a single product. Returns 404 if the product does not exist."
    )
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "200", description = "Product found")
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", description = "Product not found")
    public ProductOut findById(@PathVariable String id) { ... }

    @PostMapping
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    @Operation(summary = "Create a new product")
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "201", description = "Product created",
        headers = @Header(name = "Location", description = "URI of the new product"))
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "422", description = "Validation failed")
    public ProductOut create(@RequestBody @Valid ProductIn in) { ... }
}

In the hands-on layout the mappings live on an interface (AccountController) implemented by a @RestController (AccountResource); springdoc picks up mappings and annotations declared on the interface, so the documentation can sit next to the contract.

items.title: Request body (Record)
items.text:
@Schema(description = "Payload for creating or updating a product")
public record ProductIn(

    @Schema(description = "Product name", example = "Tomato")
    @NotBlank String name,

    @Schema(description = "Unit price", example = "10.12")
    @Positive BigDecimal price,

    @Schema(description = "Unit of sale", example = "kg")
    @NotBlank String unit
) {}

Bean Validation annotations are documented too: springdoc lists @NotNull / @NotBlank fields as required, and turns constraints such as @Size, @Min and @Max into schema limits — the document shows the rules the code enforces.

items.title: Response body
items.text:
@Schema(description = "Product as returned by the API")
public record ProductOut(

    @Schema(description = "Unique product identifier (UUID)",
            example = "0195abfb-7074-73a9-9d26-b4b9fbaab0a8")
    String id,

    @Schema(description = "Product name", example = "Tomato")
    String name,

    @Schema(description = "Unit price", example = "10.12")
    BigDecimal price,

    @Schema(description = "Unit of sale", example = "kg")
    String unit
) {}

items.title: API metadata
items.text:
Configure the springdoc endpoints in application.yml, and the global metadata (title, version, contact) with a @Bean:

application.ymlJava config 
springdoc:
  api-docs:
    path: /v3/api-docs
  swagger-ui:
    path: /swagger-ui.html
    operationsSorter: method

spring:
  application:
    name: product-service

@Configuration
public class OpenApiConfig {

    @Bean
    public OpenAPI productServiceOpenAPI() {
        return new OpenAPI()
            .info(new Info()
                .title("Product Service API")
                .version("1.0.0")
                .description("Manages the product catalogue for the platform")
                .contact(new Contact()
                    .name("Platform Team")
                    .email("platform@example.com")));
    }
}

items.title: Security scheme
items.text:
To show the Authorize button in Swagger UI and enable sending JWT tokens with requests:

@Configuration
public class OpenApiConfig {

    @Bean
    public OpenAPI openAPI() {
        return new OpenAPI()
            .addSecurityItem(new SecurityRequirement().addList("bearerAuth"))
            .components(new Components()
                .addSecuritySchemes("bearerAuth",
                    new SecurityScheme()
                        .name("bearerAuth")
                        .type(SecurityScheme.Type.HTTP)
                        .scheme("bearer")
                        .bearerFormat("JWT")));
    }
}

After adding this, Swagger UI shows an Authorize button. Paste a JWT there and all subsequent requests will include Authorization: Bearer <token>.

In the course's platform

In Hands-on 3 the gateway validates the JWT (read from a cookie) and forwards the caller's identity to the services in the id-account header. A business service therefore does not validate tokens itself: when you test it directly in its Swagger UI, fill the id-account header field that springdoc generates from the @RequestHeader parameter. The bearer scheme above is what you need when the service itself validates Authorization: Bearer.

items.title: Disabling Swagger in production
items.text:
Exposing Swagger UI in production is a security risk — it documents your entire attack surface. Disable it per environment:

application-prod.yml
springdoc:
  api-docs:
    enabled: false
  swagger-ui:
    enabled: false

Activate the profile with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod (an environment variable in compose.yaml or in the Kubernetes deployment). If the API is public on purpose, publish the generated document on a documentation site instead of serving it from the running service.

Common pitfalls

  • Documentation that lies: @ApiResponse(responseCode = "404") on a method whose code actually returns 500 for a missing product. Annotations are not checked against behaviour — test the status codes.
  • Entities in the document: if the controller returns the JPA model, the document (and the response) shows internal fields. Document DTOs.
  • No examples: a schema with only types (string, number) forces consumers to guess. Add example to @Schema.
  • Swagger UI left on in production (see above).

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• An OpenAPI document is the machine-readable contract: info, servers, paths, components (schemas and security schemes).
  • Code-first (springdoc, this course) generates the document from the code; contract-first writes the YAML first and generates code.
  • springdoc serves /v3/api-docs and /swagger-ui.html; choose the version that matches Spring Boot (3.0.x for Boot 4).
  • @Tag, @Operation, @ApiResponse and @Schema(description, example) make the generated document useful to people.
  • Keep Swagger UI off in production and test that the documented status codes are the real ones.
