items.title: O — Open/Closed Principle
items.text:
"Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification." — Bertrand Meyer

A module is open if it can be extended with new behaviour. It is closed if its source code is stable — existing consumers and tests do not break when new behaviour is added. The mechanism is abstraction: define an interface that callers depend on, then add new implementations without touching the callers.

Violation Applied — interface Applied — service DiscountService.java — modified for every new type
// VIOLATION: every new customer type requires modifying this class.
// The class is open for modification but closed for extension.
public class DiscountService {

    public double calculate(Account account) {
        if ("VIP".equals(account.type())) {
            return account.orderTotal() * 0.20;
        } else if ("EMPLOYEE".equals(account.type())) {
            return account.orderTotal() * 0.30;
        } else if ("SEASONAL".equals(account.type())) {
            // Added later — had to reopen this class
            return account.orderTotal() * 0.15;
        } else {
            return account.orderTotal() * 0.05;
        }
        // Adding "PARTNER" requires another else-if and another class modification.
    }
}
DiscountPolicy.java — extension point
// Extension point: implement this interface to add a new discount rule
// without touching DiscountService.
public interface DiscountPolicy {
    boolean appliesTo(Account account);
    double calculate(Account account);
}
DiscountService.java — closed for modification
// Closed for modification: this class never changes when a new policy is added.
// Open for extension: inject a new DiscountPolicy implementation.
public class DiscountService {

    private final List<DiscountPolicy> policies;

    public DiscountService(List<DiscountPolicy> policies) {
        this.policies = policies;
    }

    public double calculate(Account account) {
        return policies.stream()
            .filter(p -> p.appliesTo(account))
            .findFirst()                                // same rule as before: one policy applies
            .map(p -> p.calculate(account))
            .orElse(account.orderTotal() * 0.05);       // default discount
    }
}

// Each policy is a new class — DiscountService is never touched again.
class VipDiscountPolicy implements DiscountPolicy {
    public boolean appliesTo(Account a) { return "VIP".equals(a.type()); }
    public double calculate(Account a)  { return a.orderTotal() * 0.20; }
}

class EmployeeDiscountPolicy implements DiscountPolicy {
    public boolean appliesTo(Account a) { return "EMPLOYEE".equals(a.type()); }
    public double calculate(Account a)  { return a.orderTotal() * 0.30; }
}

classDiagram
    class DiscountService {
        +calculate(account) double
    }
    class DiscountPolicy {
        <<interface>>
        +appliesTo(account) bool
        +calculate(account) double
    }
    class VipDiscountPolicy
    class EmployeeDiscountPolicy
    class PartnerDiscountPolicy

    DiscountService --> DiscountPolicy
    VipDiscountPolicy ..|> DiscountPolicy
    EmployeeDiscountPolicy ..|> DiscountPolicy
    PartnerDiscountPolicy ..|> DiscountPolicy

Adding PartnerDiscountPolicy requires creating one new class — DiscountService is never touched. In Spring, annotating each policy with @Component is enough: the container injects every DiscountPolicy bean into the List<DiscountPolicy> constructor parameter.

Closed against which changes?

No class is closed against every change. OCP asks you to anticipate the likely axis of variation (here: new customer types) and put the abstraction there. Adding extension points "just in case" produces interfaces with a single implementation forever.

items.title: L — Liskov Substitution Principle
items.text:
"If S is a subtype of T, then objects of type T may be replaced with objects of type S without altering any of the desirable properties of the program." — the usual paraphrase of Barbara Liskov (1987) and Liskov & Wing (1994)

Every subtype must honour the contract of the supertype — not just the method signatures, but the behaviour. A caller that works correctly with T must work correctly with any S extends T without modification.

Violation — Square extends Rectangle Applied — common interface Rectangle.java / Square.java — contract broken
public class Rectangle {
    protected int width;
    protected int height;

    public void setWidth(int w)  { this.width  = w; }
    public void setHeight(int h) { this.height = h; }
    public int area()            { return width * height; }
}

// VIOLATION: Square overrides setters in a way that breaks Rectangle's contract.
// Client code that sets width and height independently will get wrong results.
public class Square extends Rectangle {

    @Override
    public void setWidth(int w) {
        this.width  = w;
        this.height = w; // forces both dimensions to be equal
    }

    @Override
    public void setHeight(int h) {
        this.width  = h; // forces both dimensions to be equal
        this.height = h;
    }
}

// Client code expecting Rectangle behaviour:
// rect.setWidth(5);   rect.setHeight(3);
// assert rect.area() == 15;   ← FAILS for Square: area() returns 9
Shape.java — subtypes honour the contract
// Proper design: both share a common interface without inheritance between them.
// Each type upholds its own contract independently.
public interface Shape {
    int area();
}

public class Rectangle implements Shape {
    private final int width;
    private final int height;

    public Rectangle(int width, int height) {
        this.width  = width;
        this.height = height;
    }

    @Override
    public int area() { return width * height; }
}

public class Square implements Shape {
    private final int side;

    public Square(int side) { this.side = side; }

    @Override
    public int area() { return side * side; }
}

// Any code expecting a Shape can use Rectangle or Square interchangeably.
// No surprises — each type fulfils the Shape contract correctly.

classDiagram
    class Shape {
        <<interface>>
        +area() int
    }
    class Rectangle {
        -width int
        -height int
        +area() int
    }
    class Square {
        -side int
        +area() int
    }
    Rectangle ..|> Shape
    Square ..|> Shape

LSP and testing

A practical test: if substituting a subtype causes a test written for the supertype to fail, the subtype violates LSP. This is why a test suite written against an interface (Shape) must pass for every implementation.

LSP in the store: test adapters

InMemoryAccountRepository (used in unit tests) and AccountJpaAdapter (used in production) both implement AccountRepository. If the database rejects a duplicate email through a UNIQUE constraint but the in-memory version silently overwrites it, the two are not substitutable: unit tests pass and production fails. Keep the behaviour the port promises — not just its method signatures — identical in every implementation, ideally by running one shared contract test against both.

items.title: I — Interface Segregation Principle
items.text:
"Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use." — Robert C. Martin

A fat interface forces clients to declare dependencies on methods they never call. When those methods change — for reasons unrelated to the client — the client must be recompiled and re-deployed. Smaller, focused interfaces minimise coupling.

Violation — fat interface Applied — segregated AccountRepository.java — fat interface
// VIOLATION: a single fat interface mixes read, write, admin, and reporting.
// Clients that only read data are forced to depend on write and admin methods.
public interface AccountRepository {

    // Read operations
    Optional<Account> findById(String id);
    Optional<Account> findByEmail(String email);
    List<Account> findAll();

    // Write operations
    Account save(Account account);
    void delete(String id);

    // Admin operations — not needed by most clients
    List<Account> findByRole(String role);
    void bulkImport(List<Account> accounts);

    // Reporting — not needed by most clients
    Map<String, Long> countByRegion();
    List<Account> findInactive(Duration since);
}

// A read-only client (e.g. a profile page service) now depends on all nine methods:
// a change to bulkImport() or countByRegion() affects it, and any test fake of this
// interface must stub write, admin and reporting methods it never calls.
AccountReader / AccountWriter / AccountAdmin
// Segregated interfaces: each client depends only on what it actually uses.

public interface AccountReader {
    Optional<Account> findById(String id);
    Optional<Account> findByEmail(String email);
    List<Account> findAll();
}

public interface AccountWriter {
    Account save(Account account);
    void delete(String id);
}

public interface AccountAdmin extends AccountReader {
    List<Account> findByRole(String role);
    void bulkImport(List<Account> accounts);
}

// AccountService depends only on what it needs — no unused methods.
public class AccountService {
    private final AccountReader reader;
    private final AccountWriter writer;

    public AccountService(AccountReader reader, AccountWriter writer) {
        this.reader = reader;
        this.writer = writer;
    }

    public Account findById(String id) {
        return reader.findById(id).orElseThrow(AccountNotFoundException::new);
    }

    public Account save(Account account) {
        return writer.save(account);
    }
}

// The JPA adapter implements all interfaces — no behaviour is lost.
class JpaAccountAdapter implements AccountReader, AccountWriter, AccountAdmin {
    // single implementation, multiple interfaces
}

classDiagram
    class AccountReader {
        <<interface>>
        +findById(id)
        +findByEmail(email)
        +findAll()
    }
    class AccountWriter {
        <<interface>>
        +save(account)
        +delete(id)
    }
    class AccountAdmin {
        <<interface>>
        +findByRole(role)
        +bulkImport(accounts)
    }
    AccountAdmin --|> AccountReader
    class JpaAccountAdapter
    JpaAccountAdapter ..|> AccountReader
    JpaAccountAdapter ..|> AccountWriter
    JpaAccountAdapter ..|> AccountAdmin

    class AccountService {
        -reader AccountReader
        -writer AccountWriter
    }
    AccountService --> AccountReader
    AccountService --> AccountWriter

AccountService depends only on AccountReader and AccountWriter. Changes to admin or reporting methods never affect it.

items.title: D — Dependency Inversion Principle
items.text:
"High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details. Details should depend on abstractions." — Robert C. Martin

Without DIP, high-level business logic (use cases) knows about and instantiates low-level infrastructure (databases, HTTP clients). A change to the database forces a rewrite of the business logic. DIP inverts this: the high-level module declares an interface (the abstraction), and the low-level module implements it. Both depend on the interface — the arrow of dependency points toward the business rule, not the infrastructure.

Violation — direct instantiation Applied — depends on abstraction AccountService.java — tightly coupled to MySql
// VIOLATION: high-level module directly instantiates a low-level module.
// Swapping the persistence mechanism requires modifying AccountService.
public class AccountService {

    // Direct dependency on a concrete class — impossible to substitute in tests
    private final MySqlAccountRepository repository = new MySqlAccountRepository();

    public Account findById(String id) {
        return repository.findById(id);
    }

    public Account create(AccountIn in) {
        Account account = Account.of(in);
        repository.save(account);
        return account;
    }
}

// Concrete low-level module
class MySqlAccountRepository {
    public Account findById(String id) { /* SQL query */ return null; }
    public void save(Account account)  { /* SQL insert */ }
}
AccountService.java + AccountRepository + JpaAccountRepository
// Abstraction — defined by the high-level module, implemented by the low-level module.
public interface AccountRepository {
    Optional<Account> findById(String id);
    Account save(Account account);
}

// High-level module depends on the abstraction, not on a concrete class.
// The implementation is injected at runtime by the DI container (Spring).
public class AccountService {

    private final AccountRepository repository;

    public AccountService(AccountRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    public Account findById(String id) {
        return repository.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(AccountNotFoundException::new);
    }

    public Account create(AccountIn in) {
        return repository.save(Account.of(in));
    }
}

// Low-level module also depends on the abstraction.
@Repository
public class JpaAccountRepository implements AccountRepository {

    private final AccountJpaRepository jpa;

    public JpaAccountRepository(AccountJpaRepository jpa) {
        this.jpa = jpa;
    }

    @Override
    public Optional<Account> findById(String id) {
        return jpa.findById(id).map(AccountMapper::toDomain);
    }

    @Override
    public Account save(Account account) {
        return AccountMapper.toDomain(jpa.save(AccountMapper.toTable(account)));
    }
}

flowchart LR
    subgraph bad ["❌ Before"]
        as_bad["AccountService"] -->|new| mysql["MySqlAccountRepository"]
    end
    subgraph good ["✅ After"]
        as_good["AccountService"] -->|depends on| iface["«interface»\nAccountRepository"]
        jpa["JpaAccountRepository"] -->|implements| iface
        memory["InMemoryAccountRepository\n(test)"] -->|implements| iface
    end

Notice who owns the interface: AccountRepository is declared next to AccountService (the high-level module), in business terms, and the JPA class implements it. If the interface lived in the persistence package and mirrored JPA, the dependency would not really be inverted.

DIP (a design principle) is often confused with two related mechanisms:

  • Dependency Injection — a technique: objects receive their dependencies (usually through the constructor) instead of creating them with new. Spring's container does this for every @Service, @Repository and @Component.
  • Inversion of Control — the general idea that a framework calls your code (and wires it), rather than your code calling the framework.

Dependency Injection is how DIP is usually implemented in Spring, but injecting a concrete class still couples you to it; DIP requires that the injected type be an abstraction owned by the high-level module.

DIP is the principle that makes Clean Architecture and Hexagonal Architecture possible: by inverting dependencies at every layer boundary, each layer can be developed, tested, and replaced independently.

items.title: Summary
items.text:
Principle Problem solved Mechanism SRP Classes that change for multiple reasons break unrelated callers One concern per class OCP Modifying existing code to add features breaks existing behaviour Extend via new implementations of an interface LSP Subtypes that break supertype contracts cause subtle runtime bugs Honour behavioural contracts, not just method signatures ISP Fat interfaces force callers to depend on unused methods Split interfaces by client need DIP High-level logic coupled to low-level infrastructure Both depend on an abstraction; details depend on policies

SOLID is a guide, not a goal

  • Interface for every class. An interface with exactly one implementation and no test double adds a file and nothing else. Introduce the abstraction when a second implementation (or a test fake) appears.
  • SRP taken to one method per class. Splitting too far scatters one business concept across ten files; split by reason to change, not by line count.
  • Inheritance for reuse. Most LSP violations come from extends used to share code; prefer composition and small interfaces.
  • Speculative generality. Principles applied to imagined future requirements produce complexity you pay for today (YAGNI — You Aren't Gonna Need It).

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• SOLID is about managing change: each principle limits how far a change in one place ripples through the code.
  • SRP: one reason to change (one actor) per class. OCP: add behaviour by adding classes behind an interface.
  • LSP: subtypes and implementations must keep the behaviour of the contract — including test doubles and adapters.
  • ISP: give each client a small interface with only what it uses. DIP: business code owns the interfaces; infrastructure implements them.
  • DIP + dependency injection is the bridge to Clean Architecture and Hexagonal Architecture, where the same ideas are applied to the whole service.

  1. MARTIN, R. C. Agile Software Development: Principles, Patterns, and Practices. Pearson, 2002. ↩

  2. MEYER, B. Object-Oriented Software Construction, 1st ed. Prentice Hall, 1988. ↩

  3. LISKOV, B.; WING, J. A Behavioral Notion of Subtyping. ACM TOPLAS, 1994. ↩

  4. MARTIN, R. C. The Single Responsibility Principle. The Clean Code Blog, 2014. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
Cloud computing has revolutionized how organizations build, deploy, and scale applications. The three foundational service models—Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS)—represent layers of abstraction over physical hardware, each catering to different levels of control, management responsibility, and operational efficiency. These models form a stacked hierarchy, where higher layers build upon and abstract the complexities of lower ones.

This article provides a deep technical and operational breakdown of each model, their interrelationships, shared responsibility boundaries, real-world use cases, and trade-offs. A visual diagram and authoritative references are included.

items.title: Definition
items.text: IaaS delivers virtualized computing resources over the internet. Users rent raw infrastructure—servers, storage, networking, and virtualization—on a pay-as-you-go basis.

items.title: Core Components
items.text: Component Description Examples Compute Virtual machines (VMs) or bare-metal servers AWS EC2, Azure VMs, Google Compute Engine Storage Block, file, or object storage AWS S3, EBS; Azure Blob Storage Networking VPCs, load balancers, firewalls, DNS AWS VPC, Azure VNet Virtualization Hypervisors (e.g., KVM, Xen, VMware) Managed via provider APIs

items.title: Management Responsibility (User)
items.text:
• OS installation, patching, updates
  • Middleware (web servers, databases)
  • Application runtime and data
  • Security configurations (firewalls, IAM)

items.title: Provider Responsibility
items.text:
• Physical data centers
  • Power, cooling, hardware maintenance
  • Host OS and hypervisor
  • Network infrastructure

items.title: Deep Technical Insight
items.text:
• Instance Types: Optimized for CPU, memory, GPU, or storage (e.g., AWS c6g for ARM Graviton).
  • Billing Granularity: Per-second billing (post-2017 in major providers).
  • Programmatic Control: Full root access via SSH/RDP; automation via Terraform, CloudFormation.
  • High Availability: Multi-AZ deployments, auto-scaling groups.

items.title: Use Cases
items.text:
• Lift-and-shift migrations
  • Dev/test environments
  • Disaster recovery
  • High-performance computing (HPC)

items.title: Definition
items.text: PaaS provides a managed application development and deployment platform. Developers focus on code; the provider manages the underlying infrastructure, OS, middleware, and runtime.

items.title: Core Components
items.text: Layer Managed By Examples Runtime Provider Node.js, Python, Java, .NET Middleware Provider Message queues, caching (Redis) OS Provider Linux/Windows (patched automatically) Infrastructure Provider Auto-scaled compute, storage

items.title: Management Responsibility (User)
items.text:
• Application code
  • Configuration (environment variables, scaling rules)
  • Data (in managed DBs)

items.title: Provider Responsibility
items.text:
• Everything below the application layer
  • Auto-scaling, load balancing, patching
  • Build pipelines, CI/CD integration

items.title: Deep Technical Insight
items.text:
• Stateless Architecture: Encourages 12-factor app design.
  • Buildpacks / Containers: Heroku (buildpacks), Cloud Foundry, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service.
  • Serverless Evolution: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions = PaaS extreme (no server management).
  • Polyglot Support: Multiple language runtimes with zero-downtime deployments.

items.title: Use Cases
items.text:
• Microservices deployment
  • API backends
  • Rapid prototyping
  • Mobile app backends

items.title: Definition
items.text: SaaS delivers fully functional software applications over the internet on a subscription basis. Users access via browser or API—no installation or maintenance.

items.title: Core Components
items.text: Component Managed By Examples Application Provider Gmail, Salesforce, Slack Data Provider (multi-tenant) Isolated logically Runtime & Infra Provider Fully abstracted

items.title: Management Responsibility (User)
items.text:
• User accounts, permissions
  • Data input and usage
  • Integrations (via APIs)

items.title: Provider Responsibility
items.text: • Everything: Code, servers, databases, security, updates, scaling

items.title: Deep Technical Insight
items.text:
• Multi-Tenancy: Single instance serves all customers; data isolated via tenant IDs.
  • Zero-Touch Updates: Continuous deployment with A/B testing.
  • API-First Design: REST/GraphQL APIs for integration (e.g., Zapier, Salesforce APIs).
  • Compliance Built-In: SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA (provider-managed).

items.title: Use Cases
items.text:
• CRM (Salesforce)
  • Collaboration (Microsoft 365)
  • HR (Workday)
  • Analytics (Google Analytics)

items.title: The Relationship: The Cloud Service Stack
items.text:
The models are hierarchical and interdependent:

+------------------+
|      SaaS        |  ← Fully managed application
+------------------+
|      PaaS        |  ← Development + runtime platform
+------------------+
|      IaaS        |  ← Raw infrastructure
+------------------+
| On-Premises      |  ← You manage everything
+------------------+

items.title: Key Relationships
items.text: Relationship Explanation SaaS builds on PaaS SaaS providers use PaaS internally (e.g., Salesforce runs on Heroku-like PaaS). PaaS builds on IaaS PaaS orchestrates VMs, containers, and storage from IaaS (e.g., AWS Elastic Beanstalk uses EC2). IaaS is the foundation All cloud services run on virtualized hardware. Hybrid Scenarios Use IaaS for custom OS, PaaS for apps, SaaS for productivity.

items.title: Visual Diagram: Cloud Service Responsibility Matrix
items.text:
Legend:

  • Green: Managed by Provider
  • Orange: Managed by User
  • Pink: SaaS user manages only data/config

items.title: Comparison Table
items.text: Feature IaaS PaaS SaaS Control High Medium Low Flexibility Highest High Lowest Time to Market Slow Fast Instant Scalability Manual/Automated Automatic Automatic Cost Model Pay for infra Pay for usage Pay per user/seat Maintenance User Provider Provider Examples AWS EC2, DigitalOcean Heroku, AWS Elastic Beanstalk Google Workspace, Dropbox

items.title: Trade-offs and Decision Framework
items.text: Scenario Recommended Model Need full OS control IaaS Building custom apps fast PaaS Need off-the-shelf software SaaS Compliance requires isolation IaaS or dedicated PaaS Startup MVP PaaS + SaaS tools Enterprise with legacy apps IaaS (lift-and-shift)

items.title: Conclusion
items.text:
IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS are not competitors but complementary layers in the cloud ecosystem. Choosing the right model—or combining them—depends on control needs, development speed, operational overhead, and compliance requirements. Modern architectures often use all three: IaaS for custom workloads, PaaS for application logic, and SaaS for productivity and integration.

Pro Tip: Use the shared responsibility model as your decision anchor—the less you want to manage, the higher you go in the stack.

Article by Grok (xAI) | November 05, 2025

items.title: Overview
items.text:
When a server cannot handle growing traffic, two strategies exist:

Vertical scaling (scale-up) : Replace the server with a more powerful one — more CPU, RAM, faster disk. Simple, but bounded: there is a physical limit to how large a single machine can be, and upgrades require downtime.

Horizontal scaling (scale-out) : Add more servers and distribute the load across them. Theoretically unbounded, but introduces a critical problem: consistency across environments.

flowchart LR
    subgraph vs [Vertical Scaling]
        s1["Server\n4 CPU / 8 GB"]:::small -->|upgrade| s2["Server\n32 CPU / 128 GB"]:::big
    end
    subgraph hs [Horizontal Scaling]
        lb[Load Balancer] --> n1[Server 1]
        lb --> n2[Server 2]
        lb --> n3[Server 3]
    end
    classDef small fill:#ddd
    classDef big fill:#6c6,color:#fff

With one server, you can install Java, configure the database driver and tune environment variables by hand. With ten servers behind a load balancer, every one of them must be identical — the same OS, the same Java version, the same libraries, the same configuration — or a request will behave differently depending on which server it lands on.

An application that works on a developer's laptop may fail in production because of different OS versions, library versions, or environment variables — the infamous "it works on my machine" problem.

Containerisation solves this by packaging the application together with all its dependencies into a portable, self-contained unit — a container image — that runs identically everywhere: on your laptop, on the CI server and on every production node.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Explain what a container is (an isolated process built on Linux namespaces, cgroups and a layered filesystem) and how it differs from a virtual machine.
  • Write a Dockerfile for a Spring Boot service, using a multi-stage build and a cache-friendly layer order.
  • Run, inspect and debug containers with the essential docker commands (ports, logs, exec, networks, volumes).
  • Compose a multi-service stack (service + PostgreSQL) with compose.yaml, .env files and health checks.
  • Diagnose common mistakes: localhost between containers, data lost without a volume, secrets committed in .env, unpinned latest tags.

items.title: Containers vs. Virtual Machines
items.text:
Both containers and virtual machines (VMs) provide isolation, but at different levels of the stack:

flowchart TB
    subgraph vm [Virtual Machines]
        direction TB
        hw_vm[Physical Hardware]:::infra
        hvm[Hypervisor]:::infra
        os1[Guest OS 1]:::customer
        os2[Guest OS 2]:::customer
        app1[App A]:::customer
        app2[App B]:::customer
        hw_vm --> hvm --> os1 & os2
        os1 --> app1
        os2 --> app2
    end
    subgraph ct [Containers]
        direction TB
        hw_ct[Physical Hardware]:::infra
        os_ct[Host OS + Kernel]:::infra
        engine[Container Engine]:::infra
        c1[Container A]:::customer
        c2[Container B]:::customer
        hw_ct --> os_ct --> engine --> c1 & c2
    end
    classDef infra fill:#a8e6cf,stroke:#333
    classDef customer fill:#ffd3b6,stroke:#333

Provider / shared layer    Application layer

Aspect Docker Containers Virtual Machines Isolation Process-level — share the host kernel Full OS isolation — each VM has its own kernel Resource overhead Lightweight — no duplicate OS per container Higher — each VM carries a complete OS Startup time Seconds Minutes (full OS boot) Portability High — image bundles app and all dependencies Lower — OS-specific configuration Security boundary Weaker (shared kernel) Stronger (separate kernel) Typical use Microservices, CI/CD, horizontal scaling Different guest OS, strong isolation requirements

The key insight: containers share the host kernel, so they start in seconds and consume far less memory. VMs carry their own kernel — giving stronger isolation at the cost of higher overhead2.

In practice the two are combined, not opposed: a cloud provider rents you a VM (isolation between customers), and you run several containers on it (density and portability for your services).

items.title: What a container really is
items.text:
A container is not a lightweight VM: it is an ordinary Linux process that the kernel shows a restricted view of the machine. Three kernel features make that possible:

Feature What it does What you observe Namespaces Give the process its own view of a resource: process IDs (pid), network interfaces and ports (net), mounted filesystems (mnt), hostname (uts), users (user), IPC Inside the container, ps shows your app as PID 1, and it has its own IP address and port 8080 cgroups (control groups) Limit and account for CPU, memory and I/O docker run --memory 512m — the JVM is killed (OOM) if it exceeds 512 MB Layered filesystem (OverlayFS) Stack the read-only image layers and add a thin writable layer on top (copy-on-write) Files you write inside the container disappear when the container is removed

You can verify the "just a process" claim yourself:

docker run --rm alpine ps                               # inside: ps is PID 1, nothing else is visible
docker run -d --name pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:17
docker top pg                                           # from the host: the postgres processes, with host PIDs

Docker on macOS and Windows

Namespaces and cgroups are Linux kernel features. Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows therefore runs a small Linux VM behind the scenes, and your containers run inside it. That is why bind-mounted files can be slower there, and why an image built for linux/arm64 (Apple Silicon) may need --platform linux/amd64 to match a cloud server.

Docker is one implementation of an open standard

Image format and runtime behaviour are standardised by the Open Container Initiative (OCI). An image built with docker build also runs on Podman, on containerd, and on Kubernetes — which, since version 1.24, no longer talks to Docker and runs containers through containerd or CRI-O.

items.title: The container lifecycle
items.text:
flowchart LR
    src[Source Code\n+ Dockerfile] -->|docker build| img[Image\n:tag]
    img -->|docker push| reg[(Registry\nDocker Hub / ECR)]
    reg -->|docker pull| deploy[Any Host]
    deploy -->|docker run| c1[Container 1]
    deploy -->|docker run| c2[Container 2]
    deploy -->|docker run| c3[Container 3]

A Dockerfile describes how to build the image. An image is the immutable artifact — it gets versioned, stored in a registry, and pulled onto any machine. A container is a running instance of an image — isolated, ephemeral, and disposable1.

The lifecycle in the store

In Hands-on 1 the account service is packaged this way: mvn package produces the JAR, a Dockerfile copies it onto a Java base image, and docker compose up --build builds the image and starts it next to PostgreSQL. Later, in Hands-on 4, Jenkins runs the same build and pushes the image to a registry, and in Hands-on 5 Kubernetes pulls that image and runs several containers from it.

Pitfalls

  • Treating a container like a server. Do not docker exec into a container to install packages or edit files: the change is lost on the next deploy. Change the Dockerfile and rebuild.
  • Storing data in the container. The writable layer disappears with the container — persist databases in a volume (Docker › Volumes).
  • Shipping latest. myapp:latest points to whatever was pushed last; deploy explicit versions (myapp:1.4.2 or a Git commit SHA) so you know exactly what runs and can roll back.
  • Assuming a container is a security boundary. All containers share the host kernel; a kernel exploit escapes them. Do not run untrusted code next to sensitive workloads without stronger isolation (VMs).

items.title: Containerisation in the cloud
items.text:
Docker and Compose run containers on one host. Running them across many hosts — restarting crashed containers, spreading replicas, rolling out new versions — is the job of an orchestrator such as Kubernetes3 (Hands-on 5). Cloud providers offer managed container services that add automatic scheduling, scaling, load balancing, and deep integration with other cloud services on top of the container model:

Service Provider Model ECS / Fargate AWS Managed containers — no cluster to operate EKS AWS Managed Kubernetes Cloud Run Google Serverless containers — scales to zero GKE Google Managed Kubernetes AKS Azure Managed Kubernetes Google AWSTesla Tesla

Inside a Google data center

Inside Amazon's Massive Data Center

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Horizontal scaling needs identical environments; a container image packages the app with all its dependencies and ends "it works on my machine".
  • A container is an isolated Linux process (namespaces + cgroups + layered filesystem), not a small VM: it shares the host kernel, starts in seconds and isolates less than a VM.
  • Dockerfile → image → registry → container: the image is the immutable, versioned artifact; containers are disposable.
  • Keep state out of containers (volumes) and ship explicit image versions, not latest.
  • Docker and Compose run containers on one host; orchestrators and managed cloud services run them across many.

  2. Docker vs. Virtual Machines: Differences You Should Know ↩

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Containers
items.text:
Q1. A container is "an isolated process sharing the host kernel". Which Linux features provide, respectively, its isolated view of the system and its resource limits?

  • A. Hypervisor and guest OS
  • B. Namespaces and cgroups
  • C. OverlayFS and iptables
  • D. chroot and swap
Answer

B — Namespaces and cgroups.

Namespaces give the process its own view of process IDs, network interfaces, mounts and hostname — that is why your app is PID 1 inside the container and has its own IP address. cgroups limit and account for CPU, memory and I/O (docker run --memory 512m). OverlayFS provides the layered filesystem, not isolation; a hypervisor and guest OS are what a virtual machine uses, which is exactly what containers avoid.

items.title: Docker
items.text:
Q2. What is the key difference between a Docker image and a container?

  • A. An image runs in the foreground; a container runs in the background
  • B. An image is an immutable snapshot; a container is a running instance of that image
  • C. An image includes the host OS kernel; a container uses its own kernel
  • D. An image is stored in the registry; a container is stored on the host filesystem
Answer

B — Image = immutable snapshot; container = running instance.

An image is built once from a Dockerfile and stored as a read-only artifact. A container is a live process created from that image — it has its own writable layer on top of the image layers. Multiple containers can run from the same image simultaneously without interfering with each other.

Q3. What is the primary benefit of a multi-stage Dockerfile build?

  • A. It runs all build stages in parallel, reducing total build time
  • B. It allows multiple base images to be used simultaneously in one container
  • C. The final image contains only runtime artifacts, not the build toolchain — producing a smaller and more secure image
  • D. It enables the same image to run on multiple operating systems
Answer

C — Smaller final image without the build toolchain.

In a Java project, the build stage needs Maven and JDK; the runtime only needs JRE and the compiled JAR. Multi-stage builds discard everything from intermediate stages — Maven, source code, test dependencies — leaving an image that is several times smaller (a JRE on Alpine instead of a full JDK plus Maven and its repository) and has a reduced attack surface.

Q4. To maximise Docker layer caching, where should COPY src ./src appear relative to dependency installation?

  • A. Before — so the source is available when downloading dependencies
  • B. After — a source change rebuilds only the COPY src layer and the ones after it, leaving the cached dependency layer intact
  • C. It makes no difference; Docker caches all layers equally
  • D. At the very beginning, before any other instruction
Answer

B — After dependency installation.

Docker rebuilds all layers from the first changed layer onward. If COPY src comes before RUN mvn dependency:go-offline, every source code change forces a fresh dependency download. Placing the source copy after dependency installation means the slow dependency step is only re-run when pom.xml changes.

Q5. What is the difference between a named volume and a bind mount?

  • A. A named volume is faster; a bind mount is more durable
  • B. A named volume is managed by Docker and persists beyond container removal; a bind mount maps a specific host path into the container
  • C. A bind mount requires the Docker daemon; a named volume does not
  • D. They are identical — the terms are interchangeable
Answer

B — Named volume = Docker-managed and persistent; bind mount = specific host path.

Named volumes are created and managed by Docker, survive docker rm, and do not depend on the host's directory layout. Bind mounts directly expose a host directory — useful in development for hot-reload (changes on the host immediately reflect in the container) but tied to the host's filesystem layout.

Q6. Which Docker network driver allows containers on the same network to reach each other by service name?

  • A. host — containers share the host network stack
  • B. none — containers are fully isolated
  • C. overlay — used for Swarm mode multi-host networking
  • D. A user-defined bridge network — containers attached to it resolve each other by name
Answer

D — A user-defined bridge network.

On a user-defined bridge network (docker network create …), Docker's embedded DNS server resolves container names to their IP addresses. The default bridge network (used when you pass no --network) does not provide name resolution — containers there can only use IP addresses. Docker Compose creates a user-defined network for each project, which is how services reach each other by service name (db, app, gateway) without any hardcoded IP addresses.

Q7. A Dockerfile contains EXPOSE 8080, and you start the container with docker run -d store/account:1.0. Why does http://localhost:8080 in your browser not answer?

  • A. EXPOSE only works with Docker Compose
  • B. EXPOSE is documentation; the port must be published with -p 8080:8080 to be reachable from the host
  • C. The application must listen on port 80 inside a container
  • D. Containers can never be reached from the host's browser
Answer

B — EXPOSE documents, -p publishes.

EXPOSE records which port the application listens on, but does not open anything on the host. docker run -p 8080:8080 (format host:container) maps a host port to the container port; in Compose the same is done with ports:. Other containers on the same network can reach port 8080 without any publishing.

items.title: Docker Compose
items.text:
Q8. What does depends_on with condition: service_healthy do that plain depends_on does not?

  • A. It sets a timeout after which the dependent service starts regardless
  • B. It delays the dependent service until the dependency passes its healthcheck, not just until the container process starts
  • C. It causes Compose to restart the dependency if it becomes unhealthy after startup
  • D. It runs the dependency in a separate isolated network
Answer

B — Waits for healthcheck to pass, not just container start.

Plain depends_on only waits for the dependency container to be running (process started). The database process might be running but not yet ready to accept connections. condition: service_healthy waits until the healthcheck command inside the dependency returns exit code 0 — e.g., pg_isready -U myapp.

Q9. Why should credentials never be hard-coded in compose.yaml?

  • A. Docker Compose does not support plain-text values in environment blocks
  • B. Compose strips plain-text values during the build phase for security
  • C. Credentials committed to version control are a security incident; .env files allow per-environment secrets outside the repository
  • D. Hard-coded values prevent the service from reading them at runtime
Answer

C — Credentials in VCS = security incident.

Once a secret is committed to a repository — even a private one — it can be retrieved from history even after deletion. .env files are added to .gitignore and never committed, allowing each environment (dev, staging, production) to have different secrets without them ever appearing in the codebase.

Q10. What does docker compose down -v do that docker compose down does not?

  • A. It stops containers more forcefully using SIGKILL instead of SIGTERM
  • B. It rebuilds all images before stopping
  • C. It also removes named volumes, permanently deleting any persisted data
  • D. It removes the project network but keeps the containers stopped
Answer

C — Also removes named volumes.

docker compose down stops and removes containers and networks but leaves named volumes intact (the database data survives). Adding -v also removes named volumes — permanently deleting all persisted data. This is irreversible, so use it only when you genuinely want a clean slate.

Q11. Inside a Docker Compose network, how do services address each other?

  • A. By the container's full image name and tag
  • B. By the host machine's IP address and the mapped port
  • C. By the service name defined in compose.yaml — Compose provides DNS resolution by service name
  • D. By the container ID assigned at runtime
Answer

C — By service name.

Compose automatically creates a network and configures DNS so that each service is reachable by its name in compose.yaml. A Spring Boot app configured with SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/store will resolve db to the PostgreSQL container's IP without any manual configuration.

Q12. Which two mechanisms control startup ordering in Docker Compose? Select the most complete answer.

  • A. restart: always retries until all dependencies are up; priority field sets integer startup order
  • B. depends_on for basic ordering; healthcheck with condition: service_healthy for readiness-gated ordering
  • C. order: field in volumes: block; links: for legacy dependency declaration
  • D. Environment variable injection order; port mapping order in ports: block
Answer

B — depends_on + healthcheck with condition: service_healthy.

depends_on guarantees that container B starts after container A is running. Adding condition: service_healthy guarantees that B waits until A passes its healthcheck and is actually ready. The combination is essential for databases, which take several seconds to initialise after the process starts.

Q13. The account service works when started from the IDE with spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/store. Packaged as a container in the same compose.yaml as the db service, it fails with Connection refused. What is the fix?

  • A. Publish port 5432 of db with ports: - 5432:5432
  • B. Use network_mode: host for every service
  • C. Point the URL to the service name: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/store, passed as an environment variable
  • D. Add depends_on: - db to the account service
Answer

C — Use the service name.

Inside a container, localhost is the container itself — there is no PostgreSQL there. Compose's DNS resolves the service name db to the database container, which listens on its container port 5432. Publishing the port (A) only helps clients on the host; depends_on (D) orders the start but does not change the address. Passing the URL through an environment variable (e.g. SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL) keeps the same image working in the IDE, in Compose and in Kubernetes.

Q14. A project has a .env file with DB_PASSWORD=devpass next to compose.yaml. Which statement is correct?

  • A. Every variable in .env is automatically injected into every container
  • B. .env is used to fill ${DB_PASSWORD} placeholders in compose.yaml; to inject a whole file into a container you use env_file:
  • C. .env is ignored unless you pass --env-file .env to docker compose up
  • D. Values in .env always override variables exported in your shell
Answer

B — .env is for interpolation; env_file: injects into a container.

Compose reads .env from the project directory automatically and uses it to substitute ${...} in compose.yaml — a container only receives a value if the file maps it, for example POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}. To pass every KEY=value of a file to a container, use env_file: on the service. Variables already set in the shell take precedence over .env (D is false).

items.title: Docker Compose
items.text:
Running the account service and its database with plain docker commands already takes a handful of long command lines, and the order matters:

docker network create store
docker volume create db-data
docker run -d --name db --network store \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=store -e POSTGRES_USER=store -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
  -v db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17
docker build -t store/account ./account-service
docker run -d --name account --network store -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/store store/account

Add a gateway, an auth service, Redis and Kafka, and this becomes an error-prone script that every developer must keep in their head — and that nobody can review in a pull request. Docker Compose replaces it with a file.

Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container applications using a declarative YAML file1. Instead of running multiple docker run commands with flags, you describe the entire application stack — services, networks, volumes, environment variables — in a single compose.yaml, and start everything with one command.

items.title: Basic structure
items.text:
compose.yaml
name: myapp

services:
  web:
    build: ./web          # build from a local Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "80:80"
    depends_on:
      - app

  app:
    build: ./app
    environment:
      - SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/myapp
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: myapp
      POSTGRES_USER: myapp
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  db-data:

All services share a default bridge network. Each service is reachable from other services using its service name as the hostname (db, app, web).

flowchart LR
    user[User] -->|HTTP :80| web[Web]
    subgraph myapp [172.18.0.0/16]
        web
        app[App]
        db[(Database :5432)]
    end
    web -->|API| app
    app -->|JDBC| db

The vocabulary of a Compose file2:

Key Meaning name The project name; prefixes containers, networks and volumes (myapp-db-1, myapp_db-data) services One entry per container to run. Each service is a template: you can run several replicas of it image Use an existing image from a registry (postgres:17) build Build the image from a local Dockerfile (path to the build context) ports Publish host:container ports to your machine — only what you need to reach from outside environment Environment variables passed to the container depends_on Start order between services volumes Named volumes or bind mounts; top-level volumes: declares the named ones

docker compose, not docker-compose; and no version:

Compose v2 is a plugin of the Docker CLI: the command is docker compose (with a space). The old Python docker-compose (v1) is no longer supported since 2023. The top-level version: "3.8" key you see in older tutorials is obsolete — Compose ignores it and prints a warning. The preferred file name is compose.yaml; docker-compose.yml is still accepted.

items.title: Key commands
items.text: Command Description docker compose up Create and start all services docker compose up -d Start in detached (background) mode docker compose up --build Rebuild images before starting docker compose down Stop and remove containers and networks docker compose down -v Also remove named volumes docker compose logs -f Follow logs from all services docker compose logs -f app Follow logs from a specific service docker compose ps List running services docker compose exec app sh Open a shell in a running service docker compose restart app Restart a single service docker compose config Print the final file, with all ${VARIABLES} resolved — the first thing to check when a value looks wrong

items.title: Networking: service names, not localhost
items.text:
Compose creates one network per project and registers every service in Docker's embedded DNS3. Inside that network, services talk to each other on their container port using the service name; the ports: mapping only matters for traffic coming from your machine.

From To the database URL The app container db service jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/myapp Your laptop (IDE, psql, DBeaver) published port jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/myapp (only if ports: - 5432:5432)

The most common Compose bug: localhost

A service configured with localhost:5432 works when you run it from the IDE and fails as soon as it runs inside Compose, with Connection refused: inside a container, localhost is the container itself. Use the service name (db) and pass the URL through an environment variable, so the same image works in both places.

This is also how the store keeps services private: in Hands-on 2 only the gateway publishes a port; the other services are reachable only from inside the Compose network.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
Hard-coding credentials inside compose.yaml is a security risk and prevents environment-specific configuration. Use .env files instead:

compose.yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-myapp}       # (1)!
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:-myapp}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set it in .env}   # (2)!
    volumes:
      - ${VOLUME:-./data}/db:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"                             # (3)!
  1. :-myapp is the default value if POSTGRES_DB is not set in the environment or .env file. See Compose interpolation docs.
  2. :? makes Compose fail loudly with that message if the variable is missing or empty. A plain ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} without a default would only print a warning and substitute an empty string.
  3. In production, remove this port mapping so the database is only reachable inside the Compose network.
.env
POSTGRES_DB=myapp_prod
POSTGRES_USER=myapp
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=S3cr3t!
VOLUME=/data/myapp

When you run docker compose up, Compose automatically reads .env from the project directory (the folder of compose.yaml). Variables already set in your shell take precedence over the values in .env.

.env versus env_file:

The .env file is used for interpolation: it fills the ${...} placeholders in compose.yaml and is not passed to the containers by itself. To inject every variable of a file into a container, use env_file: in the service:

services:
  account:
    env_file: account.env   # every KEY=value becomes an environment variable of the container

Never commit .env to version control

Add .env to .gitignore. Each environment (development, staging, production) should have its own .env file, kept outside the repository. Committing credentials — even to a private repo — is a security incident waiting to happen. Commit a .env.example with placeholder values instead, so others know which variables to set.

items.title: Health checks and dependency ordering
items.text:
depends_on ensures a service starts after its dependencies, but does not wait for the dependency to be ready (e.g., the database to finish initialising). Use healthcheck for that:

compose.yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U myapp"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  app:
    build: ./app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy    # wait until db passes healthcheck

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as docker compose up
    participant DB as db
    participant A as app
    C->>DB: start container
    DB-->>C: running (still initialising)
    C->>DB: healthcheck: pg_isready
    DB-->>C: unhealthy, retry in 5 s
    C->>DB: healthcheck: pg_isready
    DB-->>C: healthy
    C->>A: start container
    A->>DB: connect on db:5432

Without condition: service_healthy, app would start right after db is running and could crash with a connection error while PostgreSQL is still creating its files. Adding restart: on-failure (or unless-stopped) to a service is a complementary safety net: if it crashes anyway, Docker starts it again.

items.title: Named volumes vs. bind mounts
items.text:
compose.yaml
volumes:
  db-data:        # Docker-managed named volume — data persists across `down`

services:
  db:
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data     # named volume (production)
      - ./init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql  # bind mount (seed data)
Named volume Bind mount Data location Managed by Docker Host path you specify Persistence Survives docker compose down Survives (it's your host path) Removed by down -v Yes — data is deleted No — the host folder stays Use case Production data, databases Dev: hot-reload source, seed scripts

Init scripts run only once

The PostgreSQL image runs the scripts in /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/ only when the data directory is empty. If you change init.sql but the volume already holds data, nothing happens — remove the volume (docker compose down -v) to re-initialise.

items.title: Full example
items.text:
compose.yaml
name: myapp

services:

  web:
    build:
      dockerfile_inline: |
        FROM nginx:latest
        RUN apt update
        RUN apt install -y net-tools iputils-ping
    ports:
      - 80:80

  app:
    image: eclipse-temurin:25-jdk
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password
      POSTGRES_DB: mydb
    volumes:
      - ${VOLUME:-./volume}/db:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    ports:
      - 5432:5432

Try it:

docker compose up -d --build  # (1)!
  1. -d runs the containers in detached mode.--build forces a rebuild of images before starting.

Access the web service at http://localhost:80 and verify all containers are running with docker compose ps.

items.title: Limits of Compose
items.text:
Compose runs everything on one host. It does not spread containers across machines, does not reschedule them when a host dies, and does not perform rolling updates. It is ideal for development, CI and small single-server deployments; for a cluster, the same images are run by an orchestrator such as Kubernetes (Hands-on 5).

Common mistakes

  • depends_on without a health check, then debugging "random" startup failures.
  • docker compose down -v on a database you care about — the named volume, and all its data, is gone.
  • Publishing every port (5432:5432, 6379:6379) "just in case": each published port is a door into the stack. Publish only the entry point (the gateway).
  • Forgetting --build: docker compose up reuses the image it built last time, so your code change does not appear.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• Hands-on 1 — Containerization — the first Compose file of the store: account service and PostgreSQL.
  • Hands-on 2 — the gateway as the only published entry point.
  • Hands-on 7, Hands-on 8, Hands-on 9 — adding Nginx, Redis and Kafka to the same Compose stack.
  • Hands-on 5 — from Compose to Kubernetes.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• compose.yaml declares the whole stack — services, networks, volumes, variables — and docker compose up -d --build starts it.
  • Services reach each other by service name on the container port; localhost inside a container is the container itself.
  • .env fills ${...} placeholders (use :- for defaults, :? for required values) and must never be committed; env_file: injects variables into a container.
  • depends_on orders the start; add a healthcheck and condition: service_healthy to wait until a dependency is ready.
  • Named volumes survive down but not down -v; Compose is single-host — clusters need an orchestrator.

  2. Compose File Reference ↩

items.title: Docker
items.text:
In Hands-on 1 you run the account service with mvn spring-boot:run. That works because your laptop has the right JDK, Maven and environment variables. To run the same service on a colleague's machine, a CI server or a cloud VM, you would have to reproduce that whole setup by hand — and keep it in sync forever. Docker turns the setup into a file (the Dockerfile) and the result into an artifact (the image) that runs the same way everywhere.

Docker is a platform for building, shipping, and running applications in containers1. It standardises the packaging of an application and all its dependencies — runtime, libraries, environment variables, configuration — into a single portable unit that runs identically on any machine with the Docker Engine installed.

items.title: Core concepts
items.text:
flowchart LR
  df[Dockerfile] -->|docker build| img[Image]
  img -->|docker run| c1[Container A]
  img -->|docker run| c2[Container B]
  img -->|docker push| reg[(Registry\nDocker Hub)]
  reg -->|docker pull| img2[Image on\nanother host]

Dockerfile : A text file containing step-by-step instructions for building an image. Each instruction that changes the filesystem (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a new read-only layer.

Image : An immutable snapshot built from a Dockerfile. Images are the artifact that gets versioned, pushed to a registry, and shipped. An image is identified by a name and a tag (eclipse-temurin:25-jre-alpine, store/account:1.0); when you omit the tag, Docker assumes latest.

Container : A running instance of an image. Containers are isolated processes on the host OS — they share the kernel but have their own filesystem, network, and process namespace (see What a container really is).

Registry : A server that stores and distributes images. Docker Hub3 is the default public registry. Private registries (AWS ECR, GitHub Container Registry, GitLab Registry) are used for proprietary images.

items.title: How Docker works: client, daemon, registry
items.text:
The docker command you type is only a client. It sends each request to the Docker daemon (dockerd), a background service that builds images, pulls them from registries and asks the container runtime (containerd, which uses runc) to start the actual processes.

flowchart LR
    cli["docker CLI"] -->|REST API| daemon["dockerd daemon"]
    daemon -->|pull image| reg[(Registry)]
    daemon -->|create container| rt["containerd + runc"]
    rt -->|start process| proc["container process"]

This is why docker ps fails with "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon" when Docker Desktop is not running: the client is fine, but nobody is listening on the other side.

items.title: Dockerfile
items.text:
A Dockerfile defines the environment the application runs in. Each instruction adds a layer to the image2:

Dockerfile
# Base image — choose the smallest that fits
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy the built artifact from the host (run `mvn package` first)
COPY target/*.jar app.jar

# Expose the port the application listens on (documentation only)
EXPOSE 8080

# Command to run when the container starts
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

The Dockerfile used for the store's services in Hands-on 1 follows the same pattern: a Java 25 base image, the JAR built by Maven, and java -jar as entry point.

The instructions you will use most often:

Instruction Purpose Example FROM Base image to start from (always first) FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre-alpine WORKDIR Set (and create) the working directory WORKDIR /app COPY Copy files from the build context into the image COPY target/*.jar app.jar RUN Execute a command at build time and save the result as a layer RUN apk add --no-cache curl ENV Set an environment variable for build and run time ENV SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod ARG Build-time variable (not available when the container runs) ARG VERSION=1.0 EXPOSE Document the port the app listens on (does not publish it) EXPOSE 8080 USER Run the following instructions and the container as this user USER app ENTRYPOINT / CMD What runs when the container starts ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

RUN vs CMD vs ENTRYPOINT

RUN executes while the image is built (installing packages, compiling). ENTRYPOINT and CMD define what executes when a container starts. When both are present, CMD supplies default arguments to ENTRYPOINT, and anything you type after the image name in docker run <image> … replaces CMD. Prefer the exec form with brackets (["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]): the JVM becomes PID 1 and receives the SIGTERM sent by docker stop, so Spring Boot can shut down gracefully.

items.title: .dockerignore
items.text:
docker build . sends the whole directory (the build context) to the daemon. A .dockerignore file keeps out what the image does not need — making builds faster and preventing secrets from ending up in a layer:

.dockerignore
.git
.idea
*.iml
.env
target/*
!target/*.jar

items.title: Multi-stage builds
items.text:
Multi-stage builds separate the build environment from the runtime environment, producing a smaller final image. They also remove the need to have Maven and a JDK installed on the machine that builds the image:

Dockerfile (multi-stage)
# Stage 1: build
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-25 AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline          # cache dependencies separately
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn package -DskipTests

# Stage 2: run — only the JRE, no Maven, no source
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /build/target/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

The final image contains only the JRE and the compiled JAR — Maven and the source tree are discarded.

Why *.jar and not app.jar?

Maven names the artifact <artifactId>-<version>.jar (for example account-service-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar), not app.jar. The wildcard matches it — Spring Boot keeps the original thin JAR as *.jar.original, which the pattern does not match — and the COPY renames it to app.jar inside the image.

items.title: Layer caching
items.text:
Docker builds images layer by layer. If a layer has not changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached version — skipping that step entirely. Once a layer changes, that layer and every layer after it are rebuilt. Layer order matters: place instructions that change infrequently (dependencies) before instructions that change often (source code).

flowchart LR
    subgraph bad [Poor order — cache busted on every code change]
        direction TB
        b1["COPY src ./src\n(changes every commit)"]:::changed --> b2["RUN mvn package"]:::changed --> b3["RUN mvn dependency:go-offline"]:::changed
    end
    subgraph good [Good order — dependencies cached separately]
        direction TB
        g1["COPY pom.xml ."]:::cached --> g2["RUN mvn dependency:go-offline"]:::cached --> g3["COPY src ./src\n(changes every commit)"]:::changed --> g4["RUN mvn package\n(only rebuilds app)"]:::changed
    end
    classDef cached fill:#6c6,color:#fff
    classDef changed fill:#f66,color:#fff

The multi-stage Dockerfile above already exploits this: RUN mvn dependency:go-offline runs only when pom.xml changes, not on every code change.

items.title: Managing containers
items.text: Command Description docker run <image> Create and start a container from an image docker run -d <image> Run in detached (background) mode docker run -p 8080:8080 <image> Publish a port: host port 8080 → container port 8080 (host:container) docker run --name myapp <image> Assign a name to the container docker run -e KEY=value <image> Set an environment variable docker run --rm <image> Remove the container automatically when it exits docker ps List running containers docker ps -a List all containers (including stopped) docker stop <container> Gracefully stop a running container (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 s) docker rm <container> Remove a stopped container docker exec -it <container> sh Open an interactive shell in a running container docker logs <container> Print the container's logs (its stdout and stderr) docker logs -f <container> Follow logs in real time docker inspect <container> Full JSON metadata for a container

items.title: Managing images
items.text: Command Description docker build -t myapp:1.0 . Build an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory docker images List local images docker pull <image> Download an image from the registry docker push <image> Push an image to the registry docker rmi <image> Remove a local image docker tag <image> <new-tag> Tag an image with a new name

items.title: Housekeeping
items.text:
Command Description docker system prune Remove stopped containers, dangling images, unused networks docker volume ls List volumes docker network ls List networks

Debugging a container that does not start

A container that exits right after docker run is the most common first problem. Follow the evidence:

docker ps -a                    # STATUS shows "Exited (1) 3 seconds ago"
docker logs account             # the application's own error message (e.g. cannot reach the database)
docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' account   # 137 + true = killed for memory
docker run -it --rm --entrypoint sh store/account:1.0                 # open a shell in the image to look around

items.title: Networking
items.text:
Each container gets its own network namespace — its own IP address and its own localhost. Docker provides several network drivers4:

Driver Description bridge A private virtual network on the host. On a user-defined bridge network (docker network create …), containers reach each other by name through Docker's embedded DNS. On the default bridge (used when you pass no --network), they can only use IP addresses host Container shares the host's network stack (no isolation) none No network access 
docker network create store-net
docker run -d --name db --network store-net -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:17
docker run --rm --network store-net postgres:17 pg_isready -h db   # "db" resolves to the database container

When using Docker Compose, all services are attached to a user-defined network that Compose creates automatically, so they can reach each other by their service name as the hostname (Docker Compose).

EXPOSE does not publish a port, and localhost is not the host

  • EXPOSE 8080 is documentation. To reach the container from your browser you must publish the port with -p 8080:8080.
  • Inside a container, localhost is the container itself. A Spring Boot app configured with jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/store will not find a database running in another container — use the container (or service) name: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/store.

items.title: Volumes
items.text:
Containers are ephemeral — data written inside a container is lost when the container is removed. Volumes persist data beyond the container lifecycle:

# Named volume (managed by Docker)
docker run -v mydata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17

# Bind mount (maps a host directory)
docker run -v /host/path:/container/path myapp

Named volumes are preferred in production because Docker manages their location. Bind mounts are useful during development to reflect local file changes without rebuilding the image.

PostgreSQL 18 changed the data path

Up to postgres:17, the official image keeps its data in /var/lib/postgresql/data. From postgres:18 on, the data lives in a version-specific directory (/var/lib/postgresql/18/docker) and the volume should be mounted at /var/lib/postgresql. An image tagged postgres or postgres:latest therefore changed behaviour silently when 18 became latest — one more reason to pin the major version of the images you depend on.

items.title: Good practices and pitfalls
items.text:
Good practices

  • Pin versions: eclipse-temurin:25-jre-alpine, postgres:17 — never an implicit latest for something you deploy.
  • Small base images (-alpine, -jre, distroless): faster pulls, smaller attack surface.
  • One process per container: the service, not the service and its database.
  • Run as a non-root user (USER), so a compromised app does not run as root inside the container.
  • Configuration through environment variables, so the same image runs in every environment.

Common mistakes

  • Secrets in the image (COPY .env, ENV DB_PASSWORD=…): anyone who pulls the image can read every layer. Pass secrets at run time.
  • Building the JAR outside and forgetting to rebuild it: with a single-stage Dockerfile, docker build copies whatever is in target/ — run mvn package first, or use a multi-stage build.
  • Source copied before dependencies: every commit downloads all Maven dependencies again (see Layer caching).

items.text:
• Hands-on 1 — Containerization — the account service's Dockerfile and its Compose file.
  • Docker Compose — running several containers together.
  • Hands-on 4 — Jenkins builds and pushes images in a pipeline.
  • Hands-on 5 — Kubernetes runs these images across a cluster.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• The docker CLI talks to a daemon that builds images, pulls them from registries and starts containers through containerd/runc.
  • A Dockerfile is a recipe; each filesystem-changing instruction is a cached layer — put dependencies before source code.
  • Multi-stage builds keep Maven and the sources out of the final image; ENTRYPOINT in exec form lets the JVM shut down gracefully.
  • Publish ports with -p host:container; containers on a user-defined network find each other by name, and localhost means the container itself.
  • Containers are disposable: keep data in volumes, configuration in environment variables, and pin image versions.
