items.title: Core Concepts
items.text:
Concept Definition Example Event An immutable record of something that happened OrderCreated { orderId, customerId, timestamp } Message Generic data container sent between services Any payload in a queue Command An instruction to do something (can be rejected) PlaceOrder { items, paymentToken } Producer / Consumer The service that writes / reads messages order-service produces; notification-service consumes Broker The server that stores messages and serves them to consumers A Kafka broker (kafka:9092) Topic A named, durable, ordered log of events order-events Partition A shard of a topic for parallelism; order is kept only inside it Partition 0, 1, 2 of order-events Key Optional value that decides the partition of a message orderId Offset Sequential integer identifying a message position Offset 42 in partition 1 Consumer Group A set of consumers sharing the work of a topic notification-group

Events are facts

Unlike database records, events are never updated or deleted — the log is append-only. This immutability makes events safe to replay for rebuilding state, auditing history, or populating new projections without touching the original data.

items.title: Kafka Architecture
items.text:
Apache Kafka1 is a distributed, append-only log: producers append messages to the end, consumers read from any position they choose, and messages stay on disk after being read (until the retention policy deletes them). This is the main difference from a classic message queue such as RabbitMQ, where a message is removed once a consumer acknowledges it.

Kafka organises messages into topics, each split into ordered partitions. Multiple consumer groups can read the same topic independently — each group maintains its own offset pointer per partition.

flowchart LR
    subgraph broker ["Kafka Broker"]
        subgraph topic ["Topic: order-events"]
            P0["Partition 0\n0, 1, 2, 3, →"]
            P1["Partition 1\n0, 1, 2, →"]
            P2["Partition 2\n0, 1, →"]
        end
    end
    subgraph ng ["notification-group"]
        N0[Consumer A]
        N1[Consumer B]
        N2[Consumer C]
    end
    subgraph ag ["analytics-group"]
        A0[Consumer X]
    end
    P0 --> N0
    P1 --> N1
    P2 --> N2
    P0 --> A0
    P1 --> A0
    P2 --> A0

Each consumer group tracks its own offsets, so notification-group and analytics-group progress through the log independently. Adding a new consumer group never affects existing groups.

Retention policies control how long Kafka keeps messages:

Policy Config Behavior Time-based retention.ms=604800000 Delete messages older than 7 days Size-based retention.bytes=1073741824 Delete the oldest segments when a partition exceeds 1 GB (the limit is per partition, not per topic) Compact cleanup.policy=compact Keep only the latest message per key (useful for state snapshots)

retention.ms=604800000 (7 days) is Kafka's default; retention.bytes defaults to -1 (no size limit).

items.title: Keys, partitions and ordering
items.text:
When a producer sends a message with a key, Kafka's default partitioner hashes the key to choose the partition: the same key always goes to the same partition (as long as the number of partitions does not change). Messages without a key are spread across partitions.

Since order is only guaranteed inside a partition, the key is how you choose what must stay in order. In Hands-on 9 the order service sends kafkaTemplate.send("order-events", order.getId().toString(), event) — the orderId is the key, so OrderCreated, OrderPaid and OrderShipped of the same order are always read in sequence, while different orders are processed in parallel.

flowchart LR
    p["order-service<br/>(producer)"] -->|"key=order-7"| h{"hash(key) % 3"}
    h -->|"order-7 → P1"| P1["Partition 1"]
    h -.->|"other keys"| P0["Partition 0"]
    h -.->|"other keys"| P2["Partition 2"]
    P1 --> c["consumer B<br/>reads order-7 events in order"]

Choosing the key

  • A key with few values (e.g. country) creates hot partitions: one partition gets most of the traffic while others sit idle.
  • Adding partitions later changes hash(key) % partitions, so existing keys may move to a different partition and lose their ordering for a while — size partitions up front.
  • No key at all means no ordering between related events.

items.title: Durability: replication and acks
items.text:
In production each partition is replicated on several brokers (replication factor, typically 3). One replica is the leader and receives all writes; the others are followers that copy it. The replicas that are up to date form the ISR (in-sync replicas). If the leader's broker dies, an in-sync follower is elected leader.

The producer setting acks chooses how much of this the producer waits for:

acks The producer gets a confirmation when… Risk 0 it has sent the message (no confirmation) Lost if the broker never received it 1 the leader has written it Lost if the leader dies before followers copy it all all in-sync replicas have it (with min.insync.replicas ≥ 2) Slowest, but survives the loss of a broker

Hands-on 9 uses acks: all with enable.idempotence: true; the idempotent producer attaches a sequence number to each message so that the producer's own retries do not create duplicates in the log. (Since Kafka 3.0 both are already the producer defaults.)

ZooKeeper and KRaft

Older Kafka clusters stored their metadata in a separate ZooKeeper ensemble. Kafka now has its own Raft-based metadata quorum (KRaft; see Consensus), and Kafka 4.0 (2025) removed ZooKeeper support entirely. Hands-on 9 runs Kafka 4 in KRaft mode: a single node that is both broker and controller.

items.title: Pub/Sub (Fan-out)
items.text:
One published event is delivered to every interested consumer group. Each group receives a full, independent copy of the message. Because groups track their own offsets, a slow analytics pipeline does not affect the notification pipeline.

Use cases: email notifications, audit logs, analytics pipelines, cache invalidation.

items.title: Competing Consumers
items.text:
Multiple consumers within the same group share partitions — each partition is owned by exactly one consumer at a time, so each message is processed by exactly one consumer. This pattern enables horizontal scaling of processing without duplicated work.

Use cases: order processing, payment handling, image resizing jobs.

The maximum parallelism of a group is the number of partitions: with 3 partitions, a fourth consumer in the same group sits idle. When a consumer joins or leaves, Kafka rebalances the group and reassigns partitions.

items.title: Event Sourcing
items.text:
Instead of storing only the current state, the system stores the full history of events3. Current state is derived by replaying all events from the beginning (or from a snapshot).

sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    User->>+CommandHandler: PlaceOrder
    CommandHandler->>+EventStore: append OrderCreated
    EventStore-->>-CommandHandler: ack
    CommandHandler-->>-User: 202 Accepted
    EventStore-->>Projection: OrderCreated event
    Projection->>ReadModel: update order view

This means the write model is the event log itself. Projections (read models) are rebuilt from events at any time, enabling time travel debugging and zero-downtime schema migration.

items.title: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
items.text:
Separate the write side (commands, events, event store) from the read side (queries, projections, read model)4. The write side is optimised for consistency and auditability; the read side is optimised for query performance.

flowchart LR
    client --> |"POST /orders (Command)"| cmd["Command Handler"]
    cmd --> |"OrderCreated"| bus["Event Bus (Kafka)"]
    bus --> |"project"| view["Read Model\n(optimised for queries)"]
    client --> |"GET /orders (Query)"| view
    cmd --> |"append"| store["Event Store"]

CQRS is commonly paired with Event Sourcing because the event log is the natural write model. However, CQRS can also be applied without event sourcing — using separate read/write databases kept in sync via change-data-capture (CDC: a tool such as Debezium reads the database's transaction log and publishes every change as an event).

Event sourcing and CQRS are not defaults

Both add real complexity: events must be versioned forever, read models are eventually consistent, and rebuilding projections takes time. Use them for parts of the domain that need an audit trail or very different read and write shapes (e.g. order history, ledgers) — not for every CRUD entity of the store.

items.title: Delivery Guarantees and Idempotent Consumers
items.text:
A consumer reads a message, processes it (e.g. sends an e-mail), and commits its offset to tell Kafka "I am done up to here". A crash can happen between any two of these steps, and when you commit decides what a crash costs:

Guarantee How A crash means Typical use At-most-once Commit before processing The message is lost Metrics where a gap is acceptable At-least-once Commit after processing The message is processed again The default choice — Hands-on 9 (enable_auto_commit=False + commit() after processing) Exactly-once Kafka transactions (idempotent producer + isolation.level=read_committed) Neither — but only for read from Kafka → write to Kafka Stream processing (Kafka Streams) 
sequenceDiagram
    participant K as Kafka
    participant N as notification-service
    participant M as Mail server
    K->>N: OrderCreated (offset 42)
    N->>M: send confirmation e-mail
    Note over N: crashes before commit
    N->>K: (restart) fetch from last committed offset
    K->>N: OrderCreated (offset 42) again
    N->>N: already sent for order 7? yes → skip
    N->>K: commit offset 43

Exactly-once inside Kafka does not extend to side effects outside it: Kafka cannot "un-send" an e-mail or roll back a row in Postgres. In practice, systems use at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumers: processing the same message twice has the same effect as processing it once.

Common ways to make a consumer idempotent:

  • Processed-message table: store the event ID (or orderId + event type) in the consumer's database in the same transaction as the business change; skip events already stored.
  • Natural idempotency: write operations that are idempotent by nature — UPSERT, "set status to PAID" instead of "add 10 to the balance".
  • Unique constraints: let the database reject the second insert of the same orderId.

items.title: The dual-write problem
items.text:
In Hands-on 9 the order service saves the order in Postgres and then publishes OrderCreated to Kafka. These are two different systems, and no transaction covers both:

  • The database commit succeeds, then the service crashes before publishing → the order exists, but nobody is ever notified.
  • The event is published, then the database transaction rolls back → consumers react to an order that does not exist.

items.title: Transactional outbox
items.text:
The transactional outbox2 removes the dual write. The service writes the event into an outbox table in the same local database transaction as the order. A separate relay (a polling job, or CDC with Debezium) reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka, marking rows as sent.

sequenceDiagram
    participant O as order-service
    participant DB as Postgres
    participant R as Outbox relay
    participant K as Kafka
    O->>DB: BEGIN
    O->>DB: INSERT INTO orders ...
    O->>DB: INSERT INTO outbox (OrderCreated)
    O->>DB: COMMIT (both or neither)
    R->>DB: read unsent outbox rows
    R->>K: publish OrderCreated
    R->>DB: mark row as sent

If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking the row, the event is published again — another reason consumers must be idempotent.

items.title: Sagas
items.text:
Some business operations span several services: placing an order must reserve stock (product service) and charge the customer (payment service). Each service has its own database, so a single ACID transaction is impossible (see Microservices). A saga2 is a sequence of local transactions, one per service, where each step is triggered by the previous one's event. If a step fails, the saga runs compensating transactions that semantically undo the steps already done (release the stock, refund the payment).

sequenceDiagram
    participant O as Order
    participant I as Inventory
    participant P as Payment
    O->>I: OrderCreated
    I->>P: StockReserved
    P->>I: PaymentFailed
    I->>O: StockReleased (compensation)
    O->>O: mark order CANCELLED
Style How it is coordinated Good Watch out Choreography Each service reacts to the others' events (diagram above) No central component, loose coupling The flow is spread over many services; hard to follow and to change Orchestration A saga orchestrator sends commands and waits for replies The flow is explicit in one place The orchestrator is one more service to build and run

Sagas are not transactions

A saga gives up isolation: other requests can see the intermediate state (stock reserved, payment not yet done). Design the states explicitly (PENDING, CONFIRMED, CANCELLED) and make every step and every compensation idempotent.

items.title: Dead Letter Queue
items.text:
When a consumer fails to process a message repeatedly, it must not block the rest of the stream. A Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) is a separate topic where messages are moved after exhausting retry attempts, allowing the main stream to continue while the failing messages are investigated and reprocessed manually.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending
    Pending --> Processing : consumer picks up
    Processing --> Committed : success
    Processing --> Retry : transient failure (attempt < max)
    Retry --> Processing : after backoff
    Processing --> DLQ : max retries exceeded
    DLQ --> Processing : manual reprocessing

Spring Kafka

Spring Kafka's @RetryableTopic annotation handles retry scheduling and DLQ routing automatically. Configure attempts, backoff, and the DLQ topic name declaratively without manual error-handling boilerplate.

// default: 3 attempts in total; Spring Kafka 4 (Spring Boot 4) annotation
@RetryableTopic(backOff = @BackOff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2))
@KafkaListener(topics = "order-events", groupId = "invoice-group")
public void onOrderCreated(OrderCreatedEvent event) {
    invoiceService.create(event);   // throws → retried after 1 s, then 2 s
}

@DltHandler
public void onDeadLetter(OrderCreatedEvent event) {
    log.error("order {} sent to the dead letter topic", event.orderId());
}

Retry only failures that can succeed later (a database briefly unavailable). A message that can never be processed — invalid JSON, an unknown product ID — should go straight to the DLQ; retrying it only delays the rest of the partition.

items.title: When to Use (and Not Use) Event-Driven
items.text:
Scenario Best fit Reason Login / auth token generation REST Caller needs the token synchronously Order confirmation email Event User doesn't wait; email can lag Real-time fraud check (must block) REST Need the answer before proceeding Audit log for all order mutations Event Fire-and-forget, fan-out Payment processing Depends If idempotent retry is guaranteed: event. If blocking confirmation needed: REST + saga Analytics data pipeline Event High volume, consumers can be slow Service health check REST Synchronous by nature

Operational Complexity

Event-driven systems are harder to debug than REST. A request that spans 5 services and 3 Kafka topics requires distributed tracing (covered in the Observability class) to diagnose. Do not adopt event-driven architecture for its own sake — adopt it when the coupling and latency costs of synchronous calls become concrete problems.

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming exactly-once: duplicates will arrive; every consumer must be idempotent.
  • Dual writes: saving to the database and publishing to Kafka without an outbox loses or invents events after a crash.
  • Breaking the event schema: consumers you do not know about read your events. Only add optional fields; never rename or remove fields without a new version (OrderCreatedV2) — a schema registry with Avro or Protobuf can enforce this.
  • Ignoring consumer lag: the queue-depth chart above is real. Monitor the lag of each consumer group (Kafka UI, Prometheus) and alert when it grows.
  • Events that are commands in disguise: SendEmailToCustomer couples the producer to one consumer; publish the fact (OrderCreated) and let consumers decide.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• Hands-on 9 — Kafka in the store: OrderCreated published by the order service and consumed by the notification service, with a DLQ.
  • Microservices — database per service, the reason sagas and outboxes are needed.
  • Distributed Systems — eventual consistency, ordering and consensus (KRaft).
  • Reliability — retries, backoff and idempotency apply to consumers too.
  • Observability and Hands-on 10 — tracing a request across topics.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Use events when the caller does not need the answer to continue; use a synchronous request when it does.
  • Kafka is a replicated, partitioned log: order holds within a partition, the key decides the partition, and each consumer group keeps its own offsets — different groups fan out, the same group shares the work.
  • Delivery is realistically at-least-once: commit after processing and make every consumer idempotent.
  • Never dual-write: the transactional outbox publishes events reliably; sagas with compensations replace distributed transactions.
  • Event sourcing and CQRS are powerful for specific domains, not defaults; a DLQ keeps poison messages from blocking a partition.

  2. RICHARDSON, C. Microservices Patterns — Event Sourcing, CQRS, Saga. ↩↩

  3. FOWLER, M. Event Sourcing, 2005. ↩

items.title: Core Concepts
items.text:
Q1. Which of the following best describes the difference between an event, a command, and a message?

  • A. They are all equivalent terms for the same concept in messaging systems
  • B. A command is an instruction that can be rejected; an event is an immutable record of something that already happened; a message is a generic data container that may represent either
  • C. An event is sent to a single recipient; a command is broadcast to all consumers; a message is stored in a database
  • D. A command carries no payload; an event carries a payload; a message carries metadata only
Answer

B — Command = instruction (rejectable); event = immutable fact; message = generic container.

The distinction is semantic but important for system design. A command (PlaceOrder) expresses intent and implies a single handler that may reject it. An event (OrderCreated) is a statement of fact — it has already happened and cannot be undone. A message is the neutral transport-level term that encompasses both. Using the right vocabulary prevents ambiguity about who owns the decision.

Q2. In Kafka, when a topic has 3 partitions and a consumer group has 3 consumers, how are partitions assigned?

  • A. All 3 consumers read from all 3 partitions simultaneously, tripling throughput
  • B. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group; each consumer owns one partition
  • C. Kafka randomly delivers each message to any available consumer regardless of partition
  • D. Only one consumer is active at a time; the other two are on standby
Answer

B — Each partition is owned by exactly one consumer in the group.

Kafka's partition assignment protocol guarantees that within a consumer group, each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer at a time. This ensures ordered, non-duplicated processing within a partition. With 3 partitions and 3 consumers the assignment is 1:1. If a consumer leaves the group, Kafka triggers a rebalance and reassigns its partition to a remaining consumer.

Q3. Why are events considered immutable in event-driven systems?

  • A. Because Kafka does not support update operations at the protocol level
  • B. Because immutability allows brokers to compress events more efficiently
  • C. Because events record something that already happened — the fact cannot change — making them safe to replay, audit, and use as a reliable source of truth
  • D. Because consumer groups require a fixed schema to parse messages
Answer

C — Events are facts about the past; facts cannot be retroactively changed.

Immutability is a design principle, not just a technical constraint. If an event could be mutated after publication, consumers that already processed it would hold a different view of history than consumers processing it later — destroying consistency. The append-only log is what makes event sourcing, time-travel debugging, and zero-downtime projection rebuilds possible.

Q4. In a CQRS architecture, which side handles write operations?

  • A. The read model, because it holds the most recent state
  • B. The query handler, which reads from the event store and materialises a projection
  • C. The command handler, which validates the command, appends an event to the event store, and publishes it to the event bus
  • D. The API gateway, which routes writes and reads to the same underlying service
Answer

C — The command handler owns writes: validate, append event, publish.

CQRS separates the write path (commands → command handler → event store / event bus) from the read path (queries → read model). The command handler enforces business invariants and produces events as its output. The read model is a derived, denormalised projection updated asynchronously from those events. This separation allows each side to be optimised and scaled independently.

Q5. A user initiates a login and your service must return a session token before the HTTP response is sent. Which communication style is the correct choice and why?

  • A. Asynchronous event, because publishing to Kafka is faster than an HTTP round-trip
  • B. Synchronous REST, because the caller requires the result immediately before it can proceed
  • C. Asynchronous event with a callback, so the UI polls for the token
  • D. Either style — the choice only affects internal architecture, not latency visible to the user
Answer

B — Synchronous REST, because the caller is blocked waiting for the result.

The defining question for choosing synchronous vs asynchronous is: does the caller need the answer before it can continue? For authentication the answer is yes — without the token there is nothing to do next. Asynchronous patterns introduce latency indirection (polling, webhooks, long-polling) that adds complexity without benefit when the result is required immediately.

Q6. What is the purpose of a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)?

  • A. To store messages that have been successfully processed so they can be audited later
  • B. To buffer messages when the broker is under high load, releasing them when load drops
  • C. To capture messages that could not be processed after exhausting retry attempts, preventing them from blocking the main stream while preserving them for investigation
  • D. To compact the topic by removing duplicate messages with the same key
Answer

C — DLQ captures unprocessable messages without blocking the main stream.

Without a DLQ, a message that consistently causes a consumer to throw an exception would either be retried forever (stalling progress) or silently dropped (losing data). The DLQ is a safety valve: failing messages are moved there so the stream continues, and an operator can inspect the message, fix the root cause, and replay it. Spring Kafka's @RetryableTopic automates retry scheduling and DLQ routing.

Q7. What does consumer group offset tracking enable that a simple queue does not?

  • A. It allows multiple independent groups to read the same topic at their own pace without interfering with each other
  • B. It prevents consumers from reading the same partition more than once per day
  • C. It encrypts messages so that only the group with the correct key can decode them
  • D. It limits the rate at which producers can publish to a topic
Answer

A — Each group owns its own offset, so groups progress independently.

In a traditional queue, once a message is consumed it is gone. In Kafka, the message remains in the log and each consumer group maintains its own pointer (offset) per partition. The notification-group can be at offset 42 while the analytics-group is still at offset 10 — both reading the same topic without interfering. This is what makes fan-out (pub/sub) to multiple independent consumers possible at scale.

Q8. In event sourcing, what does "replaying events" mean, and why is it useful?

  • A. Resending failed events to consumers that did not acknowledge receipt
  • B. Re-publishing events to a new topic to trigger downstream services again
  • C. Iterating through the full history of stored events in order to reconstruct the current state of an entity, or to populate a new read model projection from scratch
  • D. Synchronising the event store with a relational database by re-executing SQL statements
Answer

C — Replay reconstructs state by iterating the event history in order.

Because the event store is append-only and immutable, the complete history is always available. Replaying means iterating events from offset 0 (or a snapshot) and applying each event to an in-memory aggregate until the current state is reached. This enables building entirely new projections, migrating to a new schema, or debugging by inspecting what the system looked like at any point in the past.

Q9. What is the key operational difference between pub/sub (fan-out) and competing consumers?

  • A. In pub/sub each consumer group receives a full copy of every message; in competing consumers multiple consumers in one group share the partitions so each message is processed by exactly one consumer
  • B. Pub/sub requires a dedicated broker per consumer; competing consumers share a single broker
  • C. Competing consumers are only possible with RabbitMQ, not Kafka
  • D. In pub/sub only one consumer can be active at a time; in competing consumers all consumers run in parallel on the same message
Answer

A — Fan-out = every group gets a copy; competing consumers = one group shares the work.

The distinction is determined by consumer group membership. Put email-service, analytics-service, and audit-service in separate groups → each receives every OrderCreated event (fan-out). Put three instances of payment-processor in the same group → Kafka assigns each partition to one instance, so each event is processed once (competing consumers). The same Kafka topic supports both patterns simultaneously.

Q10. Within a single Kafka partition, message ordering is guaranteed. Why is ordering not guaranteed across partitions of the same topic?

  • A. Because Kafka replicates partitions to different brokers, introducing variable network delays
  • B. Because each partition is an independent ordered log with its own offset sequence; a message in partition 0 at offset 5 and a message in partition 1 at offset 3 have no defined temporal relationship — the consumer receives them based on whichever is polled first
  • C. Because consumer groups read partitions in reverse order by default to balance load
  • D. Because Kafka uses timestamps instead of offsets for cross-partition ordering, and clocks are never perfectly synchronised
Answer

B — Each partition is an independent log; offsets are not comparable across partitions.

A partition is an ordered, append-only sequence. Within partition 0 you know message at offset 5 came after offset 4. But partition 0 offset 5 and partition 1 offset 3 were written independently — there is no global sequence number linking them. If strict global ordering is required, use a single partition (at the cost of parallelism) or include an application-level timestamp and sort at read time.

Q11. The order service publishes OrderCreated, OrderPaid and OrderShipped for each order to a topic with 6 partitions. The shipping consumer must see the events of the same order in sequence. What should the producer do?

  • A. Publish without a key so Kafka balances the load evenly
  • B. Use the orderId as the message key, so all events of one order land in the same partition
  • C. Use a single consumer for the whole topic
  • D. Add a timestamp to each event; Kafka orders messages by timestamp across partitions
Answer

B — Key by orderId.

The default partitioner hashes the key, so the same key always goes to the same partition, and Kafka guarantees order within a partition. Different orders still spread over the 6 partitions and are processed in parallel. Option A loses ordering; C keeps ordering only by giving up parallelism (and does not fix the order across partitions); D is false — Kafka does not reorder messages by timestamp.

Q12. The notification service commits the Kafka offset after sending the e-mail. It crashes right after sending, before committing. What happens on restart, and what should the code do about it?

  • A. The message is lost; nothing can be done
  • B. The message is read again (at-least-once delivery); the consumer must be idempotent, e.g. skip orders it already notified
  • C. Kafka detects the crash and deletes the message so it is not processed twice
  • D. The message goes to the dead letter queue automatically
Answer

B — Redelivery; make the consumer idempotent.

Committing after processing gives at-least-once delivery: the consumer resumes from the last committed offset and sees the message again. Committing before processing would give at-most-once (lost message instead of duplicate). Kafka's exactly-once transactions cover only Kafka-to-Kafka processing, not an e-mail, so the realistic design is at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer (a processed-messages table, upserts or unique constraints).

Q13. The order service saves an order in Postgres and then calls kafkaTemplate.send(...). What problem does the transactional outbox solve here?

  • A. It makes Kafka faster by batching messages in Postgres
  • B. It removes the need for consumer groups
  • C. It avoids the dual write: the order and the event are written in the same local database transaction, and a relay publishes the event afterwards, so a crash can no longer leave an order without its event (or an event without its order)
  • D. It guarantees that each event is delivered exactly once to every consumer
Answer

C — It turns two writes to two systems into one local transaction.

Without the outbox, a crash between the database commit and the publish loses the event; a rollback after the publish produces an event for an order that does not exist. With the outbox, both rows commit together, and a relay (polling or CDC) publishes the event. The relay may publish twice after a crash, so D is false — consumers still need to be idempotent.

Q14. In a choreographed saga, inventory reserves stock after OrderCreated, but the payment service then emits PaymentFailed. What should happen?

  • A. The database rolls back the stock reservation automatically, as in an ACID transaction
  • B. The inventory service runs a compensating transaction that releases the stock, and the order is marked as cancelled
  • C. The order service retries the payment forever until it succeeds
  • D. Nothing — the stock remains reserved until an operator fixes it manually
Answer

B — Compensate the steps already done.

Each saga step is a local transaction in a different service and database, so there is no global rollback (A). Instead, every step that can be undone has a compensating action — here, StockReleased — triggered by the failure event, and the order moves to CANCELLED. Compensations, like the steps, must be idempotent because events may be redelivered.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Picture the store as a single Spring Boot application: login, catalogue, orders and payments in one codebase, one database, one deployable .jar. On Black Friday only checkout is overloaded, but the only way to scale it is to run more copies of everything. A bug in the catalogue page takes login down with it. Three teams now share the codebase, and every release needs all of them to agree on the same day. Nothing is wrong with the code — the shape of the system no longer fits the organisation.

The microservices style is a response to this specific problem: as teams and codebases grow, a single monolith becomes increasingly expensive to change — a modification to one module requires understanding and testing the entire system, and a deployment requires coordinating across the whole organisation.

Microservices is an architectural style that structures an application as a collection of small, autonomous services, each modelled around a specific business domain52. Rather than building one large deployable unit (a monolith), the system is composed of independently deployable pieces that collaborate through well-defined APIs.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Compare a monolith, a modular monolith and microservices, and justify when splitting is worth its cost.
  • Explain Conway's Law and the core principles of microservices (single capability, independence, data isolation).
  • Choose between synchronous and asynchronous communication for an interaction, and estimate the availability cost of a synchronous chain.
  • Apply Domain-Driven Design (bounded contexts, aggregates, context maps) to find service boundaries.
  • Describe the infrastructure components of a microservice platform and follow one request through the course's architecture.

items.title: Monolith vs. Microservices
items.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph mono [Monolith]
        direction TB
        ui_m[UI]
        biz_m[Business Logic\nOrders · Auth · Payments · Inventory]
        data_m[Single Database]
        ui_m --> biz_m --> data_m
    end
    subgraph micro [Microservices]
        direction TB
        gw[API Gateway]
        s1[Orders\nService]
        s2[Auth\nService]
        s3[Inventory\nService]
        db1[(Orders DB)]
        db2[(Auth DB)]
        db3[(Inventory DB)]
        gw --> s1 & s2 & s3
        s1 --> db1
        s2 --> db2
        s3 --> db3
    end

Neither style is universally better. The right choice depends on team size, domain complexity, and operational maturity:

Dimension Monolith Microservices Deployment One unit — simple to ship Independent per service — complex to coordinate Scaling Scale the whole app Scale only the bottleneck service Development speed Fast initially Slower setup; faster at scale Operational complexity Low High — needs orchestration, tracing, service discovery Data consistency ACID transactions Eventual consistency across services Team fit Small, co-located team Multiple teams, each owning a service

Two terms in the table deserve a definition. An ACID transaction (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) lets the monolith change orders and stock in one database operation that either fully happens or not at all. Across services there is no shared transaction: each service commits its own data, and the system becomes consistent a moment later — eventual consistency (see CAP Theorem).

Start with a monolith

Most successful microservice systems began as monoliths. Identify stable domain boundaries (using Domain-Driven Design) before splitting. Premature decomposition creates a distributed monolith — all the complexity of microservices with none of the independence benefits.

The middle ground: a modular monolith. One deployable unit, but internally split into modules with explicit interfaces and no shared tables — each module could become a service later. It gives the team practice with boundaries before paying for the network, and it is often the right answer for a small team.

Symptoms of a distributed monolith

  • Services must be deployed together ("release train") because a change in one breaks the others.
  • Two services read and write the same tables.
  • One user request triggers a long chain of synchronous calls; if any link is down, everything is down.
  • A shared library with domain classes forces every service to upgrade at once.

items.title: Conway's Law
items.text:
"Any organisation that designs a system will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organisation's communication structure." — Melvin Conway, 19676

Service boundaries and team boundaries converge over time. The simulation below shows how an initially unified codebase fragments into services that mirror the communication patterns of the teams that built it:

2026-10-23T08:15:37.509450 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The law also works in reverse, which is how organisations use it on purpose: the inverse Conway maneuver shapes the teams first (one team per business capability) so that the architecture follows.

items.title: Key principles
items.text:
Principle Meaning Single Responsibility Each service implements exactly one business capability Independence Services can be developed, deployed, and scaled without coordinating with others Data isolation Each service owns its own database — no shared schema, no shared tables Decentralised governance Teams choose the technology that best fits their service Failure isolation A failing service does not cascade and bring down the entire system API-first communication Services interact through explicit, versioned contracts Observability Comprehensive monitoring, distributed tracing, and structured logging are prerequisites

How small is "micro"? Not a number of lines. A service is the right size when one team can own it end to end, it can be deployed without coordinating with others, and it maps to one business capability. Services that are too small ("nanoservices", e.g. one service per table) spend more time talking to each other than doing work.

items.title: The store, decomposed
items.text:
The course builds one platform step by step. Each service owns one capability and its own data4:

Service Capability Owns Talks to Built in gateway-service Single entry point, routing, authentication check — every service Hands-on 2, 3 account-service User accounts accounts schema — Hands-on 1 auth-service Register, login, issue and resolve JWTs — (uses account) account Hands-on 3 product-service Product catalogue products data — Product API order-service Orders of the current user orders data product, exchange, Kafka Order API exchange-service (Python) Currency conversion — third-party rates API Exchange API notification-service (Python) Order confirmation e-mails — Kafka Hands-on 9

Note decentralised governance in action: the exchange and notification services are written in Python, the others in Java — the contract is HTTP/JSON or a Kafka event, so the language does not leak.

items.title: Owning the data
items.text:
Database-per-service means that no service reads or writes another service's tables. It does not require one database server per service. In the hands-on, a single Postgres container hosts several schemas, and each service is the only one that touches its own (the account service sets hibernate.default_schema: accounts and runs its own Flyway migrations):

flowchart LR
    subgraph pg ["one Postgres server"]
        s1[("schema accounts")]
        s2[("schema products")]
        s3[("schema orders")]
    end
    account["account-service"] --> s1
    product["product-service"] --> s2
    order["order-service"] --> s3
    order -->|"GET /products/{id}"| product
    order -.-x|"no direct SQL"| s2

When the order service needs a product's price, it asks the product API, never the product table. That keeps the product team free to change its schema. Two consequences follow:

  • Queries across services become API calls (or a local copy of the data, kept up to date by events — see CQRS).
  • Business transactions across services cannot use one ACID transaction. They become a sequence of local transactions coordinated by events, with compensating actions when a step fails — the saga pattern4.

items.title: Inter-service communication
items.text:
Services in a microservice system communicate in two fundamentally different ways, each with distinct trade-offs:

Synchronous (HTTP / gRPC)Asynchronous (Messaging)

The caller sends a request and waits for a response. Simple to reason about, but creates temporal coupling — the caller cannot complete its operation if the callee is down.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Gateway
    participant Order Service
    participant Inventory Service

    Client->>+Gateway: POST /orders
    Gateway->>+Order Service: create order
    Order Service->>+Inventory Service: reserve items
    Inventory Service-->>-Order Service: reserved ✓
    Order Service-->>-Gateway: 201 Created
    Gateway-->>-Client: 201 Created

Use when: the caller needs the result immediately (e.g., checkout response, auth validation).

The producer publishes an event and continues. Consumers process the event independently, in their own time. This eliminates temporal coupling — services can be down and process the message when they recover.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Order Service
    participant Message Broker
    participant Inventory Service
    participant Notification Service

    Order Service->>Message Broker: OrderPlaced event
    Note over Order Service: continues immediately
    Message Broker->>Inventory Service: OrderPlaced
    Message Broker->>Notification Service: OrderPlaced
    Inventory Service->>Message Broker: InventoryReserved

Use when: strict consistency is not needed immediately (e.g., sending an email, updating analytics, inventory reservation).

In the store, the order service calls the product service synchronously (it needs the price to compute the total before answering), and publishes an OrderCreated event to Kafka asynchronously so that the notification service can send the e-mail without slowing the customer down (Hands-on 9).

Synchronous chains multiply failure

If a request must pass through three services, and each one is available 99.9% of the time, the chain is available only 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.7% of the time — from about 8.8 hours of downtime a year to about 26 hours. Every extra synchronous hop lowers availability and adds latency. Keep chains short, use timeouts and circuit breakers (Resilience Patterns), and move work that does not need an immediate answer to events (Event-Driven Architecture).

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Microservices trade operational complexity for independent deployment, scaling and team autonomy — worth it only when those are real problems.
  • Start with a (modular) monolith; split along stable domain boundaries found with DDD3, or you get a distributed monolith.
  • Conway's Law: service boundaries mirror team communication — design both together.
  • Each service owns one capability and its data; others use its API, never its tables.
  • Synchronous calls are simple but couple availability; events decouple producers from consumers.

items.title: Domain-Driven Design
items.text:
Q1. What is the primary purpose of a Bounded Context in DDD?

  • A. It limits the number of entities a single service can manage
  • B. It defines the boundary within which a domain model is valid — the same term can mean different things in different contexts
  • C. It enforces a maximum size for aggregates within the domain
  • D. It specifies which database schema a service is allowed to access
Answer

B — Defines the boundary where a domain model is valid.

A Customer in the Sales context (credit limit, region) is a completely different model from Customer in Billing (tax ID, billing address). Bounded contexts allow each team to use the term differently without creating one bloated class that satisfies none of them well. In microservices, a bounded context typically maps to one service.

Q2. Which DDD building block is the sole entry point for all modifications to the objects within it?

  • A. Domain Service
  • B. Repository
  • C. Value Object
  • D. Aggregate Root
Answer

D — Aggregate Root.

The Aggregate Root is the only object external code holds a reference to. All state changes to child entities and value objects inside the aggregate must go through the root, which enforces invariants. For example, Order.addItem() checks the "max 50 items" rule before allowing a new OrderItem to be added.

Q3. What distinguishes an Entity from a Value Object?

  • A. Entities are immutable; Value Objects change state over time
  • B. An Entity has a persistent identity that survives attribute changes; a Value Object is defined entirely by its attributes and has no identity
  • C. Entities exist only in memory; Value Objects are persisted to the database
  • D. Entities are shared between bounded contexts; Value Objects are local to one context
Answer

B — Entity has identity; Value Object is defined by its attributes.

Two Order objects with the same ID are the same order even if their status differs (entity). Two Money(10.00, BRL) objects are identical and interchangeable because they have the same attributes (value object). Value objects should be immutable — operations return new instances.

Q4. In Event Storming, what do Domain Events (orange sticky notes) represent?

  • A. Commands that users send to the system to trigger state changes
  • B. External API calls that the system makes to third-party services
  • C. Things that happened in the domain, expressed in past tense, used to trigger reactions in other bounded contexts
  • D. Business rules that enforce invariants within an aggregate
Answer

C — Things that happened, past tense.

OrderPlaced, PaymentCharged, ItemShipped — domain events describe facts. They are immutable records that other bounded contexts (Inventory, Notifications, Analytics) subscribe to and react to independently. This decouples contexts without requiring direct calls between them.

Q5. According to the DDD-to-microservices mapping, what is the natural starting point for a microservice boundary?

  • A. A database table — each table becomes one microservice
  • B. A use case — each user story maps to one service
  • C. A team — Conway's Law dictates that one team = one service
  • D. A Bounded Context — the ubiquitous language and model are internally consistent within that boundary
Answer

D — A Bounded Context.

The bounded context defines a conceptual seam where the model is self-consistent and the team owns the ubiquitous language. Starting there (rather than by table or use case) produces services that can evolve independently. However, a bounded context is a starting point — operational or team constraints may lead to merging or splitting.

Q6. In the Order API, an order item stores only the product's id (plus quantity and total), not a full Product object. Which DDD rule does this follow?

  • A. Value objects must be immutable
  • B. Aggregates reference other aggregates by identity only
  • C. Every entity needs its own repository
  • D. Domain events must be written in the past tense
Answer

B — Reference other aggregates by identity.

Order and Product are different aggregates, in different bounded contexts (and services). Holding only the product id means the order aggregate can never modify a product, and the two can be stored in different databases. It also matches the Ordering context's model: the item keeps the price paid, so a later catalogue price change does not alter past orders.

Q7. The exchange service consumes a third-party rates API whose JSON format it does not control. Which context-map pattern keeps that format from spreading through the exchange service's code?

  • A. Shared Kernel
  • B. Conformist
  • C. Anti-Corruption Layer
  • D. Published Language
Answer

C — Anti-Corruption Layer.

An ACL is a translation layer at the border: it calls the provider and converts the provider's model into the service's own (e.g. a Rate value object). If the provider changes or is replaced, only the ACL changes. A conformist would adopt the provider's model as is; a shared kernel is code shared by two cooperating teams, which is impossible with a third party.

items.title: Microservice Architecture
items.text:
Q8. What is the primary role of an API Gateway in a microservices architecture?

  • A. It stores shared configuration for all microservices
  • B. It acts as a message broker between services using async events
  • C. It is the single external entry point — handling routing, authentication, rate limiting, and SSL termination on behalf of all services
  • D. It manages the lifecycle of containers and restarts failed services
Answer

C — Single external entry point.

The gateway is the only service exposed to the internet. Internal services never directly face external traffic. By centralising cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting, SSL, logging), the gateway lets business microservices focus entirely on their domain logic.

Q9. Why does each microservice own its own database (database-per-service pattern)?

  • A. It reduces infrastructure cost by using smaller, cheaper databases
  • B. It is required by the OpenAPI specification
  • C. It ensures services can evolve their schema independently without coupling to other services' data models
  • D. It prevents services from reading each other's data, improving security
Answer

C — Independent schema evolution.

A shared database creates a hidden coupling: changing a table that Service A owns might break Service B, which also reads it. With database-per-service, each service's schema is its private implementation detail. Services communicate through APIs, never through shared tables.

Q10. What is the key trade-off between synchronous (HTTP) and asynchronous (messaging) inter-service communication?

  • A. Sync is more secure; async is less secure
  • B. Sync gives immediate results but creates temporal coupling; async decouples services but the producer does not get an immediate result
  • C. Async is always better — sync should never be used in microservices
  • D. Sync uses more CPU; async uses more memory
Answer

B — Sync = immediate result, temporal coupling; async = decoupled, no immediate result.

If the Order service calls the Inventory service synchronously and Inventory is down, Order is also broken. With async messaging, Order publishes an OrderPlaced event and continues; Inventory processes it when it recovers. Use sync when the caller needs the result immediately (e.g., auth validation); use async when strict consistency is not required (e.g., sending confirmation email).

Q11. What problem does Service Discovery solve in a dynamic microservice environment?

  • A. It prevents two services from being deployed with the same name
  • B. It allows services to find each other's current network locations dynamically, since IP addresses change as instances scale up or down
  • C. It monitors health checks and restarts unhealthy services
  • D. It routes external traffic to the correct microservice based on the URL path
Answer

B — Finding current network locations of dynamic instances.

In a containerised environment, instances are created and destroyed constantly, and their IP addresses change on every restart. A service registry (Consul, Eureka, Kubernetes DNS) maintains the current location of all instances. Services register on startup and deregister on shutdown, and callers query the registry to find them.

Q12. In the course's reference architecture, who is responsible for validating JWT tokens on each request?

  • A. Each business microservice validates the token independently on every request
  • B. The identity provider re-validates the token on every request via a callback
  • C. The Gateway delegates validation to the Auth Service and forwards the caller's identity in the id-account header; business microservices trust that header without re-validating
  • D. The load balancer validates tokens before passing requests to the gateway
Answer

C — Gateway delegates to Auth Service; business services trust the id-account header.

The gateway's AuthorizationFilter intercepts every request to a secured route, reads the JWT from the cookie, calls POST /auth/solve on the Auth Service, and forwards the resolved identity in the id-account header to the downstream service. Business microservices trust this header without calling the Auth Service themselves, keeping each service focused on its domain. This is only safe because the services are not reachable from outside: a service exposed directly could receive a forged id-account.

Q13. A checkout request passes synchronously through three services, each available 99.9% of the time. Approximately how available is the checkout as a whole?

  • A. 99.9% — the chain is as available as each service
  • B. 99.97% — redundancy across three services increases availability
  • C. 99.7% — the availabilities multiply (0.999³), roughly tripling the downtime
  • D. 97% — each hop removes one percentage point
Answer

C — about 99.7%.

In a synchronous chain the request succeeds only if every service is up, so availabilities multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.997. Downtime grows from about 8.8 hours a year to about 26 hours. This is why long synchronous chains are avoided, and why work that does not need an immediate answer is moved to events.

Q14. Which situation is a symptom of a distributed monolith?

  • A. The exchange service is written in Python and the others in Java
  • B. The product and order services must always be deployed on the same day because the order service reads the product tables directly
  • C. The order service publishes OrderCreated to Kafka and does not know who consumes it
  • D. The gateway runs three replicas behind Nginx
Answer

B — Coordinated deployments caused by shared tables.

A distributed monolith has the network costs of microservices without their independence: services share data or are so coupled that they must be released together. A is decentralised governance, C is healthy asynchronous decoupling, and D is horizontal scaling of the entry point.

items.title: Architecture & Components
items.text:
The store now has six services. Each of them needs HTTPS, must check who the user is, must be found by the others even though its containers come and go, needs configuration and secrets, and must produce logs and metrics. If every team solves these problems inside its own service, the platform ends up with six slightly different (and slightly wrong) implementations of the same thing. The answer is to move these cross-cutting concerns — concerns that every service has, but that are not part of any business domain — into shared infrastructure.

A production microservices system is more than a collection of independent services. It requires a set of infrastructure components that handle cross-cutting concerns — routing, security, discovery, configuration, and observability — so that individual services can stay focused on their business domain1.

items.title: Components
items.text: Source: System Design 101 — Microservice Architecture

items.title: Load Balancer
items.text:
Distributes incoming traffic across multiple instances of a service. Prevents any single instance from becoming a bottleneck and routes traffic away from unhealthy instances.

  • Layer 4 (TCP): Fast, routes by IP/port — used for raw throughput.
  • Layer 7 (HTTP): Routes by URL path, headers, or cookies — enables content-based routing and canary deployments.

In the course, Hands-on 7 puts Nginx in front of several gateway replicas, using the least_conn algorithm (each new request goes to the replica with the fewest active connections).

items.title: CDN (Content Delivery Network)
items.text: A geographically distributed network of caches that serves static assets (images, JS, CSS) from the location nearest to the user. Reduces latency for clients worldwide and offloads traffic from origin servers.

items.title: API Gateway
items.text:
The single entry point for all external clients. The gateway is responsible for:

Concern How Routing /orders/** → Order Service, /products/** → Product Service Authentication Validates JWT tokens before forwarding requests Rate limiting Protects services from traffic spikes or abusive clients Request/response transformation Adds headers, aggregates multiple service calls SSL termination Handles HTTPS; services communicate in plain HTTP inside the trusted network

The gateway is the boundary between the public internet and the trusted internal network. In the course it is a Spring Cloud Gateway application (Hands-on 2); routes are declared in application.yaml, e.g. Path=/accounts/** → http://account:8080.

Gateway or load balancer?

Both forward requests, but at different levels. A load balancer spreads requests for one service across its identical replicas and knows nothing about the application. A gateway decides which service a request is for and applies application rules (authentication, rate limits). The course uses both: Nginx balances the gateway replicas, and the gateway routes to the services.

items.title: Identity Provider
items.text:
Manages user authentication and authorisation using standard protocols:

  • OAuth 2.0 — delegation framework: a user grants a client access to their resources without sharing their password.
  • OpenID Connect (OIDC) — identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0: provides a JWT identity token (id_token) in addition to the access token.
  • JWT (JSON Web Token) — a signed, self-contained token that encodes claims (user ID, roles, expiry). Services validate the signature without calling the identity provider on every request.

In the course, the auth service plays this role in a simplified form: it registers and logs users in, issues a JWT (stored in a cookie), and resolves a token back to an account id for the gateway (Hands-on 3). OAuth 2.0 and OIDC are covered in Security.

items.title: Service Discovery & Registry
items.text:
In a dynamic environment where service instances scale up/down and IP addresses change, services cannot hard-code endpoints. A service registry (Consul, Eureka, Kubernetes DNS) stores the current locations of all service instances. Services register on startup and deregister on shutdown.

  • Client-side discovery: the caller queries the registry and load-balances itself.
  • Server-side discovery: the load balancer or gateway queries the registry on behalf of the caller.

In the course, the platform's DNS is the registry. Docker Compose gives every service a hostname equal to its name, so the gateway route and the Feign client both simply use http://account:8080; with several replicas, the name resolves to all of them. In Kubernetes (Hands-on 5), a Service object gets a stable DNS name and spreads traffic over the pods behind it — server-side discovery, with no Eureka or Consul to run.

items.title: Configuration Service
items.text:
Centralises configuration for all services (Spring Cloud Config, AWS Parameter Store, Vault). Changes can be pushed to running services without redeployment. Secrets (credentials, API keys) are stored encrypted and injected at runtime.

In the course, configuration follows the twelve-factor rule of keeping it in the environment3: application.yaml reads variables such as ${DATABASE_HOST}, whose values come from the .env file and compose.yaml, and later from Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets. The same image runs in every environment; only the environment changes.

items.title: Message Broker
items.text: Carries events between services asynchronously, so that the producer does not wait for — or even know — its consumers. The course uses Apache Kafka: the order service publishes OrderCreated to the order-events topic and the notification service consumes it (Hands-on 9, Event-Driven Architecture).

items.title: Distributed Cache
items.text: An in-memory store shared by all replicas of a service, used to avoid repeating expensive calls or queries. With several gateway replicas, a local cache in each JVM would hold different data; Redis gives them one shared cache (Hands-on 8).

items.title: Observability Stack
items.text: With dozens of processes, "look at the log" no longer works. The platform collects metrics (Prometheus scrapes each service's /actuator/prometheus; Grafana draws dashboards — Hands-on 6) and traces that follow one request across services (OpenTelemetry + Jaeger — Hands-on 10). See Observability.

items.title: Summary: the course's platform
items.text: Component Common options In our platform Hands-on Load balancer Nginx, HAProxy, cloud load balancers Nginx in front of the gateway replicas 7 API gateway Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, cloud API gateways Spring Cloud Gateway (gateway-service) 2, 3 Identity provider Keycloak, Auth0, Amazon Cognito auth-service issuing JWTs 3 Service discovery Eureka, Consul, Kubernetes DNS Docker Compose DNS, then Kubernetes Services 1, 5 Configuration Spring Cloud Config, Vault, ConfigMaps .env + environment variables, then ConfigMaps and Secrets 5 Message broker Kafka, RabbitMQ Kafka 9 Cache Redis, Memcached Redis 8 Observability Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Jaeger Prometheus + Grafana, OpenTelemetry + Jaeger 6, 10

items.title: Our architecture
items.text:
The diagram below shows the reference architecture used in this course:

flowchart LR
  subgraph client["Internet"]
    direction LR
    Web
    Mobile
    Desktop
  end
  subgraph Trusted Layer
    direction LR
    lb(["Load Balancer"])
    gateway["API Gateway"]
    auth["Auth Service"]
    subgraph bm ["Business Microservices"]
      direction LR
      ms1["Service 1"]
      ms2["Service 2"]
      ms3["Service 3"]
      db1[("Database 1")]
      db2[("Database 2")]
    end
  end
  subgraph third-party["Third-Party APIs"]
    direction LR
    tp1["External Service"]
  end
  client --> lb --> gateway
  gateway --> ms1
  gateway --> ms2
  gateway --> ms3
  ms1 --> db1
  ms2 --> db2
  ms2 --> ms3
  ms3 --> tp1
  gateway --> auth

In the store, the business microservices are account, product and order; the exchange service is the one that calls a third-party API.

Key design decisions in this architecture:

  • All external traffic enters through the gateway. Internal services are not reachable from the internet.
  • Auth is a separate service. The gateway delegates token validation to the Auth Service (POST /auth/solve) and forwards the caller's identity in the id-account header; business microservices trust that header and never parse the JWT themselves.
  • Each service has its own database. No shared schema. Services communicate through APIs, not through shared tables.
  • Services can call each other. Service 2 calls Service 3 for a sub-operation. In synchronous flows, this is fine; for reliability at scale, consider event-driven patterns.

items.title: Following one request
items.text:
A logged-in user places an order. Every component above plays its part, in this order:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor U as Browser
    participant N as Nginx
    participant G as Gateway
    participant A as Auth
    participant O as Order
    participant P as Product
    participant K as Kafka
    U->>N: POST /orders (JWT cookie)
    N->>G: forward to one gateway replica
    G->>A: POST /auth/solve (token)
    A-->>G: idAccount
    G->>O: POST /orders + header id-account
    O->>P: GET /products/{id}
    P-->>O: product with price
    O->>O: save order in its own schema
    O-)K: OrderCreated (async)
    O-->>G: 201 Created
    G-->>N: 201 Created
    N-->>U: 201 Created
  • 1–2 The load balancer picks a gateway replica.
  • 3–4 The gateway checks the token with the auth service and learns who the user is.
  • 5 It routes to the order service, adding the id-account header.
  • 6–7 The order service asks the product API (never the product table) for the price.
  • 8–9 It saves the order in its own schema and publishes an event to the broker, without waiting for the notification service.
  • 10–12 The response travels back. A trace in Jaeger shows exactly these hops as spans.

Common architecture pitfalls

  • Bypassing the gateway: if a business service's port is published to the internet, anyone can call it and forge the id-account header. Only the gateway (or the load balancer in front of it) may be exposed, and the gateway must overwrite any identity header the client sends.
  • A single gateway instance: the entry point becomes a single point of failure and a bottleneck — run replicas behind a load balancer (Hands-on 7).
  • Business logic in the gateway: the gateway should route and enforce cross-cutting rules, not compute order totals. Otherwise every domain change needs a gateway deployment.
  • "Trusted network" as the only defence: plain HTTP inside the cluster is a simplification; production platforms often add mutual TLS between services (Security).

items.title: Best practices
items.text:
Source: System Design 101 — Microservice Best Practices Practice Why it matters Design for failure Any downstream call can fail. Use timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers. Automate everything Manual deployments at scale are error-prone. CI/CD pipelines, IaC, and container orchestration are prerequisites. Own your data A service that shares its database with another service cannot evolve independently. Async where possible Synchronous chains amplify latency and couple availability. Events decouple producers from consumers. Observe everything Distributed traces, structured logs, and metrics are the only way to understand failures across service boundaries. Version your APIs Services are deployed independently; breaking API changes must be versioned to avoid forcing coordinated deployments.

These practices are developed in their own classes: Resilience Patterns, Deployment, Observability and REST versioning2.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Cross-cutting concerns (routing, authentication, discovery, configuration, observability) belong in shared infrastructure, not in each service.
  • The gateway is the single entry point and the trust boundary; the load balancer spreads load over identical replicas.
  • In the course, the gateway resolves the JWT through the auth service and forwards id-account; services never parse tokens.
  • Discovery is the platform's DNS (Docker Compose, then Kubernetes Services); configuration comes from the environment.
  • Kafka, Redis, Prometheus/Grafana and OpenTelemetry/Jaeger complete the platform — each one is built in a hands-on.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• Build the components: Hands-on 2 — Gateway, 3 — Security, 5 — Orchestration, 6 — Observability, 7 — Load Balancer, 8 — Cache, 9 — Kafka, 10 — Tracing.
  • Why and where to split: Microservices, Domain-Driven Design.
  • Deploying all of it: Project.

  1. XU, A. System Design 101 ↩

  2. NEWMAN, S. Building Microservices. O'Reilly, 2021. ↩

  3. WIGGINS, A. The Twelve-Factor App — III. Config. ↩

items.title: Domain-Driven Design
items.text:
You have decided to split the store into services. Where do you cut? By database table (products, orders, order_items)? By layer (one service for the UI, one for the logic)? By whatever the teams are working on this month? Each of these produces services that must change together and call each other constantly — a distributed monolith. You need a way to find the places where the business itself has a seam. That is what Domain-Driven Design gives you.

Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is a software development approach introduced by Eric Evans1 that places the domain — the specific area of business the software supports — at the centre of all design decisions. DDD provides a vocabulary and a set of patterns that help translate business complexity into code structure, and it is the primary tool for identifying the right boundaries between microservices.

DDD works at two levels:

Level Question it answers Tools Strategic design Where are the boundaries? How does the business split into parts, and how do the parts relate? Subdomains, ubiquitous language, bounded contexts, context maps, Event Storming Tactical design What goes inside one boundary? How is the model written in code? Entities, value objects, aggregates, repositories, domain events, domain services

Strategic design decides the microservices; tactical design shapes the code inside each one.

items.title: Subdomains: where to invest
items.text:
The domain of the store is online retail. It splits into subdomains, and not all of them deserve the same effort2:

Kind Meaning In the store Core What makes the business different; worth the best people and custom code Ordering, pricing, the catalogue experience Supporting Needed and specific to the business, but not a differentiator Notifications, currency display Generic Solved problems, the same for every company Authentication, payments, e-mail delivery

Generic subdomains are candidates to buy or reuse (an identity provider such as Keycloak, a payment provider). The course builds its own auth service to learn how it works, but a real store would usually not.

items.title: Ubiquitous Language
items.text:
The single most important DDD practice is establishing a Ubiquitous Language: a shared vocabulary used consistently by both developers and domain experts in conversations, documentation, and code.

Without a ubiquitous language, the same concept gets different names in different layers:

  • Business calls it a Customer, the database has a USER table, the code has a Person class.
  • Each translation is a place where understanding can diverge.

With ubiquitous language, the code reads like the business speaks:

// Without ubiquitous language
public class Person {
    private String userHandle;
    public void changeUserHandle(String newHandle) { ... }
}

// With ubiquitous language (domain uses "Account" and "username")
public class Account {
    private String username;
    public void changeUsername(String newUsername) { ... }
}

The hands-on follows this: the business talks about accounts, so the service is account-service, the resource is /accounts, and the classes are AccountIn, AccountOut and AccountService (Hands-on 1).

items.title: Bounded Context
items.text:
A Bounded Context is the boundary within which a particular model is defined and applicable. The same word can mean different things in different contexts — and that is fine, as long as each context has a clear boundary.

flowchart LR
  subgraph Sales ["Bounded Context: Sales"]
    c1[Customer\n- name\n- creditLimit\n- salesRegion]
  end
  subgraph Support ["Bounded Context: Support"]
    c2[Customer\n- name\n- ticketHistory\n- supportTier]
  end
  subgraph Billing ["Bounded Context: Billing"]
    c3[Customer\n- name\n- taxId\n- billingAddress]
  end

Each bounded context has its own model of Customer. Trying to build one unified Customer class that satisfies all three leads to a bloated object that satisfies none of them well.

The word “product” in the store

In the Catalogue context, a product has a name, a current price and a unit, and its price can change any day. In the Ordering context, what matters is the product as it was sold: its id, the quantity and the total paid. That is why, in the Order API, each order item stores its own total and only the product's id: if the catalogue price changes tomorrow, yesterday's order must not change. Same word, two models, two services.

In microservices, a bounded context typically maps to one microservice (or a small cluster of closely related services). This is why DDD is the primary tool for microservice decomposition — the bounded context gives you the natural seam.

items.title: Context maps: how contexts relate
items.text:
Bounded contexts are not islands; they exchange data. A context map draws the contexts and names the relationship between each pair3. In every relationship one side is upstream (its model influences the other) and the other is downstream (it depends on the upstream model).

Pattern Meaning Use when Customer / Supplier The downstream team's needs are taken into account in the upstream team's plans Two teams in the same company that talk to each other Open Host Service + Published Language The upstream exposes a well-defined, documented API (e.g. REST + JSON described in OpenAPI) for any consumer One provider, many consumers Conformist The downstream simply adopts the upstream model as is The upstream model is good enough, or you have no influence over it Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) The downstream writes a translation layer so that the upstream model does not leak into its own The upstream is a legacy or third-party system with a model you do not want Shared Kernel Two contexts share a small part of the model (and its code), changed only by agreement Two closely cooperating teams; use sparingly — it couples them

The store's context map:

flowchart LR
    product["Catalogue (product)"] -->|"Open Host Service: REST + JSON"| order["Ordering (order)"]
    account["Accounts (account)"] -->|"Conformist: AccountOut"| auth["Identity (auth)"]
    rates["Third-party rates API"] -->|"Anti-Corruption Layer"| exchange["Currency (exchange)"]
    exchange -->|"Open Host Service: REST"| order
    order -->|"event OrderCreated"| notification["Notification"]
  • Catalogue → Ordering: the product service publishes its API (an Open Host Service, documented with OpenAPI); the order service consumes it.
  • Accounts → Identity: the auth service reuses AccountIn / AccountOut from the account module exactly as they are — a conformist relationship.
  • Third-party rates → Currency: the exchange service must not let the provider's JSON format spread through its code. It translates it at the border:
exchange-service: anti-corruption layer (illustrative)
def get_rate(source: str, target: str) -> Rate:
    # the provider's model, e.g. {"base": "USD", "rates": {"BRL": 5.43}, "date": "..."}
    raw = provider.latest(base=source)
    # our model: one Rate value object, in our own vocabulary
    return Rate(source=source, target=target, value=Decimal(str(raw["rates"][target])))

If the provider changes its format, or is replaced, only this function changes.

items.title: Building blocks
items.text: The tactical patterns, illustrated with the Ordering context.

items.title: Entities
items.text:
Objects with a distinct identity that persists over time and across different representations. Two entities are the same if they have the same identity, regardless of whether their attributes differ.

public class Order {
    private final OrderId id;  // identity
    private OrderStatus status;
    private List<OrderItem> items;

    // Two Orders with the same id are the same Order,
    // even if their status differs.
}

items.title: Value Objects
items.text:
Objects defined entirely by their attributes — they have no identity. Two value objects with the same attributes are interchangeable.

public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {
    // No id field. Two Money(10.00, BRL) objects are equal and interchangeable.
    public Money add(Money other) {
        if (!this.currency.equals(other.currency))
            throw new CurrencyMismatchException();
        return new Money(this.amount.add(other.amount), this.currency);
    }

    public Money multiply(int quantity) {
        return new Money(this.amount.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(quantity)), this.currency);
    }
}

Value objects should be immutable. Operations return new instances rather than mutating state. Java records are a natural fit: fields are final and equals/hashCode compare the attributes.

items.title: Aggregates
items.text:
An Aggregate is a cluster of entities and value objects treated as a single unit for data changes. Every aggregate has one Aggregate Root — the only entry point for modifications.

flowchart TB
  subgraph Order [Aggregate: Order]
    root[Order\n«root»]
    item1[OrderItem]
    item2[OrderItem]
    addr[ShippingAddress\n«value object»]
    root --> item1
    root --> item2
    root --> addr
  end

Rules:

  • External code holds references only to the root, never to internal entities.
  • All invariants are enforced by the root. Example: "an order cannot have more than 50 items" is checked inside Order.addItem().
  • Aggregates are the unit of persistence — save and load the whole aggregate together.
  • Reference other aggregates by identity only. An OrderItem keeps the product's id, not a Product object; the order keeps the account id, not an Account. Otherwise one aggregate could change another, and the two could never live in different services.
  • One transaction changes one aggregate. If a use case must change two aggregates, the second change happens afterwards, triggered by a domain event (eventual consistency).

An invariant is a rule that must always hold for the aggregate to be valid. The root is where it is checked:

public class Order {                                  // aggregate root
    private static final int MAX_ITEMS = 50;

    private final OrderId id;
    private final AccountId accountId;                // other aggregate: by id only
    private final List<OrderItem> items = new ArrayList<>();
    private Money total = new Money(BigDecimal.ZERO, Currency.getInstance("USD"));

    public void addItem(ProductId productId, int quantity, Money unitPrice) {
        if (quantity <= 0)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be positive");
        if (items.size() >= MAX_ITEMS)
            throw new IllegalStateException("an order has at most " + MAX_ITEMS + " items");
        OrderItem item = new OrderItem(productId, quantity, unitPrice.multiply(quantity));
        items.add(item);
        total = total.add(item.total());              // invariant: total = sum of items
    }

    public List<OrderItem> items() {
        return List.copyOf(items);                    // callers cannot bypass the root
    }
}

items.title: Repositories
items.text:
A Repository provides a collection-like interface for retrieving and persisting aggregates. Repositories hide all database details from the domain model.

public interface OrderRepository {
    Optional<Order> findById(OrderId id);
    List<Order> findByCustomer(CustomerId customerId);
    Order save(Order order);
}

The domain declares the interface; the infrastructure provides the implementation (JPA, MongoDB, in-memory). In the hands-on, AccountRepository extends CrudRepository<AccountModel, String> is such an interface, and Spring Data generates the implementation. There is one repository per aggregate root — there is no OrderItemRepository, because items are only saved through their order.

items.title: Domain Events
items.text:
A Domain Event is a record of something that happened in the domain — past tense, immutable. Events are the primary mechanism for decoupling bounded contexts.

public record OrderPlaced(
    OrderId orderId,
    CustomerId customerId,
    Instant occurredAt
) {}

When the Order aggregate is placed, it raises OrderPlaced. Other bounded contexts (Inventory, Billing, Notifications) subscribe to this event and react independently — without the Order context knowing who is listening. In Hands-on 9 this is the OrderCreated event that the order service publishes to the Kafka topic order-events and the notification service consumes.

items.title: Domain Services
items.text:
Operations that don't naturally belong to any entity or value object — typically involving multiple aggregates or requiring external information.

// Neither Order nor Customer "owns" this logic — it needs both
public class PricingService {
    public Money calculateTotal(Order order, CustomerDiscount discount) { ... }
}
