items.title: Using DDD to find microservice boundaries
items.text:
Event Storming (Alberto Brandolini)4 is the most effective technique for discovering bounded contexts collaboratively. Domain experts and developers gather in front of a wall of sticky notes and map out the entire domain on a shared timeline.

flowchart LR
    ev1["🟠 OrderPlaced\n(domain event)"]
    ev2["🟠 PaymentCharged"]
    ev3["🟠 InventoryReserved"]
    ev4["🟠 OrderShipped"]
    cmd1["🔵 Place Order\n(command)"]
    cmd2["🔵 Charge Card"]
    cmd3["🔵 Reserve Items"]

    cmd1 --> ev1 --> cmd2 & cmd3
    cmd2 --> ev2
    cmd3 --> ev3
    ev2 & ev3 --> ev4

The process:

  1. Identify domain events (orange) — things that happened, past tense: OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed, ItemShipped
  2. Add commands (blue) — what triggered each event: Place Order, Charge Card
  3. Group by bounded context — cluster events and commands that belong together under the same ubiquitous language
  4. Draw context maps — identify how contexts interact: shared kernel, customer/supplier relationship, or anti-corruption layer (see Context maps)
  5. One context → one service as a starting point; merge or split based on operational and team constraints

Bounded context ≠ microservice (always)

A bounded context is a conceptual boundary. In practice, a small team might implement two related bounded contexts in one service to avoid the operational overhead of a separate deployment. Only split when independence of deployment or scale becomes valuable.

Common DDD mistakes

  • Entity services: one service per table or noun (OrderItemService, AddressService). They have no behaviour of their own and must always be called together.
  • Anemic domain model: entities with only getters and setters, and every rule in a service class. Nothing protects the invariants; put the rule in the aggregate root.
  • One giant model: a single Customer/Product class shared by every service through a common library — every change forces every service to redeploy.
  • Aggregates that are too big: an Account aggregate that contains all its orders. Loading an account loads thousands of orders, and two users editing different orders conflict. Keep aggregates small; link by id.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Strategic DDD finds the boundaries (subdomains, bounded contexts, context maps); tactical DDD shapes the code inside each one.
  • A ubiquitous language keeps business, code and API using the same words (Account, /accounts).
  • A bounded context is where one model is valid — the natural candidate for a microservice.
  • Context maps name the relationships; an anti-corruption layer keeps a third-party model out of your code.
  • Aggregates protect invariants through their root, reference other aggregates by id, and change in one transaction each.
  • Domain events (past tense) let other contexts react without the producer knowing them.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• Why boundaries matter: Microservices. The infrastructure around them: Architecture & Components.
  • Keeping the domain independent of frameworks inside a service: Clean Architecture and Hexagonal Architecture.
  • Domain events on a broker: Event-Driven Architecture, Hands-on 9 — Kafka.
  • Model your own contexts: Product API, Order API, Exchange API.

  1. EVANS, E. Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software. Addison-Wesley, 2003. ↩

  2. VERNON, V. Implementing Domain-Driven Design. Addison-Wesley, 2013. ↩

  3. Domain-Driven Design Reference — Eric Evans's condensed reference card. ↩

  4. BRANDOLINI, A. Introducing Event Storming. eventstorming.com. ↩

items.title: Observability
items.text:
A system you cannot observe is a system you cannot operate. Monitoring tells you that something is wrong; observability tells you why. The distinction matters in microservices: a request that touches eight services and three databases cannot be diagnosed from a single metric on a single dashboard. Observability is the property of a system that makes its internal state inferable from external outputs.

Picture a customer complaining that "checkout is slow" in the store. The request went through Nginx, the gateway, the auth check, the order service, the product service and Postgres, and maybe published an event to Kafka. Which one was slow? Was it slow for everyone or just for this customer? Without telemetry designed in advance — numbers, records and request paths emitted by every service — the only answer is guessing.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Explain the difference between monitoring and observability, and which question each pillar (metrics, logs, traces) answers.
  • Write PromQL queries for request rate, error ratio and latency percentiles of a Spring Boot service, and build RED / USE dashboards.
  • Configure structured logs that carry the trace ID, and correlate a log line with its trace.
  • Explain how trace context crosses services with the W3C traceparent header, and choose a sampling strategy.
  • Instrument a Spring Boot service with OpenTelemetry (Java agent and manual spans) and design symptom-based alerts.

items.title: Slides
items.text: Click the slides and use ← → to move through them; F goes full screen and P opens the presenter view, with the notes. Open the slides in a new tab

items.title: The Three Pillars
items.text:
Observability is built on three complementary data types. Each answers a different question about system behaviour.

Pillar Answers Toolchain Retention Metrics Is the system healthy right now? Is it trending up or down? Prometheus → Grafana Weeks to months (aggregated) Logs What exactly happened, and in what sequence? ELK / EFK / Loki Days to weeks Traces Which service in this request was slow? Where did the error originate? Jaeger / Tempo / Zipkin Days

All three describe the same events from different angles. One POST /orders that fails produces: an increment of a counter http_server_requests_seconds_count{status="500"} (metric), a JSON line {"level":"ERROR","msg":"product not found",...} (log), and a trace with one span per hop, the last one marked ERROR (trace). Metrics are cheap and tell you that something changed; logs and traces are more expensive and tell you what and where.

Observability ≠ Monitoring

Monitoring asks pre-defined questions: "Is the error rate below 1%?" Observability lets you ask questions you didn't think of at design time: "Why are exactly 7% of requests from mobile clients in São Paulo timing out on a Tuesday?" Observability requires all three pillars working together2.

items.title: Prometheus Data Model
items.text:
Every time series has a metric name and a set of key-value labels:

http_requests_total{method="GET", status="200", service="order"} 4823
Type What it measures Example Counter Monotonically increasing value; never decreases http_requests_total, errors_total Gauge Current value that can go up or down memory_bytes, active_connections Histogram Distribution of values in configurable buckets http_request_duration_seconds{le="0.1"} Summary Pre-calculated quantiles (less flexible than histogram) http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.99"}

A label is a dimension of the series: every distinct combination of label values is a separate time series stored by Prometheus.

items.title: PromQL Basics
items.text:
PromQL is Prometheus' query language. The queries below use the metric that Spring Boot (Micrometer) exports for every HTTP endpoint, http_server_requests_seconds, with the labels application, uri, method and status:

Query Meaning rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m]) Requests per second, averaged over the last 5 minutes sum by (application) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])) 5xx errors per second, per service sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) Error ratio (0–1) — the basis of an availability SLI histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m]))) P99 latency across all instances increase(http_server_requests_seconds_count[1h]) Total requests in the last hour

Two rules: apply rate() or increase() to a counter before summing (they handle counter resets when a pod restarts), and keep the le label when summing histogram buckets (sum by (le)), because histogram_quantile needs it. The _bucket series exist only if histograms are enabled: management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true.

Why percentiles, not averages

If 99 requests take 50 ms and 1 takes 5 s, the average is ~100 ms — it looks fine, but one user in a hundred waits 5 seconds. P99 (the value below which 99% of requests fall) exposes that tail; with many calls per page, most users hit the tail somewhere.

items.title: RED, USE and the Golden Signals
items.text:
Method For Metrics RED (Tom Wilkie) Services / APIs Rate (requests/sec), Errors (error rate), Duration (latency percentiles) USE (Brendan Gregg) Infrastructure / Resources Utilisation (% busy), Saturation (queue depth), Errors Four golden signals (Google SRE1) Any user-facing system Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation

Which method to use?

Use RED for service-level dashboards (what users experience), USE for infrastructure dashboards (what resources experience). Both together give complete coverage.

items.title: Metrics Pipeline
items.text:
flowchart LR
    app["Spring Boot\n(Actuator + Micrometer)"]
    prom["Prometheus"]
    grafana["Grafana\n(dashboards + alerts)"]
    prom -->|"scrapes /actuator/prometheus (e.g. every 15 s)"| app
    prom -->|"PromQL queries"| grafana

Prometheus uses a pull model: the application only exposes its current values at an HTTP endpoint, and Prometheus fetches (scrapes) them on a schedule and stores them as time series. This is what Hands-on 6 sets up for the store.

Spring Boot Actuator configuration to expose the Prometheus endpoint (it also needs the io.micrometer:micrometer-registry-prometheus dependency):

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus
  metrics:
    tags:
      application: ${spring.application.name}

Label cardinality

Never put unbounded values — user ID, order ID, e-mail, full URL with IDs — in a metric label. Each distinct value creates a new time series; 100,000 users × 10 endpoints × 5 status codes is 5 million series, and Prometheus runs out of memory. High-cardinality details belong in logs and traces. (This is why Spring Boot uses the URI template /orders/{id} as the uri label, not /orders/42.)

items.title: Alerting
items.text:
Dashboards need someone looking at them; alerts notify a human when action is needed. Prometheus evaluates alerting rules and sends firing alerts to Alertmanager (or Grafana Alerting), which routes them to e-mail, Slack or a pager.

groups:
  - name: order-service
    rules:
      - alert: OrderHighErrorRatio
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order"}[5m])) > 0.05
        for: 5m                     # must hold for 5 minutes, avoids flapping
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "More than 5% of order requests are failing"

Alert on symptoms, not causes

Page people for what users feel — error ratio, latency, an SLO error budget burning fast (see SLI / SLO / SLA) — not for "CPU above 80%". High CPU with happy users is not an emergency; an alert that fires without requiring action trains people to ignore alerts.

items.title: Structured vs Unstructured
items.text: Unstructured Structured (JSON) Example 2024-01-15 ERROR Order 42 failed {"level":"ERROR","orderId":42,"msg":"failed","traceId":"abc123"} Searchable grep / regex only Full field queries Aggregatable Hard Easy (Kibana, Loki) Machine-parseable Brittle Reliable

items.title: Log Levels
items.text: Level Use TRACE Extremely detailed — every method entry/exit. Never in production. DEBUG Diagnostic — variable values, decision points. Dev/staging only. INFO Significant events — startup, config loaded, request received WARN Something unexpected but handled — retry triggered, fallback used ERROR Failure requiring attention — exception caught, downstream unreachable

items.title: Correlation IDs and MDC
items.text:
When a request touches multiple services, a shared ID in every log line — a correlation ID — allows reconstructing the full call sequence by searching for that one value. With distributed tracing, the natural correlation ID is the trace ID.

In Java, the place to put it is the MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) of SLF4J/Logback: a per-thread map of key-value pairs that the logging framework can print in every line with %X{key}. Who fills the MDC depends on how the service is instrumented:

OpenTelemetry Java agent (automatic)Manual MDC (your own keys)

With the OTel Java agent attached (see below and Hands-on 10), you write no MDC code for the trace context. The agent's Logback/Log4j instrumentation puts the active trace_id, span_id and trace_flags into the MDC whenever a span is current, and removes them afterwards. You only reference the keys in the pattern:

%d{ISO8601} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} [trace_id=%X{trace_id} span_id=%X{span_id}] - %msg%n

Without the agent, the same keys can be filled by the opentelemetry-logback-mdc-1.0 library; Spring Boot's own Micrometer Tracing fills the keys traceId and spanId instead. Use the key names of the tool you actually run.

MDC.put is for business context that no tool can know — the customer ID, the order ID — or for a correlation ID when there is no tracing at all. Always remove what you put: threads are reused by the server's pool, and a forgotten key leaks into the next request's logs.

public Order create(OrderIn in) {
    try (var ignored = MDC.putCloseable("customerId", in.customerId())) {  // removed at the end
        log.info("creating order");   // ... [trace_id=4bf9...] customerId=c-42 ... creating order
        return repository.save(...);
    }
}

%d{ISO8601} %-5level [trace_id=%X{trace_id}] customerId=%X{customerId} %logger{36} - %msg%n

MDC is per thread

The MDC lives in a ThreadLocal. Work handed to another thread (@Async, CompletableFuture, reactive code such as the WebFlux gateway) does not see it unless the context is propagated; the OTel agent does this for the libraries it instruments, but your own MDC.put values are not copied automatically.

items.title: Log Aggregation Pipeline
items.text:
flowchart LR
    svc1["Service A\n(JSON logs → stdout)"]
    svc2["Service B\n(JSON logs → stdout)"]
    svc3["Service C\n(JSON logs → stdout)"]
    collector["Filebeat / Fluentd\n(collector)"]
    elastic["Elasticsearch\n(index + store)"]
    kibana["Kibana\n(search + dashboards)"]
    svc1 --> collector
    svc2 --> collector
    svc3 --> collector
    collector --> elastic
    elastic --> kibana

Loki as a lighter alternative

Loki (Grafana Labs) indexes only labels, not full text, making it much cheaper to operate than Elasticsearch. If you already run Prometheus and Grafana, adding Loki gives you log aggregation with zero new UI to learn — all signals live in the same Grafana dashboards.

items.title: Anatomy of a Trace
items.text:
A trace represents a single end-to-end request. It is composed of spans — one per operation (service call, DB query, cache lookup, etc.).

Field Description Example traceId Globally unique ID for the entire request (128 bits) 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736 spanId Unique ID for this operation 00f067aa0ba902b7 parentSpanId Span that triggered this one a2fb4a1d1a96d312 name Operation name GET /orders/{id} startTime / duration When it started and how long it took 2024-01-15T10:30:00Z, 45ms status OK / ERROR ERROR attributes Key-value tags http.status_code=500, db.type=postgresql

items.title: W3C traceparent Header
items.text:
The traceparent header propagates trace context across service boundaries using the format version-traceId-parentSpanId-flags:

traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
Field Value Meaning version 00 W3C spec version traceId 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736 128-bit globally unique trace ID parentSpanId 00f067aa0ba902b7 64-bit ID of the span that sent this request flags 01 Sampling flag (01 = sampled)

On every downstream call, a service keeps the version, the traceId and (normally) the flags exactly as received, and replaces the parentSpanId field with the ID of its own current span. This is how trace context crosses service boundaries without any service needing to understand the full trace. The header is defined by the W3C Trace Context recommendation5; OpenTelemetry uses it by default.

items.title: Request Flow with Spans
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor User
    participant GW as Gateway [span: root, 120ms]
    participant OS as OrderService [span: child, 95ms]
    participant DB as PostgreSQL [span: leaf, 40ms]

    User->>+GW: GET /orders/42<br/>traceparent: 00-abc...-root-01
    GW->>+OS: GET /orders/42<br/>traceparent: 00-abc...-gw_span-01
    OS->>+DB: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id=42
    DB-->>-OS: row data
    OS-->>-GW: 200 OK (95ms)
    GW-->>-User: 200 OK (120ms)

items.title: Sampling Strategies
items.text:
Recording every span of every request is expensive at scale, so tracing systems keep only a sample of traces.

Strategy How Tradeoff Head sampling The decision is made at the first span (e.g. keep 10% by trace ID: parentbased_traceidratio) and travels in the flags of traceparent, so every service agrees Cheap and simple, but blind: it drops 90% of the rare error traces too Tail sampling All spans are sent to the OTel Collector, which waits until the trace is complete and then decides Can keep every error or slow trace, but the Collector must buffer all spans in memory Rate-limiting Keep at most N traces per second Predictable cost; under a spike most traces are dropped

Production recommendation

Head and tail sampling are applied in sequence, so a trace dropped at the head can never be "rescued" by the tail. To keep every error trace, sample 100% at the head (or a high ratio) in the services, and let a tail-sampling policy in the OTel Collector keep all traces with an ERROR span or a high latency plus a small percentage (1–10%) of the normal ones. If you cannot run tail sampling, a head ratio of 1–10% is a reasonable default — accepting that some error traces will be lost and their logs are your fallback.

items.title: OpenTelemetry (OTel)
items.text:
OpenTelemetry is the CNCF standard for generating, collecting, and exporting telemetry3. It replaces vendor-specific SDKs (Zipkin client, Jaeger client, etc.) with a single neutral API, so switching backends requires only a configuration change, not a code change.

Component Role API Language-specific interfaces — Tracer, Meter, Logger SDK Implementation of the API; includes sampling, batching, exporters Collector Standalone process that receives, processes, and exports telemetry Exporter Protocol adapter that sends the data out: OTLP (the default), Zipkin, Prometheus, console OTLP The OpenTelemetry Protocol, over gRPC (port 4317) or HTTP/protobuf (port 4318); Jaeger, Tempo and most vendors accept it natively 
flowchart LR
    app["Application\n(OTel SDK)"]
    collector["OTel Collector"]
    prom["Prometheus\n(metrics)"]
    jaeger["Jaeger\n(traces)"]
    loki["Loki\n(logs)"]
    app -->|"OTLP (gRPC/HTTP)"| collector
    collector --> prom
    collector --> jaeger
    collector --> loki

items.title: Java Zero-Code Instrumentation
items.text:
The OTel Java agent instruments Spring Boot automatically via bytecode injection — no code changes required.

# pin a version: "latest" makes builds unreproducible
ADD https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java-instrumentation/releases/download/v2.4.0/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar /app/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar

ENTRYPOINT ["java", \
  "-javaagent:/app/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar", \
  "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

Configure the agent via environment variables in Docker Compose:

environment:
  OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: order-service
  OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL: grpc            # agent 2.x defaults to http/protobuf (port 4318)
  OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: http://jaeger:4317
  OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER: none
  OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER: none

Match the protocol to the port

Since version 2.0 the Java agent sends OTLP over HTTP/protobuf by default, which listens on port 4318. Either point it at http://jaeger:4318, or keep port 4317 and set OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc as above. A mismatch produces no traces and only an export error in the service log.

Why disable metrics/logs exporters?

The Java agent can export all three signals via OTLP. We disable metrics and logs here because Prometheus already scrapes metrics via Actuator and Loki (or ELK) handles logs separately. Enabling all three from the agent would duplicate data and inflate storage costs.

items.title: Manual Spans
items.text:
When automatic instrumentation is not granular enough — you want to see how long your price calculation took, not just the HTTP and SQL calls around it — add custom spans. Add the OTel API dependency (its version is managed by the opentelemetry-bom, or set it explicitly):

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.opentelemetry</groupId>
    <artifactId>opentelemetry-api</artifactId>
</dependency>

The simplest way, with the agent attached, is an annotation (dependency io.opentelemetry.instrumentation:opentelemetry-instrumentation-annotations):

@WithSpan("calculateTotal")
public BigDecimal calculateTotal(@SpanAttribute("order.items") int items, ...) { ... }

For full control, create the span yourself. The agent registers the global OpenTelemetry instance, so obtain the tracer from it (it is not a Spring bean unless you declare one):

private static final Tracer tracer =
    GlobalOpenTelemetry.getTracer("store.order");

public Order processOrder(OrderRequest request) {
    Span span = tracer.spanBuilder("processOrder").startSpan();
    try (Scope scope = span.makeCurrent()) {
        span.setAttribute("order.customerId", request.customerId());
        // ... business logic
        return order;
    } catch (Exception e) {
        span.recordException(e);
        span.setStatus(StatusCode.ERROR, e.getMessage());
        throw e;
    } finally {
        span.end();
    }
}

items.title: Grafana Unified Stack (LGTM)
items.text:
Loki + Grafana + Tempo + Mimir/Prometheus — the LGTM stack — puts all three observability signals into a single UI. The key advantage is signal correlation: you can jump from a metric spike to the traces that caused it to the log lines that explain it, all without leaving Grafana.

flowchart LR
    app["Application"]
    prom["Prometheus\n(metrics)"]
    loki["Loki\n(logs)"]
    tempo["Tempo\n(traces)"]
    grafana["Grafana"]
    app --> prom
    app --> loki
    app --> tempo
    prom --> grafana
    loki --> grafana
    tempo --> grafana

A typical drill-down workflow: a metric alert fires in Grafana → click "View Traces" to open the correlated trace in Tempo → click a span to see the correlated log lines from Loki. This cross-signal navigation is what separates an observability platform from three isolated monitoring tools.

items.title: DORA Metrics
items.text:
DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) identified four metrics that predict software delivery performance and organisational performance4. Two measure throughput (how fast changes flow) and two measure stability (how often changes break things and how fast you recover). Elite-performing teams score well on all four simultaneously — speed and stability are not a trade-off.

Metric Measures Elite benchmark (State of DevOps 2024) Deployment Frequency How often code reaches production On demand (multiple deploys per day) Change Lead Time Commit to running in production Less than one day Change Failure Rate % of deployments that need a fix or rollback ~5% Failed Deployment Recovery Time (formerly MTTR / time to restore service) How long to recover from a failed deployment Less than one hour

DORA and observability

DORA metrics are themselves telemetry. Deployment frequency comes from CI/CD logs (Hands-on 4). Recovery time requires precise incident start and end timestamps from your monitoring system. Change Failure Rate requires correlating deployment events with error-rate spikes. You cannot improve what you cannot measure — and you cannot measure it without observability infrastructure.

items.title: Observability Snapshot: Spike Simulation
items.text:
The chart below simulates what the three observability pillars look like during a traffic spike. Panel 1 shows the request rate rising sharply at steps 10–12; Panel 2 shows error events clustering in the same window; Panel 3 shows trace span durations stretching out under load.

2026-10-23T08:15:37.777668 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The three panels share a timeline: the spike visible in Panel 1 directly explains the error cluster in Panel 2, and both explain the stretched span durations in Panel 3. Without all three pillars, you would see only one piece of the picture.

Common pitfalls

  • Logging everything at INFO (or DEBUG in production): log volume and cost explode, and the useful lines drown.
  • Logging secrets or personal data: passwords, JWTs, card numbers and e-mails must never reach the log pipeline.
  • Unbounded metric labels: user or order IDs as labels crash Prometheus — put them in logs and traces.
  • Broken context propagation: one service without instrumentation (or a proxy that drops traceparent) splits every trace in two.
  • Alerting on causes, not symptoms: dozens of CPU and memory alerts nobody acts on hide the one that matters.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• Hands-on 6 — Prometheus and Grafana for the store's metrics.
  • Hands-on 10 — OpenTelemetry Java agent, Jaeger and trace_id in the logs.
  • Reliability and SLI / SLO / SLA — SLIs are PromQL queries over these metrics; burn-rate alerts use them.
  • Event-Driven Architecture — tracing across Kafka topics and monitoring consumer lag.
  • Exercise: Bottlenecks — using observability to find where the platform is slow.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Monitoring answers known questions; observability lets you investigate new ones from metrics (that), logs (what) and traces (where).
  • Prometheus scrapes /actuator/prometheus; use rate() on counters, histogram_quantile with sum by (le) for percentiles, and keep labels low-cardinality.
  • Build dashboards with RED (services) and USE (resources); alert on symptoms users feel.
  • Logs must be structured and carry the trace_id — filled automatically by the OTel agent; use MDC.put only for your own business keys.
  • A trace is a tree of spans linked by traceparent; head sampling is cheap but blind, tail sampling keeps the interesting traces.
  • OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard; measure delivery performance with the four DORA metrics.

  1. BEYER, B. et al. Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems. O'Reilly, 2016. ↩

  2. MAJORS, C.; FONG-JONES, L.; MIRANDA, G. Observability Engineering. O'Reilly, 2022. ↩

  3. OPENTELEMETRY. opentelemetry.io — specification, SDKs, Collector. ↩

  4. FORSGREN, N.; HUMBLE, J.; KIM, G. Accelerate: The Science of Lean Software and DevOps. IT Revolution, 2018. See also the yearly DORA State of DevOps reports. ↩

  5. W3C. Trace Context. W3C Recommendation. ↩

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: The Three Pillars
items.text:
Q1. A user reports that request 7f3d... returned a 500 error. Which pillar(s) would you use to diagnose the root cause?

  • A. Metrics — check the error rate counter for that time window
  • B. Logs — search for the specific request ID in the log stream
  • C. Traces — find the specific trace and inspect which span failed
  • D. Both B and C — logs for the exception detail, traces for the call path
Answer

D — Both logs and traces are needed.

The trace shows which service in the call chain caused the error and how long each hop took, narrowing the investigation to a single span. The logs inside that service then reveal the exact exception class, message, and stack trace. Neither pillar alone gives the full picture: traces without logs tell you where but not why; logs without traces make it hard to identify which service among many produced the matching log line.

Q2. Why is a Histogram preferred over a Summary for latency metrics in Prometheus?

  • A. Histograms use less storage than summaries at high cardinality
  • B. Histograms are calculated server-side, so dashboards load faster
  • C. Histograms allow quantile calculation across multiple instances and arbitrary time windows in PromQL; summaries pre-calculate quantiles in the client and cannot be aggregated
  • D. Summaries are deprecated and no longer supported by Prometheus
Answer

C — Histograms are aggregatable; summaries are not.

A Summary calculates quantiles inside the application process — once exported, the p99 value of instance A and instance B cannot be meaningfully combined. A Histogram exports raw bucket counts, so histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m]))) correctly computes the p99 across all instances and across any chosen time window. In a horizontally-scaled microservice this distinction is critical.

items.title: PromQL and Metrics
items.text:
Q3. What does rate(http_errors_total[5m]) return?

  • A. The total number of errors that occurred in the last 5 minutes
  • B. The per-second average rate of increase of http_errors_total over the last 5-minute window
  • C. The error rate as a percentage of total requests
  • D. The number of errors per minute, sampled once every 5 minutes
Answer

B — Per-second average rate of increase over the 5-minute window.

rate() divides the total increase in the counter over the window by the window duration in seconds. A counter that increased by 300 in 5 minutes returns 1.0 (one error per second). Because rate() operates on the raw counter, it handles counter resets (service restarts) correctly, which increase() also does but as an absolute count rather than a per-second rate.

items.title: Logs
items.text:
Q4. What is the purpose of MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) in logging?

  • A. It sets the log level per class at runtime without restarting the service
  • B. It attaches key-value pairs (such as traceId) to every log line produced by the current thread, enabling correlation across log entries
  • C. It compresses log output to reduce storage costs
  • D. It routes log lines to different files based on severity level
Answer

B — Attaches key-value pairs to every log line on the current thread.

MDC stores a thread-local map whose values the logging framework (Logback, Log4j2) can print in every log line using a pattern like %X{trace_id}. With the OpenTelemetry Java agent, the agent itself puts trace_id and span_id into the MDC while a span is active, so every log line of the request carries the same ID with no application code — making it trivial to filter an entire request's log history with a single query. MDC.put is still useful for your own business keys (customer ID, order ID), which you must remove at the end of the request.

items.title: Distributed Traces
items.text:
Q5. Why does every span in a distributed trace share the same traceId?

  • A. Because all spans are created by the first service, which distributes them
  • B. Because the traceId is generated once at the entry point and propagated in the traceparent header to every downstream service, which copies it unchanged into their own spans
  • C. Because the tracing backend assigns a common ID when it assembles the trace from individual spans
  • D. Because spans are stored in the same database table and inherit the row ID
Answer

B — The traceId is generated once and propagated via traceparent.

When the first service (e.g., the API gateway) receives a request with no traceparent header, it generates a 128-bit traceId and creates the root span. Every outgoing HTTP call includes traceparent: 00-<traceId>-<currentSpanId>-01. Each downstream service reads this header, keeps the traceId unchanged, generates a new spanId, and sets parentSpanId to the received spanId. The result is a tree of spans that all share the same traceId, which the tracing backend uses to assemble the full trace view.

Q6. A service receives traceparent: 00-abc123000000000000000000000000aa-def456000000000000-01 and creates a child span with ID 999888000000000000. What does the traceparent header it sends to the next downstream service look like?

  • A. 00-abc123000000000000000000000000aa-def456000000000000-01 (unchanged)
  • B. 00-999888000000000000000000000000bb-abc123000000000000-01 (new traceId)
  • C. 00-abc123000000000000000000000000aa-999888000000000000-01 (same traceId, new spanId)
  • D. 00-abc123000000000000000000000000aa-def456000000000000-999888000000000000-01 (appended)
Answer

C — Same traceId, new spanId equal to the current span's ID.

The traceId (abc123...) never changes across the entire request — that is the invariant that links all spans together. The parentSpanId field in the new header is set to the current span's ID (999888...), so the downstream service knows exactly which span triggered the call. The received def456... becomes the parentSpanId of the current span (stored in the span record), not forwarded further.

items.title: Sampling
items.text:
Q7. What is the key difference between head sampling and tail sampling?

  • A. Head sampling is done by the application; tail sampling is done by the tracing backend
  • B. Head sampling decides whether to record a trace at the very first span before any downstream calls are made; tail sampling decides after the complete trace is assembled, allowing it to favour traces with errors or high latency
  • C. Head sampling keeps 100% of traces; tail sampling discards them
  • D. They are synonyms for the same strategy applied at different layers of the stack
Answer

B — Decision timing is the core difference.

Head sampling must commit to record or drop a trace at the moment the root span is created, with no knowledge of what will happen downstream. This is fast and has near-zero overhead but will randomly discard some error traces. Tail sampling buffers spans until the trace is complete, then applies rules — for example, keep all traces where any span has status=ERROR. The tradeoff is higher memory and latency in the collector.

items.title: OpenTelemetry
items.text:
Q8. Which OpenTelemetry component can receive telemetry from multiple services, apply filtering and batching, and fan the data out to multiple backends simultaneously?

  • A. The OTel API — it abstracts over multiple backends in the application code
  • B. The OTel SDK — it batches spans before exporting
  • C. The OTel Collector — a standalone process that acts as a pipeline between producers and backends
  • D. The OTLP exporter — it can route to multiple endpoints from within the SDK
Answer

C — The OTel Collector.

The Collector is a vendor-agnostic proxy deployed as a sidecar or as a cluster-level gateway. Its pipeline has three stages: receivers (accept OTLP, Jaeger, Zipkin, etc.), processors (filter, sample, batch, add attributes), and exporters (send to Prometheus, Jaeger, Loki, Datadog, etc. simultaneously). Centralising telemetry routing in the Collector means changing backends requires only a Collector config change, not a redeployment of every application.

items.title: DORA Metrics
items.text:
Q9. Which DORA metric most directly measures how quickly a team can respond to a production incident?

  • A. Deployment Frequency — more deploys means faster response
  • B. Lead Time for Changes — measures the full commit-to-production pipeline
  • C. Change Failure Rate — tracks how often deployments cause incidents
  • D. Failed Deployment Recovery Time (formerly MTTR / time to restore service) — measures elapsed time from a failure to service restoration
Answer

D — Failed Deployment Recovery Time (formerly MTTR).

This metric is the time from when a failure starts (typically when an alert fires) to when the service is restored to normal operation. It directly captures incident response effectiveness — including detection speed, diagnosis time, fix deployment, and verification. Deployment frequency and lead time measure throughput; change failure rate measures how often changes break things, not how fast you recover. Elite teams recover in under one hour.

items.title: Java Agent Instrumentation
items.text:
Q10. The OpenTelemetry Java agent instruments Spring Boot without code changes. How does it achieve this?

  • A. It requires annotating all classes with @OtelInstrumented
  • B. It uses Java bytecode instrumentation (java.lang.instrument API) to modify loaded classes at runtime
  • C. It reads application.properties and generates proxy classes at startup
  • D. It requires rebuilding the application with a special Maven plugin
Answer

B — Java bytecode instrumentation via java.lang.instrument.

The JVM's java.lang.instrument API, combined with a ClassFileTransformer, allows a -javaagent JAR to intercept every class as it is loaded and rewrite its bytecode before it reaches the application. The OTel Java agent uses this mechanism to inject span creation, HTTP header propagation, and JDBC tracing into Spring MVC, RestTemplate, WebClient, Hibernate, and dozens of other libraries — all without touching the application source code.

items.title: Added topics
items.text:
Q11. A developer adds the label userId to the metric http_server_requests_seconds so they can see the latency of each user. The store has 200,000 users. What is the problem?

  • A. None — Prometheus compresses labels, so extra labels are free
  • B. Every distinct label value creates a new time series; hundreds of thousands of series per endpoint and status make Prometheus' memory and query cost explode (high cardinality)
  • C. Prometheus rejects labels whose name ends in Id
  • D. The metric becomes a gauge instead of a histogram
Answer

B — Unbounded label cardinality.

A time series is identified by its metric name plus the full set of label values, so 200,000 users × each URI × each status × each histogram bucket is millions of series. Per-user detail belongs in logs and traces (which are designed for high-cardinality fields); metrics should use bounded labels such as uri (the template /orders/{id}), method and status.

Q12. The services use head sampling at 10%, and the OTel Collector has a tail-sampling rule "keep 100% of traces with an ERROR span". What fraction of error traces ends up in Jaeger?

  • A. 100% — the tail rule overrides the head decision
  • B. About 10% — traces dropped by head sampling are never sent to the Collector, so the tail rule cannot recover them
  • C. 0% — head and tail sampling cannot be combined
  • D. 110% — the two rules add up
Answer

B — About 10%.

Sampling decisions are applied in sequence: a trace not sampled at the head is never recorded or exported, so the Collector never sees it. To keep all error traces, sample 100% (or a high ratio) at the head and let the Collector's tail-sampling policy keep all error/slow traces plus a small fraction of the others.

Q13. Why should histogram_quantile be applied to sum by (le) (rate(..._bucket[5m])) rather than to sum(rate(..._bucket[5m]))?

  • A. sum without by (le) merges all buckets into one number, removing the bucket boundaries that histogram_quantile needs to estimate the percentile
  • B. by (le) makes the query faster but gives the same result
  • C. le stands for "latency estimate" and is required by Grafana
  • D. Without by (le) the result is in milliseconds instead of seconds
Answer

A — The le label carries the bucket boundaries.

Each histogram bucket is a series with an le ("less than or equal") label, such as le="0.1". Summing across instances must keep le so that each bucket's counts from all instances are added together; summing everything into one number destroys the distribution and histogram_quantile returns nothing useful.

Q14. Which alert is the best one to wake up the on-call engineer at 3 a.m.?

  • A. CPU of an order-service pod above 80% for 5 minutes
  • B. JVM heap usage above 70%
  • C. More than 5% of POST /orders requests returning 5xx for 5 minutes (or the SLO error budget burning at 14.4×)
  • D. A new deployment was made
Answer

C — Alert on a symptom users feel.

Paging alerts should be urgent, actionable and tied to user impact: failing orders are exactly that. High CPU or heap usage (A, B) may be perfectly normal while users are happy — they are causes worth a dashboard or a ticket, not a page. A deployment (D) is an event to annotate on dashboards, not an alert.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Picture the store on a Black Friday evening. The product service is healthy, the database is healthy, but the payment provider starts answering in 3 seconds instead of 100 ms. Within a minute the gateway stops answering everything — login, catalogue, cart — even though nothing on those routes is broken. Nobody wrote a bug; the system simply had no defence against a slow dependency. This class is about building the defences, and about deciding with numbers how much failure is acceptable.

Reliability is the probability that a system performs its required function without failure, under stated conditions, for a specified period of time1. In distributed systems, this definition expands beyond hardware to encompass software failures, network partitions, overloaded dependencies, and incorrect deployments.

A reliable system is not one that never fails. It is one that fails gracefully, recovers quickly, and limits the blast radius of any single failure on its users. (The blast radius is the set of users and components affected by one failure.)

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Calculate availability from MTTF and MTTR, the downtime allowed by a number of "nines", and the end-to-end availability of services in series and in parallel.
  • Classify a failure (transient, permanent, intermittent, Byzantine) and explain how a cascading failure spreads through exhausted resources.
  • Define SLIs and SLOs for a service of the store and compute its error budget and burn rate.
  • Choose and configure resilience patterns — timeout, retry with backoff and jitter, circuit breaker, bulkhead, rate limiting, health checks — for a call between two services.
  • Design a chaos experiment with a steady-state hypothesis and a controlled blast radius.

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
1. This overview — availability, the "nines", composite availability, failure modes and cascading failures.
  2. SLI / SLO / SLA — how to measure reliability, set targets, and turn the gap into an error budget.
  3. Resilience Patterns — timeout, retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, rate limiting and health checks, and how to layer them.
  4. Chaos Engineering — injecting failures on purpose to prove that the patterns work.
  5. Quiz — check your understanding.

items.title: Availability
items.text:
The most visible expression of reliability is availability — the fraction of time a system is in a functioning state. Reliability and availability are related but not identical: a service that crashes for one second every minute has poor reliability (it fails often) but still about 98% availability; a service that fails once a year but takes a week to repair is very reliable and poorly available. Availability is derived from two measurable quantities:

Term Full name Meaning MTTF Mean Time To Failure Average time the system operates before a failure occurs MTTR Mean Time To Repair (or Recover) Average time to detect, diagnose, and restore service after a failure MTBF Mean Time Between Failures MTTF + MTTR — the complete failure-and-recovery cycle \[ \text{Availability} = \frac{MTTF}{MTTF + MTTR} \]

Worked example — the order service

The order service crashes on average once every 30 days (MTTF = 720 h). Each time, it takes 2 hours for someone to notice, find the cause and restart it (MTTR = 2 h).

Availability = 720 / (720 + 2) ≈ 99.72%.

Two ways to improve it:

  • Halve the failures (MTTF = 1440 h) → 1440 / 1442 ≈ 99.86%.
  • Let Kubernetes restart the pod automatically in 1 minute (MTTR ≈ 0.017 h) → 720 / 720.017 ≈ 99.998%.

Recovering faster was the bigger win — and much cheaper than never failing.

Key insight: reliability improves by either preventing failures (↑ MTTF) or recovering faster (↓ MTTR). Most engineering investments target one of these two levers. Incident response, automation, and runbooks primarily attack MTTR. Fault-tolerant design, testing, and redundancy primarily attack MTTF.

items.title: The "nines" of availability
items.text:
Availability targets are usually quoted as a number of "nines". The table below shows how much downtime each target allows, per window (year = 365.25 days, month = 1/12 of a year ≈ 30.44 days):

Availability Per year Per month Per 28 days Per week 90% ("one nine") 36.5 days 73.1 hours 2.8 days 16.8 hours 99% ("two nines") 3.65 days 7.31 hours 6.72 hours 1.68 hours 99.9% ("three nines") 8.77 hours 43.8 minutes 40.3 minutes 10.1 minutes 99.95% 4.38 hours 21.9 minutes 20.2 minutes 5.04 minutes 99.99% ("four nines") 52.6 minutes 4.38 minutes 4.03 minutes 1.01 minutes 99.999% ("five nines") 5.26 minutes 26.3 seconds 24.2 seconds 6.05 seconds 99.9999% ("six nines") 31.6 seconds 2.63 seconds 2.42 seconds 0.60 seconds

Each additional "nine" is a 10× reduction in allowable downtime. Moving from three nines to four nines is not an incremental improvement — it requires a fundamentally different operational posture. At five nines, human reaction time is too slow; detection and recovery must be fully automated.

Always state the window

"99.9%" alone is ambiguous: it allows 43.8 minutes in a calendar month but 40.3 minutes in a 28-day window. Whenever you quote an availability number, quote the window it is measured over.

items.title: Composite availability
items.text:
Real requests cross several components, so the availability the user sees depends on how the components are combined3.

In series (dependency chain)In parallel (redundant replicas)

When a request needs every component to work, their availabilities multiply. The gateway calls the order service, which calls the product service, each at 99.9%:

\[ A_{chain} = 0.999 \times 0.999 \times 0.999 \approx 99.7\% \]

The chain is worse than any individual component. Every synchronous dependency you add lowers the ceiling.

When any one of \(n\) identical, independent replicas is enough, the system is down only if all of them are down at the same time:

\[ A_{parallel} = 1 - (1 - a)^n \]

Two gateway replicas at 99% each behind Nginx (Hands-on 7): \(1 - 0.01^2 = 99.99\%\). Redundancy turns two mediocre components into a very available one — as long as their failures really are independent (same bug, same host or same zone break that assumption).

flowchart LR
    user([User]) --> lb["Nginx"]
    lb --> g1["gateway #1<br/>99%"]
    lb --> g2["gateway #2<br/>99%"]
    g1 --> order["order<br/>99.9%"]
    g2 --> order
    order --> product["product<br/>99.9%"]

This is why redundancy (multiple instances) and isolation patterns (circuit breakers) exist: to break the failure-propagation chain.

items.title: Failure modes
items.text:
Distributed systems fail in ways that single-machine systems do not. Partial failures — where some components work and others do not — are far more common than total outages, and substantially harder to handle correctly.

flowchart TD
    F[Failure] --> T["Transient<br/>Temporary, self-healing<br/>e.g. brief network blip"]
    F --> P["Permanent<br/>Requires intervention<br/>e.g. disk crash, OOM kill"]
    F --> I["Intermittent<br/>Unpredictable recurrence<br/>e.g. memory leak, GC pause"]
    P --> CS["Crash-stop<br/>Node halts and stays halted"]
    P --> BZ["Byzantine<br/>Node behaves arbitrarily or incorrectly"]
Failure class Characteristics Handling strategy Transient Self-resolves within seconds; safe to retry Retry with exponential backoff and jitter Permanent (crash-stop) Node stops responding and never recovers Circuit breaker + failover to healthy replica Intermittent Appears and disappears without a clear trigger P99 latency histograms; anomaly-based alerting Byzantine Node returns incorrect data without crashing Consensus protocols; checksums; input validation

The most common failure in practice is not a crash but a slow response: the caller cannot tell a slow node from a dead one (see Distributed Systems), so it keeps waiting.

items.title: Cascading failures
items.text:
A single slow dependency can exhaust resources in its caller — thread pool slots, connection pool entries, memory — and propagate that exhaustion upstream through the entire service graph. This is the most dangerous failure pattern in microservice architectures2.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Users
    participant O as Order service (200 threads)
    participant P as Payment service
    U->>O: POST /orders (many per second)
    O->>P: charge (normally 100 ms)
    Note over P: degrades: 3 s per call
    Note over O: threads wait 30× longer → all 200 busy
    U->>O: GET /orders/42 (no payment needed)
    O-->>U: 503 — no free thread
    Note over U,O: unrelated routes fail too

The arithmetic is simple (Little's law: requests in flight = arrival rate × time each one takes). At 60 orders per second and 100 ms per payment call, about 6 threads are busy waiting on payment. At 3 s per call, 180 threads are — almost the whole pool — and every other route of the order service starves. If the gateway in turn waits on the order service, the exhaustion climbs one more level. Timeouts, circuit breakers, and bulkheads (Resilience Patterns) are the engineering response to this failure mode.

Common pitfalls

  • No timeout on an HTTP client (or a default of minutes): one slow dependency holds threads indefinitely.
  • Retrying blindly: retries multiply the load on a service that is already struggling, turning a slowdown into an outage.
  • Shared pools: one connection or thread pool for every dependency means the worst dependency decides for all.
  • Assuming independence: two replicas on the same node, or with the same bad config, fail together.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• Distributed Systems — partial failure and the impossibility of telling slow from dead.
  • Observability — SLIs are computed from metrics; you cannot run SLOs or chaos experiments without it.
  • Event-Driven Architecture — asynchronous messaging removes the caller's wait from the chain; DLQs handle poison messages.
  • Hands-on 5 (Kubernetes self-healing), Hands-on 7 (replicas behind a load balancer) and Hands-on 6 (Prometheus and Grafana for SLIs).

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR); faster recovery is often the cheapest improvement.
  • Each extra nine is 10× less downtime — and always state the window a number refers to.
  • In series availabilities multiply (worse than any part); in parallel, redundancy gives \(1-(1-a)^n\).
  • Partial and slow failures are the norm; a slow dependency exhausts its caller's resources and cascades upstream.
  • The rest of the class measures reliability (SLOs, error budgets), contains failures (resilience patterns), and proves the containment works (chaos engineering).

  1. IEEE Standard Glossary of Software Engineering Terminology, IEEE Std 610.12-1990. ↩

  2. NYGARD, M. Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, 2nd ed. Pragmatic Programmers, 2018. ↩

  3. BEYER, B. et al. Site Reliability Engineering. Google / O'Reilly, 2016. ↩

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: SLI / SLO / SLA / Error Budget
items.text:
Q1. Why is CPU utilisation a poor Service Level Indicator (SLI)?

  • A. It is too difficult to measure accurately with modern tools
  • B. It measures infrastructure state, not user-perceived quality — a service can have 95% CPU and serve all requests correctly, or 5% CPU and be completely down
  • C. CPU metrics reset on each container restart, making trending impossible
  • D. It is not supported by Prometheus or Grafana
Answer

B — Measures infrastructure, not user experience.

A good SLI reflects whether the user is getting value from the service. CPU utilisation correlates poorly with user experience — a CPU-bound service may still respond correctly, while a service with idle CPU might be down due to a deadlock. Use request success rate, latency percentiles, or error rate instead.

Q2. For a 99.9% availability SLO over 28 days, approximately how many minutes of downtime are permitted?

  • A. ~4.03 minutes
  • B. ~40.3 minutes
  • C. ~403 minutes
  • D. ~8.77 hours
Answer

B — ~40.3 minutes.

28 days × 24 h × 60 min = 40,320 minutes, and 0.1% of that is ≈ 40.3 minutes. The figure of ~43.8 minutes that appears in many "nines" tables is for an average calendar month (365.25 / 12 ≈ 30.44 days), and 8.77 hours is the budget for a whole year. Always compute the budget for the window the SLO actually uses.

Q3. What happens to engineering work priorities when the error budget is exhausted?

  • A. The SLO is automatically relaxed to 99.5% for the remainder of the window
  • B. The operations team takes over all deployments until the next window starts
  • C. Non-essential deployments are frozen and reliability work takes priority over feature work until the budget resets
  • D. The team pages the on-call engineer who must approve all subsequent commits
Answer

C — Non-essential deploys frozen; reliability work prioritised.

The error budget is the team's licence to take risk. When it is gone, further risky deployments would push the SLO breach from "possible" to "guaranteed." The budget policy creates an objective, data-driven mechanism for the SRE and PM to agree: "we're out of budget this month, features wait."

Q4. What is the key distinction between an SLO and an SLA?

  • A. An SLO applies to APIs; an SLA applies to databases
  • B. An SLO is an internal engineering target (stricter); an SLA is a legal contract with customers that carries financial consequences if breached (more lenient)
  • C. SLOs are measured in percentages; SLAs are measured in absolute downtime minutes
  • D. SLOs expire after 28 days; SLAs are permanent until renegotiated
Answer

B — SLO = internal target (stricter); SLA = legal contract (more lenient).

The gap between SLO and SLA is intentional: if your SLO is 99.95% and your SLA is 99.9%, you can breach your internal target without triggering contractual penalties. This buffer gives the team early warning before the customer-facing commitment is at risk.

Q5. A burn rate of 14.4× on a 28-day SLO window means what in practical terms?

  • A. The service is performing 14.4× better than the SLO requires
  • B. 14.4% of the error budget has been consumed in the last hour
  • C. The error budget will be exhausted in exactly 14.4 days
  • D. The error budget will be fully consumed in approximately 48 hours — a critical alert requiring immediate response
Answer

D — Budget exhausted in ~48 hours.

Burn rate 1 = consuming the budget at exactly the rate the SLO allows. Burn rate 14.4 = consuming it 14.4× faster. A 28-day budget at 14.4× burn rate is exhausted in 28/14.4 ≈ 1.94 days ≈ 47 hours. This is the threshold where an immediate page is warranted — the incident is moving too fast for next-business-day resolution. (In one hour, a 14.4× burn consumes about 2% of the budget, which is how the SRE Workbook derives the number.)

Q6. What is the difference between MTTF and MTTR, and which lever is faster to improve in a production incident?

  • A. MTTF is failure frequency; MTTR is repair time — MTTF is faster to improve
  • B. MTTF is mean time to failure (how long before it breaks); MTTR is mean time to repair (how long to fix it) — MTTR is faster to improve during an active incident
  • C. They are equivalent; improving one automatically improves the other
  • D. MTTF measures software failures; MTTR measures hardware failures
Answer

B — MTTF = time before failure; MTTR = time to repair; MTTR is faster to improve during an incident.

During an active incident, you cannot retroactively prevent the failure (MTTF is already 0 — it happened). What you control is MTTR: faster detection (alerting), faster diagnosis (runbooks, distributed tracing), and faster mitigation (feature flags, rollback procedures). Long-term, MTTF improves through better testing and fault-tolerant design.

items.title: Resilience Patterns
items.text:
Q7. What state does a circuit breaker enter after its wait timeout expires while in the Open state?

  • A. Closed — it automatically assumes the service has recovered
  • B. Failed — it requires manual intervention to reset
  • C. Half-Open — it allows a limited number of probe requests to test whether the service has recovered
  • D. Degraded — it passes traffic at 50% of the normal rate
Answer

C — Half-Open.

The Open state blocks all requests. After a configured wait timeout (e.g., 30 seconds), the breaker moves to Half-Open and allows a small number of probe requests through. If they succeed, the service has recovered and the breaker closes. If they fail, the service is still down and the breaker returns to Open.

Q8. Why should you never retry a non-idempotent POST /orders without additional safeguards?

  • A. POST is not retryable at the HTTP protocol level
  • B. The server will return 405 Method Not Allowed on the second attempt
  • C. Each retry may create a duplicate order — retries are only safe for idempotent operations or operations protected by idempotency keys
  • D. Circuit breakers block all retries of POST requests automatically
Answer

C — Each retry may create a duplicate order.

POST /orders creates a new resource on each call. If the request succeeds on the server but the response is lost (network partition), a retry will create a second order. Safe retries for non-idempotent operations require an idempotency key — a client-generated unique ID that the server uses to detect and deduplicate replayed requests.

Q9. What problem does adding jitter to exponential backoff solve?

  • A. It prevents the backoff delay from growing indefinitely
  • B. It ensures all clients use the same retry interval for predictability
  • C. It breaks the thundering herd — without jitter, all clients that failed simultaneously retry at the same moments, spiking load on the recovering service
  • D. It randomises which backend server handles the retried request
Answer

C — Breaks the thundering herd.

Imagine 1,000 clients all failing at t=0 and retrying at t=1s, t=2s, t=4s in perfect synchrony. Each retry wave hits the recovering service with a massive spike, potentially causing it to fail again. Adding random jitter spreads retries across a time window, converting a spike into a manageable steady stream.

Q10. Which patterns combine to form a defence-in-depth call chain? Select the most complete answer.

  • A. Only circuit breaker + timeout — the others add unnecessary complexity
  • B. Rate limiter → circuit breaker → bulkhead → timeout → retry with backoff
  • C. Load balancer → health check → circuit breaker
  • D. Retry with backoff → bulkhead → rate limiter → timeout
Answer

B — Rate limiter → circuit breaker → bulkhead → timeout → retry with backoff.

Each layer handles a distinct failure scenario: the rate limiter protects against traffic spikes and abuse; the circuit breaker fast-fails calls to known-failing dependencies; the bulkhead isolates thread pools so one slow dependency cannot starve others; the timeout bounds wait time; the retry handles transient failures. In the layering shown in class, rate limiting and fast-failing happen before consuming a bulkhead thread. Libraries may nest them differently — Resilience4j's default puts Retry outermost so each attempt passes through the breaker — but the set of layers is the same, and C and D each miss essential ones.

Q11. Two gateway replicas, each available 99% of the time and failing independently, sit behind Nginx. Any one replica can serve all traffic. What is the availability of the gateway layer (ignoring Nginx)?

  • A. 98.01%
  • B. 99%
  • C. 99.5%
  • D. 99.99%
Answer

D — 99.99%.

In parallel, the layer is down only when both replicas are down at the same time: 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.0001, so availability = 1 − 0.0001 = 99.99%. Option A (0.99²) is the formula for components in series, where every one must work. The result holds only if the failures are independent — two replicas on the same node or with the same bad configuration fail together.

Q12. The order service's liveness probe calls the database and fails when it is unreachable. The database is down for 15 seconds. What happens on Kubernetes?

  • A. Nothing — Kubernetes ignores liveness failures shorter than one minute
  • B. The pods are removed from the Service's endpoints until the database is back, then receive traffic again
  • C. Every replica fails liveness at the same time and is restarted, so a short database blip becomes a full outage while all JVMs boot again
  • D. Only one replica is restarted, because Kubernetes restarts pods one at a time
Answer

C — All replicas restart together.

Liveness answers "is this process stuck?"; a failure triggers a restart. Because every replica depends on the same database, they all fail liveness together and are all restarted, turning a 15-second hiccup into minutes of downtime. Option B describes what a readiness failure does. Keep external dependencies out of liveness.

Q13. The gateway, the order service and its Feign client for the product service each retry failed calls up to 3 times. The product service starts failing. How many calls can a single user request generate to the product service in the worst case?

  • A. 3
  • B. 9
  • C. 27
  • D. 81
Answer

C — 27 (3 × 3 × 3).

Retries at each layer multiply: each of the gateway's 3 attempts reaches the order service, which makes 3 attempts, each of which the Feign client tries 3 times. This retry amplification hits the struggling service hardest exactly when it is weakest. Retry at one layer only, cap attempts, use backoff with jitter and stop retrying when the circuit breaker is open.

Q14. A client sends POST /orders with the header Idempotency-Key: k-42. The server creates the order, but the response is lost and the client retries with the same key. What should the server do?

  • A. Create a second order, because every POST creates a new resource
  • B. Return 409 Conflict and ask the client to generate a new key
  • C. Recognise the key as already processed and return the result of the first request without creating another order
  • D. Delete the first order and create a new one to keep the data consistent
Answer

C — Return the stored result for the same key.

The idempotency key identifies one logical operation. The server stores the keys it has processed (with their results), so a repeated key returns the original response instead of duplicating the order. This makes a non-idempotent POST safe to retry.

items.title: Chaos Engineering
items.text:
Q15 (bonus). The first Principle of Chaos Engineering requires establishing a steady state before injecting failures. What does "steady state" refer to?

  • A. A deployment freeze where no code changes are made during the experiment
  • B. A measurable baseline of normal system behaviour expressed as SLIs — request rate, error rate, latency — against which the experiment's impact is evaluated
  • C. A state where all services are running at exactly 50% capacity
  • D. The configuration of the system at the last known-good deployment
Answer

B — Measurable SLI baseline.

You cannot determine whether injecting a failure caused degradation unless you know what "normal" looks like. The steady-state hypothesis is: "Even with condition X injected, the system will continue to exhibit [specific SLI values]." Falsifying the hypothesis is a finding — the system does not handle that condition as designed.

items.title: Chaos Engineering
items.text:
You added timeouts, a circuit breaker and a fallback to the call from the order service to the product service. Do they work? The unit tests pass, but nobody has ever seen the breaker open in production — and the first time it matters will be during a real outage, at night, with real customers. The only way to know is to cause the failure yourself, on purpose, while you are watching.

Chaos Engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in its ability to withstand turbulent conditions in production1. Rather than waiting for failures to happen organically, practitioners inject controlled failures deliberately — and use the results to find and fix weaknesses before real incidents do.

"The best way to avoid failure is to fail constantly." — John Ciancutti, Netflix, 20105

The idea is older than the name. At Amazon in the early 2000s, Jesse Robbins (later co-founder of Opscode, the company behind Chef) ran GameDay exercises that deliberately caused major failures in production systems to expose hidden weaknesses in software and in the teams operating it4.

items.title: Origin: Netflix and the Simian Army
items.text:
In 2008 a database corruption stopped Netflix from shipping DVDs for three days. The company decided to move away from its own data centre to AWS, accepting that in the cloud individual instances can disappear at any time. During that migration (around 2010) the engineers built Chaos Monkey: a service that randomly terminates instances in production during business hours, forcing every team to build services that survive arbitrary instance loss5. Running it during working hours is deliberate — the engineers are at their desks to see and fix what breaks.

The practice was tested for real in April 2011, when a large AWS failure in the us-east-1 region took down many well-known sites for hours; Netflix kept streaming, with some degradation, largely because its services were already built to lose instances. That year Netflix described a whole Simian Army6 — a collection of tools that introduced different failure scenarios:

Tool Failure injected Chaos Monkey Terminates random EC2 instances Latency Monkey Introduces artificial delays in REST calls Conformity Monkey Shuts down instances that violate best practices Doctor Monkey Monitors health checks, isolates unhealthy instances Janitor Monkey Cleans up unused cloud resources Security Monkey Finds and reports security policy violations Chaos Gorilla Simulates failure of an entire AWS Availability Zone

The insight was transformational: failure is not a special case to be avoided; it is the environment that production systems live in, and the only way to know your system survives it is to test it there. In 2016 Netflix engineers formalised the practice and gave it its name in an IEEE Software article2; the principles below come from that work.

items.title: Principles of Chaos Engineering
items.text:
The Principles of Chaos Engineering1 define the discipline across five core ideas:

1. Build a hypothesis around steady state behaviour : Define what "normal" looks like before injecting failures — in terms of measurable outputs (request rate, error rate, latency). The hypothesis is: "This system will continue to exhibit the steady state even when condition X is introduced."

2. Vary real-world events : Simulate events that actually happen: server crashes, network partition, disk full, clock skew, dependency timeout, traffic spike. Synthetic or artificial failures that never occur in practice produce misleading confidence.

3. Run experiments in production : Staging environments do not faithfully reproduce production load, data distribution, or dependency behaviour. Weaknesses only visible under production conditions are invisible in staging. Start with small blast radius and expand as confidence grows.

4. Automate experiments to run continuously : A one-time experiment produces a one-time result. Systems change constantly; new deployments can reintroduce weaknesses. Continuous chaos experiments run automatically (often on a schedule) so regressions are caught immediately.

5. Minimise blast radius : Control the scope of each experiment carefully. Affect the minimum number of users necessary to validate the hypothesis. Expand scope only after smaller experiments produce no observable impact.

items.title: The experiment lifecycle
items.text:
Each experiment follows the scientific method3: state what you expect, change one variable, measure, and compare.

flowchart LR
    H["1. Hypothesise
Define steady state
and expected behaviour"]
    D["2. Design
Choose failure type
and blast radius"]
    I["3. Inject
Introduce the
controlled failure"]
    O["4. Observe
Measure SLIs
and system behaviour"]
    A["5. Analyse
Compare actual vs
hypothesised behaviour"]
    R["6. Improve
Fix weaknesses;
update runbooks"]

    H --> D --> I --> O --> A --> R
    R -->|"run again
with wider scope"| H

A chaos experiment that confirms the hypothesis (the system behaves as expected) builds confidence in that failure mode. An experiment that falsifies the hypothesis is a finding: the system does not handle this failure correctly, and the team now knows before a real incident teaches them.

An experiment on the store

Step Content Steady state POST /orders: availability ≥ 99.9% and P95 latency < 500 ms (from the Grafana dashboard of Hands-on 6). Hypothesis "If the product service answers in 3 s instead of 50 ms, the order service's circuit breaker opens within 30 s, orders fail fast with a clear 503, and GET /orders keeps its normal latency." Injection Put Toxiproxy between order and product and add a 3 s latency toxic — first in the Docker Compose environment, later on one replica. Blast radius One environment, 10 minutes, abort if the availability of GET /orders drops below 99%. Observe resilience4j_circuitbreaker_state, error rate and P95 per route, the order service's busy threads, traces in Jaeger. Possible findings The Feign read timeout was never configured, so the breaker only counts calls after 60 s; or the retry multiplies calls and the breaker opens too late.

Either outcome is useful: a confirmed hypothesis is evidence that the patterns work; a falsified one is a bug found on your terms.

items.title: Fault injection types
items.text: Category Examples Tools Process / instance Kill container, OOM-kill process, terminate VM Chaos Monkey, LitmusChaos Network Add latency, drop packets, corrupt packets, partition network segment Toxiproxy, Gremlin, Chaos Mesh Resource Saturate CPU, fill disk, exhaust memory, fill file descriptor table Stress-ng, Gremlin Dependency Return HTTP 500, inject timeouts, return malformed responses Wiremock, Toxiproxy State Corrupt database records, roll back a deployment, expire TLS certificates Manual, Gremlin Infrastructure Terminate an Availability Zone, lose a region, simulate CDN failure Chaos Gorilla, AWS Fault Injection Simulator

items.title: Blast radius control
items.text:
The blast radius of a chaos experiment is the set of users and systems affected by the injected failure. Controlling it is what separates engineering practice from recklessness.

flowchart TD
    S1["Stage 1\nUnit / integration tests\n(no users affected)"]
    S2["Stage 2\nStaging / canary environment\n(internal users only)"]
    S3["Stage 3\n1% of production traffic\n(small user cohort)"]
    S4["Stage 4\nFull production\n(all traffic, all regions)"]

    S1 -->|confidence increases| S2
    S2 -->|no findings| S3
    S3 -->|SLIs hold| S4

Practical controls:

  • Feature flags: enable chaos injection only for a percentage of requests.
  • Time windows: run experiments only during business hours when the team is available to abort.
  • Automated abort conditions: if an SLI drops below a threshold, halt the experiment automatically.
  • Dark reads / shadow traffic: run experiments against a copy of production data, not the primary path.

items.title: GameDay
items.text:
A GameDay is a planned, team-wide chaos exercise where engineers deliberately introduce failures and observe whether the system and the team respond correctly. Unlike automated continuous chaos experiments, GameDays are collaborative events focused on process as much as technology.

A typical GameDay:

  1. Brief: the scenario is described to the team (e.g., "The primary database fails at 10:00 AM"). Alternatively, the scenario is kept secret (a surprise GameDay) to test realistic incident response.
  2. Execute: the failure is injected. Engineers monitor dashboards, run incident response procedures, and communicate as they would in a real incident.
  3. Observe: the team tracks how long detection takes, how long recovery takes, and which runbooks were effective.
  4. Debrief: a blameless post-mortem identifies what went well, what failed, and what improvements to make to the system and the runbooks.

Blameless culture is a prerequisite

GameDays only work if engineers feel safe surfacing problems. If findings lead to blame or punishment, the team will avoid honest reporting — and the weaknesses remain hidden. The output of a GameDay is a list of improvements, not a list of culprits.

items.title: Tools
items.text: Tool Maintained by Strengths Chaos Monkey Netflix Instance termination; the original Gremlin Gremlin Inc. SaaS; broad failure library; UI-driven LitmusChaos CNCF Kubernetes-native; GitOps-friendly Chaos Mesh CNCF Kubernetes-native; broad failure library Toxiproxy Shopify TCP proxy; adds latency/drops packets; ideal for integration tests AWS FIS Amazon Native AWS integration; IAM-controlled; safe abort conditions

items.title: Prerequisites: observability first
items.text:
Chaos engineering without observability is dangerous and unproductive. Before running any experiment, the team must be able to:

  1. Measure steady state: SLI dashboards must exist and show baseline values.
  2. Detect deviations: alerts must fire within seconds of an SLI dropping.
  3. Attribute causality: distributed tracing must allow the team to identify which component introduced the latency or errors.
  4. Abort safely: an automated kill switch must be able to halt the experiment immediately if it exceeds the defined blast radius.

Start with observability. Then add resilience patterns. Then run chaos experiments to validate the patterns actually work.

Common pitfalls

  • Chaos without a hypothesis is just breaking things: if you did not say in advance what should happen, you cannot learn from what did happen.
  • Starting in production: the principle says production is the goal, not the first step. Begin in a test environment and widen the blast radius only when smaller experiments pass.
  • No abort switch: every experiment needs a way to stop it in seconds.
  • Fixing nothing: an experiment whose findings never become tickets only consumed error budget.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
• SLI / SLO / SLA — the steady state is expressed as SLIs, and experiments spend error budget.
  • Resilience Patterns — what chaos experiments verify.
  • Observability and Hands-on 10 — you need metrics and traces to observe an experiment.
  • Hands-on 5 — deleting a pod by hand (kubectl delete pod) is the simplest chaos experiment you can run on Kubernetes.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Chaos engineering is experimentation: a steady-state hypothesis, a controlled injection, measurement and analysis.
  • It grew from Netflix's Chaos Monkey (2010) and the Simian Army, and from Amazon's GameDays.
  • Inject real-world failures (instance loss, latency, dependency errors) and keep the blast radius small, widening it step by step.
  • A falsified hypothesis is a finding, not a failure.
  • Prerequisites: observability, resilience patterns, an automated abort — and a blameless culture.

  1. Principles of Chaos Engineering. principlesofchaos.org. ↩↩

  2. BASIRI, A. et al. Chaos Engineering. IEEE Software, v. 33, n. 3, p. 35–41, 2016. ↩

  3. ROSENTHAL, C.; JONES, N. Chaos Engineering: System Resiliency in Practice. O'Reilly, 2020. ↩

  4. ROBBINS, J. et al. Resilience Engineering: Learning to Embrace Failure. ACM Queue, v. 10, n. 9, 2012. ↩

  5. CIANCUTTI, J. 5 Lessons We've Learned Using AWS. Netflix Tech Blog, Dec. 2010. ↩↩

  6. IZRAILEVSKY, Y.; TSEITLIN, A. The Netflix Simian Army. Netflix Tech Blog, Jul. 2011. ↩

items.title: Resilience Patterns
items.text:
When a downstream service degrades or fails, the naive default — keep sending requests and wait for a response — reliably produces cascading failures. The calling service's threads block, its queue fills, and the failure propagates upstream to clients who had nothing to do with the broken dependency.

Resilience patterns are design decisions that interrupt this propagation. They do not prevent failures; they limit how far a failure travels through the system1.

flowchart LR
    client --> gateway
    gateway -->|"Timeout\nCircuit Breaker\nBulkhead"| downstream:::slow
    gateway -->|"fast failure\nor fallback"| client:::ok

    classDef slow fill:#f90,color:#000
    classDef ok fill:#6c6,color:#fff

The patterns below are complementary — production systems use them in combination, not in isolation. Throughout the page we use one running example from the store: the order service calls the product service (through an OpenFeign client, as in Hands-on 1) to check prices before saving an order.

Pattern Question it answers Protects against Timeout How long am I willing to wait? Hanging calls Retry Is it worth trying again? Transient failures Circuit breaker Should I even try? A dependency that is known to be down Fallback What do I answer instead? Total loss of a feature Bulkhead How much of my capacity can one dependency take? Resource exhaustion spreading Rate limiting How much traffic do I accept? Spikes and abusive clients Health checks Should traffic reach this instance? Routing to broken instances

items.title: Timeout
items.text:
A timeout is a deadline applied to an outbound call. If the downstream service does not respond within the deadline, the call is abandoned and an error is returned to the caller immediately.

Without a timeout, a single hanging dependency can hold threads indefinitely. With a timeout, the maximum damage any single slow call can do is bounded.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as Gateway
    participant P as Payment Service

    C->>+G: POST /checkout
    G->>+P: POST /charge
    Note over P: processing...
    Note over G: deadline exceeded (500 ms)
    G-->>-C: 503 Service Unavailable
    P-->>-G: (response arrives late — discarded)

items.title: Choosing timeout values
items.text:
• Percentile-based: set the timeout at the P99.9 latency of the downstream service under normal conditions. Anything slower than that is already abnormal.
  • Budget-aware: if the upstream call has its own timeout of 1 s, all downstream calls within that request must complete well under 1 s combined.
  • Distinct per dependency: a database query, a third-party API, and an internal microservice have very different latency profiles. A single global timeout value is almost always wrong.
