Coding Interview Prep System Design 2026.2 System Design & Scalability

Study material for technical interviews — how to think about, communicate and design scalable systems. Based on Cracking the Coding Interview (G. McDowell) and top-tier software engineering references, connected to the topics and hands-ons of the course.

Contents Algorithms vs. System Design Handling the Questions (8 principles) Design Step-By-Step (5 steps) Algorithms that Scale (4 steps) Back-of-the-Envelope Key Concepts Worked Example: URL Shortener Practice Problems Connection to the Course Quiz Interview Checklist References Algorithms vs. System Design

Two kinds of problem, two distinct skills — but the same structured way of reasoning.

Algorithm Questions Closed problem

They usually have a deterministic solution. The focus is on the correctness of the algorithm, its O(n) complexity and a clean implementation. Examples: "find the shortest path", "check whether a tree is a BST".

System Design Questions Open problem

There is no single answer. The focus is on tradeoffs, scalability, communication and engineering reasoning. Examples: "design Twitter", "design a URL shortening system for 100M users".

"Tackle the problem by doing it just like you would at work." Ask questions. Engage the interviewer. Discuss the tradeoffs. There is no perfect answer — there is well-articulated reasoning and justified solutions.

Essential mindset

In system design, the interviewer wants to see how you think, not just what you have memorized. A candidate who asks good questions, makes assumptions explicit and admits uncertainty with solid reasoning often outperforms a candidate who tries to recite a ready-made architecture.

What the interviewer evaluates Clear communication Structured reasoning Technical knowledge Managing tradeoffs Realistic estimates Spotting bottlenecks Aspect Algorithm Interview System Design Interview Correct answerDeterministic, usually uniqueMultiple valid solutions FocusCorrectness and complexityTradeoffs and scalability Typical length20–45 min45–60 min CommunicationImportantCritical — it is the main evaluation Whiteboard/diagramUsefulMandatory Handling the Questions

8 principles to run a system design interview with confidence and clarity.

1 Communicate Think out loud. The interviewer wants to follow your reasoning, not just see the final solution. Long silence is the biggest enemy in a system design interview — even if you don't know the answer yet, say what you are thinking: "I'm considering a cache here because..." 2 Go broad first Before diving into details, sketch the whole system at a high level. Establish the main components before going deep into any of them. Detailing a component too early, only to redesign it later, is a common mistake. 3 Use the whiteboard Draw! Diagrams help both the interviewer and you keep the reasoning organized. A clear block diagram communicates more than minutes of verbal explanation. Start simple and refine. 4 Acknowledge interviewer concerns If the interviewer raises an objection or points out a problem, don't ignore it or defend your position at all costs. Say: "good point, let me reconsider that part". This shows technical maturity and openness to feedback. 5 Be careful about assumptions Implicit assumptions are traps. If you assume the system has 1,000 users when it actually has 1 billion, your whole solution may be wrong. Ask before you assume. 6 State your assumptions explicitly When you need to assume something (which is unavoidable), say it out loud: "I'll assume the system must support 10M daily active users, peaking at 100k req/s". The interviewer can correct it, confirm it or give more context. 7 Estimate when necessary Back-of-envelope calculations are expected and valued. Know how to make quick estimates of throughput, storage and bandwidth. E.g.: "1M users × 100KB/user = ~100GB of storage". It doesn't need to be exact — the order of magnitude is what matters. 8 Drive You lead the session. Don't wait for the interviewer to tell you what to do next. Propose the next step: "I'll focus on the database layer now, OK?" or "I see two main bottlenecks — let me tackle the most critical one first". Take ownership.

Practical tip: Use explicit transitions between stages. When moving from "main components" to "identifying bottlenecks", say: "Now that we have the main components, I'll identify the critical points of this system." This keeps the interviewer oriented in your structure.

Design: Step-By-Step

A 5-step structure to design complex systems in an organized way during the interview.

1 Scope the Problem Ask questions to narrow down the problem. How many users? Which features are essential vs. nice-to-have? Is the system read-intensive or write-intensive? Is strong consistency required, or is eventual consistency enough? Define the scope before any architecture. Typical questions: "What are the main features I should design?", "What scale do we expect in 1 year?", "Are there latency constraints?" 2 Make Reasonable Assumptions With the scope defined, state explicit assumptions: "I'll assume 10M DAU, a peak of 100k req/s, 99.9% availability (at most ~8.7h of downtime per year), and that the system is far more read-heavy than write-heavy (100:1)". This anchors the rest of the conversation and shows that you think in concrete metrics. 3 Draw the Major Components Sketch the main blocks: clients → load balancers → web/app servers → caches → databases → message queues → CDN. Don't go into details yet — big picture first. Each block must have a clear purpose. Label the arrows with the kind of data flowing between components. 4 Identify the Key Issues Where are the bottlenecks? What are the single points of failure? Which components will "break" first as the system grows? Is the database the read bottleneck? Does the application server hold state that prevents horizontal scaling? Identify the critical points before proposing solutions. 5 Redesign for the Key Issues Now you go deeper: add sharding to the database, caching on hot paths, horizontal scaling of the app servers, a CDN for static assets, queues for asynchronous processing. Redesign iteratively, focusing on the problems you identified. Justify each decision with the tradeoffs involved. example — scalable URL shortener architecture CDN static Client browser/app Load Balancer App Server 1 App Server 2 App Server 3 Cache Redis miss DB Primary MySQL / PG DB Replica read-only repl. Queue Kafka/SQS Analytics workers Analytics DB step 1 scope steps 2–3 components step 4–5 bottlenecks / redesign async processing decoupling Key scoping question

Always ask: "Is this system read-heavy or write-heavy?" — it changes everything. Read-heavy (e.g. URL shortener, Twitter timeline) → aggressive caching, DB read replicas. Write-heavy (e.g. log ingestion, real-time chat) → queues + asynchronous processing, eventual consistency.

Algorithms that Scale: Step-By-Step

When the problem is algorithmic but must run at massive scale — data that does not fit in one machine.

Unlike pure system design, here you start from a correct algorithm and iterate until it works with billions of records. The key is to recognize where the solution "breaks" as it scales and to address exactly those points.

1 Ask Questions How much data? What is the distribution? What are the time and memory constraints? Does the data fit in RAM? Are there duplicates? Is it sorted? Are approximations (approximate algorithms) acceptable, or is exact precision required? The right questions reveal the real problem and the applicable techniques. 2 Make Believe Assume the data fits in a single machine and solve the problem there. Find the correct algorithm, ignoring scale for now. This gives you the baseline solution you will adapt. E.g.: for the top-K words in 1TB of logs, you would start with a HashMap + a MinHeap of size K. 3 Get Real Now face reality: the data doesn't fit in RAM, or doesn't fit on one machine's disk, or serial processing would be too slow. How do you split the problem? Hash partitioning? Sampling? Streaming? Which parts can be parallelized? 4 Solve Problems Identify which parts of the step 2 solution break at scale and fix exactly those points. Sharding, MapReduce, approximate counting (HyperLogLog for distinct counts, Count-Min Sketch for frequencies), reservoir sampling for streaming data. Full example Top-K words in 1TB of logs

Make believe: HashMap<String, Integer> to count + a MinHeap of size K for the top-K. O(N log K). Get real: 1TB doesn't fit in RAM (assume ~10GB of heap). Solve: Split the file into N chunks. Each worker processes one chunk → emits (word, count). A central reducer aggregates counts per word and keeps a global MinHeap of size K. Alternative: MapReduce — Map emits (word, 1), Reduce sums, each reducer keeps a local top-K, final merge.

Scaling techniques When to use each approach

MapReduce: batch, parallelizable data; fits word count, PageRank, joins of large tables. HyperLogLog: counts distinct elements with ~1% error using O(log log N) memory. Ideal for "how many unique users visited?" Count-Min Sketch: approximate frequency of elements. Ideal for top-K with high cardinality. Bloom Filter: probabilistic membership check. "Has this URL already been visited?" with zero false negatives.

Back-of-the-Envelope

Reference numbers for quick estimates — the order of magnitude is what matters, not precision.

1 day ~10⁵ s 86,400 s. Round it to 100k and do the math in your head. 1M req/day ~12/s That is the average. Typical peak: 2–5× the average — size for the peak. Read : Write 100:1 Typical ratio of read-heavy systems (feeds, URL shortener, catalogs). Latencies every engineer should know OperationApprox. latencyImplication L1 cache reference~1 nsCPU is practically "free" compared to I/O Main memory (RAM) access~100 nsThat's why in-memory caches (Redis) answer in sub-ms Read 1 MB sequentially from RAM~5–10 μsScanning data in memory is cheap Random SSD read (4 KB)~20–100 μs~1,000× slower than RAM Round trip within the same datacenter~0.5 msEvery call between microservices costs at least this much Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD~0.2–1 msSequential reads are much cheaper than random ones Spinning disk (HDD) seek~5–10 msAvoid random HDD access on the critical path Round trip São Paulo ↔ Virginia (us-east-1)~110–130 msAvoid synchronous cross-region calls; use CDN/edge Availability — the "nines" SLODowntime / yearDowntime / month 99%~3.65 days~7.3 h 99.9%~8.77 h~43.8 min 99.95%~4.38 h~21.9 min 99.99%~52.6 min~4.38 min 99.999%~5.26 min~26.3 s Powers of 2 Storage units

2¹⁰ ≈ 10³ → KB (thousand) 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶ → MB (million) 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹ → GB (billion) 2⁴⁰ ≈ 10¹² → TB (trillion) 2⁵⁰ ≈ 10¹⁵ → PB

Typical sizes To estimate storage

Numeric ID / timestamp: 8 B UUID: 16 B (36 B as text) "Small" record (URL, short post): ~0.5–1 KB Compressed photo: ~200 KB – 2 MB 1 min of HD video: ~50–100 MB

How to present an estimate

Round aggressively, do the math out loud and, above all, say what the number changes in the architecture. "That's ~3 TB in 5 years — it fits in one database with replicas, so sharding is a future optimization, not a day-1 requirement." An estimate that does not lead to a decision is just arithmetic.

Key Concepts

The concepts that show up in every system design interview — click each item to expand the explanation.

Horizontal vs. Vertical Scaling fundamentals ▶

Vertical scaling (scale up): adds more CPU, RAM or disk to the same machine. It is simple — no code changes required. But it has a physical and hardware limit (there is no machine with infinite RAM), creates a single point of failure, and cost grows exponentially with capacity.

Horizontal scaling (scale out): adds more machines. Theoretically unlimited and cheaper at scale. It requires stateless application servers, load balancing and coordination between nodes. Most large-scale web systems scale horizontally.

Practical strategy: start vertical (simpler, zero refactoring), but design for horizontal from the start. When vertical hits a cost or physical limit, move to horizontal. The mistake is not planning for this from the beginning.

AspectVerticalHorizontal ImplementationSimpleComplex LimitMaximum hardwarePractically unlimited CostGrows exponentiallyGrows linearly Single point of failureYesNo (with redundancy) Downtime when expandingUsually yesNo Load Balancer infrastructure ▶

Distributes requests across multiple backend servers, preventing any server from being overloaded while others sit idle. It also runs health checks and automatically removes failed servers from the pool.

Distribution algorithms:

  • Round-robin: each server receives requests in turn. Simple, but ignores the current load.
  • Weighted round-robin: more powerful servers receive a larger share of requests.
  • Least connections: forwards to the server with the fewest active connections. Better for requests of variable duration.
  • IP hash: shard = hash(client_IP) % N. Guarantees sticky sessions (same client → same server). Useful when the server holds state.

Implementation types: Hardware (F5, Cisco), software (Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy), cloud-managed (AWS ALB/NLB, GCP Cloud Load Balancing).

Watch out: the load balancer itself can become a single point of failure. Solution: active/passive pairs (primary + standby with automatic failover) or DNS-based load balancing (multiple IPs in DNS with a short TTL).

Database Denormalization & NoSQL data ▶

Denormalization: denormalizing a relational database means strategically duplicating data to avoid expensive JOINs. You trade consistency (updates must be made in several places) for read performance. It works well when reads far outnumber writes and JOINs are a proven bottleneck.

NoSQL — when and which to use:

  • Key-Value (Redis, DynamoDB): O(1) access by key. Ideal for sessions, caching, leaderboards, rate limiting.
  • Document (MongoDB, Couchbase): semi-structured data, flexible schema. Ideal for product catalogs, user profiles.
  • Column-family (Cassandra, HBase): massive distributed writes, queries by partition key. Ideal for time series, IoT, logs.
  • Graph (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune): complex relationships between entities. Ideal for social graphs, recommendation systems, fraud detection.

CAP Theorem: in a distributed system, you can guarantee at most 2 of the 3 properties: Consistency (all nodes see the same data), Availability (every request gets a response), Partition tolerance (the system keeps working despite network failures). In practice, P is unavoidable — you choose between CP (consistency) and AP (availability).

Database Partitioning (Sharding) data ▶

Splits the database across multiple nodes (shards), where each node stores a subset of the data. It lets you scale storage and query throughput horizontally beyond the limits of a single machine.

Sharding strategies:

  • Vertical partitioning: different tables on different servers. Simple, but limits the growth of individual tables.
  • Horizontal (range-based): users with id 1–1M on shard A, 1M–2M on B. Good for range queries, but can create hot spots if the distribution is uneven.
  • Hash-based: shard = hash(user_id) % N. Uniform distribution, avoids hot spots. Makes range queries harder. Consistent hashing minimizes data remapping when nodes are added or removed.
  • Directory-based: a lookup table maps key → shard. Flexible (lets you move data without rehashing), but the table becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

Classic problem: queries that span shards (cross-shard joins) are extremely expensive. Choose the sharding key based on the most frequent access patterns. If 90% of queries are by user_id, use user_id as the sharding key.

Caching performance ▶

Stores computed results or frequently accessed data in memory (much faster than disk) to avoid recomputation or database I/O. It is one of the highest-impact optimizations in read-heavy systems.

Eviction policies (when memory is full):

  • LRU (Least Recently Used): removes the item accessed longest ago. It is the default — it works well for most workloads.
  • LFU (Least Frequently Used): removes the least frequently accessed item. Better when data popularity is stable over time.
  • TTL (Time-To-Live): each item has an expiration time. Essential for time-sensitive data (e.g. prices, sessions).

Write strategies:

  • Write-through: writes to the cache and the database at the same time. Guaranteed consistency, but higher write latency.
  • Write-back (write-behind): writes to the cache immediately and propagates to the database asynchronously. Higher throughput, but risk of data loss if the cache fails.
  • Write-around: writes straight to the database, bypassing the cache. The cache is only populated on the next read. Useful when written data is rarely read right afterwards.

Classic problems: Cache stampede (many keys expiring at the same time cause a flood of database queries — use probabilistic expiration or a mutex lock), cold start (empty cache after a deploy — use warm-up scripts), cache poisoning (invalid data in the cache).

Asynchronous Processing & Queues architecture ▶

Instead of processing everything synchronously inside the user's request, you enqueue the heavy work for asynchronous execution. The user gets a fast response (an acknowledgment), and workers do the processing in the background.

Classic use cases:

  • Sending email/SMS after sign-up
  • Generating an image thumbnail after upload
  • Payment processing with automatic retry
  • Indexing content for a search engine
  • Push notifications to mobile devices

Tools and tradeoffs:

  • RabbitMQ: AMQP, delivery guarantees (at-least-once), complex routing via exchange/binding. Ideal for workloads that need delivery guarantees.
  • Apache Kafka: distributed log, persistent message retention, replay capability, very high throughput (millions of msg/s). Ideal for event streaming, auditing, multiple independent consumers.
  • Amazon SQS: managed, zero ops, SQS Standard (at-least-once, unordered) or FIFO (exactly-once, ordered). Ideal if you want simplicity on AWS.

The producer-consumer pattern decouples services, absorbs traffic spikes (the producer can be much faster than the consumer for short periods) and enables automatic retry when a worker fails.

Networking Metrics metrics ▶

Three fundamental metrics to understand and size the network capacity of a distributed system:

Bandwidth cap. Theoretical maximum capacity of the channel in bits/second. It is the ceiling — the most the link can carry. real Throughput Actual rate of successful transfer. Always ≤ bandwidth. Reduced by congestion, retransmissions and overhead. RTT Latency Time for a packet to go from A to B (one-way) or A→B→A (Round-Trip Time). Made up of propagation + transmission + processing + queuing delay.

Components of latency:

  • Propagation delay: speed of light × distance. São Paulo → New York ≈ 100ms minimum.
  • Transmission delay: packet size ÷ bandwidth. A 1GB file over a 100Mbps link takes ~80 seconds.
  • Processing delay: time routers take to process the header and decide the next hop.
  • Queuing delay: time spent waiting in the buffers of congested routers. Variable and unpredictable.

Rule of thumb: optimizing throughput (batching, compression) can increase latency. Optimizing latency (smaller requests, persistent connections) can reduce throughput. Understand which one is more critical for your system before optimizing.

MapReduce big data ▶

A programming paradigm for processing large datasets in parallel on a cluster. The programmer only defines the Map and Reduce functions; the framework takes care of distribution, parallelism, fault tolerance and the shuffle.

The flow of the two phases:

  • Map: each worker reads a chunk of the input data and emits (key, value) pairs. E.g.: for word count, each line → emits (word, 1) for every word found.
  • Shuffle & Sort: the framework automatically groups all values emitted for the same key and sends them to the same reducer.
  • Reduce: the reducer receives (key, [v1, v2, v3, ...]) and produces the final result. E.g.: (word, [1,1,1]) → (word, 3).

The framework takes care of: distributing data among workers, parallel execution, automatic re-execution of failed tasks (fault tolerance), shuffle/sort between Map and Reduce, and monitoring.

Implementations: Hadoop MapReduce (batch, disk I/O — robust but slow), Apache Spark (in-memory — 10-100x faster for iterative algorithms such as ML, streaming via Spark Streaming).

When NOT to use it: real-time queries with low-latency requirements, ACID transactions that need strong consistency, caching systems or simple lookups. MapReduce is for batch processing of large volumes.

# Pseudocode — Word Count in MapReduce
def map(document_id, text):
    for word in text.split():
        emit(word, 1)           # emits (key, value)

def reduce(word, counts):       # receives (key, [v1, v2, ...])
    emit(word, sum(counts))     # aggregates and emits the final result
Consistent Hashing data ▶

The problem: with shard = hash(key) % N, changing N (adding a node or losing one) remaps almost every key. In a distributed cache this amounts to emptying the whole cache at once — and all traffic falls on the database.

The solution: nodes and keys are placed on a hash ring (e.g. 0 … 2³²−1). Each key belongs to the first node found going clockwise. When a node is added or removed, only the keys in the neighboring range change owner — on average K/N keys.

  • Virtual nodes: each physical node takes several positions on the ring, which evens out the distribution and lets you give more weight to bigger machines.
  • Replication: the key is also stored on the next R−1 nodes of the ring (the Dynamo and Cassandra model).
  • Where it shows up: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak, Memcached clients (ketama), Nginx (hash $request_uri consistent;).
Replication & Consistency Models data ▶

Replicating data increases availability and read capacity, but forces you to choose what the client may see while the replicas converge.

Topologies:

  • Leader-follower (primary-replica): writes go to the leader, reads scale out on the replicas. With asynchronous replication there is replication lag — a read on a replica may return stale data.
  • Multi-leader: writes accepted in several regions. Requires conflict resolution (last-write-wins, CRDTs, merge in the application).
  • Leaderless (quorum): N replicas; a write is acknowledged by W and a read queries R. If R + W > N, every read hits at least one replica with the latest acknowledged write. E.g.: N=3, W=2, R=2.

Consistency models (strongest to weakest): linearizability (strong) → read-your-writes → monotonic reads → eventual consistency.

Practical trick: to guarantee read-your-writes without global strong consistency, read from the leader for a few seconds after the user's own write (e.g. after editing their profile).

In the course: CAP Theorem · Consensus & Algorithms

CDN & Edge infrastructure ▶

A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a network of edge servers that keep copies of content close to the user. It reduces latency (the RTT to the edge is much smaller than to the origin) and takes load off the origin.

  • Pull CDN: the edge fetches from the origin on the first access (cache miss) and stores it according to Cache-Control/TTL. Simple, the default in most cases.
  • Push CDN: you publish the content to the CDN explicitly. Useful for large, rarely changing files.
  • Invalidation: prefer versioning the file name (app.3f9a1c.js) over invalidating the cache — invalidation is slow and expensive.
  • Beyond static files: TLS termination, DDoS/WAF protection, edge compute and caching of dynamic responses with a short TTL.

Examples: Amazon CloudFront, Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly.

Rate Limiting resilience ▶

Limits how many requests a client (user, API key, IP) can make within a time window. It protects against abuse and accidental spikes, ensures fair use and controls cost. The standard response is HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.

Algorithms:

  • Token bucket: tokens are refilled at a fixed rate; each request consumes one. Allows bursts up to the bucket size. The most common choice for APIs.
  • Leaky bucket: requests enter a queue that is drained at a constant rate. Smooths traffic (it is the model behind Nginx's limit_req).
  • Fixed window counter: one counter per window (e.g. per minute). Simple, but allows up to 2× the limit at the window boundary.
  • Sliding window (log or counter): more accurate than the fixed window, at a higher memory/computation cost.

Distributed: with several gateway replicas, the counter must be shared — typically Redis (INCR + EXPIRE, or a Lua script for atomicity). Also decide what happens if Redis goes down: fail-open (let traffic through) or fail-closed (block it).

In the course: Hands-on 2 — Gateway · Hands-on 8 — In-Memory Cache

API Gateway & Microservices architecture ▶

API Gateway: the single entry point of the system. It concentrates cross-cutting concerns — routing, authentication (JWT validation), rate limiting, TLS, CORS, response aggregation — so internal services don't have to repeat them.

  • Communication: synchronous (REST/gRPC) when the client needs the answer now; asynchronous (events on a queue) when the work can happen later.
  • Database per service: each service owns its data. Consistency across services via Saga (orchestrated or choreographed) and the Outbox pattern to publish events reliably.
  • Service discovery: the orchestrator's DNS (Kubernetes Services) or a registry (Eureka, Consul).

A tradeoff that impresses in interviews: knowing when not to use microservices. Small team and a still-unstable domain → start with a modular monolith and extract services when there is a concrete reason (independent scaling, independent deploys, separate teams).

In the course: Microservices — Architecture & Components · Hands-on 2 — Gateway · Hands-on 3 — Security

Resilience Patterns resilience ▶

In distributed systems, partial failures are the rule. These patterns keep the failure of one dependency from bringing down the whole system (cascading failure).

  • Timeout: every remote call needs one. Without a timeout, a slow dependency exhausts the threads of its callers.
  • Retry with exponential backoff + jitter: only for transient errors and idempotent operations. Jitter keeps all clients from retrying at the same time (thundering herd).
  • Circuit breaker: closed → open (fails fast, without calling the dependency) → half-open (tests whether it is back).
  • Bulkhead: resource pools isolated per dependency, so that one cannot consume all the connections.
  • Idempotency key: the client sends a unique identifier; the server deduplicates repetitions of the same operation.
  • Fallback / graceful degradation: a degraded response (cache, default value) instead of an error.
  • Load shedding: reject part of the traffic early when saturated, instead of degrading every request.

In the course: Resilience Patterns · Chaos Engineering

Observability & SLOs metrics ▶

Designing the system is not enough: you need to know when and where it is failing. Bringing up observability at the end of the interview shows production maturity.

  • Logs: what happened, event by event. Structured (JSON) and with a trace id.
  • Metrics: how much and how often. The RED method for services (Rate, Errors, Duration) and USE for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors).
  • Traces: where the time was spent in a request that crosses several services.

SLI / SLO / SLA: the SLI is the measurement (e.g. % of requests with latency < 300 ms); the SLO is the internal target (e.g. 99.9% over 28 days); the SLA is the contract with the customer, with a penalty. The error budget (1 − SLO) defines how much risk you can spend on deploys and experiments.

Use percentiles, not averages: p50, p95 and p99. The average hides the tail — and the tail is where the unhappy users are.

In the course: Observability · SLI / SLO / SLA · Hands-on 6 · Hands-on 10

Worked Example: URL Shortener

The 5 steps applied to the system in the diagram above — the outline of a ~45-minute answer.

1 Scope the Problem Functional: shorten a long URL, redirect the short code to the original URL, custom alias and expiration (optional), click counting. Out of scope: user accounts and link editing. Non-functional: low-latency redirect (p99 < 100 ms), high availability and codes that are not trivial to guess. 2 Make Reasonable Assumptions 100M new URLs/month → ~40 writes/s. A 100:1 read:write ratio → ~4,000 redirects/s on average (peak ~10k/s). Storage over 5 years: 6B records × ~500 B ≈ 3 TB. Cache: ~350M redirects/day; keeping the 20% most accessed ≈ 35 GB of RAM — fits in a small Redis cluster. 3 Draw the Major Components API: POST /api/v1/urls {longUrl, alias?, expiresAt?} → 201 {shortUrl} and GET /{code} → 301/302 Location: longUrl. Model: urls(code PK, long_url, created_at, expires_at). Components: load balancer → stateless app servers → database. 4 Identify the Key Issues (a) Generating unique codes without collisions and without expensive coordination between servers. (b) The database takes all the read traffic. (c) Counting clicks synchronously would slow down the redirect. 5 Redesign for the Key Issues Cache-aside in Redis for the hot codes; read replicas on the database; sharding by hash of the code only if the volume requires it. Each click becomes an event on a queue (Kafka/SQS) consumed by workers that write to the analytics database — the redirect does not wait for it. How to generate the short code? Option A Hash + truncate

Hash (MD5/SHA-256) of the URL, first 7 characters in base62. Deterministic: the same URL produces the same code. Con: collisions must be detected and resolved (re-hash with a salt).

Option B Counter + base62

A unique ID (sequence, Snowflake or ranges pre-allocated per server) converted to base62. No collisions. Con: sequential codes are predictable and allow links to be enumerated.

Option C Key Generation Service

A service pre-generates random keys and hands them out in batches to the app servers. No collisions on the request path, and unpredictable. Con: one more component to operate and replicate.

# base62: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes — plenty for 6B URLs
ALPHABET = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"

def base62(n: int) -> str:
    s = ""
    while n > 0:
        n, r = divmod(n, 62)
        s = ALPHABET[r] + s
    return s or "0"
Classic tradeoff: 301 or 302?

301 (Moved Permanently) is cached by the browser: less load on the server, but subsequent clicks no longer go through you — the count is incomplete. 302 (Found) always goes through the server: accurate analytics, but more traffic. There is no right answer — choose and justify it with the requirements from step 1.

Practice Problems

Classic interview questions. Try to solve them with the 5 steps before opening the key points.

Distributed Rate Limiter medium ▶
  • Choice of algorithm (token bucket vs. sliding window) and its justification.
  • State shared across gateway replicas (Redis) and atomicity (Lua script).
  • Rules per client/endpoint, a 429 response with Retry-After.
  • Fail-open vs. fail-closed if the counter storage goes down.
News Feed (Twitter / Instagram) hard ▶
  • Fan-out on write (push to pre-computed timelines) vs. fan-out on read (build the timeline at read time).
  • Hybrid model: push for regular users, pull for celebrities with millions of followers.
  • Timeline in cache (a list of IDs in Redis), media in object storage + CDN.
  • Cursor-based pagination, not offset-based.
Chat (WhatsApp / Slack) hard ▶
  • Persistent connections (WebSocket) and a service that knows which server each user is connected to.
  • Per-conversation ordering (a sequence number per conversation_id) — global ordering is not needed.
  • Delivery to offline users (store-and-forward) and delivery/read receipts.
  • Partitioning the message storage by conversation (e.g. Cassandra).
Notification System medium ▶
  • Multiple channels (push, e-mail, SMS) with separate queues and workers per channel.
  • Retries with backoff and idempotency so nobody is notified twice.
  • User preferences and opt-out, per-user rate limit, templates.
  • Integration with external providers (APNs, FCM, SES, Twilio) and what to do when they fail.
Web Crawler medium ▶
  • URL frontier: a prioritized queue partitioned by domain.
  • Politeness: respect robots.txt and limit requests per domain.
  • Deduplication: a Bloom filter for URLs already seen, a content hash for duplicate pages.
  • DNS cache, distributed page storage, spider-trap detection.
Ride Sharing (Uber / 99) hard ▶
  • Frequent location updates (every few seconds) — a write-heavy system.
  • Geospatial index: geohash, quadtree or H3 for "nearby drivers".
  • Matching that guarantees a driver is never assigned to two rides (lock/strong consistency at that point).
  • Surge pricing, ETA and partitioning by region/city.
Distributed Key-Value Store advanced ▶
  • Partitioning with consistent hashing and virtual nodes.
  • Replication with a configurable quorum (N, R, W) and the consistency × latency tradeoff.
  • Failure detection (gossip), hinted handoff and anti-entropy (Merkle trees).
  • Conflict resolution: vector clocks or last-write-wins.

items.title: System Architecture — 2027.1
items.text:
Most systems you will build or maintain in your career have to be fast, available, consistent enough, secure and affordable — at the same time, under load, while parts of them fail. This edition of the course is about how to design such systems, how to prove with numbers that a design works, and how to explain it — to a team in a design review, and to an interviewer in a system-design interview.

What changes in 2027.1

The course is reorganized around the building blocks of modern architectures — the same palette of components you will find in the System Design Playground: client, traffic & edge, compute, storage, messaging, observability, network, AI & agents and external services.

  • Every class teaches a group of components, with the trade-offs, the numbers and the failure modes that matter in practice and in interviews.
  • Every class page embeds the playground, preloaded with a scenario, so you can see the concept under load: change a parameter, run a load test with randomness (crashes, spikes, hot keys, region outages), read the report.
  • The hands-on labs build one system along the semester — BoxOffice, a ticketing platform with a flash sale at 10:00 — and every lab ends with a "Measure it" step.
  • The Support section has the interview material, a workbook, a cheat sheet, a concept map and study cards.

items.title: The running example: BoxOffice
items.text:
A stadium show goes on sale at 10:00. Two million fans, sixty thousand seats. The catalog is read-heavy, the seat inventory must never sell the same seat twice, payments go through an external provider that sometimes slows down, confirmations go out by e-mail, bots try to buy everything, and an AI assistant answers "find me two seats under R$ 300 for Saturday and hold them". Almost every topic of the course appears in this one system.

items.title: Index
items.text:
BoxOffice has twelve engineers and merges about sixty pull requests a week. A PR waits, on average, most of a working day for its first human review; the on-sale of a stadium show is in three weeks. At the planning meeting someone says the obvious thing: "Let's put AI in the pipeline." Two weeks later the team has a bot that leaves fifteen comments on every PR (people stopped reading them on day three), an agent that "fixed" a red build by deleting the failing test, release notes announcing a refund feature nobody built, and an invoice nobody predicted.

None of that is a problem of the models. The same tools, designed well, cut review latency, find real bugs, write useful tests and shorten incidents. The difference is system design: where the AI step sits in the delivery lifecycle, what context it gets, what it is allowed to do, how its output is checked, what it costs, and how the team knows whether it helps. This class applies the course's toolbox — components, failure modes, numbers, trade-offs — to AI inside the software delivery pipeline.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Map AI capabilities to each stage of the delivery lifecycle (plan, code, review, test, build, release, operate) and place a tool on the spectrum from assistant to autonomous agent.
  • Design an AI pull-request reviewer: context, structured output, noise control, advisory vs gate, and how to measure its precision.
  • Evaluate AI-generated tests with mutation testing and explain the oracle problem, flaky-test triage and test selection.
  • Specify an agent that runs headless in CI with least privilege, budgets, idempotency, verification and an audit trail.
  • Separate decision from explanation in release and operations: risk scoring, canary analysis, incident summaries, postmortems.
  • Threat-model AI in the pipeline (prompt injection, secret exfiltration, slopsquatting, supply chain) and define a governance policy, including evaluation of the AI tools themselves.
  • Estimate the token, runner and attention cost of an AI step and predict its effect on the DORA metrics.

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
1. This overview — AI across the delivery lifecycle, the autonomy spectrum, the contract of an AI step, DORA metrics and cost.
  2. Code review — what AI review is good and bad at, context engineering, structured findings, noise control, gates, precision, architecture conformance.
  3. Testing — generated tests and mutation testing, contract and property-based tests, load scripts from OpenAPI, flaky-test triage, test selection, synthetic data, the oracle problem.
  4. Agents in CI — fix-the-build, dependency and migration agents; headless runs; sandboxing, permissions, budgets, idempotency and audit.
  5. Release & operate — release notes, change risk scoring, canary analysis, incident response, postmortems, ChatOps: AI proposes, policies and humans dispose.
  6. Security & governance — prompt injection in the pipeline, exfiltration, slopsquatting, SLSA, SBOM and signing, policy as code, licensing, privacy, cost governance and evaluation of AI tools.
  7. Quiz — check your understanding.

items.title: Prerequisites from earlier classes
items.text:
This class does not repeat two foundations; read them first if needed:

  • Cloud-native — Delivery: CI, GitOps with Argo CD, deployment strategies, canary analysis with Argo Rollouts, and the DORA metrics. Every AI step here plugs into that pipeline.
  • AI systems & agents: the LLM as a dependency (tokens, latency, cost), the LLM gateway, the agent loop, and safety and evals. Here the "users" of the model are not fans but engineers and pipelines.

items.title: AI across the delivery lifecycle
items.text:
The software delivery lifecycle is a sequence of stages, each with its own inputs, outputs and failure modes. AI can help at every stage — but what "help" means, and what can go wrong, differs a lot:

Stage What AI does BoxOffice example Main risk Control Plan Drafts specs, ADRs, splits work, estimates impact Draft ADR "Redis for seat holds vs PostgreSQL" from the discussion Confident but wrong design reasoning Human-owned ADR, review by the architect Code Completes code, writes features in the IDE or as an agent Implements GET /catalog/events?city= with tests Plausible code with subtle bugs; insecure patterns; invented packages Review, tests, SAST, dependency policy Review Reviews PRs: bugs, security, conventions, architecture rules Flags order writing to the inventory schema Noise; false sense of safety; gullible to injected text Precision measured, advisory first, human approval Test Generates tests, triages flaky ones, selects what to run Unit tests for hold expiry; picks the 40 relevant tests of 4,000 Tests that assert bugs; skipped relevant tests Mutation score, safety net of full runs Build Explains failures, proposes fixes, upgrades dependencies Fixes a compile error after a Spring Boot upgrade Agent bends tests to pass; excessive permissions Sandbox, no write token, verification, draft PRs Release Release notes, changelogs, change risk scores Notes for v1.8.0 with the new Flyway migration Invented features; wrong risk estimate Grounding in commits; risk only routes reviews Operate Explains canaries, summarises incidents, suggests runbooks, drafts postmortems "The canary of inventory fails because p99 doubled after the pool change" Wrong diagnosis followed under stress; autonomous rollbacks Policy decides; humans act; AI explains 
flowchart LR
    plan["Plan<br/>AI drafts ADR"] --> code["Code<br/>assistant / agent"]
    code --> pr["Pull request"]
    pr --> review["AI review<br/>advisory comments"]
    pr --> tests["CI tests<br/>+ AI-generated tests<br/>judged by mutation score"]
    review --> human{"Human approval<br/>(branch protection)"}
    tests --> human
    tests -->|"red build"| agent["Fix agent<br/>draft PR"]
    agent --> human
    human --> build["Build · scan · SBOM · sign"]
    build --> release["Release notes<br/>grounded draft"]
    release --> canary["Canary<br/>policy verdict + AI explanation"]
    canary --> operate["Operate<br/>AI incident summary"]
    operate -->|"postmortem draft"| plan

Notice the shape: the AI steps branch off the main path and come back through a deterministic check or a human before anything changes in production. That is the pattern the rest of the class elaborates.

items.title: The autonomy spectrum
items.text:
"AI in the pipeline" covers tools of very different autonomy. A useful scale, borrowed from how the industry talks about driving automation, is who decides the next action and who is accountable for it:

Level Name The AI… A human… BoxOffice example 0 Assistant answers when asked asks, reads, decides everything "Explain this stack trace" in a chat 1 Copilot suggests inline, in context accepts or rejects each suggestion IDE completion while writing HoldService 2 Reviewer / drafter produces an artifact on an event (comment, test, notes) reviews the artifact; nothing is applied automatically The PR reviewer and the release-notes draft 3 Supervised agent plans and executes several steps with tools, in a sandbox, and proposes a change approves the result (draft PR, change request) The fix-the-build agent opening a draft PR 4 Autonomous agent executes and applies changes within guardrails, without per-change approval sets policies and audits afterwards Auto-merged dependency patch upgrades with green CI

Moving up the scale buys throughput and costs control. The right level depends on the blast radius of a mistake and on how verifiable the output is: a typo fix in docs can be level 4; a change to seat locking in inventory stays at level 2–3 no matter how good the model is. Accountability never moves to the tool: the engineer who merges an AI-written change owns it.

Think first: which level for each?

(a) Bumping jackson-databind from 2.18.1 to 2.18.2 in all services; (b) rewriting the SELECT … FOR UPDATE in inventory; (c) translating the error messages of notification to Spanish.

(a) Level 4 is reasonable if CI is trustworthy: patch release, automated tests, canary — this is what Dependabot/Renovate auto-merge already does without AI. (b) Level 2 at most: concurrency bugs are hard to test, the blast radius is "double booking at 10:00". (c) Level 3: an agent can do it and open a PR, but a native speaker reviews it — correctness is not machine-verifiable.

items.title: The contract of an AI step
items.text:
Every AI step in a pipeline — review, test generation, fix agent, notes, canary explanation — can be designed with the same five-part contract. Writing it down for each step is the fastest way to find what is missing:

Part Question Reviewer example Trigger Which event starts it, and which must not? pull_request opened/synchronize; not drafts, not forks Context What does it read, and which of it is untrusted? Diff (untrusted), PR text (untrusted), CONVENTIONS.md, ADRs Output What shape, and how is it validated? JSON findings against a schema; only added lines; thresholds Action What does it change, with which permission? Inline comments, pull-requests: write; never approves Budget & fallback Max time, tokens, dollars? What if the model is down or wrong? 10 min, ~US$ 0.02; fail open (no comments)

Two properties follow from the contract. Least privilege: the permission of the action is the most the step can ever do, whatever the model says. Fail-safe direction: decide in advance whether an AI outage blocks the pipeline (fail closed) or skips the step (fail open). Advisory steps fail open; a security gate that you rely on must fail closed — and then it must be very reliable.

items.title: What happens to the DORA metrics
items.text:
The DORA metrics — deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore — are defined in Delivery. AI changes the inputs to all four, not always in the expected direction:

  • Lead time can fall (faster first review, faster fixes of red builds) — or rise, if PRs get bigger because code is cheap to generate and slow to review.
  • Deployment frequency follows lead time, but only if batches stay small.
  • Change failure rate can rise if review attention drops ("the bot looked at it") or generated code is merged without understanding; it can fall if AI review and tests catch real defects.
  • Time to restore can fall with good incident summaries and faster diagnosis; it can rise if a confident wrong explanation sends the on-call engineer down the wrong path.

The research so far is a warning against assuming the good direction. The 2024 DORA report estimated that a 25 % increase in AI adoption was associated with a 1.5 % decrease in delivery throughput and a 7.2 % decrease in delivery stability, even as individuals reported higher productivity and better code and documentation quality1; its authors point to larger batch sizes and weaker fundamentals as plausible causes. The 2025 DORA research describes AI as an amplifier of whatever the organization already is — strong platforms, small batches and good tests get stronger; weak ones get weaker2. And in a 2025 randomized controlled trial, experienced open-source developers took 19 % longer with AI tools while believing they were about 20 % faster3.

The engineering response is not to avoid AI but to measure it like any other change — with a baseline period and per-step metrics:

Step Leading metric Business metric it should move AI review precision (accepted ÷ rated comments), comments per PR time to first review, escaped defects AI tests mutation-score gain, tests kept after review change failure rate Fix agent proposals merged ÷ proposals, turns and US$ per proposal time a build stays red Release notes items edited or dropped by humans time to write notes; incident diagnosis time Canary explanation explanations consistent with policy; on-call feedback time to restore

items.title: The numbers: what an AI step costs
items.text:
An AI step has three costs: tokens (the provider's bill), runner minutes (CI time), and attention (every comment or proposal a human must read). The first two are easy to estimate; the third is usually the largest.

The table estimates the token cost of one review of a typical PR and the monthly bill for BoxOffice (12 engineers, ~250 reviews per month, counting re-reviews after pushes) and for a 500-engineer organization (~20,000 reviews per month). Assumptions, all illustrative: an 8,000-token stable prefix (instructions, conventions, ADRs), 6,000 tokens of diff and PR text, 1,500 output tokens (findings plus reasoning). Prices are the providers' list prices per million tokens when this page was written — check current pricing before using them.

Model US$ / review (cold cache) US$ / review (80 % prefix hits) US$ / month, 12 engineers US$ / month, 500 engineers Large model (Claude Opus 5.5) 0.0940 0.0633 15.82 1,266 Mid model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) 0.0470 0.0323 8.07 646 Small model (Claude Haiku 4.5) 0.0235 0.0161 4.04 323 Local model (Ollama on the runner) 0.0000 0.0000 0.00 0

What the numbers say:

  • Tokens are cheap relative to people. Even with the largest model, a review costs cents; the 500-engineer organization pays in a month roughly what a few engineer-days cost. The expensive failure is not the bill, it is noise: a reviewer with 40 % precision that posts four comments on each of ~5,000 reviews a week produces about 12,000 useless comments a week — at one minute each, 200 hours — five engineers' full 40-hour weeks spent reading them.
  • Output tokens are about half the bill for the large model, although they are a tenth of the tokens: each output token costs 5× an input token. Asking for "no praise, no restating the code" is also a cost optimization.
  • Caching the stable prefix helps more as the prefix grows (big conventions files, many ADRs) — but only if the prefix is byte-identical across runs.
  • Local models remove the token bill but not the cost: a CPU runner generating a few tokens per second makes the job minutes long, and lower recall means missed defects. Compare them on a golden set before choosing.
  • Runner minutes: a review job of ~1.5 minutes on a hosted Linux runner costs on the order of one US cent at typical per-minute prices (check your CI provider) — comparable to the tokens. An agent that runs the full build three times costs far more in minutes than in tokens.

Agents behave differently: each step re-sends the growing context, so the cost grows roughly quadratically with the number of steps (AI systems — the numbers). The Agents in CI page computes it for a fix-the-build agent.

items.title: The LLM gateway is shared infrastructure
items.text:
CI bots are clients of the model like the BoxOffice assistant is. At the scale of an organization they should go through the same LLM gateway: one place for keys, per-repository quotas and budgets, model routing ("small model for release notes, large model for security review"), fallbacks when a provider is down, and cost attribution per team. Without it, every repository holds its own API key, and a runaway agent loop in one repository can exhaust the organization's rate limit during the on-sale.

Try it: open the scenario below with the spike profile. Imagine the spike is not fans but a mass dependency upgrade that triggers 300 PR reviews and 300 fix agents at once. Watch the LLM gateway's queue and error rate, then lower the per-client quota and run again: the bots slow down, the assistant's fans do not.

Open the full playground to change the components yourself. The gateway component is described in the component catalog.

In the interview

"How would you add AI code review to a 500-engineer monorepo?" A strong answer follows the system-design framework instead of naming a tool:

  1. Requirements: what problems (review latency, missed classes of bugs, architecture drift)? Advisory or gating? Which languages and directories? Data that may not leave the company?
  2. Estimates: PRs per day (~500 engineers × ~1 PR/day ≈ 500, ×2 with re-reviews), tokens per review, cost per month (cents per review → a few thousand dollars per month at most), latency budget (comments before the human reviewer arrives, < 5 min).
  3. Design: trigger on PR events with path filters and CODEOWNERS-aware routing; context = diff + per-directory conventions + ADRs + ownership; structured findings; noise control (thresholds, dedup, only changed lines, cap per PR); one review per push; LLM gateway with per-team quotas; fail open.
  4. Rollout: shadow mode (findings logged, not posted) on a golden set and real PRs → advisory for volunteer teams → measure precision per category → gate only high-precision categories (for example secrets, SQL injection, cross-boundary calls), as a required check, never an approval.
  5. Risks: prompt injection from PR text, secrets in prompts, fork PRs and pull_request_target, model regressions — a golden-set eval in CI for every prompt or model change, and cost dashboards.

Common pitfalls

  • Adding AI to a weak pipeline: without fast CI, good tests and small PRs, AI amplifies the weakness (the DORA warning). Fix the fundamentals first.
  • Measuring adoption instead of outcomes: "80 % of PRs got an AI review" says nothing; precision, escaped defects and lead time do.
  • Letting the model decide: approvals, merges, rollbacks and promotions belong to policies and people. The model proposes and explains.
  • Ignoring the attention cost: every low-value comment trains people to ignore the high-value ones.
  • Granting broad permissions "to make it work": the permission of the action is the worst case of every prompt injection.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• AI fits every stage of delivery, but what it may do depends on the blast radius and the verifiability of its output: assistant → copilot → reviewer → supervised agent → autonomous agent.
  • Design each AI step with the contract: trigger, context (trusted vs untrusted), validated output, least-privilege action, budget and fail-safe direction.
  • AI changes the DORA inputs in both directions; research so far shows perceived and measured productivity can disagree — measure with baselines and per-step metrics.
  • Tokens are cheap; attention and wrong decisions are expensive. Precision beats recall for anything that talks to humans.
  • AI proposes; rules and humans dispose.
