items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
Q1. A team wants an agent to rewrite the SELECT … FOR UPDATE logic that prevents double booking in inventory, and another to bump a patch version of a logging library in all services. Which autonomy levels are appropriate?

  • A. Both autonomous (level 4): CI will catch any problem
  • B. Seat locking at most level 2–3 (draft for careful human review); the patch bump can be level 4 if CI and canary are trustworthy
  • C. Both level 0: AI must never change code
  • D. Seat locking level 4 because it is critical and needs speed; the library bump level 2
Answer

B.

Autonomy should follow the blast radius of a mistake and how verifiable the change is. Concurrency bugs are hard to test and catastrophic at an on-sale; a patch-level dependency bump is low-risk and well covered by automated checks (Renovate/Dependabot already auto-merge such updates without AI).

Q2. According to the 2024 DORA report, a 25 % increase in AI adoption was associated with which effect on software delivery?

  • A. Higher throughput and higher stability
  • B. An estimated 1.5 % decrease in delivery throughput and 7.2 % decrease in delivery stability, despite reported individual productivity gains
  • C. No measurable effect on any metric
  • D. A 25 % reduction in lead time
Answer

B.

Individuals reported benefits (code quality, documentation, review speed), but delivery throughput and stability went slightly down. The report's authors suggest causes such as larger batches and weaker fundamentals. The lesson: measure outcomes with baselines, not adoption or perception.

Q3. A review uses an 8,000-token stable prefix, 6,000 tokens of diff and 1,500 output tokens. With the page's illustrative mid-model prices — US$ 2 per million input tokens, US$ 10 per million output tokens, and a 1.25× premium to write the prefix to the prompt cache — what does one review cost with a cold cache?

  • A. About US$ 0.005
  • B. About US$ 0.047
  • C. About US$ 0.47
  • D. About US$ 4.70
Answer

B.

Prefix written to the cache: 8,000 × 2 × 1.25 / 10⁶ = US$ 0.020. Diff: 6,000 × 2 / 10⁶ = US$ 0.012. Output: 1,500 × 10 / 10⁶ = US$ 0.015. Total ≈ US$ 0.047 (0.043 without the cache-write premium; ~0.032 once 80 % of prefixes hit the cache). At 20,000 cold reviews a month that is ~US$ 940 — small next to engineers' time, which is why the attention cost of noisy comments matters more than the token bill.

Q4. Which part of the "contract of an AI step" determines the worst case of a successful prompt injection?

  • A. The trigger
  • B. The context
  • C. The action and the permission it runs with
  • D. The output schema
Answer

C.

Whatever the model is persuaded to say, the step can never do more than its credentials and tools allow. A reviewer with pull-requests: write that only posts COMMENT reviews can, at worst, post a wrong comment. The schema helps, but the permission is the hard limit.

items.title: Code review
items.text:
Q5. Your AI reviewer posts 3 comments per PR, and only 4 in 10 are rated useful. What is the most likely consequence, and the best first fix?

  • A. Developers read every comment carefully; no fix needed
  • B. Developers start ignoring all bot comments, including the useful ones; raise the confidence/severity thresholds, cap comments, and measure precision again
  • C. The bot finds too few bugs; lower the thresholds
  • D. Make it a required check so developers must address the comments
Answer

B.

A reviewer is judged by its worst comments. With 40 % precision, the rational behaviour is to skip it. Trade some recall for precision (high + medium confidence, minimum severity, a cap, dedup), measure, and only gate narrow categories with proven precision.

Q6. Why should architecture rules such as "order must not access the inventory schema" be enforced primarily by deterministic checks, with AI as a complement?

  • A. Because models cannot read SQL
  • B. Deterministic checks (database grants, ArchUnit, lint) are exact, reproducible and cannot be talked out of a verdict; AI adds explanation and catches fuzzy cases rules cannot express
  • C. Because ArchUnit is faster than any model call
  • D. Because architecture rules change too often for AI
Answer

B.

Defense in depth: the database role of order without grants on inventory.* fails the mistake even if every reviewer misses it. The AI reviewer explains why and suggests the right fix, and its recurring findings are candidates for new deterministic rules.

Q7. A 5,000-line PR exceeds the reviewer's diff budget. What should the reviewer do?

  • A. Truncate the diff at the budget and review what fits, without saying so
  • B. Keep whole files by priority (production code first), review per file or per service and merge the results, and list the files not reviewed
  • C. Refuse to review and fail the build
  • D. Send the whole repository instead
Answer

B.

Truncating mid-file produces confident comments about code the model never saw. Budgeting whole files, splitting into map/reduce calls, and being explicit about what was not reviewed keeps the review honest — and a 5,000-line PR is itself a finding worth discussing.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
Q8. A generated test suite raises line coverage of HoldService from 45 % to 95 %, but the mutation score stays at 41 %. What does this tell you?

  • A. The tests are excellent; mutation testing is unreliable
  • B. The new tests execute the code but do not check its results well enough to notice injected bugs
  • C. PIT was misconfigured, because coverage and mutation score always move together
  • D. The class has no bugs
Answer

B.

Coverage counts executed lines; mutation score counts changes the tests detect. Assertion-weak tests raise coverage and kill no mutants. Feed the surviving mutants back to the generator and review the assertions.

Q9. A model labels a failing test in seat-hold logic as "flaky" with medium confidence. What should happen?

  • A. Quarantine it automatically; the model knows best
  • B. Check deterministic signals (rerun on the same commit, failure history, correlation with the diff); quarantine only by policy, with an owner and a ticket
  • C. Delete the test
  • D. Rerun the full suite until it passes and merge
Answer

B.

Quarantine hides a test from everyone. A real race condition in holds labelled "flaky" could reach production. The model's label is evidence for a human or a rule, not a decision.

Q10. Predictive test selection runs 15 % of the suite with 95 % recall of failures. What makes this acceptable?

  • A. Nothing: any missed failure is unacceptable
  • B. A safety net that runs the full suite after merge or nightly, so missed failures are caught and attributed to a commit within hours
  • C. The model's confidence score
  • D. Running the selected tests twice
Answer

B.

Selection trades CI minutes for a small delay in detecting some failures. The full suite on main or nightly bounds that delay. Without it, the skipped test might be the one that mattered.

items.title: Agents in CI
items.text:
Q11. A fix-the-build agent with no prompt caching starts with 20,000 tokens of context and adds 2,500 tokens per turn. Roughly how does its total input tokens grow with the number of turns n?

  • A. Constant
  • B. Linearly with n
  • C. Roughly quadratically with n, because every turn re-sends the whole growing context
  • D. Logarithmically
Answer

C.

Turn i sends ≈ 20,000 + 2,500·(i−1) tokens; the sum over n turns is ≈ 20,000·n + 1,250·n². Caching the repeated prefix makes it much cheaper per token, but budgets on turns and dollars must still be enforced by the harness.

Q12. Which design keeps a CI agent safe even if a log line successfully injects instructions into it?

  • A. A strong system prompt telling the agent never to follow instructions in logs
  • B. The agent job has only a spend-limited model key and a read-only token, tools limited to reading/editing src/ and running the build; a separate job applies a verified patch as a draft PR that a human must approve
  • C. Running the agent on a bigger model
  • D. Giving the agent contents: write so it can fix things faster
Answer

B.

Prompt instructions are a mitigation; capabilities are the control. With no write token, no secrets, an allow-listed tool surface, independent verification and human approval, a successful injection can at most produce a bad patch that a person rejects.

items.title: Release & operate
items.text:
Q13. Why should an LLM not be the judge that promotes or aborts a canary?

  • A. LLMs cannot read numbers
  • B. The verdict must be reproducible, auditable, statistically sound and immune to manipulation by text in logs or labels; thresholds and statistical tests in Git provide that, and the model explains the verdict
  • C. Because Argo Rollouts does not support HTTP calls
  • D. Because LLM calls are too expensive for canaries
Answer

B.

Same data must give the same verdict, and a log line saying "promote" must have no effect. The model is valuable after the verdict: explaining it, correlating it with the change, and proposing where to look.

items.title: Security & governance
items.text:
Q14. What is the "lethal trifecta" for AI agents?

  • A. Cost, latency and accuracy
  • B. Access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally — together they let one injected instruction exfiltrate data
  • C. Prompt injection, jailbreaks and hallucinations
  • D. SBOM, signing and provenance
Answer

B.

Any one of the three is manageable. Design AI steps so that none has all three: for example, the reviewer reads untrusted PR text but holds no secrets beyond a spend-limited key and can only post comments.

Q15. An agent adds the dependency spring-boot-starter-seatlock to inventory. It does not exist on Maven Central today. What is the risk and the control?

  • A. No risk: the build will just fail
  • B. Slopsquatting: an attacker can publish a malicious package under a hallucinated name; control with dependency review, a registry proxy that quarantines new packages, and a policy that agents may not add dependencies without justification
  • C. A licensing risk only
  • D. Typosquatting of the model name
Answer

B.

Models repeatedly hallucinate the same plausible package names; once an attacker registers one, the build succeeds — with their code. Deterministic controls on new dependencies stop it regardless of how the name got there.

Back to the class

items.title: Index
items.text: The team upgrades Spring Boot across BoxOffice on a Monday morning. Fourteen services, fourteen red builds: a renamed configuration property here, a deprecated method there, a test that relied on an old default. Each fix is small and boring; together they take two engineers two days. An agent — a model that plans, uses tools, observes the result and tries again — can do most of this work while the engineers review. It can also, if badly designed, push to main, leak the deploy key, loop for an hour on a flaky test, or "fix" a red build by deleting the assertion. This page is about the design that gets the first outcome and makes the second impossible.

items.title: What agents do in a pipeline
items.text:
The agent loop — the model chooses a tool, the harness runs it, the result goes back into the context, repeat — becomes, in CI, a loop over the repository and the build:

Agentic workflow Trigger Verifiable by Typical blast radius Sensible autonomy Fix the failing build CI run failed The build and tests pass; diff is small One branch Supervised: draft PR Dependency upgrade Renovate/Dependabot PR is red Build, tests, canary Many services Supervised; auto-merge only patch versions with green CI Migration (JUnit 4 → 5, javax → jakarta, Java 17 → 21) Planned campaign Build, tests, plus a codemod for the mechanical part Whole codebase, in batches Supervised, one PR per service Issue to PR Issue labelled or @mention Tests written with the issue's acceptance criteria One feature Supervised; human review as usual Docs and config sync API or schema changed Lint, link check, OpenAPI diff Docs Can be autonomous for docs-only changes

Every row ends in the same place: a proposal (a branch, a draft PR) that deterministic checks and a human approve. That is level 3 of the autonomy spectrum. Level 4 — applying changes without per-change approval — is reserved for changes that are both low-risk and fully verifiable, and rarely needs a model at all.

items.title: Anatomy of a fix-the-build agent
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant CI as CI run
    participant Orch as Workflow (deterministic)
    participant Agent as Agent loop (sandbox)
    participant Model as Model
    participant Repo as Git host
    CI-->>Orch: run failed (event)
    Orch->>Orch: dedupe by commit SHA, check branch is not ai-fix/*
    Orch->>Agent: failed log + checkout (no write token)
    loop at most N turns, M dollars
        Agent->>Model: context + tool results
        Model-->>Agent: tool call (read / edit / run build)
        Agent->>Agent: execute allow-listed tool, log it
    end
    Agent-->>Orch: working-tree diff + transcript
    Orch->>Orch: verify: paths allowed, no test removed, build green
    Orch->>Repo: separate job with write token: branch + draft PR
    Repo-->>Orch: human reviews, CI runs, merge or close

Read it as two programs. The agent is non-deterministic and untrusted: it may be wrong, confused or manipulated by text in the log. The orchestrator around it — triggers, dedupe, verification, the PR job — is ordinary deterministic code, reviewed like any other. All the safety lives in the orchestrator.

items.title: Running agents headless
items.text:
Agents in CI run headless: no terminal, no human to answer "may I run this command?". Every decision a person would make interactively must be made in advance, as configuration.

Claude Code (CLI)Claude Code GitHub ActionGeneric loop (any provider)

claude -p "<task>" runs Claude Code non-interactively. Relevant flags from its CLI reference:

gh run view "$RUN_ID" --log-failed | tail -n 300 | \
claude --bare -p "The CI build failed; the log is on stdin. Fix the root cause with the smallest change. Never delete or weaken a test." \
  --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Write,Bash(mvn -B *)" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --max-turns 25 --max-budget-usd 1.50 \
  --output-format stream-json --verbose > transcript.jsonl

--bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md (the same behaviour on every machine, and nothing loaded from the repository you did not choose); --allowedTools uses permission-rule syntax (Bash(mvn -B *) allows only commands starting with mvn -B); dontAsk denies everything else; --max-turns and --max-budget-usd bound the loop; stream-json produces a transcript for the audit log, whose last line reports the cost.

anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 runs the same engine inside GitHub Actions. Without a prompt it answers @claude mentions in PRs and issues (only from users with write access, by default); with a prompt it runs in automation mode on any event. CLI flags go in claude_args. The interactive setup from the documentation:

name: Claude Code
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
  pull_request_review_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  claude:
    if: contains(github.event.comment.body, '@claude')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: write
      issues: write
      id-token: write
      actions: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          fetch-depth: 1
      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}

Note the permissions: this job can write code, PRs and issues — appropriate for an on-demand assistant that humans invoke, which pushes commits a human then reviews. For an unattended agent reacting to failures, prefer a job without write access that produces a patch, and a separate job that opens the PR (next section). Check the action's security documentation and current inputs before use.

An agent is a loop you can write yourself over any API with tool calling — including OpenAI-compatible endpoints via LiteLLM or a local model with Ollama. The core, without error handling:

for step in range(MAX_STEPS):
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, messages=messages, tools=TOOLS)
    msg = reply.choices[0].message
    messages.append(msg.model_dump(exclude_none=True))
    if not msg.tool_calls:
        break
    for call in msg.tool_calls:
        result = run_allow_listed(call.function.name, json.loads(call.function.arguments))
        audit(step, call, result)
        messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id, "content": result})

Writing it yourself makes the tool surface explicit: here the agent has read_file, write_file (only under src/), run_build and finish — and no shell at all. Hands-on 13 has the complete version with budgets and an audit log.

items.title: Sandboxing
items.text:
The agent executes the build, and the build executes the repository's code: tests, Maven plugins, scripts. Assume that code — or text the agent reads — may be hostile, and contain it in layers:

Layer Control Protects against Ephemeral environment Fresh hosted runner or container per run, destroyed after Persistence between runs; poisoned caches (be careful with shared build caches) Tool allow-list Read/edit files, run the build; no general shell, no curl, no git push The agent doing anything you did not foresee Filesystem scope Writes only under services/*/src/; .github/, .git/ unreachable Editing CI to remove checks; tampering with history Environment scrubbing Build and tests run without *KEY*, *TOKEN*, *SECRET* variables A malicious test reading the environment Network egress Only the package registry and the model endpoint (proxy or firewall on self-hosted runners) Exfiltration to arbitrary hosts Resource limits Job timeout, CPU/memory limits Runaway loops and builds

No single layer is perfect. A tool allow-list of Bash(mvn *) still runs whatever the project's Maven plugins do; environment scrubbing does not protect the model API key held by the agent process itself. That is why the key has a spend limit, the job has no write token, and the output is verified outside the agent.

items.title: Permissions: the token is the blast radius
items.text:
Whatever the model decides, it can never do more than its credentials allow. Design the credentials first:

  • Least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN: declare permissions: in every workflow; the job that runs the agent gets contents: read (and actions: read to fetch logs).
  • Split jobs by privilege: the agent job produces a patch artifact; a small job with contents: write and pull-requests: write applies it and opens a draft PR. The job with write access runs no model and no untrusted code.
  • No secrets in the agent's context: never paste secrets into prompts or tool results; keep deploy keys, cloud credentials and registry tokens out of the job entirely.
  • Read-only by default: an agent that only diagnoses (explains the failure as a comment) needs no write access at all — start there.
  • Branch protection and rulesets: main requires PRs, CI and a human approval; bots cannot bypass; changes to .github/workflows/ require a code owner.
  • Human approval is structural, not a prompt instruction: the agent cannot merge because its token cannot.

items.title: Budgets: turns, tokens, dollars, minutes
items.text:
Each agent turn re-sends the whole context — instructions, tool definitions, the log, every file read, every tool result so far. Context grows with every step, so total input tokens grow roughly quadratically with the number of steps (AI systems — the numbers). Prompt caching reads the repeated prefix at a fraction of the price, which changes the slope dramatically. Illustrative assumptions: a 20,000-token starting context (instructions, tool definitions, log), 2,500 tokens added per step (tool result plus the model's output), 400 output tokens per step, list prices of a large model at the time of writing (US$ 4 input, US$ 20 output, US$ 0.20 cached read per million tokens):

2026-10-23T08:15:39.348817 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Without caching, 40 turns cost more than eight times what 10 turns cost (about US$ 11 vs US$ 1.3); with caching, the curve is nearly linear and about eight times cheaper at 40 turns. Either way, the budget must be enforced by the harness, not requested in the prompt:

Budget Typical value for fix-the-build Enforced by Turns 20–30 --max-turns, or the loop bound Dollars US$ 1–2 per run --max-budget-usd, or a token counter in the loop; workspace spend limit at the provider Wall time 20–30 min timeout-minutes on the job Runs per commit 1 Dedupe on the commit SHA Runs per day per repository e.g. 20 Quota in the LLM gateway

The ratio that matters is dollars per merged fix, not per run: an agent that costs US$ 0.80 per run but produces a mergeable fix one time in four costs US$ 3.20 per useful fix — compare that with the engineer-time it saves.

items.title: Idempotency, retries and loops
items.text:
Agents are triggered by events, and events repeat: a CI run is re-run, two pushes arrive in a minute, the agent's own branch fails CI. The messaging patterns of the course apply directly (Messaging — delivery semantics):

  • Idempotency key: the failing commit SHA. One proposal per SHA (branch ai-fix/<sha8>, concurrency group on the SHA). Re-runs find the branch and stop.
  • No self-triggering: never run the agent on its own branches (ai-fix/*), and remember that pushes with the GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger new workflow runs on GitHub — a built-in loop breaker.
  • Retries are for transport, not for the task: SDKs retry 429/5xx with backoff. Re-running a failed agent is a new attempt with a new cost — make it a human decision, or at most one automatic retry with a different strategy.
  • Fail open for advisory agents: if the agent fails, the original red build is still there; nothing is worse than before.

items.title: Audit: who changed what, and why
items.text:
An agent's change must be explainable months later. Keep:

Record Where The full transcript (prompts, tool calls, results) CI artifact with a retention period Model id, prompt version, harness version In the transcript and in the PR body Cost and turns Job summary; aggregated in the LLM gateway That the commit is AI-generated Commit trailer (AI-assisted: ai-fix (claude-opus-5-5)), PR label ai-generated Who approved it The PR review — the human of record

This is the same discipline as for any production change, and it feeds the supply-chain provenance of the software: you can answer "which code in inventory was written by an agent, approved by whom?".

items.title: Dependency and migration agents
items.text:
Dependency upgrades are the most common agentic workflow in practice. Bots such as Renovate or Dependabot open the upgrade PR deterministically; the agent's job starts when that PR is red: read the changelog and the failure, adapt the code, keep the change minimal. Group related updates (all Spring artifacts together), let patch-level updates with green CI auto-merge without AI, and send major versions to an agent that proposes and a human that approves.

Migrations — JUnit 4 → 5, javax.* → jakarta.*, Java 17 → 21 — mix a large mechanical part with a long tail of special cases. Use deterministic codemods for the mechanical part (OpenRewrite recipes for Java are the standard tool) and the agent for the leftovers the recipe cannot handle. Split the campaign into one PR per service, small enough to review, behind the normal CI and canary. Large-scale changes at Google followed the same principle long before LLMs: automate the change, shard it into independently reviewable pieces, and let the owners review each piece1.

BoxOffice: the Spring Boot upgrade, again

Renovate opens one grouped PR per service. Six are green and merge after review. For the eight red ones, the fix agent runs once per failing commit, with mvn as its only shell command, a US$ 1.50 cap and 25 turns. It proposes six fixes as draft PRs (renamed properties, a changed default in a test slice); for the other two it stops and explains (a removed API that needs a design decision). Two engineers review eight PRs in a morning instead of fixing fourteen services in two days — and the two hard cases get their full attention.

In the interview

For "design an agent that fixes broken builds", draw the orchestrator around the agent, not just the loop: trigger and dedupe, sandbox and tool allow-list, budgets enforced by the harness, verification outside the agent, a separate privileged step that opens a draft PR, and the audit trail. Quantify cost per run (quadratic in turns, mitigated by caching) and per merged fix. Say which failures it should not touch (flaky tests, infrastructure, security findings) and how the system detects them.

Common pitfalls

  • One job with the agent and a write token: every prompt injection becomes a push.
  • Budgets in the prompt ("please stop after 10 steps") instead of in the harness.
  • Trusting the agent's "fixed it": verify independently; check that no test was removed or weakened.
  • Agents triggering agents: a fix branch fails CI, which triggers the fix agent, which…
  • Running agents on fork code with secrets (pull_request_target, workflow_run): see Security & governance.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    TRIG["red build event<br/>trigger + dedupe"] --> HARN["harness = orchestrator"]
    HARN --> SB["sandbox, tool allow-list,<br/>no write token"]
    HARN --> BUD["budgets: turns, tokens,<br/>dollars, minutes"]
    HARN --> LOOP["agent loop<br/>→ AI systems agents"]
    LOOP --> VER["verification<br/>outside the agent"]
    VER --> PRIV["separate privileged step<br/>opens a draft PR"]
    PRIV --> HUM["human review"]
    HARN --> IDEM["idempotency, retries, loops<br/>→ Messaging semantics"]
    HARN --> AUD["audit trail:<br/>who changed what, and why"]

Palette components: orchestrator (the harness that enforces budgets and permissions) · toolreg (the allow-list of tools the agent may call) · llmgw (quotas and cost per run) · safety (no secrets or write tokens in the agent's reach) · logs (the audit trail) · metrics (merged fixes per proposal, cost per merged fix). Scenarios: ai-assistant with the spike profile (hundreds of agents at once compete with user traffic at the gateway). Continues in: AI systems — agents, Messaging — semantics (at-least-once runs, idempotent effects), Security & governance, Cloud-native — delivery, Hands-on 13 — fix agent.

  1. WINTERS, T.; MANSHRECK, T.; WRIGHT, H. Software Engineering at Google, ch. 22 "Large-Scale Changes". O'Reilly, 2020. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
A pull request to order changes the checkout so that it confirms the seat hold with one SQL statement instead of an HTTP call to inventory — "it is faster". The code compiles, the tests pass, and the reviewer, at 18:40 on a Friday, approves. Three weeks later, during an on-sale, inventory changes its hold table and checkout breaks. The rule that was violated — one schema per service — was written in a wiki page nobody opened. A reviewer that had read that page, every time, on every PR, would have caught it.

That is the promise of AI code review: a reviewer that reads every diff in minutes, never gets tired, and can be told the team's rules. This page is about turning the promise into a tool people actually trust.

items.title: Why code review, and what it is for
items.text:
Modern code review — a lightweight, tool-based review of each change before merging — is near-universal in industry. Studies at Microsoft and Google found that its main outcomes are not only finding defects but knowledge transfer, shared code ownership and consistency; at Google the median review latency was under a day, with most changes small12. Two consequences for AI review:

  • An AI reviewer can take over part of the defect-finding and consistency work, but not the knowledge transfer: a human must still read the code to learn it.
  • Review latency matters. The first human look often waits hours; an AI review in two minutes gives the author something to fix before the human arrives, so the human review is shorter.

items.title: What AI review is good and bad at
items.text:
Good at (high precision when given context) Bad at (low precision or blind) Local bugs visible in the diff: null handling, off-by-one, wrong comparison, resource leaks Bugs that need runtime knowledge: performance under load, race conditions across services Security patterns: SQL by concatenation, secrets in code, missing authorization check, unsafe deserialization Whether the feature is the right feature: product intent is not in the diff Violations of written conventions and ADRs Conventions nobody wrote down Missing tests for risky logic; tests that assert nothing Judging whether a test asserts the correct expected value (the oracle problem) Explaining unfamiliar code to the human reviewer Large refactors spanning hundreds of files (context limits, attention dilution) Consistency: error formats, status codes, logging, naming Architecture trade-offs that require weighing business context

Two systematic weaknesses deserve names. Gullibility: the model reads text written by the author — PR description, code comments — and can be steered by it ("this was approved by security"); see prompt injection. Plausible noise: a model asked to review will find something; without explicit permission to return nothing, it pads the review with style remarks and restatements.

items.title: Anatomy of an AI reviewer
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant GH as Git host
    participant R as Reviewer job
    participant Ctx as Context builder
    participant GW as LLM gateway
    participant Post as Poster
    GH->>R: PR opened / new push
    R->>Ctx: diff + PR metadata
    Ctx->>Ctx: number lines, filter files, budget tokens
    Ctx->>Ctx: add conventions, ADRs, owners, related code
    Ctx->>GW: system (stable, cached) + user (untrusted data)
    GW-->>R: JSON findings (schema-validated)
    R->>R: filter: changed lines, severity, confidence, dedup, cap
    R->>Post: findings to post
    Post->>GH: one review with inline comments
    Post->>GH: metrics: tokens, US$, kept vs dropped

The model is one box of eight. Most of the engineering — and most of the quality — is in the context builder and the filter.

items.title: Context engineering
items.text:
A model can only review against what it is given. Context engineering is deciding what goes into the limited, priced context window, and in which order.

Context Why Cost / risk BoxOffice The diff, with line numbers The subject of the review; numbered lines let the model cite exact lines Grows with PR size; untrusted git diff base...head, each new line as L21 + … Repository conventions Turns generic advice into your rules Must be short and current; read on every run CONVENTIONS.md: schema per service, timeouts, money as cents Architecture decisions (ADRs) The why behind rules; lets the model flag decisions being reversed Long; summarise or retrieve the relevant ones 0001-schema-per-service.md, 0004-outbox-for-events.md Surrounding code The full function or class around a hunk; the callers of a changed method Token-expensive; retrieval needed in big repos The whole HoldService.java when a hunk changes expire() Ownership and service map Which service owns which data and API Small, high value "inventory owns inventory.*; order owns orders.*" History Earlier review comments, related incidents Can bias towards old issues "Incident 2026-08: hold expiry off by 2 min" PR title and description Intent of the change Untrusted — injection channel Wrapped in <untrusted_pr_description>

Three practical rules:

  1. Order for caching. Put stable content first (instructions, conventions, ADRs) and per-run content last (diff). Prompt caching is a prefix match: if the stable part is byte-identical, repeated reviews read it at a fraction of the price (LLM gateway).
  2. Budget, do not truncate. A 5,000-line PR does not fit — and should not be reviewed as one blob. Keep whole files by priority (production code before tests before config), list the skipped files in the review, or split: one call per file or per service (map), then one call to merge and deduplicate (reduce). Cutting a diff in the middle produces confident nonsense about code the model never saw.
  3. Write conventions for humans first. If a rule is unclear to a new engineer it is unclear to the model. A rule that needs a paragraph of nuance is usually better as a deterministic check (below).
Think first: retrieval for a monorepo

BoxOffice becomes a monorepo of 40 services and 2 M lines. A PR changes the signature of InventoryClient.confirmHold. Which extra context would most improve the review, and how do you find it without sending the whole repository?

The call sites of the changed method and the contract of the API it wraps. Find them deterministically — a code index (language server, ctags, a code-search service) or a simple git grep confirmHold — and add the 5–10 most relevant snippets. Embedding-based retrieval over the repository (RAG) helps for fuzzy questions ("where else do we compute seat prices?"), but for "who calls this method" a symbol index is exact and cheaper.

items.title: Structured output, posted as review comments
items.text:
Free text is for humans; the pipeline needs data. Ask for JSON that validates against a schema — with Claude, structured outputs constrain the response to the schema; with other providers, JSON mode plus validation and one repair attempt:

{
  "summary": "Adds direct SQL access from order to the inventory schema.",
  "findings": [
    {
      "file": "services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/OrderService.java",
      "line": 21,
      "severity": "blocker",
      "category": "architecture",
      "confidence": "high",
      "title": "order writes to the inventory schema",
      "explanation": "CONVENTIONS.md: a service reads and writes only its own schema. This UPDATE couples order to inventory's table layout and bypasses inventory's locking, so a hold can be confirmed after it expired.",
      "suggestion": "Call InventoryClient.confirmHold(holdId) and handle 409 Conflict."
    }
  ]
}
Field Used for file, line Inline placement; validated against the diff (comments on lines outside the diff are rejected by the Git host) severity (nit … blocker) Thresholds and ordering; gate decisions category Per-category precision; routing (security findings to the security champion) confidence Noise control; calibration over time title Deduplication fingerprint; the line people scan explanation, suggestion The comment body; a concrete fix makes a comment actionable

On GitHub, all findings of one run go into one review (POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{number}/reviews with a comments array of path, line, side), so the author gets one notification, not twelve3. A review event of COMMENT keeps the bot advisory; the code — not the model — chooses that event.

items.title: Noise control
items.text:
Every comment spends a developer's attention. A reviewer is judged by its worst comments: after a few useless ones, people stop reading — including the useful ones. The controls, in the order they act:

Control What it removes Triggers and path filters Drafts, docs-only PRs, generated files, lockfiles, vendored code Prompt: "an empty list is a good review; no praise; no restating" Padding Only changed lines Comments on code the author did not touch Minimum severity Style nits a formatter should handle Minimum confidence Speculation Deduplication by fingerprint across pushes The same comment reposted after every push Cap per PR Floods on big PRs — keep the most severe One review per push + one sticky summary Notification storms

The thresholds trade precision (the fraction of posted comments that are useful) against recall (the fraction of real problems found). The table uses an illustrative labelled sample of 100 PRs — the model emitted 60 high-, 90 medium- and 150 low-confidence findings, of which 48, 45 and 30 were real problems, out of 150 real problems in total:

Post findings with confidence ≥ Comments per PR Precision Recall high 0.6 80% 32% medium 1.5 62% 62% low 3.0 41% 82%

Posting everything finds the most problems and is ignored by everybody (3 comments per PR, 4 out of 10 useful). Posting only high confidence is trusted and misses two thirds of the problems. Most teams start at high + medium for severities ≥ minor, measure, and move per category: secrets and SQL injection can stay at medium; style never gets posted.

items.title: Advisory or gate?
items.text:
Advisory Gate (required check) Effect Comments; humans decide Merge blocked until the finding is fixed or overridden Cost of a false positive A minute of reading A blocked PR, an override, frustration — and pressure to disable the bot Cost of a false negative Same as today False sense of safety if humans relax Needs Nothing special Measured high precision in that category; an override path; fail-closed reliability Good for Everything, at first Narrow, high-precision categories: hardcoded secrets, SQL by concatenation, forbidden cross-schema access

A safe rollout: shadow (findings logged, not posted; compare with what humans found) → advisory for volunteer teams → gate per category once precision is proven. Even as a gate, an AI check is a required status check — never an approval. Approval stays human, enforced by branch protection.

items.title: Measuring the reviewer
items.text:
You cannot tune what you do not measure, and "the team likes it" is not a measurement.

Metric How Notes Precision Accepted ÷ (accepted + dismissed) comments; reactions or a resolve-with-reason button Needs people to rate; sample if necessary Recall Found ÷ planted, on a golden set of PRs with known problems Run on every prompt or model change, in CI Escaped defects Bugs found later in code the bot reviewed Slow, but the metric the business cares about Noise Comments per PR; % of PRs with zero comments Zero is often the right answer Cost and latency US$ and minutes per review From the job's token usage Behavioral Time to first review, review rounds, time to merge Needs a baseline period

An LLM can also judge comments ("was this comment correct?"), which is cheaper than human labels — but LLM-as-judge has biases (it tends to agree with confident text, and with itself). Use it to triage, and calibrate it against a human-labelled sample.

items.title: Architecture conformance
items.text:
The opening story — order writing to the inventory schema — is an architecture rule. Such rules are the most valuable thing an automated reviewer can check, because humans forget them and violations are expensive later. But many of them do not need a model at all.

Rule Deterministic check (preferred) Where AI adds value "order must not access the inventory schema" SQL lint: grep for inventory. in services/order/**; separate DB users per service with grants (the database refuses) Explaining why, suggesting the API call instead "Controllers must not call repositories directly" ArchUnit test in the build — "Every outbound HTTP client has timeouts" Custom lint, or a shared client library that requires them Spotting a new hand-rolled client that bypasses the library "Events go through the outbox" ArchUnit: no KafkaTemplate usage outside the outbox relay Recognising a disguised direct publish "Prefer idempotent operations for payment" Hard to express statically Good fit: fuzzy, semantic, context-dependent services/order/src/test/java/boxoffice/order/ArchitectureTest.java
@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "boxoffice.order")
class ArchitectureTest {

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule no_direct_kafka_outside_outbox =
        noClasses().that().resideOutsideOfPackage("..outbox..")
            .should().dependOnClassesThat().haveSimpleName("KafkaTemplate")
            .because("ADR-0004: events are published through the transactional outbox");
}

The best design combines both: deterministic rules block, because they are exact; the AI reviewer explains and catches what the rules cannot express, and its recurring findings become candidates for new deterministic rules. Defense in depth again — and the database user of order without grants on inventory.* is the last layer that does not depend on any reviewer.

BoxOffice: the reviewer catches the shortcut

With CONVENTIONS.md in its context, the reviewer of hands-on 13 flags the UPDATE inventory.hold in OrderService as a high-confidence architecture blocker, citing the rule and explaining the consequence (a hold confirmed after expiry, coupling to another service's table). The team then adds the deterministic check: a separate PostgreSQL role per service, so the same mistake fails in the integration tests even if every reviewer misses it.

In the interview

When asked to design an AI code reviewer, say early that precision beats recall for anything that talks to humans, and show how you will measure it (golden set for recall, accepted/rated for precision). Describe the context (diff + conventions + ADRs + related code by symbol search), structured findings, the filter (changed lines, severity, confidence, dedup, cap) and the rollout (shadow → advisory → gate per category). Mention that architecture rules should be deterministic checks first, with AI as the explainer.

Common pitfalls

  • No permission to stay silent: the model invents work. Say explicitly that an empty review is good.
  • Reviewing the whole repository instead of the change: expensive and off-topic.
  • Treating the bot's silence as approval: humans relax, escaped defects rise.
  • Gating before measuring: one week of false blocks and the team disables the bot.
  • Rules only in the prompt: a rule that matters must also exist as a test, a lint or a database grant.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    PR["pull request event"] --> CTX["context: diff, conventions,<br/>ADRs, symbol search"]
    CTX --> RET["retrieval<br/>→ AI systems RAG & Memory"]
    CTX --> LLM["model call<br/>→ LLM gateway, prefix cache"]
    LLM --> OUT["structured findings<br/>(JSON schema)"]
    OUT --> NOISE["noise control: changed lines,<br/>confidence, dedup, cap"]
    NOISE --> GATE{"advisory<br/>or gate?"}
    GATE --> PREC["precision + golden set<br/>→ AI systems safety & evals"]
    ARCH["architecture rules:<br/>deterministic checks first"] --> OUT
    PR --> INJ["PR text is untrusted<br/>→ Security & governance"]

Palette components: orchestrator (the reviewer job around the model) · llmgw (routing, quotas, cached prefix of conventions and ADRs) · memory (the context assembled for each diff) · safety (untrusted PR text, validated output) · metrics (precision and comments per PR). Scenarios: none specific. Continues in: AI systems — RAG & Memory, AI systems — LLM Gateway, AI systems — safety & evals, Security & governance, Hands-on 13 — the reviewer.
