items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Components and numbers
items.text:
Q1. BoxOffice's first assistant prototype calls the model provider directly from the assistant service. Which palette component should be added first so that a provider outage, a runaway retry loop and the question "how much does each conversation cost?" are all handled in one place?

  • A. Memory Fabric
  • B. LLM Gateway
  • C. Tool Registry
  • D. Vector DB
Answer

B — LLM Gateway.

Fallbacks between providers, token quotas and budgets, and per-call token/cost telemetry are cross-cutting concerns of every model call — exactly what a gateway centralizes, as the API Gateway does for HTTP. The Memory Fabric and the Tool Registry solve other problems (what the model knows; what it may do).

Q2. Which statement best explains why prompt injection is harder to prevent than SQL injection?

  • A. LLM providers do not offer input validation
  • B. Prompts are usually longer than SQL queries
  • C. In an LLM, instructions and data travel in the same channel (the prompt); there is no equivalent of a prepared statement that separates them
  • D. Prompt injection only happens with open-weight models
Answer

C — Instructions and data share one channel.

A prepared statement guarantees that user data is never parsed as SQL. A model reads the system prompt, the user message, retrieved documents and tool results as one sequence of tokens, and any of them can try to act as an instruction. That is why the defense is architectural (least privilege, isolation, confirmation) rather than a single filter.

Q3. An agent request makes 4 model calls. The stable prefix (system prompt + tool definitions) has 3,000 tokens and every tool result adds ~800 tokens to the conversation. Why do total input tokens grow faster than linearly with the number of calls?

  • A. Because output tokens are billed as input on the next call
  • B. Because each call re-sends the whole conversation so far, which grows at every step
  • C. Because the provider charges a fixed fee per call
  • D. Because embeddings are recomputed at every step
Answer

B — Each call re-sends the growing conversation.

The model is stateless: call i sends the prefix plus everything added in calls 1 … i−1. Summing a context that grows linearly gives a total that grows roughly quadratically with the number of steps — the reason fewer steps (better tools, parallel tool calls, workflows) pays twice, in cost and latency. Prompt caching lowers the price of the repeated prefix but not its growth.

Q4. A model has TTFT = 0.5 s and TPOT = 25 ms. Approximately how long does a 400-token answer take end to end, and how long until the user sees the first word if it is streamed?

  • A. 10.5 s total; 0.5 s to the first token
  • B. 10.5 s total; 10.5 s to the first token
  • C. 0.5 s total; 0.5 s to the first token
  • D. 20.5 s total; 0.5 s to the first token
Answer

A — ≈ 10.5 s total; 0.5 s to the first token.

End-to-end latency = TTFT + TPOT × (N − 1) = 0.5 + 0.025 × 399 ≈ 10.5 s. With streaming, the user starts reading after the TTFT — which is why TTFT is the interactive SLO and TPOT only needs to beat reading speed (40 tokens/s here).

Q5. A self-hosted 8-billion-parameter model uses ~128 KiB of KV cache per token. The GPU has 64 GB free after loading the weights. Roughly how many concurrent conversations of 8,000 tokens can it serve?

  • A. About 8
  • B. About 64
  • C. About 640
  • D. Unlimited — batching removes the limit
Answer

B — About 64.

8,000 tokens × 128 KiB ≈ 1 GiB per conversation; 64 GB / 1 GiB ≈ 60–64 sequences. Batching raises throughput because one read of the weights advances many sequences, but every active sequence needs its KV cache in GPU memory — so concurrency is bounded by context length × number of users.

items.title: Gateway
items.text:
Q6. Which pair correctly contrasts prompt caching and semantic caching?

  • A. Both return a previously stored answer; prompt caching is just faster
  • B. Prompt caching reuses the model's computation for an identical prompt prefix and the answer is computed normally (no correctness risk); semantic caching returns a stored answer to a similar question (risk of false hits)
  • C. Prompt caching stores embeddings; semantic caching stores KV tensors
  • D. Semantic caching works only with exact-match keys
Answer

B.

Prompt (prefix) caching saves input cost and TTFT for repeated prefixes such as the system prompt and tool definitions; the model still generates a fresh answer. A semantic cache skips the model altogether when a new question's embedding is close to a stored one — great for generic FAQ, dangerous when "refund for the Saturday show" and "refund for the Sunday show" look alike. Scope its keys and use it only for generic answers.

Q7. The gateway receives a 400 error saying the prompt exceeds the model's context window. What should it do?

  • A. Retry the same deployment with exponential backoff
  • B. Fall back to the next deployment in the chain with the same prompt, whatever its window
  • C. Not retry the same request as is: trim the history or route to a long-context model
  • D. Open the circuit breaker for that provider
Answer

C.

A 400 is a client error: retrying the identical request will fail identically, and it says nothing about the provider's health (so no circuit-breaker failure). Retries with backoff are for 429 and 5xx; context overflow needs a different request (compaction, fewer chunks) or a model with a larger window.

items.title: Agents and tools
items.text:
Q8. Each step of an agent is correct with probability 0.95, independently. What is the approximate probability that a 10-step task succeeds, and what is the main design lesson?

  • A. 95% — steps do not compound
  • B. ~60% — reduce the number of steps, validate after each step, and use workflows for the known parts
  • C. ~90% — add more agents to vote
  • D. ~5% — agents should never be used
Answer

B — 0.95¹⁰ ≈ 0.60.

Errors compound like availabilities in series. The levers are fewer steps (task-level tools, parallel calls, deterministic code for known steps), validation after each step (schemas, business rules), and recovery (errors returned to the model, re-planning).

Q9. The hold_seats tool timed out and the agent loop retried it. How should the system guarantee the fan does not end up with two holds?

  • A. Lower the model temperature so it calls the tool only once
  • B. Tell the model in the system prompt never to retry
  • C. Pass an idempotency key derived from the conversation, step and call to the tool; the inventory service returns the same hold for the same key
  • D. Use a larger model
Answer

C — Idempotency keys.

Model calls are side-effect free and safe to retry; tool calls change the world. The fix is the same as for any integration: idempotency keys enforced by the service, reversible actions (holds that expire) and compensations (release a hold) — not instructions to the model, which are probabilistic.

Q10. In the Model Context Protocol (MCP), what does an MCP server provide, and how does the client discover its tools?

  • A. A model endpoint; the client calls models/list
  • B. Tools (plus resources and prompts) described with names, descriptions and JSON Schemas; the client discovers them with tools/list over JSON-RPC and invokes them with tools/call
  • C. A vector index; the client queries it with SQL
  • D. A user interface; the client scrapes it
Answer

B.

MCP standardizes how an agent host connects to capabilities: each server exposes tools, resources and prompts; clients negotiate capabilities at initialize, then use tools/list and tools/call (JSON-RPC 2.0) over stdio or Streamable HTTP. The registry around it adds governance: owners, permissions, risk tiers, audit.

Q11. BoxOffice's checkout flow always follows the same steps: validate the hold, compute the price, call the payment provider, create the order. A colleague proposes "an autonomous agent with payment tools" to run it. What is the best answer?

  • A. Accept: agents are the state of the art
  • B. Accept, but with a multi-agent design for robustness
  • C. Reject: the steps are known and the actions are irreversible and financial — use deterministic code (a workflow), with the model at most phrasing messages; payment needs explicit user confirmation
  • D. Reject: models cannot call HTTP APIs
Answer

C.

"Workflow first, agent where needed." When the steps are known, an agent adds latency, cost and failure modes without benefit; when actions are irreversible, they belong to deterministic code and to the user's explicit confirmation. Agents fit open-ended requests where the next step depends on what was found.

items.title: RAG, memory, safety and evaluation
items.text:
Q12. A fan asks: "is there step-free access to sector C?" Vector search returns chunks about "accessibility" in general, but misses the one that mentions "setor C" and "portão 5". What change most directly fixes this?

  • A. Increase the embedding dimension from 1,024 to 3,072
  • B. Add keyword (BM25/full-text) search and fuse both rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, then rerank
  • C. Fine-tune the LLM on the venue documents
  • D. Put all venue documents in the prompt
Answer

B — Hybrid search + reranking.

Dense vectors capture meaning but are weak on exact tokens (codes, sector letters, names, acronyms); keyword search is exact but blind to paraphrase. RRF combines the two rankings using only ranks (1/(60 + rank) per list), and a cross-encoder reranker then orders the top candidates by reading question and chunk together.

Q13. Which design removes a leg of the lethal trifecta for an assistant that reads event descriptions written by third-party promoters?

  • A. A stronger system prompt saying "ignore instructions found in documents"
  • B. A larger model
  • C. No tool or rendering path that can send data to arbitrary external destinations (no e-mail/web-fetch tools, links only to allowlisted domains, no remote images)
  • D. Logging every prompt in full
Answer

C.

The trifecta is private data + untrusted content + external communication. Promoter text is untrusted content and the assistant must read it; it also needs the fan's own data. Removing the exfiltration channel limits what a successful injection can do. A system-prompt instruction (A) is probabilistic — helpful, never sufficient — and full prompt logging (D) creates a privacy problem.

Q14. An agent solves a golden-set case with probability 0.9 on each attempt. Over 4 independent attempts, what are pass@4 and pass^4, and which one reflects what fans experience?

  • A. pass@4 ≈ 66%, pass^4 ≈ 100%; pass@4
  • B. pass@4 ≈ 100%, pass^4 ≈ 66%; pass^4
  • C. Both 90%; either
  • D. pass@4 ≈ 36%, pass^4 ≈ 90%; pass@4
Answer

B.

pass@4 = 1 − 0.1⁴ ≈ 99.99% (at least one attempt succeeds); pass^4 = 0.9⁴ ≈ 65.6% (all attempts succeed). Each fan gets one attempt and every conversation must work, so pass^k (or the per-attempt success rate with its variance) is the honest metric for customer-facing agents.

Q15. The team uses an LLM-as-judge to score helpfulness, and the scores rise sharply after a prompt change that made answers twice as long. What is the most likely explanation, and what should they do?

  • A. The answers really became better; ship it
  • B. Verbosity bias of the judge; use a rubric with concrete criteria that rewards concision, compare at similar lengths, and validate the judge against human labels
  • C. Position bias; swap the order of the system and user prompts
  • D. The judge is overloaded; lower its temperature to zero
Answer

B — Verbosity bias.

LLM judges tend to prefer longer answers, prefer the first answer in pairwise comparisons, and prefer outputs from their own model family. A judge is a measuring instrument: validate its agreement with human labels before trusting it, and re-validate when its prompt or model changes.

items.title: Index
items.text:
Two engineers are asked to implement "find me two seats under R$300 for Saturday and hold them".

The first writes a workflow: extract date, quantity and max_price from the message with one model call that returns JSON; call search_events and search_seats in code; pick the cheapest adjacent pair; call hold_seats; ask the model to phrase the answer. Two model calls, every step testable, latency predictable.

The second writes an agent: give the model the tools and the goal, and let it decide what to call, in which order, and when to stop. It handles requests the first design never anticipated ("…and if there is nothing on Saturday, try Sunday, but not in the upper ring"), and it fails in ways the first design never could (it holds the wrong event, or loops forever comparing seats).

Both are correct designs — for different requests. This page is about the machinery of the second one, and about knowing when to choose the first.

items.title: Workflows and agents
items.text:
The difference is who decides the next step: your code, or the model1.

Level Who decides the next step Example in BoxOffice Model calls Predictability Single call nobody — one step summarize the reviews of an event 1 high Workflow: chain code, fixed sequence extract → search → hold → phrase answer fixed (2–4) high Workflow: routing code, after a classifier FAQ → small model; booking → booking workflow; complaint → human 1 + branch high Workflow: parallel code, fan-out then merge check 3 venues at once; vote of 3 models on a fraud signal N in parallel high Orchestrator-workers a model splits the task; code runs the workers "plan my festival weekend" → tickets + lodging + transport variable medium Agent the model, at every step, in a loop open-ended support conversation with tools variable, unbounded without limits low

Start at the top of the table and move down only when the simpler level measurably fails on your evaluation set. Most production "agents" in 2026 are workflows with one or two agentic steps.

items.title: The agent loop
items.text:
An agent is a loop around a model call. In the ReAct formulation2 the model alternates reasoning (what do I know, what do I need), acting (requesting a tool call) and observing (reading the tool result), until it can answer.

flowchart TD
    start(["user message"]) --> ctx["build context:<br/>system prompt + tools + memory + history"]
    ctx --> call["call the model (via LLM gateway)"]
    call --> decide{"tool calls<br/>in the reply?"}
    decide -- no --> answer(["final answer to the user"])
    decide -- yes --> guard["Safety Mesh:<br/>validate + authorize each call"]
    guard --> run["execute tools (in parallel if independent)"]
    run --> append["append calls + results to history"]
    append --> budget{"steps, tokens, time<br/>within budget?"}
    budget -- yes --> call
    budget -- no --> stop(["stop: partial answer or hand off to a human"])

The loop itself is ordinary code. Here is a minimal, provider-agnostic version — the three collaborators are the other palette components:

agent_loop.py
import json

MAX_STEPS, MAX_TOKENS = 8, 40_000


def run_agent(llm, registry, guard, user, question, history):
    """llm: LLM-gateway client; registry: Tool Registry; guard: Safety Mesh.
    All three are this sketch's own interfaces, not a specific SDK."""
    messages = [*history, {"role": "user", "content": question}]
    used = 0
    for step in range(MAX_STEPS):
        reply = llm.chat(alias="assistant-default", system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
                         messages=messages, tools=registry.schemas_for(user))
        used += reply.input_tokens + reply.output_tokens
        messages.append(reply.message)          # the assistant turn, with its tool calls
        if not reply.tool_calls:                # no action requested: this is the answer
            return reply.text
        for call in reply.tool_calls:           # the model may request several at once
            verdict = guard.check_tool_call(call.name, call.arguments, user)
            if verdict == "allow":
                result = registry.call(call.name, call.arguments, as_user=user)
            else:                               # denied, or needs the user's confirmation
                result = {"error": verdict}
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id,
                             "content": json.dumps(result)})
        if used > MAX_TOKENS:
            break
    return "I could not finish this request. A human agent will contact you."

Five details in those 25 lines carry most of the engineering:

  1. The model never executes anything. It returns a request (tool_calls); the orchestrator validates, authorizes as the user (as_user=user) and executes.
  2. Errors go back to the model as data. A denied or failed call becomes a tool result ({"error": ...}), so the model can recover — ask the fan, choose another seat — instead of crashing the loop.
  3. Every loop has budgets: steps, tokens and (in production) wall-clock time. Without them, a confused model loops until the quota or the invoice stops it.
  4. The tools offered depend on the user (schemas_for(user)): an anonymous visitor does not even see hold_seats. A tool the model cannot see is a tool it cannot misuse.
  5. History grows at every step — the quadratic token growth computed in the overview.

items.title: Stopping and context management
items.text:
Stop condition Why A reply without tool calls normal end: the model has an answer Step limit (e.g. 8) bounds cost and latency; a task that needs 30 steps is a workflow in disguise Token or cost budget protects the quota — see LLM Gateway Wall-clock deadline the user is waiting; return what you have Same tool + same arguments twice loop detection: the model is stuck Risky action pending pause and ask the human (human-in-the-loop)

As the history grows, context engineering keeps it useful: tools return compact results (5 seat options, not 5,000 seats); older turns are compacted into a summary; large documents are referenced by ID and fetched only when needed. A focused context is cheaper, faster, and more accurate than a long one3.

items.title: Tool calling
items.text:
Tool calling (also called function calling) is the contract between the model and your code:

  1. The request declares the tools: name, description and a JSON Schema of the arguments.
  2. The model replies either with text or with one or more tool calls: {id, name, arguments}, where arguments should match the schema. Many APIs can enforce the schema with constrained decoding (structured outputs), so the JSON is always well-formed.
  3. The orchestrator executes the call and sends the result back in a message linked to the call id.
  4. The model continues with the result in its context.

The model chooses tools by reading their names and descriptions, so the tool interface is a prompt and an API at the same time. Good tools are designed for the model, not copied from the internal API:

Principle Bad Good Task-level, not table-level run_sql(query), get_all_seats(event_id) search_seats(event_id, quantity, max_price_brl) Few and distinct 40 tools with overlapping names ~5–15 tools per agent, clearly separated Typed arguments date: string ("next Sat"?) date: string, format: date plus an enum where possible Compact results full JSON of every seat top 5 options, only the fields needed to decide Actionable errors 500 Internal Server Error "event evt_123 is sold out; 2 similar events on Sunday: ..." Descriptions with intent "hold seats" "Hold seats for 10 minutes so the fan can pay. Reversible: an unpaid hold expires." Least privilege one tool that reads and writes everything read tools and write tools separate, each with its own permission

items.title: Tools are side effects
items.text:
A model call can be retried freely. A tool call changes the world. If hold_seats times out and the loop retries, did the first hold happen? This is the integration problem of Compute & services, and it has the same answers:

  • Idempotency keys. The orchestrator derives a key from (conversation, step, call) and passes it to every write tool; the service returns the same result for the same key.
  • Reversible first. Prefer actions with a natural undo — a hold expires in 10 minutes; an order with payment does not.
  • Compensation. If a later step fails, run the inverse action (release_hold), exactly as in a saga.
  • Risk tiers decide what may run without a human:
Tier Examples Policy Read search_events, search_seats, get_order automatic Reversible write hold_seats, add_to_wishlist automatic within limits (≤ 6 seats, ≤ 1 active hold) Irreversible / financial create_order, refund_order, charge explicit user confirmation in the UI, never by text alone External communication send_email, post_review confirmation, or not offered at all

items.title: Durable execution
items.text: A conversation that waits for the fan's confirmation, or a task that runs for minutes, cannot live only in a process's memory: pods restart. Persist the agent state after every step — messages, pending tool calls, idempotency keys — in a database, and resume from the last checkpoint. For long multi-step tasks, a durable workflow engine (Temporal-style: each step recorded, retried and resumable) gives you this for free; for short chats, a conversation_state row plus the session cache in the Memory Fabric is enough.

items.title: Planning
items.text:
The agent loop plans one step at a time. For longer tasks, explicit planning helps:

Pattern How it works Model calls Strengths Weaknesses ReAct (implicit plan) decide the next action after each observation 1 per step adapts to surprises can wander; greedy Plan-and-execute a planner writes the full plan; an executor runs steps; re-plan on failure 1 plan + steps (+ re-plans) fewer large-model calls (executor may be small); plan is inspectable and approvable rigid when the world changes mid-plan Reflection / evaluator-optimizer4 a critic (another prompt or model) reviews the result; the generator retries with feedback ×2 or more catches errors before the user sees them doubles cost and latency Parallel steps independent actions issued together in one step fewer rounds lower latency only for independent actions

BoxOffice: a plan the fan can see

For "two seats under R$300 for Saturday, not in the upper ring, hold them", a plan-and-execute assistant first shows:

  1. Find events on Saturday in São Paulo.
  2. For each event, search pairs of adjacent seats ≤ R$300, excluding the upper ring. (parallel)
  3. Choose the cheapest pair; if none, check Sunday.
  4. Hold the pair (reversible, 10 min) and return the checkout link.

Showing the plan costs one call, but it lets the fan correct a misunderstanding before any action, and it gives the evaluation team a trajectory to compare with the expected one.

items.title: Why every step must be checked
items.text:
If each step is right with probability \(p\), independently, an \(n\)-step task succeeds with probability \(p^n\):

ResultSource

Per-step success1 step3 steps5 steps10 steps20 steps 99%99%97%95%90%82% 97%97%91%86%74%54% 95%95%86%77%60%36% 90%90%73%59%35%12% 

# Probability that an n-step task succeeds when each step succeeds with
# probability p, independently: P(task) = p ** n
steps = [1, 3, 5, 10, 20]
head = ["Per-step success"] + [f"{n} step{'s' if n > 1 else ''}" for n in steps]
print("<table><thead><tr>" + "".join(f"<th>{h}</th>" for h in head) + "</tr></thead><tbody>")
for p in (0.99, 0.97, 0.95, 0.90):
    cells = [f"{p:.0%}"] + [f"{p ** n:.0%}" for n in steps]
    print("<tr>" + "".join(f'<td style="text-align:right">{c}</td>' for c in cells) + "</tr>")
print("</tbody></table>")

A step that is right 95% of the time sounds good; a 10-step task built from it succeeds only 60% of the time. The levers are the same as for availability in series (Estimation): fewer steps (better tools, workflows for the known parts), validation after each step (schemas, business rules in code), and recovery (errors returned to the model, re-planning) — the agent equivalent of retries and redundancy.

items.title: Tool registry and MCP
items.text:
Without a standard, every agent needs a custom integration with every tool: N agents × M tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP)5 does for agents what the Language Server Protocol did for code editors: each tool provider writes one MCP server, each agent host embeds MCP clients, and any client can use any server — N + M integrations.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Host["Host: assistant service (orchestrator)"]
        c1["MCP client"]
        c2["MCP client"]
        c3["MCP client"]
    end
    c1 -- "Streamable HTTP + OAuth" --> s1["MCP server<br/>catalog team"]
    c2 -- "Streamable HTTP + OAuth" --> s2["MCP server<br/>inventory team"]
    c3 -- "stdio (local process)" --> s3["MCP server<br/>local files / dev tools"]
    s1 --> catalog["catalog service"]
    s2 --> inventory["inventory service"]

The essentials of the protocol:

  • Roles. The host is the application (the BoxOffice assistant); it runs one client per connection; each server exposes capabilities.
  • Server primitives. Tools (actions the model may call), resources (data the application can read into context, identified by URIs), and prompts (reusable templates offered to the user). Clients may in turn offer servers capabilities such as sampling (the server asks the host's model for a completion) and elicitation (the server asks the user for input).
  • Messages. JSON-RPC 2.0. A session starts with initialize (version and capability negotiation); then tools/list discovers tools and tools/call invokes them; servers can notify tools/list_changed.
  • Transports. stdio for a server running as a local subprocess; Streamable HTTP for remote servers, with OAuth 2.1-based authorization.

The inventory team publishes its capabilities as an MCP server. With the official Python SDK, a tool is a typed, documented function — the SDK derives the JSON Schema from the type hints and the description from the docstring:

inventory_mcp.py
# Official MCP Python SDK (package "mcp"); check its docs for the current API.
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

from inventory_client import InventoryClient  # the team's existing HTTP client

mcp = FastMCP("boxoffice-inventory")
inventory = InventoryClient("http://inventory:8080")


@mcp.tool()
def search_seats(event_id: str, quantity: int, max_price_brl: float) -> list[dict]:
    """Find available seats for an event, adjacent when possible, priced at or
    below max_price_brl each. Returns at most 5 options, cheapest first."""
    return inventory.search(event_id, quantity, max_price_brl, limit=5)


@mcp.tool()
def hold_seats(event_id: str, seat_ids: list[str], idempotency_key: str) -> dict:
    """Hold seats for 10 minutes so the fan can pay. Reversible: an unpaid hold
    expires. Calling again with the same idempotency_key returns the same hold."""
    return inventory.hold(event_id, seat_ids, ttl_seconds=600, key=idempotency_key)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")

On the wire, this is what the orchestrator's client sees when it discovers the tool (tools/list result, abridged) and then calls it:

tools/list (result, abridged)
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 2,
  "result": {
    "tools": [
      {
        "name": "hold_seats",
        "description": "Hold seats for 10 minutes so the fan can pay. Reversible: an unpaid hold expires. Calling again with the same idempotency_key returns the same hold.",
        "inputSchema": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "event_id": {"type": "string"},
            "seat_ids": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
            "idempotency_key": {"type": "string"}
          },
          "required": ["event_id", "seat_ids", "idempotency_key"]
        },
        "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": false, "idempotentHint": true}
      }
    ]
  }
}
tools/call (request, then result)
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "tools/call",
 "params": {"name": "hold_seats",
            "arguments": {"event_id": "evt_8812", "seat_ids": ["C12", "C13"],
                          "idempotency_key": "conv_51f3:step3:call1"}}}

{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7,
 "result": {"content": [{"type": "text",
                         "text": "{\"hold_id\": \"h_77a\", \"expires_at\": \"2027-03-13T10:12:00Z\", \"total_brl\": 560.00}"}],
            "isError": false}}

Notice what is not an argument: the fan's identity. The MCP server takes the user from the authenticated session (the OAuth access token the host obtained on the fan's behalf, as in Identity) — never from a field the model fills in, or a prompt injection could hold seats for someone else.

items.title: The registry around MCP
items.text:
MCP standardizes the wire; the Tool Registry component is the governance around it:

Registry concern What it records / enforces Catalog which MCP servers exist, owner team, version, endpoint, SLO Exposure which tools each agent (and each user role) may see Risk tier read / reversible / irreversible / external — feeds the Safety Mesh Authentication OAuth scopes per tool; tokens per user, not a shared super-token Limits and audit rate limits per tool; an audit log of every call with user, arguments and result Supply chain pinned versions; reviewed descriptions; allowlist of third-party servers

Annotations are hints, not security

readOnlyHint or destructiveHint come from the server. A malicious or buggy third-party server can lie, and its tool descriptions are text the model reads — a place for injected instructions (tool poisoning), which can even change after you approved the server. Treat third-party MCP servers like third-party code: review, pin, sandbox, and enforce permissions in your own registry and services.

For communication between agents owned by different teams or companies, separate protocols are emerging (for example Agent2Agent, A2A). The distinction to keep: MCP connects an agent to tools and data; agent-to-agent protocols connect an agent to another agent.

items.title: Multi-agent orchestration
items.text:
When one agent has too many tools, too long a prompt, or tasks that can run in parallel, the work is split across several agents.

Pattern Shape BoxOffice example Why use it Supervisor / orchestrator-workers one agent decomposes and delegates; workers return results "plan my festival weekend": tickets agent, travel agent, lodging agent separation of tools and prompts; parallelism Router / handoff a triage agent transfers the conversation to a specialist triage → booking agent, refunds agent, accessibility agent each specialist has a short prompt and few tools Parallel fan-out + aggregate the same input to several agents; merge or vote three reviewers check a refund decision robustness through diversity Evaluator-optimizer a generator and a critic iterate a draft reply to an angry fan, checked against policy quality on hard outputs Hierarchical supervisors of supervisors large back-office automation very large tasks — rarely needed 
sequenceDiagram
    actor F as Fan
    participant S as Supervisor agent
    participant T as Tickets agent
    participant L as Lodging agent
    F->>S: "festival weekend in Rio, budget R$2,000"
    par in parallel
        S->>T: find 2 passes ≤ R$900
        S->>L: find lodging near the venue ≤ R$1,100
    end
    T-->>S: 2 options (hold not yet placed)
    L-->>S: 3 options
    S-->>F: combined proposal: confirm?

Multi-agent systems trade money and latency for modularity. Each agent has its own context (more tokens in total), every hand-off loses information unless the state is passed explicitly, and failures become harder to trace. Pass explicit, structured artifacts between agents (a list of candidate seats with IDs), not whole transcripts, and trace the full tree of calls (Observability).

items.title: When NOT to use agents
items.text:
If… …then prefer BoxOffice the steps are known in advance a workflow (code orchestrates, model fills gaps) the hold-seats flow the decision must be exactly right every time deterministic code price calculation, seat allocation, refunds rules the latency budget is under ~1–2 s a single small-model call, or no model autocomplete in search the action is irreversible code + explicit human confirmation payment, refund volume is huge and the task is narrow a classifier, a small fine-tuned model, or rules fraud signals on every checkout you cannot evaluate the result do not automate it yet — one agent with good tools works do not add agents most support conversations

Try it

Run the AI assistant scenario with the stress profile. Each request entering the Orchestrator becomes several calls to the LLM Gateway and the Tool Registry: compare the request rate at the orchestrator with the rate at the gateway. That ratio is the number of agent steps, and it is the multiplier of your model capacity and cost.

items.title: BoxOffice: the trace of one task
items.text:
Step Model output Orchestrator action Context after the step 1 search_events(city="São Paulo", date="2027-03-13") read tool → 3 events ~3,900 tokens 2 search_seats(evt_8812, 2, 300) and search_seats(evt_8820, 2, 300) (parallel) 2 read tools → 4 pairs ~5,000 tokens 3 hold_seats(evt_8812, ["C12","C13"], key) Safety Mesh: reversible, 2 seats → allow; hold h_77a ~5,300 tokens 4 text: "I held C12–C13 for R$280 each until 10:12. Pay here: …" stream to the fan; save the turn —

Parallel tool calls saved one full round (≈ 2 s). Had the model asked for a 40-seat hold, step 3 would have returned {"error": "deny: invalid arguments: List should have at most 6 items after validation, not 40"} (the guardrail check) and the model would have explained the limit to the fan.

In the interview

Say "workflow first, agent where needed" and justify it with the compounding math (\(0.95^{10} \approx 60\%\)). Draw the loop with its budgets (steps, tokens, time) and show where tools are authorized as the user and made idempotent. Name MCP as the way teams expose tools, and add a registry for permissions, risk tiers and audit. If multi-agent comes up, give one concrete reason (tool separation or parallelism) and its cost (tokens, latency, debuggability).

Common pitfalls

  • Agents for deterministic flows — slower, costlier and less reliable than ten lines of code.
  • No budgets — a model stuck in a loop is an unbounded cost.
  • Database-shaped tools (run_sql, get_everything) — huge results, injection risk, and the model does the work your service should do.
  • Retrying write tools without idempotency keys — double holds, double orders.
  • The agent's own super-credential instead of the user's token — the "confused deputy" problem.
  • Trusting third-party MCP servers blindly — their descriptions are prompts and their annotations are claims.
  • Multi-agent by default — more tokens and more failure points with no measured gain.

items.title: Index
items.text:
Six months after the assistant launched, BoxOffice has five features that call models: the support assistant, a review summarizer, an event-description translator, a fraud-signal classifier and the nightly job that embeds the catalog. Each team picked its own provider, wrote its own retry loop and pasted an API key into its own configuration. Then three things happened in the same week: a provider had a two-hour outage and three features went down with it; the translator, stuck in a retry loop, burned a month of budget in one night; and nobody could answer the CFO's question, "how much does the assistant cost per conversation?".

The fix is the same one the course applied to HTTP traffic in Traffic & Edge: put one gateway in front of every model, and move the cross-cutting concerns into it.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Before["Before: every service talks to every provider"]
        a1["assistant"] --> p1["provider A"]
        a2["summarizer"] --> p1
        a2 --> p2["provider B"]
        a3["translator"] --> p2
        a4["embed job"] --> p3["self-hosted"]
    end
    subgraph After["After: one LLM gateway"]
        b1["assistant"] --> gw["LLM Gateway"]
        b2["summarizer"] --> gw
        b3["translator"] --> gw
        b4["embed job"] --> gw
        gw --> q1["provider A"]
        gw --> q2["provider B"]
        gw --> q3["self-hosted"]
    end

items.title: What the gateway does
items.text:
An LLM gateway is a reverse proxy specialized for model APIs. Clients send requests in one format to a model alias (assistant-default, not a vendor model name); the gateway decides which real deployment serves it, and records what happened.

Responsibility What it means Classic equivalent Unified API one request/response format for every provider; clients do not import vendor SDKs adapter / anti-corruption layer Credentials provider keys live only in the gateway (secret store); clients authenticate with their own service identity API gateway + secrets management Routing alias → model and deployment, by feature, difficulty, cost, latency or data residency L7 routing Fallbacks and retries on 429, 5xx or a slow first token, retry with backoff or move to the next deployment retry + circuit breaker Quotas and budgets requests and tokens per minute per user, team and feature; currency budgets per month rate limiter Caching exact-match and semantic response caches; prompt-cache-friendly requests cache Observability one trace span per call with model, tokens, cost, TTFT; dashboards per feature access log + metrics Policy hooks calls the Safety Mesh before and after the model (redaction, filters) WAF / filters

The gateway is on the critical path of every AI feature, so it must itself be stateless, horizontally scaled and highly available — the quota counters and caches live in Redis, exactly like a rate-limiting API gateway (Edge).

items.title: Routing
items.text:
The same prompt can be served by models that differ by an order of magnitude in price and speed. Routing chooses, per request, the cheapest deployment that is good enough.

Strategy How it decides Good for Watch out Static, per feature the alias maps to one model (translator → small model) most features; simple and predictable over-paying for easy requests By task a rule or a small classifier labels the request (FAQ, booking, complaint) and picks a model assistants with mixed traffic the classifier is one more model to evaluate Cascade try the small model first; escalate when its answer fails validation or a confidence check1 high volume, mostly easy requests worst-case latency = small + large Learned router a model trained on preference data predicts whether the small model suffices2 very high volume needs training data and monitoring Latency/cost aware send to the deployment with the lowest current TTFT or price multi-provider, multi-region oscillation; keep some stickiness Compliance personal data stays in deployments in an approved region, or self-hosted LGPD, contractual constraints fewer fallbacks available 
flowchart TD
    req["request: alias assistant-default"] --> pii{"contains personal data?"}
    pii -- yes --> region["only approved-region deployments"]
    pii -- no --> all["all deployments"]
    region --> task{"task class"}
    all --> task
    task -- "FAQ / small talk" --> small["small model"]
    task -- "booking with tools" --> large["large model"]
    small --> check{"answer valid?"}
    check -- no --> large
    check -- yes --> done(["respond"])
    large --> done

Aliases decouple applications from model names. When a new model version appears, the platform team points assistant-default at it for 5% of traffic (a canary, as in Cloud-native delivery), compares online metrics and offline evals, then rolls forward or back — with no change in the assistant's code. Pin model versions behind the alias: a provider silently updating "latest" is an untested deploy.

items.title: Fallbacks and retries
items.text:
A model call has no side effects: retrying it is always safe (tool calls are a different story — see Agents & Tools). But not every error deserves a retry, and some deserve a different model.

Error Meaning Gateway action 429 rate limited your quota at that deployment is exhausted honor Retry-After if short; otherwise fall back to another deployment 5xx, "overloaded" provider-side failure retry with exponential backoff + jitter, then fall back; count it in the circuit breaker No first token within the TTFT deadline queueing or an overloaded region cancel and fall back (or hedge: send a second request after the p95 TTFT and keep the first to answer) Stream breaks after tokens were sent connection lost mid-answer cannot retry transparently — the user already saw part of it; retry the whole answer and tell the client to replace it 400 context too long the prompt does not fit do not retry the same deployment; trim history, or route to a long-context model Refusal / content filter the model or provider declined do not fall back to a "less strict" model; return the policy answer Invalid JSON / schema output did not match the requested format one repair attempt with the validation error, then fail; prefer constrained decoding (structured outputs)

A simplified, provider-agnostic sketch of the fallback chain, combining the retry and circuit-breaker patterns of Reliability:

router.py
import random
import time

CHAIN = {  # model alias -> ordered list of deployments
    "assistant-default": ["large@provider-a", "large@provider-b", "medium@self-hosted"],
    "assistant-cheap": ["small@self-hosted", "small@provider-a"],
}
RETRYABLE = {429, 500, 502, 503, 504}


def complete(alias, request, clients, breakers, ttft_deadline_s=3.0):
    """clients and breakers are this sketch's own interfaces, not a real SDK."""
    last_error = None
    for deployment in CHAIN[alias]:
        if breakers[deployment].is_open():
            continue  # known to be failing: skip it without waiting
        for attempt in range(2):
            try:
                reply = clients[deployment].chat(request, first_token_timeout=ttft_deadline_s)
                breakers[deployment].record_success()
                return reply
            except ProviderError as error:
                breakers[deployment].record_failure()
                last_error = error
                if error.status not in RETRYABLE:
                    raise  # 400, context too long, refusal: another try will not help
                if error.status == 429 and not error.retry_after:
                    break  # quota gone here: go straight to the next deployment
                wait = error.retry_after or 0.2 * 2**attempt
                time.sleep(wait + random.uniform(0, wait))  # backoff with jitter
    raise AllDeploymentsFailed(alias) from last_error

Two traps specific to models:

  • A fallback model is a different program. Prompts tuned for one model, its tool-calling format and its refusal style may not transfer. Run the eval suite against every model in the chain, not only the primary — otherwise the fallback silently lowers quality exactly during an incident.
  • Retries multiply token spend. The retry storm of the reliability class now has a price tag: cap attempts, use a retry budget (e.g. retries ≤ 10% of calls), and count retried tokens against the caller's quota.

Try it

Load the AI assistant scenario with the spike profile and chaos set to medium. Watch the LLM Gateway when a provider starts failing: without a fallback, errors propagate to the orchestrator and the fan; with a second provider wired to the gateway, the error rate stays low but cost and latency per request change. Compare the token rate the gateway reports with the provider's limit. Open it in the full playground to add the second provider yourself.

items.title: Quotas and token budgets
items.text:
Provider limits are expressed in requests per minute (RPM), tokens per minute (TPM) — sometimes input and output separately — and concurrent requests, per account and per region. A single feature with a bug can exhaust the account's TPM and take every other feature down with it: the noisy neighbor problem, now with an invoice. OWASP lists it as unbounded consumption3; some call it denial of wallet.

The gateway enforces its own, finer limits:

Scope Example limit (BoxOffice) Why Per user 20 requests and 60,000 tokens per hour stop abuse and runaway loops from one account Per feature assistant ≤ 60% of the account TPM; nightly jobs ≤ 20% protect interactive traffic from batch jobs Per request max_tokens ≤ 600 output tokens; ≤ 8 model calls per task bound the worst case of a single request Per month US$ budget per feature with alerts at 50/80/100% finance can plan; no surprises

Counting tokens before you know them. A token bucket counts tokens instead of requests, but output tokens are only known after the call. The usual approach is reserve, then reconcile: before the call, count the input tokens with the model's tokenizer and reserve input + max_tokens from the bucket; after the call, return the unused part. Keep the counters in Redis with atomic scripts, as in the rate-limiter design of Edge.

What happens when a budget runs out is a product decision, decided in advance:

  1. Degrade: route to a smaller model or answer from the cache/FAQ.
  2. Queue: background work (summaries, embeddings) waits for the next window — the async queue pattern.
  3. Shed: return 429 with Retry-After and a friendly message; interactive traffic has priority over batch, and paying flows over browsing.

BoxOffice at 10:00

The flash sale makes the assistant's traffic 50× normal for 15 minutes. The gateway reserves 70% of the account's TPM for the assistant alias with priority interactive, pauses the nightly embedding job (priority batch), routes questions classified as FAQ to the small model and the semantic cache, and caps each fan at 5 assistant requests per minute. When the reserved TPM is 90% used, new conversations get a link to the static FAQ page instead of a model answer: the sale goes on; the assistant degrades.

items.title: Caching: three different things
items.text:
"Cache the LLM" means three different mechanisms with very different risks.

Exact-match response cache Prompt caching (prefix cache) Semantic cache Key hash of the full request (model, prompt, parameters) the longest identical prefix of the prompt embedding of the user question; hit if similarity ≥ threshold What is reused the final answer the model's internal state for the prefix (the KV cache) a stored answer to a similar question Where it lives gateway (Redis) inside the model server / provider gateway (Redis or a vector index) Saves the whole call input-token cost (cached tokens billed at a discount) and TTFT the whole call Correctness risk none (same input) none — the answer is computed normally false hits: a similar question that needs a different answer Hit ratio in a chat low (questions rarely repeat byte-for-byte) high (system prompt + tools + history repeat on every call) medium for FAQ-like traffic; ~0 for personal, tool-using requests

items.title: Prompt caching
items.text:
Processing the input (the prefill, below) produces internal key/value tensors for every token. When the next request starts with the same tokens, the server can reuse them instead of recomputing. Most major providers and open-source servers (e.g. vLLM's automatic prefix caching) support this; providers bill cached input tokens at a fraction of the normal price, require a minimum prefix length, and keep entries for minutes of inactivity. Details — automatic or explicit cache markers, discount, lifetime — differ by provider: read their documentation.

Because the match is on an exact prefix, the order of the prompt matters:

flowchart LR
    s["1. system prompt<br/>(static)"] --> t["2. tool definitions<br/>(static)"] --> k["3. retrieved documents<br/>(per conversation)"] --> h["4. conversation history<br/>(grows)"] --> u["5. new user message<br/>(changes every call)"]

Cache busters

A timestamp, a request ID or the user's name at the top of the system prompt changes the prefix on every call and silently drops the hit ratio to zero. So does re-ordering tool definitions or re-serializing JSON with unstable key order. Put everything that varies at the end, and monitor the cached-token ratio per feature.

items.title: Semantic caching
items.text:
A semantic cache embeds the user question (see RAG & Memory) and looks for a previous question whose embedding is close enough. "What time do the gates open at Arena Paulista?" and "when do doors open at Arena Paulista?" should hit. The danger is the reverse case: "can I get a refund for the Saturday show?" and "can I get a refund for the Sunday show?" are almost identical as vectors and may need different answers.

Rules that keep a semantic cache safe:

  • Scope the key: tenant, language, event or venue ID, and policy version are part of the key, not only the vector.
  • Only for generic answers: never cache answers that used tools, personal data or the user's permissions.
  • Tune the threshold with data: label a sample of (question, cached question) pairs as same/different and pick the similarity threshold for the precision you need; a hit ratio gained with wrong answers is a bug.
  • Short TTL and invalidation when the source document changes (the same problem as in Caching).

items.title: Inference performance: TTFT, TPOT and throughput
items.text:
Generating an answer has two phases with opposite profiles:

  • Prefill — the model processes all input tokens in parallel. It is compute-bound and ends when the first output token appears: it sets the time to first token (TTFT). TTFT grows with the uncached prompt length and with queueing at the server.
  • Decode — the model generates output tokens one at a time, each step reading all the model weights from GPU memory. It is memory-bandwidth-bound and sets the time per output token (TPOT), also called inter-token latency (ITL).
\[ \text{latency}_{\text{e2e}} = \text{TTFT} + \text{TPOT} \times (N_{out} - 1) \qquad \text{speed per user} = \frac{1}{\text{TPOT}}\ \text{tokens/s} \]

With TTFT = 0.6 s and TPOT = 20 ms (50 tokens/s), a 250-token answer takes 0.6 + 0.02 × 249 ≈ 5.6 s; a 1,000-token answer, ~20.6 s. Answer length is a latency decision.

ResultSource

2026-10-23T08:15:39.744896 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ 

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from io import StringIO

# Left: end-to-end latency = TTFT + TPOT x (output tokens - 1)
models = {"large model (TTFT 0.6 s, 50 tok/s)": (0.6, 0.020),
          "small model (TTFT 0.2 s, 150 tok/s)": (0.2, 1 / 150)}
tokens = list(range(1, 1001, 10))

# Right: one self-hosted replica decoding a batch of b sequences per step.
# Step time = fixed weight read + a small per-sequence cost (illustrative).
W_READ_MS, PER_SEQ_MS = 12.0, 0.15
batch = list(range(1, 257))
per_stream = [1000 / (W_READ_MS + PER_SEQ_MS * b) for b in batch]
aggregate = [b * s for b, s in zip(batch, per_stream)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
for label, (ttft, tpot) in models.items():
    ax[0].plot(tokens, [ttft + tpot * (n - 1) for n in tokens], label=label)
ax[0].set_xlabel("output tokens")
ax[0].set_ylabel("end-to-end latency (s)")
ax[0].set_title("Latency grows with the answer length")
ax[0].legend()

twin.plot(batch, per_stream, color="tab:red", label="per-user speed (tok/s)")
twin.set_ylabel("per-user speed (tokens/s)", color="tab:red")

items.title: Streaming
items.text:
Since the answer arrives token by token, the gateway streams it to the client — usually with Server-Sent Events (SSE) over HTTP, as seen in Protocols. The fan starts reading after the TTFT instead of after the full latency, which is why TTFT is the interactive SLO (e.g. p95 TTFT < 1.5 s) and TPOT only needs to beat reading speed (people read roughly 4–8 words per second, so ~15–20 tokens/s already feels fluent).

Streaming has architectural consequences:

  • Long-lived connections. By Little's law, 33 requests/s × 12 s per streamed answer ≈ 400 open connections per instance pool. Use asynchronous servers (FastAPI/uvicorn, Netty), and raise idle timeouts on load balancers and proxies that would cut a slow stream.
  • Tool calls and JSON cannot be acted on until complete. Only the final natural-language answer benefits from streaming.
  • Output guardrails and streaming conflict. Checking the whole answer before showing it removes the TTFT benefit; checking chunk by chunk may show a problematic sentence before it is caught. Common compromise: stream, check in windows of a few sentences, and retract if needed — and never stream content of high-risk actions before validation.

items.title: Batching and the KV cache
items.text:
If you self-host a model (or just want to understand provider limits), one number explains most behavior: decode is limited by memory bandwidth, not by compute. Every decode step reads all the weights. An 8-billion-parameter model in 16-bit precision is ~16 GB; a GPU with ~3 TB/s of memory bandwidth needs at least ~5 ms to read it — so a single sequence cannot exceed ~200 tokens/s however powerful the GPU.

Batching amortizes that read: one pass over the weights advances b sequences at once. Replica throughput grows almost linearly with b while each user's speed degrades slowly (right plot above). Two techniques made this practical:

  • Continuous (in-flight) batching4: instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish, the server adds and removes sequences at every token step, so a short answer does not wait for a long one.
  • PagedAttention5: the KV cache of each sequence is stored in fixed-size pages, like virtual memory, eliminating fragmentation and allowing prefix sharing across requests (which is how self-hosted prompt caching works).

The limit is memory for the KV cache, the key/value tensors kept for every token of every active sequence:

\[ \text{KV bytes per token} = 2 \times \text{layers} \times \text{KV heads} \times \text{head dim} \times \text{bytes per value} \]

For a Llama-3-8B-class model (32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, 16-bit values): 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 128 KiB per token. An 8,000-token conversation needs ~1 GiB. On an 80 GB GPU with ~16 GB of weights, ~64 GB remain: ~64 concurrent 8k-token conversations, or ~512 of 1k tokens. Concurrency is bounded by context length × users, which is why long prompts are expensive even when they are cheap per token.

Other serving techniques you will see in 2026 (all trade something for throughput or latency):

Technique Idea Trade-off Quantization (8-bit, 4-bit weights) fewer bytes per weight → less memory, faster decode some quality loss; must be evaluated Speculative decoding6 a small draft model proposes several tokens; the large model verifies them in one step extra compute; gain depends on how often the draft is right Chunked prefill split long prefills so they do not stall ongoing decodes slightly higher TTFT for long prompts Prefill/decode disaggregation7 run the two phases on different GPU pools KV cache must move between pools; more moving parts

items.title: Self-hosted or API?
items.text:
Criterion Provider API Self-hosted (vLLM, SGLang, Ollama for dev) Cost model per token; zero when idle per GPU-hour; paid when idle Best when traffic is spiky or small; best-quality models needed traffic is high and steady; smaller open-weight models suffice Latency control limited (shared infrastructure, rate limits) full (batch size, hardware, region) Data control contractual (retention, region) full Operations none GPUs, drivers, autoscaling, model updates, on-call

A back-of-the-envelope check: a GPU that costs US$ c per hour and sustains T output tokens/s at your batch size costs \(c / (3600 \cdot T \cdot u)\) per token at utilization u. At 10% utilization it is 10× more expensive per token than at 100%. Self-hosting wins only with steady load — or when data cannot leave your network. For offline work (embedding the catalog, running evals), many providers also offer batch APIs: asynchronous, results within hours, at a discount.

items.title: Observability at the gateway
items.text: Because every call passes through it, the gateway is the natural place to emit the LLM telemetry described in Safety, Evals & Observability: one span per call with model, tokens (input, cached, output), cost, TTFT and finish reason, plus metrics aggregated per alias, feature and user tier. The dashboards answer the CFO's question directly: US$ per conversation, by feature, per day.

items.title: Products
items.text:
The gateway is a pattern, not a product. Examples, to explore — check each product's current documentation for capabilities:

Open sourceManaged / cloud
  • LiteLLM (proxy server): unified API, routing, fallbacks, budgets, spend tracking — used in Hands-on 12.
  • Envoy AI Gateway: LLM traffic management built on Envoy Gateway.
  • Serving engines behind the gateway: vLLM, SGLang, Ollama (local development).
  • Cloud model platforms with routing and cross-region capacity: Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, Azure AI Foundry.
  • API-management products with LLM policies (token limits, semantic caching): Azure API Management, Kong AI Gateway, Cloudflare AI Gateway.

In the interview

Put an LLM gateway between every service and the models, and name four of its jobs: routing by alias, fallbacks with circuit breakers, token quotas with priorities, and cost/latency telemetry. Separate TTFT (interactive SLO, streamed) from TPOT (speed) in your latency estimate, and distinguish prompt caching (safe, cuts input cost and TTFT) from semantic caching (risky, only for generic answers). If the interviewer asks about self-hosting, answer with the KV-cache memory and utilization arguments.

Common pitfalls

  • Model names hard-coded in services — every model change is a multi-team deploy. Use aliases.
  • Unpinned "latest" models — quality changes without a deploy, and nobody knows why the evals dropped.
  • Retrying 400s and refusals, or falling back to a weaker-guarded model on a refusal.
  • Rate limiting by requests only — one 100k-token request costs as much as a thousand small ones.
  • Variable data at the top of the prompt — the prompt cache never hits.
  • A semantic cache keyed only by the vector — leaks answers across events, users or tenants.
  • Proxy idle timeouts shorter than the longest stream — answers cut in the middle under load.
