items.text:
• Databases — the source of truth the cache protects; read replicas are the other way to scale reads.
  • Traffic & Edge — DNS and CDN — HTTP caching and CDNs, the outermost cache layers.
  • Hands-on 5 — Caching — Redis cache-aside on the catalog service; measure the hit ratio and p99; reproduce and fix a stampede.
  • Exercise — cache + replica — before/after measurements of a cache and a read replica.
  • Case studies: distributed cache, URL shortener, search autocomplete.
  • Playground — scenario read-heavy-cache.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Caches work because of locality and skew: a cache holding 1% of a Zipf-distributed catalog can absorb most reads.
  • A request crosses many cache layers (client, CDN, gateway, in-process, distributed, database); closer to the user is faster but harder to invalidate.
  • \(t_{\text{eff}} = h \cdot t_{\text{hit}} + (1-h) \cdot t_{\text{miss}}\) and \(\text{QPS}_{\text{DB}} = (1-h) \cdot \text{QPS}\): think in miss ratio — each extra nine is 10× less database load.
  • Size for the working set, measure item sizes, watch evictions, and keep headroom.
  • Cache what you display, not what you decide on: seat holds, payments and balances go to the source of truth.

  1. BRESLAU, L. et al. Web Caching and Zipf-like Distributions: Evidence and Implications. IEEE INFOCOM, 1999. ↩

  2. DEAN, J. Designs, Lessons and Advice from Building Large Distributed Systems. Keynote, LADIS, 2009 ("latency numbers every programmer should know"). Network and SSD values updated to current hardware as orders of magnitude. ↩

  3. FIELDING, R.; NOTTINGHAM, M.; RESCHKE, J. RFC 9111 — HTTP Caching. IETF, 2022. ↩

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Why caching works and hit-ratio math
items.text:
Q1. BoxOffice's event page receives 40,000 reads per second. With the current cache the hit ratio is 95%. The team improves it to 99%. What happens to the number of reads that reach the database?

  • A. It drops by about 4%, from 2,000 to 1,920 QPS
  • B. It drops from 2,000 to 400 QPS — five times less
  • C. It drops from 38,000 to 39,600 QPS
  • D. It does not change; the hit ratio only affects latency
Answer

B — From 2,000 to 400 QPS.

The database receives the misses: \((1-h) \times \text{QPS}\). At 95%, 0.05 × 40,000 = 2,000 QPS; at 99%, 0.01 × 40,000 = 400 QPS. Four points of hit ratio became a 5× cut in database load. Always reason with the miss ratio — that is the number the database feels.

Q2. A cache hit costs 0.5 ms and a miss costs 10.5 ms (failed lookup + database). What is the average (effective) latency of a read at a 90% hit ratio?

  • A. 0.5 ms
  • B. 1.5 ms
  • C. 5.5 ms
  • D. 9.5 ms
Answer

B — 1.5 ms.

\(t_{\text{eff}} = h \cdot t_{\text{hit}} + (1-h) \cdot t_{\text{miss}} = 0.9 \times 0.5 + 0.1 \times 10.5 = 0.45 + 1.05 = 1.5\) ms. Note that the 10% of misses contribute more than twice as much as the 90% of hits — and they also define the tail (p95/p99) of the latency.

Q3. Why can a cache that holds only 1% of a catalog of 100,000 events answer more than half of the reads?

  • A. Because Redis compresses the values, so 1% of the memory holds the whole catalog
  • B. Because popularity is skewed (approximately Zipf): a few items receive most of the requests, and the cache keeps those
  • C. Because the database also has a cache, so the two together cover 100%
  • D. It cannot; a cache holding 1% of the data answers at most 1% of the reads
Answer

B — Skewed popularity.

Web workloads follow Zipf-like distributions: the item of rank \(i\) is requested with probability ∝ \(1/i^s\). With \(s \approx 1\), the top 1% of items gets around 60% of the requests. With a weak skew (many items with similar popularity), the same small cache would help much less — check the access pattern before adding a cache.

Q4. Which piece of BoxOffice data should never be decided from a cached value?

  • A. The event description shown on the event page
  • B. The list of events "this weekend in São Paulo"
  • C. Whether seat A-12 can be held for the fan who just clicked it
  • D. The venue's seating layout
Answer

C — The seat hold.

The seat map can be cached for display (a stale map only produces a "seat no longer available" message), but the decision to give the seat to a fan must be made on the source of truth, in a SQL transaction, or two fans can get the same seat. Rule of thumb: cache what you display, not what you decide on.

items.title: Patterns
items.text:
Q5. An organizer edits event 42. The catalog service uses cache-aside. Which write sequence is the standard, safest choice?

  • A. Delete the cache key, then update the database
  • B. Update the database, commit, then delete the cache key
  • C. Update the cache with the new value, then update the database
  • D. Update the database and the cache in any order — both will end up equal
Answer

B — Write the database, commit, then delete.

Deleting first (A) lets a reader refill the cache with the old row before the update. Updating the cache (C, D) lets concurrent writers reorder: the database ends with one value and the cache with the other. Deleting after the commit is idempotent and order-independent; the next read loads the fresh row. A TTL remains as a safety net for the rare race that is still possible.

Q6. A product manager wants to count views per event and show "1,834 people viewed this event today", at tens of thousands of increments per second. Which pattern fits best?

  • A. Write-through to PostgreSQL on every view
  • B. Write-behind: INCR in Redis, flushed to the database in batches every few seconds
  • C. Cache-aside with a 5-minute TTL
  • D. Write-around: write every view to the database and never cache
Answer

B — Write-behind.

Counters are the textbook case for write-behind: increments are coalesced in memory and persisted in batches, protecting the database from the write rate. Losing a few seconds of counts on a cache failure is acceptable for this data. The same pattern would be unacceptable for orders, payments or seat holds.

Q7. What is the main risk of write-behind (write-back) caching?

  • A. Reads after a write always miss
  • B. Writes acknowledged to the client can be lost if the cache node fails before flushing to the database
  • C. It requires a distributed lock for every read
  • D. It cannot be used with Redis
Answer

B — Acknowledged writes can be lost.

Write-behind confirms the write when it reaches the cache's memory; the database only receives it later. If the node dies (or fails over with asynchronous replication) before the flush, the write is gone even though the client was told it succeeded.

items.title: Invalidation and eviction
items.text:
Q8. In cache-aside, the code already deletes the key after every write. Why should cached events still have a TTL?

  • A. Redis requires a TTL on every key
  • B. Because explicit invalidation will eventually miss something — a race, a crashed process, a batch job or a manual SQL fix — and the TTL bounds how long the stale value lives
  • C. Because without a TTL the hit ratio would be 100%, which overloads Redis
  • D. It should not; a TTL only adds misses
Answer

B — The TTL is the safety net.

The cache-aside race (a slow reader storing an old value after the writer's delete), writes that bypass the application, or a failover that loses a DEL all leave stale entries. Without a TTL, these errors are permanent. With one, they are bounded.

Q9. A nightly report reads every event once, in id order, through the same cache used by the website. The next morning the hit ratio is very low for the first minutes. Which eviction policy was most likely in use, and what would resist this?

  • A. LFU was in use; switch to LRU
  • B. LRU was in use; the scan replaced the hot items with items read once. LFU or W-TinyLFU (or bypassing the cache for the report) would resist it
  • C. Random eviction was in use; switch to FIFO
  • D. noeviction was in use; switch to volatile-ttl
Answer

B — Scan pollution of LRU.

LRU treats "read once a second ago" as more valuable than "read a thousand times a minute ago", so a sequential scan larger than the cache evicts the whole hot set. Frequency-based policies (LFU, W-TinyLFU) keep the steadily popular items. The simplest fix is often to keep batch reads out of the shared cache.

Q10. BoxOffice runs 20 replicas of catalog, each with an in-process (L1) Caffeine cache in front of Redis. An organizer fixes a typo in the event name. Why might some users still see the typo after Redis was invalidated, and what fixes it?

  • A. Redis replicates asynchronously; the fix is WAIT
  • B. Each replica's L1 cache still has its own copy; fix with a short L1 TTL and/or a broadcast invalidation (pub/sub or CDC) to every replica
  • C. The CDN cached the database; purge the database
  • D. Caffeine ignores TTLs; replace it with a HashMap
Answer

B — Twenty private copies.

Deleting the Redis key does not reach the 20 local caches. A two-level cache needs its own invalidation: a short L1 TTL (accepting a few seconds of staleness), a message broadcast to every replica (Redis pub/sub, client-side caching with tracking, or a CDC pipeline), or both.

items.title: Failure modes
items.text:
Q11. The cached event page for the stadium show is read 20,000 times per second. Recomputing it takes 200 ms. When the key expires and nothing protects it, about how many requests hit the database for the same query?

  • A. 1
  • B. 20
  • C. About 4,000
  • D. 20,000 every second, forever
Answer

C — About 4,000 (a cache stampede).

By Little's law, requests arriving during the recompute window = rate × time = 20,000 × 0.2 s = 4,000, each missing and running the same query. Under that load the query slows down, so the real number tends to be larger. Fixes: request coalescing, a lock/lease so only one recomputes, stale-while-revalidate, or probabilistic early expiration (XFetch).

Q12. At 09:50 a job warms the cache with the 5,000 hottest pages, all with TTL = 600 s. The on-sale starts at 10:00. What is the problem and the fix?

  • A. No problem; a warm cache is always good
  • B. All 5,000 keys expire together at 10:00, the peak — a cache avalanche. Add random jitter to the TTLs (e.g. 600 + random 0–120 s)
  • C. The TTL is too long; use 60 s
  • D. The keys will be evicted by LRU before 10:00
Answer

B — Avalanche, fixed with TTL jitter.

Keys written together with the same TTL expire together. Spreading expirations with jitter (and refreshing the hottest keys ahead of time) avoids a synchronized wave of misses at the worst possible moment.

Q13. Bots request GET /events/{random id} for ids that do not exist, at 5,000 requests per second. The hit ratio of the cache is fine for real traffic, but the database load jumps. What is happening and what helps?

  • A. Hot key; use key replication
  • B. Cache penetration: missing ids are never cached, so every request reaches the database. Validate input, cache "not found" with a short TTL, use a Bloom filter of valid ids, and rate-limit at the edge
  • C. Cache avalanche; add TTL jitter
  • D. Big key; split the value
Answer

B — Cache penetration.

There is nothing to cache for a key that does not exist, so plain cache-aside sends every such request to the database. Negative caching stores the absence; a Bloom filter (~9.6 bits per id for 1% false positives) rejects ids that certainly do not exist before touching the cache or the database.

items.title: Redis
items.text:
Q14. In Redis Cluster, a Lua script must update seats:42 and prices:42 atomically, but fails with a CROSSSLOT error. What is the fix?

  • A. Increase the number of hash slots
  • B. Rename the keys with a hash tag, e.g. {event:42}:seats and {event:42}:prices, so only event:42 is hashed and both keys land in the same slot
  • C. Use KEYS * to find the slots first
  • D. Disable cluster mode for Lua scripts
Answer

B — Hash tags.

Redis Cluster maps each key to one of 16,384 slots with CRC16(key) mod 16384; multi-key operations require all keys in the same slot. With a hash tag, only the text inside {...} is hashed. Choose tags with high cardinality (one per event), or the tag becomes a hot spot.

Q15. A colleague proposes to implement seat holds only in Redis with SET hold:42:A-12 fan:1017 NX PX 600000, replicated with Sentinel, to avoid touching PostgreSQL during the flash sale. What is the strongest objection?

  • A. SET NX is not atomic
  • B. Redis replication is asynchronous: after a failover the new primary may not have a hold that was already granted, so the seat can be granted again — the decision must stay in the database, with Redis only as a fast pre-filter
  • C. Redis cannot store keys with colons
  • D. PX only accepts seconds
Answer

B — Asynchronous replication can lose acknowledged holds.

SET NX is atomic on one node, which makes it a great filter that rejects most competing clicks in microseconds. But a failover, an eviction or a flush can erase a hold silently, and then two fans can both succeed. The seat hold is taken in a SQL transaction with a constraint that makes double booking impossible; Redis only reduces how many requests reach it.

items.title: Index
items.text:
A cache changes how the system fails. Without it, the database degrades smoothly as load grows. With it, the database is sized for the misses — and anything that suddenly turns hits into misses (a restart, an expiry, a new kind of request, a cache node dying) sends the full load to a database that was never sized for it. Most cache incidents are not bugs in the cache; they are the moment the system discovers how much it depended on the cache.

This page goes through the classic failure modes in the order they tend to appear in a flash sale, each with its symptom and its fix.

Failure What happens Main fix Cold cache empty cache after restart or deploy warm-up, gradual traffic shift Stampede a hot key expires; thousands recompute it at once lock/lease, coalescing, stale-while-revalidate, XFetch Avalanche many keys expire at the same moment TTL jitter Penetration requests for keys that never exist negative caching, Bloom filter, validation Hot key one key overloads one cache node local L1 cache, key replication Big key huge values block the cache split, compress, UNLINK Cache down the cache cluster fails timeouts, fallback with load shedding, replicas, gutter pool Memory pressure evictions and fragmentation sizing, separate instances, eviction policy

items.title: Cold cache
items.text:
A cold cache is an empty one: after a restart of Redis without persistence, a deploy that changes the key version (:v3 → :v4), a new region, or a cache node replaced by autoscaling. The hit ratio starts at zero and climbs as keys are read.

The danger is the gap between the load the database was sized for (the misses) and the load it receives (everything). With 50,000 reads/s and a usual 98% hit ratio, the database is sized for ~1,000 QPS; a cold start sends it 50,000.

Think first: when is the safest moment to deploy a new cache key version?

BoxOffice needs to change the format of the cached event (:v3 → :v4). The release is ready at 09:30; the stadium on-sale starts at 10:00.

Not at 09:30. A new key version is a cold cache for every event, and the hottest moment of the month is half an hour away. Deploy after the on-sale peak (or before, with a warm-up and enough time to verify the hit ratio). More generally: schedule cache-invalidating deploys outside known peaks, and roll them out gradually so old and new versions warm up in parallel.

Fixes:

  • Warm-up: before a known peak, preload the keys you know will be hot — the events going on sale today, the home page lists — with a job that reads them through the normal path.
  • Gradual traffic shift: send 5%, then 25%, then 100% of traffic to a new cache node or region (canary), so it warms under a fraction of the load.
  • Persistence for big caches: a Redis restart that reloads an RDB snapshot comes back warm (Redis — persistence).
  • Never restart all cache nodes at once.
  • Capacity floor: know how many QPS the database can take with an empty cache, and protect it with load shedding (see cache down). The Google SRE book lists cold caches among the classic triggers of cascading failures1.

items.title: Cache stampede
items.text:
A cache stampede (also thundering herd or dog-piling) happens when a hot key expires or is deleted. Every request that arrives before someone puts the value back misses — and each one goes to the database to recompute the same value.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as 4,000 requests
    participant R as Redis
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    Note over R: event:42 expires at 10:00:00.000
    A->>R: GET event:42 (×4,000 within 200 ms)
    R-->>A: miss (×4,000)
    A->>D: same SELECT (×4,000)
    Note over D: CPU 100%, query time 3 ms to 2 s
    D-->>A: rows, slowly
    A->>R: SET event:42 (×4,000, all identical)

The arithmetic is Little's law. If event 42 is read 20,000 times per second and recomputing it takes 200 ms, then about \(20{,}000 \times 0.2 = 4{,}000\) requests miss before the first one finishes. Worse: under that load the query slows down, the window grows, and more requests pile in. A stampede can take down a database that was serving the same page comfortably one second before.

There are four standard fixes. They are complementary.

items.title: 1. Lock (or lease): only one recomputes
items.text:
On a miss, a request tries to acquire a short lock for the key. The winner recomputes; the others wait a few milliseconds and read the cache again (or serve a stale copy).

catalog/stampede_lock.py
import json
import time
import uuid

RELEASE = """
if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
end
return 0
"""


def get_event(event_id: int, db, r) -> dict:
    key = f"boxoffice:catalog:event:{event_id}:v3"
    lock = f"lock:{key}"
    for _ in range(50):                                   # wait at most ~1 s
        cached = r.get(key)
        if cached is not None:
            return json.loads(cached)
        token = str(uuid.uuid4())
        if r.set(lock, token, nx=True, px=5_000):          # only one winner
            try:
                event = db.fetch_event_with_venue_and_prices(event_id)
                r.set(key, json.dumps(event), ex=300)
                return event
            finally:
                r.eval(RELEASE, 1, lock, token)             # release only our own lock
        time.sleep(0.02)                                    # losers wait and re-read
    return db.fetch_event_with_venue_and_prices(event_id)   # last resort
  • SET ... NX PX 5000 is atomic: set only if absent, with a 5 s expiry so a crashed winner does not block the key forever.
  • The release checks the token, so a slow winner whose lock already expired does not delete someone else's lock.
  • Cost: losers wait (latency) and poll the cache. Facebook's memcache leases are a refined version of this, built into the cache server2.

items.title: 2. Request coalescing (single-flight)
items.text:
Inside one process, concurrent misses for the same key can share one in-flight computation: the first caller starts it, the others wait for the same future. Caffeine's LoadingCache and AsyncLoadingCache do this automatically; Go has singleflight; in Java you can use a ConcurrentHashMap<Key, CompletableFuture<V>>.

Coalescing does not need Redis: with 20 replicas, a stampede of 4,000 requests becomes 20 database queries — usually harmless. It is the cheapest fix and should be the default for hot paths.

items.title: 3. Stale-while-revalidate
items.text: Keep two expirations: a soft TTL stored inside the value (e.g. 60 s) and a longer hard TTL on the key (e.g. 10 min). After the soft TTL, the first reader triggers a background refresh (guarded by a lock) and everyone, including that reader, keeps getting the stale value until the new one arrives. Readers never wait; the database sees one query. The same idea exists in HTTP as Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=600.

items.title: 4. Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch)
items.text:
Instead of a lock, let each reader decide at random to refresh the value a little before it expires, with a probability that grows as expiry approaches. Vattani, Chierichetti and Lowenstein showed that the following rule is optimal in a precise sense3. Store with the value the time \(\delta\) it took to compute it and its expiry time; on each read, recompute if

\[ t_{\text{now}} - \delta \cdot \beta \cdot \ln(u) \;\geq\; t_{\text{expiry}}, \qquad u \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1] \]

Since \(-\ln u\) is an exponential random variable with mean 1, each read "looks ahead" by a random amount of about \(\delta \beta\). The parameter \(\beta\) (default 1) trades earlier refreshes for fewer stampedes. The probability that a single read refreshes, with \(r\) seconds left before expiry, is \(e^{-r/(\delta \beta)}\).

2026-10-23T08:15:40.202138 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The right panel is the elegant part. If reads arrive at rate \(\lambda\), the probability that nobody refreshed early before expiry is \(e^{-\lambda \delta \beta}\). A hot key (hundreds of reads per second) is almost surely refreshed just before it expires — by one reader, with no lock and no coordination — while a cold key, where a stampede cannot happen anyway, simply expires. The algorithm adapts to the traffic by itself.

catalog/xfetch.py
import json
import math
import random
import time


def xfetch(r, key: str, recompute, ttl: int = 300, beta: float = 1.0):
    entry = r.hgetall(key)                     # {"data": ..., "delta": ..., "expiry": ...}
    now = time.time()
    if entry:
        delta, expiry = float(entry["delta"]), float(entry["expiry"])
        u = 1.0 - random.random()              # in (0, 1], so log(u) is defined
        if now - delta * beta * math.log(u) < expiry:
            return json.loads(entry["data"])   # serve the cached value
    start = time.time()
    value = recompute()                        # miss, or chosen to refresh early
    delta = time.time() - start
    r.hset(key, mapping={"data": json.dumps(value), "delta": delta, "expiry": start + ttl})
    r.expire(key, ttl)
    return value
Fix Readers wait? DB queries per expiry Complexity Best for Lock / lease yes (losers) 1 medium any shared hot key Coalescing yes, per process 1 per replica low (library) always, as a baseline Stale-while-revalidate no 1 medium data that tolerates seconds of staleness XFetch no ~1 low hot keys with a known recompute cost

items.title: Cache avalanche
items.text:
A cache avalanche is a stampede on many keys at once: a large set of keys expires at the same moment, or the cache is flushed, and the misses for all of them hit the database together.

BoxOffice: the warm-up that caused the outage

To prepare for the 10:00 on-sale, a job warms the cache at 09:50 with the 5,000 hottest pages, all with TTL = 600 s. Every one of them expires at 10:00:00 — the exact moment 2 million fans press F5. The warm-up made things worse than no warm-up at all.

The fix is jitter: add a random component to every TTL, e.g. ttl = 600 + random(0, 120), so expirations spread over two minutes. Combine with refresh-ahead or XFetch for the very hottest keys, and with stampede protection for each individual key.

items.title: Cache penetration
items.text:
Cache penetration is traffic for keys that do not exist in the database. They are never cached (there is nothing to cache), so every request goes through to the database. A bot enumerating GET /events/1, /events/2, …, /events/99999999, or a buggy client asking for an id that was deleted, can generate a database query per request at the rate of the cache.

Fixes, in layers:

  1. Validate input before touching anything: malformed or out-of-range ids are rejected at the gateway.
  2. Negative caching: cache "not found" with a short TTL (e.g. 30–60 s) — see patterns.
  3. Bloom filter of existing ids: a compact probabilistic set that answers "definitely not present" or "probably present". A request for an id the filter says is absent never reaches the cache or the database. Sizing: about \(-\ln p / (\ln 2)^2 \approx 9.6\) bits per element for a 1% false-positive rate — ~120 KB for 100,000 events4. Redis Stack / Redis 8 offer Bloom filters natively (BF.ADD, BF.EXISTS).
  4. Rate limiting and bot mitigation at the edge (WAF), since penetration is often abuse (Traffic & Edge).

items.title: Hot keys
items.text:
A distributed cache spreads keys over nodes, but one key lives on one node. When a single key is extremely popular, that node saturates while the rest of the cluster is idle.

BoxOffice: one key, one node

Illustrative numbers: 2 million fans refresh the event page about every 5 seconds → 400,000 reads/s of event:42. The cached value is 4 KB. On a single Redis node that means 400,000 × 4 KB ≈ 1.6 GB/s ≈ 13 Gbit/s of outgoing traffic — more than a 10 Gbit/s network interface — plus far more commands than one node's main thread is comfortable with. Adding nodes to the cluster does nothing: the key still lives on one of them.

Fixes:

  • L1 in-process cache with a short TTL (1–2 s) in each catalog replica (two-level cache). With 50 replicas and a 1 s TTL, Redis sees ~50 reads/s for that key instead of 400,000. This is by far the most effective fix.
  • Key replication: store N copies under different keys (event:42#0 … event:42#7), which hash to different nodes; readers pick one at random. Writes and invalidations must touch all N copies.
  • Read replicas of the cache shard (Redis replicas with READONLY reads in Cluster), accepting slightly staler reads.
  • Shrink the value: send the static part (description, images) through the CDN and cache only the small dynamic part.
  • Cache higher up: the public event page can be cached at the CDN or gateway for a few seconds, so the hot key never reaches the application.

Detecting hot keys: client-side metrics per key prefix, redis-cli --hotkeys (requires an LFU eviction policy), or the MONITOR command on a replica for a few seconds (never on a busy primary).

items.title: Big keys
items.text:
A big key is a value of megabytes, or a collection (hash, list, set, sorted set) with millions of members. Redis executes commands on a single main thread, so reading, writing, expiring or deleting a big key blocks every other client for its duration; transferring it saturates the network.

  • Find them with redis-cli --bigkeys or MEMORY USAGE key.
  • Split large objects (one key per section instead of one per venue), paginate collections (HSCAN, ZRANGE ... LIMIT), compress values above a few KB.
  • Delete with UNLINK (frees memory in a background thread) instead of DEL.
  • Keep values small — a common guideline is to stay well below 100 KB per value and avoid collections with more than ~10,000 elements; treat these as rules of thumb, not limits.

items.title: The cache goes down
items.text:
Sooner or later, the Redis primary fails, the network partitions, or a failover takes 10–30 seconds. What happens next depends on decisions made long before:

flowchart TD
    F["Redis unavailable"] --> T{"Cache calls have<br/>a short timeout?"}
    T -->|"no"| X1["threads block on Redis<br/>whole service stalls"]
    T -->|"yes"| B{"Fallback on error?"}
    B -->|"no"| X2["every read fails<br/>outage"]
    B -->|"read the DB"| C{"Can the DB take<br/>the full load?"}
    C -->|"yes"| OK1["slower but correct"]
    C -->|"no"| S["shed load and serve degraded:<br/>static page, waiting room,<br/>rate-limited misses"]

The uncomfortable truth: once the database is sized for the misses, the cache is no longer optional. It is a load-bearing dependency, and it needs the same reliability engineering as the database:

  • Timeouts on every cache call (tens of milliseconds, not the client default) and a circuit breaker, so a sick cache fails fast instead of holding threads (Reliability).
  • Replication with automatic failover (Redis Sentinel or Cluster; managed services do this for you) — see Redis.
  • Protected fallback: falling back to the database for every miss during an outage is a self-inflicted stampede. Limit concurrent fallback queries (a bulkhead), serve degraded content for non-essential parts, and put the waiting room in front of the on-sale.
  • Gutter pool: Facebook keeps a small pool of idle cache servers; when a server fails, clients send its keys to the gutter pool (with short TTLs) instead of to the database2.
  • Know the number: test what the database can take with the cache off. That number is your real capacity floor.

items.title: Memory pressure, evictions and stale failovers
items.text:
• Eviction storms: when the working set outgrows maxmemory, the cache evicts keys that will be needed again; the hit ratio falls, the database load rises. Watch evicted_keys and the hit ratio together.
  • Fragmentation: memory used by the process can exceed the data size (mem_fragmentation_ratio in INFO memory); leave headroom.
  • Snapshot fork: an RDB snapshot or AOF rewrite forks the process; with copy-on-write, a write-heavy instance can need up to twice its memory during the snapshot. Size for it, or run persistence on a replica.
  • Stale data after failover: Redis replication is asynchronous. If the primary acknowledged a DEL and failed before replicating it, the promoted replica still has the old value — invalidations can be lost. One more reason every key needs a TTL.

items.title: See it in the playground
items.text:
Try it: this scenario runs the read-heavy-cache design under a spike. First watch the steady state: hit ratio, database QPS and p99. Then (1) flush the cache at the peak and watch the database load jump to the full request rate — a cold cache under load; (2) shorten the TTL of the hot keys and look for stampede spikes in the database QPS each time they expire; (3) enable chaos and watch what happens to p99 while the cache is unavailable.

The full playground lets you add a second cache layer or a waiting room and compare.

BoxOffice: an on-sale, minute by minute

Time Event Failure mode avoided 09:30 no cache-invalidating deploys until 11:00 cold cache 09:45 warm-up job loads today's on-sale events, TTL 600 s + jitter 0–120 s cold cache, avalanche 09:59 2 M fans on the event page; catalog serves it from a 1 s L1 cache in each replica hot key 10:00 the price table is edited; delete after commit, CDC broadcasts to L1 caches stale data 10:02 event:42 reaches its soft TTL; one replica refreshes it in the background, others serve stale stampede 10:05 bots probe /events/<random id>; WAF rate-limits, Bloom filter and negative cache absorb the rest penetration 10:11 Redis primary fails; failover in 15 s; cache calls time out at 50 ms; circuit breaker opens; misses are limited to 2,000 QPS, the rest see the waiting room cache down

In the interview

After you draw a cache, the interviewer will often ask "what happens when a hot key expires?" or "what if Redis goes down?". Name the failure (stampede, avalanche, hot key, penetration), give the number that makes it dangerous (Little's law: reads/s × recompute time), and the fix (coalescing or a lock, TTL jitter, L1 cache, negative caching / Bloom filter). For "Redis goes down", say that the database is sized for the misses, so you need timeouts, a circuit breaker and load shedding — not a naive fallback.

Common pitfalls

  • Warm-ups with identical TTLs — they schedule an avalanche.
  • Locks without expiry — a crashed winner blocks the key forever. Always PX.
  • Fallback to the database on every cache error — a cache outage becomes a database outage.
  • Default client timeouts (seconds) on cache calls — a slow Redis stalls every thread.
  • Ignoring keys that do not exist — bots will find them.
  • Scaling the cluster to fix a hot key — the key still lives on one node.
  • DEL of a huge collection, KEYS *, MONITOR on the primary — they block the single main thread.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    COLD["cold cache<br/>warm before traffic"] --> DB["the database takes the misses"]
    STAMP["stampede: a hot key expires<br/>reads/s × recompute time"] --> FIX["lock, coalescing,<br/>stale-while-revalidate, XFetch"]
    AVA["avalanche: many keys<br/>expire together"] --> JIT["TTL jitter"]
    PEN["penetration: keys<br/>that never exist"] --> NEG["negative caching,<br/>Bloom filter"]
    HOT["hot key: one node"] --> L1["L1, key copies, CDN<br/>→ Patterns, Edge"]
    DOWN["the cache goes down"] --> RES["timeouts, circuit breaker,<br/>bulkhead → Reliability"]
    DOWN --> DB
    DB --> SHED["shed load, waiting room<br/>→ Messaging"]

Palette components: cache (a load-bearing dependency once the database is sized for the misses) · sql (what it can take with the cache off is the real capacity floor) · app (single-flight, an L1, short cache timeouts) · cdn · apigw (cache the hot public page higher up) · queue (the waiting room when the fallback would drown the database) · metrics (hit ratio, evicted_keys). Scenarios: read-heavy-cache, flash-sale, cascading-failure. items.title: Index
items.text:
"There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things." — Phil Karlton1

Filling a cache is easy. The hard part is knowing when a copy stopped being true. The database changes; the copy in Redis, in twenty JVMs, in a CDN and in a million browsers does not know it. Every caching design is, at its core, an answer to two questions:

  1. How stale may each piece of data be? (the staleness budget)
  2. How does a change in the source reach every copy within that budget? (the invalidation mechanism)

And because memory is finite, a third question follows: when the cache is full, what do we throw away? (the eviction policy). This page covers the three.

items.title: The staleness budget
items.text:
Before choosing a mechanism, decide — with the product team, not alone — how wrong each kind of data may be, and for how long. The answer is different for every entity.

BoxOffice: staleness budget per data type

Data Changes Acceptable staleness Mechanism Why Event description, images, line-up rarely (organizer edits) ~1 minute delete on write + TTL 5 min a typo fix may take a minute to appear Venue geometry almost never hours TTL 1 h + versioned key on change immutable in practice Price table dynamic pricing, during sales seconds TTL 30 s + delete on write; price re-read from DB at checkout displaying an old price is tolerable; charging it is not Seat map (display) every hold and sale 1–2 s TTL 1 s, or no cache a stale map only causes "seat no longer available" Availability counter ("1,203 left") every sale a few seconds TTL 2 s approximate is fine for display User profile rarely ~1 minute, but read-your-writes for the owner delete on write; owner reads bypass the cache briefly the user must see their own edit Session on login/logout none (logout must work) written to Redis as the source of truth for sessions, not a cache security Seat hold, order, payment — zero not cached correctness

Writing this table is half of the design: once each row has a budget, the mechanism follows.

items.title: TTL: the safety net
items.text:
A TTL (time to live) makes every entry expire after a fixed time. It is the simplest mechanism and the one you should always have, even when you also invalidate explicitly — because explicit invalidation will eventually miss something (a bug, a manual SQL fix, a crashed process between the commit and the delete), and the TTL bounds how long the error lives.

Choosing the TTL is a trade-off between freshness and hit ratio:

  • Too long: stale data lives long after a change.
  • Too short: the long tail of keys always misses (a key read once every 10 minutes never hits with a 60 s TTL), and hot keys expire often, which risks a stampede.

Practical rules:

  • Start from the staleness budget: TTL ≤ budget when there is no explicit invalidation; TTL = a few × budget when there is (the TTL then only bounds the damage of a missed invalidation).
  • Add jitter — TTL = base ± 10% — so that keys written together do not expire together (cache avalanche).
  • Absolute vs. sliding expiration: an absolute TTL expires a fixed time after the write; a sliding one is extended on every read (GETEX key EX 300 in Redis). Sliding expiration keeps hot keys forever — good for sessions, dangerous for data that changes, since a hot stale key may never be refreshed.

items.title: Explicit invalidation
items.text: To get freshness better than the TTL, the code that writes to the database also tells the cache that the value changed. Two decisions matter: delete or update, and in which order.

items.title: Delete, don't update
items.text:
When the event changes, the writer can either update the cache with the new value or delete the key and let the next read fill it. Deleting is safer. Consider two organizers editing event 42 at the same time:

sequenceDiagram
    participant W1 as Writer 1
    participant W2 as Writer 2
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    participant R as Redis
    W1->>D: UPDATE price = 100
    W2->>D: UPDATE price = 120
    W2->>R: SET event:42 price 120
    W1->>R: SET event:42 price 100
    Note over D,R: DB says 120, cache says 100 until the TTL expires

The writes reached the database in one order and the cache in the other. With delete, both writers send DEL event:42: the operations are idempotent and their order does not matter; the next reader loads 120 from the database. Updating the cache is also wasteful when the value is written more often than it is read.

items.title: Write first, then delete
items.text: Order What can go wrong Delete cache → write DB between the two, a reader misses, reads the old row and puts it back. The cache is stale until the TTL. Avoid. Write DB → delete cache (after commit) a narrow race remains (next section), but this is the standard choice Write DB → update cache concurrent writers can reorder (above) Write DB, delete inside the transaction the delete can happen before the commit is visible; a reader refills the old value. Delete after commit.

items.title: The cache-aside race
items.text:
Even "write DB, then delete after commit" leaves one race. It needs a slow reader:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Rd as Reader
    participant R as Redis
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    participant W as Writer
    Rd->>R: GET event:42
    R-->>Rd: miss
    Rd->>D: SELECT event 42
    D-->>Rd: old row v1
    Note over Rd: reader pauses (GC, slow network)
    W->>D: UPDATE event 42 to v2 and COMMIT
    W->>R: DEL event:42
    Rd->>R: SET event:42 v1
    Note over R: stale v1 stays until the TTL expires

The reader read before the write and stored after the delete. It is rare — the reader must be slower than a whole write plus a delete — but at tens of thousands of reads per second, rare things happen every day. The fixes, from simplest to most robust:

  1. A TTL as safety net — bounds the damage. For most data, this is enough.
  2. Delayed double delete — the writer deletes, and deletes again a short time later (e.g. 500 ms, longer than a typical read). The second delete removes what a slow reader put back. Cheap, but probabilistic.
  3. Versioned values — store the row version with the value and only write to the cache if the version is newer than what is there. Since versions come from the database (version column, or the commit LSN), a slow reader with v1 cannot overwrite v2. With versions, updating on write is safe too.
  4. Leases — on a miss, the cache hands the reader a lease token; a delete invalidates outstanding tokens, and a SET with an invalid token is rejected. Facebook's memcache uses leases both for this race and to limit stampedes (only one lease per key every few seconds)2.
set_if_newer.lua — versioned set in Redis
-- KEYS[1] = cache key; ARGV[1] = version; ARGV[2] = value; ARGV[3] = TTL in seconds
local current = redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'version')
if current and tonumber(current) >= tonumber(ARGV[1]) then
  return 0                       -- a newer (or equal) version is already cached
end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'version', ARGV[1], 'data', ARGV[2])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[3])
return 1

The script runs atomically inside Redis (Redis — atomicity), so the compare and the set cannot interleave with another writer.

items.title: Invalidation from the database log (CDC)
items.text:
Invalidation in application code has a structural weakness: it only covers writes that go through that code. A batch job, another service, a migration or a DBA fixing a row by hand will change the database without deleting anything.

Change data capture (CDC) moves invalidation to the source: a connector reads the database's replication log (the PostgreSQL write-ahead log, WAL) and publishes every committed change as an event. An invalidator consumes the events and deletes the affected keys.

flowchart LR
    APP["catalog service"] -->|"UPDATE events"| DB[("PostgreSQL")]
    ADM["admin script"] -->|"UPDATE events"| DB
    DB -->|"WAL"| DBZ["Debezium<br/>CDC connector"]
    DBZ -->|"change event<br/>events id=42"| K[["Kafka topic<br/>catalog.events"]]
    K --> INV["cache invalidator"]
    INV -->|"DEL event:42"| R[("Redis")]
    INV -->|"publish invalidate 42"| PS(("pub/sub<br/>L1 caches"))
  • Complete: every committed change is seen, whatever wrote it; uncommitted changes never are.
  • Ordered per key: the log is in commit order, so invalidations cannot be reordered (with Kafka partitioned by key).
  • Decoupled: the writer does not know which caches exist.
  • Costs: an extra pipeline to run (Debezium, Kafka); invalidation lags the commit by milliseconds to seconds; still needs a TTL in case the pipeline stops.

CDC and the outbox pattern are covered in Messaging.

items.title: Invalidating many copies
items.text:
A value may be cached in several places at once. Each needs its own mechanism:

Copy How to invalidate Notes Redis (shared) DEL key one call reaches every reader In-process L1 in each replica broadcast via pub/sub (Redis PUBLISH, Kafka) or Redis client-side caching (CLIENT TRACKING); or a very short TTL a replica that misses the message stays stale until its TTL CDN purge API (by URL or by tag / surrogate key) purges take seconds to propagate worldwide and may be rate-limited; prefer versioned URLs for assets Browser / mobile app impossible to recall only Cache-Control: max-age (short for data) and versioned URLs (for assets)

Tag-based invalidation helps when one change affects many keys: tag every cached response that contains event 42 with event-42 and purge by tag. Some CDNs support it natively; in Redis you can keep a set of keys per tag (SADD tag:event-42 key1 key2) and delete them together.

items.title: Eviction policies
items.text:
A cache has a memory limit. When it is full and a new value arrives, the eviction policy chooses a victim. A good policy keeps the items that will be read again soonest — which nobody knows, so every policy is a guess based on the past.

Policy Evicts Strength Weakness LRU (least recently used) the item unused for the longest time adapts fast to change; simple a single scan of cold items flushes the hot ones LFU (least frequently used) the item with fewest accesses keeps steadily popular items; resists scans slow to adapt: yesterday's hit lingers (needs aging); new items are evicted before they prove themselves FIFO (first in, first out) the oldest insertion trivial, cheap ignores popularity Random a random item no metadata at all ignores popularity, but surprisingly decent with skew TTL-based (volatile-ttl) the item closest to expiry uses the developer's hint only as good as the TTLs W-TinyLFU admission by frequency estimate + small LRU window near-optimal hit ratio on many real traces; scan-resistant and adaptive more complex (built into Caffeine)

W-TinyLFU, used by Caffeine, combines both worlds: new items enter a small LRU window; to move into the main cache, an item must have a higher estimated frequency than the victim it would replace. Frequencies are kept in a compact probabilistic sketch (a Count-Min sketch) and periodically halved, so old popularity fades3.

The simulation below shows why the policy matters. A cache of 1,000 entries serves Zipf-distributed reads over 20,000 items; in the middle of the run, a reporting job scans 2,000 items that nobody else reads.

2026-10-23T08:15:40.894634 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

How to read it:

  • During the scan, every policy misses — the scanned items were never cached. What matters is what the cache looks like afterwards.
  • LRU and FIFO filled the whole cache with the 2,000 scanned items (more than its capacity), evicting every hot item; the hit ratio needs a while to climb back.
  • LFU evicted scanned items among themselves (each had frequency 1) and kept the hot set: it recovers immediately and has a higher hit ratio overall, because with a stable Zipf workload frequency is a better predictor than recency.
  • The weakness of plain LFU does not show here: if popularity changes (yesterday's sold-out show), it keeps old favourites too long. That is why real LFU implementations age their counters — and why W-TinyLFU exists.

items.title: Eviction in Redis
items.text:
Redis applies a policy only when memory reaches maxmemory. Its LRU and LFU are approximated: instead of a global ordered list, Redis samples a few keys (maxmemory-samples, default 5) and evicts the best candidate among them; LFU uses a small logarithmic counter per key that decays over time4.

maxmemory-policy Evicts Use when noeviction nothing — writes fail with an error when full Redis holds data that must not disappear (sessions, queues, locks) allkeys-lru any key, least recently used a pure cache — the usual default for caching allkeys-lfu any key, least frequently used a pure cache with stable popularity (catalogs) volatile-lru keys with a TTL, LRU mixed instance: keys without TTL are protected volatile-lfu keys with a TTL, LFU same, with frequency allkeys-random any key, at random uniform access, cheapest volatile-random keys with a TTL, at random rarely the best choice volatile-ttl keys with a TTL, shortest remaining TTL first the TTLs encode priority

Mixed instances

With a volatile-* policy and keys that have no TTL, Redis may find nothing it is allowed to evict and start rejecting writes, exactly like noeviction. Prefer separate instances (or databases in separate clusters) for "cache" and "must keep" data.

items.title: What consistency can a cache offer?
items.text:
A cache-aside cache in front of a database is eventually consistent: after a write, readers may see the old value until the invalidation arrives or the TTL expires. You can strengthen specific guarantees, at a cost:

Guarantee Meaning How to get it with a cache Bounded staleness no value older than T TTL ≤ T (and nothing else is needed) Read-your-writes after I write, I see my write write-through for that key; or mark the session "recently wrote" and bypass the cache for a few seconds; for L1 caches, route the user to the same replica Monotonic reads I never see a value go back in time avoid mixing caches with different freshness for the same user (e.g. L1 with 30 s TTL and L2 with 5 s) Linearizability everyone sees the latest write not with a cache. Read the source of truth.

These are the same consistency models seen in Distributed Systems — a cache is just another replica, with weaker guarantees and no replication protocol.

BoxOffice: a price change during the on-sale

Dynamic pricing raises the price of section B from R$ 300 to R$ 350 at 10:07. The catalog service commits the change and deletes prices:42:BRL; CDC also publishes an invalidation for the in-process caches of the event details that embed the price. The event page may show R$ 300 for up to ~2 s on replicas that missed the message (L1 TTL = 2 s for event details during on-sales; the price table itself is not kept in L1, see Patterns).

At checkout, the order service does not use the cached price: it reads the price in the same SQL transaction that confirms the hold. If it differs from what the fan saw, the fan is asked to confirm the new price. The cache made the page fast; the database kept the money correct.

In the interview

When you add a cache, the follow-up question is always "how do you keep it consistent?". A strong answer has three layers: (1) the staleness budget for this data ("prices: a few seconds; descriptions: a minute"); (2) the mechanism — TTL as the safety net, delete after commit, CDC if many writers; (3) the escape hatch for decisions — "the checkout reads the price from the database". Mention the cache-aside race and how the TTL (or versions, or leases) bounds it, and you are ahead of most candidates.

Common pitfalls

  • No TTL "because we invalidate explicitly" — the first missed delete becomes permanent.
  • Deleting before writing the database, or inside the transaction before it commits.
  • Updating instead of deleting without versions — concurrent writers reorder.
  • Forgetting derived keys: the event changed, but the search results, the "events this weekend" list and the venue page that embed it did not. Use tags, CDC, or short TTLs for aggregate keys.
  • Purging the CDN for every change — slow and rate-limited; version the URLs instead.
  • LRU caches next to batch jobs — a nightly scan evicts the hot set; give batch jobs their own path or bypass the cache.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    BUD["staleness budget<br/>per data item"] --> TTL["TTL: the safety net"]
    BUD --> EXP["explicit invalidation<br/>delete, don't update"]
    EXP --> RACE["write first, then delete<br/>the cache-aside race"]
    EXP --> CDC["CDC from the WAL<br/>Debezium → Kafka"]
    CDC --> MANY["many copies: L1 via pub/sub,<br/>CDN purge, versioned URLs"]
    CDC -.-> MSG["change streams<br/>→ Messaging patterns"]
    EV["eviction: LRU, LFU,<br/>W-TinyLFU"] --> MEM["maxmemory policy<br/>→ Redis"]
    TTL --> CONS["what consistency a cache offers<br/>→ Distributed consistency"]
    RACE --> CONS

Palette components: cache (TTLs, deletes, eviction policy) · app (deletes after the commit, keeps L1 copies) · sql (its write-ahead log is the source of invalidations) · kafka (Debezium change events, ordered per key) · pubsub (broadcast to in-process caches) · cdn (purge by URL or tag — or better, versioned URLs). Scenarios: read-heavy-cache, cdn-static, event-fanout. Continues in: Failure Modes, Distributed — consistency, Messaging — patterns (CDC, outbox), Edge — DNS & CDN, Hands-on 5.
