items.title: Index
items.text:
Putting a cache in front of a database raises two questions that have nothing to do with Redis itself: who fills the cache when a value is missing, and what happens to the cache when the data is written. The answers form a small set of named patterns. They are worth knowing by name: in a design review or an interview, "cache-aside with delete-on-write and a 5-minute TTL" says in one sentence what would otherwise take a paragraph2.

Pattern Who reads the DB on a miss What happens on a write Cache-aside the application app writes the DB, then deletes the key Read-through the cache (through a loader) combined with one of the write patterns Write-through — cache and DB written synchronously, together Write-behind — cache written now, DB written later, in batches Write-around — DB written, cache not touched (filled on the next read) Refresh-ahead the cache, before expiry —

Throughout the page the example is the BoxOffice catalog service: GET /events/{id} returns an event with its venue and price table, and organizers occasionally edit an event with PUT /events/{id}.

items.title: Cache-aside
items.text:
Cache-aside (also called lazy loading) is the default pattern and the one you should assume unless there is a reason not to. The application talks to both the cache and the database; the cache is a passive key-value store that knows nothing about the database1.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as catalog service
    participant R as Redis
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    A->>R: GET event:42
    R-->>A: nil (miss)
    A->>D: SELECT event, venue, prices WHERE id = 42
    D-->>A: row
    A->>R: SET event:42 json EX 300
    A->>R: GET event:42 (next request)
    R-->>A: json (hit)

Read path: look in the cache; on a hit, return it; on a miss, read the database, store the result with a TTL, return it. Write path: update the database, then delete the key (not update it — see Invalidation). The next read repopulates it.

Why it is the default:

  • Only what is read gets cached — no memory wasted on data nobody asks for.
  • The cache is optional: if Redis is down, reads go to the database (slower, but correct). The application keeps working, provided the database can take the load.
  • Simple to reason about: the database is always the source of truth — the cache holds derived data that can be rebuilt at any time3.

Its costs:

  • The first read of each key is slow (miss + database + SET): three round trips instead of one.
  • Staleness window: between the database write and the delete, and in a few race conditions (Invalidation), readers can see an old value — bounded by the TTL.
  • Cache logic is spread through the application code — unless a framework hides it.

items.title: Cache-aside in Spring Boot
items.text:
Spring's cache abstraction implements cache-aside with annotations: @Cacheable wraps the read path, @CacheEvict the delete on write. This is the setup used in Hands-on 5.

catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/EventService.java
@Service
public class EventService {

    private final EventRepository repository;

    public EventService(EventRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    // Read path: key "events::42"; runs the method only on a miss
    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "events", key = "#id", unless = "#result == null")
    public EventDto findById(long id) {
        return repository.findWithVenueAndPrices(id)
                .map(EventDto::from)
                .orElse(null);
    }

    // Write path: update the database first, then delete the key
    @Transactional
    @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "events", key = "#id")
    public EventDto update(long id, EventUpdate change) {
        Event event = repository.findById(id).orElseThrow();
        event.apply(change);
        return EventDto.from(repository.save(event));
    }
}
catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/CacheConfig.java
@Configuration
@EnableCaching
public class CacheConfig {

    @Bean
    public RedisCacheManager cacheManager(RedisConnectionFactory factory) {
        RedisCacheConfiguration defaults = RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig()
                .entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(5))
                .disableCachingNullValues()
                .serializeValuesWith(RedisSerializationContext.SerializationPair
                        .fromSerializer(RedisSerializer.json()));

        return RedisCacheManager.builder(factory)
                .cacheDefaults(defaults)
                .withCacheConfiguration("events", defaults.entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(5)))
                .withCacheConfiguration("prices", defaults.entryTtl(Duration.ofSeconds(30)))
                .build();
    }
}

When does @CacheEvict run?

By default @CacheEvict runs after the method returns — but @Transactional may commit even later, when the proxy chain unwinds. If the eviction happens before the commit, a concurrent reader can miss, read the old row (still uncommitted change), and put it back in the cache. Make sure the delete happens after the commit: order the proxies so the transaction commits first, use TransactionAwareCacheManagerProxy (or RedisCacheManager.builder(...).transactionAware()), or evict in an @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT).

items.title: Cache-aside by hand (Python)
items.text:
Without a framework, the pattern is a dozen lines. This is what @Cacheable does behind the scenes:

assistant/catalog_cache.py
import json
import redis

r = redis.Redis(host="redis", port=6379, decode_responses=True)
TTL_SECONDS = 300


def get_event(event_id: int, db) -> dict | None:
    key = f"boxoffice:catalog:event:{event_id}:v3"
    cached = r.get(key)
    if cached is not None:                       # hit
        return json.loads(cached)
    event = db.fetch_event_with_venue_and_prices(event_id)   # miss → source of truth
    if event is not None:
        r.set(key, json.dumps(event), ex=TTL_SECONDS)
    return event


def update_event(event_id: int, change: dict, db) -> None:
    db.update_event(event_id, change)            # 1. commit to the database
    r.delete(f"boxoffice:catalog:event:{event_id}:v3")   # 2. then invalidate

items.title: Read-through
items.text:
In read-through, the application only talks to the cache. On a miss, the cache itself loads the value from the database, using a loader function you register. The logic moves from the application into the cache layer.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as catalog service
    participant C as Cache with loader
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    A->>C: get(42)
    C->>D: loader(42): SELECT ...
    D-->>C: row
    C-->>A: value (now cached)
    A->>C: get(42)
    C-->>A: value (hit)

In-process caches implement this natively — Caffeine's LoadingCache, Guava, .NET MemoryCache with a factory. Distributed caches rarely do (Redis has no idea how to query PostgreSQL), so "read-through Redis" in practice is a library in the application that behaves as if it were the cache.

Read-through with Caffeine (in-process)
LoadingCache<Long, Venue> venues = Caffeine.newBuilder()
        .maximumSize(10_000)
        .expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
        .build(id -> venueRepository.findById(id).orElse(null));   // the loader

Venue v = venues.get(7L);   // miss → loader runs once, even with 100 concurrent callers

A useful property: a good read-through cache coalesces concurrent misses on the same key — 100 threads asking for venue 7 trigger a single loader call. That is the cure for the stampede described in Failure Modes.

items.title: Write-through
items.text:
In write-through, every write goes to the cache and to the database as part of the same operation, before the client gets an answer. The cache is always warm with the latest value for every key written.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as catalog service
    participant C as Cache
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    A->>C: put(42, new event)
    C->>D: UPDATE events SET ... WHERE id = 42
    D-->>C: ok
    C-->>A: ok (cache and DB both updated)
  • Good: reads right after a write hit the cache with the fresh value (read-your-writes through the cache); no miss penalty after updates.
  • Bad: every write pays two latencies; values that are written but never read still take memory (combine with a TTL); the two writes are not atomic — if the database write fails after the cache write, the cache holds a value that never existed. Write to the database first, and delete the key if anything fails.

Write-through fits data that is read soon after it is written: a user's profile after editing, the organizer's dashboard.

items.title: Write-behind
items.text:
Write-behind (or write-back) acknowledges the write as soon as the cache has it and persists to the database later, asynchronously, often in batches.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as service
    participant C as Cache
    participant W as Flusher
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    A->>C: INCR views:event:42
    C-->>A: ok (fast, in memory)
    A->>C: INCR views:event:42
    C-->>A: ok
    W->>C: every 10 s: read and reset counters
    W->>D: UPDATE event_stats SET views = views + 1834
  • Good: writes are as fast as memory; many writes to the same key are coalesced into one database write; the database is protected from write bursts.
  • Bad: acknowledged writes can be lost if the cache node dies before flushing; the database is always behind; ordering and failures of the flusher need careful engineering.

Use it only for data where losing a few seconds of writes is acceptable: view counters, "people looking at this event right now", analytics events, rate-limit counters. Never for orders, payments or seat holds.

Think first: write-behind for seat holds?

During the flash sale, writing every seat hold to SQL is the bottleneck. A colleague proposes: "write holds to Redis, acknowledge the fan, and flush to PostgreSQL every second". What can go wrong?

If the Redis primary fails before the flush, holds that fans already saw as confirmed vanish — and the seats can be sold again: double booking, the one bug BoxOffice must never have. Even with Redis replication, replication is asynchronous (Redis) and the last acknowledged writes can be lost on failover. The right tools for the hold bottleneck are elsewhere: a waiting room to cap the arrival rate, fine-grained row locks, and partitioning the inventory (Databases).

items.title: Write-around
items.text:
In write-around, writes go straight to the database and the cache is not touched (or the key is simply deleted). The value enters the cache only when someone reads it.

This is what cache-aside does on the write path, and it is the right choice when written data is rarely read soon after: the ticket a fan just bought (read a handful of times, by one person), audit logs, order history. Writing those to the cache would only evict useful entries.

items.title: Refresh-ahead
items.text:
Refresh-ahead reloads a hot entry before it expires, so readers never see the miss. A background task (or the first reader after a threshold, e.g. when 80% of the TTL has passed) fetches the fresh value while the current one is still served.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Reader
    participant C as Cache
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    A->>C: get(event:42), TTL 300 s, age 250 s
    C-->>A: current value (served immediately)
    C->>D: async reload (age > 80% of TTL)
    D-->>C: fresh value, TTL reset to 300 s
  • Good: hot keys never expire under load — no latency spike, no stampede.
  • Bad: if the prediction is wrong, the cache refreshes keys nobody will read (wasted database load). Works best for a small, known set of hot keys — like the events going on sale today.

Caffeine implements it with refreshAfterWrite; the probabilistic version, which needs no background job, is XFetch (Failure Modes). A related HTTP idea is Cache-Control: stale-while-revalidate, which lets a CDN serve the old copy while it fetches a new one.

items.title: Comparing the patterns
items.text:
Cache-aside Read-through Write-through Write-behind Write-around Refresh-ahead Consistency with DB eventual (TTL-bounded) eventual strong-ish (two writes, not atomic) DB lags the cache eventual eventual Read latency on miss high (3 round trips) high (hidden in cache) rare misses after writes rare misses high on first read almost never misses Write latency DB + delete — DB + cache memory only DB only — Risk of data loss none none none yes (unflushed writes) none none Complexity low low (in-process) / medium medium high low medium Cache survives outage? app falls back to DB depends on library writes fail or degrade writes are lost yes falls back to misses BoxOffice use event details, search results venue geometry (Caffeine) organizer's own dashboard view counters, "N people viewing" tickets, order history today's on-sale events

In practice, systems combine them: cache-aside + write-around (delete on write) is the common baseline; refresh-ahead is added for the few hottest keys; write-behind is reserved for counters.

items.title: Designing cache keys and values
items.text:
The patterns say when to read and write the cache; the key and value design decides whether it works at scale.

Namespaced, structured keys. Use a prefix per service and entity, and include anything that changes the answer:

boxoffice:catalog:event:42:v3                 # one event, schema version 3
boxoffice:catalog:prices:42:BRL               # price table in a given currency
boxoffice:search:q=rock+sp:page=1:lang=pt     # a search result page
boxoffice:session:9f1c2e...                   # a session
  • Version in the key (:v3): when the object's format changes in a deploy, bump the version — old and new replicas no longer read each other's incompatible values, and old keys simply expire.
  • Everything that changes the result must be in the key: language, currency, page, the user's permissions. Forgetting one is how a page in Portuguese is served to an English user — or one user's data to another.
  • Keep keys short but readable; avoid unbounded user input in keys (normalize and hash long search queries).

What to cache.

Granularity Example Pro Con Database row / object event:42 reusable by many pages; easy to invalidate page needs several lookups Query result search:q=rock saves the most expensive work hard to invalidate (which queries contain event 42?) — rely on TTL Rendered fragment / response HTML of the event card, full JSON response fastest most duplicated; invalidation is coarse

Values. JSON is readable and debuggable; binary formats (Protocol Buffers, MessagePack, Kryo) are smaller and faster to parse. Compress values above a few kilobytes (e.g. with LZ4 or Zstandard). Large values hurt more than they seem: a 1 MB value takes ~1 ms of network transfer per read on a 10 Gbit/s link and blocks Redis while it is being copied (Failure Modes — big keys).

Negative caching. If GET /events/999999 does not exist, cache the absence too (a sentinel such as "∅" with a short TTL, e.g. 30 s). Otherwise, every request for a missing id — from a bug or a bot — goes straight to the database. This is the first defence against cache penetration.

items.title: Two-level cache (near cache)
items.text:
Each replica of the catalog service can keep a small in-process cache (L1) in front of the shared Redis (L2):

flowchart LR
    REQ["request"] --> L1["L1: Caffeine<br/>in the JVM, ~1 µs"]
    L1 -->|"miss"| L2[("L2: Redis<br/>shared, ~0.5 ms")]
    L2 -->|"miss"| DB[("PostgreSQL<br/>~5 ms")]
    DB --> L2
    L2 --> L1
  • Why: a hit in L1 costs a hash-map lookup (microseconds, no network), and it absorbs hot keys that would otherwise hammer a single Redis shard (Failure Modes — hot keys).
  • The catch — invalidation: with 20 replicas, a write must invalidate 20 private L1 caches plus Redis. Options: a very short L1 TTL (1–5 s) and accept that staleness; or broadcast invalidations over Redis pub/sub (or Redis client-side caching with tracking, CLIENT TRACKING) so each replica drops its local copy.

BoxOffice: what goes where

Data L1 (Caffeine) L2 (Redis) Why Venue geometry (sections, rows, seats layout) yes, 10 min yes, 1 h almost immutable; read on every seat-map render Event details yes, 2 s yes, 5 min, delete on write hot during on-sales; edits must show up quickly Price table no yes, 30 s changes during dynamic pricing; a stale price at checkout is a business problem Search results no yes, 60 s many distinct keys, low reuse per replica Session no yes (separate instance, noeviction) must be shared by all replicas; must not be evicted Seat hold never never (decided in SQL) strong consistency required

In the interview

Name the pattern and the invalidation in one breath: "cache-aside on Redis for event details, TTL 5 minutes, delete on write after commit, and a 2-second in-process L1 for the hottest events during an on-sale". Then show that you know the costs: the miss penalty, the staleness window and the race that TTL bounds. If the interviewer pushes on consistency, say what you do not cache and why.

Common pitfalls

  • Updating the cache on write instead of deleting: two concurrent writers can leave the older value in the cache forever (see Invalidation).
  • Evicting before the transaction commits (@CacheEvict + @Transactional in the wrong order).
  • Caching null without meaning to — or never caching it, and letting missing ids hit the database.
  • Write-behind for data you cannot lose.
  • Keys that forget a dimension (language, currency, user) — the cache serves the wrong answer, quickly.
  • Java serialization of entities with lazy relations — serializing a JPA entity can trigger queries or fail; cache DTOs, not entities.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    CA["cache-aside<br/>the app fills on a miss"] --> INV["delete after commit<br/>→ Invalidation"]
    RT["read-through<br/>the cache library loads"] --> INV
    WA["write-around<br/>write the DB, skip the cache"] --> CA
    WT["write-through<br/>cache and DB together"] --> FRESH["fresh reads,<br/>slower writes"]
    WB["write-behind<br/>flush later, in batches"] --> LOSS["may lose acked writes:<br/>counters yes, seats never"]
    LOSS -.-> TX["seat holds stay in SQL<br/>→ Databases"]
    RA["refresh-ahead"] --> STAMP["no expiry spikes<br/>→ Failure modes"]
    KEYS["keys: namespace,<br/>version, small values"] --> CA
    L1["two-level cache<br/>Caffeine L1 + Redis"] --> HOT["hot keys<br/>→ Failure modes"]

Palette components: cache (Redis, the shared copy) · app (catalog runs cache-aside and keeps a Caffeine L1 per replica) · sql (the source of truth behind every pattern) · worker (the flusher of write-behind counters) · pubsub (tells every L1 copy to drop a key). Scenarios: read-heavy-cache, search-autocomplete. Continues in: Invalidation and Eviction, Failure Modes, Databases — the double-booking bug, Hands-on 5, Exercise: cache + database.

  1. AMAZON WEB SERVICES. Database Caching Strategies Using Redis. AWS Whitepaper. ↩

  2. XU, A. System Design Interview — An Insider's Guide, vol. 1. Byte Code LLC, 2020. Chapter 1 (cache tier) and chapter 6 (key-value store). ↩

  3. KLEPPMANN, M.; RICCOMINI, C. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd ed. O'Reilly. Chapters on storage and derived data. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text: Redis (REmote DIctionary Server) is the default answer to "which distributed cache?" — and much more than a cache. It is an in-memory server of data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams and more, each with atomic operations. BoxOffice uses it as the catalog cache, but also as the session store, the rate limiter, the waiting-room line and the "people viewing now" counter. Knowing what each structure costs, how Redis persists and replicates, and how Redis Cluster spreads keys is what lets you use it well — and recognise when it is the wrong tool.

items.title: What makes Redis fast
items.text:
• Everything is in RAM. A read is a hash-table lookup plus a memory copy; disk is only used for persistence, in the background.
  • One thread executes commands. Commands run one at a time on a single main thread (since Redis 6, separate I/O threads can handle network reads and writes). There are no locks inside the server, and every command is atomic: no other command runs in the middle of an INCR.
  • Simple protocol, small values. Most commands are O(1) or O(log n). In the same data center, a round trip of a small GET costs a fraction of a millisecond, dominated by the network.

The single thread is also Redis's main constraint: one slow command (an O(n) scan of a big key, a long Lua script) blocks every client. Throughput per node is high — on the order of 100,000 simple commands per second or more on typical hardware, an illustrative figure you should verify with redis-benchmark on your own setup — and scaling beyond one node means Redis Cluster.

items.title: Redis, Valkey and the alternatives (2026)
items.text:
In 2024 Redis changed from the open-source BSD license to source-available licenses (RSALv2/SSPLv1). In response, the Linux Foundation started Valkey, a fork of Redis 7.2 backed by several cloud providers, which stays BSD-licensed and protocol-compatible. In 2025, Redis 8 added the open-source AGPLv3 as a license option. For this course — and in most interviews — "Redis" means the protocol and data model, which Redis and Valkey share12.

Redis / Valkey Memcached Dragonfly Data model rich data structures strings only Redis-compatible Threads single command thread (+ I/O threads) multi-threaded multi-threaded, shared-nothing Persistence RDB, AOF none snapshots Replication / cluster built-in (Sentinel, Cluster) none (clients shard) built-in replication When default choice a pure, simple, very large cache of blobs when one big node must replace a cluster

items.title: Data structures and what BoxOffice does with them
items.text:
Type Key commands Complexity BoxOffice use String GET SET INCR EXPIRE MGET O(1) cached event JSON; counters; idempotency markers Hash HSET HGET HGETALL HINCRBY O(1) per field session (session:9f1c → user, roles, cart); event fields updated separately List LPUSH RPOP LRANGE O(1) at the ends simple work queues; "last 10 events viewed" Set SADD SISMEMBER SMEMBERS O(1) per member tags of an event; ids already notified Sorted set ZADD ZRANK ZRANGE ZPOPMIN O(log n) waiting room: fans ordered by arrival time; top-selling events HyperLogLog PFADD PFCOUNT O(1), ~12 KB per counter unique visitors per event (~0.81% standard error) Bitmap SETBIT BITCOUNT O(1) per bit daily active users by user id Geo GEOADD GEOSEARCH O(log n) "events near me" Stream XADD XREADGROUP XACK O(1) append lightweight event log with consumer groups (Kafka is covered in Messaging) redis-cli — a tour with BoxOffice data
> SET boxoffice:catalog:event:42:v3 '{"id":42,"name":"Stadium Show"}' EX 300
OK
> TTL boxoffice:catalog:event:42:v3
(integer) 300
> HSET session:9f1c user 1017 roles fan cart 3
(integer) 3
> INCR views:event:42
(integer) 1
> ZADD waitingroom:42 1760695200123 fan:1017 1760695200456 fan:2203
(integer) 2
> ZRANK waitingroom:42 fan:2203
(integer) 1
> ZPOPMIN waitingroom:42 1
1) "fan:1017"
2) "1760695200123"
> PFADD visitors:event:42 fan:1017 fan:2203 fan:1017
(integer) 1
> PFCOUNT visitors:event:42
(integer) 2

The waiting room is a good example of choosing a structure: a sorted set with the arrival time (in milliseconds) as the score gives each fan their position in O(log n) (ZRANK), and lets the admission job take the next 500 fans in one command (ZPOPMIN waitingroom:42 500).

items.title: Round trips: pipelining and multi-key commands
items.text: At 0.5 ms per round trip, reading 100 keys one by one costs 50 ms. MGET (or pipelining — sending many commands without waiting for each reply) does it in about one round trip. A page that needs many cached objects should fetch them together.

items.title: Atomicity
items.text:
Because commands run one at a time, a single command is atomic. For more than one command, Redis offers three tools:

Tool What it gives Limits Single command (INCR, SET ... NX, ZPOPMIN) atomic read-modify-write one key, one operation MULTI / EXEC (+ WATCH) queue commands and run them together, without interleaving; WATCH aborts if a watched key changed (optimistic locking) no rollback: if a command fails, the others still run; cannot use a read result inside the transaction Lua scripts (EVAL) / functions (FCALL, Redis 7+) arbitrary logic executed atomically on the server blocks the server while it runs — keep scripts short

A fixed-window rate limiter for the API gateway in two commands:

redis-cli — 100 requests per minute per client
> INCR rl:client:abc:202610171000
(integer) 1
> EXPIRE rl:client:abc:202610171000 60 NX
(integer) 1

If the counter returned by INCR exceeds 100, the request is rejected. (EXPIRE ... NX sets the expiry only the first time. More refined algorithms — token bucket, sliding window — are in Traffic & Edge.)

items.title: A seat pre-hold in Redis — and why SQL still decides
items.text:
During the flash sale, thousands of fans click the same good seats. A Redis pre-hold can reject most of the losers in microseconds, before they reach the database:

redis-cli — pre-hold seat A-12 of event 42 for 10 minutes
> SET hold:42:A-12 fan:1017 NX PX 600000
OK
> SET hold:42:A-12 fan:2203 NX PX 600000
(nil)

NX makes the set succeed only if nobody holds the key; PX 600000 releases it automatically after 10 minutes. The second fan gets nil immediately: "seat taken".

It is tempting to stop there. Do not. The fan who got OK still goes to the inventory service, which takes the hold in a PostgreSQL transaction with a constraint that makes double booking impossible (Databases — the double-booking bug). Redis is a fast filter; the database decides. Why:

  • Redis replication is asynchronous: after a failover, the new primary may not have the hold that was just granted — two fans could both get OK (replication).
  • Memory pressure, a FLUSHALL by mistake, or a cache restart without persistence erase holds silently.
  • The order, the payment and the ticket live in SQL; the seat state must be in the same transaction as them.

If Redis loses a pre-hold, the worst case is that two fans reach the database and one of them loses there. Correctness never depended on Redis.

items.title: Persistence
items.text:
Redis keeps data in memory but can write it to disk, so a restart does not start cold.

Mode How it works Data loss on crash Restart Use None memory only everything cold, fast pure cache that can be rebuilt RDB (snapshot) forks and writes a point-in-time snapshot every N minutes / M writes since the last snapshot (minutes) fast load of a compact file caches that should restart warm; backups AOF (append-only file) logs every write; appendfsync everysec (default) or always ~1 s with everysec; ~none with always (slow) replays the log (slower) Redis as a primary store for non-critical data (sessions) RDB + AOF both as AOF AOF used for recovery the recommended setting when data matters

For a cache, RDB or nothing is usually enough. If you find yourself tuning appendfsync always, ask whether this data belongs in a database.

items.title: Replication and failover
items.text:
A Redis primary can have several replicas that receive a stream of its writes. Replicas serve reads (slightly stale) and are candidates for promotion if the primary fails.

flowchart LR
    APP["catalog service"] -->|"writes and reads"| P[("Redis primary")]
    P -->|"async replication"| R1[("replica 1")]
    P -->|"async replication"| R2[("replica 2")]
    S1["Sentinel 1"] -.->|"monitor"| P
    S2["Sentinel 2"] -.->|"monitor"| P
    S3["Sentinel 3"] -.->|"monitor"| P
    S1 -.->|"quorum agrees: promote"| R1
  • Replication is asynchronous: the primary acknowledges a write before the replicas have it. If the primary dies, the last acknowledged writes may be lost. WAIT numreplicas timeout makes a client wait until N replicas have its writes — it reduces the window but does not make Redis strongly consistent.
  • Redis Sentinel is a group of processes (at least 3) that monitor the primary; when a quorum agrees it is down, they promote a replica and tell clients the new address. Failover takes seconds — the cache is unavailable or read-only meanwhile.
  • min-replicas-to-write makes the primary refuse writes when it cannot reach enough replicas, limiting loss during a partition.

For a cache this is fine: a lost write is a future miss. For data that must not be lost, it is the reason to keep the source of truth in a database.

items.title: Redis Cluster
items.text:
When one node is not enough — memory or throughput — Redis Cluster shards the keyspace over several primaries, each with its own replicas3.

  • The keyspace is divided into 16,384 hash slots. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384.
  • Each primary owns a set of slots (e.g. three primaries: 0–5460, 5461–10922, 10923–16383).
  • Clients are cluster-aware: they cache the slot → node map and send each command directly to the right node. If the map is outdated, the node answers MOVED <slot> <address> and the client updates its map; during a slot migration, ASK redirects a single request.
  • Adding a node = moving some slots to it, live, without rehashing every key.
flowchart LR
    C["cluster-aware client<br/>slot map cached"] -->|"event:42 → slot 16271"| N3
    C -->|"prices:42 → slot 9049"| N2
    N1[("primary A<br/>slots 0–5460")] --- R1[("replica A")]
    N2[("primary B<br/>slots 5461–10922")] --- R2[("replica B")]
    N3[("primary C<br/>slots 10923–16383")] --- R3[("replica C")]
redis-cli — which slot does a key go to?
> CLUSTER KEYSLOT event:42
(integer) 16271
> CLUSTER KEYSLOT prices:42
(integer) 9049
> CLUSTER KEYSLOT {event:42}:seats
(integer) 16271
> CLUSTER KEYSLOT {event:42}:prices
(integer) 16271

Multi-key operations (MGET, MULTI/EXEC, Lua scripts touching several keys) only work when all keys are in the same slot — otherwise Redis answers CROSSSLOT. Hash tags solve this: if a key contains {...}, only the part inside the braces is hashed. {event:42}:seats and {event:42}:prices land in the same slot, so a script can update both atomically.

Hash tags concentrate load

Everything with the same tag lives on one node. Tag by something with many values (one event, one user), never by something with few ({boxoffice} would put the whole application on one node — a self-made hot key).

items.title: Hash slots vs. consistent hashing
items.text:
Memcached takes a different approach: the servers do not know about each other, and the client decides which server holds a key, usually with consistent hashing (the ketama algorithm) so that adding a server remaps only ~1/N of the keys (Databases — consistent hashing). Redis Cluster uses a fixed number of slots instead: the mapping key → slot never changes, only slot → node does, and the nodes themselves coordinate failover and redirects.

Redis Cluster (hash slots) Client-side consistent hashing (Memcached) Who knows the mapping servers + cluster-aware clients clients only Adding a node move some slots, live ~1/N of keys remap (become misses) Replication / failover built-in none (a dead node = misses) Multi-key operations within one slot (hash tags) none

items.title: Managed Redis
items.text:
AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS, Valkey, Memcached): managed cache with replication, automatic failover, Cluster mode and a serverless option.
  • Amazon MemoryDB: Redis/Valkey-compatible with a durable, multi-AZ transaction log — designed to be a primary database, not just a cache.
  • Memorystore for Redis, Memorystore for Redis Cluster and Memorystore for Valkey: managed instances with replicas and automatic failover.
  • Memorystore for Memcached.
  • Azure Managed Redis (based on Redis Enterprise) and the older Azure Cache for Redis tiers, with replication, clustering and geo-replication options.
  • Self-hosted Redis or Valkey: a single node with Docker for development (Hands-on 5); Sentinel or Cluster on VMs; on Kubernetes with an operator or a Helm chart (StatefulSet + persistent volumes).
  • Memcached and Dragonfly as alternatives.

Managed services take care of failover, patching and backups; you still own sizing, eviction policy, key design, timeouts and what happens when it fails.

items.title: Sizing a Redis deployment
items.text:
Worked example — the BoxOffice cache cluster

Illustrative assumptions: 2 million cached keys (events, prices, search results, fragments); average key 50 bytes; average value 2 KB; per-key overhead (dictionary entry, object headers, expiry) ~100 bytes.

  • Data: 2,000,000 × (50 + 2,048 + 100) B ≈ 4.4 GB.
  • Fragmentation and growth headroom (+30%): ≈ 5.7 GB.
  • Fork headroom for RDB snapshots on a write-heavy primary: keep memory use ≤ ~70% of RAM → ≈ 8 GB per copy.
  • Throughput: 300,000 reads/s at peak after the L1 caches; assume (to be benchmarked) ~100,000 ops/s per primary → 3 primaries, each with 1 replica.
  • Result: Redis Cluster with 3 primaries × ~1.5 GB of data each (≈ 2.7 GB of RAM with the headroom above) + 3 replicas — 6 nodes with 4–8 GB of RAM. The constraint is throughput, not memory.

Sessions (2 M fans × 0.5 KB ≈ 1 GB) go to a separate small instance with noeviction and AOF, so cache evictions can never log a fan out.

items.title: Connecting from Spring Boot
items.text:
The configuration used in Hands-on 5:

catalog/src/main/resources/application.yaml
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: ${REDIS_HOST:redis}
      port: 6379
      timeout: 50ms            # command timeout: fail fast if Redis is slow
      connect-timeout: 200ms
      # cluster:
      #   nodes: redis-0:6379,redis-1:6379,redis-2:6379
  cache:
    type: redis
    redis:
      time-to-live: 5m         # default TTL for @Cacheable caches
      cache-null-values: false
      key-prefix: "boxoffice:catalog:"
compose.yaml (excerpt)
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:8-alpine
    command: ["redis-server", "--maxmemory", "256mb", "--maxmemory-policy", "allkeys-lru"]
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"

In the interview

When you say "Redis", be ready for three follow-ups. Data model: pick the structure that matches the access pattern ("a sorted set for the waiting room, a hash for sessions"). Scaling: Redis Cluster with 16,384 hash slots, hash tags for multi-key operations, and replicas for failover — and why a hot key is not fixed by adding nodes. Durability: replication is asynchronous, so Redis is a cache or a store for data you can afford to lose; the seat hold and the payment live in the database.

Common pitfalls

  • KEYS * in production — O(n) over the whole keyspace, blocks the server. Use SCAN.
  • Keys without TTL in a cache — memory grows until evictions or OOM errors start.
  • Big values and huge collections — see big keys.
  • Redis as the only copy of money data — orders, payments, seat holds belong in the database.
  • Default timeouts — a slow or failing Redis must not stall the service.
  • One instance for cache and sessions — the cache's eviction policy will evict sessions.
  • Hash tags with low cardinality — the whole application on one node.

items.title: Index
items.text:
It is 10:00 and BoxOffice opens the sale of a stadium show: two million fans, sixty thousand seats. Over the semester you built every piece needed to survive that morning — a CDN and a WAF at the edge, stateless services behind a load balancer, a cache, a database that never sells a seat twice, a queue, a payment integration, observability, a load test that found the knee. This class puts the pieces together the way an interviewer asks for them: a one-sentence prompt, a blank whiteboard and 45 minutes.

The twelve case studies below are the classic system-design interview problems. They are not twelve unrelated systems: they are the same few ideas — cache the hot reads, take slow work off the critical path, choose a partition key, make retries safe, protect the one resource that cannot scale — combined in different proportions. Studying them is how the vocabulary of the course becomes a reflex.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Apply the interview framework of class 1 to an unseen problem within 45 minutes: clarify, estimate, API and data model, high-level design, deep dives, bottlenecks and wrap-up.
  • Estimate the load of a system from a few assumptions and derive design decisions from the numbers.
  • Compose palette components (edge, compute, storage, messaging, observability, AI) into a design and justify each one.
  • Analyze a design for bottlenecks and failure modes and defend its trade-offs out loud.
  • Validate a design under load in the System Design Playground and explain what the metrics show.
  • Evaluate your own answer against a junior / mid / senior rubric.

items.title: How to study a case
items.text:
Every case page follows the interview framework of class 1, section by section, so you can rehearse the order until it is automatic. The timing below is for a 45-minute interview; the case pages use the same numbering.

# Step Minutes What you produce Typical mistake 1 Clarify the requirements 5 Functional list, non-functional targets with numbers, out of scope Designing before knowing whether it is 1 k or 1 M users 2 Estimate 5 QPS (average and peak), storage, bandwidth, memory — and one sentence on what they imply Computing numbers and never using them 3 API and data model 5–7 A handful of endpoints, main entities, the store for each and why Twenty endpoints, no idempotency, no pagination 4 High-level design 10 One diagram with the read path and the write path Boxes without data flows; every component "because big systems have it" 5 Deep dives 10–15 Two or three hard parts solved with alternatives and a choice Going deep on the easy part 6 Bottlenecks, failure modes, trade-offs 5 What breaks first, what happens when X dies, what you gave up "It scales horizontally" with no evidence 7 Wrap-up 2–3 Summary, what you would do next, how you would measure it Running out of time mid-sentence

The ten sections of each case page map onto these steps: requirements (1), estimates (2), API and data model (3), high-level design (4), deep dives (5), bottlenecks and trade-offs (6), and then three study aids — Try it in the playground, Follow-up questions and a self-assessment rubric.

A study method that works

  1. Attempt first. Read only the prompt (the quote at the top of the page). Set a timer for 40 minutes and solve it on paper or on the playground canvas, out loud, as if an interviewer were there.
  2. Compare section by section. Open the page and compare your requirements, numbers, API, diagram and deep dives. Note what you missed, not what you got right.
  3. Run the scenario. Load the matching playground scenario, predict what will break, run it, and check your prediction (next section).
  4. Answer the follow-ups before opening them; they are the questions that decide between levels.
  5. Grade yourself with the rubric, then repeat a week later without looking. Spaced repetition beats rereading.
  6. Practice in pairs with the mock interview script: one plays the interviewer, using the follow-ups as probes.

items.title: How to use the playground with a case
items.text:
Each case embeds the System Design Playground preloaded with its scenario. The playground is a simulator, not a benchmark: its numbers are illustrative, but the shapes (where the queue grows, when p99 bends, which component saturates first) are the ones you will see in real systems and in the labs.

flowchart LR
    p["Predict<br/>what breaks first?"] --> r["Run<br/>load / spike profile"]
    r --> o["Observe<br/>utilization, p99,<br/>errors, backlog, cost"]
    o --> c["Change one thing<br/>replicas, cache, queue,<br/>timeout, partition"]
    c --> e["Explain<br/>with the numbers<br/>of section 2"]
    e --> p
  • Predict before you run. Write down which component you expect to saturate and at what load. Being wrong is the useful part.
  • Change one thing at a time. Add a cache or replicas or a queue, never all three, so you know which change moved the metric.
  • Use the profiles: load for steady state, spike for the BoxOffice 10:00 moment, stress and breakpoint to find the knee, chaos (or the chaos level) to kill or slow components and watch failure modes.
  • Connect it to the estimates. If the page says the cache must absorb 95% of reads, look at the hit ratio; if Little's Law says 40 calls are in flight, look at the concurrency of the dependency.
  • Export your design (JSON) when you like it: it is the format of the playground exercise.

items.title: Patterns that repeat
items.text:
After a few cases you will notice that the deep dives are drawn from a short list. Recognizing the pattern in a new problem is most of the work.

Pattern The problem it solves Where it appears Cache the hot reads (cache-aside, CDN, L1 in-process) Read-heavy traffic with a skewed popularity URL shortener, news feed, autocomplete, video, ticketing catalog Take slow work off the critical path (queue/stream + workers) Spikes and slow side effects (analytics, e-mail, transcoding) URL shortener clicks, notifications, news-feed fan-out, video, payments outbox Make retries safe (idempotency keys, dedupe, conditional writes) Networks and clients retry; providers call back twice Payments, ticketing, chat, notifications, ride requests Choose the partition key (by user, conversation, city, event, code) One node cannot hold the data or the traffic Chat (conversation), ride sharing (city), ticketing (event), cache (key ring) Protect what cannot scale (admission control, rate limits, bulkheads) A hot row, a primary, a provider's limit Ticketing waiting room, rate limiter, payments, AI assistant quotas Precompute vs. compute on read Latency of reads vs. cost of writes News feed fan-out, autocomplete top-k, video renditions Stateful edges, stateless core Long-lived connections Chat gateways, ride-sharing driver connections, live streams Strong consistency only where it matters Correctness vs. availability and cost Seats, payments and driver assignment strong; feeds, counters, positions eventual

BoxOffice everywhere

Every case page has a BoxOffice connection: short links in ticket SMS (URL shortener), "5 holds per minute" (rate limiter), the "Following" tab when an artist announces a tour (news feed), fan groups during a festival (chat), 60 000 fans leaving the stadium (ride sharing), trailers on event pages (video), "doors open in 2 h" (notifications), the payment adapter (payments), search-as-you-type for artists (autocomplete), the support assistant (AI) and, of course, the flash sale itself (ticketing).

Common pitfalls in design interviews

  • Jumping to the solution ("we use Kafka and Cassandra") before requirements and numbers.
  • Numbers that change nothing. Every estimate should end in a decision: "so the hot set fits in memory", "so we need a queue".
  • Ignoring the write path or the failure path — the interviewer will ask "what happens when X is down?".
  • Over-engineering: microservices, multi-region and five databases for a system with 100 requests per second. Saying "a single PostgreSQL is enough here, and this is when it stops being enough" is a senior answer.
  • Monologue. Check in with the interviewer at the end of each step; they often steer you toward the deep dive they care about.
