items.title: 6.1 Partitioning: why hash % N breaks, and consistent hashing
items.text:
With node = hash(key) % N, going from 4 to 5 nodes changes the owner of almost every key — a cache with 80% of its keys suddenly in the wrong place is, for the database, the same as an empty cache. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on the same ring of hash values; a key belongs to the first node clockwise. Adding a node only takes keys from its neighbors — about 1/N of them. Each physical node gets many virtual nodes (points on the ring) so that load is even and a failed node's keys spread over all the others, not just one neighbor (partitioning).

ResultSource scheme keys_moved_pct max_load_vs_avg hash % N 80.1% 1.01 ring, 1 vnodes/node 20.9% 1.96 ring, 10 vnodes/node 17.5% 1.53 ring, 100 vnodes/node 19.9% 1.14 ring, 1000 vnodes/node 20.7% 1.04 
import bisect
import hashlib

def h(s: str) -> int:
    return int.from_bytes(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).digest()[:8], "big")

keys = [f"event:{i}" for i in range(50_000)]
kh = {k: h(k) for k in keys}

def mod_n(n):
    return {k: kh[k] % n for k in keys}

def ring(nodes, vnodes):
    points = sorted((h(f"node{n}#{v}"), n) for n in range(nodes) for v in range(vnodes))
    hashes = [p for p, _ in points]
    owner = {}
    for k in keys:
        i = bisect.bisect(hashes, kh[k]) % len(points)
        owner[k] = points[i][1]
    return owner

def moved(a, b):
    return sum(a[k] != b[k] for k in keys) / len(keys)

def max_over_avg(owner, nodes):
    counts = [0] * nodes
    for n in owner.values():
        counts[n] += 1
    return max(counts) / (len(keys) / nodes)

print("| scheme | keys_moved_pct | max_load_vs_avg |\n|---|---:|---:|")
a, b = mod_n(4), mod_n(5)
print(f"| `hash % N` | {moved(a, b):.1%} | {max_over_avg(b, 5):.2f} |")
for v in (1, 10, 100, 1000):
    a, b = ring(4, v), ring(5, v)
    print(f"| `ring, {v} vnodes/node` | {moved(a, b):.1%} | {max_over_avg(b, 5):.2f} |")

Read the table in two columns. Keys moved going from 4 to 5 nodes: hash % N moves ~80%; the ring moves ~20% — the theoretical minimum, 1/5. Load balance (the busiest node relative to the average): with one point per node the ring is very uneven (the busiest node holds almost twice its share); with hundreds of virtual nodes it approaches 1.0.

Ring with virtual nodesFixed hash slots (Redis Cluster)Rendezvous hashing

Used by Dynamo, Cassandra and many client libraries (e.g. ketama for Memcached). Each node owns many arcs; adding/removing a node moves ~1/N of the keys, taken from or given to all other nodes.

The key space is split into a fixed number of slots (16 384); each node owns a set of slots. Rebalancing moves slots, not individual hash ranges, and the cluster tells clients with MOVED/ASK redirects. Same benefit as the ring (only moved slots change owner), simpler to reason about and to migrate gradually.

For each key, compute hash(key, node) for every node and pick the highest. No ring, perfect 1/N movement, but O(N) per lookup — fine for tens of nodes.

items.title: 6.2 Eviction, TTL and memory
items.text:
When memory is full, something must go. The policy decides the hit ratio you get from the same RAM (caching failure modes):

Policy Keeps Good for Weakness LRU (least recently used) Recently used keys Recency-driven workloads A one-off scan of many keys flushes the hot set LFU (least frequently used) Often used keys Stable popularity Slow to forget yesterday's hits; needs decay W-TinyLFU (Caffeine) A small LRU "window" + an admission filter by approximate frequency Mixed workloads; resists scans More complex; mostly in-process caches TTL-only Everything until it expires Small, bounded data sets Memory grows with traffic Random Random keys Very cheap Lower hit ratio
  • Real engines approximate: Redis samples a few keys and evicts the best candidate among them (approximated LRU or LFU with decaying counters) instead of maintaining a perfect global order.
  • TTL is a consistency tool, eviction is a memory tool. Always set a TTL (so stale data has a bound), and add jitter to TTLs written in bulk (e.g. 300 s ± 10%) so they do not expire at the same second.
  • Leave headroom: plan for ~70–80% of RAM for data. Fragmentation, replication buffers and forking for snapshots need the rest; a node that swaps to disk is slower than no cache at all.

items.title: 6.3 Replication and failover
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as App
    participant P as Primary (node-b)
    participant R as Replica (node-e)
    participant S as Failure detector
    A->>P: SET seats:42 v7
    P-->>A: OK
    P--)R: replicate v7 (async)
    Note over P: primary crashes before v7 reaches the replica
    S->>S: node-b missed heartbeats → majority agrees
    S->>R: promote node-e to primary
    A->>R: GET seats:42
    R-->>A: v6 (the acknowledged write v7 is lost)
  • Replication is usually asynchronous: fast writes, but a failover can lose the last acknowledged writes. For a cache that is acceptable — the next miss reloads from the database. If a stale value is dangerous (seat availability), keep TTLs short or delete keys on write (invalidation).
  • Failure detection needs a majority (Redis Sentinel, or the cluster nodes voting) so that one isolated observer does not promote a replica on its own.
  • Split brain: after a partition, the old primary may still accept writes from clients on its side. Mitigate by having a primary stop accepting writes when it cannot see enough replicas/peers (min-replicas-to-write), and by epochs/terms so clients and nodes reject the stale primary.
  • Warm replicas also serve reads (if stale reads are acceptable) and avoid the cold-node stampede after failover.

items.title: 6.4 Hot keys, big keys and stampedes
items.text:
• Hot key — one key (the event page during an on-sale, a celebrity's profile) receives so many requests that its node saturates while the rest are idle. Consistent hashing cannot help: one key lives on one node. Fixes: a small in-process L1 cache with a TTL of seconds on every app server; replicate the key under several names (event:42#1 … #8) and read a random copy; serve it from replicas.
  • Big key — a 5 MB value read 1 000 times per second is 5 GB/s on one node. Split it (paginate, compress), or cache the rendered fragments instead of the whole object.
  • Stampede (thundering herd) — a hot key expires and thousands of requests miss at once and all hit the database. Fixes (caching failure modes):
    • Request coalescing / leases: the first miss gets a lease (SET lock:key NX EX 5) and reloads; the others wait briefly or get the stale value. Memcache at Facebook used leases for exactly this.
    • Probabilistic early expiration: each reader may refresh before the TTL with a probability that grows as expiry approaches, so one request refreshes early instead of all at once.
    • Serve stale while revalidating for data where a few seconds of staleness are fine.
import math, random, time

def should_refresh_early(expires_at: float, recompute_s: float, beta: float = 1.0) -> bool:
    """XFetch: refresh before expiry with a probability that grows near the deadline."""
    return time.time() - recompute_s * beta * math.log(random.random()) >= expires_at

items.title: 6.5 Routing: who knows where a key lives?
items.text:
Client-side routing (smart client) Proxy (twemproxy, mcrouter, Envoy) Server-side redirects (Redis Cluster) Hops 1 (client → node) 2 (client → proxy → node) 1, plus a redirect after rebalancing Client complexity High (map, retries, pooling in every language) Low (looks like one server) Medium (cluster-aware client) Config changes Pushed to every client Only to proxies Learned through MOVED Extra features — Pooling, replication, shadow traffic Slot migration built in

Facebook's memcache deployment, for example, put routing in a proxy (mcrouter) so that thousands of web servers did not each manage connections to every cache node.

items.title: 7. Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs
items.text:
Where What goes wrong Mitigation Trade-off Adding/removing nodes hash % N remaps almost every key → mass misses Consistent hashing or hash slots; migrate gradually Rebalancing traffic for a while Node failure Its keys go cold; database spike Replicas with automatic failover; spread keys with vnodes; L1 cache absorbs some reads Replicas double the memory cost Async replication Acknowledged writes lost on failover Accept it for a cache; short TTLs or delete-on-write for sensitive keys Stale or missing values briefly Network partition Two primaries (split brain) Majority-based failover; primary stops writes without quorum; epochs Writes rejected on the minority side Hot key One node saturated L1 cache, key replication with suffixes, read from replicas Staleness, more memory Big key Network link saturated; slow commands block the node Split/compress; avoid O(N) commands on big structures More keys to manage Stampede on expiry Thousands of misses for one key Leases/coalescing, early refresh, TTL jitter, serve stale Slight staleness Memory pressure Eviction storms, fragmentation, swapping Headroom (~70–80%), right policy, alerts on evictions and memory Fewer bytes per node used

The trade-offs to say out loud: availability and speed over consistency (a cache may be stale or lose writes, the database is the truth), memory vs. throughput (size by both), and even distribution vs. hot keys (hashing spreads keys, not popularity).

items.title: 8. Try it in the playground
items.text:
Two scenarios cover the two halves of this case: the cache in front of a database, and the partitioning of data over nodes.

Try it — cache in front of the database

  1. Run read-heavy-cache with the load profile and note the hit ratio, the database utilization and the p99.
  2. Lower the hit ratio (or shrink the cache) by 5 points and run again: compare the change in database load with the estimate in section 2.
  3. Turn chaos on to fail the cache (or flush it): watch the cold-cache stampede on the database and how long p99 takes to recover.

Try it — partitions and hot keys

  1. Run sharding with the load profile and compare utilization across partitions.
  2. Concentrate traffic on one key/partition (a hot key): one node saturates while the others idle — more partitions do not help.
  3. Add partitions/nodes with an even workload and observe how throughput scales; then fail one node and see where its traffic goes.

Open the full playground

items.title: 9. Follow-up questions an interviewer asks
items.text:
Why not just use hash(key) % N? It is simpler.

It distributes keys well while N is fixed. The moment N changes — a node fails, you scale for an on-sale — about 1 - 1/N of the keys change owner (80% going from 4 to 5 nodes), which is equivalent to flushing the cache in the middle of the peak. Consistent hashing or fixed slots move only the keys that must move (~1/N).

A node fails during the BoxOffice on-sale. Walk me through what happens.

Clients get timeouts/connection errors for that node's slots. The failure detector (a majority of nodes or Sentinels) marks it failed after a few seconds and promotes its replica; clients learn the new owner (redirect or config push) and continue. Writes acknowledged by the old primary but not yet replicated are lost — harmless for a cache. Without a replica, that node's keys would be misses until refilled; L1 caches, request coalescing and a database with headroom keep that spike survivable.

How do you keep the cache consistent with the database?

You don't make it strongly consistent — you bound the inconsistency. Cache-aside with: write to the database, then delete the key (not update it, to avoid racing writers putting an old value back); a TTL as a safety net; and, for critical data, invalidation driven by change data capture from the database log. Short TTLs for data that changes often (seat availability), long ones for data that rarely does (venue descriptions).

LRU or LFU?

LRU when recent use predicts future use and the workload has no big scans; LFU (with decay) when popularity is stable and you must protect the hot set from one-off traffic, like a crawler reading every event page once. Modern in-process caches use W-TinyLFU, which combines a small recency window with a frequency-based admission filter and is robust to both. In Redis, allkeys-lfu or allkeys-lru are the usual choices for a pure cache.

How would you make the cache survive a whole-cluster restart without hammering the database?

Avoid it being cold: persist snapshots and reload them on start (Redis RDB), restart nodes one by one with replicas serving meanwhile, or warm the cache from the database with a background job (top-N keys from access logs) before sending traffic. Rate-limit the misses that reach the database during warm-up.

When should you not add a cache?

When the hit ratio would be low (uniform random access over a huge key space), when data must be strongly consistent on every read, when the database already serves the load comfortably, or when the added operational complexity (invalidation bugs, stampedes, a new failure mode) costs more than the latency it saves. Measure first (performance engineering).

items.title: 10. Self-assessment rubric
items.text:
Level What the answer contains Junior A key-value map in memory with get/set and TTL; several nodes with hash % N; LRU eviction. Does not notice what happens when N changes. Mid Consistent hashing with virtual nodes (or hash slots); eviction and TTL choices; primary/replica with failover; cache-aside and stampede protection; sizing by memory. Senior Sizes by memory and ops/s and links hit ratio to database load; explains key movement and load balance quantitatively; async replication loss and split brain with quorum-based failover; hot keys (L1, key replication) and big keys; routing options with trade-offs; leases/early expiration; warm-up and operational metrics; knows when a cache is the wrong tool.

Related: Caching, Redis, Caching failure modes, Partitioning, Hands-on 5 (Redis cache-aside, hit ratio and stampede).

items.title: Index
items.text:
"Design the home feed of a social network like Instagram or X: users follow other users and, when they open the app, see the latest posts of the people they follow."

The news feed is the classic read-heavy, fan-out problem. One write (a post) must become visible in the feeds of everybody who follows the author — two people for most users, fifty million for a pop star. The interview turns on one decision — do the work when the post is written, or when the feed is read? — and on what happens at the extremes of that decision: celebrities, inactive users, deleted posts and ranking.

BoxOffice has the same shape: fans follow artists and venues, and the "Following" tab shows tour announcements, new dates and presale codes. When a stadium-level artist with millions of followers announces a tour, BoxOffice faces exactly the celebrity problem of this page — at the worst moment, because everyone will open the app at once.

Difficulty hard Key concepts fan-out on write (push) vs. on read (pull) vs. hybrid, the celebrity problem, timeline cache of IDs, hydration, ranking pipeline, cursor pagination, media via CDN Palette components lb, app, cache, nosql, kafka, worker, objstore, cdn Playground scenario news-feed

What this case trains

  • Estimate the write amplification of fan-out and the memory of a timeline cache.
  • Compare fan-out on write, fan-out on read and the hybrid model, and justify a threshold for celebrities.
  • Design the read path: timeline IDs from a cache, hydration with batched lookups, merge and ranking within a latency budget.
  • Explain why feeds paginate with cursors, not offsets.
  • Handle edge cases: inactive users, deletions, privacy changes, new users with an empty feed.

items.title: 1. Clarify the requirements
items.text: (interview framework)

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text:
1. A user publishes a post (text, optional images/video).
  2. A user follows / unfollows other users (asymmetric: following is not friendship).
  3. A user opens the home feed: posts of the people they follow, newest first (or ranked), paginated with infinite scroll.
  4. Posts show author, counts (likes, comments) and media.

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.text: Quality Target Latency Feed p99 < 300 ms (it is the first screen of the app) Freshness A new post appears in followers' feeds within a few seconds (eventual consistency is fine) Scale 100 M daily active users; heavy-tailed follower counts (up to tens of millions) Availability 99.95%; a degraded feed (slightly stale, fewer items) beats an error page Durability A published post is never lost; feeds themselves can be rebuilt

items.title: Out of scope (say it explicitly)
items.text:
Comments and likes as features (we only show counts), search, notifications, ads ranking, direct messages. Each is its own design problem.

Questions to ask the interviewer Question Why it matters Chronological or ranked feed? Ranking adds a candidate → score → re-rank pipeline and changes what you cache. Max followers? Max followees? The tail of the distribution decides push vs. pull. How fresh must the feed be? Seconds allow asynchronous fan-out; "immediately" pushes toward pull. Mostly text or media-heavy? Media goes to object storage + CDN; the feed carries URLs. How many users are daily active vs. registered? Fan-out to inactive users is wasted work and memory. Can posts be edited, deleted, made private? Pushed copies must be filtered or invalidated on read.

items.title: 2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates
items.text:
ResultSource quantity value unit posts_day 20,000,000 posts write_qps 231 posts/s read_qps 11,574 req/s peak_read_qps 34,722 req/s fanout_qps 46,296 inserts/s timeline_gb 1,280 GB posts_tb_year 7.30 TB media_tb_day 1.00 TB/day 
# News feed: assumptions (illustrative)

peak_factor    = 3
avg_followers  = 200          # average fan-out per post (the tail is much larger)
timeline_len   = 800          # post IDs kept per cached feed
id_b           = 8            # one post ID (64-bit)
cache_overhead = 2            # data-structure overhead in the cache
post_b         = 1_000        # text + metadata
media_share    = 0.1          # posts with an image
image_b        = 500_000

posts_day      = dau * posts_per_dau
write_qps      = posts_day / 86_400
read_qps       = dau * reads_per_dau / 86_400
peak_read_qps  = read_qps * peak_factor

posts_tb_year  = posts_day * post_b * 365 / 1e12
media_tb_day   = posts_day * media_share * image_b / 1e12

rows = [
    ("posts_day", posts_day, "posts"), ("write_qps", write_qps, "posts/s"),
    ("read_qps", read_qps, "req/s"), ("peak_read_qps", peak_read_qps, "req/s"),
    ("fanout_qps", fanout_qps, "inserts/s"), ("timeline_gb", timeline_gb, "GB"),
    ("posts_tb_year", posts_tb_year, "TB"), ("media_tb_day", media_tb_day, "TB/day"),
]
print("| quantity | value | unit |\n|---|---:|---|")
for name, value, unit in rows:
    v = f"{value:,.0f}" if abs(value) >= 100 else f"{value:,.2f}"
    print(f"| `{name}` | {v} | {unit} |")

What the numbers tell us:

  • Reads (~12 k/s, ~35 k/s at peak) outnumber posts (~230/s) by 50:1. ⇒ make reads cheap, even at the cost of more work on writes.
  • But push fan-out turns 230 posts/s into ~46 k timeline inserts/s on average — and the average hides the tail: one post by an account with 50 M followers is 50 M inserts by itself. ⇒ the write path must be asynchronous (queue + workers), and celebrities need special handling.
  • Cached timelines of 800 IDs for every daily user take ~1.3 TB of RAM — a large but ordinary cache cluster (tens of nodes). Keeping only IDs, not posts, is what makes this affordable; caching for active users only cuts it further.
  • Posts are ~7 TB/year (a partitioned store), media ~1 TB/day (object storage + CDN — never in the database).

items.title: 3. API
items.text:
POST /v1/posts                               → 201 {postId, createdAt}
     {"text": "Tour announced! Presale Friday 10:00", "mediaIds": ["m_81f…"]}
POST /v1/media                               → 201 {mediaId, uploadUrl}   (pre-signed PUT to object store)

GET  /v1/feed?limit=20&cursor=eyJ0cyI6…      → 200 {items: [Post…], nextCursor}
GET  /v1/users/{id}/posts?cursor=…           → 200 {items: [Post…], nextCursor}   (profile timeline)

PUT    /v1/users/{id}/followers/me           → 204   (follow)
DELETE /v1/users/{id}/followers/me           → 204   (unfollow)
  • Cursor, not page number: cursor encodes (score or timestamp, postId) of the last item seen. New posts arriving at the top do not shift the pages (no duplicates, no gaps) and the query is an index seek, not OFFSET 4000.
  • Media is uploaded directly to object storage with a pre-signed URL; the post only references mediaId.

items.title: 4. Data model
items.text:
-- Posts: partitioned by author, newest first (wide-column, e.g. Cassandra)
CREATE TABLE posts_by_author (
    author_id  BIGINT,
    post_id    BIGINT,          -- Snowflake-style: time-ordered, unique
    text       TEXT,
    media      LIST<TEXT>,
    visibility TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY ((author_id), post_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (post_id DESC);

-- Social graph, stored in both directions
CREATE TABLE followers (user_id BIGINT, follower_id BIGINT, PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), follower_id));
CREATE TABLE following (user_id BIGINT, followee_id BIGINT, PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), followee_id));

# Timeline cache (Redis sorted set, score = post timestamp), trimmed to 800 entries
feed:{user_id}   →  { (1767261600123, 918273645), (1767261598001, 918273511), ... }

# Post cache for hydration (hash per post) and counters
post:{post_id}   →  { author_id, text, media, created_at }
likes:{post_id}  →  1532
Data Store Why Posts Wide-column NoSQL (nosql), partition = author Write-heavy, append-only, read "latest N of author" — one partition scan Social graph NoSQL tables in both directions (or a graph service, e.g. TAO-style) "Followers of X" for fan-out, "followees of Y" for pull Home timelines Cache (cache): sorted set of IDs per user Rebuildable, read on every feed open, ~1.3 TB Post objects Cache (cache) in front of the posts store Hydration does multi-gets of 20–50 posts per feed page Media Object store (objstore) + CDN (cdn) Large immutable blobs, served at the edge Fan-out jobs Kafka (kafka) topic post-created Decouples posting from fan-out; absorbs bursts

items.text:
flowchart LR

Write path: the post service stores the post and publishes post-created; it returns 201 immediately. Fan-out workers read the author's followers in pages and push the post ID into each active follower's timeline (ZADD + ZREMRANGEBYRANK to trim).

Read path:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as App
    participant F as Feed service
    participant T as Timeline cache
    participant C as Celebrity posts
    participant P as Post cache
    participant R as Ranking
    A->>F: GET /v1/feed?limit=20
    F->>T: ZREVRANGE feed:42 0 199
    T-->>F: 200 post IDs (pushed)

    C-->>F: 30 post IDs
    F->>F: merge, drop deleted / blocked

    P-->>F: post objects

    R-->>F: top 20

items.title: 6.1 Fan-out on write, on read, or both
items.text:
Fan-out on write (push)Fan-out on read (pull)Hybrid (what large networks do)

When a post is created, insert its ID into every follower's precomputed timeline. Reading the feed is a single cache read — fast and predictable. Costs: write amplification proportional to followers, wasted work for followers who never log in, and a delay of minutes for an account with tens of millions of followers.

Store posts only by author. When a user opens the feed, fetch the latest posts of each of their followees and merge them. Writes are trivial and always fresh. Costs: every feed open does hundreds of queries (one per followee, or a scatter-gather over partitions) — slow and expensive at 35 k reads/s.

Push for ordinary authors; pull for celebrities (authors above a follower threshold). At read time, merge the pushed timeline with the latest posts of the few celebrities the user follows — usually a handful of cheap, highly cached queries (a celebrity's recent posts are read by millions, so they are always in cache).

Push Pull Hybrid Read latency Lowest (one cache read) Highest (N queries + merge) Low (cache read + few celebrity reads) Write cost Followers × posts One insert Followers × posts, capped at threshold Freshness Seconds to minutes (queue) Immediate Seconds Celebrity post Millions of inserts Free Free (pulled) Inactive users Wasted inserts Free Skip them; rebuild on login

How much work does a threshold save? With a heavy-tailed distribution of followers, a tiny share of authors produces most of the fan-out:

ResultSource

median followers: 143 · max: 50,000,000

threshold celebrities celebrities_pct writes_avoided_pct 10,000 3,380 1.69% 91.6% 100,000 535 0.27% 83.9% 1,000,000 81 0.04% 71.2% 
# Who pays for push fan-out? Synthetic heavy-tailed follower counts (illustrative)
import random

random.seed(42)
authors = 200_000
followers = [min(50_000_000, int(60 / (1 - random.random()) ** 1.25)) for _ in range(authors)]
total = sum(followers)                  # timeline inserts if every author posts once
followers.sort()

print(f"median followers: {followers[authors // 2]:,}  ·  max: {followers[-1]:,}\n")
print("| threshold | celebrities | celebrities_pct | writes_avoided_pct |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|")
for threshold in (10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000):
    celeb = [f for f in followers if f >= threshold]
    print(f"| {threshold:,} | {len(celeb):,} | {len(celeb) / authors:.2%} | {sum(celeb) / total:.1%} |")

Pulling the posts of a fraction of a percent of the authors removes most of the fan-out writes. The threshold is a tuning knob: lower it and reads get a bit more expensive (more celebrities to merge per user), raise it and celebrity posts take longer to fan out.

items.title: 6.2 The timeline cache and hydration
items.text:
• Store IDs, not posts. A post can be edited, deleted or have its counters change; copying it into 200 timelines would make every change a fan-out. A timeline is a list of (score, post_id); the content is hydrated at read time with one batched multi-get from the post cache.
  • Trim each timeline to a few hundred entries (ZREMRANGEBYRANK). Nobody scrolls back 5 000 posts through the home feed; older history comes from the pull path.
  • Active users only. Fan-out workers skip users who have not opened the app in, say, 30 days. When such a user returns, the feed service rebuilds the timeline with a pull (slow once, then cached) — a classic cache-miss path (caching patterns).
  • Filter on read. Deleted posts, blocked authors and posts that became private are removed during hydration (the post cache says deleted), so the timeline itself never needs to be cleaned synchronously.
  • Partition the timeline cache by user_id (consistent hashing); a user's feed lives on one shard, so the read is a single round trip.

items.title: 6.3 Ranking
items.text:
A chronological feed is "sort by time". A ranked feed is a small pipeline that must fit in the latency budget:

flowchart LR
    cand["Candidates<br/>~500 IDs<br/>(pushed + pulled)"] --> feat["Features<br/>author affinity, age,<br/>engagement, media type"]
    feat --> score["Scoring model<br/>(lightweight)"]
    score --> rerank["Re-rank<br/>diversity, dedupe,<br/>business rules"]
    rerank --> page["Top 20"]
  • Candidate generation is the timeline (push + pull); features come from precomputed stores (affinity between user and author computed offline), never from expensive live queries.
  • Precompute when possible: rank the first page when the user is likely to open the app (or right after fan-out) and cache it for a few minutes.
  • Keep a fallback: if the ranking service is slow, return the chronological order. A feed that is less clever but on time is better than a spinner (reliability patterns).

items.title: 6.4 Pagination and freshness
items.text:
• Cursor pagination: the cursor is (score, post_id) of the last item; the next page is ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:42 (score -inf LIMIT 0 20. New posts arriving at the top do not shift the next page, unlike OFFSET.
  • New posts while scrolling are shown with a "new posts" pill that reloads from the top (a separate request with since=), not inserted under the user's finger.
  • Read-your-writes: after posting, the author must see the post in their own feed immediately even if fan-out takes seconds — insert it into the author's own timeline synchronously, or merge the author's latest posts on read (consistency models).

items.title: 7. Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs
items.text:
Where What goes wrong Mitigation Trade-off Celebrity post Millions of inserts; followers see it minutes late Hybrid: pull above a threshold Reads merge a few extra sources Fan-out workers Queue lag after a burst of posts; feeds stale Scale consumers on lag; partition post-created by author; prioritize active users More workers, cost Timeline cache shard loss Users on that shard get empty feeds Replicas; rebuild on miss via pull; degrade to "latest from followees" Slow first load after failover Hydration fan-out Feed needs 200+ post lookups Batched multi-get; post cache; hydrate only the top candidates Ranking sees fewer features Ranking service slow Feed p99 above budget Timeout + fallback to chronological; precomputed first page Less relevant feed Hot post Viral post read by millions; its cache key is hot Replicate hot keys; local in-process cache for seconds Counters slightly stale Deletes / privacy Removed post still in timelines Filter on read via post state; lazy cleanup Small extra work per read Media traffic Bandwidth dominates the bill CDN, responsive image sizes, lazy loading CDN cost, cache invalidation of edits

The trade-offs to say out loud: write amplification vs. read latency (push pays at write time so reads are cheap), freshness vs. cost (asynchronous fan-out means seconds of delay), and relevance vs. latency (ranking must fall back to chronological when it is slow).

items.title: 8. Try it in the playground
items.text:
The news-feed scenario contains the post service, a fan-out path through a queue and workers, a timeline cache and the feed service.

Try it

  1. Run with the load profile; note the feed p99, the cache hit ratio and the fan-out backlog (queue depth / consumer lag).
  2. Increase the write share (or switch to spike) to simulate a celebrity post: does the backlog grow? How long until it drains — that is the freshness your users see.
  3. Add workers and watch the backlog drain faster; then remove the timeline cache and see the read path collapse onto the database (that is fan-out on read).
  4. Turn chaos on to slow the workers: reads should keep working with stale timelines — the system degrades instead of failing.

Open the full playground

items.title: 9. Follow-up questions an interviewer asks
items.text:
A user follows 5 000 accounts, 300 of them celebrities. Does the hybrid still work?

Merging 300 celebrity timelines on every read would be slow. Options: cap the number of pulled sources per read (take the most recent/most relevant 50 celebrities by affinity), precompute a per-user "celebrity digest" every few minutes, or lower the push threshold for users with many celebrity followees. Edge cases like this are why real systems decide push vs. pull per (author, follower) pair, not only per author.

A user returns after six months. What does the first feed open do?

Their timeline is not in the cache (fan-out skipped inactive users). The feed service builds it with fan-out on read: fetch recent posts of followees (in parallel, with a time bound), merge, rank, return the first page, and write the timeline to the cache so later opens are fast. The first open is slower (say 500 ms instead of 100 ms) — show a skeleton screen.

How do you delete a post that was pushed into ten million timelines?

You do not touch the timelines synchronously. Mark the post as deleted in the posts store and the post cache; hydration drops it, so it disappears from every feed on the next read. A background job may remove the ID from timelines later, but it is optional: timelines are trimmed and the entry ages out anyway.

How would you show like counts that update in real time?

Counters are a separate, write-heavy concern. Keep them in a counter service with sharded counters (or Redis INCR per post, aggregated periodically to the database), accept a few seconds of staleness, and push updates only for posts currently visible on screen (via WebSocket/SSE), if at all. Never store the count inside the timeline.

What changes for a brand-new user with no follows?

The cold start feed comes from recommendations: popular posts in their region, accounts similar to the ones they picked at sign-up, trending content. Architecturally, it is a different candidate source plugged into the same ranking pipeline.

How do you go multi-region?

Users are served by their home region. Posts are replicated asynchronously across regions; fan-out runs in each region for the followers who live there (a post created in São Paulo is fanned out in Frankfurt to European followers). Timelines are per-region caches and can be rebuilt; a few seconds of cross-region delay is acceptable for a feed.

Why not store timelines in the database instead of a cache?

You can (some systems keep a durable materialized timeline in a wide-column store), but timelines are derived data: they can always be recomputed from posts and the graph. Keeping them in memory makes the hot path fast; making them durable buys faster recovery after a cache loss at the cost of write load on the database. Either is defensible if you say why.

items.title: 10. Self-assessment rubric
items.text:
Level What the answer contains Junior Posts and follows tables; the feed as a query SELECT … WHERE author IN (followees) ORDER BY time LIMIT 20; a cache in front. Does not notice the cost at scale. Mid Fan-out on write with a queue and workers; timeline cache of IDs; recognizes the celebrity problem and proposes the hybrid; cursor pagination; media on CDN. Senior Quantifies write amplification and memory; chooses a threshold with reasoning; designs hydration, filtering on read, active-user fan-out and rebuild on miss; ranking pipeline with latency budget and fallback; read-your-writes for the author; failure modes (worker lag, cache loss) and multi-region fan-out.

Related: Messaging, Caching patterns, Partitioning, Hands-on 7 (asynchronous processing with Kafka), Hands-on 5 (caching).

items.title: Index
items.text:
"Design a notification system that sends push notifications, e-mails and SMS for many product teams: order confirmations, reminders and marketing campaigns. Users must be able to choose what they receive."

The notification system is the classic asynchronous fan-out to unreliable third parties problem. Nothing here is computationally hard; what makes it interesting is that every interesting part sits outside your control: Apple's and Google's push gateways, e-mail and SMS providers with their own rate limits, phones that uninstall the app, inboxes that bounce. The interview checks whether you can build a pipeline that absorbs bursts, never sends the same message twice (or explains when it might), keeps urgent messages fast while a marketing blast is draining, and respects what the user asked for.

BoxOffice sends three very different kinds of notification, and they make the requirements concrete:

  • Transactional — "your tickets for Saturday" seconds after the payment webhook (ticketing case). Low volume, must arrive fast, must not be lost.
  • Scheduled — "doors open in 2 hours" to the 60 000 ticket holders of tonight's show. Known in advance, all at the same moment.
  • Campaign — "presale for the stadium tour starts Friday at 10:00" to the 5 million followers of an artist. Huge, not urgent, and dangerous: if everyone taps at once, the notification DDoSes your own app.
Difficulty medium Key concepts queue per channel and per priority, workers, device-token registry, templates and preferences (opt-out, quiet hours, frequency caps), idempotency and deduplication, retries with backoff + jitter, DLQ, provider failover and circuit breakers, per-provider rate limits, scheduler and campaign batching, delivery tracking via webhooks Palette components scheduler, queue, worker, notifications, email, thirdparty, nosql, sql, analytics Playground scenario notification-system

What this case trains

  • Estimate the burst of a bulk campaign and show that a third-party rate limit, not your servers, sets how long it takes.
  • Design a pipeline of queues and workers per channel and priority, so marketing never delays a password reset.
  • Guarantee at-most-once effect on the user where possible, using notification IDs, idempotent consumers and provider features — and explain where duplicates can still happen.
  • Apply retries with backoff and jitter, dead-letter queues, circuit breakers and provider failover to external integrations.
  • Spread scheduled and bulk sends over time to protect providers and your own backend.

items.title: 1. Clarify the requirements
items.text: (interview framework)

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text:
1. Internal services trigger notifications through one API (order, inventory, auth…), by user and type, with data for the template.
  2. Channels: push (iOS via APNs, Android via FCM), e-mail and SMS.
  3. Scheduled notifications (send at a time) and campaigns (send to an audience, e.g. all followers of an artist).
  4. Templates per type, channel and language.
  5. User preferences: opt-out per category and channel, quiet hours, unsubscribe link in every marketing e-mail.
  6. Tracking: sent, delivered, opened, bounced, per notification and per campaign.

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.text: Quality Target Latency Transactional: handed to the provider in p99 < 5 s. Campaigns: minutes to an hour is fine. Reliability No accepted notification is silently lost (retry, then DLQ with an alert) Duplicates A user should not receive the same notification twice; rare duplicates are tolerated, systematic ones are bugs Scale ~12 M notifications/day, bursts of millions in one campaign Isolation A campaign must never delay transactional messages Compliance Respect opt-outs and unsubscribes immediately; transactional vs. marketing rules differ

items.title: Out of scope (say it explicitly)
items.text:
Building our own push or e-mail infrastructure (we use providers), the content editor for marketing, A/B testing of copy, the in-app inbox UI (mentioned as a follow-up).

Questions to ask the interviewer Question Why it matters Which channels, and which are mandatory per type? Fan-out per channel and different providers, costs and limits. How big is the biggest campaign? How fast must it go out? Sizes queues and workers; a provider limit may make "fast" impossible. Transactional and marketing in the same system? Separate priorities or queues so marketing never blocks transactional. Is a duplicate worse than a loss? Order confirmation: a duplicate is fine, a loss is not. Marketing: the opposite. Do we need open/click tracking? Webhooks, tracking pixels, link redirection, analytics store. Time zones and quiet hours? The scheduler must defer messages per user.

items.title: 2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates
items.text:
ResultSource quantity value unit campaign_msgs 7,500,000 msgs daily_msgs 12,500,000 msgs/day avg_rate 145 msgs/s blast_rate_1m 125,000 msgs/s spread_rate 4,167 msgs/s taps_blast 8,333 req/s taps_spread 278 req/s email_drain_min 41.67 min log_gb_day 6.25 GB/day dedup_gb 5.25 GB

    print(f"| `{name}` | {v} | {unit} |")

What the numbers tell us:

  • The average is tiny (~145 messages/s) and the peak is huge: one presale campaign is 7.5 M messages, 125 k/s if fired in one minute. ⇒ a queue between the trigger and the senders, and workers that drain at a controlled rate. This is a burst-absorption problem, not a throughput problem.
  • Blasting in one minute also makes ~8 k app requests/s from fans who tap the notification — on the same backend that is preparing the presale. Spreading over 30 minutes cuts that to ~280 req/s. ⇒ spread campaigns over a window: the notification system must protect the rest of BoxOffice, not only itself.
  • With an e-mail provider that accepts 1 000 messages/s, the 2.5 M e-mails take ~42 minutes no matter how many workers we run. ⇒ the provider's limit decides the duration; we need per-provider rate limiting, and transactional e-mails need reserved capacity (a separate priority) or they wait 40 minutes behind the campaign.
  • The notification log is ~6 GB/day and the dedup keys for a week ~5 GB — small. Storage is not the problem; ordering the work is.

items.title: 3. API
items.text:
POST /v1/notifications                                   → 202 {notificationId, status: ACCEPTED}
     Idempotency-Key: order-81f3-confirmed
     {"userId": 42, "type": "order.confirmed", "priority": "transactional",
      "data": {"orderId": "81f3", "event": "Rock in Rio — Day 2", "seats": ["A-12-07", "A-12-08"]}}

POST /v1/campaigns                                       → 202 {campaignId, status: SCHEDULED}
     {"audience": {"followersOf": "artist:77"}, "type": "presale.alert",
      "sendAt": "2027-03-10T15:00:00Z", "spreadOver": "30m", "channels": ["push", "email"]}
POST /v1/campaigns/{campaignId}/cancel                   → 200 {sent, cancelled}

PUT  /v1/users/{userId}/preferences                      → 204
     {"marketing": {"push": true, "email": false}, "quietHours": {"from": "22:00", "to": "08:00"},
      "timezone": "America/Sao_Paulo", "locale": "pt-BR"}
POST   /v1/devices  {"userId": 42, "platform": "ios", "token": "…"}    → 201
DELETE /v1/devices/{token}                                              → 204

POST /v1/webhooks/{provider}                             ← delivered / bounced / complaint / opened (signed)
GET  /v1/notifications/{notificationId}                  → 200 {channel statuses, attempts}
  • The trigger is asynchronous: 202 Accepted means "durably queued", not "delivered". Producers never wait for Apple or the e-mail provider.
  • The Idempotency-Key comes from the business event (order-81f3-confirmed), so a producer that retries — or an event consumed twice from Kafka — creates one notification.
  • priority is set by type (configured centrally), not chosen freely by each team — otherwise everything becomes "transactional".

items.title: 4. Data model
items.text:
-- Preferences, templates, campaigns: small, relational, read-mostly (SQL)
CREATE TABLE preference (
    user_id     BIGINT, category TEXT, channel TEXT,       -- 'marketing' | 'reminders' | 'transactional'
    enabled     BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, category, channel)
);
CREATE TABLE user_settings (
    user_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, timezone TEXT, locale TEXT,
    quiet_from TIME, quiet_to TIME, email TEXT, phone TEXT, email_suppressed BOOLEAN DEFAULT false
);
CREATE TABLE device (
    token TEXT PRIMARY KEY, user_id BIGINT NOT NULL, platform TEXT NOT NULL,   -- ios | android | web
    active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT true, last_seen TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE TABLE template (
    type TEXT, channel TEXT, locale TEXT, version INT,
    subject TEXT, body TEXT,                                -- e.g. Mustache/Handlebars source
    PRIMARY KEY (type, channel, locale, version)
);
CREATE TABLE campaign (
    campaign_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, audience JSONB, type TEXT, send_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    spread_over INTERVAL, status TEXT, cursor TEXT          -- where the audience expansion stopped
);

# Notification log (NoSQL, partition = user_id, clustering = created_at DESC): write-heavy, append-only
notification {notification_id, user_id, type, channel, status: ACCEPTED|SENT|DELIVERED|FAILED|SKIPPED,
              provider, provider_msg_id, attempts, created_at, sent_at, reason}

# Dedup keys (cache) — one per notification and channel
SET notif:order-81f3-confirmed:push 1 NX EX 604800     → OK (first time) | nil (already sent)

# Per-user frequency cap (cache)
INCR cap:42:marketing:2027-03-10  → 2      EXPIRE … 86400
Data Store Why Preferences, settings, devices, templates, campaigns SQL (sql) + cache in workers Small, relational, changed by users and admins; read on every send Notification log / status NoSQL (nosql), partitioned by user Millions of appends per day, read by user ("what did we send to 42?") and by id Dedup keys, frequency caps, provider rate limits In-memory KV with TTL (cache) Atomic SET NX / INCR, expire by themselves Work in flight Queues (queue) per channel × priority, plus retry and dead-letter queues Absorb bursts, isolate channels and priorities Delivery events Analytics (analytics) / data warehouse Campaign reports, bounce rates, provider comparison

items.title: 5. High-level design
items.text:
flowchart LR
    ord["order / inventory /<br/>auth services"] --> api["Notification API<br/>validate, idempotency"]
    camp["Campaign service"] --> sch["Scheduler<br/>sendAt, spread, quiet hours"]
    sch --> api
    api --> route["Router<br/>preferences, templates,<br/>devices, caps"]
    route --> qt[["Queues: transactional<br/>push · email · sms"]]
    route --> qm[["Queues: bulk<br/>push · email · sms"]]
    qt --> wp["Push workers"]
    qm --> wp
    qt --> we["E-mail workers"]
    qm --> we
    qt --> ws["SMS workers"]
    wp --> apns[["APNs / FCM"]]
    we --> esp[["E-mail provider A / B"]]
    ws --> sms[["SMS provider"]]
    wp -. failed after retries .-> dlq[["DLQ"]]
    esp -. webhooks .-> trk["Tracking"]
    trk --> an[("Analytics")]
    route --> log[("Notification log")]

One order confirmation, end to end:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as order (Kafka consumer)
    participant A as Notification API
    participant R as Router
    participant Q as Queue (transactional email)
    participant W as E-mail worker
    participant P as E-mail provider
    participant T as Tracking
    O->>A: POST /notifications (Idempotency-Key order-81f3-confirmed)
    A->>A: first time? store ACCEPTED
    A-->>O: 202
    A->>R: route(user 42, order.confirmed)
    R->>R: preferences ok, render pt-BR template
    R->>Q: enqueue email job
    Q->>W: job (attempt 1)
    W->>P: send (timeout 3 s)
    P--xW: 503 Service Unavailable
    W->>Q: re-enqueue with backoff 2 s ± jitter
    Q->>W: job (attempt 2)
    W->>P: send
    P-->>W: 202 accepted, provider id
    W->>W: status SENT
    P-->>T: webhook delivered

items.title: 6.1 Channels, queues and priorities
items.text:
Each channel has its own provider, failure modes and limits, so each gets its own queue and worker pool — a slow SMS provider must not stop push notifications (a bulkhead). Each channel also has (at least) two priorities: transactional and bulk.

Push (APNs / FCM)E-mailSMS

The device registers its token with our API after login. Workers send to Apple Push Notification service (iOS) or Firebase Cloud Messaging (Android, web). Payloads are small (a few kB). The providers tell you when a token is dead (APNs answers 410 Unregistered, FCM UNREGISTERED): deactivate the token, or you keep paying for sends to uninstalled apps. Push is best-effort: delivery to a phone that is off is deferred or dropped by the platform.

Sent through an e-mail service provider (Amazon SES, SendGrid, Mailgun…). Deliverability depends on your domain reputation: SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, a suppression list for hard bounces and spam complaints (never send to them again), and a one-click unsubscribe header on marketing mail (RFC 8058). Throughput is limited by the provider's sending rate.

The most expensive channel per message and the most regulated (sender IDs, opt-in rules per country). Use it only for what really needs it (one-time codes, critical changes such as "your event was cancelled"). Providers have per-second limits and delivery receipts arrive by webhook.

Channel Typical latency Cost per message Reliability signal Main limit Push Seconds ~Free Provider accepted; device delivery not guaranteed Token validity, payload size E-mail Seconds to minutes Low Delivered / bounced / complaint webhooks Provider rate, domain reputation SMS Seconds High Delivery receipts (DLR) Cost, carrier rules, provider rate

Priorities. Two separate queues per channel (or one queue system with strict priority) and separate worker pools or reserved capacity for transactional. A campaign of 2.5 M e-mails then drains at the provider's limit minus the share reserved for transactional, and the order confirmation still leaves in seconds.

items.title: 6.2 Delivering once: idempotency, retries, DLQ and failover
items.text:
The pipeline is at-least-once end to end — queues redeliver when a worker crashes, workers retry when a provider times out (delivery semantics). To make the effect "once" for the user:

  1. Notification ID from the business event. The API stores Idempotency-Key → notificationId; a second trigger for order-81f3-confirmed returns the existing notification.
  2. Idempotent workers. Before calling the provider, a worker claims notif:{id}:{channel} with SET NX; a redelivered job finds the key and only checks the status.
  3. Provider-side guards where they exist. APNs apns-collapse-id makes the device show only the latest notification with that ID; several e-mail and SMS APIs accept an idempotency key or a client reference.
def handle(job):
    key = f"notif:{job.notification_id}:{job.channel}"
    if not cache.set(key, "sending", nx=True, ex=7 * 86_400):
        return ack(job)                                   # already handled: duplicate delivery
    try:
        provider_id = provider.send(job.payload, timeout=3, idempotency_key=job.notification_id)
        log.update(job.notification_id, job.channel, status="SENT", provider_id=provider_id)
        return ack(job)
    except (Timeout, ProviderUnavailable, RateLimited) as err:
        cache.delete(key)                                 # allow the retry to claim it again
        if job.attempt >= MAX_ATTEMPTS:
            return dead_letter(job, reason=str(err))      # alert + manual or automatic replay
        delay = min(300, 2 ** job.attempt) * random.uniform(0.5, 1.5)   # backoff + jitter
        return retry_later(job, delay)
    except InvalidRecipient:
        devices.deactivate(job.token)                     # permanent: do not retry
        log.update(job.notification_id, job.channel, status="FAILED", reason="invalid recipient")
        return ack(job)

Where duplicates can still happen

If the provider accepted the message but the response was lost (timeout), the worker cannot know whether it was sent. Retrying risks a duplicate; not retrying risks a loss. For transactional messages choose retry (a duplicate "your tickets" e-mail is harmless) and lean on provider idempotency keys and collapse IDs. Say this explicitly in the interview: "exactly-once delivery" to a third party does not exist; exactly-once effect is engineered with idempotency where the other side supports it.

Failures by type. Distinguish transient errors (timeouts, 429, 5xx: retry with exponential backoff and jitter), permanent errors (invalid token, hard bounce: do not retry, fix the data) and poison messages (a template that fails to render: straight to the DLQ). The dead-letter queue is monitored; a non-empty DLQ alerts someone and has a replay tool.

Provider outage. A circuit breaker per provider opens when errors pile up (integrations). For e-mail and SMS, keep a second provider and fail over transactional traffic to it (bulk can simply wait). For push there is no alternative to APNs/FCM: queue and wait, and drop marketing pushes that become stale (a presale alert after the presale is noise).

items.title: 6.3 Preferences, templates and limits
items.text:
The router applies a fixed sequence of checks before anything is queued — cheap filters first:

flowchart LR
    t["Trigger<br/>user 42, presale.alert"] --> p{"Opted in for<br/>marketing push?"}
    p -->|no| skip1["SKIPPED (log)"]
    p -->|yes| c{"Frequency cap<br/>≤ 3 marketing/day?"}
    c -->|exceeded| skip2["SKIPPED (log)"]
    c -->|ok| qh{"Quiet hours<br/>in user's timezone?"}
    qh -->|yes| def["Defer to scheduler<br/>(08:00 local)"]
    qh -->|no| r["Render template<br/>(locale pt-BR)"]
    r --> d["Look up devices"]
    d --> q[["Queue push (bulk)"]]
  • Preferences are cached in the router (they are read on every send and change rarely); an opt-out must still take effect within seconds, so invalidate on change.
  • Transactional bypasses frequency caps and quiet hours (a ticket confirmation at 23:00 is expected); marketing never does. The category is fixed per type, centrally.
  • Templates are versioned per type, channel and locale; render in the router (or the worker) with the data from the trigger, and fall back to a default locale. A rendering error is a poison message.
  • Frequency caps (INCR with a daily TTL per user and category) protect users from five teams each sending "just one" push per day.
  • Provider rate limits are enforced by the workers with a shared token bucket per provider and account (rate limiter case), so we slow down before the provider starts answering 429.

items.title: 6.4 Scheduled sends and campaigns
items.text:
Scheduled notifications ("doors open in 2 h") are stored with a send_at; the scheduler polls a time-bucketed index (WHERE send_at <= now() AND status = 'PENDING', claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so several scheduler instances do not double-send) or uses a delayed queue. 60 000 reminders at exactly 18:00 is itself a mini-campaign: spread them over a few minutes.

Campaigns are expanded in batches, never as one giant job:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Campaign service
    participant G as Followers (social graph)
    participant S as Scheduler
    participant R as Router
    C->>G: page of followers of artist:77 (cursor, 10 000)
    G-->>C: user ids + next cursor
    C->>C: save cursor (resumable)
    C->>S: batch with send times spread over 30 min (jittered)
    S->>R: due batches, at a controlled rate
    R->>R: preferences, caps, quiet hours, render
    Note over C,R: repeat until the cursor is exhausted (or the campaign is cancelled)
  • Resumable: the cursor is saved after each page; if the campaign service restarts, it continues instead of starting over (and duplicates are stopped by dedup keys anyway).
  • Spread with jitter: each batch gets send times distributed over the window, so the providers see a flat rate and BoxOffice sees ~280 taps/s instead of 8 000 (section 2). The same reasoning as the waiting room: turn a spike into a flow.
  • Kill switch: cancel stops the expansion and makes workers drop jobs of that campaign — essential when the copy has a wrong date.
  • Time zones: "at 10:00 local time" means one batch schedule per time zone.

Tracking. Providers report delivered, bounced, complaint (and for e-mail, opens via a tracking pixel and clicks via redirected links) through signed webhooks. The tracking service updates the notification log and streams events to the analytics store for campaign reports. Opens are approximate: some mail clients pre-fetch images (Apple Mail Privacy Protection, for example), inflating open rates.

items.title: 7. Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs
items.text:
Where What goes wrong Mitigation Trade-off Campaign burst Millions of jobs flood queues and providers Batched expansion; spread over a window; per-provider token bucket Campaign takes tens of minutes Priority inversion Order confirmation waits behind a campaign Separate queues/worker pools per priority; reserved provider capacity Idle reserved capacity Provider slow / down Workers block; queue grows Timeouts, circuit breaker, second provider for e-mail/SMS, drop stale marketing Two providers to integrate and pay Duplicates Redelivery or retry after an unknown outcome Idempotency key from the event, SET NX claim, provider idempotency/collapse IDs Dedup state; rare duplicates remain Poison messages A broken template is retried forever Classify errors; DLQ for non-retryable; alert on DLQ depth Manual replay work Dead tokens / bounces Paying for undeliverable sends; reputation drops Deactivate tokens on 410/UNREGISTERED; suppression list Must handle re-registration Self-inflicted DDoS Everyone taps the push at once Spread sends; pre-warm caches of the target page Later recipients learn later Preferences cache stale Opted-out user still notified Invalidate on change; check at send time for marketing One extra lookup

The trade-offs to say out loud: duplicates vs. losses (for transactional, retry and accept rare duplicates), speed vs. protection (a campaign spread over 30 minutes is slower but safe for providers and for BoxOffice), and isolation vs. utilization (separate pools per channel and priority waste some capacity but make failures local).

items.title: 8. Try it in the playground
items.text:
The notification-system scenario has a scheduler and producers feeding a queue, workers per channel and external e-mail/push providers.

Try it

  1. Run with the spike profile (a campaign) and watch the queue depth and the consumer lag: how long does the backlog take to drain?
  2. Add workers: does the drain time improve, or does the external provider become the limit? (That is the email_drain_min number of section 2.)
  3. Turn chaos to medium to slow down or fail the e-mail provider: do retries pile up? Where would a circuit breaker and a DLQ help?
  4. Compare the latency of the first and the last notification of the burst — that gap is what a transactional message would suffer without a separate priority queue.

Open the full playground

items.title: 9. Follow-up questions an interviewer asks
items.text:
How do you make sure a user does not get the same notification twice?

Layers: an idempotency key derived from the business event at the API (one notification per event); a SET NX claim per notification and channel in the worker (one send per redelivered job); provider features (collapse IDs, idempotency keys) for the case where the provider accepted but we did not get the answer. And be honest: when the outcome of a send is unknown, you choose between a possible duplicate and a possible loss — for transactional messages, prefer the duplicate.

The e-mail provider is down for an hour. What happens?

The circuit breaker opens after a burst of failures, so workers stop hammering it. Transactional e-mail fails over to the secondary provider (pre-configured, with its own domain authentication). Bulk e-mail stays queued and resumes when the breaker half-opens and probes succeed; marketing messages whose content expired (a presale that already started) are dropped. Push and SMS are unaffected because they have their own queues and workers.

A user has a phone, a tablet and the web app. Who gets the push?

All active devices of the user, by default — the device registry has one row per token. Use a collapse ID so the same notification replaces itself instead of stacking, and when the user opens it on one device, send a silent update to clear it from the others (the same receipt idea as in the chat case). Tokens that the provider reports as dead are deactivated.

How do you send 'doors open in 2 hours' exactly on time for 60 000 people?

The event time is absolute, so send_at = doors_open - 2 h is the same instant for everyone; the scheduler starts the batch a few minutes earlier and spreads it (nobody notices 18:00 vs. 17:57). Use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (or a partitioned delayed queue) so multiple scheduler instances share the work without double-sending, and mark each row as ENQUEUED in the same transaction that claims it.

Marketing sent a campaign with the wrong date. Can you stop it?

Yes, if the system was built for it: campaigns expand in batches with a saved cursor, so cancel stops the expansion; workers check the campaign status (cached for seconds) before sending each job and drop jobs of cancelled campaigns. Messages already handed to providers cannot be recalled — which is another reason to spread campaigns over time instead of blasting them.

Do notifications need to be ordered?

Usually not globally, but some pairs matter: "payment received" should not arrive after "order cancelled". Avoid depending on order: make each notification self-contained (it states the current state, rendered at send time), use a per-user ordering key in the queue when it really matters, and collapse superseded notifications (a newer status replaces the older one).

How would you add an in-app notification inbox?

Store every notification for the in-app channel in the notification log (partitioned by user, newest first) with a read flag, expose GET /v1/users/{id}/inbox?cursor=…, and push "you have a new item" over the app's real-time connection when it is open. The inbox becomes just another channel with its own worker, which writes to the store instead of calling a provider.

items.title: 10. Self-assessment rubric
items.text:
Level What the answer contains Junior An API that calls the push or e-mail provider directly when a service asks; a table of notifications. No queue, no retries; the producer waits for the provider. Mid Asynchronous pipeline with queues and workers per channel; templates and preferences; retries with backoff; DLQ; device-token registry; mentions idempotency and rate limits of providers. Senior Estimates the campaign burst and identifies the provider limit as the bottleneck; separates priorities so transactional is never delayed; idempotency end to end with honest discussion of unknown outcomes; error classification (transient, permanent, poison); circuit breakers and provider failover; frequency caps and quiet hours; resumable batched campaigns spread over time to protect the backend; tracking via webhooks and suppression lists.

Related: Queues and pub/sub, Delivery semantics, Asynchronous work and schedulers, External integrations, Hands-on 7 (idempotent notification consumer and DLQ), Ticketing case.

items.title: Index
items.text:
"Design the payment system of a ticketing platform. Fans pay by card or Pix through an external payment provider; promoters get paid after the show. Nobody may be charged twice, and every cent must be accounted for."

Payments are where "eventually consistent" stops being an acceptable answer. A fan charged twice calls the bank; a promoter paid twice is money you will never see again; a ticket issued without payment is a gift. Yet the system talks to an external provider over an unreliable network, which means timeouts with unknown outcomes, duplicated webhooks and money that arrives days later in a settlement file. The interview tests whether you can turn an at-least-once world into an exactly-once effect, and whether you know how money is recorded: a double-entry ledger, not a balance column.

This is BoxOffice's payment service — the adapter behind the order flow of the ticketing case. That page models the order as a state machine (HELD → PENDING_PAYMENT → CONFIRMED) and uses webhooks and reconciliation; this page goes one level deeper into what happens inside payment: idempotency, the ledger, the provider integration and the daily reconciliation.

Difficulty hard Key concepts idempotency keys, exactly-once effect over at-least-once delivery, payment state machine with an UNKNOWN state, double-entry ledger, PSP integration (hosted page, tokenization, 3-D Secure, signed webhooks), reconciliation with settlement files, transactional outbox, retries with backoff and DLQ Palette components apigw, app, sql, kafka, queue, worker, scheduler, payment, dwh Playground scenario payment-system

What this case trains

  • Explain why "exactly-once delivery" does not exist and build an exactly-once effect from retries plus idempotency.
  • Design an idempotency-key store that handles concurrent duplicates, replays and changed payloads.
  • Record money movements in a double-entry ledger and verify that every transaction balances.
  • Integrate with a payment service provider (PSP) while staying out of most of the PCI DSS scope, and handle timeouts whose outcome is unknown.
  • Design reconciliation between the ledger and the provider's settlement reports.

items.title: 1. Clarify the requirements
items.text: Payments have more hidden requirements than any other case. Ask (interview framework).

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text:
1. Pay-in: charge the fan for an order (card, Pix, wallet) through an external PSP; support 3-D Secure challenges.
  2. Refunds: full or partial, e.g. when a show is cancelled.
  3. Ledger: record every money movement (charge, PSP fee, platform fee, promoter payable, refund, payout).
  4. Payouts: pay promoters their share after the event (batch, out of the request path).
  5. Reconciliation: every day, match the provider's settlement report against the ledger and flag differences.
  6. Notify the order service of outcomes (confirm, fail) so tickets are issued.

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.text: Quality Target Correctness Never charge twice for one order; never issue a ticket without a captured payment; the ledger always balances Durability A recorded payment or ledger entry is never lost (RPO = 0) Auditability Immutable history: corrections are new entries, never updates Availability 99.95% for checkout; when the PSP is down, fail fast and clearly Latency Checkout API p99 < 1 s excluding the provider and the 3-D Secure challenge Security / compliance Card numbers never touch our servers (PCI DSS scope minimized); secrets in a vault; webhooks authenticated Scale ~300 k payments/day, peaks of ~300 payments/s during several simultaneous on-sales

items.title: Out of scope (say it explicitly)
items.text:
Building our own card processing (we are not an acquirer), fraud models (mention a fraud check hook), multi-currency FX, invoicing and taxes, chargeback disputes in detail.

Questions to ask the interviewer Question Why it matters Do we process cards ourselves or use a PSP (Stripe, Adyen, Mercado Pago, Pagar.me…)? A PSP with a hosted page or tokenization keeps raw card data out of our systems. Authorize and capture together, or authorize now and capture later? Two-step capture lets us release the money if the seat hold fails. Which payment methods? Pix / boleto are asynchronous Asynchronous methods make webhooks the only way to learn the outcome. Who gets paid, when? Platform fee? Defines ledger accounts (promoter payable, platform revenue) and payouts. One PSP or several (failover, cost routing)? Multiple PSPs multiply integration and reconciliation work. What is the refund policy? Partial refunds? Refunds are ledger transactions too; partial ones need amounts per line.

items.title: 2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates
items.text:
ResultSource quantity value unit avg_tps 3.47 payments/s inflight_peak 600 calls ledger_lines 1,200,000 lines/day ledger_gb_year 87.60 GB/year idem_mb_day 300 MB/day webhooks_day 600,000 events/day gmv_day_m 69.00 M/day dup_charges 300 charges/day

peak_tps       = 300          # payments/s when several on-sales open at 10:00
avg_order      = 230.0        # currency units per order (tickets + fees)

dup_rate       = 0.001        # share of payments that would be duplicated without idempotency

avg_tps        = orders_day / 86_400
inflight_peak  = peak_tps * psp_s                 # Little's Law: L = λ·W
ledger_lines   = orders_day * entries_per
ledger_gb_year = ledger_lines * entry_b * 365 / 1e9
idem_mb_day    = orders_day * idem_b / 1e6
webhooks_day   = orders_day * webhooks_per
gmv_day_m      = orders_day * avg_order / 1e6     # millions per day
dup_charges    = orders_day * dup_rate

rows = [
    ("avg_tps", avg_tps, "payments/s"), ("inflight_peak", inflight_peak, "calls"),
    ("ledger_lines", ledger_lines, "lines/day"), ("ledger_gb_year", ledger_gb_year, "GB/year"),
    ("idem_mb_day", idem_mb_day, "MB/day"), ("webhooks_day", webhooks_day, "events/day"),
    ("gmv_day_m", gmv_day_m, "M/day"), ("dup_charges", dup_charges, "charges/day"),
]
print("| quantity | value | unit |\n|---|---:|---|")
for name, value, unit in rows:
    v = f"{value:,.0f}" if abs(value) >= 100 else f"{value:,.2f}"
    print(f"| `{name}` | {v} | {unit} |")

What the numbers tell us:

  • On average only ~3.5 payments/s; the peak of 300/s is set by on-sales. With a 2 s provider, ~600 calls are in flight at the peak (Little's Law). ⇒ size the adapter's connection pool and bulkhead for that, and remember the provider has its own rate limit.
  • The ledger grows by 1.2 M lines/day, ~88 GB/year: a single, well-indexed PostgreSQL with a standby holds years of it. Payments are a correctness problem, not a scale problem.
  • Idempotency records take ~300 MB/day; keep them for 24 h–7 days and they fit anywhere.
  • Even a 0.1% duplicate rate would mean ~300 double charges per day — 300 angry fans and chargebacks. That is the number that justifies idempotency everywhere.
  • ~69 M currency units/day flow through the system: reconciliation differences of a fraction of a percent are still real money.

items.title: 3. API
items.text:
POST /v1/payments                                   → 201 {paymentId, status, nextAction?}
     Idempotency-Key: order-7f3c…                    (one key per order attempt)
     {"orderId": "7f3c…", "amount": 23000, "currency": "BRL",
      "method": "card", "paymentToken": "tok_1Q…", "returnUrl": "https://…"}
     status: REQUIRES_ACTION (3-D Secure) | PROCESSING | SUCCEEDED | FAILED

GET  /v1/payments/{paymentId}                       → 200 {status, amount, refundedAmount, events[]}
POST /v1/payments/{paymentId}/refunds               → 201 {refundId, status}
     Idempotency-Key: refund-…
     {"amount": 10000, "reason": "event_cancelled"}

POST /v1/webhooks/psp                               ← provider → us, HMAC-signed
     PSP-Signature: t=1767261600,v1=5257a8…
     {"id": "evt_9a…", "type": "payment.captured", "data": {"pspPaymentId": "pi_3N…", …}}
  • The fan's card data goes from the browser straight to the PSP (hosted fields or a redirect); we receive only a token (paymentToken). That is what keeps our servers out of most of the PCI DSS scope.
  • nextAction tells the client to run the 3-D Secure challenge with the issuing bank; the result arrives later as a webhook.
  • Every mutating call takes an Idempotency-Key; webhooks carry an event id that we deduplicate on.

items.title: 4. Data model
items.text:
CREATE TABLE payment (
    payment_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id        UUID        NOT NULL UNIQUE,      -- one payment per order attempt
    amount_cents    BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    currency        CHAR(3)     NOT NULL,
    status          TEXT        NOT NULL,             -- CREATED | REQUIRES_ACTION | PROCESSING
                                                      -- | UNKNOWN | SUCCEEDED | FAILED | REFUNDED
    psp             TEXT        NOT NULL,
    psp_payment_id  TEXT        UNIQUE,
    version         INT         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE idempotency_key (
    key             TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    request_hash    TEXT        NOT NULL,             -- SHA-256 of method + path + body
    status          TEXT        NOT NULL,             -- IN_PROGRESS | DONE
    response_code   INT,
    response_body   JSONB,
    locked_until    TIMESTAMPTZ,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE ledger_entry (                           -- append-only: no UPDATE, no DELETE
    entry_id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    txn_id          UUID        NOT NULL,             -- groups the lines of one transaction
    account         TEXT        NOT NULL,             -- 'psp_receivable', 'promoter_payable:88', …
    amount_cents    BIGINT      NOT NULL,             -- debit > 0, credit < 0
    currency        CHAR(3)     NOT NULL,
    payment_id      UUID,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE processed_webhook (event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, received_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now());
CREATE TABLE outbox (id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, topic TEXT, payload JSONB, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now());
Data Store Why Payments, idempotency keys, ledger, processed webhooks SQL (sql), one database ACID transactions across payment state, ledger lines and outbox; unique constraints are the last line of defense against duplicates Outcome events (PaymentSucceeded, PaymentFailed) Kafka (kafka) via outbox The order and notification services react asynchronously, never by polling the payment DB Retries to the PSP, refunds, payouts Queue (queue) + workers (worker) Backoff, rate limits toward the provider, dead-letter queue for manual review Settlement files, ledger history Data warehouse (dwh) Reconciliation queries and finance reports, off the transactional database

flowchart LR
    fan([Fan browser]) -->|"card data"| psp[["PSP<br/>hosted fields, 3-D Secure"]]
    fan --> gw["API gateway"]
    gw --> ord["order"]
    ord --> pay["payment service"]
    pay --> db[("PostgreSQL<br/>payment, idempotency,<br/>ledger, outbox")]
    pay -->|"charge(token, key)"| psp
    psp -. "signed webhook" .-> wh["webhook handler"]
    wh --> db
    db -. outbox relay .-> k[["Kafka<br/>payment events"]]
    k --> ord
    k --> notif["notification"]
