    pay --> q
    wk --> psp
    sched["scheduler<br/>reconciliation"] --> rec["reconciliation job"]
    psp -. "settlement file (daily)" .-> rec
    rec --> dwh[("Data warehouse")]
    rec --> db

A card payment with 3-D Secure, end to end:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant F as Fan
    participant O as order
    participant P as payment
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    participant S as PSP
    F->>S: card data (hosted fields) → token
    F->>O: POST /orders/{id}/pay {token}
    O->>P: POST /payments (Idempotency-Key = order attempt)
    P->>D: insert idempotency key IN_PROGRESS + payment CREATED
    P->>S: create payment (idempotency key = paymentId)
    S-->>P: requires_action (3-D Secure)
    P->>D: status REQUIRES_ACTION, key DONE + stored response
    P-->>F: nextAction: 3-D Secure challenge
    F->>S: completes challenge with the bank
    S-->>P: webhook payment.captured (signed)
    P->>D: one transaction: status SUCCEEDED + 4 ledger lines + outbox
    D-)O: PaymentSucceeded (via Kafka)
    O-->>F: order CONFIRMED, tickets issued

items.title: 6.1 Exactly-once effect: idempotency keys
items.text:
There is no exactly-once delivery over a network: a request whose response was lost may or may not have been executed. What we can build is an exactly-once effect: the client retries until it gets an answer (at-least-once), and the server makes the operation idempotent — executing it twice has the same effect as once (delivery semantics).

The server-side algorithm for POST /v1/payments with Idempotency-Key: K:

flowchart TD
    r["Request with key K"] --> ins{"INSERT key K<br/>IN_PROGRESS<br/>(unique)"}
    ins -->|"inserted"| run["Execute: create payment,<br/>call PSP"]
    run --> save["Store response,<br/>status DONE"]
    save --> ok["Return response"]
    ins -->|"conflict"| chk{"Same request_hash?"}
    chk -->|"no"| e422["422: key reused<br/>with different body"]
    chk -->|"yes, DONE"| replay["Replay stored response"]
    chk -->|"yes, IN_PROGRESS"| e409["409: still processing,<br/>retry later"]
Situation What the server does Why First request with K Insert IN_PROGRESS (unique constraint wins the race), execute, store the response The unique insert is the lock: two concurrent duplicates cannot both execute Retry of a finished request Return the stored response (same status code and body) The client cannot tell a replay from the original — that is the point Retry while the first is still running 409 Conflict (or wait briefly) Never run the side effect twice in parallel Same K, different body 422 A client bug; executing it would be silently wrong Crash in the middle (IN_PROGRESS forever) locked_until expires; a recovery path checks the PSP for the payment before retrying The PSP call may have happened — never assume it did not

The same idea applies outward: our call to the PSP carries our idempotency key (the paymentId), so if the adapter times out and retries, the provider returns the existing payment instead of charging again. Stripe-style APIs accept an Idempotency-Key header; with providers that do not, use a unique merchant reference and look it up before creating a new charge.

# key choice matters
Idempotency-Key: order-7f3c-attempt-1   ✔ one key per (order, attempt): a retry of the same attempt is a no-op,
                                           a new card after a decline is a new attempt
Idempotency-Key: <random per HTTP call> ✘ every retry looks new → double charge
Idempotency-Key: user-42                ✘ blocks every future purchase of that user

items.title: 6.2 The unknown outcome
items.text:
The adapter calls the PSP and gets a timeout. Was the card charged? You do not know — and this is the single most important sentence of the interview.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CREATED
    CREATED --> PROCESSING: call PSP
    PROCESSING --> REQUIRES_ACTION: 3-D Secure
    REQUIRES_ACTION --> PROCESSING: challenge done
    PROCESSING --> SUCCEEDED: PSP ok / webhook captured
    PROCESSING --> FAILED: declined
    PROCESSING --> UNKNOWN: timeout / 5xx
    UNKNOWN --> SUCCEEDED: status query or webhook says captured
    UNKNOWN --> FAILED: status query says not found / failed
    SUCCEEDED --> REFUNDED: refund
    SUCCEEDED --> [*]
    FAILED --> [*]
  • Never map a timeout to FAILED: if the charge went through, the fan pays for nothing; if you retry with a new key, they pay twice.
  • Keep the payment in UNKNOWN and resolve it: retry with the same idempotency key (safe), query the PSP by your reference, or wait for the webhook. A scheduler job sweeps payments stuck in UNKNOWN for more than a few minutes.
  • Meanwhile the order stays PENDING_PAYMENT and the seat hold is extended (see the ticketing state machine); the fan sees "confirming your payment…".
  • Timeouts on the PSP call are long enough for the provider's normal p99 (seconds), wrapped in a circuit breaker and a bulkhead so a slow provider cannot exhaust the payment service (reliability patterns).

items.title: 6.3 The double-entry ledger
items.text:
A balance column that you UPDATE loses history, cannot explain itself to an auditor and breaks silently under concurrent updates. Accounting solved this centuries ago: double-entry bookkeeping. Every transaction is a set of lines, each moving money into (debit) or out of (credit) an account, and the lines of every transaction sum to zero. Balances are derived by summing lines; nothing is ever updated or deleted — a mistake is fixed by a new, reversing transaction.

A fan buys a 200.00 ticket plus a 30.00 service fee; the PSP keeps a 2.5% fee; the promoter is paid after the show:

ResultSource transaction lines sum T1 capture 4 0 T2 settlement 2 0 T3 payout 2 0 account balance bank 24.25 platform_revenue -30.00 promoter_payable 0.00 psp_fees 5.75 psp_receivable 0.00

Sum of all balances: 0

# Double-entry ledger for one BoxOffice ticket sale (amounts in cents; debit > 0, credit < 0)
from collections import defaultdict

transactions = {
    "T1 capture": [                       # fan pays 230.00 through the PSP
        ("psp_receivable",   +22_425),    # PSP owes us 230.00 minus its fee
        ("psp_fees",          +575),      # 2.5% of 230.00 is our expense
        ("promoter_payable", -20_000),    # we owe the promoter the ticket price
        ("platform_revenue", -3_000),     # the service fee is ours
    ],
    "T2 settlement": [                    # PSP pays out to our bank two days later
        ("bank",             +22_425),
        ("psp_receivable",   -22_425),
    ],
    "T3 payout": [                        # after the show we pay the promoter
        ("promoter_payable", +20_000),
        ("bank",             -20_000),
    ],
}

balances = defaultdict(int)
print("| transaction | lines | sum |\n|---|---:|---:|")
for name, lines in transactions.items():
    total = sum(amount for _, amount in lines)
    assert total == 0, f"{name} does not balance"
    for account, amount in lines:
        balances[account] += amount
    print(f"| {name} | {len(lines)} | {total} |")

print("\n| account | balance |\n|---|---:|")
for account, cents in sorted(balances.items()):
    print(f"| `{account}` | {cents / 100:,.2f} |")
print(f"\nSum of all balances: {sum(balances.values())}")

Read the result: after the three transactions the bank holds 24.25 — exactly the platform revenue (30.00) minus the PSP fee (5.75); the receivable from the PSP and the payable to the promoter are zero, as they should be once settled. If any of these balances is not what the business expects, the ledger tells you which transaction caused it.

Engineering rules for the ledger:

  • Append-only at the database level (revoke UPDATE/DELETE for the application role). Refunds and corrections are new transactions.
  • Write all lines of a transaction in one database transaction, together with the payment state change and the outbox row. Check the zero-sum invariant in code and with a periodic query (SELECT txn_id FROM ledger_entry GROUP BY txn_id HAVING sum(amount_cents) <> 0 must return nothing).
  • Integer minor units (cents) and an explicit currency — never floating point for money.
  • Account per counterparty where needed (promoter_payable:88) so the payout job knows what each promoter is owed.

items.title: 6.4 Webhooks, outbox and reconciliation
items.text:
Webhooks are how asynchronous methods (Pix, 3-D Secure, bank transfers) report outcomes. The handler must:

  1. Verify the signature (HMAC over timestamp + body with a shared secret) and reject old timestamps — otherwise anyone can POST "payment succeeded".
  2. Deduplicate on the provider's event id (INSERT INTO processed_webhook … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING): providers deliver at least once.
  3. Apply the change as a conditional transition (… WHERE status IN ('PROCESSING','UNKNOWN')), so out-of-order events (a failed after a captured) cannot move the state backwards.
  4. Return 2xx quickly and do heavy work asynchronously; a slow handler makes the provider retry, multiplying load.

Outbox. The payment state, ledger lines and an outbox row are committed together; a relay publishes the outbox to Kafka. The order service never learns about a payment that was rolled back, and never misses one that was committed (messaging patterns).

Reconciliation is the safety net for everything above. Once a day the PSP publishes a settlement report (every captured payment, refund, fee and payout). A scheduled job loads it into the warehouse and matches it, line by line, against the ledger:

Mismatch Likely cause Action In PSP report, not in our ledger Lost webhook; payment stuck in UNKNOWN Create the missing transaction; confirm or refund the order In our ledger, not in PSP report Recorded success that never captured; timing (cut-off) Re-check next day; then investigate and reverse Amounts differ Fees changed, partial capture, currency rounding Adjusting transaction + alert finance Duplicate charge in PSP report Idempotency bug Refund immediately; postmortem

Retries toward the provider (refunds, payouts, status queries) run from a queue with exponential backoff and jitter; after N attempts the message goes to a dead-letter queue watched by humans. Money operations are never retried forever blindly.

In the interview

Say the three sentences that interviewers wait for: "A timeout means unknown, not failed." — "Retries are safe because every call, ours and the PSP's, carries an idempotency key." — "Money is recorded as balanced, append-only ledger transactions, and a daily reconciliation against the provider catches whatever slipped through."

items.title: 7. Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs
items.text:
Where What goes wrong Mitigation Trade-off PSP timeout Outcome unknown; risk of double charge or unpaid ticket UNKNOWN state, retry with same key, status query, webhook, reconciliation Fan waits "confirming…" for seconds or minutes PSP outage All checkouts fail Circuit breaker, clear error, pause admissions (ticketing), optional second PSP A second PSP doubles integration and reconciliation PSP rate limit at on-sale peak 429s from the provider Bulkhead + concurrency limit in the adapter; queue non-urgent calls (refunds, payouts) Refunds slower during peaks Duplicate webhooks / retries Double ledger entries Event-id dedupe, conditional transitions, unique order_id / psp_payment_id Extra tables and lookups Concurrent duplicates Two requests with the same key run in parallel Unique insert of the key as a lock; 409 for in-progress Clients must handle 409 Database primary failure Payments cannot be recorded Synchronous standby (RPO = 0); fail closed — never "record later" Short unavailability during failover Ledger drift Balances do not match reality Zero-sum invariant checks, daily reconciliation, append-only Operational process for mismatches Webhook spoofing Fake "succeeded" events HMAC signature, timestamp tolerance, allow-list, fetch status from PSP before confirming high-value orders Small extra latency

The trade-offs to say out loud: consistency over availability (if the payment database is down, stop taking payments rather than record them "later"), latency over certainty at the edge (answer the fan with "processing" and resolve asynchronously instead of holding the request until the truth is known), and outsourcing card handling to the PSP (less PCI scope and fraud work, in exchange for dependency and fees).

items.title: 8. Try it in the playground
items.text:
The payment-system scenario models the payment service, its database and an external payment provider with retries and idempotency.

Try it

  1. Run with the load profile and note the p99 of the payment path and the number of in-flight calls to the provider.
  2. Turn chaos to medium to make the provider slow and flaky. Without timeouts/circuit breaker, watch in-flight calls pile up (Little's Law) and the service saturate.
  3. Add a queue + workers in front of the provider for non-urgent calls (refunds, retries) and observe how the checkout path stays responsive.
  4. Increase retries without backoff: does the provider's error rate get worse? This is the retry storm — and in payments, without idempotency keys, every retry could be a second charge.

Open the full playground

items.title: 9. Follow-up questions an interviewer asks
items.text:
Why not just use a database transaction that includes the PSP call?

A database transaction cannot include an HTTP call to another company: you cannot roll back a charge by rolling back your BEGIN. Distributed transactions (two-phase commit) are not offered by payment providers. The pattern is a local transaction for our state (payment, ledger, outbox), an idempotent call to the provider, and compensation (a refund) when a later step fails — a saga (messaging patterns).

The fan's payment succeeded, but the seat hold had already expired and the seat was resold. What now?

The webhook handler finds the order EXPIRED. Options, in order: if the seat (or an equivalent one) is still available, confirm the order; otherwise refund automatically (a new ledger transaction reversing T1 and a refund request to the PSP, both idempotent) and notify the fan. Reconciliation catches the case where even the webhook was lost. The design point: payment and inventory are separate systems, so the inconsistency window exists and must have a defined resolution.

How long do you keep idempotency keys?

Long enough to cover every realistic retry: client retries happen within minutes, queued retries within hours. 24 hours is common for public APIs; for internal payment-to-PSP calls, keep the mapping (our paymentId ↔ psp_payment_id) forever as part of the payment record. Expired keys are deleted by a scheduled job; they are small.

How do you pay promoters?

A scheduled payout job after the event computes each promoter's balance from the ledger (promoter_payable:88), creates a payout transaction (debit payable, credit bank) and sends the transfer request through the provider or bank with an idempotency key. Payouts are batched, rate limited and go through the same queue + DLQ path; failures leave the payable balance untouched, so nothing is lost.

Do we need event sourcing for payments?

The ledger already is an append-only log of financial facts, and the payment table records a state machine with its history (events[]). Full event sourcing of every aggregate is optional; what matters is immutability of money movements and the ability to explain every balance. Many payment systems combine a relational state table with an immutable ledger — simpler to query and audit.

How would you add a second payment provider?

Put an adapter interface in front of providers (create, query, refund, parse webhook, parse settlement file) and a router that chooses by method, cost or health. The hard parts are not the API calls: each provider has its own webhook semantics, settlement format and fee model, so reconciliation and the ledger must track which provider handled each payment. Failover only for new payments; a payment never moves between providers once started.

How do you test that nobody is ever charged twice?

Unit tests of the idempotency algorithm (replay, concurrent duplicates, changed body); integration tests against the provider's sandbox with injected timeouts after the request was accepted; chaos tests with Toxiproxy dropping responses between payment and the PSP stub (Hands-on 9); and a production invariant: a daily query proving there is at most one captured payment per order and that every ledger transaction sums to zero.

items.title: 10. Self-assessment rubric
items.text:
Level What the answer contains Junior Calls the PSP from the order service; stores a paid flag; maybe retries on error. Treats a timeout as a failure; no ledger. Mid Idempotency key on the API and to the PSP; webhooks verified and deduplicated; payment state machine; outbox to notify the order service; mentions reconciliation and the PCI benefit of tokenization. Senior Explains why exactly-once delivery is impossible and builds the exactly-once effect; designs the idempotency store for races, replays and changed bodies; the UNKNOWN state and its resolution paths; a double-entry ledger with invariants and corrections as new transactions; reconciliation workflow with mismatch types; bulkheads and rate limits toward the PSP during on-sales; payout batches; compensation (refund) as a saga step; explicit CP choice for the payment database.

Related: Integrations (webhooks, idempotency), Messaging patterns (outbox, saga), Ticketing case, Hands-on 7 (outbox), Hands-on 9 (resilience between order and payment).

items.title: Index
items.text:
"Design a rate limiter for a public API. It must work across many API gateway replicas, add almost no latency, and let us set different limits per user, per IP and per partner."

Every public API needs one, and every large system has several: at the edge against floods, at the gateway per client, inside services to protect a fragile dependency. The problem is small enough to design end to end in 45 minutes and deep enough to separate levels: a junior candidate names "token bucket"; a senior one explains why a sliding-window counter is accurate enough, how to make the check atomic across 20 gateway replicas, what happens when the counter store is down, and why rate limiting alone does not stop an overload.

In BoxOffice, the rate limiter is the second line of defense of the flash sale: the WAF stops obvious floods, the waiting room meters admissions, and the gateway enforces "5 hold attempts per minute per account" and the quotas of reseller partners.

Difficulty medium Key concepts token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, sliding window (log and counter), GCRA, atomic counters in Redis with Lua, 429 + Retry-After, fail-open vs. fail-closed, local vs. global limits Palette components apigw, lb, waf, app, cache, metrics Playground scenario rate-limiter

What this case trains

  • Compare the five classic rate-limiting algorithms on accuracy, memory and burst behavior.
  • Implement an atomic, distributed check with Redis and a Lua script, and explain the race it avoids.
  • Decide where limits live (edge, gateway, service, client) and how they are configured per user, IP and plan.
  • Design the failure behavior (fail-open vs. fail-closed) and the client contract (429, Retry-After, backoff with jitter).
  • Distinguish rate limiting from load shedding and concurrency limiting.

items.title: 1. Clarify the requirements
items.text: The word "rate limiter" hides several different products. Ask before drawing (interview framework).

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text:
1. Limit the number of requests a client can make in a time window; the client can be a user ID, an API key, an IP address, or a combination.
  2. Several rules per request, e.g. 10 req/s per user and 1 000 req/min per API key and 100 req/s per IP on /login.
  3. Rejected requests get HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a hint of when to retry.
  4. Rules are configurable without redeploying (per endpoint, per plan: free, partner, internal).
  5. Expose metrics: allowed vs. rejected per rule and client.

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.text: Quality Target Latency Adds < 1 ms at p99 to each request (it is on every request) Throughput 50 k req/s at peak (BoxOffice on-sale day), across ~20 gateway replicas Accuracy A client can exceed its limit by a small margin (say ≤ 10%) during races or bursts; never by 2× Availability A failure of the limiter must not take the API down Memory State for ~1 M active clients must fit comfortably in RAM

items.title: Out of scope (say it explicitly)
items.text:
DDoS protection at the network layer (that is the WAF/CDN's job), billing based on usage, abuse detection with machine learning. Mention that they exist in the layers around the limiter.

Questions to ask the interviewer Question Why it matters Client-side, server-side, or gateway? A client-side limiter is courtesy, not protection: the server side is mandatory. What identifies the client: user, API key, IP? IPs are shared (NAT, mobile carriers) and spoofable through proxies; user/key is fairer. Hard limit or soft (allow a burst)? Token bucket allows bursts; leaky bucket smooths them. How many gateway replicas, how many regions? A per-replica limit is wrong by a factor N; a global limit needs shared state. What should happen if the limiter's storage is down? Fail-open (availability) vs. fail-closed (protection). Is the limit about rate or about concurrency or cost? "10 requests/s" vs. "5 in flight" vs. "100 k LLM tokens/min" are different mechanisms.

items.title: 2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates
items.text:
ResultSource quantity value unit counter_ops 100,000 ops/s script_calls 50,000 calls/s counters_mb 200 MB log_gb 30.00 GB redis_nodes 1.50 nodes local_error 20.00 x limit added_ms 0.50 ms 
# Rate limiter: assumptions (illustrative)
peak_rps       = 50_000      # API requests per second at peak
gateways       = 20          # gateway replicas
active_clients = 1_000_000   # distinct keys active in a window
rules_per_req  = 2           # e.g. per-user + per-IP
bucket_b       = 100         # one counter in Redis: key + 2 numbers + overhead, bytes
user_limit_min = 600         # per-user limit: 600 requests per minute
log_entry_b    = 50          # one timestamp in a sorted set, with overhead
redis_ops_node = 100_000     # simple ops/s one Redis node sustains (order of magnitude)
rtt_ms         = 0.5         # gateway → Redis round trip in the same zone

counter_ops    = peak_rps * rules_per_req           # one atomic op per rule (or 1 script)
script_calls   = peak_rps                            # all rules in one Lua call
counters_mb    = active_clients * rules_per_req * bucket_b / 1e6
log_gb         = active_clients * user_limit_min * log_entry_b / 1e9
redis_nodes    = script_calls * 3 / redis_ops_node   # a script costs ~3 simple ops
local_error    = gateways                             # per-replica limits: worst-case factor
added_ms       = rtt_ms

rows = [
    ("counter_ops", counter_ops, "ops/s"), ("script_calls", script_calls, "calls/s"),
    ("counters_mb", counters_mb, "MB"), ("log_gb", log_gb, "GB"),
    ("redis_nodes", redis_nodes, "nodes"), ("local_error", local_error, "x limit"),
    ("added_ms", added_ms, "ms"),
]
print("| quantity | value | unit |\n|---|---:|---|")
for name, value, unit in rows:
    v = f"{value:,.0f}" if abs(value) >= 100 else f"{value:,.2f}"
    print(f"| `{name}` | {v} | {unit} |")

What the numbers tell us:

  • Counters for a million clients take ~200 MB — one Redis node holds them easily. A sliding-window log (one timestamp per request) would need ~30 GB for the same clients: that is why the log is rarely used at scale.
  • 50 k script calls/s at ~3 operations each is ~1.5 Redis nodes of work ⇒ a small Redis Cluster (3 primaries + replicas), sharded by client key, with headroom.
  • One round trip in the same zone adds ~0.5 ms — within budget, as long as the gateway talks to Redis over persistent, pipelined connections and all rules go in a single script call.
  • Enforcing limit independently on each of 20 replicas lets a client get up to 20× the limit when the load balancer spreads its requests. ⇒ either a shared counter, or a local limit of limit / N with sticky routing, or a hybrid (see 6.3).

items.title: 3. API
items.text:
The limiter is usually not a public API but a filter inside the gateway; still, define its contract — internal and external.

# Internal (gateway → limiter library or sidecar)
check(rules=[("user:42", 10, 1s), ("ip:203.0.113.7", 100, 1s)], cost=1)
    → {allowed: true|false, remaining: 7, resetMs: 380, retryAfterMs: 0}

# External: what the API client sees
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 2
RateLimit-Policy: "per-user";q=10;w=1
RateLimit: "per-user";r=0;t=2
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type": "https://bx.example/problems/rate-limited", "title": "Too many requests",
 "detail": "Limit of 10 requests per second per user exceeded", "retryAfterSeconds": 2}
  • 429 (RFC 6585) plus Retry-After (seconds or a date) is the contract. Well-behaved clients retry after that time, with exponential backoff and jitter.
  • The RateLimit / RateLimit-Policy header fields are being standardized by the IETF HTTPAPI working group; many APIs still use the older X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset. Either way: tell clients their budget before they hit the wall.
  • Rules are data, not code, e.g. stored in a config service and cached by every gateway:
rules:
  - match: { path: "/v1/events/*/holds", method: POST }
    key: user
    limit: { requests: 5, per: 60s }          # 5 hold attempts per minute per account
  - match: { path: "/v1/*" }
    key: api_key
    limit: { requests: 1000, per: 60s, burst: 200 }
    plans: { partner: 10000, internal: unlimited }
  - match: { path: "/v1/auth/login" }
    key: ip
    limit: { requests: 10, per: 60s }
    on_store_failure: closed                   # security-sensitive: fail closed

items.title: 4. Data model
items.text:
The state is tiny and short-lived: per (rule, client) a counter or a token count with a timestamp, expiring automatically.

# Token bucket (Redis hash)              key TTL = time to refill completely × 2
rl:tb:user:42          → { tokens: 7.4, ts: 1767261600123 }

# Fixed window counter (Redis string)    key TTL = window
rl:fw:user:42:29454360 → 9            (window id = floor(now / 60 s))

# Sliding window counter: two fixed windows, current and previous
rl:sw:user:42:29454360 → 4
rl:sw:user:42:29454359 → 9

# Sliding window log (Redis sorted set)  score = timestamp
rl:log:user:42         → { 1767261600123, 1767261600201, ... }
Data Store Why Counters / buckets In-memory KV with TTL and atomic scripts: Redis (cache) Sub-millisecond, atomic, expires by itself; losing it costs only a few extra requests Rules Config service or SQL, cached in every gateway (refresh every few seconds) Read on every request: must be local Allowed / rejected events Metrics (metrics), sampled logs Dashboards, alerting on unusual rejection rates, tuning limits

items.title: 5. High-level design
items.text:
flowchart LR
    c([Clients]) --> waf["WAF / CDN<br/>coarse per-IP limits"]
    waf --> lb["Load balancer"]
    lb --> gw1["API gateway #1<br/>rate-limit filter"]
    lb --> gw2["API gateway #N<br/>rate-limit filter"]
    gw1 --> r[("Redis Cluster<br/>counters, Lua")]
    gw2 --> r
    cfg["Rules config<br/>service"] -. pushed / cached .-> gw1
    cfg -. pushed / cached .-> gw2
    gw1 --> svc["Backend services"]
    gw2 --> svc
    gw1 -. allowed / 429 .-> m["Metrics"]

One request through the filter:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant G as API gateway
    participant R as Redis
    participant S as Service
    C->>G: POST /v1/events/42/holds (user 42)
    G->>G: match rules (local cache)
    G->>R: EVALSHA token_bucket {user:42, ip:…} now cost=1
    R-->>G: allowed=1, remaining=4
    G->>S: forward request
    S-->>G: 201 Created
    G-->>C: 201 + RateLimit: r=4
    C->>G: 6th attempt within the minute
    G->>R: EVALSHA token_bucket …
    R-->>G: allowed=0, retry after 9 s
    G-->>C: 429 Too Many Requests, Retry-After: 9

items.title: 6.1 The algorithms
6.2 Making it atomic across replicas
items.text:
The naive implementation has a race:

gateway A: GET rl:user:42      → 9          gateway B: GET rl:user:42 → 9
gateway A: 9 < 10 → allow, SET 10           gateway B: 9 < 10 → allow, SET 10
                       → 11 requests allowed, counter says 10

Read-check-write must be one atomic operation on the store. In Redis, use INCR (atomic) for counters, or a Lua script, which runs atomically on the shard that owns the key:

-- token_bucket.lua   KEYS[1] = bucket key   ARGV: capacity, refill per second, cost
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate     = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local cost     = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local t        = redis.call('TIME')                       -- server clock: no skew between gateways
local now      = tonumber(t[1]) * 1000 + math.floor(tonumber(t[2]) / 1000)

local b      = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or capacity
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * rate)

local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then
  tokens  = tokens - cost
  allowed = 1
end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity / rate * 1000) * 2)
local retry_ms = 0
if allowed == 0 then retry_ms = math.ceil((cost - tokens) / rate * 1000) end
return { allowed, tostring(tokens), retry_ms }               -- floats → string (Redis truncates numbers)

Details that show seniority:

  • One call per request for all rules (pass several keys) — but in Redis Cluster all keys of one script must hash to the same slot: use a hash tag, e.g. rl:{user:42}:tb and rl:{user:42}:fw; rules keyed by different entities (user and IP) need separate calls, pipelined.
  • Use the server's clock (TIME) instead of each gateway's: 20 gateways with clocks 50 ms apart would refill the bucket inconsistently.
  • TTL on every key: idle clients disappear by themselves; memory stays proportional to active clients.
  • Load the script once (SCRIPT LOAD) and call it with EVALSHA to avoid sending the source on every request.

items.title: 6.3 Where to enforce, and local vs. global
items.text:
flowchart LR
    cl["Client SDK<br/>courtesy limit"] --> edge["Edge / WAF<br/>per IP, coarse"]
    edge --> gw["API gateway<br/>per user / key / plan"]
    gw --> mesh["Service mesh<br/>per caller service"]
    mesh --> svc["Service<br/>concurrency limit<br/>to its DB / provider"]
Placement Protects Strength Weakness Client SDK Our service from well-behaved clients Cheap, smooths traffic Not enforceable Edge / WAF Everything behind it from floods Absorbs attacks far from origin Knows only IP, not user API gateway Services from any single client Knows identity and plan Needs shared state across replicas Inside the service A fragile dependency (DB, payment provider) Knows the real cost Late: the request already used resources

Global vs. local. A shared Redis gives an exact global limit at the cost of a network hop. Alternatives when that hop is too expensive (multi-region, very high rates):

  • Local buckets with limit / N: no network, but wrong when traffic is unevenly spread; acceptable with consistent-hash routing of each client to one gateway.
  • Local + periodic sync: each gateway counts locally and pushes deltas to the shared store every 100 ms, reading back the global total — approximate (overshoots by at most one sync interval of traffic), very fast. This is roughly how large CDNs do it.
  • Per-region limits: limit per region and accept that a client using two regions gets up to 2× — usually fine.

items.title: 6.4 When the limiter itself fails
items.text:
• Fail-open (allow when Redis is unreachable) keeps the API available — the right default for ordinary limits, because the limiter exists to protect the backend, and a short period without limits is rarely worse than a full outage. Pair it with a local fallback bucket so the protection degrades instead of disappearing.
  • Fail-closed (reject) for limits that guard security: login attempts, password reset, OTP verification — otherwise an attacker who can overload Redis also disables brute-force protection.
  • Put a tight timeout (a few ms) on the Redis call and a circuit breaker around it: a slow limiter is worse than none, because it adds latency to every request (reliability patterns).

Rate limiting is not overload protection

A per-client limit of 10 req/s does nothing when a million legitimate clients each send 1 req/s — the 10:00 on-sale. Protecting the backend from total load needs load shedding (reject when the service's own queue or latency is too high), concurrency limits (at most N in-flight calls to the payment provider), and, for BoxOffice, the waiting room. Say this in the interview: it shows you know what the rate limiter does not do.

items.title: 7. Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs
items.text:
Where What goes wrong Mitigation Trade-off Redis round trip Adds latency to every request Same-zone Redis, pipelining, one script per request, local cache of "blocked until" Small staleness on blocks Redis down or slow Every request blocked or slowed Timeout + breaker; fail-open with local fallback bucket; fail-closed for security rules Brief over-admission Hot client key One huge partner saturates one Redis shard Local pre-aggregation for that key; split key into sub-buckets Approximate limit for that client Fixed-window boundaries 2× bursts at window edges Token bucket or sliding window counter Slightly more state Shared IPs (NAT, mobile carriers) Many users blocked together Prefer user/key limits; generous IP limits only on unauthenticated routes Attackers can rotate accounts Retry storms Rejected clients retry immediately, multiplying load Retry-After, client backoff + jitter, SDKs that respect it Clients wait longer Rule changes Bad rule blocks everybody Rules as versioned config, dry-run ("shadow") mode, gradual rollout Slower to react Multi-region Global limit needs cross-region coordination Per-region limits or async sync Up to N× the limit across N regions

The trade-offs to say out loud: accuracy vs. latency (exact global counters cost a network hop; approximate local ones are free), availability vs. protection (fail-open vs. fail-closed, chosen per rule), and fairness vs. simplicity (per-IP limits are easy but punish users behind a shared NAT).

items.title: 8. Try it in the playground
items.text:
The rate-limiter scenario places an API gateway with rate limiting in front of a backend that has a fixed capacity.

Try it

  1. Run with the spike profile and the limiter disabled (or bypassed): watch the backend's utilization reach 100% and p99 and errors explode for everybody.
  2. Enable the limiter and run again: rejections (429) appear at the gateway, while the backend stays below saturation and the p99 of accepted requests stays flat.
  3. Raise the limit step by step and find the value where the backend starts to saturate — that is the capacity your limit must stay under.
  4. Turn chaos on to fail the counter store (cache): does the gateway fail open or closed in the simulator, and what does that do to the backend?

Open the full playground

items.title: 9. Follow-up questions an interviewer asks
items.text:
Token bucket or sliding window — which one would you pick and why?

For an API limit, token bucket: two numbers per client, exact, and it allows short bursts (a page load firing 8 requests at once), which is what users actually do. Configure capacity (burst) and refill rate separately. Pick the sliding window counter when the product says "N requests per minute" and you want the semantics of a window with almost no burst, at the cost of a small approximation. Avoid fixed windows except for coarse daily quotas.

How do you rate limit by cost instead of by request count?

Make the token cost a parameter: a cheap GET costs 1, an export costs 50, an LLM call costs its number of tokens. The token bucket handles it unchanged (cost argument in the script). For LLM calls the cost is only known after the response, so reserve an estimate up front and settle the difference afterwards (debit or credit the bucket).

The limit must hold across two regions. What do you do?

Options in increasing cost: (1) split the limit per region (limit / 2 each, or proportional to traffic) — no coordination, slightly unfair; (2) count locally and replicate counts asynchronously between regions every few hundred ms — approximate global limit; (3) a single global store — exact but adds a cross-region round trip (tens of ms) to every request, which usually violates the latency requirement. Most systems choose (1) or (2) and state the error bound.

A client complains it got 429s while it was under the limit. How can that happen?

Common causes: the client's clock or its own counting differ from ours (window alignment); requests went to two regions with separate limits; a shared key (IP behind NAT, an API key used by several services); retries counted as requests; or the limit uses a token bucket and the client sent a burst bigger than the capacity. The RateLimit headers on every response let the client see its real budget — the best way to avoid this conversation.

How do you test the rate limiter?

Unit tests of the algorithm with a fake clock (boundaries, bursts, refill); concurrency tests with many goroutines/threads against a real Redis to prove atomicity (count allowed requests: must be ≤ limit); a load test (k6) with a known arrival rate per client and a check that rejections start at the configured limit; and a chaos test that kills Redis to verify fail-open/closed behavior (performance engineering).

What is the difference between rate limiting, throttling and backpressure?

Rate limiting rejects requests above a configured rate for a client. Throttling slows them down instead (delays, queues, leaky bucket). Backpressure is a signal from a saturated consumer to its producer to slow down (TCP windows, reactive streams, a full queue blocking the producer). Rate limiting is policy about clients; backpressure is a property of the system's capacity. A robust API uses both.

Why not just let the backend autoscale instead of rejecting requests?

Autoscaling takes minutes and costs money; an abusive client can grow as fast as you scale. Some resources do not scale at all (a database primary, a partner's API limit). Rate limiting is about fairness between clients and protecting fixed resources; autoscaling is about capacity for legitimate demand. You want both.

items.title: 10. Self-assessment rubric
items.text:
Level What the answer contains Junior A counter per user with a fixed window in Redis or in memory; returns 429. May keep the counter in each server's memory without noticing the N× problem. Mid Compares token bucket, fixed window and sliding window; uses a shared Redis with atomic operations; per-rule configuration; 429 with Retry-After; mentions fail-open. Senior Explains the race and fixes it with a Lua script (hash tags in Cluster, server clock, TTLs); chooses placement per layer; discusses local vs. global limits and multi-region error bounds; fail-open vs. fail-closed per rule; cost-based limits; distinguishes rate limiting from load shedding and concurrency limiting; client contract with backoff and jitter; observability of rejections.

Related: API gateway, Hands-on 3 (Nginx rate limiting), Hands-on 4 (gateway and identity), Redis, Reliability patterns.

items.title: Index
items.text:
"Design a ride-hailing service like Uber or 99: a rider requests a ride, the system finds a nearby driver, and both see each other on the map until the trip ends."

Ride sharing is the classic geospatial, write-heavy, real-time problem. Hundreds of thousands of phones report their position every few seconds; most of those writes are useless a few seconds later, and the only query that matters — which available drivers are near this point? — must answer in milliseconds. On top of that sits a small but strict consistency problem: one driver, one ride. The interview tests whether you can pick a spatial index, keep the hot data in memory, partition the world sensibly, and protect the one place where correctness is not negotiable.

BoxOffice meets the same problems twice. Its "events near me" search uses the same geo index ideas, and every stadium show ends with 60 000 fans leaving at once — a ride-hailing app sees a single map cell go from a handful of requests to thousands in minutes. That hot cell is one of the follow-ups below.

Difficulty hard Key concepts write-heavy location ingestion, latest-position store, geohash vs. quadtree vs. H3, neighbor-cell search, matching/dispatch with a per-driver lock and offer timeout, trip state machine, partitioning by city, surge pricing per cell Palette components mobile, apigw, app, stream, cache, sql, nosql, notifications, payment Playground scenario ride-sharing

What this case trains

  • Estimate the location-update rate and show why only the latest position belongs on the hot path.
  • Compare geohash, quadtree and H3 for "nearby" queries, including the cell-border problem.
  • Design matching so that a driver is never assigned to two rides, with offers that time out.
  • Model the trip as a state machine and partition the system by geography.
  • Identify hot spots (stadium exits, airports) and failure modes (phones going offline mid-trip, a region down).

items.title: 1. Clarify the requirements
items.text: (interview framework)

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text:
1. Drivers go online/offline and, while online, send their location every few seconds.
  2. A rider sees nearby drivers on the map and an ETA and price estimate.
  3. A rider requests a ride; the system matches a driver, who accepts or declines within a few seconds.
  4. During the trip, both apps show live location; the trip ends with payment and a rating.
  5. Trip history for riders, drivers and support.

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.text: Quality Target Latency Nearby-drivers query p99 < 100 ms; match found in a few seconds Correctness A driver is never assigned two rides at the same time; a rider is never charged twice Scale ~1 M drivers online at peak worldwide, location every 4 s; ~20 M trips/day Freshness Positions on the map at most a few seconds old Availability 99.99% for requesting and matching; a city must keep working if another region fails Durability Trips and payments are never lost; raw location history may be sampled

items.title: Out of scope (say it explicitly)
items.text:
Routing/maps engine (we call one), driver onboarding and documents, fraud detection, shared rides (pooling) — mention pooling as an extension.

Questions to ask the interviewer Question Why it matters How many drivers online, how often do they report? Sizes the write path: 1 M every 4 s is 250 k writes/s. One city or global? Partitioning by city/region keeps every query local. Does the driver accept, or is the ride assigned? Offers with timeouts need a lock per driver. How precise must "nearby" be? Straight line or road ETA? Spatial index for candidates, routing engine for ranking. Must we keep every GPS point? Hot path keeps only the latest; history goes to cheap storage, maybe sampled. Surge pricing? Scheduled rides? Pooling? Each adds a component; agree on what is in the 45 minutes.

items.title: 2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates
items.text:
ResultSource quantity value unit loc_writes 250,000 writes/s ingest_mb_s 25.00 MB/s history_tb_day 2.16 TB/day latest_mb 100 MB trip_rps 231 req/s peak_trip_rps 694 req/s active_trips 277,778 trips trip_push_rps 138,889 msgs/s writes_city 500 writes/s 
# Ride sharing: assumptions (illustrative)
drivers_online = 1_000_000     # at peak, worldwide
update_s       = 4             # driver location interval
loc_b          = 100           # driver id, lat, lon, heading, speed, ts
trips_day      = 20_000_000
peak_factor    = 3
trip_min       = 20            # average trip duration
rider_poll_s   = 2             # rider app refreshes driver position during the trip
cities         = 500

loc_writes     = drivers_online / update_s
ingest_mb_s    = loc_writes * loc_b / 1e6
history_tb_day = loc_writes * 86_400 * loc_b / 1e12
latest_mb      = drivers_online * loc_b / 1e6
trip_rps       = trips_day / 86_400
peak_trip_rps  = trip_rps * peak_factor
active_trips   = trip_rps * trip_min * 60             # Little's Law: L = λ·W
trip_push_rps  = active_trips / rider_poll_s
writes_city    = loc_writes / cities                   # average; big cities are 10-50x this

rows = [
    ("loc_writes", loc_writes, "writes/s"), ("ingest_mb_s", ingest_mb_s, "MB/s"),
    ("history_tb_day", history_tb_day, "TB/day"), ("latest_mb", latest_mb, "MB"),
    ("trip_rps", trip_rps, "req/s"), ("peak_trip_rps", peak_trip_rps, "req/s"),
    ("active_trips", active_trips, "trips"), ("trip_push_rps", trip_push_rps, "msgs/s"),
    ("writes_city", writes_city, "writes/s"),
]
print("| quantity | value | unit |\n|---|---:|---|")
for name, value, unit in rows:
    v = f"{value:,.0f}" if abs(value) >= 100 else f"{value:,.2f}"
    print(f"| `{name}` | {v} | {unit} |")

What the numbers tell us:

  • 250 k location writes/s — far beyond what a relational primary should absorb as row updates. But the latest position of every driver is only ~100 MB: it fits in memory many times over. ⇒ keep the latest position in an in-memory geo index; stream the raw points to cheap storage.
  • Raw history is ~2 TB/day if kept in full ⇒ object storage / data lake, compressed and possibly sampled, never on the hot path.
  • Ride requests are only ~230/s (~700/s at peak) — the matching path is low volume but must be correct.
  • Little's Law gives ~280 k trips in progress at any time, each pushing the driver's position to the rider: ~140 k messages/s of real-time fan-out (persistent connections, as in the chat case).
  • Divided by city the write rate is small (~500 writes/s on average, a few tens of thousands in the largest metros). ⇒ partition by city/region: every query is local to one shard.

items.title: 3. API
items.text:
# Driver app (in practice over a persistent connection: WebSocket / gRPC stream / MQTT)
PUT  /v1/drivers/me/status        {"status": "AVAILABLE|OFFLINE"}                 → 204
PUT  /v1/drivers/me/location      {"lat": -23.5475, "lon": -46.6361, "heading": 90,
                                   "speed": 8.3, "ts": 1767261600123}             → 204
POST /v1/offers/{offerId}/accept                                                  → 200 {rideId}
POST /v1/offers/{offerId}/decline                                                 → 204

# Rider app
GET  /v1/drivers/nearby?lat=…&lon=…&radius=2000                                   → 200 [{driverId, lat, lon, etaS}]
POST /v1/rides  {"pickup": {...}, "dropoff": {...}, "product": "economy"}
     Idempotency-Key: 5b1e…                                                       → 202 {rideId, status: MATCHING, fareEstimate}
GET  /v1/rides/{rideId}                                                           → 200 {status, driver, driverLocation, etaS}
POST /v1/rides/{rideId}/cancel                                                    → 200 {cancellationFee}
  • Location updates are fire-and-forget: if one is lost, the next arrives in 4 s. No retries, no acknowledgments per point.
  • Ride creation is idempotent (Idempotency-Key): a rider tapping twice on a slow network must not get two cars.

items.title: 4. Data model
items.text:
# Latest positions, one geo set per city (Redis GEO = sorted set of geohash-encoded scores)
GEOADD drivers:sao-paulo -46.6361 -23.5475 driver:42
GEOSEARCH drivers:sao-paulo FROMLONLAT -46.6361 -23.5475 BYRADIUS 2 km ASC COUNT 20

# Driver state (hash), with TTL refreshed by each update: no update for 30 s → stale
driver:42 → { status: AVAILABLE, city: sao-paulo, lat, lon, ts, rideId: null }

CREATE TABLE ride (
    ride_id        UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    city           TEXT        NOT NULL,
    rider_id       BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    driver_id      BIGINT,
    status         TEXT        NOT NULL,   -- MATCHING | ACCEPTED | ARRIVING | IN_PROGRESS | COMPLETED | CANCELLED
    pickup         POINT       NOT NULL,
    dropoff        POINT       NOT NULL,
    fare_cents     INT,
    surge          NUMERIC(3,2),
    idempotency_key TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    requested_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    completed_at   TIMESTAMPTZ
);

-- At most one active ride per driver: the database enforces it
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_ride_per_driver ON ride (driver_id)
    WHERE status IN ('ACCEPTED', 'ARRIVING', 'IN_PROGRESS');
Data Store Why Latest driver positions In-memory geo index (cache, e.g. Redis GEO), sharded by city 250 k writes/s, sub-ms radius queries, only the last value matters Location stream Event stream (stream/Kafka), partitioned by city Feeds the geo index, ETA models, surge and the history Location history Object store / data lake (via the stream) Cheap, append-only, for disputes and analytics Rides, payments SQL (sql), partitioned by city Transactions, unique constraints, state machine Driver/rider profiles SQL or NoSQL (nosql) Read-mostly, cached

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant R as Rider app

items.title: 6.1 Ingesting locations: keep only what matters
items.text:
• The latest position is the product; the trail is analytics. The location service validates the point (plausible speed, not in the ocean), writes the latest value to the geo index and appends it to the stream. Nothing on the hot path reads history.
  • Batch and coalesce. The gateway can coalesce updates per driver (if two arrive in the same 100 ms window, keep the newest) and write to the geo index in pipelined batches.
  • Adaptive frequency. An available driver standing still does not need to report every 4 s; a driver approaching a pickup needs more. The app adapts the interval to speed and state — fewer writes, better freshness where it matters.
  • Staleness. Each driver state has a TTL refreshed by updates; a phone that goes silent for 30 s drops out of the candidate set automatically, without a cleanup job.
  • Partition by city. The stream topic, the geo index and the rides database are all partitioned by city (or region), so a query in São Paulo never touches Lisbon's shards (partitioning).

items.title: 6.2 The spatial index: geohash, quadtree or H3
items.text:
A B-tree on (lat, lon) cannot answer "within 2 km" efficiently: it orders by one dimension at a time. Spatial indexes map 2-D space to cells (specialized databases).

GeohashQuadtreeH3 (hexagons)

Interleave the bits of longitude and latitude and encode in base32: nearby points share a prefix (6gyf4…). Prefix = cell, so "nearby" becomes "same prefix", which any sorted key-value store can answer (Redis GEO uses a 52-bit geohash as the sorted-set score). Fixed grid, simple, but cells are rectangles whose size depends on latitude, and two points across a cell border can have totally different prefixes.

Recursively split a square into four children until each leaf has at most k drivers. Adapts to density: downtown gets small cells, the countryside one big cell. Usually an in-memory structure rebuilt or updated per city; moving drivers make updates frequent.

Uber's open-source hierarchical index divides the globe into hexagons at 16 resolutions. Every neighbor of a hexagon is at the same distance from its center (squares have edge and corner neighbors), which makes "k rings around me" searches, smoothing and surge maps cleaner. Cells are IDs (64-bit integers) — easy to use as keys in any store.

Geohash Quadtree H3 Cell shape Rectangles, fixed grid Squares, adaptive Hexagons, fixed hierarchy Adapts to density No (pick a precision) Yes No (pick a resolution) Neighbor search 8 neighbors + self (edges and corners differ in distance) Tree traversal k-ring, uniform distances Storage String/integer key in any KV store In-memory tree 64-bit ID in any KV store Typical use Redis GEO, Elasticsearch geo, simple services In-memory spatial services Surge maps, analytics, dispatch at scale

How big is a geohash cell? It depends on the precision (characters) and the latitude — computed here for São Paulo:

ResultSource precision cell width (km) cell height (km) 4 35.876 19.436 5 4.485 4.859 6 1.121 0.607 7 0.140 0.152 8 0.035 0.019 
import math

lat = -23.55                       # São Paulo
print("| precision | cell width (km) | cell height (km) |\n|---:|---:|---:|")
for p in range(4, 9):
    bits = 5 * p                   # base32: 5 bits per character
    lon_bits, lat_bits = (bits + 1) // 2, bits // 2
    width = 360 / 2 ** lon_bits * 111.32 * math.cos(math.radians(lat))
    height = 180 / 2 ** lat_bits * 110.57
    print(f"| {p} | {width:.3f} | {height:.3f} |")

Precision 6 (~1.1 × 0.6 km) is a good bucket for "drivers within a couple of km". Border problem: a rider at the edge of a cell may be 50 m from a driver in the next cell — always search the cell plus its 8 neighbors (or an H3 k-ring), then filter by real distance. If too few drivers are found, expand the ring (precision 5, or k + 1) until enough candidates appear or a maximum radius is reached.

items.title: 6.3 Matching without double assignment
items.text:
The dangerous moment: two riders' matchers pick the same nearest driver at the same time. The rule one driver, one ride needs an atomic guard (consensus and locks):

  1. Candidates come from the geo index (fast, slightly stale — fine).
  2. Before offering, lock the driver: SET lock:driver:42 <rideId> NX PX 15000 — only one matcher wins; the lock expires if the driver ignores the offer or the matcher crashes.
  3. The driver accepts → the ride service assigns with a conditional update (UPDATE ride SET driver_id = 42, status = 'ACCEPTED' WHERE ride_id = $1 AND status = 'MATCHING'), and the partial unique index guarantees the driver has no other active ride — the durable last line of defense if the lock ever misbehaves.
  4. The driver declines or the offer times out → release the lock and offer the next candidate.

Greedy vs. batched matching. Greedy (each request takes its nearest available driver) is simple and fast. Batched matching collects requests for 1–2 seconds and solves an assignment problem over all of them (minimizing total pickup time), which is globally better in dense areas — a classic trade-off of latency for efficiency.

items.title: 6.4 The trip as a state machine
items.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> MATCHING: rider requests
    MATCHING --> ACCEPTED: driver accepts offer
    MATCHING --> CANCELLED: no driver / rider cancels
    ACCEPTED --> ARRIVING: driver en route
    ARRIVING --> IN_PROGRESS: rider picked up
    ARRIVING --> CANCELLED: rider no-show (fee)
    IN_PROGRESS --> COMPLETED: drop-off
    COMPLETED --> [*]: payment captured
    CANCELLED --> [*]
  • Every transition is a conditional update on the current state (idempotent under retries) and emits an event (stream) for notifications, ETA updates, receipts and analytics.
  • Payment: authorize an estimate when the ride is accepted, capture the final fare on COMPLETED through the payment provider with an idempotency key (see the payment system case).
  • Phones go offline mid-trip (tunnels): the trip continues on the server; the driver app buffers GPS points and uploads them later so the fare can be computed from the real route.

Surge pricing fits the same pipeline: a stream job counts open requests (demand) and available drivers (supply) per H3 cell per minute and publishes a multiplier per cell, smoothed in space and time so prices do not flicker.

items.title: 7. Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs
items.text:
Where What goes wrong Mitigation Trade-off Location writes 250 k/s overload a database Latest value in memory, history to the stream; coalesce and batch; adaptive interval Map positions a few seconds old Hot cell (stadium exit, airport) Thousands of requests and a dense cluster in one cell Finer cells / quadtree split there; batched matching; queue riders with honest ETA; surge to attract supply Some riders wait or pay more Double assignment Two matchers offer the same driver Per-driver lock with TTL + conditional update + partial unique index Extra round trip per offer Matcher crash after offer Driver locked to a ride nobody tracks Lock TTL; ride stuck in MATCHING is re-matched by a sweeper A few seconds lost Stale positions Offering drivers who went offline TTL on driver state; drop candidates older than N s Fewer candidates City shard down Rides in that city fail Replicas per city; failover; other cities unaffected (isolation) Cross-region replication cost Real-time fan-out 140 k position pushes/s to riders Persistent connections, push only to active trips, coarser rate when far away Map less smooth ETA service slow Matching blocked Timeout + fall back to straight-line distance × factor Worse ranking for a moment

The trade-offs to say out loud: freshness vs. write cost (positions every 4 s, not every second), eventual consistency for positions, strong consistency for assignment (the geo index may be stale; the driver lock and the ride row may not), and greedy vs. batched matching (latency vs. global efficiency).

items.title: 8. Try it in the playground
items.text:
The ride-sharing scenario models write-heavy location updates flowing through a stream into a geo index, and a matching path that reads it.

Try it

  1. Run with the load profile and watch the write throughput on the stream and the geo index versus the much smaller ride-request path.
  2. Increase the number of drivers (load) until the geo index saturates; then add partitions/replicas (sharding by city) and compare.
  3. Switch to spike to imitate the end of a stadium show: which component turns into the bottleneck — the matcher or the store holding rides?
  4. Turn chaos on to fail one node of the geo index: do matches stop everywhere or only for the affected partition?

Open the full playground

items.title: 9. Follow-up questions an interviewer asks
items.text:
A BoxOffice stadium show ends: 60 000 people leave at once. What happens to your system?

One cell (or a few) gets a burst of thousands of requests while drivers are scarce and arriving from outside. Mitigations: anticipate it — the event schedule is known, so surge and driver incentives can start before the show ends; split the hot cell into finer cells for matching; use batched matching to assign efficiently; create pickup zones a few blocks away to avoid gridlock; and be honest with riders (queue position and ETA instead of repeated failed matches). The infrastructure side is a hot partition: make sure the city shard has headroom, because the spike is predictable.

Why not just use PostgreSQL with PostGIS?

For one city with a few thousand drivers, PostGIS with a GiST index is an excellent answer — simple and correct. The problem at scale is the update rate: hundreds of thousands of row updates per second, each rewriting index entries and producing WAL, for data that is obsolete in 4 seconds. An in-memory geo index for the latest positions plus SQL for rides gives each store the workload it is good at.

A driver crosses from one city shard into another.

Shards should follow operational regions with a margin, so crossings are rare. When it happens, the location service writes the driver to the new shard and removes them from the old one (the TTL removes leftovers anyway); an active trip stays owned by the shard where it started until it ends. For queries near a border, search both shards.

How do you compute ETA?

Straight-line distance is only a filter. ETA comes from a routing engine over the road graph with live traffic (speeds learned from the location stream of all drivers), usually with precomputed shortcuts (contraction hierarchies) to answer in milliseconds. Matching asks for ETAs of the top 10–20 candidates, not all of them.

How long do you keep location history and why?

Trip routes are kept as long as receipts, disputes and regulations require (fare calculation, safety investigations). Points of drivers who are idle can be sampled or dropped after short-term analytics. Store them compressed in object storage, partitioned by city and day, and treat them as personal data (access control, retention policy).

How would you add shared rides (pooling)?

Matching becomes harder: the candidate is a driver already on a trip whose route can absorb a detour within limits for both riders. The geo index must include drivers on pooled trips with remaining seats, and the matcher evaluates insertion cost on the route. The state machine gains per-rider legs. It is a good place to show you know when a problem changes class (from nearest-neighbor to a constrained optimization).

items.title: 10. Self-assessment rubric
items.text:
Level What the answer contains Junior Drivers table with lat/lon updated on every report; "find drivers where distance < 2 km"; ride table. Misses the write rate and the double-assignment race. Mid Latest positions in an in-memory geo index (Redis GEO/geohash), history in a stream; nearby search with neighbor cells; ride state machine; a lock or conditional update to avoid double assignment; partitioning by city. Senior Quantifies writes and memory; compares geohash, quadtree and H3 with the border problem and ring expansion; offer locks with TTL plus a durable unique constraint; greedy vs. batched matching; adaptive update frequency; hot-cell handling with surge and pickup zones; failure modes (matcher crash, stale drivers, city shard down); payment integration with idempotency.

Related: Partitioning, Specialized databases, Chat case (persistent connections), Payment system case, Hands-on 6 (transactions and locking).

items.title: Index
items.text:
"Design the search box suggestions of a large site: as the user types, show the 5–10 most likely completions of what they are typing, fast enough to feel instantaneous."

Autocomplete (also called typeahead or search-as-you-type) looks like a small UI feature and is a very instructive system. Every keystroke is a request, so it is one of the highest-QPS endpoints of any site; the answer must arrive in well under 100 ms or it is useless (the user already typed the next letter); and the suggestions are derived data — computed offline from millions of past searches, then served from memory. The interview tests whether you separate the serving path (a read-only, in-memory index) from the data path (logs → aggregation → index build), and whether you know which data structure answers "top-k completions of a prefix" without scanning.

BoxOffice needs exactly this: fans type col… and expect Coldplay, Coldplay São Paulo, Coala Festival, mixing artists, venues and cities. When a tour is announced, searches for that artist jump within minutes — and yesterday's suggestions do not know it yet. That freshness problem is one of the deep dives below.

Difficulty medium Key concepts trie with top-k cached per node, prefix hash table, finite-state transducers, offline aggregation with time decay, immutable index snapshots and atomic swap, trending overlay, sharding by prefix and skew, browser/CDN caching, client debouncing, blocklists Palette components client, cdn, apigw, search, cache, analytics, stream, dwh, worker Playground scenario search-autocomplete

What this case trains

  • Estimate keystroke traffic and show how debouncing and caching cut it before it reaches the servers.
  • Explain how a trie with top-k cached in every node answers a prefix in O(length of the prefix), and compare it with a prefix hash table.
  • Design the data pipeline that turns search logs into an index: aggregation, time decay, snapshot build, atomic swap.
  • Decide between replicating the whole index and sharding it by prefix, accounting for skew.
  • Handle freshness (trending queries), filtering of offensive or blocked terms, and a latency budget of tens of milliseconds.

items.title: 1. Clarify the requirements
items.text: (interview framework)

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text:
1. As the user types, return up to k = 8 suggestions that start with the typed prefix, ranked by popularity.
  2. Suggestions can be typed entities (artist, venue, city, event) with an ID, so the UI can show an icon and jump straight to the page.
  3. Suggestions reflect what people search: popular queries first, with recent trends surfacing within minutes.
  4. Offensive, illegal or blocked terms never appear.
  5. Results may depend on locale (pt-BR vs. en) and, optionally, on the user's city.

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.text: Quality Target Latency p99 < 100 ms as perceived by the user; < 10–20 ms inside our servers Throughput Tens of thousands of requests/s at peak (every keystroke is a request) Availability 99.9%; if autocomplete fails, the search box still works — it degrades gracefully Freshness Popularity updated daily; trending queries visible within ~15 minutes Consistency Not required: two users may see slightly different suggestions for a few minutes

items.title: Out of scope (say it explicitly)
items.text:
The full search results page (ranking, inverted index — see the search component), spelling correction beyond simple typo tolerance, voice search, ads in suggestions.

Questions to ask the interviewer Question Why it matters Prefix match only, or also matches in the middle of words ("paulo" → "Coldplay São Paulo")? Prefix → trie/FST; infix → n-gram or inverted index, more memory. How many suggestions, and ranked by what? Top-k per prefix is precomputed with a fixed k and a fixed score. How fresh must suggestions be? Daily rebuild vs. a streaming "trending" layer. Personalized per user? Personalized results cannot be cached at the CDN. Multiple languages and regions? One index per locale/region, or a filter at serve time. Typo tolerance? Fuzzy matching multiplies the work per keystroke.

items.title: 2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates
items.text:
ResultSource quantity value unit naive_rps 13,889 req/s rps 4,630 req/s peak_rps 23,148 req/s origin_peak 11,574 req/s trie_nodes 30,000,000 nodes trie_gb 6.00 GB logs_gb_day 10.00 GB/day 
# Search autocomplete: assumptions (illustrative)
dau             = 20_000_000
searches_per    = 5           # searches per user per day
chars_per_query = 12          # average characters typed
req_per_search  = 4           # requests actually sent after debouncing (not 12)
peak_factor     = 5           # tour announcement spikes
distinct_q      = 5_000_000   # distinct queries kept after a minimum-count filter
prefixes_per_q  = 6           # new trie nodes per query (prefixes are shared)
node_b          = 200         # node: children map + top-10 ids + overhead
log_b           = 100         # one logged search (query, ts, locale, city)
cdn_hit         = 0.5         # share of prefix requests answered by browser/CDN caches

naive_rps   = dau * searches_per * chars_per_query / 86_400
rps         = dau * searches_per * req_per_search / 86_400
peak_rps    = rps * peak_factor
origin_peak = peak_rps * (1 - cdn_hit)
trie_nodes  = distinct_q * prefixes_per_q
trie_gb     = trie_nodes * node_b / 1e9
logs_gb_day = dau * searches_per * log_b / 1e9

rows = [
    ("naive_rps", naive_rps, "req/s"), ("rps", rps, "req/s"),
    ("peak_rps", peak_rps, "req/s"), ("origin_peak", origin_peak, "req/s"),
    ("trie_nodes", trie_nodes, "nodes"), ("trie_gb", trie_gb, "GB"),
    ("logs_gb_day", logs_gb_day, "GB/day"),
]
print("| quantity | value | unit |\n|---|---:|---|")
for name, value, unit in rows:
    v = f"{value:,.0f}" if abs(value) >= 100 else f"{value:,.2f}"
    print(f"| `{name}` | {v} | {unit} |")

What the numbers tell us:

  • One request per character would be ~14 k req/s on average. Debouncing in the client (send only after the user pauses ~100–150 ms) cuts it to ~4.6 k req/s; a tour announcement multiplies it by 5, to ~23 k req/s. ⇒ the cheapest request is the one never sent.
  • Short prefixes (c, co, col) are the same for everybody: if browser and CDN caches answer half of the requests, the origin sees ~12 k req/s at peak.
  • The whole index — ~30 M trie nodes, ~6 GB — fits in the memory of one server. ⇒ the default is to replicate the full index on every serving node, not to shard it; sharding is a later step if the index grows (more locales, more entity types).
  • Logs are ~10 GB/day — modest. Aggregating them is a batch/stream job; it never touches the serving path.

In the interview

Split the problem out loud: "There are two systems here. A serving system — read-only, in-memory, answering a prefix in a few milliseconds — and a data pipeline that rebuilds what it serves from the search logs. They only meet at the index snapshot."

items.title: 3. API
items.text:
GET /v1/autocomplete?q=col&limit=8&locale=pt-BR&city=sao-paulo
    → 200 Cache-Control: public, max-age=60
      {"prefix": "col",
       "suggestions": [
         {"text": "Coldplay", "type": "artist", "id": "a-118"},
         {"text": "Coldplay São Paulo", "type": "event", "id": "e-4410"},
         {"text": "Coldplay Rio", "type": "event", "id": "e-4411"}
       ]}

POST /v1/search/events      (batched, asynchronous; or simply the access logs)
    {"query": "coldplay sao paulo", "selected": "e-4410", "position": 2, "ts": 1767261600123}
  • The response is cacheable for public, non-personalized prefixes (Cache-Control: public, max-age=60): browsers and the CDN answer repeated prefixes without reaching us (DNS & CDN).
  • Normalize the prefix before caching and lookup (lowercase, trim, strip accents: Colé → cole) so equal prefixes share a cache key.
  • Personalization (the user's own recent searches) is merged in the client, keeping the server response shareable.

items.title: 4. Data model
items.text:
# Serving: an immutable in-memory index per locale, loaded from a snapshot file
trie node "col" → children {d, o, …}, top: [(98000, a-118 "Coldplay"), (41000, e-4410 …), …]

# Snapshot files in object storage, one per build
s3://…/autocomplete/pt-BR/2027-03-14T10:00Z/index.bin     (+ manifest with checksum)

# Trending overlay (cache, refreshed every minute by the stream job)
trending:pt-BR → [("coldplay 2027", 15400), ("metallica rio", 8200)]   TTL 30 min

-- Aggregated counts in the data warehouse, input of the index build
CREATE TABLE query_counts_daily (
    locale     TEXT,
    query      TEXT,          -- normalized
    day        DATE,
    searches   BIGINT,
    selections BIGINT,        -- suggestion clicked / result opened
    PRIMARY KEY (locale, query, day)
);
Data Store Why Serving index In-memory trie/FST in the autocomplete service (search), loaded from a snapshot Microsecond lookups; read-only, so no locks; ~6 GB fits in RAM Snapshots Object store Versioned, immutable, easy to roll back Search events Event stream (stream) → data warehouse (dwh) Append-only logs, aggregated in batch Daily counts Data warehouse (dwh) Large scans and group-bys for the build Trending overlay, hot prefixes Cache (cache) Small, frequently updated, shared by all serving nodes

One keystroke, from typing to suggestions:

sequenceDiagram

    participant U as Browser
    participant C as CDN
    participant A as Autocomplete service
    participant T as Trending cache
    U->>U: user types "col", waits 120 ms (debounce)

    else miss
