items.title: 6.1 The data structure: trie with top-k per node
items.text:
A trie stores strings character by character; every path from the root is a prefix. Finding the best completions of col naively means walking to the node col and then visiting its whole subtree to rank every query below it — far too slow for c, whose subtree is a large part of the index.

The fix is to cache the top-k completions in every node at build time. A lookup becomes: walk len(prefix) nodes, return the list stored there — no subtree walk (specialized data stores):

ResultSource prefix top_3 c coldplay, coldplay sao paulo, concert tickets co coldplay, coldplay sao paulo, concert tickets col coldplay, coldplay sao paulo, coldplay rio m metallica, madonna, maroon 5 ma madonna, maroon 5, maracana mar maroon 5, maracana, marisa monte x — 
# A tiny trie that caches the top-k completions in every node
K = 3
counts = {                         # aggregated query counts (illustrative)
    "coldplay": 9_800, "coldplay sao paulo": 4_100, "coldplay rio": 2_900,
    "colombia festival": 600, "coala festival": 1_200, "concert tickets": 3_300,
    "maroon 5": 2_500, "madonna": 3_900, "maracana": 2_200, "marisa monte": 1_700,
    "metallica": 5_200, "metallica 2027": 1_100,
}

class Node:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}
        self.top = []                # [(count, query)], best first, at most K

def insert(root, query, count):
    node = root
    for ch in query:
        node = node.children.setdefault(ch, Node())
        node.top = sorted(node.top + [(count, query)], reverse=True)[:K]

def suggest(root, prefix):
    node = root
    for ch in prefix:
        node = node.children.get(ch)
        if node is None:
            return []
    return [q for _, q in node.top]  # O(len(prefix)): no subtree walk at query time

root = Node()
for q, c in counts.items():
    insert(root, q, c)

print("| prefix | top_3 |\n|---|---|")
for p in ("c", "co", "col", "m", "ma", "mar", "x"):
    print(f"| `{p}` | {', '.join(suggest(root, p)) or '—'} |")

The price is memory (k entries per node, most of them repeated along a path) and rebuild instead of update: changing one count can change the top-k of every ancestor. That is why the index is built offline and served read-only.

Trie with top-k per nodePrefix hash tableFST / completion suggester

Lookup O(length of prefix); compact because prefixes are shared; natural for "starts with". Updates are expensive (ancestors' lists), so it is rebuilt as a snapshot. Store IDs or offsets in the lists, not full strings, to save memory.

Precompute a map prefix → top-k list for every prefix (e.g. a Redis hash or a key-value store). O(1) lookup, trivial to shard by key and to serve from any KV store; uses more memory (no sharing between prefixes) and the same rebuild cost. A pragmatic choice when you would rather not run a custom in-memory service.

A finite-state transducer shares both prefixes and suffixes, so it is much smaller than a trie; Lucene's completion suggester (used by Elasticsearch and OpenSearch) builds one per index segment, with weights and optional fuzzy matching. The off-the-shelf answer for a team that already runs a search cluster.

Trie + top-k Prefix hash table FST (search engine) Lookup O(prefix length) O(1) O(prefix length) Memory Medium Highest Lowest Sharding By prefix range By key (any KV store) By index/shard of the engine Build Custom job Custom job Engine indexing Typo tolerance Custom Hard Built-in (fuzzy)

items.title: 6.2 The data pipeline: from logs to snapshots
items.text:
flowchart LR
    logs[["Search events<br/>stream"]] --> raw[("Raw logs<br/>object store")]
    raw --> agg["Daily aggregation<br/>count per normalized query"]
    agg --> decay["Score with time decay<br/>+ selections weight"]
    decay --> filt["Filter<br/>min count, blocklist"]
    filt --> build["Build index<br/>per locale"]
    build --> snap[("Snapshot vN<br/>+ checksum")]
    snap --> canary["Canary node<br/>sanity checks"]
    canary --> fleet["All nodes<br/>load + atomic swap"]
  • Normalize queries (lowercase, accents, whitespace) and aggregate per day; keep only queries above a minimum count — this removes typos, one-off searches and most personal data (an e-mail typed into the search box should never become a suggestion).
  • Score with time decay: score = Σ count_day × 0.5^(age_days / half_life), e.g. a 7-day half-life, plus a weight for selections (a suggestion that people click is better than one they ignore).
  • Build the index per locale into an immutable snapshot in object storage, with a checksum and a manifest. Serving nodes download it, build the in-memory structure next to the current one and switch a pointer — an atomic swap, with no lock on the read path and an instant rollback to the previous version if metrics drop.
  • Validate before shipping: size within ±10% of the last build, top suggestions for a fixed set of prefixes present, no blocklisted term — on a canary node first (asynchronous work).

items.title: 6.3 Serving at scale: replicate, cache, debounce
items.text:
• Replicate first. With ~6 GB per locale, every node holds the full index; adding nodes adds throughput linearly, and any node can answer any prefix — no routing, no hot shards.
  • Shard when it no longer fits, by prefix range — but by traffic, not by alphabet: s and c get far more traffic than x and q, so split ranges like ca–ce, cf–cz until each shard has similar load. Alternatively shard by locale/region first, which is a natural split.
  • Caches at every layer: the browser (max-age=60 and an in-memory map of prefixes already seen in this session), the CDN for short public prefixes, a small LRU inside the service for the hottest prefixes (caching patterns).
  • Client discipline: debounce (~100–150 ms), start only after 1–2 characters, cancel in-flight requests when the prefix changes, and discard responses for stale prefixes (responses can arrive out of order).
  • Latency budget: of a 100 ms p99 perceived by the user, the network round trip takes most; the service must answer in a few milliseconds — which an in-memory, read-only structure does easily, and a database query per keystroke does not.

items.title: 6.4 Freshness, filtering and personalization
items.text:
• Trending overlay. A daily index cannot know a tour announced an hour ago. A stream job counts queries over a sliding window (say 15 minutes) and flags those growing much faster than their baseline; the serving nodes merge this small list (hundreds of entries) with the static top-k at request time (Kafka and streams).
  • Filtering happens twice: at build time (blocklist, minimum count) and at serve time (a small blocklist pushed to all nodes within minutes), because removing an offensive suggestion cannot wait for tomorrow's build.
  • Entities over strings. For BoxOffice, suggestions that point to an artist, venue or event (with an ID) are more useful than raw query strings: build part of the index from the catalog (names and aliases, weighted by ticket sales) and merge it with the query-log index.
  • Personalization (recent searches, the user's city) is merged in the client or with a small per-user list — so the shared, cacheable response stays the same for everybody.
  • Typo tolerance (coldpaly) needs fuzzy matching — edit distance 1 on the FST, or n-gram indexes. It multiplies the work per keystroke, so apply it only after a few characters or when exact matches are few.

items.title: 7. Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs
items.text:
Where What goes wrong Mitigation Trade-off Keystroke volume One request per character overloads the origin Debounce, minimum prefix length, cancel stale requests Suggestions appear ~100 ms later Short prefixes a, c, s are the hottest keys Browser/CDN caching; precomputed responses in a local LRU Up to 60 s staleness Index too big for one node More locales and entity types Shard by locale, then by prefix range balanced by traffic Routing layer, uneven shards Bad build Empty or corrupted index pushed to all nodes Checksums, size checks, canary node, keep the previous snapshot for rollback Slower rollout Stale popularity Tour announced, suggestions do not show it Trending overlay from the stream (minutes) Another job to operate Offensive suggestions Manipulated or offensive queries rise to the top Blocklist at build and serve time, minimum count, rate-limit query logging per user Some legitimate terms blocked Out-of-order responses co answer arrives after col answer Client discards responses that do not match the current prefix — Service down Search box without suggestions Degrade silently; search still works Worse experience, no outage

The trade-offs to say out loud: freshness vs. simplicity (daily immutable snapshots plus a small trending overlay instead of a mutable index), memory vs. latency (top-k cached in every node), and replication vs. sharding (replicate while it fits in RAM; shard by traffic when it does not).

items.title: 8. Try it in the playground
items.text:
The search-autocomplete scenario puts a search service behind a cache, with a read-heavy, spiky keystroke workload.

Try it

  1. Run with the load profile: note the cache hit ratio and the p99 of the search service.
  2. Remove the cache (or lower its hit ratio) and run again: how much more load reaches the search service? Does the p99 still fit a keystroke budget of a few tens of milliseconds?
  3. Switch to spike (a tour announcement): add replicas of the search service until p99 recovers — the index is replicated, so throughput grows with nodes.
  4. Turn chaos on to fail the search service: autocomplete should degrade (no suggestions), never break the page.

Open the full playground

items.title: 9. Follow-up questions an interviewer asks
items.text:
Why not run SELECT … WHERE query LIKE 'col%' ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 8 on the database?

A B-tree index on query can find the range col… quickly, but it must then read every row in that range to sort by count — for c that is a large fraction of the table — at thousands of requests per second. Precomputing the top-k per prefix moves that sorting to the offline build, so the online path is a constant-time read. A database query per keystroke also puts a heavy, spiky load on a system that has better things to do.

A new artist explodes on social media. How fast can suggestions react?

The daily index reacts tomorrow; the trending overlay reacts in minutes: a stream job compares each query's count in the last 15 minutes with its baseline and publishes the fastest risers to a cache that every serving node merges at request time. Protect it from manipulation (count distinct users, not raw searches; minimum volume; blocklist).

How do you keep personal data out of suggestions?

Suggestions come only from queries typed by many distinct users (a k-anonymity-style threshold), after normalization; anything that looks like an e-mail, phone number or document number is dropped by the pipeline; raw logs have a short retention. Per-user history, if offered, stays per user and is merged on the client.

How do you support suggestions for 'paulo' matching 'Coldplay São Paulo'?

That is infix matching. Index each word (or each suffix of the phrase) as an additional entry pointing to the same suggestion, or use an n-gram/inverted index in a search engine. Memory grows (several entries per suggestion), so restrict it to entity names (artists, venues, cities) rather than all queries.

How do you roll out a new index without hurting latency?

Build it offline, distribute the snapshot, have each node load it into memory beside the current one (requires memory headroom for two copies), run checks, then swap an atomic reference. Readers never lock; the old copy is freed after in-flight requests finish. Roll out to a canary node first and compare click-through rate before going fleet-wide.

How would you measure if suggestions are good?

Online metrics: share of searches that use a suggestion, position of the clicked suggestion, keystrokes saved, searches with zero results after a suggestion. Offline: replay last week's queries against the new index and check that the query actually searched appears in the top-k for its prefixes. A/B test ranking changes.

items.title: 10. Self-assessment rubric
items.text:
Level What the answer contains Junior An endpoint that queries the database with LIKE 'prefix%' and sorts by count; maybe a cache. Misses the keystroke volume and the latency budget. Mid Trie (or prefix table) in memory with top-k per node; offline build from logs; caching and debouncing; replication of the index. Senior Separates serving and data pipelines explicitly; time-decayed scoring with selections; immutable snapshots with validation, canary and atomic swap; trending overlay from a stream; filtering at build and serve time; sharding by traffic-balanced prefix ranges only when needed; CDN/browser caching with normalized keys; personalization in the client; out-of-order responses; quality metrics.

Related: Specialized data stores, Caching patterns, DNS & CDN, Kafka and streams, Hands-on 5 (caching).

items.title: Index
items.text:
"Design a ticketing platform like Ticketmaster. A stadium show goes on sale at 10:00: two million fans, sixty thousand seats. Nobody may get the same seat twice."

This is the flagship case of the course because it is BoxOffice itself, and because it packs into one problem the hardest ideas of the semester: a spike that is 100× the normal load and arrives in seconds, a hot, strongly consistent resource (the seats) that cannot be cached away, an external dependency (the payment provider) that is slow and occasionally down, and adversarial traffic (bots and scalpers). Most of the system is a boring read-heavy catalog; the interview is decided in the ten minutes after 10:00.

Difficulty hard (senior favorite) Key concepts waiting room / virtual queue, admission control with Little's Law, seat holds with TTL, concurrency control (pessimistic, optimistic, conditional update), idempotency, order state machine, payment webhooks Palette components cdn, waf, apigw, queue, app, sql, cache, scheduler, kafka, payment, notifications, email Playground scenario flash-sale

What this case trains

  • Estimate the arrival rate of an on-sale and derive the admission rate of a waiting room with Little's Law.
  • Design seat holds that never double-book, and compare pessimistic locking, optimistic locking and conditional updates.
  • Model the checkout as a state machine that survives payment timeouts, retries and late webhooks.
  • Identify the bottlenecks of a flash sale (hot rows, connection pools, the payment provider, bots) and defend the trade-offs (fairness vs. throughput, user experience vs. consistency).

items.title: 1. Clarify the requirements
items.text: Spend the first five minutes here (see the interview framework). A ticketing system can mean "a box office for a theater with 300 seats" or "the Eras Tour on-sale": the answers below change the design completely.

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text:
1. Fans browse events and venues (catalog) and see the seat map with live availability.
  2. A fan selects seats and gets a hold: the seats are reserved for them for a few minutes (e.g. 10 min) while they pay.
  3. The fan pays through an external payment provider; on success the order is confirmed and the tickets are issued (e-mail + app).
  4. Unpaid holds expire and the seats return to sale.
  5. During high-demand on-sales, fans wait in a waiting room and are admitted in order.

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.text: Quality Target (state it, the interviewer will push on it) Correctness Zero double booking. A seat is sold at most once — strong consistency on the inventory. Scalability Absorb 2 M fans arriving within ~2 minutes without collapsing; normal days are ~100× quieter. Latency Hold a seat in p99 < 300 ms for admitted fans; catalog pages p99 < 200 ms. Availability 99.95% for browse and checkout; the waiting room must stay up even if the backend is saturated (it is the shock absorber). Fairness First-come-first-served (or a declared lottery), with per-account limits; bots must not win. Durability A confirmed order is never lost (payment taken ⇒ ticket exists).

items.title: Out of scope (say it explicitly)
items.text:
Event creation by promoters, dynamic pricing, resale marketplace, physical ticket scanning at the gate, refunds. Mention them in one sentence and move on.

Questions to ask the interviewer Question Why it matters Reserved seats or general admission (GA)? Reserved seats = many rows with low contention each; GA = one hot counter. Different concurrency designs. How big is the biggest on-sale? Do several happen at once? Sizes the waiting room and tells whether to partition by event. Can a fan pick the exact seat, or do we assign "best available"? "Best available" lets the server batch and avoid conflicts. How long is a hold? Max tickets per account? Hold TTL and limits drive Little's Law and fairness. Do we own payments or use a provider (Stripe, Adyen, Mercado Pago…)? External provider ⇒ webhooks, idempotency, reconciliation. Is the waiting room FIFO or a randomized lottery for early arrivals? Fairness policy; FIFO rewards bots with fast networks.

items.title: 2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates
items.text:
The numbers are what make this problem interesting: the total work is tiny (60 k seats fit in a few megabytes), but the peak is brutal. State the assumptions, then compute. The block below is the estimate as code — open the Source tab, change an assumption and redo it on paper.

ResultSource quantity value unit orders 30,000 join_rate 16,667 req/s no_queue_rps 166,667 req/s naive_poll 200,000 req/s admit_rate 33.33 fans/s admits 50,000 fans sellout_min 25.00 min order_rate 20.00 orders/s pay_inflight 40.00 calls seat_map_rps 3,333 req/s edge_gb 200 GB inventory_mb 6.00 MB 
# BoxOffice flash sale: assumptions (illustrative, change them freely)
fans        = 2_000_000   # fans who show up for the on-sale
arrival_s   = 120         # most of them arrive within ~2 min of 10:00
seats       = 60_000
per_order   = 2           # tickets per order (average)
checkout_s  = 300         # time an admitted fan spends choosing + paying
active_cap  = 10_000      # shoppers the inventory + payment path can serve at once
conversion  = 0.6         # admitted fans who end up buying
poll_s      = 10          # waiting-room status refresh interval
page_kb     = 100         # waiting-room page + assets
psp_s       = 2.0         # payment provider latency

orders       = seats / per_order
join_rate    = fans / arrival_s                 # joins per second at the door
no_queue_rps = fans * 5 / 60                    # 5 requests/fan in the 1st minute, no queue
naive_poll   = fans / poll_s                    # status polls if all hit the origin
admit_rate   = active_cap / checkout_s          # Little's Law: L = λ·W  →  λ = L / W
admits       = orders / conversion
sellout_min  = admits / admit_rate / 60
order_rate   = admit_rate * conversion
pay_inflight = order_rate * psp_s               # Little's Law again
seat_map_rps = active_cap / 3                   # each shopper refreshes the map every 3 s
edge_gb      = fans * page_kb / 1e6
inventory_mb = seats * 100 / 1e6                # ~100 B per seat row

rows = [
    ("orders", orders, ""), ("join_rate", join_rate, "req/s"),
    ("no_queue_rps", no_queue_rps, "req/s"), ("naive_poll", naive_poll, "req/s"),
    ("admit_rate", admit_rate, "fans/s"), ("admits", admits, "fans"),
    ("sellout_min", sellout_min, "min"), ("order_rate", order_rate, "orders/s"),
    ("pay_inflight", pay_inflight, "calls"), ("seat_map_rps", seat_map_rps, "req/s"),
    ("edge_gb", edge_gb, "GB"), ("inventory_mb", inventory_mb, "MB"),
]
print("| quantity | value | unit |\n|---|---:|---|")
for name, value, unit in rows:
    v = f"{value:,.0f}" if abs(value) >= 100 else f"{value:,.2f}"
    print(f"| `{name}` | {v} | {unit} |")

What the numbers tell us — this paragraph is the part the interviewer is listening for:

  • Without a waiting room the inventory would see ~170 k requests/s for a minute. A single PostgreSQL primary does a few thousand small write transactions per second; no amount of app servers fixes that, because the bottleneck is a handful of hot rows. ⇒ we need admission control.
  • With 10 k concurrent shoppers and 5 minutes each, Little's Law gives an admission rate of ~33 fans/s (2 000/min), a sell-out in ~25 minutes and only ~20 orders/s — easy for one well-indexed database.
  • The waiting room itself must take ~17 k joins/s and, if everybody polls the origin, 200 k polls/s. ⇒ serve the page from the CDN and make the status endpoint cheap (a signed token + a single counter read, cacheable for a second).
  • About 40 payment calls are in flight at any time (20/s × 2 s). ⇒ size the connection pool and bulkhead of the payment adapter for that, not for the 2 M fans.
  • The entire inventory is ~6 MB: storage is not a problem; contention is.

items.title: 3. API
items.text:
Keep it short and resource-oriented; the interesting fields are the tokens and the idempotency key.

POST /v1/events/{eventId}/queue                      → 201 {queueToken, position, etaSeconds}
GET  /v1/queue/{queueToken}                          → 200 {status: WAITING|ADMITTED, position, accessToken?}

GET  /v1/events/{eventId}                            → 200 event, venue, price levels   (CDN, minutes)
GET  /v1/events/{eventId}/availability?section=A     → 200 {seatsBitmap, version}      (cache, 1 s)

POST /v1/events/{eventId}/holds                      → 201 {holdId, seats, expiresAt} | 409 SEAT_TAKEN
     Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>
     Idempotency-Key: 7f3c…
     {"seatIds": ["A-12-07", "A-12-08"]}
DELETE /v1/holds/{holdId}                            → 204

POST /v1/orders                                      → 202 {orderId, status: PENDING_PAYMENT, paymentUrl}
     Idempotency-Key: 9a41…
     {"holdId": "…"}
GET  /v1/orders/{orderId}                            → 200 {status: CONFIRMED|PENDING_PAYMENT|EXPIRED|FAILED}

POST /v1/webhooks/payments                           ← provider callback, signed (HMAC)
  • The accessToken is what the waiting room hands out: a short-lived signed token (e.g. a JWT with eventId, userId, exp = 15 min). The gateway rejects hold/order calls without a valid one, so nobody can skip the queue by calling the API directly.
  • Idempotency-Key on holds and orders: mobile networks retry, users double-click; the server stores the key with the response and replays it instead of creating a second hold or order.
  • POST /v1/orders returns 202 Accepted: payment is asynchronous; the client polls the order (or gets a push) until it is CONFIRMED.

items.title: 4. Data model
items.text:
The inventory is small, relational and needs transactions ⇒ SQL (PostgreSQL), partitioned by event_id if there are many events. The catalog is read-mostly and can live in the same database behind a cache, or in a document store.

CREATE TABLE seat (
    event_id     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    seat_id      TEXT        NOT NULL,             -- 'A-12-07' (section-row-number)
    section      TEXT        NOT NULL,
    price_cents  INT         NOT NULL,
    status       TEXT        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'AVAILABLE',  -- AVAILABLE | HELD | SOLD
    hold_id      UUID,
    held_until   TIMESTAMPTZ,
    version      INT         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_id)
);

CREATE TABLE hold (
    hold_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    event_id     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    user_id      BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    expires_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    status       TEXT        NOT NULL               -- ACTIVE | CONVERTED | EXPIRED | RELEASED
);

CREATE TABLE ticket_order (
    order_id        UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    hold_id         UUID UNIQUE NOT NULL,           -- one order per hold
    user_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
    total_cents     INT    NOT NULL,
    status          TEXT   NOT NULL,                -- PENDING_PAYMENT | CONFIRMED | FAILED | EXPIRED
    payment_ref     TEXT,                           -- provider's id
    idempotency_key TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE outbox (                               -- transactional outbox → Kafka
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, topic TEXT, payload JSONB, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
Data Store Why Seats, holds, orders SQL (sql) Transactions, unique constraints, conditional updates. Tiny volume, high contention. Waiting-room queue Redis sorted set or a managed queue (queue) Millions of entries, O(log n) position lookups, disposable after the sale. Availability snapshot Cache (cache), 1 s TTL 3 k reads/s per hot event; slightly stale is fine — the hold is the real check. Event pages, images CDN (cdn) + object store Static, identical for everybody. Order events Kafka (kafka) via outbox Fan-out to notification, analytics, fraud — off the critical path.

items.title: 5. High-level design
items.text:
Read the diagram as two paths. The cheap path (catalog, waiting page, availability) is served by the CDN and caches and never touches the hot rows. The expensive path (hold → order → payment) is protected by the waiting room, which lets in only what the database and the payment provider can take.

flowchart LR
    fan([Fan / mobile]) --> cdn["CDN<br/>event pages, waiting page"]
    cdn --> waf["WAF<br/>bots, DDoS"]
    waf --> gw["API Gateway<br/>auth, rate limit,<br/>access token check"]
    gw --> wr["Waiting room"]
    wr --> q[("Queue<br/>Redis sorted set")]
    gw --> cat["catalog"]
    cat --> cache[("Cache<br/>availability 1 s")]
    gw --> inv["inventory<br/>holds"]
    inv --> sql[("PostgreSQL<br/>seat, hold, order")]
    gw --> ord["order"]
    ord --> sql
    ord --> pay["payment adapter"]
    pay --> psp[["Payment provider"]]
    psp -. webhook .-> pay
    sql -. outbox .-> kafka[["Kafka<br/>order events"]]
    kafka --> notif["notification"] --> email[["E-mail / push"]]
    kafka --> an["analytics"]
    sched["scheduler<br/>expire holds"] --> sql

The happy path of one fan, step by step:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant F as Fan
    participant W as Waiting room
    participant I as inventory
    participant O as order
    participant P as Payment provider
    participant N as notification
    F->>W: join (10:00:03)
    W-->>F: queueToken, position 48 210
    F->>W: poll status (every 10 s, cached)
    W-->>F: ADMITTED + accessToken (15 min)
    F->>I: POST /holds {A-12-07, A-12-08} + accessToken
    I->>I: conditional UPDATE (both seats or none)
    I-->>F: 201 holdId, expiresAt = now + 10 min
    F->>O: POST /orders {holdId} + Idempotency-Key
    O->>P: create payment (idempotency key = orderId)
    O-->>F: 202 PENDING_PAYMENT, paymentUrl
    P-->>O: webhook: payment succeeded
    O->>O: seats SOLD, order CONFIRMED, outbox row (one transaction)
    O-)N: OrderConfirmed (Kafka)
    N-->>F: e-mail + push with tickets

items.title: 6. Deep dives
items.text: The interviewer will pick one or two of these. Lead with the one that protects correctness (holds), then the one that protects availability (the waiting room).

items.title: 6.1 Seat holds without double booking
items.text:
Two fans click seat A-12-07 in the same millisecond. Exactly one must win. There are four classic ways to guarantee it (transactions & isolation):

Conditional update (recommended)Pessimistic lockOptimistic lockRedis first, SQL as truth

One statement, atomic per row, no explicit lock held across a round trip. Expired holds are reclaimed in the same statement (lazy expiration).

BEGIN;
UPDATE seat
   SET status = 'HELD', hold_id = $1, held_until = now() + interval '10 minutes',
       version = version + 1
 WHERE event_id = $2
   AND seat_id = ANY($3)
   AND (status = 'AVAILABLE' OR (status = 'HELD' AND held_until < now()));
-- the app checks: rows updated == number of seats requested, otherwise ROLLBACK → 409
INSERT INTO hold (hold_id, event_id, user_id, expires_at, status)
     VALUES ($1, $2, $4, now() + interval '10 minutes', 'ACTIVE');
COMMIT;

Lock the rows, check, then update. Simple to reason about; the lock is held for the whole transaction, so keep it short and always lock in the same order (sort seat_id) to avoid deadlocks.

BEGIN;
SELECT seat_id, status, held_until FROM seat
 WHERE event_id = $1 AND seat_id = ANY($2)
 ORDER BY seat_id
   FOR UPDATE;            -- NOWAIT or SKIP LOCKED for "best available"
-- app checks every row is free, then UPDATE ... ; COMMIT

Read without locking, write only if the version did not change. No lock waits, but under heavy contention most attempts fail and retry — bad for the hottest seats.

UPDATE seat SET status = 'HELD', hold_id = $1, version = version + 1
 WHERE event_id = $2 AND seat_id = $3 AND version = $4;   -- 0 rows → somebody won, retry

SET hold:{event}:{seat} <holdId> NX EX 600 in Redis gives a sub-millisecond, self-expiring hold; the order is still written in SQL with a UNIQUE (event_id, seat_id) on sold tickets as the final guard. Faster, but two stores must agree (what if Redis fails over and loses the key?). Use when the SQL path is measured to be the bottleneck — not by default.

SET hold:42:A-12-07 3f9a... NX EX 600   →  OK  (you got it)  |  nil (taken)
Approach Contention behavior Pitfalls Use when Conditional UPDATE … WHERE status='AVAILABLE' Losers fail fast (0 rows) Must check the row count Default for reserved seats SELECT … FOR UPDATE Losers wait for the lock Deadlocks, long lock holds, pool exhaustion Multi-step checks in one transaction Optimistic (version) Losers retry Retry storms on hot rows Low contention (normal days) Redis SET NX EX Fastest, TTL built in Two sources of truth Extreme rates, measured need

Expiration. A hold must end even if the fan closes the browser. Combine (a) lazy expiration in the hold statement (an expired HELD seat counts as available), (b) a scheduler job that sweeps hold rows with expires_at < now() every few seconds and flips seats back to AVAILABLE so the seat map is accurate, and (c) extending the hold while a payment is in flight, so a fan who is paying does not lose the seat at second 601.

General admission: the one hot row

With GA tickets there are no seat rows, only remaining = 60 000. UPDATE pool SET remaining = remaining - 2 WHERE remaining >= 2 is correct but serializes every buyer on one row. Fixes: split the pool into N sub-counters (shards) and pick one at random; or keep the counter in Redis (DECRBY in a Lua script) and write orders to SQL asynchronously; or pre-allocate the stock into the waiting room tokens (each admitted fan carries the right to buy up to 4).

items.title: 6.2 The waiting room (virtual queue)
items.text:
The waiting room is load shedding with good manners: instead of letting 2 M requests hit the inventory and fail randomly, it turns the burst into a steady, measured flow and tells each fan where they stand.

flowchart LR
    j["Fans join<br/>~17 k/s"] --> rq[("Queue<br/>sorted by<br/>random or arrival")]
    rq --> d{"Admitter<br/>every second"}
    d -->|"admit λ = L / W<br/>≈ 33 fans/s"| tok["accessToken<br/>(signed, 15 min)"]
    tok --> shop["Shopping<br/>≤ 10 k at once"]
    shop -->|"buys or times out"| out([leaves])
    out -. frees a slot .-> d

Design points:

  1. Static page on the CDN. The waiting page is HTML + JS cached at the edge; the only dynamic call is the status poll, answered from Redis (ZRANK for the position) or from a cached "now serving number" — the client compares it with its own number, so the origin answers one value for everybody.
  2. Admission rate from Little's Law. The admitter lets in λ = L / W fans per second, where L is the number of shoppers the checkout path can serve (measured in the load test, e.g. 10 k) and W the time each spends (5 min). It is a closed loop: admit more when shoppers leave early, admit fewer when p99 of POST /holds rises or the payment provider slows down.
  3. Fairness. Pure FIFO rewards whoever has the fastest connection — usually bots. A common policy: everyone who arrives before 10:00 gets a random position at 10:00 (a lottery), and late arrivals go to the back in FIFO order.
  4. Tokens, not sessions. Admission produces a signed accessToken (event, user, expiry). The gateway verifies the signature locally — no shared session store on the hot path — and enforces "max 6 tickets per account".
  5. Bots. The WAF does bot scoring, rate limits per IP/ASN and challenges; requiring a logged-in, verified account to join is the strongest filter. Queue-it, Cloudflare Waiting Room and the AWS Virtual Waiting Room solution are real products built on these ideas.

Why not just autoscale?

App servers scale in a minute or two; the seat rows do not scale at all — there is one row per seat and the best seats are wanted by everybody. The database primary, the connection pool and the payment provider's rate limit are fixed for the next 30 minutes. Autoscaling helps the cheap path (catalog, waiting room); the expensive path needs admission control.

items.title: 6.3 Checkout and payment: a state machine, not a function call
items.text:
A payment provider answers in seconds, times out, and sometimes calls you back before your HTTP request returns. Model the order as a state machine whose transitions are idempotent (integrations, payment system case).

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> HELD: POST /holds
    HELD --> PENDING_PAYMENT: POST /orders (extend hold)
    HELD --> EXPIRED: TTL (10 min) elapses
    PENDING_PAYMENT --> CONFIRMED: webhook succeeded
    PENDING_PAYMENT --> FAILED: webhook failed / declined
    PENDING_PAYMENT --> CONFIRMED: reconciliation finds payment
    FAILED --> HELD: retry with another card (hold still valid)
    EXPIRED --> [*]
    CONFIRMED --> [*]
  • Idempotency key to the provider = orderId. If the adapter times out and retries, the provider returns the same payment instead of charging twice.
  • Webhooks are the source of truth for the outcome; they are signed (HMAC), may arrive twice or out of order, so the handler is UPDATE ticket_order SET status='CONFIRMED' WHERE order_id=$1 AND status='PENDING_PAYMENT' — a second delivery changes nothing.
  • Confirm in one transaction: seats HELD → SOLD, order CONFIRMED, an outbox row. A relay publishes the outbox to Kafka; notification consumes it idempotently (dedupe by orderId) and sends the e-mail (messaging patterns).
  • Reconciliation. A scheduler job lists PENDING_PAYMENT orders older than N minutes and asks the provider for their status. This fixes lost webhooks — and the nasty case "payment succeeded after the hold expired": either the seats are still free (confirm) or they were resold (refund automatically and apologize).
  • Resilience. Timeout + circuit breaker + bulkhead around the provider (reliability patterns); if the breaker is open, stop admitting new fans instead of letting them hold seats they cannot pay for.

items.title: 6.4 The read path: seat map and catalog
items.text:
Fans hammer the seat map. Serving it from the seat table would put reads on the same hot rows as the holds.

  • Keep a per-section availability bitmap (one bit per seat — 60 k seats = 7.5 kB) in the cache, rebuilt every second from the database or updated from hold/sold events. Clients poll it (or receive it via SSE) with a version number.
  • Accept staleness: the map may show a seat as free that was taken 800 ms ago. The hold request is the real check; return 409 SEAT_TAKEN with the fresh bitmap so the UI updates.
  • Pre-warm the CDN and the cache before 10:00 (event page, images, bitmaps): a cold cache at the moment of the spike is a self-inflicted stampede (caching failure modes).
  • Offer "best available": the server picks seats with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so concurrent buyers never wait on each other's rows.

items.title: 7. Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs
items.text:
Where What goes wrong at 10:00 Mitigation Trade-off Inventory hot rows Lock waits on the best sections; p99 explodes Admission control; conditional updates; "best available" with SKIP LOCKED; GA counter sharding Fans wait longer in the queue DB connection pool Requests wait for a connection, threads pile up PgBouncer; small fixed pool sized by Little's Law; timeouts Rejecting early (503) vs. waiting Waiting-room status 200 k polls/s on the origin Static page on CDN; cached "now serving" number; poll interval with jitter Position updates every 10 s, not real time Payment provider Slow (5 s) or down; its rate limit Bulkhead + timeout + breaker; slow the admitter; extend holds while paying Sale takes longer; some fans lose holds Webhooks Lost, duplicated, out of order Idempotent handler; reconciliation job Extra moving part (scheduler) Mass expiry 5 k holds expire at 10:10 together; seats flap Jittered TTLs; release in batches; show "seats may come back" Slightly unfair to late fans Bots Bots fill the queue and hold seats to resell WAF bot scoring, verified accounts, per-account limits, lottery at open Friction for real fans Cold caches Stampede on event page at 10:00:00 Pre-warm, request coalescing, long TTL on static content Must invalidate if the event changes Single region Region outage during the sale Multi-AZ primary with synchronous standby; pause the sale (queue holds everyone) Cross-region active-active inventory is much harder (consensus)

The two trade-offs to say out loud: consistency over availability for the inventory (if the database is unreachable, stop selling; never sell from a stale replica), and fairness and stability over raw speed (a sale that takes 25 orderly minutes beats one that crashes at minute 2).

items.title: 8. Try it in the playground
items.text:
The flash-sale scenario wires a waiting room (queue) in front of the inventory (SQL) and the payment provider, and replays a 10:00 spike.

Try it

  1. Run the scenario with the spike profile and look at the SQL utilization, the queue backlog and the p99 of the checkout path.
  2. Bypass the queue (connect the gateway straight to the inventory app) and run again: watch the database saturate and errors climb — this is the "no waiting room" number from section 2.
  3. Restore the queue and change the number of workers/replicas behind it: find the admission rate where p99 stays under the SLO and the backlog still drains.
  4. Turn chaos to medium to slow down the payment provider: what happens to in-flight requests (Little's Law), and what should the admitter do?

Open the full playground

items.title: 9. Follow-up questions an interviewer asks
items.text:
The payment provider goes down at 10:05. What happens?

The circuit breaker around the payment adapter opens after a few failures; POST /orders answers quickly with "payments are temporarily unavailable" instead of hanging. The admitter pauses (no point admitting fans who cannot pay), and the holds of fans already in checkout are extended for the outage window so nobody loses a seat through no fault of their own. When the breaker half-opens and probes succeed, admission resumes slowly. If the outage is long, a second provider (failover) is the business decision to discuss.

How do you stop scalpers' bots?

Layers: (1) require a logged-in, verified account (phone/card) before joining the queue; (2) WAF bot scoring, device fingerprinting and challenges at the edge; (3) a lottery for everyone who joins before the on-sale, which removes the advantage of millisecond-fast scripts; (4) per-account and per-payment-instrument limits enforced at hold and order time; (5) post-sale analysis to cancel suspicious orders. No single layer is enough; the goal is to make bots expensive, not impossible.

Why not keep the whole inventory in Redis?

You can — 60 k seats are tiny — and some platforms do hold seats in memory. The cost is a second source of truth: a Redis failover can lose the last writes (asynchronous replication), so a seat could be held twice. If you do it, keep a durable guard in SQL (a unique constraint on (event_id, seat_id) for sold tickets) so the worst case is a failed checkout, never a double sale. Start with SQL and conditional updates; they handle the ~20 orders/s that admission control lets through.

The primary database fails in the middle of the sale.

With a synchronous standby in another availability zone, failover takes seconds to a minute and loses no committed transactions (RPO = 0). During the failover, holds and orders fail; the waiting room keeps everybody in place (it does not depend on the inventory database), and the admitter pauses. Clients retry with the same idempotency keys, so no duplicate holds appear. Never fail over to an asynchronous replica for the inventory without accepting that recent holds may be lost.

Ten big on-sales start at 10:00 on the same day. Does the design change?

Partition by event_id: each event gets its own queue and admitter, and the inventory can be sharded by event (events never share seats, so there are no cross-shard transactions). The shared parts are the edge (CDN, WAF), the payment provider's global rate limit and notification capacity — allocate them per event (bulkheads) so one hot sale does not starve the others.

How do you test this before the real on-sale?

A load test that reproduces the spike (k6 with an arrival-rate executor ramping to the expected join rate in seconds), with realistic data (hot sections, 2 tickets per order) and the payment provider replaced by a stub with configurable latency (performance engineering). Find the breaking point of the checkout path, then set the admission rate below it with margin. Add a chaos test: provider slow, database failover, cache flush — during the load test.

How would you show fans an accurate ETA in the queue?

ETA ≈ position / admission rate. Because the admission rate is adjusted dynamically, smooth it (moving average) and show a range ("about 20–30 minutes"). Also show when tickets are likely to be gone: if remaining seats / tickets per order is smaller than the number of fans ahead of you, tell the fan the truth early.

items.title: 10. Self-assessment rubric
items.text:
Level What the answer contains Junior Catalog + inventory + orders on an app server and a SQL database; a lock or transaction so two people cannot buy the same seat; mentions caching for the catalog. Misses the spike or tries to solve it with "more servers". Mid All of the above plus holds with TTL and expiration, idempotent order creation, asynchronous payment with webhooks, outbox to notifications; estimates the peak and recognizes the hot-row problem; proposes a waiting room. Senior Derives the admission rate with Little's Law and closes the loop on p99 and provider health; compares concurrency-control options with their contention behavior; designs the order state machine with reconciliation and the "paid after expiry" case; discusses fairness (lottery vs. FIFO), bots, GA counter sharding, failover semantics (RPO = 0 for inventory), multi-event isolation, and how to load-test it. States the CP choice for the inventory explicitly.

Related: Hands-on 6 (seat holds and transactions), Hands-on 7 (outbox and waiting-room queue), Hands-on 9 (resilience around payment), team project.

items.title: Index
items.text:
"Design a URL shortener like bit.ly or TinyURL: users submit a long URL and get a short one; anybody who opens the short URL is redirected to the original."

The URL shortener is the "hello world" of system design interviews, and it is usually the first problem you get as a junior or the warm-up in a senior loop. It looks trivial — a key-value lookup — and that is exactly the trap: the interviewer wants to see whether you drive the conversation (requirements, numbers, API, data, design, deep dives) instead of jumping to "use a hash". It exercises three ideas you will reuse in almost every other case: unique ID generation, read-heavy caching, and taking side work (analytics) off the critical path.

BoxOffice uses one too: the SMS that says "your tickets for Saturday" carries a short link such as https://bx.example/aB3x9Kq, because an SMS has 160 characters and a signed ticket URL has 300.

Difficulty easy (warm-up, junior favorite) Key concepts base62 encoding, unique ID generation (counter ranges, Snowflake, key generation service) vs. hashing, collisions, 301 vs. 302, cache-aside for hot links, asynchronous click analytics Palette components dns, lb, app, cache, nosql, kafka, analytics Playground scenario url-shortener

What this case trains

  • Run the full interview framework on a small problem, inside 35–45 minutes.
  • Estimate read/write rates, storage over five years and the size of the hot set.
  • Compare ID-generation strategies (hash, counter + base62, key generation service, Snowflake) on collisions, coordination and predictability.
  • Design a redirect path that serves most requests from a cache and justify 301 vs. 302.
  • Move click analytics off the critical path with an event stream.

items.title: 1. Clarify the requirements
items.text: Even for a "simple" problem, spend 3–5 minutes here (interview framework). The requirements decide whether codes may be predictable, whether analytics must be exact, and whether the same long URL always gets the same code.

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text:
1. Shorten: given a long URL, return a short URL with a unique code (e.g. 7 characters).
  2. Redirect: GET /{code} sends the browser to the long URL.
  3. Custom alias (optional): the user chooses the code (/boxoffice-rock-in-rio).
  4. Expiration (optional): links can expire at a given date.
  5. Click statistics: number of clicks per link, per day, per country.

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.text: Quality Target Latency Redirect p99 < 100 ms (it sits in front of every click) Availability 99.99% for redirects — a broken short link breaks the campaign, the SMS, the printed QR code Scale 100 M new links per month; read-heavy (100:1) Durability A created link works for years (until it expires) Security Codes should not be trivially guessable (no enumeration of private links); block malicious destinations Analytics Eventually consistent; minutes of delay are fine; small loss is acceptable

items.title: Out of scope (say it explicitly)
items.text:
User accounts and link editing UI, billing, QR-code rendering, A/B testing of destinations. They are features on top of the same core.

Questions to ask the interviewer Question Why it matters How many new links per month? Read:write ratio? Sizes everything: QPS, storage, cache. How short must the code be? Which characters? 7 characters of base62 give 3.5 trillion codes; base64 adds + and / (unsafe in URLs). Same long URL twice → same code, or a new one? Deterministic (hash) vs. unique per request (counter). Per-user stats usually need distinct codes. Must codes be unpredictable? Sequential counters leak volume and allow enumeration. Do analytics need to be exact? Real time? Exact + real time is expensive; approximate + delayed is cheap. Do links expire? Can they be deleted? Cleanup jobs, cache invalidation, code reuse (usually: never reuse).

items.title: 2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates
items.text:
State the assumptions, then compute. All numbers are illustrative — open the Source tab, change one and recompute.

ResultSource quantity value unit write_qps 38.58 req/s read_qps 3,858 req/s peak_read 11,574 req/s records 6,000,000,000 links storage_tb 3.00 TB codes_7 3,521,614,606,208 codes used_pct 0.17 % cache_gb 33.33 GB clicks_gb 66.67 GB/day 
# URL shortener: assumptions (illustrative)
new_per_month = 100_000_000   # new short links per month
read_write    = 100           # redirects per created link
peak_factor   = 3             # peak / average traffic
years         = 5             # retention
record_b      = 500           # code + long URL + metadata, bytes
hot_fraction  = 0.2           # share of a day's redirects worth caching (80/20 rule)
click_b       = 200           # one click event (code, time, country, referrer)

write_qps  = new_per_month / (30 * 86_400)
read_qps   = write_qps * read_write
peak_read  = read_qps * peak_factor
records    = new_per_month * 12 * years
storage_tb = records * record_b / 1e12
codes_7    = 62 ** 7
used_pct   = records / codes_7 * 100
cache_gb   = read_qps * 86_400 * hot_fraction * record_b / 1e9
clicks_gb  = read_qps * 86_400 * click_b / 1e9

rows = [
    ("write_qps", write_qps, "req/s"), ("read_qps", read_qps, "req/s"),
    ("peak_read", peak_read, "req/s"), ("records", records, "links"),
    ("storage_tb", storage_tb, "TB"), ("codes_7", codes_7, "codes"),
    ("used_pct", used_pct, "%"), ("cache_gb", cache_gb, "GB"),
    ("clicks_gb", clicks_gb, "GB/day"),
]
print("| quantity | value | unit |\n|---|---:|---|")
for name, value, unit in rows:
    v = f"{value:,.0f}" if abs(value) >= 100 else f"{value:,.2f}"
    print(f"| `{name}` | {v} | {unit} |")

What the numbers tell us:

  • ~40 writes/s and ~4 k redirects/s (peak ~12 k/s): a single database could take the writes; the reads are what we design for. ⇒ cache in front of the store, stateless app servers behind a load balancer.
  • 6 billion links, ~3 TB in 5 years: too much for comfort on one node with replicas and indexes, trivial for a partitioned key-value store. The access pattern is a single-key lookup, so a KV store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) or a sharded SQL table both work.
  • 7 base62 characters = 3.5 trillion codes; we use 0.17% of them in 5 years. Short codes are not the scarce resource — uniqueness without coordination is the design problem.
  • The hot set is ~33 GB: it fits in the RAM of one or two cache nodes. With a Zipf-like popularity (a few links get most clicks), the hit ratio will be high.
  • Click events are ~67 GB/day — more than the links themselves. ⇒ they go to a stream and an analytics store, never to the main table.

In the interview

Say the conclusion, not only the number: "4 k reads per second against 40 writes, and the hot set fits in memory — so this is a caching problem with an ID-generation problem attached."

items.title: 3. API
items.text:
POST /v1/urls                          → 201 {code, shortUrl, expiresAt}
     {"longUrl": "https://boxoffice.example/events/42?utm_source=sms",
      "customAlias": null, "expiresAt": "2027-12-31T23:59:59Z"}
     (409 ALIAS_TAKEN, 422 INVALID_URL, 429 TOO_MANY_REQUESTS)

GET  /{code}                           → 302 Found, Location: <longUrl>
                                         (404 not found, 410 Gone when expired)

GET  /v1/urls/{code}/stats?from=…&to=… → 200 {clicks, byDay[], byCountry[]}
DELETE /v1/urls/{code}                 → 204   (owner only)
  • Creation is authenticated (API key or user token) and rate limited per client — a shortener is a favorite tool of spammers.
  • The redirect is public and does one thing: look up and answer. Everything else (counting, geo lookup, bot detection) happens asynchronously.

items.title: 4. Data model
items.text:
The core access pattern is code → longUrl, a point lookup by primary key, at thousands per second, over billions of rows. No joins, no range scans.

-- Logical model (a KV/wide-column table, or a sharded SQL table)
CREATE TABLE short_url (
    code        VARCHAR(16) PRIMARY KEY,   -- partition key
    long_url    TEXT        NOT NULL,
    owner_id    BIGINT,
    created_at  TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL,
    expires_at  TIMESTAMP
);

-- Only for the counter-based generator: one row per range allocation
CREATE TABLE id_range (
    name        VARCHAR(32) PRIMARY KEY,   -- 'short_url'
    next_start  BIGINT      NOT NULL
);
Data Store Why code → long_url NoSQL key-value / wide-column (nosql), partitioned by code Point lookups, horizontal scale, no joins; 3 TB spread over nodes Hot codes Cache (cache), cache-aside, TTL hours ~33 GB hot set; most redirects never touch the database ID ranges Small SQL table or a coordination service (etcd, ZooKeeper) A few writes per minute; needs atomic increments Click events Kafka (kafka) → analytics store / data warehouse High volume, append-only, read in aggregate

Why not one PostgreSQL?

For BoxOffice's own SMS links (thousands per day) one PostgreSQL table with a B-tree on code is perfect. For 100 M links per month the answer is still "SQL works", as long as you shard by code — the point of the interview is to show you know when a single node stops being enough and what you would partition by.

items.title: 5. High-level design
items.text:
flowchart LR
    u([Browser / app]) --> dns["DNS"]
    dns --> lb["Load balancer"]
    lb --> app["Shortener app<br/>(stateless, N replicas)"]
    app --> cache[("Cache<br/>hot codes")]
    app --> db[("NoSQL<br/>code → long_url")]
    app --> ids["ID allocator<br/>(ranges)"]
    app -. click event .-> k[["Kafka<br/>clicks"]]
    k --> agg["Analytics workers<br/>aggregate"]
    agg --> dwh[("Analytics store")]

The write path asks the ID allocator for a code (from a range already leased in memory — no network call most of the time), stores the row, and returns the short URL. The read path is shown below; notice that the click event is fired after the response and never waits.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant A as Shortener app
    participant C as Cache
    participant D as NoSQL
    participant K as Kafka
    B->>A: GET /aB3x9Kq
    A->>C: GET url:aB3x9Kq
    alt cache hit (most requests)
        C-->>A: long_url
    else cache miss
        C-->>A: nil
        A->>D: get(code = aB3x9Kq)
        D-->>A: long_url, expires_at
        A->>C: SET url:aB3x9Kq long_url EX 86400
    end
    A-->>B: 302 Location: long_url
    A-)K: click {code, ts, ip, user-agent}

items.title: 6.1 Generating the code
items.text:
This is the deep dive every interviewer expects. Four families, each with a different trade-off:

Hash + truncateCounter + base62Key generation service (KGS)Snowflake-style IDs

base62(sha256(longUrl))[:7]. Deterministic: the same URL gives the same code, so duplicates are free. But 7 characters keep only ~42 bits of the hash, so collisions happen and must be detected: insert with a conditional put (IF NOT EXISTS); on conflict, rehash longUrl + salt and try again. Two users shortening the same URL share a code — and share statistics.

A unique integer, encoded in base62. No collisions by construction. The problem is the counter: a single sequence is a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Fix it with range allocation: each app server leases a block (e.g. 10 000 ids) with one atomic update and hands them out from memory. A crash wastes at most one block — harmless with 3.5 trillion codes.

UPDATE id_range SET next_start = next_start + 10000
 WHERE name = 'short_url'
RETURNING next_start - 10000 AS block_start;

A separate service pre-generates random unused codes into a table and hands batches to app servers, marking them used. Unpredictable codes, no collisions on the request path. Costs: one more stateful service to replicate, and careful handling so two servers never get the same batch (move keys from unused to used atomically).

64-bit IDs built from timestamp | machine id | sequence (Twitter Snowflake): generated locally, roughly time-ordered, no coordination except assigning machine IDs. In base62 a 64-bit ID needs up to 11 characters — longer than 7. Good for internal IDs, less good when shortness is the product.

Strategy Collisions Coordination Predictable? Code length Same URL → same code Hash + truncate Yes, must retry None (but a conditional write) No 7 Yes Counter + base62 (ranges) No One atomic update per block Yes (sequential) 7 No KGS No KGS service No 7 No Snowflake No Machine IDs only Partially (time-ordered) ~11 No

The base62 encoding itself is a few lines:

ALPHABET = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"

def base62(n: int) -> str:
    s = ""
    while n > 0:
        n, r = divmod(n, 62)
        s = ALPHABET[r] + s
    return s or "0"

# 62**7 = 3_521_614_606_208 codes; base62(3_521_614_606_207) == "ZZZZZZZ"

Sequential codes leak information

With a plain counter, aB3x9Kq is followed by aB3x9Kr: anyone can enumerate links (including private ones) and estimate your volume. Keep the counter but scramble it with a bijection before encoding — e.g. multiply by a large constant coprime with 62 (odd and not a multiple of 31) modulo 62^7, or a small Feistel cipher — so consecutive ids give unrelated codes, still without collisions.

Recommendation for the interview: counter with range allocation + scrambling for generated codes; a conditional insert (IF NOT EXISTS) for custom aliases. Mention hashing and why you did not choose it (collisions, shared stats).

items.title: 6.2 The redirect: 301 or 302, and caching
items.text:
301 Moved Permanently 302 Found (or 307) Browser caches it? Yes, potentially forever No (unless Cache-Control says so) Load on our servers Lower: repeat clicks never reach us Every click reaches us Analytics Undercounts repeat visits Complete Changing/expiring the link later Hard: browsers keep the old answer Easy

Most commercial shorteners answer 302 (or 301 with a short Cache-Control: max-age) because analytics and the ability to disable a malicious link are part of the product. Whatever you choose, say why (HTTP semantics).

Caching the lookup (cache-aside):

  • Cache-aside with a TTL of hours: the mapping almost never changes, so staleness is not a problem; on delete or expiration, delete the key explicitly.
  • Negative caching: cache "not found" for a short time (url:zzzzzzz → ∅, 60 s), otherwise a bot scanning random codes goes straight to the database.
  • Zipf popularity: a viral link can receive thousands of clicks per second — a hot key on one cache shard. Mitigate with a small in-process cache (L1, a few seconds) on each app server in front of the shared cache.
  • Expiration: check expires_at on every read (cached together with the URL) and answer 410 Gone; a background job deletes expired rows later.

items.title: 6.3 Click analytics off the critical path
items.text:
Counting clicks synchronously (UPDATE stats SET clicks = clicks + 1) would turn every read into a write on a hot row. Instead:

flowchart LR
    app["Shortener app"] -->|"fire-and-forget<br/>click event"| k[["Kafka topic clicks<br/>partitioned by code"]]
    k --> s["Stream aggregation<br/>1-min windows"]
    s --> olap[("Analytics store<br/>clicks per code/day/country")]
    k --> lake[("Object store<br/>raw events")]
    olap --> api["GET /stats"]
  • The app produces the event after answering (or buffers it in memory and sends batches): the redirect does not depend on Kafka being healthy. If Kafka is down, drop or buffer — analytics may lose a few events; redirects must not fail (messaging semantics).
  • A stream job aggregates per code per minute and writes counters to an analytics store; raw events land in object storage for later analysis.
  • Unique visitors need a distinct count: use HyperLogLog (≈1–2% error, a few kB per counter) instead of storing every visitor ID.

items.title: 7. Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs
items.text:
Where What goes wrong Mitigation Trade-off Database reads Every redirect hits the store; p99 grows with load Cache-aside + L1 in-process cache; read replicas Staleness after delete (bounded by TTL) Viral link One hot key saturates one cache shard L1 cache with seconds of TTL; replicate the hot key More memory, slightly staler data ID allocator Single counter = bottleneck and SPOF Range leasing; allocator replicated (SQL with failover) Gaps in the sequence after crashes (harmless) Code scanning Bots try random codes → misses hit the DB Negative caching; rate limit per IP; non-sequential codes Little memory for negative entries Malicious destinations Shortener used to hide phishing Check URLs against a reputation list at creation and asynchronously later; disable link (302 makes this effective) Creation latency; false positives Analytics pipeline Kafka slow or down Fire-and-forget with a bounded buffer; drop on overflow Some clicks lost (acceptable by requirement) Region outage Redirects fail everywhere Multi-region read path: replicated KV, GeoDNS, cache per region Writes need a home region or conflict-free IDs (ranges per region)

The trade-offs to say out loud: availability and latency over strict consistency for the redirect path (a link deleted a few seconds ago may still redirect from the cache), 302 over 301 because analytics and control matter, and counter ranges over hashing because uniqueness without collision retries is simpler to reason about.

items.title: 8. Try it in the playground
items.text:
The url-shortener scenario has the read path of this page: load balancer, app replicas, a cache in front of the store, and an event stream for clicks.

Try it

  1. Run with the load profile and note the cache hit ratio, the database utilization and the redirect p99.
  2. Remove the cache (or set its hit ratio low) and run again: how many times higher is the database load? Does p99 still meet the 100 ms target?
  3. Switch to the stress profile and add app replicas until the bottleneck moves: is it the app tier, the cache, or the store?
  4. Turn chaos on and kill the stream/analytics consumer: do redirects keep working? (They should — that is the point of section 6.3.)

Open the full playground

items.title: 9. Follow-up questions an interviewer asks
items.text:
How do you support custom aliases without clashing with generated codes?

Use a conditional insert (INSERT … IF NOT EXISTS or a unique constraint) and answer 409 when the alias is taken. To avoid a generated code ever colliding with an alias, put them in different spaces: generated codes have exactly 7 characters from base62, aliases must be longer or contain a -; or reserve aliases in the same table so the generator's conditional insert would fail and fetch the next id.

The same user shortens the same URL twice. Same code?

It depends on the requirement you clarified. With a counter, you get two codes (and two sets of statistics), which is what campaign tools want. If deduplication is required, keep a secondary index hash(longUrl, owner) → code and check it before allocating — one extra lookup on the (rare) write path.

How would you go multi-region?

Redirects are reads: replicate the KV store to every region (asynchronous replication is fine), keep a cache per region, and route users with GeoDNS/anycast to the nearest one. For writes, give each region its own id ranges (or a region bit in the id) so codes never collide without cross-region coordination. A link created in São Paulo may take a second to work in Frankfurt — acceptable if you say it.

How do you count unique clicks per link?

Exact unique counts need the set of visitor IDs — huge for popular links. Use HyperLogLog per link per day (Redis PFADD/PFCOUNT, or the analytics store's approximate distinct function): ~1% error with a few kilobytes per counter, and HLLs can be merged across days.

How do you clean up expired links? Can codes be reused?

Read-time check (answer 410 if expires_at < now) makes expiration exact; a background job deletes expired rows in batches (or the store's native TTL does it). Do not reuse codes: old copies of the short URL are printed, cached in browsers (301) and in other people's messages — reusing them would send users to an unrelated page. With 3.5 trillion codes there is no need.

What if someone uses your shortener for phishing?

Check the destination against reputation lists at creation, rate limit and require authentication for creation, rescan popular links asynchronously, and keep a "disabled" flag that the redirect respects. This is one more reason to prefer 302: you can still stop sending people to a link after it turns malicious.

Why not just use the database auto-increment column?

It works at small scale and is a perfectly good answer for BoxOffice's internal links. At 100 M links per month with a sharded store there is no single auto-increment, and the primary becomes a write bottleneck and SPOF. Range leasing keeps the same idea (a counter) while touching the shared counter once per 10 000 ids.

items.title: 10. Self-assessment rubric
items.text:
Level What the answer contains Junior API with create and redirect; a table code → url; some way to generate codes (often a hash) without handling collisions; "add a cache". Mid Requirements and estimates driving the design (read-heavy, hot set fits in memory); base62 with a collision-free generator (counter ranges or KGS); cache-aside with TTL; 301 vs. 302 discussed; analytics asynchronous. Senior Compares the four generators on collisions, coordination and predictability, and scrambles sequential ids; negative caching and hot-key mitigation; data partitioning by code; multi-region with per-region id ranges; abuse handling; explicit consistency choice for the redirect path; knows when a single PostgreSQL is still the right answer.

Related: Caching, Hands-on 5 (cache-aside and hit ratio), Messaging, interview practice problems.
