items.title: Index
items.text:
"Design a video platform like YouTube: creators upload videos, the platform processes them, and millions of viewers watch them smoothly on any device and any network."

Video is the case where bandwidth, not requests, is the bottleneck. A redirect is 500 bytes; one minute of HD video is tens of megabytes. Almost every design decision follows from that: viewers never touch your servers (a CDN delivers the bytes), uploads never pass through your servers (they go straight to object storage), and the heavy CPU work (transcoding) is a batch pipeline of workers that can take minutes. The interesting parts are the pipeline, adaptive bitrate streaming and the economics of egress.

BoxOffice uses video on every event page — artist trailers, venue tours, replays of livestreamed shows. Its volume is small next to YouTube, but the architecture is the same, and the day an artist announces a tour with a video, the CDN is what keeps the event page alive.

Difficulty hard Key concepts pre-signed and resumable multipart uploads, transcoding as a DAG of queue-driven workers, renditions and the bitrate ladder, adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH), per-title encoding, CDN with origin shield, egress cost, long-tail popularity, asynchronous view counting Palette components client, cdn, apigw, app, objstore, queue, worker, sql, nosql, analytics Playground scenario video-streaming

What this case trains

  • Estimate egress bandwidth, storage and transcoding capacity, and explain why bandwidth dominates cost.
  • Design an upload path that bypasses the application servers and survives flaky networks.
  • Build a transcoding pipeline as a DAG of idempotent, queue-driven tasks.
  • Explain adaptive bitrate streaming: renditions, segments, manifests and how the player switches.
  • Design delivery with a CDN, an origin shield and a strategy for the popularity long tail.

items.title: 1. Clarify the requirements
items.text: (interview framework)

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text:
1. Creators upload videos (up to a few GB) from web and mobile, and see processing progress.
  2. The platform transcodes each upload into several resolutions and formats, with thumbnails.
  3. Viewers watch with smooth playback that adapts to their connection; they can seek.
  4. Basic metadata: title, description, owner; view counts.

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.text: Quality Target Playback Start in < 2 s; rebuffering rare (it is the metric viewers feel) Scale 50 M daily viewers, 30 min/day each; 500 k uploads/day Processing time A 10-minute video playable within minutes of upload (low resolutions first) Availability 99.99% for playback; uploads may be retried Durability Originals never lost (11 nines-class object storage) Cost Bandwidth is the largest bill: design for cache hit ratio and efficient encoding

items.title: Out of scope (say it explicitly)
items.text:
Recommendations, comments, monetization/ads, live streaming (a follow-up), copyright detection (mention it as an asynchronous step), DRM details.

Questions to ask the interviewer Question Why it matters Video on demand only, or live too? Live has seconds of budget: no time for a full transcoding pipeline. Max upload size and duration? Multipart/resumable uploads, chunked transcoding. Which devices? Formats (HLS for Apple, DASH elsewhere, CMAF for both), codecs (H.264 everywhere, AV1/HEVC where supported). Global audience? CDN footprint, multi-CDN, regional storage. Is it OK if high resolutions appear later than low ones? Lets you publish fast and finish the ladder in the background. How accurate must view counts be? Exact and real-time is expensive; approximate and delayed is cheap.

items.title: 2. Back-of-the-envelope estimates
items.text:
ResultSource quantity value unit egress_pb_day 33.75 PB/day concurrent 1,041,667 streams peak_streams 3,125,000 streams peak_tbps 9.38 Tbit/s origin_tb_day 1,688 TB/day raw_tb_day 375 TB/day encoded_tb_day 398 TB/day encode_workers 20,833 workers cdn_usd_day 337,500 USD/day 
# Video streaming: assumptions (illustrative; prices are placeholders, not quotes)
dau          = 50_000_000
watch_min    = 30            # minutes watched per viewer per day
bitrate_mbps = 3.0           # average delivered bitrate
peak_factor  = 3
uploads_day  = 500_000
video_min    = 10            # average upload duration
source_mbps  = 10            # bitrate of the uploaded original
ladder_mbps  = 10.6          # sum of all rendition bitrates (240p..1080p)
renditions   = 6
cdn_hit      = 0.95          # share of bytes served from CDN caches
usd_per_gb   = 0.01          # illustrative blended CDN price

egress_pb_day  = dau * watch_min * 60 * bitrate_mbps / 8 / 1e9
concurrent     = dau * watch_min / 1_440                   # Little's Law: viewers watching now
peak_streams   = concurrent * peak_factor
peak_tbps      = peak_streams * bitrate_mbps / 1e6
origin_tb_day  = egress_pb_day * 1e3 * (1 - cdn_hit)
raw_tb_day     = uploads_day * video_min * 60 * source_mbps / 8 / 1e6
encoded_tb_day = uploads_day * video_min * 60 * ladder_mbps / 8 / 1e6
encode_workers = uploads_day * video_min * renditions / 1_440   # 1 rendition-minute per worker-minute
cdn_usd_day    = egress_pb_day * 1e6 * usd_per_gb

rows = [
    ("egress_pb_day", egress_pb_day, "PB/day"), ("concurrent", concurrent, "streams"),
    ("peak_streams", peak_streams, "streams"), ("peak_tbps", peak_tbps, "Tbit/s"),
    ("origin_tb_day", origin_tb_day, "TB/day"), ("raw_tb_day", raw_tb_day, "TB/day"),
    ("encoded_tb_day", encoded_tb_day, "TB/day"), ("encode_workers", encode_workers, "workers"),
    ("cdn_usd_day", cdn_usd_day, "USD/day"),
]
print("| quantity | value | unit |\n|---|---:|---|")
for name, value, unit in rows:
    v = f"{value:,.0f}" if abs(value) >= 100 else f"{value:,.2f}"
    print(f"| `{name}` | {v} | {unit} |")

What the numbers tell us:

  • Viewers pull ~34 PB per day, ~9 Tbit/s at peak. No data center serves that from a few servers. ⇒ the CDN delivers the bytes, close to viewers; our origin must only see the misses.
  • Even with a 95% CDN hit ratio, the origin (object storage) serves ~1.7 PB/day ⇒ an origin shield (a mid-tier cache) between the CDN edges and storage, so that a miss in 300 edge locations becomes one fetch.
  • Uploads add ~375 TB/day of originals and ~400 TB/day of encoded renditions ⇒ object storage with lifecycle rules (move old, rarely watched renditions to colder tiers; keep originals in archive storage to re-encode later).
  • Transcoding needs on the order of ~20 k encoding workers busy all day (under this illustrative speed). ⇒ elastic, queue-driven workers, ideal for cheap preemptible/spot capacity.
  • With an illustrative price of 1 cent per GB, delivery costs hundreds of thousands of dollars per day: every percent of bitrate saved by better encoding or every percent of cache hit ratio is real money. ⇒ the "boring" optimizations (codec choice, per-title encoding) are architecture.

items.title: 3. API
items.text:
POST /v1/videos                                   → 201 {videoId, uploadId, partSize, partUrls[]}
     {"title": "Rock in Rio 2027 — official trailer", "sizeBytes": 734003200, "contentType": "video/mp4"}
PUT  <pre-signed partUrl #n>   (bytes of part n, straight to object storage) → 200 ETag
POST /v1/videos/{videoId}/complete  {"parts": [{"n": 1, "etag": "…"}, …]}   → 202 {status: PROCESSING}
GET  /v1/videos/{videoId}                          → 200 {status: PROCESSING|READY|FAILED,
                                                          progress, manifestUrl, thumbnails[]}

GET  https://cdn.example/vod/{videoId}/master.m3u8         (manifest, from the CDN)
GET  https://cdn.example/vod/{videoId}/720p/seg_00042.m4s  (segment, from the CDN)

POST /v1/events/playback   [{"videoId": "…", "type": "start|heartbeat|rebuffer|end", "ts": …}]  → 202
  • The application never proxies video bytes: it signs URLs. The object store and the CDN do the heavy lifting.
  • Multipart upload: the file is split into parts (e.g. 8–64 MB) uploaded in parallel and retried independently; complete assembles them. A dropped connection costs one part, not the whole file.
  • Playback beacons are batched and asynchronous: they feed view counts and quality metrics (startup time, rebuffering).

items.title: 4. Data model
items.text:
CREATE TABLE video (
    video_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    owner_id     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    title        TEXT        NOT NULL,
    status       TEXT        NOT NULL,   -- UPLOADING | PROCESSING | READY | FAILED | BLOCKED
    duration_s   INT,
    source_key   TEXT,                   -- raw/{video_id}/source.mp4
    manifest_key TEXT,                   -- vod/{video_id}/master.m3u8
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE transcode_task (
    video_id   UUID,
    task       TEXT,                     -- 'split', 'encode:720p:chunk-007', 'package', 'thumbs'
    status     TEXT NOT NULL,            -- PENDING | RUNNING | DONE | FAILED
    attempts   INT  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    output_key TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (video_id, task)
);

# Object storage layout
raw/{video_id}/source.mp4                    original, kept (archive tier after 30 days)
vod/{video_id}/master.m3u8                   master manifest (lists renditions)
vod/{video_id}/{rendition}/index.m3u8        media playlist per rendition
vod/{video_id}/{rendition}/seg_00001.m4s     ~4 s segments (CMAF fragments)
thumbs/{video_id}/{n}.jpg
Data Store Why Originals, segments, thumbnails Object store (objstore) Huge, immutable blobs; cheap, durable, served via CDN Video metadata, task state SQL (sql) Small, relational, status transitions View counts, playback metrics Stream → NoSQL counters (nosql) and analytics (analytics) Very high write rate, approximate is fine Transcoding work Queue (queue) Spreads tasks over elastic workers; retries Delivery CDN (cdn) with origin shield Bytes close to viewers; protects the origin

items.title: 5. High-level design
items.text:
flowchart LR
    cr([Creator]) --> api["Video API"]
    api --> meta[("Metadata<br/>SQL")]
    cr -. "parts via<br/>pre-signed URLs" .-> raw[("Object store<br/>raw/")]
    raw -. upload completed .-> q[["Transcode queue"]]
    q --> w["Transcoding workers<br/>split · encode · package"]
    w --> vod[("Object store<br/>vod/")]
    w --> meta
    v([Viewer]) --> cdn["CDN edge"]
    cdn --> shield["Origin shield"]
    shield --> vod
    v -. playback beacons .-> an["Analytics<br/>views, QoE"]

Upload to first playback:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Creator app
    participant A as Video API
    participant S as Object store
    participant Q as Queue
    participant W as Workers
    participant V as Viewer
    participant E as CDN
    C->>A: POST /videos (size, type)
    A-->>C: videoId + pre-signed part URLs
    C->>S: PUT parts in parallel (retry failed parts)
    C->>A: POST /complete
    A->>Q: enqueue split(videoId)
    Q->>W: split into chunks, enqueue encode tasks
    W->>S: write 240p/360p first → status READY
    W->>S: write 720p/1080p later, update manifest
    V->>E: GET master.m3u8, then segments
    E->>S: miss → fetch once via shield
    E-->>V: segments (cached for everybody)

items.title: 6.1 Uploads that bypass the application
items.text:
• Pre-signed URLs: the API authorizes the upload and returns URLs that let the client PUT directly into the object store for a few minutes. App servers handle kilobytes of JSON, never gigabytes of video (object storage).
  • Multipart and resumable: parts upload in parallel and are retried individually; the client stores uploadId so it can resume after the app is closed. Incomplete uploads are cleaned up by a lifecycle rule.
  • Integrity and safety: a checksum per part; after complete, an asynchronous step validates the container, scans for malware and runs content checks before publishing.
  • Upload close to the user: object stores offer accelerated/edge ingestion; for a global audience, upload to the nearest region and replicate.

items.title: 6.2 Transcoding as a DAG of tasks
items.text:
Encoding a 2-hour video on one machine takes too long. Split it, encode the pieces in parallel, put them back together:

flowchart LR
    src["source.mp4"] --> split["Split into<br/>~10 s chunks<br/>(at keyframes)"]
    split --> e1["encode 240p…1080p<br/>chunk 1"]
    split --> e2["encode 240p…1080p<br/>chunk 2"]
    split --> e3["encode 240p…1080p<br/>chunk N"]
    src --> th["Thumbnails"]
    src --> au["Audio tracks"]
    e1 --> pkg["Package<br/>HLS / DASH (CMAF)"]
    e2 --> pkg
    e3 --> pkg
    au --> pkg
    pkg --> pub["Publish<br/>manifest + status"]
    th --> pub
  • Queue-driven: each node of the DAG is a task message; a small orchestrator (or a workflow engine) enqueues a task when its inputs are ready (async work).
  • Idempotent tasks: a task writes to a deterministic key (vod/{id}/720p/chunk-007) — running it twice produces the same object, so retries and duplicate deliveries are harmless.
  • Prioritize: encode low resolutions first and publish as soon as they exist; higher rungs and expensive codecs (AV1) follow. Popular creators or BoxOffice's official trailers can go to a high-priority queue.
  • Elastic and cheap: encoding is CPU/GPU-bound and restartable — run it on autoscaled preemptible instances; a preempted task is simply retried.

items.title: 6.3 Adaptive bitrate streaming
items.text:
Each video is encoded into a ladder of renditions, each cut into short segments (2–6 s). The player downloads a manifest that lists the renditions, measures its throughput and buffer, and picks the rendition of the next segment — switching up or down without stopping (HLS, MPEG-DASH).

Rendition Resolution Bitrate (H.264, illustrative) Typical network 240p 426×240 0.4 Mbit/s Weak mobile 360p 640×360 0.8 Mbit/s 3G / congested 480p 854×480 1.4 Mbit/s Average mobile 720p 1280×720 3.0 Mbit/s Good mobile / Wi-Fi 1080p 1920×1080 5.0 Mbit/s Wi-Fi / broadband 2160p (4K) 3840×2160 ~15 Mbit/s (less with HEVC/AV1) Fast broadband, TVs 
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:7
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360,CODECS="avc1.4d401e,mp4a.40.2"
360p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=3000000,RESOLUTION=1280x720,CODECS="avc1.4d401f,mp4a.40.2"
720p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080,CODECS="avc1.640028,mp4a.40.2"
1080p/index.m3u8
  • Start low, climb fast: the first segment comes from a low rung so playback starts in under 2 s; the player climbs as its buffer fills.
  • Per-title encoding: a cartoon needs far fewer bits than a concert with confetti and strobes for the same visual quality. Analyzing each video and choosing its own ladder (Netflix's "per-title encode optimization") saves a large share of bandwidth for simple content.
  • Codecs: H.264 plays everywhere; HEVC and AV1 deliver the same quality with notably fewer bits but cost much more CPU to encode and are not supported on every device. Encode the expensive codecs only for videos that get enough views to pay for it.

items.title: 6.4 Delivery: CDN, shield and the long tail
items.text:
• CDN edges cache manifests and segments near viewers. Segments are immutable (new content = new key), so they can be cached for a long time without invalidation (DNS and CDN).
  • Origin shield: one regional cache layer in front of the object store; all edges miss to the shield, which misses to the origin at most once per object — essential for a video that goes viral minutes after upload.
  • Popularity is a long tail: a small fraction of videos gets most views. Push (pre-position) the head to edges ahead of demand — e.g. BoxOffice's trailer before a tour announcement — and let the long tail be pulled on demand, accepting a slower first start.
  • Multi-CDN and ISP-embedded caches (as Netflix does with Open Connect) are the next steps at very large scale, for cost and resilience.
  • View counts come from playback beacons through a stream into aggregated counters, deduplicated per session and filtered for bots; exact real-time counts are not needed.

In the interview

Say early: "The bytes never go through my servers: uploads go to object storage with pre-signed URLs, and playback comes from the CDN. My servers handle metadata, orchestration and signatures." It shows you found the real bottleneck.

items.title: 7. Bottlenecks, failure modes and trade-offs
items.text:
Where What goes wrong Mitigation Trade-off Egress bandwidth Cost and capacity explode CDN, high hit ratio, efficient codecs, per-title encoding Encoding CPU cost; device support Viral new video Cold CDN: all edges miss together Origin shield, request collapsing, pre-positioning Shield is one more tier Upload over bad networks Large uploads fail at 95% Multipart + resumable uploads Client complexity Transcoding backlog Upload spike; videos stuck in PROCESSING Autoscale on queue depth, priorities, publish low rungs first Cost of extra workers; HD appears later Worker failure / preemption Task lost mid-encode Idempotent tasks with deterministic outputs; retries with attempt limit; DLQ Wasted partial work Poison input Corrupt file crashes encoders repeatedly Validation step; DLQ after N attempts; mark FAILED and tell the creator Some uploads rejected Rebuffering Player picks too-high rendition ABR with buffer-based logic; short segments; more low rungs More segments/requests Storage growth Hundreds of TB/day Lifecycle tiers; drop rarely watched high rungs and re-encode on demand from the original Slower first view for old videos

The trade-offs to say out loud: encoding cost vs. delivery cost (spend CPU once to save bandwidth on every view — worth it only for videos that get watched), time to publish vs. completeness (low resolutions first), and push vs. pull to the edge (pre-position the head, pull the tail).

items.title: 8. Try it in the playground
items.text:
The video-streaming scenario has the object store, a CDN in front of it, and a queue of transcoding workers fed by uploads.

Try it

  1. Run with the load profile and look at the CDN hit ratio and the egress from the object store (origin).
  2. Lower the CDN hit ratio (or remove the CDN): how much more traffic does the origin take? That is why the shield and pre-positioning exist.
  3. Switch to spike to simulate an upload wave: watch the transcoding queue grow; add workers and find how many keep the backlog flat.
  4. Turn chaos on to kill workers mid-task: does the queue redeliver, and do retries finish the videos?

Open the full playground

items.title: 9. Follow-up questions an interviewer asks
items.text:
What changes for live streaming (e.g. a BoxOffice livestreamed concert)?

The budget drops from minutes to seconds. The encoder ingests a live feed (RTMP/SRT/WebRTC) and produces the ladder in real time — no chunk-parallel DAG; segments are published as they are produced, and playlists are updated continuously. Low-latency HLS / chunked CMAF deliver partial segments to reach a few seconds of glass-to-glass latency. The CDN still carries the bytes, and the audience spike at the show's start is predictable, so pre-warm capacity. A replay is just the recorded segments turned into VOD.

A creator's video goes viral ten minutes after upload. What happens?

Only low resolutions may exist yet; the higher rungs are being encoded — bump the video to the high-priority queue. On delivery, every CDN edge misses at once: the origin shield and request collapsing (one fetch for many concurrent misses of the same segment) protect the object store. Manifests have short TTLs so new renditions appear; segments are immutable and cached long.

How do you reduce the delivery bill?

In order of impact: raise the cache hit ratio (shield, pre-positioning, longer TTLs for immutable segments); spend fewer bits per view (per-title encoding, HEVC/AV1 for popular videos, capping resolution on small screens); negotiate or mix CDNs; and at very large scale, place caches inside ISPs. Measure cost per hour watched as the metric.

How do you count views accurately?

Define a view (e.g. ≥ 30 s watched), send batched beacons, deduplicate per session/device in the stream, filter bots and replays, aggregate into counters asynchronously. Show an approximate, slightly delayed count publicly; keep the exact, audited count for payments to creators.

Do you keep the original upload? Why?

Yes, in cheap archive storage. Codecs improve (H.264 → HEVC → AV1) and ladders change; re-encoding from the original gives better quality than transcoding an already compressed rendition. It also allows dropping rarely watched renditions and recreating them on demand.

How do you protect premium content?

Signed URLs or tokens with short expiry on manifests (the CDN validates them at the edge), and DRM (Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady) encrypting segments with keys delivered by a license server only to authorized players. It adds a license-server dependency to playback start, so it must be highly available.

items.title: 10. Self-assessment rubric
items.text:
Level What the answer contains Junior Upload through the app server into storage; serve the file through the app or a CDN; a videos table. One format, no adaptation. Mid Pre-signed uploads to object storage; queue + transcoding workers producing several resolutions; HLS/DASH with a CDN; metadata in SQL; asynchronous view counts. Senior Quantifies egress and cost; multipart/resumable uploads; chunked DAG pipeline with idempotent tasks, priorities and low-rungs-first publishing; ABR mechanics and per-title encoding; codec trade-offs; origin shield, request collapsing, pre-positioning of the head vs. pulling the tail; storage lifecycle; live-streaming differences.

Related: DNS and CDN, Specialized storage (object stores), Async work, FinOps, Hands-on 7 (queues and workers).

items.title: Index
items.text:
BoxOffice runs on a laptop: nine services, PostgreSQL, Redis and Kafka, all started with one docker compose up. Then reality arrives. On a normal Tuesday the platform serves a few hundred requests per second; on the morning a stadium show goes on sale it must absorb twenty times that for thirty minutes, and shrink back afterwards so nobody pays for idle machines. The team wants to ship a fix to inventory at 09:55 without taking the site down at 10:00, and to know before the invoice arrives how much the whole thing costs.

None of these is an application problem. They are platform problems: where the code runs, how it gets there, how it scales, and who pays for it. This class is about the set of practices and tools — containers, Kubernetes, infrastructure as code, continuous delivery, GitOps, progressive delivery and FinOps — that the industry calls cloud-native.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Explain what "cloud-native" means and which properties of an application (stateless processes, configuration in the environment, disposability) make it portable across platforms.
  • Map each BoxOffice component to a service model (IaaS, CaaS, PaaS, FaaS, DBaaS, SaaS) and justify the trade-off between control and operational effort.
  • Build a small, secure container image for a Java service and describe what an OCI image is made of.
  • Write the Kubernetes manifests (Deployment, Service, probes, resources, HPA, PodDisruptionBudget, Ingress) that run a BoxOffice service, and predict what the control plane does when a pod dies.
  • Design a delivery pipeline — infrastructure as code, CI, GitOps and a canary rollout gated by metrics — and choose a deployment strategy for a given risk.
  • Estimate the monthly cost of the BoxOffice architecture, identify its fixed and variable costs, and propose optimizations backed by numbers.

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
1. This overview — what cloud-native means, the twelve-factor properties, service models and platform engineering.
  2. Containers — namespaces and cgroups, OCI images and layers, a production Dockerfile for a Spring Boot service, supply-chain hygiene.
  3. Kubernetes — the control loop, the core objects, probes, resources, autoscaling (HPA, cluster autoscaling, KEDA) and BoxOffice's manifests.
  4. Delivery — Terraform/OpenTofu, GitHub Actions, GitOps with Argo CD, deployment strategies and a canary with automated metrics analysis.
  5. FinOps — cloud pricing models, a cost model of BoxOffice, unit economics and how to cut the bill.
  6. Quiz — check your understanding.

items.title: What "cloud-native" means
items.text:
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) defines cloud-native technologies as those that "empower organizations to build and run scalable applications in modern, dynamic environments such as public, private, and hybrid clouds", citing containers, service meshes, microservices, immutable infrastructure and declarative APIs as the typical building blocks1. Stripped of the marketing, the definition rests on four ideas:

Idea What it means BoxOffice example Immutable artifacts You never patch a running server; you build a new image and replace the old instances inventory:1.8.3 is built once and promoted unchanged from staging to production Declarative desired state You describe what you want (5 replicas of catalog), and a controller continuously makes reality match Kubernetes restarts a crashed order pod without anyone being paged Elasticity Capacity follows demand, automatically, in minutes or seconds catalog goes from 4 to 40 replicas during the flash sale and back to 4 at lunch Automation end to end Infrastructure, builds, tests, deploys and rollbacks are code, versioned in Git A merged pull request reaches production through a pipeline, not a checklist

The opposite is a pet server: a machine with a name, configured by hand over years, that nobody dares to reboot. Cloud-native systems treat instances as cattle — numbered, identical and replaceable. The phrase is an old operations joke, but it captures the shift: an instance failure becomes a routine event handled by software, not an incident handled by people.

items.title: The application has to cooperate
items.text:
A platform can only restart, move and multiply a process that allows it. The Twelve-Factor App methodology, written by Heroku engineers in 2011, lists the properties that make an application portable across platforms2. Six of the twelve matter most for this class:

Factor Rule What breaks if you ignore it III. Config Configuration (URLs, credentials, feature switches) comes from the environment, not from the code One image per environment; secrets end up in Git IV. Backing services PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka and the payment provider are attached resources, addressed by URL Moving from Compose to a managed database requires code changes VI. Processes Processes are stateless; state lives in backing services A user loses the cart when the pod holding it in memory is replaced IX. Disposability Start fast, shut down gracefully on SIGTERM Rolling updates drop in-flight requests; autoscaling reacts too slowly X. Dev/prod parity Keep development, staging and production as similar as possible "Works on my machine"; load tests that measure the wrong system XI. Logs Write logs to stdout as an event stream; the platform collects them Logs vanish with the container; disks fill up

BoxOffice: the seat hold that lived in memory

An early version of inventory kept seat holds in a ConcurrentHashMap inside the JVM. It worked with one instance. With three replicas behind a load balancer, a fan who held seat A-12 on replica 1 could see it as free on replica 2 — and during a rolling update every hold on the replaced pod disappeared. Moving holds to PostgreSQL (with an expiry column) or to Redis (with a TTL) made the service stateless (factor VI) and therefore safe to scale and to replace. See Databases — transactions for how the hold itself is made consistent.

items.title: Service models: who operates what
items.text:
Every component of BoxOffice has to run somewhere, and for each one the team chooses how much of the stack it operates itself. The NIST definition of cloud computing introduced three service models3; practice has added several more. All of them can be read on the same stack of layers:

Layer On-premises IaaS CaaS PaaS FaaS SaaS Data and access rules you you you you you you Application code you you you you you provider Runtime (JVM, Python) you you you (in the image) provider provider provider Container orchestration and scaling you you provider (control plane) provider provider provider Operating system you you shared (nodes) or provider (Fargate, Autopilot) provider provider provider Virtualization, hardware, data centre you provider provider provider provider provider
  • IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service. Virtual machines, disks and networks (Amazon EC2, Google Compute Engine, Azure VMs). Maximum control, maximum toil: you patch the OS, install the JDK, configure the firewall.
  • CaaS — Containers as a Service. You hand over container images; the provider runs the scheduler (Amazon EKS/ECS, Google GKE, Azure AKS). With serverless variants (AWS Fargate, GKE Autopilot) you do not see nodes at all.
  • PaaS — Platform as a Service. You hand over code or an image plus a little configuration; the platform builds, runs, scales and routes (Heroku, Google App Engine, Azure App Service, Railway, Fly.io).
  • FaaS — Functions as a Service. You hand over a function; the platform runs it per event and bills per invocation and millisecond (AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Run functions, Azure Functions). Scales to zero, but has cold starts and concurrency limits (see Compute — serverless and autoscaling).
  • DBaaS — Database as a Service. Managed databases (Amazon RDS/Aurora, Cloud SQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL): backups, failover, patching and replicas are buttons, not projects.
  • SaaS — Software as a Service. A finished product used through an API or a browser: the payment provider, the e-mail provider, the observability vendor.

The rule that never changes, in any column: your data, your identities and access rules, and your configuration remain your responsibility4. A public S3 bucket is a customer mistake, not a provider failure.

items.title: BoxOffice, component by component
items.text:
There is no single "right" model for a whole system. Each component gets the model that minimizes total effort for the control it needs:

Component Palette Chosen model Why Alternative gateway, catalog, inventory, order, search services App Server CaaS (managed Kubernetes) Many services, shared tooling, fine control of scaling and rollout PaaS while the team is small Seat inventory and orders SQL Database DBaaS (managed PostgreSQL, Multi-AZ) Backups and failover are hard to get right; the data is the business Self-managed on Kubernetes with an operator — only with a strong DBA team Holds, sessions, hot catalog pages Cache DBaaS (managed Redis-compatible) Same reasons; the cache is on the critical path Redis in a pod (dev only) Events (orders, notifications) Kafka Managed Kafka (Amazon MSK, Confluent Cloud) Running Kafka well is a specialty Strimzi operator on Kubernetes Ticket PDFs, event images Object Store IaaS-level storage service (S3, GCS, Blob) Practically unlimited, cheap, durable — Image thumbnails, webhook receivers Serverless FaaS Bursty, event-driven, idle most of the time A worker deployment Card payments Payment SaaS (payment provider) Card data compliance (PCI DSS) is not BoxOffice's core business — Transactional e-mail Email SaaS Deliverability and reputation are a business of their own — Think first: why not run everything on FaaS and never think about servers again?

Three reasons. (1) Long-lived connections and pools: inventory keeps a warm connection pool to PostgreSQL; thousands of short-lived function instances would each open their own connections and exhaust the database (a proxy such as RDS Proxy mitigates this). (2) Cold starts and concurrency limits hurt exactly at the flash-sale peak, when the platform must scale from almost nothing to thousands of concurrent executions in seconds. (3) Cost at steady load: per-request billing is cheap for spiky, mostly idle work, but a service busy 24/7 is usually cheaper on always-on containers. The FinOps page computes the break-even point.

Try it: open the scenario below and press Run with the spike profile. Watch the number of serverless instances, the cold-start latency at the beginning of the spike, and what happens to the error rate when the concurrency limit is reached. Then raise the limit (or enable provisioned concurrency) and run again.

Open the full playground to change the components yourself.

items.title: Platform engineering
items.text:
With fifteen services, three environments and five teams, every team rediscovering how to write a Dockerfile, a Helm chart, a pipeline and an alert is wasteful. Platform engineering answers with an internal developer platform (IDP): a product, built by a platform team for the other engineering teams, that offers golden paths — paved, supported ways of doing common things5.

flowchart LR
    dev["Product team<br/>(order, inventory…)"] -->|"uses"| portal["Developer portal<br/>(e.g. Backstage)"]
    portal --> tmpl["Service template<br/>Dockerfile · manifests · pipeline"]
    portal --> env["Self-service environments<br/>(namespace, database, queue)"]
    portal --> obs["Built-in observability<br/>dashboards · SLO alerts"]
    tmpl --> plat["Platform: Kubernetes · Argo CD · Terraform modules · policies"]
    env --> plat
    obs --> plat

A good golden path is optional but attractive: a new BoxOffice service created from the template gets a hardened image, Kubernetes manifests with probes and resource limits, a CI pipeline with tests and image scanning, a canary rollout, a RED dashboard and an SLO alert — on day one. The team can leave the path when it has a reason; most never need to.

Approach Strength Risk Every team does its own operations ("you build it, you run it") Autonomy, ownership Duplicated effort, uneven quality, high cognitive load Central operations team receives tickets Consistency Becomes a bottleneck; slow lead time Platform team offers self-service golden paths Autonomy and consistency The platform must be treated as a product with users — otherwise it becomes the ticket queue again

In the interview

Cloud-native details rarely drive a system-design interview, but they show maturity in the wrap-up. Spend one or two sentences on them: "Services are stateless containers on managed Kubernetes with an HPA on CPU and requests per second; the database is managed PostgreSQL Multi-AZ; we deploy through GitOps with canaries gated on the p99 and error-rate SLOs; at peak the cost is dominated by X." If asked "why not serverless?", answer with connection pools, cold starts at the peak and steady-load cost, not with taste.

Common pitfalls

  • Lift-and-shift and call it cloud-native: moving a stateful VM image into a container changes nothing about disposability or elasticity.
  • Kubernetes for a team of two: a PaaS gives the same benefits with far less operational load until the service count and scale justify the cluster.
  • Ignoring the fixed costs: control planes, load balancers and NAT gateways bill by the hour with zero traffic.
  • Snowflake environments: staging built by hand differs from production, and every test result becomes doubtful.
  • Forgetting that the data is yours: managed services do not decide who may read your tables or buckets.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Cloud-native = immutable artifacts + declarative desired state + elasticity + automation; the application must be stateless and disposable for the platform to help.
