items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Cloud-native and service models
items.text:
Q1. An early version of BoxOffice's inventory kept seat holds in a map inside the JVM. Which twelve-factor property did it violate, and what was the visible symptom with three replicas?

  • A. Config — the database URL was hard-coded, so replicas used different databases
  • B. Processes (stateless) — a hold made on one replica was invisible to the others and was lost when that pod was replaced
  • C. Logs — holds were written to a local file that filled the disk
  • D. Dev/prod parity — the map behaved differently in production
Answer

B — Processes must be stateless.

State kept in process memory ties a user to one instance. Behind a load balancer the next request may go to another replica, and any restart, rolling update or scale-in destroys the state. Moving holds to PostgreSQL (with an expiry) or Redis (with a TTL) makes every replica equivalent and disposable.

Q2. For which BoxOffice component is SaaS the most defensible service model?

  • A. The inventory service
  • B. The seat-inventory database
  • C. Card payment processing
  • D. The Kubernetes worker nodes
Answer

C — Card payments.

Handling card data brings heavy compliance obligations (PCI DSS), fraud detection and banking integrations that are not BoxOffice's core business. A payment provider offers all of it as a product through an API. The inventory service and its database are the core of the business and stay under the team's control (CaaS and DBaaS).

Q3. Which responsibility stays with the customer in every service model, including SaaS?

  • A. Patching the operating system
  • B. Deciding who may access the data, and the configuration of the service
  • C. Replacing failed disks
  • D. Scaling the runtime
Answer

B — Data access and configuration.

The provider may operate everything from the hardware to the application, but it cannot decide who in your organization should read which data, or whether a bucket should be public. Most cloud data leaks are configuration mistakes on the customer side.

items.title: Containers
items.text:
Q4. Two containers run on the same host. What do they share that two virtual machines on the same host would not share?

  • A. The CPU
  • B. The physical memory
  • C. The operating-system kernel
  • D. The network card
Answer

C — The kernel.

Containers are isolated processes (namespaces) with resource limits (cgroups) on a single shared kernel. VMs each boot their own kernel on a hypervisor. This is why containers start in milliseconds and are denser, and also why their isolation boundary is weaker — multi-tenant platforms wrap them in micro-VMs such as Firecracker or gVisor.

Q5. In the catalog Dockerfile, COPY pom.xml and mvn dependency:go-offline come before COPY src. Why?

  • A. Maven requires the POM to be in a separate layer
  • B. So that a code change invalidates only the later layers, and the dependency download is reused from the build cache
  • C. To make the final image smaller
  • D. Because distroless images do not support COPY src
Answer

B — Layer caching.

Each instruction produces a layer, and a layer is rebuilt only if its inputs (or a previous layer) changed. Dependencies change rarely; source code changes on every commit. Ordering from least to most frequently changing keeps the expensive steps cached. (Image size is reduced by the multi-stage build, not by this ordering.)

Q6. A team uses ENTRYPOINT java -jar app.jar (shell form). During every rolling update a few requests fail. What is the most likely cause?

  • A. The JVM starts too slowly
  • B. /bin/sh is PID 1, does not forward SIGTERM to Java, and the container is killed with SIGKILL after the grace period, dropping in-flight requests
  • C. The image is too large to pull in time
  • D. The readiness probe is too strict
Answer

B — Signals do not reach the JVM.

With the shell form, the shell becomes PID 1 and Java a child process that never sees SIGTERM, so Spring Boot's graceful shutdown never runs. The exec form (ENTRYPOINT ["java", …]) makes Java PID 1. Combine it with server.shutdown: graceful and a short preStop sleep so endpoints are updated before shutdown begins.

items.title: Kubernetes
items.text:
Q7. A node running two catalog pods loses power. Which mechanism brings the Deployment back to its 4 desired replicas?

  • A. The kubelet on the failed node restarts the pods when power returns
  • B. Controllers compare desired and actual state; the ReplicaSet controller creates new pods and the scheduler places them on healthy nodes
  • C. The HPA detects the CPU drop and scales up
  • D. Argo CD re-applies the manifests from Git
Answer

B — Reconciliation by controllers.

Kubernetes is a set of control loops. The node controller marks the node as not ready, its pods are eventually evicted, the ReplicaSet sees 2 actual vs 4 desired, creates two pods, and the scheduler binds them to nodes with free capacity. No human and no Git sync is required.

Q8. The readiness probe of inventory checks that PostgreSQL is reachable. PostgreSQL fails over and is unreachable for 20 seconds. What happens?

  • A. Only the pods connected to the old primary are removed from the Service
  • B. Every inventory pod becomes unready at the same time, the Service has no endpoints, and all requests fail — including those that a cache or a graceful error could have served
  • C. The pods are restarted, which speeds up recovery
  • D. Nothing, because readiness probes are ignored during failovers
Answer

B — A shared dependency makes all pods unready together.

Readiness should answer "can this pod serve traffic?". A dependency shared by all pods turns a 20-second database blip into a total outage of the service, with no chance of degraded responses. Keep readiness local (application started, warmed up, not overloaded), and handle dependency failures in the code (timeouts, circuit breakers, fallbacks). Putting the database in the liveness probe would be worse: it restarts every pod.

Q9. The HPA targets 60 % average CPU utilization. catalog has 5 pods at 96 %. How many replicas will the HPA request (ignoring min/max and stabilization)?

  • A. 6
  • B. 8
  • C. 10
  • D. 96
Answer

B — 8.

desired = ⌈current × current metric / target⌉ = ⌈5 × 96 / 60⌉ = ⌈8.0⌉ = 8. Note that the percentage is relative to the pods' CPU request: without requests, CPU utilization-based autoscaling cannot work.

Q10. A latency-sensitive Java service has a CPU limit of 1 core. Average CPU usage is 45 %, but p99 latency is high and spiky. What should you look at first?

  • A. The memory limit, because Java uses a lot of memory
  • B. CPU throttling: many threads can consume the 100 ms CFS quota early in each period and then wait, adding latency even at a low average
  • C. The number of replicas in the PodDisruptionBudget
  • D. The image size
Answer

B — CFS throttling.

A CPU limit is enforced per scheduling period (100 ms by default). Bursty multi-threaded work (request handling plus GC) can exhaust the quota early and stall for the rest of the period. The average looks fine; the tail does not. Check container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total; consider raising or removing the CPU limit while keeping the request.

items.title: Delivery and FinOps
items.text:
Q11. Which property distinguishes pull-based GitOps (Argo CD) from a CI job that runs kubectl apply?

  • A. GitOps only works with Helm
  • B. An agent inside the cluster continuously reconciles the cluster to the state in Git; CI never holds cluster credentials, and manual drift is detected or reverted
  • C. GitOps deploys faster because it skips tests
  • D. With GitOps you cannot roll back
Answer

B — Continuous, pull-based reconciliation.

The cluster pulls its desired state from Git, so the audit trail is git log, rollback is git revert, drift is visible, and the CI system — a frequent attack target — has no permission to change production.

Q12. A canary of order receives 5 % of 400 req/s. The baseline error rate is 0.1 %. Why is a 30-second canary step not enough to promote safely?

  • A. Because Argo Rollouts requires at least 10 minutes per step
  • B. Because 30 s at 20 req/s is only ~600 requests — too few to distinguish a small error-rate regression (e.g. 0.1 % → 0.2 %) from noise
  • C. Because the JVM needs 30 s to start
  • D. Because canaries must always receive 50 % of the traffic
Answer

B — Not enough samples.

At 0.1 % you expect fewer than one error in 600 requests in either version; detecting a doubling of a rare event needs many thousands of requests (≈ 18 000 for 80 % power in the page's estimate — about 15 minutes at 5 %). Large regressions show up quickly; small ones need time, more weight, or longer pauses.

Q13. A schema change renames orders.total to orders.amount_cents. Why should it not be shipped in the same release as the code that uses the new name?

  • A. Flyway cannot rename columns
  • B. During a rolling update or canary, old and new versions run side by side; the old version would break the moment the column is renamed. Use expand/contract: add the new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, drop the old column later
  • C. Renaming columns locks the table for hours in PostgreSQL
  • D. Because the canary analysis cannot read the database
Answer

B — Two versions coexist; the database does not roll back.

Any progressive strategy (rolling, canary, blue/green with a shared database) requires schema changes to be compatible with both the old and the new code. Expand/contract spreads a breaking change over several backward-compatible releases.

Q14. In the BoxOffice cost model, four 2-hour on-sales need 24 extra nodes. Why do they add so little to the monthly bill, and what is the lesson?

  • A. Because peak nodes are free on AWS
  • B. Because 24 nodes × 8 hours is a tiny fraction of 24 nodes × 730 hours; elastic capacity costs in proportion to the time it exists, so autoscaling and pre-scaling for known peaks beat provisioning for the peak permanently
  • C. Because the on-sales run on spot instances
  • D. Because the database handles the peak alone
Answer

B — You pay for capacity × time.

24 × $0.192 × 8 h ≈ $37, versus ≈ $3,364 per month to keep the same nodes always on. The economic case for elasticity is exactly this peak-to-average ratio. The same model shows that data services, CDN egress and log ingestion — not peak compute — dominate the bill.

Q15. Below which average traffic level is a pay-per-request function usually cheaper than two always-on container tasks behind a load balancer, in the page's model?

  • A. About 10 requests per second on average
  • B. About 1 000 requests per second
  • C. Functions are always cheaper
  • D. Containers are always cheaper
Answer

A — Around ten requests per second on average (with the page's assumptions).

Containers have a fixed monthly floor (tasks + load balancer) and a low marginal cost; functions have no floor and a higher cost per request. The crossing point depends on request duration, memory and the front door's per-request price, so recompute it for your workload — but the shape of the trade-off is general: low or very spiky traffic favours per-request pricing, steady load favours always-on capacity.

items.title: Index
items.text: The inventory service works on Ana's laptop with Java 21.0.4 and fails on Bruno's with Java 17; the staging server has a different time zone; production has an older libc. Every environment is a slightly different machine, and every difference is a bug waiting for a deploy. A container packages the application together with everything it needs to run — runtime, libraries, configuration defaults — into one immutable artifact that behaves the same on a laptop, in CI and in a Kubernetes cluster.

items.title: Containers are processes, not small VMs
items.text:
A virtual machine (VM) emulates hardware: each VM boots its own kernel on top of a hypervisor. A container is an ordinary Linux process that the kernel isolates and limits. All containers on a host share the host's kernel.

flowchart TB
    subgraph VMs["Virtual machines"]
        direction TB
        hw1["Hardware"] --> hv["Hypervisor"]
        hv --> g1["Guest OS kernel"] --> a1["catalog"]
        hv --> g2["Guest OS kernel"] --> a2["inventory"]
    end
    subgraph CT["Containers"]
        direction TB
        hw2["Hardware"] --> k["Host OS kernel<br/>namespaces + cgroups"]
        k --> c1["catalog<br/>(process)"]
        k --> c2["inventory<br/>(process)"]
    end

Two kernel features do the work4:

Feature What it does Example Namespaces Give the process its own view of the system: process IDs (pid), network interfaces (net), mount points (mnt), hostname (uts), users (user), IPC Inside the container, catalog is PID 1 and sees only its own files and its own eth0 Control groups (cgroups v2) Limit and account the resources the process can use: CPU time, memory, I/O, number of processes inventory may use at most 1 CPU and 1 GiB; above 1 GiB the kernel kills it (OOMKilled) Virtual machine Container Isolation boundary Hardware (hypervisor) — strong Kernel (namespaces) — weaker; one kernel bug affects all Start time Tens of seconds to minutes (boot an OS) Milliseconds to seconds (start a process) Size Gigabytes (a full OS) Megabytes to a few hundred MB Density per host Tens Hundreds Typical use Multi-tenant isolation, different kernels/OSes Packaging and running services

Because the isolation is weaker, cloud providers that run other customers' containers on shared hosts wrap them in lightweight VMs (AWS Firecracker under Lambda and Fargate, gVisor under Google Cloud Run). For your own services on your own nodes, plain containers are the norm.

The JVM must know it is in a container

A JVM that sizes its heap from the host's memory (64 GB) inside a container limited to 1 GiB will be killed by the kernel the first time it grows. Modern JVMs (Java 10+) read the cgroup limits; size the heap as a percentage of the container limit with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 and leave room for metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers.

items.title: What an image is
items.text:
An image is a read-only template from which containers are started. The Open Container Initiative (OCI) standardizes its format, so an image built with Docker runs on containerd, CRI-O or Podman1. An OCI image is:

  • a list of layers — compressed tar archives, each holding the file-system changes of one build step;
  • a config — environment variables, the default command, the user, exposed ports;
  • a manifest that lists the config and the layers by their digests (SHA-256 hashes of the content).
flowchart LR
    m["Manifest<br/>sha256:9f2c…"] --> cfg["Config<br/>ENTRYPOINT, USER, ENV"]
    m --> l1["Layer 1: base OS files<br/>(distroless / Alpine)"]
    m --> l2["Layer 2: Java runtime"]
    m --> l3["Layer 3: dependencies (jars)"]
    m --> l4["Layer 4: application classes"]

Layers are content-addressed and shared: ten BoxOffice services built on the same base image store and download the base layers once. When a container starts, the runtime stacks the read-only layers with an overlay file system and adds a thin writable layer on top — which disappears with the container. That is why state must live in volumes or backing services.

items.title: Tags move, digests do not
items.text: boxoffice/inventory:1.8.3 is a tag: a human-friendly pointer that anyone with push rights can move to another image. boxoffice/inventory@sha256:9f2c… is a digest: it identifies exactly one content. Production deployments should reference digests (or immutable tags enforced by the registry) so that "the image we tested" is provably "the image we run".

items.title: A production Dockerfile for a BoxOffice service
items.text:
The catalog service is a Spring Boot 4 application on Java 21. A naive Dockerfile copies the source and runs Maven inside the final image — producing a large image that contains the compiler, the Maven cache and the source code. A multi-stage build compiles in one stage and copies only the result into a minimal runtime stage2:

catalog/Dockerfile
# ---- build stage: JDK + Maven, discarded at the end ----
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /src
# 1. dependencies first: this layer is cached until pom.xml changes
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -q dependency:go-offline
# 2. then the source code, which changes on every commit
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -q package -DskipTests \
 && java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/catalog.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination target/extracted

# ---- runtime stage: only a JRE, no shell, non-root ----
FROM gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12:nonroot
WORKDIR /app
# Spring Boot layers: rarely-changing first, application classes last
COPY --from=build /src/target/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /src/target/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build /src/target/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /src/target/extracted/application/ ./
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
EXPOSE 8080
USER nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]

Each line has a reason:

Choice Effect Copy pom.xml and resolve dependencies before copying src A code change rebuilds only the last layers; CI builds drop from minutes to seconds Spring Boot layered jar extraction The ~60 MB of dependencies become a layer that changes rarely3; a deploy pushes only the few-hundred-KB application layer Distroless base image No shell, no package manager: smaller attack surface and fewer CVEs to patch (Alpine or eclipse-temurin:21-jre are common alternatives) USER nonroot A compromised process is not root inside the container MaxRAMPercentage=75 Heap follows the container memory limit ExitOnOutOfMemoryError A JVM in a bad state dies fast and is replaced, instead of limping Exec-form ENTRYPOINT (JSON array) Java runs as PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly, so graceful shutdown works

Add a .dockerignore (with target/, .git/, *.log, .env) so the build context sent to the builder stays small and secrets do not leak into layers.

docker build -t boxoffice/catalog:1.4.0 catalog/
docker image ls boxoffice/catalog            # check the size
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 --memory=512m --cpus=1 \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/catalog boxoffice/catalog:1.4.0

BoxOffice: what multi-stage bought us

With the naive single-stage image (JDK + Maven + sources) the team measured an image of roughly 800 MB; the multi-stage distroless image was under 250 MB, and a typical code change pushed a single small layer. Your numbers will differ — measure them with docker image ls and docker history — but the order of magnitude is typical. Smaller images matter for scaling speed: when the HPA adds 20 pods during the flash sale, each new node must pull the image before the pod can start.

items.title: Graceful shutdown: the other half of disposability
items.text:
When Kubernetes replaces a pod it sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 s by default), then sends SIGKILL. A service that dies instantly drops every in-flight request — including someone's payment. Spring Boot handles it with two properties:

catalog/src/main/resources/application.yaml
server:
  shutdown: graceful            # stop accepting, finish in-flight requests
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 20s

items.title: Registries and the supply chain
items.text:
Images are stored in a registry (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Harbor). Because an image is everything that will run in production, the path from source to registry — the software supply chain — is an attack target. The minimum hygiene for BoxOffice's pipeline5:

Practice Tool examples Protects against Scan images for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and fail on critical ones Trivy, Grype, registry scanning Shipping a base image with a known exploit Generate an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials: the list of every package in the image) Syft, docker buildx --sbom, CycloneDX, SPDX Not knowing whether you are affected by the next Log4Shell Sign images and verify the signature at deploy time Sigstore Cosign, Kyverno / admission policies A tampered image pushed to your registry Record provenance (who built what, from which commit) SLSA provenance attestations, GitHub artifact attestations An image built outside the pipeline Pin base images and dependencies; rebuild regularly Renovate, Dependabot Silent drift and stale patches

The Network & security class discusses supply-chain security in depth; the Delivery page wires these steps into the CI pipeline.

items.title: Docker Compose: the whole system on one machine
items.text:
Compose describes a multi-container application in one YAML file. For BoxOffice it is the local development and test environment, not the production platform:

compose.yaml (excerpt)
services:
  catalog:
    build: ./catalog
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/boxoffice
      SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST: redis
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits: { cpus: "1.0", memory: 512M }
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: boxoffice
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
    volumes: [ "pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data" ]
  redis:
    image: redis:8-alpine
volumes:
  pgdata: {}

Services find each other by service name (db, redis) through Compose's internal DNS — never localhost, which inside a container means the container itself. Compose has no multi-host scheduling, no self-healing across machines and no rolling updates; when you need those, you need an orchestrator — the subject of the next page.

items.title: Trade-offs
items.text:
Decision Option A Option B Rule of thumb Base image Distroless / minimal Full OS image (Debian, Ubuntu) Minimal in production; full image only when you need debugging tools inside (use ephemeral debug containers instead) Build Dockerfile Buildpacks (spring-boot:build-image), Jib Buildpacks/Jib give good layering without a Dockerfile; a Dockerfile gives full control Java startup JIT JVM GraalVM native image / CRaC Native images start in milliseconds and use less memory (good for FaaS and fast scale-out), at the cost of longer builds and reflection configuration Reference Tag Digest Digests (or immutable tags) in production

In the interview

Containers come up when you talk about deployment and scaling speed. Two crisp points are enough: "Services are packaged as immutable OCI images, promoted by digest from staging to production" and "new replicas start in seconds because images are small and layered — pull time matters when we scale out for the spike". If pressed on isolation, mention that containers share the kernel and that multi-tenant platforms add micro-VMs (Firecracker, gVisor).

Pitfalls

  • latest in production: you do not know what is running, and rollback is ambiguous.
  • Secrets baked into layers: a COPY .env or ARG PASSWORD stays in the image history forever — even if a later layer deletes the file.
  • Running as root and with a full shell: one RCE becomes a foothold.
  • No memory limit, or a heap larger than the limit: random OOMKilled restarts under load.
  • Shell-form ENTRYPOINT (ENTRYPOINT java -jar app.jar): sh becomes PID 1, swallows SIGTERM, and every deploy kills requests mid-flight.
  • Writing state to the container file system: it is gone at the next restart.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    NS["namespaces + cgroups"] --> CT["container =<br/>isolated process"]
    IMG["OCI image: layers,<br/>config, manifest"] --> CT
    IMG --> DIG["digest, not tag:<br/>build once, promote"]
    DIG --> DEL["CI and GitOps<br/>→ Delivery"]
    IMG --> SC["scan, SBOM, sign<br/>→ Network & security"]
    CT --> MEM["memory limit → OOMKilled<br/>JVM MaxRAMPercentage"]
    CT --> SIG["SIGTERM, graceful shutdown<br/>→ safe rolling updates"]
    MEM --> K8S["pods, probes, limits<br/>→ Kubernetes"]
    SIG --> K8S
    CMP["Docker Compose:<br/>local environment"] --> CT
    CT --> VM["Firecracker, gVisor<br/>under FaaS → Compute"]

Palette components: app (every BoxOffice service is an image) · worker · serverless (containers wrapped in micro-VMs). Scenarios: scale-out (small images start replicas fast), serverless-burst (cold starts). Continues in: Kubernetes, Delivery, Network & security — supply-chain security, Compute — serverless and autoscaling, Hands-on 1 — container.

  1. Open Container Initiative. OCI Image Format Specification. ↩

  2. Docker. Multi-stage builds and Dockerfile best practices. ↩

  3. Spring Boot reference. Efficient container images. ↩

  4. KERRISK, M. Namespaces in operation. LWN.net, 2013. ↩

  5. OpenSSF. SLSA — Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
It is 09:40 on on-sale day. A bug in inventory lets a seat hold expire two minutes early, and the fix is a one-line change. In a team without a delivery pipeline, the fix waits: someone must build it, someone must copy the jar, someone must restart servers one by one, and nobody wants to do that twenty minutes before the biggest traffic peak of the year. In a team with a good pipeline, the fix is merged, built, scanned, rolled out to 5 % of the traffic, checked automatically against the SLOs, and promoted — or rolled back — without a human touching a server.

This page builds that pipeline in four layers: the infrastructure is code, every change is integrated and tested continuously, the cluster pulls its desired state from Git, and each release is exposed gradually and judged by metrics.

flowchart LR
    pr["Pull request<br/>inventory fix"] --> ci["CI: build · test · scan<br/>SBOM · sign · push image"]
    ci --> cfg["Config repo:<br/>image digest bumped"]
    cfg --> argo["Argo CD:<br/>sync cluster to Git"]
    argo --> canary["Canary 5 % → 25 % → 50 %"]
    canary --> an{"Metrics analysis<br/>error rate, p99"}
    an -->|"healthy"| full["100 % — promoted"]
    an -->|"degraded"| rb["Automatic rollback"]

items.title: Infrastructure as code
items.text:
The BoxOffice production environment has a VPC, subnets, a Kubernetes cluster, a managed PostgreSQL, a managed Redis, a Kafka cluster, buckets, DNS records and IAM roles — a few hundred resources. Created by clicking in a console, they cannot be reviewed, reproduced or rebuilt after a disaster, and staging silently drifts away from production. Infrastructure as code (IaC) describes those resources in versioned files that a tool applies.

Property Why it matters for BoxOffice Declarative You write what should exist; the tool computes the create/update/delete plan Reviewable A change to the database instance size is a pull request with a diff and an approver Reproducible Staging and a load-test environment are the same modules with different variables — parity for performance tests Recoverable After a region loss, the environment is re-created from code (data comes from backups — see Disaster recovery)

Terraform (HashiCorp) is the most widely used IaC tool. In 2023 HashiCorp changed its license to the Business Source License; the community fork OpenTofu, hosted by the Linux Foundation, keeps the open-source MPL 2.0 license and the same language (HCL) and CLI workflow1. The snippet below works in both:

infra/modules/data/main.tf
variable "env"            { type = string }                 # "staging" | "prod"
variable "db_instance"    { type = string }                 # e.g. "db.r6g.large"
variable "private_subnets" { type = list(string) }

resource "aws_db_subnet_group" "boxoffice" {
  name       = "boxoffice-${var.env}"
  subnet_ids = var.private_subnets
}

resource "aws_db_instance" "inventory" {
  identifier                  = "boxoffice-inventory-${var.env}"
  engine                      = "postgres"
  engine_version              = "17"
  instance_class              = var.db_instance
  allocated_storage           = 100
  multi_az                    = var.env == "prod"           # standby in another AZ
  db_subnet_group_name        = aws_db_subnet_group.boxoffice.name
  username                    = "boxoffice"
  manage_master_user_password = true                        # password kept in Secrets Manager
  backup_retention_period     = 7
  deletion_protection         = var.env == "prod"
  tags = { project = "boxoffice", env = var.env, service = "inventory" }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "tickets" {
  bucket = "boxoffice-tickets-${var.env}"
  tags   = { project = "boxoffice", env = var.env }
}

output "inventory_endpoint" { value = aws_db_instance.inventory.endpoint }
infra/envs/prod/main.tf
terraform {
  backend "s3" {                                  # shared, locked state
    bucket       = "boxoffice-tfstate"
    key          = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "us-east-1"
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}

module "data" {
  source          = "../../modules/data"
  env             = "prod"
  db_instance     = "db.r6g.large"
  private_subnets = module.network.private_subnet_ids
}

tofu init          # download providers, configure the state backend
tofu plan          # show what would change — reviewed in the pull request
tofu apply         # apply exactly the reviewed plan

The tool keeps a state file mapping each resource in the code to a real resource ID. It must be remote and locked (two engineers applying at once corrupt it) and is sensitive (it may contain secrets). When someone changes a resource by hand, the next plan shows drift — a scheduled plan in CI that alerts on drift keeps the console honest.

Tool Style Notes Terraform / OpenTofu Declarative HCL, any provider The common default; huge provider ecosystem Pulumi General-purpose languages (TypeScript, Python, Go, Java) Loops and abstractions in a real language; same plan/apply model AWS CloudFormation / CDK, Azure Bicep, GCP Infrastructure Manager Provider-native No state file to manage; one cloud only Crossplane Kubernetes custom resources reconciled by controllers Infrastructure managed by the same GitOps loop as the applications

items.title: Continuous integration
items.text:
Continuous integration (CI) means every change is merged to the main branch frequently and verified automatically by building and testing it. Continuous delivery (CD) means every verified change is releasable at any time; continuous deployment goes one step further and releases every change automatically2.

BoxOffice's CI runs on GitHub Actions. On a pull request it builds and tests; on main it also publishes a signed image and proposes the new version to the configuration repository:

.github/workflows/inventory.yaml
name: inventory
on:
  pull_request: { paths: [ "inventory/**" ] }
  push:         { branches: [ main ], paths: [ "inventory/**" ] }

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write        # push to GitHub Container Registry
  id-token: write        # keyless signing with Sigstore
  attestations: write

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: "21", cache: maven }
      - name: Unit and integration tests (Testcontainers)
        run: mvn -B -f inventory/pom.xml verify
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with: { registry: ghcr.io, username: "${{ github.actor }}", password: "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" }
      - name: Build and push image
        id: push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: inventory
          push: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
          tags: ghcr.io/boxoffice/inventory:${{ github.sha }}
          sbom: true                      # SBOM attached to the image
          provenance: mode=max            # SLSA provenance
      - name: Scan for critical vulnerabilities
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.28.0
        with:
          image-ref: ghcr.io/boxoffice/inventory:${{ github.sha }}
          severity: CRITICAL
          exit-code: "1"
      - name: Sign image (keyless)
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/boxoffice/inventory@${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}

  propose-release:
    needs: build
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Bump the image digest in the config repo (staging overlay)
        run: |
          git clone https://x-access-token:${{ secrets.CONFIG_REPO_TOKEN }}@github.com/<your-org>/boxoffice-config.git
          cd boxoffice-config/apps/inventory/overlays/staging
          kustomize edit set image inventory=ghcr.io/boxoffice/inventory@${{ needs.build.outputs.digest }}
          git commit -am "inventory: ${{ github.sha }}" && git push

Notice what the pipeline does not do: it never runs kubectl apply against production and holds no cluster credentials. It only writes to Git. The cluster pulls. Hands-on 11 builds this workflow step by step and adds a k6 performance budget gate (see Capacity planning — performance budgets).

Keep CI fast

A pipeline that takes 40 minutes is a pipeline people bypass. Cache dependencies (cache: maven), run unit tests before slow integration tests, build images with layer caching, and run independent jobs in parallel. The DORA research associates short lead times with better stability, not worse3.

items.title: GitOps with Argo CD
items.text:
GitOps applies the Kubernetes control loop to delivery itself. The OpenGitOps principles are: the desired state is declarative, versioned and immutable (in Git), pulled automatically by an agent in the cluster, and continuously reconciled4.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Engineer
    participant Git as Config repo (Git)
    participant Argo as Argo CD (in the cluster)
    participant K8s as Kubernetes API
    Dev->>Git: PR "inventory → sha256:ab12…" (reviewed, merged)
    Argo->>Git: poll / webhook: new commit
    Argo->>K8s: diff desired vs live → apply
    K8s-->>Argo: resources healthy
    Note over Argo,K8s: someone runs kubectl edit by hand…
    Argo->>K8s: drift detected → reverted to Git (self-heal)
config/argocd/inventory-prod.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: inventory-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: boxoffice
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/<your-org>/boxoffice-config.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/inventory/overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: boxoffice
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true        # delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true     # revert manual changes
    syncOptions: [ CreateNamespace=true ]
Push-based CD (CI runs kubectl apply) Pull-based GitOps (Argo CD, Flux) Credentials CI holds cluster-admin credentials — a juicy target Only the in-cluster agent can change the cluster Drift Undetected until the next deploy Detected and optionally reverted continuously Audit trail Spread across CI logs git log of the config repo Rollback Re-run an old pipeline git revert Multi-cluster One pipeline step per cluster Each cluster pulls its own path

Promotion between environments becomes a pull request that copies the digest from overlays/staging to overlays/prod — reviewed, auditable and trivially reversible.

items.title: Deployment strategies
items.text:
Deploying (putting new code on servers) and releasing (exposing it to users) are different steps. The strategies below differ in how they separate them:

Strategy How Downtime Extra capacity Rollback Blast radius Recreate Stop all old, start all new Yes None Redeploy old (slow) 100 % Rolling update Replace pods a few at a time (maxSurge, maxUnavailable) No Small (surge) Roll forward/back gradually Grows with the rollout Blue/green Run the full new version beside the old; switch the router at once No 2× during switch Switch back — seconds 100 % at the switch, but instant undo Canary Send a small % of traffic to the new version, increase while metrics stay healthy No Small Set weight to 0 — seconds 1–5 % at first Shadow (mirroring) Copy live traffic to the new version; discard its responses No Up to 2× Nothing to roll back 0 % (beware side effects: payments!) Feature flags Deploy code dark; enable per user/segment at runtime No None Flip the flag Chosen segment

Rolling updates are the Kubernetes default and are enough for most changes. For risky changes on the purchase path — inventory, order, payment — BoxOffice uses canaries, and for product features feature flags (with a vendor-neutral API such as OpenFeature), which decouple deploy from release entirely: the code ships on Tuesday, the feature turns on for 1 % of fans on Thursday.

The database does not roll back

Two versions of order run side by side during any rolling update or canary, so every schema change must be backward compatible. Use expand/contract (parallel change): (1) expand — add the new column, nullable; (2) deploy code that writes both and reads the new one with a fallback; (3) backfill; (4) contract — drop the old column in a later release. Never rename or drop a column in the same release that stops using it.

items.title: Canary with automated metrics analysis
items.text:
A canary is only as good as the decision to promote it. Looking at a dashboard and "feeling fine" is not a decision. Argo Rollouts replaces a Deployment with a Rollout that shifts traffic in steps and runs an analysis at each step, querying the metrics backend and aborting automatically when the canary is worse than its thresholds5.

config/apps/inventory/base/rollout.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata: { name: inventory }
spec:
  replicas: 10
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: inventory } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: inventory } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: inventory
          image: ghcr.io/boxoffice/inventory@sha256:ab12c3d4e5f6
  strategy:
    canary:
      canaryService: inventory-canary
      stableService: inventory-stable
      trafficRouting:
        plugins:
          argoproj-labs/gatewayAPI: { httpRoute: inventory, namespace: boxoffice }
      analysis:                                  # runs in the background from step 1
        templates: [ { templateName: inventory-slo } ]
        startingStep: 1
      steps:
        - setWeight: 5
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
config/apps/inventory/base/analysis.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata: { name: inventory-slo }
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: error-rate
      interval: 1m
      failureLimit: 2                       # two bad minutes → abort and roll back
      successCondition: result[0] < 0.005   # < 0.5 % of requests fail
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{service="inventory-canary",status=~"5.."}[2m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{service="inventory-canary"}[2m]))
    - name: p99-latency
      interval: 1m
      failureLimit: 2
      successCondition: result[0] < 0.300   # p99 below 300 ms (the hold SLO)
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (
              rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket{service="inventory-canary"}[2m])))

items.title: How long must a canary run?
items.text:
A canary at 5 % sees few requests, and rare errors need many requests to become visible. Before choosing pause durations, estimate how many canary requests you need to tell a real regression from noise. The table uses the standard normal-approximation sample size for comparing two proportions (one-sided α = 5 %, power 80 %), with an illustrative baseline error rate of 0.1 % and 400 requests per second reaching inventory:

Regression to detect Canary requests needed Time at 5 % weight Time at 25 % weight 0.1% → 1.0% errors 835 0.7 min 0.1 min 0.1% → 0.5% errors 2,312 1.9 min 0.4 min 0.1% → 0.2% errors 18,527 15.4 min 3.1 min

Large regressions show up in a minute or two; a doubling of a small error rate needs a quarter of an hour at 5 %. That is why canary steps are measured in minutes, not seconds, why the analysis compares the canary with the stable baseline running at the same time (same traffic, same hour), and why low-traffic services are better served by longer pauses or synthetic traffic. Google's SRE workbook discusses these trade-offs in its chapter on canarying releases6.

BoxOffice: no canaries during the on-sale

Even with automated analysis, BoxOffice declares a change freeze on the purchase path from 30 minutes before an on-sale until it ends: the traffic is too unusual for the baseline to mean anything, and the cost of a bad rollout is highest. The 09:40 fix from the introduction is therefore deployed through an expedited canary (5 % → 100 % with a 5-minute analysis) at 09:42 — or it waits. Writing that rule down in advance is part of delivery engineering.

items.title: Measuring delivery: the DORA metrics
items.text:
The DORA research program (DevOps Research and Assessment) found four metrics that predict software-delivery performance and that move together in high-performing teams3:

Metric Question Throughput or stability Deployment frequency How often do we deploy to production? Throughput Lead time for changes How long from commit to running in production? Throughput Change failure rate What fraction of deployments cause a failure needing remediation? Stability Time to restore service How long to recover from such a failure? Stability

The key finding — speed and stability are not a trade-off — is the argument for everything on this page: small, frequent, automatically verified changes are both faster and safer than large, rare, manual ones.

items.title: AI in the pipeline
items.text: Pipelines increasingly include AI steps: automated pull-request review, generated tests, agents that propose fixes for failing builds, AI-assisted canary analysis, release notes and incident summaries — and the security and governance questions they raise. These are covered in their own class: AI-Assisted Delivery. The foundations on this page — reproducible builds, GitOps, metric-gated rollouts — are what make those AI steps safe to adopt.

items.title: Trade-offs
items.text:
Decision Choose A when… Choose B when… Rolling vs canary Low-risk change, good tests, fast rollback Critical path, hard-to-test behaviour under real traffic Blue/green vs canary You need an instant all-or-nothing switch (e.g. a protocol change) and can afford 2× capacity briefly You want to limit blast radius and judge with metrics Feature flag vs canary Exposing product behaviour to chosen users Validating a new build as a whole Monorepo pipeline vs per-service Shared tooling, atomic cross-service changes Independent teams and release cadences

In the interview

When the interviewer asks "how do you roll this out safely?", answer in layers: immutable images built once, GitOps so production equals Git, canary on the critical path with automatic rollback on SLO metrics (error rate and p99 compared with the baseline), feature flags for product changes, and expand/contract migrations so two versions can run side by side. Mention that canary duration depends on traffic volume — it shows you understand the statistics, not just the tool.

Pitfalls

  • Building a different artifact per environment: what you tested is not what you ship. Build once, promote by digest.
  • Canary without automated analysis: a human looking at graphs promotes everything.
  • Canary judged on CPU: judge on user-facing SLIs (errors, latency), compared with the stable baseline.
  • Shadowing a service with side effects: mirrored POST /payments charge real cards twice.
  • IaC state on a laptop: lost, unlocked or full of secrets.
  • Long-lived feature flags: every flag is a branch in the code; remove flags after the rollout.

items.title: Index
items.text:
The first real invoice of BoxOffice's production environment arrives, and it is three times the estimate. Nobody can say why: the costs are spread over forty line items, half of them have names like USE1-NatGateway-Bytes and DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes, and no resource is tagged with the service that created it. In the cloud, every architectural decision is also a purchasing decision — and the bill is the one metric that every executive reads.

FinOps (cloud financial operations) is the practice of bringing financial accountability to the variable spending model of the cloud, so that engineering, finance and business make trade-offs between speed, cost and quality together1. For a system designer it comes down to three skills: estimate what an architecture will cost, attribute what it actually costs, and optimize without breaking the SLOs2.

items.title: The FinOps lifecycle
items.text:
The FinOps Foundation organizes the practice in three phases that repeat continuously1:

flowchart LR
    inform["Inform<br/>visibility: tags, allocation,<br/>showback, unit costs"] --> optimize["Optimize<br/>rightsizing, commitments,<br/>spot, architecture changes"]
    optimize --> operate["Operate<br/>budgets, anomaly alerts,<br/>policies, reviews"]
    operate --> inform
  • Inform — you cannot optimize what you cannot see. Every resource carries tags (project, env, service, team); Kubernetes costs are split by namespace and label using the pods' resource requests (tools such as the CNCF project OpenCost4, or Kubecost). The result is showback (teams see their costs) or chargeback (teams are billed internally).
  • Optimize — reduce waste (idle and oversized resources) and pay less per unit (commitments, spot, cheaper architectures).
  • Operate — budgets with alerts, anomaly detection on daily spend, policies (no untagged resources, no GPU instances in dev), and a monthly cost review next to the SLO review.

items.title: Anatomy of a cloud bill
items.text: Cost type Billed by BoxOffice examples Watch out for Compute vCPU-hour and GB-hour (VMs, containers), or request + GB-second (FaaS) Kubernetes nodes, Lambda thumbnails Idle replicas, oversized requests Managed services Instance-hour + storage + I/O PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka Multi-AZ doubles the instance; replicas add up Storage GB-month, plus requests S3 ticket PDFs, database volumes, snapshots Snapshots and logs kept forever Data transfer GB moved CDN egress to fans, cross-AZ traffic between services, NAT processing Internet egress and cross-AZ traffic are charged; ingress usually is not Fixed hourly items Hour, whether used or not Kubernetes control plane, load balancers, NAT gateways, public IPv4 addresses They dominate small and non-production environments Observability GB ingested, retained, queried; active series Logs, metrics, traces High-cardinality metrics and debug logs in production Third-party SaaS Per transaction or per seat Payment fees (a percentage of the ticket price), e-mail per thousand Often larger than the whole infrastructure — but a business cost

items.title: Pricing models
items.text:
Model Discount vs on-demand Commitment Good for On-demand — None Spiky and unknown workloads; the reference price Commitments (AWS Savings Plans / Reserved Instances, GCP committed use discounts, Azure reservations) Substantial (often tens of percent) for 1 or 3 years Pay for a baseline whether you use it or not The steady baseline: the 6 always-on nodes, the databases Spot / preemptible Large, variable None, but the provider can reclaim the capacity with short notice (two minutes on AWS) Stateless, interruptible work: workers, batch, CI runners, part of the stateless fleet Serverless / per request — None Low or very spiky traffic; scale to zero

The usual portfolio is commit for the floor, on-demand for the daily wave, spot for the interruptible part — which only works if you know your baseline, i.e., after the Inform phase.

items.title: A cost model of BoxOffice
items.text:
The model below estimates the monthly bill of the production architecture designed in this course. Every number is an assumption you can change — that is the point of a model: it makes the drivers explicit and lets you ask "what if?". Prices are approximate on-demand list prices for AWS us-east-1; confirm them with the provider's calculator before quoting them, and remember that other regions (including sa-east-1, São Paulo) are more expensive.

Assumptions

  • Production only (staging and load-test environments are extra), running 24/7 (730 h per month).
  • Steady state: 6 worker nodes run all services. Four on-sales per month, each needing 24 extra nodes for 2 hours.
  • Not included: payment-provider fees, taxes, support plans, free tiers and discounts, cross-AZ transfer between services.
ComponentPaletteSizing (assumption)Steady $/monthOn-sale extraShareKubernetes control plane—1 cluster$73$01%Worker nodes (services)app6 × m6i.xlarge, +24 at peak$841$3717%PostgreSQL primary, Multi-AZsqldb.r6g.large ×2 + 2 × 200 GB$374$07%PostgreSQL read replicasqldb.r6g.large + 200 GB$187$04%Redis (primary + replica)cache2 × cache.r6g.large$301$06%Kafka (managed)kafka3 brokers + 3 × 500 GB$610$012%Load balancerlb1 ALB, ~5 LCU (×20 at peak)$46$61%NAT gatewaysnat3 AZs + 2 TB processed$189$04%Object storageobjstore500 GB tickets and images$12$00%CDN egresscdn20 TB/month$1,700$034%Logs ingestionlogs1 TB/month$500$010%Serverless thumbnailsserverless2 M runs × 0.5 s × 1 GB$17$00%Transactional e-mailemail1.5 M e-mails$150$03%Total$4,999$43100%

Total ≈ $5,042/month. The four on-sales add only $43 because the 24 extra nodes exist for 8 hours; keeping them 24/7 'just in case' would add ≈ $3,364/month. At 400,000 tickets per month the platform costs ≈ $0.013 per ticket sold.

2026-10-23T08:15:42.116838 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

items.title: Reading the model
items.text:
• The peak is cheap; the baseline is not. Elastic capacity for the on-sales costs almost nothing because it exists for eight hours. Provisioning for the peak permanently would cost more than the entire rest of the compute bill. This is the economic argument for autoscaling, pre-scaling and waiting rooms (Capacity planning).
  • Data services dominate compute. PostgreSQL, Redis and Kafka together cost more than the nodes running nine services. Before adding a fourth data store, ask whether an existing one can do the job.
  • Bytes cost more than CPUs. CDN egress and log ingestion are two of the largest lines. Image compression, longer cache lifetimes, sampling debug logs and shorter retention change the bill more than tuning Java.
  • Unit economics turns the bill into a business metric: cost per ticket sold (or per 1 000 requests, per active user). A bill that doubles while tickets triple is good news; a bill that grows while tickets are flat is a regression — track it like a performance regression.

items.title: Pay per request or pay per hour?
items.text:
When is FaaS cheaper than always-on containers? The plot compares a function (100 ms per request at 512 MB, behind an HTTP API front door) with a minimum of two small container tasks behind a load balancer, each serving 50 requests per second:

2026-10-23T08:15:42.273837 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Below roughly ten requests per second on average, paying per request wins — idle containers are pure waste. Above it, the per-request premium accumulates and always-on containers win, more so with commitments. Spiky traffic shifts the picture: what matters is the average, while containers must be sized for the peak (or autoscale). This is why BoxOffice runs the thumbnail generator and webhook receivers as functions and the purchase path as containers.

items.title: Optimization levers
items.text:
The levers below follow the cost-optimization practices of the cloud providers' well-architected frameworks3. Each one saves money and each one, except the last, can hurt an SLO if applied blindly.

Lever What to do Typical effect Risk to the SLOs Rightsizing Set requests from measured usage (e.g. p95 of CPU and max of memory over two weeks), not guesses Fewer nodes for the same pods Too tight → throttling and OOMKilled; re-run the load test Autoscaling and scale to zero HPA + node autoscaling; KEDA scale-to-zero for workers; turn off staging at night and weekends Non-production hours: 730 → ~250 per month Cold starts; scale-up lag at peaks Commitments Cover the measured baseline with 1-year commitments Lower unit price on the floor Paying for unused commitment if the architecture changes Spot capacity Run workers, CI and a share of stateless replicas on spot, spread across instance types Large discount on that share Interruptions: needs graceful shutdown, PDBs, on-demand fallback ARM instances Graviton/Axion/Ampere nodes for JVM and Python services (multi-arch images) Lower price per vCPU for similar performance on many workloads Verify with a benchmark; native libraries must exist for ARM Reduce data transfer CDN with long TTLs; keep chatty services in the same AZ; VPC endpoints for S3/ECR instead of NAT Lower egress and NAT processing Zone affinity reduces spreading Storage lifecycle Move old ticket PDFs to infrequent-access/archive tiers; expire snapshots Lower GB-month Slower, priced retrieval Observability hygiene Sample traces, drop debug logs in production, cap metric cardinality, shorter retention Lower ingestion bill Less detail when debugging — keep exemplars and error traces Delete idle resources Unattached volumes, old load balancers, forgotten test clusters Pure savings None

Cost and reliability pull in opposite directions

Multi-AZ doubles the database cost; a second region roughly doubles everything. Those are not waste — they buy availability. FinOps is not "spend less", it is "know what each dollar buys". Write the trade-off in the design document: "Multi-AZ PostgreSQL costs $187/month more and turns a zone failure from a multi-hour outage into a one-minute failover."

items.title: Estimating in a system-design interview
items.text:
Interviewers rarely want dollars, but cost-awareness is a strong signal. A three-step habit is enough:

  1. Name the drivers: "Cost is dominated by egress for images (CDN), the data tier, and peak compute."
  2. Order of magnitude from your capacity estimate: "30 nodes for 8 hours a month is cheap; 30 nodes for 730 hours is not — so we autoscale and pre-scale."
  3. One optimization with its trade-off: "Spot for workers, because they are idempotent and retry; never for the primary database."

In the interview

Cost questions often come disguised: "Do we really need Kafka here?", "Why three replicas?", "Could this be serverless?". Answer with utilization and peak-to-average ratio: always-on capacity is cheapest when it is busy; per-request pricing is cheapest when traffic is low or very spiky. Mention that data transfer and managed data stores usually dominate before compute does.

Pitfalls

  • No tags: costs that cannot be attributed cannot be owned or optimized.
  • Estimating compute only: the fixed hourly items, data transfer and observability are where surprises come from.
  • Rightsizing without a load test: the savings show up in the bill, the throttling shows up in the p99 at the next peak.
  • Commitments before measuring the baseline: locking in capacity for an architecture you are about to change.
  • Non-production environments running 24/7: often a large share of the total bill.
  • Optimizing cents while the NAT gateway processes terabytes: sort by cost before optimizing.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    BILL["the bill: compute, managed services,<br/>storage, transfer, fixed items"] --> INF["Inform: tags,<br/>cost by pod requests"]
    INF --> OPT["Optimize: rightsizing,<br/>commitments, spot, ARM"]
    OPT --> OPS["Operate: budgets,<br/>anomalies, monthly review"]
    BASE["baseline vs peak<br/>→ autoscaling, pre-scaling"] --> OPT
    FAAS["per request vs per hour<br/>→ serverless break-even"] --> OPT
    UNIT["unit economics:<br/>cost per ticket sold"] --> OPS
    OPT --> SLO["every lever can hurt an SLO<br/>→ Reliability"]
    OPT --> LT["re-run the load test<br/>→ Performance"]
    BILL --> MAZ["Multi-AZ, second region:<br/>cost that buys availability"]
    BILL --> OBS["observability bill:<br/>cardinality, retention"]

Palette components: sql · cache · kafka (the data tier dominates compute) · cdn (egress) · nat (fixed hourly + per GB processed) · objstore (lifecycle tiers) · logs (ingestion) · serverless · worker (spot candidates) · payment (fees, a business cost). Scenarios: serverless-burst, multi-region (what a second region costs). Continues in: Compute — containers or serverless, Performance — capacity planning, Reliability — disaster recovery, Network & security — the cloud network (NAT gateways), Observability — signals (cardinality), Project — cost report.

items.title: Index
items.text:
Docker Compose starts BoxOffice on one machine. Production needs more: forty containers spread over several machines, a replacement started within seconds when one dies, a new version rolled out without downtime, and capacity added automatically when the on-sale begins. Doing that by hand — SSH into a node, docker run, update the load balancer — does not survive the first night on call. An orchestrator does it for you, and Kubernetes is the de facto standard5.

Kubernetes descends from Google's internal cluster managers, Borg and Omega; its designers summarized the lesson of a decade of running containers at scale as declarative state reconciled by independent control loops1.

items.title: The control loop: desired state vs actual state
items.text:
You never tell Kubernetes "start a container". You tell it "there should be five replicas of catalog, version 1.4.0, each with 1 CPU" — the desired state — and store it in the API server. Controllers then run forever:

loop:
    desired = read spec from the API server
    actual  = observe the cluster
    if actual != desired:
        act to reduce the difference (create, delete, update)

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as kubectl / Argo CD
    participant API as API server (+ etcd)
    participant RS as ReplicaSet controller
    participant S as Scheduler
    participant K as kubelet (node 2)
    U->>API: apply Deployment catalog, replicas = 5
    API->>RS: watch: desired 5, actual 4 (a node died)
    RS->>API: create Pod catalog-7f9c
    API->>S: watch: unscheduled pod
    S->>API: bind catalog-7f9c to node 2 (enough free CPU)
    API->>K: watch: new pod for this node
    K->>K: pull image, start container, run probes
    K->>API: status: Running, Ready
    Note over RS,API: actual = desired → nothing to do

This is why Kubernetes self-heals: a crashed process, a deleted pod or a dead node all appear as "actual ≠ desired", and the same loop fixes them. It is also why the API is declarative and idempotent: applying the same manifest twice changes nothing.

items.title: The pieces of a cluster
items.text:
Component Where Role API server Control plane The only entry point; validates and stores objects; everything else watches it etcd Control plane Strongly consistent key-value store (Raft consensus) holding the cluster state Scheduler Control plane Chooses a node for each new pod (free resources, affinity, spread constraints) Controller manager Control plane Runs the controllers (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Job, Node, HPA…) kubelet Every node Starts the pod's containers through the container runtime (containerd), runs probes, reports status kube-proxy / CNI plugin Every node Implements Service virtual IPs and pod networking (iptables, IPVS or eBPF, e.g. Cilium)

With a managed service (EKS, GKE, AKS) the provider runs and upgrades the control plane; you manage the nodes — or, with GKE Autopilot or EKS on Fargate, not even those.

items.title: The core objects
items.text: Object What it is BoxOffice use Pod One or more containers that share network and volumes; the unit of scheduling. Ephemeral One catalog instance (plus, sometimes, a sidecar) Deployment Keeps N identical pods running and rolls out new versions (through ReplicaSets) catalog, inventory, order, gateway Service A stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of pods, selected by labels http://inventory:8080 always works, whatever pods exist Ingress / Gateway API HTTP routing from outside the cluster to Services (host, path, TLS) api.boxoffice.example/catalog/** → catalog ConfigMap / Secret Configuration and credentials injected as environment variables or files Database URL; database password (from a secret manager) StatefulSet Pods with stable identity and their own persistent volume Kafka or PostgreSQL if self-hosted Job / CronJob Run-to-completion work, once or on a schedule Release expired seat holds every minute; nightly reconciliation with the payment provider HorizontalPodAutoscaler Adjusts a Deployment's replica count from metrics catalog 4 → 40 replicas during the on-sale PodDisruptionBudget Limits how many pods voluntary disruptions (node drains, upgrades) may take down at once Never fewer than 3 inventory pods during a node upgrade

items.title: BoxOffice's catalog on Kubernetes
items.text:
The manifests below are the heart of Hands-on 10. Read them top to bottom; each block answers one operational question.

k8s/catalog/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: catalog
  labels: { app: catalog }
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: catalog }
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0 }   # never below 4 ready pods
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: catalog }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      topologySpreadConstraints:                           # spread replicas across zones
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: catalog } }
      containers:
        - name: catalog
          image: ghcr.io/boxoffice/catalog@sha256:9f2c0d7e1b4a   # digest, not a tag
          ports: [ { containerPort: 8080 } ]
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: catalog-config }
            - secretRef:    { name: catalog-db }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "768Mi" }      # what the scheduler reserves
            limits:   { memory: "768Mi" }                   # hard ceiling (OOMKilled above)
          startupProbe:                                     # JVM warm-up: up to 60 s
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 12
          readinessProbe:                                   # receive traffic?
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 3
          livenessProbe:                                    # restart me?
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          lifecycle:
            preStop: { sleep: { seconds: 5 } }              # let endpoints update before SIGTERM
k8s/catalog/service-hpa-pdb.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: catalog }
spec:
  selector: { app: catalog }
  ports: [ { port: 8080, targetPort: 8080 } ]
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: catalog }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: catalog }
  minReplicas: 4
  maxReplicas: 40
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 }   # % of the CPU request
  behavior:
    scaleUp:   { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0,   policies: [ { type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 15 } ] }
    scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300, policies: [ { type: Pods,    value: 2,   periodSeconds: 60 } ] }
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: { name: catalog }
spec:
  minAvailable: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: catalog } }
k8s/edge/httproute.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: { name: boxoffice-api }
spec:
  parentRefs: [ { name: public-gateway } ]
  hostnames: [ "api.boxoffice.example" ]
  rules:
    - matches: [ { path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /catalog } } ]
      backendRefs: [ { name: catalog, port: 8080 } ]
    - matches: [ { path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /inventory } } ]
      backendRefs: [ { name: inventory, port: 8080 } ]

The Gateway API (Gateway + HTTPRoute) is the successor of the older Ingress object: it separates the infrastructure owner (who runs the Gateway) from the application teams (who own routes), and supports weighted backends natively3 — which is how canaries split traffic (see Delivery). The Edge class covers the Ingress component.

items.title: Probes: three different questions
items.text:
Probe Question On failure Common mistake Startup Has the application finished starting? Keeps the other probes disabled; after failureThreshold, restarts the container Missing → a slow JVM is killed by liveness before it ever starts Readiness Should this pod receive traffic now? Removed from the Service endpoints (no restart) Checking downstream dependencies: when PostgreSQL blinks, all pods become unready and the whole service disappears Liveness Is the process stuck beyond repair? Container restarted Making it depend on the database: a DB outage triggers restart storms that make recovery slower

Keep liveness local (is the JVM responsive?) and make readiness reflect only what this pod itself needs to serve. Spring Boot Actuator exposes /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness with exactly these semantics. The Observability class treats health checks as a palette component (Health Check).

items.title: Requests, limits and quality of service
items.text:
• Request — what the scheduler reserves on a node. It decides where a pod fits and is the base of the HPA's utilization percentage.
  • Limit — the ceiling. Above the memory limit the container is killed (OOMKilled); above the CPU limit it is throttled — it simply waits, which shows up as latency, not as errors.
QoS class Rule Evicted under node pressure Guaranteed requests = limits for CPU and memory Last Burstable some requests set, lower than limits Middle BestEffort nothing set First

CPU limits and latency

A Java service with a 1-CPU limit that keeps 4 threads (GC and requests) busy in parallel on a multi-core node can consume its 100 ms quota in the first 25 ms of each 100 ms period and then stall for 75 ms. The p99 grows while average CPU looks fine. Watch the cgroup metric nr_throttled (exposed by cAdvisor as container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total). Many teams set a CPU request but no CPU limit for latency-sensitive services, and always set a memory limit. The Performance class shows how to spot throttling in a load test.

items.title: Autoscaling at three levels
items.text:
flowchart LR
    load["k6 / fans<br/>requests per second ↑"] --> hpa["HPA<br/>more pods"]
    hpa --> pend["Pods Pending<br/>(no room on nodes)"]
    pend --> ca["Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter<br/>more nodes"]
    ca --> run["Pods scheduled<br/>image pulled, JVM warm"]
    run --> ready["Ready → receive traffic"]

1. Pods — Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA). Every 15 s the HPA computes2

\[ \text{desired} = \left\lceil \text{current} \times \frac{\text{current metric}}{\text{target metric}} \right\rceil \]

With 4 catalog pods at 90 % CPU (of request) and a 60 % target: ⌈4 × 90/60⌉ = 6 pods. Scaling on CPU works for CPU-bound services; for I/O-bound services scale on requests per second per pod or on queue lag through custom/external metrics.

2. Nodes — Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter. When pods stay Pending because no node has room, a node autoscaler provisions new machines (Karpenter chooses instance types per workload and can use spot capacity). This takes minutes: VM boot, node join, image pull.

3. Events — KEDA. The Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaler scales on external sources (Kafka consumer lag, queue length, cron windows) and can scale to zero — natural for the notification workers4.

BoxOffice: why the HPA alone does not save the on-sale

The HPA reacts after CPU rises; the node autoscaler needs minutes; each JVM needs ~20–40 s to start and warm up. A flash sale goes from 5 % to 100 % of peak in seconds. So the team pre-scales before 10:00 — a CronJob or KEDA's cron scaler sets minReplicas to the expected peak at 09:45 — keeps a buffer of spare nodes (low-priority "balloon" pods that are evicted when real pods need room), and puts a waiting room in front so that admission, not autoscaling, controls the rate. The capacity numbers come from the Capacity planning page.

Try it: in the scenario below, run the spike profile with 2 replicas, then with 6. Watch p99 latency and errors while the replicas are busy; then enable autoscaling (if offered) and observe the lag between the start of the spike and the moment new replicas are healthy.

items.title: Where to run Kubernetes
items.text:
AWSGoogle CloudAzureLocal / open source

Amazon EKS — managed control plane (billed per cluster-hour), nodes as EC2 managed node groups, Karpenter, or Fargate. AWS Load Balancer Controller for Ingress/Gateway; IAM Roles for Service Accounts for pod credentials.

GKE Standard (you manage node pools) or Autopilot (billed per pod resource request; Google manages nodes). Gateway API is supported natively.

AKS — managed control plane, node pools on VM scale sets, KEDA available as an add-on, Azure Container Apps as a simpler serverless alternative built on Kubernetes.

kind (Kubernetes in Docker) and minikube for the labs; k3s for small edge or single-VM clusters. Same API — the manifests above run unchanged.

items.title: Trade-offs
items.text:
Question Kubernetes Simpler alternative (ECS, Cloud Run, PaaS) Team and service count Pays off with many services and teams sharing tooling Better for a few services and a small team Portability Same API on every cloud and on-premises Tied to one provider Ecosystem Huge: Argo CD, KEDA, operators, service mesh, policy engines Smaller, but integrated Operational load Upgrades every few months, add-ons, networking, security policies Most of it is the provider's Fixed cost Control plane + system pods + spare node capacity Close to zero at idle (scale to zero on Cloud Run)

In the interview

You rarely draw Kubernetes in a system-design interview — you draw stateless service replicas behind a load balancer with autoscaling. Kubernetes is the implementation detail you mention when asked "how do you deploy and scale this?". Good signals: distinguishing readiness from liveness, knowing that autoscaling has lag (and pre-scaling for known peaks), keeping databases out of the cluster or on operators with care, and spreading replicas across availability zones.

Pitfalls

  • No requests/limits: the scheduler packs pods blindly and one noisy pod starves its neighbours.
  • Liveness depending on downstream services: a database blip restarts the whole fleet.
  • No PodDisruptionBudget: a routine node upgrade drains every inventory pod at once.
  • All replicas in one zone or on one node: "redundancy" that fails together.
  • HPA on CPU for an I/O-bound service: CPU stays low while latency explodes; scale on RPS or lag.
  • kubectl apply from laptops in production: nobody knows what is deployed — use GitOps (Delivery).
