items.title: Index
items.text:
It is 09:59 on the day a stadium tour goes on sale on BoxOffice. Two million fans are refreshing the event page; 60 thousand seats exist. In the next ten minutes the platform must render the catalog for millions of page views, hold and sell seats without double booking, charge cards through an external payment provider, generate 60 thousand tickets and e-mails, and release seats whose holds expired. At 03:00 the same platform serves a few hundred requests per second.

The edge (class 4) decides where each request goes. This class is about what happens when it arrives: where the code runs, how it is split into services, how those services talk, what runs outside the request, how the fleet grows and shrinks on its own, and how to depend safely on systems you do not control — the payment provider, the e-mail provider, any third-party API.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Explain why application servers should be stateless and move each kind of state (sessions, files, caches, schedules) to the right place.
  • Estimate how many replicas a service needs for a given peak, using per-instance capacity and a target utilization.
  • Compare a monolith, a modular monolith and microservices, and justify service boundaries with bounded contexts and Conway's law.
  • Choose an API style (REST, gRPC, GraphQL, asynchronous) for an interaction and evolve a contract without breaking its consumers.
  • Design background work with queues, workers and schedulers that are safe under retries and multiple replicas.
  • Decide between containers and serverless, and configure autoscaling (target tracking, HPA, queue-based, scheduled) for a spiky workload.
  • Integrate an external provider safely: idempotency keys, verified webhooks, retries with backoff, reconciliation and a plan for provider outages.

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
1. This overview — the compute palette, stateless app servers, horizontal scaling and how many replicas you need.
  2. Services — monolith, modular monolith and microservices; DDD bounded contexts; Conway's law; the architecture inside a service; auth, search, notifications and analytics as services.
  3. API styles — REST, gRPC, GraphQL and asynchronous APIs for the same BoxOffice resource; contracts, OpenAPI and versioning.
  4. Async work — workers and background jobs, job design, schedulers, distributed locks and leader election.
  5. Serverless & autoscaling — functions as a service, cold starts and concurrency; autoscaling policies, HPA and why reactive scaling lags a flash sale.
  6. External integrations — 3rd-party APIs, payment and e-mail providers: webhooks with signatures, idempotency keys, retries, reconciliation and provider outages.
  7. Quiz — check your understanding.

items.title: Slides
items.text: Click the slides and use ← → to move through them; F goes full screen and P opens the presenter view, with the notes. Open the slides in a new tab

items.title: The compute palette
items.text:
In the System Design Playground, the COMPUTE category groups every component that runs your code. Each one is a different answer to the question "where does this piece of logic execute, and how does it scale?":

Component What it runs BoxOffice example Scales on App Server Request/response handlers behind a load balancer catalog, inventory, order requests per second, CPU Worker Jobs pulled from a queue, outside any user request ticket PDF generation, e-mail sending queue depth, consumer lag Serverless Short functions started per event by the platform resize an artist image on upload; receive webhooks concurrent invocations Auth Service Login, tokens, sessions, identity auth issues JWTs for fans and staff logins per second (spikes at on-sale) Search Full-text and faceted queries over an index "coldplay são paulo" → events queries per second, index size Scheduler Time-triggered work (cron, delayed jobs) open the sale at 10:00; release expired holds number of jobs, precision Notifications Fan-out to e-mail, push and SMS providers "your tickets are here" messages per second, provider limits Analytics Event ingestion and aggregation sales per minute dashboard events per second

The rest of this page is about the most common of them — the app server — and the property that makes everything else possible: being stateless.

items.title: Stateless app servers
items.text:
A server is stateless when it keeps nothing between requests that another replica would need: any replica can serve any request, because everything that must survive lives outside the process — in a database, a cache, an object store or the client itself. That one property is what lets a load balancer send each request anywhere, lets you add replicas in seconds, and lets you kill a replica without losing anything.

flowchart LR
    fan([Fan]) --> lb["Load balancer"]
    lb --> a1["catalog #1"]
    lb --> a2["catalog #2"]
    lb --> a3["catalog #3"]
    a1 --> redis[("Redis<br/>sessions, cache")]
    a2 --> redis
    a3 --> redis
    a1 --> pg[("PostgreSQL")]
    a2 --> pg
    a3 --> pg
    a3 --> s3[("Object store<br/>images, PDFs")]

The replicas are interchangeable boxes; the state is in the shared stores on the right. Every kind of state that tends to "stick" to a server has a standard new home:

State that sticks to a server Why it breaks scaling Where it should live HTTP session in memory (cart, login) The next request may hit another replica → "you were logged out" A signed token on the client (JWT) or a session store (Redis) Uploaded files on local disk Other replicas cannot see them; lost when the pod dies Object store (S3, GCS, MinIO) In-process cache Each replica has a different, stale copy A distributed cache (Redis) — or accept short TTLs per replica Scheduled jobs inside the app (@Scheduled) With 10 replicas the job runs 10 times A scheduler with a lock or a leader Counters and rate limits in memory Each replica counts only its share Redis (INCR) or the API gateway WebSocket connections A connection is state, pinned to one replica Keep it, but publish messages through pub/sub so any replica can reach any user

BoxOffice: the seat hold

When a fan picks seat C-14, the inventory service creates a hold that expires in 10 minutes. A tempting first version keeps the hold in a ConcurrentHashMap inside the replica. It works on a laptop and fails in production: the next click goes to another replica, which does not know the hold; a restart forgets every hold; two replicas sell the same seat. The hold must live in the shared store that guarantees "one seat, one hold" — a row in PostgreSQL with a unique constraint (or a Redis key set with NX and an expiry). Class 6 (databases) shows the transaction that makes it safe.

This is factor VI of the Twelve-Factor App: "execute the app as one or more stateless processes"1. It does not mean the system has no state — it means the state is concentrated in a few components built to hold it, which you then scale with different techniques (replicas, partitions, caches: classes 6 and 7).

Sticky sessions are a crutch

A load balancer can pin each user to one replica (session affinity). It hides the problem without solving it: load becomes uneven (one replica gets the heavy users), and when that replica dies or is scaled in, its users lose their state. Use affinity only for connection-oriented traffic (WebSockets) or as a temporary step while moving state out.

items.title: Scaling up or out
items.text:
There are two ways to give a service more capacity:

Vertical scaling (scale up) Horizontal scaling (scale out) How A bigger machine: more vCPUs, more memory More machines (replicas) behind a load balancer Limit The biggest instance type; price grows faster than size The shared stores behind the replicas Availability One box: its failure is your outage Replicas cover for each other Downtime to change Usually a restart None — add and remove replicas live Requires Nothing from the code Stateless app servers Good for Databases, quick fixes, small systems App servers, workers, anything stateless

App servers are scaled out almost by default, because statelessness makes it trivial. Databases are usually scaled up first, then with replicas and partitions — which is why the data tier, not the app tier, is where most bottlenecks end up.

items.title: How many replicas?
items.text:
The question every design has to answer with a number. Start from one replica's capacity, measured with a load test (hands-on 2), and the peak load from your estimate (class 2):

\[ N = \left\lceil \frac{\text{peak RPS}}{\text{RPS per replica} \times \text{target utilization}} \right\rceil + \text{spare} \]

Why a target utilization (typically 50–70%)? Because latency is not linear in load. As a server approaches 100% busy, requests start to queue, and waiting time explodes — the "knee" of the curve (queueing). The target leaves headroom for bursts and for losing a replica.

Worked example — the catalog service at on-sale

Assume (illustrative numbers): one catalog replica has 10 vCPUs and spends 20 ms of CPU per request, so it can complete at most 10 / 0.020 = 500 requests/s. The edge caches most of the static page, and the API receives 4,000 requests/s at peak.

  • At 100% utilization you would need 4,000 / 500 = 8 replicas — with zero headroom, every burst queues.
  • At a 65% target: 4,000 / (500 × 0.65) ≈ 12.3 → 13 replicas.
  • Add N + 1 spare (or one zone's worth, if you run in three zones): 14 replicas.

The chart below makes the knee visible. It models each replica as a 10-core server with 20 ms of work per request (an M/M/10 queue) and spreads 4,000 requests/s evenly over N replicas:

2026-10-23T08:15:42.678573 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

With 8 replicas the queue grows without limit (100% busy). With 9 replicas (89% busy) the mean latency is about 31 ms — 60% above the 20 ms of real work; from about 12 replicas on, adding more barely changes the mean. And the tail (p99) degrades much earlier and much faster than the mean (percentiles) — another reason to keep utilization moderate.

Think first: why not just run 100 replicas?

Three reasons. Cost: you pay for idle capacity all day to cover ten minutes of peak — the motivation for autoscaling. Shared stores: 100 replicas × a pool of 20 database connections = 2,000 connections, more than a PostgreSQL server should accept (each connection is a process with its own memory); the bottleneck simply moves to the database. Diminishing returns: once queueing is gone, extra replicas do not make a request faster — the 20 ms of work remain.

items.title: Try it in the playground
items.text:
Open the scale-out scenario: a load balancer in front of N app replicas.

  1. Run the load profile with 2 replicas and note p99 and the error rate.
  2. Add replicas one at a time and watch p99 fall until it flattens — the point where queueing is gone.
  3. Turn chaos to medium to kill replicas at random: health checks remove dead replicas from the pool, and the remaining ones absorb the load only if you left headroom.

Open the full simulator

items.title: A replica's life cycle
items.text:
Scaling out means replicas are created and destroyed all the time — by deploys, by the autoscaler, by node failures. A replica that behaves well during its life cycle is as important as a stateless one:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Starting : scheduled on a node
    Starting --> Ready : startup + readiness probe pass
    Ready --> NotReady : readiness fails (e.g. DB unreachable)
    NotReady --> Ready : readiness passes again
    Ready --> Draining : SIGTERM (deploy, scale-in)
    Draining --> [*] : in-flight requests done
    Ready --> [*] : crash / liveness fails → restart
  • Start fast, warm up before taking traffic. A JVM service may need several seconds to start; the readiness probe should pass only once connection pools are open and caches are warm. Slow starts make autoscaling slow (serverless & autoscaling).
  • Shut down gracefully. On SIGTERM, stop accepting new requests, finish the in-flight ones, then exit. In Spring Boot, server.shutdown=graceful with spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=20s does this.
  • Be disposable (Twelve-Factor IX): nothing important should depend on a replica living long. Health checks (liveness, readiness, startup) are covered in reliability.

items.title: Compute shapes
items.text:
The same stateless service can run on very different substrates. The choice changes who manages what, how fast you scale and how you pay:

Shape Unit you deploy Scaling speed You manage Pay for Typical use Virtual machine VM image minutes OS, runtime, app provisioned hours legacy, special hardware, databases Containers on Kubernetes container image seconds (pod) to minutes (node) the cluster (or a managed one), the app nodes, even when idle the default for services Serverless containers (Cloud Run, Fargate, Container Apps) container image seconds, to zero the app per request or per vCPU-second APIs with idle periods Functions (FaaS) (Lambda, Cloud Functions) a function sub-second to seconds, to zero a function per invocation and duration event glue, webhooks, bursty work

Class 12 (cloud-native) covers containers and Kubernetes in depth; this class covers the decisions that depend on the workload: serverless and autoscaling.

items.text:
Every compute component answers where a piece of logic runs and how it scales; the external components are the logic you call but do not run. The map links each palette component (green) to the concepts it relies on (blue):

flowchart LR
    app["app"]:::comp -.- c1["stateless, scale out,<br/>replica life cycle"]:::tech
    app -.- c2["REST, gRPC, GraphQL,<br/>async APIs"]:::tech

    queue --> worker["worker"]:::comp

    classDef comp fill:#1e9e5a22,stroke:#1e9e5a
    classDef tech fill:#2f6fed22,stroke:#2f6fed
Palette component Question it answers Concepts Taught in Scenarios app Where does request/response logic run, and how does it scale? stateless replicas, sizing at 50–70%, life cycle, API contracts this overview, API Styles monolith, scale-out worker What runs outside the user's request? jobs on a queue, workers = rate × time per job, at least once, DLQ Async Work async-queue scheduler What runs at a given time — once, not once per replica? CronJob, distributed lock, leader election, fencing tokens, lazy expiry Async Work — schedulers notification-system serverless What should scale per request, and down to zero? FaaS, cold starts, concurrency = rate × duration, cost per use Serverless & Autoscaling serverless-burst auth Who is the caller? identities and tokens, buy before build, validation at the gateway Services flash-sale (login bursts) search · analytics How do derived views stay off the request path? derived data, fed by events, rebuildable from the source of truth Services search-autocomplete, event-fanout notifications · email How do messages reach fans despite provider limits? queue-driven workers, provider rate limits, bounces, a secondary provider Services, Integrations — provider outages notification-system payment · thirdparty How do we depend on systems we do not control? adapters, idempotency keys, UNKNOWN outcomes, webhooks, reconciliation Integrations payment-system, cascading-failure, retry-storm (the whole tier) How many replicas, and when? HPA, KEDA, queue-depth scaling, scheduled scaling, autoscaling lag Serverless & Autoscaling — lag scale-out, flash-sale

In the interview

State the compute tier in one sentence and move on to the interesting parts: "The API tier is stateless — sessions are JWTs, files go to the object store — so it sits behind a load balancer and autoscales on CPU and requests per second; I'd size it at about 65% target utilization, which is 13–14 replicas for our 4 k RPS peak." Interviewers want to hear that you know where the state went, and a number. Spend the remaining time on the stateful parts (database, cache, queue), where the real trade-offs are.

Common pitfalls

  • Hidden state: an in-memory map, a local file or an in-process @Scheduled job that silently assumes one replica.
  • Scaling the stateless tier into a wall: more app replicas multiply connections to the database, which is the real bottleneck.
  • Sizing for the average: a fleet sized for 03:00 or for the daily mean melts at 10:00 on sale day.
  • No headroom for failures: 100% of capacity used means losing one replica (or one zone) is an outage.
  • Slow, heavy start-up: a replica that needs 90 s to become ready cannot help with a spike that lasts 5 minutes.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• The compute tier is easy to scale because it is stateless: sessions, files, caches, schedules and counters live in stores built for state.
  • App servers scale out; size them as peak / (capacity per replica × target utilization) plus spare, and keep utilization around 50–70% because latency explodes near 100%.
  • Replicas are disposable: fast start, readiness before traffic, graceful shutdown.
  • The next pages decide how to split the code into services, how they talk, what runs in the background, how the fleet scales itself, and how to depend on providers you do not control.

  1. WIGGINS, A. The Twelve-Factor App, factors VI (processes) and IX (disposability). 2011. ↩

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Stateless servers and scaling
items.text:
Q1. BoxOffice's first inventory version keeps seat holds in a ConcurrentHashMap inside each replica. Everything works on a developer laptop. What happens with three replicas behind a round-robin load balancer?

  • A. A fan's next request may reach a replica that does not know the hold, a restart forgets every hold, and two replicas can hold the same seat for different fans
  • B. Nothing changes: each replica has its own map, so holds are three times faster
  • C. The load balancer automatically synchronizes the three maps
  • D. Only performance degrades, because the maps must be copied between replicas
Answer

A — The state is stuck in one process.

A stateless replica keeps nothing another replica would need. The hold is shared state with an invariant ("one seat, one hold"), so it must live in a store that enforces it — a PostgreSQL row with a unique constraint, or a Redis key set with NX and an expiry. Sticky sessions would only hide part of the problem and still lose holds on restarts.

Q2. One catalog replica completes at most 500 requests/s. The peak is 6,000 requests/s and the team targets 60% utilization, plus one spare replica. How many replicas?

  • A. 12
  • B. 20
  • C. 21
  • D. 24
Answer

C — 21 replicas.

At the target, each replica should serve 500 × 0.6 = 300 requests/s, so 6,000 / 300 = 20 replicas, plus one spare = 21. Option A (12) is the count at 100% utilization (6,000 / 500), which leaves no headroom: latency explodes near saturation and losing one replica means overload. Option B forgets the spare.

Q3. Why do teams target 50–70% utilization on app servers instead of running them close to 100%?

  • A. Cloud providers charge more for CPUs above 70%
  • B. Queueing delay grows sharply as utilization approaches 100%, so headroom keeps latency (especially the tail) low and absorbs bursts and replica failures
  • C. The JVM garbage collector does not run above 70% CPU
  • D. Load balancers stop sending traffic to replicas above 70% utilization
Answer

B — Latency is not linear in load.

In a queue, waiting time grows like 1 / (1 − ρ): at 50% utilization a request waits about as long as its service time, at 90% about ten times as long, and the p99 degrades even earlier. The headroom also covers bursts and the loss of a replica or a zone.

items.title: Services and boundaries
items.text:
Q4. BoxOffice has three teams and one Spring Boot codebase. Which situation is the strongest reason to extract inventory into its own service?

  • A. The codebase has more than 100,000 lines
  • B. A new developer prefers Kotlin
  • C. Microservices are the modern standard
  • D. During on-sale, inventory is write-hot and needs strong consistency and its own scaling and tuning, while catalog is read-heavy and cacheable; one team owns inventory and must release independently
Answer

D — A real force: different scaling/consistency profile and team autonomy.

Size alone (A) and fashion (C) are not reasons; a language preference (B) is weak. Splitting pays off when you can name the force — independent scaling, team autonomy, failure isolation, compliance scope, different technology — and that force tells you where to cut.

Q5. In BoxOffice, the word Event means "artist, date, venue, images" in the catalog and "seat map, sections, holds" in inventory. What does DDD recommend?

  • A. Let each bounded context have its own Event model, exchanging ids and events between contexts
  • B. Create one shared Event class in a common library used by all services
  • C. Rename one of them so the word is unique across the company
  • D. Store everything in one events table that both services read and write
Answer

A — One model per bounded context.

A bounded context is the boundary inside which one model and one meaning of each word apply. A shared class (B) or a shared table (D) couples the teams and produces a bloated model — the classic path to a distributed monolith. Contexts reference each other by id and communicate through APIs and events.

Q6. The payment service talks to an external provider whose API uses statuses such as requires_action and processing. Where should those strings appear in BoxOffice's code?

  • A. Everywhere a payment status is checked, so developers learn the provider's vocabulary
  • B. In the database, as the payment status column values
  • C. Only inside the provider adapter (anti-corruption layer), which translates them into BoxOffice's own payment states behind a port such as PaymentGateway
  • D. In the front-end, which shows them to the fan
Answer

C — Inside the adapter only.

The port (PaymentGateway) belongs to the core and speaks BoxOffice's language; the adapter is the only class that knows the provider's API. This keeps use-case tests independent of the provider and makes adding a second provider a new adapter instead of a rewrite.

items.title: API styles
items.text:
Q7. The internal order service calls inventory thousands of times per second during on-sale; both are owned by BoxOffice. Which style fits best, and what is its main operational catch?

  • A. GraphQL; the catch is that it cannot be used between services
  • B. Webhooks; the catch is that they need signatures
  • C. REST with XML; the catch is payload size
  • D. gRPC; the catch is that its long-lived HTTP/2 connections defeat L4 load balancing, so you need an L7 proxy, a mesh or client-side balancing
Answer

D — gRPC, with L7 or client-side load balancing.

gRPC gives generated typed clients, compact protobuf payloads, multiplexing and deadlines — ideal for internal high-volume calls. Because all calls from one client share one HTTP/2 connection, an L4 balancer pins them to one replica; balance per request with Envoy, a service mesh, or client-side load balancing.

Q8. Which change to a public REST API is breaking?

  • A. Adding a new optional query parameter ?city=
  • B. Adding the field doorsOpenAt to the event response
  • C. Changing price from reais (450.00) to cents (45000) in the same field
  • D. Adding a new endpoint GET /v1/venues/{id}
Answer

C — Changing a field's meaning.

Existing clients would show prices 100 times too high without any error. Additions (A, B, D) are compatible as long as clients are tolerant readers that ignore unknown fields. A breaking change needs a new version (or a new field) and an expand-and-contract migration.

Q9. A mobile event page built on GraphQL lists 20 events, each with its availability resolved by the inventory service. Latency is poor and inventory receives 21 calls per page view. What is the problem and the usual fix?

  • A. The N+1 problem; batch the 20 lookups into one call with a DataLoader
  • B. Over-fetching; switch to REST
  • C. Missing indexes in the catalog database
  • D. GraphQL cannot call other services; move the data into the BFF's own database
Answer

A — N+1, fixed with batching (DataLoader).

One query for the list plus one resolver call per item is the N+1 pattern. A DataLoader collects the ids requested during one execution step and resolves them in a single batched call (and caches them per request).

items.title: Async work
items.text:
Q10. After the on-sale opens, 100 orders/s arrive for ticket rendering; each job takes 0.8 s of one worker. There are 40 workers. After 10 minutes of peak, approximately how large is the backlog?

  • A. 0 — 40 workers are enough
  • B. 3,000 jobs
  • C. 30,000 jobs
  • D. 60,000 jobs
Answer

C — about 30,000 jobs.

40 workers / 0.8 s = 50 jobs/s of capacity. The backlog grows at 100 − 50 = 50 jobs/s; over 600 s that is 30,000 jobs. Keeping up would need 100 × 0.8 = 80 workers (Little's law) — and only if the downstream (e.g. the e-mail provider's rate limit) allows it.

Q11. inventory runs 10 replicas, and a @Scheduled(fixedRate = 30_000) method releases expired holds. What is wrong, and what does a correct fix require?

  • A. Nothing is wrong; Spring runs scheduled methods on one replica only
  • B. The job runs on all 10 replicas; a distributed lock with an expiry (e.g. ShedLock) reduces duplicates, but because locks can expire during a pause, the release itself must also be idempotent (a conditional UPDATE) or fenced
  • C. The job runs 10 times; using a bigger replica fixes it
  • D. The job never runs, because @Scheduled is disabled in containers
Answer

B — Runs N times; locks alone are not a correctness guarantee.

Spring schedules the method in every replica. A CronJob, a lock or leader election stops the duplication in the normal case, but a lock holder that pauses past the lock expiry can run concurrently with the next holder. Correctness comes from idempotent, conditional writes (... WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' AND expires_at < now()) or fencing tokens.

items.title: Serverless and autoscaling
items.text:
Q12. A function handles 1,500 requests/s with an average duration of 200 ms on AWS Lambda (one request per execution environment). How many concurrent environments does it need, and what risk does that create for a PostgreSQL database behind it?

  • A. 30 environments; no risk
  • B. 1,500 environments; one per request per second
  • C. 7,500 environments; Lambda will reject the requests
  • D. 300 environments; up to 300 simultaneous database connections unless a pooler (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer) or reserved concurrency limits them
Answer

D — 300 concurrent environments.

Concurrency = rate × duration = 1,500 × 0.2 = 300 (Little's law). Each environment typically opens its own database connection, so the function tier can exhaust the database's connections; put a pooler in between or cap the function with reserved concurrency.

Q13. A stadium on-sale opens at 10:00 and traffic jumps 20× within seconds. The Kubernetes HPA targets 60% CPU. Why do fans still see errors in the first minutes, and what is the best mitigation for this known event?

  • A. Reactive scaling needs metrics, a decision, possibly new nodes, image pulls and JVM warm-up — minutes in total; scale on a schedule (e.g. at 09:45) to the forecast and pre-warm caches and pools
  • B. The HPA is broken; replace it with a VPA
  • C. CPU is the wrong metric for every service; scale on latency instead
  • D. Set maxReplicas to 1,000 so the HPA can react faster
Answer

A — Autoscaling lag; pre-scale on a schedule.

Each step of reactive scaling is small, but together they take one to a few minutes, while the spike arrives in seconds. For announced peaks, raise the minimum ahead of time; for unknown spikes, rely on headroom, a waiting room and load shedding. Raising maxReplicas (D) does not make scaling faster and may overload the database.

items.title: External integrations
items.text:
Q14. payment calls the provider to create a charge; the call times out. What should the service do?

  • A. Mark the payment as failed and release the fan's seats
  • B. Mark the payment as succeeded, since most charges succeed
  • C. Mark it UNKNOWN, then retry with the same idempotency key or query the provider's status, and also accept the outcome by webhook
  • D. Retry immediately with a new idempotency key so the provider does not reject it as a duplicate
Answer

C — The outcome is unknown; resolve it safely.

A timeout after sending means the charge may or may not exist. Failing (A) releases seats of a fan who may have been charged; succeeding (B) gives tickets that may not be paid. A new key (D) is exactly how double charges happen. The same key makes the retry safe: the provider returns the original payment if it was created.

Q15. Which webhook receiver design is correct?

  • A. Parse the JSON, re-serialize it, verify the HMAC on the result, process the payment inline, then answer 200
  • B. Answer 500 to duplicate events so the provider stops sending them
  • C. Skip signature verification if the request comes over HTTPS
  • D. Verify the HMAC over the raw body (with the timestamp and a constant-time comparison), store the event with a unique event id, enqueue it, answer 2xx immediately, and apply it in a worker as a monotonic state transition
Answer

D — Verify, deduplicate, acknowledge fast, process asynchronously.

Re-serialized JSON (A) changes bytes and breaks the signature; inline processing causes provider timeouts and retries. HTTPS (C) protects the channel, not the sender's identity. Answering 500 (B) makes the provider retry more. Duplicates should get a 2xx and be ignored.

Q16 (bonus). Webhooks and idempotency keys are in place. Why does BoxOffice still run a reconciliation job against the provider's reports?

  • A. To recalculate the exchange rate of every payment
  • B. Because the provider requires it for the API key to stay valid
  • C. Because webhooks can be lost after the provider's retries, refunds can be made in the provider's dashboard, bugs can skip updates, and fees and chargebacks appear only in reports — the two sides must be compared and differences resolved
  • D. Reconciliation is only needed when there is no idempotency
Answer

C — Per-interaction safety does not guarantee that the books agree.

Reconciliation compares BoxOffice's payments with the provider's records (a near-real-time sweeper for stuck payments plus a daily report check), fixes the known mismatch types automatically (e.g. confirm or refund a payment whose webhook was lost) and sends the rest to an exception queue.

items.title: Index
items.text:
Four different clients need the same information from BoxOffice — "which events are on sale, and how many seats are left?":

  • the web app, rendering an event page that combines catalog data, the seat map and availability;
  • the mobile app, on a congested 4G connection in a stadium queue, where every kilobyte and round trip counts;
  • a reseller partner that integrates once and then expects the API never to break;
  • the internal order service, which asks inventory to confirm holds thousands of times per second during on-sale.

One API style does not fit all four. This page compares the four families you will meet in practice — REST, gRPC, GraphQL and asynchronous APIs — on the same BoxOffice resource, and then covers what matters more than the style: designing the contract well and evolving it without breaking anyone.

items.title: An API is a contract
items.text:
An API (Application Programming Interface) is the contract between a provider (the service that implements it) and its consumers (the code that calls it): which operations exist, what they accept and what they return — and nothing about how they are implemented. A stable contract is what lets the catalog team rewrite its persistence layer without telling anybody, and what lets the mobile team ship without waiting for the backend.

Three consequences shape everything below:

  • Expose DTOs, not entities. A DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a class whose only job is to cross the boundary. Returning the JPA entity ties the contract to the database schema and leaks internal fields.
  • The contract is a document, not just code. OpenAPI (REST), .proto files (gRPC), the GraphQL schema and AsyncAPI (events) describe it in a machine-readable way, from which clients, servers, mocks and tests are generated.
  • Changing the contract is a negotiation. Anything a consumer can observe — a field name, a status code, the order of a list — is part of it.

items.title: One resource, four styles
items.text:
The resource: an event with its availability (seats left per section). Here is how each style expresses "give me event evt_42 with its availability".

REST + OpenAPIgRPC + Protocol BuffersGraphQLAsync (events + AsyncAPI)

Resources are identified by URLs, operations by HTTP methods, results by status codes; the contract is an OpenAPI document.

GET /v1/events/evt_42?include=availability HTTP/1.1
Accept: application/json
openapi.yaml (excerpt)
openapi: 3.1.0
info: { title: BoxOffice Catalog API, version: 1.4.0 }
paths:
  /v1/events/{eventId}:
    get:
      operationId: getEvent
      parameters:
        - { name: eventId, in: path, required: true, schema: { type: string } }
        - { name: include, in: query, schema: { type: string, enum: [availability] } }
      responses:
        "200":
          description: The event
          content:
            application/json:
              schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Event" }
        "404": { $ref: "#/components/responses/NotFound" }
components:
  schemas:
    Event:
      type: object
      required: [id, title, startsAt, venue]
      properties:
        id: { type: string, example: evt_42 }
        title: { type: string, example: "Stadium Tour — São Paulo" }
        startsAt: { type: string, format: date-time }
        venue: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/VenueRef" }
        availability:
          type: array
          items:
            type: object
            properties:
              section: { type: string, example: "PISTA" }
              seatsLeft: { type: integer, example: 1180 }
              priceCents: { type: integer, example: 45000 }

Any HTTP client can call it — a browser, curl, a partner's script — and GET responses can be cached by browsers and CDNs.

Operations are remote procedure calls declared in a .proto file; code for client and server is generated, and messages travel as compact binary over HTTP/2.

inventory.proto
syntax = "proto3";
package boxoffice.inventory.v1;

import "google/protobuf/timestamp.proto";

service InventoryService {
  rpc GetAvailability (GetAvailabilityRequest) returns (Availability);
  // server streaming: the seat map pushes changes while the fan looks at it
  rpc WatchAvailability (GetAvailabilityRequest) returns (stream AvailabilityChange);
}

message GetAvailabilityRequest {
  string event_id = 1;
}

message Availability {
  string event_id = 1;
  repeated Section sections = 2;
  google.protobuf.Timestamp as_of = 3;
}

message Section {
  string name = 1;
  int32 seats_left = 2;
  int64 price_cents = 3;
}

message AvailabilityChange {
  string section = 1;
  int32 seats_left = 2;
}

The numbers (= 1, = 2) are field tags: on the wire only the tag and the value travel, not the field name — which is why protobuf messages are compact, and why a tag must never be reused.

One endpoint (POST /graphql) and a typed schema; the client chooses the fields it wants, possibly crossing several services in one request.

schema.graphql (excerpt)
type Query {
  event(id: ID!): Event
  events(city: String, first: Int = 20, after: String): EventConnection!
}

type Event {
  id: ID!
  title: String!
  startsAt: DateTime!
  venue: Venue!
  availability: [SectionAvailability!]!   # resolved by the inventory service
}

type SectionAvailability {
  section: String!
  seatsLeft: Int!
  priceCents: Int!
}
the mobile app's query
query EventCard {
  event(id: "evt_42") {
    title
    startsAt
    availability { section seatsLeft }
  }
}

The mobile app gets exactly title, startsAt and two fields per section — no venue description, no images, no prices it does not display.

No request at all: the provider publishes a fact when something changes, and interested consumers subscribe. The contract is the message schema and the channel, described in AsyncAPI.

asyncapi.yaml (excerpt)
asyncapi: 3.0.0
info: { title: BoxOffice Inventory Events, version: 1.0.0 }
channels:
  availabilityChanged:
    address: inventory.availability.v1
    messages:
      AvailabilityChanged:
        payload:
          type: object
          required: [eventId, section, seatsLeft, occurredAt]
          properties:
            eventId: { type: string, example: evt_42 }
            section: { type: string, example: PISTA }
            seatsLeft: { type: integer, example: 1179 }
            occurredAt: { type: string, format: date-time }
operations:
  publishAvailabilityChanged:
    action: send
    channel: { $ref: "#/channels/availabilityChanged" }

search and analytics consume this topic to keep their own copies up to date; nobody calls inventory to ask.

items.title: REST in practice
items.text: REST (Representational State Transfer) was defined by Roy Fielding as an architectural style on top of HTTP semantics12. In practice "REST API" means Richardson maturity level 2: resources with their own URLs, correct HTTP methods and status codes3.

items.title: Resources and methods for BoxOffice
items.text:
Method + path Meaning Safe Idempotent Success GET /v1/events?city=sao-paulo&cursor=… list events yes yes 200 GET /v1/events/{id} one event yes yes 200 POST /v1/events/{id}/holds hold seats for 10 min no no → needs an Idempotency-Key 201 + Location DELETE /v1/holds/{holdId} release a hold no yes 204 POST /v1/orders check out a hold no no → needs an Idempotency-Key 202 (payment pending) or 201 GET /v1/orders/{id} order status yes yes 200 PATCH /v1/fans/me update profile fields no not guaranteed 200

Safe means the request does not change server state (caches and crawlers may call it freely). Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once, so it is safe to retry. POST is neither — which is why every POST that creates money-related state in BoxOffice requires an idempotency key (integrations).

items.title: Status codes that carry meaning
items.text:
Code BoxOffice meaning Client should… 200 OK / 201 Created done / created (with Location) proceed 202 Accepted order received, payment still being processed poll GET /orders/{id} or wait for a push 400 Bad Request / 422 Unprocessable Content malformed / semantically invalid (7 seats, max is 6) fix the request — never retry 401 / 403 not authenticated / not allowed log in / give up 404 Not Found no such event give up 409 Conflict seat already held by someone else pick other seats 429 Too Many Requests rate limited (bots at on-sale) wait Retry-After, then retry 503 Service Unavailable overloaded or dependency down retry with backoff + jitter

Errors deserve a uniform body. RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs defines one (application/problem+json) that Spring Boot (3 and later) supports out of the box via ProblemDetail4:

409 Conflict — application/problem+json
{
  "type": "/problems/seat-unavailable",
  "title": "Seat unavailable",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "Seat C-14 is held by another fan.",
  "instance": "/v1/events/evt_42/holds",
  "unavailableSeats": ["C-14"]
}

items.title: Pagination: offset vs cursor
items.text:
Offset (?page=3&size=20) Cursor / keyset (?after=eyJpZCI6...&limit=20) Query ORDER BY starts_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40 WHERE (starts_at, id) > (:t, :id) ORDER BY starts_at, id LIMIT 20 Deep pages slow: the DB still walks the skipped rows fast: an index seek Inserts during paging rows shift → duplicates or gaps stable Jump to page 37 yes no (next/previous only) Use for small admin tables feeds, catalogs, anything large or live

The cursor is an opaque string (often base64 of the last row's sort key) that the client sends back unchanged.

items.title: Caching and long-running operations
items.text:
• Conditional requests: catalog returns ETag: "v17" and Cache-Control: public, max-age=30; a client that repeats the request with If-None-Match: "v17" gets 304 Not Modified with no body. The CDN (edge) does the same at scale — another reason to keep reads as cacheable GETs.
  • Long-running operations: never hold a connection for 30 s. Answer 202 Accepted with a Location: /v1/orders/ord_9 status resource, and let the client poll it or receive a push. Checkout uses exactly this while the payment provider decides.

items.title: The contract in code
items.text:
With springdoc-openapi, the OpenAPI document is generated from the annotated controller (code-first); alternatively the YAML is written first and the controller interface is generated from it (contract-first, e.g. with openapi-generator). Contract-first fits APIs consumed by partners; code-first is faster for internal ones.

catalog: EventController.java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/v1/events")
@Tag(name = "Events")
class EventController {

    private final EventQueries queries;

    EventController(EventQueries queries) { this.queries = queries; }

    @GetMapping("/{eventId}")
    @Operation(summary = "Get one event, optionally with seat availability")
    ResponseEntity<EventDto> get(@PathVariable String eventId,
                                 @RequestParam(required = false) Include include) {
        EventDto event = queries.find(eventId, include == Include.AVAILABILITY)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ErrorResponseException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND));
        return ResponseEntity.ok()
                .eTag(event.version())
                .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofSeconds(30)).cachePublic())
                .body(event);
    }
}

Hands-on 1 builds this service, serves the document at /v3/api-docs and the Swagger UI at /swagger-ui.html.

items.title: gRPC in practice
items.text:
gRPC is an RPC framework from Google built on HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers5. What you get:

  • Generated, typed clients in a dozen languages from one .proto — calling inventory.getAvailability(req) looks like a local method call.
  • Compact binary messages and cheap parsing: protobuf payloads are typically several times smaller than the equivalent JSON, which matters for chatty internal traffic.
  • Multiplexing: many concurrent calls over one HTTP/2 connection.
  • Streaming: unary, server streaming (WatchAvailability above), client streaming and bidirectional.
  • Deadlines that propagate: the caller says "I need an answer within 300 ms", and every hop knows how much time is left.

And what it costs:

  • Browsers cannot call it directly: you need gRPC-Web or Connect through a proxy, or a REST/GraphQL facade at the edge.
  • Load balancing is subtle: one long-lived HTTP/2 connection carries all calls, so an L4 load balancer pins all traffic of a client to one server. Use an L7 proxy (Envoy, a service mesh) or client-side load balancing (edge).
  • Harder to debug by hand: binary on the wire; use grpcurl and server reflection.

Typical use: high-volume, internal, service-to-service calls — order → inventory during on-sale — where both sides are yours.

items.title: GraphQL in practice
items.text:
GraphQL is a query language and runtime for APIs6. The client sends a query describing the shape of the data it wants; the server's resolvers fetch each field, possibly from different services.

  • No over-fetching or under-fetching: one round trip returns exactly what a screen needs — attractive for mobile.
  • A typed schema with introspection: great tooling and self-documentation.
  • Evolution without versions: add fields freely, mark old ones @deprecated, remove them when usage drops to zero.

The problems to plan for:

  • The N+1 problem: listing 20 events, each with availability, naively triggers 1 + 20 calls to inventory. Batch them with a DataLoader (collect the 20 ids, make one call).
  • Caching is harder: queries usually go as POST to one URL, so HTTP caches and CDNs do not help by default. Persisted queries (the client sends a hash of a pre-registered query, possibly with GET) restore cacheability and block arbitrary queries.
  • Abusive queries: a deeply nested query can be very expensive. Limit depth and compute a query cost budget per client.
  • Authorization per field, not per endpoint.

Typical use: a BFF (Backend for Frontend) — one GraphQL layer per front-end that composes catalog, inventory and search for the screens. Large organizations use federation to let each team own part of one graph.

items.title: Asynchronous APIs
items.text:
Not every interaction is a question that needs an immediate answer. Asynchronous styles remove the caller's wait:

Style Direction BoxOffice use Covered in Events on a broker (Kafka, Pub/Sub) provider publishes, many consumers OrderConfirmed → notification, analytics, search messaging Commands on a queue one producer, one of N workers "render ticket PDF for order 9" async work Webhooks provider calls your URL when something happens the payment provider tells payment a charge succeeded integrations WebSocket / SSE server pushes to a connected client live seat map, "your place in the queue: 18,204" edge — protocols

The contract still matters: event schemas need the same discipline as REST payloads — documented (AsyncAPI), versioned and evolved compatibly (schema registry, messaging).

items.title: Choosing a style
items.text:
REST gRPC GraphQL Async (events/queues) Transport HTTP/1.1, 2, 3 HTTP/2 HTTP broker protocol (Kafka, AMQP), HTTP for webhooks Payload JSON (text) protobuf (binary) JSON JSON, Avro, protobuf Contract OpenAPI (optional!) .proto (mandatory) schema (mandatory) AsyncAPI, schema registry Browser-native yes no (gRPC-Web/Connect) yes WebSocket/SSE for push HTTP caching excellent (GET, ETag, CDN) none hard (persisted queries) not applicable Streaming SSE, chunked built in (4 kinds) subscriptions inherent Coupling request/response, temporal request/response, temporal, codegen request/response, temporal none in time: consumers can be down Best for public & partner APIs, CRUD, cacheable reads internal high-QPS calls, polyglot services, streaming front-ends composing many services (BFF) side effects, fan-out, work that can wait 
flowchart TD
    q1{"Does the caller need<br/>the result to continue?"} -->|no| async["Async: event or queue<br/>(or a webhook to a partner)"]
    q1 -->|yes| q2{"Who is the consumer?"}
    q2 -->|"browser, partner,<br/>public"| q3{"Does one screen need data<br/>from many services?"}
    q3 -->|yes| gql["GraphQL BFF<br/>(REST underneath)"]
    q3 -->|no| rest["REST + OpenAPI"]
    q2 -->|"internal service,<br/>high volume or streaming"| grpc["gRPC"]
    q2 -->|"internal service,<br/>moderate volume"| rest

Real systems mix them. BoxOffice: REST at the public edge and for partners, a GraphQL BFF for the web and mobile apps, gRPC between order and inventory, events for everything that happens because an order was confirmed, and webhooks in from the payment provider.

items.title: Evolving a contract
items.text:
APIs change. The first question for every change is whether it is breaking — whether an existing, unchanged consumer would stop working:

Compatible (no new version) Breaking (needs a new version or a migration) add an endpoint, RPC or query field remove or rename an endpoint, RPC or field add an optional request field add a required request field add a response field remove a response field, or change its type or meaning (price in cents instead of reais) accept a new enum value in input return a new enum value consumers cannot handle add a new event type change the meaning of an existing event

Compatible changes rely on consumers being tolerant readers: they ignore fields they do not know (Jackson does by default in Spring Boot — keep it so). Each style has its own rules:

  • REST/JSON: tolerant readers + optional fields; breaking changes go to a new major version.
  • Protobuf: never change or reuse a field tag; when you delete a field, mark its tag reserved so nobody reuses it; adding fields is always safe.
  • GraphQL: no versions — add fields, deprecate with @deprecated(reason: …), remove when usage telemetry says nobody asks for them.
  • Events: the schema registry checks compatibility on every new version; old events stay in the log forever, so consumers must read every version that was ever written.

When a breaking change is unavoidable, version and migrate:

Strategy Example Notes URI path /v1/orders → /v2/orders most visible; easiest to route and test — the common choice Header / media type Accept: application/vnd.boxoffice.v2+json cleaner URLs; harder to test by hand Package (gRPC) boxoffice.inventory.v1 → .v2 both services can run side by side

Then expand and contract (parallel change): ship v2 next to v1, migrate consumers, watch v1 traffic fall to zero, announce the date with the Sunset header (RFC 8594)7, and only then remove v1.

Consumer-driven contract tests

How do you know a change is compatible before deploying it? Each consumer publishes the interactions it relies on ("order calls GET /v1/holds/{id} and reads status and expiresAt"); the provider's CI replays them against the new version and fails the build if any breaks. Tools: Pact, Spring Cloud Contract. This turns "did we break someone?" from a production incident into a red build.

In the interview

The API step of the interview framework takes 3–5 minutes: list the few endpoints that matter, with method, path, key parameters and response — not the whole CRUD. For BoxOffice:

  • GET /v1/events/{id}/availability → sections and seats left (cacheable for a few seconds)
  • POST /v1/events/{id}/holds {seats} + Idempotency-Key → 201 {holdId, expiresAt} or 409
  • POST /v1/orders {holdId, paymentToken} + Idempotency-Key → 202 {orderId, status: PENDING}
  • GET /v1/orders/{id} → status

Mention pagination (cursor), idempotency for writes, rate limits, and say why you picked the style ("REST at the edge for cacheability and partners; gRPC internally between order and inventory"). Interviewers notice when you know which calls are retried and which must not duplicate.

Common pitfalls

  • Leaking the implementation: returning entities, database ids or internal enum names that you will never be able to change.
  • Chatty APIs: a screen that needs 12 sequential calls is slow on mobile; aggregate in a BFF or design coarser resources.
  • Verbs in URLs (/createOrder, /getEvents): RPC disguised as REST; use methods on resources.
  • 200 OK with {"error": ...}: breaks retries, monitoring and caches — use the status code.
  • Non-idempotent writes without keys: a timeout plus a retry equals a double charge.
  • Silent breaking changes: renaming a field passes the provider's tests and breaks every consumer — use contract tests.
  • gRPC behind an L4 load balancer: all calls stick to one replica.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    CON["API = contract<br/>OpenAPI, proto, schema"] --> REST["REST<br/>public, cacheable"]
    CON --> GRPC["gRPC<br/>internal, high volume"]
    CON --> GQL["GraphQL BFF<br/>one screen, many services"]
    CON --> ASYNC["async: events, queues,<br/>webhooks → Messaging"]
    REST --> HTTP["status codes, cursor pagination,<br/>Cache-Control → CDN"]
    REST --> IDEM["idempotency keys<br/>→ Integrations"]
    GRPC --> H2["HTTP/2, streaming, deadlines<br/>→ Edge protocols"]
    CON --> EVO["compatible evolution,<br/>contract tests"]
    EVO --> VER["breaking change: new version,<br/>expand and contract"]
    ASYNC --> SCH["event schemas evolve too<br/>→ Messaging semantics"]

Palette components: app (every service publishes a contract) · client · mobile (consumers of the REST API and the GraphQL BFF) · cdn (caches the cacheable GETs) · queue (commands) · kafka (events such as OrderConfirmed) · payment (calls BoxOffice back by webhook). Scenarios: event-fanout, payment-system, chat (server push). Continues in: Edge — protocols, Edge — API gateway, Messaging — schema evolution, Integrations — idempotency keys, Hands-on 1.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• An API is a contract; describe it in a machine-readable form (OpenAPI, .proto, GraphQL schema, AsyncAPI) and expose DTOs, not entities.
  • REST for public and cacheable APIs, gRPC for internal high-volume calls, GraphQL for front-ends composing many services, async when the caller does not need to wait — real systems mix them.
  • Design REST with correct methods and status codes, Problem Details errors, cursor pagination, caching headers, 202 for long operations and idempotency keys for unsafe writes.
  • Evolve compatibly (tolerant readers, optional fields, never reuse protobuf tags, @deprecated); version only for breaking changes, then expand and contract; catch breaks with contract tests.

  1. RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics. IETF, 2022. ↩

  2. FIELDING, R. T. Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures. Doctoral dissertation, UC Irvine, 2000. ↩

  3. FOWLER, M. Richardson Maturity Model. martinfowler.com, 2010. ↩

  4. RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs. IETF, 2023. ↩

  5. gRPC — Core concepts, architecture and lifecycle; Protocol Buffers — Language guide (proto 3). ↩

  6. GraphQL Specification; OpenAPI Specification; AsyncAPI Specification. ↩

  7. RFC 8594 — The Sunset HTTP Header Field. IETF, 2019. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
When the payment for an order succeeds, BoxOffice has a lot to do: mark the order confirmed, turn the hold into sold seats, render a ticket PDF with a QR code (about 800 ms of CPU), e-mail it through the provider (300 ms, sometimes 5 s), send a push notification, update the sales dashboard, and re-index availability for search. If the checkout request does all of that before answering, the fan waits seconds, every slow provider slows checkout, and an e-mail outage fails ticket sales.

None of that work changes the answer the fan is waiting for — "your order is confirmed". It can happen a moment later, somewhere else. This page is about that "somewhere else": workers that process jobs from a queue, and schedulers that start work at a given time — and about making both correct when jobs are retried and replicas run in parallel.

items.title: What belongs in the request path?
items.text:
Ask one question about every step: does the user's answer depend on it?

Step after "pay" Answer depends on it? Where it runs Verify payment succeeded, confirm hold → order CONFIRMED yes — it is the answer in the request (or the payment webhook handler) Render ticket PDF no worker Send e-mail with the ticket no worker (notification) Push notification no worker (notification) Update sales dashboard no analytics consumer Update search availability no search consumer

Everything below the first row becomes a job (a unit of work described by a small message) placed on a queue and executed by workers (processes that pull jobs and run them).

sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fan
    participant O as order
    participant Q as Queue / Kafka
    participant W as ticket worker
    participant N as notification worker
    participant E as E-mail provider
    F->>O: POST /orders/ord_9/confirm
    O->>O: order CONFIRMED (one DB transaction)
    O->>Q: OrderConfirmed {orderId: ord_9}
    O-->>F: 200 Your order is confirmed
    Q->>W: render tickets for ord_9
    W->>W: PDF + QR → object store
    W->>Q: TicketsIssued {orderId: ord_9}
    Q->>N: TicketsIssued
    N->>E: send e-mail with link
    E-->>N: 202 queued

What you gain:

  • Latency: checkout answers in tens of milliseconds instead of seconds.
  • Availability: the e-mail provider can be down for 20 minutes; jobs wait in the queue and checkout keeps selling.
  • Load leveling: the queue absorbs the on-sale spike; workers drain it at their own, steady pace.
  • Independent scaling: ticket rendering is CPU-heavy, e-mail is I/O-bound — each worker pool scales on its own.

What you pay: the result is eventually there, not immediately; you need to show status ("your tickets are being issued"), handle failures without a user to show an error to, and make every job safe to run more than once.

Publishing reliably

"Commit the order, then publish the event" has a gap: if the process dies between the two, the order exists and no ticket is ever issued. The transactional outbox closes it — write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the order, and let a relay publish it. Class 8 (messaging) covers it; hands-on 7 builds it.

items.title: How many workers?
items.text:
Workers are sized like any server, with Little's law: the number of jobs in progress equals the arrival rate times the time each job takes.

\[ \text{workers needed} = \text{job arrival rate} \times \text{time per job} \]

When arrivals exceed capacity, the excess accumulates as backlog, and the backlog drains only at the difference between capacity and arrivals:

\[ \text{backlog growth} = \lambda_{\text{in}} - \mu_{\text{workers}}, \qquad \text{drain time} = \frac{\text{backlog}}{\mu_{\text{workers}} - \lambda_{\text{in}}} \]

Worked example — ticket rendering at on-sale

Assume (illustrative) 60,000 seats sell in about 10 minutes → 100 orders/s; off-peak, 10 orders/s. Rendering one order's tickets takes 0.8 s of a worker.

  • To keep up at peak: 100 × 0.8 = 80 workers busy all the time.
  • With only 40 workers (capacity 50/s), the backlog grows by 50 jobs/s: after 10 minutes, 30,000 jobs are waiting. The last fan waits about 30,000 / 50 = 600 s = 10 minutes for the tickets, and after the peak the backlog drains at 50 − 10 = 40 jobs/s, taking another 12.5 minutes.
  • Is that acceptable? Only the SLO can say. If the promise is "tickets in your inbox within 5 minutes", 40 workers are not enough.
2026-10-23T08:15:42.534155 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Two lessons from the plot. First, a queue converts a capacity problem into a delay: nothing failed with 40 workers, fans just waited. Second, the downstream sets the real limit: if the e-mail provider accepts at most, say, 100 messages per second on your plan, 500 notification workers do not send faster — they only collect 429 Too Many Requests. Size the worker pool for the slowest dependency and let the queue hold the rest.

Scale workers on queue depth or consumer lag, not CPU: a worker waiting on a slow provider uses no CPU but is not free. Serverless & autoscaling shows how (KEDA).

items.title: Try it in the playground
items.text:
Open the async-queue scenario: producers write to a queue drained by a pool of workers.

  1. Run the spike profile and watch backlog and consumer lag climb during the burst, then fall.
  2. Double the worker replicas: the peak backlog drops and drains sooner — check it against the formula above.
  3. Lower the downstream's rate limit: more workers stop helping, and errors appear instead.

items.title: Designing jobs that survive the real world
items.text:
A queue is not magic: workers crash in the middle of jobs, brokers redeliver, providers time out. Most brokers give at-least-once delivery: a job is removed (acknowledged) only after the worker says it finished, so a crash before the ack means the job is delivered again. Every rule below follows from that.

Rule Why BoxOffice example Make jobs idempotent the same job will run twice before rendering, check whether ord_9 already has tickets; e-mail with a dedupe key ord_9:tickets Ack after the work, not before acking first turns a crash into a lost job commit the Kafka offset after the PDF is stored Put ids in the message, not data messages stay small; the worker reads the current state {"orderId": "ord_9"}, not the whole order Retry with backoff, then park transient errors heal; permanent ones must not block the queue 4 attempts at 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, then the dead-letter queue (DLQ) Set a timeout per job a stuck job holds a worker forever PDF rendering aborts after 10 s Separate queues by priority a bulk job must not delay urgent ones tickets (urgent) and marketing-emails (bulk) on different queues and pools Record job status users and support need to see progress ticket_status = PENDING / ISSUED / FAILED on the order Respect downstream limits more parallelism than the provider allows = errors a rate limiter in the notification worker

A poison message is one that fails every time (a malformed payload, a bug). Without a retry limit it is retried forever and, on ordered partitions, blocks every message behind it. The DLQ parks it for a human (or a fixed version of the code) and lets the queue move on. Monitor the DLQ size: a growing DLQ is an incident.

With Spring for Apache Kafka, retries with backoff and a dead-letter topic are a few annotations3:

ticket-worker: TicketJobListener.java
@Component
class TicketJobListener {

    private final TicketService tickets;

    TicketJobListener(TicketService tickets) { this.tickets = tickets; }

    @RetryableTopic(
        attempts = "4",                                    // 1 try + 3 retries
        backOff = @BackOff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2.0), // 1 s, 2 s, 4 s (Spring Kafka 4)
        dltTopicSuffix = ".dlt")
    @KafkaListener(topics = "order.confirmed.v1", groupId = "ticket-worker")
    void onOrderConfirmed(OrderConfirmed event) {
        if (tickets.alreadyIssued(event.orderId())) {
            return;                                        // idempotent: duplicate delivery
        }
        tickets.renderAndStore(event.orderId());           // PDF + QR → object store
    }

    @DltHandler
    void onDeadLetter(OrderConfirmed event) {
        tickets.markFailed(event.orderId());               // visible to support; alert on rate
    }
}

items.title: Where jobs live
items.text:
Option Durable? Good for Watch out In-process (@Async, a thread pool) no — lost on crash or deploy fire-and-forget work you can afford to lose not a queue; no retries, no visibility Redis-based queues (Sidekiq, Celery, BullMQ) mostly (depends on persistence settings) simple job queues with retries and schedules Redis memory and persistence configuration Broker queues (SQS, RabbitMQ, Cloud Tasks) yes one job → one worker, per-message ack, delays, DLQ ordering is weak or per group Event log (Kafka, Pub/Sub, Kinesis) yes, replayable many consumers of the same facts, high throughput, ordering per key parallelism capped by partitions; offset-based acks Workflow engines (Temporal, AWS Step Functions) yes, with state multi-step processes that last minutes to days, with compensations a new platform to learn and operate

Durable execution engines deserve a mention: when a process has many steps and waits — "event cancelled → refund 60,000 orders → e-mail each fan → wait 7 days → close the accounting" — writing it as a workflow, whose progress the engine persists after every step, is simpler and safer than chaining queues by hand4.

items.title: Schedulers
items.text:
Some work is triggered by time, not by a request or an event:

  • every 30 s, release expired holds so their seats can be sold again;
  • at 10:00:00, open the sale for an event;
  • 24 h before each show, send a reminder to every ticket holder;
  • every night, reconcile payments with the provider's report (integrations).

items.title: The duplicate-cron problem
items.text:
The obvious implementation is a @Scheduled method in the service. It works on one replica. With 10 replicas, the job runs 10 times: 10 reminder e-mails per fan, 10 concurrent sweeps fighting over the same rows. The same happens with a cron entry copied to every VM. There are four standard fixes:

Kubernetes CronJobDistributed lock (ShedLock)Leader electionManaged scheduler

Run the job as its own short-lived pod, created by the cluster on a schedule, so the service replicas never run it.

release-holds-cronjob.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: release-expired-holds
spec:
  schedule: "* * * * *"              # every minute (cron's finest granularity)
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid          # never two runs at the same time
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 30        # skip a run that could not start in time
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 50      # kill a run that hangs
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: sweeper
              image: ghcr.io/boxoffice/inventory:1.8.2
              args: ["--job=release-expired-holds"]

Simple and visible (kubectl get jobs). Granularity is one minute and a pod start costs seconds, so it suits jobs that run every minute or less often.

Every replica tries to run the job, but only the one that acquires a lock in a shared store (PostgreSQL, Redis) actually does.

inventory: HoldSweeper.java
@Component
class HoldSweeper {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(HoldSweeper.class);
    private final HoldRepository holds;

    HoldSweeper(HoldRepository holds) { this.holds = holds; }

    @Scheduled(fixedRate = 30_000)
    @SchedulerLock(name = "releaseExpiredHolds",
                   lockAtMostFor = "PT25S",   // lock expires even if this replica dies
                   lockAtLeastFor = "PT5S")   // absorb small clock differences
    void releaseExpiredHolds() {
        int released = holds.releaseExpired(Instant.now(), 5_000);   // batch of 5,000
        log.info("released {} expired holds", released);
    }
}

ShedLock stores the lock as a row (name, lock_until, locked_by) and acquires it with a conditional UPDATE, so it needs no extra infrastructure beyond the service's own database2.

The replicas elect one leader that runs all scheduled work; if it dies, another takes over after the lease expires. Kubernetes offers Lease objects for this (the same mechanism its own controllers use), and Spring Integration, etcd and ZooKeeper provide election recipes.

Fits services with many periodic tasks, or tasks that must keep running state (a leader that holds a connection to a provider's stream).

The cloud calls you on a schedule: AWS EventBridge Scheduler, Google Cloud Scheduler, Azure Logic Apps / Functions timers. It invokes an HTTP endpoint, a queue or a function — at most once per schedule as far as the scheduler is concerned, still at least once from your endpoint's point of view if it retries.

Zero infrastructure; supports one-off schedules ("at 2027-03-14T10:00:00-03:00"), which cron cannot express.

items.title: Locks expire: fencing tokens
items.text:
A distributed lock with an expiry has a subtle hole, described by Martin Kleppmann1: a replica takes the lock, then pauses (a long garbage collection, a VM migration) beyond the lock's expiry. Another replica takes the lock and starts the job. The first one wakes up, still believing it holds the lock, and both write.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Replica A
    participant L as Lock store
    participant B as Replica B
    participant DB as Database
    A->>L: acquire (token 33), expires in 25 s
    Note over A: GC pause: 40 s
    B->>L: lock expired → acquire (token 34)
    B->>DB: release holds (token 34)
    A->>DB: release holds (token 33) — still thinks it owns the lock
    DB-->>A: rejected: token 33 < 34 already seen

The fix is a fencing token: the lock store hands out an increasing number with each acquisition, and the protected resource rejects writes carrying an older token. When the resource cannot check tokens, the job itself must be idempotent — which you need anyway. A lock is an optimization that avoids duplicated effort; correctness must come from idempotency or from the database (a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' AND expires_at < now() releases each hold at most once, no matter how many sweepers run).

items.title: Delayed work: three ways to expire a hold
items.text:
Releasing a hold 10 minutes after it was created is a delayed job. Three designs, often combined:

Design How Pros Cons Sweeper a scheduled job releases WHERE expires_at < now() in batches simple, catches everything seats return up to one period late; batch load on the DB Delayed message on hold, enqueue "release H-7" with a 10-min delay (SQS delay, Redis sorted set by due time, RabbitMQ delayed exchange) precise timing, no scanning one message per hold; must still be idempotent (hold may be confirmed) Lazy expiry treat a hold as free when expires_at < now() at read time correct immediately, no job needed for correctness expired rows remain until cleaned

BoxOffice uses lazy expiry for correctness (availability and new holds ignore expired holds) and a sweeper for cleanup. The scheduler is then not on the critical path: if it is down for 5 minutes, no seat is lost.

Opening the sale at 10:00

Do not make "the sale opens" depend on a cron firing exactly at 10:00:00 — schedulers are late by seconds, and a missed run would mean no sale. Store onSaleAt = 10:00:00 with the event; inventory simply rejects holds before that instant (a check against the clock, with clocks synchronized by NTP — distributed). The scheduler only does the preparation: at 09:45 it scales the fleet up and warms the caches (serverless & autoscaling).

The notification-system scenario combines a scheduler, a queue and the e-mail/push providers. Try raising the scheduler's job count to simulate the 24-hour reminder burst, and watch where the backlog builds up.

Open the full simulator

items.title: Trade-offs at a glance
items.text:
Do it in the request Do it in a worker Latency for the user sum of every step only the essential steps Failure of a non-essential step fails the request retried later; user unaffected Consistency immediate eventual — show status Load spikes hit every dependency at once absorbed by the queue Debugging one stack trace follow a job through queues (tracing) Operational parts none broker, workers, DLQ, monitoring of lag

In the interview

Whenever a design has a slow, failure-prone or bursty step that does not change the user's answer, say: "I'd move it off the request path: the API writes the order and an event in one transaction (outbox), and a worker pool consumes it — idempotent, with retries, exponential backoff and a DLQ. I'd scale the workers on consumer lag." For scheduled work, mention that cron on every replica runs N times, and pick CronJob, a lock or leader election — plus idempotency because locks expire. Then give a number: "100 jobs/s × 0.8 s = 80 workers at peak".

Common pitfalls

  • @Async treated as a queue: work disappears on every deploy or crash.
  • Non-idempotent jobs: at-least-once delivery turns a retry into a second e-mail or a second charge.
  • No retry limit and no DLQ: one poison message blocks a partition forever.
  • Scaling workers on CPU: I/O-bound workers look idle while the backlog grows.
  • More workers than the provider allows: only produces 429s.
  • @Scheduled on every replica: the job runs N times.
  • Trusting a lock for correctness: locks expire; use fencing tokens or idempotent, conditional writes.
  • The scheduler on the critical path: if "the sale opens" or "the hold expires" requires a job to fire on time, a late job becomes an outage.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    RP["request path: only what<br/>the answer depends on"] --> Q["jobs on a queue<br/>→ Messaging"]
    Q --> W["workers<br/>rate × time per job"]
    W --> JOB["idempotent jobs, ack after work,<br/>retries with backoff"]
    JOB --> DLQ["DLQ for poison messages"]
    W --> SCALE["scale on queue lag<br/>→ Autoscaling"]
    CRON["scheduled work<br/>on N replicas"] --> LOCK["CronJob, distributed lock,<br/>leader election"]
    LOCK --> FENCE["locks expire: fencing tokens<br/>→ Distributed consensus"]
    CRON --> LAZY["lazy expiry + sweeper<br/>seat holds → Databases"]

Palette components: queue (jobs and delayed messages) · worker (consumers sized by Little's law) · scheduler (cron and delayed work, once per cluster) · kafka (commit the offset after the work) · sql (ShedLock row, holds that expire lazily) · objstore (ticket PDFs) · notifications · email (the ticket e-mail, off the request path). Scenarios: async-queue, notification-system. Continues in: Serverless & Autoscaling — scaling on queue depth, Messaging — queues and pub/sub, Messaging — delivery semantics, Distributed — consensus (fencing), Hands-on 7.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Keep only what the user's answer depends on in the request; move the rest to jobs on a queue processed by workers.
  • Size workers with Little's law (rate × time per job); a queue turns overload into delay, and the slowest downstream sets the real limit.
  • Delivery is at least once: idempotent jobs, ack after work, retries with backoff, a DLQ for poison messages, priorities by queue.
  • Scheduled work on N replicas runs N times: use a CronJob, a distributed lock (ShedLock) or leader election — and stay idempotent, because locks expire (fencing tokens).
  • Design time-based rules so that correctness does not depend on a job firing on time (lazy expiry + sweeper).

  1. KLEPPMANN, M. How to do distributed locking. 2016. See also KLEPPMANN, M. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, chapter 8 (fencing tokens). ↩

  2. Kubernetes — CronJob; ShedLock. ↩

  3. Spring for Apache Kafka — Non-blocking retries. ↩

  4. Temporal documentation — Durable execution. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
At 10:03 on sale day a fan clicks Pay. BoxOffice's payment service calls the payment provider, and the call times out after 5 seconds. Did the card get charged? The fan, seeing a spinner, clicks Pay again. Thirty seconds later the provider sends a notification that the first charge succeeded — and then another one for the second. Meanwhile, the e-mail provider is rate-limiting BoxOffice because 40 thousand confirmation e-mails were sent in 5 minutes, and a venue-map API used on the event page is down.

BoxOffice deliberately buys its generic subdomains (services) — card processing, e-mail delivery, maps. That is the right call, and it turns each of them into a dependency you do not control: its latency, its availability, its limits, its API changes and, most importantly, the fact that it decides some outcomes asynchronously. This page covers the techniques that make such integrations safe: idempotency keys, verified webhooks, retries that cannot duplicate, reconciliation, and a plan for provider outages. The palette's EXTERNAL category — 3rd Party API, Payment, Email — is what this page is about.

items.title: What you do not control
items.text:
Property Internal service External provider Latency low, predictable, measured by you higher, heavy tail, on the public internet Availability your SLO, your on-call their SLA (credits, not your lost sales) Limits you set them rate limits and quotas per API key Changes coordinated, contract-tested versioned by them, deprecated on their calendar Outcome of a call known when the call returns may be decided later (3-D Secure, bank review) Failure visibility your logs and traces their status page, their error codes Cost infrastructure often per call or per message

Each row maps to a design rule:

  • Isolate the provider behind an adapter (an anti-corruption layer, services): the provider's model, status names and SDK stop at one class.
  • Every call has a timeout, and retries are safe (idempotency keys) — sections below.
  • Protect yourself from the provider with a circuit breaker and a bulkhead per provider (reliability), so a slow provider cannot exhaust your threads (the cascading-failure scenario).
  • Respect their limits: throttle on your side, honor 429 and Retry-After.
  • Assume outcomes arrive asynchronously: model states explicitly, accept webhooks, reconcile.
  • Observe each provider separately: latency, error rate by error code, rate-limit hits, cost.

items.title: Anatomy of a payment
items.text:
Card payments are the hardest integration BoxOffice has, so we use them as the guide. The card number never touches BoxOffice: the app collects it with the provider's hosted fields and receives a token, which keeps BoxOffice out of most of the PCI DSS scope7. The payment service then creates a payment with that token.

sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fan (app)
    participant O as order
    participant P as payment
    participant X as Payment provider
    F->>X: card details in hosted fields → token tok_abc
    F->>O: POST /v1/orders {holdId, token} + Idempotency-Key k-1
    O->>P: charge order ord_9 (key ord_9)
    P->>X: create payment 450.00 BRL, token, Idempotency-Key ord_9
    X-->>P: status processing
    P-->>O: PENDING
    O-->>F: 202 Accepted — order ord_9 PENDING
    Note over X: bank authorizes (maybe after 3-D Secure)
    X->>P: webhook payment.succeeded (signed)
    P->>O: PaymentSucceeded ord_9
    O->>O: confirm hold → order CONFIRMED
    O-->>F: push: your tickets are being issued

Notice what is not in the picture: a synchronous "charge succeeded" answer on which checkout depends. The provider may answer processing, may ask the fan to authenticate with the bank (requires_action, 3-D Secure), or may simply time out. The definitive outcome often arrives later, by webhook. So BoxOffice models the payment as an explicit state machine:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CREATED
    CREATED --> PENDING : provider accepted the request
    CREATED --> UNKNOWN : timeout — outcome not known
    UNKNOWN --> PENDING : status query / webhook
    PENDING --> REQUIRES_ACTION : 3-D Secure needed
    REQUIRES_ACTION --> PENDING : fan authenticated
    PENDING --> SUCCEEDED : webhook payment.succeeded
    PENDING --> FAILED : webhook payment.failed
    SUCCEEDED --> REFUNDED : hold expired / event cancelled

The UNKNOWN state is the honest answer to "the call timed out": the request may or may not have reached the provider. Never treat a timeout as a failure (you would release the seats of a fan who was charged) nor as a success. Resolve it by querying the provider or waiting for the webhook — and make sure that retrying cannot charge twice.

items.title: Idempotency keys
items.text:
An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. POST /payments is not — unless both sides agree on an idempotency key: a unique identifier of one logical operation, sent with every attempt of that operation. The server remembers the keys it has processed and, on a repeat, returns the stored result instead of executing again12.

BoxOffice needs keys in both directions:

  • Inbound — fans and apps retry: a double click, a mobile app retrying on a flaky connection, the gateway retrying a 503. BoxOffice's POST /v1/orders and POST /v1/events/{id}/holds require an Idempotency-Key header, generated by the client once per logical action (a UUID created when the fan presses Pay, reused on every retry of that press).
  • Outbound — BoxOffice retries the provider. Every call that creates a charge or a refund carries a key derived from BoxOffice's own id (ord_9, or ord_9:refund:1), so a retry after a timeout reuses it and the provider returns the original payment instead of creating a second one.
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as payment
    participant X as Payment provider
    P->>X: create payment, Idempotency-Key ord_9
    Note over X: charge created (pay_77)
    X--xP: response lost (timeout)
    Note over P: state UNKNOWN → retry with the SAME key
    P->>X: create payment, Idempotency-Key ord_9
