    X-->>P: pay_77 succeeded (stored result, no new charge)

items.title: Implementing it on your own API
items.text:
The provider does this for you on its side; on BoxOffice's side you implement it. The core is a table whose primary key makes "first one wins" a database guarantee:

V7__idempotency_keys.sql
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
    client_id     text        NOT NULL,              -- keys are scoped per caller
    key           text        NOT NULL,
    request_hash  text        NOT NULL,              -- SHA-256 of method + path + body
    status        text        NOT NULL,              -- IN_PROGRESS | COMPLETED
    response_code int,
    response_body jsonb,
    locked_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (client_id, key)
);
CREATE INDEX idempotency_keys_created_at ON idempotency_keys (created_at);  -- purge after 24 h
order: IdempotentExecutor.java
@Component
class IdempotentExecutor {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final TransactionTemplate tx;

    IdempotentExecutor(JdbcTemplate jdbc, TransactionTemplate tx) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.tx = tx;
    }

    StoredResponse execute(String clientId, String key, String requestHash,
                           Supplier<StoredResponse> operation) {
        // 1. Claim the key. The primary key guarantees that only one request wins.
        int claimed = jdbc.update("""
                INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (client_id, key, request_hash, status)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'IN_PROGRESS')
                ON CONFLICT (client_id, key) DO NOTHING
                """, clientId, key, requestHash);

        if (claimed == 0) {                                   // 2. Seen before.
            Map<String, Object> row = jdbc.queryForMap("""
                    SELECT request_hash, status, response_code, response_body::text AS body
                      FROM idempotency_keys WHERE client_id = ? AND key = ?
                    """, clientId, key);
            if (!requestHash.equals(row.get("request_hash")))
                throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY,
                        "Idempotency-Key reused with a different request");
            if ("IN_PROGRESS".equals(row.get("status")))
                throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.CONFLICT,
                        "a request with this Idempotency-Key is still being processed");
            return new StoredResponse((Integer) row.get("response_code"), (String) row.get("body"));
        }

        // 3. First time: run the operation and store its response in ONE transaction.
        try {
            return tx.execute(status -> {
                StoredResponse response = operation.get();
                jdbc.update("""
                        UPDATE idempotency_keys
                           SET status = 'COMPLETED', response_code = ?, response_body = ?::jsonb
                         WHERE client_id = ? AND key = ?
                        """, response.code(), response.body(), clientId, key);
                return response;
            });
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {                        // nothing was committed:
            jdbc.update("DELETE FROM idempotency_keys WHERE client_id = ? AND key = ?",
                        clientId, key);                       // let the client retry
            throw e;
        }
    }
}

The decisions hidden in those lines are the ones an interviewer will probe:

Case Behavior Why Same key, same request, completed return the stored response (same status code and body) the client cannot tell a replay from the original Same key, still in progress 409 Conflict — "try again shortly" two concurrent attempts must not both run Same key, different request 422 a client bug; executing it would be surprising Operation failed before committing delete the key nothing happened; a retry should run again Process crashed while IN_PROGRESS after a timeout (locked_at older than, e.g., 1 min), allow a new attempt to take over otherwise the key is stuck forever Old keys purge after 24 h (or the retry window you document) storage; the IETF draft and providers use similar windows

When the operation also calls the provider, step 3 is not purely local: the provider call cannot be rolled back with the transaction. That is why the outbound call carries its own idempotency key derived from the order id — if BoxOffice's transaction fails after the provider charged, the retry asks the provider again with the same key and gets the same payment back. For longer multi-step operations, Brandur Leach's "atomic phases and recovery points" design generalizes this3.

Keys must identify the logical operation

A key generated per HTTP attempt (a new UUID on each retry) protects nothing. A key derived from the content ("fan 42 buys seat C-14") blocks a fan who legitimately buys twice. Generate it when the user decides to act, and reuse it for every retry of that decision.

items.title: Retries and unknown outcomes
items.text:
Not all failures are equal. What you may do next depends on whether the request could have had an effect:

What happened Could it have taken effect? What to do Connection refused, DNS failure, TLS handshake failed no — nothing was sent retry (with backoff) Timeout after sending the request unknown retry with the same idempotency key, or query the status first 5xx from the provider unknown (possibly partial) retry with the same key, with backoff and jitter 429 Too Many Requests no wait for Retry-After, then retry; throttle yourself 400, 401, 402 card declined, 422 no, and it will not succeed do not retry; surface the error

Retries follow the rules from reliability: exponential backoff with full jitter, a small maximum number of attempts, at one layer only, and inside the caller's time budget. For a user-facing checkout that budget is short — a few seconds; after that, the payment becomes UNKNOWN/PENDING and the fan sees "we are confirming your payment", while a background job resolves it.

items.title: Webhooks
items.text:
A webhook is an HTTP request that the provider sends to your URL when something happens on its side — payment.succeeded, payment.failed, charge.refunded, email.bounced. It is how asynchronous outcomes reach you without polling. Treat each delivery as an untrusted, possibly duplicated, possibly late message:

Property of webhook delivery Consequence for the receiver Anyone on the internet can call your URL verify the signature before trusting anything A captured request can be sent again later check the timestamp (reject old ones) At-least-once: retried until you answer 2xx, for hours or days deduplicate by event id No ordering guarantee apply monotonic state transitions; ignore stale events Your slow handler causes provider timeouts and retries acknowledge fast, process asynchronously Deliveries can be lost after the provider gives up reconcile (next section) 
sequenceDiagram
    participant X as Payment provider
    participant H as Webhook receiver
    participant DB as inbox table
    participant Q as Queue
    participant W as payment worker
    X->>H: POST /webhooks/payments (signed)
    H->>H: verify signature + timestamp
    H->>DB: INSERT event (unique event id)
    H->>Q: enqueue event id
    H-->>X: 200 OK (within milliseconds)
    X->>H: same event again (retry)
    H->>DB: INSERT → duplicate, ignored
    H-->>X: 200 OK
    Q->>W: process event
    W->>W: PENDING → SUCCEEDED (conditional update)

items.title: Verifying signatures
items.text:
Providers sign each delivery with a secret shared only with you, usually an HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body plus a timestamp and a message id. The Standard Webhooks specification, adopted by several providers, defines the headers webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature, and signs the string id.timestamp.body4; other providers use the same idea with their own header names (Stripe's Stripe-Signature, for instance5). A receiver in Python with FastAPI:

payment-webhooks/main.py
import base64
import hashlib
import hmac
import json
import os
import time

from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, HTTPException, Request

from adapters import inbox, queue        # the service's own persistence and queue adapters

app = FastAPI()
SECRET = base64.b64decode(os.environ["WEBHOOK_SECRET"].removeprefix("whsec_"))
TOLERANCE_S = 300                        # reject deliveries older than 5 minutes


def verify(body: bytes, msg_id: str, timestamp: str, signatures: str) -> None:
    if abs(time.time() - int(timestamp)) > TOLERANCE_S:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="timestamp outside tolerance")   # replay
    signed = f"{msg_id}.{timestamp}.".encode() + body
    expected = base64.b64encode(hmac.new(SECRET, signed, hashlib.sha256).digest()).decode()
    for candidate in signatures.split():                  # several during secret rotation
        version, _, value = candidate.partition(",")
        if version == "v1" and hmac.compare_digest(value, expected):                # constant time
            return
    raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="invalid signature")


@app.post("/webhooks/payments")
async def payment_webhook(
    request: Request,
    webhook_id: str = Header(...),
    webhook_timestamp: str = Header(...),
    webhook_signature: str = Header(...),
):
    body = await request.body()          # the RAW bytes: re-serialized JSON would not match
    verify(body, webhook_id, webhook_timestamp, webhook_signature)
    event = json.loads(body)
    if await inbox.insert_if_absent(event_id=webhook_id, payload=event):   # unique event id
        await queue.publish("payment.provider-events", {"eventId": webhook_id})
    return {"received": True}            # 2xx fast; a worker does the real processing

Details that matter: verify over the raw bytes (parsing and re-serializing JSON changes whitespace and key order); compare with a constant-time function (hmac.compare_digest) so the comparison time does not leak the signature; accept several signatures during secret rotation; keep the handler tiny so it always answers within the provider's timeout.

items.title: Out of order and stale events
items.text:
The worker applies each event as a conditional state transition, so a late or duplicated event cannot move a payment backwards:

apply payment.succeeded
UPDATE payments
   SET status = 'SUCCEEDED',
       provider_updated_at = :occurred_at
 WHERE provider_payment_id = :provider_payment_id
   AND status IN ('CREATED', 'UNKNOWN', 'PENDING', 'REQUIRES_ACTION');
-- 0 rows updated = already final (duplicate or stale event): acknowledge and ignore

Many teams also treat the webhook as a notification only ("something changed on pay_77") and fetch the current object from the provider's API before acting. It costs one call, but the state you act on is always the latest and authoritative one.

items.title: Webhooks or polling?
items.text:
Webhooks (push) Polling (pull) Latency of the outcome seconds the polling interval Load one request per event requests even when nothing changed Needs a public endpoint yes (signature, TLS, availability) no Missed updates possible — needs reconciliation none, if the query is complete Typical use primary channel for outcomes fallback for stuck items, reconciliation

Use both: webhooks as the fast path, and a sweeper that polls the provider for payments still UNKNOWN or PENDING after, say, 10 minutes.

When BoxOffice sends webhooks

Resellers subscribe to BoxOffice events (order.confirmed, event.cancelled). Now BoxOffice is the provider and must offer what it expects from others: signed deliveries with a unique id and timestamp, retries with exponential backoff for a documented period, a dead-letter store, a dashboard to replay deliveries, and the promise that delivery is at-least-once and unordered. A queue with one worker pool per subscriber keeps one slow reseller from delaying the rest.

items.title: Reconciliation
items.text:
Idempotency and webhooks make each interaction safe. They do not guarantee that, at the end of the day, BoxOffice's records agree with the provider's: a webhook may be lost after the provider's retries ran out, a support agent may refund a payment in the provider's dashboard, a bug may skip a state update, and the provider deducts fees and chargebacks you only learn about from reports.

Reconciliation is the periodic job that compares the two sides and resolves differences — standard practice in any system that moves money6.

flowchart LR
    report["Provider report<br/>or list API since T"] --> load["Load into<br/>provider_payments"]
    ours[("payments<br/>(BoxOffice)")] --> match{"Match by<br/>provider id"}
    load --> match
    match -->|"equal"| ok["Matched ✓"]
    match -->|"theirs SUCCEEDED,<br/>ours PENDING"| fix["Auto-fix:<br/>confirm or refund"]
    match -->|"only in one side,<br/>amount differs"| human["Exception queue<br/>(finance on-call)"]
find mismatches for one day
SELECT coalesce(p.id, r.reference)  AS payment,
       p.status                      AS ours,
       r.status                      AS theirs,
       p.amount_cents                AS our_amount,
       r.amount_cents                AS their_amount
  FROM payments p
  FULL OUTER JOIN provider_payments r
         ON r.provider_payment_id = p.provider_payment_id
 WHERE (p.created_at >= :day AND p.created_at < :day + interval '1 day'
        OR r.created_at >= :day AND r.created_at < :day + interval '1 day')
   AND (p.id IS NULL
        OR r.provider_payment_id IS NULL
        OR p.status <> r.status
        OR p.amount_cents <> r.amount_cents);
Mismatch Likely cause Resolution Provider succeeded, BoxOffice PENDING lost webhook confirm the order if the hold is still valid; otherwise refund automatically Provider refunded, BoxOffice SUCCEEDED refund made in the provider's dashboard cancel the tickets, update the order BoxOffice SUCCEEDED, provider has nothing bug or test data in production exception queue — investigate Amounts differ currency, fees, partial capture exception queue; check the fee model

Run it at two speeds: a near-real-time sweeper (every few minutes, for payments stuck in UNKNOWN/PENDING, by querying the provider's API) and a daily reconciliation against the provider's settlement report, which also checks fees and payouts against the bank. Larger systems record every money movement in a double-entry ledger so that the books always balance and every difference has an explanation.

items.title: Provider outages
items.text:
Providers fail like everything else — and their outage arrives on your busiest day, because your busiest day is their busiest day too. Decide in advance, per provider, what BoxOffice does:

Strategy How Fits Cost Fail fast, clearly circuit breaker opens; checkout answers "payments temporarily unavailable" in milliseconds payments when nothing else is possible lost sales during the outage — but no hung threads, no cascading failure Queue and retry later accept the work, deliver when the provider is back e-mail, push, analytics exports delayed delivery; backlog to drain (rate limits!) Fail over to a second provider route by provider health; same port, two adapters e-mail (stateless sends); payments for large businesses two integrations, two reconciliations, card tokens are often provider-specific Degrade the feature hide the optional part venue maps, recommendations, fraud score (fall back to rules) reduced experience Protect the user's state extend seat holds while the payment provider is down BoxOffice checkout seats unavailable to others for longer 
flowchart LR
    n["notification worker"] --> cb{"circuit breaker<br/>primary ESP"}
    cb -->|"closed"| p["Primary e-mail provider"]
    cb -->|"open"| s["Secondary e-mail provider"]
    p -.->|"429 / 5xx"| retry["retry queue<br/>(backoff)"]
    s -.->|"429 / 5xx"| retry
    retry --> n

The BoxOffice decisions:

  • Payment provider down → the breaker opens after a burst of failures; new checkouts fail fast with a clear message, and active holds are extended by the outage duration so fans do not lose their seats while waiting. Payments already in flight stay UNKNOWN and are resolved by the sweeper when the provider returns. (A second payment provider is on the roadmap, behind the same PaymentGateway port.)
  • E-mail provider down or rate-limiting → messages wait in the queue; the notification worker throttles to the provider's limit; after a sustained outage, traffic fails over to a secondary provider. Ticket links remain available in the app, so a late e-mail is an inconvenience, not a lost sale.
  • Venue-map API down → the event page renders without the interactive map (cached image fallback).

E-mail is an integration with its own rules

Sending e-mail reliably is more than an API call. Providers enforce rate limits per account; they report bounces (address does not exist) and complaints (marked as spam) by webhook, and BoxOffice must stop sending to those addresses (a suppression list) or the provider will suspend the account. Domain authentication with SPF, DKIM and DMARC decides whether messages reach the inbox at all. And transactional mail (tickets, password resets) should use a separate stream or subdomain from marketing mail, so that a bad campaign does not hurt ticket delivery.

items.title: Try it in the playground
items.text:
Open the payment-system scenario: checkout calls a payment service that calls an external provider, with retries and idempotency.

  1. Raise the chaos level to high so the provider has outages and slow periods; watch checkout p99 and the error rate.
  2. Set retries without backoff on the payment edge: the provider receives a retry storm and stays down longer. Switch to exponential backoff with jitter.
  3. Add a timeout and a circuit breaker on the edge to the provider: checkout fails fast instead of piling up threads, and recovers when the provider does.

Open the full simulator

items.title: Security of integrations
items.text:
• Secrets (API keys, webhook secrets) live in a secret manager, never in the repository; rotate them, and use restricted keys with only the permissions a service needs (network & security).
  • Minimize PCI DSS scope: tokenize with the provider's hosted fields or payment page so that card numbers never cross BoxOffice's network.
  • Egress control: calls to providers leave through a NAT gateway with fixed IPs (some providers allowlist them); deny other outbound traffic.
  • Treat provider responses as input: validate them; a compromised or buggy provider must not be able to inject data into your system unchecked.

items.title: Trade-offs at a glance
items.text:
Decision Option A Option B Confirming a payment synchronous answer: simple UX, but checkout depends on the provider's latency and fails on timeouts 202 + webhook: robust and honest about uncertainty, but needs states, push/poll in the UI and reconciliation Learning outcomes webhooks: fast, efficient, can be lost polling: simple, complete, slow and wasteful Provider redundancy one provider: simpler, cheaper two providers: survives outages, doubles integration and reconciliation work Webhook processing inline: simpler inbox + queue: fast acks, retries under your control

In the interview

The payment-system follow-ups are predictable — have the answers ready:

  • "The call to the provider timed out. Was the customer charged?" → We don't know: state UNKNOWN; retry with the same idempotency key or query the status; never charge twice, never assume failure.
  • "The user double-clicked Pay." → client-generated Idempotency-Key per logical action; the second request returns the first result.
  • "How do you know the payment succeeded?" → signed webhook, verified, deduplicated by event id, applied as a monotonic state transition; plus a sweeper that polls stuck payments.
  • "What if the webhook never arrives?" → reconciliation against the provider's API and settlement reports, at two speeds.
  • "The provider is down." → circuit breaker, fail fast, extend holds, queue what can wait; a second provider if the business justifies it.

Common pitfalls

  • No timeout on provider calls: the provider's slow day becomes your outage (cascading-failure).
  • Retrying writes without an idempotency key: double charges, double refunds, duplicate e-mails.
  • Treating a timeout as a failure and releasing the seats of a fan who was charged.
  • Trusting unsigned webhooks, or verifying the signature over re-serialized JSON.
  • Slow webhook handlers doing all the work inline: provider timeouts, retries and duplicates.
  • Assuming webhook order: a late processing event overwriting succeeded.
  • No reconciliation: small disagreements accumulate silently until the accounting does not close.
  • Leaking the provider's model (status strings, ids, SDK types) throughout the code instead of one adapter.
  • Ignoring rate limits and bounces: the e-mail provider suspends the account on sale day.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    ADP["one adapter per provider<br/>ports and adapters"] --> RES["timeouts, circuit breaker,<br/>bulkhead → Reliability"]
    IK["idempotency keys<br/>inbound and outbound"] --> RETRY["safe retries"]
    TO["a timeout means UNKNOWN"] --> SM["payment state machine"]
    RETRY --> SM
    SM --> WH["webhooks: signature,<br/>dedup by event id"]
    SM --> REC["reconciliation with<br/>the provider's records"]
    WH --> ASYNC["ack fast, process async<br/>→ Messaging"]
    OUT["provider outages"] --> STRAT["fail fast, queue, fail over,<br/>degrade, extend holds"]
    STRAT --> RES
    IK -.-> DIST["idempotency<br/>→ Distributed systems"]

Palette components: payment (the provider behind the payment adapter) · email (rate limits, bounces, a secondary provider) · thirdparty (the venue-map API: degrade without it) · app (the adapter service) · sql (idempotency keys under a unique constraint, payment states) · queue (deliver later; process webhooks asynchronously) · scheduler (sweepers and reconciliation jobs) · serverless (a cheap webhook receiver). Scenarios: payment-system, cascading-failure, retry-storm, notification-system. Continues in: Reliability — circuit breaker, Distributed — idempotency, Distributed — transactions, Case study: payment system, Hands-on 9.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• External providers add latency, limits, changes and asynchronous outcomes you do not control; isolate each one behind an adapter with timeouts, circuit breaker and bulkhead.
  • Idempotency keys — inbound from clients, outbound to providers, derived from the logical operation — make retries safe; implement them with a unique key, stored responses, in-progress and mismatch handling.
  • A timeout means UNKNOWN, not failed: model the payment as a state machine and resolve uncertainty by query, webhook or sweeper.
  • Webhooks: verify the signature over raw bytes with a timestamp, deduplicate by event id, acknowledge fast, process asynchronously, apply monotonic transitions.
  • Reconcile with the provider's records periodically; webhooks and retries are not enough on their own.
  • Plan each provider outage in advance: fail fast, queue, fail over, degrade — and protect the user's state (extend holds).

  2. Stripe. Idempotent requests. Stripe API reference. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
Look at a day of BoxOffice traffic. From midnight to 09:45 the API serves a few hundred requests per second. At 10:00, when a stadium tour goes on sale, it jumps to tens of thousands — in seconds. By 10:30 it is back to normal. The same shape repeats a few times a week, at times announced in advance, plus surprises (an artist posts the link on social media at 23:00).

Two bad options: size the fleet for the peak and pay for idle machines 99% of the time, or size it for the average and fall over at 10:00. This page covers the two families of tools that avoid both — serverless platforms, which scale per request and charge per use, and autoscaling, which grows and shrinks a fleet of replicas based on metrics or schedules — and the uncomfortable truth they share: scaling takes time, and a flash sale does not wait.

items.title: Serverless
items.text:
Serverless means you deploy code and the platform provisions, scales and bills the machines underneath, including scaling to zero when there is no traffic. Two shapes dominate:

  • Functions as a Service (FaaS) — AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Run functions, Azure Functions: you deploy a function, the platform calls it once per event (an HTTP request, a queue message, a file upload, a schedule).
  • Serverless containers — Google Cloud Run, AWS Fargate (with ECS), Azure Container Apps: you deploy a container image that serves HTTP; the platform runs as many instances as the traffic needs, down to zero.

The idea has been described as "cloud programming simplified"1: no servers to patch, no capacity to plan, pay only for what runs. The constraints are the price.

items.title: How a function runs
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant E as Event source
    participant P as Platform
    participant X as Execution environment
    E->>P: invoke (request 1)
    P->>X: no warm environment → create sandbox
    Note over X: INIT: download code, start runtime, run init code (cold start)
    X-->>P: ready
    P->>X: handle request 1
    X-->>E: response
    E->>P: invoke (request 2)
    P->>X: reuse the warm environment
    X-->>E: response (no cold start)
    Note over X: idle for a while → frozen, later destroyed

Each execution environment (a lightweight VM or sandbox) handles one request at a time in Lambda; a burst of 300 simultaneous requests needs 300 environments. Environments are reused while traffic continues and destroyed after some idle time2. Everything follows from that model:

  • Cold start: the first request on a new environment pays for creating it. For a small Python or Node.js function this is typically a few hundred milliseconds; for a Spring Boot application on a plain JVM it can be several seconds (illustrative ranges — measure your own).
  • Concurrency = rate × duration (Little's law again): 2,000 requests/s × 0.2 s = 400 concurrent environments. Halving the duration halves the concurrency — and the bill.
  • State dies with the environment: anything kept in memory or on the local disk may vanish between requests; it is the stateless rule from the overview, enforced.

items.title: Cold starts and how to reduce them
items.text:
Technique What it does Cost Keep init cheap fewer dependencies, lazy loading, smaller package engineering time Initialize outside the handler DB clients and SDKs created once per environment, reused by every request none — always do it Provisioned concurrency / minimum instances the platform keeps N environments warm you pay for them while idle — partly undoing "pay per use" Snapshot restore (Lambda SnapStart) starts from a snapshot of an already-initialized runtime (Java, Python, .NET) restrictions on unique state at init (random seeds, connections) Native compilation (GraalVM native image, Spring AOT) a Java service starts in tens of milliseconds longer builds; some reflection limits Choose the runtime Go, Node.js and Python start faster than a full JVM may not match the team's stack

Cold starts matter on latency-critical, user-facing paths with spiky traffic. They do not matter for a queue consumer rendering ticket PDFs, where an extra second is invisible.

items.title: Concurrency limits protect — and throttle
items.text:
Serverless scales fast, but not infinitely:

  • Account and function limits: AWS Lambda has a default quota of 1,000 concurrent executions per Region shared by all functions of the account (it can be raised), and each function scales up by at most 1,000 environments every 10 seconds2. Beyond the limit, invocations are throttled (429), and asynchronous events are retried later.
  • Reserved concurrency caps one function so it cannot starve the others — and also caps the load it can put on a downstream.
  • Instance concurrency: serverless containers such as Cloud Run let one instance serve several requests at once (80 by default)3, which means far fewer instances — and fewer cold starts — for I/O-bound services.

Serverless scales; your database does not

1,000 concurrent functions, each opening a connection, means 1,000 connections to a PostgreSQL server that comfortably handles a few hundred. The function tier scaled perfectly and took the database down. Put a connection pooler (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer) or a queue between them, and set reserved concurrency to what the downstream can take.

items.title: Cost: per use vs always on
items.text:
FaaS bills per invocation plus GB-seconds (memory × duration). Containers bill for provisioned capacity whether used or not. Which is cheaper depends on how busy the service is. The chart uses illustrative list prices (AWS Lambda x86 in us-east-1 at the time of writing: US$ 0.20 per million requests and US$ 0.0000166667 per GB-second; a container replica at an assumed US$ 60/month, each handling up to 300 requests/s, minimum two for availability) — check current prices before using them in a real decision.

2026-10-23T08:15:43.000793 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

With these assumptions each invocation costs about US$ 1 per million, so functions are far cheaper below roughly a hundred million requests per month (a few dozen requests per second on average), and containers win for steady, busy services. Spiky, mostly idle workloads favor serverless; steady high-volume ones favor provisioned capacity. FinOps (cloud-native) builds on this calculation.

items.title: The landscape
items.text:
AWSGoogle CloudAzureOpen source / Kubernetes
  • Lambda (functions; triggers from API Gateway, SQS, S3, EventBridge, Kinesis/Kafka).
  • Fargate (serverless containers under ECS or EKS).
  • App Runner (container web services). Edge: CloudFront Functions, Lambda@Edge.
  • Cloud Run (serverless containers, concurrency per instance, scale to zero) and Cloud Run functions.
  • Triggers via Eventarc, Pub/Sub, Cloud Scheduler, Cloud Tasks.
  • Azure Functions (consumption and premium plans with pre-warmed instances).
  • Azure Container Apps (serverless containers, KEDA-based scaling).
  • Knative (serverless containers on Kubernetes, scale to zero).
  • KEDA (event-driven autoscaling of any Deployment, including to zero).
  • OpenFaaS. Edge runtimes: Cloudflare Workers (V8 isolates with very fast start).

Where BoxOffice uses serverless

  • Webhook receiver for the payment provider: bursty, tiny, must always answer — verify the signature, store the event, enqueue, return 200 (integrations).
  • Image processing when the marketing team uploads artist photos: triggered by the object store, minutes of idle between bursts.
  • Not for inventory: it holds hot connections to the database, needs predictable p99 during on-sale and runs all day — containers with autoscaling fit better.

items.title: Try it in the playground
items.text:
Open the serverless-burst scenario: a serverless function behind an API receives a burst.

  1. Run the spike profile and look at p99 during the first seconds: the cold-start penalty.
  2. Lower the function's concurrency limit until throttled requests (errors) appear; then raise it and watch what happens to the database behind it.
  3. Compare the live cost with the same load on a container tier (swap the node for an App Server with autoscaling).

Open the full simulator

items.title: Autoscaling
items.text:
Autoscaling adjusts capacity automatically. It operates at three levels, which must work together:

Level What changes Kubernetes Cloud VMs Horizontal number of replicas HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA), KEDA Auto Scaling groups, managed instance groups Vertical CPU/memory of each replica VerticalPodAutoscaler (VPA) instance type (usually with a restart) Infrastructure number of nodes the replicas run on Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter —

The HPA adds pods, but if no node has room, the pods stay Pending until the cluster autoscaler adds a node — which takes much longer. Both loops matter for the response time.

items.title: Policies
items.text: Policy How it decides Good for Weakness Target tracking keep a metric near a target ("CPU at 60%") most services reacts after the load arrives Step scaling add k replicas when a metric crosses thresholds coarse, explicit rules tuning; still reactive Scheduled change min/max at given times known events: on-sale at 10:00, business hours only as good as the calendar Predictive forecast from history (e.g. daily cycles) and scale ahead strong, regular daily or weekly patterns useless for one-off events Queue-based replicas proportional to backlog or lag workers (async work) max parallelism may be capped (Kafka partitions)

items.title: The Kubernetes HPA
items.text:
Every 15 seconds (by default) the HPA computes4:

\[ \text{desiredReplicas} = \left\lceil \text{currentReplicas} \times \frac{\text{currentMetric}}{\text{targetMetric}} \right\rceil \]

Six catalog replicas at 90% CPU with a 60% target: ⌈6 × 90 / 60⌉ = 9 replicas. It ignores changes within a 10% tolerance, and uses stabilization windows so that it does not oscillate (scale-down waits 5 minutes by default).

catalog-hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: catalog
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: catalog
  minReplicas: 4                 # never below N+1 across zones
  maxReplicas: 40                # bounded by what the database can take
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60   # % of the CPU *request* of each pod
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 100               # at most double every 15 s
          periodSeconds: 15
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 20                # remove at most 20% per minute
          periodSeconds: 60

CPU utilization is measured relative to the pod's CPU request, so the HPA only works if requests are set (and realistic). Hands-on 10 runs this HPA under a k6 load.

items.title: Choosing the metric
items.text: Metric Use when Caveat CPU utilization CPU-bound services (rendering, JSON-heavy APIs) I/O-bound services look idle while saturated Requests per second per replica you know a replica's capacity from load tests needs custom metrics (Prometheus adapter) In-flight requests / concurrency I/O-bound services, long requests needs instrumentation Queue depth or consumer lag workers the max useful replicas may be capped (partitions) Latency almost never alone it rises for many reasons, including a slow downstream that more replicas would make worse

items.title: Scaling workers on queue depth
items.text:
KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) feeds the HPA with metrics from event sources — Kafka lag, SQS depth, RabbitMQ queue length, Prometheus queries, cron — and can scale a Deployment to zero when there is nothing to do5:

ticket-worker-scaledobject.yaml
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: ticket-worker
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: ticket-worker            # the Deployment
  minReplicaCount: 1
  maxReplicaCount: 24              # = partitions of order.confirmed.v1
  cooldownPeriod: 120
  triggers:
    - type: kafka
      metadata:
        bootstrapServers: kafka:9092
        consumerGroup: ticket-worker
        topic: order.confirmed.v1
        lagThreshold: "200"        # target lag per replica

With a lag of 4,800 messages and a threshold of 200, KEDA asks for 24 replicas — the cap, because a Kafka consumer group cannot use more consumers than the topic has partitions (messaging).

items.title: Autoscaling lag
items.text:
Reactive autoscaling has a built-in delay: the load must arrive, be measured, trigger a decision, and the new capacity must start and warm up. Each step is small; together they are minutes:

Step Typical duration (illustrative) Metrics collected and aggregated 15–60 s HPA evaluation loop up to 15 s Pod scheduled — if a node has room ~1 s New node provisioned — if not 30–120 s Image pulled (not cached on the node) 5–60 s JVM start, Spring context, connection pools, cache warm-up 10–60 s Readiness probe passes, load balancer adds the pod 5–10 s Total ~1 to 4 minutes

A flash sale goes from 1× to 20× in seconds (here, 1,000 to 20,000 req/s in 20 s). The simulation below compares a reactive autoscaler (target 60%, doubling at most every 15 s, new replicas ready after 90 s) with the same autoscaler plus a scheduled pre-scale at 09:45 to the forecast, 20,000 / (500 × 0.6) ≈ 67 replicas:

2026-10-23T08:15:43.244910 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The red area is demand above capacity: requests that queue, time out or are rejected — in the first minutes of the sale, exactly when it matters most. Reactive scaling eventually catches up, but after the fans had a bad time.

items.title: Scheduled and predictive scaling
items.text:
When you know the spike is coming, do not wait for metrics:

  • Scheduled scaling: at 09:45 raise minReplicas (or the Auto Scaling group's minimum) to the forecast for 10:00, and bring it back down at 10:45. With KEDA, a cron trigger does exactly this.
  • Pre-warm everything the replicas need: nodes (overprovisioning with low-priority "placeholder" pods that get evicted when real pods need the room), images pulled, caches filled, database connection pools opened.
  • Predictive scaling (e.g. AWS predictive scaling) learns daily and weekly cycles from history and scales ahead of them. It helps with the regular evening peak, not with a one-off on-sale.

And when even that is not enough — two million fans for 60 thousand seats — capacity is not the answer at all: a waiting room admits fans at the rate the system can serve, rate limiting stops bots, and load shedding rejects excess early and cheaply (edge, reliability). The flash-sale scenario in the playground combines all of them.

items.title: Scaling in, safely
items.text:
Scaling down causes incidents too:

  • Flapping: scaling down as soon as load dips, then up again; stabilization windows and slow scale-down policies prevent it.
  • Killing in-flight work: replicas must drain on SIGTERM (graceful shutdown, overview); workers must stop taking jobs and finish or release the current one.
  • Scaling to zero saves money but brings back the cold start for the next request; keep a minimum on user-facing paths.

Do not autoscale into a wall

Set maxReplicas from the downstream budget, not from hope. If PostgreSQL accepts 500 connections and each replica holds a pool of 20, more than 25 replicas will fail to connect — and the autoscaler, seeing high latency, will add more. Use a connection pooler (PgBouncer), smaller pools, or caches to reduce database load, and alert when the HPA sits at its maximum.

items.title: Containers or serverless?
items.text:
Containers + HPA (Kubernetes) Serverless containers (Cloud Run, Fargate) Functions (Lambda) Scale-up speed pods: seconds; nodes: minutes seconds sub-second to seconds per environment Scale to zero with KEDA/Knative yes yes Cold start per new pod (JVM: seconds) per instance per environment, more frequent Concurrency per instance many requests many requests (configurable) one request (Lambda) Long-lived connections, WebSockets yes limited via a managed gateway only Max request duration unlimited minutes (platform limit) 15 min (Lambda) Cost shape pay for provisioned nodes pay per use (CPU-seconds), min instances optional pay per invocation + GB-seconds Operational effort highest (cluster) low lowest Best for steady, busy core services APIs with idle periods, small teams event glue, webhooks, bursty jobs

In the interview

When the problem has spikes, say explicitly that autoscaling is not instantaneous: "Reactive scaling takes one to a few minutes — metrics, decision, node, image, JVM warm-up — so for a known on-sale I'd pre-scale on a schedule at 09:45, and for unknown spikes rely on headroom, a waiting room and load shedding while the HPA catches up." Name the metric ("CPU for catalog, consumer lag for the ticket workers via KEDA"), the bounds ("max replicas limited by the database's connections") and, if you propose serverless, its limits ("cold starts, concurrency quotas, connections to the database — I'd put RDS Proxy in front").

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming instant elasticity: the first minutes of a spike are served by whatever was already running.
  • No CPU requests on pods: the HPA has nothing to compute utilization against.
  • Scaling on the wrong metric: CPU for I/O-bound services; latency that rises because of a slow downstream.
  • maxReplicas above what the database can take: the autoscaler turns slowness into an outage.
  • Serverless in front of a fixed-size database without a pooler or reserved concurrency.
  • Heavy initialization inside the handler instead of once per environment.
  • Runaway cost: a function that triggers itself (writes to the bucket that triggers it) or an unbounded retry loop scales to the quota and bills accordingly — set budgets and alarms.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    FAAS["functions per event"] --> COLD["cold starts,<br/>provisioned concurrency"]
    FAAS --> CONC["concurrency = rate × duration<br/>quotas, throttling"]
    CONC --> DOWN["the database does not scale with it<br/>→ Databases"]
    FAAS --> COST["per use vs always on<br/>→ FinOps"]
    AS["autoscaling"] --> HPA["HPA, KEDA, VPA, node autoscalers<br/>→ Kubernetes"]
    HPA --> MET["metric: CPU, RPS,<br/>concurrency, queue lag"]
    AS --> LAG["minutes of lag"]
    LAG --> SCHED["scheduled scaling + pre-warm<br/>for the 10:00 on-sale"]
    LAG --> PROT["waiting room, rate limiting,<br/>load shedding → Reliability"]
    HPA --> MAX["maxReplicas from<br/>the downstream budget"]
    MAX --> DOWN

Palette components: serverless (webhooks, image resizing, bursty glue) · app (the containers the HPA scales) · worker (KEDA on queue lag) · queue (the lag signal) · sql (the connection budget that caps maxReplicas) · apigw (rate limiting while capacity catches up) · metrics (what the autoscaler reads). Scenarios: serverless-burst, scale-out, async-queue, flash-sale. Continues in: Cloud-native — Kubernetes, Cloud-native — FinOps, Reliability — load shedding, Estimation — queueing, Exercise: Kubernetes autoscaling.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Serverless scales per request and bills per use; mind cold starts, concurrency = rate × duration, account quotas and the downstream that does not scale with it.
  • It is cheapest for spiky, mostly idle work; always-on containers win for steady, busy services.
  • Autoscaling works on replicas (HPA, KEDA), replica size (VPA) and nodes (Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter); pick the metric that reflects saturation — CPU, RPS, concurrency or queue lag.
  • Reactive scaling lags by minutes; for known peaks, scale on a schedule and pre-warm; for unknown ones, keep headroom and protect the system with waiting rooms, rate limiting and load shedding.
  • Bound the autoscaler by what the shared stores can take.

items.title: Index
items.text:
BoxOffice started, like most companies, as one Spring Boot application: events, seats, orders, payments and e-mails in one codebase, one PostgreSQL database, one deployable .jar. For the first year that was exactly right. Then three things happened at once. On sale days only the seat map and checkout were overloaded, but the only way to scale them was to run more copies of everything. A bug in the venue-image upload took checkout down with it. And four teams now shared one codebase: every release needed all of them to agree on the same day.

Nothing was wrong with the code. The shape of the system no longer fitted the load or the organization. This page is about choosing that shape: how big a deployable unit should be, where to draw the boundaries between services, and how to organize the code inside one service so that it survives years of change.

items.title: The spectrum: monolith to microservices
items.text:
"Monolith or microservices" is not a binary choice; it is a spectrum of how many independently deployable units the system has, and how strongly their boundaries are enforced.

flowchart LR
    subgraph mono ["Monolith"]
        direction TB
        m1["one app<br/>catalog · inventory · order · payment"] --> mdb[("one database")]
    end
    subgraph modular ["Modular monolith"]
        direction TB
        mm["one app"] --- c1["module catalog"]
        mm --- c2["module inventory"]
        mm --- c3["module order"]
        c1 --> s1[("schema catalog")]
        c2 --> s2[("schema inventory")]
        c3 --> s3[("schema order")]
    end
    subgraph micro ["Microservices"]
        direction TB
        gw["gateway"] --> x1["catalog"]
        gw --> x2["inventory"]
        gw --> x3["order"]
        x1 --> d1[("catalog DB")]
        x2 --> d2[("inventory DB")]
        x3 --> d3[("order DB")]
    end
    mono --> modular --> micro
Dimension Monolith Modular monolith Microservices Deployable units 1 1 many (one per service) Boundaries enforced by discipline (often none) the build: modules, package visibility, ArchUnit tests the network: a service can only call another's API Calls between parts in-process, nanoseconds in-process, nanoseconds network, ~0.5–5 ms in a datacenter, can fail Transactions one ACID transaction across everything one database, but each module owns its tables no shared transaction: sagas, eventual consistency Scaling the whole app the whole app each service on its own profile Failure isolation a memory leak kills everything a memory leak kills everything one service fails, others degrade Team autonomy low beyond ~10 engineers medium: separate modules, shared release high: own code, data, release cadence Operational cost lowest low high: discovery, tracing, CI/CD per service, on-call

The modular monolith deserves more attention than it gets. It gives you the main benefit of microservices — clear boundaries, each module owning its data — without paying for the network. If a module later needs independent scaling or a different team, it can be extracted along a boundary that already exists. Shopify, for example, publicly described its choice to modularize a large Rails monolith rather than split it into services7.

Monolith first

Most successful microservice systems began as monoliths: you rarely know the right boundaries on day one, and moving a boundary inside one codebase is a refactoring, while moving it between services is a migration2. Start with a (modular) monolith; split when one of the forces below becomes real.

items.title: When splitting pays off
items.text:
Split a part of the system into its own service when at least one of these forces is strong — and write down which one, because it tells you where to cut:

Force BoxOffice example Why a separate service helps Different scaling profile catalog is read-heavy (thousands of reads per write), inventory is write-hot during on-sale Scale and tune each on its own; cache one aggressively, protect the other Team autonomy the search team ships twice a day; payments ships monthly after review Independent releases, no release train Failure isolation the AI assistant can be slow or down without blocking ticket sales A failure stays inside a boundary (with timeouts and breakers, see reliability) Security / compliance scope only payment talks to the payment provider and holds provider tokens Smaller audit scope (PCI DSS), tighter network policies Different technology assistant is Python + FastAPI + pgvector; the core is Java Each service picks its runtime; the contract is HTTP or events

And the costs you accept when you split:

  • Every call can fail or be slow (distributed systems): timeouts, retries, circuit breakers become mandatory.
  • No cross-service transactions: "hold seat, create order, charge card" becomes a saga with compensations (messaging).
  • Availability multiplies down along synchronous chains: three services at 99.9% in series give ≈ 99.7%.
  • Operations multiply: N pipelines, N dashboards, distributed tracing to debug one request (observability).

Symptoms of a distributed monolith

All the costs of microservices, none of the benefits:

  • Services must be deployed together because a change in one breaks the others.
  • Two services read and write the same tables.
  • One user request triggers a long chain of synchronous calls; if any link is down, everything is down.
  • A shared library of domain classes forces every service to upgrade at once.

How small is "micro"? Not a number of lines. A service is the right size when one team can own it end to end, it can be deployed without coordinating with others, and it maps to one business capability. Services that are too small ("nanoservices", e.g. one per table) spend more time talking to each other than working.

items.title: Finding boundaries with Domain-Driven Design
items.text:
You have decided to split. Where do you cut? By database table (events, seats, orders)? By layer (a "UI service", a "logic service")? Each produces services that must change together. Domain-Driven Design (DDD)1 gives a better answer: cut where the business itself has a seam.

DDD works at two levels:

Level Question Tools Strategic design Where are the boundaries? subdomains, ubiquitous language, bounded contexts, context maps, Event Storming Tactical design What goes inside one boundary? entities, value objects, aggregates, repositories, domain events

Strategic design decides the services; tactical design shapes the code inside each one.

items.title: Subdomains: where to invest
items.text:
Not every part of the business deserves the same effort:

Kind Meaning In BoxOffice Strategy Core What makes the business different seat inventory and holds under a flash sale, the waiting room, pricing build it, with the best people Supporting Specific to the business, not a differentiator catalog of events and venues, notifications, search tuning build simply, or customize a product Generic Solved problems, the same for every company identity/login, card payments, e-mail delivery buy or reuse: an identity provider, a payment provider, an e-mail provider

That last row is why BoxOffice has an external integrations problem at all: it deliberately does not build its own card processing or mail servers.

items.title: Ubiquitous language and bounded contexts
items.text:
The ubiquitous language is the vocabulary shared by developers and domain experts and used verbatim in code: if the box-office staff say hold, on-sale, seat map and allocation, the code says Hold, OnSale, SeatMap and Allocation — not TempReservation or Lock.

But the same word often means different things in different parts of the business. A bounded context is the boundary inside which one model, and one meaning of each word, applies:

flowchart LR
    subgraph cat ["Catalog context"]
        e1["Event<br/>artist · date · venue · description · images"]
    end
    subgraph inv ["Inventory context"]
        e2["Event<br/>seat map · sections · holds · capacity"]
    end
    subgraph ord ["Order context"]
        e3["Event (as sold)<br/>event id · seat · price paid · fees"]
    end
    cat -. "same word,<br/>different model" .- inv
    inv -. "same word,<br/>different model" .- ord

Trying to build one Event class that serves all three — with images, a seat map and historical prices — produces a bloated object that serves none well and couples three teams. Instead each context owns its own model, and they exchange ids and events. Note the Order context in particular: an order stores the price paid, not a reference to the current price, because if the catalog changes a price tomorrow, yesterday's order must not change.

A bounded context typically maps to one service (or a small group of closely related ones). That is the main heuristic for service boundaries.

items.title: Context maps: how contexts relate
items.text:
Contexts exchange data, and the relationship between each pair is a design decision. A context map draws them3:

Pattern Meaning Use when Customer / Supplier the upstream team plans with the downstream team's needs in mind two teams in the same company Open Host Service + Published Language the upstream publishes a documented API or event schema for any consumer one provider, many consumers Conformist the downstream adopts the upstream model as is the upstream model is fine, or you have no influence Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) the downstream translates the upstream model at the border a third-party or legacy model you do not want leaking in Shared Kernel two contexts share a small piece of model and code rarely; it couples the two teams 
flowchart LR
    catalog["Catalog"] -->|"Open Host: REST + OpenAPI"| order["Order"]
    catalog -->|"Published Language:<br/>EventPublished events"| search["Search"]
    inventory["Inventory"] -->|"Customer / Supplier:<br/>hold & confirm API"| order
    order -->|"OrderConfirmed event"| notification["Notification"]
    psp["Payment provider"] -->|"Anti-Corruption Layer"| payment["Payment"]
    payment -->|"PaymentSucceeded event"| order
    mail["E-mail provider"] -->|"Anti-Corruption Layer"| notification

The two anti-corruption layers matter most in practice: the payment provider's model (its "payment intents", its status names, its error codes) must not spread through BoxOffice. The payment service translates it into BoxOffice's own Payment model at the border — the integrations page shows that adapter.

items.title: Aggregates: the unit of consistency
items.text:
Inside a context, an aggregate is a cluster of objects changed together as one unit, with one root as the only entry point. The root enforces the invariants — rules that must always hold. Two rules make aggregates fit microservices:

  • Reference other aggregates by id only. A Hold keeps the seatId and the fanId, never a Fan object. That is what lets the two live in different services.
  • One transaction changes one aggregate. If a use case must change two aggregates, the second change happens afterwards, triggered by a domain event (eventual consistency).
inventory: the Hold aggregate root (illustrative)
public class Hold {                                   // aggregate root
    private static final Duration TTL = Duration.ofMinutes(10);
    private static final int MAX_SEATS = 6;           // per fan, per event

    private final HoldId id;
    private final EventId eventId;                    // other aggregates: by id only
    private final FanId fanId;
    private final Set<SeatId> seats;
    private final Instant expiresAt;
    private HoldStatus status = HoldStatus.ACTIVE;

    public static Hold place(EventId event, FanId fan, Set<SeatId> seats, Clock clock) {
        if (seats.isEmpty() || seats.size() > MAX_SEATS)
            throw new HoldRejected("between 1 and " + MAX_SEATS + " seats");
        return new Hold(HoldId.random(), event, fan, Set.copyOf(seats),
                        clock.instant().plus(TTL));
    }

    public void confirm(Clock clock) {                // called when the payment succeeds
        if (status != HoldStatus.ACTIVE || clock.instant().isAfter(expiresAt))
            throw new HoldExpired(id);
        status = HoldStatus.CONFIRMED;
    }
}

The invariant "a seat belongs to at most one active hold" spans all holds of an event, so it cannot be checked inside one Hold object; it is enforced by the database (a unique constraint on (event_id, seat_id) for active holds) — exactly the kind of decision class 6 is about.

Event Storming in one paragraph

To find contexts with the business, put domain experts and engineers in front of a wall and write every domain event on an orange sticky note, in the past tense: EventPublished, SaleOpened, FanQueued, SeatsHeld, HoldExpired, PaymentSucceeded, OrderConfirmed, TicketIssued, TicketScanned. Order them in time, add the commands (blue) and actors (yellow) that cause them, and look where the vocabulary changes or where one group of people hands over to another. Those seams are your candidate bounded contexts6.

items.title: Conway's law
items.text:
"Any organization that designs a system will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure." — Melvin Conway, 19684

Boundaries in the code drift to match boundaries between teams, because communication within a team is cheap and communication between teams is expensive. The plot below shows BoxOffice's evolution: as teams form around business capabilities, the codebase splits along the same lines.

2026-10-23T08:15:43.416988 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Two practical consequences:

  • If boundaries and teams disagree, the teams win. A service owned by three teams becomes a coordination bottleneck; three services owned by one team tend to merge back into a distributed monolith.
  • The inverse Conway maneuver: shape the teams first — one stream-aligned team per business capability, plus a platform team that provides deployment, observability and databases as self-service — so that the architecture follows5.

items.title: Owning the data
items.text:
Database per service means no service reads or writes another service's tables. It does not require one database server per service: one PostgreSQL cluster can host several schemas, as long as each schema has exactly one owner.

flowchart LR
    order["order"] -->|"POST /holds/{id}/confirm"| inventory["inventory"]
    inventory --> inv[("inventory schema")]
    order --> ord[("order schema")]
    order -.-x|"no direct SQL"| inv

When order needs to confirm a hold, it calls the inventory API, never the holds table. That keeps the inventory team free to change its schema, add a cache or move to another database. Two consequences follow:

  • Queries across services become API calls — or a local, read-only copy of the other service's data kept up to date by events (CQRS, messaging). search keeps its own index of events this way.
  • Business transactions across services become a sequence of local transactions coordinated by events or an orchestrator, with compensations when a step fails: the saga pattern. "Payment failed → release the hold" is a compensation.

items.title: Talking to each other
items.text:
Synchronous (request/response)Asynchronous (events)

The caller waits for the answer. Simple, but temporally coupled: if inventory is down, order cannot confirm.

sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fan
    participant O as order
    participant I as inventory
    F->>O: POST /orders
    O->>I: confirm hold H-7
    I-->>O: confirmed
    O-->>F: 201 Created

Use when the caller needs the answer now to respond (confirm the hold before saying "you have tickets").

The producer publishes a fact and moves on; consumers react in their own time. No temporal coupling — notification can be down for five minutes and catch up.

sequenceDiagram
    participant O as order
    participant K as Kafka
    participant N as notification
    participant A as analytics
    O->>K: OrderConfirmed
    Note over O: answers the fan immediately
    K->>N: OrderConfirmed → e-mail tickets
    K->>A: OrderConfirmed → sales dashboard

Use when the work does not change the answer to the user (e-mail, analytics, search indexing).

Class 8 (messaging) goes deep on events; the API styles page covers the request/response options.

items.title: Inside one service: internal architecture
items.text: Splitting the system decides the boundaries between services. Each service still needs a structure inside, and the same principle applies at a smaller scale: protect the business rules from things that change more often — frameworks, databases, protocols, providers.

items.title: SOLID in one table
items.text:
The five SOLID principles8 are class-level rules that make that protection possible:

Principle One sentence Violation in BoxOffice Single responsibility a class has one reason to change OrderService that also renders the e-mail HTML and calls the payment provider Open/closed add behavior by adding code, not editing working code a switch (provider) that grows with each new payment provider Liskov substitution a subtype must work wherever its parent does a FreeTicketPayment that throws on refund() Interface segregation clients should not depend on methods they do not use one InventoryRepository with 40 methods used by every class Dependency inversion business code depends on abstractions it owns, not on infrastructure HoldService importing the JPA EntityManager or the provider's SDK

items.title: Layered, clean and hexagonal
items.text:
Most Spring Boot services start layered: controller → service → repository → database. It separates HTTP from business logic, but the business layer still depends on the persistence layer. Clean Architecture (Robert C. Martin) and Hexagonal Architecture, a.k.a. ports and adapters (Alistair Cockburn), invert that one arrow: the core defines interfaces (ports) in business terms, and infrastructure (adapters) implements them910.

flowchart LR
    rest["REST controller<br/>(driving adapter)"] --> uc["PayForOrder<br/>use case"]
    kafka["Kafka listener<br/>(driving adapter)"] --> uc
    uc --> port1["«port»<br/>PaymentGateway"]
    uc --> port2["«port»<br/>PaymentRepository"]
    stripe["ProviderAdapter<br/>(HTTP client)"] -.->|implements| port1
    fake["FakeGateway<br/>(tests)"] -.->|implements| port1
    jpa["JpaPaymentRepository"] -.->|implements| port2

For the payment service this is not academic. The port is the anti-corruption layer from the context map:

payment: a port owned by the core, an adapter per provider
// core — knows nothing about HTTP, JSON or any provider SDK
public interface PaymentGateway {
    ChargeResult charge(PaymentId id, Money amount, PaymentMethodToken method,
                        IdempotencyKey key);
}

// adapter — the only class that knows the provider's API and vocabulary
@Component
class ProviderPaymentGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    private final ProviderClient client;   // generated or hand-written HTTP client

    @Override
    public ChargeResult charge(PaymentId id, Money amount, PaymentMethodToken method,
                               IdempotencyKey key) {
        var response = client.createPayment(amount.cents(), amount.currency().code(),
                                            method.value(), key.value());
        return switch (response.status()) {            // translate THEIR states to OURS
            case "succeeded"       -> ChargeResult.succeeded(response.id());
            case "requires_action" -> ChargeResult.needsCustomerAction(response.nextActionUrl());
            case "processing"      -> ChargeResult.pending(response.id());
            default                -> ChargeResult.failed(response.failureCode());
        };
    }
}

The payoff: use-case tests run in milliseconds with a FakeGateway; adding a second provider for failover is a new adapter, not a rewrite; and the provider's status names stop at one class.

Layered Clean / Hexagonal Business code depends on the persistence framework interfaces it owns Unit tests need a database or framework mocks plain in-memory fakes Swapping DB / provider / protocol touches business classes a new adapter Cost fewest classes more interfaces, mappers, indirection

Do not over-architect a CRUD service

Ports, adapters and mappers cost classes and indirection. A service that only stores and returns records (the venue list, a lookup table) can stay layered. The structure pays off where business rules are rich (inventory), integrations are external (payment, notification) or the service will live for years. Microservices let each service choose.

items.title: Shared capabilities as services
items.text:
Some capabilities are needed by many parts of the system and appear as their own components in the palette. They are usually the first services extracted — and often the first ones bought:

Capability Palette What it owns Build or buy? Scaling notes Auth auth identities, credentials, sessions, token signing keys usually buy/reuse: Keycloak, Auth0, Cognito, Entra ID stateless token validation at the gateway; login spikes at on-sale Search search an inverted index, derived from the catalog build on Elasticsearch/OpenSearch or a managed search index updated from EventPublished events; read-heavy, cache popular queries Notifications notifications templates, user preferences, delivery log build the service, buy the delivery (e-mail/push/SMS providers) queue-driven workers; throttled by provider rate limits Analytics analytics an event stream and aggregates build the pipeline on Kafka + a data warehouse append-only, high write volume, never on the request path Scheduler scheduler job definitions and their next run Kubernetes CronJob, a cloud scheduler, or a library with locks see async work

Two patterns repeat: these services are mostly fed by events rather than called synchronously, and their data is often derived — search and analytics can be rebuilt from the source of truth, which makes them cheaper to operate.

items.title: BoxOffice service map
items.text:
Service Capability Owns Called by Scaling profile gateway single entry point, auth check, rate limits — clients requests/s auth login, tokens users, credentials gateway login bursts at on-sale catalog events, venues, artists catalog DB gateway, order read-heavy, cache + CDN inventory seat maps, holds seats, holds gateway, order write-hot during on-sale; correctness first order orders, checkout saga orders gateway follows sales payment adapter to the payment provider payments, provider ids order follows sales; bounded by the provider notification e-mail and push templates, delivery log events queue-driven bursts search full-text search derived index gateway read-heavy assistant AI support (Python) conversations, embeddings gateway GPU/LLM-bound, isolated

In the interview

You rarely need to draw twenty microservices. Draw the few services whose boundaries matter for the problem and justify each split with a force: "I'd keep catalog and inventory separate because catalog is read-heavy and cacheable while inventory is write-hot and must be strongly consistent — different scaling and consistency needs." If asked "monolith or microservices?", answer with the trade-off, not a slogan: team size, independent scaling needs, and operational maturity. Saying "I'd start as a modular monolith and extract inventory first" is a strong, defensible answer.

Common pitfalls

  • Splitting by technical layer ("UI service", "DB service") instead of by business capability: every feature touches every service.
  • Shared database between services: the schema becomes a contract nobody can change.
  • Entity services (EventService, SeatService, PriceService) that are just CRUD over one table and must call each other for every use case.
  • Synchronous chains of five services for one click: availability and latency multiply.
  • Splitting before the domain is understood: boundaries drawn too early are expensive to move.
  • Ignoring the teams: boundaries that do not match ownership decay (Conway).

Scenarios: monolith, event-fanout. Continues in: API Styles, Databases (one database per service), Messaging — patterns (outbox, saga), Distributed — transactions, Hands-on 1.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Monolith → modular monolith → microservices is a spectrum; start modular and split when a force (scaling profile, team autonomy, failure isolation, compliance, technology) is real.
  • Find boundaries with DDD: subdomains tell you what to build or buy, bounded contexts tell you where one model ends; aggregates reference each other by id.
  • Conway's law: services take the shape of the teams — design both together.
  • Each service owns its data; others use its API or its events, never its tables.
  • Inside a service, ports and adapters keep business rules independent of frameworks and providers — essential for integrations, optional for CRUD.
  • Auth, search, notifications, analytics and scheduling are shared capabilities, usually event-fed and often bought.

items.title: Index
items.text:
BoxOffice started like most products: one service and one PostgreSQL database holding everything — events, venues, seats, orders, users, even the poster images as bytea columns. It worked for a year. Then the stadium show went on sale at 10:00. Two million fans opened the event page, the search box was hammered with "taylor", the marketing team ran a "sales per minute" report on the same database, and 60,000 seats had to be sold exactly once each. At 10:02 the database CPU was at 100%, the report query held locks for 40 seconds, and two fans received tickets for seat A-12.

Nothing was "wrong" with PostgreSQL. The problem was that different data has different shapes, and one store was asked to be good at all of them at once. This class is about recognizing those shapes and choosing — and scaling — the right store for each.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Classify the data of a system by access pattern, volume, consistency need and query flexibility, and map each kind to a storage component (SQL, NoSQL, search, object store, data warehouse, vector database).
  • Compare relational, key-value, document, wide-column and graph models, and justify a SQL-vs-NoSQL choice with a decision guide instead of a slogan.
  • Explain how B-tree and LSM-tree storage engines and indexes work, and predict their effect on read and write cost.
  • Diagnose isolation anomalies (lost update, write skew, phantoms) and fix a double-booking bug with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, conditional updates, optimistic locking or constraints.
  • Design replication (leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless) and partitioning (range, hash, consistent hashing) for a workload, and anticipate replication lag, hot partitions and resharding.
  • Decide when a search engine, object storage, a data warehouse or a vector database belongs in the architecture, and how data flows into it (CDC, ETL/ELT, embeddings).

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
1. This overview — the data map of BoxOffice, the questions that choose a store, polyglot persistence, and the database scaling ladder.
  2. Data Models & Storage Engines — relational, key-value, document, wide-column, graph; the SQL-vs-NoSQL decision guide; B-trees vs LSM-trees; indexes and EXPLAIN.
  3. Transactions & Isolation — ACID, isolation levels and their anomalies, the double-booking bug and four ways to fix it, seat holds.
  4. Replication — leader-follower, synchronous vs asynchronous, replication lag, failover, multi-leader and leaderless quorums.
  5. Partitioning & NewSQL — range, hash and consistent hashing, hot partitions, secondary indexes, resharding, Spanner and CockroachDB.
  6. Specialized Stores — search engines, object storage, data warehouses and lakehouses, vector databases.
  7. Quiz — check your understanding.
