items.title: Data has a shape
items.text:
Before picking a database, describe the data. Four properties decide almost everything:

Property Question to ask Why it matters Access pattern How is it read and written? By key? By range? Full-text? Aggregations over millions of rows? Each store is fast for a few patterns and slow for the rest. Read/write ratio and volume How many reads and writes per second, at peak? How many bytes, growing how fast? Decides whether one node is enough, and whether to scale reads (replicas, cache) or writes (partitioning). Consistency need What breaks if a reader sees data that is a few seconds old? If two writers race? Money and inventory need strong guarantees; a "views" counter does not. Query flexibility Are the queries known in advance, or will analysts invent new ones every week? Fixed queries allow denormalized NoSQL tables; ad hoc queries need SQL and indexes.

Applying them to BoxOffice gives a data map. The volumes below are illustrative assumptions for a mid-size ticketing company — the point is the order of magnitude and the contrast between rows, not the exact values.

Data Example Volume (assumed) Access pattern Consistency need Palette component Seat inventory and holds seat A-12 of event 42 is HELD by Alice until 10:07 60 k rows per stadium event; bursts of thousands of writes/s at on-sale point read/update by (event_id, seat_id); "best available" range scan strong — never sell a seat twice sql Orders and payments order 9001: 2 tickets, R$ 980, PAID ~100 k orders/day (≈ 36 M/year) × ~1 KB ≈ 37 GB/year by id, by customer; joins with tickets strong — money sql Event catalog name, venue, date, lineup, prices ~20 k events/year, a few KB each read-heavy (≫ 100 reads per write), by id and by listing stale by seconds is fine sql + cache Search "taylor são paulo december" same events, as an inverted index full-text, typo-tolerant, ranked, autocomplete eventual (seconds) search Event posters and tickets as PDF posters/42/hero.webp, 2 MB posters: ~20 k events × ~5 images ≈ 100 GB/year; ticket PDFs: ~7 TB/year (or render on demand) whole object by key, served through a CDN write once, read many objstore Clickstream and sales analytics page_view, add_to_cart, purchase events ~100 M events/day × ~200 B ≈ 20 GB/day aggregations over months ("sales per minute per city") minutes of delay is fine dwh Sessions, rate-limit counters, waiting-room position session:abc → user 7 millions of small keys key lookup, sub-millisecond, with TTL losing some is tolerable cache / nosql Assistant knowledge FAQ chunks, refund policy, event descriptions as embeddings ~100 k vectors × 1,024 dims × 4 B ≈ 400 MB nearest-neighbour by meaning eventual vectordb

Notice that the rows differ by orders of magnitude in every column. A store tuned for the first row (small, hot, transactional) is a poor fit for the sixth (huge, append-only, scanned in bulk), and vice versa.

flowchart LR
    gw["gateway"] --> inv["inventory"]
    gw --> ord["order"]
    gw --> cat["catalog"]
    gw --> srch["search"]
    gw --> ast["assistant"]
    inv --> sqlI[("SQL<br/>seats, holds")]
    ord --> sqlO[("SQL<br/>orders, payments")]
    cat --> cache[("Cache")]
    cache -->|miss| sqlC[("SQL<br/>events, venues")]
    sqlC -->|"CDC"| idx[("Search index")]
    srch --> idx
    cat -->|"poster URLs"| obj[("Object store")]
    sqlO -->|"CDC / ELT"| dwh[("Data warehouse")]
    ast --> vec[("Vector DB")]

This is polyglot persistence: each service keeps its data in the store that fits its access pattern, and data flows between stores through change streams rather than shared tables.

Think first: is the search index a second source of truth?

No. The catalog SQL database is the system of record; the search index, the cache, the warehouse and the vector database are derived data — they can be rebuilt from the system of record. That distinction tells you where writes go (only to the system of record), what to back up carefully, and what you may throw away and rebuild after a bug. Kleppmann calls this split "systems of record vs derived data"1.

items.title: Five questions that choose a store
items.text:
When a requirement arrives — in a design review or in an interview — walk through these questions in order. Most of the time the answer is "a relational database", and you only leave it with a reason.

  1. What is the system of record, and what are its invariants? Seats must never be sold twice; an order total must equal the sum of its items. Invariants that span several rows want transactions — a relational database is the default.
  2. What are the top 3 queries, and are they known in advance? Known key lookups at huge scale fit a key-value or wide-column store; unknown, ad hoc queries fit SQL.
  3. How big, how fast, growing how? Estimate peak QPS and bytes (see Estimation). If one node with replicas can hold it for the next two to three years, you do not need to partition yet.
  4. How stale can a read be? Seconds of staleness unlock replicas, caches and asynchronous indexes — the cheapest scaling tools there are.
  5. What can the team operate? A managed PostgreSQL that everybody understands beats an exotic store that one person can debug at 3 a.m.

BoxOffice: applying the questions to the seat inventory

  1. Invariant: one seat, at most one valid hold or ticket → needs atomic check-and-set → transactions.
  2. Top queries: hold seat by (event_id, seat_id); list available seats of a section; release expired holds → known, but the second one is a range scan → SQL with a composite index fits.
  3. Volume: the whole inventory of a stadium event is 60 k rows — tiny. The challenge is write bursts on a single event, not size.
  4. Staleness: the seat map shown to fans can be seconds old; the hold decision must read the current state.
  5. Team: PostgreSQL is in every hands-on of the course.

Decision: PostgreSQL for inventory, with row-level locking (see Transactions) and a cached, slightly stale seat map for display.

items.title: The database scaling ladder
items.text:
The database is usually the first component to saturate, because it is the one component that is hard to make stateless. The classic mistake is to jump straight to sharding. Climb the ladder one step at a time, and measure before each step2:

Step What you do What it buys What it costs 1. Fix the queries Add the missing index, remove N+1 queries, read EXPLAIN Often 10–100× on the slow query Almost nothing 2. Pool connections PgBouncer or the driver pool; cap connections per service Stops the database from drowning in connections A config file 3. Scale up Bigger instance: more RAM (working set in memory), faster SSD 2–4× with no code change Money; there is a largest instance 4. Cache reads Cache-aside for hot, read-mostly data (Caching) Removes most read traffic Staleness and invalidation 5. Read replicas Route reads to followers (Replication) Read throughput × replicas Replication lag; reads may be stale 6. Split by function One database per service (catalog, inventory, order) Isolates workloads; smaller databases No cross-service joins or transactions 7. Partition (shard) Spread one table across nodes by key (Partitioning) Write throughput and storage × shards Cross-shard queries, resharding, operations 8. Specialized stores Search, warehouse, object store, vector DB for derived data Each query on the engine built for it More systems and pipelines to run

Steps 1–5 are cheap and reversible; steps 6–8 change the architecture. In 2026 a single well-tuned relational node with a few replicas comfortably serves a large majority of products; sharding is for the few that outgrow it, and managed distributed SQL (see NewSQL) has made that last step less painful than it used to be.

Try it. The scenario below is the one-node starting point: client → app → SQL. Raise the load until the database saturates and watch the p99 latency bend upward (the "knee" from Queueing). Then think about which rung of the ladder you would climb first — and check it in the db-replicas scenario on the Replication page.

The full simulator, with every storage component in the palette, is in the Playground.

items.title: One database per service, or one database for everything?
items.text:
Two opposite pieces of advice coexist, and both are right in their context.

Database per service. In a microservice architecture each service owns its data and nobody else reads its tables (Compute & Services). The catalog can change its schema without breaking inventory; a slow analytics query cannot lock the order tables. The price: no joins and no transactions across services — you need events, sagas and the transactional outbox (Messaging patterns).

"Just use Postgres". Modern PostgreSQL covers a surprising range3: JSONB documents with GIN indexes, full-text search (tsvector), geospatial (PostGIS), time series (partitioned tables, TimescaleDB), queues (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), and vector search (pgvector). Fewer systems means fewer things to operate, back up, secure and learn.

One engine for many needs Specialized store per need Operations one thing to run, monitor and back up one more system per need Consistency can update everything in one transaction derived stores lag behind (CDC, ETL) Peak performance good enough up to medium scale best for that access pattern at large scale Features basic full-text, basic vector search relevance tuning, facets, billions of vectors, columnar scans Team skills one skill set several

The pragmatic path for BoxOffice: start with PostgreSQL per service (owned schemas, separate databases or at least separate users), and add a specialized store when a measured need appears — the search relevance team needs facets and typo tolerance, analysts need to scan two years of clicks, the assistant needs tens of millions of vectors.

Palette component Question it answers Concepts Taught in Scenarios sql Where does data with invariants live? ACID, isolation levels, conditional UPDATE, SELECT … FOR UPDATE, indexes, EXPLAIN Data Models, Transactions monolith, flash-sale sql (replicas) How do we scale reads and survive a dead leader? leader–follower, sync vs async, replication lag, read-your-writes, pooling, failover Replication db-replicas nosql Which access pattern forces us out of a relational database? key-value, document, wide-column, graph, LSM-trees, partition and sort keys Data Models — decision guide sharding nosql (partitioned) How do writes and storage grow past one node? range vs hash, consistent hashing, hot partitions, resharding, leaderless quorums, NewSQL Partitioning, Replication — leaderless sharding search How do fans find "rock in São Paulo"? inverted index, ranking, kept in sync by CDC, derived data Specialized — search engines search-autocomplete objstore Where do posters and ticket PDFs live? objects by key, presigned URLs, a CDN in front Specialized — object storage cdn-static, video-streaming dwh Where do the analysts' queries run? OLTP vs OLAP, columnar storage, star schema, ETL/ELT, lakehouse Specialized — warehouses event-fanout vectordb How does the assistant find text by meaning? embeddings, exact vs approximate search, HNSW, pgvector first Specialized — vector databases ai-assistant cache · stream How do reads skip the database, and derived stores stay in sync? the scaling ladder, cache-aside, CDC, outbox this overview, Caching read-heavy-cache

In the interview

Interviewers listen for why you chose a store, not for brand names. A strong pattern is: "Seats and orders go to a relational database because the invariant 'one seat, one ticket' needs transactions; the catalog is read-heavy, so a cache in front of it; search goes to an inverted index fed by CDC; posters in object storage behind the CDN; analytics in a warehouse, never on the OLTP database." Then estimate: "60 k seats per event is tiny — the problem is write contention, not size", which shows you know which dimension is hard.

Common pitfalls

  • Sharding first. Partitioning a 50 GB database adds months of complexity to solve a problem an index and a replica would have solved.
  • Analytics on the OLTP database. A report that scans millions of rows competes with checkout for CPU, I/O and locks. Move it to a replica at least, to a warehouse at best.
  • Blobs in the database. Images and PDFs bloat backups and the buffer pool; store them in object storage and keep only the key.
  • Choosing NoSQL "for scale" without knowing the queries. NoSQL tables are designed around access patterns; if you do not know them yet, you will design the wrong table.
  • Treating derived data as the source of truth. If the search index or cache is the only place where a value lives, a rebuild loses data.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Describe data by access pattern, volume, consistency need and query flexibility before choosing a store.
  • Separate the system of record from derived data (cache, search index, warehouse, vectors) that can be rebuilt.
  • The relational database is the default for data with invariants; leave it for a measured reason.
  • Climb the scaling ladder in order: queries and indexes → pooling → scale up → cache → replicas → split by function → shard → specialized stores.
  • Polyglot persistence buys performance per access pattern at the price of operations and pipelines.

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Models and storage engines
items.text:
Q1. BoxOffice must guarantee that a seat is never sold twice, and analysts keep inventing new questions about orders. Which storage choice fits the orders and seat inventory best?

  • A. A wide-column store, because it scales writes horizontally
  • B. A document database, embedding every ticket inside the event document
  • C. A relational database, because the invariant spans rows and needs transactions and constraints, and ad hoc queries need SQL
  • D. A key-value store with a TTL on each seat
Answer

C — A relational database.

The deciding factors are the invariant ("one seat, one ticket" — enforceable with a transaction and a unique constraint) and query flexibility (ad hoc questions need joins and indexes). Wide-column and key-value stores scale well but are designed around queries known in advance and offer limited transactions; embedding every ticket in the event document makes the document grow without bound and every purchase contend on one document.

Q2. Why does a B-tree index on a table with one billion rows usually answer a point lookup with only one or two disk reads?

  • A. Because B-trees keep the entire table in memory
  • B. Because with a fan-out of a few hundred keys per page the tree is only about 4 levels deep, and the upper levels stay cached in memory
  • C. Because B-trees hash the key directly to the page on disk
  • D. Because PostgreSQL compresses the index to fit in one page
Answer

B — Shallow tree, cached top levels.

With 8 KiB pages and ~16 bytes per key + pointer, each page points to ~500 children: 500³ = 125 million, 500⁴ = 62.5 billion. A billion rows fit in 4 levels; the root and internal pages are hot and stay in the buffer pool, so only the leaf (and maybe one internal page) comes from disk.

Q3. A team is choosing a storage engine for gate scans: millions of tiny append-only writes per hour, read back by (event, gate) and time. Which statement is correct?

  • A. A B-tree is better because in-place updates avoid compaction
  • B. An LSM-tree fits well: writes are sequential appends to a memtable and SSTables, and Bloom filters keep point reads cheap; compaction is the price
  • C. Neither: append-only data must go to object storage
  • D. An LSM-tree, because it never needs to read more than one file per query
Answer

B — LSM-tree.

LSM-trees turn random small writes into sequential appends and batch them, which is why write-heavy stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, RocksDB) use them. Reads may consult several levels — Bloom filters skip most SSTables, but D overstates it — and background compaction rewrites data (write amplification) and can cause I/O spikes.

Q4. An index exists on seats(event_id, section, status). Which query cannot use it efficiently?

  • A. WHERE event_id = 42
  • B. WHERE event_id = 42 AND section = 'B'
  • C. WHERE section = 'B' AND status = 'AVAILABLE'
  • D. WHERE event_id = 42 AND section = 'B' AND status = 'AVAILABLE'
Answer

C.

A composite B-tree is sorted by its first column, then the second, and so on (the leftmost-prefix rule). Without event_id, the matching entries are scattered across the whole index — like searching a phone book sorted by surname for everyone named "Ana".

items.title: Transactions and isolation
items.text:
Q5. Two requests run this on PostgreSQL (read committed) for seat A-12: SELECT status … → AVAILABLE, then UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :me WHERE event_id = 42 AND seat_id = 'A-12'. Both report success. What is the anomaly, and which single change fixes it?

  • A. Dirty read; switch to read uncommitted
  • B. Phantom read; add an index on status
  • C. Lost update (check-then-act race); add AND status = 'AVAILABLE' to the UPDATE and check that exactly 1 row was updated
  • D. Deadlock; retry both transactions
Answer

C — Lost update; make the update conditional.

Both transactions decided on a stale read; the row lock only serialized the two UPDATEs, and the second overwrote the first. With the condition inside the UPDATE, PostgreSQL re-checks the WHERE on the latest row version after the first transaction commits: the second update matches 0 rows and the application tells that fan the seat is taken.

Q6. Under PostgreSQL repeatable read (snapshot isolation), a customer with 4 tickets opens two tabs; each counts the customer's tickets (4), checks 4 + 2 ≤ 6, and holds two different seats. Both commit. What happened, and what prevents it?

  • A. Nothing wrong: repeatable read prevents every anomaly
  • B. Write skew; use serializable isolation (with retries) or lock a shared row such as a per-customer limit row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE
  • C. Dirty read; use read committed
  • D. Lost update; add a version column to seats
Answer

B — Write skew.

The two transactions wrote different rows, so there was no write–write conflict for snapshot isolation to detect, yet together they broke the invariant "at most 6 tickets". Serializable snapshot isolation detects the read/write dependency and aborts one (SQLSTATE 40001); alternatively, materialize the conflict so both transactions must lock the same row.

Q7. For the "best available" feature, hundreds of fans per second ask for "any 2 free seats in section B". Which query avoids making them queue behind each other?

  • A. SELECT … WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE' LIMIT 2 FOR UPDATE
  • B. SELECT … WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE' LIMIT 2 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  • C. SELECT … WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE' LIMIT 2 in serializable isolation
  • D. LOCK TABLE seats IN EXCLUSIVE MODE
Answer

B — FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.

Plain FOR UPDATE makes every fan wait for the same first free rows; SKIP LOCKED hands each transaction rows nobody else is holding, so they proceed in parallel. Serializable would cause aborts and retries under this contention, and a table lock serializes everything.

Q8. Each hold transaction decrements a single events.seats_left counter and holds that row lock for about 5 ms. Ignoring everything else, what is the maximum hold rate for the whole event?

  • A. About 20 holds/s
  • B. About 200 holds/s
  • C. About 2,000 holds/s
  • D. Unlimited, because PostgreSQL uses MVCC
Answer

B — About 200 holds/s.

A row lock serves one transaction at a time: 1 / 0.005 s = 200 per second, regardless of hardware. MVCC lets readers proceed without blocking, but two writers to the same row still serialize. The fix is to remove the hot row from the hot path (per-section or sharded counters, computed asynchronously).

items.title: Replication
items.text:
Q9. After adding asynchronous read replicas, fans sometimes see an empty My tickets page right after paying. Which fix provides read-your-writes consistency?

  • A. Add more replicas to reduce the load on each one
  • B. Route each user to the same replica every time (sticky replica)
  • C. For a short period after a user writes, route that user's reads to the primary (or to a replica that has replayed the write's log position)
  • D. Increase the cache TTL of the page
Answer

C.

The problem is replication lag: the read reached a replica that had not yet applied the write. Reading from the primary after a write — or waiting until the replica's replayed LSN passes the write's LSN — guarantees the user sees their own write. A sticky replica gives monotonic reads (time does not go backwards) but can still be behind; more replicas do not reduce lag.

Q10. The inventory primary uses asynchronous replication and crashes; a replica is promoted automatically. What is the specific risk for BoxOffice?

  • A. None, because WAL replay guarantees no data loss
  • B. Holds acknowledged by the old primary but not yet shipped are lost, so the new primary may sell those seats again
  • C. The replica refuses to be promoted while the old primary is down
  • D. Reads become slower because the new primary has a cold cache, but data is safe
Answer

B — Lost acknowledged writes.

With asynchronous replication, "committed" means "on the leader's disk". Writes in flight to the replicas disappear on failover. For data where a lost write means a double booking or lost money, use a synchronous standby (or quorum commit) and accept one extra round trip per commit. (D is a real but secondary effect.)

Q11. A leaderless store has N = 3 replicas per key. Which configuration guarantees that a read overlaps the latest acknowledged write while tolerating one replica being down for both reads and writes?

  • A. W = 1, R = 1
  • B. W = 2, R = 2
  • C. W = 3, R = 1
  • D. W = 1, R = 3
Answer

B — W = 2, R = 2.

R + W = 4 > N = 3, so read and write sets always share at least one replica, and both operations still succeed with one node down. A gives no overlap; C blocks writes and D blocks reads when any single node is down.

items.title: Partitioning and specialized stores
items.text:
Q12. A distributed cache with 9 nodes uses node = hash(key) mod N. One node is added. Roughly what fraction of keys now maps to a different node, and what would consistent hashing give?

  • A. About 10% with mod N; about 90% with consistent hashing
  • B. About 90% with mod N; about 10% with consistent hashing
  • C. About 50% with both
  • D. 0% with both, because hashes do not change
Answer

B — ~90% vs ~10%.

A key keeps its node under mod N only when hash mod 9 = hash mod 10, which happens for about 1 in 10 keys — so ~90% move, effectively flushing the cache onto the database. With consistent hashing, the new node takes over only its arcs of the ring: about 1/N = 1/10 of the keys.

Q13. The inventory is partitioned by event_id. At 10:00 the stadium show's partition is at 100% while the others idle. Which change addresses the hot partition without making every hold a cross-partition transaction?

  • A. Partition by hash(seat_id) instead
  • B. Add more nodes to the cluster
  • C. Partition by (event_id, section), keep group holds inside one section, and put a waiting room in front to cap the hold rate
  • D. Switch the partition to asynchronous replication
Answer

C.

A finer key spreads the big event over ~40 sections while keeping each hold transaction local, and the waiting room limits concurrency to what one partition can serve. Partitioning by seat (A) spreads load but turns "available seats in section B" into scatter/gather and group holds into cross-shard transactions; more nodes (B) do not help when the load targets one key.

Q14. Marketing wants "tickets sold per minute per city for the last two years" every morning. Where should this query run, and why?

  • A. On the order primary, with an index on created_at
  • B. In a column-oriented data warehouse fed by CDC/ELT, because it scans few columns of very many rows and must not compete with checkout
  • C. In the search engine, because it has aggregations
  • D. In the vector database, because it is fast
Answer

B — In the warehouse.

This is an OLAP query: few columns, billions of rows, seconds of latency acceptable. A column store reads only the needed columns, compresses them well and scans in parallel. Running it on the OLTP primary competes with checkout for CPU, I/O and locks.

Q15. The support assistant must find the policy paragraph for "can I get my money back if the show changes date?", which shares almost no words with "Refunds for rescheduled events". Which component and technique fit?

  • A. A full-text search index with BM25 and stemming
  • B. Embeddings stored in a vector database (for example pgvector with an HNSW index), queried by cosine similarity
  • C. A LIKE '%money back%' query on the policies table
  • D. A key-value store keyed by the question text
Answer

B — Embeddings + approximate nearest-neighbour search.

Lexical search (A, C) matches words, and the two texts share few. Embeddings place texts with similar meaning close together; an ANN index such as HNSW finds the nearest ones quickly at the cost of slightly imperfect recall. In practice, hybrid search (BM25 + vectors) and a reranker often work best.

items.title: Index
items.text:
"Should we use SQL or NoSQL?" is the most common storage question in design reviews and interviews, and also the most badly posed. "NoSQL" is not one thing: a key-value store, a document database, a wide-column store and a graph database are as different from each other as each is from PostgreSQL. And underneath the data model sits a second choice that matters just as much for performance — the storage engine that lays the bytes on disk.

This page takes one piece of BoxOffice — events, venues, seats and orders — and stores it in each model, then opens the engine room: B-trees, LSM-trees and indexes.

items.title: The relational model
items.text:
The relational model stores data as tables (relations) of rows with a fixed set of typed columns. Relationships are expressed by foreign keys, and queries combine tables with joins. The schema is declared up front and enforced on every write (schema-on-write)1.

BoxOffice core schema (PostgreSQL)
CREATE TABLE venues (
    id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name      TEXT NOT NULL,
    city      TEXT NOT NULL,
    capacity  INT  NOT NULL CHECK (capacity > 0)
);

CREATE TABLE events (
    id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    venue_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES venues(id),
    title     TEXT NOT NULL,
    starts_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    on_sale_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE seats (
    event_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES events(id),
    seat_id   TEXT   NOT NULL,              -- 'A-12'
    section   TEXT   NOT NULL,
    price_cents INT  NOT NULL,
    status    TEXT   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'AVAILABLE'
              CHECK (status IN ('AVAILABLE', 'HELD', 'SOLD')),
    held_by   BIGINT,
    hold_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
    version   INT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_id)
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    event_id    BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES events(id),
    total_cents INT    NOT NULL,
    status      TEXT   NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE tickets (
    order_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
    event_id  BIGINT NOT NULL,
    seat_id   TEXT   NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_id),        -- one ticket per seat, enforced by the database
    FOREIGN KEY (event_id, seat_id) REFERENCES seats(event_id, seat_id)
);

Three properties make the relational model the default for a system of record:

  • Normalization — each fact is stored once (the venue's city lives in venues, not copied into every event), so an update cannot leave two copies disagreeing.
  • Constraints — PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_id) on tickets makes double-selling a seat impossible, no matter how buggy the application code is.
  • Declarative queries — you say what you want; the query planner decides how, using whatever indexes exist. New questions do not need new tables.
An ad hoc question, answered with joins
-- Revenue per city for shows in December, best first
SELECT v.city, SUM(o.total_cents) / 100.0 AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN events e ON e.id = o.event_id
JOIN venues v ON v.id = e.venue_id
WHERE o.status = 'PAID'
  AND e.starts_at >= '2026-12-01' AND e.starts_at < '2027-01-01'
GROUP BY v.city
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

The costs: rows that belong together (an event and its lineup and prices) are spread across tables and reassembled by joins; the schema must be migrated (with Flyway in Hands-on 1) before new fields appear; and scaling writes beyond one node needs partitioning, which breaks cross-partition joins and transactions (see Partitioning).

items.title: Document databases
items.text:
A document database stores self-contained, nested documents — usually JSON or a binary form of it — addressed by a key. Everything you need to render an event page can live in one document:

events/42 as a document
{
  "_id": 42,
  "title": "Stadium Tour 2027",
  "venue": { "id": 7, "name": "Allianz Parque", "city": "São Paulo" },
  "startsAt": "2027-03-14T21:00:00-03:00",
  "lineup": ["Main act", "Opening act"],
  "priceTiers": [
    { "section": "Pista", "priceCents": 49000 },
    { "section": "Cadeira Superior", "priceCents": 29000 }
  ],
  "tags": ["pop", "stadium"]
}
  • Locality: one read returns the whole page; no joins. Great for "load the aggregate by id".
  • Flexible schema (schema-on-read): a festival can carry a stages array that a football game does not have.
  • Weakness — many-to-many relationships: the venue is copied into every event. Renaming the venue means updating thousands of documents, or accepting stale copies. Queries that cut across documents ("all events at venue 7") need secondary indexes or a different collection.

Products: MongoDB, Couchbase, Google Firestore, Azure Cosmos DB, Amazon DocumentDB — and PostgreSQL itself with JSONB columns and GIN indexes, which is often enough.

items.title: Key-value stores
items.text:
The simplest model: an opaque value looked up by a key — GET, PUT, DELETE, sometimes with a TTL. No queries by value, no joins, so the store can be extremely fast and easy to partition by key.

Store Typical use at BoxOffice Redis / Valkey (in memory) sessions, rate-limit counters, cached event pages, waiting-room position (see Caching) Amazon DynamoDB, Azure Cosmos DB (key-value / document APIs) huge, predictable lookups at any scale, e.g. "tickets of customer X" etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul small, strongly consistent configuration and leader election

DynamoDB deserves a note because it is a common interview answer. It is a managed, partitioned key-value and document store: each item has a partition key (hashed to choose the partition) and an optional sort key (items with the same partition key are stored sorted, so range queries within a partition are cheap). You design the table around the queries — the opposite of normalization.

Access pattern Partition key Sort key Tickets of a customer, newest first CUSTOMER#7 ORDER#2027-03-01T10:02#9001 Seats of an event section EVENT#42#SEC#B SEAT#A-12

The design starts from the list of queries; a new query that does not fit the keys needs a global secondary index — or a new table.

items.title: Wide-column stores
items.text:
Wide-column stores (Apache Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Google Bigtable, Apache HBase) organize rows into partitions by a partition key, and sort rows inside a partition by clustering columns. They are built for very high write throughput across many nodes, with tunable consistency (see Replication).

Cassandra (CQL): one table per query
-- Query: "the last 50 scans at gate 3 of event 42" (anti-fraud at the stadium)
CREATE TABLE gate_scans_by_event (
    event_id   bigint,
    gate       int,
    scanned_at timestamp,
    ticket_id  uuid,
    result     text,
    PRIMARY KEY ((event_id, gate), scanned_at, ticket_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (scanned_at DESC, ticket_id ASC);

SELECT * FROM gate_scans_by_event
WHERE event_id = 42 AND gate = 3
LIMIT 50;

The syntax looks like SQL, but the rules are different: you can only filter by the partition key (and then by clustering columns in order); there are no joins; each query gets its own denormalized table. In exchange, writes are appends to an LSM-tree (see below) and spread over every node — ideal for time series, event logs, IoT and messaging at large scale.

items.title: Graph databases
items.text:
When the questions are about relationships — paths, neighbours, communities — a graph database stores nodes and edges as first-class citizens. Neo4j (query language Cypher), Amazon Neptune and the ISO standard query language GQL (2024) are examples.

Fans who bought this show also bought…
MATCH (e:Event {id: 42})<-[:BOUGHT]-(f:Fan)-[:BOUGHT]->(other:Event)
WHERE other.startsAt > datetime()
RETURN other.title, count(f) AS fans
ORDER BY fans DESC
LIMIT 5;

In SQL the same query is a self-join of orders with itself; it works for one hop but grows painful for "friends of friends of friends" or fraud rings (cards, devices and accounts linked across many hops). Most systems never need a graph database; recommendation and fraud teams sometimes do.

items.title: Comparing the models
items.text: Model Data unit Best at Weak at Examples Relational rows in tables, joins invariants, transactions, ad hoc queries horizontal write scaling (without NewSQL) PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle Key-value opaque value by key the fastest lookups, easy partitioning any query not by key Redis, Valkey, DynamoDB, etcd Document nested JSON by key aggregates read together, evolving schemas many-to-many, cross-document invariants MongoDB, Firestore, Cosmos DB, Postgres JSONB Wide-column rows sorted inside partitions massive write throughput, time-ordered data joins, ad hoc queries, strong consistency by default Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable, HBase Graph nodes and edges multi-hop relationship queries bulk scans and aggregations Neo4j, Neptune Time series (series, timestamp, value) metrics, downsampling, retention general-purpose queries Prometheus, InfluxDB, TimescaleDB

items.title: SQL or NoSQL? A decision guide
items.text:
The guide below encodes the questions from the overview. Read it as "the default is relational; each arrow out of it needs a reason".

flowchart TD
    A["New data to store"] --> B{"Invariants across rows?<br/>money, stock, uniqueness"}
    B -->|yes| SQL["Relational database<br/>PostgreSQL / MySQL"]
    B -->|no| C{"Queries known in advance<br/>and mostly by key?"}
    C -->|no, ad hoc| SQL
    C -->|yes| D{"Scale beyond one node<br/>for writes or storage?"}
    D -->|no| SQL
    D -->|yes| E{"Shape of the data?"}
    E -->|"blob: images, PDFs"| OBJ["Object storage"]
    E -->|"key → value, TTL"| KV["Key-value<br/>Redis, DynamoDB"]
    E -->|"aggregate as JSON"| DOC["Document<br/>MongoDB, Firestore"]
    E -->|"time-ordered, huge writes"| WC["Wide-column<br/>Cassandra, Bigtable"]
    E -->|"multi-hop relationships"| GR["Graph<br/>Neo4j"]
    SQL --> F{"Outgrows one primary?"}
    F -->|"yes, need SQL + scale"| NEW["Distributed SQL<br/>Spanner, CockroachDB"]

And for the derived data, the question is the query, not the scale: full-text → search engine, aggregations over history → data warehouse, similarity by meaning → vector database.

Some myths to retire before an interview:

Myth Reality "NoSQL has no schema." It has an implicit schema in the application code — and every reader must handle every old version of it. "SQL does not scale." Read replicas, partitioning and distributed SQL scale relational databases to very large workloads; most companies never outgrow one primary. "NoSQL has no transactions." DynamoDB, MongoDB and Cosmos DB offer multi-item transactions, with limits on size and scope. "NoSQL is faster." A key lookup is fast on any engine. NoSQL is faster at the patterns it was designed for and slower (or unable) at the rest. "Pick one for the whole company." Polyglot persistence: choose per service and per access pattern. Think first: where would you store BoxOffice's seat inventory if it had to serve a 200 k-seat festival with 50 entry gates?

Still a relational database — the invariant (one seat, one ticket) is the deciding factor, and 200 k rows is small. The gate scans, on the other hand, are append-only, time-ordered, written by 50 gates at once and queried by (event, gate) → a wide-column store (or a partitioned SQL table) fits them. Same event, two different stores, decided by access pattern.

items.title: Storage engines: how bytes reach the disk
items.text: A database is, at its core, two operations: store this key and value and give me the value for this key (or this range of keys). How it lays the data on disk determines the cost of each. Two families dominate: B-trees (update pages in place) and LSM-trees (append, then merge)2.

items.title: B-trees
items.text:
A B-tree keeps keys sorted in fixed-size pages (8 KiB in PostgreSQL, 16 KiB in MySQL InnoDB). Each internal page holds hundreds of keys and pointers to child pages; leaves hold the rows or pointers to them. Lookups walk from the root to a leaf3.

flowchart TD
    R["root page<br/>… | 30 | 60 | …"] -->|"key 42"| I["internal page<br/>31 … 40 | 41 … 50 | …"]
    I -->|"key 42"| L["leaf page<br/>41, 42, 43 … → rows"]
    L -->|"update in place:<br/>rewrite the 8 KiB page"| D[("disk")]
    W["write-ahead log (WAL)<br/>append the change first"] --> D

The numbers explain why B-trees are everywhere. With 8 KiB pages and ~16 bytes per key + pointer, one page has a fan-out of ~500:

Levels Keys reachable (500^levels) 2 250 thousand 3 125 million 4 62.5 billion

A billion-row table is 4 levels deep, and the top levels stay cached in memory, so a point lookup costs one or two disk reads. Writes, though, modify a page in place: changing a 100-byte row dirties a whole 8 KiB page that is later written back, and the change is also appended to the write-ahead log (WAL) for crash recovery. Used by PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server, Oracle, SQLite.

items.title: LSM-trees
items.text:
A log-structured merge-tree (LSM-tree) never updates in place4. Writes go to the WAL and to an in-memory sorted table (the memtable); when it fills, it is flushed to disk as an immutable sorted file (an SSTable). Background compaction merges SSTables into larger, sorted levels and drops overwritten and deleted values.

flowchart LR
    W["write key=42"] --> WAL["WAL<br/>append"]
    W --> M["memtable<br/>in memory, sorted"]
    M -->|"full → flush"| L0["L0 SSTables"]
    L0 -->|"compaction"| L1["L1 (10× bigger)"]
    L1 -->|"compaction"| L2["L2 (10× bigger)"]
    R["read key=42"] --> M
    R -->|"bloom filter says<br/>'maybe here'"| L1

Writes are sequential appends — very fast, even on slow disks. Reads may have to check the memtable and several levels; Bloom filters (a compact probabilistic set per SSTable that answers "definitely not here" or "maybe here") skip most of them. Used by RocksDB (inside many systems), Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, Bigtable, LevelDB, and CockroachDB's Pebble.

items.title: Write amplification
items.text:
Write amplification is the number of bytes the engine writes to disk for each byte the application writes. It drives SSD wear, I/O cost and peak write throughput. The model below is a back-of-the-envelope intuition, not a benchmark: a B-tree that rewrites a whole 8 KiB page per random small update (plus the WAL), and a leveled LSM-tree with size ratio 10 where each record is rewritten about 5 times per level during compaction (plus the WAL and the flush).

2026-10-23T08:15:43.649556 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Read the plot as intuition:

  • For small records updated at random (counters, statuses, events), the B-tree pays for a whole page per tiny change, and the LSM-tree's sequential, batched writes win. That is why write-heavy stores (Cassandra, RocksDB) are LSM-based.
  • For large records, the page cost is amortized and the LSM-tree's repeated compaction dominates. Real B-tree engines also batch many updates to the same page before writing it, which lowers their curve a lot for workloads with locality.
  • More data means more LSM levels, so its write amplification grows slowly with the dataset.
B-tree LSM-tree Point read 1–2 page reads (upper levels cached) memtable + one SSTable per level, mostly skipped by Bloom filters Range scan excellent: leaves are sorted and linked good, but merges several levels Random small writes in-place page writes; amplification depends on record size sequential appends; amplification ≈ levels × size ratio Space some free space inside pages (fragmentation) obsolete versions until compaction; compressed files Latency predictability stable compaction can cause background I/O spikes Typical engines PostgreSQL, InnoDB, SQL Server, SQLite RocksDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, Pebble

items.title: Indexes
items.text:
An index is an additional data structure — usually a B-tree — that maps column values to the rows that contain them, so the database finds rows without scanning the whole table. The primary key is always indexed; every other index is your decision, and each one speeds up reads and slows down writes (every INSERT/UPDATE must update every index on the table).

Index kind What it is BoxOffice example Single-column B-tree on one column orders(customer_id) for "my orders" Composite B-tree on several columns, sorted by the first, then the second… seats(event_id, section, status) Covering composite index that also stores the columns the query returns (INCLUDE), so the table is not touched seats(event_id, section) INCLUDE (seat_id, price_cents) Partial indexes only rows matching a condition seats(event_id, hold_expires_at) WHERE status = 'HELD' — only holds, tiny Unique rejects duplicates tickets(event_id, seat_id) — the anti-double-booking guarantee GIN / full-text inverted index on words or JSON keys events USING GIN (to_tsvector('portuguese', title)) Vector (HNSW, IVF) approximate nearest neighbours pgvector index for the assistant (Specialized)

A composite index follows the leftmost-prefix rule: an index on (event_id, section, status) helps queries that filter by event_id, by event_id AND section, or by all three — but not by section alone, just as a phone book sorted by surname then first name does not help you find everyone named "Ana".

items.title: Reading EXPLAIN
items.text:
EXPLAIN shows the plan the database chose; EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and reports real times. The output below is illustrative, for a seats table with 3 million rows (50 events of 60 k seats):

Before: no index on section/status
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT seat_id, price_cents FROM seats
WHERE event_id = 42 AND section = 'B' AND status = 'AVAILABLE';

-- Seq Scan on seats  (cost=0.00..71842.00 rows=310 width=12)
--                    (actual time=0.031..212.448 rows=287 loops=1)
--   Filter: ((event_id = 42) AND (section = 'B') AND (status = 'AVAILABLE'))
--   Rows Removed by Filter: 2999713
-- Execution Time: 212.502 ms
After: a composite index that matches the filter
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY seats_event_section_status_idx
    ON seats (event_id, section, status) INCLUDE (seat_id, price_cents);

-- Index Only Scan using seats_event_section_status_idx on seats
--                    (cost=0.43..18.10 rows=310 width=12)
--                    (actual time=0.025..0.391 rows=287 loops=1)
--   Index Cond: ((event_id = 42) AND (section = 'B') AND (status = 'AVAILABLE'))
-- Execution Time: 0.430 ms

Reading guide: Seq Scan with a large "Rows Removed by Filter" means a missing index; Index Scan walks the index and fetches rows from the table; Index Only Scan answers from the index alone; cost is the planner's estimate in arbitrary units, actual time is what happened. CONCURRENTLY builds the index without blocking writes — essential on a live table. You will do this in Hands-on 6.

BoxOffice: the index budget of the seats table

The on-sale workload is write-heavy on seats (thousands of holds per second on one event), so every extra index costs throughput exactly when it hurts most. The team keeps three:

  1. the primary key (event_id, seat_id) — every hold is a point update by it;
  2. (event_id, section, status) INCLUDE (seat_id, price_cents) — the "available seats in this section" query;
  3. a partial index on (hold_expires_at) WHERE status = 'HELD' — the job that releases expired holds scans only the few thousand held rows.

An index on held_by was proposed for "my current holds" and rejected: that query is rare and can be served from the order service instead.

In the interview

  • Do not say "NoSQL because it scales". Say which access pattern forces you out of a relational database, and name the model that fits it: "gate scans are time-ordered appends at high rate, queried by (event, gate) — a wide-column table partitioned by that pair".
  • When you add a NoSQL store, list its queries first and derive the partition and sort keys from them.
  • Mention indexes with their cost: "a composite index on (event_id, section, status); I keep the index count low on seats because it is write-hot".
  • If asked about storage engines: B-tree = read-optimized, in-place; LSM = write-optimized, append + compaction, Bloom filters for reads.

Common pitfalls

  • An index per column "just in case": slower writes, more memory, and the planner still cannot combine them as well as one good composite index.
  • Wrong column order in a composite index ((status, event_id) when every query filters by event_id): the leftmost-prefix rule makes it useless for most queries.
  • Functions on indexed columns (WHERE lower(email) = …) bypass a plain index; create an expression index instead.
  • Documents that grow forever (an event document with every ticket embedded): reads and writes get slower as the array grows, and many databases cap document size (16 MB in MongoDB).
  • Modeling NoSQL like SQL (normalized tables, joins in the application): you pay the network round trips and lose both models' strengths.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    REL["relational model<br/>tables, joins, constraints"] --> GUIDE["SQL or NoSQL?<br/>access pattern first"]
    DOC["document"] --> GUIDE
    KV["key-value"] --> GUIDE
    WC["wide-column"] --> GUIDE
    GR["graph"] --> GUIDE
    IDX["indexes: composite order,<br/>EXPLAIN"] --> BT["B-tree<br/>read-optimized, in place"]
    BT -.-> REL
    LSM["LSM-tree<br/>write-optimized, compaction"] -.-> WC
    GUIDE --> TX["invariants<br/>→ Transactions"]
    GUIDE --> PART["known keys at scale<br/>→ Partitioning"]
    KV --> CACHE["in memory<br/>→ Caching, Redis"]

Palette components: sql (the default for data with invariants and ad hoc queries) · nosql (key-value, document, wide-column or graph — chosen by access pattern, keys derived from the queries) · cache (a key-value store in memory) · vectordb (an ANN index is one more index type). Scenarios: monolith, sharding. Continues in: Transactions, Partitioning, Caching — Redis, Estimation — numbers, Hands-on 6 (indexes and EXPLAIN).

  1. CODD, E. F. A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks. Communications of the ACM, 13(6), 1970. ↩

  2. KLEPPMANN, M.; RICCOMINI, C. Designing Data-Intensive Applications. 2nd ed. O'Reilly. Chapter "Storage and Retrieval". ↩

  3. BAYER, R.; McCREIGHT, E. Organization and Maintenance of Large Ordered Indexes. Acta Informatica, 1(3), 1972. ↩

  4. O'NEIL, P. et al. The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree). Acta Informatica, 33(4), 1996. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
Three years after launch, BoxOffice sells in 30 countries. The orders and tickets tables grow by hundreds of millions of rows a year, the primary's disk is measured in terabytes, and the write rate during big on-sales is close to what one machine can absorb. Replicas no longer help: they scale reads, and every replica must still apply every write. The next rung of the scaling ladder is to split the data itself across machines.

Partitioning — also called sharding — divides a dataset so that each record belongs to exactly one partition (shard), and different partitions live on different nodes. Each node handles only its share of the reads, writes and storage. The words vary by product — shard in MongoDB and Elasticsearch, region in HBase, tablet in Bigtable, range in CockroachDB, vnode in Cassandra — but the questions are always the same: by what key, how to spread it evenly, how to find it, and how to move it when nodes change1.

flowchart LR
    R["router<br/>partition = f(key)"] -->|"customer 7"| S1[("shard 1<br/>+ replicas")]
    R -->|"customer 1042"| S2[("shard 2<br/>+ replicas")]
    R -->|"customer 98311"| S3[("shard 3<br/>+ replicas")]

Partitioning is usually combined with replication: each partition has its own leader and followers, so a node can be leader for some partitions and follower for others.

items.title: Partitioning by key range
items.text:
Assign each partition a continuous range of keys, like the volumes of an encyclopedia: A–F, G–M, N–S, T–Z. Within a partition, keys are kept sorted.

  • Range queries are cheap: "orders from 2027-03-01 to 2027-03-07" reads one or two partitions.
  • Boundaries adapt to the data: when a range grows too large, it is split in two (Bigtable tablets, HBase regions, CockroachDB and TiDB ranges do this automatically).
  • Danger — sequential keys. If the key is a timestamp or an auto-increment id, all new writes go to the last range. Today's clickstream lands on one node while the others idle. Fix it by prefixing the key with something else: (event_id, timestamp) instead of timestamp.

items.title: Partitioning by hash
items.text:
Apply a hash function to the key and use the hash to choose the partition. A good hash spreads even sequential keys uniformly.

  • Even load for writes and point reads.
  • Range queries scatter: adjacent keys hash to unrelated partitions, so "orders this week" must ask every partition.
  • Compound keys recover some locality: Cassandra hashes only the partition key and keeps rows sorted by the clustering columns inside it — PRIMARY KEY ((event_id), scanned_at) gives an even spread across events and cheap time ranges within one event.

The naive implementation, partition = hash(key) mod N, has a fatal flaw: when N changes, almost every key changes partition.

items.title: Consistent hashing
items.text:
Consistent hashing2 places both nodes and keys on the same circular hash space (a ring, e.g. 0 to 2^64 − 1). Each key belongs to the first node found walking clockwise from the key's position.

flowchart LR
    K1["key seat:A-12<br/>hash = 0x1F…"] -->|"walk clockwise"| N1["node B<br/>at 0x40…"]
    K2["key seat:C-07<br/>hash = 0x9A…"] -->|"walk clockwise"| N2["node C<br/>at 0xB0…"]
    K3["key seat:Z-99<br/>hash = 0xF3…"] -->|"wraps around"| N0["node A<br/>at 0x10…"]
    NEW["new node D at 0x80…"] -.->|"takes only keys<br/>between 0x40 and 0x80"| N2

When a node joins, it takes over only the keys between itself and its predecessor; when a node leaves, only its keys move to its successor. On average 1/N of the keys move, the minimum possible — compared with almost all of them under mod N.

With only one position per node, the arcs are uneven and one node can own far more than its share. Virtual nodes (vnodes) fix this: each physical node takes many positions on the ring (100–256 is common), so its total share averages out, and a node with twice the capacity can simply take twice the vnodes.

The simulation below hashes 20,000 keys with MD5. On the left, the percentage of keys that change node when the cluster grows from N − 1 to N nodes; on the right, how unbalanced 10 nodes are (busiest node ÷ average) as the number of virtual nodes grows:

2026-10-23T08:15:44.015064 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Going from 9 to 10 nodes with mod N moves about 90% of the keys — in a distributed cache, that is the same as flushing the whole cache onto the database at once. With consistent hashing, about 10% move. And with a single position per node, the busiest node carries several times its fair share; a few hundred vnodes bring it close to 1.

Consistent hashing is used by Dynamo and DynamoDB, Cassandra and ScyllaDB, Riak, client-side Memcached sharding (the ketama algorithm), Nginx's hash … consistent upstreams and many load balancers. Two relatives are worth recognizing: rendezvous hashing (highest random weight: each key picks the node with the highest hash(key, node))3 and jump consistent hash (no ring, near-perfect balance, but nodes can only be added or removed at the end)4.

items.title: Fixed number of partitions
items.text:
A simpler alternative many systems use: create many more partitions than nodes up front and assign whole partitions to nodes. Adding a node means moving some whole partitions to it; the key → partition mapping never changes.

  • Redis Cluster: 16,384 hash slots, slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384; slots are moved between nodes (see Redis).
  • Elasticsearch / OpenSearch: the number of primary shards is fixed when the index is created.
  • Kafka: a topic's partitions (see Kafka).

The catch: choose the count well. Too few partitions limits how far you can scale; too many adds per-partition overhead.

Strategy Key → partition Range queries Adding a node Used by Key range sorted boundaries, split when large efficient split and move ranges Bigtable, HBase, CockroachDB, TiDB, MongoDB (ranged) Hash mod N hash(k) mod N scatter to all moves almost everything nothing serious — avoid Consistent hashing first node clockwise on a ring scatter to all ~1/N of keys move Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak, Memcached clients Fixed partitions hash(k) mod P, P fixed and large scatter to all move whole partitions Redis Cluster, Elasticsearch, Kafka, Couchbase Directory lookup table key → shard depends update the table custom sharding, Vitess (vindexes)

items.title: Choosing the partition key
items.text:
The partition key is the most consequential and the least reversible decision of a sharded design. A good key has:

  1. High cardinality — many distinct values, so the data can be cut into many pieces.
  2. Even distribution of both data and traffic across values.
  3. Query locality — the most frequent queries and every transaction touch one partition.
BoxOffice data Candidate key Locality Distribution Verdict orders, tickets customer_id "my orders" and checkout touch one shard millions of customers, even good; event-level reports scatter → run them in the warehouse orders created_at time ranges are local all of today's writes on one shard bad (sequential key) seats (inventory) event_id a hold transaction stays in one shard one stadium show = one hot shard good locality, dangerous skew — see below seats (event_id, section) a hold of seats in one section stays local the stadium show spreads over ~40 sections better for big events gate_scans (event_id, gate) the gate's recent scans are local 50 gates spread the load good Think first: why not partition seats by seat_id alone?

The distribution would be perfect, but the main query — "available seats of event 42, section B" — would scatter to every shard, and a group hold of 4 adjacent seats would become a cross-shard transaction. Locality of the dominant query and of transactions beats a perfect spread.

items.title: Hot partitions
items.text:
Even with a perfect hash, traffic is rarely uniform. A hot partition (or hot key) receives far more load than the others: the celebrity whose posts everyone reads, the product on a Black Friday deal, the stadium show at 10:00. Hashing cannot spread load that targets one key.

Try it. The sharding scenario spreads a NoSQL table over several partitions. Run it with uniform traffic and note the per-partition load; then make the key distribution skewed (one hot key) and watch a single partition saturate and its latency climb while the others are idle — adding partitions does not help.

Mitigations, from the least to the most invasive:

Technique How Cost Cache the reads the hot event page is served from the cache or CDN, not the shard (Caching) staleness Throttle and queue the writes a waiting room admits fans at the rate the shard can serve (flash-sale scenario) users wait Finer key (event_id, section) instead of event_id queries over the whole event scatter over ~40 partitions Key salting / write sharding append a suffix 0–9 to a hot key (event:42#7); writes pick a random suffix, reads merge all ten reads do 10× the work Sharded counters "seats left" kept as 10 sub-counters, summed on read approximate reads during updates Dedicated capacity move the hot partition to its own node; managed stores may split it automatically (DynamoDB adaptive capacity) operations, cost

BoxOffice: the inventory partition plan

  • Partition key (event_id, section). A normal concert has 5–10 sections; the stadium show has ~40, spread over many nodes.
  • Holds and confirms are single-partition transactions (all seats of a group hold are in the same section by design of the UI).
  • "Seats left" for the event page is a sharded counter per section, aggregated every second into the cache — never a hot row.
  • The waiting room limits concurrent hold attempts to what the busiest partition can serve.

items.title: Secondary indexes on partitioned data
items.text:
Partitioning by customer_id makes "orders of customer 7" fast. What about "orders of event 42"? A secondary index is needed, and on partitioned data it comes in two flavours:

flowchart TB
    subgraph local ["Local (document-partitioned) index"]
        Q1["query: event_id = 42"] --> P1["shard 1<br/>+ its own index"]
        Q1 --> P2["shard 2<br/>+ its own index"]
        Q1 --> P3["shard 3<br/>+ its own index"]
    end
    subgraph global ["Global (term-partitioned) index"]
        Q2["query: event_id = 42"] --> IX["index partition<br/>for event_id 42"]
        IX --> D1["shard 1"]
        IX --> D3["shard 3"]
    end
Local index Global index Write updates the index on the same shard — cheap, transactional updates an index partition elsewhere — often asynchronous Read by indexed column scatter/gather to every shard; tail latency of the slowest one one index partition, then only the shards that hold matches Examples MongoDB, Cassandra secondary indexes, Elasticsearch DynamoDB global secondary indexes (eventually consistent), Spanner/CockroachDB indexes (transactional)

Scatter/gather is more dangerous than it looks: a query to 20 shards is as slow as the slowest of the 20. The chance that all 20 answer within their own p99 is 0.99²⁰ ≈ 82 %, so a shard's p99 is only about the p82 of the query — 18 % of queries are slower. For the query p99 to stay under a target, each shard must meet it at its p99.95 (0.99^(1/20) ≈ 0.9995) (see Percentiles).

items.title: Rebalancing and resharding
items.text:
Nodes are added, removed and fail; data grows unevenly. Rebalancing moves partitions so that load stays even, ideally while the database keeps serving traffic and moving only the data that must move.

  • Prefer schemes where the key → partition mapping is stable (fixed partitions, consistent hashing, range splits), so rebalancing moves partitions, not individual keys.
  • Rebalancing competes with live traffic for network and disk; throttle it, and avoid fully automatic rebalancing triggered by a node that is merely slow (it can cascade).
  • Changing the partition key (resharding) is a migration project. The common recipe is online:
flowchart LR
    A["1. create new shards<br/>with the new key"] --> B["2. dual-write:<br/>old + new"]
    B --> C["3. backfill history<br/>(copy + CDC catch-up)"]
    C --> D["4. verify:<br/>compare reads"]
    D --> E["5. switch reads<br/>to new shards"]
    E --> F["6. stop old writes,<br/>delete old shards"]

Sharding layers automate much of this for existing relational databases: Vitess for MySQL (built at YouTube) and Citus for PostgreSQL handle routing, resharding and distributed queries.

items.title: Request routing
items.text:
Some component must know which node holds which partition:

Approach How Examples Any node forwards the client contacts any node; it forwards or redirects Cassandra, Redis Cluster (MOVED redirects) Routing tier a stateless proxy knows the map MongoDB mongos, Vitess vtgate, Citus coordinator Partition-aware client the client library caches the map Kafka clients, DynamoDB SDK via endpoints, smart Redis clients

The map itself is small, critical metadata — kept in a consensus store such as etcd or ZooKeeper, or gossiped between nodes (see Consensus).

items.title: Cross-partition queries and transactions
items.text:
Partitioning works beautifully until an operation needs several partitions at once:

  • Joins and aggregates across shards become scatter/gather, done by a coordinator — slower, and limited by the slowest shard.
  • Transactions across shards need a coordination protocol — two-phase commit or consensus-based commit — with extra round trips and failure modes (see Transactions).
  • Unique constraints on non-key columns (unique e-mail when sharding by customer_id) need a global index or a separate lookup table.

So the design goal is: choose keys so that the hot path is single-partition, and send the rest to systems built for it (a warehouse for analytics, a search index for cross-cutting lookups).

items.title: NewSQL: distributed SQL databases
items.text:
What if you want partitioning and SQL transactions across partitions, without writing a sharding layer? NewSQL or distributed SQL databases do this5:

  • Google Spanner6 splits tables into ranges, replicates each range with Paxos across zones or regions, and runs distributed transactions with two-phase commit over those groups. Its TrueTime API exposes clock uncertainty (a few milliseconds, bounded by GPS and atomic clocks); a commit waits out that uncertainty, which gives external consistency (linearizable transactions) across the world.
  • CockroachDB7 (PostgreSQL wire protocol) splits data into ranges of a few hundred megabytes, replicates each with Raft, and uses hybrid logical clocks instead of special hardware; serializable isolation is the default.
  • YugabyteDB (PostgreSQL-compatible) and TiDB (MySQL-compatible) follow similar designs; cloud providers offer managed and serverless distributed SQL as well.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as Gateway node
    participant R1 as Range 1 leader (orders)
    participant R2 as Range 2 leader (tickets)
    C->>G: BEGIN, INSERT order, INSERT tickets, COMMIT
    G->>R1: write intent (replicated by Raft)
    G->>R2: write intent (replicated by Raft)
    R1-->>G: ok (majority acked)
    R2-->>G: ok (majority acked)
    G->>G: commit record (atomic)
    G-->>C: COMMIT ok
Single-node SQL + replicas Sharded SQL (Citus, Vitess) Distributed SQL (Spanner, CockroachDB…) NoSQL (Cassandra, DynamoDB) Write scaling one primary per shard automatic, per range automatic, per partition Cross-partition transactions n/a (one node) limited / 2PC yes, serializable limited or none Write latency lowest low + consensus round trip (more if multi-region) low, tunable SQL and joins full most, with caveats most none / limited Operations simple sharding layer to run managed or complex managed or complex

Distributed SQL is not free: every write is replicated by consensus, so latency is higher than on a single node, and a transaction that spans regions pays inter-region round trips. It is the right answer when you need both SQL transactions and more write capacity or geographic resilience than one primary can give — not as a default.

In the interview

  • Introduce sharding only after estimating: "~1 B orders × 1 KB ≈ 1 TB, ~5 k writes/s at peak — beyond one comfortable primary, so I partition orders by customer_id".
  • Justify the key with the three criteria (cardinality, distribution, locality of the hot path) and name what scatters ("event-level reports go to the warehouse").
  • Say "consistent hashing with virtual nodes" and why: adding a node moves ~1/N of the keys, not all of them.
  • Always raise the hot partition before the interviewer does — the celebrity, the flash sale — and give a concrete mitigation (cache, finer key, salting, queue).
  • If transactions must span partitions, mention distributed SQL (Spanner, CockroachDB) and its cost: consensus round trips.

Common pitfalls

  • hash mod N for anything that will ever resize.
  • Sequential partition keys (timestamps, auto-increment) on range partitioning: one hot shard takes every write.
  • A key that ignores the hot path: transactions that become cross-shard on day one.
  • Too few fixed partitions: you cannot scale past one node per partition later.
  • Scatter/gather on the hot path: p99 of the query becomes the p99 of the slowest shard.
  • Sharding too early: you pay the complexity for years before you need the capacity.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    RANGE["by key range"] --> KEY["choosing the partition key<br/>cardinality, distribution, locality"]
    HASH["by hash"] --> KEY
    CH["consistent hashing<br/>virtual nodes"] --> HASH
    KEY --> HOT["hot partitions<br/>the on-sale event"]
    HOT --> MIT["cache, finer key, salting,<br/>queue → Caching, Messaging"]
    KEY --> SEC["secondary indexes<br/>local vs global"]
    KEY --> RESH["rebalancing,<br/>request routing"]
    KEY --> XP["cross-partition queries<br/>reports → warehouse"]
    XP --> NEW["NewSQL: Spanner, CockroachDB<br/>consensus per range → Distributed"]
    CH -.-> LB["the same ring in load balancers<br/>→ Edge"]

Palette components: nosql (Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB partition by key) · sql (sharded PostgreSQL, or distributed SQL) · cache (Redis Cluster hash slots; serves the hot event page instead of the shard) · search (Elasticsearch shards) · kafka (partitions by key) · queue (the waiting room in front of a hot partition) · lb (consistent hashing for affinity) · dwh (where scatter-gather reports belong). Scenarios: sharding, flash-sale. Continues in: Specialized Stores, Distributed — consensus, Edge — load balancing, Caching — Redis Cluster, Case study: distributed cache.
