items.title: Index
items.text:
Ten minutes before the on-sale, the catalog database is at 90% CPU — almost all of it from SELECTs for the event page. The team adds two read replicas and routes reads to them. CPU drops to 30%. Then the support channel lights up: "I paid, the confirmation e-mail arrived, but My tickets is empty!" Nothing was lost. The fan's next read simply went to a replica that had not yet received the write.

Replication — keeping a copy of the same data on several machines — is the most used scaling and availability tool in databases, and it comes with exactly this kind of surprise. This page covers the three ways to replicate (single-leader, multi-leader, leaderless), what replication lag does to users, and what happens when the leader dies.

items.title: Why replicate
items.text:
Goal How replication helps BoxOffice example Availability if one node dies, another has the data and takes over the inventory primary crashes at 10:01; a standby is promoted in seconds Read scaling reads are spread over several copies catalog reads go to 2–5 replicas Latency a copy close to the user a replica in another region for the event pages Durability a disk or machine loss does not lose committed data a synchronous standby holds every committed hold

Replication does not scale writes: every copy must apply every write. For that you need partitioning.

items.title: Single-leader replication
items.text:
One node, the leader (primary), accepts all writes. It records each change in its log — the write-ahead log (WAL) in PostgreSQL, the binlog in MySQL — and ships the log to followers (replicas, standbys), which replay it in the same order. Reads can go to any node1.

flowchart LR
    app["catalog service"] -->|"writes"| P[("primary")]
    P -->|"WAL stream"| R1[("replica 1")]
    P -->|"WAL stream"| R2[("replica 2")]
    app -->|"reads"| R1
    app -->|"reads"| R2
    app -->|"reads that must be fresh"| P

This is the model of PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL replication, SQL Server Always On, MongoDB replica sets and most managed services (Amazon RDS read replicas, Cloud SQL, Azure Database). It is simple to reason about because there is exactly one order of writes — the leader's.

items.title: Synchronous, asynchronous, semi-synchronous
items.text:
The key decision is when the leader tells the client "committed":

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant P as Primary
    participant S as Sync standby
    participant A as Async replica
    C->>P: COMMIT hold A-12
    P->>P: write WAL locally
    P->>S: ship WAL
    S-->>P: flushed
    P-->>C: committed
    P->>A: ship WAL (later)
    Note over A: may lag ms … s behind
Mode Leader answers "committed" after… Durability on leader loss Write latency Availability risk Asynchronous its own disk flush the last writes not yet shipped are lost lowest none from replicas Synchronous (all replicas) every replica confirms no loss highest: slowest replica decides any replica down blocks writes Semi-synchronous / one sync standby one replica confirms, others async no loss if that standby survives + one network round trip if the sync standby dies, another must take its role Quorum storage (Aurora: 4 of 6 copies across 3 zones)4 a write quorum of storage nodes confirms survives a zone loss + round trip to the quorum tolerates slow nodes

In PostgreSQL this is the synchronous_commit and synchronous_standby_names settings5; ANY 1 (s1, s2) means "wait for any one of the two standbys" — a quorum that tolerates one slow standby. Within one region, a synchronous round trip costs around a millisecond; across continents it costs tens to hundreds of milliseconds, which is why cross-region replicas are almost always asynchronous.

items.title: Replication lag and its anomalies
items.text:
An asynchronous replica is behind the leader by the replication lag: usually milliseconds, but seconds or minutes when the leader takes a burst of writes, a replica replays a huge transaction, or the network is congested. Lag creates three user-visible anomalies2:

Anomaly What the user sees Guarantee that prevents it Reading your own write fails pays, opens My tickets, sees nothing read-your-writes (read-after-write) consistency Time goes backwards refreshes the page: the ticket appears, refreshes again: gone (second read hit a more-lagged replica) monotonic reads Effect before cause sees the reply "refund approved" before the refund request in a chat thread consistent prefix reads 
sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fan
    participant O as order service
    participant P as Primary
    participant R as Replica (lag 800 ms)
    F->>O: POST /orders/9001/confirm
    O->>P: UPDATE orders SET status = 'PAID'
    P-->>O: committed
    O-->>F: 200 "Payment confirmed"
    F->>O: GET /me/tickets
    O->>R: SELECT … WHERE customer_id = 7
    R-->>O: (no row yet)
    O-->>F: "You have no tickets"

How likely is it? Under an illustrative model — lag exponentially distributed around a mean, and the fan's next click going to a replica — the answer depends entirely on the lag at that moment:

2026-10-23T08:15:44.226299 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

On a quiet day the bug is invisible; during the on-sale — exactly when the most fans are watching — most of them hit it. That is why lag bugs survive testing.

items.title: Fixing read-your-writes
items.text:
Technique How Trade-off Read from the leader after a write for N seconds after a user writes, route that user's reads to the primary (a timestamp in the session or a cookie) simple; the primary takes some extra reads Read from the leader for owned data "my orders", "my tickets" always on the primary; catalog on replicas simple rule; does not scale if most reads are "mine" Wait for the replica to catch up the write returns its log position (PostgreSQL LSN, MySQL GTID); the next read goes to a replica only once it has replayed that position (pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()) precise; needs plumbing in the data access layer Sticky replica per user hash the user to one replica gives monotonic reads, not read-your-writes Synchronous replica for reads read from a sync standby no lag, but writes pay the latency

Monitor lag as a first-class metric — pg_stat_replication.replay_lag in PostgreSQL, ReplicaLag in Amazon RDS — and alert on it (see Observability). A replica that is minutes behind is worse than no replica.

Try it. In the db-replicas scenario, a primary takes the writes and replicas serve the reads. Add replicas and watch read throughput rise while the primary's load stays flat; then increase the write rate and watch the replication lag grow — and with it, the share of stale reads.

items.title: Connection pooling
items.text:
Replicas multiply where queries can go; connection pools decide how many can run at once. In PostgreSQL each connection is a separate operating-system process with its own memory, so thousands of idle connections cost real RAM and CPU — and the database does not get faster beyond a few concurrent queries per CPU core.

Size pools with Little's Law, not with guesses: busy connections = queries per second × query time. At 2,000 queries/s × 5 ms = 10 connections busy on average. A pool of 20–30 handles bursts; a pool of 500 only adds contention.

The catch in microservices: 20 pods × a pool of 50 = 1,000 connections to one primary. A connection pooler such as PgBouncer (or RDS Proxy, or Cloud SQL Auth Proxy with pooling) sits between them, multiplexing thousands of client connections onto a few dozen server connections. In transaction pooling mode a server connection is lent per transaction, so session state (SET, temporary tables, some prepared-statement uses) must not leak across transactions. You will measure this in Hands-on 6.

items.title: Failover: when the leader dies
items.text:
If a follower dies, it reconnects and catches up from the log. If the leader dies, the system must fail over:

sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Failover manager (e.g. Patroni + etcd)
    participant P as Old primary
    participant S as Standby
    participant A as Apps
    M->>P: health check
    Note over P: no answer for 10 s
    M->>S: promote to primary
    S-->>M: promoted (new timeline)
    M->>A: update DNS / virtual IP / proxy
    A->>S: writes resume
    Note over P: if it comes back, it must be fenced<br/>and rejoin as a follower

Each step hides a hard problem:

  • Detection uses timeouts. Too short: a GC pause or network blip triggers an unnecessary failover. Too long: minutes of write downtime.
  • Lost writes. With asynchronous replication, writes acknowledged by the old leader but not yet shipped are gone. If those were seat holds, the new primary may sell the same seats again.
  • Split brain. If the old leader was only partitioned, not dead, two nodes may accept writes. Systems prevent this with consensus on who the leader is (Patroni stores the leader key in etcd; see Consensus) and fencing: the old leader is cut off (STONITH, "shoot the other node in the head") or its writes are rejected by fencing tokens.
  • Clients must follow. Through DNS, a virtual IP, a proxy or a driver that knows the topology.

Managed services package all of this — Amazon RDS Multi-AZ with a synchronous standby, Aurora with quorum storage, Cloud SQL high availability, Azure zone-redundant HA — with failovers that typically take from tens of seconds to a couple of minutes; the design question for you is what the application does meanwhile (retries with backoff, see Reliability).

items.title: Multi-leader replication
items.text:
In multi-leader (multi-primary, active-active) replication, several nodes accept writes and replicate to each other asynchronously. Typical reasons: one leader per region so writes are local; offline-first clients (a mobile app or a collaborative editor is effectively a leader); a second data center that must accept writes during a partition.

The price is write conflicts: two leaders accept different writes to the same record concurrently.

Resolution strategy How it works Risk Last write wins (LWW) keep the write with the highest timestamp silently drops the other write; clocks drift (see Time & Clocks) Merge application-specific merge (union of tags, sum of counters) only works for mergeable data CRDTs conflict-free replicated data types that merge automatically (counters, sets, text) limited data types; more metadata Avoid conflicts route all writes for a record to one "home" leader back to single-leader, per record

BoxOffice: where multi-leader fits — and where it must not

Event descriptions edited by venue staff in two regions: conflicts are rare and LWW or a "last editor wins, keep history" rule is acceptable.

Seat inventory: a conflict is a double booking. Two regions accepting holds for the same seat is exactly the bug of the transactions page, at continental scale. Inventory stays single-leader per event — if BoxOffice expands to another continent, each event's inventory lives in one "home" region.

items.title: Leaderless replication
items.text:
Amazon's Dynamo paper (2007)3 popularized a third design, used by Cassandra, ScyllaDB and Riak: no leader at all. The client (or a coordinator node) sends each write to all N replicas of a key and considers it successful when W of them acknowledge; it reads from R replicas and takes the newest version.

flowchart LR
    C["coordinator<br/>N = 3, W = 2, R = 2"] -->|"write v2"| A[("replica A ✓")]
    C -->|"write v2"| B[("replica B ✓")]
    C -.->|"write v2 (node down)"| X[("replica C ✗")]
    C -->|"read"| B
    C -->|"read"| X
    B -->|"v2 is newer"| C

If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write (with caveats under concurrent writes and failures — quorums alone are not linearizable). With N = 3:

W R R + W > N? Behaviour 1 1 no fastest, highest availability; reads may be stale 2 2 yes the usual "quorum" setting; tolerates 1 node down for reads and writes 3 1 yes fast reads; a single node down blocks writes 1 3 yes fast writes; a single node down blocks reads

Missed writes are repaired by read repair (a read that sees an old version writes the new one back), hinted handoff (a neighbour holds writes for a down node and replays them later; with a sloppy quorum those temporary holders even count toward W) and anti-entropy (background comparison of replicas with Merkle trees). Cassandra exposes the choice per query as consistency levels ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL.

items.title: Comparing the designs
items.text:
Single-leader Multi-leader Leaderless Writes accepted by one node several leaders any W of N replicas Write conflicts none (one order) yes — must be resolved yes — versions, LWW or siblings Failover needed, delicate another leader keeps going not needed Read-your-writes via routing tricks per leader with R + W > N, mostly Good for most OLTP: orders, inventory, users multi-region writes, offline clients high write availability, time series, carts Examples PostgreSQL, MySQL, RDS, MongoDB MySQL group replication (multi-primary), CouchDB, collaborative editors Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak, DynamoDB internally

BoxOffice: the replication plan

  • catalog: primary + 2 asynchronous read replicas; event pages read from replicas (staleness of a second is fine) behind the cache.
  • inventory: primary + one synchronous standby in another availability zone — a lost hold is a double booking, so no acknowledged write may be lost on failover. All holds and confirms go to the primary; the seat map may be served from a replica or the cache.
  • order: primary + async replica for reports; My tickets reads from the primary for 30 seconds after a purchase (session timestamp), from the replica otherwise.
  • Lag alert: page the on-call if any replica is more than 5 s behind for 2 minutes.

In the interview

  • "Add read replicas" is never the whole answer: add "…and I handle replication lag: reads that must reflect the user's own writes go to the primary".
  • State the durability choice: async (may lose the last writes on failover) vs a synchronous standby (no loss, + one round trip per commit). Tie it to the data: money and seats → sync standby.
  • For leaderless stores, write R + W > N and say what it buys and what it does not (it is not a transaction).
  • Mention failover time and what clients do meanwhile: retries with backoff, idempotent writes.

Common pitfalls

  • Reading your own writes from a replica — the empty My tickets page.
  • Using replicas for decisions: checking seat availability on a replica and then writing on the primary reintroduces the check-then-act race with extra lag.
  • Replicas as backups: a DELETE without WHERE replicates in milliseconds. Backups and point-in-time recovery are separate (see Disaster Recovery).
  • Unmonitored lag: a replica hours behind still answers queries — with hours-old data.
  • Too many connections from many pods with big pools; use a pooler and size pools with Little's Law.
  • Automatic failover without fencing: split brain is worse than downtime.

    SL --> LAG["replication lag"]
    LAG --> RYW["read-your-writes,<br/>monotonic reads"]

Palette components: sql (a primary with read replicas; a synchronous standby for seats and money) · nosql (leaderless quorums: Cassandra, DynamoDB) · app (routes reads and writes, retries with backoff during a failover) · cache (sits in front of the catalog replicas) · dns (one way clients follow the new leader). Scenarios: db-replicas, multi-region. items.title: Index
items.text:
A fan types "tayler swift sp dezembro" into the BoxOffice search box. Marketing wants "tickets sold per minute, per city, for the last two years" every morning. The event page shows a 2 MB poster to millions of visitors. The support assistant must find the refund policy paragraph that answers "can I get my money back if the show moves to another date?" — a sentence that shares almost no words with the policy text.

A relational database can do a weak version of each of these, and that is often the right start. But each one has an engine designed for it: a search engine, object storage, a data warehouse and a vector database. All four hold derived data (see the overview): copies of the system of record, reshaped for one kind of question.

items.title: How derived data flows
items.text:
The system of record stays in the services' relational databases. Changes flow out to the specialized stores through change data capture (CDC): a connector reads the database's log (the PostgreSQL WAL, the MySQL binlog) and publishes every insert, update and delete as an event.

flowchart LR
    DB[("catalog + order<br/>PostgreSQL")] -->|"WAL"| CDC["CDC connector<br/>(Debezium)"]
    CDC --> K[["event stream<br/>(Kafka)"]]
    K --> IDX["indexer"] --> S[("search index")]
    K --> ELT["loader"] --> W[("data warehouse")]
    K --> EMB["embedding worker"] --> V[("vector DB")]
    UP["poster upload"] --> O[("object storage")]

Why not have the service write to the database and to the search index directly (a dual write)? Because the two writes can fail independently or arrive in different orders under concurrency, leaving the stores permanently inconsistent. CDC (or the transactional outbox, see Messaging patterns) gives one ordered source of changes, and any derived store can be rebuilt by replaying it.

items.title: Why LIKE '%taylor%' is not search
The inverted index
items.text:
A search engine builds an inverted index: for each term, the list (postings list) of documents that contain it — the index at the back of a book1.

Term Postings (event ids) taylor 42, 77 swift 42 sao 42, 51, 77 paulo 42, 51, 77 stadium 42, 51

A query intersects or unions postings lists, which is fast because they are sorted and compressed. Before indexing, text goes through an analyzer:

  1. Tokenize: "Taylor Swift — São Paulo" → Taylor, Swift, São, Paulo.
  2. Normalize: lowercase and strip accents → taylor, swift, sao, paulo.
  3. Stem (language-specific): shows → show, ingressos → ingress.
  4. Synonyms: sp ↔ sao paulo.

The same analyzer runs on the query, so "SÃO PAULO" and "sao paulo" match the same terms. Fuzzy matching accepts terms within an edit distance (tayler → taylor, distance 1), and edge n-grams or completion suggesters index prefixes (tay, tayl, …) for autocomplete.

items.title: Ranking
items.text:
Matching documents are scored for relevance. The default in Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Lucene is BM252, which grows with how often a query term appears in a document (with diminishing returns), shrinks for terms common to every document (show, ingresso), and normalizes for document length. Products then blend it with business signals: popularity, date proximity, ticket availability.

Elasticsearch / OpenSearchPostgreSQL full-text POST /events/_search
{
  "query": {
    "function_score": {
      "query": {
        "multi_match": {
          "query": "tayler swift sp dezembro",
          "fields": ["title^3", "lineup^2", "city", "description"],
          "fuzziness": "AUTO"
        }
      },
      "functions": [
        { "field_value_factor": { "field": "popularity", "modifier": "log1p" } }
      ]
    }
  },
  "aggs": { "by_city": { "terms": { "field": "city.keyword" } } }
}
Good enough for a small catalog
ALTER TABLE events ADD COLUMN search tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('portuguese', unaccent_immutable(title)), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('portuguese', unaccent_immutable(coalesce(description, ''))), 'B')
  ) STORED;
CREATE INDEX events_search_idx ON events USING GIN (search);

SELECT id, title, ts_rank(search, q) AS rank
FROM events, websearch_to_tsquery('portuguese', 'taylor swift dezembro') q
WHERE search @@ q
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- unaccent_immutable: an IMMUTABLE wrapper around unaccent(), required in generated columns

items.title: Running a search cluster
items.text:
• An index is split into shards (fixed at creation, see Partitioning) with replicas for availability and read throughput. A query fans out to one copy of every shard and merges the top results — scatter/gather.
  • Search is near real time: new documents become searchable after a refresh (1 second by default in Elasticsearch), and the CDC pipeline adds its own lag. The event the venue just created may take a few seconds to appear — acceptable for search, not for inventory.
  • The index is derived: when the mapping or analyzer changes, build a new index from the stream or a snapshot and switch an alias to it.

Try it. The search-autocomplete scenario puts a search service and a cache behind the gateway. Run it and watch what fraction of keystrokes the cache absorbs (popular prefixes like "tay" repeat a lot); then raise the load and see which component saturates first when the cache is cold.

The full design — top-k prefix tries, debouncing on the client, per-prefix caching — is in the search autocomplete case study.

items.title: Object storage
items.text:
Object storage keeps blobs — images, videos, PDFs, backups, data-lake files — as immutable objects in buckets, addressed by a key and accessed over HTTP (PUT, GET, DELETE, LIST)3. The namespace is flat: posters/42/hero.webp looks like a path, but there are no real directories.

Property Object storage Block storage (a disk) Database Unit whole object (bytes to terabytes) 4 KiB blocks rows Access HTTP API, from anywhere mounted by one machine query language Update replace the whole object in place in place, transactional Scale effectively unlimited one volume one cluster Cost per GB lowest, with cold tiers medium highest Durability Amazon S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) per year, by storing copies across several facilities one volume, replicate yourself your replication and backups

Since 2020, Amazon S3 offers strong read-after-write consistency for all operations, and the other major clouds do as well. What object storage does not do: append to an object, rename cheaply (rename = copy + delete), lock, or query inside objects (except through engines that read files, like a warehouse).

The pattern that keeps blobs off your servers is the presigned URL: the service authorizes the upload, but the bytes go straight from the browser to the bucket.

sequenceDiagram
    participant V as Venue admin (browser)
    participant C as catalog service
    participant S as Object storage
    participant W as Thumbnail worker
    V->>C: POST /events/42/poster (name, type, size)
    C->>C: check permission, choose key posters/42/hero.webp
    C-->>V: presigned PUT URL (valid 5 min)
    V->>S: PUT posters/42/hero.webp (2 MB)
    S-->>V: 200 OK
    S->>W: event: object created
    W->>S: PUT posters/42/hero-400w.webp
    Note over C,S: the database stores only the key,<br/>the CDN serves the images
Presigned upload URL (boto3; works with any S3-compatible store)
import boto3

s3 = boto3.client("s3")

def poster_upload_url(event_id: int) -> str:
    return s3.generate_presigned_url(
        "put_object",
        Params={"Bucket": "boxoffice-media",
                "Key": f"posters/{event_id}/hero.webp",
                "ContentType": "image/webp"},
        ExpiresIn=300,  # seconds
    )

Reads go through the CDN (see DNS & CDN) with long cache lifetimes and versioned keys (hero.v3.webp), so the bucket sees a tiny fraction of the traffic. Lifecycle rules move old objects to cheaper tiers (infrequent access, archive) and delete temporary ones automatically; multipart upload sends large files in parallel parts that can be retried individually.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source / self-hosted

Amazon S3 (storage classes Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier), CloudFront as CDN.

Google Cloud Storage (Standard, Nearline, Coldline, Archive), Cloud CDN.

Azure Blob Storage (Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive tiers), Azure Front Door.

S3-compatible servers such as Ceph Object Gateway, SeaweedFS or Garage — useful in labs and on-premises; the S3 API is the de facto standard.

items.title: OLTP vs OLAP
items.text:
The services run OLTP (online transaction processing): many small reads and writes of individual rows, by key, with transactions. Analysts run OLAP (online analytical processing): few, huge queries that aggregate millions of rows over a few columns. They want opposite things from storage4:

OLTP (inventory, order) OLAP (warehouse) Typical query UPDATE seats … WHERE event_id = 42 AND seat_id = 'A-12' SELECT city, date_trunc('minute', sold_at), count(*) … GROUP BY 1, 2 over 2 years Rows touched a few, by index millions to billions, scanned Columns touched most of the row a few of many Latency target milliseconds seconds to minutes Writers the application, constantly batch or streaming loads Layout row-oriented column-oriented Data current state history, often append-only

items.title: Why columns
items.text:
A column store keeps each column in its own files. A query that reads 3 of 30 columns reads about a tenth of the bytes, and a column of similar values (city, status) compresses extremely well (dictionary and run-length encoding)5. With illustrative numbers for BoxOffice's clickstream — 20 GB/day for two years ≈ 15 TB raw:

Layout Bytes read for a query on 3 of 30 columns Row store ~15 TB (every row, every column) Column store ~1.5 TB (3 columns of 30) Column store + compression (assume 5–10×) ~150–300 GB + partition pruning (last 30 days only) a few GB

That difference — and running the scan in parallel on many machines — is why a warehouse answers in seconds what would take hours on the OLTP database (while hurting checkout).

items.title: Modelling: the star schema
items.text:
Warehouses are usually modelled as a star schema: a central fact table of events (one row per ticket sold) with foreign keys to dimension tables that describe them.

erDiagram
    FACT_TICKET_SALES }o--|| DIM_EVENT : "event_key"
    FACT_TICKET_SALES }o--|| DIM_VENUE : "venue_key"
    FACT_TICKET_SALES }o--|| DIM_DATE : "date_key"
    FACT_TICKET_SALES }o--|| DIM_CUSTOMER : "customer_key"
    FACT_TICKET_SALES {
        bigint ticket_id
        timestamp sold_at
        int price_cents
        string channel
    }
    DIM_EVENT {
        bigint event_key
        string title
        string genre
    }
    DIM_VENUE {
        bigint venue_key
        string city
        string country
    }
Sales per minute per city on on-sale day (warehouse SQL)
SELECT v.city,
       date_trunc('minute', f.sold_at) AS minute,
       count(*)                        AS tickets,
       sum(f.price_cents) / 100.0      AS revenue
FROM fact_ticket_sales f
JOIN dim_venue v ON v.venue_key = f.venue_key
WHERE f.sold_at >= '2027-03-01 10:00' AND f.sold_at < '2027-03-01 12:00'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 2, 1;

items.title: Getting data in: ETL, ELT, streaming
items.text: Approach How Freshness Typical tools ETL (extract, transform, load) transform outside, load clean tables hours (batch) Spark, custom jobs, Airflow ELT (extract, load, transform) load raw data, transform inside the warehouse with SQL hours to minutes Fivetran / Airbyte + dbt Streaming CDC change events continuously appended seconds to minutes Debezium + Kafka, cloud streaming ingestion

items.title: Lakes and lakehouses
items.text:
A data lake stores raw files — usually Parquet, a columnar file format — in object storage, cheaply and in any shape. The weakness of a plain lake is that files have no transactions or schema. Open table formats — Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, Apache Hudi — add a transaction log, schema evolution and time travel on top of those files, so several engines (Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, cloud warehouses) can query the same tables. That combination is the lakehouse6.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source / independent

Amazon Redshift (warehouse), Athena (SQL on S3), S3 Tables / Iceberg.

BigQuery (serverless warehouse, also over Iceberg tables in Cloud Storage).

Microsoft Fabric / Azure Synapse, Azure Databricks.

ClickHouse, DuckDB (in-process), Apache Spark, Trino; Snowflake and Databricks run on all three clouds.

items.title: Embeddings: meaning as geometry
items.text:
An embedding model turns a piece of text (or an image) into a vector of numbers — typically hundreds to a few thousand dimensions — such that texts with similar meaning end up close to each other. "Can I get my money back if the show moves to another date?" and "Refunds for rescheduled events" share few words but have nearby embeddings. Closeness is usually measured with cosine similarity:

\[ \cos(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert \, \lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert} \]

This powers semantic search and the retrieval step of RAG (retrieval-augmented generation), where the BoxOffice assistant fetches the most relevant policy chunks and gives them to the language model (see AI Systems — RAG & memory).

flowchart LR
    Q["fan question"] --> E["embed<br/>(embedding model)"]
    E --> V[("vector DB<br/>top-k nearest")]
    V --> RR["rerank<br/>(optional)"]
    RR --> L["LLM prompt:<br/>question + chunks"]
    L --> A["answer with sources"]

items.title: Exact vs approximate search
items.text:
The exact answer compares the query with every vector: for 10 million vectors of 1,024 dimensions, that is about 10 billion multiply-adds per query — fine offline, too slow for interactive traffic. Vector databases use approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes that look at a small fraction of the vectors and accept missing a few true neighbours. The quality measure is recall@k: of the true k nearest, how many did the index return?

  • IVF (inverted file): cluster the vectors (e.g. with k-means); at query time scan only the nprobe clusters closest to the query.
  • HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world)7: a layered graph in which each vector links to its near neighbours; a search starts at the sparse top layer and greedily walks toward the query, layer by layer. Very good recall/latency trade-off, at the cost of memory for the graph and slower inserts. Parameters: m (links per node), ef_construction, and ef_search (how wide the search is — the recall knob at query time).
  • Quantization (product quantization, scalar or binary) compresses vectors 4–32× to fit more in memory, trading a little recall.

A small, real experiment makes the trade-off visible: 20,000 synthetic 64-dimensional vectors around 200 topics, an IVF index with one bucket per topic, and 60 queries. Each point is a value of nprobe:

2026-10-23T08:15:44.606617 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Comparing about 8% of the vectors already returns roughly 9 of the 10 true neighbours; each extra point of recall costs more work. Real embeddings and HNSW behave differently in detail, but the shape — a tunable recall-versus-cost curve — is the same, and it is a product decision: for RAG, a reranker after the ANN step forgives a slightly lower recall.

items.title: Where to keep vectors
Choosing among them
items.text:
Store Answers Fed by Freshness Not for Search engine "which documents match these words, ranked?" CDC / indexer ~seconds system of record, transactions Object storage "give me this blob" direct upload (presigned URL) immediate small records, queries inside objects Data warehouse / lakehouse "aggregate history across millions of rows" ELT / streaming CDC minutes to hours serving the app's hot path Vector database "what is closest in meaning?" embedding worker ~seconds exact matches, structured filters alone

BoxOffice: the specialized stores in place

  • Search: OpenSearch index of events, fed by Debezium from the catalog database; Portuguese analyzer, sp ↔ sao paulo synonym, fuzzy matching, popularity boost; autocomplete prefixes cached.
  • Object storage: posters uploaded with presigned URLs, resized by a worker, served through the CDN with versioned keys; ticket PDFs generated on demand and stored for 1 year by a lifecycle rule.
  • Warehouse: order and clickstream events land in Iceberg tables on object storage; dbt builds the star schema; the "sales per minute" dashboard reads the warehouse, never the order database.
  • Vectors: the assistant's knowledge base (policies, FAQs, event descriptions) in pgvector in its own PostgreSQL, with an HNSW index; re-embedded by a worker whenever a document changes.

In the interview

  • For any "search" requirement, say inverted index and how it is kept in sync (CDC, eventual consistency of seconds) — and that the index is derived data you can rebuild.
  • Images, video and files → object storage + CDN + presigned URLs; the database stores only keys and metadata.
  • "Analytics" or "reports" → OLAP in a warehouse, column storage, fed by CDC/ELT — "never on the OLTP primary".
  • Semantic search or RAG → embeddings + ANN index (HNSW), and mention recall vs latency and the option of pgvector before a dedicated product.

Common pitfalls

  • Dual writes from the application to the database and the index: they drift apart; use CDC or an outbox.
  • Treating the search index as the source of truth: a mapping change or a corrupted index must be fixable by a rebuild.
  • Serving blobs through the application servers: every image byte costs app CPU and bandwidth; use presigned URLs and the CDN.
  • Reports on the production database: long scans compete with checkout; use the warehouse (or at least a replica).
  • Vectors without a re-embedding plan: when the embedding model changes, every vector must be recomputed — old and new vectors are not comparable.

items.title: Index
items.text:
At 10:00:03 on sale day, Alice and Bob both click seat A-12 of the stadium show. Both see "Seat held — you have 10 minutes to pay". Both pay. At the gate, one of them is turned away. The code that did this had been in production for a year, had 100% test coverage and passed every code review — because the bug only exists when two requests interleave in the database, which never happens in a unit test.

This page explains why, using the vocabulary every database engineer shares: transactions, isolation levels and anomalies. Then it fixes the bug four different ways and builds the seat-hold flow BoxOffice really uses.

items.title: ACID, concretely
items.text:
A transaction groups several reads and writes into one logical unit. The classic guarantees are summarized as ACID1:

Letter Guarantee What it means for a seat hold What it does not mean Atomicity all writes of the transaction happen, or none the seat is marked HELD and the hold row is created, or neither nothing about concurrency Consistency the database moves from one valid state to another constraints (CHECK, UNIQUE, foreign keys) hold after every commit it is mostly your invariants, enforced by A, I and D plus constraints Isolation concurrent transactions do not interfere as defined by the isolation level Bob's transaction does not see Alice's half-done work it does not mean "as if run one at a time" — unless the level is serializable Durability once committed, the data survives a crash after "Seat held", a power cut does not undo the hold survival of a disk or region loss — that needs replication (Replication)

The trap is in the I: most databases do not run transactions as if one at a time by default. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server default to read committed; MySQL InnoDB defaults to repeatable read. Both permit anomalies — including the one that sold seat A-12 twice.

items.title: The double-booking bug
items.text:
This is the code path, written as the SQL each request sends (the application checks the result of the SELECT before issuing the UPDATE):

Hold a seat — naive version (check, then act)
BEGIN;  -- PostgreSQL default: READ COMMITTED

SELECT status FROM seats
WHERE event_id = 42 AND seat_id = 'A-12';
-- application: if status != 'AVAILABLE' then ROLLBACK and show "seat taken"

UPDATE seats
SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :customer_id,
    hold_expires_at = now() + interval '10 minutes'
WHERE event_id = 42 AND seat_id = 'A-12';

COMMIT;

Now interleave two requests:

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Alice (T1)
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant B as Bob (T2)
    A->>DB: SELECT status … A-12
    DB-->>A: AVAILABLE
    B->>DB: SELECT status … A-12
    DB-->>B: AVAILABLE
    A->>DB: UPDATE … SET HELD, held_by = Alice
    Note over DB: T1 locks row A-12
    B->>DB: UPDATE … SET HELD, held_by = Bob
    Note over DB: T2 waits for T1's row lock
    A->>DB: COMMIT
    DB-->>A: ok — "seat held"
    Note over DB: lock released: T2's UPDATE runs<br/>and overwrites Alice's hold
    B->>DB: COMMIT
    DB-->>B: ok — "seat held"

Both requests read AVAILABLE before either wrote; both decided "free"; the second UPDATE overwrote the first. This is the check-then-act race, and the anomaly is called a lost update: Alice's write was silently lost. The row lock did not help, because it only serialized the two UPDATEs — the decision had already been made on stale reads.

If the tickets table has PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_id) (see Data Models), the second ticket insert fails at payment confirmation — after the money was taken. The constraint saved the stadium from two people in one seat, but turned the bug into a refund and an angry customer. Constraints are the last line of defense, not the design.

Think first: would wrapping the code in a transaction with a stricter isolation level fix it?

In PostgreSQL, yes: under repeatable read, T2's UPDATE fails with could not serialize access due to concurrent update because the row changed after T2's snapshot; the application retries, reads HELD and tells Bob the seat is taken. Under serializable the same happens. In MySQL InnoDB, repeatable read does not detect it: the UPDATE reads the latest committed row and overwrites it. Isolation levels have the same names across databases but not the same behaviour — test yours, or use one of the fixes below that work everywhere.

items.title: Isolation levels and their anomalies
items.text:
An anomaly is an outcome that could never happen if transactions ran one at a time (serially). Each weaker isolation level permits some of them in exchange for more concurrency2.

Anomaly What happens BoxOffice example Dirty read T2 reads data T1 wrote but has not committed the seat map shows A-12 sold; Alice's card is declined and T1 rolls back — the seat was never sold Non-repeatable read (read skew) T reads the same data twice and gets different values, because another transaction committed in between a report counts 59,990 sold seats, then sums paid orders and gets 60,002 tickets — the two numbers disagree Lost update two transactions read, modify and write the same row; one write is lost the double booking above Phantom a query's set of matching rows changes because another transaction inserted or updated rows "how many tickets does customer 7 hold?" returns 2, while another transaction adds 2 more Write skew two transactions read the same data, then write different rows based on it; each is fine alone, together they break an invariant the ticket limit below

The levels, as implemented by PostgreSQL (other databases differ — check the documentation3):

Level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom Lost update Write skew Read uncommitted (behaves as read committed in PostgreSQL) no possible possible possible possible Read committed (default) no possible possible possible possible Repeatable read (snapshot isolation) no no no detected → error, retry possible Serializable (serializable snapshot isolation) no no no no no — aborts with error 40001, retry

items.title: How snapshots work: MVCC
items.text:
PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle and most modern engines use multi-version concurrency control (MVCC): an update writes a new version of the row instead of overwriting it, tagged with the transaction that created it. Each transaction reads from a snapshot — the versions committed before it (repeatable read) or before each statement (read committed) started.

Row A-12 version Created by Visible to status = AVAILABLE T100 (loading the event) transactions whose snapshot predates T205's commit status = HELD, held_by = Alice T205 (Alice) transactions that start after T205 commits

The payoff: readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. The cost: old versions accumulate and must be cleaned up (VACUUM in PostgreSQL), and two writers to the same row still serialize on a row lock.

items.title: Write skew: the ticket limit
items.text:
BoxOffice allows at most 6 tickets per customer per event. Alice already holds 4 and opens two browser tabs, each trying to hold 2 more seats:

Time Tab 1 (T1) Tab 2 (T2) 1 SELECT count(*) … WHERE held_by = 7 → 4 2 SELECT count(*) … WHERE held_by = 7 → 4 3 4 + 2 ≤ 6 → UPDATE seats … 'B-1', 'B-2' 4 4 + 2 ≤ 6 → UPDATE seats … 'C-7', 'C-8' 5 COMMIT COMMIT Alice now holds 8 tickets

No row was written by both transactions, so no row lock conflicts and snapshot isolation sees nothing wrong. This is write skew, and it is driven by a phantom: each transaction's count(*) would have changed had it seen the other's writes. Two fixes:

  • Serializable isolation: PostgreSQL's serializable snapshot isolation (SSI)4 tracks read/write dependencies and aborts one transaction with ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions (SQLSTATE 40001). The application must retry it.
  • Materialize the conflict: make both transactions lock the same row first, e.g. a per-customer-per-event row:
Turn write skew into a plain row-lock conflict
BEGIN;
SELECT tickets_held FROM customer_event_limits
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND event_id = 42
FOR UPDATE;                         -- the second tab waits here
-- application: if tickets_held + 2 > 6 then ROLLBACK
UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', held_by = 7,
                 hold_expires_at = now() + interval '10 minutes'
WHERE event_id = 42 AND seat_id IN ('B-1', 'B-2') AND status = 'AVAILABLE';
UPDATE customer_event_limits SET tickets_held = tickets_held + 2
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND event_id = 42;
COMMIT;

items.title: Four ways to fix the double booking
items.text: All four work on any mainstream relational database at read committed, which is why they are preferred over "just raise the isolation level".

items.title: 1. Atomic conditional update (compare-and-set)
items.text:
Put the check inside the write, so check and act are one atomic statement:

Fix 1 — conditional UPDATE
UPDATE seats
SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :customer_id,
    hold_expires_at = now() + interval '10 minutes'
WHERE event_id = 42 AND seat_id = 'A-12'
  AND status = 'AVAILABLE';
-- 1 row updated → the hold is yours; 0 rows → someone else got it

When Bob's UPDATE waits for Alice's lock and then runs, PostgreSQL re-checks the WHERE clause against the new row version: status is now HELD, so 0 rows are updated. One round trip, no explicit lock, no retry loop. This is the BoxOffice default.

items.title: 2. Pessimistic locking: SELECT … FOR UPDATE
items.text:
Lock the row when you read it, so nobody can change it until you commit:

Fix 2 — lock on read
BEGIN;
SELECT status FROM seats
WHERE event_id = 42 AND seat_id = 'A-12'
FOR UPDATE;                 -- Bob blocks here until Alice commits
-- application: if status != 'AVAILABLE' then ROLLBACK
UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :customer_id,
                 hold_expires_at = now() + interval '10 minutes'
WHERE event_id = 42 AND seat_id = 'A-12';
COMMIT;

Use it when the decision needs application logic between the read and the write (pricing rules, the ticket limit). Variants matter under load:

  • FOR UPDATE NOWAIT fails immediately instead of waiting — good for "seat taken, choose another".
  • FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED skips rows other transactions hold — perfect for "best available": hand each fan different free seats without them queuing on the same rows.
Best available: two free seats in section B, without waiting on other fans
SELECT seat_id FROM seats
WHERE event_id = 42 AND section = 'B' AND status = 'AVAILABLE'
ORDER BY seat_id
LIMIT 2
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

When one transaction locks several rows (a group of 4 seats), always lock them in the same order (e.g. ORDER BY seat_id). Otherwise T1 locks A-1 then waits for A-2 while T2 locks A-2 then waits for A-1 — a deadlock; the database kills one of them.

items.title: 3. Optimistic locking with a version column
items.text:
Do not lock at all; detect conflicts at write time with a version counter:

Fix 3 — optimistic concurrency control
SELECT status, version FROM seats
WHERE event_id = 42 AND seat_id = 'A-12';     -- AVAILABLE, version 7

UPDATE seats
SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :customer_id, version = version + 1,
    hold_expires_at = now() + interval '10 minutes'
WHERE event_id = 42 AND seat_id = 'A-12' AND version = 7;
-- 0 rows → somebody changed the seat since you read it: reload and retry

JPA/Hibernate does this automatically with an @Version field and throws OptimisticLockException. It shines when conflicts are rare (editing an event description) and holds no locks during user think time. It is a poor fit for a flash sale, where thousands of fans collide on the same few rows and most attempts fail and retry.

items.title: 4. Let a constraint decide
items.text:
Make the invariant a unique constraint, and let the database reject the loser. With a separate holds table, an expired hold can even be taken over atomically:

Fix 4 — unique key + upsert that only steals expired holds
CREATE TABLE seat_holds (
    event_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
    seat_id    TEXT   NOT NULL,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_id)
);

INSERT INTO seat_holds (event_id, seat_id, customer_id, expires_at)
VALUES (42, 'A-12', :customer_id, now() + interval '10 minutes')
ON CONFLICT (event_id, seat_id) DO UPDATE
    SET customer_id = EXCLUDED.customer_id, expires_at = EXCLUDED.expires_at
    WHERE seat_holds.expires_at < now();   -- only if the old hold expired
-- 1 row → hold acquired; 0 rows → a live hold exists

items.title: Comparing the fixes
items.text: Approach How conflicts are resolved Under heavy contention Round trips Best for Conditional UPDATE the WHERE is re-checked; loser updates 0 rows good: short lock, no retries 1 single-row check-and-set (seat hold) SELECT … FOR UPDATE losers wait for the lock waits pile up; use NOWAIT / SKIP LOCKED 2+ logic between read and write; multi-row decisions Optimistic (version) loser detects the change and retries many failed attempts and retries 2 + retries rare conflicts, long user think time Unique constraint / upsert loser gets a constraint violation or 0 rows good 1 "at most one" invariants; last line of defense Serializable + retry database aborts one transaction aborts grow with contention n + retries complex invariants across many rows

items.title: Seat holds, end to end
items.text:
A hold is a lease: a temporary, expiring claim. The seat's life cycle:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> AVAILABLE
    AVAILABLE --> HELD: hold (conditional UPDATE)
    HELD --> SOLD: payment confirmed
    HELD --> AVAILABLE: hold expired or cancelled
    SOLD --> AVAILABLE: refund (rare, audited)
    SOLD --> [*]

Two design decisions make it robust:

  1. Lazy expiry. The hold query treats an expired hold as available, so a seat is never stuck because a cleanup job is late:

    InventoryRepository.java (Spring Data JPA)
    @Modifying
@Query("""
    UPDATE Seat s
       SET s.status = 'HELD', s.heldBy = :customerId, s.holdExpiresAt = :expiresAt
     WHERE s.eventId = :eventId AND s.seatId = :seatId
       AND (s.status = 'AVAILABLE'
            OR (s.status = 'HELD' AND s.holdExpiresAt < CURRENT_TIMESTAMP))
    """)
int tryHold(@Param("eventId") long eventId, @Param("seatId") String seatId,
            @Param("customerId") long customerId, @Param("expiresAt") Instant expiresAt);

    The service throws SeatTakenException when tryHold returns 0. A background job still flips expired holds back to AVAILABLE (using the partial index on hold_expires_at) so the seat map stays accurate.

  2. Confirm conditionally, too. Payment confirmation runs UPDATE seats SET status = 'SOLD' WHERE … AND status = 'HELD' AND held_by = :customer_id AND hold_expires_at > now(). If the hold expired while the fan was paying, 0 rows are updated and the payment is refunded or the fan is offered another seat. Never assume the state you saw minutes ago is still true.

items.title: Contention: why hot rows cap throughput
items.text:
A row lock behaves like a server that serves one transaction at a time. If each transaction holds it for t seconds, that row admits at most 1 / t transactions per second, no matter how big the machine is (Little's Law, from Queueing). The plot compares three designs under illustrative assumptions (load spread evenly over the contended rows; the database itself tops out at 10,000 transactions per second):

2026-10-23T08:15:44.824304 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The lessons:

  • Never keep a global counter in the hot path. Decrementing events.seats_left in every hold serializes the whole on-sale on one row: at 5 ms per transaction, 200 holds per second, for 2 million fans. Compute "seats left" asynchronously (or with per-section counters) and show it from a cache.
  • Keep transactions short. A transaction that calls the payment provider (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds) while holding a seat lock multiplies lock time by 100. Hold the seat, commit, call the provider outside any transaction, then confirm in a new short transaction.
  • Fine-grained rows spread contention. One row per seat means fans only collide when they want the same seat.

Try it. The flash-sale scenario puts a waiting room (queue) in front of the inventory database. Run it, then remove the queue or raise the arrival rate and watch the SQL node's utilization and p99 latency: the queue exists precisely to keep the number of concurrent hold transactions below what the database can serve.

items.title: Transactions across services
items.text:
The hold lives in the inventory database, the order in the order database, and the payment at an external provider. No single ACID transaction spans them.

  • Two-phase commit (2PC) coordinates several databases: a coordinator asks every participant to prepare (promise to commit), then tells all of them to commit. It is atomic, but a participant that prepared must wait — holding locks — until the coordinator answers; if the coordinator crashes at the wrong moment, they block. It is used inside some databases and with XA transactions, rarely across microservices, and never across an external payment provider.
  • Sagas split the business transaction into local transactions, each with a compensation (release the hold, refund the payment), coordinated by events or an orchestrator. Combined with the transactional outbox (write the event in the same local transaction as the state change), they give atomicity eventually. See Messaging patterns.
  • Calls to the payment provider carry an idempotency key, so a retry never charges twice. See Integrations.

BoxOffice: the checkout, transaction by transaction

  1. inventory: conditional UPDATE → seat HELD for 10 minutes. Commit. (~2 ms of lock time)
  2. order: insert the order as PENDING + an outbox event OrderCreated. Commit.
  3. payment: call the provider with idempotency key = order id. No database transaction open.
  4. On PaymentSucceeded: inventory runs the conditional confirm (HELD by this customer and not expired → SOLD) and inserts the ticket (unique key). Commit.
  5. On failure or timeout: compensations release the hold and cancel the order.

Every step is short, idempotent and safe to retry, and no lock is held while waiting for the network.

In the interview

  • When a design has a scarce resource (seats, stock, usernames, coupon codes), say the words "check-then-act race" and show the fix: "a conditional UPDATE … WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE' and I check the affected row count", plus "a unique constraint as the last line of defense".
  • Know the default isolation level of the database you name (PostgreSQL: read committed; MySQL InnoDB: repeatable read) and one anomaly it allows.
  • For "best available" or job queues on SQL, mention FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
  • For flows across services, say saga + outbox + idempotency keys, not distributed transactions.
  • Mention contention: "a single counter row would cap the on-sale at 1 / lock-time — I avoid it".

Common pitfalls

  • Check in the application, act in the database — the double booking. Move the check into the WHERE clause or a constraint.
  • Long transactions: a transaction open during an HTTP call, a user's think time, or a big report holds locks and old MVCC versions for its whole duration.
  • Retrying without idempotency: serializable and optimistic strategies require retries; the retried code must be safe to run twice.
  • Raising the isolation level as a magic fix: it changes behaviour per database, adds aborts under load, and still needs a retry loop.
  • Inconsistent lock order when locking several rows: deadlocks under exactly the load you are testing for.
  • Caching the decision: the seat map may come from a cache; the hold must always hit the database (see Caching).

items.text:
flowchart LR
    ACID["ACID"] --> ISO["isolation levels<br/>MVCC snapshots"]
    ISO --> ANOM["anomalies: lost update,<br/>write skew"]
    ANOM --> BUG["the double-booking bug<br/>check-then-act race"]

Palette components: sql (the inventory database decides: conditional updates, row locks, constraints) · app (inventory answers 409 to the losers; transactions stay short) · queue (the waiting room bounds contention on hot rows) · scheduler (the job that flips expired holds back) · stream (outbox events between order, inventory and payment) · payment (called with an idempotency key, never inside a transaction). Scenarios: flash-sale, payment-system. Continues in: Replication, Distributed — transactions, Messaging — patterns, Compute — schedulers, Case study: ticketing, Hands-on 6.

items.title: Index
items.text:
It is 10:00:00 and the stadium show goes on sale. Two million fans press "Hold seat" in the BoxOffice app at roughly the same second, and 60,000 seats have to be shared among them — each seat sold exactly once. One fan, on a train, presses the button, the spinner turns for five seconds, and the app shows "Something went wrong, try again". She presses again. Did the first request hold a seat? Is she about to hold two? Will she be charged twice?

On a single machine that question would not exist: the function either returned or threw. BoxOffice, however, runs on dozens of machines — gateways, several replicas of the inventory service, a replicated PostgreSQL, Redis, a Kafka cluster — and the only thing connecting them is a network that can lose, delay and duplicate messages. That makes BoxOffice a distributed system, and this class is about what that changes.

A distributed system is a set of independent computers (nodes) that cooperate only by exchanging messages over a network, with no shared memory and no shared clock, and that appear to their users as a single coherent system1. Leslie Lamport's half-joking definition is the most useful one for an engineer: "a distributed system is one in which the failure of a computer you didn't even know existed can render your own computer unusable"2.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Justify when to distribute a system (scale, fault tolerance, latency, isolation) and list what it costs.
  • Classify failures with the standard failure models (crash, omission, timing, Byzantine, gray) and recognise the 8 fallacies of distributed computing in a design.
  • Explain why a caller cannot tell a slow node from a dead one, and design retried operations to be idempotent (idempotency keys, conditional writes).
  • Compare replication models and consistency models (linearizable → causal → read-your-writes → eventual) and choose one per data domain.
  • Apply CAP and PACELC to justify a trade-off between consistency, availability and latency.
  • Size a consensus cluster (Raft, quorums R + W > N) and explain leader election, split brain and fencing.
  • Choose between two-phase commit and a saga (with compensations, reservations and an outbox) for an operation that spans several services.
  • Order events across machines without trusting wall clocks (Lamport, vector and hybrid clocks, TrueTime).

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
1. This overview — why distribute, what it costs, failure models, the unreliable network (8 fallacies), timeouts, delivery semantics and idempotency.
  2. Replication & Consistency — single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication; the consistency spectrum from linearizable to eventual; session guarantees such as read-your-writes.
  3. CAP & PACELC — the consistency-versus-availability choice during a partition, the latency-versus-consistency choice the rest of the time, and multi-region designs.
  4. Consensus & Quorums — majorities, Raft (election and log replication), R + W > N, leases and fencing tokens, and the tools that do it for you.
  5. Distributed Transactions — atomicity across services: two-phase commit and why it blocks, sagas with compensations, try–confirm–cancel reservations, and the transactional outbox.
  6. Time & Clocks — NTP and clock drift, Lamport and vector clocks, hybrid logical clocks, TrueTime, and how to order events in practice.
  7. Quiz — check your understanding.

items.title: Slides
items.text: Click the slides and use ← → to move through them; F goes full screen and P opens the presenter view, with the notes. Open the slides in a new tab

items.title: Why distribute?
items.text:
Nobody distributes a system for fun: a single process with a single database is easier to write, test, debug and reason about. We pay the price of distribution only when one machine can no longer deliver a non-functional requirement:

Reason What one machine cannot do In BoxOffice Scalability Serve more requests, store more data or run more computation than its CPU, memory, disk or network card allow 2 M fans in the first minute of an on-sale; one server cannot even accept that many TLS connections Fault tolerance / availability Survive its own failure — a disk, a power supply, a kernel panic, a deploy gone wrong If the only inventory machine dies at 10:00:05, the sale stops Latency Be close to every user; light in fibre needs ~100 ms to cross half the planet (~20,000 km) one way Fans in Lisbon and in São Paulo both expect a fast seat map Isolation and organisation Let teams deploy independently, or contain a failure to one part of the product A bug in search should not stop payment Data residency Keep personal data in a jurisdiction (e.g. LGPD in Brazil, GDPR in Europe) European fans' data stays in an EU region

Vertical scaling — a bigger machine — is the first answer and often the right one for a while. It stops working for three reasons: there is a largest machine you can buy; the price grows faster than the capacity at the top end; and, however big it is, it is still one machine — a single point of failure (SPOF).

Think first: if one machine is simpler, why not run BoxOffice on the largest server money can buy?

It would probably handle the average day. But (1) the 10:00 on-sale peak is orders of magnitude above the average, and the machine would be idle (and paid for) the rest of the time; (2) any failure — hardware, operating system, a bad deploy — takes the whole company offline, which violates any reasonable availability target; (3) fans far away from that machine pay the round-trip time on every request. You still use vertical scaling for components that are hard to split (a primary database), but you add replicas and spread stateless work across many machines.

items.title: At scale, failure is the norm
items.text:
The second argument hides a paradox: distributing for fault tolerance means using more machines, and more machines means more failures. If each machine fails on a given day with a small probability \(p\), independently, the probability that at least one of \(N\) machines fails that day is \(1 - (1-p)^N\):

2026-10-23T08:15:45.383902 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

With an (illustrative) 0.1% chance of failure per machine per day, three machines see a failure on about 0.3% of days, but a fleet of 3,000 machines sees at least one failure on about 95% of days. Google's early reports describe exactly this experience: at fleet scale, hardware failures are a daily routine, not an exception3. The conclusion shapes the rest of the course: a distributed system must treat failure as a normal event and keep working through it — it cannot hope to avoid it.

items.title: What distribution costs
items.text: Cost Why Where it comes back in the course Partial failure Some nodes work while others do not; every call can fail on its own Failure models, Reliability Unreliable network Messages are lost, delayed, duplicated, reordered The network is unreliable, Idempotency No global clock Each node has its own clock, and they disagree Time & Clocks Consistency Copies of the same data can diverge Replication & Consistency, CAP Coordination Agreeing on anything (a leader, a lock, an order, a commit) needs messages and majorities Consensus, Distributed Transactions Operations More processes to deploy, observe and debug Observability, Cloud-native

items.title: BoxOffice is a distributed system
items.text:
Follow one click on "Hold seat A-12" through BoxOffice. Every arrow is a message over the network; every box is a process that can fail, pause or slow down on its own:

flowchart LR
    fan([Fan's phone]) -->|"POST /holds"| gw[gateway]
    gw -->|"validate token"| auth[auth]
    gw -->|"forward"| inv[inventory]
    inv -->|"UPDATE seat ... (transaction)"| pg[("PostgreSQL primary")]
    pg -->|"replicate WAL"| rep[("PostgreSQL replica")]
    inv -->|"cache seat map"| redis[("Redis")]
    inv -->|"SeatHeld event"| kafka[["Kafka (3 brokers)"]]
    kafka -->|"consume"| notif[notification]

Nothing in that picture shares memory or a clock. If Redis is slow, inventory waits; if the replica lags, a read from it is stale; if Kafka is unreachable, the hold may be committed in PostgreSQL but the SeatHeld event never published. Each of these is a partial failure, and the rest of this page is about naming them precisely.

items.title: Failure models
items.text:
A failure model states what a faulty component may do. It matters because every algorithm is only correct under some model: a protocol that tolerates crashes can be fooled by a node that lies.

Model What the faulty node (or link) does Example in BoxOffice Typical defence Crash-stop Halts and never comes back A VM is terminated Replicas + failover Crash-recovery Halts, later restarts with what it had on disk An inventory pod is OOM-killed and restarted Durable logs; idempotent replays Omission Silently drops some messages it should send or receive A full socket buffer drops the SeatHeld event Acknowledgements, retries, timeouts Timing (performance) Responds, but too late A 3-second garbage-collection pause in payment Timeouts, hedging, circuit breakers Byzantine Behaves arbitrarily: corrupts, lies, equivocates A bit flip corrupts a message; a compromised client forges tickets Checksums, signatures, validation; BFT protocols (3f + 1 nodes) Gray failure Looks healthy to the health check but fails for users /health returns 200 while every real query times out Health checks that exercise the real path; client-side signals

Two more ideas complete the vocabulary:

  • Partial failure: on one machine, a program usually works or crashes as a whole. In a distributed system, part of it fails while the rest keeps running, and nobody has a complete view of which part. Gray failures, studied by Microsoft in Azure, are the worst case — the system's own monitoring disagrees with its users4.
  • Timing assumptions: in a synchronous model, messages and processing have known upper bounds; in an asynchronous model, there are no bounds at all. Real networks are partially synchronous: they behave well most of the time, with occasional unbounded delays (a congested switch, a GC pause, a VM migration). Practical algorithms (Raft, for example) are designed to be safe under asynchrony and to make progress only when the network behaves.

The most common failure is not a crash

Crashes are easy: the process is gone, connections are refused, the orchestrator restarts it. The failures that hurt in production are slow responses, partial failures and gray failures — the node is there, answering some requests, holding your threads.

items.title: The 8 fallacies of distributed computing
items.text:
In the 1990s, L. Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun Microsystems listed the assumptions that newcomers to distributed systems make — all of them false5:

Fallacy Reality In BoxOffice 1. The network is reliable Packets are dropped, links fail, switches reboot The inventory → PostgreSQL connection resets mid-transaction 2. Latency is zero Same data centre ≈ 0.5 ms round trip; across continents ≈ 150 ms6 Six sequential service calls of 30 ms each make a 180 ms checkout 3. Bandwidth is infinite Links saturate, especially at peaks Returning the full 60,000-seat map as JSON to 2 M fans 4. The network is secure Traffic can be read, modified or forged Services trust any caller inside the cluster 5. Topology doesn't change Nodes come and go; IPs change A Kubernetes pod is rescheduled with a new IP during the on-sale 6. There is one administrator Many teams, accounts, providers and policies The payment provider changes a TLS setting on their side 7. Transport cost is zero Serialisation costs CPU; cloud egress costs money Cross-zone traffic on the monthly bill 8. The network is homogeneous Different protocols, versions, encodings Java services, a Python assistant, Kafka's binary protocol

Every one of them shows up in later classes: fallacy 1 in Reliability, 2 in Estimation, 3 in Traffic & Edge, 4 in Network & Security, 5 in Cloud-native.

items.title: Slow or dead?
items.text:
When inventory sends a request to payment and no reply arrives, it cannot know which of these happened:

sequenceDiagram
    participant I as inventory
    participant P as payment
    I->>P: authorise R$ 450 (request 1)
    Note over I,P: (a) request lost  (b) payment crashed<br/>(c) reply lost  (d) payment just slow
    I-->>I: no reply after 2 s: timeout
    I->>P: authorise R$ 450 (retry)
    P-->>I: OK
    Note over I,P: in cases (c) and (d) the fan was charged twice

From the caller's side, a lost request, a crashed server, a lost reply and a very slow server all look the same: silence. The only practical tool is a timeout — after a deadline, assume failure. But a timeout does not tell you whether the operation ran, so two things follow:

  1. Choosing the timeout is a trade-off. Too long and the caller's threads pile up waiting (the cascading failure of Reliability); too short and you declare healthy-but-slow nodes dead, retry, and add load exactly when the system is struggling. A common starting point is slightly above the downstream's p99.9 latency, within the caller's own latency budget. Systems such as Cassandra and Akka go further and use adaptive failure detectors (the φ accrual detector) that learn the normal distribution of heartbeat delays7.
  2. Retries must be safe. If the retry can apply the operation a second time, it must be harmless to do so — the operation must be idempotent.

items.title: At most once, at least once, exactly once
items.text:
Whenever a message crosses an unreliable network, the sender chooses a delivery semantics:

Semantics How Risk Use for At most once Send once, never retry Messages lost Metrics samples, "fan is typing…" signals At least once Retry until acknowledged Duplicates Almost everything: orders, events, e-mails Exactly once Not achievable by the network alone — Obtained as at least once + idempotent processing ("effectively once")

"Exactly-once delivery" over an unreliable network is impossible in general — the sender can never be sure the receiver did not process a message whose acknowledgement was lost. What systems such as Kafka call exactly-once is exactly-once processing: duplicates may arrive, but their effect is applied once, through deduplication or transactions8. The Messaging class covers this in depth.

items.title: Idempotent operations
items.text:
An operation is idempotent if applying it several times has the same effect as applying it once: \(f(f(x)) = f(x)\).

Operation Idempotent? Why GET /events/42 Yes Reads change nothing PUT /holds/A-12 {fan: 42} Yes Sets the state to a value; repeating sets the same value DELETE /holds/A-12 Yes The hold is gone after the first call; the second may return 404, but the state is the same POST /orders No Each call creates a new order UPDATE seats SET sold = sold + 1 No Each call increments again UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', fan = 42 WHERE id = 'A-12' AND status = 'FREE' Yes A conditional write: the second call matches no row

Two techniques make non-idempotent operations safe to retry:

  1. Rewrite it as a state transition with a condition (compare-and-set): "set the seat to HELD if it is FREE", "set version 8 if the current version is 7". A duplicate fails the condition and changes nothing.
  2. Idempotency keys: the client generates a unique key per intended operation and sends it with every attempt; the server stores the key with the result and, on a duplicate, returns the stored result instead of executing again. Stripe's public API popularised the Idempotency-Key header9, and there is an IETF draft standardising it.
sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fan's app
    participant O as order
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    F->>O: POST /orders, Idempotency-Key: 7f3a…
    O->>DB: INSERT key 7f3a… (unique) + order 981
    DB-->>O: committed
    O--xF: 201 Created (reply lost on the train)
    F->>O: retry: POST /orders, Idempotency-Key: 7f3a…
    O->>DB: INSERT key 7f3a…
    DB-->>O: unique violation: key exists
    O->>DB: SELECT stored response for 7f3a…
    O-->>F: 201 Created, order 981 (same order, no duplicate)

The key and the business change must be stored in the same transaction; otherwise a crash between the two writes reopens the window for duplicates:

idempotency.sql
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
    key           UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    request_hash  TEXT        NOT NULL,   -- reject the same key with a different body
    response      JSONB,                  -- what we answered the first time
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, request_hash)
VALUES ('7f3a…', 'sha256:…')
ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING;            -- 0 rows inserted → duplicate: return stored response
INSERT INTO orders (id, fan_id, total) VALUES (981, 42, 450.00);
UPDATE idempotency_keys SET response = '{"orderId": 981}' WHERE key = '7f3a…';
COMMIT;

BoxOffice: holding a seat safely

The app generates a UUID when the fan taps Hold seat and reuses it for every retry of that tap. inventory executes UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', fan_id = :fan, hold_key = :key WHERE id = :seat AND (status = 'FREE' OR hold_key = :key). The first attempt holds the seat; a retry with the same key matches the row again and changes nothing; a different fan's request matches no row and gets 409 Conflict. The payment adapter forwards the same key to the external provider, so a retried charge is not charged twice (Integrations).

Think first: the fan's retry arrives at a different order replica than the first attempt. Does the idempotency key still work?

Only if the deduplication state is shared — stored in the database (as above) or in a shared store such as Redis, not in the memory of one replica. A per-replica in-memory set of "seen keys" breaks as soon as the load balancer sends the retry elsewhere, which is the normal case. Keys also need a retention period (Stripe keeps them for 24 hours) long enough to cover every retry the client can make.

items.title: Putting it together: the concept map
items.text:
The three root problems — partial failure, an unreliable network, and no global clock — explain almost every design decision in the rest of the course. The map below connects each problem to the techniques of this class (blue), to the subpage that teaches it, and to the palette components where you will meet it in the playground (green):

flowchart LR
    PF["Partial failure"]:::problem --> REP["Replication<br/>(keep copies)"]
    NET["Unreliable network"]:::problem --> IDEM["Timeouts, retries,<br/>idempotency"]
    CLK["No global clock"]:::problem --> ORD["Ordering:<br/>logical / hybrid clocks"]
    REP --> CM["Consistency models<br/>linearizable … eventual"]
    CM --> CAP["CAP / PACELC<br/>C vs A, L vs C"]
    CAP --> CONS["Consensus, quorums,<br/>fencing"]
    IDEM --> TX["Sagas, outbox,<br/>2PC"]
    CONS --> TX
    ORD --> CONS
    REP -.-> sql["sql · nosql"]:::comp
    CM -.-> cache["cache · cdn"]:::comp
    CONS -.-> kafka["kafka · scheduler"]:::comp
    IDEM -.-> pay["payment · queue"]:::comp
    TX -.-> stream["stream · kafka"]:::comp
    CAP -.-> dns["dns (multi-region)"]:::comp

Technique Taught in Palette components where it shows up Other classes that build on it Timeouts, retries, idempotency keys this overview payment, thirdparty, queue Reliability, Compute — integrations Replication, consistency models Replication & Consistency sql, nosql, cache, cdn Databases — replication, Caching CAP, PACELC, multi-region CAP & PACELC dns, sql, nosql Reliability, Traffic & Edge Consensus, quorums, leases, fencing Consensus & Quorums kafka, scheduler, sql (failover) Cloud-native — Kubernetes (etcd), Databases — partitioning 2PC, sagas, outbox, reservations Distributed Transactions stream, kafka, payment Messaging — patterns, Case study: payment system Clocks, ordering, unique ids Time & Clocks kafka, sql, scheduler Messaging — Kafka, Case study: URL shortener

In the interview

You will rarely be asked "what is a distributed system?". You will be asked "the client times out — what happens?" or "how do you avoid charging twice?". Strong answers: (1) name the ambiguity ("a timeout doesn't tell me whether the charge happened"); (2) make the operation idempotent with an idempotency key stored atomically with the result; (3) retry with backoff and jitter only at one layer; (4) state the delivery semantics explicitly ("at-least-once delivery, effectively-once processing"). Saying "exactly-once delivery" without qualification is a red flag for interviewers.

Pitfalls

  • Treating a remote call like a local function call — no timeout, no retry policy, no thought about partial failure.
  • Retrying non-idempotent operations (POST, increments) without a key: duplicates, double charges, double-sold seats.
  • Deduplicating in memory on one replica: the retry goes to another replica.
  • Health checks that lie: /health returns 200 because the process is alive, while every request fails (gray failure).
  • Assuming failures are independent: replicas in the same rack, zone or with the same bad configuration fail together.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Distribute for scale, fault tolerance, latency, isolation or data residency — and only then: you pay with partial failures, an unreliable network and no global clock.
  • At scale, failure is the normal case: \(1-(1-p)^N\) approaches 1 quickly.
  • Know the failure models; the dangerous ones in practice are slow, partial and gray failures, not clean crashes.
  • A caller cannot distinguish slow from dead: use timeouts, and accept that a timed-out operation may have happened.
  • Exactly-once delivery is impossible; build at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing with conditional writes or idempotency keys stored atomically.
