items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Failures, networks and idempotency
items.text:
Q1. BoxOffice's inventory calls payment and gets no reply within 2 s. What can inventory conclude?

  • A. The payment service has crashed and must be restarted
  • B. The request was lost, so it is safe to retry without any precaution
  • C. Nothing certain: the request may have been lost, the server may have crashed, the reply may have been lost, or the server may just be slow — the charge may or may not have happened
  • D. The network is partitioned, so the system must switch to AP mode
Answer

C — Nothing certain.

A lost request, a crashed server, a lost reply and a slow server all look like silence to the caller. A timeout lets the caller assume failure and move on, but it does not tell whether the operation was executed. That is why a retry must be made safe — the operation must be idempotent (for example, with an idempotency key the provider deduplicates).

Q2. Each machine in a fleet fails on a given day with probability 0.1%, independently. Approximately what is the probability that at least one of 1,000 machines fails today?

  • A. 0.1%
  • B. 1%
  • C. About 63%
  • D. 100%
Answer

C — About 63%.

P(at least one failure) = 1 − (1 − 0.001)^1000 ≈ 1 − e^(−1) ≈ 0.63. With 3,000 machines it is about 95%. At scale, failures are a daily event, so the system must keep working through them instead of trying to avoid them.

Q3. The /health endpoint of the search service returns 200 OK, the load balancer keeps it in rotation, but every real search query times out. Which failure model is this?

  • A. Crash-stop
  • B. Byzantine failure
  • C. Gray failure
  • D. Omission failure of the load balancer
Answer

C — Gray failure.

A gray failure is one where the system's own monitoring sees the component as healthy while users experience failures. The fix is a health check that exercises the real dependency path (a readiness check that runs a cheap query) plus client-side signals such as error rates and passive outlier detection at the load balancer.

Q4. Which of these operations is idempotent?

  • A. POST /orders creating a new order for fan 42
  • B. UPDATE seats SET sold = sold + 1 WHERE event_id = 42
  • C. UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', fan_id = 42 WHERE id = 'A-12' AND status = 'FREE'
  • D. Sending a "your ticket is ready" e-mail
Answer

C — The conditional write.

Running it twice leaves the same state: the second execution matches no row (the seat is no longer FREE). POST creates a new order each time, the increment adds again, and each e-mail send is a new e-mail — all need an idempotency key or deduplication to be safely retried.

Q5. An order service stores idempotency keys in an in-memory HashSet on each replica. Three replicas run behind a load balancer. What goes wrong?

  • A. Nothing; the set is fast and correct
  • B. A retry may reach a different replica that has never seen the key, so the order is created twice
  • C. The keys use too much memory
  • D. The load balancer rejects requests that carry an Idempotency-Key header
Answer

B — The retry hits another replica.

Deduplication state must be shared (a unique key in the database, written in the same transaction as the order, or a shared store such as Redis). Per-replica memory also loses every key on restart. And the key must be stored atomically with the business change — otherwise a crash between the two writes reopens the duplicate window.

items.title: Replication and consistency
items.text:
Q6. A fan pays and is redirected to My tickets, which reads from an asynchronous read replica. The list is empty. Which guarantee is violated, and what is the cheapest fix?

  • A. Linearizability; make all reads and writes go through consensus
  • B. Read-your-writes; read the user's own data from the primary (or pass the write's log position and wait for a replica that has applied it)
  • C. Monotonic writes; send writes in order
  • D. Eventual consistency; the replica will never receive the write
Answer

B — Read-your-writes.

The fan does not need the whole system to be linearizable — she needs to see her own writes. Routing her reads of her own data to the primary (or for a few seconds after a write), or using a version token such as the PostgreSQL WAL LSN, provides read-your-writes at a much lower cost than global strong consistency.

Q7. Refreshing the event page, a fan sees "95 seats left", then "340 seats left", then "90 seats left", because each refresh hits a different replica. Which session guarantee is missing?

  • A. Read-your-writes
  • B. Monotonic reads
  • C. Monotonic writes
  • D. Linearizability of writes
Answer

B — Monotonic reads.

Monotonic reads promise that a session never sees data go back in time. Pinning the session to one replica (hash of the session id) or tracking the last version seen and only accepting replicas at least that fresh fixes it. The counter may still lag — that is fine for this screen — but it must not jump backwards.

Q8. Which statement about replication modes is correct?

  • A. Asynchronous replication with automatic failover never loses acknowledged writes
  • B. Fully synchronous replication to every follower makes writes highly available
  • C. Semi-synchronous replication (leader + at least one follower acknowledge) avoids losing acknowledged writes on failover if a synchronous follower is promoted, at the cost of one extra round trip
  • D. Multi-leader replication eliminates write conflicts
Answer

C — Semi-synchronous.

Asynchronous replication can lose the last acknowledged writes when the leader dies before followers received them. Fully synchronous replication blocks every write if any follower is down or slow. Multi-leader replication accepts writes in several places and therefore creates conflicts. Semi-synchronous (or quorum) replication is the usual compromise for data you cannot lose.

items.title: CAP and PACELC
items.text:
Q9. BoxOffice's seat inventory is replicated across two regions, and the link between them drops. A fan in region 2 asks to hold a seat whose latest state lives in region 1. A CP configuration will:

  • A. Hold the seat in region 2 and reconcile later
  • B. Refuse the request (error or timeout) until it can confirm the latest state
  • C. Return the seat as free and let the payment provider decide
  • D. Automatically become CA until the partition heals
Answer

B — Refuse until it can confirm.

During a partition, a CP system sacrifices availability on the side that cannot reach the latest state (typically the minority) rather than risk an inconsistent answer — here, a double-sold seat. An AP system would answer and reconcile later. "CA" is not an option for replicated data.

Q10. Why do most designs replicate synchronously across availability zones but asynchronously across regions?

  • A. CAP forbids synchronous replication between regions
  • B. Because of PACELC's else branch: an extra round trip across zones costs ~1–2 ms, while across continents it costs ~150 ms on every write
  • C. Availability zones never partition
  • D. Regions use different database engines
Answer

B — Latency (the "EL/EC" choice).

Even with no partition, consistency costs latency: a write must wait for the confirming replicas. A cross-zone round trip is cheap enough to pay on every write; a cross-continent one is not. Across regions, systems choose latency (async replication) or avoid the question by giving each record a home region.

items.title: Consensus and quorums
items.text:
Q11. An etcd cluster must keep accepting writes if any two nodes fail at the same time. What is the minimum cluster size?

  • A. 3
  • B. 4
  • C. 5
  • D. 6
Answer

C — 5.

N nodes tolerate ⌊(N−1)/2⌋ failures: 3 tolerate 1, 4 still tolerate only 1, 5 tolerate 2. Even sizes add cost without adding fault tolerance. The 5 nodes should be spread across zones so that no single zone holds a majority.

Q12. A Cassandra table uses N = 3 replicas. Which read/write settings guarantee that a read overlaps with the latest acknowledged write?

  • A. W = 1, R = 1
  • B. W = 1, R = 2
  • C. W = 2, R = 2
  • D. W = 2, R = 1
Answer

C — W = 2, R = 2.

The overlap condition is R + W > N: 2 + 2 = 4 > 3. Options A (2), B (3) and D (3) are not greater than N. Remember the overlap is necessary but not sufficient for linearizability: concurrent writes, sloppy quorums and LWW with skewed clocks still cause anomalies.

Q13. A scheduler replica holds a lease from etcd, pauses for 15 s in garbage collection, and wakes up after its lease has expired and another replica took it. What prevents the old holder from corrupting the shared state?

  • A. A longer lease TTL
  • B. A fencing token that increases with every grant and is checked by the storage, which rejects writes with an older token
  • C. Synchronised clocks with NTP
  • D. Running the scheduler with more memory
Answer

B — A fencing token.

A paused process cannot know it was paused. Longer TTLs only make the window rarer; clocks do not help a process that is not running. The storage must reject stale holders by comparing a monotonically increasing token (etcd revision, ZooKeeper zxid, a Raft term).

items.title: Distributed transactions
items.text:
Q14. In two-phase commit, the coordinator crashes after every participant voted yes but before sending the decision. What happens to the participants?

  • A. They commit on their own, since everybody voted yes
  • B. They abort on their own after a timeout
  • C. They stay in doubt, holding their locks, until the coordinator recovers and tells them the decision
  • D. They elect a new coordinator with Raft and continue
Answer

C — In doubt, holding locks.

A participant that voted yes has promised to commit if told so, and cannot know whether the coordinator decided commit (and others already committed) or abort (maybe someone else voted no). It must wait — this is 2PC's blocking problem. Systems such as Spanner and CockroachDB avoid it by replicating the coordinator's state with consensus; option D describes that design, not plain 2PC.

Q15. BoxOffice's checkout spans inventory, payment (an external provider) and order. The card is declined after the seat was moved to RESERVED_FOR_PAYMENT. In an orchestrated saga, what should happen?

  • A. Nothing: sagas are isolated, so the seat was never visible as reserved
  • B. The orchestrator runs compensations in reverse order: release the seat, then cancel the order
  • C. The orchestrator asks the payment provider to roll back its prepared transaction
  • D. The whole checkout is retried until the card is accepted
Answer

B — Compensate in reverse order.

A saga is a sequence of local transactions; when a step fails, the already-completed steps are undone by compensating transactions. Sagas are not isolated — other fans saw the seat as reserved, which is why the intermediate state works as a semantic lock with an expiry. An external provider has no "prepared transaction" to roll back (it cannot join 2PC), and retrying a declined card forever is not a business rule.

items.title: Time and clocks
items.text:
Q16. Two inventory nodes resolve conflicting writes to the same seat with last-write-wins using their own wall clocks. Node 1's clock is 50 ms ahead. What happens to two conflicting writes made 20 ms apart, the later one on node 2?

  • A. The later write always wins, because NTP corrects the clocks
  • B. The earlier write (on node 1) can win, because its timestamp is higher; the later write is silently lost
  • C. Both writes are kept as siblings
  • D. The database rejects both writes
Answer

B — The earlier write can win.

With clocks that disagree by more than the gap between the events, timestamps order them wrongly, and LWW silently discards one write — always biased towards the node with the fastest clock. For seats and money, let a single authority decide (a conditional write on one primary), or detect concurrency with version vectors.

Q17. Lamport clock values satisfy L(a) = 7 and L(b) = 9. What can you conclude?

  • A. a happened before b
  • B. b happened before a
  • C. Either a happened before b, or a and b are concurrent — but b did not happen before a
  • D. a and b are concurrent
Answer

C — Not "b → a", but a may be concurrent with b.

Lamport clocks guarantee that if a → b then L(a) < L(b). Contrapositive: if L(a) < L(b), b did not happen before a. They cannot distinguish "a → b" from "concurrent". Vector clocks can.

items.title: Index
items.text:
BoxOffice expands to Europe. To give fans in Lisbon the same fast experience as fans in São Paulo, the team runs the inventory database in two regions, each with a full copy of the seats, replicating to each other. One afternoon, during the on-sale of a festival, the transatlantic link between the regions degrades and then drops. Both regions are alive; both keep receiving "Hold seat A-12" requests. Each region now has two options for each request: answer with what it knows (and risk selling seat A-12 on both sides of the ocean) or refuse until the link comes back (and lose the sale). There is no third option. That dilemma is what the CAP theorem formalises.

The CAP theorem, conjectured by Eric Brewer in 2000 and proven by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch in 20021, states that a replicated data store cannot simultaneously guarantee all three of the following properties:

CAP theorem Three overlapping circles: Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance. The overlaps are CP and AP, the two real choices, and CA, which only exists without partitions. The centre, all three at once, is impossible. Consistency every read sees the latest write Availability every request gets a non-error answer Partition tolerance works while the network is split CP ZooKeeper, etcd AP Cassandra, DNS CA no partitions (single node) all three: impossible Partitions will happen, so the real choice is CP or AP — during a partition.

items.title: The three properties
items.text:
Consistency (C) : Every read returns the most recent write, or an error. In CAP, "consistency" means linearizability: the replicas behave as if there were a single copy (see Linearizability).

Availability (A) : Every request received by a non-failing node gets a non-error response — even if it does not contain the most recent write. Note the strictness: every non-failing node, not "most of the time".

Partition tolerance (P) : The system keeps operating when the network partitions — splits the nodes into groups that are alive but cannot exchange messages (or exchange them with unbounded delay).

P is not optional

Partitions are not a design choice; they happen — a switch fails, a cable is cut, a cloud region's link degrades, a long GC pause makes a node look unreachable. Any system whose data lives on more than one machine must decide what to do when they happen. So the real choice is C or A, during a partition. Brewer himself, twelve years later, stressed that partitions are rare and that the interesting design work is in detecting them, operating in a limited mode while they last, and recovering afterwards4.

The C in CAP is not the C in ACID

In ACID transactions, consistency means "the transaction preserves the invariants" (constraints, foreign keys, CHECK). In CAP it means linearizability. A single PostgreSQL server is ACID-consistent and CAP does not even apply to it — CAP is about replicas.

items.title: A partition, step by step
items.text:
The same request, handled by a system that chooses consistency (CP) and by one that chooses availability (AP):

sequenceDiagram
    participant FA as Fan in São Paulo
    participant SP as sa-east (region 1)
    participant EU as eu-west (region 2)
    participant FB as Fan in Lisbon
    Note over SP,EU: transatlantic link is down
    FA->>SP: hold seat A-12
    SP-xEU: replicate (cannot reach)
    FB->>EU: hold seat A-12
    alt CP: choose consistency
        SP-->>FA: 503: cannot confirm with the other region
        EU-->>FB: 503: cannot confirm with the other region
    else AP: choose availability
        SP-->>FA: held!
        EU-->>FB: held!
        Note over SP,EU: link returns: conflict, seat sold twice
    end

Neither answer is "wrong" in the abstract: the CP system refuses rather than risk a double sale; the AP system serves every fan and must reconcile later. Which one is acceptable depends on the data and the business — not on the database brand.

Think first: is there a way to keep selling seats on both sides of the ocean and never sell a seat twice?

Yes — by not replicating the decision. Give each event a home region (the region of the venue) and send every hold for that event to its home region's primary. Inside one region, the data is consistent; across regions, there is no shared decision to disagree on. During a transatlantic partition, a Lisbon fan buying a São Paulo show cannot reach the home region and is refused (CP for that event), but every event whose home is reachable keeps selling. You have not escaped CAP — you have shrunk the blast radius of the C/A choice to the requests that really cross the partition. See Multi-region designs.

items.title: CP — consistent and partition-tolerant
items.text:
During a partition, the nodes that cannot confirm the latest state (typically the minority side) refuse requests. After the partition heals, they catch up before serving again.

flowchart LR
    CA(["Fan A"]) -->|"1 · hold A-12"| A[("Node A (majority)<br/>A-12 = HELD")]
    A -.-x|"2 · replicate ✗ partition"| B[("Node B (minority)<br/>A-12 = FREE")]
    CB(["Fan B"]) -->|"3 · is A-12 free?"| B
    B -->|"4 · error: no quorum"| CB
  • Examples: etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, Spanner, CockroachDB; PostgreSQL with synchronous replication; MongoDB with majority reads and writes.
  • Use when: a wrong answer is worse than no answer — inventory, money, identity, leadership, locks.

items.title: AP — available and partition-tolerant
items.text:
During a partition, every node keeps answering with the data it has. Replicas diverge and converge after the partition heals (eventual consistency), resolving conflicts with LWW, version vectors or CRDTs (Eventual consistency).

flowchart LR
    CA(["Fan A"]) -->|"1 · like event 42"| A[("Node A<br/>likes = 101")]
    A -.-x|"2 · replicate ✗ partition"| B[("Node B<br/>likes = 100")]
    CB(["Fan B"]) -->|"3 · read likes"| B
    B -->|"4 · 100 (stale)"| CB
    A ==>|"5 · partition heals: merge"| B
  • Examples: Cassandra and DynamoDB at default settings, CouchDB, Riak, DNS, CDNs, most caches.
  • Use when: a slightly stale answer is better than no answer — catalogue, recommendations, counters, carts, feeds.

items.title: "CA"
items.text:
A system that is consistent and available as long as there are no partitions — in practice, a single node, or a cluster that simply has not decided what to do in a partition. It is not a real third option for a distributed system.

CP AP During a partition Minority side refuses (errors, timeouts) Every node answers, maybe stale After the partition Minority catches up, nothing to reconcile Replicas converge; conflicts must be resolved Guarantee Linearizable Eventual (or causal at best) User-visible failure "Try again later" Wrong or outdated data, later corrected Examples etcd, ZooKeeper, Spanner, CockroachDB, PostgreSQL sync replication Cassandra, DynamoDB (defaults), DNS, CDN, caches BoxOffice data Seats, holds, orders, payments, auth sessions Catalogue, images, counters, recommendations

CP and AP describe a configuration, not a product

Most databases let you tune the trade-off — even per request. Cassandra with QUORUM reads and writes behaves much more like a CP system; PostgreSQL serving reads from an asynchronous replica returns stale data during a partition. Many real systems are, strictly, neither CP nor AP: they may be unavailable and return stale data in some failure modes2. Ask "how is it configured, and what do my requests see during a partition?" rather than "is this database CP or AP?".

items.title: PACELC: the trade-off you pay every day
items.text:
CAP only talks about partitions, which are rare. Daniel Abadi's PACELC (2010–2012)3 adds the trade-off that exists all the time:

If there is a Partition, choose between Availability and Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose between Latency and Consistency.

flowchart LR
    Q{"Is there a<br/>partition?"} -->|"yes · P"| PAC{"Availability<br/>or Consistency?"}
    PAC -->|A| PA["PA: answer, maybe stale"]
    PAC -->|C| PC["PC: refuse or wait"]
    Q -->|"no · E (else)"| ELC{"Latency<br/>or Consistency?"}
    ELC -->|L| EL["EL: answer before<br/>the replicas confirm"]
    ELC -->|C| EC["EC: wait for<br/>the replicas"]

The else branch exists because of replication itself: to be consistent, a write must wait for other replicas to acknowledge (one or more network round trips, maybe to another continent); to be fast, it must answer before they do and accept that a replica may lag.

items.title: How much latency does consistency cost?
items.text:
The answer is "a round trip to wherever the other replicas are". Round-trip times (RTT) below are typical orders of magnitude, used here as illustrative assumptions:

Where the confirming replicas are Typical RTT Cost of an EC write (one extra round trip) Same machine / same rack < 0.5 ms Negligible Another availability zone, same region ~1–2 ms Small: the standard for production databases Another region, same continent ~10–40 ms Noticeable on every write Another continent (e.g. São Paulo ↔ Europe) ~150–200 ms Dominates the request; a 5-write checkout costs a second

This table is why most systems choose EC inside a region (synchronous or quorum replication across zones costs a millisecond or two) and EL across regions (asynchronous replication, or partitioning data by home region).

System (typical configuration) During partition Else PACELC Cassandra, ScyllaDB (ONE) A L PA/EL DynamoDB (eventually consistent reads) A L PA/EL MongoDB (majority read/write concern) C C PC/EC PostgreSQL + synchronous standby C C PC/EC Spanner, CockroachDB C C PC/EC PostgreSQL + async read replicas, reads on replicas (failover may lose writes) L —/EL

items.title: Multi-region designs
items.text:
Regions fail — rarely, but entirely — and BoxOffice wants to survive that. The C/A/L trade-offs become concrete in five common topologies:

Topology Writes During a region loss Consistency Cost and complexity Single region, multi-AZ One primary, sync standby in another zone Region down = BoxOffice down Strong Lowest; the default starting point Active–passive (warm standby) Primary region only; async replica in region 2 Fail over (DNS) to region 2; lose the last seconds of writes (RPO > 0) Strong in normal operation Moderate; failover must be rehearsed Active–active, partitioned by home Each record has a home region; writes go there Records homed in the dead region are unavailable; others unaffected Strong per record Higher; routing by home region Active–active, everything everywhere Any region writes any record All regions keep writing Eventual; conflicts to resolve Highest; only for conflict-tolerant data Globally consistent database Consensus across regions (Spanner, CockroachDB) Survives a region if a majority of replicas remain Strong everywhere Write latency ≥ cross-region RTT; premium cost

Try it. In the multi-region scenario, run the load profile, then fail the primary region. Watch how long DNS takes to shift traffic (the TTL), how many requests fail during the switch, and what happens to writes that had not yet replicated. Then lower the DNS TTL and repeat.

Open the full playground

BoxOffice: the chosen design

  • Seats, holds, orders, payments — active–active partitioned by home region: each event's inventory lives in the region of its venue, in a PostgreSQL primary with a synchronous standby in another zone (PC/EC inside the region). A Lisbon fan buying a São Paulo show pays one transatlantic round trip on the hold — acceptable for a once-in-a-while action.
  • Catalogue, images, search index — replicated asynchronously to every region and cached at the CDN (PA/EL). A new event appears in Europe a few seconds later; nobody notices.
  • Accounts / auth — read-mostly; replicated everywhere, with writes (password change, logout everywhere) going to a home region.
  • Disaster recovery — each region's database ships backups and an async replica to another region (active–passive per region); the RPO/RTO targets are discussed in Reliability — disaster recovery.

In the interview

Never say "I'll pick CP" (or AP) for the whole system. Say it per data, and say what the user sees: "Seat inventory is CP: during a partition, the minority side returns 503 and the app says 'try again'; double booking is unacceptable. The catalogue is AP: it may be seconds stale." Then bring up PACELC — the interviewer usually cares more about everyday latency than about partitions: "inside a region I replicate synchronously across zones (~1–2 ms); across regions I partition by home region instead of paying 150 ms per write." Mentioning that CAP's C is linearizability (not ACID's C) is a cheap, strong signal.

Pitfalls

  • "We chose CA." If data lives on more than one machine, partitions will happen; "CA" only means nobody decided what happens then.
  • Treating CAP as a permanent label. The C/A choice only applies during a partition; the daily trade-off is latency (PACELC).
  • Forgetting caches and replicas. A cache in front of a CP store makes those reads AP; an async read replica makes them EL.
  • Cross-region synchronous replication by default. It makes every write pay an intercontinental round trip — and a degraded link makes the whole system slow.
  • Unrehearsed failover. Active–passive only works if failover (and failback) is tested; otherwise the passive region is a theory.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    REP["Replication<br/>(Replication & Consistency)"] --> Q{"partition?"}
    Q -->|yes| CA{"C or A"}
    Q -->|no| LC{"L or C"}
    CA -->|C| MAJ["majority side only<br/>→ Consensus & Quorums"]
    CA -->|A| MERGE["diverge, then merge<br/>LWW · CRDTs → Time & Clocks"]
    LC -->|C| SYNC["sync replication<br/>across zones"]
    LC -->|L| ASYNC["async replication,<br/>caches, CDN"]
    MAJ --> MR["multi-region design<br/>home region per event"]
    ASYNC --> MR
    MR --> DR["failover & DR<br/>→ Reliability"]

Palette components where the C/A/L choice is made: sql (sync standby or async replicas) · nosql (tunable quorums) · cache and cdn (always EL) · dns (failover between regions, scenario multi-region). Continues in: Consensus & Quorums, Reliability — disaster recovery, Traffic & Edge — DNS.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• CAP: during a network partition, a replicated store must choose between consistency (refuse) and availability (answer, maybe stale). P is not optional.
  • CAP's C is linearizability, not ACID's C; "CA" is not an option for distributed data.
  • PACELC: else (no partition) the choice is latency vs consistency — and you pay it on every request.
  • Choose per data domain: seats, money and identity CP/EC; catalogue and counters AP/EL.
  • In multi-region designs, partitioning data by home region keeps strong consistency local and limits the blast radius of a partition.

  1. GILBERT, S.; LYNCH, N. Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services. ACM SIGACT News, 2002. ↩

  2. KLEPPMANN, M. Please stop calling databases CP or AP, 2015. ↩

  3. ABADI, D. Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design. IEEE Computer, 2012. ↩

  4. BREWER, E. CAP Twelve Years Later: How the "Rules" Have Changed. IEEE Computer / InfoQ, 2012. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
At 10:00:03, three seconds into the on-sale, the machine running the PostgreSQL primary of inventory freezes. Its synchronous standby is healthy. Someone — or something — must decide that the old primary is dead, promote the standby, and make every inventory replica write to the new one. Now imagine the old primary was not dead, only paused for eight seconds by a storage hiccup: it wakes up, still believes it is the primary, and accepts a hold on seat A-12 that the new primary has already given to someone else. Two primaries at once is called split brain, and in a ticketing system it means double-sold seats.

Deciding "who is the primary now" is an instance of the consensus problem: getting a group of nodes to agree on a single value — despite lost and delayed messages and despite some nodes failing. Consensus is the foundation of leader election, distributed locks, replicated configuration (etcd behind every Kubernetes cluster), and of every strongly consistent replicated database.

items.title: Consensus and replicated state machines
items.text:
The most useful form of consensus is agreeing on a log: an ordered sequence of commands. If every node starts in the same state and applies the same commands in the same order, every node ends in the same state — a replicated state machine:

flowchart LR
    C([clients]) --> L
    subgraph L["leader"]
        LL["log: hold A-12 · hold B-3 · release A-12"] --> LS[("state")]
    end
    subgraph F1["follower 1"]
        F1L["same log"] --> F1S[("same state")]
    end
    subgraph F2["follower 2"]
        F2L["same log"] --> F2S[("same state")]
    end
    L -->|"replicate entries"| F1
    L -->|"replicate entries"| F2

A correct consensus algorithm guarantees:

Safety — "nothing bad happens" : All nodes that decide, decide the same value (the same log entry at each position), and that value was proposed by someone.

Liveness — "something good eventually happens" : Non-faulty nodes eventually decide.

items.title: Why it is hard: FLP
items.text: The FLP impossibility result (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985)1 proves that in a fully asynchronous system — no bound on message delay — no deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus if even one node may crash: some unlucky schedule of delays keeps it undecided forever. The way out, used by Paxos and Raft, is to never compromise safety and to guarantee progress only when the network behaves "well enough" (partial synchrony), using timeouts to suspect failures. A timeout can be wrong (the node was just slow), which is why the algorithms must remain safe even when suspicions are false.

items.title: Majorities: why clusters have 3 or 5 nodes
items.text:
The central trick is the majority quorum: a decision is valid only if more than half of the N nodes accept it. Any two majorities of the same cluster share at least one node — so two conflicting decisions can never both gather a majority: the shared node would have to vote for both, and the protocol forbids it.

Cluster size N Majority ⌊N/2⌋ + 1 Failures tolerated ⌊(N−1)/2⌋ 1 1 0 2 2 0 3 2 1 4 3 1 5 3 2 7 4 3

Use an odd number of nodes

Going from 3 to 4 nodes adds cost and one more machine that can fail, but tolerates no extra failure. A 2-node cluster is worse than one node: losing either node stops it. That is why etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul and Kafka controller quorums are sized 3 or 5 — and spread across 3 availability zones so that losing one zone leaves a majority.

What does the majority buy in availability? If each node is up with probability \(a\) (independently), the cluster is up when at least a majority is:

\[ A_{cluster}(N) = \sum_{k=\lfloor N/2 \rfloor + 1}^{N} \binom{N}{k}\, a^{k} (1-a)^{N-k} \] 2026-10-23T08:15:45.017479 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

With nodes at 99% each, one node gives 2 nines, two nodes give less (98.01% — both must be up), three nodes give ≈ 99.97% and five ≈ 99.999%. The independence assumption is optimistic — nodes in the same zone, on the same version, or overloaded by the same traffic fail together — which is why the nodes are spread over failure domains.

items.title: Split brain, and why the majority prevents it
items.text:
A partition splits a 5-node cluster 3/2. Only the side with 3 nodes can form a majority, elect a leader and commit writes; the side with 2 knows it is a minority and stops accepting writes:

flowchart LR
    subgraph maj ["Majority side (3 of 5)"]
        n1[node 1: leader] --- n2[node 2]
        n2 --- n3[node 3]
    end
    subgraph min ["Minority side (2 of 5)"]
        n4[node 4] --- n5[node 5]
    end
    n3 -.-|partition| n4
    maj -->|"can elect and commit"| ok([keeps selling seats])
    min -->|"cannot reach 3 votes"| ko([rejects writes: 503])

This is exactly the CP behaviour of CAP: the minority side is unavailable, so the system stays consistent.

items.title: Raft
items.text:
Raft (Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014)2 was designed to be understandable, and it is the consensus algorithm you are most likely to meet: etcd (Kubernetes), Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV, YugabyteDB and Kafka's KRaft controller all use it. It splits the problem into three parts:

  1. Leader election — exactly one leader per term; all writes go through it.
  2. Log replication — the leader appends commands to its log and replicates them to followers.
  3. Safety — an entry acknowledged by a majority (committed) is never lost or overwritten.

items.title: Roles and terms
items.text:
Each node is a follower, a candidate or the leader. Time is divided into terms numbered 1, 2, 3…, each starting with an election; a term has at most one leader. Terms act as a logical clock (Time & Clocks): any node that sees a message with a higher term than its own updates its term and steps down to follower — which is how a stale leader that wakes up after a pause discovers it has been replaced.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Follower
  Follower --> Candidate : election timeout (no heartbeat)
  Candidate --> Leader : votes from a majority
  Candidate --> Follower : sees a leader or a higher term
  Candidate --> Candidate : split vote, new timeout
  Leader --> Follower : sees a higher term

items.title: Leader election
items.text:
The leader sends periodic heartbeats (empty AppendEntries messages). A follower that hears nothing for an election timeout assumes the leader is dead, increments the term, votes for itself and asks the others for votes:

sequenceDiagram
  participant N1 as node 1 (follower)
  participant N2 as node 2 (follower)
  participant N3 as node 3 (old leader, frozen)
  Note over N1,N3: term 4: node 3 stops sending heartbeats
  N1->>N1: election timeout: term 5, candidate, votes for itself
  N1->>N2: RequestVote(term 5, last log index 812, term 4)
  N1->>N3: RequestVote(term 5, ...)
  N2-->>N1: vote granted (my log is not newer than yours)
  Note over N1: 2 of 3 votes: leader of term 5
  N1->>N2: AppendEntries(term 5, heartbeat)
  N1->>N3: AppendEntries(term 5, heartbeat)
  Note over N3: wakes up, sees term 5 > 4: steps down to follower

Three rules make it safe:

  • One vote per node per term — so at most one candidate can collect a majority in a term.
  • Election restriction — a node only votes for a candidate whose log is at least as up-to-date as its own. Since every committed entry is on a majority, and the winner needs votes from a majority, the new leader is guaranteed to hold every committed entry.
  • Randomised election timeouts (the paper suggests 150–300 ms) — if all followers timed out together they would split the votes forever; with random timeouts, one usually fires first and wins before the others start.

How long are writes unavailable when a leader dies? Roughly election timeout + one round of voting. etcd's defaults are a 100 ms heartbeat and a 1,000 ms election timeout3 (tuned up for cross-zone latency), so a crashed leader means about one to two seconds without writes — a number to remember when a client's timeout is shorter than that.

items.title: Log replication
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as inventory
  participant L as leader
  participant F1 as follower 1
  participant F2 as follower 2
  C->>L: hold A-12 for fan 42
  L->>L: append to log at index 813 (term 5)
  L->>F1: AppendEntries(index 813, prev = 812/term 4)
  L->>F2: AppendEntries(index 813, prev = 812/term 4)
  F1-->>L: OK (written to disk)
  Note over L: 2 of 3 have it: committed, apply to state
  L-->>C: OK, seat held
  F2-->>L: OK (later)
  L->>F1: next heartbeat carries commit index 813
  • The leader answers the client only after a majority (counting itself) has durably written the entry: committed entries survive the loss of any minority.
  • Each AppendEntries carries the index and term of the previous entry; a follower rejects it if its log does not match there, and the leader walks back until the logs agree, then overwrites the follower's uncommitted divergent suffix. This log matching keeps all logs identical up to the commit index.
  • Followers learn the commit index from later messages and apply entries to their own state machine.

Reads in Raft are not free either

A leader that answers reads from its local state might be a stale leader that has not yet noticed a newer term. Linearizable reads must confirm leadership — by a round of heartbeats to a majority (etcd's ReadIndex) or by a time-based leader lease, which depends on bounded clock drift. Serving reads from followers is faster but only eventually consistent, unless the follower first asks the leader for the current commit index.

Think first: a 5-node etcd cluster spread over 3 zones (2 + 2 + 1). Zone A, with 2 nodes, goes down. Can the cluster still accept writes? And if it were 3 + 1 + 1 and the 3-node zone failed?

In the first case, 3 nodes remain — a majority of 5 — so yes: a new leader is elected (if needed) and writes continue. In the second case only 2 nodes remain, which is not a majority of 5, so the cluster stops accepting writes, even though 2 machines are perfectly healthy. Placement matters as much as N: with 3 zones, spread as evenly as possible so that no single zone holds a majority.

items.title: Paxos, in one paragraph
items.text: Paxos (Lamport, 1989/1998; "Paxos Made Simple", 2001)4 is the original consensus algorithm with the same guarantees. Its single-decree form agrees on one value in two phases (prepare/promise, then accept/accepted) among proposers and acceptors with numbered ballots; production systems run Multi-Paxos — a stable leader skipping the first phase — which looks a lot like Raft. Paxos is proven and widely deployed (Google's Chubby and Spanner), but famously hard to implement; Raft's contribution was not new guarantees but a structure that engineers can follow. ZooKeeper uses a related protocol, ZAB (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast).

items.title: Quorums in leaderless stores: R + W > N
items.text:
Leaderless databases in the Dynamo family (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak) use quorums per request, without a leader. With N replicas of each key, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read queries R replicas and keeps the newest version:

Parameter Meaning N Number of replicas of each key W Replicas that must acknowledge a write R Replicas that must answer a read Overlap condition R + W > N — every read set intersects every write set

When R + W > N, at least one replica in any read set holds the latest acknowledged write. With N = 3:

Setting W R R + W > N? Behaviour write ONE, read ONE 1 1 No Fastest; reads may be stale; available with 2 nodes down write QUORUM, read QUORUM 2 2 Yes Reads see the latest acknowledged write; tolerates 1 node down write ALL, read ONE 3 1 Yes Fast reads, but one node down blocks every write write ONE, read ALL 1 3 Yes Fast writes, but one node down blocks every read

Three mechanisms make leaderless replicas converge: read repair (a read that sees an old version writes back the newest), hinted handoff (a write meant for a dead node is held by another and delivered later — a sloppy quorum that breaks the overlap guarantee meanwhile), and anti-entropy (background comparison of replicas using Merkle trees)5.

R + W > N is necessary, not sufficient

The overlap guarantees that a read contacts a replica with the latest write. It does not make the store linearizable: concurrent writes, a write that reached fewer than W replicas and was reported as failed (but stays on some), sloppy quorums and LWW with skewed clocks all produce anomalies. Quorum stores offer tunable consistency, not consensus. Use a consensus-based store when you need a single agreed order.

items.title: Leases, locks and fencing tokens
items.text:
A common use of consensus is a distributed lock or lease: "only one scheduler replica sends the 09:55 on-sale starts soon push". You take a lease from etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul with a time-to-live and renew it while you are alive. But a lock holder can pause — a long garbage collection, a VM migration — and keep working after its lease expired and someone else took it6:

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as worker A
    participant LK as lock service (etcd)
    participant B as worker B
    participant S as storage
    A->>LK: acquire lease
    LK-->>A: granted, fencing token 33
    Note over A: GC pause 15 s: lease expires
    B->>LK: acquire lease
    LK-->>B: granted, fencing token 34
    B->>S: write (token 34)
    S-->>B: OK, highest token seen = 34
    Note over A: wakes up, still thinks it holds the lock
    A->>S: write (token 33)
    S-->>A: rejected: 33 < 34

The fix is a fencing token: a number that increases with every grant (etcd's revision, ZooKeeper's zxid), sent with every write; the storage rejects any token lower than the highest it has seen. The same idea — a monotonically increasing epoch or term — protects the PostgreSQL failover of the opening story: the old primary, fenced off (its writes rejected, or its machine forcibly isolated — "STONITH", shoot the other node in the head), cannot corrupt the new one.

fenced-write.sql
-- The storage enforces the fence: a write carrying an old token changes nothing
UPDATE scheduled_jobs
   SET last_run_at = now(), fencing_token = :token
 WHERE job_id = 'onsale-reminder-42'
   AND fencing_token <= :token;     -- 0 rows updated → a newer token exists: we are a stale holder

items.title: In practice: use, don't build
items.text:
Tool What you use it for Consensus etcd Kubernetes state, leader election, config, locks Raft Apache ZooKeeper Coordination for older Hadoop/Kafka-era systems ZAB Consul Service discovery, KV config, locks Raft Kafka (KRaft) Cluster metadata and controller election; ZooKeeper mode removed in Kafka 4.0 Raft-based Patroni (for PostgreSQL) Automatic primary failover, with leader key in etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper Delegates to the DCS Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, TiDB SQL with consensus per data range Paxos (Spanner) / Raft

BoxOffice: who is the primary?

The inventory PostgreSQL runs under Patroni, with a 3-node etcd cluster spread across 3 availability zones. The primary holds a leader key in etcd with a TTL of ~30 s (Patroni's default), renewed every ~10 s. If it stops renewing — crash, freeze, network loss — the key expires, the healthiest synchronous standby takes it (an atomic compare-and-set in etcd: only one can win), promotes itself, and clients follow the new leader through the service endpoint. An old primary that wakes up finds it no longer holds the key and demotes itself (Patroni can also use a watchdog to reset the machine). The seat decision itself stays a plain UPDATE … WHERE status = 'FREE' on the single primary — consensus is used only to decide which node that is.

In the interview

Use consensus as a component, not a topic to re-derive. Say: "leader election and the cluster metadata go in etcd/ZooKeeper (Raft, 3 or 5 nodes across 3 zones); the data path stays on a single leader per shard." Know the numbers: N nodes tolerate ⌊(N−1)/2⌋ failures; a leader failover costs about an election timeout (~1 s in etcd defaults); every committed write pays a majority round trip. If you mention locks, mention fencing tokens — it is the follow-up question that separates candidates.

Pitfalls

  • Implementing Paxos or Raft yourself for an application. Use etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, or the database's own guarantees (a unique constraint, SELECT … FOR UPDATE, an advisory lock).
  • Putting bulk data through consensus. Every write goes through one leader and waits for a majority; consensus stores hold small, critical data (leaders, config, locks) — not the catalogue.
  • Even-sized clusters and bad placement: 4 nodes tolerate what 3 do; a zone that holds a majority is a single point of failure.
  • Locks without fencing: a paused process will eventually write after losing its lease.
  • Client timeouts shorter than a failover: a 500 ms client timeout against a store that needs ~1–2 s to elect a leader turns every failover into a burst of errors (and retries).

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    MAJ["majority quorums<br/>no split brain"] --> RAFT["Raft / Paxos<br/>replicated log"]
    RAFT --> ETCD["etcd · ZooKeeper · KRaft"]
    ETCD --> LE["leader election<br/>(DB failover, scheduler)"]
    ETCD --> LOCK["leases & locks"]
    LOCK --> FT["fencing tokens"]
    RAFT --> NEWSQL["Spanner · CockroachDB<br/>(consensus per range)"]
    NEWSQL --> TX2["2PC over consensus groups<br/>→ Distributed Transactions"]
    Q["R + W > N<br/>leaderless quorums"] --> TUNE["tunable consistency<br/>(Cassandra, Dynamo)"]
    TERMS["terms / epochs"] --> FT
    TERMS -.-> CLK["logical clocks<br/>→ Time & Clocks"]

Palette components that rely on consensus: kafka (KRaft controller, partition leaders) · sql (Patroni + etcd failover) · nosql (quorums) · scheduler (one leader runs the jobs). Continues in: Distributed Transactions, Cloud-native — Kubernetes (etcd), Compute — async work (scheduler leader election).

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Consensus makes nodes agree on one value — in practice, one log — despite failures; it underlies leader election, locks, configuration and strongly consistent databases.
  • FLP: no deterministic algorithm always terminates in an asynchronous system; Paxos and Raft are always safe and use timeouts for liveness.
  • Majorities overlap: N nodes tolerate ⌊(N−1)/2⌋ crashes; use 3 or 5, spread so no zone holds a majority; the minority side of a partition stops (no split brain).
  • Raft: terms, randomised election timeouts, one vote per term, election restriction, commit after a majority writes.
  • Leaderless quorums need R + W > N for overlap, but give tunable consistency, not linearizability.
  • Leases need fencing tokens; and above all: use a proven coordination service, don't build one.

  1. FISCHER, M.; LYNCH, N.; PATERSON, M. Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process. Journal of the ACM, 1985. ↩

  2. ONGARO, D.; OUSTERHOUT, J. In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm. USENIX ATC, 2014. Interactive visualisation: raft.github.io. ↩

  3. ETCD. Tuning — heartbeat interval and election timeout. ↩

  4. LAMPORT, L. Paxos Made Simple. ACM SIGACT News, 2001. ↩

  5. DECANDIA, G. et al. Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store. SOSP, 2007. ↩

  6. KLEPPMANN, M. How to do distributed locking, 2016. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
A fan pays for two tickets at 10:00:41. The confirmation screen says "Order 981 confirmed". She taps My tickets — and the list is empty. In a panic she buys again. Nothing was lost and nothing was buggy in the usual sense: the payment was written to the PostgreSQL primary, while My tickets was served by a read replica that had not yet received the write. BoxOffice had silently chosen a consistency model, and it was the wrong one for that screen.

This page explains how data is copied between nodes (replication) and what a reader is allowed to see while the copies disagree (consistency models). The two are inseparable: the replication design decides which consistency models are cheap, which are expensive and which are impossible.

items.title: Why replicate?
items.text:
Keeping a copy of the same data on several nodes serves three different goals, and it helps to say which one you want:

Goal How replication helps BoxOffice Availability / durability If one node dies, another has the data The inventory database survives the loss of a machine or a zone Read throughput Reads are spread over many copies The event catalogue is read ~100× more than it is written (illustrative ratio) Latency A copy close to the user answers faster A catalogue copy in a European region for fans in Lisbon

All three are easy if the data never changes. The difficulty is entirely in handling changes: each write must reach every copy, and while it travels, the copies disagree.

items.title: Replication models
items.text: There are three families, distinguished by who accepts writes1.

items.title: Single-leader (primary–replica)
items.text:
One node, the leader (primary), accepts all writes and streams a log of changes to the followers (replicas). Reads can go to the leader or to followers. This is the default in PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis and Kafka (one leader per partition).

flowchart LR
    w([order: write]) -->|"INSERT order 981"| L[("leader<br/>(primary)")]
    L -->|"WAL stream"| F1[("follower 1")]
    L -->|"WAL stream"| F2[("follower 2")]
    r1([My tickets: read]) -->|"SELECT"| F1
    r2([catalogue: read]) -->|"SELECT"| F2

items.title: Multi-leader
items.text: Several nodes accept writes — typically one leader per data centre or region — and replicate to each other asynchronously. Writes are fast and local everywhere, but two leaders can accept conflicting writes to the same record, which must be resolved later. Typical uses: multi-region deployments, offline-first apps (each phone is a "leader"), collaborative editing.

items.title: Leaderless
items.text:
Any replica accepts reads and writes. The client (or a coordinator) sends each write to several replicas and each read to several replicas, and quorums decide what counts as success (R + W > N, see Consensus & Quorums). This is the design of Amazon's Dynamo paper2, Cassandra and ScyllaDB.

Single-leader Multi-leader Leaderless Who accepts writes One leader One leader per region/site Any replica Write conflicts None (the leader orders writes) Yes — must be resolved Yes — must be resolved Write latency Round trip to the leader (maybe far away) Local Round trip to W replicas Leader failure Failover needed (seconds) Other leaders continue No leader to lose Strong consistency possible? Yes (read from leader, sync replication) Not across leaders Only approximately (quorums) Typical systems PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Kafka partitions Multi-region MySQL/Postgres setups, CouchDB, Active-Active Redis Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak, DynamoDB (internally) BoxOffice use inventory, order, payment — (avoid for seats!) Fan activity, view counters

items.title: Synchronous or asynchronous?
items.text:
Independently of who leads, the leader must decide when to tell the client "OK":

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as order
    participant L as leader
    participant F1 as follower 1 (sync)
    participant F2 as follower 2 (async)
    C->>L: INSERT order 981
    L->>F1: replicate
    L->>F2: replicate
    F1-->>L: written to disk
    L-->>C: OK (after 1 sync follower)
    Note over F2: still applying...<br/>a read here is stale
    F2-->>L: written (later)
Mode Client gets OK when… If the leader dies right after OK Write latency Availability of writes Asynchronous the leader wrote locally Recent writes may be lost Lowest High: followers can be down Synchronous (all) every follower wrote Nothing lost Slowest follower decides Low: any follower down blocks writes Semi-synchronous the leader + k followers wrote Nothing lost if a sync follower is promoted One extra round trip Good: tolerates other followers down Quorum (consensus) a majority wrote Nothing lost Median of the fastest majority Tolerates a minority down

PostgreSQL exposes this choice in synchronous_commit and synchronous_standby_names (for example ANY 1 (replica_a, replica_b) — semi-synchronous with one of two). In practice, "fully synchronous" is rare: one slow follower would stall every write. Semi-synchronous or quorum replication is the usual compromise.

items.title: Replication lag
items.text:
With asynchronous followers, the delay between a write on the leader and its visibility on a follower is the replication lag. On a healthy system it is usually milliseconds; under heavy write load, during a long transaction or after a network hiccup, it can grow to seconds or minutes. The time between a write and a following read decides whether that read is stale:

2026-10-23T08:15:45.135408 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

With an (assumed) exponential lag, the same screen that is almost never stale on a quiet day is stale for about 69% of fans who open it 300 ms after paying during the on-sale, when the mean lag grows to 800 ms. The bug of the opening story is not rare under load — it is the expected behaviour.

Try it. Load the db-replicas scenario, run the load profile and watch the replica lag metric. Then raise the write rate (or switch to spike) and see the lag — and the fraction of stale reads — grow. Finally route the reads to the primary and compare the primary's CPU and p99.

Open the full playground

items.title: Consistency models: a contract
items.text:
A consistency model is a contract between a data store and its programmers: if you follow these rules, the results of reads will be predictable in this way3. Stronger models are easier to program against and cost more coordination (latency, availability); weaker models are cheaper and push the complexity into the application.

flowchart TD
    LIN["Linearizable<br/>(strong consistency)"] --> SEQ["Sequential"]
    SEQ --> CAU["Causal"]
    CAU --> RYW["Read-your-writes"]
    CAU --> MR["Monotonic reads"]
    CAU --> CP["Consistent prefix"]
    RYW --> EV["Eventual"]
    MR --> EV
    CP --> EV

An arrow from A to B means "A guarantees everything B guarantees, and more". The three middle-row models are session guarantees: they hold for one client's session, not for everyone.

items.title: Linearizability (strong consistency)
items.text:
Linearizability makes a replicated system behave as if there were a single copy of the data, and every operation took effect atomically at one instant between its start and its end4. Once any read has returned a new value, every later read (by anyone, on any replica) must return that value or a newer one.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Fan A
    participant N1 as replica 1
    participant N2 as replica 2
    participant B as Fan B
    A->>N1: hold seat A-12
    N1-->>A: OK (hold committed)
    Note over A,B: the write has completed
    B->>N2: is seat A-12 free?
    N2-->>B: yes, FREE (stale)
    Note over N2,B: violates linearizability:<br/>B started after A's write finished
    B->>N2: hold seat A-12
    Note over N2: double booking if N2 accepts

Linearizability is what you need when correctness depends on one up-to-date answer:

  • uniqueness and inventory — a seat, a username, the last unit of stock;
  • leader election and locks — only one node may believe it is the leader;
  • cross-channel timing — a fan pays, then the notification service (reading elsewhere) must see the paid order.

It is obtained by routing all reads and writes for a key through one leader that is itself elected by consensus (with care about stale leaders), or by consensus on every operation. Its price: every operation pays at least one round trip to the leader or to a majority, and nodes that cannot reach the leader/majority must refuse — the C-or-A choice of CAP.

Serializable is not linearizable

Serializability is an isolation guarantee for transactions over many objects (the result equals some serial order of the transactions). Linearizability is a recency guarantee for single objects (reads see the latest write in real time). A database can offer one, both ("strict serializability", as in Spanner) or neither. Isolation levels are covered in Databases — transactions.

items.title: Sequential consistency
items.text: All nodes see all operations in the same order, and each node's operations appear in its program order — but that order need not respect real time. A read may return a value that is "old" in wall-clock terms, as long as everyone agrees on the sequence. It is mainly a hardware-memory and theory concept; in system design you rarely choose it explicitly.

items.title: Causal consistency
items.text:
Operations that are causally related — one could have influenced the other — are seen by everyone in that order; concurrent operations may be seen in different orders by different nodes.

The classic example is a conversation: if Ana posts "Is the 10:00 sale delayed?" and the organiser replies "No, it starts on time", nobody may see the reply without the question. In BoxOffice: a SeatReleased event caused by a HoldExpired event must not be applied before it.

Causal consistency is interesting because it is the strongest model that remains available during a network partition5: nodes can keep accepting reads and writes on both sides and still respect causality. It is tracked with logical clocks — see Time & Clocks.

items.title: Session guarantees
items.text:
Most "my data disappeared" bugs are violations of one of these four guarantees, defined for a single client session (Terry et al., Bayou project)6:

Guarantee Promise Violation in BoxOffice Read-your-writes After you write, your reads see that write The opening story: you paid, My tickets is empty Monotonic reads You never see the data go back in time Remaining seats shows 120, then 340, then 95 as you hit different replicas Monotonic writes Your writes are applied in the order you made them "Change e-mail" then "send ticket" — the ticket goes to the old address Writes-follow-reads (causal) A write you make after reading X is ordered after X You reply to a support message that other replicas have not received yet 
sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fan's app
    participant R1 as replica 1 (lag 10 ms)
    participant R2 as replica 2 (lag 2 s)
    F->>R1: GET /events/42/availability
    R1-->>F: 95 seats left
    F->>R2: refresh (load balancer picks R2)
    R2-->>F: 340 seats left
    Note over F: the count went back in time:<br/>monotonic reads violated

How to provide them on top of asynchronous replicas:

  • Read from the leader after a write: for a short window (e.g. 1–5 s) after the fan writes, route her reads to the primary — or always read data the user owns (My tickets) from the primary.
  • Version tokens: the write returns the leader's log position (in PostgreSQL, the WAL LSN — Log Sequence Number); the client sends it with the next read, and a replica only answers once it has applied at least that position (otherwise it waits or forwards to the leader). Many databases expose this as causal sessions or read-after-write tokens (MongoDB causal consistency sessions, Cosmos DB session consistency).
  • Sticky replica: pin each session to one replica (hash of the session id) — gives monotonic reads, not read-your-writes.

items.title: Eventual consistency
items.text:
Eventual consistency only promises that if writes stop, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value. It says nothing about when, and nothing about what you read meanwhile. It is the guarantee of DNS, of most caches and CDNs, of asynchronous replicas, and of leaderless stores at low quorum settings.

It is perfectly fine for many domains — the event description, the poster image, the "312 people are looking at this event" counter. The hard part is what happens when replicas accepted concurrent writes to the same item and must converge:

Strategy How Trade-off Last-write-wins (LWW) Keep the write with the highest timestamp Simple; silently drops concurrent writes and depends on clocks that drift (Time & Clocks) Version vectors / siblings Detect concurrent versions, keep all, let the application merge No silent loss; the application must write merge logic (Dynamo's shopping cart merged by union) CRDTs Data types whose merge is commutative, associative and idempotent Automatic, provably convergent; only for data that fits a CRDT (counters, sets, registers, text) Avoid conflicts Route all writes for a key to one leader (a "home" region) No conflicts at all; that key's writes pay the latency to its home

A CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type)7 is designed so that replicas can exchange state in any order, any number of times, and still end up equal. The simplest is the grow-only counter: each replica increments only its own slot, and merge takes the element-wise maximum.

GCounter.java
// Grow-only counter CRDT: e.g. "fans interested in event 42", counted in 3 regions
class GCounter {
    private final long[] counts;   // one slot per replica
    private final int me;          // this replica's index

    GCounter(int replicas, int me) { this.counts = new long[replicas]; this.me = me; }

    void increment() { counts[me]++; }

    long value() { return java.util.Arrays.stream(counts).sum(); }

    // merge = element-wise max: commutative, associative, idempotent
    void merge(GCounter other) {
        for (int i = 0; i < counts.length; i++)
            counts[i] = Math.max(counts[i], other.counts[i]);
    }
}

If São Paulo counted [3, 0, 0] and Lisbon [0, 2, 0], both merge to [3, 2, 0] and report 5 — no increment lost, no coordination needed. A single shared number with LWW would report 3 or 2.

items.title: The spectrum at a glance
items.text:
Model Guarantee Coordination cost Available during a partition? Typical implementation Linearizable Single-copy, real-time recency Highest: leader or majority round trip per operation No (minority side must refuse) Raft/Paxos-based stores (etcd, Spanner, CockroachDB), single leader with reads at the leader Sequential One global order for all High No Mostly theory / hardware memory models Causal Cause before effect, for everyone Medium: track dependencies Yes Logical/vector clocks, causal sessions Read-your-writes, monotonic reads Per-session sanity Low: route or wait per session Yes, if the session stays on its side Leader reads after write, LSN tokens, sticky replicas Eventual Converge if writes stop Lowest Yes Async replication, caches, DNS, leaderless at ONE

BoxOffice: one consistency model per data domain

Data Model Why How Seat status and holds Linearizable Two fans must never hold the same seat Single PostgreSQL primary per event; conditional UPDATE/SELECT … FOR UPDATE Payments Linearizable + idempotent A double charge is unacceptable Primary only; idempotency key forwarded to the provider My tickets, My orders Read-your-writes The fan must see what she just bought Read from the primary for the fan's own data, or LSN token Remaining-seats counter on the event page Monotonic reads (eventual is tolerable) It may lag, but must not jump backwards Sticky replica or cache with a short TTL Event catalogue, images, descriptions Eventual Seconds of staleness hurt nobody Replicas, cache, CDN "Fans interested" counters, analytics Eventual (CRDT) Approximate is fine, availability matters Per-region counters merged

The design principle: strong where money or uniqueness is at stake, weak everywhere else — because strong consistency is paid on every request.

In the interview

When the interviewer says "and the user should see their update immediately", translate it into a model: "that's read-your-writes, not global strong consistency — I'll read the user's own data from the leader, or pass the write's log position as a token." Then name the one place that does need linearizability (inventory, balances, uniqueness) and explain how you get it (single leader + consensus-based failover, conditional writes). Interviewers reward precise vocabulary and a per-domain choice; they penalise "everything is strongly consistent" (slow, expensive) and "everything is eventually consistent" (double bookings).

Pitfalls

  • Read/write split by default: sending all reads to replicas breaks read-your-writes on the first screen after a write.
  • Caches are replicas too: putting Redis or a CDN in front of a linearizable store makes those reads eventually consistent (Caching).
  • Load balancers break session guarantees: two consecutive reads may hit two different replicas with different lag.
  • Async replication + automatic failover = lost writes: the promoted follower may not have the last acknowledged writes. Use semi-synchronous replication for data you cannot lose.
  • Confusing "eventual" with "soon": eventual consistency has no time bound; under load the lag can reach minutes. Monitor replication lag and alert on it.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    W["write on the leader"] --> REPL{"replication<br/>sync or async?"}
    REPL -->|"sync / quorum"| LIN["linearizable reads"]
    LIN --> COST["pays latency and availability<br/>→ CAP & PACELC"]
    REPL -->|"async: lag"| STALE["stale reads"]
    STALE --> SG["session guarantees<br/>read-your-writes, monotonic reads"]
    W2["writes on several leaders"] --> CONF["concurrent writes"]
    CONF --> RES["LWW · version vectors · CRDTs<br/>→ Time & Clocks"]
    LIN --> CONS["leader chosen by consensus<br/>→ Consensus & Quorums"]

Palette components that are replicas (and therefore have a consistency model): sql (primary + read replicas, scenario db-replicas) · nosql (leaderless, scenario sharding) · cache (scenario read-heavy-cache) · cdn (scenario cdn-static) · stream (replicated partitions). Builds on: failure models. Continues in: CAP & PACELC, Databases — replication, Caching — invalidation.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Replication serves availability, read throughput and latency; all the difficulty is in propagating writes.
  • Single-leader avoids write conflicts; multi-leader and leaderless accept writes everywhere and must resolve conflicts (LWW, version vectors, CRDTs, or avoid them with a home leader).
  • Synchronous vs asynchronous replication trades write latency and availability for durability on failover; semi-synchronous or quorum is the usual compromise.
  • Consistency models range from linearizable (single-copy illusion) through causal and session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads) to eventual.
  • Choose per data domain: linearizable for seats and money, read-your-writes for a user's own data, eventual for the catalogue and counters.

  2. DECANDIA, G. et al. Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store. SOSP, 2007. ↩

  3. Consistency Models — Jepsen (Kyle Kingsbury), a clickable map of the models and their relationships. ↩
