items.title: Index
items.text:
Seat A-12 is held by Bruno. At 10:00:00.040 (real time) he gives up and releases it through inventory-1; twenty milliseconds later, at 10:00:00.060, Carla grabs it through inventory-2. Both updates replicate to the other nodes, and the store resolves the conflict with the most common rule there is — last write wins by timestamp. But inventory-1's clock runs 50 ms ahead: Bruno's release is stamped 10:00:00.090, Carla's hold 10:00:00.060. The release "wins", the seat shows as FREE, and Carla — who has already been charged — has no seat. No message was lost and no code had a bug: the system simply trusted two clocks that disagreed.

A distributed system has no global clock. Every machine has its own, they drift apart, and the network delay between them is variable and unknown — so "which happened first?" has no free answer. This page shows what physical clocks can and cannot do, and the tools that order events without trusting them: logical clocks, vector clocks, hybrid clocks, TrueTime, and plain single authorities.

items.title: Two clocks in every machine
items.text:
Every operating system offers two different clocks, and mixing them up is a classic bug:

Time-of-day (wall) clock Monotonic clock Answers "What date and time is it?" "How much time has passed?" Java System.currentTimeMillis(), Instant.now() System.nanoTime() Linux CLOCK_REALTIME CLOCK_MONOTONIC Can jump? Yes — NTP steps it, an admin changes it, leap seconds Never goes backwards Comparable across machines? Roughly (within the sync error) No — its zero is arbitrary per machine Use for Timestamps shown to people, dates, expiry deadlines stored in a database Timeouts, durations, rate limiting, latency metrics Durations.java
// Wrong: if NTP steps the wall clock during the call, the "duration" can be negative or huge
long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
callPaymentProvider();
long elapsedMs = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;

// Right: the monotonic clock only measures elapsed time, and never goes backwards
long t0 = System.nanoTime();
callPaymentProvider();
long elapsedNs = System.nanoTime() - t0;

items.title: Physical clocks drift
items.text:
A computer's clock is a quartz oscillator, and quartz is imperfect: its frequency depends on temperature and on the crystal. Drift is measured in ppm (parts per million): 20 ppm means 20 µs gained or lost per second — about 1.7 seconds per day. Google assumes a bound of 200 ppm for its servers1. Left alone, two machines' clocks diverge without limit.

NTP (Network Time Protocol) corrects this by periodically asking time servers (organised in strata, stratum 0 being atomic or GPS clocks) and adjusting the local clock — gradually (slewing) for small offsets, by a jump (stepping) for large ones. Its accuracy is limited by the network delay it cannot measure exactly: NTP assumes the request and the response took equally long, so asymmetric delays become clock error.

2026-10-23T08:15:45.589739 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The synchronised servers stay within a couple of milliseconds of each other (a sawtooth: drift, correct, drift); the one that lost NTP silently walks away — 24 ms after ten minutes at 40 ppm, and over three seconds after a day. Nothing alerts by default. Typical orders of magnitude (illustrative, they depend heavily on the setup):

Synchronisation Typical accuracy Notes None (free-running quartz) Seconds per day Never acceptable for servers NTP over the public internet Milliseconds to tens of ms Asymmetric routes add error NTP inside a data centre / cloud time service Sub-millisecond to ~1 ms E.g. Amazon Time Sync Service, Google's internal NTP PTP (Precision Time Protocol, IEEE 1588) with hardware timestamps Microseconds Needs NIC/switch support; offered on some cloud instances GPS + atomic clocks per data centre (Google TrueTime) ε of a few ms, with a known bound See TrueTime

Leap seconds and smearing

Every few years a leap second was added to UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), and naïve clocks either repeated a second or jumped — crashing software in 2012. Google, AWS and others now smear it: they slow their clocks slightly over ~24 hours so no second is repeated. In 2022 the General Conference on Weights and Measures decided to stop adding leap seconds by 20352. Lesson: even "what time is it" has operational edge cases.

items.title: Why timestamps cannot order events
items.text:
The opening story, step by step. Each node stamps its write with its own wall clock; replication delivers both writes to both nodes; last-write-wins (LWW) keeps the higher timestamp:

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Bruno
    participant I1 as inventory-1 (clock +50 ms)
    participant I2 as inventory-2 (clock accurate)
    participant C as Carla
    B->>I1: release A-12 (real time .040)
    Note over I1: stamped .090
    C->>I2: hold A-12 (real time .060)
    Note over I2: stamped .060
    I1->>I2: replicate release @ .090
    I2->>I1: replicate hold @ .060
    Note over I1,I2: LWW: .090 > .060, the release wins<br/>Carla's hold is silently discarded

With clocks synchronised to within ε, two events less than ε apart cannot be ordered by their timestamps — and in an LWW store, the node with the fastest clock wins every conflict. Cassandra uses LWW per column by default, and so does any "updated_at wins" merge logic you write yourself. LWW is acceptable when losing one of two concurrent writes is harmless (a profile picture); it is dangerous for seats and money.

The way out is to stop asking clocks when something happened and ask instead what could have influenced what.

items.title: Lamport clocks
items.text:
Leslie Lamport's 1978 paper3 — one of the most cited in computer science — observed that what matters is the happened-before relation (→):

  • if a and b happen in the same process and a comes first, then a → b;
  • if a is the sending of a message and b its receipt, then a → b;
  • if a → b and b → c, then a → c (transitivity).

If neither a → b nor b → a, the events are concurrent (a ∥ b): neither could have influenced the other.

A Lamport clock is a counter per process with three rules:

  1. Before each local event, increment the counter.
  2. When sending a message, attach the counter.
  3. When receiving a message carrying t, set the counter to max(local, t) + 1.
sequenceDiagram
    participant O as order
    participant K as Kafka consumer (inventory)
    participant N as notification
    Note over O: create order 981 (L=1)
    O->>K: OrderPaid (L=2)
    Note over K: receive: max(0, 2) + 1 = 3
    Note over N: unrelated local event (L=1)
    K->>N: TicketIssued (L=4)
    Note over N: receive: max(1, 4) + 1 = 5

The guarantee is one-directional: if a → b then L(a) < L(b). The converse does not hold — L(a) < L(b) does not prove that a happened before b; they may be concurrent. Breaking ties by node id gives a total order consistent with causality, which is enough for many algorithms (Raft's term is a Lamport-style counter). What a Lamport clock cannot do is detect concurrency.

items.title: Vector clocks
items.text:
A vector clock keeps one counter per node. Each node increments its own entry on a local event, attaches the whole vector to messages, and on receipt takes the element-wise maximum (then increments its own entry). Comparing two vectors answers the question Lamport clocks cannot:

  • V(a) ≤ V(b) element-wise (and different) → a → b;
  • V(b) ≤ V(a) → b → a;
  • neither → concurrent: a real conflict that needs resolution.

Three replicas of Carla's cart ([SP, LIS, NYC] counters):

Step Replica Operation Vector Relation 1 SP add ticket for event 42 [1, 0, 0] — 2 LIS receives step 1, adds parking pass [1, 1, 0] step 1 → step 2 3 NYC receives step 1, removes the ticket [1, 0, 1] step 1 → step 3 4 compare step 2 vs step 3 [1,1,0] vs [1,0,1] concurrent: neither ≤ the other

The store keeps both versions (siblings) and asks the application to merge them — exactly what Amazon's Dynamo did for the shopping cart (merge by union, which is why deleted items occasionally came back)4. Riak exposed the same model.

sequenceDiagram
    participant SP as replica SP
    participant LIS as replica LIS
    participant NYC as replica NYC
    Note over SP: add ticket [1,0,0]
    SP->>LIS: replicate [1,0,0]
    SP->>NYC: replicate [1,0,0]
    Note over LIS: add parking [1,1,0]
    Note over NYC: remove ticket [1,0,1]
    LIS->>NYC: replicate [1,1,0]
    Note over NYC: [1,1,0] vs [1,0,1]: concurrent<br/>keep both, merge in the application

The cost is size: the vector grows with the number of nodes (or clients) that write. Practical systems use version vectors with one entry per replica (not per client) and prune old entries.

items.title: Hybrid logical clocks
items.text:
Logical clocks capture causality but have nothing to do with real time — you cannot ask "what was the state at 10:00:00?". Physical clocks are close to real time but do not capture causality. A hybrid logical clock (HLC, Kulkarni et al., 2014)5 combines both into one fixed-size timestamp (l, c):

  • l is the largest physical time the node has seen (its own clock or any message's);
  • c is a logical counter that breaks ties when l does not advance.
hlc.py
import time

class HLC:
    def __init__(self):
        self.l, self.c = 0, 0                 # (physical part in ms, logical counter)

    def now(self):                             # local event or send
        pt = int(time.time() * 1000)
        if pt > self.l:
            self.l, self.c = pt, 0
        else:
            self.c += 1                        # wall clock did not advance: count
        return (self.l, self.c)

    def update(self, ml, mc):                  # on receiving a message stamped (ml, mc)
        pt = int(time.time() * 1000)
        new_l = max(self.l, ml, pt)
        if new_l == self.l == ml:
            self.c = max(self.c, mc) + 1
        elif new_l == self.l:
            self.c += 1
        elif new_l == ml:
            self.c = mc + 1
        else:
            self.c = 0
        self.l = new_l
        return (self.l, self.c)

HLC timestamps respect causality (like Lamport clocks), stay within the clock-sync error of real time (so they can be used for "read as of 10:00:00" snapshots), and fit in 64 bits. CockroachDB, YugabyteDB and MongoDB (cluster time) use them. They still rely on a bound on clock skew: CockroachDB, for example, has a configured maximum offset (500 ms by default) and a node that detects it is further off than that shuts itself down rather than risk inconsistency6.

items.title: TrueTime and Spanner
items.text:
Google's Spanner1 took the opposite route: instead of avoiding physical time, make it trustworthy. Each data centre has GPS receivers and atomic clocks, and the TrueTime API does not return a time but an interval: TT.now() = [earliest, latest], guaranteed to contain the true time, with an uncertainty ε that the paper reports as typically 1–7 ms.

To make transactions externally consistent (if T1 commits before T2 starts, T2's timestamp is larger), Spanner uses commit wait: it picks the commit timestamp s = TT.now().latest and then waits until TT.now().earliest > s before making the commit visible — i.e. until s is guaranteed to be in the past everywhere.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as client
    participant S as Spanner leader
    participant TT as TrueTime
    C->>S: commit T1
    S->>TT: now()
    TT-->>S: [10:00:00.100, 10:00:00.106]
    Note over S: s = .106 (latest), replicate via Paxos meanwhile
    S->>TT: now() until earliest > .106
    TT-->>S: [10:00:00.107, 10:00:00.113]
    S-->>C: committed at s = .106
    Note over C,S: any later transaction gets s' > .106

The cost of correctness is literally waiting out the uncertainty (on average ~2ε per commit, overlapped with the Paxos replication). Smaller ε means faster commits, which is why Google invests in clocks. AWS later published a similar open-source API, ClockBound, that returns error bounds on EC2 instances.

items.title: Ordering in practice
items.text:
Most systems never implement vector clocks or TrueTime. They get order from simpler sources — and it is worth knowing what each one guarantees:

Technique What it orders Guarantee Typical use Single authority (one DB primary, now() and sequences on it) Everything that goes through it Total order, one clock Seat holds, order numbers, hold expiry Kafka partition offsets Messages within one partition Total order per partition (per key) All events of one BoxOffice event in one partition Lamport / Raft terms Causally related events Causal → smaller number Leader epochs, fencing tokens Vector / version vectors Versions of one item Detects concurrency Leaderless stores, sync/offline apps HLC All events in a cluster Causal + close to real time CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, MongoDB TrueTime All transactions globally External consistency Spanner Time-ordered IDs (Snowflake, UUIDv7, ULID) IDs by creation time, roughly Sortable, unique; not causal across machines Primary keys, log/event ids

A Snowflake ID (Twitter, 2010) packs a 64-bit integer with a 41-bit millisecond timestamp, a 10-bit machine id and a 12-bit per-millisecond sequence — up to 4,096 ids per millisecond per machine, unique without coordination, and roughly sortable by time. UUIDv7 (RFC 9562, 2024)7 standardises the same idea in a 128-bit UUID with a 48-bit Unix-millisecond prefix: B-tree indexes stay compact because new keys are appended at the end instead of scattered like random UUIDv4.

Snowflake.java
// 64-bit id: 41 bits of ms since a custom epoch | 10 bits machine id | 12 bits sequence
final class Snowflake {
    private static final long EPOCH = 1735689600000L;   // 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z
    private final long machineId;                         // 0..1023, assigned per instance
    private long lastMs = -1, seq = 0;

    Snowflake(long machineId) { this.machineId = machineId; }

    synchronized long next() {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        if (now < lastMs) now = lastMs;                   // clock stepped back: do not go backwards
        if (now == lastMs) {
            seq = (seq + 1) & 0xFFF;                      // 4096 ids per ms
            if (seq == 0) while ((now = System.currentTimeMillis()) <= lastMs) { }  // wait next ms
        } else {
            seq = 0;
        }
        lastMs = now;
        return ((now - EPOCH) << 22) | (machineId << 12) | seq;
    }
}
Think first: two orders get Snowflake ids 7.31e17 and 7.29e17 from two different order replicas. Can you conclude which order was placed first?

Only approximately. The ids embed each machine's wall clock, so with clocks synchronised to within a few milliseconds, ids generated more than that apart are correctly ordered — but two orders a millisecond apart on different machines can come out in either order. Time-ordered ids are great for index locality and "roughly newest first" listings; they are not a source of causal or total order across machines. If the order matters (who got the last seat), let a single authority decide — the inventory primary's conditional UPDATE.

BoxOffice: where time and order come from

  • Who got seat A-12 — decided by the single inventory primary for that event (conditional UPDATE); no timestamps compared at all.
  • Hold expiry — expires_at = now() + interval '10 minutes' computed by PostgreSQL on the primary, and the sweeper compares against the same database's now(): one clock, so skew between app servers is irrelevant.
  • Event ordering — every event about one show (SeatHeld, SeatReleased, OrderPaid) is published with Kafka key = eventId, so they land in one partition and every consumer sees them in the same order.
  • Ids — orders and tickets use UUIDv7: unique without coordination, index-friendly, roughly time-sortable — never used to decide who was first.
  • Durations and timeouts — measured with the monotonic clock (System.nanoTime()), never with wall-clock differences.
  • Monitoring — an alert on NTP offset per node (e.g. > 50 ms), because a machine that lost NTP is silent otherwise.

In the interview

When a design compares timestamps from different machines ("the latest update wins", "sort the chat messages by created_at"), say it out loud: "clocks drift, so timestamps from different servers can't order events less than the skew apart." Then offer the fix that fits: a single authority (sequence or conditional write on one leader), a per-key ordered log (Kafka partition by key), a logical/version counter (optimistic concurrency with a version column), or an HLC-based database if you need global order. For "design a unique ID generator", Snowflake / UUIDv7 with their bit layouts is the expected answer (Alex Xu, vol. 1, ch. 7)8.

Pitfalls

  • Measuring durations with the wall clock — negative or huge latencies when NTP steps the clock; use the monotonic clock.
  • LWW on data where both writes matter — silent data loss, biased towards the node with the fastest clock.
  • Expiry computed on one machine and checked on another — a 10-minute hold may expire early or late by the skew; compute and compare on the same clock (the database's).
  • Assuming time-ordered ids are causally ordered — Snowflake/UUIDv7 order is only as good as clock sync.
  • Not monitoring clock offset — a node that lost NTP drifts silently until something breaks.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• There is no global clock: quartz clocks drift (ppm), NTP keeps them within ms of each other — not identical, and not if it stops.
  • Use the monotonic clock for durations and timeouts, the wall clock only for human-facing timestamps.
  • Timestamps from different machines cannot order events closer than the skew; LWW loses writes.
  • Lamport clocks: a → b ⇒ L(a) < L(b); vector clocks also detect concurrency; HLC gives causality close to real time in 64 bits; TrueTime bounds the uncertainty and waits it out.
  • In practice, get order from a single authority, a partitioned log keyed by entity, or a version column — and use Snowflake/UUIDv7 for unique, sortable ids, not for deciding who came first.

items.title: Index
items.text:
The fan has held seat A-12 and taps Pay R$ 450. Three things must now happen together: inventory turns the seat from HELD into SOLD, payment charges the card through an external provider, and order records a confirmed order. Inside one PostgreSQL database this would be a single transaction — BEGIN … COMMIT, all or nothing. But the three pieces live in three services with three databases (and one of them is someone else's company). What happens when the charge succeeds and the inventory database is down? Or the seat is marked SOLD and the charge is declined?

A distributed transaction is a unit of work that changes data on several nodes and must be atomic: either every change happens, or none does. This page shows the classic protocol that achieves it — two-phase commit (2PC) —, why it is rarely used across microservices, and what replaces it in practice: sagas, the reservation (try–confirm–cancel) pattern and the transactional outbox.

items.title: Atomicity across nodes: the problem
items.text:
On one node, atomicity is provided by the database's log: a transaction's changes become durable and visible at a single point, the commit record. Across nodes there is no single log, and each participant can fail independently — so a naïve "commit everywhere, one after the other" leaves a window where some participants committed and others did not:

sequenceDiagram
    participant O as order (checkout)
    participant I as inventory DB
    participant P as payment provider
    O->>I: UPDATE seat A-12 to SOLD, then COMMIT
    I-->>O: committed
    O->>P: charge R$ 450
    P-->>O: declined (card limit)
    Note over O,P: the seat is SOLD but nobody paid:<br/>no single place can roll both back

Two families of solutions exist:

Approach Idea Isolation Availability Atomic commitment (2PC) Everyone prepares, then a coordinator decides commit/abort for all Full ACID across participants All participants and the coordinator must be up at the same time Sagas and compensations A sequence of local transactions; on failure, run compensating transactions that undo the earlier steps None between steps (intermediate states are visible) Each step only needs its own service

items.title: Two-phase commit (2PC)
items.text:
2PC introduces a coordinator (often the service or database node that started the transaction) and splits the commit into two phases1:

  1. Prepare (voting): the coordinator asks every participant "can you commit?". A participant that answers yes must first write all the changes and a prepared record durably to disk and keep the locks: from that moment it has promised to commit if asked — it can no longer abort on its own.
  2. Commit (decision): if all voted yes, the coordinator writes commit to its own log and tells everyone to commit; if anyone voted no (or timed out), it decides abort.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as coordinator
    participant I as inventory DB
    participant R as order DB
    C->>I: PREPARE (seat A-12 → SOLD)
    C->>R: PREPARE (order 981 → CONFIRMED)
    I-->>C: YES (changes + prepared record on disk, locks held)
    R-->>C: YES
    Note over C: all YES: write COMMIT to the coordinator log
    C->>I: COMMIT
    C->>R: COMMIT
    I-->>C: done (locks released)
    R-->>C: done

PostgreSQL exposes the participant side as PREPARE TRANSACTION 'id' followed later by COMMIT PREPARED 'id' or ROLLBACK PREPARED 'id'; the X/Open XA standard defines the same protocol for databases and message brokers coordinated by a transaction manager (as in Jakarta EE).

items.title: The blocking problem
items.text:
The weak point is the moment after a participant voted yes and before it hears the decision. If the coordinator crashes there, the participant is in doubt: it cannot commit (maybe someone voted no) and cannot abort (maybe the coordinator decided commit and others already committed). It must wait, holding its locks, until the coordinator recovers:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as coordinator
    participant I as inventory DB
    participant R as order DB
    C->>I: PREPARE
    C->>R: PREPARE
    I-->>C: YES (locks on seat A-12 held)
    R-->>C: YES
    Note over C: crashes before sending the decision
    Note over I: in doubt: cannot commit, cannot abort
    Note over I,R: seat A-12 stays locked until<br/>the coordinator comes back

During the 10:00 on-sale, a locked seat row blocks every other fan trying to hold it, and a crashed coordinator can freeze a whole block of seats. Three-phase commit (3PC) tries to remove the blocking but assumes bounded network delays, which real networks do not guarantee; production systems instead make the coordinator itself fault-tolerant by replicating its decision with consensus — exactly what Google Spanner (2PC over Paxos groups) and CockroachDB (over Raft) do2.

items.title: What 2PC costs
items.text:
• Latency: two round trips to every participant, plus forced disk writes (fsync) at each prepare and at the decision. Locks are held for the whole duration — the slowest participant decides how long.
  • Availability: the coordinator and every participant must be up at the same time. Availabilities multiply, like services in series:
2026-10-23T08:15:45.718040 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/
  • Coupling: every participant must speak the same protocol and expose "prepared" state. An external payment provider will never join your 2PC: its API charges or declines, with no "prepare and wait for my decision" step.

Where 2PC is alive and well

2PC is the standard inside a distributed database or broker, where one vendor controls all participants and the coordinator is replicated: Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, TiDB, and Kafka transactions (atomic writes to several partitions plus consumer offsets). What is discouraged is 2PC across independently deployed microservices and third parties.

Think first: inventory and order share the same PostgreSQL cluster but use different schemas. Do you need 2PC between them?

No — if both tables are in the same database, a single local transaction covers both, and that is far simpler and faster than any distributed protocol. Splitting data into separate databases is a decision with a price; when two pieces of data must change atomically all the time, that is a strong hint they belong to the same service or at least the same database (see Compute — services).

items.title: Sagas
items.text:
A saga (Garcia-Molina and Salem, 1987)3 splits a long transaction into a sequence of local transactions \(T_1, T_2, …, T_n\), each committed in its own service's database. If step \(T_k\) fails, the saga runs compensating transactions \(C_{k-1}, …, C_1\) that semantically undo the steps already done. There is no global lock and no global commit point.

The BoxOffice checkout as a saga:

Step Local transaction (service) Compensation 1 Create order PENDING (order) Mark order CANCELLED 2 Confirm the hold: seat HELD → RESERVED_FOR_PAYMENT (inventory) Release the seat → FREE 3 Charge the card (payment → provider) Refund the charge 4 Seat → SOLD, order → CONFIRMED, issue ticket (last step: no compensation; it must succeed — retried until it does) 
sequenceDiagram
    participant O as order (orchestrator)
    participant I as inventory
    participant P as payment
    participant N as notification
    O->>O: T1: order 981 PENDING
    O->>I: T2: reserve seat A-12 for payment
    I-->>O: reserved
    O->>P: T3: charge R$ 450 (idempotency key)
    P-->>O: declined
    Note over O: T3 failed: compensate in reverse order
    O->>I: C2: release seat A-12
    I-->>O: seat FREE
    O->>O: C1: order 981 CANCELLED
    O->>N: tell the fan "payment declined"

Two ways to coordinate the steps:

OrchestrationChoreography

A central orchestrator (here, the order service or a workflow engine such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions) tells each participant what to do and decides when to compensate. The saga's logic is in one place, easy to read, monitor and change; the orchestrator must persist its state so it survives restarts. Preferred when there are more than a few steps.

No central brain: each service reacts to events from the others (OrderCreated → inventory reserves → SeatReserved → payment charges → PaymentFailed → inventory releases…). Loosely coupled and simple for two or three steps; with more, the flow is spread over many services and hard to follow ("who compensates what?"). Covered with Kafka in Messaging — patterns.

items.title: Sagas give up isolation
items.text:
Between steps, other transactions see intermediate states: an order PENDING, a seat RESERVED_FOR_PAYMENT. Sagas are ACD without the I. Design countermeasures explicitly4:

  • Semantic locks: the intermediate state is the lock — while a seat is RESERVED_FOR_PAYMENT, no other fan can hold it, and the hold expires after 10 minutes if the saga never finishes.
  • Commutative and idempotent steps: every step and compensation may be retried (at-least-once), so each one needs an idempotency key (Idempotency).
  • Order the steps by risk: do the cheap, invisible, easily reversed steps first, and the steps that are hard or impossible to compensate (a charge, an e-mail) last, so that a failure late in the saga has little to undo. A refund is a compensation the fan sees; releasing a seat is invisible.
  • Pivot step: the step after which the saga can only go forward (here, the successful charge) — after it, the remaining steps must be retried until they succeed, never compensated.

items.title: Reservation: try, confirm, cancel
items.text: The TCC pattern (try–confirm–cancel) makes each participant offer a tentative operation with a timeout. BoxOffice already works this way: the hold is the try (the seat is reserved for 10 minutes), the sale is the confirm, and expiry or release is the cancel. Payment providers offer the same shape: authorise (reserve funds) → capture (take them) or void (release them). Because every tentative state expires by itself, a crash anywhere leaves the system converging to a safe state instead of blocking.

items.title: The dual-write problem and the outbox
items.text:
Every saga step does two things: change its own database and tell the next step (send an event or a command). Doing them as two separate writes is the dual-write problem — if the service crashes between them, the database says "seat reserved" but no event is ever sent, and the saga stalls:

sequenceDiagram
    participant I as inventory
    participant DB as inventory DB
    participant K as Kafka
    I->>DB: UPDATE seat + INSERT INTO outbox (SeatReserved), one COMMIT
    Note over I,DB: one local transaction: both or neither
    DB-->>I: committed
    Note over DB,K: a relay (poller or CDC such as Debezium)<br/>reads the outbox table
    DB->>K: publish SeatReserved
    K-->>DB: ack: mark outbox row as sent

The transactional outbox writes the event into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the business change; a separate relay publishes outbox rows to the broker and marks them sent. Publishing is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent. The details (polling vs change data capture, ordering, cleanup) are in Messaging — patterns and Hands-on 7.

items.title: Choosing
items.text:
Local transaction 2PC / distributed DB Saga (orchestrated) Saga (choreographed) TCC / reservation Atomicity Yes Yes Eventually, via compensation Eventually, via compensation Eventually, via confirm/cancel Isolation Yes Yes No (semantic locks) No Partial (the reservation) Availability One DB All participants at once Each step independently Each step independently Each step independently Latency Lowest 2 round trips + fsyncs, locks held Sum of steps, asynchronous possible Asynchronous Try now, confirm later Works with third parties — No Yes Yes Yes, if they offer reserve/capture Complexity Lowest In the database (if it offers it) Orchestrator state, compensations Event flow spread across services Timeouts and expiry logic BoxOffice use Hold a seat; seat + outbox row Inside CockroachDB/Spanner if used Checkout Notifications, analytics Seat hold; card authorise/capture

BoxOffice: the checkout, end to end

  1. Hold (TCC try): inventory runs one local transaction — conditional UPDATE of the seat to HELD with expires_at, plus an outbox row SeatHeld.
  2. Checkout saga, orchestrated by order: create order PENDING → inventory moves the seat to RESERVED_FOR_PAYMENT → payment authorises the card with an idempotency key → inventory marks the seat SOLD → payment captures → order CONFIRMED → notification sends the ticket.
  3. Failures: card declined → release the seat, cancel the order. Timeout talking to the provider → query the provider by idempotency key before deciding (the charge may have happened — see Slow or dead?). Orchestrator crash → it resumes from its persisted state. Abandoned hold → expires after 10 minutes and the sweeper releases the seat.
  4. No 2PC anywhere across services — the external provider could not join one anyway.

In the interview

When a design touches several services' data "atomically", say: "I won't use 2PC across services — it blocks if the coordinator fails, couples availability of every participant, and the payment provider can't participate. I'll use an orchestrated saga with compensations, idempotent steps, a semantic lock on the seat, and a transactional outbox to publish each step's event." Then name the pivot step and what happens on a timeout with the provider. If the data can live in one database, say so — the best distributed transaction is the one you avoid.

Pitfalls

  • Dual writes (database, then broker) without an outbox: a crash between them silently stalls the saga.
  • Non-idempotent steps or compensations: retries double-charge or double-refund.
  • Forgetting that compensations can fail: they must be retried until they succeed, and alerted on when they cannot.
  • Treating sagas as isolated: another fan sees RESERVED_FOR_PAYMENT; design for it (semantic locks, expiry).
  • 2PC with a non-replicated coordinator: a coordinator crash leaves participants in doubt with locks held.

items.text:
flowchart LR
    IDEM["idempotency keys<br/>(overview)"] --> SAGA["saga steps<br/>retried safely"]
    OUT["transactional outbox"] --> SAGA
    SAGA --> ORCH["orchestration<br/>(workflow engine)"]
    SAGA --> CHOR["choreography<br/>(events on Kafka)"]
    TCC["reservations: hold, authorise"] --> SAGA
    TPC["2PC"] --> BLOCK["blocks if the<br/>coordinator fails"]
    BLOCK --> CONS["replicate the coordinator<br/>→ Consensus"]
    CONS --> NEWSQL["inside Spanner,<br/>CockroachDB, Kafka txns"]

Palette components involved: stream / kafka (saga events, outbox relay) · queue (commands to participants) · payment (authorise / capture / void) · sql (local transactions + outbox table) · worker (orchestrator, relay). Try the payment-system and flash-sale scenarios in the playground. Continues in: Messaging — patterns, Compute — integrations, Case study: ticketing.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• A distributed transaction must be atomic across nodes; there is no single log to make it so.
  • 2PC (prepare, then commit) gives ACID across participants but blocks when the coordinator fails, holds locks for two round trips, and needs every participant up at once — use it inside distributed databases, not across microservices.
  • Sagas chain local transactions with compensations; they trade isolation for availability — use semantic locks, idempotent steps and a pivot step.
  • TCC / reservations (hold → sell / expire; authorise → capture / void) make tentative states expire safely.
  • The transactional outbox solves the dual-write problem between a database and a broker.

  1. GRAY, J.; LAMPORT, L. Consensus on Transaction Commit. ACM TODS, 2006. ↩

  2. CORBETT, J. C. et al. Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database. OSDI, 2012. ↩

  3. GARCIA-MOLINA, H.; SALEM, K. Sagas. ACM SIGMOD, 1987. ↩

  4. RICHARDSON, C. Pattern: Saga and Microservices Patterns. Manning, 2018. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
It is 09:59:58 on a Tuesday. BoxOffice has announced that tickets for a stadium show go on sale at 10:00: 60 thousand seats, about 2 million fans with the page open, many of them pressing "refresh" every second. At 10:00:00 every phone sends a request at once. Most of those requests should never reach the inventory service that holds the seats — and the ones that do must arrive at a healthy replica, in a fair order, from real fans and not from scalper bots.

Everything that happens between the fan's phone and the first BoxOffice service is the edge: name resolution, content delivery, traffic filtering, load balancing, and the API gateway. This class is about that path. It decides how fast the first byte arrives, how much load the core services see, and whether a flash sale is a success or a 10-minute outage on the evening news.

In this course, the edge means the set of components that receive, filter, route and distribute traffic before it reaches the application services. In the course simulator they form the TRAFFIC & EDGE category of the palette: dns, cdn, waf, lb, apigw and ingress1.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Trace a request from a client to a service through DNS, CDN, WAF, load balancer, API gateway and ingress, and explain what each hop decides.
  • Configure DNS records and TTLs, and CDN caching (Cache-Control, cache keys, invalidation) for a read-heavy page, and compute the origin load for a given hit ratio.
  • Compare L4 and L7 load balancing and choose a balancing algorithm (round robin, least connections, power of two choices, consistent hashing) for a workload.
  • Design a rate-limiting policy with token bucket or sliding window, and place it at the right layer.
  • Contrast HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 (QUIC), WebSockets, SSE and gRPC, and select one for a given interaction.
  • Defend an edge architecture against bots and DDoS attacks with WAF rules, rate limits, challenges and a waiting room.

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
1. This overview — the request's journey through the edge, reverse proxies, TLS termination, a latency budget, and edge security (WAF, bots, DDoS).
  2. DNS & CDN — name resolution, TTLs, GeoDNS and anycast; content delivery networks, cache keys, invalidation and edge compute.
  3. Load Balancing — L4 vs L7, algorithms, consistent hashing, service discovery, health checks, and Kubernetes Ingress / Gateway API.
  4. API Gateway & Rate Limiting — what a gateway centralises, the BFF pattern, and the rate-limiting algorithms.
  5. Protocols — HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC, TLS 1.3, WebSockets, SSE and gRPC.
  6. Quiz — check your understanding.

items.title: The request's journey
items.text:
A fan opens https://boxoffice.com/events/stadium-show and taps "Choose seats". Before any Java code runs, the request crosses several components, each one with a precise job. Press play and follow it:

sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fan's phone
    participant D as DNS
    participant C as CDN edge
    participant W as WAF
    participant L as Load balancer
    participant G as API gateway
    participant I as Ingress
    participant S as inventory service
    F->>D: boxoffice.com? (A/AAAA)
    D-->>F: 203.0.113.10 (nearest edge, TTL 60 s)
    F->>C: GET /events/stadium-show (TLS)
    C-->>F: HTML, JS, images from the edge cache
    F->>C: GET /api/events/42/seats
    C->>W: cache miss: forward to origin
    W->>L: request passed the rules (not a bot)
    L->>G: pick a healthy gateway replica
    G->>I: token valid, under the rate limit
    I->>S: route /api/events/** to inventory
    S-->>F: seat map (JSON)

Read the diagram as a series of decisions, made as early (and as cheaply) as possible:

  1. DNS decides where the client goes: which IP address, which region, which edge location.
  2. The CDN (Content Delivery Network) decides whether the request needs to go further at all: if the response is cached at the edge, the journey ends here, a few milliseconds from the fan.
  3. The WAF (Web Application Firewall) decides whether the request is allowed: malformed, malicious or abusive traffic is dropped here.
  4. The load balancer decides which replica serves the request, and only sends it to healthy ones.
  5. The API gateway decides whether the caller is allowed and within its quota: authentication, rate limits, routing to the right service.
  6. The ingress (inside Kubernetes) decides which Service in the cluster receives the request, by host and path.

Each hop removes work from the next one. In a well-designed flash sale, the vast majority of requests end at the CDN (static assets, the event page, even a seat map cached for one second), many bots end at the WAF, and only a controlled, fair stream reaches inventory.

Palette id Component Job Layer Typical products dns DNS name → IP; geographic and health-based routing application protocol over UDP/TCP 53 Route 53, Cloud DNS, Azure DNS, Cloudflare DNS cdn CDN cache content near users; absorb load and attacks L7 (HTTP) CloudFront, Cloud CDN, Azure Front Door, Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly waf WAF filter malicious or abusive HTTP requests L7 AWS WAF, Cloud Armor, Azure WAF, Cloudflare WAF, ModSecurity / Coraza lb Load Balancer spread connections or requests over healthy replicas L4 (TCP/UDP) or L7 (HTTP) ALB/NLB, Cloud Load Balancing, Azure Load Balancer, Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy apigw API Gateway single entry point for APIs: auth, rate limits, routing L7 API Gateway, Apigee, Azure API Management, Kong, Spring Cloud Gateway ingress Ingress HTTP routing into a Kubernetes cluster L7 Gateway API implementations (Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium), Traefik, cloud ingress controllers

Layers, briefly

"L4" and "L7" refer to the OSI model: layer 4 is the transport layer (TCP, UDP — connections, ports), layer 7 is the application layer (HTTP — methods, paths, headers, cookies). A component that works at L4 sees connections; one that works at L7 sees requests. The difference matters for load balancing and is detailed in Load Balancing.

Real deployments merge some of these boxes. Cloudflare or CloudFront combine DNS, CDN, WAF and DDoS protection in one product; an AWS Application Load Balancer can terminate TLS and route by path, doing part of the gateway's job; in Kubernetes the ingress controller often is the L7 load balancer. In an interview, draw the responsibilities as separate boxes first; then say which ones a single product covers.

items.title: Reverse proxies
items.text:
Almost every box on the edge is a reverse proxy: a server that receives requests on behalf of other servers, forwards them, and returns the answer as if it were its own. The client only knows the proxy's address; the backends stay hidden in a private network.

flowchart LR
    c1([Fan 1]) --> rp["Reverse proxy<br/>boxoffice.com:443"]
    c2([Fan 2]) --> rp
    c3([Bot]) -.->|blocked| rp
    rp --> a1[gateway replica 1]
    rp --> a2[gateway replica 2]
    rp --> a3[gateway replica 3]

Because every request passes through it, a reverse proxy is the natural place to put cross-cutting concerns once instead of in every service:

Concern What the proxy does TLS termination decrypts HTTPS once, so services do not each manage certificates Load balancing spreads requests over replicas, skips unhealthy ones Caching serves repeated responses without touching the backend Compression gzip / Brotli responses for slow mobile networks Security hides internal topology, filters requests, enforces limits Observability one place to log every request and measure latency and errors

The opposite, a forward proxy, sits in front of clients (a corporate proxy, for example). On the edge we only care about reverse proxies.

items.title: Where TLS terminates
items.text:
TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts the traffic between two endpoints. On the edge, there are three common choices of where the encrypted connection ends:

Option How it works Pros Cons Terminate at the edge CDN / LB decrypts; plain HTTP inside the private network simple; the proxy can read headers and cache traffic inside the network is readable by anyone who gets in Re-encrypt (TLS bridging) edge decrypts, inspects, opens a new TLS connection to the backend inspection and encryption in transit two handshakes, certificates on the backends Pass-through L4 LB forwards encrypted bytes; the service terminates TLS end-to-end encryption no L7 routing, caching or WAF at the LB

Modern architectures follow a zero-trust posture: terminate public TLS at the edge, and encrypt again inside the cluster — often automatically, with mutual TLS (mTLS) from a service mesh (see Network & Security).

Think first: can a CDN cache a page if TLS goes all the way to the service?

No. To cache a response, the CDN must read it, and to read it, it must hold the certificate and decrypt the traffic. With TLS pass-through, the CDN only sees encrypted bytes and can neither cache nor filter them. That is why CDNs and WAFs terminate TLS: you trust your edge provider with your certificate (or a certificate issued for it) in exchange for caching and filtering.

items.title: A latency budget for the edge
items.text:
Every hop adds time. Suppose BoxOffice wants the seat map API to answer in under 200 ms at p99 for fans in Brazil. Where does the time go? The figures below are illustrative assumptions for a São Paulo user and a São Paulo region; the method matters more than the numbers.

Step Cold (first visit) Warm (connection reused) DNS lookup (resolver cache miss / hit) 30 ms 0 ms (cached) TCP + TLS 1.3 handshake to the edge (2 RTT × 10 ms) 20 ms 0 ms (connection reused) CDN edge → WAF → LB (same metro) 5 ms 5 ms API gateway: JWT check + rate-limit lookup in Redis 5 ms 5 ms Ingress → inventory → PostgreSQL 40 ms 40 ms Response transfer (60 KB of JSON over mobile) 30 ms 30 ms Total ≈ 130 ms ≈ 80 ms

Three lessons come out of this kind of table:

  • Connection setup is expensive and avoidable. DNS caching, keep-alive and TLS session resumption remove about a third of the cold cost. HTTP/3 removes even more (Protocols).
  • Distance dominates. If the origin were in Virginia instead of São Paulo, each round trip would cost about 120 ms instead of 10 ms, and a cold request would pay several of them. This is why CDNs and edge locations exist.
  • The cheapest request is the one that never reaches the origin. A cache hit at the edge answers in the time of one RTT to the nearest point of presence.

items.title: Edge security: WAF, bots and DDoS
items.text: On sale day, BoxOffice does not only receive fans. It receives scalper bots that try to grab the best seats in the first second, credential-stuffing scripts that test leaked passwords against /login, and possibly a DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack from someone who wants the sale to fail. The edge is the first and cheapest place to stop all of them, because it sees all the traffic before it costs anything to the core.

items.title: Web Application Firewall (WAF)
items.text:
A WAF inspects HTTP requests (L7) and blocks the ones that match rules. Rules come in three families:

  • Managed rule sets that detect common attacks — SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), path traversal, known vulnerable endpoints. The reference is the OWASP Core Rule Set (CRS), used by ModSecurity and Coraza and mirrored by the cloud WAFs2.
  • Reputation rules: block or challenge IP addresses from known botnets, anonymising proxies, or data-centre ranges that real fans do not use.
  • Custom rules for your application: "at most 5 POST /login per IP per minute", "only allow PUT /holds with a valid waiting-room token", "block requests without a User-Agent".

WAF rules start in count (log-only) mode, are tuned against real traffic to remove false positives, and only then switched to block. A WAF that blocks real fans during the sale is worse than no WAF.

items.title: Bot mitigation
items.text:
Bots are not all bad (search engine crawlers, uptime monitors), and the bad ones increasingly look like humans. Mitigation combines several signals, cheapest first:

Technique How it works Stops Cost / risk Rate limiting per IP / per account cap requests per time window (API Gateway) naive scripts botnets spread over thousands of IPs IP reputation and ASN rules block known-bad IPs and hosting providers cheap bot farms residential proxies slip through Fingerprinting TLS fingerprint (e.g. JA3/JA4), header order, JavaScript-collected device signals headless browsers, scripted clients privacy concerns; arms race Challenges invisible JavaScript proof-of-work or CAPTCHA when the score is suspicious most automated traffic friction for real users Behavioural analysis mouse/touch patterns, navigation speed, purchase velocity advanced bots needs data and models Virtual waiting room admit users to the sale at a controlled rate, in random or arrival order the "first second" advantage of bots users wait; must be fair and transparent Business rules max 6 tickets per account, verified phone, identity checks scalping at scale product decision, not only technical

The waiting room deserves a special mention for BoxOffice: when 2 million fans arrive for 60 thousand seats, letting all of them into the seat map at once guarantees an outage and rewards whoever is fastest — usually a bot. A waiting room at the edge hands each visitor a signed token with a position, and admits, say, 2 000 users per minute to the purchase flow. The core sees a steady, sized load; the rest of the fans see a progress bar served from the CDN. You will model it with a queue in the messaging class and the ticketing case study.

items.title: DDoS
items.text:
A denial-of-service attack tries to exhaust a resource — bandwidth, connections, CPU — so that legitimate users cannot be served. "Distributed" means it comes from many sources at once (a botnet), so blocking a single IP does not help3.

Attack type Layer Example Defence Volumetric L3/L4 UDP floods, DNS/NTP amplification reaching hundreds of Gbit/s absorb with capacity: anycast spreads the flood over hundreds of edge locations; upstream scrubbing centres filter it Protocol L4 SYN floods that fill connection tables SYN cookies, stateless L4 filtering at the edge Application L7 many valid-looking GET /search?q=… requests that are expensive for the backend WAF rules, rate limits, challenges, caching, autoscaling with limits

The key idea is asymmetry: you cannot out-provision an attacker with your own servers, but a large CDN/DDoS provider has more edge capacity than any single attack. With anycast, the same IP address is announced from every edge location, so traffic from each bot goes to the nearest location and the flood is divided among all of them (DNS & CDN). Volumetric attacks are therefore a problem you buy a solution for (AWS Shield, Cloud Armor, Azure DDoS Protection, Cloudflare)4; L7 attacks are a problem you also have to design for — expensive endpoints must be cacheable, rate-limited or protected by a challenge.

BoxOffice: 10:00, the sale opens

The edge configuration for the stadium sale, layer by layer:

  • DNS: boxoffice.com points to the CDN's anycast addresses; TTL 60 s so that the team can redirect traffic quickly if a region fails.
  • CDN: the event page, JavaScript and images are cached with long TTLs and fingerprinted file names; the seat-availability JSON is micro-cached for 1 second — 2 million fans polling every 5 s become, at most, one origin request per second per edge location.
  • WAF: OWASP managed rules on; a custom rule allows POST /api/holds only with a valid waiting-room token; POST /login limited per IP and per account.
  • Bots: JavaScript challenge on suspicious fingerprints; data-centre ASNs challenged before entering the queue.
  • Waiting room: admits a fixed number of users per minute, sized from the capacity of inventory and payment measured in the load tests.
  • API gateway: JWT validation and a token bucket of 10 requests/s per user with bursts of 20, and a limit of 6 seats per hold.

The result: the core services see thousands of requests per second instead of millions, and they see them in the order the waiting room decided — not in the order the fastest bot decided.

Try it. Load the flash-sale scenario and run the spike profile. First observe what happens to inventory without the waiting room (remove the queue between the gateway and the services): latency and errors explode at the start of the sale. Then put the queue back and compare p99 latency, error rate and the number of seats sold per minute.

In the interview

When you draw the high-level design, put the edge in one line: "client → DNS → CDN → load balancer → API gateway → services". Then spend words only where the problem needs them: a read-heavy system (news feed, catalogue) deserves a sentence on CDN caching and hit ratio; a public API deserves rate limiting; a flash sale or ticketing problem deserves WAF, bots and a waiting room. Always say what each hop removes from the core — that is the signal interviewers look for.

Pitfalls

  • Treating the edge as a single box. "We put a load balancer in front" does not answer "how do you survive 2 million users at 10:00?" Say what is cached, what is filtered and what is limited.
  • Forgetting that every edge component can fail. A load balancer, a gateway or a WAF in a single instance is a single point of failure. Managed edge services are replicated for you; self-hosted ones must run in pairs or clusters.
  • Blocking real users. Aggressive WAF and bot rules turned on without a "count mode" period produce false positives exactly when traffic is most valuable.
  • Doing business logic at the edge. Edge functions and gateways are for cross-cutting concerns. Pricing rules or seat allocation in a gateway plugin become an untestable, unversioned second application.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• The edge is everything between the client and the first service: dns, cdn, waf, lb, apigw, ingress. Each hop makes a decision and should remove work from the next one.
  • Most edge components are reverse proxies, the natural place for TLS termination, load balancing, caching, security and observability.
  • Latency on the edge is dominated by round trips and distance; caching, connection reuse and modern protocols attack exactly that.
  • WAF rules filter malicious requests, bot mitigation combines rates, fingerprints, challenges and a waiting room, and DDoS defence relies on anycast capacity for volumetric attacks and on design (caching, limits) for L7 attacks.
  • In an interview, draw the edge quickly, then go deep only where the problem demands it — and say what each component removes from the core.

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: The edge and its security
items.text:
Q1. In the BoxOffice request path fan → DNS → CDN → WAF → load balancer → API gateway → ingress → inventory, which component should reject a request whose JWT has expired?

  • A. The CDN, because it is closest to the fan
  • B. The load balancer, because it already terminates TLS
  • C. The API gateway, which centralises authentication for every service
  • D. The ingress, because it knows which Kubernetes Service owns the route
Answer

C — The API gateway.

Validating identity (JWT signature, expiry, audience) is the classic cross-cutting job of the API gateway: it is done once, consistently, before any service runs. The CDN and the load balancer do not know about users (although an edge function can pre-validate tokens), and the ingress only routes by host and path. The services should still check authorisation for their own resources (zero trust), but rejecting an expired token belongs at the gateway.

Q2. At 10:00 a botnet of 50 000 residential IP addresses sends valid-looking GET /api/search?q=… requests, each of them expensive for the backend. Which defence is least effective on its own?

  • A. A rate limit of 100 requests per minute per IP address
  • B. Caching search results at the CDN for a few seconds
  • C. A JavaScript challenge for clients with a suspicious fingerprint
  • D. A virtual waiting room that admits users at a controlled rate
Answer

A — A per-IP rate limit.

Each bot can send up to 100 requests per minute and never trip the limit: 50 000 × 100 = 5 million requests per minute (about 83 000 per second), all accepted. This is an application-layer (L7) DDoS distributed across many sources: per-IP limits barely notice it. Caching makes repeated expensive requests cheap, challenges filter automated clients, and a waiting room caps the rate that reaches the core regardless of how many sources there are.

Q3. Why is anycast effective against volumetric DDoS attacks?

  • A. It encrypts traffic, so attackers cannot read the responses
  • B. The same IP address is announced from many locations, so traffic from a global botnet is split across all of them instead of concentrating on one
  • C. It blocks UDP traffic, which is used by most attacks
  • D. It changes the site's IP address every few seconds
Answer

B — The flood is divided among many locations.

With anycast, routing delivers each packet to the nearest location announcing the address. A botnet spread around the world therefore hits hundreds of edge locations, each receiving a fraction of the attack — a fraction that a large CDN can absorb. This is why volumetric DDoS protection is usually bought from providers with large anycast networks.

items.title: DNS & CDN
items.text:
Q4. BoxOffice uses DNS failover between two regions. Health checks run every 10 s, the primary is declared unhealthy after 3 consecutive failures, and the record's TTL is 60 s. In the best case, roughly how long after the primary region fails do clients that respect the TTL start using the secondary?

  • A. About 10 seconds
  • B. About 30 seconds
  • C. About 90 seconds
  • D. About 10 minutes
Answer

C — About 90 seconds.

Detection takes about 3 × 10 s = 30 s; after that, resolvers may still hold the old answer for up to one TTL (60 s). Total ≈ 30 + 60 = 90 s in the best case. In practice it is longer: some resolvers and clients keep answers longer than the TTL, and open connections keep using the old region until they break. DNS failover is suitable for regional disasters, not for fast instance-level failover.

Q5. The edge receives 200 000 requests per second for static content. The CDN hit ratio improves from 95% to 99%. What happens to the load on the origin?

  • A. It drops by about 4%, from 10 000 to 9 600 requests per second
  • B. It drops by about 80%, from 10 000 to 2 000 requests per second
  • C. It does not change; the hit ratio only affects latency
  • D. It drops by half, from 10 000 to 5 000 requests per second
Answer

B — From 10 000 to 2 000 req/s.

The origin sees the miss rate: 5% of 200 000 = 10 000 req/s before, 1% of 200 000 = 2 000 req/s after — five times fewer. Small changes in hit ratio near 100% are large changes in miss rate, which is the number that sizes the origin.

Q6. BoxOffice deploys a new JavaScript bundle. Which strategy guarantees that no fan runs a mix of the old HTML and the new JavaScript, without depending on CDN purges?

  • A. Keep the name app.js and set Cache-Control: no-store on it
  • B. Keep the name app.js, deploy, and purge it from every PoP
  • C. Give the bundle a content-based name (app.b71e02.js) cached with max-age=31536000, immutable, and reference it from an HTML page with a short TTL
  • D. Set max-age=60 on app.js and wait one minute after each deploy
Answer

C — Fingerprinted (versioned) URLs.

A new version gets a new URL, so caches can never serve an old file under the new name; old and new versions coexist while the short-lived HTML switches from one to the other. Purges are slow, may fail and never reach browser caches; no-store throws away the benefit of the CDN; a 60 s TTL still leaves a window of mixed versions.

Q7. During the sale, the seat-availability endpoint receives 400 000 requests per second from fans polling. The response may be up to one second old. With Cache-Control: s-maxage=1 and 40 CDN PoPs serving those fans (no origin shield), what is the maximum request rate this endpoint sends to the origin?

  • A. About 40 requests per second
  • B. About 4 000 requests per second
  • C. About 400 000 requests per second
  • D. Zero, because the CDN never contacts the origin for cached content
Answer

A — About 40 req/s.

Each PoP fetches the object at most once per second when it expires (one PoP × 1 req/s × 40 PoPs). This is micro-caching: a short TTL on a hot dynamic endpoint turns hundreds of thousands of requests per second into a handful at the origin, at the cost of up to one second of staleness. An origin shield would reduce it further to about one request per second. The hold itself must still go to the origin and be checked against the database.

items.title: Load balancing
items.text:
Q8. Which statement about L4 and L7 load balancers is correct?

  • A. An L4 load balancer can route /api/holds to inventory and /api/orders to order
  • B. An L7 load balancer chooses a backend per HTTP request and can route by path, host or header; an L4 load balancer chooses per connection and only sees IPs and ports
  • C. L4 load balancers always terminate TLS
  • D. L7 load balancers are always faster than L4 ones because they understand the protocol
Answer

B.

L4 works with connections (TCP/UDP): fast and protocol-agnostic, but blind to paths and headers, and usually passing TLS through. L7 terminates the connection, reads each request and can route, retry, rewrite and balance per request — at a higher CPU cost per request.

Q9. A cache tier uses server = hash(key) mod N with N = 4 servers. A fifth server is added. Approximately what fraction of keys now map to a different server, and what would it be with consistent hashing?

  • A. 20% with mod N; 80% with consistent hashing
  • B. About 80% with mod N; about 20% with consistent hashing
  • C. 25% in both cases
  • D. 100% with mod N; 0% with consistent hashing
Answer

B — About 80% vs about 20%.

With mod N, a key keeps its server only if hash mod 4 = hash mod 5, which happens for about 1 key in 5, so ~80% move — almost every cache entry misses at once. With consistent hashing, the new server takes over only the keys between itself and its predecessors on the ring: about 1/(N+1) = 1/5 = 20%, exactly the share it must own anyway.

Q10. Why do consistent-hashing implementations place each server on the ring many times (virtual nodes)?

  • A. To encrypt the keys
  • B. To make the arcs between points average out, so each server owns close to its fair share of keys, and to spread a removed server's keys over all remaining servers
  • C. To allow the same key to be stored on several servers for durability
  • D. To make lookups O(1) instead of O(log N)
Answer

B — Balance.

With one point per server, random positions create arcs of very different lengths: one server can own half of the keys and another almost none. With 100–200 points per server, the ownership of each server is the sum of many small arcs and approaches 1/N. When a server leaves, its many small arcs are inherited by many different servers. Replication (C) is a separate design choice built on top of the ring.

Q11. The order service calls inventory over gRPC through an L4 load balancer. After scaling inventory from 3 to 6 pods, the new pods receive almost no traffic. What is the most likely cause?

  • A. The new pods failed their readiness probes
  • B. gRPC uses long-lived HTTP/2 connections, and an L4 load balancer chooses a backend only when a connection is opened; the existing connections stay on the old pods
  • C. gRPC does not support more than three servers
  • D. The L4 load balancer uses consistent hashing on the request path
Answer

B — Connection-level balancing of long-lived connections.

order multiplexes all its calls over a few HTTP/2 connections opened before the scale-out. Fixes: per-request L7 balancing (Envoy, a service mesh), client-side load balancing in the gRPC client, or a maximum connection age so clients reconnect and spread over the new pods.

items.title: API gateway and rate limiting
items.text:
Q12. A token bucket has capacity 20 and a refill rate of 10 tokens/s. A fan who has been idle for a minute sends 50 requests in the same instant. How many are accepted immediately, and what is the maximum sustained rate afterwards?

  • A. 50 accepted; then 20 per second
  • B. 20 accepted; then 10 per second
  • C. 10 accepted; then 10 per second
  • D. 30 accepted; then 20 per second
Answer

B — 20 now, 10 per second afterwards.

After a long idle period the bucket is full (capacity 20, never more). The instant burst consumes the 20 tokens; the other 30 requests are rejected with 429. From then on, tokens arrive at 10 per second, so that is the maximum sustained rate: capacity sets the burst, refill sets the average.

Q13. A fixed window limiter allows 100 requests per minute per user. What is the largest number of requests a user can get accepted in any 2-second interval?

  • A. 100
  • B. About 3, because 100 per minute is under 2 per second
  • C. 200, by sending 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next
  • D. Unlimited, because the counter resets every minute
Answer

C — 200.

This is the boundary problem of fixed windows: 100 requests at 10:00:59 fill the 10:00 window, and 100 more at 10:01:00 fill the 10:01 window — 200 accepted in about one second, twice the intended rate. The sliding window log (exact) or the sliding window counter (weighted approximation) fix it.

Q14. BoxOffice runs 6 gateway replicas behind a load balancer, and each replica keeps its rate-limit counters in local memory with a limit of 10 req/s per user. Requests are spread evenly across replicas. What limit does a user actually get, and what is the usual fix?

  • A. 10 req/s; no fix needed
  • B. Up to about 60 req/s; store the counters in a shared store such as Redis and update them atomically (e.g. with a Lua script)
  • C. About 1.7 req/s; increase the limit to 60
  • D. 10 req/s, but only if sticky sessions are enabled
Answer

B — Up to 6× the limit; use a shared, atomic counter.

Each replica sees one sixth of the user's requests and applies the full limit to them, so the effective limit is ~60 req/s. A shared store (Redis) with an atomic read-modify-write (a Lua script, or INCR with expiry for windows) gives one consistent count. Alternatives accept approximation: each replica enforces limit / replicas, or replicas sync counters asynchronously. Sticky sessions would help only partially and harm load balancing.

items.title: Protocols
items.text:
Q15. The seat map must show, to millions of browsers, each seat that becomes held or sold within about one second. Clients never send data back on this channel. Which choice is the simplest that meets the requirement?

  • A. WebSockets, because they are the fastest real-time protocol
  • B. Server-Sent Events: one long-lived HTTP response streaming events, with automatic reconnection and resume via Last-Event-ID
  • C. gRPC bidirectional streaming from the browser
  • D. Long polling with a 60-second timeout and no caching
Answer

B — Server-Sent Events.

The traffic is one-way (server → client), so SSE fits exactly: it is plain HTTP (works through CDNs, proxies and HTTP/2 multiplexing), and EventSource reconnects and resumes on its own. WebSockets would work but add a stateful bidirectional channel, upgrade handling and custom reconnection for no benefit. gRPC is not natively available in browsers. Polling with CDN micro-caching is also a valid, even cheaper design if a couple of seconds of delay are acceptable.

items.title: Index
items.text:
BoxOffice has nine services. Without a gateway, the mobile app would need to know nine addresses, every service would validate JWTs on its own (with nine slightly different bugs), every service would implement its own rate limit, and a fan's script hammering POST /api/holds 500 times per second would go straight to inventory. The API gateway is the single front door that solves all of this in one place — and it is also the place where many architectures quietly grow a bottleneck or a second monolith.

An API gateway is an L7 reverse proxy specialised for APIs: it is the single entry point for clients, routes each request to the right service, and applies cross-cutting policies — authentication, rate limits, quotas, transformations, observability — before the request reaches any business code1. It is the apigw component of the palette.

items.title: What a gateway does
items.text:
flowchart LR
    app([Mobile app]) --> gw
    web([Web app]) --> gw
    partner([Partner API client]) --> gw
    subgraph gw [API gateway]
        direction TB
        a["Authenticate: JWT / API key"] --> r["Rate limit and quota"]
        r --> t["Route + transform"]
        t --> o["Log, metrics, trace"]
    end
    gw --> catalog[catalog]
    gw --> inventory[inventory]
    gw --> order[order]
    gw --> assistant[assistant]
Responsibility What it means BoxOffice example Routing map host/path/method to a service and version /api/holds/** → inventory, /api/v2/orders/** → order v2 Authentication (authN) offload validate the JWT signature and expiry, or the API key, once reject expired tokens before they reach any service; pass X-User-Id downstream Coarse authorisation (authZ) route-level rules: scopes, roles /api/admin/** requires the admin role; fine-grained rules ("can this user cancel this order?") stay in the service Rate limiting and quotas requests per second per user/IP/key; monthly quotas per plan 10 req/s per fan, bursts of 20; partner plans of 1 M calls/month Request/response transformation rename headers, strip internal fields, convert protocols (REST ↔ gRPC) expose inventory's gRPC API as REST to the web app Aggregation one client call fans out to several services and merges the answers GET /api/events/42/page returns event + venue + availability Caching cache GET responses for a short time event details for 30 s Observability access logs, RED metrics per route, start the distributed trace p99 per route, traceparent header injected Resilience timeouts, retries, circuit breakers per route 2 s timeout to inventory; no retries on POST API products API keys, developer portal, plans, usage billing ticket resale partners

The key word is cross-cutting: concerns that are the same for every service. Anything that depends on the business — prices, seat allocation, refund rules — belongs in a service, not in gateway configuration.

items.title: Gateway, load balancer, ingress or service mesh?
items.text:
These four components overlap, and products blur the lines (Envoy is the engine of many of them). What distinguishes them is which traffic they handle and what they know:

Load balancer (lb) Ingress / Gateway API (ingress) API gateway (apigw) Service mesh (mesh) Traffic north-south (into the system) north-south into a Kubernetes cluster north-south, API traffic east-west (service to service) Main job spread load over healthy replicas route HTTP by host/path to Services API policies: auth, limits, keys, transformations mTLS, retries, timeouts, telemetry between services Knows about backends, health Services, hosts, paths consumers, API keys, plans, routes every service identity Typical products ALB/NLB, Nginx, HAProxy Envoy Gateway, Traefik, cloud controllers Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway, Azure APIM, Spring Cloud Gateway Istio, Linkerd, Cilium

A typical BoxOffice request crosses a load balancer (managed, at the region entrance), the API gateway (policies), and, between services, the mesh. On Kubernetes the gateway is often deployed as the Gateway API implementation, merging the ingress and gateway roles. The mesh is studied in Network & Security.

items.title: Backend for Frontend (BFF)
items.text:
The mobile app and the web app need different things: the app shows a compact event card and works on slow networks; the web page shows the full seat map and venue details. A single, generic API either over-fetches for mobile or forces the web app to make many calls.

The Backend for Frontend pattern gives each client type its own thin gateway layer, owned by the team that builds that frontend2:

flowchart LR
    m([Mobile app]) --> bm[Mobile BFF]
    w([Web app]) --> bw[Web BFF]
    p([Partners]) --> pg[Public API gateway]
    bm --> catalog[catalog]
    bm --> inventory[inventory]
    bw --> catalog
    bw --> inventory
    bw --> order[order]
    pg --> catalog

Each BFF aggregates and shapes the responses its client needs (one call for the "event screen" on mobile, with smaller images and fewer fields) and evolves at the speed of that frontend. GraphQL servers are often used as BFFs, because the client describes the exact shape it needs (see API styles).

One general-purpose gateway BFF per client Responses generic; clients over-fetch or make many calls tailored per screen Ownership platform team; a shared bottleneck for changes frontend team owns its BFF Duplication none some shared logic duplicated across BFFs Number of components one one per client type

Use a BFF when clients differ significantly and are owned by different teams; keep cross-cutting policies (auth, rate limits) in the shared gateway in front of the BFFs.

items.title: Rate limiting
items.text:
Rate limiting caps how many requests a client may make in a period of time. It protects the backend from overload and abuse, keeps one noisy client from hurting the others (fairness), and enforces commercial plans. It answers with 429 Too Many Requests — "you, specifically, are sending too much" — unlike 503 Service Unavailable, which means "the server is overloaded for everyone".

Every rate limiter has to decide three things:

  1. Who is being limited — the key: the user id (from the JWT), the API key, the client IP, or a combination such as user + route.
  2. How much — the policy: 10 requests per second with bursts of 20; 1 000 per hour; 4 holds per event per user.
  3. How to count — the algorithm, below.

items.title: Token bucket
items.text:
The most widely used algorithm3. Each key has a bucket that holds at most capacity tokens (the burst size) and is refilled at a constant rate (the sustained limit). Each request takes a token; if the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.

flowchart LR
    req([Request from fan 7]) --> chk{"Token in<br/>fan 7's bucket?"}
    refill(["Refill: +10 tokens/s<br/>up to capacity 20"]) -.-> chk
    chk -->|"yes: take 1 token"| fwd[Forward to inventory]
    chk -->|"no: bucket empty"| rej["429 Too Many Requests<br/>Retry-After: 1"]

The implementation does not need a timer: store the token count and the time of the last update, and on each request add elapsed × rate tokens (capped at capacity) before checking. Two numbers per key, O(1) work per request.

The simulation below shows one fan's bucket (capacity 20, refill 10/s) under an illustrative traffic pattern: normal browsing at 4 req/s, a 2-second burst at 40 req/s (the fan mashes "refresh" at 10:00), and then 8 seconds at 14 req/s.

2026-10-23T08:15:45.910815 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Read the two panels together:

  • During the burst, the first second accepts about 29 requests — the 20 saved tokens plus the refill — and then the limiter settles at the refill rate of 10/s; the excess is rejected.
  • During the sustained phase at 14 req/s, the bucket drains slowly (it loses 4 tokens per second) and accepts everything for about five seconds; after that, it accepts exactly 10/s.
  • When traffic calms down (4 req/s, so a net refill of 6 tokens/s), the bucket is full again in about three seconds and the next burst will be absorbed again.

This is the behaviour you usually want: short bursts are tolerated, sustained excess is not. The two parameters map directly to product language — "10 requests per second, bursts of up to 20".

Think first: a bucket has capacity 50 and refills at 5 tokens/s. A client that was idle for a long time sends 100 requests at once. How many are accepted immediately? And how long until it can send another 50 at once?

50 are accepted (the full bucket); the other 50 are rejected. The bucket is empty, so it needs 10 s (50 tokens ÷ 5 tokens/s) to be full again. Over a long period, the client can never average more than 5 req/s, whatever its pattern.

items.title: Leaky bucket
items.text: Requests enter a queue of fixed size and leave it at a constant rate, like water leaking from a bucket with a hole. If the queue is full, new requests are dropped. The output is perfectly smooth — the backend sees exactly the leak rate — at the cost of added latency for queued requests and no bursts reaching the backend. Nginx's limit_req is a leaky bucket; with burst=… nodelay it behaves much like a token bucket.

items.title: Fixed window counter
items.text: Count requests per key in fixed windows — "minute 10:00", "minute 10:01" — with a counter that resets at each boundary: INCR ratelimit:fan7:202610171000 with a 60 s expiry. Simple and cheap, but it has a boundary problem: with a limit of 100 per minute, a client can send 100 at 10:00:59 and another 100 at 10:01:00 — 200 requests in two seconds, twice the intended rate, all accepted.

items.title: Sliding window log
items.text: Store the timestamp of every request (for example in a Redis sorted set); on each request, drop timestamps older than the window and count the rest. Exact — there is no boundary problem — but memory grows with the limit: a limit of 1 000 per hour stores up to 1 000 timestamps per key.

items.title: Sliding window counter
items.text:
A cheap approximation that fixes the boundary problem: keep the counters of the current and previous fixed windows and weight the previous one by how much of it still overlaps the sliding window:

\[ \text{estimate} = \text{current} + \text{previous} \times \left(1 - \frac{\text{elapsed in current window}}{\text{window size}}\right) \]

Example: limit 100/min. The previous minute had 80 requests; 15 s into the current minute there have been 30. Estimate = 30 + 80 × (1 − 15/60) = 30 + 60 = 90 → the request is allowed. It assumes the previous window's requests were evenly spread, which is close enough in practice; Cloudflare reported that this approximation misjudged a tiny fraction of requests on real traffic4.

items.title: Comparing the algorithms
items.text: Algorithm Memory per key Bursts Accuracy Typical use Token bucket 2 numbers allowed, up to capacity good API gateways (AWS API Gateway, Spring Cloud Gateway, Envoy) Leaky bucket a queue smoothed out good protecting a backend that needs a constant rate; Nginx limit_req Fixed window 1 counter up to 2× at boundaries weak at boundaries simple quotas (per day / per month) Sliding window log 1 timestamp per request none beyond the limit exact low limits where exactness matters (login attempts) Sliding window counter 2 counters approximately limited very good high-volume APIs (Cloudflare)

items.title: Distributed rate limiting
items.text:
BoxOffice runs six gateway replicas. If each keeps its counters in memory, a fan whose requests are spread across them gets six times the limit. A rate limit that must hold across replicas needs a shared counter store, almost always Redis: fast (sub-millisecond in the same zone), with atomic operations and expiry.

The read-modify-write of a token bucket must be atomic — two gateway replicas reading "1 token left" at the same time would both accept. A Lua script runs atomically inside Redis:

token_bucket.lua
-- KEYS[1] = bucket key (e.g. "rl:user:7:holds")
-- ARGV[1] = capacity, ARGV[2] = refill rate (tokens/s), ARGV[3] = cost of this request
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate     = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local cost     = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local t   = redis.call("TIME")                        -- Redis clock: no skew between gateways
local now = tonumber(t[1]) * 1000 + math.floor(tonumber(t[2]) / 1000)

local b      = redis.call("HMGET", KEYS[1], "tokens", "ts")
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or capacity
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now

tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * rate)   -- refill since last call
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then
  tokens = tokens - cost
  allowed = 1
end

redis.call("HSET", KEYS[1], "tokens", tokens, "ts", now)
redis.call("PEXPIRE", KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity / rate * 1000) * 2)  -- idle keys disappear
return { allowed, tostring(tokens) }

Design points worth saying out loud:

  • One round trip per request (a few hundred microseconds to a millisecond) — acceptable at the gateway, but it is on the critical path of every request.
  • Time comes from Redis (TIME), not from each gateway: gateway clocks drift (see Time & clocks).
  • Fail open or fail closed? If Redis is unreachable, should the gateway accept everything (protecting availability) or reject everything (protecting the backend)? Most APIs fail open with a local, per-replica fallback limit.
  • Hot keys and scale: a Redis Cluster shards keys by hash; a single very hot key (a global limit) lands on one shard. Per-user keys spread naturally.
  • Approximate alternatives: each replica enforces limit / replicas locally, or syncs counters asynchronously every 100 ms. Less exact, no extra round trip.

items.title: Where to rate limit
items.text:
