Layer Key Protects against Example Edge / CDN / WAF IP, fingerprint, ASN floods, scrapers, credential stuffing — before any cost 100 req/10 s per IP on /login API gateway user id, API key, route abusive users, plan quotas, fairness 10 req/s per fan, bursts of 20 Service business entity business abuse the gateway cannot see max 6 seats per hold, 1 active hold per event per user Outbound (client side) the provider's quota exceeding a 3rd-party limit (payment, e-mail) 100 req/s to the payment provider

Use several layers: coarse and cheap at the edge, identity-aware at the gateway, business rules in the services. Rate limiting is also one of the resilience patterns of class 9 — there, the point of view is protecting a service from overload (load shedding).

items.title: Telling the client
items.text:
A good limiter tells well-behaved clients how to behave:

429 response
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 2
RateLimit-Policy: "per-user";q=20;w=1
RateLimit: "per-user";r=0;t=2
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type": "https://boxoffice.example/problems/rate-limited", "title": "Too many requests", "status": 429}

Retry-After (seconds, or a date) is standard HTTP. Many APIs also send X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset; the IETF is standardising RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy fields for the same purpose5. Clients should respect Retry-After and back off with jitter — otherwise every rejected client retries at the same instant.

items.title: Configuration examples
Trade-offs at a glance
items.text:
Decision Option A Option B Choose A when… Entry point one API gateway BFF per client clients have similar needs, or one team owns all clients Algorithm token bucket sliding window counter bursts are acceptable and you want simple, clear parameters Counter store shared (Redis) local per replica the limit must be accurate across replicas Redis down fail open fail closed availability matters more than strict protection Gateway product managed (AWS API GW, Apigee, APIM) self-hosted (Kong, Spring Cloud Gateway, Envoy) you want plans, keys and portals without operating them Logic in gateway only cross-cutting policies business rules always A

BoxOffice: the gateway on sale day

  • Routing: /api/events/** → catalog, /api/holds/** → inventory, /api/orders/** → order, /api/assistant/** → assistant.
  • Authentication: the gateway validates the JWT issued by auth (signature with the cached public keys, expiry, audience) and forwards X-User-Id; catalog GETs are public.
  • Rate limits (several layers):
    • edge/WAF: 100 requests per 10 s per IP on /login; waiting-room token required on /api/holds;
    • gateway: token bucket per user, 10 req/s with bursts of 20 on /api/**, and 1 req/s with bursts of 3 on POST /api/holds;
    • inventory: at most 6 seats per hold and one active hold per user per event (a business rule, enforced with the database).
  • Store: Redis (with a replica) for the buckets; if it fails, gateways fail open with a local limit of 1/6 of the global one.
  • Answers: 429 with Retry-After; the app backs off with jitter and shows "too many attempts, try again in a few seconds".
  • Assistant: a separate, lower limit and a token-cost-based quota, because an LLM call is far more expensive than a catalog read (see AI systems).

In the interview

  • Put the API gateway in the high-level design and list what it centralises: routing, authentication, rate limiting, observability. Then move on — unless the question is a rate limiter.
  • If asked to design a rate limiter: clarify key, limit and scope (per user? per IP? global?), pick token bucket (bursts) or sliding window counter (accuracy), store counters in Redis with an atomic Lua script, and discuss fail open vs closed, multi-region (local limits per region or async sync) and the 429 + Retry-After response.
  • Know the fixed window boundary problem (2× burst) — it is a classic follow-up question.
  • Mention BFF when the question has very different clients (mobile, web, TV, partners).

Pitfalls

  • Gateway as a single point of failure or bottleneck: it is on the path of every request. Run several replicas across zones, size it in load tests, and keep its per-request work small.
  • Business logic in the gateway: scripts and plugins that compute prices or allocate seats create a second, hidden monolith that nobody tests. Keep the gateway dumb and the services smart.
  • Trusting the gateway alone: services must still verify identity and authorisation (zero trust); an attacker inside the network bypasses the gateway.
  • Per-replica counters that silently multiply the limit by the number of replicas.
  • Rate-limiting by IP only: thousands of fans behind one mobile carrier's NAT share an IP; botnets have thousands of IPs. Prefer user/API-key keys, with IP limits only at the edge and generous.
  • Retrying 429 immediately: clients without backoff turn a limit into a retry storm.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    GW["API gateway"] --> AUTH["JWT validation<br/>→ Network & Security"]
    GW --> RL["rate limiting"]
    RL --> TB["token bucket in Redis<br/>→ Caching (Redis)"]
    RL --> SHED["load shedding, 429<br/>→ Reliability"]
    RL --> RETRY["client retries with backoff<br/>→ retry storms"]
    GW --> BFF["BFF per client"]
    BFF --> STYLES["REST, GraphQL, gRPC<br/>→ Compute: API styles"]
    GW --> OBS["access logs, RED metrics<br/>→ Observability"]
    GW --> WR["waiting room<br/>→ Messaging (queue)"]

Palette components: apigw · auth (issues the tokens the gateway validates) · cache (shared rate-limit counters) · queue (the waiting room) · waf (coarse limits per IP, before the gateway). Scenarios: rate-limiter, retry-storm, flash-sale. Continues in: Case study: rate limiter, Reliability — patterns, Network & Security — identity, Hands-on 4.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• An API gateway is the single entry point for APIs: routing, authentication offload, rate limits, transformations, aggregation and observability — cross-cutting concerns only.
  • The BFF pattern gives each client type its own tailored layer.
  • Token bucket (capacity = burst, refill = sustained rate) is the default rate-limiting algorithm; leaky bucket smooths output; fixed window allows 2× bursts at boundaries; sliding window log is exact but memory-heavy; sliding window counter is a cheap, accurate approximation.
  • Across replicas, keep counters in Redis and update them atomically (Lua); decide whether to fail open or closed.
  • Limit in layers (edge, gateway, service), answer 429 with Retry-After, and make clients back off with jitter.

  1. RICHARDSON, C. Pattern: API Gateway / Backends for Frontends. microservices.io. ↩

  2. NEWMAN, S. Backends For Frontends, 2015. See also NEWMAN, S. Building Microservices, 2nd ed. O'Reilly, 2021. ↩

  3. XU, A. System Design Interview — An Insider's Guide, vol. 1, ch. 4 "Design a rate limiter". Byte Code LLC, 2020. ↩

  4. CLOUDFLARE. How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains. Cloudflare Blog, 2017. ↩

  5. IETF HTTPAPI WG. RateLimit header fields for HTTP. Internet-Draft. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
At 10:00 the BoxOffice stadium sale opens and 2 million phones ask the same two questions almost at once: "where is boxoffice.com?" and "give me the event page". If both questions travel all the way to the BoxOffice servers in São Paulo, the servers drown before a single seat is sold. The Domain Name System (DNS) and a Content Delivery Network (CDN) exist so that most of those questions are answered close to the fan, by machines that BoxOffice does not even operate.

This page covers the first two hops of the request's journey: DNS decides where a client goes; the CDN decides whether the request needs to go any further.

items.title: DNS: the Internet's phone book
items.text:
Computers talk to IP addresses (203.0.113.10, 2001:db8::10); people type names (boxoffice.com). DNS translates the name into addresses. It is one of the oldest and largest distributed systems in existence: a hierarchical, delegated, heavily cached database1.

  • Hierarchical: names are read from right to left. The root (.) knows who is responsible for com.; com. knows who is responsible for boxoffice.com.; boxoffice.com. knows the address of api.boxoffice.com.
  • Delegated: each level is run by a different organisation. BoxOffice controls only its own zone, boxoffice.com, through its authoritative name servers (usually a managed service such as Route 53 or Cloudflare DNS).
  • Cached: every answer carries a TTL (time to live, in seconds). Resolvers keep the answer for that long, so the vast majority of lookups never reach the authoritative servers.

items.title: Resolution, step by step
items.text:
When the fan's phone needs api.boxoffice.com, it does not walk the hierarchy itself. A tiny stub resolver in the operating system asks a recursive resolver (the one from the mobile carrier, or a public one such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8), which does the work and caches the results:

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Phone (stub resolver)
    participant R as Recursive resolver
    participant Root as Root server
    participant TLD as .com TLD server
    participant A as boxoffice.com authoritative
    P->>R: A? api.boxoffice.com
    Note over R: cache miss
    R->>Root: A? api.boxoffice.com
    Root-->>R: ask .com (NS a.gtld-servers.net)
    R->>TLD: A? api.boxoffice.com
    TLD-->>R: ask boxoffice.com (NS ns1.boxoffice-dns.net)
    R->>A: A? api.boxoffice.com
    A-->>R: 203.0.113.10, TTL 60
    Note over R: cache for 60 s
    R-->>P: 203.0.113.10
    P->>R: A? api.boxoffice.com (another fan, 5 s later)
    R-->>P: 203.0.113.10 (from cache)

A cold lookup costs several round trips (tens to hundreds of milliseconds); a cached one costs a single round trip to the resolver, or nothing at all when the answer is in the operating system or browser cache. In practice the root and .com answers are almost always cached too (their TTLs are one to two days), so a typical miss costs just one trip from the resolver to the authoritative server.

Think first: 2 million fans look up boxoffice.com at 10:00. How many queries reach BoxOffice's authoritative servers?

Far fewer than 2 million. Fans share a few thousand recursive resolvers (their mobile carriers, ISPs and public resolvers). Each resolver asks the authoritative server once per TTL and serves everyone else from its cache. With a 60 s TTL and, say, 5 000 active resolvers, the authoritative servers see on the order of 5 000 queries per minute — about 80 per second. DNS caching is the first and most effective load shield on the Internet.

items.title: Record types
items.text: Type Maps Example Used for A name → IPv4 address api.boxoffice.com → 203.0.113.10 the basic lookup AAAA name → IPv6 address api.boxoffice.com → 2001:db8::10 IPv6 clients (most mobile networks) CNAME name → another name (alias) www.boxoffice.com → d123.cloudfront.net pointing at a CDN or load balancer whose IPs change ALIAS / ANAME apex name → another name (provider feature) boxoffice.com → my-alb.amazonaws.com a CNAME is not allowed at the zone apex; providers flatten it NS zone → its name servers boxoffice.com → ns1.boxoffice-dns.net delegation MX domain → mail servers boxoffice.com → mail.provider.com receiving e-mail TXT name → free text v=spf1 include:… domain ownership proofs, SPF/DKIM/DMARC for e-mail SRV service → host + port _sip._tcp.boxoffice.com service discovery (Kubernetes DNS uses it internally) CAA domain → allowed certificate authorities 0 issue "letsencrypt.org" restricts who may issue TLS certificates for the domain

items.title: TTL: freshness versus load
items.text:
The TTL is a classic trade-off between how fast a change propagates and how much load and latency the lookups cost:

TTL Change propagates in Lookup load / latency Good for 5–60 s about a minute many more queries; more cold lookups for users failover records, records you plan to change 5–60 min about an hour low ordinary records 1–2 days days minimal NS records, things that never change

Lower the TTL before a migration

If you are going to move api.boxoffice.com to a new load balancer next Tuesday, lower its TTL from 1 hour to 60 seconds on Monday (at least one old TTL in advance). Resolvers that cached the old record with the 1-hour TTL will have expired it by Tuesday, and the switch will take about a minute instead of an hour. Raise the TTL again after the migration.

items.title: Routing with DNS: GeoDNS, latency, weights and failover
items.text:
Because the authoritative server chooses the answer, it can give different answers to different clients. Managed DNS services offer several routing policies4:

Policy The answer depends on BoxOffice use Simple nothing; always the same records development environments Geolocation (GeoDNS) the client's country or continent (estimated from the resolver's IP, or from the EDNS Client Subnet option) send fans in Europe to the EU region for data-residency rules Latency-based the region with the lowest measured latency from the client's network São Paulo fans to sa-east-1, Lisbon fans to eu-west-1 Weighted a configured percentage send 5% of traffic to a new region or stack (DNS-level canary) Failover the result of a health check the secondary region answers only when the primary is unhealthy

DNS failover is the simplest form of multi-region disaster recovery: the DNS provider probes https://sa.boxoffice.com/health every 10–30 s from several locations; after a few failures it stops returning the primary's address and returns the secondary's.

sequenceDiagram
    participant HC as DNS health checker
    participant P as Region SP (primary)
    participant S as Region US (secondary)
    participant F as Fan's resolver
    HC->>P: GET /health
    P-->>HC: 200 OK
    F->>HC: A? api.boxoffice.com
    HC-->>F: SP address (TTL 60)
    Note over P: region outage
    HC->>P: GET /health
    Note over HC: 3 failures in a row: mark SP unhealthy
    F->>HC: A? api.boxoffice.com (after its TTL expired)
    HC-->>F: US address (TTL 60)
    F->>S: traffic now goes to the secondary

DNS failover is not instant

The time to fail over is roughly detection + TTL: with a 30 s health-check interval, 3 failures to declare the primary down and a 60 s TTL, clients move after about 90 s + 60 s = 2.5 minutes in the best case. In practice it is longer: some resolvers and clients ignore low TTLs (ISP resolvers that enforce a minimum TTL, applications that resolve a name once and keep the address in a connection pool, older devices), and long-lived connections keep talking to the dead region until they break. DNS failover is good for regional disasters; for failing servers inside a region, use a load balancer with health checks, which reacts in seconds (Load Balancing).

Try it. Open the multi-region scenario and run the load profile. Then trigger the outage of the primary region (chaos high, or disable the region in the panel). Watch how long errors last before DNS sends traffic to the secondary, and change the DNS TTL to see how it stretches or shortens that window.

Open the full playground

items.title: Anycast
items.text:
With ordinary (unicast) addressing, one IP address belongs to one place. With anycast, the same IP address is announced over BGP (the Border Gateway Protocol that glues the Internet's networks together) from many locations at once, and each packet is delivered by the network to the nearest one, in routing terms.

flowchart LR
    f1([Fan in São Paulo]) --> sp["Edge São Paulo<br/>announces 198.51.100.1"]
    f2([Fan in Lisbon]) --> li["Edge Lisbon<br/>announces 198.51.100.1"]
    f3([Fan in Tokyo]) --> tk["Edge Tokyo<br/>announces 198.51.100.1"]

Anycast gives three things at once, without any DNS trick:

  • Low latency: every client reaches a nearby location.
  • Automatic failover: if a location stops announcing the address, routing converges to the next-nearest one, typically within seconds.
  • DDoS absorption: an attack from a global botnet is split among all the locations instead of hitting one (see edge security).

The root DNS servers, public resolvers like 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8, and every large CDN use anycast. Anycast works best with short, mostly stateless exchanges (DNS over UDP, HTTP requests at an edge cache); a route change in the middle of a long TCP connection can break it, which large providers mitigate with careful routing.

items.title: CDN: bring the content to the fan
items.text:
A CDN is a network of caching reverse proxies — points of presence (PoPs), hundreds of them around the world — that store copies of your content close to users3. A fan in Recife who asks for the BoxOffice logo receives it from a PoP in Recife or Fortaleza, not from the origin in São Paulo; a fan in Lisbon receives it from Lisbon, not from across the Atlantic.

A CDN does three jobs at once5:

  1. Latency: content travels a few kilometres instead of thousands. A round trip across the Atlantic costs around 100–150 ms; to a PoP in the same city, a few milliseconds.
  2. Offload: every cache hit is a request the origin (your servers) never sees. This is often the main reason for a CDN in a system design.
  3. Protection: the CDN's capacity and anycast network absorb traffic spikes and attacks before they reach you.
sequenceDiagram
    participant F1 as Fan 1 (Recife)
    participant E as CDN PoP Recife
    participant O as Origin (São Paulo)
    participant F2 as Fan 2 (Recife)
    F1->>E: GET /img/stadium.webp
    Note over E: MISS: not in cache
    E->>O: GET /img/stadium.webp
    O-->>E: 200, Cache-Control: max-age=86400
    E-->>F1: 200 (stored for 1 day)
    F2->>E: GET /img/stadium.webp
    Note over E: HIT
    E-->>F2: 200 from the PoP (origin untouched)

items.title: Pull versus push
items.text:
Model How content gets to the PoPs Pros Cons Good for Pull (origin pull) the PoP fetches from the origin on the first miss, then caches it zero upload work; only popular content occupies the cache the first request in each PoP is slow (a miss) websites, APIs, almost everything Push you upload content to the CDN storage in advance no cold misses; predictable you manage uploads, versions and deletion large files known in advance: video, software downloads, game patches

Most designs use pull in front of an origin, and that origin is frequently an object store (S3, Cloud Storage, Azure Blob — the objstore component) for static files and media.

items.title: The cache key
items.text:
The CDN stores each response under a cache key — by default, the host plus the URL path plus the query string. Two requests with the same key share the cached copy. Getting the key right is most of the work:

  • Too specific a key fragments the cache: /events/42?utm_source=instagram and /events/42?utm_source=email are the same page, but with the default key they are cached twice and both miss. Remove tracking parameters from the key, or sort query parameters.
  • Too generic a key leaks data: if the response depends on a cookie (session=…) or a header (Accept-Language) that is not in the key, one fan may receive a page personalised for another.
  • The Vary response header tells caches which request headers change the response (Vary: Accept-Encoding is normal; Vary: Cookie effectively disables shared caching).

items.title: Cache-Control: the origin decides
items.text:
The origin tells every cache — the browser, the CDN, any proxy in between — what it may do with a response through the Cache-Control header2:

Directive Meaning max-age=N the response is fresh for N seconds (in any cache) s-maxage=N freshness for shared caches (CDN, proxies) only; overrides max-age there public / private may be stored by shared caches / only by the user's browser no-cache may be stored, but must be revalidated with the origin before each use no-store must not be stored anywhere (personal data, payment pages) stale-while-revalidate=N after expiry, serve the stale copy for up to N s while fetching a fresh one in the background stale-if-error=N if the origin fails, keep serving the stale copy for up to N s immutable the content will never change at this URL; do not even revalidate

Revalidation uses validators: the origin sends an ETag (a version identifier) or Last-Modified; the cache asks If-None-Match: "v42", and the origin answers 304 Not Modified with no body when nothing changed — cheap for both sides.

Typical BoxOffice responses
# fingerprinted JavaScript bundle: cache "forever"
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# event page HTML: short in browsers, longer at the CDN, survive origin hiccups
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60, stale-if-error=3600

# seat availability JSON during the sale: micro-cache at the CDN for one second
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=1, stale-while-revalidate=1

# the fan's order and payment pages: never cache
Cache-Control: private, no-store

items.title: Invalidation: purge or version?
items.text:
The event's poster image changed. How do the 300 PoPs learn about it? There are two strategies:

  • Purge (invalidation): call the CDN API to remove /img/stadium.webp (or a tag, or a prefix) from every PoP. The next request misses and fetches the new version. Purges are not instantaneous — they propagate in seconds to minutes, depending on the provider — and browsers that already cached the old version with max-age will not be purged at all.
  • Versioned (fingerprinted) URLs: never change a file in place. The build produces app.3f9a1c.js; a new build produces app.b71e02.js and the HTML references the new name. Old and new versions coexist, caches never serve the wrong one, and the files can be cached with immutable for a year. Only the small HTML that references them needs a short TTL.

Prefer versioned URLs for every static asset and keep purges for the exceptional cases (an error on a published page, legal take-downs). This is the edge version of the oldest joke in computing — there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things — and versioned URLs solve the first by doing the second. Invalidation in general is studied in the caching class.

items.title: Origin shield and tiered caching
items.text:
With 300 PoPs, a new file can cause 300 misses — one per PoP — that all hit the origin. A tiered cache (or origin shield) adds a middle layer: PoPs ask a regional cache, and only the regional cache asks the origin. The origin sees one request per object instead of one per PoP, and request collapsing at the shield merges simultaneous misses for the same object into a single origin fetch.

flowchart LR
    p1[PoP Recife] --> sh[Origin shield<br/>São Paulo]
    p2[PoP Porto Alegre] --> sh
    p3[PoP Manaus] --> sh
    sh --> o[(Origin)]

items.title: How much does the hit ratio matter?
items.text:
The fraction of requests the CDN serves from cache is the hit ratio. The load on the origin is the miss fraction times the traffic, so every extra "nine" of hit ratio divides the origin load by ten. Suppose (illustrative assumption) 200 000 requests per second reach the edge during the sale:

2026-10-23T08:15:46.104732 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Going from 90% to 99% hit ratio looks like a small improvement ("only nine points"), but it cuts the origin load from 20 000 to 2 000 requests per second — ten times fewer servers. When you discuss a CDN in an interview, talk about the miss rate, not the hit rate: it is the number that sizes the origin.

Try it. Load the CDN scenario and run the load profile. Lower the CDN hit ratio (or the TTL) step by step and watch the request rate and p99 latency at the app servers grow; then raise it and see how few app replicas you need. Finally, purge the cache during the run: the sudden wave of misses is a small-scale stampede on the origin.

Open the full playground

items.title: Caching dynamic content: micro-caching
items.text: "Dynamic" does not mean "uncacheable". The seat-availability JSON of the stadium show changes all the time, but nobody is harmed if it is one second old. If every PoP caches it for 1 s (s-maxage=1), the origin receives at most one request per second per PoP (or per shield, with tiered caching), no matter how many fans are polling. With 2 million fans polling every 5 seconds — 400 000 requests per second — and 50 PoPs serving Brazil, the origin sees about 50 requests per second for that endpoint. The seat map is at most a second stale; the hold itself (POST /api/holds) is never cached and is checked against the database, so a stale map can never cause a double booking.

items.title: Edge compute
items.text:
Modern CDNs also run your code in the PoPs: Cloudflare Workers, AWS CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge, Fastly Compute, Akamai EdgeWorkers. These are small functions (milliseconds of CPU, limited memory, usually JavaScript or WebAssembly) executed on each request, before the cache or the origin. Good uses:

  • Validate a waiting-room token or a JWT signature at the edge and reject invalid requests before they cross the ocean.
  • Rewrite and redirect: A/B tests, language redirects, normalising the cache key (removing utm_* parameters).
  • Assemble responses from cached fragments, or add security headers.
  • Serve a waiting-room page entirely from the edge while the origin is protected.

Bad uses: anything that needs your database on every request (the function is far from the data, so each call crosses the network anyway), long computations, and business logic that would be better tested and versioned in a service.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source / other
  • DNS: Route 53 (latency, geolocation, weighted and failover routing; health checks).
  • CDN: CloudFront, with CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge for edge compute; Origin Shield.
  • Origin: S3 for static files and media; Application Load Balancer for APIs.
  • Protection: AWS WAF and AWS Shield (Standard is included; Advanced is paid).
  • DNS: Cloud DNS (with geolocation and failover routing policies).
  • CDN: Cloud CDN, attached to the global external Application Load Balancer; Media CDN for video.
  • Origin: Cloud Storage buckets or backend services behind the load balancer.
  • Protection: Cloud Armor (WAF rules and DDoS protection).
  • DNS: Azure DNS; Traffic Manager for DNS-based routing (performance, priority, weighted, geographic).
  • CDN: Azure Front Door (global L7 entry point with CDN, WAF and routing).
  • Origin: Blob Storage, App Service, AKS behind Application Gateway.
  • Protection: Azure WAF and Azure DDoS Protection.
  • DNS: BIND, PowerDNS, CoreDNS (the DNS inside Kubernetes); managed: Cloudflare DNS, NS1.
  • CDN: Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, Bunny; self-hosted caching with Varnish or Nginx proxy_cache.
  • Edge compute: Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, Akamai EdgeWorkers.

items.title: Trade-offs at a glance
items.text:
Decision Option A Option B Choose A when… DNS TTL short (30–60 s) long (hours) you need fast failover or plan a change Routing latency-based / GeoDNS anycast you need per-region control (data residency, canaries) Failover DNS failover anycast / global LB a few minutes of failover time is acceptable and cheap matters CDN model pull push content is requested unpredictably (most web traffic) Freshness purge on change versioned URLs the URL cannot change (the HTML page itself, an API) Dynamic data micro-cache (1–5 s) no cache slightly stale data is acceptable and the endpoint is hot Logic edge function origin service the logic is small, stateless and must run before the origin

BoxOffice: DNS and CDN for the stadium sale

  • boxoffice.com and www → ALIAS/CNAME to the CDN, which answers from anycast addresses. api.boxoffice.com has latency-based records for the São Paulo and Virginia regions, with failover health checks and a 60 s TTL.
  • Static assets (JavaScript, CSS, fonts) are fingerprinted and cached for a year with immutable. Event posters live in the object store and are cached for a day; the rare change uses a new file name.
  • The event page HTML: s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60, stale-if-error=3600. If the origin goes down during the sale, fans still see the page.
  • Seat availability: micro-cached for 1 s at the CDN, with an origin shield in São Paulo. Holds, orders and payments: private, no-store, never cached, always go to the origin.
  • An edge function checks the waiting-room token on every /api/* request; requests without a valid token receive the waiting-room page from the edge.

Back-of-the-envelope: 2 M fans × (1 page + 30 assets) at the opening, plus polling, is millions of requests per minute; with a 99% hit ratio on assets and micro-caching on the seat map, the origin sees a few thousand requests per second, almost all of them holds and orders — the requests that actually need the origin.

In the interview

  • Say what you cache at the CDN and for how long: "static assets and images with versioned URLs and long TTLs; the event page for minutes with stale-while-revalidate; the seat map micro-cached for 1 s; nothing user-specific."
  • Quantify with the miss rate: "at 99% hit ratio, 200 k req/s at the edge become 2 k at the origin."
  • Mention DNS in one sentence — "latency-based DNS to the nearest region, with health-checked failover" — and know its limit: failover takes about detection + TTL, minutes, not seconds.
  • For a global, read-heavy system (news feed, video streaming, URL shortener redirects), the CDN is often the most important component of the design.

Pitfalls

  • Caching personalised responses in a shared cache because a cookie or Authorization header is not in the cache key: one user sees another's data. Mark them private or no-store.
  • Purging as a deploy strategy: purges are slow, can fail and do not reach browsers. Use versioned file names.
  • Cache-busting by accident: random query parameters, timestamps in URLs or Vary: Cookie silently drop the hit ratio to zero.
  • Thundering herd on expiry: if a hot object expires in every PoP at the same time, they all miss together. Origin shield, request collapsing and stale-while-revalidate prevent it.
  • Trusting DNS failover for fast recovery: low TTLs are not always respected; long-lived connections do not re-resolve.
  • Forgetting that the CDN is a dependency: a CDN outage takes your site down too. Very large sites use two CDNs (multi-CDN) with DNS steering between them.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    TTL["DNS TTL"] --> FO["failover speed<br/>→ multi-region (class 3)"]
    ANY["anycast"] --> DDOS["DDoS absorption<br/>→ edge security"]
    GEO["GeoDNS / latency routing"] --> HOME["home region per event<br/>→ CAP & PACELC"]
    HIT["CDN hit ratio"] --> ORIGIN["origin load<br/>→ Estimation"]
    CC["Cache-Control, TTL"] --> STALE["staleness = eventual consistency<br/>→ Replication & Consistency"]
    INV["invalidation, versioned URLs"] --> CACHE["cache invalidation<br/>→ Caching"]
    EC["edge compute"] --> WR["waiting-room token check<br/>→ API gateway"]

Palette components: dns · cdn · objstore (the usual CDN origin for images and video) · cache (the next cache layer behind the CDN). Scenarios: cdn-static, multi-region, video-streaming. Continues in: Caching — patterns, Distributed Systems — CAP & PACELC, Case study: video streaming.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• DNS is a hierarchical, delegated, cached database; caching by recursive resolvers means the authoritative servers see one query per resolver per TTL.
  • The TTL trades change propagation against lookup load; lower it before a planned change.
  • DNS can route by geography, latency, weight or health; DNS failover takes about detection + TTL, and some clients ignore TTLs.
  • Anycast announces the same IP from many locations: low latency, fast failover and DDoS absorption.
  • A CDN cuts latency, offloads the origin and absorbs attacks; most CDNs pull from the origin and cache by a cache key you must design.
  • The origin controls caching with Cache-Control; prefer versioned URLs to purges; micro-caching makes hot dynamic endpoints cheap.
  • Every extra nine of hit ratio divides the origin load by ten.

  1. MOCKAPETRIS, P. RFC 1034 — Domain Names: Concepts and Facilities and RFC 1035 — Implementation and Specification. IETF, 1987. ↩

  2. FIELDING, R.; NOTTINGHAM, M.; RESCHKE, J. RFC 9111 — HTTP Caching. IETF, 2022. See also NOTTINGHAM, M. RFC 5861 — HTTP Cache-Control Extensions for Stale Content, 2010. ↩

  3. CLOUDFLARE. What is a CDN? and What is anycast? — Cloudflare Learning Center. ↩

  4. AWS. Amazon Route 53 — Choosing a routing policy. AWS Documentation. ↩

  5. XU, A. System Design Interview — An Insider's Guide, vol. 1, ch. 1 (CDN, DNS). Byte Code LLC, 2020. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
One inventory replica handles, say, 800 holds per second before its latency climbs (an illustrative number — in hands-on 2 you measure the real one for catalog). The stadium sale needs 5 000. The answer is obvious — run seven or eight replicas — but it immediately raises the questions this page answers: who decides which replica gets each request? What happens when one replica dies, or is slow, or is being redeployed? And what if the request needs to land on a specific replica?

A load balancer (LB) is the component that spreads work across a pool of interchangeable servers — the backends, targets or upstreams — so that the pool behaves like a single, larger and more reliable server1. It is the lb component of the palette, and, in Kubernetes, the ingress component plays the same role for HTTP traffic entering the cluster.

items.title: Why load balance?
items.text:
A load balancer gives you three things at once:

  • Scalability: add replicas to handle more traffic (horizontal scaling, or scale-out), instead of buying a bigger machine (vertical scaling, or scale-up).
  • Availability: when a replica fails its health checks, the LB stops sending it traffic; users do not notice.
  • Operability: you can drain, replace and upgrade replicas one at a time (rolling deploys), with no downtime.

This only works if the replicas are interchangeable — any one of them can serve any request. That is why application servers should be stateless: session data, carts and seat holds live in a shared store (Redis, PostgreSQL), not in the memory of one replica. Statelessness is the precondition for everything on this page.

flowchart LR
    f([Fans]) --> lb{{Load balancer}}
    lb --> a1[inventory-1]
    lb --> a2[inventory-2]
    lb --> a3[inventory-3]
    lb -.->|"health check fails: skipped"| a4["inventory-4 ✗"]
    a1 --> db[(PostgreSQL)]
    a2 --> db
    a3 --> db

items.title: L4 versus L7
items.text:
Load balancers differ in how much of the traffic they understand.

A layer-4 (L4) load balancer works with TCP connections or UDP datagrams. It sees IP addresses and ports, picks a backend when a connection opens, and forwards the bytes of that connection to it. It does not read HTTP: it cannot route by path, it cannot see that one connection carries 1 000 requests, and it does not need to decrypt TLS.

A layer-7 (L7) load balancer speaks HTTP. It terminates the client's connection, reads each request (method, path, headers, cookies), picks a backend per request, and opens (or reuses) its own connection to it. It is a full reverse proxy.

L4 (transport) L7 (application) Unit of balancing connection (or packet flow) request Sees IPs, ports, TCP/UDP method, path, host, headers, cookies, body TLS usually passes through encrypted usually terminates (decrypts) Routing by path or host no yes: /api/holds → inventory, /api/orders → order Retries, header rewrites, caching, compression no yes Performance very high (millions of connections, microseconds) high, but more CPU per request Long-lived connections (gRPC, HTTP/2, WebSockets) balanced once, at connect time can balance each request/stream Examples AWS NLB, GCP passthrough Network LB, Azure Load Balancer, Linux IPVS, HAProxy in TCP mode AWS ALB, GCP Application LB, Azure Application Gateway, Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik

A common production layout uses both: an L4 load balancer (or anycast) at the front for raw capacity and DDoS resilience, spreading connections over a fleet of L7 proxies (Envoy, Nginx) that do TLS, routing and per-request balancing. This is how Google's and Cloudflare's front ends are built.

Think first: the order service calls inventory over gRPC through an L4 load balancer. There are 4 inventory replicas, but one of them receives almost all the traffic. Why?

gRPC runs over HTTP/2, which multiplexes many requests over one long-lived TCP connection. An L4 load balancer chooses a backend once per connection, so if order opened one connection (or a few) and keeps it for hours, all its requests go to the same replica. Fixes: an L7 load balancer that balances per request (Envoy, a service mesh), client-side load balancing in the gRPC library, or limiting connection age (max_connection_age) so clients reconnect periodically. More in Protocols.

items.title: Balancing algorithms
items.text:
Once the LB has a list of healthy backends, it needs a rule to pick one. The rule matters most when requests have different costs or backends have different speeds.

Algorithm How it picks Strength Weakness Round robin next backend in a fixed cycle simple, fair when requests and servers are uniform ignores load: a slow server gets as many requests as a fast one Weighted round robin cycle proportional to weights (e.g. 2:1) mixes machine sizes; canaries (5% weight) weights are static Random uniform random choice stateless, works across many LB instances short-term imbalance Least connections backend with the fewest active connections/requests adapts to slow requests and slow servers needs shared state; misleading with long-lived idle connections Least response time / EWMA lowest recent latency (exponentially weighted moving average) × load routes around degraded servers can herd onto a server that just became fast Power of two choices (P2C) pick two backends at random, send to the less loaded near-optimal balance with almost no coordination needs a load signal (in-flight requests) IP hash / source hash hash(client IP) mod N same client → same backend, no cookie uneven with NATs and proxies; reshuffles when N changes Consistent hashing hash(key) placed on a ring of backends same key → same backend; adding a node moves only ~1/N keys needs virtual nodes for balance; hot keys stay hot

Two of these deserve more attention.

items.title: Power of two choices
items.text: Choosing the least-loaded backend among all of them sounds ideal, but with many load balancer instances (each with a slightly stale view) they all pick the same "least loaded" server at once and overload it — a herd. Picking a backend at random avoids the herd but leaves some servers much busier than others by chance. Mitzenmacher showed that a tiny compromise gets almost the best of both: sample two backends at random and pick the less loaded one2. The maximum load drops exponentially compared with pure random choice, and there is no herd, because different LB instances sample different pairs. Envoy, Nginx (random two least_conn), HAProxy and the gRPC libraries implement it; it is the default choice of many modern proxies.

items.title: Consistent hashing
items.text:
Sometimes you want the same key to go to the same backend: a cache server that holds a user's data, a WebSocket server that holds a chat room, a shard of a key-value store. The naive way is server = hash(key) mod N. It works until N changes: going from 5 to 6 servers changes the result of mod for most keys, so almost every key moves — every cache misses at once.

Consistent hashing (Karger et al., 1997)3 places both servers and keys on a circle of hash values (the ring). A key belongs to the first server found walking clockwise from its position.

flowchart LR
    A["node A<br/>position 10"] -->|clockwise| B["node B<br/>position 40"]
    B -->|clockwise| D["new node D<br/>position 55"]
    D -->|clockwise| C["node C<br/>position 75"]
    C -->|"clockwise (wraps to 0)"| A
    k1(["hold:42 → 30"]) -.->|owner| B
    k2(["hold:77 → 50"]) -.->|"owner: was C, now D"| D
    k3(["hold:91 → 90"]) -.->|"owner (wraps)"| A

In the diagram, positions go from 0 to 99: hold:42 hashes to 30 and belongs to B (the first node at or after 30); hold:91 hashes to 90 and wraps around to A. When node D joins at position 55, only the keys between 40 and 55 — such as hold:77 — move from C to D; nothing else changes. In general, when a server is added, it only takes over the keys between itself and its predecessor — about 1/(N+1) of them; when one is removed, only its keys move, to its successor.

With one point per server, the arcs of the ring have very different lengths, so some servers own much more than their share. The fix is virtual nodes5: each physical server is placed on the ring many times (100–200 points, for example), so the arcs average out. Virtual nodes also make it easy to give a bigger machine more points (weights) and, when a server leaves, spread its keys over all the others instead of dumping them on one neighbour.

The simulation below hashes 40 000 seat-hold keys onto 5 nodes. On the left, one point per node versus 200 virtual nodes per node; on the right, the fraction of keys that change owner when a 6th node joins:

2026-10-23T08:15:46.407206 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Two lessons from the figure. With a single point per node, one node owns about half of all keys and another almost none — the ring is badly unbalanced. With 200 virtual nodes, every node is close to the ideal 20%. And when the 6th node arrives, hash mod N remaps about 83% of the keys (5/6 of them, as theory predicts), while the ring remaps about 17% — the 1/6 that the new node must own anyway.

Consistent hashing appears all over system design: Nginx hash $key consistent, Envoy's ring hash and Maglev balancers, memcached clients, Amazon's Dynamo and Cassandra for data partitioning (studied in Databases — partitioning), and Discord-style chat servers that pin a channel to a node.

Consistent hashing does not fix hot keys

It balances many keys. If one key is very popular — the stadium show's seat map — all its requests still go to one node. Hot keys need other tools: caching, replicating the hot key, or splitting it.

items.title: Service discovery: how the LB knows the replicas
items.text:
Replicas come and go — autoscaling adds them at 09:58, a deploy replaces them, a crash removes one — and their IP addresses change every time. Before a load balancer can pick a healthy replica, something must tell it which replicas exist right now. That is service discovery, and it has two shapes:

flowchart LR
    subgraph server ["Server-side discovery"]
        C1([gateway]) -->|"inventory.svc"| LB1["load balancer / kube-proxy"]
        LB1 --> R1[inventory-1]
        LB1 --> R2[inventory-2]
        REG1[("registry<br/>(K8s endpoints)")] -.->|"watch"| LB1
    end
    subgraph client ["Client-side discovery"]
        C2([gateway]) -->|"1 · who serves inventory?"| REG2[("registry<br/>(Consul, Eureka)")]
        REG2 -->|"2 · [10.0.1.7, 10.0.2.9]"| C2
        C2 -->|"3 · picks one itself"| R3[inventory-3]
    end
Server-side discovery Client-side discovery Who chooses the replica a load balancer or proxy in the path the calling service, with a client library Registry the platform (Kubernetes endpoints, cloud target groups) Consul, Eureka, etcd, DNS SRV records Extra hop yes (the proxy) no Language coupling none: any client just calls a name every language needs the library (or a sidecar does it — the service mesh) Typical today Kubernetes Service + DNS, cloud LBs gRPC clients with xDS, service meshes, older Spring Cloud Netflix stacks

Registration happens either by the platform (Kubernetes adds a pod's IP to the Service's endpoints when its readiness probe passes) or by the instance itself (it registers on start and sends heartbeats; a missed heartbeat removes it). Either way, discovery and health checks are two halves of the same question — which replicas can serve now? — and the registry is a small, strongly consistent store (etcd, Consul's Raft) for the reasons in Distributed Systems — consensus.

items.title: Health checks
items.text:
A load balancer is only as good as its knowledge of which backends are healthy. There are two complementary ways to find out:

Type How Reacts to Example Active the LB probes each backend periodically (GET /actuator/health/readiness every 5 s; 2 failures → unhealthy; 3 successes → healthy again) crashed, hung or not-ready backends, even with no traffic AWS target groups, Nginx Plus health_check, HAProxy check, Kubernetes readiness probes Passive (outlier detection) the LB watches real responses; a backend that returns many 5xx or timeouts is ejected for a while backends that pass the probe but fail real requests Envoy outlier detection, Nginx max_fails / fail_timeout

Design the health endpoint carefully. Readiness ("can I serve traffic now?") should check what the instance needs to answer requests — but if it checks a shared dependency such as the database, a database blip marks every replica unhealthy at once and the LB has nothing left to route to. The usual compromise: readiness reflects the instance's own state (started, warmed up, not overloaded, not shutting down); dependency failures are handled by timeouts and circuit breakers (Reliability — patterns).

items.title: Connection draining
items.text: When a replica is removed — scaled in, or replaced by a deploy — cutting it off abruptly fails every request in flight. Connection draining (deregistration delay) fixes this: the LB stops sending new requests to the replica, waits for the in-flight ones to finish (up to, say, 30 s), and only then removes it. In Kubernetes, the pod becomes not ready, is removed from the Service endpoints, and receives SIGTERM; the application should finish its current requests before exiting (Spring Boot: server.shutdown=graceful).

items.title: Sticky sessions
items.text:
Session affinity ("sticky sessions") makes the LB send every request from the same client to the same backend, using a cookie set by the LB or a hash of the client IP. It exists for applications that keep state in memory — a server-side session, an in-process cache, a WebSocket.

Sticky sessions Stateless replicas + shared store Where state lives in one replica's memory Redis / database / client token (JWT) A replica dies its users lose their session nothing is lost Balance uneven: heavy users stick to one replica any replica takes any request Scaling in / deploys must wait for sessions to end or lose them drain in seconds Extra cost none one network call to the shared store

Prefer stateless replicas. Use affinity only where the state is inherently local and cheap to rebuild — a WebSocket connection, a local cache that only improves hit ratio — and prefer consistent hashing on a meaningful key (user id, room id) to cookie stickiness, because it survives LB restarts and scales smoothly.

items.title: The load balancer must not be the weak point
items.text:
A single load balancer in front of ten replicas is a single point of failure. How the LB itself stays up depends on who runs it:

  • Managed cloud load balancers (ALB/NLB, Google Cloud Load Balancing, Azure Load Balancer) are distributed systems run by the provider across several availability zones; you get a DNS name or an IP, and the provider scales and replaces the underlying machines.
  • Self-hosted (Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy on VMs): run at least two, in an active-passive pair sharing a virtual IP (VIP) moved by VRRP (keepalived) when the active one fails, or active-active behind DNS or an L4 tier.
  • Anycast at the edge: the same IP announced from many locations (DNS & CDN).

There is also a hierarchy of scopes: a global load balancer (anycast or DNS-based) chooses the region; a regional load balancer chooses the zone and instance; inside Kubernetes, the Service and ingress choose the pod.

flowchart TB
    u([Fans worldwide]) --> g["Global LB / DNS<br/>chooses the region"]
    g --> r1["Regional LB São Paulo<br/>across 3 zones"]
    g --> r2["Regional LB Virginia"]
    r1 --> i1["Ingress / Gateway<br/>in the cluster"]
    i1 --> p1[inventory pods]
    i1 --> p2[order pods]

Try it. Load the scale-out scenario and run the load profile with 2 replicas; note p99 latency and errors. Increase the replica count until p99 stabilises. Then kill one replica while the test runs (chaos medium, or stop it in the panel): watch the health checks remove it, the error spike that lasts until they do, and the remaining replicas absorb the load. Try a different balancing algorithm and compare p99.

Open the full playground

items.title: A load balancer in practice: Nginx
items.text:
Hands-on 3 puts Nginx in front of three replicas of catalog. The core of the configuration is an upstream block:

nginx.conf
upstream catalog {
    least_conn;                                    # or: random two least_conn;  hash $arg_event consistent;
    server catalog-1:8080 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;   # passive health check
    server catalog-2:8080 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    server catalog-3:8080 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    keepalive 32;                                  # reuse connections to the backends
}

server {
    listen 80;

    location /api/events/ {
        proxy_pass http://catalog;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_connect_timeout 1s;
        proxy_read_timeout 5s;
        proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503;  # retry another replica (not POST/PATCH by default)
    }
}

Note what is configured besides the algorithm: timeouts toward the backends, keep-alive connections to them, and proxy_next_upstream, which retries a failed request on another replica. Nginx does not retry non-idempotent requests (such as POST) by default — retrying a POST /holds on another replica could create two holds.

items.title: Load balancing in Kubernetes
items.text:
In Kubernetes, three objects share the load-balancing work.

Service — a stable virtual IP and DNS name (inventory.boxoffice.svc.cluster.local) in front of the pods that match a label selector. Only ready pods are listed as endpoints. Traffic to the Service IP is spread across them at L4, by kube-proxy (iptables/IPVS rules) or by an eBPF data plane such as Cilium. A Service of type LoadBalancer also asks the cloud provider for an external L4 load balancer.

inventory-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: inventory
spec:
  selector:
    app: inventory
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

Ingress — the original API for L7 HTTP routing into the cluster: rules by host and path, TLS termination, all implemented by an ingress controller (Traefik, HAProxy, cloud controllers; the community ingress-nginx controller was very popular but has been retired by the Kubernetes project). The Ingress API is simple but limited: anything beyond host/path routing (header matching, traffic splitting, timeouts) requires controller-specific annotations, which are not portable.

ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: boxoffice
spec:
  ingressClassName: traefik
  tls:
    - hosts: [api.boxoffice.com]
      secretName: boxoffice-tls
  rules:
    - host: api.boxoffice.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api/holds
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: inventory
                port:
                  number: 80

Gateway API — the successor of Ingress, generally available since 20234. It splits the configuration by role, so that each team owns its part:

Resource Owned by Defines GatewayClass infrastructure provider which implementation (Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium, NGINX Gateway Fabric, cloud gateways) Gateway platform / cluster operators listeners: ports, protocols, hostnames, TLS certificates HTTPRoute (and GRPCRoute, TLSRoute, …) application teams routing rules: path, header and method matching, weights, filters, timeouts

Features that needed annotations in Ingress are part of the standard: weighted traffic splitting (canaries), header-based routing, request mirroring, timeouts and gRPC routing.

gateway.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: public
spec:
  gatewayClassName: envoy
  listeners:
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      hostname: api.boxoffice.com
      tls:
        certificateRefs:
          - name: boxoffice-tls
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: inventory
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /api/holds
      timeouts:
        request: 2s
      backendRefs:
        - name: inventory        # stable version: 95% of requests
          port: 80
          weight: 95
        - name: inventory-canary # new version: 5% of requests
          port: 80
          weight: 5

In hands-on 10 you deploy BoxOffice on a local cluster and expose it through an ingress; canary releases come back in the cloud-native class.

items.title: Trade-offs at a glance
items.text:
Decision Option A Option B Choose A when… Layer L4 L7 you need raw throughput, non-HTTP protocols or TLS pass-through Algorithm round robin least connections / P2C requests and servers are uniform Affinity consistent hashing on a key none (stateless) a backend holds useful per-key state (cache, room, shard) Health checks active only active + passive (outlier detection) traffic is low and failures are clean crashes Operation managed cloud LB self-hosted Nginx / HAProxy / Envoy you are on a cloud and want HA and scaling solved for you Kubernetes Ingress Gateway API a simple, existing setup; new designs should prefer Gateway API

BoxOffice: load balancing the core

  • A regional managed L7 load balancer terminates TLS for api.boxoffice.com, spreads requests across three availability zones and forwards them to the Kubernetes Gateway (Envoy Gateway), which routes by path: /api/events/** → catalog, /api/holds/** → inventory, /api/orders/** → order.
  • Algorithm: P2C on in-flight requests (least-request, the Envoy Gateway default), because hold requests vary in cost when there is lock contention on popular sections.
  • Health: readiness probes on /actuator/health/readiness (instance state only) plus outlier detection that ejects a pod returning 5 consecutive 5xx for 30 s.
  • Stateless services: holds live in PostgreSQL, sessions are JWTs; no sticky sessions. The one exception is the waiting-room WebSocket/SSE service, where connections are long-lived and balanced at connection time.
  • Deploys: graceful shutdown (30 s) and a 5% weighted canary route before the sale day.

In the interview

  • Draw the load balancer in front of every stateless tier, and say "the app servers are stateless, so the LB can send any request anywhere" — this justifies horizontal scaling.
  • Name the algorithm only when it matters: least connections / P2C for uneven request costs; consistent hashing when requests should reach the server that holds their data (cache nodes, chat rooms, shards). Know the 1/(N+1) property and why virtual nodes exist.
  • Mention health checks and draining when asked about failures or deploys.
  • If asked "isn't the LB a single point of failure?": managed LBs are replicated across zones; self-hosted ones run as an active-passive pair with a floating IP, or behind anycast/DNS.

Pitfalls

  • Stateful replicas behind a round-robin LB: logins "randomly" disappear because the session lives in another replica. Externalise state.
  • Readiness that checks shared dependencies: a database blip ejects every replica at once.
  • L4 balancing of long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connections: all traffic sticks to the first replicas; new replicas receive nothing after a scale-out.
  • Retrying non-idempotent requests at the LB: duplicated holds or orders.
  • No draining: every deploy causes a burst of 502s.
  • Forgetting the LB's own limits: connection tables, TLS handshakes per second and bandwidth are finite; managed LBs may also need pre-warming before a known spike — ask the provider before the sale.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    SD["service discovery"] --> LB["load balancer"]
    HC["health checks<br/>(readiness)"] --> LB
    LB --> ALG["algorithm: RR, least conn,<br/>P2C, consistent hashing"]
    ALG --> STATELESS["stateless replicas<br/>→ Compute"]
    ALG --> CH["consistent hashing<br/>→ sharding (class 6)"]
    LB --> HA["LB redundancy, anycast<br/>→ Reliability"]
    LB --> K8S["Service, Ingress, Gateway API<br/>→ Cloud-native"]
    STATELESS --> AS["autoscaling<br/>→ Compute"]
    HC --> OBS["health endpoints<br/>→ Observability"]

Palette components: lb · ingress · app (the replicas behind it) · healthcheck · mesh (client-side balancing in a sidecar). Scenarios: scale-out, chat (long-lived connections). Continues in: Compute — services, Databases — partitioning (consistent hashing for data), Cloud-native — Kubernetes, Hands-on 3.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• A load balancer turns a pool of stateless, interchangeable replicas into one scalable, highly available service.
  • L4 balances connections (fast, protocol-agnostic); L7 balances requests (routing, TLS, retries, per-request decisions).
  • Round robin for uniform work; least connections / power of two choices for uneven work; consistent hashing with virtual nodes when a key must stick to a server — adding a node moves only about 1/(N+1) of the keys.
  • Active and passive health checks remove failed replicas; draining makes deploys invisible.
  • Avoid sticky sessions; keep state in a shared store.
  • In Kubernetes: Service (L4, ready pods), Ingress (basic L7) and Gateway API (role-based, portable L7 routing with weights and timeouts).

  1. BEYER, B. et al. Site Reliability Engineering, ch. 19 "Load Balancing at the Frontend" and ch. 20 "Load Balancing in the Datacenter". O'Reilly, 2016. ↩

  2. MITZENMACHER, M. The Power of Two Choices in Randomized Load Balancing. IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems, 2001. ↩

  3. KARGER, D. et al. Consistent Hashing and Random Trees. ACM STOC, 1997. ↩

  4. KUBERNETES SIG NETWORK. Gateway API. Kubernetes documentation. ↩

  5. XU, A. System Design Interview — An Insider's Guide, vol. 1, ch. 5 "Design consistent hashing". Byte Code LLC, 2020. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
The BoxOffice seat map has a problem. During the sale, seats change colour every second as other fans hold them. The first version of the web app asked GET /api/events/42/seats every 2 seconds: 2 million fans × 0.5 requests per second = 1 million requests per second, most of them answering "nothing changed". Meanwhile, fans on a train in São Paulo complain that the app "freezes" every time the phone switches between cell towers. Both problems are protocol problems — the choice of how bytes travel between the phone and the edge — and both have good modern answers.

This page reviews the protocols that run on the edge: the three generations of HTTP, the TLS handshake that protects them, the options for real-time updates (polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events, WebSockets), and gRPC for service-to-service calls. The goal is not to memorise headers, but to know what each protocol costs in round trips and connections, and what it is good for.

items.title: Round trips are the currency
items.text:
Bandwidth keeps growing; the speed of light does not. A round-trip time (RTT) is the time a packet takes to go to the server and back: around 1–10 ms inside a city, around 30–60 ms across a continent, around 100–200 ms between continents. Every protocol exchange that waits for an answer costs at least one RTT, and on a new connection there are several of them before the first byte of data: one to open TCP, one or two for TLS7.

That is why the history of web protocols is mostly a history of removing round trips and using connections better.

items.title: HTTP/1.1
items.text:
HTTP/1.1 (1997, current specification RFC 9112) is a text protocol: the client writes GET /api/events/42 HTTP/1.1, headers, a blank line; the server answers with a status line, headers and a body1.

  • Persistent connections (keep-alive): one TCP connection can carry many requests one after the other, avoiding a new handshake for each.
  • One request at a time per connection: a second request must wait until the first response has arrived completely. If the first response is slow, everything behind it waits — head-of-line (HOL) blocking. (Pipelining, which was meant to fix this, was never usable in practice.)
  • Browsers work around it by opening about 6 parallel connections per host, and developers used to work around that with tricks like domain sharding, sprites and bundling.
  • Headers are plain text and repeated on every request: cookies and user agents can add hundreds of bytes per request.

HTTP/1.1 is still everywhere — between a load balancer and its backends, in simple clients, in curl — and it is perfectly fine for low-concurrency, request-response traffic.

items.title: HTTP/2
items.text:
HTTP/2 (2015, RFC 9113) keeps the same semantics — methods, status codes, headers — but changes how they travel2:

  • Binary framing: messages are split into frames, each tagged with a stream id.
  • Multiplexing: many requests and responses travel at the same time over one TCP connection, their frames interleaved. A slow response no longer blocks the others at the HTTP level.
  • Header compression (HPACK): repeated headers are sent as small references to a table shared by both ends.
  • Stream priorities and flow control per stream.

One connection per origin is enough, so the domain-sharding tricks become counterproductive. But one problem remains, one layer down: TCP delivers bytes in order. If a single packet is lost, TCP holds back all the bytes after it — of every stream — until the retransmission arrives. On a lossy mobile network, HTTP/2's single connection can be slower than HTTP/1.1's six. This is TCP head-of-line blocking, and it is the reason for HTTP/3.

items.title: HTTP/3 and QUIC
items.text:
HTTP/3 (2022, RFC 9114) runs over QUIC (RFC 9000), a transport protocol built on top of UDP3. QUIC moves into user space what TCP did in the kernel, and redesigns it:

  • Independent streams in the transport: a lost packet only delays the stream it belongs to; the others keep flowing. No TCP head-of-line blocking.
  • TLS 1.3 built in: the transport and cryptographic handshakes are combined, so a new connection needs 1 RTT before sending data — and a resumed one can send data in the very first packet (0-RTT).
  • Connection migration: a QUIC connection is identified by a connection ID, not by the (IP, port) pair. When the phone moves from Wi-Fi to 4G, its IP changes but the connection survives — no new handshake, no "freeze".
  • Always encrypted, including most of the transport headers, which also makes it harder for middleboxes to interfere.

The costs: UDP is sometimes blocked or throttled by corporate networks (browsers fall back to HTTP/2 automatically), QUIC uses more CPU than kernel TCP, and load balancers must route by connection ID to keep migrating connections on the same server. Browsers, CDNs and the big platforms adopted it quickly; inside the data centre, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 remain the norm.

HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3 Transport TCP TCP QUIC over UDP Format text binary frames binary frames Concurrency on one connection one request at a time multiplexed streams multiplexed, independent streams Head-of-line blocking HTTP and TCP level TCP level only none across streams Header compression none HPACK QPACK Handshake before data (new connection) TCP + TLS: 2–3 RTT TCP + TLS: 2–3 RTT 1 RTT (0-RTT on resumption) Survives IP change no no yes (connection migration) Typical place backends, simple clients browsers, gRPC, internal browsers and mobile ↔ CDN/edge

items.title: TLS 1.3: the handshake
items.text:
Every connection on the edge is encrypted with TLS. Before any HTTP data, client and server must agree on keys and the client must verify the server's certificate (that it really is boxoffice.com). TLS 1.2 needed two round trips for that; TLS 1.3 (2018, RFC 8446) needs one, by having the client guess the key-exchange parameters and send its key share immediately4.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Fan's phone
    participant S as CDN edge (boxoffice.com)
    C->>S: TCP SYN
    S-->>C: SYN-ACK
    C->>S: ACK + TLS ClientHello (key share, supported ciphers, SNI = boxoffice.com)
    S-->>C: ServerHello (key share) + certificate + Finished (encrypted)
    Note over C: verify certificate, derive keys
    C->>S: Finished + GET /api/events/42 (encrypted)
    S-->>C: 200 OK (encrypted)

With QUIC, the TCP exchange disappears: the first QUIC packet already carries the ClientHello, so the request goes out after one round trip. With 0-RTT resumption, a client that talked to the server recently reuses a pre-shared key and sends the request in the first flight — with a caveat: 0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker, so servers only accept idempotent requests (GET) in 0-RTT.

The chart counts the round trips before the first response byte on a new connection (server processing time ignored), at three distances:

2026-10-23T08:15:46.599187 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Two conclusions. First, the protocol matters most when the server is far away — 600 ms versus 150 ms intercontinental — which is also why CDNs terminate connections close to the user: with an edge in the same city, even TLS 1.2 costs only 40 ms. Second, the best handshake is the one you do not repeat: keep-alive and connection pooling (between the gateway and the services, too) make the setup cost disappear for every request after the first.

Think first: the mobile app makes 30 small API calls when the event screen opens. The API is in Virginia (RTT 150 ms from São Paulo) and the app opens a new HTTP/1.1 connection with TLS 1.2 for each call, 6 at a time. Roughly how long does it take?

Each call on a fresh connection costs 4 RTT ≈ 600 ms; 30 calls in batches of 6 means 5 batches ≈ 3 seconds, before any server time. Fixes, in order of impact: reuse connections (keep-alive) and multiplex them with HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 (all 30 calls over one connection: 1 handshake + roughly 1 RTT ≈ 300–450 ms); terminate TLS at an edge close to the fan; and aggregate the 30 calls into one screen-level call in a BFF (API gateway).

items.title: Real-time: getting updates to the client
items.text: HTTP is request-response: the client asks, the server answers. For the seat map, the waiting-room position or a chat, the server knows when something changed. There are four ways to get that information to the client.

items.title: Short polling
items.text: The client asks every N seconds: "anything new?". Trivial to implement and to cache, but wasteful (most answers are "no") and slow to react (up to N seconds of delay). Polling with micro-caching at the CDN (DNS & CDN) is a perfectly good design for the seat map when a few seconds of delay are acceptable.

items.title: Long polling
items.text: The client asks, and the server holds the request open until there is news (or a timeout of, say, 30 s), then answers; the client immediately asks again. Near real-time over plain HTTP, but every message costs a full request, and servers must hold many open requests.

items.title: Server-Sent Events (SSE)
items.text:
The client opens one ordinary HTTP request with Accept: text/event-stream; the server keeps the response open and streams events as lines of text, for as long as it wants:

GET /api/events/42/seats/stream
event: seat
id: 1842
data: {"seat": "B-12", "status": "held"}

event: seat
id: 1843
data: {"seat": "B-13", "status": "sold"}

SSE is one-way (server → client), text-only, and runs over normal HTTP — so it passes through proxies, CDNs and load balancers, works over HTTP/2 multiplexing, and the browser's EventSource API reconnects automatically, sending the last received id in a Last-Event-ID header so the server can resume. It is the simplest good answer for "push updates to many clients": live scores, notifications, the waiting-room position, and the token-by-token stream of an LLM response.

items.title: WebSockets
items.text:
A WebSocket (RFC 6455) starts as an HTTP/1.1 request that asks to upgrade the connection; after the 101 Switching Protocols answer, the TCP connection becomes a full-duplex channel of messages in both directions, with very low per-message overhead5:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Browser
    participant L as Load balancer (L7)
    participant W as ws service
    C->>L: GET /ws (Upgrade: websocket, Sec-WebSocket-Key)
    L->>W: forward the upgrade request
    W-->>C: 101 Switching Protocols (Sec-WebSocket-Accept)
    Note over C,W: same TCP connection, now a two-way message channel
    C->>W: {"type": "join", "room": "event-42"}
    W-->>C: {"type": "seat", "seat": "B-12", "status": "held"}
    C->>W: {"type": "ping"}
    W-->>C: {"type": "pong"}

WebSockets are the tool for interactive, bidirectional traffic: chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing. They come with operational costs: connections are stateful and long-lived (a server restart disconnects thousands of users, who all reconnect at once), load balancers must support the upgrade and long idle timeouts, and you need a pub/sub backbone so that a message published on one server reaches clients connected to the others (the chat case study).

Short polling Long polling SSE WebSockets Direction client pulls client pulls (server holds) server → client both ways Latency of updates up to the interval low low lowest Cost per update a full request (often empty) a full request a few bytes a few bytes Through proxies/CDN easy, cacheable easy easy (plain HTTP) needs upgrade support Reconnection and resume n/a manual built in (Last-Event-ID) manual Binary data yes yes no (text) yes Good for dashboards, low-frequency status legacy clients feeds, notifications, progress, LLM streaming chat, games, collaboration

WebTransport

WebTransport is a newer browser API over HTTP/3 that offers multiple streams and unreliable datagrams — useful for games and media. It is still maturing; for most designs in 2026, SSE and WebSockets are the safe choices.

items.title: gRPC: calls between services
items.text:
Between BoxOffice's own services, the priorities are different: no browsers, both sides under our control, many calls per user action, and a need for strict contracts. gRPC is an RPC (Remote Procedure Call) framework from Google that runs over HTTP/2 and encodes messages with Protocol Buffers (protobuf), a compact binary format generated from a schema6:

inventory.proto
syntax = "proto3";
package boxoffice.inventory.v1;

service Inventory {
  rpc HoldSeats (HoldRequest) returns (Hold);                   // unary
  rpc WatchSeats (WatchRequest) returns (stream SeatEvent);     // server streaming
}

message HoldRequest {
  string event_id = 1;
  repeated string seat_ids = 2;
  string user_id = 3;
  string idempotency_key = 4;
}

message Hold {
  string hold_id = 1;
  int64 expires_at_epoch_ms = 2;
}

message WatchRequest { string event_id = 1; }
message SeatEvent { string seat_id = 1; string status = 2; }

From this file, the protobuf compiler generates client and server code in Java, Python, Go and others. gRPC offers four call types — unary, server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional streaming — and has deadlines built in: the caller says "I need an answer within 300 ms", and the deadline propagates through the chain of calls, so downstream services stop working on requests nobody is waiting for anymore.

REST + JSON gRPC + protobuf GraphQL Contract OpenAPI (optional) .proto (mandatory, code-generated) schema (mandatory) Payload text JSON, human-readable binary, compact, fast to parse JSON Transport HTTP/1.1, 2 or 3 HTTP/2 usually HTTP POST Streaming via SSE / WebSockets native, both directions subscriptions (WebSockets) Browser support native needs gRPC-Web or a proxy native Caching by CDN/HTTP natural for GET no hard (POST) Sweet spot public APIs, web and mobile internal service-to-service, low latency clients that need flexible aggregation (BFF)

The full comparison of API styles, with versioning and design advice, is in Compute — API styles.

items.title: Long-lived connections and load balancing
items.text:
HTTP/2, gRPC, SSE and WebSockets all keep connections open for a long time. That has a consequence that surprises many teams: load is balanced when a connection is opened, not when a request is sent — unless an L7 proxy balances each request or stream.

  • After a scale-out, the new replicas get no traffic: the existing clients are still attached to the old ones.
  • After a deploy or a crash, all clients of a server reconnect at the same moment — a reconnection storm.
  • An L4 load balancer sees one gRPC connection and sends all of the caller's requests to one replica (Load Balancing).

Remedies: L7 balancing per request (Envoy, service mesh) or client-side balancing for gRPC; a maximum connection age so clients rotate periodically; jittered reconnection backoff on the client; and draining that closes connections gradually during deploys.

items.title: Trade-offs at a glance
items.text:
Need Prefer Why Browsers and mobile apps → edge HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (let the CDN negotiate) multiplexing, fewer round trips, connection migration Edge → backends inside the region HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 with keep-alive pools simple; RTTs are tiny; connection reuse removes the setup cost Server → many clients, one-way updates SSE plain HTTP, auto-reconnect, works through the edge Interactive, bidirectional, low latency WebSockets full duplex, small messages Updates every few seconds are fine polling + CDN micro-caching stateless, cacheable, cheapest to operate Service-to-service, high volume, strict contract gRPC binary, code-generated, streaming, deadlines Public API for third parties REST + JSON (OpenAPI) universal, cacheable, easy to debug

BoxOffice: one protocol per interaction

  • Fan ↔ CDN: HTTP/3 with fallback to HTTP/2; TLS 1.3 terminated at the edge. Connection migration keeps the app working on the train.
  • Seat map: before 10:00, polling every 10 s with micro-caching; during the sale, an SSE stream per event (/api/events/42/seats/stream) fed by a pub/sub topic of seat changes. One held event replaces 2 million "nothing changed" answers.
  • Waiting room: an SSE stream with the fan's position, served by a dedicated service; reconnection with Last-Event-ID and jitter.
  • Order → inventory: gRPC HoldSeats with a 300 ms deadline and an idempotency key; client-side load balancing over the inventory pods.
  • Assistant: the LLM answer is streamed token by token with SSE; a WebSocket would only be needed for a voice or two-way collaborative mode.
  • Partners: REST + JSON with OpenAPI, versioned paths, rate-limited per API key at the gateway.

In the interview

  • When a problem has real-time requirements (chat, live scores, ride tracking, notifications), state the options and choose explicitly: "SSE for one-way updates; WebSockets because the chat is bidirectional; polling would cost N requests per second for nothing." Then mention the consequence: stateful connections need a pub/sub layer between servers and a plan for reconnection storms.
  • For internal calls, "REST between services" is fine; say "gRPC" when latency, volume or streaming matter, and mention deadlines.
  • If latency for distant users comes up, count round trips: "TLS 1.3 and HTTP/3 cut the handshake to 1 RTT, and an edge close to the user makes that RTT small."

Pitfalls

  • WebSockets by default: choosing WebSockets for one-way updates buys stateful servers, custom reconnection and proxy configuration that SSE gives for free.
  • Idle timeouts: load balancers close idle connections (often after 60 s); SSE and WebSocket streams need heartbeats (comments or pings) to stay open.
  • Reconnection storms after a deploy: thousands of clients reconnecting at once. Add jitter and drain gradually.
  • Balancing gRPC at L4: one replica gets all the traffic.
  • 0-RTT for non-idempotent requests: replayable. Only GETs in early data.
  • Assuming UDP works everywhere: always keep an HTTP/2 fallback for HTTP/3.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    RTT["round trips"] --> TLS["TLS 1.3, 0-RTT"]
    RTT --> QUIC["HTTP/3 over QUIC"]
    RTT --> LAT["latency budget<br/>→ Estimation"]
    H2["HTTP/2 streams"] --> GRPC["gRPC between services<br/>→ Compute: API styles"]
    RT["real-time push"] --> SSE["SSE: seat map, queue position"]
    RT --> WS["WebSockets: chat, assistant"]
    WS --> PS["pub/sub fan-out<br/>→ Messaging"]
    WS --> LL["long-lived connections<br/>→ load balancing"]
    TLS --> MTLS["mTLS inside the cluster<br/>→ service mesh"]

Palette components: client and mobile (choose the protocol) · cdn and lb (terminate TLS, speak HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) · pubsub (fan-out behind WebSockets) · mesh (mTLS between services). Scenarios: chat, video-streaming, ai-assistant (streamed tokens). Continues in: Compute — API styles, Case study: chat, Network & Security — service mesh.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Latency on new connections is counted in round trips: TCP + TLS 1.2 costs 4 RTT to the first byte, TLS 1.3 costs 3, QUIC 2, and QUIC 0-RTT 1. Reuse connections and terminate them close to the user.
  • HTTP/1.1: one request at a time per connection. HTTP/2: multiplexed streams over one TCP connection, but TCP head-of-line blocking. HTTP/3/QUIC: independent streams over UDP, built-in TLS 1.3, connection migration.
  • For real-time updates: polling (simple, cacheable), long polling, SSE (one-way, plain HTTP, auto-reconnect), WebSockets (bidirectional, stateful).
  • gRPC (HTTP/2 + protobuf) suits internal service-to-service calls: contracts, streaming, deadlines.
  • Long-lived connections are balanced at connect time: watch for imbalance after scale-out and reconnection storms after deploys.

  1. FIELDING, R.; NOTTINGHAM, M.; RESCHKE, J. RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics and RFC 9112 — HTTP/1.1. IETF, 2022. ↩

  2. THOMSON, M.; BENFIELD, C. RFC 9113 — HTTP/2. IETF, 2022. ↩
