items.title: Index
items.text:
The BoxOffice team is arguing about the stadium on-sale. "One PostgreSQL can't take that, we need a distributed database." — "Of course it can, Postgres is fast." Both engineers are guessing. Neither has said how many requests per second the on-sale generates, how long one seat hold keeps the database busy, how full the database can run before latency explodes, or what happens to the fans' experience when one of the ten calls behind a page is slow.

This class gives you the tools to settle that argument in five minutes on a whiteboard: the numbers every engineer should carry in their head, the formulas that connect load, latency and capacity, and the methods to turn a fuzzy question ("will it hold?") into an order-of-magnitude answer that drives a design decision. These are the same tools that you will use to read load tests (lab 2 and class 15), size clusters (class 12), set SLOs (class 9) and pass the estimation step of a system-design interview.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Recall the orders of magnitude of latency (memory, SSD, network in a data centre, across continents) and of common data sizes, and use powers of two and ten fluently.
  • Estimate requests per second (average and peak), storage, bandwidth and number of servers for a system from a few stated assumptions.
  • Apply Little's Law and the utilization law to size thread pools, connection pools and queues, and to validate a load test.
  • Explain why latency explodes near full utilization (the knee) and choose a safe operating utilization.
  • Interpret latency percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9), compute tail amplification under fan-out, and propose tail-tolerant techniques.
  • Calculate the availability of components in series and in parallel and the downtime allowed by a number of nines; reason about scalability limits with Amdahl's law and the Universal Scalability Law.

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
1. This overview — why estimate, the five-step method, and one complete back-of-the-envelope capacity check for the on-sale.
  2. Numbers Every Engineer Should Know — powers of two, latency numbers, sizes, and estimating requests per second, storage and bandwidth.
  3. Queueing, Little's Law and Scalability — concurrency, utilization, the knee of the latency curve, Amdahl and the Universal Scalability Law.
  4. Percentiles and Tail Latency — why averages lie, how fan-out amplifies the tail, and how to fight it.
  5. Availability Math — nines, MTTF/MTTR, components in series and in parallel, correlated failures.
  6. Quiz — check your understanding.

items.title: Why estimate?
items.text:
Architectural decisions differ by orders of magnitude, not by percentages. A design for 10 requests per second and one for 10,000 are different designs; 40 GB and 40 TB of data are different problems. You rarely need the exact number — you need to know which side of a threshold you are on:

If the estimate says… …the design decision is 40 GB of orders per year one PostgreSQL primary is fine for years — don't shard 40 TB per year plan partitioning or an object store from the start 1,200 catalog reads/s, 99% repeated cache them; the database only sees the misses 100,000 hold attempts/s on 60,000 seats the inventory cannot absorb it — queue fans in a waiting room 8 Gbit/s of images serve them from a CDN, not from the app servers one synchronous dependency at 99.9% on every request the service cannot promise more than 99.9% — remove it from the critical path or make it redundant

Estimation is also how you check a design and a measurement. If your load test says one server handles 50,000 requests per second while each request takes 20 ms on a single thread, something is wrong with the test — and Little's Law will tell you so in one line.

items.title: The method: five steps
items.text:
Back-of-the-envelope estimation is a form of Fermi estimation (named after the physicist Enrico Fermi, famous for estimating quantities like "how many piano tuners are there in Chicago?" from a chain of reasonable guesses). The errors in a chain of rough guesses tend to partially cancel, and an answer within a factor of 2–3 is good enough to choose between designs that differ by 10× or more1.

  1. Name the decision. What will the number decide? "Do we need to shard the orders table?" — not "how much data is there?".
  2. State the assumptions out loud and write them down: users, actions per user, sizes, peak factor. Use round numbers.
  3. Compute with powers of ten. One day ≈ 10⁵ seconds; 1 million per day ≈ 12 per second. Keep one significant digit.
  4. Sanity-check against a number you know: "1,200 req/s — that is about what one well-tuned app server handles; OK, a few servers."
  5. Conclude: state the implication for the design, and the assumption it is most sensitive to.

Rounding rules that keep you fast

  • 1 day = 86,400 s ≈ 10⁵ s; 1 month ≈ 2.5 × 10⁶ s; 1 year ≈ 3 × 10⁷ s.
  • 1 million requests per day ≈ 12 per second on average.
  • 2¹⁰ ≈ 10³: KB, MB, GB, TB, PB are each ~1,000× the previous one.
  • Keep exponents, round mantissas: 2 M × 20 = 4 × 10⁷; 4 × 10⁷ / 10⁵ = 400.

items.title: A complete capacity check: can one database take the on-sale?
items.text:
Let us settle the argument from the beginning of the page. Every step uses a tool from one of the subpages — follow the links when a step is not obvious yet.

BoxOffice — the 10:00 on-sale on one inventory database

Decision: is a single PostgreSQL primary enough for the seat inventory during a stadium on-sale, or do we need something else?

Assumptions (illustrative, to be validated with a load test in lab 2):

  • 2 M fans arrive within the first 60 s; 60 k seats; each successful fan holds 2 seats on average.
  • One seat-hold transaction keeps the database busy for S = 5 ms (a conditional UPDATE on a few rows, plus the commit).
  • The database can run about c = 8 of these transactions in parallel productively (CPU cores and row-lock contention limit it).

1. Demand (numbers): 2 M fans / 60 s ≈ 33,000 hold attempts per second, if every fan clicks once — and they click more than once.

2. Capacity (queueing): each "slot" completes 1 / 5 ms = 200 holds/s; 8 slots ≈ 1,600 holds/s at 100% utilization. To keep latency sane we run at ≤ 70%: ≈ 1,100 holds/s.

3. Verdict: demand exceeds capacity by ~30×. No tuning closes a 30× gap. Without a queue, requests pile up, latency explodes long before errors appear, and timeouts cause retries that make it worse.

4. Design: a waiting room admits fans at ~1,000/s. With 60 k seats and ~2 seats per fan, at most ~30 k successful fans are needed; at 1,000 admissions per second they are served in about 30 s, while the queue tells the rest, in near real time, how far they are from the front — and, once seats run out, that the show is sold out.

5. Check the experience (percentiles, availability): an admitted fan's hold goes through gateway → inventory → database; at 70% utilization, with the 8 slots sharing one queue (M/M/c), the database's p99 is about 25 ms — a few multiples of 5 ms, far inside the 300 ms target (one slot alone at 70% would give 15 × 5 ms ≈ 75 ms, see the queueing table). And because the on-sale depends on all of them in series, each must be more available than the 99.95% promised for checkout.

Conclusion: one PostgreSQL primary is enough if a waiting room shapes the demand; a "distributed database" would not remove the hot-row contention anyway, since everyone wants the same seats.

Notice that the most important number — 5 ms per hold — is an assumption. Estimation tells you which number to measure first. Lab 2 measures it.

items.title: See it in the playground
items.text:
The monolith scenario is a single app server and a single SQL database. The breakpoint profile ramps the load up steadily until something breaks — the standard way to find the capacity of a system.

Try it: run the breakpoint profile and watch three curves at once: throughput, p99 latency and database utilization. Note the request rate at which p99 starts to rise sharply (the knee) and the rate at which errors appear. Then read the database's service time in the component panel and compute its capacity by hand (capacity = parallel slots / service time). How close is the knee to ~70–80% of that capacity?

What should you have observed? (open after trying)

Throughput grows linearly with the offered load while latency stays flat; then, as the most-loaded component approaches saturation, latency bends upward (the knee) while throughput flattens. Past saturation, throughput stops growing at all, queues grow without bound, and timeouts turn into errors. Latency is the early warning; errors are the late one. That is why capacity is defined by the latency target ("the highest throughput at which p99 < 300 ms"), not by the point where the system crashes. The queueing page derives the shape of the curve.

In the interview

Spend 3–5 minutes on estimates, right after clarifying requirements, and do them out loud on the board: assumptions in one column, results in another. Always finish each line with its consequence — "≈ 400 reads/s average, 1,200 at peak: one database could serve it, but a cache makes it trivial" — and move on. If the interviewer gives you numbers, use them; if not, propose round ones and ask "does that sound right?". Precision is not the goal; orders of magnitude that drive decisions are.

Common pitfalls

  • Estimating the average and designing for it: systems fail at the peak. Always apply a peak factor, and for event-driven businesses like BoxOffice, estimate the spike separately.
  • False precision: "1,157.4 req/s" signals you missed the point. Say "about 1,000".
  • Forgetting replication and indexes in storage estimates (×3 for replicas, often ×1.5–2 for indexes and overhead).
  • Mixing bits and bytes: network links are in bits per second (Gbit/s), storage in bytes (GB). 1 GB/s = 8 Gbit/s.
  • Numbers without a conclusion: an estimate that does not change the design was not needed.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Design decisions change by orders of magnitude; estimation tells you which side of a threshold you are on.
  • Five steps: decision → assumptions → powers of ten → sanity check → conclusion.
  • Capacity is roughly parallel slots / service time, and you run well below it (≈ 60–75%) because latency explodes near saturation.
  • The most important output of an estimate is often which number to measure next.
  • Percentiles and availability math tell you what the users experience, not just what the servers do.

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Numbers and estimation
items.text:
Q1. BoxOffice has 2 M daily active fans, each viewing about 20 pages per day. What is the average read rate, and what should you size for?

  • A. ~40 reads/s; size for the average
  • B. ~400 reads/s on average; size for the peak hour, ~2–3× higher (~1,000–1,200 reads/s)
  • C. ~4,000 reads/s; size for the average
  • D. ~40,000 reads/s; size for 10× the average
Answer

B — ~400 reads/s average, sized for the peak.

2 × 10⁶ × 20 = 4 × 10⁷ reads/day; one day ≈ 10⁵ s, so ≈ 400 reads/s (463 with the exact 86,400). Traffic is not flat: the busiest hour is typically 2–3× the average, and that is what capacity must handle. On-sale spikes are estimated separately.

Q2. Which ordering of latencies, from fastest to slowest, is correct?

  • A. SSD random read < RAM reference < same-zone round trip < cross-continent round trip
  • B. RAM reference < SSD random read < same-zone round trip < cross-continent round trip
  • C. RAM reference < same-zone round trip < SSD random read < cross-continent round trip
  • D. Same-zone round trip < RAM reference < SSD random read < cross-continent round trip
Answer

B — ~100 ns < ~20–100 µs < ~0.1–0.5 ms < ~100+ ms.

Memory is about a thousand times faster than an SSD random read, which is somewhat faster than a network round trip inside a data centre; a round trip between continents is hundreds of times slower still, bounded by the speed of light in fibre (~5 µs per km).

Q3. A page handler makes 40 sequential calls to Redis in the same availability zone, each doing almost no work on the server. Roughly how long does the handler spend on those calls, and what is the fix?

  • A. ~40 µs; nothing to fix
  • B. ~4–20 ms, dominated by network round trips; batch the calls (MGET, pipelining) or cache in process
  • C. ~4 s; replace Redis with a database
  • D. ~400 ms; add Redis replicas
Answer

B — Round trips dominate.

Each call costs a same-zone round trip of ~0.1–0.5 ms, so 40 of them cost ~4–20 ms even though Redis does microseconds of work per call. Batching turns 40 round trips into one.

Q4. BoxOffice issues 200 k ticket PDFs per day, ~100 KB each, and wants to keep them for 5 years. Approximately how much storage is that, and where should it live?

  • A. ~36 GB, in the orders table
  • B. ~3.6 TB, in Redis
  • C. ~36 TB, in an object store (or generate the PDFs on demand instead of storing them)
  • D. ~360 TB, in the data warehouse
Answer

C — ~36 TB.

2 × 10⁵ × 10⁵ B = 2 × 10¹⁰ B = 20 GB/day; × 365 ≈ 7.3 TB/year; × 5 ≈ 36 TB. Large, immutable files belong in an object store (cheap, durable, effectively unlimited) — and since a PDF can be regenerated from the order, storing them at all is a design choice worth questioning.

Q5. Event pages load ~1 MB of images, and the peak is 1,200 page views per second. What bandwidth does the origin need without a CDN?

  • A. ~1.2 Mbit/s
  • B. ~120 Mbit/s
  • C. ~10 Gbit/s
  • D. ~1 Tbit/s
Answer

C — ~10 Gbit/s.

1,200 × 1 MB = 1.2 GB/s; × 8 bits = 9.6 Gbit/s. That saturates a 10 Gbit/s link and is expensive in egress — a strong reason to serve images from a CDN, where a 95% edge hit ratio leaves ~0.5 Gbit/s for the origin. Remember: networks in bits, storage in bytes.

items.title: Queueing and scalability
items.text:
Q6. The inventory service receives 1,000 holds/s and each hold spends 40 ms inside the service. On average, how many holds are in flight?

  • A. 25
  • B. 40
  • C. 400
  • D. 40,000
Answer

B — Little's Law: L = λ × W = 1,000 × 0.040 = 40.

This is the minimum concurrency the service needs (threads, or slots in an event loop) — plus headroom for bursts and for losing a replica.

Q7. Two million fans are in the BoxOffice waiting room, which admits 1,000 fans per second to the inventory. How long does the last fan in line wait?

  • A. ~33 seconds
  • B. ~3.3 minutes
  • C. ~33 minutes
  • D. ~5.5 hours
Answer

C — W = L / λ = 2,000,000 / 1,000 = 2,000 s ≈ 33 min.

In practice the 60 k seats run out long before, and the waiting room should tell the rest of the line that the show is sold out instead of making them wait.

Q8. A load test runs 100 virtual users in a closed loop, with no think time. The server's response time is 50 ms. What is the maximum throughput this test can generate — and what happens if the server slows to 500 ms?

  • A. 2,000 req/s; with 500 ms, still 2,000 req/s
  • B. 2,000 req/s; with 500 ms, it drops to 200 req/s — the test reduces load exactly when the system struggles
  • C. 100 req/s in both cases
  • D. 20,000 req/s; unaffected by response time
Answer

B — N = X × (R + Z), so X = 100 / 0.05 = 2,000 req/s, then 100 / 0.5 = 200 req/s.

Closed-loop tests are throttled by the system under test. To test a target arrival rate, use an open model (constant arrival rate) and check results with Little's Law.

Q9. A single database server (modelled as M/M/1) has a service time of 5 ms. What is its mean response time at 50% and at 90% utilization?

  • A. 5 ms and 5 ms
  • B. 7.5 ms and 9.5 ms
  • C. 10 ms and 50 ms
  • D. 10 ms and 500 ms
Answer

C — R = S / (1 − ρ): 5 / 0.5 = 10 ms; 5 / 0.1 = 50 ms.

Less than double the load made the mean 5× worse; the p99 (≈ 4.6 × the mean in M/M/1) goes from ~46 ms to ~230 ms. That is the knee of the latency curve.

Q10. Why do latency-sensitive services usually target ~50–70% utilization at peak instead of ~95%?

  • A. Because CPUs overheat above 70%
  • B. Because cloud providers charge more above 70%
  • C. Because response time grows like 1 / (1 − ρ), exploding near saturation, and the remaining replicas must absorb the load of one that fails
  • D. Because utilization above 70% cannot be measured accurately
Answer

C — Stay left of the knee, and keep headroom for failover.

With 4 replicas at 60%, losing one moves the others to 80% — still serviceable. At 80% each, losing one asks for ~107%: the survivors collapse.

Q11. Load tests of a service give relative throughput C(1) = 1, C(8) = 5.5, C(32) = 9 and C(64) = 8. Which model and cause fit best?

  • A. Linear scaling; the measurements are noise
  • B. Amdahl's law only; there is a serial fraction but no other cost
  • C. The Universal Scalability Law: contention plus a coherency cost (nodes coordinating with each other) that makes throughput fall past a peak
  • D. Little's Law; the test used too few virtual users
Answer

C — Throughput decreasing with more nodes is the signature of the coherency term (κ).

Amdahl's law alone flattens at 1/σ but never decreases. A fall past N* = √((1 − σ)/κ) indicates crosstalk: distributed locks, cache-coherence traffic, all-to-all communication. The fix is to partition work so nodes share less, not to add nodes.

items.title: Percentiles and availability
items.text:
Q12. Server A reports p99 = 100 ms and server B reports p99 = 1,000 ms; they served the same number of requests. What is the p99 of the two servers combined?

  • A. 550 ms, the average
  • B. 1,000 ms, the maximum
  • C. It cannot be computed from these two numbers; merge the latency histograms and compute the percentile from the result
  • D. 100 ms, the minimum
Answer

C — Percentiles cannot be averaged.

The combined p99 depends on the full shape of both distributions. Monitoring systems store histograms precisely so they can be merged across servers and time windows.

Q13. The search service queries 100 shards in parallel and waits for all of them. Each shard is slower than 200 ms in 1% of its calls (its p99), independently. Approximately what fraction of user searches take more than 200 ms?

  • A. 1%
  • B. 10%
  • C. 63%
  • D. 99%
Answer

C — 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 63%.

Under fan-out, the backend's tail becomes the user's typical experience. Mitigations: hedged requests after the p95, partial results after a deadline, fewer shards on the critical path.

Q14. Checkout synchronously calls five components, each 99.9% available, with independent failures. What is the best estimate of checkout availability, and the best first improvement?

  • A. 99.9%; nothing to improve
  • B. ~99.5%; remove from the critical path any component the user does not need to wait for (for example, send the e-mail asynchronously)
  • C. ~95%; add a cache in front of each component
  • D. ~99.99%; components in series improve availability
Answer

B — 0.999⁵ ≈ 99.5%.

In series, availabilities multiply, so the chain is worse than any link. The cheapest improvement is usually to remove hard dependencies from the path (async work, fallbacks); then add redundancy to weak links, and make each remaining link about one nine better than the target.

Q15. The inventory service has three replicas, each 99.5% available. The parallel formula gives 1 − 0.005³ ≈ 99.99999%. Why might the real availability be far lower?

  • A. Because the formula should use addition, not multiplication
  • B. Because replicas often fail together — same release, same configuration, same zone or a shared dependency — breaking the independence assumption
  • C. Because three replicas are always slower than one
  • D. Because load balancers reduce availability by half
Answer

B — Correlated failures.

A bad deploy rolled out to all replicas within minutes, a zone outage, or an expired certificate take down every replica at once. Spread replicas across zones, roll out changes gradually (canary), and reduce MTTR with fast rollback.

items.title: Index
items.text: BoxOffice promises organizers that checkout will be available 99.95% of the time. Every team proudly reports that its service runs at "three nines and a half" — gateway, auth, inventory, order, all at 99.95%. The payment provider's contract says 99.9%. And the checkout still calls the e-mail service synchronously to send the ticket. At the end of the month, checkout was available only 99.2% of the time — almost six hours of failures — and no single team missed its target. This page is the arithmetic that predicts that result in advance, and shows the design moves that change it.

items.title: Availability, MTTF and MTTR
items.text:
Availability is the fraction of time — or of requests — in which a system does its job. Two ways of measuring it are common:

Kind Formula Good for Time-based uptime / (uptime + downtime) infrastructure, "is it up?" Request-based successful requests / valid requests services; what users actually experience; the basis of SLOs2

For a component that alternates between working and being repaired, availability follows from two averages:

\[ A = \frac{\text{MTTF}}{\text{MTTF} + \text{MTTR}} \]
  • MTTF (Mean Time To Failure): how long it runs, on average, before failing.
  • MTTR (Mean Time To Recovery/Repair): how long it takes, on average, to detect, diagnose and restore service.
  • MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) = MTTF + MTTR.

BoxOffice — two ways to improve the inventory service

The inventory service fails about once a month (MTTF ≈ 720 h); each time, it takes 2 h until someone is paged, finds the problem and restarts it (MTTR = 2 h).

A = 720 / 722 ≈ 99.72%.

  • Make failures half as frequent (MTTF = 1,440 h): A = 1,440 / 1,442 ≈ 99.86%.
  • Detect the failure with a health check and replace the instance automatically in 2 minutes (MTTR ≈ 0.033 h): A = 720 / 720.033 ≈ 99.995%.

Recovering faster is usually the cheaper lever. Automation (health checks, automatic restarts, failover) attacks MTTR; testing and redundancy attack MTTF.

items.title: The nines
items.text:
Availability targets are quoted as a number of "nines". The table is computed for several windows — the same percentage allows different downtimes depending on the period it is measured over:

A 365.25 d 30.44 d 28 d 7 d 1 d 90% 36.5 d 3.04 d 2.8 d 16.8 h 2.4 h 99% 3.65 d 7.31 h 6.72 h 1.68 h 14.4 min 99.5% 1.83 d 3.65 h 3.36 h 50.4 min 7.2 min 99.9% 8.77 h 43.8 min 40.3 min 10.1 min 1.44 min 99.95% 4.38 h 21.9 min 20.2 min 5.04 min 43.2 s 99.99% 52.6 min 4.38 min 4.03 min 1.01 min 8.64 s 99.999% 5.26 min 26.3 s 24.2 s 6.05 s 0.864 s 99.9999% 31.6 s 2.63 s 2.42 s 0.605 s 0.0864 s

Each column header is the length of the window (a year of 365.25 days, an average month, 28 days, a week, a day); each cell is the downtime allowed in that window.

Each additional nine is a 10× reduction in allowed downtime — and roughly a change in how the system must be operated:

Target Allowed per month What it takes, roughly 99% ~7 h one server, manual recovery, backups 99.9% ~44 min redundancy, health checks, on-call humans, practiced recovery 99.99% ~4 min automatic failover (humans are too slow to be in the loop), multi-zone, safe deploys (canary, instant rollback) 99.999% ~26 s multi-region active-active, everything automated, extreme change discipline — very expensive

A useful sanity check: at 99.99% you cannot afford one 5-minute incident per month. If your recovery procedure involves a human reading a dashboard, you are not a four-nines system.

Request-based numbers are big numbers

At 2,000 requests per second, "99.9% of requests succeed" still means 2 failed requests every second, ~170,000 per day. Availability targets are about rates, never about "no errors" — 100% is neither achievable nor a sensible goal. The gap to 100% is the error budget (class 9).

items.title: Components in series
items.text:
When a request needs every component in a chain to work (a synchronous dependency chain), the system works only if all of them work. If failures are independent, availabilities multiply:

\[ A_{series} = a_1 \times a_2 \times \dots \times a_n = \prod_{i=1}^{n} a_i \]

The chain is always worse than its weakest link, and every extra synchronous dependency lowers the ceiling. The plot shows \(a^n\) for n identical components:

2026-10-23T08:15:46.842395 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Ten components at 99.9% give 99.0%; thirty give 97.0%. A microservice architecture in which a request synchronously crosses ten services needs each of them to be much better than the target of the whole.

items.title: Components in parallel
items.text:
When any one of n redundant, independent components is enough (replicas behind a load balancer, a primary with a standby, two payment providers), the system fails only if all of them fail at the same time:

\[ A_{parallel} = 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{n} (1 - a_i) \qquad \text{(identical: } 1 - (1 - a)^n \text{)} \] One replica Two replicas Three replicas 99% 1 − 0.01² = 99.99% 1 − 0.01³ = 99.9999% 99.5% 1 − 0.005² = 99.9975% 1 − 0.005³ ≈ 99.99999%

Redundancy turns mediocre components into very available systems — if the failures are independent (see below) and if failover actually works (the load balancer notices the failure and stops sending traffic, the standby really takes over).

items.title: k-of-n: quorums
items.text:
Some systems need a majority of replicas, not just one — consensus protocols and quorum-replicated databases (class 3). With 3 replicas of availability a, a 2-of-3 quorum is available when all 3 or exactly 2 are up:

\[ A_{2\text{-of-}3} = a^3 + 3a^2(1 - a) \]

With a = 99%: 0.970299 + 0.029403 = 99.97% — better than one node, worse than "any one of three" (99.9999%). The price of consistency is paid in availability, even in the arithmetic.

items.title: BoxOffice checkout, computed
items.text:
The checkout path, as described at the top of the page (availabilities are illustrative assumptions):

flowchart LR
    fan([Fan]) --> edge["Edge + gateway<br/>99.99%"]
    edge --> auth["auth<br/>99.95%"]
    auth --> order["order<br/>99.95%"]
    order --> inv["inventory<br/>99.95%"]
    inv --> db[("inventory DB<br/>99.95%")]
    order --> pay["payment provider<br/>99.9%"]
    order --> mail["email (sync)<br/>99.5%"]
Design Calculation Availability Failures per 30 days Naive (everything synchronous, in series) 0.9999 × 0.9995⁴ × 0.999 × 0.995 99.19% ~5.8 h E-mail made asynchronous (queue + worker; off the critical path) 0.9999 × 0.9995⁴ × 0.999 99.69% ~2.2 h + second payment provider (fail over when the first is down) 0.9999 × 0.9995⁴ × (1 − 0.001²) 99.79% ~1.5 h + every internal component at 99.99% (replicas, automatic failover, safe deploys) 0.9999⁵ × (1 − 0.001²) 99.95% ~22 min

Three lessons, in decreasing order of cost-effectiveness:

  1. Remove dependencies from the critical path. Making the e-mail asynchronous gained more than any other single change — and cost almost nothing. If the user does not need it to finish before the response, it should not be in the chain.
  2. Add redundancy where a dependency is weak and critical. A second payment provider turns a 99.9% dependency into an effectively 99.9999% one (if their failures are independent).
  3. Make each remaining link better than the target. A chain of five components can only meet 99.95% if each is around 99.99%. This is the "rule of the extra nine": a service's critical dependencies should each be roughly one nine more available than the service itself1.

Soft dependencies are not in the chain

A dependency whose failure the service can tolerate — by serving a cached value, a default, or a partial page — does not multiply into the availability of the critical path. Recommendations, view counters and the AI assistant should all be soft dependencies of checkout: if they fail, checkout still works. Turning hard dependencies into soft ones (fallbacks, caches, async) is a design skill you will practise in class 9.

items.title: The independence assumption
items.text:
All the formulas above assume that components fail independently. Real failures are often correlated, and correlation destroys the parallel formula:

  • Two replicas on the same host, rack or availability zone go down together with it.
  • Two replicas running the same buggy release crash on the same input.
  • A bad configuration pushed everywhere at once breaks every replica at once.
  • A shared dependency — the same DNS provider, the same certificate that expires, the same database — is a single point of failure hidden behind apparent redundancy.
  • Overload: when one replica dies, its traffic moves to the others, which may then fail too (a cascading failure).

BoxOffice — three replicas, one outage

The inventory service runs 3 replicas, each 99.5% available on its own: the parallel formula promises 1 − 0.005³ ≈ 99.99999%. In practice, the year's worst outage came from a release with a connection-pool misconfiguration, deployed to all three replicas within 2 minutes. All three failed together, for 40 minutes, until the rollback. The redundancy did not help, because the failure was not independent. The fixes are not more replicas, but diversity in time and space: canary deploys (one replica first, watch, then the rest), replicas spread across zones, and fast rollback (lower MTTR).

Designing for independence — separate failure domains (zones, regions), staged rollouts, no hidden shared dependencies — is as important as adding replicas.

items.title: Detection and failover time
items.text:
Redundancy only helps after the failure is detected and traffic is moved. If a load balancer checks health every 10 s and needs 3 consecutive failures to mark a replica down, users hit the failed replica for up to ~30 s each time. With frequent small failures this matters:

\[ \text{downtime per year} \approx \text{failures per year} \times (\text{detection time} + \text{failover time}) \]

Ten failovers a year at 30 s + 30 s each is 10 minutes: fine for 99.99% (52 minutes per year), but it consumes a fifth of the budget. Faster health checks, client-side retries to another replica, and connection draining reduce it.

Think first: is a second region worth it?

BoxOffice runs in one region with three availability zones. The provider's documentation suggests that a full-region outage is rare, but when it happens it can last hours. A second region (active-passive, with DNS failover) would roughly double infrastructure cost. How would you decide?

Answer sketch: estimate the expected cost of downtime versus the cost of the second region. If a region outage of ~4 h happens about once every two years (an assumption to validate with your provider's history), the expected downtime is ~2 h/year — almost half of the ~4.4 h/year that a 99.95% target allows, before any other incident. Then consider when it happens: a region outage during a stadium on-sale costs the business far more than one at 4 a.m. on a Tuesday. If the SLA with organizers carries penalties, or one lost on-sale costs more than a year of a second region, it is worth it — and then the hard part is the data (class 3 and class 9), not the servers.

In the interview

When you draw a high-level design, do the series calculation out loud for the critical path: "the request crosses five components; at 99.9% each that is about 99.5%, so to promise 99.9% overall I need redundancy in each and I'd take the e-mail off the path." Then mention correlated failures — "replicas in different zones, canary deploys" — which shows you know where the formulas stop being true. Quote downtime with a window: "four nines is about four minutes a month".

Common pitfalls

  • Quoting a target without a window: 99.9% is 43.8 min per average month but 40.3 min per 28 days.
  • Ignoring the chain: each team meets its target and the product misses its own.
  • Assuming independence: replicas in the same zone, on the same release, behind the same DNS.
  • Counting redundancy without failover: a standby that is never tested is not redundancy.
  • Chasing nines everywhere: different paths deserve different targets; five nines for the recommendations widget is wasted money.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    MT["A = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR)"] --> NINES["nines over a window<br/>→ Reliability SLOs"]
    SER["series: ∏ aᵢ"] --> CHAIN["critical path: edge, auth,<br/>order, inventory, provider"]
    CHAIN --> ASYNC["move deps off the path<br/>queue + worker → Messaging"]
    PAR["parallel: 1 − ∏(1 − aᵢ)"] --> RED["replicas,<br/>a second provider"]
    QUO["k-of-n quorums<br/>→ Distributed"] --> RED
    RED --> IND["independent? zones,<br/>releases, config"]
    IND --> DR["multi-AZ, multi-region<br/>→ Reliability"]
    MT --> DET["detection + failover time<br/>health checks"]
    DET --> RED

Palette components: lb · healthcheck (detection time = interval × failures to mark down) · app (replicas in parallel, if failures are independent) · sql (primary + standby with automatic failover) · payment (a 99.9% dependency; a second provider) · email (moved off the critical path) · queue · worker (the asynchronous path) · dns (multi-region failover). Scenarios: scale-out, multi-region, payment-system, notification-system. Continues in: Distributed — consensus (quorums), Reliability — SLOs, Reliability — multi-AZ and multi-region, Compute — provider outages, Exercise: design doc.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• A = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR); reducing MTTR through automation is often the cheapest lever.
  • Each nine is 10× less downtime; always state the window.
  • Series multiplies (worse than the weakest link); parallel gives 1 − ∏(1 − aᵢ); quorums lie in between.
  • Improve a chain by removing hard dependencies from the critical path, adding redundancy to weak links, and making each link ~one nine better than the target.
  • The formulas assume independent failures; correlated failures (same zone, same release, same config) are what actually take systems down.

  1. TREYNOR, B.; DAHLIN, M.; RAU, V.; BEYER, B. The Calculus of Service Availability. ACM Queue, 15(2), 2017. ↩

  2. BEYER, B. et al. Site Reliability Engineering. Google / O'Reilly, 2016. Chapter 3 (embracing risk). ↩

items.title: Index
items.text: How long does it take to read a seat from memory? From an SSD? From a database in the same data centre? From a server in Virginia, while the fan is in São Paulo? The answers span eight orders of magnitude — from a nanosecond to a hundred milliseconds — and most architectural rules of thumb ("cache it", "batch it", "don't call across regions synchronously") are just consequences of that spread. This page collects the numbers worth memorizing and shows how to turn them, together with a few assumptions about users, into requests per second, storage and bandwidth.

items.title: Powers of two (and ten)
items.text:
Data sizes are powers of two; estimates are easier in powers of ten. Since 2¹⁰ = 1,024 ≈ 10³, you can switch freely for estimation purposes:

Power of two Exact value ≈ Power of ten Unit Something that size 2¹⁰ 1,024 10³ (thousand) 1 KB a short JSON response; a seat record ×10 2²⁰ 1,048,576 10⁶ (million) 1 MB an event poster (compressed photo) 2³⁰ ≈ 1.07 × 10⁹ 10⁹ (billion) 1 GB a year of BoxOffice seat data (illustrative) 2⁴⁰ ≈ 1.10 × 10¹² 10¹² (trillion) 1 TB a large single-node database 2⁵⁰ ≈ 1.13 × 10¹⁵ 10¹⁵ (quadrillion) 1 PB a video platform's catalog

Strictly, 2¹⁰ bytes is a kibibyte (KiB) and 10³ bytes a kilobyte (kB); the difference (2.4% at KB, 10% at TB) does not matter for back-of-the-envelope work.

Bits vs bytes

Network speeds are quoted in bits per second (a "10 Gbit/s" network interface), storage and payloads in bytes. Divide by 8: a 10 Gbit/s link carries at most 1.25 GB/s. Mixing the two is the most common estimation error.

items.title: Time
items.text:
Period Seconds Round to 1 minute 60 — 1 hour 3,600 4 × 10³ 1 day 86,400 10⁵ 1 month (30 days) 2,592,000 2.5 × 10⁶ 1 year 31,536,000 3 × 10⁷

A handy conversion table, using 1 day ≈ 10⁵ s (the exact factor is 86,400, which makes the real rates about 15% higher):

Per day ≈ Per second (average) 1 million ~12 10 million ~120 100 million ~1,200 1 billion ~12,000

items.title: Latency numbers every engineer should know
items.text:
In 2009, Jeff Dean (Google) popularized a list of "numbers everyone should know" — the cost of basic operations in a computer and a network1. Hardware has changed since (SSDs replaced spinning disks on the hot path, networks got faster), but the ratios have stayed remarkably stable, because some limits — the speed of light, the physics of memory — do not improve. The table uses 2020s orders of magnitude, compiled from Dean's list, its later updates2 and Gregg's Systems Performance3; your hardware may differ by 2–3×, which is fine for estimates.

Operation Latency (order of magnitude) If 1 ns were 1 second… L1 cache reference ~1 ns 1 s Branch mispredict ~3 ns 3 s L2 cache reference ~4 ns 4 s Mutex lock/unlock (uncontended) ~20 ns 20 s Main memory (RAM) reference ~100 ns 1.7 min Compress 1 KB with a fast compressor ~2 µs 33 min Read 1 MB sequentially from RAM ~10–50 µs 3–14 h Random 4 KB read from an NVMe SSD ~20–100 µs 6–28 h Round trip inside one data centre / availability zone ~0.1–0.5 ms 1–6 days Read 1 MB sequentially from an NVMe SSD ~0.2 ms 2.3 days Redis GET or primary-key SQL query, same zone (mostly network) ~0.2–1 ms 2–12 days Round trip between availability zones of one region ~1–2 ms 12–23 days Spinning disk (HDD) seek ~5–10 ms 2–4 months Read 1 MB sequentially from an HDD ~5 ms 2 months Round trip São Paulo ↔ US East (Virginia) ~110–130 ms ~4 years Round trip across the Atlantic / Pacific ~80–200 ms 3–6 years TCP + TLS handshake to a far server 2–3 round trips —

items.title: What the table teaches
items.text:
1. Memory is ~1,000× faster than SSD, and SSD ~100× faster than HDD for random reads. This is why caches (Redis keeps everything in RAM) and in-memory indexes exist.
  2. Inside a data centre, the network costs more than the work. A Redis GET takes microseconds of CPU on the server; the round trip is what you wait for. A page that makes 50 sequential calls to Redis spends ~10–25 ms just on round trips — batch them (MGET, pipelining) or cache in process.
  3. Across regions, physics wins. Light in optical fibre travels at about 200,000 km/s, i.e. ~5 µs per km, so every 100 km adds about 1 ms of round trip before any router or server touches the packet. São Paulo to Virginia is ~7,500 km in a straight line, so the theoretical minimum round trip is ~75 ms; real routes give ~110–130 ms. No technology removes this: avoid synchronous cross-region calls on the critical path and serve users from nearby (CDN, regional deployments).
  4. Sequential beats random. Reading 1 MB sequentially from an SSD costs about as much as a few random 4 KB reads. Log-structured storage, Kafka's append-only log and batch processing all exploit this.
  5. Round trips add up; bandwidth rarely limits small requests. For a 2 KB API response, latency is dominated by round trips (connection setup, TLS, the request itself), not by transfer time. Reusing connections (keep-alive, HTTP/2) matters more than a fatter pipe.

BoxOffice — the seat map, three ways

The seat map of a stadium event needs ~60,000 seat states.

  • 60,000 individual queries from the app to PostgreSQL in the same zone: 60,000 × ~0.5 ms ≈ 30 s. Unusable.
  • One query returning 60,000 rows of ~50 bytes (3 MB): one round trip + ~10–30 ms of database work + ~3 ms to transfer over a 10 Gbit/s link ≈ 20–40 ms.
  • One cached, compressed blob in Redis (~300 KB after compression), refreshed every second: one round trip + a fraction of a millisecond of transfer ≈ 1–2 ms.

Same data, four orders of magnitude apart — decided entirely by the number of round trips and where the data lives.

items.title: Throughput rules of thumb
items.text:
Latency tells you how long one operation takes; capacity planning also needs how many operations per second a component can sustain. These vary much more with hardware, configuration and workload than latencies do, so treat the table as illustrative starting assumptions that you must replace with measurements (that is what lab 2 is for):

Component Order of magnitude (simple operations, one node) What limits it App server (JVM, simple JSON endpoint) 10³–10⁴ requests/s CPU per request, threads, downstream calls Nginx serving cached/static content 10⁴–10⁵ requests/s CPU, network Relational database, primary-key reads 10⁴–10⁵ queries/s CPU, buffer cache hit ratio Relational database, durable write transactions 10³–10⁴ commits/s log flush (fsync), locks Redis, simple GET/SET ~10⁵ operations/s per instance single-threaded command loop, network Kafka, one partition ~10 MB/s order of magnitude disk, network, replication 10 Gbit/s network interface 1.25 GB/s the wire

The pattern to remember: reads are cheaper than durable writes, memory is cheaper than disk, and anything that must flush to disk or cross the network to commit (durable writes, replication, consensus) has a lower ceiling.

items.title: Typical sizes
items.text:
Item Size Note Boolean / byte 1 B — Integer / timestamp 4–8 B bigint, epoch millis UUID 16 B (36 B as text) store binary when you can Short string (name, e-mail) 20–100 B UTF-8 BoxOffice seat row ~100 B ids, status, price, hold id, version BoxOffice order ~1 KB with items and payment reference BoxOffice event (description, metadata) ~2–5 KB — JSON API response (a page of results) 2–50 KB before compression Ticket PDF ~100 KB — Compressed photo (poster) 200 KB – 2 MB multiple resolutions 1 minute of HD video 50–100 MB depends on bitrate One embedding vector (1,024 dims × 4 B) ~4 KB relevant for vector DBs (class 13)

Two multipliers are easy to forget: replication (a database usually keeps 3 copies; object stores replicate internally) and indexes and overhead (often 1.5–2× the raw data in a relational database).

items.title: Estimating requests per second (QPS)
items.text:
QPS (queries per second, used loosely for requests per second) is the starting point of every capacity estimate:

\[ \text{QPS}_{avg} = \frac{\text{daily active users} \times \text{actions per user per day}}{86{,}400} \qquad \text{QPS}_{peak} = \text{QPS}_{avg} \times \text{peak factor} \]
  • Peak factor: traffic is not flat over the day. For consumer products the busiest hour is typically 2–3× the daily average; that is the number you size for. For event-driven businesses, the peak is a spike that has nothing to do with the daily average — estimate it separately.
  • Read/write ratio: split the actions into reads and writes. Reads can be cached and replicated; writes go to a primary. A product at 100:1 and one at 1:1 are different designs.

BoxOffice — requests per second (assumptions in italics)

Normal day

  • 20 M registered fans, 2 M daily active; each views ~20 pages (events, seat maps, searches).
  • Reads: 2 M × 20 = 4 × 10⁷ per day → 4 × 10⁷ / 10⁵ ≈ 400 reads/s average.
  • Peak hour ≈ 3× average → ~1,200 reads/s.
  • Writes: 100 k orders/day, each ~5 writes (hold, order, payment, tickets, outbox) → 5 × 10⁵ / 10⁵ ≈ 5 writes/s average, ~15 at peak.
  • Read/write ratio ≈ 100:1 → cache and replicate reads; a single primary handles writes easily.

On-sale spike

  • 2 M fans arrive in the first 60 s; each sends ~3 requests in that minute (page, refresh, hold attempt).
  • 2 × 10⁶ × 3 / 60 ≈ 100,000 requests/s at the edge — ~80× the normal peak, for a few minutes.
  • Only 60 k seats exist: at most ~30 k fans can succeed (2 seats each). Almost all of the spike must be absorbed before it reaches the inventory: CDN for static content, cache for the event page, waiting room for holds.

items.title: Estimating storage
items.text:
\[ \text{storage} = \text{items per day} \times \text{size per item} \times \text{retention (days)} \times \text{replication factor} \;(\times \text{index overhead}) \]

BoxOffice — storage for 5 years

Data Volume Size each Per year 5 years, ×3 replicas Store Orders 100 k/day 1 KB 100 MB/day × 365 ≈ 37 GB ≈ 550 GB SQL Seats 20 k events/year × 5 k seats = 10⁸ rows 100 B 10 GB ≈ 150 GB SQL (hot only during on-sale) Ticket PDFs 200 k tickets/day 100 KB 20 GB/day ≈ 7 TB object store (replicated internally) ≈ 35 TB Object Store Event images 20 k events × 5 images 1 MB 100 GB ≈ 0.5 TB Object Store + CDN Access logs 10⁸ requests/day 500 B 50 GB/day ≈ 18 TB keep 30 days hot ≈ 1.5 TB log platform / object store

Conclusions: the transactional data (orders, seats) is well under a terabyte even after 5 years with replicas — a single PostgreSQL primary with replicas fits; sharding is not a day-one requirement. The bulky data is files and logs, which belong in an object store (cheap, durable, effectively unlimited) — and you might decide to generate ticket PDFs on demand instead of storing 35 TB of them.

items.title: Estimating bandwidth
items.text:
\[ \text{bandwidth} = \text{requests per second} \times \text{bytes per response} \]

BoxOffice — bandwidth at the normal peak

  • API responses: 1,200 req/s × 20 KB ≈ 24 MB/s ≈ 0.2 Gbit/s — trivial for the origin.
  • Images: each page view loads ~1 MB of images → 1,200 × 1 MB ≈ 1.2 GB/s ≈ 10 Gbit/s — saturates a 10 Gbit/s link and costs a lot in egress. Serve images from a CDN: with a 95% edge hit ratio, the origin sends only ~0.5 Gbit/s.
  • On-sale spike: 100 k req/s × 5 KB (a lightweight waiting-room page) ≈ 500 MB/s ≈ 4 Gbit/s — must be served from the edge (CDN or edge compute), not from the app servers.

items.title: Estimating servers and memory
items.text:
Once you know the peak load and the per-node capacity, the number of nodes follows — with headroom and redundancy:

\[ \text{nodes} = \left\lceil \frac{\text{peak QPS}}{\text{capacity per node} \times \text{target utilization}} \right\rceil + \text{spares} \]
  • Target utilization of 60–75% for latency-sensitive services — the queueing page explains why running closer to 100% destroys p99.
  • Spares (N+1, N+2): if one node fails or is being deployed, the others must absorb its load without crossing the knee.

For cache memory, a common rule of thumb is the 80/20 rule: a small fraction of the items receives most of the traffic, so caching the hot set — often ~20% of the items, sometimes far less — captures most of the reads.

BoxOffice — catalog servers and cache

  • One catalog instance handles ~1,000 req/s at 100% CPU (to be measured). Peak 1,200 req/s at 60% target → 1,200 / 600 = 2 → 2 + 1 spare = 3 instances.
  • Hot set: the ~2,000 events on sale this month × 5 KB (event JSON) + seat-map summaries (~300 KB each) ≈ 10 MB + 600 MB ≈ ~0.6 GB — fits in a small Redis instance with a replica.
Think first: estimate a URL shortener

100 M new short URLs per month; reads are 100× writes; each record ~500 B; keep for 5 years.

Answer sketch

  • Writes: 10⁸ / (2.5 × 10⁶ s) ≈ 40 writes/s; reads ≈ 4,000 reads/s (peak ×2–3 → ~10 k/s).
  • Storage: 10⁸ × 12 × 5 = 6 × 10⁹ records × 500 B = 3 TB (≈ 9 TB with 3 replicas).
  • Implications: reads dominate and are highly cacheable (popular links) → cache; 3 TB is large for one node's working set, so plan partitioning or a key-value store; key space: 6 × 10⁹ URLs need ≥ 6 characters in base 62 (62⁶ ≈ 5.7 × 10¹⁰). The case study develops it.

In the interview

Carry a small "numbers card" in your head: 1 day ≈ 10⁵ s; 1 M/day ≈ 12/s; RAM ~100 ns; SSD ~100 µs; same-zone round trip ~0.5 ms; cross-continent ~100+ ms; 1 Gbit/s ≈ 125 MB/s. Write assumptions before results, round everything to one significant digit, and finish every line with its consequence. If you are unsure of a number, say so and give a range: "a primary-key lookup is around a millisecond including the network — let's say 1 ms."

Common pitfalls

  • Treating latency numbers as exact: they are orders of magnitude; your hardware and your cloud will differ.
  • Forgetting round trips: 100 sequential calls at 0.5 ms are 50 ms, even if each call does almost nothing.
  • Sizing for the daily average instead of the peak — or forgetting the spike altogether.
  • Ignoring replication, indexes and retention in storage.
  • Bits vs bytes, and 86,400 vs 10⁵ when precision matters (e.g. SLA calculations — use the exact value there).

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    P2["powers of two and ten<br/>1 day ≈ 10⁵ s"] --> QPS["QPS: average and peak<br/>the spike estimated apart"]
    LAT["latency numbers<br/>RAM, SSD, network"] --> CACHE["cache the hot set<br/>→ Caching"]
    LAT --> RT["count round trips<br/>→ Edge protocols"]
    QPS --> NODES["nodes = peak / capacity × U<br/>+ spares → Compute"]
    QPS --> BW["bandwidth = QPS × size<br/>→ CDN"]
    SIZES["typical sizes"] --> STO["storage × retention<br/>× replication"]
    STO --> SHARD["shard or not?<br/>→ Databases"]
    STO --> OBJ["bulky files and logs<br/>→ object store"]
    NODES --> KNEE["target utilization<br/>→ Queueing"]

Palette components: app (instances = peak / capacity per node, plus spares) · sql (orders and seats stay under a terabyte; the durable-write ceiling) · cache (the hot set, ~0.6 GB for the catalog) · cdn (image bandwidth off the origin) · objstore (ticket PDFs, images, logs) · kafka (~10 MB/s per partition) · vectordb (~4 KB per embedding). Scenarios: monolith, read-heavy-cache, cdn-static, url-shortener. Continues in: Queueing, Edge — DNS & CDN, Caching, Databases — partitioning, Case study: URL shortener, Exercise: estimation.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• 2¹⁰ ≈ 10³; 1 day ≈ 10⁵ s; 1 M per day ≈ 12 per second.
  • Latencies span eight orders of magnitude: RAM ~100 ns, SSD ~100 µs, same-zone network ~0.5 ms, cross-continent ~100 ms; most design rules follow from these ratios.
  • QPS = users × actions / 86,400 × peak factor; estimate spikes separately.
  • Storage = items × size × retention × replication (× overhead); bandwidth = QPS × size.
  • Nodes = peak / (capacity × target utilization) + spares; cache the hot set.

  1. DEAN, J. Designs, Lessons and Advice from Building Large Distributed Systems. Keynote, LADIS workshop, 2009 ("numbers everyone should know"). ↩

  2. SCOTT, C. Latency numbers every programmer should know (interactive), University of California, Berkeley. ↩

  3. GREGG, B. Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud, 2nd ed. Addison-Wesley, 2020. Chapter 2 (methodologies: latency scale and known numbers). ↩

items.title: Index
items.text: The BoxOffice dashboard says the seat-map endpoint has an average latency of 55 ms. Everyone is happy — except the fans, who complain on social media that the seat map "takes forever" during on-sales. Both are right. The average is 55 ms; but one request in a hundred takes more than half a second, and a fan who opens the seat map, refreshes it, zooms into two sections and tries three holds makes enough requests to hit one of those slow ones almost every visit. This page is about the slow requests: how to measure them, why they matter more than the average suggests, and why they get worse as systems become more distributed.

items.title: Why averages lie
items.text:
Latency distributions are not bell curves. Most requests are fast and similar; a minority — hitting a cache miss, a garbage-collection pause, a lock, a retry, a cold connection — are much slower. The result is a long tail to the right. The plot shows a synthetic but realistic distribution for 100,000 requests: 97% are "normal" (around 40 ms) and 3% hit a slow path (around 400 ms):

2026-10-23T08:15:47.123877 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

The mean (about 55 ms) describes no actual request: it is pulled up by the tail, yet it hides how bad the tail is. The median says what a typical request experiences. The p99 and p99.9 say what the unlucky requests experience — and they are roughly 12× and 28× slower than the median (≈ 510 ms and ≈ 1.1 s vs ≈ 40 ms). A dashboard that shows only the average would never reveal that.

items.title: Percentiles
items.text:
The p-th percentile (written pXX) of a set of latencies is the value below which XX% of them fall1:

Percentile Meaning Also called What it tells you p50 half the requests are faster median the typical experience p90, p95 90% / 95% are faster — the common "slow-ish" experience p99 99% are faster; 1 in 100 is slower "two nines" tail the experience of the unlucky — and of heavy users p99.9 1 in 1,000 is slower "three nines" tail rare but real; dominates when requests fan out max the slowest one seen p100 outliers; noisy, but worth a look

To compute a percentile exactly, sort the values and take the one at position ⌈p × n⌉ (the nearest-rank method): with 1,000 requests, p99 is the 990th fastest. In production, systems do not store every latency; they record histograms — counts of requests per latency bucket (0–5 ms, 5–10 ms, …) — and estimate percentiles from the buckets. Prometheus histograms, HdrHistogram and OpenTelemetry exponential histograms all work this way (class 10).

You cannot average percentiles

If server A has p99 = 100 ms and server B has p99 = 1,000 ms, the p99 of the fleet is not 550 ms; it depends on how many requests each served and on the shape of both distributions. The same is true across time: the average of 60 per-minute p99 values is not the p99 of the hour. To aggregate, merge the histograms (add the bucket counts) and compute the percentile from the merged histogram. Dashboards that average percentiles are among the most common — and most misleading — mistakes in monitoring.

items.title: Why the tail matters more than "1%" suggests
items.text:
1. Users make many requests. A fan's visit during an on-sale (event page, seat map, refreshes, holds, payment, confirmation) easily involves 50 requests. The probability that at least one is slower than the p99 is \(1 - 0.99^{50} \approx 39\%\). The "1% tail" is felt by four in ten visits.
  2. The slowest users are often the best customers. Fans with many orders, organizers with large events, accounts with a lot of data — their requests do more work and land in the tail. Amazon famously set its internal latency targets at the p99.9 for this reason2.
  3. The tail is where overload starts. As the queueing curves show, the p99 rises long before the mean when a component approaches saturation. It is the earliest warning you get.

items.title: Tail amplification under fan-out
items.text:
Modern backends rarely answer a request with a single call. The BoxOffice seat-map page calls inventory (availability), catalog (venue layout and prices), order (the fan's existing tickets) and a recommendations service, in parallel; the search service queries 20 index shards in parallel and merges the results. A request that fans out to N backends in parallel is as slow as the slowest of them.

If each backend call is slow (above its p99) with probability q = 1%, independently, the probability that the user request waits for at least one slow call is:

\[ P(\text{user request is slow}) = 1 - (1 - q)^N \] Fan-out N q = 1% (backend p99) q = 0.1% (backend p99.9) 1 1% 0.1% 5 4.9% 0.5% 20 18% 2% 100 63% 9.5% 500 99% 39% 2026-10-23T08:15:47.305691 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

This is the central observation of Dean and Barroso's The Tail at Scale3: with a fan-out of 100, a backend whose p99 is 1 second makes 63% of user requests take more than 1 second. In a large distributed system, the backend's tail becomes the user's median. The more you split a system into parallel pieces (shards, microservices), the more the rare slowness of each piece dominates.

BoxOffice — search across 20 shards

The search service splits the event index into 20 shards to keep each one small and fast. Each shard answers in 15 ms at p50 and 120 ms at p99 (a merge or a cache miss now and then). The user's search waits for all 20:

  • P(at least one shard above 120 ms) = 1 − 0.99²⁰ ≈ 18% — so the user-facing p82 is already ≥ 120 ms, and the user-facing p99 is driven by the shards' p99.9 or worse.
  • Halving the number of shards to 10 cuts that probability to ~10%, but makes each shard bigger and slower. Keeping 20 shards and hedging (below) is usually the better trade.

items.title: Where the tail comes from
items.text:
Tail latency is rarely caused by the "normal" code path. Typical causes3:

Source Example Mitigation Queueing a burst arrives while a server is busy headroom (lower utilization), load balancing on least-loaded Shared resources noisy neighbours on the same host, disk or network isolation, dedicated capacity for critical paths Garbage collection a JVM pauses for 200 ms GC tuning, low-pause collectors, smaller heaps Background work database compaction, log rotation, backups schedule off-peak, rate-limit background tasks Cache misses cold cache after deploy; rare keys pre-warming, larger cache, request coalescing Retries and timeouts the first attempt times out at 1 s, the retry succeeds well-tuned timeouts, hedging instead of waiting Cold starts a new container or serverless function initializes warm pools, provisioned concurrency Slow dependencies the payment provider has a bad minute timeouts, circuit breakers, async processing

items.title: Taming the tail
items.text:
You cannot eliminate variability; you can design so that it does not reach the user.

  • Hedged requests: send the request to one replica; if it has not answered within, say, the p95 latency, send a second copy to another replica and use whichever answers first. Only ~5% of requests are duplicated, but the tail shrinks dramatically. Dean and Barroso report a Google case where hedging after 10 ms cut the p99.9 of a 1,000-key read from 1,800 ms to 74 ms with only 2% more requests3. Hedge only idempotent reads.
  • Tied requests: send to two replicas at once, each knowing about the other; the first to start processing cancels the other. Removes queueing variability at the cost of a little coordination.
  • Reduce fan-out: fewer, larger partitions for latency-critical paths; precompute aggregates (a materialized seat-map summary instead of calling five services).
  • Degrade gracefully: give each backend a deadline and return a partial answer — the seat map without the recommendations panel is still a seat map.
  • Take work off the critical path: what does not need to finish before the response (e-mails, analytics, search indexing) goes to a queue.
  • Keep utilization low on latency-critical components, and isolate them from batch work.

items.title: Latency budgets
items.text:
A user-facing target must be split across the components on the path. For BoxOffice checkout (p99 < 1.5 s):

Step Budget (p99) Notes Edge (CDN, WAF, gateway) 50 ms TLS termination near the user order service logic 50 ms validation, idempotency check inventory (confirm hold) 100 ms one transaction on the primary payment → provider 1,000 ms the provider dominates; timeout at 1.2 s Write order + outbox 50 ms one transaction Slack 250 ms network variance, retries Total 1,500 ms —

Summing p99s is pessimistic (they rarely all happen on the same request), which is exactly what you want in a budget. When a step exceeds its budget, you know whose problem it is. Each budget also sets that component's timeout — a timeout longer than the caller's whole budget protects nothing.

items.title: Measuring percentiles honestly
items.text:
Two traps make tail latency look better than it is:

  • Coordinated omission: a load generator that sends the next request only after the previous one returns stops sending when the server stalls — so it never records the requests that would have arrived during the stall, and the tail disappears from the results. Use tools that keep a constant arrival rate (open model: k6's constant-arrival-rate, wrk2) and compare intended vs actual send times4. Class 15 covers it in depth.
  • Measuring at the wrong place: the server's own timer misses the time spent in the accept queue, the load balancer and the network. Measure where the user is (client-side, or at the edge), and compare with server-side numbers.

Try it: in the scale-out scenario, run the load profile and note the p50 and p99. Then use chaos at low to make one replica occasionally slow. Which percentile moves first? By how much does the p99 move compared with the p50?

Think first: SLO for the seat map

BoxOffice wants an SLO for the seat-map endpoint. Option A: "average latency < 100 ms". Option B: "99% of requests < 300 ms, measured at the gateway over 28 days". Which one, and why?

Answer: B. It is stated as a percentile (it constrains the tail, which users feel), it has a threshold that matters to users, a measurement point (the gateway, closer to the user than the service) and a window. Option A can be met while 3% of requests take more than a second — exactly the complaint on social media. SLOs are developed in class 9.

In the interview

Always state latency targets as percentiles ("p99 < 200 ms for reads"), and when your design fans out (sharded search, a page aggregating several services, scatter-gather), mention tail amplification and one mitigation: "with 20 shards, the slowest shard dominates, so I'd add hedged requests after the p95 and return partial results after a deadline." It shows you understand how distributed systems behave, not just how they are drawn.

Common pitfalls

  • Reporting averages for latency — or SLOs on averages.
  • Averaging percentiles across servers or time windows instead of merging histograms.
  • Ignoring fan-out: the backend's p99 is not the user's p99 when one request makes many calls.
  • Hedging non-idempotent requests: duplicating a POST /orders duplicates the order.
  • Coordinated omission in load tests: the tail you do not measure is the tail you do not fix.

items.text:

Scenarios: scale-out (with chaos), search-autocomplete. Continues in: Availability Math, Reliability — SLOs, Reliability — timeouts, Observability — signals, Performance — load testing, Hands-on 2.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Latency distributions have long tails; the mean hides them — use p50, p99, p99.9.
  • Percentiles come from histograms; aggregate by merging histograms, never by averaging percentiles.
  • Users and heavy customers make many requests, so the "1% tail" touches a large share of visits.
  • Under fan-out N, P(slow) = 1 − (1 − q)ᴺ: with 20 calls the backend's p99 hits 18 % of user requests; from ~70 calls on, it is the user's median.
  • Fight the tail with hedging, partial results, less fan-out, headroom and async work; split end-to-end targets into latency budgets and matching timeouts.

  1. KLEPPMANN, M.; RICCOMINI, C. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd ed. O'Reilly. Chapter 2 (describing performance: response time percentiles and tail latency amplification). ↩

  2. DeCANDIA, G. et al. Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store. SOSP, 2007 (service-level agreements expressed at the 99.9th percentile). ↩

  3. DEAN, J.; BARROSO, L. A. The Tail at Scale. Communications of the ACM, 56(2), 2013, pp. 74–80. ↩↩↩

  4. TENE, G. How NOT to Measure Latency. Talk, Strange Loop, 2015. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text: The BoxOffice inventory database is at 70% CPU during a normal on-sale and holds take about 75 ms at p99. The team decides it has "30% to spare". At the next, bigger on-sale the CPU reaches 92% — only 22 points more — and the p99 jumps to almost 300 ms, four times worse and right at the 300 ms hold target. Timeouts fire, clients retry, and the extra load pushes the database to 100%. Nothing was "broken"; the team simply did not know the shape of the curve that relates load to latency. This page derives that curve from a few simple laws, and then uses the same laws to answer the questions that every capacity decision asks: how many requests are in flight? how big must this pool be? how full can this component run? will adding nodes help?

items.title: The vocabulary of a queue
items.text:
Every component that serves requests — a CPU core, a thread pool, a database connection, a payment API — can be seen as a queue in front of one or more servers (in queueing theory, a "server" is anything that serves a request):

flowchart LR
    arrivals(["Arrivals<br/>λ requests/s"]) --> queue["Queue<br/>(waiting: Wq)"]
    queue --> s1["Server 1<br/>(service: S)"]
    queue --> s2["Server 2"]
    queue --> s3["Server c"]
    s1 --> out(["Completions<br/>X requests/s"])
    s2 --> out
    s3 --> out
Symbol Name Meaning BoxOffice example λ arrival rate requests arriving per second 1,000 holds/s S service time time a server spends on one request (no waiting) 5 ms of database work per hold μ service rate requests one server completes per second: μ = 1/S 200 holds/s per connection c servers parallel servers (cores, threads, connections) 8 productive connections ρ utilization fraction of time servers are busy: ρ = λ / (c·μ) = λ·S / c 1,000 × 0.005 / 8 = 62.5% Wq waiting time time spent in the queue before service starts — R (or W) response time waiting + service: R = Wq + S what the client measures L number in system requests waiting or in service ("in flight", concurrency) — X throughput completions per second (= λ in steady state, if nothing is dropped) —

items.title: Little's Law
items.text:
The most useful formula in capacity planning is also the simplest1:

\[ L = \lambda \times W \]

The average number of requests in a system equals the average arrival rate times the average time each request spends in the system. It holds for any stable system (arrivals do not exceed capacity in the long run), regardless of the distribution of arrivals or service times, the number of servers, or the scheduling order. You can apply it to a thread pool, a whole service, a queue, a database — or a coffee shop: if 2 customers arrive per minute and each stays 15 minutes, there are on average 30 customers inside.

Its three forms answer three different questions:

Form Question BoxOffice example L = λ × W How many requests are in flight? How big must the pool be? 1,000 holds/s × 20 ms inside the service = 20 holds in flight → at least 20 worker threads W = L / λ How long does each request (or person) wait? 2 M fans in the waiting room, admitted at 1,000/s → the last one waits 2 M / 1,000 = 2,000 s ≈ 33 min λ = L / W What throughput can this concurrency sustain? 8 connections, each hold occupies one for 5 ms → at most 8 / 0.005 = 1,600 holds/s

BoxOffice — sizing the inventory service

The inventory service receives λ = 1,000 holds/s. Each hold spends W = 40 ms inside the service (validation, the database call, serializing the response), of which 10 ms hold a database connection (the transaction plus round trips).

  • Requests in flight in the service: 1,000 × 0.040 = 40 → with one thread per request, the service needs at least 40 worker threads; with 4 replicas, ~10 each, plus headroom.
  • Connections in use: 1,000 × 0.010 = 10 → a connection pool of ~15 across all replicas suffices. A pool of 200 would not make anything faster — it would only let more transactions contend for the same rows.

Now the payment provider slows down from 300 ms to 3 s, and the order service calls it synchronously at 100 orders/s: in-flight payment calls go from 100 × 0.3 = 30 to 100 × 3 = 300. If the order service has 200 threads, it is exhausted — and every other route of the order service fails with it. This is the arithmetic of a cascading failure (class 9), and it is why timeouts and bulkheads exist.

items.title: Little's Law as a lie detector for load tests
items.text:
A load-testing tool with a fixed number of virtual users (VUs) that each send a request, wait for the response, "think" for Z seconds and repeat is a closed system. Little's Law applied to it says:

\[ N_{users} = X \times (R + Z) \]

With 100 VUs, no think time (Z = 0) and R = 50 ms, the test cannot produce more than 100 / 0.05 = 2,000 req/s, whatever the server could take. If the server slows down to R = 500 ms, the test generates only 200 req/s — the load drops exactly when the system struggles, hiding the problem. Check every load-test result with this formula; lab 2 does it, and class 15 discusses open vs closed workload models.

items.title: The utilization law
items.text:
A second, equally simple law connects throughput and utilization:

\[ U = X \times S \]

The utilization of a resource equals its throughput times the service time per request. A database that serves 1,000 holds/s at 5 ms of CPU each needs 5 CPU-seconds per second: 5 cores at 100%, or 62.5% of 8 cores. Turned around, it gives the capacity of a resource: utilization cannot exceed 100% per server, so

\[ X_{max} = \frac{c}{S} \]

That is the "parallel slots divided by service time" rule used in the overview. The resource with the highest utilization (the largest ratio of demand to capacity) is the bottleneck: it saturates first and caps the throughput of the whole system.

items.title: Why latency explodes before 100%: the knee
items.text:
If requests arrived at perfectly regular intervals and each took exactly S, a server could run at 99% utilization with no waiting at all. Real traffic is random: requests arrive in bursts, and some take longer than others. During a burst, requests queue; the queue drains during quiet moments. The busier the server, the fewer quiet moments it has to catch up — and the longer the queues grow.

The simplest model of this is the M/M/1 queue: random (Poisson) arrivals, random (exponential) service times, one server. Its mean response time is2:

\[ R = \frac{S}{1 - \rho} \] Utilization ρ Mean response time R p99 response time (≈ 4.6 R) With S = 5 ms 10% 1.1 S 5 S R ≈ 6 ms 50% 2 S 9 S R = 10 ms 70% 3.3 S 15 S R ≈ 17 ms 80% 5 S 23 S R = 25 ms 90% 10 S 46 S R = 50 ms, p99 ≈ 230 ms 95% 20 S 92 S R = 100 ms, p99 ≈ 460 ms 99% 100 S 460 S R = 500 ms, p99 ≈ 2.3 s

(In M/M/1 the response time is exponentially distributed, so its p99 is ln(100) ≈ 4.6 times its mean.) Going from 50% to 90% utilization — less than double the load — makes the response time 5× worse; from 90% to 99% — 10% more load — another 10× worse. That is exactly the story of the BoxOffice inventory at the top of this page.

The plot shows R / S as a function of utilization for one server (M/M/1, mean and p99), and for 4 and 16 servers sharing one queue (M/M/c, computed with the Erlang C formula):

2026-10-23T08:15:47.444546 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/

Three lessons from the curves:

  1. The knee. Latency is almost flat at low utilization, then bends sharply. For a single server the bend is around 70–80%; past it, small increases in load cause huge increases in latency, and the tail (p99) explodes first.
  2. Pooling helps. With 16 servers sharing one queue, the knee moves far to the right: a request only waits if all servers are busy. That is one reason why one big pool behind a load balancer behaves better than many small, separate queues (for example, sticky routing of users to specific servers).
  3. Variability is the enemy. The M/M/1 model assumes very random arrivals and service times. More regular traffic queues less; burstier traffic (an on-sale!) queues more. Kingman's approximation for a single server makes this explicit3:
\[ W_q \approx \frac{\rho}{1 - \rho} \times \frac{C_a^2 + C_s^2}{2} \times S \]

where \(C_a\) and \(C_s\) are the coefficients of variation (standard deviation / mean) of the inter-arrival and service times. The first factor is the utilization effect; the second is the variability effect. A waiting room that admits fans at a steady rate lowers \(C_a\); cutting slow outliers (a heavy query that takes 50× the normal time) lowers \(C_s\). Both reduce queueing without adding a single server.

items.title: What utilization should you run at?
items.text:
Component Typical sustained target Why Latency-sensitive service (API, database primary) ~50–70% at peak stay left of the knee; absorb bursts and the loss of one replica Batch / asynchronous workers 80–90%+ latency of individual jobs matters little; throughput and cost do Network links < 70–80% queues in routers add latency and drop packets near saturation

Redundancy pushes in the same direction: with 4 replicas at 60%, losing one moves the other three to 80% — still serviceable. With 4 replicas at 80%, losing one asks for 107%: the remaining replicas collapse. Headroom is what makes failover work.

BoxOffice — reading the knee from the playground

In the overview, the monolith scenario with the breakpoint profile ramps load until it breaks. Suppose the database has 8 slots and S = 5 ms: capacity = 8 / 0.005 = 1,600 req/s. The knee (p99 rising sharply) should appear around 70–85% of that, ~1,100–1,350 req/s, and errors only near 1,600 req/s. If you see the knee much earlier, the bottleneck is somewhere else (the app server's thread pool, perhaps) — find the component with the highest utilization.

Try it: run the breakpoint profile, then double the database's capacity (or add app replicas) and run again. Does the knee move? By how much? If adding app replicas does not move it, which component is the bottleneck?

items.title: When more servers stop helping
items.text: Little's Law and the utilization law suggest that capacity grows linearly with the number of servers: X_max = c / S. In practice it does not, because servers coordinate. Two classic models describe how scaling bends.

items.title: Amdahl's law
items.text:
If a fraction σ of the work is inherently serial (cannot be parallelized — a global lock, a single primary, a sequential step), then with N parallel workers the speedup is bounded4:

\[ \text{Speedup}(N) = \frac{N}{1 + \sigma (N - 1)} \;\le\; \frac{1}{\sigma} \]

With 5% serial work, no number of nodes gives more than 20× speedup; with 1%, 100×. For BoxOffice: if every hold must pass through the same lock on the same "section counter" row for even 5% of its time, adding inventory replicas stops paying off long before 20 replicas.

items.title: The Universal Scalability Law
items.text:
Neil Gunther's Universal Scalability Law (USL) adds a second term, κ (coherency), for the cost of keeping nodes consistent with each other — cache invalidation messages, distributed locks, cluster membership chatter, replication — which grows with the number of pairs of nodes, roughly N²5:

\[ C(N) = \frac{N}{1 + \sigma (N - 1) + \kappa N (N - 1)} \]

With κ > 0, throughput does not just flatten — it reaches a peak at \(N^* = \sqrt{(1 - \sigma)/\kappa}\) and then decreases: adding nodes makes the system slower.

2026-10-23T08:15:47.542149 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ Model Parameters Shape Real-world causes Linear — doubles with N shared-nothing, perfectly partitioned work (rare) Amdahl σ (contention) flattens at 1/σ a single primary, a global lock, a sequential step USL σ, κ (coherency) peaks at N*, then falls lock contention across nodes, cache coherence traffic, all-to-all chatter

The practical use of the USL is to fit σ and κ to a few load-test measurements (throughput at N = 1, 2, 4, 8…) and predict where scaling stops before buying the hardware (class 15). The design lesson is broader: shared-nothing designs scale. Partition the work so that nodes do not need to talk to each other — BoxOffice partitions inventory by event, so that holds for different events never contend — and both σ and κ shrink.

Think first: will a second inventory database help?

The on-sale for one stadium show is limited by row-lock contention on that event's seats in the inventory database. The team proposes adding a second database node with multi-primary replication. Use Amdahl and the USL to argue.

Answer: the bottleneck is contention on the same rows (σ), not CPU. A second primary does not split that contention — both nodes still need to agree on the same seats, which adds coherency cost (κ: cross-node conflict detection or distributed locking). Throughput for that event would likely drop. What helps is reducing σ: shorter transactions, holding seats with one conditional UPDATE, admitting fans at a steady rate (waiting room), or splitting the event into independently allocated sections. A second node does help with different events (partitioning by event), where there is no shared state.

In the interview

Use Little's Law whenever you size a pool, a queue or a fleet: "1,000 req/s × 40 ms = 40 concurrent requests, so 4 instances with 16 threads each leave headroom". When proposing capacity, say the target utilization and why: "I'd size for 60% at peak so we stay left of the knee and survive losing one node." If asked "what if we add more servers?", mention the bottleneck and Amdahl: "app servers scale linearly until the single primary saturates; after that, we need to cache, partition or queue."

Common pitfalls

  • Planning for 90–100% utilization of latency-sensitive components: the p99 collapses long before the CPU graph looks alarming.
  • Oversized pools: a pool of 500 database connections does not add capacity; it moves the queue into the database, where contention makes everything slower.
  • Ignoring Little's Law in load tests: closed-loop tools with few VUs cannot generate the intended load against a slow system.
  • Assuming linear scaling: serial sections and coordination costs bend the curve; measure at several N.
  • Unbounded queues: a queue that grows without limit turns overload into ever-growing latency; bound it and shed load early (class 9).

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Little's Law L = λ × W gives concurrency, waiting time or throughput from the other two — for pools, services, queues and load tests.
  • Utilization law U = X × S; capacity ≈ c / S; the most loaded resource is the bottleneck.
  • Response time grows like S / (1 − ρ): flat at low load, explosive past the knee (≈ 70–80% for one server); the tail explodes first.
  • Run latency-sensitive components at ~50–70% at peak; pooling and lower variability push the knee right.
  • Amdahl (serial fraction σ) caps speedup at 1/σ; the USL (coherency κ) makes throughput fall past N*; shared-nothing partitioning is how you scale.

  1. LITTLE, J. D. C. A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW. Operations Research, 9(3), 1961, pp. 383–387. ↩

  2. HARCHOL-BALTER, M. Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems: Queueing Theory in Action. Cambridge University Press, 2013. ↩

  3. KINGMAN, J. F. C. The single server queue in heavy traffic. Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, 57(4), 1961, pp. 902–904. ↩

  4. AMDAHL, G. M. Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities. AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference, 1967. ↩
