items.title: Index
items.text:
Friday, 10:00. BoxOffice, a small ticketing start-up, opens the sale for the year's biggest stadium show: 60,000 seats, 2 million fans refreshing the page at the same second. At 10:00:04 the site answers in 9 seconds. At 10:00:20 it answers nothing. At 10:03 it comes back — and 312 seats have been sold twice. The code had no bug that a unit test could catch: every function did exactly what it was written to do. What failed was the system: how many machines, which database, where the data lives, what waits for what, and what happens when 2 million people arrive at once.

This course is about that layer — the decisions that sit above the code and decide whether the code survives contact with reality. By the end of the semester you will be able to design BoxOffice so that 10:00 on Friday is a non-event, measure that it works, and defend every decision with numbers, in a design review or in a system-design interview.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Explain what system design is, how it differs from software (code-level) design, and why it is a trade-off discipline rather than a search for the "right" architecture.
  • Distinguish functional from non-functional requirements and write measurable quality-attribute targets (scalability, availability, latency, consistency, durability, cost, security, operability) for a system.
  • Trace the evolution of a system from one server to millions of users, identifying the symptom that triggers each new component.
  • Apply a time-boxed framework (clarify → estimate → API & data model → high-level design → deep dives → bottlenecks & trade-offs → wrap-up) to an open-ended design problem in 45 minutes.
  • Use the System Design Playground to build an architecture from the component palette, load it, and read its metrics.

  2. Requirements — functional vs non-functional requirements; the quality attributes and how to make them measurable.
  3. The Scaling Journey — BoxOffice from 1 user to 10 million: monolith first, then one component per symptom.
  4. The Interview Framework — a 7-step, 45-minute method for open-ended design problems.
  5. Quiz — check your understanding.

items.title: What is system design?
items.text:
System design is the process of defining the components of a system, the interfaces between them, and the data that flows through and is stored by them, so that the system satisfies its requirements — both what it must do and how well it must do it1. It answers questions like:

  • How many servers do we need, and what happens when one dies?
  • Where does each piece of data live, who is allowed to change it, and how fast must every reader see the change?
  • Which work must happen now, while the user waits, and which can happen later?
  • What will this cost per month, and what breaks first if traffic doubles?

It is useful to place system design next to the design work you already know:

Level Typical question Unit of design Example from BoxOffice Algorithm How do I compute this efficiently? function, data structure find the best available block of 4 adjacent seats Software design How do I organize this code so it is easy to change? classes, modules, packages OrderService depends on a PaymentGateway interface System design How do these running processes and machines cooperate under load and failure? services, databases, queues, caches, networks inventory in PostgreSQL with row locks; catalog served from a cache and a CDN

The jump from software design to system design is a jump from one process to many processes on many machines, connected by an unreliable network. That jump brings three new realities:

  1. Load — the system must keep working when many users arrive at once. Ten users and ten million users need different architectures, not just more of the same.
  2. Partial failure — some parts fail while others keep running. A disk fills, a node reboots, a third-party API slows down. The system must keep its promises anyway.
  3. Trade-offs — almost every decision buys one quality with another. A cache buys latency with freshness; a replica buys availability with consistency; a queue buys resilience with immediacy.

There is no right architecture — only justified ones

The question "what is the best database?" has no answer. "Which database fits a seat inventory that must never double-sell, at 5,000 writes per second at peak, with a two-person team and a R$ 20k monthly budget?" has a few good answers and many bad ones. System design is the skill of turning the first kind of question into the second, then choosing — and saying out loud what you gave up.

items.title: Why it matters to you
items.text:
• At work, almost every feature eventually raises a system question: Will this query be fast with 50 million rows? Should this e-mail be sent synchronously? What happens if the payment provider is down? Engineers who can answer with numbers make better decisions and are trusted with bigger ones.
  • In interviews, system design is a standard round for software engineering roles at most technology companies. It is open-ended on purpose: the interviewer watches how you think — how you clarify, estimate, structure, and handle trade-offs2.
  • In this course, it is the thread that ties together everything from DNS to AI agents: each topic is a component you add to a design for a reason you can measure.

items.title: BoxOffice, the running example
items.text:
Every class, lab, quiz and slide deck uses the same fictional system, so that each new concept lands on a problem you already know. BoxOffice sells tickets for concerts, games and festivals. It was chosen because it has, on purpose, every hard property a real system can have — and they are intuitive:

Property Where it shows up in BoxOffice Course topic Extreme spikes the flash sale at 10:00: 2 M fans, 60 k seats estimation, edge, messaging, performance Read-heavy traffic browsing events, venues, seat maps caching, CDN, replicas Strong consistency a seat can be sold exactly once databases, distributed systems External dependencies payment provider, e-mail, push notifications compute & integrations, reliability Search "rock shows in São Paulo next weekend" databases (search engines) Abuse bots buying tickets to resell edge (WAF, rate limiting), security Asynchronous work tickets by e-mail, waiting room, analytics messaging AI a support assistant that answers "can I change my seat?" AI systems

Its services — which you will build, measure and break in the labs — are gateway, auth, catalog (events and venues), inventory (seats and holds), order, payment (adapter to an external provider), notification, search and assistant (AI). The code lives in the course repository, https://github.com/repo-classes/pma271.

How the semester runs

Every week has a theory meeting (a class like this one) and a practice meeting (a hands-on lab). The theory introduces a palette group and the reasoning behind it; the lab builds the same idea into the real BoxOffice code (Java 21 + Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, Nginx, Kubernetes…) and measures it with k6. Individual exercises make you practice estimation, playground designs and load-test reports; the team project takes one system from a design document to a load-tested, observable deployment with a chaos game day.

items.title: The System Design Playground
items.text:
Reading about a cache is not the same as watching the p99 latency fall when its hit ratio climbs. The course comes with a simulator, the System Design Playground, where every component of the palette is a block you can drop on a canvas, connect, and put under load. It is a model — it does not run real code — but it reproduces the behaviour that matters for design: queues that grow when a component is saturated, latency that explodes near full utilization, failures that cascade when there are no timeouts, cost that grows with every replica.

The workflow is always the same:

  1. Build — pick components from the palette and connect them (client → load balancer → app → database…).
  2. Configure — set capacities, replicas, cache hit ratios, timeouts.
  3. Load — choose a load profile: smoke (a trickle, to check it works), load (expected traffic), stress (beyond it), spike (a sudden jump, like 10:00 on Friday), soak (hours at a steady rate), breakpoint (ramp until something breaks), chaos (inject failures).
  4. Read — watch throughput, latency percentiles (p50, p99), error rate, per-component utilization and monthly cost.
  5. Change one thing and run again. That is the scientific method applied to architecture, and it is exactly what you will do with real systems in the labs.

Throughout the course, pages embed the playground preloaded with a scenario. Here is the first one: BoxOffice as a single application server and a single SQL database.

Try it: start with the load profile and note the p99 latency and the utilization of the app and the database. Then switch to spike. Which component saturates first? What happens to latency before errors appear? Write down the request rate at which things went wrong — you will compute it by hand in class 2.

What did you see? (open after trying)

As the load approaches the capacity of the most-loaded component, latency grows slowly at first and then explodes — long before the error rate rises. Requests queue up in front of the saturated component; each new request waits for all the ones ahead of it. This "knee" in the latency curve is one of the most important shapes in the course: class 2 explains it with queueing theory, and every capacity decision you make afterwards (how many replicas? how big a connection pool?) is about staying to the left of it.

The second scenario puts a load balancer in front of several replicas of the application.

Try it: run the stress profile with 1 replica, then 2, then 4. Does throughput double each time? Watch the database: at some point adding app replicas stops helping. Why? Then kill one replica (or use the chaos profile) and watch what the health checks do.

BoxOffice — what the two scenarios teach

Horizontal scaling (more app servers) only helps while the app servers are the bottleneck. Once the single database saturates, extra replicas just queue at the database instead of at the app. The next move is not "more of the same" but a different component: a cache for the catalog reads, read replicas, or a queue in front of the seat inventory. Choosing which one, and proving it with numbers, is what The Scaling Journey and the rest of the course are about.

items.title: How to study system design
items.text:
• Draw. Every concept in this course has a picture. If you cannot draw it, you do not understand it yet.
  • Estimate before you design. A design for 100 requests per second and one for 100,000 are different designs. Class 2 gives you the numbers and formulas.
  • Name the trade-off. For every component you add, say what it buys and what it costs: "the cache cuts catalog p99 from 80 ms to 5 ms, at the price of showing a price up to 60 s stale".
  • Break things on purpose. In the playground and in the labs, find the breaking point, then fix it. You learn more from one saturation than from ten diagrams.
  • Practise out loud. System design is a conversation. Use the interview framework with a classmate every week, starting now.

Common pitfalls when starting

  • Jumping to technology names ("Kafka! Kubernetes! microservices!") before understanding the problem and its numbers.
  • Designing for Google scale when the problem has 1,000 users. Over-engineering is as wrong as under-engineering — and more expensive.
  • Treating the diagram as the answer. The boxes are the easy part; the reasoning about load, failure and trade-offs is the design.
  • Ignoring cost and operability. An architecture the team cannot afford or cannot operate at 3 a.m. is not a good architecture.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• System design decides components, interfaces and data so that a system meets functional and non-functional requirements under load and partial failure.
  • It is a trade-off discipline: every component buys one quality with another; good designs say which.
  • The course is organized around a component palette of ten categories; each theory class teaches one group, and the catalog is your dictionary.
  • BoxOffice — a ticketing platform with a 10:00 flash sale — is the example everywhere.
  • The playground lets you build, load and break architectures in minutes; the labs do the same with real code and real measurements.

  1. KLEPPMANN, M.; RICCOMINI, C. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd ed. O'Reilly. Chapter 1 (trade-offs in data systems architecture). ↩

  2. XU, A. System Design Interview — An Insider's Guide, vol. 1. Byte Code LLC, 2020. Chapter 3 (a framework for system design interviews). ↩

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: System design and requirements
items.text:
Q1. Which question is a system design question rather than a software (code-level) design question?

  • A. Should OrderService depend on an interface or on a concrete payment client class?
  • B. Which sorting algorithm should rank events by date?
  • C. Should seat holds and the event catalog live in the same database, given that one is strongly consistent and write-hot and the other is read-heavy and cacheable?
  • D. Should a method throw a checked or an unchecked exception?
Answer

C — It is about running components, data placement and load.

System design decides components, interfaces between running processes, and where data lives, so that the system meets its requirements under load and partial failure. A and D are code-level design; B is an algorithm question.

Q2. Which of the following is a non-functional requirement?

  • A. A fan can hold up to 6 seats for 10 minutes.
  • B. Organizers can schedule an on-sale date.
  • C. Seat holds complete in under 300 ms at the 99th percentile while handling 5,000 holds per second.
  • D. Fans receive their tickets by e-mail.
Answer

C — It describes how well, with a number, a percentile and a load level.

A, B and D describe what the system does (functional). C is a measurable latency target at a stated throughput — a quality attribute.

Q3. Why is "the system must be scalable" a poor requirement?

  • A. Scalability cannot be achieved with relational databases.
  • B. It does not say which load parameter grows, by how much, or what performance must be kept while it grows.
  • C. Scalability is a functional requirement, not a non-functional one.
  • D. Modern clouds scale automatically, so the requirement is redundant.
Answer

B — Scalability is meaningless without a load parameter and a target.

A useful version names the load ("2 M fans in the first minute of an on-sale", "1,500 catalog reads/s") and the performance to keep ("hold p99 < 300 ms"). Clouds provide resources, not an architecture that can use them.

Q4. BoxOffice needs strong consistency for which data?

  • A. The event description shown in search results.
  • B. The "1,234 people are looking at this event" counter.
  • C. The state of each seat (free, held, sold).
  • D. The list of recommended events on the home page.
Answer

C — Two fans must never buy the same seat.

Strong consistency costs latency and availability, so it is paid only where the business requires it. Descriptions and recommendations can be seconds or minutes stale; the viewer counter is only a hint.

Q5. A database is unreachable for 20 minutes because of a network problem, but no confirmed data is lost. Which statement is correct?

  • A. Durability was violated, availability was not.
  • B. Availability was violated, durability was not.
  • C. Both availability and durability were violated.
  • D. Neither was violated, because the data is still there.
Answer

B — Unavailable, but durable.

Availability is about serving requests when needed; durability is about never losing confirmed data. A system can be down without losing anything (this case), or up while keeping nothing durable (a cache).

Q6. Which statement best describes the trade-off introduced by caching the event catalog?

  • A. It improves consistency at the cost of latency.
  • B. It improves latency and reduces database load at the cost of freshness (readers may see stale data).
  • C. It improves durability at the cost of availability.
  • D. It has no trade-off if the TTL is short.
Answer

B — Speed and offload are bought with freshness.

A cached page can be stale until its TTL expires or the key is invalidated. A shorter TTL reduces staleness but also the hit ratio — it moves along the trade-off, it does not remove it.

items.title: The scaling journey
items.text:
Q7. BoxOffice runs three app server replicas behind a load balancer. After a login, fans are randomly "logged out" on the next page. What is the most likely cause?

  • A. The load balancer's health checks are too frequent.
  • B. Session state is kept in the memory of the app server that handled the login.
  • C. The database has no read replicas.
  • D. The CDN is caching the login page.
Answer

B — The app servers are not stateless.

The next request lands on another replica that does not know the session. Keep session state in a signed token (JWT) or a shared store (Redis). Stateless app servers are the precondition for horizontal scaling and rolling deploys.

Q8. The catalog database is at 80% CPU, and 95% of its queries are reads of data that changes a few times per day. Adding which component gives the biggest reduction in database load per real (R$) spent?

  • A. More app server replicas.
  • B. A cache with cache-aside, reaching a 95% hit ratio.
  • C. A message queue between the app and the database.
  • D. Sharding the catalog database.
Answer

B — A 95% hit ratio sends only 5% of reads to the database (a 20× reduction).

More app replicas (A) would only add load on the database. A queue (C) does not help synchronous reads. Sharding (D) adds a lot of complexity for a problem that is read volume, not data size or write volume.

Q9. After adding read replicas, a fan pays, is redirected to "My orders" and does not see the new order. What is happening, and what is a standard fix?

  • A. The order was lost; enable synchronous replication everywhere.
  • B. Replication lag: the read hit a replica that has not applied the write yet; read the fan's own recent data from the primary (read-your-writes).
  • C. The CDN cached the page; disable the CDN.
  • D. The load balancer sent the request to an unhealthy server; reduce the health-check interval.
Answer

B — Replication lag; use read-your-writes.

Replicas apply the primary's changes asynchronously, milliseconds to seconds later. Routing a user's reads of their own recent writes (or the whole critical flow) to the primary fixes the symptom without giving up replicas for everything else.

Q10. Why does BoxOffice put a waiting room (a queue) in front of the inventory for big on-sales?

  • A. To store tickets durably.
  • B. To convert a spike of millions of concurrent requests on hot rows into a steady admission rate that the inventory can sustain.
  • C. To make seat holds eventually consistent.
  • D. To cache the seat map.
Answer

B — It shapes the spike into a flat, sustainable load.

60 k seats cannot accept 2 M concurrent holds: the rows are hot and the database has a finite capacity. The waiting room admits fans at that capacity and keeps the inventory strongly consistent.

Q11. A team of four engineers is starting a new product with an uncertain domain and a few hundred users. Which architecture is the most sensible starting point?

  • A. Twelve microservices on Kubernetes with Kafka between them.
  • B. A modular monolith with one database, extracting services later when a measured symptom justifies it.
  • C. One serverless function per database table.
  • D. A multi-region active-active deployment.
Answer

B — Monolith first.

Distribution has a large fixed cost (network failures, distributed data, many deployables, platform work). With an uncertain domain the service boundaries are not known yet; a modular monolith keeps them cheap to change.

items.title: The interview framework
items.text:
Q12. In a 45-minute system-design interview, what is the main purpose of the estimation step?

  • A. To show that you can multiply large numbers quickly.
  • B. To compute exact server counts for the final design.
  • C. To get orders of magnitude that change design decisions — for example, whether to cache, shard or queue.
  • D. To fill time while thinking about the design.
Answer

C — An estimate that leads to no decision is just arithmetic.

"40 GB/year of orders fits one database for years — no sharding" or "100 k req/s at the on-sale — the inventory needs a waiting room" are the kind of conclusions an estimate exists for.

Q13. Twenty minutes into the interview, the candidate has a detailed SQL schema but no diagram of the overall system. Which principle was violated?

  • A. Think out loud.
  • B. Go broad first, then deep — a complete simple design before any deep dive.
  • C. State assumptions explicitly.
  • D. Estimate before designing.
Answer

B — Breadth first.

The interviewer cannot evaluate depth on a design they have not seen. Draw a high-level design that covers every functional requirement (step 4) before the deep dives (step 5), and watch the clock at each transition.

Q14. During the deep dive on double booking, which answer shows the strongest trade-off reasoning?

  • A. "I'll use Redis locks, because Redis is fast."
  • B. "I'll use a database, because databases are consistent."
  • C. "Options: pessimistic locks, a conditional UPDATE … WHERE status = 'FREE', or a distributed lock. The conditional update is atomic in the single source of truth and holds no long locks; a Redis lock adds a second system that must agree with the database. I'll use the conditional update."
  • D. "Double booking is rare, so I'll fix it later with refunds."
Answer

C — Alternatives, comparison, choice, and what is given up.

A and B name a technology without comparing it to anything. D ignores a requirement the candidate wrote on the board ("no double booking, ever").

Q15. The interviewer asks: "What happens if the payment provider becomes very slow?" What is the best reaction?

  • A. Explain that the provider has an SLA, so it will not happen.
  • B. Treat it as a hint about failure handling: add timeouts and a circuit breaker on the payment call, keep the hold alive while payment is pending, and explain the cost (seats locked longer).
  • C. Replace the provider with an in-house payment system.
  • D. Ask the interviewer to move on to another topic.
Answer

B — Questions from the interviewer are hints about what they want to evaluate.

A slow dependency without timeouts exhausts the caller's threads and cascades (class 9). Naming the mitigation and its cost shows both depth and trade-off reasoning.

items.title: Index
items.text:
"Design a ticketing system like BoxOffice. You have 45 minutes." The prompt is one sentence long on purpose. There is no single correct answer, no hidden test suite, and the interviewer will not tell you what to do next. What they evaluate is how you get from a vague sentence to a defensible design: the questions you ask, the numbers you estimate, the structure you impose, and how you reason about trade-offs when they push back1.

Without a method, 45 minutes disappear fast: 20 minutes on the database schema, then a panic to draw the rest. This page gives you a seven-step framework with a time budget, applies it end to end to BoxOffice, and lists what interviewers look for at each step. The same framework is useful outside interviews — it is the skeleton of a good design review or design document.

items.title: What the interviewer is looking for
items.text:
Interviewers usually score a few dimensions, with different names in different companies but similar content12:

Signal What it looks like in practice Problem navigation asks clarifying questions; scopes the problem; identifies what is hard about this problem Solution design a working high-level design that covers the requirements, built from appropriate components Technical depth can go deep on the critical parts: data model, consistency, scaling, failure handling Trade-off reasoning names alternatives, compares them with numbers, states what is given up Communication thinks aloud, drives the session, structures the board, adapts to feedback

Expectations grow with seniority. A rough guide:

Level Expected Intern / junior a reasonable high-level design with guidance; knows the main components and what they do Mid-level drives the whole design; goes deep in one or two areas; spots the main bottleneck Senior and above drives and prioritizes: finds the hardest parts quickly, goes deep with numbers, anticipates failure modes, operations and cost, and discusses evolution

items.title: The framework at a glance
items.text:
# Step Time (45 min) Output on the board 1 Clarify requirements 0–5 min functional list (3–5 items) + non-functional targets 2 Estimate 5–10 min requests/s (average and peak), storage, bandwidth — and what they imply 3 API & data model 10–15 min 4–6 endpoints; main entities with keys 4 High-level design 15–25 min box-and-arrow diagram covering every functional requirement 5 Deep dives 25–37 min detail of the 1–3 hardest parts 6 Bottlenecks & trade-offs 37–42 min what breaks first, how to fix it, what each choice costs 7 Wrap-up 42–45 min summary, open issues, how it evolves

The times are a budget, not a law: if the interviewer wants to spend 15 minutes on one deep dive, follow them. But check the clock at each transition — running out of time before drawing a complete high-level design is the most common way to fail.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Candidate
    participant I as Interviewer
    I->>C: "Design BoxOffice"
    C->>I: 1. Clarifying questions (users, scale, consistency, scope)
    I-->>C: answers / "you decide"
    C->>C: 2. Estimate out loud
    C->>I: 3. Proposes API and data model
    C->>I: 4. Draws the high-level design
    I-->>C: "How do you avoid double booking?"
    C->>I: 5. Deep dive (with alternatives)
    I-->>C: "What if traffic grows 10×?"
    C->>I: 6. Bottlenecks and trade-offs
    C->>I: 7. Wrap-up: summary and next steps

Notice the arrows from the interviewer: deep dives and bottlenecks are often steered by their questions. Treat every question as a hint about what they want to evaluate, not as an attack.

items.title: Step 1 — Clarify requirements (≈ 5 min)
items.text:
Goal: turn the one-sentence prompt into a problem with boundaries. Ask, then write the answers on the board.

  • Users and scale: how many users, daily active users, peak events?
  • Core features: which 3–5 must I design? What is out of scope?
  • Read/write mix and access patterns: read-heavy or write-heavy? Spiky?
  • Consistency: what must never be wrong? What can be stale?
  • Latency and availability expectations; any regulation (payments, personal data)?

BoxOffice — step 1

Functional (in scope): browse/search events; view seat map; hold seats (10-min expiry); pay via external provider; receive ticket. Out of scope: resale, dynamic pricing, organizer tools beyond creating events.

Non-functional: 20 M registered fans, 2 M daily active; big on-sales with 2 M fans for 60 k seats in the first minute; no double booking, ever; catalog may be ~1 min stale; hold p99 < 300 ms; checkout available 99.95%.

"So the interesting part is the on-sale: a huge spike of contention on a small, strongly consistent inventory. I'll focus the design there, OK?"

That last sentence matters: naming what is hard about this problem shows problem navigation and tells the interviewer where you will spend your deep-dive time.

items.title: Step 2 — Estimate (≈ 5 min)
items.text:
Goal: get orders of magnitude that change decisions. Round aggressively and say the conclusion, not just the arithmetic. Class 2 teaches the method; here is how it sounds in the interview:

BoxOffice — step 2

  • Normal day: 2 M fans × 20 page views = 40 M reads/day ≈ 40 M / 10⁵ s ≈ 400 reads/s, peak ×3 ≈ 1,200 reads/s. Orders: 100 k/day ≈ 1 write/s. Read-heavy: cache the catalog.
  • On-sale: 2 M fans in 60 s ≈ 33 k arrivals/s, each polling a few times ≈ 100 k+ req/s at the edge. Only 60 k seats ⇒ at most 60 k successful orders. "The inventory cannot see 100 k req/s on the same rows — I need a waiting room that admits a few thousand per second."
  • Storage: orders 100 k/day × 1 KB ≈ 100 MB/day ≈ 40 GB/year — fits one PostgreSQL primary for years; no sharding needed for orders. Seat rows per event ≤ 100 k × 100 B ≈ 10 MB — tiny, but hot.

Two decisions came out of four lines of arithmetic: a cache for the catalog and a waiting room for the inventory. That is the purpose of estimating.

items.title: Step 3 — API and data model (≈ 5 min)
items.text:
Goal: make the functional requirements concrete. List the main endpoints (or messages) and the main entities with their keys. Don't write every field — just enough to reason about access patterns and consistency.

GET  /events?q=&city=&date=           search and browse (cacheable)
GET  /events/{eventId}/seats          seat map with availability
POST /events/{eventId}/holds          { seatIds }        → { holdId, expiresAt }
POST /orders                          { holdId }         → { orderId, paymentUrl }
POST /payments/webhook                provider → BoxOffice: paid | declined
GET  /orders/{orderId}                status and tickets
Entity Key Main fields Store event event_id name, venue, date, on-sale time SQL (catalog), cached seat (event_id, seat_id) section, row, price, status (free / held / sold), hold_id, version SQL (inventory) hold hold_id fan_id, event_id, seat list, expires_at SQL (inventory) order order_id fan_id, hold_id, amount, status, idempotency key SQL (orders) ticket ticket_id order_id, seat, QR code SQL / Object Store (PDF)

Mention the access pattern next to each entity: the seat map is read by event_id; holds update a few seats of one event; orders are read by fan_id. Those patterns drive indexes and, later, partition keys.

items.title: Step 4 — High-level design (≈ 10 min)
items.text:
Goal: a diagram that serves every functional requirement end to end. Start simple, then add what the estimates demand. Walk through one request at a time as you draw ("the fan opens the event page: CDN, gateway, catalog, cache…").

flowchart LR
    fan([Fan]) --> cdn["CDN<br/>static + images"]
    fan --> gw["API Gateway<br/>auth, rate limit"]
    gw --> catalog["catalog"]
    catalog --> cache[("Cache")]
    cache --> catdb[("Catalog SQL<br/>+ replicas")]
    gw --> wr["Waiting room"]
    wr --> inventory["inventory"]
    inventory --> invdb[("Inventory SQL<br/>primary")]
    inventory --> order["order"]
    order --> psp["Payment provider"]
    psp -->|webhook| order
    order --> stream["Event stream"]
    stream --> notification["notification"]
    stream --> search["search"]

Draw the happy path first

Draw the components needed by the main flow, label the arrows (sync call, async message, replication), and only then decorate (replicas, caches, monitoring). An interviewer cannot evaluate a deep dive into a design they have not seen completely.

items.title: Step 5 — Deep dives (≈ 12 min)
items.text:
Goal: show technical depth on the 1–3 hardest parts. Choose them yourself (the ones you named in step 1), or follow the interviewer. For each one: state the problem, present two or three alternatives, compare them, choose.

BoxOffice — deep dive 1: never sell a seat twice

Problem: thousands of fans try to hold the same seats concurrently.

Option How Trade-off Pessimistic lock SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the seat rows inside a transaction simple and correct; locks queue under contention Conditional update (optimistic) one atomic UPDATE … WHERE status = 'FREE'; check the row count no long locks; a loser just retries other seats Distributed lock (Redis) lock per seat in Redis, then write to SQL extra component, and two systems must agree — avoid when the DB can do it

Choice: conditional update in the inventory database — the database is the single source of truth, and the check-and-set is one atomic statement:

UPDATE seat
   SET status = 'HELD', hold_id = :holdId, version = version + 1
 WHERE event_id = :eventId
   AND seat_id IN (:seatIds)
   AND status = 'FREE';
-- rows updated = number requested → hold created; otherwise roll back and answer 409

Expired holds are released by a scheduled job (status = 'HELD' AND expires_at < now()), or lazily at read time.

BoxOffice — deep dive 2: the 10:00 spike

The waiting room admits fans at the rate the inventory sustains. If one hold takes 5 ms of database time on a hot event and the database runs ~8 of them in parallel productively, the inventory completes about 8 / 0.005 = 1,600 holds/s at full utilization — say ~1,000/s to keep latency low (class 2 explains why). With ~2 seats per fan, 60 k seats need ~30 k successful fans: about 30 s of admissions. The other ~2 M fans wait in line, and the waiting room tells them as early as possible that the show is sold out. The catalog page for the event is pre-warmed in the cache and the CDN before 10:00 to avoid a cold-cache stampede.

BoxOffice — deep dive 3: paying exactly once

The fan clicks "pay" twice, or the network drops the response and the client retries. Each POST /orders carries an idempotency key; the order service stores it with a unique constraint and returns the existing order for a repeated key. The payment provider's webhook may also arrive twice — the handler is idempotent by provider transaction id.

items.title: Step 6 — Bottlenecks and trade-offs (≈ 5 min)
items.text:
Goal: critique your own design before the interviewer does. Go through the diagram and ask, for each component: what breaks first? what is the single point of failure? what happens if it is slow?

Concern Mitigation Cost of the mitigation Hot event = hot rows in one database waiting room; seats of one event on one partition (sharding by event_id across events) queueing delay for fans Payment provider slow or down timeout + circuit breaker; hold extended while payment is pending complexity; seats locked longer Catalog cache stampede at 10:00 pre-warm; request coalescing more moving parts Inventory primary failure synchronous standby + automatic failover write latency; a few seconds of unavailability Bots WAF, rate limit per fan/card, CAPTCHA at queue entry friction for real fans

Then name the main trade-offs explicitly: "I chose strong consistency for seats over availability: if the inventory primary is unreachable, holds fail rather than risk a double sale. The catalog is the opposite: I accept 60 s staleness for speed."

items.title: Step 7 — Wrap-up (≈ 3 min)
items.text: Goal: leave a clear final picture. In three or four sentences: what you designed, how it meets the key requirements, what you would do next with more time (monitoring and SLO alerts, multi-region, the AI assistant…), and any open questions. Do not introduce new components now.

items.title: How to communicate
items.text:
The structure above is necessary but not sufficient. These habits make the difference3:

  • Think out loud. Silence is the worst signal; say what you are considering and why, even when unsure.
  • Go broad, then deep. A complete simple design beats a perfect half design.
  • State assumptions explicitly. "I'll assume 2 M daily fans; tell me if that's off."
  • Use the board as your memory. Requirements in one corner, numbers in another, diagram in the middle — refer back to them.
  • Welcome pushback. "Good point — if the provider is down for an hour, holds expire; let me revisit that." Changing your mind with a reason is a strong signal.
  • Drive. Announce transitions: "I have the high-level design; I'd like to deep-dive into the double-booking problem, then the spike."
  • Quantify trade-offs. "This adds ~1 ms per request but cuts database load by 10×."

In the interview

Memorize the seven steps and their time budget, and say them out loud at the start: "I'll clarify requirements, do some quick estimates, sketch the API and data, draw a high-level design, then deep-dive into the hardest parts and discuss bottlenecks." The interviewer immediately knows you have a plan — and you have a checklist to fall back on when nerves hit.

items.title: Practising with the playground
items.text:
The playground is a good sparring partner for steps 4–6. After designing a problem on paper, rebuild your high-level design from the palette, run the load profile that matches your estimates (spike for an on-sale, soak for a steady service), and look for the first saturated component. If it is not the one you named in step 6, find out why. The practice problems and mock interview guide are organized to be used in pairs: one candidate, one interviewer, then swap.

Common pitfalls

  • Jumping into the design without clarifying — solving a problem the interviewer did not ask.
  • Estimating for the sake of it — numbers that lead to no decision waste minutes.
  • Going deep too early — 20 minutes on the schema, no time for the architecture.
  • Buzzword architecture — naming technologies without saying what problem each solves.
  • One option only — a deep dive with no alternatives shows no trade-off reasoning.
  • Defending every decision to the end — treating hints as attacks.
  • Ignoring failures — a design that only works when every component is up.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    S1["1. Clarify<br/>→ Requirements"] --> S2["2. Estimate<br/>→ Estimation"]
    S2 --> S3["3. API & data model<br/>→ Compute, Databases"]
    S3 --> S4["4. High-level design<br/>palette components"]
    S4 --> S5["5. Deep dives"]
    S5 --> S6["6. Bottlenecks<br/>& trade-offs"]
    S6 --> S7["7. Wrap-up"]
    S5 --> D1["no double booking<br/>sql conditional update"]
    S5 --> D2["the 10:00 spike<br/>waiting-room queue"]
    S5 --> D3["pay exactly once<br/>idempotency key, webhook"]
    S6 --> PG["rehearse in the playground<br/>→ Case studies"]

Palette components of the BoxOffice high-level design: cdn (static files and images) · apigw (auth, rate limit) · app (catalog, inventory, order) · cache (catalog) · sql (inventory primary, catalog replicas) · queue (waiting room) · payment (provider and webhook) · stream (events to notification and search) · waf (bots). Scenarios: flash-sale, payment-system, url-shortener (a first practice problem). Continues in: Case studies, Ticketing — the BoxOffice flash sale, Databases — the double-booking bug, Compute — idempotency keys, Interview prep — framework.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• The system-design interview evaluates process: navigation, design, depth, trade-offs and communication.
  • Use seven steps with a time budget: clarify → estimate → API & data model → high-level design → deep dives → bottlenecks & trade-offs → wrap-up.
  • Clarifying should end with what is hard about this problem — that is where your deep dives go.
  • Estimates exist to change decisions (cache? shard? queue?).
  • Deep dives compare alternatives and choose; the wrap-up summarizes and points to next steps.

  1. XU, A. System Design Interview — An Insider's Guide, vol. 1. Byte Code LLC, 2020. Chapter 3 (a framework for system design interviews). ↩↩

  2. XU, A.; LAM, S. System Design Interview — An Insider's Guide, vol. 2. Byte Code LLC, 2022. ↩

  3. McDOWELL, G. L. Cracking the Coding Interview, 6th ed. CareerCup, 2015. Chapter 9 (system design and scalability). ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
Two BoxOffice engineers receive the same request from the product team: "We need a ticketing platform that is fast, scalable and reliable." The first one starts drawing boxes. The second one asks: How many events per month? How many fans at the peak of an on-sale? What does "fast" mean — for browsing or for paying? Can we ever sell the same seat twice? What happens if the payment provider is down? Three months later the first engineer has a beautiful architecture for the wrong problem. The second has a less impressive diagram that survives 10:00 on Friday.

Requirements are the input of every design. A design can only be judged against them: "is this a good architecture?" is unanswerable; "does this architecture keep checkout p99 under 1 s with 60,000 seats and 2 million fans, without double booking, for less than R$ 40k per month?" is a question you can test.

items.title: Two kinds of requirements
items.text:
Functional requirements Non-functional requirements Describe what the system does — features, behaviours how well it does it — qualities and constraints Typical form "A fan can hold up to 6 seats for 10 minutes" "Seat holds succeed in under 300 ms (p99) at 5,000 holds/s" Answered by use cases, APIs, data model architecture: components, replication, caching, queues If missing the system does the wrong thing the system does the right thing — for 10 users, on a good day Also called features, behavioural requirements quality attributes, "-ilities", NFRs

Functional requirements decide which APIs and data exist. Non-functional requirements decide which architecture delivers them. In system design, the non-functional side drives almost every decision: the same "sell a ticket" feature can be a single PostgreSQL table for a theatre with 200 seats, or a waiting room, a sharded inventory and an event stream for a stadium.

items.title: Functional requirements
items.text:
Start from actors (who uses the system) and their goals. For BoxOffice:

Actor Goals Fan browse and search events; see the seat map; hold seats; pay; receive the ticket; transfer or cancel Organizer create an event; configure venue sections and prices; schedule the on-sale; follow sales live Venue staff validate tickets at the gate (QR code), even with a poor network Support answer fans' questions (helped by the AI assistant); issue refunds External systems the payment provider confirms or declines charges; e-mail/push providers deliver messages

Then turn the goals into a short, prioritized list. In practice — and in an interview — you cannot design everything, so you pick the core path and say explicitly what is out of scope:

BoxOffice — functional requirements (first release)

In scope (core path)

  1. Fans browse and search events by city, date, artist and category.
  2. Fans see the seat map with live availability for an event.
  3. Fans hold up to 6 seats; a hold expires after 10 minutes if not paid.
  4. Fans pay through an external payment provider; a paid hold becomes an order with tickets.
  5. Fans receive tickets by e-mail and in the app.
  6. Organizers create events and schedule on-sales.

Out of scope (for now): resale marketplace, dynamic pricing, loyalty programme, gate validation offline mode, the AI assistant (added in class 13).

A good way to check that a functional requirement is complete is to sketch its API. If you cannot write the request and the response, the requirement is still vague:

GET  /events?city=sao-paulo&from=2027-03-01&q=rock      → 200 [ {eventId, name, venue, date, minPrice} ]
GET  /events/{eventId}/seats                            → 200 { sections: [...], available: [...] }
POST /events/{eventId}/holds   { seatIds: [...] }       → 201 { holdId, expiresAt }   | 409 seat taken
POST /orders                   { holdId, paymentToken } → 201 { orderId, status }     | 402 declined
GET  /orders/{orderId}                                  → 200 { status, tickets: [...] }

You will detail APIs and data models in class 5 and class 6; at this stage the goal is only to make the scope concrete.

items.title: Non-functional requirements: the quality attributes
items.text:
Non-functional requirements describe qualities of the system. Software architecture literature calls them quality attributes1 (ISO/IEC 25010 standardizes a long list of them2). For system design, eight carry most of the weight:

Quality attribute Question it answers How to measure BoxOffice target (assumption) Palette components that help Scalability Can it handle more load by adding resources? max sustainable throughput at the latency target 2 M fans arriving in 1 min at an on-sale; 1,500 catalog req/s on a normal day Load Balancer, App Server replicas, Cache, CDN, Queue, NoSQL partitions Availability Is it up when users need it? % of successful requests over a window 99.95% for checkout per rolling 28 days replicas, Health Check, multi-AZ, DNS failover Latency How long does a user wait? percentiles (p50, p99) of response time catalog p99 < 200 ms; hold p99 < 300 ms; checkout p99 < 1.5 s Cache, CDN, async work, indexes Consistency Do all readers see the same, latest data? anomalies allowed (stale reads, double writes) a seat is sold at most once; catalog may be 60 s stale SQL transactions, single leader, consensus Durability Is confirmed data ever lost? data-loss events; RPO zero confirmed orders lost; RPO = 0 for orders replication, backups, Object Store Cost How much does it cost to run? money per month; cost per unit of business < R$ 0.10 of infrastructure per ticket sold right-sizing, autoscaling, Serverless, CDN offload Security Is it protected against misuse and attack? threats mitigated; audit findings no card data stored (PCI scope minimized); bots blocked WAF, Auth Service, API Gateway, VPC, Safety Mesh Operability Can the team run, change and fix it? MTTR, deploy frequency, alert quality deploy daily without downtime; MTTR < 30 min Metrics, Logs, Tracing, Alerting, CI/CD

The rest of this section gives each attribute a precise meaning — "scalable" and "available" are used loosely in everyday speech, and loose words make bad requirements.

items.title: Scalability
items.text:
Scalability is the ability to handle more load by adding resources, keeping performance acceptable. It is not a yes/no property: "is it scalable?" is meaningless until you say which load parameter grows and by how much3. For BoxOffice the load parameters differ per part of the system:

  • catalog: page views per second (read-heavy, highly cacheable);
  • inventory: seat holds per second on a single event (write-heavy, all on the same hot rows);
  • notification: e-mails per minute after an on-sale (bursty, can be delayed).

Each one scales with a different technique: caching and CDN for the first, partitioning and a waiting room for the second, a queue and workers for the third. Two directions exist, and you will use both:

  • Vertical scaling (scale up): a bigger machine. Simple, no code change, but limited by the largest machine you can buy and still a single point of failure.
  • Horizontal scaling (scale out): more machines. Practically unlimited for stateless components, but requires a load balancer, stateless servers, and — for data — partitioning and replication.

items.title: Availability
items.text:
Availability is the fraction of time (or of requests) in which the system serves users correctly. It is quoted in "nines" and always over a window: 99.9% per rolling 28 days allows about 40 minutes of downtime; 99.99% allows about 4 minutes. Each extra nine costs much more than the previous one — class 2 gives you the math, and class 9 the engineering.

Availability is not uniform either: BoxOffice can live with the recommendation widget down for an hour, but not with checkout down during an on-sale.

items.title: Latency (and throughput)
items.text:
Latency (response time) is how long a request takes, as seen by the client. Throughput is how many requests per second the system completes. They are linked — near saturation, latency explodes (class 2) — so a latency target is only meaningful at a given throughput.

Always state latency as a percentile, not an average: "p99 < 300 ms" means 99% of requests finish in under 300 ms. Averages hide the slow requests that users remember (percentiles and tail latency). Classic usability research gives useful anchors for user-facing targets: about 0.1 s feels instantaneous, about 1 s keeps the user's flow of thought, and beyond about 10 s users lose attention4.

items.title: Consistency
items.text:
Consistency (in the system-design sense) is about what readers see after a write. With strong consistency, once a write is acknowledged every subsequent read sees it — the system behaves as if there were a single copy of the data. With eventual consistency, replicas may disagree for a while, but converge if writes stop.

The key insight is that not all data needs the same consistency:

BoxOffice data Required consistency Why Seat state (free / held / sold) strong two fans must never buy the same seat Order and payment status strong (per order) a fan must see "paid" after paying Event description, prices shown in listings eventual (seconds to a minute) a slightly stale description harms no one; the hold re-checks the price "1,234 people are looking at this event" approximate it is a hint, not a promise

Strong consistency costs latency and availability (you will see why with CAP and PACELC in class 3), so you pay for it only where the business needs it.

items.title: Durability
items.text:
Durability means that data, once confirmed, is not lost — even if disks, machines or a whole data centre fail. It is achieved with replication (several copies, ideally in different failure domains), write-ahead logs, backups and tested restores. Its requirement is usually expressed as an RPO (Recovery Point Objective — how much recent data you may lose in a disaster): for BoxOffice orders, RPO = 0; for analytics events, a few minutes is acceptable.

Do not confuse durability with availability: a database can be down (unavailable) without losing anything (durable), and vice-versa a cache can be up while keeping nothing durable.

items.title: Cost
items.text: Every component has a price: machines, managed services, storage, network egress, third-party fees, and the people to operate it. Cost is a first-class requirement — an architecture that meets every other target at ten times the budget is a failed architecture. Good cost requirements are tied to the business: cost per ticket sold, cost per active user, or a monthly ceiling. Note also that BoxOffice traffic is spiky: paying all month for the capacity of a 10-minute on-sale is wasteful, which is why autoscaling, queues and serverless matter (class 12 covers FinOps).

items.title: Security
items.text: Security protects confidentiality (only the right people read data), integrity (only the right people change it) and availability (attackers cannot take it down) — the CIA triad. For BoxOffice it translates into concrete requirements: fans authenticate before buying; an organizer only sees their own events; bots cannot buy 500 tickets in one second; card numbers never touch BoxOffice servers (the payment provider tokenizes them, which keeps BoxOffice out of most of the PCI DSS scope5); personal data follows Brazil's data-protection law, the LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados)6.

items.title: Operability
items.text: Operability groups the qualities that make a system runnable by real people: observability (can we tell what is wrong?), deployability (can we ship a change safely, many times a day?), maintainability (can a new engineer understand and change it?), and recoverability (how fast do we restore service — the MTTR, Mean Time To Recovery). It is the attribute most often forgotten in diagrams and most often blamed in post-mortems.

items.title: Making non-functional requirements measurable
items.text:
"The system must be fast" cannot be tested, so it cannot be designed for. A practical template from software architecture is the quality attribute scenario1, which forces six parts into one sentence:

flowchart LR
    source["Source<br/>who/what"] --> stimulus["Stimulus<br/>what happens"]
    stimulus --> artifact["Artifact<br/>which part, in which<br/>environment"]
    artifact --> response["Response<br/>what the system does"]
    response --> measure["Response measure<br/>the number"]
Part BoxOffice scenario: the on-sale Source 2 M fans, from web and mobile Stimulus arrive within 60 s of 10:00 and request seat holds Environment normal operation, flash sale in progress Artifact waiting room + inventory service + seats database Response every fan gets a place in line; admitted fans can hold seats; no seat is held twice Response measure admission page p99 < 500 ms; hold p99 < 300 ms; 0 double bookings; error rate < 0.1%

Written as requirements, a measurable set for BoxOffice looks like this:

BoxOffice — non-functional requirements (first release, assumptions)

  • Load: normal day 1,500 req/s at peak hour; on-sale: 2 M fans in the first minute, 60 k seats.
  • Latency: catalog p99 < 200 ms; seat map p99 < 300 ms; hold p99 < 300 ms; checkout p99 < 1.5 s (the payment provider takes most of it).
  • Availability: checkout and holds 99.95% per rolling 28 days; catalog 99.9%; recommendations best-effort.
  • Consistency: seats strongly consistent (no double booking, ever); catalog up to 60 s stale.
  • Durability: zero loss of paid orders (RPO = 0); analytics RPO 15 min.
  • Security: no card data stored; bot purchases blocked at the edge; LGPD compliant.
  • Cost: < R$ 0.10 of infrastructure per ticket sold; idle cost < R$ 15k/month.
  • Operability: zero-downtime deploys; on-call alerted within 5 min of an SLO burn; MTTR < 30 min.

Each line is testable — with a load test, a chaos experiment or a monthly bill — and each line will drive a design decision in the coming classes.

Think first: rewrite these requirements so they are measurable
  1. "Search must be fast."
  2. "The system must never go down."
  3. "Tickets must be delivered quickly."

Possible answers

  1. "Search returns the first page of results in p99 < 250 ms at 800 queries/s; results may lag the catalog by up to 5 minutes." (Note the consistency part: a search index is usually updated asynchronously.)
  2. "Holds and checkout are available 99.95% of requests per rolling 28 days; during a region outage, service is restored in another region within 15 minutes (RTO) without losing paid orders (RPO = 0)." Never is not a requirement; it is an infinite budget.
  3. "95% of tickets reach the fan's inbox within 2 minutes of payment, 99.9% within 30 minutes; a delayed e-mail never blocks checkout." This tells the designer the e-mail can go through a queue.

items.title: Trade-offs between quality attributes
items.text:
Quality attributes pull against each other. Recognizing the tension before choosing a component is the essence of system design:

Improving… …usually costs BoxOffice example Consistency latency and availability a seat hold waits for the primary database; if the primary is unreachable, holds fail rather than risk a double sale Latency (caching) freshness (consistency) the cached event page shows a price up to 60 s old Availability (redundancy) cost and complexity a second region doubles infrastructure and needs failover tests Durability (synchronous replication) write latency each paid order waits for two replicas to confirm Security (more checks) latency and usability WAF inspection and bot challenges add milliseconds and friction Scalability (partitioning) simplicity, cross-partition queries sharding orders by fan makes "all orders of an event" a scatter-gather query Cost (fewer resources) headroom for spikes running at 80% utilization saves money and kills p99 during the on-sale

This is why the same company runs different architectures for different parts of the same product. BoxOffice's catalog is an AP-leaning, cache-everything system; its inventory is a CP-leaning, transaction-everything system; its notifications are an asynchronous, retry-until-delivered system.

items.title: Constraints and assumptions
items.text:
Requirements come with constraints — decisions already made for you — and assumptions — things you take as true to move on:

  • Team and skills: a team of six that knows Java and PostgreSQL should not adopt five new databases.
  • Time: "on-sale in 8 weeks" rules out rewriting everything as microservices.
  • Budget: a monthly ceiling, or a cost-per-ticket target.
  • Regulation: LGPD for personal data; PCI DSS for payments; tax rules for invoices.
  • Existing systems: the payment provider's API and its rate limits; the organizer's ERP.
  • Assumptions: "fans per on-sale follow last year's distribution", "the provider answers in 300–800 ms". Write them down — when an assumption is wrong, you know which part of the design to revisit.

In the interview

Spend the first 3–5 minutes on requirements, and write them on the board in two columns:

  • Functional: 3–5 core features, each one sentence ("hold seats", "pay", "get ticket"). Say what you leave out: "I'll skip resale and dynamic pricing unless you want them."
  • Non-functional: scale (users, requests/s, data size), latency targets, availability, consistency needs, and anything special (spikes, abuse, regulation).

Good clarifying questions for almost any problem: Who are the users and how many? What is the read/write ratio? What must be strongly consistent? What is the latency the user tolerates? Is the load steady or spiky? What is out of scope? If the interviewer says "you decide", state an assumption and move on: "I'll assume 10 M daily users and a read/write ratio of 100:1."

Common pitfalls

  • Unmeasurable adjectives: "fast", "scalable", "highly available" without numbers and windows.
  • One target for everything: requiring strong consistency or five nines for the whole system, when only one path needs it.
  • Forgetting the peak: designing for the daily average when the business lives on spikes.
  • Ignoring cost and operability until the first bill or the first 3 a.m. incident.
  • Gold-plating the scope: designing ten features superficially instead of the core path well.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    FR["functional requirements<br/>actors, core path"] --> API["API & data model<br/>→ Compute, Databases"]
    NFR["quality attributes"] --> QAS["quality attribute scenario<br/>a measurable target"]
    QAS --> EST["load numbers<br/>→ Estimation"]
    NFR --> SC["scalability<br/>lb, cache, queue"]
    NFR --> LAT["latency percentiles<br/>→ Estimation"]
    NFR --> AV["availability nines<br/>→ Reliability"]
    NFR --> CO["consistency per data item<br/>→ Distributed systems"]
    NFR --> SEC["security<br/>→ Network & Security"]
    NFR --> OPS["operability<br/>→ Observability"]
    CO --> TO["trade-offs: CP inventory,<br/>AP catalog"]
    LAT --> TO

Palette components: client · mobile (the actors' entry points) · sql (strong consistency for seats, durability of orders) · cache · cdn (latency bought with freshness) · lb (scalability and availability through replicas) · waf · auth (security) · payment (an external constraint: no card data stored) · metrics (operability). Scenarios: monolith, flash-sale. Continues in: Estimation — numbers, Estimation — percentiles, Estimation — availability math, Distributed — CAP and PACELC, Reliability — SLOs, Exercise: design doc.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Functional requirements define what (APIs, data); non-functional requirements define how well — and drive the architecture.
  • Eight quality attributes carry most design decisions: scalability, availability, latency, consistency, durability, cost, security, operability.
  • Make each requirement measurable: a number, a percentile, a window, a load level — the quality attribute scenario helps.
  • Different parts of the system need different qualities: strong consistency for seats, freshness traded for speed in the catalog.
  • Every improvement costs something; name the trade-off before choosing the component.

  1. BASS, L.; CLEMENTS, P.; KAZMAN, R. Software Architecture in Practice, 4th ed. Addison-Wesley, 2021. Part II (quality attributes and quality attribute scenarios). ↩↩

  2. ISO/IEC 25010:2023. Systems and software engineering — Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product quality model. ↩

  3. KLEPPMANN, M.; RICCOMINI, C. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd ed. O'Reilly. Chapter 2 (defining nonfunctional requirements: describing load and performance). ↩

  4. NIELSEN, J. Usability Engineering. Morgan Kaufmann, 1993. Chapter 5 (response time limits: 0.1 s, 1 s, 10 s). ↩

  5. PCI SECURITY STANDARDS COUNCIL. Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), v4.0, 2022. ↩

  6. BRASIL. Lei nº 13.709, de 14 de agosto de 2018 — Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD). ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
Most famous architectures were not designed; they evolved. They started as one program and one database on one machine, and each new component was added because a specific symptom — a saturated CPU, a slow page, an outage during a deploy — made it necessary. This page follows BoxOffice along that path, from its first user to ten million, one symptom at a time1.

Two rules guide the whole journey:

  1. Add a component only when a measured symptom calls for it. Every component has a price: money, latency, new failure modes, and something else to operate.
  2. Every fix creates a new problem. A replica brings replication lag; a cache brings invalidation; a queue brings duplicate messages. Knowing the next problem before you meet it is what separates design from guesswork.
Stage Scale (illustrative) Symptom What is added New problem it brings 0 first users — one server: app + database everything fails together 1 ~10 k users app and DB fight for CPU and memory separate SQL Database network hop; two things to run 2 ~100 k daily users a deploy or a crash takes the site down Load Balancer + stateless App Server replicas + Health Check session state must leave the server 3 ~1 M daily users database CPU high, mostly reads read replicas replication lag, stale reads 4 same catalog p99 grows with traffic Cache invalidation, cold cache, stampede 5 same bandwidth bill and page weight CDN + Object Store cache invalidation at the edge 6 first big on-sale checkout slowed by e-mail; spike crushes inventory Message Queue + Worker; waiting room duplicates, backlog, ordering 7 many teams, many features one bug or one deploy affects everything split into services; API Gateway; Event Stream network calls fail; distributed data 8 ~10 M daily users one database is too big / too hot partitioning, Search, Data Warehouse hot partitions, cross-shard queries 9 national scale bots, attacks, a region outage WAF, rate limiting, multi-region + DNS failover data replication across regions

The numbers are orders of magnitude for a read-heavy web product, not thresholds: a different workload hits each wall at a different point. Measure, then decide.

items.title: Stage 0 — one box
items.text:
The first version of BoxOffice is a single Spring Boot application and a PostgreSQL database on the same virtual machine. DNS points the domain to its IP address.

flowchart LR
    fan([Fan]) --> dns["DNS"]
    dns -.->|IP address| fan
    fan --> vm["One VM<br/>app + PostgreSQL + files"]

This is the right architecture for the first users: one thing to deploy, monitor and back up; transactions are local; there is no network between the code and the data. It is also fragile: the machine is a single point of failure (SPOF), and the application and the database compete for the same CPU, memory and disk.

items.title: Stage 1 — separate the database
items.text:
Symptom: under load, the database's buffer cache and the JVM fight for memory; a heavy report slows down every page; restarting the app for a deploy also risks the database.

Change: move PostgreSQL to its own machine — or better, a managed database service that handles backups, patches and failover. Now the web tier and the data tier can be sized and scaled independently: the app needs CPU, the database needs memory and fast disks.

New problem: every query now crosses the network (about 0.5 ms round trip inside a data centre — see class 2). Code that runs 200 queries per page (the classic N+1 problem) suddenly takes 100 ms more.

items.title: Stage 2 — load balancer and stateless replicas
items.text:
Symptom: BoxOffice is now a real business. A single app server is a SPOF: a crash, or simply a deploy, means downtime. At the peak hour the CPU sits at 85% and the p99 latency climbs.

Change: put a load balancer in front of two or more identical app server replicas. The load balancer spreads requests, runs health checks, and stops sending traffic to a replica that fails them. Deploys become rolling: update one replica at a time.

flowchart LR
    fan([Fan]) --> lb["Load Balancer<br/>+ health checks"]
    lb --> a1["App #1"]
    lb --> a2["App #2"]
    lb --> a3["App #3"]
    a1 --> db[("SQL Database")]
    a2 --> db
    a3 --> db

New problem — state: if the logged-in session or the shopping cart lives in the memory of App #1, the next request may land on App #2 and the fan is "logged out". The fix is to make app servers stateless: keep session data in a signed token (JWT) or a shared store (Redis), never in the server. Statelessness is the precondition for horizontal scaling — any replica can serve any request, so you can add or kill replicas freely.

You explored this stage in the overview with the scale-out scenario: replicas multiply app capacity, but the single database stays a single database.

items.title: Stage 3 — read replicas
items.text:
Symptom: the database CPU is at 70% at the peak hour. Looking at the query log, ~95% of the queries are reads — event pages, venue info, seat maps.

Change: add read replicas. The primary receives all writes and streams its changes to the replicas; reads go to the replicas. Read capacity grows with each replica; write capacity does not change.

flowchart LR
    app["App servers"] -->|writes| primary[("Primary")]
    primary -->|replication| r1[("Replica 1")]
    primary -->|replication| r2[("Replica 2")]
    app -->|reads| r1
    app -->|reads| r2

New problem — replication lag: replicas are a few milliseconds (or, under load, seconds) behind the primary. A fan pays, is redirected to "My orders", the page reads from a replica… and the order is not there yet. Fixes include read-your-writes (read the fan's own recent data from the primary) or routing whole critical flows to the primary. And the seat inventory, which must never be stale, keeps reading from the primary.

Try it: add read replicas and watch the primary's utilization fall; then increase the replication lag and look for stale reads. Which BoxOffice pages could tolerate them?

items.title: Stage 4 — a cache
items.text:
Symptom: even with replicas, every event page runs the same five queries — for data that changes a few times a day. Catalog p99 grows with traffic, and each new replica costs a full database machine.

Change: add a cache (Redis) in front of the database, using cache-aside: the app looks in the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and stores the result with a TTL (time to live).

The arithmetic is what makes caches the most powerful tool in the palette. With a hit ratio of 90%, only 10% of reads reach the database — a 10× reduction. At 99%, it is 100×. And a cache hit costs well under a millisecond, versus several milliseconds for a query.

New problems: invalidation (when the organizer changes a price, the cached page is stale until the TTL expires or the key is deleted), cold start (an empty cache after a restart sends 100% of reads to the database at once), and stampede (a popular key expires and 1,000 requests miss at the same instant). Class 7 is dedicated to them.

Try it: vary the hit ratio from 0% to 90% to 99% and watch database utilization and p99. Then flush the cache under load — what happens in the first seconds?

items.title: Stage 5 — CDN and object storage
items.text:
Symptom: event pages carry posters and venue photos — about 1 MB per page view. At 1,000 page views per second that is 1 GB/s (8 Gbit/s) leaving BoxOffice's servers, most of it identical bytes sent again and again. Fans far from the data centre wait for every image.

Change: move images and static files (JavaScript, CSS) to an object store (S3-like: cheap, durable, unlimited) and serve them through a CDN (Content Delivery Network), a network of edge servers near the users that cache those files. The origin serves each file once per edge location instead of once per fan.

New problem: a changed poster stays cached at hundreds of edge locations. The common fix is versioned file names (poster.v2.jpg, or a content hash) instead of trying to purge every edge.

Try it: run the scenario with and without the CDN in front of the origin and compare origin bandwidth and latency for distant users.

items.title: Stage 6 — asynchronous work and the first on-sale
items.text:
Symptom 1: checkout takes 2–3 s, and most of it is not paying — it is generating the PDF ticket and sending the e-mail while the fan waits. When the e-mail provider is slow, checkout is slow; when it is down, checkout fails.

Change: anything that does not need to finish before the response goes to a message queue. Checkout writes the order, publishes a TicketIssued message and answers immediately; workers consume the queue, render the PDF and send the e-mail at their own pace, retrying on failure.

Symptom 2 — the first stadium on-sale: 2 M fans arrive in one minute. Even a perfectly cached catalog cannot make 60,000 seats accept 2 million concurrent holds: the inventory rows are hot — everyone wants the same front sections.

Change: a waiting room — itself a queue. Fans get a place in line and are admitted at the rate the inventory can sustain (say, 1,000 per second). The spike becomes a long, flat, predictable load. Class 2 computes how long the line is with Little's Law.

flowchart LR
    fan([Fans]) --> wr["Waiting room<br/>(queue)"]
    wr -->|"admit 1,000/s"| inv["inventory"]
    inv --> db[("Seats<br/>SQL")]
    inv --> order["order"]
    order --> q["Message Queue"]
    q --> w["Workers"]
    w --> email["Email provider"]

New problems: queues deliver messages at least once, so consumers must be idempotent (sending the same ticket twice must not create two tickets); a backlog can grow faster than workers drain it; ordering is not guaranteed. Class 8 covers all of them.

Try it: run the spike profile and watch the queue backlog grow and drain. Add workers: how does the drain time change?

items.title: Stage 7 — services where they pay off
items.text:
Symptom: BoxOffice has now five teams working in one codebase. A memory leak in the recommendations code takes down checkout. Every deploy needs coordination across teams. The on-sale traffic hammers the inventory code, but scaling it means scaling the whole application.

Change: extract services along business boundaries — first the ones with clearly different needs: inventory (hot, strongly consistent, scaled for on-sales), notification (asynchronous), search (a different database). An API Gateway becomes the single entry point (routing, authentication, rate limiting). Services communicate through APIs and through an event stream (Kafka) for facts like OrderPaid, which several consumers (notification, analytics, search) react to.

New problems: what used to be a function call is now a network call that can be slow or fail; a transaction across services is no longer a database transaction (sagas, outbox — class 8); a request touches several services, so you need distributed tracing to debug it (class 10).

Monolith first

Splitting into services is a response to organizational and scaling symptoms, not a starting point. Teams that start with microservices pay the full cost of distribution — network failures, distributed data, many deployables, a platform to run them — before they know where the real boundaries of their domain are2. A well-structured modular monolith (clear modules with explicit interfaces inside one deployable) gets most of the benefits and keeps the option to extract a module later, when a symptom justifies it. Class 5 discusses this in depth.

items.title: Stage 8 — partition the data and specialize storage
items.text:
Symptom: the orders table has billions of rows and the primary's disk and write throughput are near their limits; full-text search with LIKE '%rock%' scans millions of rows; the organizers' sales dashboards run heavy aggregations on the production database.

Change: use the right store for each job, and partition what must grow:

  • Partitioning (sharding) splits data across several database nodes by a key — orders by fanId, seat inventory by eventId — so writes scale with the number of shards.
  • A search engine (inverted index) for full-text and faceted search, fed asynchronously from catalog events.
  • A data warehouse for analytics, fed by change data capture (CDC) or events, so dashboards never touch the transactional database.

New problems: a hot partition (one stadium on-sale lands all writes on one shard), queries across shards, rebalancing when adding nodes. Class 6.

items.title: Stage 9 — the edge and multiple regions
items.text:
Symptom: bots buy 30% of the tickets for popular shows in the first second; a DDoS attack hits the week of a big on-sale; a cloud region outage takes BoxOffice down for four hours.

Change: a WAF (Web Application Firewall) and bot mitigation at the edge; rate limiting in the API Gateway (per fan, per IP, per card); deployment across multiple availability zones first, then multiple regions with DNS failover.

New problem: data now lives far apart. Replicating the seat inventory across regions synchronously costs tens of milliseconds per write (the speed of light is a hard limit); asynchronously, it risks selling a seat twice during a failover. The usual compromise: each event's inventory has one home region, and other regions forward holds to it. Class 3 explains why there is no free lunch here (CAP and PACELC).

Try it: the final scenario puts several of these components together for the 10:00 on-sale — waiting room, inventory in SQL, payment. Run the spike profile and find the first bottleneck.

items.title: What is constant along the journey
items.text:
Some things do not belong to any single stage — they must be there from day one and grow with the system:

  • Observability — metrics, logs and traces. Every decision above starts with "the symptom is…": without measurement, there is no symptom, only opinions.
  • Automation — infrastructure as code, CI/CD, automated tests. Ten servers configured by hand are ten different servers.
  • Security — authentication, least privilege, secrets out of the code, from the first commit.
  • Cost awareness — knowing what each component costs per month, and per ticket sold.
Think first: in which order would you add components for a write-heavy system?

Consider an IoT platform that receives a temperature reading from 1 million sensors every 10 seconds (100,000 writes/s) and shows dashboards to a few hundred users.

Answer sketch: the read-side components of stages 3–5 (replicas, cache, CDN) barely help — reads are rare. The early moves are a queue or event stream to absorb and batch writes (stage 6), a write-optimized, partitioned store (time-series or wide-column, stage 8), and pre-aggregation for the dashboards. The journey above is the typical order for read-heavy web products, not a universal recipe: the workload decides the order.

In the interview

Interviewers often ask "how would this evolve?" or "what changes at 10× the traffic?". Use the journey as a mental checklist, but always tie each step to a symptom and a number: "At ~1,000 catalog reads/s the primary's CPU would be the bottleneck; with a 95% cache hit ratio only 50 reads/s reach it, so I'd add Redis before adding replicas." Start the high-level design simple (one service, one database, a cache) and add complexity only where the requirements or your estimates demand it — an interviewer is more impressed by a justified simple design than by an unjustified complex one.

Common pitfalls

  • Résumé-driven architecture: Kafka, Kubernetes and twelve microservices for a system with 100 users.
  • Scaling the wrong tier: adding app replicas when the database is the bottleneck.
  • Stateful app servers: sessions in memory make horizontal scaling and rolling deploys break users.
  • Ignoring the new problem: adding a replica without handling lag, a cache without an invalidation plan, a queue without idempotent consumers.
  • Treating the stages as fixed: they are a typical sequence for read-heavy systems; measure your own workload.

items.text:
flowchart LR
    S0["one box<br/>app + database"] --> S1["separate sql"]
    S1 --> S2["lb + stateless app<br/>+ healthcheck"]

    S2 --> WRITES["tame writes and spikes"]
