items.title: As code
items.text:
Networks are declared with infrastructure as code (IaC) so they can be reviewed, versioned and recreated. A trimmed Terraform/OpenTofu sketch of one AZ (the real module loops over the AZs):

resource "aws_vpc" "boxoffice" {
  cidr_block           = "10.20.0.0/16"
  enable_dns_hostnames = true
  tags = { Name = "boxoffice-prod" }
}

resource "aws_subnet" "public_a" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.boxoffice.id
  cidr_block        = "10.20.0.0/24"
  availability_zone = "sa-east-1a"
}

resource "aws_subnet" "app_a" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.boxoffice.id
  cidr_block        = "10.20.32.0/19"
  availability_zone = "sa-east-1a"
}

resource "aws_subnet" "data_a" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.boxoffice.id
  cidr_block        = "10.20.8.0/22"
  availability_zone = "sa-east-1a"
}

resource "aws_internet_gateway" "igw" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.boxoffice.id
}

resource "aws_eip" "nat_a" {
  domain = "vpc"
}

resource "aws_nat_gateway" "a" {
  subnet_id     = aws_subnet.public_a.id # NAT lives in the PUBLIC subnet
  allocation_id = aws_eip.nat_a.id       # fixed egress IP for the PSP allow-list
}

resource "aws_route_table" "public" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.boxoffice.id
  route {
    cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
    gateway_id = aws_internet_gateway.igw.id
  }
}

resource "aws_route_table" "app_a" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.boxoffice.id
  route {
    cidr_block     = "0.0.0.0/0"
    nat_gateway_id = aws_nat_gateway.a.id # egress only, same AZ
  }
}

# data subnets get a route table with no 0.0.0.0/0 route at all

resource "aws_route_table_association" "public_a" {
  subnet_id      = aws_subnet.public_a.id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.public.id
}

resource "aws_route_table_association" "app_a" {
  subnet_id      = aws_subnet.app_a.id
  route_table_id = aws_route_table.app_a.id
}

resource "aws_security_group" "app" {
  name   = "sg-app"
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.boxoffice.id
}

resource "aws_security_group" "db" {
  name   = "sg-db"
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.boxoffice.id

  ingress {
    description     = "PostgreSQL only from the app nodes"
    from_port       = 5432
    to_port         = 5432
    protocol        = "tcp"
    security_groups = [aws_security_group.app.id] # reference, not a CIDR
  }
}

Read it as a diagram: the only 0.0.0.0/0 → igw route is in the public table; the app table sends the Internet to NAT; the data subnets have no default route; the database accepts 5432 only from members of sg-app.

Try it. Open the payment-system scenario. The payment service calls an external provider. Increase the load and inject chaos on the provider: note that every call crosses the network boundary (in the real deployment, through the NAT gateway). Ask yourself which failures belong to the network (NAT in one AZ, egress IP not allow-listed) and which to the provider. Rebuild the design in the full playground with vpc, subnet and nat components to make the boundaries visible.

items.title: Private connectivity: reaching other networks
items.text:
BoxOffice soon needs to talk to networks it does not own: the office, the data team's VPC, a partner, a second region.

Option What it connects Traffic goes over Strengths Limits VPC peering two VPCs, one-to-one the provider's backbone simple, no bandwidth bottleneck, cheap not transitive; CIDRs must not overlap; becomes a mesh of N² links Transit gateway (hub) many VPCs and VPNs, hub-and-spoke the provider's backbone central routing, scales to hundreds of VPCs per-attachment and per-GB cost; a central component to operate PrivateLink / interface endpoint one service exposed into consumer VPCs the provider's backbone consumer sees only one IP, no routing between networks, overlapping CIDRs OK one service at a time, one direction Site-to-site VPN (IPsec) an on-prem network or another cloud the public Internet, encrypted quick to set up, cheap bandwidth limited per tunnel, Internet latency/jitter Client VPN / WireGuard individual engineers' laptops the Internet, encrypted access for people a VPN puts the laptop "inside" — classic perimeter trust Dedicated link (Direct Connect / Interconnect / ExpressRoute) a data center to the cloud a private physical circuit stable latency, high bandwidth weeks to provision, expensive; usually paired with a VPN as backup

items.title: Getting engineers in: bastion vs session manager
items.text: The old answer is a bastion host: a small VM in a public subnet with SSH open, from which engineers jump into the private network. It is an attack surface (port 22 on the Internet) and a key-management problem. The modern answer is an agent-based session service (AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, GCP IAP TCP forwarding, Azure Bastion): the engineer authenticates with the company identity provider and MFA, the session is opened by an agent from the inside, no inbound port is open, and every command is logged. For Kubernetes, kubectl through the cluster's authenticated API plays the same role. This is Zero Trust applied to people (Zero Trust).

items.title: DNS inside the VPC
items.text: Services find each other by name. The VPC provides a resolver (in AWS, at the VPC base address + 2); private hosted zones give internal names like db.boxoffice.internal that resolve only inside the VPC. Inside Kubernetes, CoreDNS resolves payment.boxoffice.svc.cluster.local. Interface endpoints rely on private DNS so that secretsmanager.sa-east-1.amazonaws.com resolves to the private endpoint IP instead of the public one.

items.title: The same ideas in other clouds
items.text:
The vocabulary changes between providers, the building blocks do not3. The biggest real difference: a Google Cloud VPC is global, while AWS and Azure networks are regional.

AWSGoogle CloudAzureKubernetes / on-prem

VPC (regional) · Subnet (per AZ) · Route table · Internet Gateway · NAT Gateway · Security Group + Network ACL · Gateway/Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink) · VPC Peering · Transit Gateway · Site-to-Site VPN · Direct Connect · Systems Manager Session Manager.

VPC network (global; subnets are regional, not per zone) · Routes · Cloud NAT (a managed service, no per-zone instance to place) · VPC firewall rules and hierarchical firewall policies (stateful, can target service accounts or network tags) · Private Service Connect · VPC Network Peering · Network Connectivity Center · Cloud VPN · Cloud Interconnect · Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP).

Virtual Network (VNet, regional) · Subnet · Route table (User-Defined Routes) · NAT Gateway · Network Security Group (NSG) + Application Security Groups · Private Endpoint / Private Link · VNet Peering · Virtual WAN / hub-spoke · VPN Gateway · ExpressRoute · Azure Bastion.

A cluster network (CNI: Calico, Cilium) with pod and service CIDRs · NetworkPolicy as the firewall · an egress gateway (Cilium, Istio) for a stable source IP · WireGuard or IPsec tunnels between sites · MetalLB for load balancer IPs on bare metal.

items.title: Trade-offs at a glance
items.text:
Decision Option A Option B Choose B when… NAT topology one NAT for the VPC (cheap) one NAT per AZ (resilient) outbound calls are on the critical path (payment!) Egress to cloud services through NAT VPC endpoints traffic is heavy or must not cross the Internet Pod addressing overlay network (few VPC IPs) VPC-native pod IPs you need SGs/flow logs per pod and have address space Connecting VPCs peering transit gateway more than a handful of VPCs, or VPNs too Admin access bastion + SSH session manager / IAP almost always Firewall granularity SG per tier per-pod SG / NetworkPolicy / mesh policy multi-tenant clusters, sensitive services

In the interview

When you draw the high-level design, put a box around it labeled VPC and split it into public (load balancer, NAT) and private (services, data) subnets across at least two AZs. Say one sentence about egress: "outbound calls to the payment provider go through a NAT gateway per AZ with a fixed IP the provider allow-lists." If the interviewer asks about cost, mention VPC endpoints to keep object-storage and registry traffic off the NAT. That is enough to signal you have run real systems.

Common pitfalls

  • SSH or RDP open to 0.0.0.0/0 — scanned within minutes; use a session manager instead.
  • Database in a public subnet "just to connect from my laptop" — one weak password away from a breach.
  • A single NAT gateway for every AZ — an AZ outage silently becomes a checkout outage.
  • Overlapping CIDRs (10.0.0.0/16 everywhere) — discovered the day you need to peer with the data team or a partner.
  • Subnets too small for VPC-native pod IPs — the cluster stops scheduling pods during the flash sale.
  • Ignoring NAT data-processing charges — registry pulls and log shipping through NAT can cost more than the servers.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    VPC["VPC + CIDR plan"] --> SUB["public / private / isolated<br/>subnets, one per AZ"]
    SUB --> RT["route tables:<br/>IGW, NAT or none"]
    RT --> NAT["NAT gateway per AZ<br/>stable egress IP"]
    NAT --> PSP["provider allow-list<br/>→ Compute integrations"]
    SUB --> SG["security groups + NACLs"]
    SG --> NOID["not an identity: NetworkPolicy,<br/>mesh policy → Service mesh"]
    SUB --> AZ["AZ and region outages<br/>→ Reliability"]
    VPC --> CON["peering, transit, PrivateLink,<br/>VPN, session manager"]
    CON --> ZT["access for people<br/>→ Zero Trust"]
    VPC --> IAC["Terraform / OpenTofu<br/>→ Cloud-native"]

Palette components: vpc · subnet · nat · vpn · lb (the ALB in the public subnets) · payment (reached through the NAT). Scenarios: payment-system, multi-region, scale-out. Continues in: Service mesh, Zero Trust, Compute — integrations, Reliability — disaster recovery, Cloud-native — delivery (infrastructure as code).

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• A VPC is your private network in a region; subnets live in one AZ; a subnet is public only because its route table points 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway.
  • Private subnets reach the Internet outbound only through a NAT gateway, which also gives a stable egress IP for allow-lists; use one per AZ for critical paths.
  • Security groups are stateful and can reference each other; NACLs are stateless subnet-level guard rails. Neither is a workload identity.
  • Plan CIDRs with room and without overlaps; AWS reserves 5 addresses per subnet; pods may need many IPs.
  • Use VPC endpoints for cloud services, peering/transit/PrivateLink between networks, VPN or dedicated links to on-prem, and session managers instead of bastions.

  1. AMAZON WEB SERVICES. Amazon VPC User Guide — subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, security groups, network ACLs. ↩↩

  2. REKHTER, Y. et al. RFC 1918 — Address Allocation for Private Internets. IETF, 1996. ↩

  3. GOOGLE CLOUD. VPC network overview; MICROSOFT. Azure Virtual Network overview. ↩

  4. AMAZON WEB SERVICES. AWS Well-Architected Framework — Security Pillar: Infrastructure protection. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text: BoxOffice launches its mobile app. Someone proposes the obvious design: a login screen in the app, the app sends e-mail and password to POST /login, keeps the password in the phone "so the user does not have to type it again", and sends it on every request. Within a week the product team also wants "Sign in with Google", a web checkout, a nightly reconciliation job in order that calls inventory with no user behind it, and an AI assistant that acts on the user's behalf. A homemade login cannot express any of this safely. This page is about the standards that can: sessions and tokens, JWT, OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect, and the authorization models that decide what an authenticated caller may do.

items.title: Authentication vs authorization
items.text:
Two different questions are asked on every request:

Authentication (authN) Authorization (authZ) Question Who are you? What are you allowed to do? Input a credential: password, passkey, certificate, token the identity + a policy (roles, scopes, ownership) Failure 401 Unauthorized 403 Forbidden (or 404 to hide existence) In BoxOffice the auth service (an identity provider) logs the user in; the gateway validates the token order checks that order 1042 belongs to the caller; admin routes require the organizer role

Vocabulary used below: a principal is the authenticated entity (a user or a workload); a credential is what it presents to prove it; a token is what it receives after authenticating and presents instead of the credential; a claim is a statement inside a token ("sub": "acc-42"). A bearer token works for whoever holds it, like cash.

items.title: Sessions vs tokens
items.text:
After login, the server must remember the user on the next request. Two families of designs:

flowchart LR
    subgraph s ["Server-side session"]
        B1(["Browser"]) -->|"Cookie: sid=9f2c…"| A1["app"]
        A1 -->|"GET session:9f2c"| R[("Redis")]
    end
    subgraph t ["Self-contained token (JWT)"]
        B2(["App"]) -->|"Authorization: Bearer eyJ…"| A2["gateway"]
        A2 -->|"verify signature locally<br/>(cached public key)"| A2
    end
Server-side session (opaque id → store) Self-contained token (JWT) What the client holds a random session id a signed document with the claims Validation lookup in a shared store (Redis) signature check with a public key, no lookup Revocation (logout, stolen) immediate: delete the key hard: valid until exp unless you add a denylist or introspection Horizontal scaling needs a shared, highly available store stateless; any instance validates Cross-service use services must call the session store any service with the public key can verify Size per request ~32 bytes often 0.5–2 KB in every request header Best for classic web apps, the BFF pattern APIs, mobile apps, service-to-service

Neither is "the modern one". Large systems combine them: a short-lived JWT (minutes) for APIs and a revocable refresh token or session stored server-side. Revocation latency then equals the access-token lifetime — a number you choose.

Think first: a user's phone is stolen at 14:00 and they log out from the web at 14:05. Access tokens live 15 minutes and are validated locally. Until when can the thief call the API?

The refresh token is revoked at 14:05, so the thief cannot get new access tokens. But the last access token issued — say at 13:58 — stays valid until 14:13, because the gateway validates it locally and cannot know it was "logged out". The exposure window is up to one access-token lifetime after revocation. Shorter tokens shrink it; introspection or a denylist (by jti, the token id) closes it at the cost of a lookup.

items.title: JSON Web Token (JWT)
items.text:
A JWT (RFC 7519) is three Base64URL-encoded parts separated by dots: header.payload.signature. Decoded, a BoxOffice access token looks like this:

header:  { "alg": "RS256", "typ": "at+jwt", "kid": "2026-10-a" }
payload: {
  "iss": "https://auth.boxoffice.com/realms/boxoffice",
  "sub": "acc-42",
  "aud": "boxoffice-api",
  "client_id": "boxoffice-mobile",
  "scope": "orders:read orders:write",
  "iat": 1792310400,
  "exp": 1792311300,
  "jti": "5b0e7c1a-6d1f-4c1e-9a43-0d6c2f6c9e10"
}
signature: RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5( SHA-256( base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload) ), private key )

The payload is encoded, not encrypted — anyone can read it. Never put secrets or personal data there you would not show the user.

With asymmetric algorithms (RS256, ES256, EdDSA) the identity provider signs with a private key that never leaves it, and anyone verifies with the public key, published as a JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) at the provider's jwks_uri. With symmetric HMAC (HS256), every verifier holds the same secret and can therefore also forge tokens — acceptable only when issuer and verifier are the same service.

items.title: Validation checklist
items.text:
RFC 8725 (JWT Best Current Practices) is the reference1. A resource server must check:

Check Why Signature with an allow-listed algorithm (never alg: none, never let the token header choose) algorithm-confusion attacks forge tokens Key selected by kid from your JWKS, re-fetched on unknown kid key rotation without downtime iss equals your identity provider tokens from another issuer are rejected aud contains this API a token minted for another API cannot be replayed here exp and nbf, with a small clock skew (≈ 30–60 s) expired tokens rejected typ is at+jwt for access tokens (RFC 9068) an ID token cannot be used as an access token required scopes / roles for the endpoint least privilege

items.title: OAuth 2.1
items.text:
OAuth is a framework for delegated authorization: a client application obtains a limited, short-lived access token to call an API on behalf of a user — or on its own behalf — without ever handling the user's password. The user authenticates only at the authorization server2.

Role Description In BoxOffice Resource owner the user who owns the data Ana, a fan Client the application requesting access mobile app, web checkout (BFF), reconciliation job, AI assistant Authorization server (AS) authenticates the user, asks for consent, issues tokens the auth service (Keycloak in the course; Auth0, Cognito, Entra ID in industry) Resource server (RS) API that validates tokens and serves data gateway + order, inventory, …

Clients are confidential (run on a server, can keep a secret: the BFF, a batch job) or public (run on the user's device, cannot keep a secret: the mobile app, a single-page app — anyone can decompile or read them).

items.title: What OAuth 2.1 changes
items.text:
OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749, 2012) accumulated a decade of security lessons in separate documents. OAuth 2.1 — an IETF draft that consolidates them, together with the Security Best Current Practice (RFC 9700) — is what new systems should follow34:

OAuth 2.0 allowed OAuth 2.1 requires Authorization Code with or without PKCE PKCE for every client using the authorization code, including confidential ones Implicit grant (token in the URL fragment) removed — tokens leaked through history, referrers, logs Resource Owner Password Credentials (the app collects the password) removed — defeats delegation, blocks MFA, trains users to type passwords anywhere redirect URIs matched by prefix or pattern exact string matching of redirect URIs bearer tokens in query strings never in the URL; header or body only long-lived refresh tokens for public clients refresh tokens sender-constrained or rotated on every use

items.title: Choosing the grant
items.text:
flowchart TD
    q1{"Is a user<br/>involved?"} -->|no| cc["Client Credentials<br/>(reconciliation job)"]
    q1 -->|yes| q2{"Can the device<br/>open a browser?"}
    q2 -->|yes| pkce["Authorization Code + PKCE<br/>(mobile app, web BFF)"]
    q2 -->|no| dev["Device Authorization<br/>(smart TV, CLI)"]
    pkce --> q3{"A service must call another<br/>on the user's behalf?"}
    q3 -->|yes| tx["Token Exchange<br/>(assistant → order)"]

items.title: Authorization Code + PKCE for the mobile app
items.text:
The app never sees the password. It opens the system browser (not an embedded WebView, where the app could read keystrokes — RFC 82525) at the authorization server, the user logs in there (with MFA or a passkey), and the app receives a short-lived, single-use authorization code through a redirect. The app then exchanges the code for tokens in a direct back-channel request.

PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, "pixy", RFC 76366) binds the code to the app instance that started the flow:

  1. The app generates a random code_verifier (43–128 characters) and keeps it in memory.
  2. It sends only code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA-256(code_verifier)) in the authorization request.
  3. At the token exchange it sends the original code_verifier; the server hashes and compares.

A malicious app that registered the same redirect scheme and intercepts the code does not have the verifier, so the code is useless.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Ana
    participant App as BoxOffice app
    participant Br as System browser
    participant AS as auth (Keycloak)
    participant GW as API gateway
    participant O as order
    Ana->>App: tap "Log in"
    App->>App: create state, nonce, code_verifier, code_challenge (S256)
    App->>Br: open /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=boxoffice-mobile&scope=openid orders:write&code_challenge&state&nonce
    Br->>AS: GET /authorize
    AS->>Ana: login page (password + MFA, or passkey)
    Ana->>AS: credentials
    AS-->>Br: 302 https://app.boxoffice.com/cb?code=XYZ&state
    Br-->>App: redirect delivered to the app (claimed HTTPS link)
    App->>App: check state
    App->>AS: POST /token {code, code_verifier, redirect_uri}
    AS->>AS: SHA-256(code_verifier) == code_challenge?
    AS-->>App: access_token (15 min) + refresh_token (rotating) + id_token
    App->>GW: POST /orders  Authorization: Bearer access_token
    GW->>GW: verify signature (cached JWKS), iss, aud, exp, scope
    GW->>O: POST /orders + X-Account-Id: acc-42
    O-->>App: 201 Created

The state parameter prevents an attacker from injecting their code into Ana's session (CSRF on the callback); the nonce is echoed inside the ID token and prevents replaying an old one.

Computing a PKCE pair by hand 
# 64 random URL-safe characters
verifier=$(openssl rand -base64 48 | tr -d '=+/\n' | cut -c1-64)
# BASE64URL(SHA-256(verifier)), without '=' padding
challenge=$(printf '%s' "$verifier" | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary \
            | openssl base64 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=')
echo "verifier=$verifier"; echo "challenge=$challenge"

Where the mobile app keeps tokens. The access token lives in memory; the refresh token in the platform's secure storage (iOS Keychain, Android Keystore-backed storage). The authorization server rotates the refresh token on every use: if a stolen copy and the legitimate app both try to use the same one, the server detects the reuse and revokes the whole family.

items.title: OpenID Connect: who is the user?
items.text:
OAuth answers "may this client call this API?". It deliberately does not tell the client who the user is — the access token is addressed to the API. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds an identity layer on top of OAuth7:

  • the openid scope in the authorization request;
  • the ID token — a JWT addressed to the client (aud = its client_id) with sub, iss, exp, nonce, auth_time and, with the profile/email scopes, name and e-mail;
  • the UserInfo endpoint for more profile claims;
  • discovery at /.well-known/openid-configuration, which lists the endpoints and the jwks_uri, so clients and resource servers bootstrap from the issuer URL alone.
Token Audience Purpose Typical lifetime ID token the client "the user who logged in is acc-42, at 14:02, with MFA" minutes, used once at login Access token the API (resource server) "this client may orders:write for acc-42" 5–60 minutes Refresh token the authorization server only obtain new access tokens without a new login hours to weeks, rotated

items.title: Web checkout: OIDC through a Backend-for-Frontend
items.text:
For the browser, the current recommendation is to keep no tokens in JavaScript at all. A BFF (Backend for Frontend) is a confidential client on the server: it runs the OIDC flow, keeps the tokens, and gives the browser only an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite session cookie8.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Ana
    participant Br as Browser (checkout SPA)
    participant BFF as web BFF (confidential client)
    participant AS as auth (OIDC provider)
    participant GW as API gateway
    Ana->>Br: click "Log in"
    Br->>BFF: GET /login
    BFF-->>Br: 302 to AS /authorize (code + PKCE, scope openid, nonce)
    Br->>AS: login (passkey)
    AS-->>Br: 302 to BFF /callback?code&state
    Br->>BFF: GET /callback?code&state
    BFF->>AS: POST /token {code, code_verifier, client secret or private_key_jwt}
    AS-->>BFF: id_token + access_token + refresh_token
    BFF->>BFF: validate id_token (sig, iss, aud, exp, nonce), store tokens server-side
    BFF-->>Br: Set-Cookie: session=… HttpOnly Secure SameSite=Lax
    Br->>BFF: GET /api/orders (cookie)
    BFF->>GW: GET /orders  Bearer access_token
    GW-->>BFF: 200 orders
    BFF-->>Br: 200 orders
Where the browser keeps credentials Readable by JS? Main risk localStorage / sessionStorage yes any XSS (cross-site scripting) steals the token HttpOnly cookie with the token no CSRF (cross-site request forgery); mitigated by SameSite + CSRF tokens BFF session cookie, tokens on the server no token in the browser session theft; the BFF is a component to scale

items.title: Client Credentials: the reconciliation job
items.text:
When no user is involved, the client authenticates as itself and receives a token that represents the service. The order reconciliation job asks for exactly the scope it needs:

curl -s -X POST https://auth.boxoffice.com/realms/boxoffice/protocol/openid-connect/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials \
  -d client_id=order-reconciler \
  -d client_secret="$ORDER_RECONCILER_SECRET" \
  -d scope=inventory:read

Better than a client secret: authenticate the client with a signed JWT (private_key_jwt) or with its workload identity (mTLS certificate or the Kubernetes service-account token) — no shared secret to leak (Zero Trust).

items.title: Token Exchange: the assistant acting for the user
items.text: The AI assistant must call order on behalf of Ana, with less power than Ana's own token. Token Exchange (RFC 8693) lets a service trade the token it received for a new one with a different audience and narrower scope (aud=order, scope=orders:read), keeping sub=acc-42 and recording the actor (act: assistant). The audit log then shows "assistant, acting for acc-42, read order 1042".

items.title: Sender-constrained tokens
items.text: A bearer token works for anyone who steals it. Sender-constrained tokens are bound to a key the legitimate client holds: with DPoP (RFC 9449) the client signs a small proof for every request with a private key on the device; with mTLS-bound tokens (RFC 8705) the token is tied to the client certificate. A stolen token alone is then useless. Financial-grade APIs require them; for BoxOffice they are worth it on payment endpoints.

items.title: Passkeys
items.text: Passkeys (WebAuthn/FIDO2) replace passwords with a key pair per site, kept on the device and unlocked with biometrics. The private key never leaves the device and the signature is bound to the site's origin, so they resist phishing. They change how the user authenticates at the authorization server; the OAuth/OIDC flows after it stay the same.

items.title: Validating tokens at the gateway
items.text:
The gateway is the first enforcement point: it rejects requests without a valid token and forwards a trusted identity downstream (see Edge — API gateway).

Local validation (JWKS) Remote validation (introspection, RFC 7662) Extra hop none — signature checked with a cached public key one call to the AS per request (cacheable for seconds) AS outage requests keep working every request fails (or uses the cache) Revocation effective only at exp immediate Token type JWT JWT or opaque Typical use most API traffic sensitive operations, opaque tokens

With Spring Security (also in Spring Cloud Gateway), local validation is configuration:

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://auth.boxoffice.com/realms/boxoffice  # discovers jwks_uri, checks iss
          audiences: boxoffice-api                                 # rejects tokens for other APIs

Strip identity headers at the edge

If the gateway forwards X-Account-Id: acc-42 to services, it must remove any X-Account-Id sent by the client, and services must be unreachable except through the gateway (or must verify the token themselves). Otherwise anyone who reaches a service directly can become any user.

items.title: Authorization models
items.text:
Authentication produced an identity. Now: may this identity do this action on this object?

Model Decides by BoxOffice example Good for Weak at RBAC (role-based) the user's roles organizer may create events; support may read any order coarse, stable permissions per-object rules ("only their events") ABAC (attribute-based) attributes of user, resource, context refunds allowed if order.eventDate > now + 48h and user.country == order.country rich, contextual rules harder to audit "who can access X?" ReBAC (relationship-based) a graph of relationships Ana may view order 1042 because she owns it; Bruno because Ana shared the ticket with him sharing, organizations, hierarchies needs a relationship store (Google Zanzibar, OpenFGA, SpiceDB)

OAuth scopes are not a replacement: a scope limits what the client may do (orders:read), not which objects the user may touch. The ownership check — the fix for OWASP API1: BOLA — always runs in the service that owns the data9:

In code (order service)Policy as code (OPA / Rego)Policy as code (Cedar) 
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_orders:read')")
public OrderOut get(@PathVariable UUID id, @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    Order order = repository.findById(id)
        .filter(o -> o.getAccountId().equals(jwt.getSubject()))  // ownership (BOLA)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND));
    return OrderOut.from(order);                                 // explicit DTO (BOPLA)
}

package boxoffice.orders

import rego.v1

default allow := false

# owners can read their own orders
allow if {
    input.action == "read"
    input.resource.owner_id == input.user.sub
}

# support staff can read any order, never modify it
allow if {
    input.action == "read"
    "support" in input.user.roles
}

permit (
  principal,
  action == Action::"ReadOrder",
  resource
)
when { resource.owner == principal };

permit (
  principal in Role::"support",
  action == Action::"ReadOrder",
  resource
);

Policy engines (OPA, Cedar, OpenFGA) move the rules out of the code into a reviewable, testable artifact that several services share. The service still asks the question for every object.

In the interview

Whenever the design has users, say in one breath: "users log in through an OIDC provider; the mobile app uses Authorization Code with PKCE; the gateway validates short-lived JWT access tokens locally against the provider's JWKS; refresh tokens rotate; service-to-service calls use client credentials or the mesh identity; and every service checks object ownership." If they ask about logout or revocation, explain the trade-off between local validation and introspection — and the exposure window equal to the token lifetime.

Common pitfalls

  • Implicit or password (ROPC) grants in new code — removed in OAuth 2.1; use Authorization Code + PKCE.
  • Skipping aud — a token issued for another API is accepted by yours.
  • Long-lived access tokens (24 h) — a stolen bearer token is a 24-hour master key.
  • Tokens in localStorage or in URLs and logs — XSS and log leaks.
  • Calling APIs with the ID token — it is for the client; APIs accept access tokens only.
  • Authorization only at the gateway — BOLA: GET /orders/{id} returns any order to any logged-in user.
  • Sharing an HMAC secret across services — every verifier can forge tokens.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    AS["auth: OIDC provider<br/>(authorization server)"] --> PKCE["Authorization Code + PKCE<br/>mobile app, web BFF"]
    AS --> CC["Client Credentials<br/>reconciliation job"]
    AS --> TX["Token Exchange<br/>assistant → order"]
    PKCE --> JWT["short-lived JWT access token<br/>+ rotating refresh token"]
    PKCE --> SESS["BFF session cookie<br/>shared store → Caching"]
    JWT --> GW["gateway validates via JWKS<br/>iss, aud, exp → Edge"]
    GW --> SVC["each service checks ownership<br/>RBAC / ABAC / ReBAC"]
    SVC --> BOLA["fixes OWASP API1 (BOLA)"]
    CC --> WI["workload identity<br/>→ Zero Trust"]
    TX --> AI["agents acting for users<br/>→ AI systems"]

Palette components: auth · apigw (the first enforcement point) · client · mobile · cache (server-side sessions) · orchestrator (the assistant acting on the user's behalf). Scenarios: rate-limiter, flash-sale, ai-assistant. Continues in: Edge — API gateway, Zero Trust, Caching — Redis, AI systems — agents, Hands-on 4 — Gateway & identity.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• AuthN (who) ≠ authZ (what). The gateway authenticates; each service still authorizes access to its own objects.
  • Sessions revoke instantly but need a shared store; JWTs scale statelessly but stay valid until exp. Combine short access tokens with revocable refresh tokens.
  • Validate JWTs properly: allow-listed algorithm, kid from your JWKS, iss, aud, exp, typ, scopes.
  • OAuth 2.1: Authorization Code + PKCE for every user-facing client (system browser for mobile, BFF for web), Client Credentials for jobs, Token Exchange for delegation; no Implicit, no ROPC.
  • OIDC adds the ID token, UserInfo and discovery. Choose RBAC, ABAC or ReBAC for authorization, and always check ownership (BOLA).

  1. SHEFFER, Y.; HARDT, D.; JONES, M. RFC 8725 — JSON Web Token Best Current Practices. IETF, 2020. See also RFC 9068 — JWT Profile for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens. ↩

  2. HARDT, D. (ed.). RFC 6749 — The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework. IETF, 2012. ↩

  3. HARDT, D.; PARECKI, A.; LODDERSTEDT, T. The OAuth 2.1 Authorization Framework. IETF Internet-Draft. ↩

  4. LODDERSTEDT, T. et al. RFC 9700 — Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security. IETF, 2025. ↩

  5. DENNISS, W.; BRADLEY, J. RFC 8252 — OAuth 2.0 for Native Apps. IETF, 2017. ↩

  6. SAKIMURA, N.; BRADLEY, J.; AGARWAL, N. RFC 7636 — Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients. IETF, 2015. ↩

  7. SAKIMURA, N. et al. OpenID Connect Core 1.0. OpenID Foundation. ↩

  8. PARECKI, A.; DE RYCK, P. OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications. IETF Internet-Draft. ↩

  9. OWASP. API1:2023 — Broken Object Level Authorization. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text: BoxOffice now runs nine services in Kubernetes. Each team has re-implemented the same things in its own way: order has a 2-second timeout to payment, inventory has none; catalog retries three times, search retries forever; nobody encrypts traffic inside the cluster because "it's internal"; and when security asks "which services can call payment?", the honest answer is "any pod that knows the URL". A service mesh moves these cross-cutting concerns — encryption, identity, authorization, timeouts, retries, traffic splitting, telemetry — out of the application code and into a uniform infrastructure layer.

items.title: What a service mesh is
items.text:
A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication1. It has two parts:

  • Data plane — proxies that sit in the path of every request between services. They terminate and originate TLS, enforce policies, retry, time out, balance load and emit metrics and traces.
  • Control plane — the brain that configures the proxies: it distributes routing rules and policies, and acts as a certificate authority that issues each workload its identity.
flowchart TB
    subgraph cp ["Control plane (istiod / linkerd-control-plane)"]
        CFG["config + policy"]
        CA["certificate authority"]
    end
    subgraph dp ["Data plane"]
        subgraph po ["pod: order"]
            O["order app"] --- PO["proxy"]
        end
        subgraph pp ["pod: payment"]
            PP["proxy"] --- P["payment app"]
        end
    end
    PO <-->|"mTLS"| PP
    CFG -.->|"routes, policies"| PO & PP
    CA -.->|"certificates (rotated)"| PO & PP

The application still calls http://payment:8080/charges in plain HTTP. The proxy on the way out upgrades it to mutual TLS, the proxy on the way in verifies the caller's identity, checks the policy and hands plain HTTP to payment. Neither application changed a line.

items.title: What you get
items.text:
Capability Without a mesh With a mesh Encryption in transit each team configures TLS (usually nobody does inside the cluster) mTLS everywhere, certificates rotated automatically Service identity IP addresses, shared secrets a cryptographic identity per workload (SPIFFE) Authorization between services in code, if at all declarative policies: "only order may POST /charges on payment" Timeouts, retries, circuit breaking libraries in each language (Resilience4j, Polly…) uniform config per route Traffic splitting (canary, mirroring) in the load balancer or in code weights per route, header-based routing Golden-signal telemetry each service instruments itself request rate, errors and latency for every hop, out of the box

The mesh is the natural home of three topics of the course: reliability patterns (see Reliability), observability of every hop (see Observability) and Zero Trust between services (Zero Trust).

items.title: Data-plane architectures: sidecar, ambient, eBPF
items.text:
Where does the proxy run? Three designs are in production today23.

SidecarAmbient (Istio)eBPF / sidecarless (Cilium)

One proxy container (Envoy for Istio, linkerd2-proxy for Linkerd) is injected into every pod. All traffic in and out of the pod is redirected through it.

  • Every hop is full L7 (HTTP-aware): retries, header routing, per-path policies.
  • Cost: one proxy per pod — memory and CPU multiplied by the number of pods, an extra hop on each side of every call, and the sidecar's lifecycle is coupled to the app (upgrading the mesh means restarting every pod; jobs need the sidecar to exit).

The mesh is split into two layers:

  • ztunnel — one per node, a small proxy that handles L4: mTLS, identity, L4 authorization and telemetry for all pods on the node.
  • waypoint proxy — an optional Envoy deployed per namespace or per service only when L7 features are needed (HTTP routing, retries, path-based policies).

Pods are not modified; adding a namespace to the mesh is a label. You pay for L7 only where you use it.

The eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) programs in the Linux kernel handle L3/L4 — routing, NetworkPolicy, load balancing, transparent encryption (WireGuard or IPsec) — with no proxy per pod. L7 features go through a shared per-node Envoy. Identity is tied to Kubernetes labels and, for mutual authentication, to SPIFFE-style identities.

Sidecar Ambient eBPF (Cilium) Proxy placement one per pod ztunnel per node + optional waypoint kernel + shared Envoy per node L7 everywhere? yes only where a waypoint is deployed only where L7 policy is configured Resource overhead (qualitative) highest — grows with pod count low for L4, pay per waypoint lowest for L3/L4 Added latency per hop two proxies on the path node-level hop; +waypoint for L7 kernel fast path Upgrade impact restart every pod upgrade node agents and waypoints upgrade the node agent Blast radius of a proxy bug one pod all pods on the node (ztunnel) the node Maturity longest in production GA in Istio since 1.24 (2024) widely used as CNI; mesh features newer

Proxyless gRPC

A fourth option skips the proxy entirely: gRPC libraries can receive mesh configuration directly from the control plane (the xDS protocol). It is efficient but only works for gRPC services written with a supporting library.

Think first: BoxOffice has 9 services × 6 replicas, and each sidecar reserves 50 MB of memory. What does the mesh cost in memory?

54 pods × 50 MB ≈ 2.7 GB just for sidecars (an illustrative reservation; measure yours), plus CPU proportional to the traffic. During a flash sale, when the autoscaler takes order and inventory to 40 replicas each, the sidecars scale too. That linear cost is the main motivation for ambient and eBPF data planes.

items.title: Identity and mTLS
items.text:
How does payment know that a call really comes from order? IP addresses prove nothing — pods are recreated with new IPs, and the attacker in the compromised search pod can send from any IP it likes. The mesh gives each workload a cryptographic identity.

  • TLS (Transport Layer Security) — the server proves its identity with an X.509 certificate signed by a certificate authority; the channel is encrypted.
  • mTLS (mutual TLS) — the client also presents a certificate. Both sides are authenticated.
  • SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework For Everyone)4 — a standard name for workload identities, spiffe://<trust-domain>/<path>. Istio uses spiffe://cluster.local/ns/<namespace>/sa/<service-account>: the identity is the Kubernetes service account.
  • SVID (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document) — the short-lived X.509 certificate that carries that identity, rotated automatically (Istio's default lifetime is 24 hours; SPIRE's default is one hour).
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant O as order (proxy)
    participant CA as Mesh CA (istiod)
    participant P as payment (proxy)
    O->>CA: CSR + proof of service account token
    CA-->>O: SVID spiffe://cluster.local/ns/boxoffice/sa/order (24 h)
    P->>CA: CSR + proof of service account token
    CA-->>P: SVID spiffe://cluster.local/ns/boxoffice/sa/payment
    O->>P: ClientHello
    P-->>O: payment certificate + CertificateRequest
    O->>O: verify payment's SVID against the trust bundle
    O->>P: order certificate + proof of private key
    P->>P: verify order's SVID, read its SPIFFE ID
    P->>P: authorization policy: may sa/order POST /charges? → allow
    Note over O,P: encrypted channel, both identities proven, policy applied

items.title: Turn on strict mTLS
items.text:
By default Istio accepts both plain-text and mTLS (permissive mode) so that services can migrate gradually. Once every workload has a proxy, make it strict:

apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT        # reject any plain-text connection to pods in this namespace

items.title: mTLS authenticates; a policy authorizes
items.text:
A valid certificate says who is calling — not whether they may. That is an authorization policy, evaluated by the proxy on every request. Only order may charge cards:

IstioLinkerd 
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: payment-allow-order
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payment
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            principals: ["cluster.local/ns/boxoffice/sa/order"]
      to:
        - operation:
            methods: ["POST"]
            paths: ["/charges", "/refunds"]

Once a workload has at least one ALLOW policy, any request that matches no rule is denied. The compromised search pod gets 403 RBAC: access denied.

# API versions change between Linkerd releases: check yours
apiVersion: policy.linkerd.io/v1beta3
kind: Server
metadata:
  name: payment-http
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payment
  port: 8080
  proxyProtocol: HTTP/1
---
apiVersion: policy.linkerd.io/v1alpha1
kind: MeshTLSAuthentication
metadata:
  name: order-only
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  identities:
    - "order.boxoffice.serviceaccount.identity.linkerd.cluster.local"
---
apiVersion: policy.linkerd.io/v1alpha1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: payment-allow-order
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  targetRef:
    group: policy.linkerd.io
    kind: Server
    name: payment-http
  requiredAuthenticationRefs:
    - group: policy.linkerd.io
      kind: MeshTLSAuthentication
      name: order-only

Linkerd names the identity after the service account too; the policy attaches to a Server (a port of a set of pods).

BoxOffice — the service call graph as policy

Draw the allowed edges once and turn each into a policy: gateway → order, catalog, search, auth; order → inventory, payment, notification (via Kafka); assistant → catalog, order (read-only). Everything else is denied. The diagram in the design document and the policies in the repository are the same thing — reviewable in a pull request.

items.title: Traffic policy
items.text: The second big job of a mesh is shaping traffic: timeouts, retries, circuit breaking and splitting.

items.title: Timeouts and retries per route
items.text:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: payment
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  hosts: ["payment"]
  http:
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: payment
            subset: v1
          weight: 90
        - destination:
            host: payment
            subset: v2        # canary: 10% of the traffic
          weight: 10
      timeout: 3s             # total budget for the call
      retries:
        attempts: 2
        perTryTimeout: 1s
        retryOn: connect-failure,refused-stream,unavailable

Three decisions are encoded here: a canary sends 10% of the calls to v2; the whole call has a 3-second budget; and retries happen only on failures where the request certainly did not reach the application (connect-failure, refused-stream, unavailable). Retrying a POST /charges after a timeout could charge the customer twice — that is what idempotency keys are for (see Compute — integrations).

items.title: Circuit breaking with outlier detection
items.text:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: payment
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  host: payment
  subsets:
    - name: v1
      labels: { version: v1 }
    - name: v2
      labels: { version: v2 }
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      http:
        http2MaxRequests: 200          # bulkhead: max concurrent requests
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 50
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5          # eject a replica after 5 errors in a row
      interval: 10s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50           # never eject more than half the replicas

Outlier detection removes a misbehaving replica from the load-balancing pool for a while — a per-instance circuit breaker. The connection pool limits are a bulkhead: when payment is slow, at most 200 requests wait on it, instead of every thread of order.

Try it. Open the cascading-failure scenario: a slow third-party dependency with no timeouts exhausts the caller's threads, and unrelated requests start failing. Turn on the timeout and the circuit breaker, run again, and compare the error rate and p99 of the other routes. In BoxOffice, the mesh VirtualService timeout and DestinationRule limits are one way to apply exactly that fix without touching the code.

Retries in two places multiply

If order uses Resilience4j with 3 attempts and the mesh adds 2 more per attempt, one user click can become 3 × 3 = 9 calls to a struggling payment — a retry storm. Decide one layer that retries (usually the mesh, or the client library, not both) and keep a retry budget.

items.title: Gateway API for the mesh (GAMMA)
items.text:
The Kubernetes Gateway API started as the successor of Ingress for north–south traffic (see Edge). The GAMMA initiative extends the same HTTPRoute resource to east–west traffic inside the mesh, so a canary looks the same in Istio, Linkerd or Cilium:

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: payment-canary
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - group: ""
      kind: Service           # attach to a Service = mesh (east-west) routing
      name: payment
      port: 8080
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: payment-v1
          port: 8080
          weight: 90
        - name: payment-v2
          port: 8080
          weight: 10

items.title: Mesh policy and NetworkPolicy: two layers
items.text:
A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is a firewall for pods at L3/L4 (IP and port), enforced by the CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium)5. A mesh authorization policy works at L7 with cryptographic identity. They are complementary layers of defense in depth:

NetworkPolicy Mesh authorization policy Layer L3/L4 — IPs, ports L7 — identity, method, path, headers Identity pod labels → IPs SPIFFE identity in the certificate Enforced by the CNI, in the kernel the proxy (sidecar, ztunnel, waypoint) Survives a bypassed proxy? yes no Can say "only POST /charges"? no yes

Start with default deny at the network layer, then open only the edges of the call graph:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: payment-from-order
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payment
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: order
      ports:
        - port: 8080

Egress is the forgotten half

Most teams write ingress policies only. Egress policies (and an egress gateway) decide what a pod may reach outside: only payment should reach the provider's address; search should reach nothing on the Internet. That is what turns a compromised pod into a dead end instead of a data-exfiltration channel.

items.title: Costs and when not to use a mesh
items.text:
A mesh is powerful and expensive to run. It adds a control plane to operate and upgrade, proxies that consume CPU and memory, a few milliseconds per hop, a new class of failures ("the proxy rejected it"), and a steep learning curve for debugging.

Situation Recommendation 3–5 services, one team, one language probably no mesh: TLS at the ingress, NetworkPolicy, a resilience library Many services, several languages and teams a mesh gives uniform mTLS, policy and telemetry Compliance requires encryption in transit everywhere a mesh (or CNI-level encryption) is the cheapest way to prove it Latency-critical hot path (microseconds) measure; consider ambient/eBPF or proxyless gRPC Only need mTLS + L4 policy ambient (ztunnel only) or Cilium, without L7 proxies

In the interview

Bring up a mesh when the design has many services and someone asks about service-to-service security or resilience: "inside the cluster, a service mesh gives every service an identity and mutual TLS; authorization policies say only order can call payment; timeouts, retries and outlier detection are configured per route." Then show you know the cost: "it adds a proxy hop and operational complexity — ambient or eBPF data planes reduce the per-pod overhead; for a handful of services I'd skip it."

Common pitfalls

  • Leaving mTLS in permissive mode forever — plain text is still accepted, so the mesh encrypts nothing an attacker cares about.
  • mTLS without authorization policies — every workload in the mesh can still call payment; you only encrypted the attack.
  • Double retries (library + mesh) — retry storms on the first incident.
  • Retrying non-idempotent calls after a timeout — double charges.
  • Assuming the mesh replaces user authorization — the mesh knows the service; only order knows whether this user owns order 1042.
  • Forgetting egress — the mesh protects calls between services, but the compromised pod can still reach the Internet unless egress is restricted.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    CP["control plane<br/>config + CA"] --> DP["data plane:<br/>sidecar, ambient, eBPF"]
    CP --> SVID["SPIFFE identity (SVID)<br/>from the service account"]
    SVID --> MTLS["strict mTLS"]
    MTLS --> AUTHZ["authorization policy<br/>only order → payment"]
    AUTHZ --> NP["NetworkPolicy L3/L4<br/>default deny + egress"]
    AUTHZ --> ZT["PEP for workloads<br/>→ Zero Trust"]
    DP --> TP["timeouts, retries,<br/>outlier detection"]
    TP --> REL["resilience patterns<br/>→ Reliability"]
    DP --> CAN["HTTPRoute weights (GAMMA)<br/>→ canary in Cloud-native"]
    DP --> TEL["golden signals per hop<br/>→ Observability"]

Palette components: mesh · app (the services behind each proxy) · ingress (Gateway API, north–south) · metrics · tracing (telemetry of every hop). Scenarios: cascading-failure, retry-storm. Continues in: Zero Trust, Reliability — patterns, Observability — signals, Edge — load balancing in Kubernetes, Cloud-native — delivery (canary).

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• A service mesh = data plane (proxies on every call) + control plane (config + certificate authority); it moves mTLS, policy, resilience and telemetry out of the code.
  • Sidecar gives full L7 everywhere at a per-pod cost; ambient splits L4 (ztunnel per node) from optional L7 (waypoints); eBPF does L3/L4 in the kernel.
  • mTLS authenticates workloads with SPIFFE identities derived from service accounts; an authorization policy decides who may call what.
  • Traffic policy — timeouts, retries, outlier detection, canary weights — is declared per route; retry in only one layer, and only idempotent calls.
  • NetworkPolicy (L3/L4, default deny, ingress and egress) and mesh policy (L7, identity) are complementary layers. For a handful of services, a mesh may not be worth it.

  1. MORGAN, W. What's a service mesh? And why do I need one?. Buoyant. See also the Linkerd documentation. ↩

  2. ISTIO. Ambient mode overview and Security — authorization policy. ↩

  3. CILIUM. Cilium Service Mesh. ↩

  4. SPIFFE. SPIFFE Overview. ↩

  5. KUBERNETES. Network Policies; Gateway API — GAMMA (service mesh). ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
A vulnerable image-parsing library lets an attacker run code inside one search pod. Now replay the default setup. From that pod, the attacker calls order with the header X-Account-Id: acc-42 and reads Ana's orders, because "only the gateway can reach order". They read the environment variables and find DATABASE_URL with the one password every service shares. They find PSP_API_KEY, because the payment key was put in a ConfigMap "temporarily". They open a connection to https://attacker.example and upload everything, because the private subnet has a NAT route and nothing restricts egress. Every step was possible because something trusted the network.

This page is about the architecture that removes that trust — Zero Trust — and about two places where trust hides in every system: secrets and the software supply chain.

items.title: From perimeter to Zero Trust
items.text:
The perimeter model ("castle and moat") protects the edge — firewall, VPN — and trusts everything inside. Once an attacker is inside, through a stolen laptop, a phished password or a vulnerable dependency, they move from machine to machine: lateral movement.

Zero Trust removes the idea of a trusted network. Its motto is "never trust, always verify": every request — from the Internet, from the office, from the pod next door — is authenticated, authorized and encrypted on its own merits1. Google built its corporate network this way in the BeyondCorp project after 20112; NIST standardized the architecture in SP 800-2071.

flowchart LR
    subgraph perimeter ["Perimeter model"]
        fw["Firewall / VPN"] -->|"inside = trusted"| int["search, order, payment, DB<br/>(trust each other)"]
    end
    subgraph zt ["Zero Trust model"]
        any["Any request<br/>(user or workload)"] -->|"identity + context"| pep["Policy Enforcement Point<br/>(gateway, mesh proxy)"]
        pep -->|"ask"| pdp["Policy Decision Point<br/>(policies, identity, device, risk)"]
        pdp -->|"allow, least privilege"| res["Resource"]
        pdp -->|"deny"| rej["Rejected + logged"]
    end

NIST names the moving parts: a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) sits in the path of every request and blocks or forwards it; a Policy Decision Point (PDP) decides from identity and context. In BoxOffice, the API gateway is the PEP for users, and the mesh proxy next to each service is the PEP for workloads (Service mesh).

items.title: Principles
items.text: Principle What it means BoxOffice mechanisms Verify explicitly every user and every workload proves who it is on every request OIDC tokens, mTLS with SPIFFE identities, signed webhooks Least privilege the minimum access, for the minimum time narrow scopes, one DB user per service, short-lived credentials, egress allow-lists Assume breach design as if an attacker is already inside; limit the blast radius default-deny NetworkPolicy, isolated subnets, per-service secrets, audit logs Continuous evaluation trust is re-checked, not granted once short token lifetimes, re-authentication for sensitive actions, anomaly alerts

items.title: The compromised search pod, again
items.text:
Attacker step Perimeter model Zero Trust control Where Call order with a forged X-Account-Id accepted — "only internal callers" order accepts calls only from the gateway's mesh identity; header stripped at the edge Service mesh, Identity Connect to PostgreSQL with the shared password works search has no route/SG/NetworkPolicy to the DB, and no DB credential at all Cloud networking Read PSP_API_KEY from the environment it is there the key exists only in payment pods, fetched from a secrets manager Secrets Exfiltrate to the Internet NAT route, no egress rules egress default-deny; only payment may reach the provider Service mesh Stay hidden nobody looks at internal traffic denied calls are logged and alerted Observability

The attack still started — Zero Trust does not prevent the first compromise. It makes the compromised pod a dead end.

items.title: Workload identity: no more long-lived keys
items.text:
Zero Trust needs every workload to have an identity it can prove without a static secret. Three common forms:

Workload Identity mechanism What it replaces Pod → pod SPIFFE ID in an mTLS certificate issued by the mesh or SPIRE, rotated hourly to daily IP allow-lists, shared API tokens Pod → cloud API (S3, Secrets Manager, KMS) the Kubernetes service account federated to a cloud role: EKS Pod Identity / IRSA, GKE Workload Identity Federation, Azure Workload Identity access keys in environment variables CI pipeline → cloud the CI system's OIDC token exchanged for short-lived cloud credentials cloud access keys stored as CI secrets

The third is a small change with a big effect: GitHub Actions can request an OIDC token that says "I am workflow release.yaml of this repository on branch main", and the cloud trusts that claim for a role valid only for the job's duration3:

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write          # allow the job to request an OIDC token
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/boxoffice-deploy
          aws-region: sa-east-1
      - run: aws eks update-kubeconfig --name boxoffice-prod

No AWS key is stored in GitHub; the role's trust policy accepts only tokens whose sub matches repo:<org>/<repo>:ref:refs/heads/main. A forked repository or another branch cannot assume it.

People are workloads too

For engineers, Zero Trust means: single sign-on with MFA or passkeys, device posture checks, and access through an identity-aware proxy or session manager instead of a VPN that puts the laptop "inside" (Cloud networking). Every access is per application and logged.

items.title: Secrets management
items.text:
A secret is any value that grants access: the payment provider API key, database passwords, the signing key of the identity provider, webhook HMAC secrets, registry tokens. Secrets must not live where things get copied, versioned or logged: source code, container images, plain ConfigMaps, CI logs.

Kubernetes Secrets are base64, not encrypted

A Kubernetes Secret stores values base64-encoded. Anyone who can get Secrets in the namespace — or create a pod that mounts them — reads them in one command:

kubectl get secret psp-api-key -n boxoffice -o jsonpath='{.data.PSP_API_KEY}' | base64 -d

By default they are also stored unencrypted in etcd. Minimum hygiene: encryption at rest for etcd (with a KMS provider), tight RBAC on Secrets, and never committing Secret manifests to Git unencrypted4.

items.title: Where secrets should live
items.text:
Approach Pros Cons Kubernetes Secrets only simple, native base64; rotation and audit are on you Encrypted in Git (Sealed Secrets, SOPS) GitOps-friendly, reviewed in PRs rotation still manual; key management for the sealing key Cloud secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault) managed, versioned, audit log, rotation hooks, IAM per secret tied to one cloud; per-secret and per-call cost HashiCorp Vault / OpenBao dynamic secrets, any cloud, fine-grained policies and audit a critical, stateful system to operate

The External Secrets Operator (ESO) bridges both worlds: the source of truth is the secrets manager; ESO syncs values into native Secrets that pods read as usual.

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: psp-api-key
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
    name: aws-secrets-manager
  target:
    name: psp-api-key            # Kubernetes Secret created and kept in sync by ESO
  data:
    - secretKey: PSP_API_KEY
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/boxoffice/payment/psp-api-key

items.title: The life of the payment API key
items.text:
The payment provider lets a merchant hold two active keys at once — the standard trick for rotation without downtime. The lifecycle of BoxOffice's most valuable secret:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Ops as Payments on-call
    participant PSP as Payment provider
    participant SM as Secrets Manager
    participant ESO as External Secrets Operator
    participant K8s as Secret psp-api-key
    participant Pay as payment pods
    Ops->>PSP: create key 2 (key 1 still active)
    Ops->>SM: put key 2 as a new version of prod/boxoffice/payment/psp-api-key
    ESO->>SM: refresh (every 1 h, or forced)
    SM-->>ESO: version 2
    ESO->>K8s: update Secret
    K8s-->>Pay: mounted file changes → app reloads (or rolling restart)
    Pay->>PSP: charges now signed with key 2
    Ops->>Ops: confirm in metrics: zero calls with key 1 for 24 h
    Ops->>PSP: revoke key 1

Notice what the design gives you: only the payment service account may read that secret (IAM); every read is in the audit log; the key never appears in Git, images or CI logs; and if it leaks, the same procedure runs in minutes instead of days.

BoxOffice — leaked key runbook (short version)

  1. Revoke first, investigate second: create a new key, roll it out (sequence above), revoke the leaked one.
  2. Search the provider's dashboard for calls from unknown IPs (BoxOffice only calls from its NAT Elastic IPs).
  3. Find how it leaked (Git history, logs, a laptop) and close that path.
  4. Write a blameless postmortem (Observability — incident response).

items.title: Dynamic secrets
items.text:
Even better than rotating a shared secret is not having one. Dynamic secrets (Vault's database engine, cloud IAM database authentication) create a unique, short-lived credential per requester:

$ vault read database/creds/order
Key                Value
lease_id           database/creds/order/8sTt3lV0b2yL
lease_duration     1h
username           v-k8s-order-x7Qa2
password           A1a-4kd0s8f7GQpz

Each order pod gets its own database user that expires in an hour. A credential stolen from a pod stops working by itself, and the database logs show exactly which pod did what.

items.title: Encryption at rest with envelope encryption
items.text:
Databases, object storage and backups are encrypted at rest with envelope encryption: each object is encrypted with a data key; the data key is itself encrypted with a key-encryption key that never leaves a KMS (Key Management Service) or HSM (hardware security module).

flowchart LR
    D["order data"] -->|"AES-256-GCM with data key"| E["ciphertext"]
    DK["data key (plaintext, in memory only)"] -->|"encrypt via KMS API"| EDK["encrypted data key<br/>(stored next to the ciphertext)"]
    KMS["KMS master key<br/>(never leaves the KMS/HSM)"] -.-> EDK

Rotating or revoking the master key in KMS controls access to all the data without re-encrypting terabytes; every decrypt call is authorized by IAM and logged.

items.title: Keep secrets out of Git
items.text: Scan before they land: a pre-commit hook and a CI job with a secret scanner (gitleaks, trufflehog, GitHub secret scanning with push protection) block commits that look like keys. If a secret is ever committed, rotate it — deleting the commit does not delete clones, forks or caches.

items.title: Supply-chain security
items.text:
BoxOffice's order image contains a few hundred libraries written by strangers, built by a CI system, stored in a registry, and pulled by the cluster. Each step is an attack path: a malicious or compromised dependency (the 2024 xz-utils backdoor), a vulnerable one (Log4Shell, 2021), a compromised build system (SolarWinds, 2020), typosquatting (spring-boot-strater) and dependency confusion (a public package with the name of your internal one). Supply-chain security answers three questions: what is inside?, is it vulnerable?, did it come from our pipeline, unmodified?

flowchart LR
    src["Source<br/>(reviewed PR)"] --> build["CI build<br/>(isolated runner)"]
    build --> sbom["SBOM<br/>(syft → CycloneDX)"]
    build --> scan["Scan<br/>(trivy / grype)"]
    scan -->|"no critical CVEs"| sign["Sign + provenance<br/>(cosign keyless, SLSA)"]
    sbom --> sign
    sign --> reg[("Registry<br/>image@sha256 + attestations")]
    reg --> adm{"Admission policy<br/>(Kyverno)"}
    adm -->|"signature valid"| run["Pod runs"]
    adm -->|"unsigned / wrong signer"| deny["Rejected"]

items.title: What is inside: the SBOM
items.text: An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) is the ingredient list of an artifact: every package, version and license, in a standard format — CycloneDX (OWASP) or SPDX (Linux Foundation, ISO/IEC 5962)5. When the next Log4Shell is announced, the question "which of our images contain this version?" becomes a query instead of a week of panic.

items.title: Is it vulnerable: scanning
items.text: Scanners (Trivy, Grype, Dependabot/Renovate for upgrades) match the SBOM against vulnerability databases (CVE identifiers, GitHub advisories). Gate the pipeline on a policy — e.g. "no critical vulnerability with a fix available" — not on zero findings, which never happens.

items.title: Did it come from us: signing and provenance
items.text:
Sigstore cosign signs container images. In keyless mode, the CI job proves its identity with its OIDC token, a short-lived certificate is issued by Sigstore's CA (Fulcio), and the signature is recorded in a public transparency log (Rekor) — no long-lived signing key to protect6. SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) defines levels of build integrity; its provenance attestation records which source, workflow and builder produced the artifact7.

SLSA Build level Requirement Protects against L1 provenance exists, describing how the artifact was built "nobody knows how this binary was produced" L2 provenance is signed by a hosted build platform tampering after the build L3 hardened build platform: isolated runs, signing keys not accessible to the build steps a compromised build step forging provenance

The BoxOffice release job, trimmed to the security steps (tool installation omitted):

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write
  id-token: write                      # keyless signing uses the job's OIDC identity
jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          push: true
          tags: registry.example.com/boxoffice/order:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: SBOM
        run: syft registry.example.com/boxoffice/order@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }} -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.cdx.json
      - name: Scan (fail on fixable critical CVEs)
        run: trivy image --severity CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 registry.example.com/boxoffice/order@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
      - name: Sign and attest
        run: |
          IMAGE=registry.example.com/boxoffice/order@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          cosign sign --yes "$IMAGE"
          cosign attest --yes --type cyclonedx --predicate sbom.cdx.json "$IMAGE"

The last link is verification at deploy time. An admission controller (Kyverno, Sigstore policy-controller, OPA Gatekeeper) rejects any pod whose image was not signed by our release workflow:

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: verify-boxoffice-images
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: signed-by-release-workflow
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
              namespaces: ["boxoffice"]
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences: ["registry.example.com/boxoffice/*"]
          mutateDigest: true             # pin the tag to the verified digest
          attestors:
            - entries:
                - keyless:
                    issuer: "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
                    subject: "https://github.com/repo-classes/pma271/.github/workflows/release.yaml@refs/heads/main"

Other habits that close common gaps: pin by digest (image@sha256:…, actions by commit SHA), use minimal or distroless base images, run containers as non-root with a read-only filesystem, use a private package proxy with scoped names to prevent dependency confusion, and follow the NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) as the checklist for the process8.

Try it. Open the ai-assistant scenario. The assistant calls tools (catalog, order) on the user's behalf: list every identity in the path (user, assistant, tool registry, services) and what each one should be allowed to do. Where would you put the PEP for a tool call? Which secrets does the LLM gateway hold? (The AI systems class goes deeper into the safety mesh.)

items.title: A defense checklist for BoxOffice
items.text:
Area Control Done when… Network isolated data subnets, per-AZ NAT, egress default-deny search cannot open a TCP connection to the DB or the Internet Workload identity mesh mTLS STRICT + authorization policies curl payment/charges from search returns 403 User identity OIDC, PKCE, 15-minute access tokens, rotating refresh tokens no password ever touches the app or our services Authorization ownership checks; admin API separated test "user A reads user B's order" fails Secrets secrets manager + ESO, per-service IAM, dual-key rotation PSP_API_KEY readable only by payment; rotation runbook tested Data KMS encryption at rest, TLS in transit backups and snapshots are encrypted Supply chain SBOM, scan gate, keyless signing, admission verification an unsigned image cannot start in boxoffice Detection audit logs, denied-request alerts a denied call from search pages someone

In the interview

"Zero Trust" is a buzzword unless you make it concrete. Say three things: every call carries an identity (tokens for users, mTLS for services), every resource checks a policy (least privilege, default deny, including egress), and credentials are short-lived (workload identity, dynamic secrets, no static keys in CI). If the design has a payment provider, add: "the API key lives in a secrets manager, only the payment service can read it, and we rotate with two active keys." For supply chain, one line is enough: "CI produces an SBOM, scans, and signs images; the cluster only runs signed images."

Common pitfalls

  • "It's internal, so it's safe" — the definition of the perimeter model.
  • One shared credential for all services — when it leaks, you cannot tell who used it, and rotation breaks everyone at once.
  • Secrets in Git, images, ConfigMaps or CI logs — and "deleting the commit" instead of rotating.
  • Static cloud keys in CI — use the CI's OIDC token and short-lived roles.
  • Signing without verifying — a signature nobody checks at deploy time protects nothing.
  • Scanning without a policy — 400 findings and no gate means nothing changes.

    PER["perimeter model:<br/>inside = trusted"] -->|"replaced by"| ZT["Zero Trust:<br/>never trust, always verify"]
    ZT --> PEP["PEP: gateway for users,<br/>mesh proxy for workloads"]
    PEP --> MESH["mTLS + authorization policy<br/>→ Service mesh"]

Palette components: apigw and mesh (the enforcement points) · payment (the key only payment may read) · logs · alerting (audit and denied-call alerts) · llmgw · toolreg (identities in an agent's tool calls). Scenarios: ai-assistant, payment-system. Continues in: Service mesh, Identity, Cloud-native — delivery, Observability — incident response, AI systems — safety & evals, Hands-on 13 — security.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Zero Trust: no trusted network; every request is authenticated, authorized and encrypted at a PEP using a PDP's decision. It turns a compromised pod into a dead end.
  • Workload identity (SPIFFE/mTLS, cloud roles for service accounts, CI OIDC) replaces static keys with short-lived, verifiable credentials.
  • Secrets belong in a secrets manager or Vault, scoped per service, audited, rotated (dual keys) — ideally dynamic; Kubernetes Secrets are base64, not encryption.
  • Envelope encryption with a KMS protects data at rest; secret scanning keeps keys out of Git.
  • Supply chain: SBOM (what is inside), scanning (is it vulnerable), signing + provenance + admission verification (did it come from us, unmodified).

items.title: Index
items.text:
Saturday, 09:59. A stadium show goes on sale at 10:00 on BoxOffice: 2 million fans for 60 thousand seats. At 10:04 the support channel fills with "checkout spins forever". The team opens the dashboards: every pod is green, CPU sits at 45%, the error rate is 0.3%, the health checks pass. And yet the median fan waits nine seconds to pay. Is it the gateway? The seat holds in inventory? The external payment provider? The database? Four teams join a call and each one shows a dashboard proving that their service is fine.

This is the moment observability exists for. The system is not down — it is slow in a way nobody predicted, and the only way out is to ask new questions of the running system and get answers in minutes, not days. This class is about designing a system so that those questions can be answered: which signals to emit, how to carry context across services, when to wake a human, and how to run the incident once someone is awake.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Distinguish monitoring from observability and map the five observability components of the palette (metrics, logs, tracing, alerting, health checks) to the questions they answer.
  • Instrument a service with the right signal for each question, applying RED, USE and the golden signals, and estimate the cost and cardinality of the telemetry it produces.
  • Explain how OpenTelemetry propagates trace context across HTTP and Kafka, and configure a Collector pipeline with sampling.
  • Design SLO-based alerts with multiwindow, multi-burn-rate rules and route them to the right people.
  • Configure liveness, readiness and startup probes without causing cascading restarts.
  • Run an incident with clear roles and write a blameless postmortem with actionable follow-ups.

items.text:
1. This overview — monitoring vs observability, the observability palette, the investigation loop, health checks, and what telemetry costs.
  2. Signals — metrics, logs, traces and profiles; RED, USE and golden signals; cardinality; dashboards.
  3. OpenTelemetry — the vendor-neutral standard: context propagation, instrumentation, the Collector, sampling and backends.
  4. Alerting — symptom-based alerts, SLO burn rate, multiwindow rules, routing and runbooks.
  5. Incident Response — on-call, severities, incident roles, mitigation first, postmortems.
  6. Quiz — check your understanding.
