items.title: Monitoring vs observability
items.text:
The two words are often used as synonyms, but they describe different capabilities.

Monitoring watches a set of pre-defined indicators and tells you when one crosses a threshold: "error rate above 1%", "disk above 90%". It answers questions you knew to ask when you built the dashboard — the known unknowns.

Observability is a property of the system: how well you can infer its internal state from its external outputs1. The term comes from control theory (Kalman, 1960); in software it means that, without shipping new code, you can ask a question you never thought of — "why are only checkouts with more than four tickets, paid with one card brand, slow since 10:02?" — and answer it from the telemetry the system already emits2. Those are the unknown unknowns, and distributed systems are full of them.

Monitoring Observability Question type known in advance ("is X above Y?") discovered during the investigation ("what do the slow requests have in common?") Typical output dashboard, threshold alert ad-hoc query, trace, high-dimensional breakdown Data needed aggregated metrics metrics plus rich events: logs, traces, profiles with many attributes Works well for failures you have seen before novel failures, emergent behaviour of many services Failure mode green dashboards while users suffer high cost if every detail is kept forever

Monitoring is not obsolete — it is a subset. You still need dashboards and alerts on known symptoms; observability is what lets you go from "the alert fired" to "this is the cause" when the cause is new.

Think first: why were the BoxOffice dashboards green?

The dashboards watched causes chosen in advance — CPU, memory, pod status, the error rate — averaged over every endpoint. The checkout problem was a latency problem on one route, concentrated in the tail (p99), caused by a dependency outside BoxOffice. An average over all routes hides it twice: other routes dilute the checkout route, and the median request hides the slow ones. The fix is not "more dashboards": it is measuring what users feel per journey (latency percentiles of POST /checkout) and having traces to see where inside the request the time went.

items.title: The observability palette
items.text:
In the System Design Playground, the OBSERVABILITY category has five components. Each one answers a different question, and each one is consumed by someone different — a human investigating, a human being woken up, or a machine making a routing decision.

Component Question it answers Consumer Relative cost Details Metrics Is something wrong? How much, since when, trending where? dashboards, alert rules low (aggregated numbers) Signals Logs What exactly happened in this event? humans investigating, audits high (one record per event) Signals Tracing Where in the request path did the time or the error go? humans investigating medium–high (sampled) Signals, OpenTelemetry Alerting Does a human need to act now? on-call engineer low Alerting Health Check Should this instance receive traffic, or be restarted? load balancer, Kubernetes very low below

All of them describe the same events from different angles. A single slow POST /checkout at 10:04 produces:

  • a sample in the latency histogram of order (metric) — cheap, aggregated, no idea which checkout;
  • a structured log line {"level":"WARN","msg":"payment call slow","trace_id":"4bf9…","duration_ms":8120} — precise, expensive at volume;
  • a trace with spans for gateway → order → inventory → payment, the payment span taking 8.1 s — shows where;
  • possibly a profile sample showing threads parked in the HTTP client — shows which code;
  • and, if enough checkouts are slow for long enough, an alert that pages the on-call engineer.

The glue between them is context: the same trace_id in the log line, in the trace and attached to the metric sample (an exemplar). Without shared context, you have three disconnected tools; with it, you have one investigation.

items.title: The investigation loop
items.text:
Observability pays off as a repeatable loop that moves from cheap, aggregated signals to expensive, detailed ones — narrowing the search at each step. Play the diagram:

flowchart LR
    A["Alert<br/>checkout SLO burning 14×"] --> D["RED dashboard<br/>which service? which route?"]
    D --> E["Exemplar<br/>one slow request's trace_id"]
    E --> T["Trace<br/>which span is slow?"]
    T --> L["Logs of that span<br/>why? (error, retry, timeout)"]
    L --> P["Profile<br/>which code path?"]
    P --> M["Mitigate<br/>rollback, breaker, failover"]
    M --> PM["Postmortem<br/>prevent the class of failure"]
  1. Detect with an SLO-based alert on a symptom users feel (Alerting).
  2. Localize with metrics: the RED dashboard shows POST /checkout p99 went from 400 ms to 9 s; other routes are normal.
  3. Pick an example: a latency panel with exemplars links a slow sample to its trace_id.
  4. Find the hop: the trace waterfall shows 8 of the 9 seconds inside the payment span, in the call to the external provider.
  5. Explain: the logs of that span show connection pool exhausted, waited 7.9 s — the provider is slow, and payment has a pool of 20 connections.
  6. Mitigate first, understand later (Incident Response): open the circuit breaker, put checkouts in a queue, or switch providers.
  7. Learn: the postmortem asks why a slow provider could hold the whole checkout hostage — and adds a timeout, a bulkhead, and an alert on provider latency.

BoxOffice — the critical path of a checkout

The flash-sale checkout crosses five BoxOffice services and one external dependency: gateway → order → inventory (confirm the seat hold, PostgreSQL) → payment (adapter) → external payment provider, and then order publishes OrderConfirmed to Kafka, consumed by notification (e-mail/push). Every arrow is a place where time can disappear, and the external provider is the one place where BoxOffice cannot add instrumentation — only measure the calls it makes.

items.title: See it in the simulator
items.text:
Try it. Press Run with the load profile and watch the metrics panel: requests per second, error rate and p99 per component. Then set chaos to medium and look at which signal reacts first — the health checks, the latency percentiles or the error rate. Notice that a slow component can keep passing a shallow health check while p99 explodes.

The full simulator is in the System Design Playground.

items.title: Health checks
items.text:
A health check is the simplest signal and the only one consumed by machines: a load balancer, an orchestrator or a service discovery system calls an endpoint and decides whether an instance should receive traffic or be restarted. Because machines act on it automatically and at scale, a badly designed health check is one of the classic causes of total outages.

Kubernetes distinguishes three probes3, and the distinction is the whole point:

Probe Question On failure Should check Startup Has the process finished starting? keep waiting (other probes are paused); kill after the budget the app is initialized (JVM warm-up, migrations done) Liveness Is the process stuck beyond repair? restart the container only the process itself: event loop / thread pool responds Readiness Can this instance serve requests right now? remove from the load balancer (no restart) can do useful work: warmed caches, required local resources 
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Starting : container created
    Starting --> Ready : startup ok, readiness ok
    Starting --> Restarting : startup budget exceeded
    Ready --> NotReady : readiness fails (overloaded, draining)
    NotReady --> Ready : readiness ok again
    Ready --> Restarting : liveness fails (deadlock)
    NotReady --> Restarting : liveness fails
    Restarting --> Starting : new container

With Spring Boot Actuator, the probes are separate health groups, exposed at /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness4:

# application.yaml (order service)
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState
        liveness:
          include: livenessState

# Deployment (excerpt) — the order container
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 24        # up to 2 minutes to start
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3         # 30 s of failures before a restart
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 2

items.title: Shallow vs deep checks
items.text:
A shallow check answers "is my process alive?". A deep check also calls the dependencies — the database, Redis, the payment provider. Deep checks look more honest, and that is exactly the trap.

The deep-check cascade

Suppose the readiness probe of order includes the PostgreSQL connection. The database has a 20-second failover. Every order pod fails readiness at the same moment, Kubernetes removes all of them from the Service, and the gateway now returns 503 for every route — including the ones that only read from Redis. Worse, if the liveness probe includes the database, Kubernetes restarts every pod at once; they all start cold, hammer the database together as it comes back, and the outage extends itself.

Rules of thumb: liveness never checks dependencies; readiness checks only what this instance needs locally and what a different instance would not fix; dependency health belongs in metrics and alerts, and degraded dependencies are handled with timeouts, circuit breakers and fallbacks (Resilience patterns).

Shallow (process only) Deep (process + dependencies) Detects crashed or deadlocked process broken dependency too Risk instance "healthy" but useless if a dependency is down correlated failure: all instances fail together → total outage, restart storms Cost trivial each probe calls the dependency (N pods × every 5 s) Use for liveness, load-balancer checks readiness only for dependencies one instance owns; otherwise a separate status endpoint for humans

Load balancers at the edge use the same idea (see Load balancing): they remove a backend after N failed checks and add it back after M successes — the hysteresis avoids flapping.

items.title: What telemetry costs
items.text:
Observability is not free, and in an interview — or in the cloud bill — you must reason about its volume like any other workload. A back-of-the-envelope estimate for BoxOffice on a normal day, with illustrative assumptions:

Assumption Value Average traffic 500 requests/s Spans per request (gateway, order, inventory, DB, payment, Kafka…) 8 Average span size (with attributes) 500 bytes Log lines per request (all services) 5, of 300 bytes each \[ \text{traces} = 500 \times 8 \times 500\ \text{B} = 2\ \text{MB/s} \approx 173\ \text{GB/day} \qquad \text{logs} = 500 \times 5 \times 300\ \text{B} = 0.75\ \text{MB/s} \approx 65\ \text{GB/day} \]

At 100% trace sampling that is over 5 TB of traces a month — before the flash sale multiplies the traffic by 50. Hence the three cost levers you will see in this class:

  • Sampling traces (keep the interesting ones — errors and slow requests — and a small share of the rest), see OpenTelemetry.
  • Bounded cardinality for metrics (no user IDs in labels), see Signals.
  • Levels, sampling and retention tiers for logs (DEBUG off in production, 7–30 days hot, then cheap object storage).

items.title: The observability concept map
items.text:
The five observability components describe the same requests from different angles, and shared context (exemplars, trace_id) turns them into one investigation. The map links each palette component (green) to the concepts it relies on (blue) and to the classes that continue them:

flowchart LR

    svc --> tracing["tracing"]:::comp
    svc --> logs["logs"]:::comp
    metrics -->|"exemplar"| tracing
    tracing -->|"trace_id"| logs
    metrics --> alerting["alerting"]:::comp
    hc["healthcheck"]:::comp -->|"probes"| svc
    metrics -.- c1["RED, USE, golden signals,<br/>histograms, cardinality"]:::tech
    logs -.- c2["structured logs,<br/>levels, redaction"]:::tech
    tracing -.- c3["traceparent, Collector,<br/>tail sampling"]:::tech
    alerting -.- c4["SLO burn rate, multiwindow,<br/>routing, runbooks"]:::tech
    hc -.- c5["liveness, readiness, startup,<br/>shallow vs deep"]:::tech
    c4 --> c6["incident roles, mitigate first,<br/>postmortems"]:::tech
    c4 -.- d1["SLI, SLO, error budget<br/>(class 9)"]
    c5 -.- d2["Kubernetes probes, LB checks<br/>(classes 4 and 12)"]
    classDef comp fill:#1e9e5a22,stroke:#1e9e5a
    classDef tech fill:#2f6fed22,stroke:#2f6fed
Palette component Question it answers Concepts Taught in Scenarios metrics Is something wrong? How much, since when? counters, gauges, histograms, RED, USE, golden signals, cardinality, PromQL Signals — metrics, cardinality observability-stack, event-fanout (consumer lag) logs What exactly happened in this event? structured logs, levels, trace_id / span_id, Loki vs Elasticsearch, retention tiers Signals — logs observability-stack tracing Where did the time or the error go? spans, critical path, traceparent, Collector, head vs tail sampling, exemplars Signals — traces, OpenTelemetry observability-stack, cascading-failure (the slow provider span) alerting Does a human need to act now? symptoms vs causes, burn rate, multiwindow rules, routing, dead man's switch, runbooks Alerting, Incident Response observability-stack, flash-sale healthcheck Should this instance get traffic, or be restarted? startup, liveness, readiness, shallow vs deep checks, hysteresis this overview scale-out, observability-stack

In the interview

Observability is the standard answer to "how would you know it works?" and belongs in the wrap-up of every design. Say it concretely, in one breath: "I'd define an SLO on checkout — 99.9% of checkouts succeed in under 2 s over 28 days — and alert on its burn rate; RED dashboards per service; OpenTelemetry traces with tail sampling that keeps every error and slow trace; structured logs with the trace ID; and readiness probes that do not depend on the database." Then mention one thing you would watch specific to the problem: consumer lag for a queue, hit ratio for a cache, replication lag for replicas.

Common pitfalls

  • Dashboards of causes, alerts on causes: CPU, memory and pod counts are green while users suffer. Measure what users feel.
  • Averages: an average latency hides the tail; use percentiles or "fraction of requests faster than X".
  • No shared context: logs without trace_id and metrics without exemplars force you to correlate by timestamp — by hand, at 3 a.m.
  • Deep liveness probes: a dependency outage becomes a restart storm.
  • Instrumenting after the incident: telemetry must be designed in, like any other requirement; you cannot query data you did not emit.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Monitoring answers known questions; observability lets you investigate new ones from the telemetry the system already emits.
  • The five palette components answer different questions: metrics (is something wrong?), logs (what happened?), traces (where?), alerting (must a human act now?), health checks (should this instance get traffic?).
  • The investigation loop goes from cheap aggregates to expensive detail: alert → dashboard → exemplar → trace → logs → profile → mitigate → postmortem. Shared context (trace_id) makes it one investigation.
  • Liveness never checks dependencies; deep checks turn a dependency blip into a total outage or a restart storm.
  • Telemetry is a workload: estimate its volume and control it with sampling, bounded cardinality and retention tiers.

  1. KALMAN, R. E. On the general theory of control systems. Proceedings of the First IFAC Congress, 1960. The term was brought to software operations by Twitter's and Honeycomb's engineers in the 2010s. ↩

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Observability and health checks
items.text:
Q1. During the BoxOffice on-sale, every pod is green, CPU is at 45% and the overall error rate is 0.3%, but fans wait nine seconds to pay. Which statement best explains why the dashboards did not show the problem?

  • A. The metrics backend was sampling too aggressively
  • B. The dashboards watched causes averaged over all routes; the problem was tail latency on one route, caused by an external dependency
  • C. Kubernetes health checks are not reliable under load
  • D. Error rates below 1% cannot be measured with Prometheus
Answer

B — Causes, averaged over everything, hide a tail-latency symptom on one journey.

CPU and pod status are causes, chosen in advance. The fans' experience was a latency symptom on POST /checkout, concentrated in the p99, caused by the payment provider. Averaging over all routes dilutes the checkout route, and the median hides the tail. Measure what users feel — per-journey latency percentiles and SLIs — and use traces to find where the time went.

Q2. The readiness probe of order checks the PostgreSQL connection. The database performs a 20-second failover. What happens?

  • A. Nothing: readiness failures only affect new pods
  • B. Kubernetes restarts every order pod, which is the desired self-healing behaviour
  • C. Every order pod becomes unready at the same time and is removed from the Service, so even routes that do not need the database return errors
  • D. The load balancer keeps sending traffic, because readiness is only checked at startup
Answer

C — A correlated readiness failure removes every instance at once.

A dependency shared by all instances makes all of them fail the probe together: the Service has no endpoints and every route fails, including those served from Redis. (Had the liveness probe checked the database, Kubernetes would also restart every pod — a restart storm.) Liveness should never check dependencies; readiness should check only what a different instance would fix; dependency health belongs in metrics, alerts, timeouts and circuit breakers.

Q3. Which probe should fail if a JVM is deadlocked and will never recover by itself?

  • A. Startup
  • B. Liveness
  • C. Readiness
  • D. None — deadlocks must be handled by an alert to a human
Answer

B — Liveness.

Liveness answers "is the process stuck beyond repair?" and its failure restarts the container. Readiness only removes the instance from the load balancer (useful when it is temporarily unable to serve, e.g. overloaded or draining). Startup protects slow-starting applications by pausing the other probes until initialization finishes.

items.title: Signals
items.text:
Q4. A team adds the label customer_id (about 1 million values) to the checkout latency histogram, which already has 204,000 series. What is the most likely consequence?

  • A. Queries become slightly slower but otherwise nothing changes
  • B. The number of series is multiplied by up to a million, and the metrics backend runs out of memory or the bill explodes
  • C. Prometheus automatically drops the label because it is high-cardinality
  • D. Nothing, because histograms store only buckets, not labels
Answer

B — Cardinality multiplies.

Every distinct combination of label values is a separate series; adding an unbounded label multiplies the series count by its number of values. Per-customer questions belong in traces and logs, where customer_id is an attribute queried on demand, not a pre-aggregated metric dimension.

Q5. Four order pods report their own p99 latency: 180 ms, 180 ms, 180 ms and 1,260 ms (the slow pod handles 10% of the traffic). What is the correct way to obtain the fleet p99?

  • A. Average the four values: 450 ms
  • B. Take the maximum: 1,260 ms
  • C. Sum the histogram buckets of all pods (sum by (le)) and compute the percentile from the total
  • D. Take the median of the four values: 180 ms
Answer

C — Aggregate buckets first, then compute the percentile.

Percentiles do not compose: neither the average nor the maximum of per-pod p99s is the fleet p99. Histogram buckets are counters, so they can be summed across pods; histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(..._bucket[5m]))) estimates the true percentile. In the simulation of the Signals page, the true fleet p99 is about 750 ms, while the average of the p99s is about 450 ms.

Q6. Which pairing of method and target is correct?

  • A. RED for the PostgreSQL connection pool; USE for the POST /checkout endpoint
  • B. RED for the POST /checkout endpoint; USE for the PostgreSQL connection pool
  • C. RED and USE are synonyms of the four golden signals
  • D. USE applies only to CPU and memory
Answer

B — RED for request-driven services, USE for resources.

RED (rate, errors, duration) describes what callers of a service experience. USE (utilization, saturation, errors) describes a resource — CPU, disks, but also pools and queues. For the connection pool, saturation (pending acquisitions, wait time) is often the earliest warning that checkout latency is about to rise.

Q7. In a checkout trace, the payment span takes 8.95 s, of which a child span pool.acquire takes 7.9 s and the HTTP call to the provider takes 1.0 s. What is the main conclusion?

  • A. The provider is responsible for the 9 seconds
  • B. Most of the time is spent waiting for a connection inside BoxOffice: the pool is saturated because each slow call holds a connection longer
  • C. The trace is broken, because child spans cannot be longer than the provider call
  • D. The database is the bottleneck
Answer

B — Queueing inside the service dominates the critical path.

The provider got slower (1 s), so by Little's law each call holds a connection longer, the pool of 20 saturates, and new calls wait 7.9 s in line. The fix is a bounded wait and a short timeout on the provider call (plus a bulkhead), not only a complaint to the provider. Without a span for the wait, the provider would be blamed for all nine seconds.

items.title: OpenTelemetry
items.text:
Q8. A request passes through gateway → order → inventory. What happens to the W3C traceparent header at each hop?

  • A. Each service generates a new trace-id
  • B. The trace-id and flags are kept; the parent-id is replaced with the ID of the caller's current span
  • C. The header is forwarded unchanged so the backend can identify the root span
  • D. The callee returns the header in the response, and the caller merges it
Answer

B — Same trace-id, new parent-id at every hop.

traceparent: 00-<trace-id>-<parent-id>-<flags>. Keeping the trace-id groups all spans of the request; replacing the parent-id lets the backend rebuild the tree. No service needs to know the whole trace.

Q9. BoxOffice handles 2,000 requests/s and 1% of them fail. Which sampling setup keeps every error trace while storing fewer than 10% of all traces?

  • A. Head sampling at 10% in every service
  • B. Rate limiting at 100 traces per second
  • C. 100% head sampling in the services and a tail-sampling policy in the Collector: all errors, all slow traces and 5% of the rest
  • D. Head sampling at 1% plus tail sampling of errors in the Collector
Answer

C — Tail sampling with full head sampling.

Head sampling decides before knowing the outcome, so it keeps errors at the same ratio as everything else (A and D lose 90% or 99% of error traces; D's tail sampler only sees the 1% that survived the head). Tail sampling decides after the trace completes; with 1% errors, 2% slow and 5% of the rest, about 7.8% of traces are stored — and 100% of the errors. Metrics should be computed from all traffic before sampling.

Q10. A team runs three replicas of a gateway Collector behind a round-robin load balancer, each with the tail-sampling processor. What goes wrong?

  • A. Nothing; tail sampling is stateless
  • B. Spans of the same trace land on different replicas, so each replica decides on fragments of the trace
  • C. The Collectors cannot receive OTLP over gRPC behind a load balancer
  • D. Tail sampling forces every replica to keep 100% of the traces
Answer

B — Tail sampling needs the whole trace in one place.

The decision ("does this trace contain an error?") requires every span of the trace. Use a first tier that routes by trace ID (the loadbalancing exporter) to a second tier that samples, so all spans of a trace reach the same instance.

items.title: Alerting
items.text:
Q11. The checkout SLO is 99.9% over a rolling 28-day window. The observed error ratio over the last hour is 1.44%. What is the burn rate, and how much of the budget did that hour consume?

  • A. Burn rate 1.44; 1.44% of the budget
  • B. Burn rate 14.4; about 2% of the budget
  • C. Burn rate 144; about 20% of the budget
  • D. Burn rate 14.4; about 14.4% of the budget
Answer

B — 14.4×, about 2%.

Burn rate = 1.44% ÷ 0.1% = 14.4. Budget consumed = burn rate × duration ÷ window = 14.4 × 1 h ÷ 672 h ≈ 2.1%, about 2%. This is the classic fast-burn paging threshold: at this pace the whole 28-day budget is gone in about 2 days (28 ÷ 14.4 ≈ 1.9).

Q12. Why does the recommended SLO alert combine a long window (1 h) with a short window (5 min) at the same burn rate?

  • A. The short window catches slow burns that the long window misses
  • B. The long window proves the burn is significant; the short window proves it is still happening, so the alert stops soon after the problem is fixed
  • C. Prometheus cannot evaluate windows longer than one hour on its own
  • D. The two windows are averaged to reduce noise
Answer

B — Significance from the long window, fast reset from the short one.

A 1-hour average stays high for up to an hour after a short outage ends, so a long-window-only alert keeps firing (slow reset). Requiring the 5-minute window too means the alert clears as soon as the errors stop. Slow burns are caught by other rules (6× over 6 h, 1× over 3 days), not by the short window.

Q13. Which of these should page the on-call engineer at 3 a.m.?

  • A. CPU of the PostgreSQL primary above 90% while all SLIs are within target
  • B. One of 30 catalog pods restarted and is healthy again
  • C. The checkout SLO burning at 20× confirmed by the 1-hour and 5-minute windows
  • D. A Kafka broker disk projected to be full in 4 days
Answer

C — Urgent, actionable and user-visible.

A and B are causes without user impact (dashboard, maybe a capacity review). D is actionable but not urgent: a ticket for working hours. A page must be urgent, actionable and about something users feel — the SLO burning fast.

items.title: Incident response
items.text:
Q14. Twelve minutes into a SEV1, the operations lead has a hypothesis but no proof; switching to the secondary payment provider is documented and tested. What should the incident commander decide?

  • A. Keep investigating until the root cause is confirmed, to avoid an unnecessary change
  • B. Switch to the secondary provider now to mitigate impact; investigate the root cause afterwards
  • C. Ask every engineer in the channel to test their own hypothesis in production in parallel
  • D. Wait for the provider's status page before acting
Answer

B — Mitigate first.

Users feel the time to mitigation. A generic, rehearsed mitigation (failover, rollback, flag) that works regardless of the exact cause should be taken as soon as it is safe. Parallel uncoordinated changes (C) make the incident worse and the timeline unreadable; understanding comes later, in the postmortem.

Q15. Which statement best describes a blameless postmortem?

  • A. It does not record who did what, so the timeline is anonymous and vague
  • B. It assumes people acted reasonably with what they knew, and asks how the system made the failure possible, producing owned and dated action items
  • C. It is written only when nobody made a mistake
  • D. It identifies the single root cause using five whys and closes the incident
Answer

B — System-focused, honest, and actionable.

Blameless does not mean vague: the timeline is precise, including who did what. The point is that people are not punished for honest accounts, so the organisation learns how failures really happen. Complex incidents have several contributing factors; a single "five whys" chain often stops at the one factor you cannot fix (here, the external provider).

items.title: Index
items.text: An alert is a request for a human's attention, often at 3 a.m. That makes it the most expensive signal in the system: it costs sleep, focus and, over time, trust. Two failure modes kill alerting. Too many alerts — "CPU above 80%" on every pod, every blip of every dependency — and the on-call engineer learns to ignore the pager; the real incident drowns in the noise. Too few, or the wrong ones — and the first person to notice the broken checkout is a fan on social media. This page is about alerts that fire when, and only when, users are being hurt enough that someone must act.

items.title: What deserves a page
items.text:
A good page is urgent, actionable, and about a user-visible problem1. If any of the three is missing, it should be something else:

Situation Urgent? Actionable? Users affected? Destination Checkout failing for 5% of fans during an on-sale yes yes yes page the on-call Error budget burning slowly: will run out in 10 days no yes a little ticket for the team, this week Disk of the Kafka broker will be full in 4 days at this rate no yes not yet ticket One of 30 catalog pods restarted and recovered no no no dashboard / log only CPU at 85% while all SLIs are fine no no no nothing — or a capacity review The alerting pipeline itself is broken yes yes indirectly page (via a dead man's switch, below)

items.title: Symptoms, not causes
items.text:
Alert on symptoms — what users experience: errors, latency, freshness, correctness. Use causes — CPU, memory, a pod restart, a full queue — for dashboards and diagnosis, not for pages.

Symptom-based alert Cause-based alert Example "checkout success ratio below SLO" "PostgreSQL CPU > 90%" Fires when users are fine? no often (high CPU, happy users) Misses real problems? rarely — whatever the cause, users feel it often — the failure you did not predict has no alert Number of rules few, per user journey many, per component and resource Tells you where to look? no — that is what dashboards and traces are for yes, but only for known failure modes

The exception is a leading indicator that will certainly become a symptom and gives time to act — a disk filling up, a certificate expiring in 7 days. Those are tickets, not pages, unless the deadline is hours away.

items.title: From the SLO to the alert
items.text:
The SLO already says how much failure is acceptable: with 99.9% of checkouts succeeding over a rolling 28-day window (the window used throughout Reliability), the error budget is 0.1% of checkouts. The question an alert must answer is therefore not "are there errors?" — there always are — but "are we spending the budget fast enough to be in trouble?".

The natural measure is the burn rate:

\[ \text{burn rate} = \frac{\text{error ratio observed over a window}}{1 - \text{SLO}} \]

A burn rate of 1 spends exactly the whole budget in the whole window; a burn rate of 14.4 spends it 14.4 times faster. If a burn rate \(b\) is sustained for a time \(t\), the fraction of the budget consumed is

\[ \text{budget consumed} = \frac{b \cdot t}{\text{SLO window}} \] Burn rate Error ratio (SLO 99.9%) Budget exhausted in Budget spent in 1 h in 6 h 1× 0.10% 28.0 days 0.1% 0.9% 2× 0.20% 14.0 days 0.3% 1.8% 3× 0.30% 9.3 days 0.4% 2.7% 6× 0.60% 4.7 days 0.9% 5.4% 14.4× 1.44% 46.7 h 2.1% 12.9% 36× 3.60% 18.7 h 5.4% 32.1% 1000× 100.00% 40 min 100.0% 100.0%

A burn rate of 1000× is a total outage (100% errors against a 0.1% budget): the whole 28-day budget is gone in about 40 minutes. That is why fast alerts must fire within minutes — and why slow burns can wait for office hours.

items.title: Six ways to write the alert
items.text:
The SRE Workbook2 compares six progressively better designs for an SLO alert. Their quality is measured by four properties: precision (fraction of alerts that were real problems), recall (fraction of real problems that alerted), detection time and reset time (how long the alert keeps firing after the problem ends).

# Rule Precision Recall Detection Reset Problem 1 error ratio > 0.1% over 10 min low high fast fast pages for blips that barely touch the budget 2 error ratio > 0.1% over 36 h high high very slow very slow a total outage takes ~2 min to alert, and the alert lasts 36 h 3 rule 1 + for: 1h medium low slow fast a 100% outage still waits an hour 4 burn rate 14.4× over 1 h high medium good slow slow burns (3×) never alert; reset takes up to an hour 5 several burn rates (14.4× / 6× / 1×) high high good slow complex; still slow to reset 6 multiwindow, multi-burn-rate high high good fast the most rules — generate them with a tool

items.title: Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate
items.text:
The recommended design combines, for each severity, a long window that proves the burn is significant and a short window (1/12 of the long one) that proves it is still happening — so the alert stops quickly once the problem is fixed:

Severity Long window Short window Burn rate Budget spent when it fires page 1 h 5 min 14.4× 2% page 6 h 30 min 6× 5% ticket 3 days 6 h 1× 10%

The plot shows the detection time for a sudden failure of a given error ratio, for the two paging rules. Note the trade-off it encodes: the worse the incident, the faster the alert — and for a given rule, the budget spent at the moment it fires is always the same (2% and 5%).

2026-10-23T08:15:48.779338 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ 1 0 0 1 0 1 1 0 2 error ratio of the incident (%) 1 0 0 1 0 1 1 0 2 time to fire (minutes) SLO 99.9% — how fast the burn-rate alerts fire page: 14.4× over 1 h (+5 min) page: 6× over 6 h (+30 min)

A total outage (100% errors) fires the fast rule in under a minute; an incident failing 2% of checkouts takes about 43 minutes to fire the fast rule, and one failing 0.7% never fires it, but fires the 6-hour rule after about 5 hours. Below 0.6% — a burn rate under 6× — only the ticket rule catches it.

items.title: The rules in PromQL
items.text:
Recording rules precompute the error ratio of the checkout journey over each window; the alert rules compare them with the thresholds. (Tools such as Sloth, Pyrra or the OpenSLO specification generate these rules from a short SLO definition, which avoids copy-paste mistakes.)

# prometheus-rules.yaml — checkout availability SLO: 99.9% over 28 days
groups:
  - name: slo-checkout-recordings
    rules:
      - record: slo:checkout_errors:ratio_rate5m
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order", http_route="/checkout", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order", http_route="/checkout"}[5m]))
      - record: slo:checkout_errors:ratio_rate1h
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order", http_route="/checkout", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[1h]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order", http_route="/checkout"}[1h]))
      # ... the same expression for 30m, 6h and 3d

  - name: slo-checkout-alerts
    rules:
      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn
        expr: |
          slo:checkout_errors:ratio_rate1h > (14.4 * 0.001)
          and
          slo:checkout_errors:ratio_rate5m > (14.4 * 0.001)
        labels:
          severity: page
          team: checkout
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout is burning its 28-day error budget at more than 14.4x"
          runbook_url: "runbooks/checkout-slo.md"
      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetSlowBurn
        expr: |
          slo:checkout_errors:ratio_rate6h > (6 * 0.001)
          and
          slo:checkout_errors:ratio_rate30m > (6 * 0.001)
        labels:
          severity: page
          team: checkout
      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetTicket
        expr: |
          slo:checkout_errors:ratio_rate3d > (1 * 0.001)
          and
          slo:checkout_errors:ratio_rate6h > (1 * 0.001)
        labels:
          severity: ticket
          team: checkout

A latency SLO works the same way: the "bad events" are the requests slower than the threshold, computed from the histogram bucket that ends at the threshold:

# fraction of checkouts slower than 2 s over 1 h (the "error ratio" of a latency SLO)
1 - (
  sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="order", http_route="/checkout", le="2"}[1h]))
  /
  sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order", http_route="/checkout"}[1h]))
)

BoxOffice — the 10:00 on-sale, through the alert's eyes

At 10:02 the payment provider slows down; at 10:03 the checkout error ratio (timeouts returned as 504) reaches 4%. That is a burn rate of 40×: the fast rule's 1-hour average crosses 1.44% after about 60 × 1.44 / 4 ≈ 22 minutes of a constant 4%… far too slow for an on-sale that is over in 30 minutes. The team therefore adds a dedicated on-sale SLO with a shorter window (for example 99% of checkouts under 2 s during the on-sale hour, alerting on 5-minute and 1-minute windows) — the general rules are tuned for a 28-day budget and cannot react to an event that lasts half an hour. Different journeys, different SLOs.

items.title: Routing: from a firing rule to a person
items.text:
An alert rule only produces a firing alert. Something must decide who hears about it, how, and how often. In the Prometheus ecosystem this is Alertmanager3 (Grafana Alerting has the same concepts): it groups related alerts into one notification, deduplicates them, applies inhibitions and silences, and routes them by labels to receivers.

flowchart LR
    R["Rule evaluation<br/>Prometheus / Mimir ruler"] --> F["Firing alert<br/>severity=page, team=checkout"]
    F --> G["Alertmanager<br/>group · dedupe"]
    G --> S{"Silenced or<br/>inhibited?"}
    S -->|yes| X["Dropped<br/>(still visible in the UI)"]
    S -->|no| RT{"Route by labels"}
    RT -->|severity=page| PD["Pager<br/>on-call phone"]
    RT -->|severity=page| SL["Slack #incidents"]
    RT -->|severity=ticket| TK["Ticket queue"]
    PD --> ACK["On-call acknowledges<br/>or escalates after 5 min"]
# alertmanager.yaml (sketch)
route:
  receiver: slack-observability          # default for anything unmatched
  group_by: [alertname, team]
  group_wait: 30s                        # wait to batch related alerts into one notification
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity="page"]
      receiver: pager-checkout
      continue: true                     # also evaluate the next route
    - matchers: [severity="page"]
      receiver: slack-incidents
    - matchers: [severity="ticket"]
      receiver: ticket-queue

inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [alertname="RegionDown"]
    target_matchers: [severity=~"page|ticket"]
    equal: [region]                      # one page for the region, not fifty for its services

receivers:
  - name: pager-checkout
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/pager-checkout
  - name: slack-incidents
    slack_configs:
      - api_url_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/slack-incidents
        channel: "#incidents"
  - name: slack-observability
    slack_configs:
      - api_url_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/slack-observability
        channel: "#observability"
  - name: ticket-queue
    webhook_configs:
      - url: http://ticket-bridge:8080/alerts
Mechanism What it does BoxOffice use Grouping many alerts with the same labels → one notification 40 order pods failing → one page, not 40 Inhibition an alert suppresses others while it fires RegionDown silences the per-service alerts of that region Silence mute matching alerts for a period, with an author and a reason planned database maintenance on Tuesday 02:00–03:00 Escalation (in the paging tool) if not acknowledged in N minutes, page the secondary, then the manager primary asleep or out of signal

items.title: Who watches the watcher?
items.text:
If Prometheus or Alertmanager is down, nothing alerts — and silence looks exactly like health. Two standard protections:

  • A dead man's switch: a rule that always fires (expr: vector(1), often named Watchdog), sent to an external service that pages if the heartbeat stops arriving.
  • Absent data alerts: absent(up{job="order"}) or absent_over_time(...) fire when a metric disappears — a crashed exporter, a renamed metric, a job that stopped being scraped.

For journeys with little traffic at night, a ratio of zero requests is undefined; synthetic probes (a k6 or Blackbox Exporter check that buys a test ticket on a fake event every minute) keep the SLI meaningful at any hour.

items.title: Runbooks
items.text:
Every page must link a runbook: a short document that tells a tired engineer what the alert means and what to try first. Runbooks reduce MTTR because the first 10 minutes stop being improvisation.

# CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn

**Meaning**: checkout is failing at more than 14.4x the rate the 99.9% SLO allows;
at this pace the 28-day budget is gone in about 2 days.

**Impact**: fans cannot buy tickets. During an on-sale, declare an incident immediately (SEV1).

**First checks (5 minutes)**
1. Checkout dashboard: which status codes? which route? since when? any deploy or flag change?
2. Payment provider panel: latency and error ratio of the provider call.
3. Open an exemplar trace of a failed checkout: which span fails or waits?

**Mitigations**
- Recent deploy → roll back (`argocd app rollback order`).
- Provider slow or failing → switch to the secondary provider (flag `payment.provider=secondary`).
- Database saturated → enable the waiting room (flag `waiting-room.enabled=true`).

**Escalate to**: payments team (secondary on-call), then the incident commander rotation.

items.title: Trade-offs
items.text:
Decision Option A Option B Guidance What to alert on causes (CPU, restarts) symptoms (SLO burn) symptoms page; causes go to dashboards and tickets Thresholds static error ratio burn rate against the SLO burn rate — the threshold follows the business target Windows one window long + short window multiwindow: precise and resets quickly Sensitivity page early (more false alarms) page late (more budget lost) tune to the budget: fast burns page, slow burns ticket Notification everything to Slack page / ticket / dashboard by severity a channel everyone mutes is no alerting at all

In the interview

When the interviewer asks "how would you know if this is broken?", answer with an SLO and its burn-rate alert, not with a list of metrics: "Checkout SLO 99.9% over 28 days; page when the 1-hour burn rate exceeds 14.4× confirmed by the 5-minute window, ticket for slow burns; every alert links a runbook." Mention that you alert on symptoms and use dashboards and traces for causes, and that a dead man's switch protects the alerting pipeline itself. That is a senior-level answer in four sentences.

Common pitfalls

  • Paging on causes: CPU, memory and restarts wake people up for nothing and train them to ignore the pager.
  • for: 1h to reduce noise: it also delays the page for a total outage by an hour; use burn rates instead.
  • One SLO window for every situation: a 28-day budget cannot protect a 30-minute on-sale; give critical events their own SLO.
  • Alerts without runbooks or owners: the alert fires, nobody knows what to do, the incident lasts longer.
  • No dead man's switch: the monitoring stack dies silently, and silence looks like health.
  • Never deleting alerts: review every page after the shift — if it was not actionable, fix it or delete it.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    SLO["SLO 99.9% over 28 days<br/>→ Reliability: SLOs"] --> BUD["error budget 0.1%"]
    SLI["SLI from metrics<br/>(RED, histograms)"] --> BR["burn rate =<br/>error ratio ÷ budget"]
    BUD --> BR
    BR --> MW["multiwindow rules:<br/>14.4× and 6× page, 1× ticket"]
    MW --> AM["Alertmanager: group,<br/>inhibit, silence, route"]
    AM --> PAGE["page + runbook"]
    AM --> TK["ticket"]
    PAGE --> IR["Incident Response"]
    DMS["dead man's switch,<br/>absent(), synthetic probes"] --> AM
    MW -.-> ONS["on-sale SLO,<br/>short windows"]

Palette components: alerting · metrics (the SLI and the recording rules) · payment (the slow provider that burns the on-sale budget) · kafka (a broker disk filling up: a ticket, not a page). Scenarios: observability-stack, flash-sale (a 30-minute on-sale needs its own SLO). Continues in: Reliability — SLOs (SLI, SLO, error budget policy), Incident Response, Cloud-native — delivery (rollbacks named in the runbook), Hands-on 8 — SLO and burn-rate alert.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• A page must be urgent, actionable and user-visible; everything else is a ticket, a dashboard, or nothing.
  • Alert on symptoms derived from the SLO; causes are for diagnosis.
  • Burn rate = observed error ratio ÷ error budget; with a 28-day window, 14.4× spends about 2% of the budget in an hour (14.4 ÷ 672 h).
  • Use multiwindow, multi-burn-rate rules: 14.4× (1 h + 5 min) and 6× (6 h + 30 min) page, 1× (3 d + 6 h) opens a ticket.
  • Alertmanager groups, deduplicates, inhibits, silences and routes; a dead man's switch and absent() alerts watch the watcher.
  • Every alert has an owner and a runbook.

  1. EWASCHUK, R. My Philosophy on Alerting. Google, 2013. Its rules are summarized in BEYER, B. et al. Site Reliability Engineering — Monitoring Distributed Systems. O'Reilly, 2016. Chapter 6. ↩

  2. BEYER, B. et al. The Site Reliability Workbook — Alerting on SLOs. O'Reilly, 2018. Chapter 5. ↩

  3. PROMETHEUS. Alertmanager and Alerting rules. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text: 10:03, Saturday. The phone of the on-call engineer vibrates: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn. Two million fans are in the waiting room, the payment provider is answering in seconds, and the company's social media is already lighting up. What happens in the next thirty minutes decides whether this becomes a bad morning or a news story. Good telemetry tells you what is wrong; it does not decide who does what, who talks to the outside world, or when you stop investigating and start mitigating. That is incident response — a practice borrowed from firefighters and emergency services, adapted to software1.

items.title: What counts as an incident
items.text:
An incident is an unplanned event that degrades or threatens a service users depend on, and that needs a coordinated response. Not every alert is an incident; an incident is declared when the response needs more than one person working the normal way. Severity levels make that decision fast and consistent — nobody should debate the definition at 3 a.m.

Severity Criteria (BoxOffice) Example Response SEV1 core journey down or badly degraded for many users; data loss or security breach; any on-sale affected checkout failing for 10% of fans during an on-sale page immediately, incident commander, status page, updates every 15–30 min SEV2 significant degradation, workaround exists, or a non-core journey down search returns stale results; e-mails delayed by 1 h page the owning team, incident channel, internal updates SEV3 minor impact, few users, no deadline pressure the seat map is slow for one venue ticket, fix in working hours SEV4 no user impact yet; a near miss a certificate expiring in 7 days ticket

Declare early, downgrade freely

Declaring an incident is cheap; declaring it late is expensive. A SEV1 that turns out to be a SEV3 costs a few people twenty minutes. A SEV3 that was really a SEV1 costs an on-sale. Make "declare and downgrade later" the norm, and never punish anyone for declaring.

items.title: On-call
items.text:
On-call means a named person is responsible, for a period, for responding to pages for a set of services. It is a production requirement, not a heroic act, and it must be sustainable.

  • Rotations: a primary and a secondary (escalation if the primary does not acknowledge within a few minutes), usually week-long shifts with a written handoff — open issues, risky deploys, silences in place.
  • Follow-the-sun: teams in different time zones split the day so nobody is paged at night; it needs at least two sites.
  • Sustainable load: Google's SRE practice caps on-call work so that engineers spend most of their time on engineering, and aims for at most about two incidents per 12-hour shift — an incident takes hours of follow-up, not just the response2. More than that means the alerting or the system needs work, not more stamina.
  • You build it, you run it: the team that owns a service carries its pager. It is the strongest incentive to build operable software.
  • Preparation: runbooks, access already granted (never "I'm waiting for production access"), dashboards bookmarked, and practice in game days (Chaos engineering).

items.title: The incident lifecycle
items.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Detected : alert, customer report, or engineer notices
    Detected --> Triaged : on-call acknowledges, assesses impact
    Triaged --> Declared : severity set, commander and channel assigned
    Triaged --> Closed : false alarm or no impact (tune the alert)
    Declared --> Mitigating : stop the bleeding
    Mitigating --> Monitoring : impact gone, SLIs recovering
    Monitoring --> Mitigating : impact returns
    Monitoring --> Resolved : stable, root fix scheduled
    Resolved --> Reviewed : blameless postmortem, action items
    Reviewed --> [*]
    Closed --> [*]

Each transition has a timestamp, and the gaps between them are the metrics that matter:

Metric From → to Improved by MTTD — mean time to detect impact starts → someone knows SLO burn-rate alerts, synthetic probes MTTA — mean time to acknowledge page → human on it sane paging load, escalation policies MTTM — mean time to mitigate impact starts → users no longer affected runbooks, rollbacks, feature flags, generic mitigations MTTR — mean time to resolve / recover impact starts → resolved all of the above, plus fast diagnosis (traces)

Users only feel impact: the time until mitigation is the number that shapes availability (recall from Reliability that availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR)). The root cause can be fixed on Monday.

items.title: Roles
items.text:
The most common way an incident goes wrong is not a missing tool — it is five engineers debugging the same thing in parallel, nobody deciding, and nobody telling customers what is going on. The Incident Command System (ICS), created for wildfire response in the 1970s, solved this with explicit roles; Google, PagerDuty and others adapted it to software13.

Role Does Does not Incident Commander (IC) owns the incident: sets severity, assigns roles, decides (rollback? failover?), keeps the timeline moving, declares the end debug — the IC's attention is on the whole response Operations / Tech lead leads the investigation and mitigation; the only one changing production (or coordinating who does) talk to customers Communications lead internal updates on a cadence, status page, support and business stakeholders speculate about causes in public Scribe records the timeline: what was seen, decided, changed — with timestamps filter what "looks bad" Subject-matter experts join when called (payments, database, network) start parallel, uncoordinated changes

In a small team, one person can hold several roles; the IC and the operations lead should still be different people whenever possible. Roles are handed over explicitly ("I am now IC") when shifts change or the incident escalates.

Play the first fifteen minutes of the flash-sale incident:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant AM as Alertmanager
    participant OC as On-call (primary)
    participant IC as Incident commander
    participant OPS as Ops lead (payments)
    participant COM as Comms lead
    participant ST as Status page
    AM->>OC: page: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn
    OC->>OC: ack, open dashboard: 504s on /checkout, on-sale live
    OC->>IC: declare SEV1, open channel inc-onsale-0313
    IC->>OPS: you lead mitigation, payments on-call joins
    IC->>COM: you own updates, every 15 min
    COM->>ST: "Some fans see errors at checkout. We are working on it."
    OPS->>OPS: exemplar trace: 7.9 s in payment pool.acquire
    OPS->>IC: provider slow, propose switch to secondary provider
    IC->>OPS: approved, go
    OPS->>OPS: flag payment.provider=secondary, waiting room throttled
    OPS->>IC: error ratio back under 0.5%, p99 1.4 s
    IC->>COM: mitigated, monitoring
    COM->>ST: "Checkout is working again. Monitoring."

items.title: Mitigate first
items.text:
During an incident the goal is to stop the impact, not to understand it. Understanding comes later, with the postmortem — and is much easier once the pressure is gone. The best mitigations are generic: they work regardless of the exact cause, and they are rehearsed in advance.

Mitigation When BoxOffice example Prerequisite Roll back a change preceded the impact (the most common case) revert order 1.4.2 → 1.4.1 fast, tested rollbacks; deploy annotations on dashboards Turn off a feature flag a new feature misbehaves disable "seat upgrade suggestions" features behind flags Fail over / drain one zone, region or provider is bad switch to the secondary payment provider; drain sa-east-1a a tested secondary and the switch documented Shed load demand exceeds capacity throttle the waiting room admission rate a waiting room / rate limiter in place Scale out saturation, the code is fine more inventory replicas, bigger connection pool if the DB can take it headroom, autoscaling limits known Block bad traffic abusive bots or an attack WAF rule for the scalper ASN WAF and rate limits at the edge Degrade gracefully a non-critical dependency fails hide recommendations, keep checkout fallbacks designed in

Do not debug in production during the incident unless it mitigates

"Let me add a log line and redeploy to understand" turns a 15-minute incident into a 2-hour one. If a mitigation is available, take it; if not, investigate with the telemetry you already have. Every change during an incident goes through the operations lead and into the timeline.

items.title: Communication
items.text:
Silence during an incident is read as incompetence or indifference. Updates have a fixed cadence (for a SEV1, every 15–30 minutes) even when there is nothing new, and a fixed shape:

[SEV1] Checkout errors during the 10:00 on-sale — update #3, 10:21
Impact:   since 10:02, ~12% of checkout attempts failed; fans in the waiting room were not affected.
Status:   MITIGATED at 10:14 — traffic moved to the secondary payment provider.
Next:     monitoring until 10:45; the primary provider is investigating on their side.
Next update: 10:45 or earlier if anything changes.
IC: @ana   Ops: @bruno   Comms: @carla

Outside the company, the status page states impact and progress, never internal names, guesses or blame ("our provider failed").

items.title: The BoxOffice incident, by the numbers
items.text:
Time Event Metric 10:00 on-sale opens 10:02 the payment provider slows down; the payment pool saturates; checkouts start failing impact starts 10:03 fast-burn page fires MTTD ≈ 1 min 10:04 on-call acknowledges MTTA ≈ 1 min 10:06 SEV1 declared, IC and roles assigned 10:11 exemplar trace shows time inside pool.acquire; switch proposed 10:14 secondary provider active, waiting room throttled; errors back to normal MTTM ≈ 12 min 10:40 stable, incident resolved MTTR ≈ 38 min

What did it cost in SLO terms? With illustrative numbers — 200 checkout attempts per second during the on-sale and an average of 12% failures for the 12 minutes of impact:

\[ 200 \times 720\ \text{s} \times 0.12 \approx 17\,300 \text{ failed checkouts} \]

If BoxOffice handles about 2 million checkouts in a normal 28-day window (the SLO window used in Reliability), a 99.9% SLO allows 2,000 failures. This one incident spent more than eight 28-day budgets — over seven months' worth — in twelve minutes. The error budget policy now applies: feature work on checkout pauses until the reliability action items are done. That is the error budget doing its job — turning one bad morning into a funded engineering priority.

items.title: Postmortems
items.text: A postmortem (also called incident review or retrospective) is a written analysis of an incident, done after it is resolved, with one goal: reduce the chance and the impact of the next one. Write one for every SEV1/SEV2, any data loss, any significant budget spend — and for interesting near misses.

items.title: Blameless
items.text: A postmortem is blameless4: it assumes everyone acted reasonably given what they knew at the time, and it asks how the system made the mistake easy, not who made it. This is not about being nice. If people are punished for honest accounts, they stop giving them, and the organisation loses the only accurate source of information about how its systems really fail. "The engineer ran the wrong command" becomes "the tool allowed a destructive command against production without confirmation, and the runbook showed it next to a harmless one".

items.title: Root cause — or contributing factors?
items.text:
Complex systems rarely fail for one reason; incidents need several factors lining up5. In the BoxOffice incident:

  • the provider slowed down (external trigger, outside BoxOffice's control);
  • the payment adapter had no timeout shorter than the provider's own, and a pool of 20 connections shared by every call;
  • the secondary provider existed, but switching was a manual, undocumented step;
  • the general 28-day SLO alerts were not designed for a 30-minute on-sale;
  • the load test before the on-sale used a provider mock that always answered in 100 ms.

Asking "five whys" down a single chain would have stopped at "the provider was slow" — the one factor BoxOffice cannot fix. Looking for all contributing factors finds four that it can.

items.title: Template
items.text:
# Postmortem: checkout errors during the 13 March on-sale (SEV1)

**Status**: final · **Authors**: … · **Reviewed**: …

## Summary
Two to four sentences: what happened, impact, how it was mitigated.

## Impact
Users affected, duration, failed checkouts, revenue and SLO budget consumed, support tickets.

## Timeline (UTC-3)
10:02 provider latency rises … 10:03 page … 10:14 mitigated … 10:40 resolved.

## Contributing factors
Technical, process and organisational factors — no names, no blame.

## What went well / what went poorly / where we got lucky

## Action items
| Action | Type (prevent / detect / mitigate) | Owner | Due | Ticket |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Timeout 800 ms + bulkhead on the provider client | prevent | payments | 27/03 | PAY-312 |
| Automatic failover to the secondary provider | mitigate | payments | 10/04 | PAY-313 |
| On-sale SLO with 1 min / 5 min burn-rate alerts | detect | SRE | 20/03 | OBS-88 |
| Provider latency injected in the pre-sale load test | prevent | performance | 27/03 | PERF-41 |

Action items are the only part of a postmortem that changes anything. Each one is specific, has one owner and a date, and is tracked like any other work. A postmortem whose actions are never done is a story, not a fix.

items.title: Closing the loop
items.text:
• Review meeting: the authors walk the team through the document; questions are about the system, not the people.
  • Share widely: other teams have the same pool, the same missing timeout.
  • Look for trends: many incidents from deploys → invest in canaries and rollbacks (Delivery); many from one dependency → bulkheads and fallbacks.
  • Practice: turn the incident into a game day scenario — inject provider latency with Toxiproxy and check that the new timeout, breaker and alert behave (Hands-on 9).
  • Measure delivery health: the DORA metrics change failure rate and failed deployment recovery time6 show whether incidents caused by changes are becoming rarer and shorter.

AI assistants in incident response

In 2026 many teams use LLM-based assistants to summarise the incident channel into a draft timeline, suggest queries, or search past postmortems for similar incidents. They are useful scribes and search tools. They are not incident commanders: an assistant can produce a confident but wrong root cause, so every claim must be checked against the telemetry, and decisions stay with the humans in the roles above.

items.title: Trade-offs
items.text:
Decision Option A Option B Guidance Who carries the pager central ops team the team that builds the service "you build it, you run it", with a central SRE team for platforms and coaching When to declare only when sure early, downgrade later early — declaring is cheap During the incident find the root cause mitigate first mitigate first; understand afterwards Postmortem tone find who erred blameless, system-focused blameless — it is the only way to get accurate accounts Analysis single root cause (5 whys) contributing factors contributing factors; complex failures have several

In the interview

Interviews rarely ask "how do you run an incident?" directly, but they often ask "what happens when X fails?" A strong answer covers three layers: how the system degrades (timeouts, fallbacks, waiting room), how you find out (SLO burn-rate alert, before customers tell you), and how you recover (a generic mitigation — failover, rollback, flag — that is documented and tested). In behavioural interviews, a well-told incident story — your role, how you mitigated, what the postmortem changed — is one of the strongest signals of real experience (see Interview preparation).

Common pitfalls

  • No incident commander: everyone debugs, nobody decides, nobody communicates.
  • Investigating before mitigating: users keep suffering while the team understands a problem a rollback would have stopped.
  • Silent incidents: no updates for an hour; support and business invent their own story.
  • Blameful postmortems: people hide what they did, and the real contributing factors stay hidden.
  • Action items without owners or dates: the same incident happens again next on-sale.
  • Unsustainable on-call: too many pages burn people out, and tired people make the next incident worse.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    AL["burn-rate page<br/>→ Alerting"] --> TRI["triage: severity<br/>SEV1 to SEV4"]
    TRI --> ROLES["IC, ops lead,<br/>comms lead, scribe"]
    ROLES --> MIT["mitigate first"]
    MIT --> RB["rollback, flag off<br/>→ Cloud-native delivery"]
    MIT --> FO["failover, shed load,<br/>degrade → Reliability"]
    MIT --> BLK["block bad traffic<br/>→ Edge (WAF)"]
    MIT -->|"timestamps"| MTT["MTTD, MTTM, MTTR<br/>→ availability"]
    MTT --> BUD["error budget spent<br/>→ SLO policy"]
    MIT --> PM["blameless postmortem,<br/>action items"]
    PM --> GD["game day<br/>→ Chaos engineering"]

Palette components: alerting (the page that starts it) · tracing (the exemplar trace that found pool.acquire) · payment (failover to the secondary provider) · queue (the waiting room, throttled to shed load) · waf (blocking abusive traffic) · app (rollback or scale-out of a service). Scenarios: flash-sale (the on-sale incident), cascading-failure (a slow provider without timeouts). Continues in: Reliability (availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR)), Reliability — SLOs, Reliability — chaos engineering, Cloud-native — delivery (rollbacks, canaries, DORA), Project — game day, Interview preparation.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• An incident needs coordination; severity levels with clear criteria make declaring fast — declare early, downgrade freely.
  • On-call must be sustainable: primary/secondary, handoffs, runbooks, and a page load that leaves time for engineering.
  • Measure MTTD, MTTA, MTTM, MTTR; users feel the time to mitigation.
  • Roles — incident commander, ops lead, comms lead, scribe — prevent chaos; the IC coordinates and does not debug.
  • Mitigate first with generic, rehearsed mitigations (rollback, flag, failover, shed load); communicate on a fixed cadence.
  • Blameless postmortems look for all contributing factors and produce owned, dated action items; the loop closes with game days.

  1. BEYER, B. et al. Site Reliability Engineering — Managing Incidents. O'Reilly, 2016. Chapter 14. ↩↩

  2. BEYER, B. et al. Site Reliability Engineering — Being On-Call. O'Reilly, 2016. Chapter 11. ↩

  3. PAGERDUTY. Incident Response Documentation. ↩

  4. ALLSPAW, J. Blameless PostMortems and a Just Culture. Etsy Code as Craft, 2012. See also Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 15 — Postmortem Culture. ↩

  5. COOK, R. I. How Complex Systems Fail. Cognitive Technologies Laboratory, University of Chicago, 1998. ↩

  6. DORA. DORA's software delivery metrics. Google Cloud. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text: BoxOffice is written in Java (gateway, order, inventory, payment, catalog), Python (the AI assistant), runs Nginx at the edge, Kafka in the middle and PostgreSQL at the bottom. Ten years ago, tracing a checkout across all of that meant a vendor agent per language, a proprietary header per vendor, and a full re-instrumentation the day the company changed vendors. Worse, a trace broke at the first component that spoke a different dialect. OpenTelemetry (OTel) fixed this by standardising the boring parts — the API, the wire protocol, the context header and the names of things — so that every library and every backend can speak the same language1. (The ideas themselves — trace IDs, spans, parent links, sampling — come from Google's Dapper paper4.)

items.title: What OpenTelemetry is (and is not)
items.text:
OpenTelemetry is a CNCF project that defines how telemetry is produced and transported. It is not a backend: it does not store or display anything. You still choose where the data goes — Prometheus, Tempo, Jaeger, Loki, a cloud service or a vendor — and you can change that choice without touching application code.

Piece What it is BoxOffice example API interfaces to create spans, metrics and logs; safe no-ops if no SDK is installed Tracer, Meter used inside payment SDK the implementation: sampling, batching, resource detection, exporters configured by the Java agent from environment variables Instrumentation libraries ready-made spans/metrics for frameworks: Spring MVC, JDBC, Kafka clients, FastAPI, HTTP clients the SELECT seat_holds span, created without any code Semantic conventions standard names for attributes and metrics: http.route, db.system, messaging.destination.name every service names the route the same way, so one dashboard works for all OTLP the OpenTelemetry Protocol, over gRPC (port 4317) or HTTP/protobuf (port 4318) all services export to the Collector over OTLP Collector a standalone process that receives, processes and exports telemetry redacts card numbers, applies tail sampling, fans out to backends

The signals have matured at different speeds: traces and metrics are stable, logs became stable later (OTel mostly bridges existing logging libraries, adding the trace context), and profiles were added as the fourth signal and are still maturing.

flowchart LR
    subgraph services ["BoxOffice services"]
        J["Java services<br/>OTel Java agent"]
        PY["assistant (Python)<br/>OTel SDK"]
        NG["Nginx<br/>OTel module"]
    end
    subgraph col ["OTel Collector"]
        R["receivers<br/>otlp"] --> PR["processors<br/>memory_limiter, k8s attrs,<br/>redaction, tail sampling, batch"] --> E["exporters"]
    end
    J -- OTLP --> R
    PY -- OTLP --> R
    NG -- OTLP --> R
    E --> TEMPO[("Tempo / Jaeger<br/>traces")]
    E --> PROM[("Prometheus / Mimir<br/>metrics")]
    E --> LOKI[("Loki<br/>logs")]

items.title: Context propagation
items.text: A trace exists only if every hop knows which trace it belongs to. Context propagation is the mechanism: the caller injects the current trace context into the outgoing request, and the callee extracts it and creates its own span as a child.

items.title: The traceparent header
items.text:
OpenTelemetry uses the W3C Trace Context standard2 by default. One header carries the context:

traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
             │  │                                │                └─ flags: 01 = sampled
             │  │                                └─ parent-id: the caller's current span (64 bits)
             │  └─ trace-id: same for the whole request (128 bits)
             └─ version

On every outgoing call, a service keeps the trace-id and the flags and replaces the parent-id with the ID of its own current span. No service needs to understand the whole trace; the tree is rebuilt by the backend from the parent links. A second header, tracestate, carries vendor-specific data, and baggage (baggage: tenant=festival-x,channel=mobile) carries business key-value pairs that every downstream service can read — useful, but every byte travels on every request, so keep it small and never put secrets in it.

items.title: Following a checkout
items.text:
Play the diagram and watch the parent-id change at each hop while the trace-id stays the same — including across Kafka, where the context travels in a message header:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant GW as gateway
    participant O as order
    participant I as inventory
    participant P as payment
    participant X as payment provider
    participant K as Kafka
    participant N as notification
    GW->>O: POST /orders<br/>traceparent: 00-4bf9…-a1a1…-01
    O->>I: PUT /holds/h7/confirm<br/>traceparent: 00-4bf9…-b2b2…-01
    I-->>O: 200 OK (90 ms)
    O->>P: POST /charges<br/>traceparent: 00-4bf9…-c3c3…-01
    P->>X: POST /v1/charges (CLIENT span recorded by payment)
    X-->>P: 200 OK (1.0 s)
    P-->>O: 201 Created
    O->>K: produce OrderConfirmed<br/>header traceparent: 00-4bf9…-d4d4…-01
    O-->>GW: 201 Created
    K->>N: consume OrderConfirmed (CONSUMER span, parent d4d4…)
    N->>N: send e-mail and push

Three details matter in practice:

  • The external provider is a black box. It will not send its spans to you. The CLIENT span recorded by payment around the call is all you will ever see of it — which is why that span's duration and status are worth an alert of their own. Many teams also strip traceparent and baggage at egress, so internal IDs do not leak to third parties.
  • Asynchronous hops propagate through message headers. A consumer that handles one message continues the producer's trace (parent-child). A consumer that processes a batch of 500 messages cannot have 500 parents; it starts its own trace and adds span links to each producer's span.
  • The trace ends where propagation breaks. One component that drops the header splits every trace in two.

Where propagation usually breaks

Place Symptom Fix A proxy or gateway that rebuilds requests and drops unknown headers traces start at the service behind it forward traceparent, tracestate, baggage; instrument the proxy Work handed to another thread (@Async, executors, reactive code) child spans appear as separate traces use instrumented executors (the Java agent wraps common ones) or pass Context explicitly Messaging without headers (old clients, custom envelopes) consumers start new traces use headers; or carry the context in the message envelope A homemade HTTP client the call has no CLIENT span and the callee starts a new trace use an instrumented client or inject the context manually

items.title: Zero-code: the Java agent
items.text:
The OpenTelemetry Java agent attaches to the JVM and instruments hundreds of libraries — Spring MVC/WebFlux, JDBC, HikariCP, Kafka clients, HTTP clients, Logback — by bytecode injection, with no code changes. It also puts trace_id and span_id into the logging context (MDC), so structured logs carry them automatically.

# Dockerfile (excerpt) — pin a version; check the latest release before upgrading
ADD https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java-instrumentation/releases/download/v2.32.0/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar /otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-javaagent:/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

# docker-compose.yaml (excerpt) — the order service
environment:
  OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: order
  OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES: service.namespace=boxoffice,service.version=1.4.2,deployment.environment.name=dev
  OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: http://otel-collector:4318   # agent 2.x default protocol: http/protobuf
  OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER: parentbased_always_on                 # keep all; the Collector decides (tail sampling)
  OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL: "15000"

service.name is the most important attribute in OpenTelemetry: without it, every service appears as unknown_service:java and no dashboard can tell them apart. service.version and deployment.environment.name let you compare a canary with the stable version, or staging with production.

items.title: Zero-code: the Python assistant
items.text:
uv add opentelemetry-distro opentelemetry-exporter-otlp
uv run opentelemetry-bootstrap -a requirements > otel-instrumentations.txt   # instrumentations for the libraries found (FastAPI, httpx, psycopg…)
uv add -r otel-instrumentations.txt
OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=assistant \
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4318 \
uv run opentelemetry-instrument uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

items.title: Manual spans where the agent cannot see
items.text:
Automatic instrumentation sees I/O. It cannot see business steps or waiting inside your code — the connection pool of the payment adapter in the Signals waterfall. A few manual spans in the right places are worth more than hundreds of automatic ones:

private static final Tracer tracer = GlobalOpenTelemetry.getTracer("boxoffice.payment");

ProviderConnection acquire() throws TimeoutException {
    Span span = tracer.spanBuilder("pool.acquire").startSpan();
    try (Scope ignored = span.makeCurrent()) {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        ProviderConnection c = pool.borrow(Duration.ofMillis(500));   // bounded wait, never forever
        span.setAttribute("pool.wait_ms", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000);
        return c;
    } catch (TimeoutException e) {
        span.recordException(e);
        span.setStatus(StatusCode.ERROR, "pool exhausted");
        throw e;
    } finally {
        span.end();
    }
}

With the agent attached, the simplest alternative is an annotation on a method: @WithSpan("seatmap.render"), with @SpanAttribute on the parameters you want recorded.

Attributes: rich, but not dangerous

Span attributes can have high cardinality — order.id, event.id, customer.tier are what make a trace searchable. They must not contain secrets or personal data: no card numbers, tokens or full e-mails. Redact at the source and add a redaction processor in the Collector as a second barrier.

items.title: The Collector
items.text:
Services could export directly to each backend, but then every service must know every backend, its credentials and its retry policy. The Collector decouples them: services send OTLP to one place, and the Collector's pipelines decide what happens next. A pipeline has three stages per signal: receivers (how data gets in), processors (what is done to it, in order), exporters (where it goes).

# otel-collector.yaml — gateway Collector for BoxOffice (sketch)
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc: { endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317 }
      http: { endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318 }

processors:
  memory_limiter:                 # first: refuse data instead of being OOM-killed
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_percentage: 80
    spike_limit_percentage: 20
  k8sattributes: {}               # add k8s.pod.name, k8s.namespace.name, k8s.deployment.name
  attributes/redact:
    actions:
      - key: payment.card_number
        action: delete
      - key: enduser.email
        action: hash
  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 10s            # wait for the trace's spans before deciding
    policies:
      - name: keep-errors
        type: status_code
        status_code: { status_codes: [ERROR] }
      - name: keep-slow
        type: latency
        latency: { threshold_ms: 2000 }
      - name: some-of-the-rest
        type: probabilistic
        probabilistic: { sampling_percentage: 5 }
  batch: {}                       # last: send in batches

exporters:
  otlp/tempo:
    endpoint: tempo:4317
    tls: { insecure: true }
  otlphttp/prometheus:
    endpoint: http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/otlp
  otlphttp/loki:
    endpoint: http://loki:3100/otlp

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, attributes/redact, tail_sampling, batch]
      exporters: [otlp/tempo]
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/prometheus]
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, attributes/redact, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/loki]

The order of processors matters: memory_limiter first, so an overloaded Collector sheds data instead of crashing; batch last, so it batches what survived.

items.title: Deployment patterns
items.text:
Pattern Where it runs Good for Watch out No Collector (SDK → backend) — demos, one backend every service holds backend config and credentials Agent DaemonSet (one per node) or sidecar local batching, host metrics, adding node/pod attributes per-node resources; cannot see whole traces Gateway a Deployment behind a Service, scaled horizontally central policy: redaction, tail sampling, routing, credentials a new critical component: size it and monitor it Agent + gateway (two tiers) both large clusters tail sampling needs all spans of a trace on the same gateway instance — route by trace ID (loadbalancing exporter)

The Collector is production infrastructure

During the flash sale, telemetry volume rises with traffic. A Collector without memory_limiter, without enough replicas, or exporting synchronously to a slow backend becomes a bottleneck — and if SDKs block on export, it can even slow the services. SDKs export asynchronously and drop data when their queue is full: losing telemetry is acceptable; slowing checkout to report on it is not. Monitor the Collector's own metrics (accepted vs refused vs dropped spans, queue size).

items.title: Sampling
items.text:
Keeping every span of every request is rarely affordable (see what telemetry costs). Sampling keeps a subset of traces — complete traces, not random spans, otherwise the trees break.

Strategy Where the decision is made Pros Cons Head sampling (e.g. parentbased_traceidratio 10%) at the first span, from the trace ID; travels in the sampled flag so every service agrees cheap; no buffering; consistent across services blind: it drops 90% of the rare error and slow traces too Tail sampling3 in the Collector, after the whole trace has arrived (decision_wait) keeps interesting traces: every error, every slow request, plus a sample of the rest every span must reach the Collector; memory to buffer; all spans of a trace on one instance Rate limiting SDK or Collector: at most N traces per second predictable cost during a spike, almost everything is dropped — exactly when you need it

Head and tail sampling are applied in sequence: a trace dropped at the head can never be rescued by the tail. The comparison below uses illustrative numbers for a busy BoxOffice day — 2,000 requests/s, 8 spans per request of 500 bytes, 1% of requests failing and 2% slower than the 2 s threshold:
