Strategy Traces kept Storage per day Error traces kept per day keep everything 100.0% 691.2 GB 1,728,000 (100%) head sampling 10% 10.0% 69.1 GB 172,800 (10%) head sampling 1% 1.0% 6.9 GB 17,280 (1%) tail: all errors + all slow + 5% of the rest 7.8% 54.3 GB 1,728,000 (100%)

Tail sampling stores less than 10% head sampling and still keeps every error trace — at the price of shipping 100% of the spans over the network to the Collector and buffering them for the decision window. A common production recipe: head sampling at 100% (or a high ratio) in the services, tail sampling in a gateway Collector, and metrics computed from all requests before sampling, so dashboards and SLOs are exact even though most traces are discarded.

Exemplars: from a metric to a trace

An exemplar is a trace_id attached to a sample of a metric — for instance, to the latency histogram bucket where a 9 s checkout landed. In Grafana, the latency panel shows exemplars as dots; clicking one opens that exact trace in Tempo. It is the bridge between "p99 is high" and "here is one request that was slow" — make sure the exemplar's trace was kept by your sampler (tail sampling of slow requests guarantees it).

items.title: Backends and a local stack
items.text:
OpenTelemetry leaves the backend to you. The same OTLP data can go to any of them:

Open sourceAWSGCPAzureSaaS

Grafana LGTM: Loki (logs), Grafana (UI), Tempo (traces), Mimir or Prometheus (metrics), plus Pyroscope (profiles). Alternatives: Jaeger for traces, OpenSearch for logs, ClickHouse-based stacks (SigNoz) for everything. You operate the storage.

CloudWatch (metrics, logs, alarms), X-Ray / CloudWatch Application Signals (traces), Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and Managed Grafana. AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) packages the Collector.

Cloud Monitoring, Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace (Google Cloud Observability); Managed Service for Prometheus. Accepts OTLP through the Collector.

Azure Monitor: Application Insights (traces, requests), Log Analytics (logs), Managed Prometheus and Managed Grafana. The Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry distro instruments applications.

Datadog, Honeycomb, New Relic, Grafana Cloud, Dynatrace, Elastic Cloud and others accept OTLP. You pay per volume (spans, series, GB of logs) — the sampling and cardinality decisions of this class are also cost decisions.

For development — and in Hands-on 8 — a single container bundles a Collector with the whole LGTM stack:

# docker-compose.yaml (excerpt)
services:
  otel-lgtm:
    image: grafana/otel-lgtm
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"   # Grafana
      - "4317:4317"   # OTLP gRPC
      - "4318:4318"   # OTLP HTTP

items.title: Trade-offs
items.text:
Decision Option A Option B Guidance Instrumentation zero-code agent manual SDK calls start with the agent; add manual spans for business steps and internal waits Export path SDK → backend SDK → Collector → backend a Collector as soon as there are two services or one policy (redaction, sampling) Collector topology agent per node central gateway agents for local enrichment; a gateway for tail sampling and credentials Sampling head tail head for cost simplicity; tail to keep every error and slow trace Protocol OTLP gRPC (4317) OTLP HTTP (4318) either; HTTP is friendlier to proxies and browsers Backend self-hosted managed / SaaS managed until the bill or data-residency rules say otherwise

In the interview

"How do you trace a request across microservices?" — "Every service is instrumented with OpenTelemetry; the W3C traceparent header (and Kafka message headers for async hops) propagates the trace ID; spans go over OTLP to a Collector that applies tail sampling — keep all errors and slow traces, a few percent of the rest — and exports to a tracing backend. Logs carry the trace ID, and the latency histograms carry exemplars, so I can jump from a dashboard to a trace to its logs." Then add the cost angle: metrics are computed from 100% of the traffic; traces are sampled.

Common pitfalls

  • Protocol and port mismatch: the Java agent 2.x defaults to OTLP over HTTP (4318); pointing it at 4317 without OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc silently produces no data.
  • Missing service.name: everything shows up as unknown_service.
  • Head sampling at 1% and no tail sampling: the one trace you need during the incident was dropped.
  • Tail sampling behind a round-robin load balancer: spans of the same trace land on different Collectors, and every decision is made on fragments.
  • No memory_limiter: the Collector is OOM-killed exactly during the traffic peak.
  • Secrets and personal data in attributes or baggage: telemetry is copied to many systems and kept for weeks.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    KH["Kafka message headers,<br/>span links → Messaging"] --> CTX["context propagation:<br/>traceparent, baggage"]
    CTX --> SVC["services: Java agent,<br/>Python SDK, Nginx"]
    SVC -->|"OTLP 4317 / 4318"| COL["Collector:<br/>receivers → processors → exporters"]
    COL --> RD["redaction:<br/>no cards, no e-mails"]
    COL --> TS["tail sampling:<br/>errors + slow + 5%"]
    TS --> TR["traces backend<br/>Tempo / Jaeger"]
    COL --> MET["metrics from all traffic<br/>→ SLOs, Alerting"]
    COL --> LG["logs backend<br/>Loki"]
    MET -->|"exemplars"| TR
    COL --> OPS["memory_limiter, gateway replicas<br/>→ Cloud-native"]

Palette components: tracing · metrics · logs · app (instrumented services) · apigw (must forward traceparent) · kafka (context in message headers) · payment (a black box: only the CLIENT span). Scenarios: observability-stack, event-fanout (traces that cross Kafka). Continues in: Signals, Alerting, Messaging — Kafka, Cloud-native — Kubernetes (Collector as DaemonSet or Deployment), Hands-on 8 — instrument everything.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• OpenTelemetry standardises the API, SDK, semantic conventions, protocol (OTLP) and Collector — not the backend; change backends without re-instrumenting.
  • Context propagation with W3C traceparent (and message headers for Kafka) is what makes a trace; one hop that drops it splits every trace.
  • Start with zero-code instrumentation, then add manual spans for business steps and for time spent waiting inside services.
  • The Collector pipelines (receivers → processors → exporters) centralise redaction, enrichment, sampling and routing; treat it as production infrastructure.
  • Tail sampling keeps every error and slow trace at a fraction of the storage; compute metrics from all traffic before sampling, and use exemplars to jump from metrics to traces.

  1. OPENTELEMETRY. What is OpenTelemetry? and Collector documentation. ↩

  2. W3C. Trace Context. W3C Recommendation. See also W3C Baggage. ↩

  3. OPENTELEMETRY COLLECTOR CONTRIB. Tail Sampling Processor. ↩

  4. SIGELMAN, B. H. et al. Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure. Google Technical Report, 2010. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text: The first question during an incident is never "why?" — it is "is something wrong, and where should I look?". The second is "what exactly happened to this request?". The third is "which line of code is burning the time?". Each question needs a different kind of data, with a different cost. Emitting every detail of every request answers all of them and bankrupts you; emitting only CPU graphs is cheap and answers none. This page is about choosing the right signal for each question.

items.title: Four signals, one spectrum
items.text:
Signal Unit of data Answers Volume / cost Typical retention Backends Metrics a number per time series per interval is something wrong? how much, since when? low and independent of traffic months (downsampled: years) Prometheus, Mimir, Thanos, CloudWatch Logs one record per event what happened in this event? grows linearly with traffic days to weeks hot, months cold Loki, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Cloud Logging Traces a tree of spans per request where did the time / error go across services? grows with traffic × hops (sampled) days to weeks Tempo, Jaeger, X-Ray, Honeycomb Profiles stack samples per process over time which code uses CPU / memory / locks? roughly constant per process days to weeks Pyroscope, Parca, cloud profilers

Think of it as a spectrum from aggregated and cheap to detailed and expensive. Metrics compress a million requests into a few numbers per interval — you can keep them for months, but you cannot ask about one request. Logs and traces keep each request — you can ask anything about it, but you must sample, filter or expire them.

flowchart LR
    M["Metrics<br/>aggregate · cheap · long retention"] --> T["Traces<br/>per request · sampled"]
    T --> L["Logs<br/>per event · verbose"]
    L --> P["Profiles<br/>per code path"]

Names used in this class

BoxOffice is instrumented with the OpenTelemetry Java agent (Hands-on 8), which follows the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions1. Its HTTP server metric http.server.request.duration (a histogram, in seconds) arrives in Prometheus as http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket, _count and _sum, with the labels http_route, http_request_method and http_response_status_code; the service name becomes the job label. Spring Boot's own Micrometer metrics use other names (http_server_requests_seconds with uri, status, application). The queries are the same idea — check which names your stack emits before copying a query.

items.title: The data model
items.text:
A metric is a time series: a name, a set of key-value labels (also called attributes or dimensions), and a sequence of (timestamp, value) samples.

http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order", http_route="/orders", http_request_method="POST", http_response_status_code="201"}  48213

Every distinct combination of label values is a separate time series that the database must index and keep in memory. This single fact explains most of the operational problems with metrics (see cardinality).

Type Behaviour Use for BoxOffice example Counter only goes up (resets to 0 on restart) events: requests, errors, bytes tickets sold, 5xx responses Gauge goes up and down current state seats left in a hold pool, queue depth, open connections Histogram counts observations in buckets (le = less or equal) plus _sum and _count latency and size distributions, percentiles checkout duration Summary quantiles computed in the process legacy; a single instance's percentiles — avoid: cannot be aggregated

Histograms are the important one. Each bucket is a counter "how many observations were ≤ this bound": with bounds 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5 s, a 0.3 s checkout increments the buckets 0.5, 1, 2.5 and +Inf. Because buckets are counters, histograms from 20 pods can be summed and a percentile estimated from the total. Newer formats — Prometheus native histograms and OpenTelemetry exponential histograms — choose bucket bounds automatically with bounded relative error, which removes the most common mistake: buckets that do not cover your SLO threshold.

items.title: Pull vs push
items.text:
Pull (scrape) Push How Prometheus calls GET /metrics on every target every 15–60 s the process sends metrics (OTLP, StatsD) to a collector Discovers dead targets yes — a failed scrape is itself a signal (up == 0) only by absence of data Short-lived jobs, serverless awkward (needs a push gateway) natural Behind NAT / many networks the scraper must reach every target targets only need to reach the collector Typical stack Prometheus + Kubernetes service discovery OpenTelemetry SDK → Collector → Prometheus/Mimir (OTLP)

Both are fine; modern stacks mix them. With OpenTelemetry the default is push over OTLP to a Collector, which can also scrape existing Prometheus endpoints (OpenTelemetry).

items.title: RED, USE and the four golden signals
items.text:
You do not need hundreds of metrics per service. Three well-known checklists tell you which few matter:

Method Applies to Signals Origin RED request-driven services (APIs) Rate, Errors, Duration Tom Wilkie (Weaveworks/Grafana)2 USE resources (CPU, disk, pools, queues) Utilization, Saturation, Errors Brendan Gregg3 Four golden signals any user-facing system latency, traffic, errors, saturation Google SRE book4

The golden signals are essentially RED + saturation. Saturation is the subtle one: how full a resource is, usually visible as waiting — a queue, a pool with pending requests, threads blocked. Utilization near 100% is not a problem by itself; work waiting in line is.

BoxOffice — RED for services, USE for resources

Component Method What to plot order (POST /checkout) RED checkouts/s; fraction of 5xx; p50/p95/p99 duration payment → external provider RED (client side) calls/s; fraction failed or timed out; p99 of the provider call PostgreSQL connection pool of inventory USE active / max connections; pending acquisitions and wait time; acquisition timeouts Kafka topic order-events USE produce rate vs consume rate; consumer lag (messages and seconds); failed deliveries / DLQ size order JVM USE CPU; heap after GC; GC pause time; thread pool queue

During the flash sale, the payment pool's pending acquisitions (saturation) rose two minutes before the checkout p99 alert fired. Saturation is the leading indicator; RED is what users feel.

items.title: RED in PromQL
items.text:
PromQL is the query language of Prometheus (and of Mimir, Thanos and most compatible backends). Two rules prevent most wrong queries: apply rate() to a counter before summing it (it handles counter resets when a pod restarts), and keep the le label when summing histogram buckets.

# Rate: requests per second, per route, of the order service
sum by (http_route) (
  rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order"}[5m])
)

# Errors: fraction (0..1) of 5xx responses
sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order"}[5m]))

# Duration: p99 latency per route, aggregated across all pods
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum by (le, http_route) (
    rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="order"}[5m])
  )
)

# SLI style: fraction of checkouts faster than 2 s (needs a bucket at le="2")
sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="order", http_route="/checkout", le="2"}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order", http_route="/checkout"}[5m]))

items.title: Percentiles, not averages — and never average percentiles
items.text:
An average latency hides the tail: if 99 checkouts take 100 ms and one takes 10 s, the average is ~200 ms and looks fine, but one fan in a hundred waits ten seconds — and a page that makes 20 calls hits that tail on most loads (see Percentiles).

A subtler mistake is to compute p99 per pod and then average across pods. Percentiles do not compose: the p99 of the whole fleet is not the mean of the pods' p99s. The simulation below has four order pods; one of them shares a node with a noisy neighbour and is slow, and it receives 10% of the traffic.

Pod Requests p99 (ms) pod-a 30,000 179 pod-b 30,000 180 pod-c 30,000 181 pod-d (noisy neighbour) 10,000 1,260 average of the four p99s 450 true fleet p99 (from all requests) 100,000 756

Averaging the pods' percentiles understates the tail users actually experience. Histograms avoid the problem because their buckets are counters that can be summed before the percentile is estimated — which is exactly what sum by (le) does in the query above.

items.title: Cardinality
items.text:
Cardinality is the number of distinct time series a metric produces: the product of the number of values of each label. It is the main driver of the memory, cost and query speed of a metrics backend — and the most common way teams accidentally take down their monitoring.

The table below grows the checkout latency histogram label by label. Each histogram series is really 17 series (15 buckets, _sum, _count); the memory column assumes, for illustration, about 4 KB per active series in the time-series database.

Label added × values Series Memory one histogram (15 buckets + _sum + _count) 17 17 68.0 KB http_request_method (4 values) 4 68 272.0 KB http_route (25 route templates) 25 1,700 6.6 MB http_response_status_code (6 values seen) 6 10,200 39.8 MB pod (20 replicas) 20 204,000 796.9 MB customer_id (1,000,000 fans) 1,000,000 204,000,000,000 760.0 TB

The first five labels are bounded: their number of values is small and known (routes are templates such as /orders/{id}, not /orders/42). Together they produce at most about 200 thousand series (an upper bound: not every route returns every status code) — a normal load for one Prometheus server. The last label is unbounded: it grows with the number of users, and it multiplies everything before it. No metrics system survives that.

Label Bounded? Where it belongs http_route (template), method, status_code, region, pod yes metric labels event_id (≈ thousands of events on sale) borderline — only if small and you need per-event SLOs usually traces customer_id, order_id, email, full URL, trace_id no traces and logs (high-cardinality data is their job) error message text no (free text) logs; use an error class as the label

High cardinality is not bad — it is in the wrong place

"Which fans had slow checkouts?" is a great question. It is answered by traces and wide events with customer_id as an attribute, queried on demand — not by a metric label that pre-aggregates every possible value forever. Metrics answer "how many / how fast"; traces and logs answer "which ones".

items.title: Logs
items.text: A log is a timestamped record of a discrete event. Logs are the most familiar signal and the easiest to abuse: they are free to write and expensive to keep.

items.title: Structured logs
items.text:
Write logs as structured records (JSON, or the OpenTelemetry log data model) with fixed field names, not as free text.

Unstructured Structured Example 10:04:12 WARN payment slow for order 9912 (8120ms) see below Query grep and regular expressions field filters and aggregations Correlation by timestamp, by hand by trace_id / span_id fields Parsing brittle; breaks when a message changes stable 
{
  "timestamp": "2027-03-13T10:04:12.481Z",
  "level": "WARN",
  "service.name": "payment",
  "message": "provider call slow",
  "trace_id": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
  "span_id": "00f067aa0ba902b7",
  "order_id": "ord_9912",
  "provider": "acme-pay",
  "duration_ms": 8120,
  "pool_wait_ms": 7900
}

The trace_id and span_id fields are what turn a log line into part of an investigation: from a slow span you jump to exactly its log lines, and from an error line you jump to the full trace. With the OpenTelemetry Java agent, they are added to the logging context automatically (OpenTelemetry).

items.title: What (not) to log
items.text:
Level Use Production? ERROR a failure that needs attention: exception, dependency unreachable yes WARN unexpected but handled: retry, fallback, slow call yes INFO significant business or lifecycle events: order confirmed, service started yes, but not one per inner step DEBUG / TRACE diagnostic detail off by default; enable per service or per request when investigating
  • Log events, not steps. One line "checkout completed" with ten fields beats ten lines "entering method X".
  • Never log secrets or personal data: passwords, tokens, card numbers, full e-mails. Mask at the source and, as a second barrier, redact in the Collector.
  • Log the decision, not just the outcome: "fallback to provider B because breaker open" explains the next hour of graphs.
  • Errors once: log an exception where it is handled, not at every layer it passes through.

items.title: Querying logs
items.text:
With Loki (the "L" of the Grafana LGTM stack), labels select streams and the rest of the line is parsed at query time, which keeps indexing cheap:

{service_name="payment"} | json | level="WARN" | duration_ms > 5000
Loki Elasticsearch / OpenSearch Indexes only labels (stream selectors) the full text of every field Storage compressed chunks in object storage — cheap inverted index on disks — expensive Fast for "logs of service X around time T", trace-ID lookups arbitrary full-text search across everything Cost driver volume scanned per query index size

items.title: Traces
items.text:
A trace records the path of one request through the system as a tree of spans. A span is one timed operation — an HTTP call received or sent, a database query, a message produced or consumed — with a start time, a duration, a status and attributes.

Field Meaning Example trace_id same for every span of the request (128 bits) 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736 span_id / parent_span_id build the tree 00f067aa0ba902b7 / a2fb4a1d1a96d312 name the operation, low cardinality POST /checkout, SELECT seat_holds kind SERVER, CLIENT, PRODUCER, CONSUMER, INTERNAL CLIENT for the call to the provider status OK, ERROR (unset by default) ERROR attributes key-value details — high cardinality is fine here order.id=ord_9912, http.response.status_code=504 events timestamped annotations inside the span exception with stack trace, retry links references to spans of other traces a batch consumer linking to each producer's trace

items.title: Reading a waterfall
items.text:
The trace of one slow checkout during the flash sale, drawn as the waterfall that Tempo or Jaeger shows:

trace 4bf92f35…   POST /checkout                       total 9.12 s
                                         0s        3s        6s        9s
gateway    SERVER POST /checkout          |██████████████████████████████|  9.12 s
 order     SERVER POST /orders            | █████████████████████████████|  9.08 s
  inventory CLIENT PUT /holds/{id}        | ▌                            |  0.09 s
   postgres CLIENT UPDATE seat_holds      | ▏                            |  0.02 s
  payment  SERVER POST /charges           |  ████████████████████████████|  8.95 s
   payment INTERNAL pool.acquire          |  ██████████████████████████  |  7.90 s
   payment CLIENT POST provider/charges   |                          ███▌|  1.02 s
  order    PRODUCER order-events publish  |                             ▏|  0.01 s

Read it top-down and look for the critical path — the chain of spans that determines the total time. Here it is not the provider call (1 s, slow but not dramatic): it is 7.9 s waiting for a connection from the payment adapter's pool. The provider got slower, every call held its connection longer, and by Little's law (concurrency = throughput × time) the pool of 20 connections saturated — so most of the time was spent queueing inside BoxOffice. Without the pool.acquire span you would blame the provider for nine seconds; with it, you know a bounded pool plus a timeout is the fix (Resilience patterns).

Spans for waiting, not just for doing

Automatic instrumentation creates spans for I/O (HTTP, SQL, Kafka). Queueing inside a service — a connection pool, a semaphore, a thread pool queue, a rate limiter — is invisible unless you add a span or at least an attribute for the wait time. Those are exactly the places where saturation hides.

items.title: Profiles
items.text:
A profile samples, many times per second, what each thread of a process is executing — the full call stack — and aggregates the samples. Continuous profiling does this all the time in production with low overhead (the tools typically target around 1–2% CPU), so you can compare "10:00 today" with "10:00 last week".

The usual visualization is the flame graph5: each box is a function, its width is the fraction of samples in which it was on the stack, and children sit on top of their callers. Wide plateaus at the top are where the CPU actually goes.

Profile type Shows BoxOffice question CPU where CPU time is spent why does search use 4 cores for autocomplete? Allocation / heap who allocates memory what triggers the GC pauses in order during the on-sale? Lock / mutex where threads wait for locks is the seat-map cache lock contended? Wall-clock where time passes, including waiting where do checkout threads sleep?

Profiling became the fourth OpenTelemetry signal (still maturing in 2026), and eBPF-based profilers (Parca, Pyroscope, cloud profilers) can profile every process on a node without changing the application. Traces tell you which service and operation is slow; profiles tell you which function inside it.

items.title: Dashboards
items.text:
A dashboard is a set of saved queries arranged to answer a question quickly. Most dashboards fail because they try to show everything; the useful ones are designed top-down, from what users feel to what resources do.

flowchart TB
    L1["1 · User journeys and SLOs<br/>search, seat hold, checkout: SLI, budget left"]
    L2["2 · Services — RED<br/>per service and route: rate, errors, p50/p99"]
    L3["3 · Dependencies<br/>provider latency, DB, cache hit ratio, Kafka lag"]
    L4["4 · Resources — USE<br/>CPU, memory, pools, queues per pod/node"]
    L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> L4
  • One dashboard, one purpose. The on-call "is checkout healthy?" view fits on one screen; deep dives live elsewhere.
  • Same time axis, same units: seconds for latency, ratios (0–1) or percentages for errors, never mixed on one panel.
  • Show percentiles and the SLO threshold as a line on the latency panel, so the eye compares at once.
  • Annotate deploys and feature flags: most incidents start at a change.
  • Dashboards as code (Grafana JSON in Git, Jsonnet/Grafonnet, Terraform): reviewed, versioned and reproducible, instead of clicked by hand and lost.

items.title: Trade-offs
items.text:
Decision Option A Option B Rule of thumb Latency metric summary (quantiles in-process) histogram (buckets) histogram — it aggregates across pods Per-user detail metric label trace / log attribute attribute; labels must be bounded Logs free text structured with trace_id structured, always Coverage log every step log events + traces events + traces; turn on DEBUG when needed Collection pull (scrape) push (OTLP) either; OTLP is the portable default Retention keep everything long tiers: hot (days) → cold object storage tiers; metrics long, raw logs/traces short

In the interview

When you add a component to a design, name its one key metric in the same sentence — it shows you have operated systems: cache → hit ratio; queue → consumer lag / age of oldest message; database replica → replication lag; connection pool → pending acquisitions; API → RED. If asked "how do you debug a slow request across services?", the answer is distributed tracing with propagated context, then the logs of the slow span. And if you propose a metric with user_id as a label, expect the follow-up question about cardinality.

Common pitfalls

  • Unbounded labels (user_id, order_id, raw URLs): the metrics backend runs out of memory or the bill explodes.
  • Averages and averaged percentiles: use histograms, aggregate buckets, then compute the percentile.
  • Histogram buckets that miss the SLO: if the SLO is "under 2 s" and no bucket ends at 2 s, the SLI cannot be computed exactly.
  • Logging personal data and secrets: logs are copied, indexed and retained — a leak multiplier.
  • Only automatic spans: waiting inside the service (pools, locks, queues) stays invisible.
  • Dashboards nobody owns: a hundred stale panels slow down every investigation.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    REQ["one checkout:<br/>gateway → order → payment"] --> MET["metrics: RED per route,<br/>USE per pool and topic"]
    REQ --> TR["trace: spans,<br/>critical path"]
    REQ --> LOG["structured log<br/>with trace_id"]
    MET --> HIST["histograms → p99<br/>→ Estimation: percentiles"]
    MET --> CARD["bounded labels<br/>(cardinality)"]
    CARD -->|"high-cardinality detail"| TR
    TR --> WAIT["pool.acquire wait<br/>→ Little's law"]
    WAIT --> RES["timeout + bulkhead<br/>→ Reliability patterns"]
    TR --> PROF["profiles: which function<br/>→ Performance"]
    MET --> SLI["SLI per journey<br/>→ Alerting, SLOs"]

Palette components: metrics · logs · tracing · app (RED per service) · sql (USE of the connection pool) · kafka (consumer lag) · payment (client-side RED of the provider call). Scenarios: observability-stack, event-fanout (consumer lag), cascading-failure (a slow provider saturating a pool). Continues in: OpenTelemetry, Alerting, Estimation — percentiles, Estimation — queueing, Reliability — patterns, Performance — bottlenecks (flame graphs), Hands-on 8 — RED dashboard.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Four signals on a cost–detail spectrum: metrics (cheap, aggregate), traces (per request, sampled), logs (per event), profiles (per code path).
  • RED for services, USE for resources, the golden signals for anything user-facing; saturation (waiting) is the leading indicator.
  • Use histograms, aggregate buckets with sum by (le), then compute percentiles; never average percentiles.
  • Cardinality is the product of label values; keep metric labels bounded and put high-cardinality detail in traces and logs.
  • Logs must be structured and carry the trace_id; traces show the critical path, including time spent waiting; profiles show the function.
  • Design dashboards top-down: journeys/SLOs → RED → dependencies → USE.

  1. OPENTELEMETRY. Semantic conventions for HTTP metrics. ↩

  2. WILKIE, T. The RED Method: key metrics for microservices architecture. Grafana Labs, 2018. ↩

  3. GREGG, B. The USE Method. See also Systems Performance, 2nd ed. Addison-Wesley, 2020. ↩

  4. BEYER, B. et al. Site Reliability Engineering. O'Reilly, 2016. Chapter 6 — Monitoring Distributed Systems. ↩

  5. GREGG, B. Flame Graphs. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
Last year BoxOffice's biggest on-sale went down at 10:02. The team had load-tested: 200 virtual users against staging, p95 of 180 ms, "all green". In the post-mortem they found five problems with that test. Staging had a tenth of production's data, so every query hit a warm cache. The virtual users waited for each response before sending the next request, so when the system slowed down, the test politely slowed down with it and never saw the queue that real fans built. The test lasted ten minutes and never reached the point where the database connection pool ran out. Nobody had written down what "good enough" meant before running it. And the report showed averages.

Performance engineering is the discipline that prevents that post-mortem. It is not "run a tool and look at a graph": it is a method — state the objective, model the workload, generate load that behaves like real users, measure what users feel, find the one resource that limits the system, fix it, and measure again. This class teaches the method and the tools, using BoxOffice's flash sale as the running test case.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Define latency, service time, throughput, concurrency, utilization and saturation, and relate them with Little's Law.
  • Read a throughput–latency curve, locate the knee and the saturation point, and explain why latency explodes as utilization approaches 100 %.
  • Apply a performance methodology — workload characterization, the USE method, RED metrics — to find the bottleneck of a system instead of guessing.
  • Design and write smoke, load, stress, spike, soak and breakpoint tests in k6, choosing between open (arrival-rate) and closed (virtual-user) workload models, with thresholds that encode the SLOs.
  • Detect coordinated omission and other measurement errors (unrealistic data, cold caches, a saturated load generator) that make a test lie.
  • Diagnose a bottleneck with profiling (flame graphs from async-profiler and py-spy), database tools (EXPLAIN ANALYZE, pg_stat_statements) and pool sizing.
  • Plan capacity with Little's Law and headroom, and enforce performance budgets in CI.

items.title: The vocabulary of performance
items.text:
Precise words prevent most performance arguments. The Estimation class introduced them; here they become measurement targets.

Term Definition BoxOffice example Service time (S) Time a resource spends actually working on one request 4 ms of CPU and 6 ms of database time to place a seat hold Waiting (queueing) time Time a request spends waiting for a busy resource Waiting for a free connection in the pool Latency / response time (R) What the client measures: waiting + service + network POST /holds took 230 ms end to end Throughput (X) Completed requests per unit of time 1 800 holds per second Concurrency (N) Requests in the system at the same moment (in service or waiting) 120 holds in flight Utilization (U) Fraction of time a resource is busy Database CPU busy 82 % of the time Saturation Work the resource cannot serve yet — the queue length 40 requests waiting for a connection Percentile (p50, p99, p99.9) The value below which that fraction of observations falls p99 = 300 ms: 1 hold in 100 is slower than 300 ms Error rate Fraction of failed requests — including timeouts 0.3 % of holds returned 503

Three relations hold for any stable system and are worth memorizing:

  • Little's Law: \(N = X \times R\) — concurrency equals throughput times response time1. At 1 800 holds/s and 0.12 s each, there are on average 216 holds in flight: that is how many threads, connections or async slots the path needs.
  • Utilization law: \(U = X \times S\) — a database spending 0.4 ms of CPU per query (per core) at 2 000 queries/s on one core is 80 % busy.
  • Response time = service time + waiting time: tuning code shortens service time; adding capacity or reducing load shortens waiting time. Near saturation, waiting dominates.

Averages lie

A mean of 120 ms is compatible with "everyone waits 120 ms" and with "99 % wait 20 ms and 1 % wait 10 s". Users — and SLOs — live in the tail. Report percentiles from histograms (HDR or native histograms), never the average of percentiles from different machines or intervals: percentiles cannot be averaged. See Percentiles and tail latency.

items.title: The throughput–latency curve and its knee
items.text:
Every system, from one thread to a data centre, shows the same shape when you increase the load. The left plot models one inventory pod with 8 worker threads and 20 ms of mean service time — capacity 400 requests per second — as an M/M/8 queue. The right plot uses the Universal Scalability Law (USL), which adds contention (σ, waiting for shared resources) and coherency (κ, the cost of keeping shared state consistent) to the ideal linear scaling2:

\[ X(N) = \frac{\lambda N}{1 + \sigma (N-1) + \kappa N (N-1)} \] 2026-10-23T08:15:49.627961 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ 0 50 100 150 200 250 300 350 400 offered load (req/s); capacity = 400 0 50 100 150 200 250 300 350 400 response time (ms) the knee: > 75 % busy Latency vs load (M/M/8, 20 ms) mean p99 0 20 40 60 80 100 120 concurrent requests N 0 100 200 300 400 500 600 700 throughput (req/s) peak at N ≈ 40 then retrograde Throughput vs concurrency (USL) USL throughput linear (ideal)

Read the two plots together:

  1. The flat region. At low load, latency is just service time. Doubling the load barely changes it. Most systems spend most of their life here, which is why they seem fast.
  2. The knee. Past roughly 70–80 % utilization, requests start finding all servers busy and queue. Latency — and the p99 first — bends upward. The knee is the useful capacity of the system: the highest throughput at which the latency SLO still holds.
  3. Saturation. As offered load approaches capacity, queues grow without bound; latency goes vertical and timeouts turn into errors. Throughput stops growing.
  4. Retrograde scaling. With contention and coherency costs, adding more concurrency past the peak reduces throughput — threads fight over locks, caches thrash, connections time out and retry. A system pushed beyond its peak can serve fewer tickets per second than one held just below it, which is the core argument for admission control and waiting rooms.

BoxOffice: the knee is the number you plan with

If one inventory pod keeps p99 under 300 ms up to 275 req/s and collapses at 360, the capacity number for planning is 275, not 360. For an on-sale expecting 4 500 hold requests per second at peak, that means ⌈4 500 / 275⌉ = 17 pods before headroom — 22 at 75 % of the knee, 33 to survive the loss of one of three zones — and a database that can take 33 pods' worth of connections. The Capacity planning page builds this model end to end.

Try it: this playground scenario is the simplest possible system — client → app server → SQL database — running the breakpoint profile, which increases the arrival rate step by step until something breaks. Press Run and watch three numbers together: throughput, p99 latency and the utilization of each component. Note the rate at which p99 starts to bend (the knee) and which component reaches 100 % first (the bottleneck). Then give that component more capacity and run again: does the knee move, and which component becomes the new bottleneck?

Open the full playground to add a cache or read replicas and see how the curve changes.

items.title: The performance-engineering loop
items.text:
Performance work is a scientific loop, not a one-off event before launch3:

flowchart LR
    slo["1. Objectives<br/>SLOs per endpoint,<br/>expected peak"] --> model["2. Workload model<br/>mix, arrival pattern,<br/>data"]
    model --> test["3. Test<br/>k6 scenario in a<br/>production-like env"]
    test --> analyze["4. Analyze<br/>curve, USE, RED,<br/>profiles"]
    analyze --> fix["5. Change ONE thing<br/>(code, config,<br/>capacity)"]
    fix --> test
    analyze --> ship["6. Ship + budget in CI<br/>monitor in production"]
    ship --> slo
  • Objectives first. "Fast" is not a requirement. "POST /holds: p99 < 300 ms and errors < 0.1 % at 4 500 req/s" is. Without it, no test can pass or fail.
  • Change one thing at a time and re-run the same test — otherwise you cannot attribute the improvement.
  • Production closes the loop. Real traffic is the best workload model: production metrics and traces feed the next test, and the performance budget in CI keeps regressions from coming back.
Level Question Tools Micro-benchmark Is this function/data structure faster? JMH (Java), pytest-benchmark Component test How many req/s does one inventory pod sustain within the SLO? k6 against one pod, profiler attached System test Does the whole purchase path hold at the on-sale peak? k6 scenarios against a production-like environment4 Production Is it holding right now? Where is the tail coming from? RED dashboards, traces, continuous profiling, SLO alerts

In the interview

When an interviewer asks "how would you know this design handles the peak?", do not say "we would load-test it". Say what you would test and how you would read it: "An open-model k6 test at the expected peak arrival rate with the realistic endpoint mix, thresholds on p99 and error rate per endpoint, run long enough to reach steady state on warm caches; then a breakpoint test to find the knee and compute the headroom; the USE method on the database and the connection pool to find what saturates first."

Common pitfalls

  • No objective: a test without pass/fail criteria produces graphs, not decisions.
  • Testing the wrong system: tiny data sets, warm caches, a different instance size, no TLS, no gateway.
  • Closed-model tests for open-world traffic: the load generator slows down with the system and hides the queue (coordinated omission).
  • Averages and single runs: report percentiles from histograms; repeat runs and look at the variance.
  • Tuning without a bottleneck: optimizing a component at 20 % utilization changes nothing.
  • A saturated load generator: if the k6 machine is at 100 % CPU, you measured k6.

items.title: Key takeaways
items.text:
• Response time = service time + waiting; near saturation, waiting dominates. \(N = X \times R\) and \(U = X \times S\) connect the numbers.
  • Every system has a knee: plan with the throughput at which the latency SLO still holds, not with the maximum.
  • Past the peak, more concurrency can mean less throughput (USL) — admission control beats overload.
  • Performance engineering is a loop: objectives → workload model → test → analyze → change one thing → re-test → budget in CI.

  1. LITTLE, J. D. C. A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW. Operations Research, v. 9, n. 3, p. 383–387, 1961. ↩

  2. GUNTHER, N. J. Guerrilla Capacity Planning. Springer, 2007. ↩

  3. GREGG, B. Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud. 2nd ed. Addison-Wesley, 2020. ↩

  4. Grafana Labs. k6 documentation — Test types. ↩

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Vocabulary and the curve
items.text:
Q1. inventory completes 2 000 holds per second and each hold spends on average 150 ms in the service. How many holds are in progress at any moment, on average?

  • A. 13
  • B. 150
  • C. 300
  • D. 2 150
Answer

C — 300.

Little's Law: N = X × R = 2 000/s × 0.15 s = 300. This is the concurrency the path must accommodate — threads, async slots or connections — and the number of VUs a load generator needs to sustain that rate when each iteration lasts 150 ms.

Q2. A breakpoint test of POST /holds shows: up to 1 100 req/s the p99 stays under the 300 ms SLO; at 1 200 req/s the p99 is 650 ms; the maximum achieved throughput is 1 250 req/s; beyond that throughput drops. Which number should capacity planning use per deployment?

  • A. 1 250 req/s, the maximum throughput
  • B. 1 100 req/s, the knee — the highest rate that still meets the SLO
  • C. 1 200 req/s, the first point above the knee
  • D. The average of all steps
Answer

B — The knee.

At 1 200–1 250 req/s the system "works" but breaks its SLO; beyond 1 250 it is saturated and retrograde. Plan with the throughput at which the SLO holds, and then add headroom below it.

Q3. According to the Universal Scalability Law, why can throughput decrease when you add more concurrent requests past a certain point?

  • A. Because the load generator becomes slower
  • B. Because of coherency costs (κ): keeping shared state consistent grows with N², so past a peak each extra request costs more than it contributes — locks, cache invalidation, retries
  • C. Because Little's Law stops being valid at high load
  • D. It cannot: throughput always grows or stays flat
Answer

B — Coherency (and contention) costs.

The USL adds a contention term σ(N−1) and a coherency term κN(N−1) to the denominator. The quadratic term eventually dominates, producing a peak and then retrograde scaling. This is why overload makes systems less productive and why admission control (a waiting room) helps.

items.title: Methodology
items.text:
Q4. During a test, inventory has 45 % CPU, all 200 Tomcat threads busy, its Hikari pool at 10/10 active with 180 threads pending, and PostgreSQL at 35 % CPU with most sessions in wait_event = Lock: tuple. What is the bottleneck?

  • A. inventory CPU — add pods
  • B. PostgreSQL CPU — use a larger instance
  • C. Row-lock contention in the database, which makes transactions hold connections longer and exhausts the pool and the threads
  • D. The Tomcat thread pool — raise it to 800
Answer

C — Lock contention.

Following the USE method downstream: CPU is not saturated anywhere; the threads and the pool are saturated because they wait; the waits end in row locks. More pods or threads add more waiters; a bigger instance has idle CPU already. Shorten transactions, use SKIP LOCKED, and control admission.

Q5. What is the main difference between the USE and RED methods?

  • A. USE is for Java, RED for Python
  • B. USE checks each resource (utilization, saturation, errors) from the inside; RED checks each service (rate, errors, duration) as users experience it — RED tells you which service hurts, USE which resource inside it is the cause
  • C. RED replaces USE in Kubernetes
  • D. USE measures latency, RED measures CPU
Answer

B.

They are complementary. In a load test the RED metrics become the thresholds (per endpoint), and when a threshold fails, USE on the resources — including software resources such as pools and locks — locates the bottleneck.

Q6. The staging database used for a load test has 1 000 seats for one event; production will have 60 000 seats for the stadium show plus all other events. Which result is most likely to be misleading?

  • A. The error rate of GET /search
  • B. The latency of seat queries and the cache hit ratio: small tables fit in memory and make missing indexes and cold-cache effects invisible
  • C. The TLS handshake time
  • D. The size of the container image
Answer

B.

Data volume and distribution decide index depth, plan choices, whether the working set fits in memory and the cache hit ratio. Test with production-sized, production-shaped (skewed) synthetic data.

items.title: Load testing
items.text:
Q7. A closed-model test has 200 VUs with 1 s of think time. When the system's response time goes from 0.1 s to 2 s, what happens to the load the test generates?

  • A. It stays at ~182 req/s
  • B. It increases, because VUs retry
  • C. It drops from ~182 req/s to ~67 req/s — the test backs off exactly when the system struggles
  • D. It drops to zero
Answer

C.

X = N / (R + Z): 200 / 1.1 ≈ 182 req/s, and 200 / 3.0 ≈ 67 req/s. Real fans arriving from the internet do not slow down because the system did; an open model (arrival rate) keeps sending ~182 req/s and reveals the queue.

Q8. Which k6 executor implements an open workload model?

  • A. constant-vus
  • B. ramping-vus
  • C. per-vu-iterations
  • D. ramping-arrival-rate
Answer

D — ramping-arrival-rate (and constant-arrival-rate).

Arrival-rate executors start iterations on a schedule, independent of how long previous iterations take. VU-based executors are closed: each VU waits for its iteration to finish before starting the next.

Q9. An arrival-rate k6 test at 1 000 iterations/s reports dropped_iterations = 48 000. What does it mean?

  • A. 48 000 requests failed with 5xx
  • B. k6 did not have enough VUs to start iterations on schedule, so the test did not deliver the intended load — it degenerated into a closed-like test. Increase preAllocatedVUs/maxVUs (VUs ≈ rate × iteration duration) or distribute the generator
  • C. The thresholds aborted the test
  • D. The server dropped 48 000 TCP connections
Answer

B.

Dropped iterations are load that was never sent. Add a threshold dropped_iterations: ['count==0'] so such a test cannot pass, and size VUs with Little's Law.

Q10. A server freezes for 1.5 s four times in a minute. A closed-loop tester reports p99 = 1 ms; an open-model tester measuring from the intended send time reports p99 ≈ 1.4 s. Which statement is correct?

  • A. The closed-loop number is right; the open model double-counts slow requests
  • B. The closed-loop tester suffered coordinated omission: it stopped sending during the freezes, so it omitted the very requests that would have been slow; users experience the open-model number
  • C. Both are wrong because the test was too short
  • D. The difference is caused by network jitter
Answer

B — Coordinated omission.

The tester coordinated with the server's stalls: one slow sample per freeze instead of ~150. Use open-model generators (k6 arrival-rate executors, wrk2, vegeta, Gatling injectOpen), measure from the intended start time, and count timeouts at their full duration.

Q11. Which test type is designed to find memory or connection leaks?

  • A. Smoke
  • B. Spike
  • C. Soak
  • D. Breakpoint
Answer

C — Soak (endurance).

Leaks and slow growth need time. A soak test holds a realistic load for hours and is read as trends: heap after GC, open connections, latency in hour 8 vs hour 1.

Q12. A sold-out seat makes POST /holds return 409 Conflict. By default k6 counts it in http_req_failed. What should the test do?

  • A. Ignore http_req_failed entirely
  • B. Declare 409 an expected status (http.setResponseCallback(http.expectedStatuses({ min: 200, max: 399 }, 409))) so that only real failures count, and check the business outcome separately (seats held)
  • C. Retry 409s until they succeed
  • D. Remove the hold flow from the test
Answer

B.

Decide explicitly which statuses are correct behaviour. Counting 409 as errors makes a correct system fail its thresholds; counting 503 as success hides an overloaded one. A business metric such as seats_held confirms that useful work happened.

items.title: Bottlenecks and capacity
items.text:
Q13. inventory has low CPU but high latency under load. Which profile is most useful?

  • A. A CPU (on-CPU) flame graph
  • B. A wall-clock (off-CPU) profile, e.g. asprof -e wall, which also samples threads that are waiting on locks, sockets and pools
  • C. An allocation profile
  • D. No profile: add pods
Answer

B — Wall-clock.

On-CPU profiles only show running code; when the time is spent waiting, they point at whatever little CPU work exists (JSON, logging) — the wrong fix. A wall-clock profile shows that the time is spent in HikariPool.getConnection, a socket read inside a locking query, or an HTTP call inside a transaction.

Q14. In EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) you see Seq Scan on seats … Rows Removed by Filter: 5968520 and Buffers: shared read=59861 for a query that returns 8 rows. What is the most likely fix?

  • A. Increase work_mem
  • B. An index matching the filter (and the sort), e.g. a partial index on (event_id, section, row_label, seat_number) WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE', created CONCURRENTLY
  • C. Add a read replica
  • D. Raise the connection-pool size
Answer

B.

The scan reads 6 million rows and ~60 000 pages to return 8. An index that matches the predicate and the order lets PostgreSQL read the first 8 matching rows directly — in the page's example, from 412 ms to under 0.1 ms.

Q15. Holds peak at 4 500/s. One inventory pod's knee is 275 holds/s, you plan to run at 75 % of the knee, and replicas are spread over 3 zones so that losing one zone leaves enough capacity. How many pods do you need?

  • A. 17
  • B. 22
  • C. 33
  • D. 45
Answer

C — 33.

⌈4 500 / (275 × 0.75)⌉ = ⌈21.8⌉ = 22 pods for the load. To survive losing one of three zones, the remaining two thirds must still hold 22: ⌈22 × 3/2⌉ = 33. Then check the shared resources: 33 pods × a pool of 10 = 330 client connections → PgBouncer.

Q16. A team adds a k6 budget test to every pull request, but it fails randomly about once a week and developers re-run it until it passes. What is the best improvement?

  • A. Remove the test
  • B. Reduce noise (fixed arrival rate, warm-up, same runner type, automatic single retry), compare relative to main's baseline with a tolerance, and add deterministic budgets such as SQL statements per request
  • C. Raise the thresholds to 10 s
  • D. Run the full breakpoint test on every pull request
Answer

B.

A gate people do not trust is worse than no gate. Keep the PR gate short and stable, catch big regressions with a relative comparison, use deterministic checks (query counts catch N+1 reliably), and run the full campaign nightly or before events in the performance environment.

items.title: Index
items.text: The breakpoint test is done: POST /holds keeps its p99 under 300 ms up to about 1 100 requests per second, and the on-sale needs 4 500. Now what? Adding pods blindly may change nothing — or make things worse. This page is about the step between measuring and fixing: reading the results correctly, locating the limiting resource, seeing which code or query consumes it, and changing one thing at a time until the bottleneck sits where you want it.

items.title: The stepped curve
items.text:
A breakpoint test that holds each rate for a couple of minutes produces one point per step: offered load, achieved throughput, p99 and errors. The table and the plot below are typical (synthetic data with noise):

Offered (req/s)Achieved (req/s)p99 (ms)ErrorsVerdict 200201590.0 %within SLO 400396650.0 %within SLO 600594780.0 %within SLO 8008111050.0 %within SLO 10009941400.0 %within SLO 110011052370.0 %within SLO ← knee 120012046580.0 %SLO broken 1300123150005.4 %saturated ← max throughput 14001179465015.0 %saturated 16001118478930.6 %saturated 2026-10-23T08:15:49.197684 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ 200 400 600 800 1000 1200 1400 1600 offered load (req/s) 200 400 600 800 1000 1200 1400 1600 throughput (req/s) knee ≈ 1100 req/s Stepped breakpoint test of POST /holds offered = achieved (ideal) achieved throughput p99 latency 1 0 2 1 0 3 p99 (ms, log) SLO p99 < 300 ms

Three regions are visible, and each has a name you should use in reports:

  • Up to the knee (≈ 1 100 req/s): achieved = offered, p99 within the SLO. This is the usable capacity of this deployment.
  • Between the knee and the maximum: achieved still ≈ offered, but the p99 breaks the SLO — the system is working, just too slowly; queues are building.
  • Past the maximum (≈ 1 250 req/s): achieved throughput falls while offered keeps growing, requests time out, errors appear. The system is saturated and, here, retrograde: overload makes it less efficient (timeouts, retries, lock convoys).

The capacity you report is the knee: "one inventory deployment of 4 pods sustains 1 100 holds/s within the SLO; it saturates at ~1 250 and degrades beyond".

items.title: Profiling: from "which resource" to "which code"
items.text:
Metrics tell you that inventory spends its time waiting or burning CPU; a profiler tells you which code does it. Modern profilers are sampling profilers: many times per second they record the stack trace of each thread, and the code that appears in many samples is where the time goes. The overhead is low enough (typically a few percent) to profile under load, even in production.

Two kinds of profile answer different questions:

  • On-CPU profiles sample only threads that are running. They find CPU-heavy code — serialization, regexes, hashing, TLS.
  • Off-CPU / wall-clock profiles sample threads whatever they are doing, including waiting for locks, sockets and pools. When CPU is low but latency is high — the common case — only a wall-clock profile shows where the time goes.

items.title: Reading a flame graph
items.text:
A flame graph draws the sampled stacks as nested boxes1:

  • each box is a function (a stack frame); the box below it is its caller;
  • the width is the share of samples in which the function was on the stack — wider means more time;
  • the x-axis is not time: frames are sorted alphabetically to merge identical stacks;
  • look for wide boxes near the top (where time is actually spent) and for unexpectedly wide subtrees.
2026-10-23T08:15:49.324540 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ 0 % 25 % 50 % 75 % 100 % of samples HoldController.hold 100% HoldService.hold 100% TransactionTemplate.execute 91% HikariPool.getConnection 24% PricingClient.quote 28% HttpClient.send 28% SocketInputStream.read 28% SeatRepository.lockSeats 33% PgStatement.execute 33% SocketInputStream.read 33% Wall-clock flame graph of POST /holds (simplified)

Reading this wall-clock profile of POST /holds top-down: almost all the time is inside TransactionTemplate.execute — and inside it, a third of the samples wait on a socket read inside SeatRepository.lockSeats (the database is making us wait for row locks), more than a quarter wait on a socket read inside PricingClient.quote (an HTTP call inside the transaction, holding the connection and the locks), and almost a quarter wait in HikariPool.getConnection (pool exhaustion, caused by the two previous items). JSON and logging, the usual suspects, are thin slivers. A CPU flame graph of the same service would have shown mostly JSON and logging, and pointed at the wrong fix.

items.title: async-profiler for the JVM
items.text:
async-profiler is a low-overhead sampling profiler for Java that avoids the safepoint bias of older JVM profilers and produces flame graphs directly2. It attaches to a running JVM:

# distroless images have no shell: attach an ephemeral debug container that shares
# the pod's process namespace, built from an image that contains async-profiler
kubectl debug -it inventory-7f9c-x2k8p --image=<your-debug-image-with-async-profiler> --target=inventory

asprof -d 30 -e cpu   -f /tmp/cpu.html   1    # on-CPU samples, 30 s, JVM is PID 1
asprof -d 30 -e wall  -t -f /tmp/wall.html 1  # wall-clock, split by thread: includes waiting
asprof -d 30 -e lock  -f /tmp/lock.html  1    # contended Java monitors and locks
asprof -d 30 -e alloc -f /tmp/alloc.html 1    # allocation hot spots (GC pressure)

Run the profiler while the load test is at the plateau — a profile of an idle service shows only idle code. If perf_events are not permitted in the container, -e itimer (or ctimer) is a CPU-sampling fallback. The JDK's built-in Java Flight Recorder is the alternative with no extra tool (jcmd 1 JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/inventory.jfr settings=profile); open the recording in JDK Mission Control or convert it to a flame graph with async-profiler's converter.

items.title: py-spy for Python
items.text:
The assistant service is Python (FastAPI). py-spy is a sampling profiler that reads the interpreter's memory from outside the process — no code changes, no restart3:

py-spy top    --pid 1                                   # live "top" of Python functions
py-spy record --pid 1 --duration 30 -o cpu.svg          # flame graph (SVG) of running code
py-spy record --pid 1 --duration 30 --idle -o wall.svg  # include idle/waiting threads
py-spy dump   --pid 1                                   # current stack of every thread, once

In a container py-spy needs the SYS_PTRACE capability (add it to the debug container, not to the application). For asyncio code, remember that waiting coroutines are not threads: a wall-clock view of the event loop shows where the loop is blocked — the classic bug being a synchronous call (a blocking HTTP client, CPU-heavy parsing) inside an async def handler.

items.title: Continuous profiling
items.text: Profiling only during incidents means you have no "before" to compare with. Continuous profiling samples every instance all the time at low frequency and stores the profiles like metrics (Grafana Pyroscope, cloud profilers; OpenTelemetry is adding profiles as a fourth signal). It enables differential flame graphs — this version vs the previous one — which make performance regressions in a canary obvious.

items.title: Database bottlenecks
items.text: The database is the most common bottleneck of a system like BoxOffice, because it is the one component that is hard to scale horizontally and that every write must reach.

items.title: Which queries?
items.text:
Start from the aggregate, not from a guess. The pg_stat_statements extension records statistics for every normalized query:

SELECT left(query, 70)                         AS query,
       calls,
       round(total_exec_time)                  AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)       AS mean_ms,
       round(100 * total_exec_time / sum(total_exec_time) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

Sort by total time, not mean: a 2 ms query called 3 000 times per second costs more than a 2 s report run once an hour.

items.title: Why is it slow? EXPLAIN ANALYZE
items.text:
EXPLAIN shows the plan the optimizer chose; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) executes the query and reports real times, real row counts and pages read4. The seat-map query of the on-sale:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, section, row_label, seat_number, price_cents
FROM seats
WHERE event_id = 4242 AND status = 'AVAILABLE'
ORDER BY section, row_label, seat_number
LIMIT 8;
Before: no suitable index (illustrative output, simplified)
Limit  (cost=187432.10..187432.12 rows=8 width=40) (actual time=412.551..412.555 rows=8 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=2112 read=59861
  ->  Sort  (cost=187432.10..187507.10 rows=30000 width=40) (actual time=412.549..412.551 rows=8 loops=1)
        Sort Key: section, row_label, seat_number
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 26kB
        ->  Seq Scan on seats  (cost=0.00..186832.00 rows=30000 width=40) (actual time=0.031..405.127 rows=31480 loops=1)
              Filter: ((event_id = 4242) AND (status = 'AVAILABLE'::text))
              Rows Removed by Filter: 5968520
Planning Time: 0.142 ms
Execution Time: 412.601 ms

How to read it, bottom-up (the innermost node runs first):

  • Seq Scan with Rows Removed by Filter: 5968520 — PostgreSQL read all 6 million seats of all events to keep 31 480. That is the problem.
  • Buffers: … read=59861 — about 60 000 pages (8 KB each, ≈ 470 MB) came from disk or the OS cache rather than PostgreSQL's buffer cache. Under load, this is I/O saturation.
  • Sort … top-N heapsort — sorting 31 480 rows to keep 8; cheap here, but avoidable.
  • Compare estimated rows=30000 with actual rows=31480: close, so statistics are fine. A large mismatch (100× off) would point at stale statistics (ANALYZE) or correlated columns.

A partial index that matches both the filter and the sort order lets PostgreSQL read the first 8 available seats directly, in order:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY seats_available_idx
    ON seats (event_id, section, row_label, seat_number)
    WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE';
After: index scan (illustrative output, simplified)
Limit  (cost=0.43..9.87 rows=8 width=40) (actual time=0.041..0.058 rows=8 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=5
  ->  Index Scan using seats_available_idx on seats  (cost=0.43..35392.11 rows=30000 width=40) (actual time=0.040..0.055 rows=8 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (event_id = 4242)
Planning Time: 0.210 ms
Execution Time: 0.079 ms

From 412 ms to 0.08 ms and from ~62 000 pages to 5. CONCURRENTLY builds the index without blocking writes — essential on a live table. (Indexes are not free: each one slows down writes and uses memory; index what the workload model says is hot.)

items.title: Lock contention and hot rows
items.text:
When everyone wants the same seats, transactions queue for row locks. Find who waits for whom:

SELECT pid,
       pg_blocking_pids(pid)        AS blocked_by,
       wait_event_type, wait_event,
       now() - query_start          AS waiting_for,
       left(query, 60)              AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

Three changes reduce contention, in order of effort:

  1. Keep transactions short. Never call another service (pricing, payment) while holding a transaction: compute the price before BEGIN, call the payment provider after COMMIT (with an outbox or a saga — see Messaging — patterns).

  2. Do not fight for the same row. When the fan asks for "2 seats in section A", any two free seats will do. SKIP LOCKED lets concurrent transactions take different free rows instead of queuing on the first one:

    BEGIN;
SELECT id FROM seats
WHERE event_id = 4242 AND section = 'A' AND status = 'AVAILABLE'
ORDER BY row_label, seat_number
LIMIT 2
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
UPDATE seats
   SET status = 'HELD', held_by = $1, hold_expires_at = now() + interval '10 minutes'
 WHERE id = ANY($2);
COMMIT;

  3. Control admission. If 50 000 fans try to hold seats in the same second, no locking strategy makes PostgreSQL happy. A waiting room admits fans at the rate the inventory can absorb — turning contention into an orderly queue (Messaging — queues).

items.title: Sizing the connection pool
items.text:
A connection pool can be a bottleneck in both directions: too small and requests wait for a connection; too large and the database spends its time switching between hundreds of sessions, fighting over locks and memory. Size it with Little's Law — connections needed = throughput × time each request holds a connection:

Design of POST /holds Connection held for At 1 500 holds/s Per pod (10 pods) Pricing call inside the transaction 6 ms SQL + 40 ms HTTP = 46 ms 1 500 × 0.046 ≈ 69 connections busy ~7, more for bursts Pricing call before the transaction 6 ms 1 500 × 0.006 ≈ 9 connections busy ~1, keep a small pool

The first fix is not a bigger pool — it is holding the connection for less time. Then size for the database's capacity: PostgreSQL works best with a number of active connections in the order of a few times its CPU cores (HikariCP's often-quoted starting point is connections ≈ cores × 2 + effective spindles)5. Twenty pods × a pool of 20 = 400 connections is far beyond that; put PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode between the pods and the database so that hundreds of client connections share a few dozen server connections. And fail fast:

inventory/src/main/resources/application.yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10
      minimum-idle: 10            # a fixed-size pool: no ramp-up during the spike
      connection-timeout: 2000    # wait at most 2 s for a connection (the default is 30 s)

items.title: One change at a time: an optimization log
items.text:
Keep a log of every run: what changed, the new knee, and what saturated next. A bottleneck removed reveals the next one; the goal is not "no bottleneck" (there is always one) but the bottleneck in the right place with enough capacity. The log below is illustrative of a typical campaign on POST /holds:

Run Change (one per run) Knee (holds/s within SLO) What saturated next 1 Baseline: 4 pods, pool 10 400 PostgreSQL I/O (seat-map Seq Scan) 2 Partial index on available seats 700 Hikari pool: 10/10 active, 150 pending 3 Pricing call moved out of the transaction 1 100 Row-lock waits on hot sections 4 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for seat selection 1 800 inventory CPU 85 % (JSON, TLS) 5 4 → 10 pods (HPA min), PgBouncer 3 400 PostgreSQL primary CPU 80 % 6 Waiting room admitting 3 000 holds/s 3 000 admitted, p99 140 ms — by design: admission is the limit

After run 6 the bottleneck is deliberate: the waiting room's admission rate, set below the database's knee. Scaling further would require partitioning inventory by event or venue (Databases — partitioning) — a much bigger change, now justified by numbers.

In the interview

In the "bottlenecks and trade-offs" step, walk the request path and name the first resource to saturate with a number: "At 4 500 holds/s the primary database is the bottleneck — every hold is a locking write. I would keep transactions short, use SKIP LOCKED so fans do not queue on the same row, size pools with Little's Law behind PgBouncer, and put a waiting room in front so admission never exceeds what the database can take." Mentioning wall-clock vs CPU profiling and EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows you have actually found bottlenecks, not just drawn boxes.

Pitfalls

  • Profiling an idle system: profile at the load-test plateau.
  • CPU flame graphs for a waiting problem: use wall-clock (off-CPU) profiles when CPU is low.
  • Optimizing by mean query time: sort by total time; frequent cheap queries dominate.
  • EXPLAIN without ANALYZE on a slow query: estimates are not measurements.
  • Growing the pool to fix pool waits: first shorten what holds the connection; bigger pools move the queue into the database.
  • Changing three things at once: you will not know which one helped — or which one hurt.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    CURVE["stepped curve<br/>and symptoms"] --> RES["which resource?<br/>USE → Methodology"]
    RES --> PROF["which code? flame graphs,<br/>async-profiler, py-spy"]
    RES --> DBQ["which query? pg_stat_statements,<br/>EXPLAIN ANALYZE"]
    DBQ --> IDX["indexes, N+1<br/>→ Databases models"]
    DBQ --> LOCK["hot rows, SKIP LOCKED<br/>→ Databases transactions"]
    DBQ --> POOL["pool sizing by Little's Law,<br/>PgBouncer"]
    RES --> CACHE["low hit ratio, stampede<br/>→ Caching failure modes"]
    RES --> DEP["slow dependency<br/>→ Reliability patterns"]
    PROF --> LOG["one change at a time:<br/>the optimization log"]

Palette components: app (CPU, GC, thread pools, serialization) · sql (indexes, locks, connection pools) · cache (hit ratio, hot keys, stampedes) · queue (taking contended writes off the request path) · thirdparty (slow dependencies) · tracing (N+1 queries show up as dozens of identical spans) and metrics (pool and throttling counters). Scenarios: monolith (breakpoint profile: find the first resource to saturate), read-heavy-cache, flash-sale (hot seat rows). Continues in: Databases — transactions, Databases — partitioning, Caching — failure modes, Messaging — queues and pub/sub, Reliability — patterns, Capacity planning.
