items.title: Index
items.text:
It is 10:02, two minutes into the stadium on-sale. BoxOffice is holding up: the waiting room admits fans at a steady pace, inventory is at 60% of its capacity. Then the external payment provider starts answering in 4 seconds instead of 200 ms. Within a minute, order has no free threads; the gateway, waiting on order, has none either; and fans who only wanted to browse the catalog get errors. Nothing in BoxOffice is broken — no bug, no crash, no full disk. The system simply had no defence against a slow dependency, and the slowness spread until it took everything down.

This class is about building those defences, and about deciding with numbers how much failure is acceptable. Reliability is the probability that a system performs its required function without failure, under stated conditions, for a stated period of time1. In distributed systems that definition covers much more than hardware: software bugs, overloaded dependencies, network partitions, bad deploys, lost data centres and operator mistakes.

A reliable system is not one that never fails. It is one that fails gracefully, recovers quickly and limits the blast radius of any single failure — the blast radius being the set of users and components affected by one failure.

Learning objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

  • Calculate availability from MTTF and MTTR, the downtime allowed by a number of "nines", and the end-to-end availability of components in series and in parallel.
  • Explain how a slow dependency causes a cascading failure, and estimate the resources it exhausts with Little's Law.
  • Define SLIs and SLOs for BoxOffice's user journeys, and compute error budgets and burn rates.
  • Choose and configure resilience patterns — timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding and rate limiting — for a call between two services, and predict what each one does under failure.
  • Design a disaster-recovery strategy from RPO and RTO targets, choosing between backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active.
  • Plan a chaos experiment and a game day with a steady-state hypothesis and a controlled blast radius.

items.title: Roadmap
items.text:
1. This overview — availability, MTTF/MTTR, the "nines", composite availability, redundancy and failover, failure modes and cascading failures.
  2. SLIs, SLOs and error budgets — how to measure reliability from the user's point of view, set targets, and spend the budget.
  3. Resilience patterns — timeout, retry with backoff and jitter, circuit breaker, bulkhead, load shedding, rate limiting, health checks, with Resilience4j.
  4. Disaster recovery — RPO and RTO, backups, multi-AZ and multi-region, and the four DR strategies.
  5. Chaos engineering — injecting failures on purpose to prove that the defences work; game days.
  6. Quiz — check your understanding.

items.title: Slides
items.text: Click the slides and use ← → to move through them; F goes full screen and P opens the presenter view, with the notes. Open the slides in a new tab

items.title: Availability
items.text:
The most visible face of reliability is availability: the fraction of time (or of requests) in which the system works. Reliability and availability are related but not the same. A service that crashes for one second every minute fails often (poor reliability) but is still about 98% available; a service that fails once a year but takes a week to repair is very reliable and poorly available. Availability comes from two measurable quantities:

Term Full name Meaning MTTF Mean Time To Failure Average time the system runs before a failure MTTR Mean Time To Repair (or Recover) Average time to detect, diagnose and restore service after a failure MTBF Mean Time Between Failures MTTF + MTTR — the whole failure-and-recovery cycle \[ \text{Availability} = \frac{MTTF}{MTTF + MTTR} \]

BoxOffice: two ways to improve inventory

inventory crashes on average once every 30 days (MTTF = 720 h). Each time, it takes 2 hours for someone to be paged, find the problem and restart it (MTTR = 2 h).

Availability = 720 / (720 + 2) ≈ 99.72%.

  • Halve the failures (MTTF = 1440 h): 1440 / 1442 ≈ 99.86%.
  • Let Kubernetes detect the crash and restart the pod in 1 minute (MTTR ≈ 0.017 h): 720 / 720.017 ≈ 99.998%.

Recovering faster was the bigger win — and much cheaper than never failing.

Reliability work pulls one of two levers. Raising MTTF (fewer failures): testing, code review, redundancy, fault-tolerant design, careful deploys. Lowering MTTR (faster recovery): good alerts, dashboards and traces, runbooks, automatic restarts and failover, quick rollbacks. In modern systems MTTR is usually the cheaper lever, and MTTR is itself a sum — time to detect + time to diagnose + time to fix — each part attacked by a different practice (see Observability).

items.title: The "nines"
items.text:
Availability targets are quoted as a number of "nines". The table shows the downtime each target allows (year = 365.25 days, month = 1/12 of a year ≈ 30.44 days):

Availability Per year Per month Per 28 days Per week 99% ("two nines") 3.65 days 7.31 hours 6.72 hours 1.68 hours 99.9% ("three nines") 8.77 hours 43.8 minutes 40.3 minutes 10.1 minutes 99.95% 4.38 hours 21.9 minutes 20.2 minutes 5.04 minutes 99.99% ("four nines") 52.6 minutes 4.38 minutes 4.03 minutes 1.01 minutes 99.999% ("five nines") 5.26 minutes 26.3 seconds 24.2 seconds 6.05 seconds

Each additional nine is 10× less downtime, and it is not an incremental improvement: it changes how you operate. At three nines, a human can be paged, open a laptop and roll back. At four nines, the whole monthly budget is shorter than it takes to wake up; detection and recovery must be automatic. At five nines, even automatic failover must complete in seconds, and a single bad deploy can spend a year's budget.

Always state the window

"99.9%" alone is ambiguous: 43.8 minutes in a calendar month, 40.3 minutes in a 28-day window. Whenever you quote availability, say over which window — and whether it counts time or requests (see SLOs).

items.title: Composite availability
items.text:
A request crosses many components, and the availability the user sees depends on how they are combined2. Two rules cover almost every case (see also Availability math).

In series (all are needed)In parallel (any one is enough)

When a request needs every component, availabilities multiply:

\[ A_{\text{series}} = A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_n \]

Three services at 99.9% each give \(0.999^3 \approx 99.7\%\). The chain is worse than its worst link, and every synchronous dependency you add lowers the ceiling. A service can never promise more availability than the product of the dependencies it calls synchronously.

When any one of \(n\) independent replicas is enough, the system fails only if all fail together:

\[ A_{\text{parallel}} = 1 - (1 - a)^n \]

Two replicas at 99% give \(1 - 0.01^2 = 99.99\%\); three give 99.9999%. Redundancy turns mediocre components into very available ones — as long as their failures are independent. The same bug, the same bad config, the same host or the same zone breaks that assumption.

Apply both rules to the BoxOffice purchase path. The numbers are illustrative assumptions, but the shape of the result is general:

2026-10-23T08:15:50.488482 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ 0 200 400 600 800 expected minutes per month in which a purchase cannot complete + second payment provider as fallback 99.940% + SQL with automatic failover (Multi-AZ) 99.840% 3 replicas of the stateless services 99.790% 1 instance each 98.301% 26 min/month 70 min/month 92 min/month 745 min/month

Reading the chart from top to bottom:

  • With one instance of everything, the three services at 99.5% dominate: about 98.3%, over 12 hours a month without purchases.
  • Three replicas of the stateless services make them practically perfect, and the bottleneck moves to the components that are not replicated: the database and the external payment provider.
  • Automatic database failover (a standby in another zone) and a second payment provider attack those. Each step removes the current weakest link — and the next weakest becomes visible.
flowchart LR
    fan(["fan"]) --> lb["load balancer<br/>99.99%"]
    lb --> g1["gateway #1"]
    lb --> g2["gateway #2"]
    lb --> g3["gateway #3"]
    g1 --> o["order × 3"]
    g2 --> o
    g3 --> o
    o --> i["inventory × 3"]
    i --> db[("SQL primary<br/>+ standby in AZ-b")]
    o --> p1["payment provider A<br/>99.9%"]
    o -.->|"fallback"| p2["payment provider B<br/>99.9%"]

Redundancy has a price tag

Each step in the chart costs money (three times the instances, a standby database, a second provider contract) and complexity (failover logic, testing the fallback). Reliability is bought, not free: the error budget is how you decide how much to buy.

items.title: Redundancy and failover
items.text:
Redundancy only helps if traffic actually moves away from the failed component — that is failover — and if the redundant copy is ready to take it.

Pattern How it works Failover time Cost BoxOffice example Active-active All copies serve traffic; the load balancer stops sending to a failed one Seconds (health-check interval) Each copy must absorb the extra load Stateless gateway, order, catalog replicas Active-passive (hot standby) A standby receives replicated state and is promoted on failure Seconds to a few minutes Standby is paid for but idle PostgreSQL primary + synchronous standby in another zone Cold standby Copy is started (or restored) only after a failure Minutes to hours Cheapest Analytics workers, rebuilt from images

Two rules make redundancy work:

  • N + 1 (or N + 2) capacity. If the flash sale needs 6 order replicas, run 7 or 8: after losing one (or during a rolling deploy), the rest must still carry the peak. With replicas spread over 3 availability zones, losing a whole zone removes a third of capacity — plan for it.
  • Stateless where possible. Stateless services fail over trivially. State (databases, caches, queues) needs replication, and replication brings the hard questions: synchronous or asynchronous, how much data can be lost, and how to avoid two primaries at once (split brain; see Consensus). The disaster recovery page treats failover across regions.

Availability zones and regions

An availability zone (AZ) is one or more data centres with independent power, cooling and networking, a few kilometres from the other zones of the same region; latency between zones is about a millisecond. Spreading replicas across zones protects against a data-centre failure at almost no latency cost. Spreading across regions (hundreds or thousands of kilometres apart) protects against a regional disaster, but every synchronous call between regions costs tens of milliseconds.

items.title: Failure modes
items.text:
Distributed systems fail in ways a single machine does not. Partial failures — some components work and others do not — are far more common than total outages, and harder to handle.

Failure class Characteristics Handling strategy Crash (fail-stop) The process dies and stays dead Health checks, restart, failover to a replica Transient Self-resolves within seconds (network blip, leader election) Retry with backoff and jitter Slow / gray failure Still answering, but slowly or with some errors; health checks may still pass Timeouts, circuit breakers, outlier detection, latency SLIs Intermittent Appears and disappears (GC pauses, a leaking resource) Percentile latency, anomaly detection, profiling Byzantine / incorrect Returns wrong data without crashing (bit flips, corrupted cache, bug) Checksums, validation, reconciliation Correlated Many components fail together (bad deploy, expired certificate, zone outage) Gradual rollouts, diversity, multi-zone, chaos tests

The most dangerous of these is not the crash but the slow component. A crashed dependency answers immediately — with a connection error — and the caller moves on. A slow dependency holds the caller's resources while it thinks. The caller cannot tell slow from dead (see Distributed systems), so without a deadline it waits.

items.title: Cascading failures
items.text:
A slow dependency exhausts a resource in its caller — threads, connections, memory — and the exhausted caller becomes slow for its callers. The exhaustion climbs the call graph until unrelated features fail. This is the most common way microservice systems go down3.

sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fans
    participant G as gateway
    participant O as order (200 threads)
    participant P as payment provider
    F->>G: POST /orders (100 per second)
    G->>O: create order
    O->>P: charge (normally 200 ms)
    Note over P: degrades: 4 s per call
    Note over O: 100/s × 4 s = 400 calls in flight > 200 threads
    F->>G: GET /events/ev-88 (catalog)
    G->>O: (gateway threads also waiting on order)
    G-->>F: 503 — no free thread
    Note over F,G: browsing fails too, although catalog is healthy

The arithmetic is Little's Law (see Queueing): calls in flight = arrival rate × time each call takes.

Payment latency Calls in flight at 100 purchases/s order thread pool (200) 200 ms (normal) 100 × 0.2 = 20 10% busy 1 s 100 × 1 = 100 50% busy 4 s 100 × 4 = 400 exhausted: requests queue, then time out

Nothing about the purchase rate changed. A 20× increase in a dependency's latency became a 20× increase in occupied threads. When the pool is full, every route of order waits — including the ones that never call payment — and the gateway, waiting on order, fills its own pool.

Three things stop the cascade, each covered in Resilience patterns:

  • A timeout caps how long one call can hold a thread (1 s timeout → at most 100 threads, not 400).
  • A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is failing, so calls fail in microseconds instead of seconds.
  • A bulkhead gives payment calls their own limited pool, so they cannot take the threads of other routes.

Try it in the playground

The cascading-failure scenario has an app calling a slow 3rd-party API with no timeouts. Press Run and watch the app's busy threads climb, then its latency and errors, then the errors of routes that do not even use the 3rd party. Now add a timeout to the 3rd-party call and run again; then enable the circuit breaker and compare the error rate and p99 of the healthy routes. Open the full playground to try a bulkhead.

items.title: Other amplifiers
items.text:
Cascades are one example of a broader family: failures that feed themselves.

  • Retry storms. Every caller retries failed calls, multiplying the load on a dependency exactly when it is weakest (patterns).
  • Thundering herd on recovery. A service comes back and every client, cache and queue consumer hits it at the same instant; it falls over again.
  • Death spiral of autoscaling or health checks. Overloaded instances fail their health checks and are removed, so the remaining ones get more load and fail too.
  • Metastable failures. The system stays broken after the trigger is gone, because the work generated by the failure (retries, timeouts, cache misses) keeps it overloaded4. The fix is to drop load until it recovers — load shedding, retry budgets, circuit breakers.

items.title: The reliability concept map
items.text:
Reliability is not one component: it is a property you buy, piece by piece, across the whole palette. The map links each palette component (green) to the reliability concepts it carries (blue); the arrows show how the class builds up — redundancy and probes keep instances serving, patterns contain slow dependencies, DR covers what redundancy cannot, SLOs say how much is enough, and chaos proves it all works:

flowchart LR

    tp["thirdparty · payment"]:::comp -.- casc["cascading failures<br/>(Little's Law)"]:::tech
    casc --> pat["timeout, retry + jitter,<br/>circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback"]:::tech
    apigw["apigw"]:::comp -.- shed["rate limiting,<br/>load shedding"]:::tech
    hc["healthcheck"]:::comp -.- probes["liveness, readiness,<br/>startup"]:::tech
    data["sql · objstore"]:::comp -.- dr["RPO / RTO, PITR backups,<br/>DR strategies"]:::tech
    dns["dns"]:::comp -.- dr
    obs["metrics · alerting"]:::comp -.- slo["SLI, SLO, error budget,<br/>burn rate"]:::tech
    probes --> red
    pat --> shed
    pat --> chaos["chaos experiments,<br/>game days"]:::tech
    dr --> chaos
    slo --> chaos

    classDef tech fill:#2f6fed22,stroke:#2f6fed
Palette component Question it answers Concepts Taught in Scenarios lb, app Does losing a replica or a zone stop the purchase? MTTF/MTTR, nines, series vs parallel, active-active, N+1, multi-AZ this overview scale-out thirdparty, payment What if a dependency gets slow? cascading failures, timeout, retry + backoff + jitter, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback this overview, Resilience patterns cascading-failure, retry-storm, payment-system apigw Which work do we refuse under overload? rate limiting per client, load shedding by priority, waiting room Resilience patterns rate-limiter, flash-sale healthcheck Should traffic reach this instance? liveness, readiness, startup; no dependencies in liveness Resilience patterns scale-out metrics, alerting Are we reliable enough? In the interview

When you finish a design, interviewers often ask "what happens if X fails?" or "what if X becomes slow?". Answer with a chain: who calls X, what resource they hold while waiting, what the timeout is, what the fallback is, and what the user sees. For BoxOffice: "payment is called by order with a 2 s timeout, a circuit breaker and its own bulkhead of 50 concurrent calls; when it opens, the fan sees 'payment temporarily unavailable, your seats stay held for 10 minutes' — and the catalog is unaffected." Also quote availability math: "two dependencies at three nines in series cap us at 99.8%".

Common pitfalls

  • No timeout on an HTTP client, or a default of minutes: one slow dependency holds threads indefinitely.
  • Assuming independence: three replicas on the same node, or with the same bad configuration, fail together.
  • Redundancy without failover tests: a standby nobody has ever promoted is a hope, not a plan.
  • Shared pools: one thread or connection pool for every dependency lets the worst one decide for all.
  • Measuring only crashes: a gray failure (slow, partially wrong) passes health checks and hurts users.

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Availability and failure
items.text:
Q1. The catalog service fails on average every 500 hours and takes 30 minutes to recover. What is its availability?

  • A. 99%
  • B. 99.5%
  • C. 99.9%
  • D. 99.99%
Answer

C — 99.9%.

Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) = 500 / 500.5 ≈ 0.999. Notice the lever: cutting MTTR to 3 minutes (automatic restart) would give 500 / 500.05 ≈ 99.99% without changing how often it fails.

Q2. The product team asks for 99.99% monthly availability on the purchase path. What does that imply operationally?

  • A. Nothing special: it is only 0.09% better than 99.9%
  • B. About 4.4 minutes of downtime per month — less than it takes to page someone and roll back by hand, so detection and recovery must be automated
  • C. About 43 minutes per month, enough for one manual rollback
  • D. Zero downtime: deploys must be done at night
Answer

B — about 4.4 minutes per month; automation is mandatory.

Each nine is 10× less downtime: 99.9% allows ≈ 43.8 min per month, 99.99% ≈ 4.38 min. A human response (alert, wake up, diagnose, roll back) does not fit in that budget, so failover, rollback and health-based routing must be automatic — and synchronous dependencies at 99.9% (like a payment provider) make the target impossible without redundancy.

Q3. The gateway runs 3 independent replicas at 99% each, and every request also needs a database at 99.95%. What is the approximate availability of the path?

  • A. 97%
  • B. 99%
  • C. 99.95%
  • D. 99.9999%
Answer

C — about 99.95%.

The replicas are in parallel: \(1 - 0.01^3 = 99.9999\%\). The database is in series: \(0.999999 \times 0.9995 \approx 99.95\%\). Once a component is replicated, the non-replicated components dominate; the next improvement must target the database (e.g. a standby with automatic failover).

Q4. order receives 50 requests/s that call payment, and has a pool of 100 threads. Payment latency goes from 100 ms to 5 s and there is no timeout. What happens?

  • A. Nothing: 50 requests/s is well below 100 threads
  • B. About 250 calls would be in flight (50 × 5), more than the pool: order exhausts its threads and its other routes start failing too
  • C. 25 threads are used, so 75 remain free
  • D. Payment calls fail fast with an error
Answer

B — thread exhaustion and a cascade.

Little's Law: calls in flight = arrival rate × time per call. At 100 ms, 5 threads are busy; at 5 s, 250 would be — beyond the pool of 100. Requests queue, every route of order slows down (including routes that do not call payment), and callers of order start to exhaust their own pools. A timeout, a circuit breaker and a bulkhead each break this chain.

items.title: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
items.text:
Q5. Which of these is the best SLI for the seat-hold journey?

  • A. Average CPU usage of the inventory pods
  • B. Number of inventory pods running
  • C. Proportion of POST /holds requests, measured at the gateway, that return non-5xx in under 500 ms
  • D. Average latency of POST /holds over the day
Answer

C — a ratio of good events to valid events, measured near the user.

CPU and pod count are infrastructure metrics: a service can be at low CPU and fully broken. An average hides the tail (5% of fans waiting 4 s barely moves it). A good SLI says what fraction of user requests were good — fast enough and successful — and can be compared with a target.

Q6. The purchase path serves 2,000,000 requests per day with an SLO of 99.95% over 28 days. How many failed requests does the error budget allow in the window?

  • A. 1,000
  • B. 28,000
  • C. 56,000
  • D. 2,800
Answer

B — 28,000.

Requests in the window: \(2\,000\,000 \times 28 = 56\,000\,000\). Budget: \((1 - 0.9995) \times 56\,000\,000 = 0.0005 \times 56\,000\,000 = 28\,000\) failed requests.

Q7. With an SLO of 99.9% over 28 days, the error rate is steady at 0.6%. What is the burn rate, and when is the budget exhausted?

  • A. 0.6×; never
  • B. 6×; in about 4.7 days
  • C. 60×; in about 11 hours
  • D. 6×; in 6 hours
Answer

B — 6×, about 4.7 days.

Burn rate = error rate / (1 − SLO) = 0.006 / 0.001 = 6. The budget lasts the window divided by the burn rate: 28 / 6 ≈ 4.7 days. In the SRE Workbook's scheme, a 6× burn sustained over 6 hours (5% of the budget) is a paging alert.

items.title: Resilience patterns
items.text:
Q8. The gateway, order and the payment adapter each retry failed calls, with up to 3 attempts per layer. The provider is down. How many calls can one fan click generate to the provider?

  • A. 3
  • B. 9
  • C. 27
  • D. 81
Answer

C — 27.

Attempts multiply across layers: \(3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27\). Retries at every layer turn an outage into a storm exactly when the dependency is weakest. Retry at one layer (close to the dependency), cap attempts, use backoff with jitter and a retry budget, and let the circuit breaker stop retries when the dependency is known to be down.

Q9. After a database failover, 1,000 clients get a connection error at the same instant and all retry with exponential backoff (0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s…) without jitter. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?

  • A. Nothing: exponential backoff already spreads the retries
  • B. All clients retry at the same instants, creating synchronized spikes above capacity; most fail again. Full jitter randomizes each wait so retries spread out
  • C. The retries are too slow; retry immediately instead
  • D. The database must be scaled to handle 1,000 concurrent connections
Answer

B — synchronized waves; add full jitter.

Backoff without jitter keeps clients that failed together in lockstep: 1,000 requests at 0.5 s, the survivors at 1.5 s, and so on, each wave above capacity. Full jitter (\(\text{random}(0, \text{base} \cdot 2^n)\)) spreads them so most succeed in the first round.

Q10. The payment circuit breaker opens several times a day although the provider is healthy. Investigation shows that waves of declined cards (bots testing stolen cards) are counted as failures. What should be changed?

  • A. Raise the failure threshold to 95%
  • B. Remove the circuit breaker
  • C. Configure business errors such as "card declined" as ignored exceptions, so only technical failures (errors, timeouts, slow calls) count
  • D. Retry declined cards three times
Answer

C — do not count correct business answers as failures.

A declined card is a valid response from a healthy provider. Counting it opens the breaker for every honest fan. Retrying it (D) is never right: the answer is final. Breakers should count technical failures — and slow calls, to catch gray failures.

Q11. At peak, order makes 100 payment calls per second with a normal latency of 200 ms. The team sets a payment bulkhead of 50 concurrent calls. What does that give?

  • A. Payment calls are limited to 50 per second
  • B. About 20 calls are normally in flight; the bulkhead tolerates latency growing about 2.5× before rejecting, and when payment is very slow at most 50 threads wait on it, leaving the rest for other routes
  • C. 50 threads are reserved and always busy
  • D. Payment calls will be retried 50 times
Answer

B — headroom of about 2.5× and a cap on the damage.

Little's Law: \(100 \times 0.2 = 20\) concurrent calls normally. With 50 permits, latency can reach about 500 ms before calls are rejected. If payment goes to 4 s, at most 50 threads wait (instead of 400), and calls beyond that fail immediately into the fallback while seat holds and the catalog keep working.

Q12. A team adds a database check to the liveness probe of order. The database has a 20-second blip. What happens?

  • A. Nothing: Kubernetes ignores probes shorter than a minute
  • B. Every order replica fails liveness at the same time and is restarted; a 20-second database blip becomes a multi-minute outage while all JVMs boot
  • C. Only the replica that noticed the blip is restarted
  • D. The replicas are removed from the load balancer and added back when the database returns
Answer

B — a fleet-wide restart.

Liveness failure means "restart the container". A shared dependency in liveness makes all replicas fail together. Liveness should only detect a stuck process; readiness removes an instance from the load balancer (D describes readiness) — and even readiness must be used carefully with shared dependencies.

items.title: Disaster recovery and chaos
items.text:
Q13. At 22:00 a script deletes every row of orders in production. The synchronous standby in another zone replicated the delete. What restores the data, and which objective does the restore time affect?

  • A. Promote the standby; it affects the RPO
  • B. A point-in-time restore from backups (base backup + WAL replay up to 21:59:59); the restore duration determines the RTO, the archiving delay the RPO
  • C. Nothing can restore it: replication is the backup
  • D. Fail over to another region; it affects the RPO
Answer

B — PITR from backups.

Replicas (in-zone or cross-region) copy the mistake. Recovering from a logical failure needs a copy from before it: a base backup plus archived WAL replayed to the instant before the delete. RPO is bounded by how often WAL is archived; RTO by how long the restore takes — which must be measured (2 TB at 200 MB/s is almost 3 hours).

Q14. For the BoxOffice purchase path the business asks for RTO ≤ 15 minutes and RPO of seconds in case of a regional outage, at a reasonable cost. Seats must never be sold twice. Which strategy fits best?

  • A. Backup and restore in another region
  • B. Pilot light with services scaled to zero
  • C. Warm standby: databases replicated asynchronously to a second region, a scaled-down copy of the services running there, promoted and scaled up on failover (with fencing of the old primary)
  • D. Multi-site active-active with both regions accepting seat holds and replicating to each other
Answer

C — warm standby.

Backup and restore (A) takes hours; pilot light (B) needs services started and scaled from zero, which is hard to fit in 15 minutes reliably. Active-active with writes in both regions (D) risks double-selling a seat unless a globally consistent database or a home region per event is used — at a much higher cost. A warm standby meets RPO (replication lag of seconds) and RTO (detect + decide + promote + scale + DNS TTL), provided it is rehearsed in DR drills.

Q15. The team wants to verify that the payment circuit breaker really protects the catalog. Which plan is a proper chaos experiment?

  • A. Kill random production pods during the next stadium on-sale and see what happens
  • B. State the steady state (catalog p99 < 300 ms, purchase success ≥ 99.9%) and the hypothesis (with 3 s of provider latency the breaker opens within 30 s and catalog latency stays flat); inject the latency with Toxiproxy under k6 load, first in staging, with an abort condition on the burn rate
  • C. Write a unit test that mocks the breaker as open
  • D. Wait for the next real provider incident and read the postmortem
Answer

B — hypothesis, controlled injection, small blast radius, abort condition.

Chaos engineering is an experiment: predict the steady state, inject one realistic fault, observe the SLIs, compare. A (random failures during an on-sale, no hypothesis, no abort) is reckless; C does not exercise timeouts, pools and real traffic; D is waiting for production to run the experiment for you, at the worst moment.

items.title: Index
items.text:
BoxOffice now has timeouts, a retry with jitter, a circuit breaker, a bulkhead, a fallback, a warm standby region and a backup policy. Do they work? The unit tests pass. But nobody has ever seen the payment breaker open with real traffic, nobody has ever promoted the standby database, and nobody knows how long the regional failover really takes. The first time any of it matters will be during a real stadium on-sale, with two million fans watching. The only way to know is to cause the failures yourself, on purpose, while you are watching and ready.

Chaos engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in its ability to withstand turbulent conditions in production1. Instead of waiting for failures to happen, you inject them deliberately, in a controlled way, and use what you learn to fix weaknesses before real incidents find them.

"The best way to avoid failure is to fail constantly." — John Ciancutti, Netflix, 20104

items.title: Where it came from
items.text:
The idea is older than the name. At Amazon in the early 2000s, Jesse Robbins ran GameDay exercises that deliberately caused major failures in production to expose hidden weaknesses — in the software and in the teams operating it3.

Netflix gave the practice its name and its tools. After moving from its own data centre to AWS around 2010 — where any instance can disappear at any time — it built Chaos Monkey, a service that terminates random production instances during business hours, so that every team had to build services that survive instance loss, and engineers were at their desks to see what broke4. A whole Simian Army followed: Latency Monkey injected delays into calls, Chaos Gorilla simulated the loss of a whole availability zone. In 2016 Netflix engineers formalized the discipline in an IEEE Software article2, from which the principles below come.

The insight: failure is not a special case to avoid; it is the environment production systems live in, and the only way to know a system survives it is to test it there.

items.title: Principles
items.text:
The Principles of Chaos Engineering1 define the discipline with five ideas:

1. Build a hypothesis around steady-state behaviour : Describe "normal" with measurable outputs users care about — the SLIs (SLOs): purchase success rate, seat-hold p99, e-mail freshness. The hypothesis: "the steady state continues even when X happens."

2. Vary real-world events : Inject failures that actually happen: instance and zone loss, latency, packet loss, a dependency returning errors, a full disk, clock skew, a traffic spike, an expired certificate.

3. Run experiments in production : Staging rarely has production's traffic shape, data volume or dependency behaviour. Production is the goal — reached gradually, not the first step.

4. Automate experiments to run continuously : Systems change every day; a weakness fixed today can return with next week's deploy. Repeat experiments automatically.

5. Minimize blast radius : Affect as few users as possible, have an abort switch, and widen the scope only after smaller experiments pass.

items.title: The experiment lifecycle
items.text:
Each experiment follows the scientific method: predict, change one variable, measure, compare5.

flowchart LR
    H["1. Hypothesis<br/>steady state + expected behaviour"] --> D["2. Design<br/>fault, scope, abort conditions"]
    D --> I["3. Inject<br/>the controlled fault"]
    I --> O["4. Observe<br/>SLIs, traces, breaker state"]
    O --> A["5. Analyse<br/>expected vs actual"]
    A --> F["6. Improve<br/>fix, update runbooks"]
    F -->|"repeat with a wider scope"| H

An experiment that confirms the hypothesis is evidence that a defence works. One that falsifies it is a finding: a weakness discovered on your schedule, with the team ready, instead of at 10:00 on a sale day.

Experiment: the payment provider slows down

Step Content Steady state Purchase success ≥ 99.9% and seat-hold p99 < 500 ms; catalog p99 < 300 ms (gateway dashboard of Hands-on 8). Hypothesis "If the payment provider answers in 3 s instead of 200 ms, the payment circuit breaker opens within 30 s, purchases fail fast with 'payment temporarily unavailable, seats held', the bulkhead caps payment calls at 50, and catalog and seat holds keep their latency." Injection Toxiproxy between payment and the provider stub: a latency toxic of 3 s ± 0.5 s, under a k6 load of 100 purchases/s. Scope and abort Compose environment first; later one canary pod. Abort if catalog p99 > 1 s or the purchase error budget burns faster than 10×. Observe resilience4j_circuitbreaker_state, bulkhead available permits, error rate and p99 per route, order busy threads, traces of slow purchases. Possible findings The read timeout was never set, so slow calls are not counted until 60 s; the retry at the gateway multiplies calls; the fallback message is a raw 500; the bulkhead is shared with inventory calls.

items.title: Toxiproxy: chaos on your laptop
items.text:
Toxiproxy is a TCP proxy with an API to add "toxics" — latency, timeouts, bandwidth limits, connection resets — to a connection. Put it between payment and the provider stub in Docker Compose, and point payment at the proxy:

# docker-compose.yaml (excerpt)
services:
  toxiproxy:
    image: ghcr.io/shopify/toxiproxy:2.9.0
    ports:
      - "8474:8474"           # Toxiproxy API
  payment:
    environment:
      PROVIDER_URL: http://toxiproxy:8666   # instead of http://provider-stub:8080

# create the proxy: toxiproxy:8666 -> provider-stub:8080
toxiproxy-cli create -l 0.0.0.0:8666 -u provider-stub:8080 provider

# experiment 1: 3 s of latency (+/- 500 ms) on every response
toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=3000 -a jitter=500 provider

# experiment 2: connections hang forever (a "black hole")
toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t timeout -a timeout=0 provider

# end of the experiment
toxiproxy-cli toxic remove -n latency_downstream provider
toxiproxy-cli toxic remove -n timeout_downstream provider

Run k6 before, during and after each toxic and compare the numbers — that is the "Measure it" step of Hands-on 9.

items.title: Chaos Mesh: chaos on Kubernetes
items.text:
On Kubernetes, experiments are declared as resources, versioned in Git and bounded in time:

apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1
kind: NetworkChaos
metadata:
  name: payment-latency
  namespace: boxoffice
spec:
  action: delay
  mode: one                  # affect a single pod: small blast radius
  selector:
    namespaces: [boxoffice]
    labelSelectors:
      app: payment
  delay:
    latency: "3s"
    jitter: "500ms"
  duration: "10m"            # the experiment ends by itself

items.title: Controlling the blast radius
items.text:
The blast radius of an experiment is the set of users and systems it can affect. Controlling it is what separates engineering from recklessness.

flowchart LR
    S1["1. Local / Compose<br/>no users"] -->|"hypothesis holds"| S2["2. Staging under k6 load<br/>internal users"]
    S2 -->|"no findings"| S3["3. One canary pod in production<br/>a few % of traffic"]
    S3 -->|"SLIs hold"| S4["4. Wider production<br/>a zone, then a region"]
  • Abort conditions tied to SLOs: stop automatically if the error-budget burn rate passes a threshold or a key SLI drops (AWS FIS and Chaos Mesh support stop conditions; at minimum, a human with a button).
  • Time-boxed: every experiment has a duration and cleans up after itself.
  • Business hours, never during an on-sale: the team must be present; the error budget policy decides whether you can afford it.
  • Announce it: the on-call and the support team know an experiment is running.

items.title: Game days
items.text:
A game day is a planned, team-wide exercise in which failures are injected and the people respond as in a real incident. Automated experiments test the software; game days also test the runbooks, the dashboards, the alerts and the communication.

BoxOffice flash-sale game day

Goal: rehearse a stadium on-sale in staging at production scale (k6 replaying the 10:00 spike) and verify that the purchase path meets its SLOs under five failures injected one at a time.

Time Injection Expected behaviour Measure 10:00 Spike starts (no fault) Waiting room admits at the configured rate; SQL < 70% Baseline SLIs 10:10 Payment provider latency 3 s Breaker opens < 30 s; seats held; catalog unaffected Time to detect (alert), purchase error rate 10:25 One order pod killed per minute Readiness removes it; N+1 capacity absorbs it Errors during restarts 10:40 Kafka broker stopped Producers retry; outbox backlog grows and drains; no lost e-mails Outbox age, consumer lag, e-mail freshness SLI 10:55 Database failover to the standby ~30 s of errors on writes, then recovery Actual RTO vs expected 11:10 Redis cache flushed Stampede protection holds; SQL load spike stays below limit SQL CPU, catalog p99

Roles: a game master (injects, keeps time, calls the abort), the on-call responders (they are not told the schedule), observers per service, and a scribe (timeline). Afterwards: a blameless debrief (what we expected, what happened, what surprised us), with action items owned and dated.

Try it in the playground

Load the flash-sale scenario with chaos set to medium: the simulator injects random latency spikes and instance failures while the on-sale traffic runs. Press Run and watch which component degrades first and whether the SLO panel stays green. Then make your design more resilient (more replicas, a cache, a lower admission rate) and run the same seed again to compare.

Blameless culture is a prerequisite

Chaos experiments and game days only work if people can surface problems safely. If a finding leads to blame, teams stop reporting honestly and weaknesses stay hidden. The output of a game day is a list of improvements, not a list of culprits (see Incident response).

items.title: Continuous verification
items.text:
Once an experiment passes, keep it passing:

  • In CI: integration tests with Toxiproxy (Testcontainers has a Toxiproxy module) assert that the client gives up after its timeout and that the breaker opens — cheap, every build.
  • Scheduled in staging: Chaos Mesh or LitmusChaos workflows run the standard experiments nightly against the latest deploy.
  • In production, small: a recurring pod-kill on a canary, a monthly backup restore, a twice-yearly regional failover drill (Disaster recovery).

items.title: Observability first
items.text:
Chaos without observability is just breaking things. Before injecting anything you must be able to:

  1. See the steady state — SLI dashboards with baselines.
  2. Detect the deviation — alerts that fire within minutes (burn-rate alerts).
  3. Explain it — traces that show which call got slow, metrics of breakers and pools.
  4. Stop it — an abort switch that works in seconds.

Observability first, then resilience patterns, then chaos experiments to prove the patterns work.

Tool Maintained by Strengths Toxiproxy Shopify (open source) Simple TCP proxy; ideal for local and CI tests Chaos Mesh CNCF Kubernetes-native; network, pod, stress, time, I/O faults; workflows LitmusChaos CNCF Kubernetes-native; experiment hub; GitOps-friendly AWS Fault Injection Service Amazon Managed; AWS-level faults (AZ power, API errors); stop conditions Azure Chaos Studio Microsoft Managed chaos for Azure resources Gremlin Gremlin Inc. Commercial platform; broad fault library; reliability scoring Chaos Monkey Netflix Random instance termination; the original

In the interview

After proposing resilience mechanisms, add how you would verify them: "I'd run a chaos experiment with a steady-state hypothesis on the purchase SLO — inject 3 s of latency on the payment provider for one canary pod, expect the breaker to open within 30 s and catalog latency to stay flat, with an automatic abort if the burn rate exceeds 10×". It shows you know that untested failover and untested fallbacks are the most common reason resilient-looking designs fail.

Common pitfalls

  • Chaos without a hypothesis: if you did not say what should happen, you cannot learn from what did.
  • Starting in production with a large blast radius — production is the destination, not the starting point.
  • No abort switch, or an abort that depends on the system being tested.
  • Running during an on-sale or with an exhausted error budget.
  • Findings that never become tickets: the experiment consumed budget and taught nothing.
  • Testing only crashes: latency and partial failures are the ones that cascade.

items.text:
flowchart LR
    SS["steady state = SLIs<br/>→ SLOs"] --> HYP["hypothesis"]
    HYP --> INJ["inject: Toxiproxy,<br/>Chaos Mesh, AWS FIS"]
    LOAD["k6 load during the run<br/>→ Performance"] --> INJ

Palette components: thirdparty (the provider stub behind Toxiproxy) · app (order pods killed during the game day) · kafka (a broker stopped) · sql (failover to the standby) · cache (Redis flushed: stampede protection) · metrics · tracing · alerting (you cannot run chaos without them). items.title: Index
items.text:
Two bad nights, two very different disasters.

On the first, the cloud region where BoxOffice runs has a major outage: networking inside the region is degraded for hours. Every replica of every service is in that region — three availability zones, all affected. Redundancy inside the region does not help.

On the second, everything is up. At 22:00 an engineer runs a cleanup script against what they believe is the staging database. It is production: DELETE FROM orders WHERE created_at < now() — every order is gone. The PostgreSQL standby in another zone faithfully replicates the delete within milliseconds. Redundancy does not help here either; it spread the damage.

Disaster recovery (DR) is the set of strategies, tools and procedures to restore service and data after events like these — events larger than what the resilience patterns of the previous page absorb. It starts with two numbers.

items.title: RPO and RTO
items.text:
RPO — Recovery Point Objective : The maximum amount of data, measured in time, you accept to lose. RPO = 5 minutes means that after recovery, at most the last 5 minutes of writes may be missing.

RTO — Recovery Time Objective : The maximum time from the disaster until service is restored. RTO = 1 hour means fans can buy tickets again at most one hour after the failure.

flowchart LR
    lb["last good<br/>recovery point"] -->|"RPO: data lost"| d(("disaster<br/>22:00"))
    d -->|"RTO: service down"| r["service<br/>restored"]

They are business decisions expressed in minutes, and they map to money: every minute of RTO during an on-sale is lost sales; every minute of RPO is orders (and payments!) that must be reconstructed by hand or refunded. Lower numbers cost more, roughly exponentially.

BoxOffice: RPO and RTO per service

Service / data Why RPO RTO order + payment ledger Money; fans were charged ≈ 0 for confirmed payments (reconcile with the provider) 15 min inventory (seats, holds) No double booking after recovery ≈ seconds; holds can be lost, sold seats cannot 15 min catalog (events, venues) Changes are rare and can be redone 1 h 1 h (and served stale from the CDN meanwhile) search index Rebuilt from the catalog n/a (derived data) 4 h Analytics / warehouse Not customer-facing 24 h 2 days

Different data deserves different targets. Giving everything the strictest target is the most expensive possible plan.

Think first: the standby replicated the DELETE. Which number did redundancy help with?

Neither. A synchronous standby gives an excellent RPO and RTO for infrastructure failures (the primary's machine dies: promote the standby, lose nothing). For logical failures — a bad script, a buggy deploy writing garbage, ransomware encrypting rows — the standby is an exact copy of the damage. Recovering needs a copy of the data as it was before the mistake: a backup, with point-in-time recovery. Replication and backups solve different problems; you need both.

items.title: Backups
items.text:
A backup is a copy of data, kept independently from the original, from which you can restore. The kinds:

Type What it copies Restore needs Trade-off Full Everything Just it Slow and big; taken rarely (e.g. weekly) Incremental Changes since the last backup of any kind Last full + every incremental since Small and fast to take; slower to restore Differential Changes since the last full Last full + last differential In between Snapshot Point-in-time image of a disk or volume (copy-on-write) The snapshot Fast; crash-consistent unless the database is told Continuous archiving (PITR) A base backup + every write-ahead log (WAL) segment Base backup + WALs replayed up to the chosen instant Restores to any moment, e.g. 21:59:30

Point-in-time recovery (PITR) is what saves the second night. PostgreSQL continuously archives its WAL3 to object storage (with tools such as pgBackRest or WAL-G, or automatically in managed databases like Amazon RDS and Cloud SQL). To undo the 22:00 delete, restore the latest base backup and replay the WAL up to just before it:

# restore the order database to 21:59:30, just before the accidental DELETE at 22:00
pgbackrest --stanza=order --type=time "--target=2027-03-14 21:59:30-03" \
  --target-action=promote restore

RPO is then the WAL archiving delay (seconds to a minute), and RTO is the restore time, which you must estimate — and measure:

\[ t_{\text{restore}} \approx \frac{\text{base backup size}}{\text{restore throughput}} + \frac{\text{WAL to replay}}{\text{replay throughput}} \]

BoxOffice: how long does the restore take?

The order database has 2 TB. Restoring from object storage at 200 MB/s takes \(2\,000\,000 / 200 = 10\,000\) s ≈ 2.8 hours, before replaying a day of WAL. That breaks the 15-minute RTO. Options: restore into a database that is already provisioned and close to the target (smaller daily base backups, faster storage), keep a delayed replica (a standby that applies WAL with a 1-hour delay, so a mistake can be caught before it reaches it), or split the data so the critical part (open orders, the payment ledger) is small. The number decides the design.

items.title: Rules for backups that actually work
items.text:
• 3-2-1: at least 3 copies of the data, on 2 different kinds of storage, 1 of them off-site (another region or account). Modern practice adds one immutable copy (object lock / WORM — write once, read many) that even an attacker with admin credentials cannot delete, against ransomware.
  • Separate the blast radius. Backups in the same account, with the same credentials, as production can be deleted by the same mistake or the same attacker.
  • Encrypt backups and manage the keys separately; a backup is a full copy of your customers' data (LGPD/GDPR apply).
  • Test restores regularly. A backup that has never been restored is a hope. Automate a periodic restore into a scratch environment and check the data (row counts, checksums, a smoke test of the application).
  • Monitor backup jobs and WAL archiving lag; alert when they fail or fall behind.

The GitLab lesson

In January 2017, GitLab.com lost about six hours of production database data after an engineer deleted the data directory on the wrong server during an incident. Of the several backup and replication mechanisms in place, none could be used as intended — some had been silently failing for a long time. The company published a candid postmortem4 that is worth reading: backups you do not test are not backups.

items.title: Multi-AZ and multi-region
items.text:
Multi-AZ (one region) Multi-region Protects against Loss of a data centre / zone Loss of a whole region; some regional dependencies Distance and latency Kilometres, ~1 ms Hundreds to thousands of km, tens of ms or more Replication Synchronous is affordable (RPO ≈ 0) Usually asynchronous (RPO = replication lag) Failover Automatic, seconds to minutes (managed databases do it) A bigger decision: DNS, data, capacity; minutes to hours Cost Moderate High: a second copy of (part of) everything, plus data transfer Complexity Low High: data consistency, deploys to two regions, testing

Synchronous replication across regions puts a cross-region round trip in every write: \(\approx 30\)–\(100\) ms per commit is often unacceptable for the seat-hold path. So multi-region DR usually means asynchronous replication, and an RPO equal to the replication lag at the moment of the disaster. That is why "RPO = 0 across regions" is either very expensive (synchronous replication, or a globally consistent database such as Spanner or CockroachDB paying the latency) or a misunderstanding.

Multi-region is also a legal question: personal data may be subject to residency rules (LGPD in Brazil, GDPR in the EU), which constrain which regions can hold the copy.

items.title: The four DR strategies
items.text:
The AWS disaster-recovery whitepaper describes a spectrum of four strategies, from cheap and slow to expensive and instant1. The same ideas apply on any cloud2.

Strategy What runs in the recovery region before the disaster Typical RPO Typical RTO Cost Backup and restore Nothing but backups (and infrastructure as code) Hours Hours to a day $ Pilot light Data replicated continuously; core infrastructure provisioned but off or at minimum (no app servers) Minutes Tens of minutes to hours $$ Warm standby A complete, scaled-down copy running and serving nothing (or test traffic) Seconds to minutes Minutes $$$ Multi-site active-active Full copies in two or more regions, all serving production traffic ≈ 0 to seconds ≈ 0 (traffic shifts) $$$$ Backup and restorePilot lightWarm standbyMulti-site active-active 
flowchart LR
    subgraph A ["Region A (primary)"]
        appA["services"] --> dbA[("databases")]
    end
    subgraph B ["Region B (recovery)"]
        bk[("backups + WAL<br/>(object storage)")]
        iac["infrastructure as code<br/>(nothing running)"]
    end
    dbA -->|"backups, WAL archive"| bk

After a disaster, create the infrastructure from code, restore the databases, deploy the services, switch DNS. Cheapest; RTO dominated by restore time and by how well-rehearsed the procedure is.

flowchart LR
    subgraph A ["Region A (primary)"]
        appA["services"] --> dbA[("databases")]
    end
    subgraph B ["Region B (recovery)"]
        dbB[("database replicas<br/>(running)")]
        appB["services<br/>(off: 0 replicas)"]
    end
    dbA -->|"async replication"| dbB

The "pilot light" is the data, always on and current. On a disaster, promote the replicas, start the services (scale from 0), switch DNS.

flowchart LR
    subgraph A ["Region A (primary, 100%)"]
        appA["services × 12"] --> dbA[("databases")]
    end
    subgraph B ["Region B (standby, ~10%)"]
        appB["services × 2<br/>(running, idle)"] --> dbB[("replicas")]
    end
    dbA -->|"async replication"| dbB

Everything already runs in region B at small scale and is continuously tested. On a disaster, promote, scale up, switch traffic. Scaling up must not depend on region A (images, secrets, quotas available in B).

flowchart LR
    dns["GeoDNS / global LB"] --> A
    dns --> B
    subgraph A ["Region A (serving)"]
        appA["services"] --> dbA[("data")]
    end
    subgraph B ["Region B (serving)"]
        appB["services"] --> dbB[("data")]
    end
    dbA <-->|"replication both ways"| dbB

Both regions serve users all the time; losing one means sending its traffic to the other (which must have the capacity). The hard part is the data: two regions accepting writes to the same records need conflict resolution or a globally consistent database.

items.title: Active-active and the seat inventory
items.text:
Active-active is easy for read-mostly data: the catalog can be read in any region from local replicas and the CDN. It is hard for data with strong invariants: if São Paulo and Virginia both accept holds for seat B-12 and replicate asynchronously, two fans can buy the same seat — exactly what BoxOffice must never do (see Consistency). The options:

  • Home region per entity: each event (show) is owned by one region; all holds and sales for it go there; the other region is its warm standby. Fans in other regions pay a little latency for that show. Ownership moves only during a failover.
  • A globally consistent database (Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB): consensus across regions on every write, at the cost of cross-region latency on the seat-hold path.
  • Multi-leader with conflict resolution (last-writer-wins, CRDTs): fine for a shopping cart or a "favorites" list, unacceptable for seats.

items.title: Failover between regions
items.text:
A regional failover is a sequence of steps, each with a duration that adds to the RTO:

sequenceDiagram
    participant M as external monitors
    participant OC as on-call
    participant DNS as DNS (health-checked)
    participant A as region A
    participant B as region B (warm standby)
    Note over A: region degraded at 22:00
    M->>OC: purchase probes failing from 3 locations (2 min)
    OC->>OC: confirm it is regional, declare disaster (5 min)
    OC->>A: fence: stop writes in A (if reachable)
    OC->>B: promote database replicas (1 min)
    OC->>B: scale services from 2 to 12 replicas (5 min)
    OC->>DNS: point boxoffice.example to region B
    Note over DNS: clients follow after the TTL (60 s)
    DNS-->>B: traffic arrives, RTO ≈ 14 min
\[ \text{RTO} \approx t_{\text{detect}} + t_{\text{decide}} + t_{\text{promote}} + t_{\text{scale}} + t_{\text{DNS TTL}} \]

Points that decide whether it works:

  • Detection from outside. Probes that run inside the failing region may fail with it. Use external synthetic checks of the purchase journey.
  • Automatic or human decision? Automatic failover is fast but risky: a network blip that triggers a regional failover (and then a failback) can cause more damage than it prevents ("flapping"). Many teams automate within a region and keep a human decision, with a rehearsed runbook, across regions.
  • Fencing. Before the standby accepts writes, make sure the old primary cannot (revoke its credentials, stop it, or use a lease). Two primaries accepting holds is split brain: double-sold seats.
  • DNS TTL. Clients and resolvers cache DNS answers for the TTL; a 1-hour TTL means a 1-hour tail of traffic going to the dead region. Health-checked DNS records (e.g. Amazon Route 53 failover records) with short TTLs on the entry point (see DNS and CDN).
  • Static stability. The recovery region must not depend on the failed one: container images, secrets, configuration and capacity quotas must already be in region B.
  • Failback. Coming back is another migration: resynchronize data from B to A, then switch at a quiet time. Plan and rehearse it too.

Try it in the playground

The multi-region scenario has DNS failover between two regions. Run it with the load profile, then trigger a region outage on the primary. Watch the error rate until the DNS health check fails over, and note how long it takes. Change the DNS TTL and the health-check interval and measure the new recovery time; then reduce the standby region's capacity and see what happens to latency right after the failover.

items.title: The BoxOffice DR plan
items.text:
Tier Services Strategy RPO RTO Tier 0 — revenue order, payment, inventory Multi-AZ synchronous standby in the region + warm standby in a second region (async replication), PITR backups with 35-day retention, immutable copy in another account Seconds (in region: 0) 15 min Tier 1 — browsing catalog, gateway, auth, waiting room Active-active reads (CDN + replicas in both regions); catalog writes only in the primary 1 h for catalog edits 5 min (mostly DNS) Tier 2 — derived search, notification Pilot light: rebuild the index from the catalog; replay unsent notifications from Kafka Derived / replayable 4 h Tier 3 — internal analytics, warehouse Backup and restore 24 h 2 days

And the practices that keep the plan honest:

  • A runbook per scenario (region loss, database corruption, compromised account) with the exact commands, owners and the decision criteria.
  • DR drills twice a year: actually fail over to region B for an hour in a quiet period, and restore a production backup into a scratch environment every month. The chaos engineering page covers how to run them as game days.
  • Review RPO/RTO with the business yearly: the stadium contract may demand more, or the analytics tier may accept less.

In the interview

When asked "what if the region goes down?" or "what if someone deletes the table?", start with RPO and RTO per data class — then pick the cheapest strategy that meets them. Distinguish clearly: replication protects against infrastructure loss, backups with PITR against logical corruption. For a system with strong invariants (seats, balances), say why active-active is hard (conflicting writes) and propose a home region per entity with a warm standby. Quote the RTO as a sum of steps, including the DNS TTL.

Common pitfalls

  • "We have replicas, so we have backups." Replicas copy the mistake.
  • Never testing a restore — or measuring its time only during the disaster.
  • Backups in the same account and region as production, deletable by the same credentials.
  • A recovery region that depends on the failed region (images, secrets, the CI system, the DNS provider's control plane in that region).
  • Ignoring capacity: a warm standby that cannot scale up because the region has no spare quota on a busy day.
  • No fencing: the old primary comes back and accepts writes — split brain, double-sold seats.

items.title: How it connects
items.text:
flowchart LR
    BIZ["RPO and RTO<br/>per data class"] --> STRAT["backup and restore · pilot light ·<br/>warm standby · active-active"]
    INFRA["infrastructure loss<br/>(zone, region)"] --> REPL["replication, multi-AZ<br/>→ Databases — replication"]
    LOGIC["logical corruption<br/>(the bad DELETE)"] --> PITR["PITR backups, 3-2-1,<br/>immutable copy"]
    REPL --> STRAT
    PITR --> STRAT
    STRAT --> AA["active-active vs the seat invariant<br/>→ Distributed — consistency"]
    STRAT --> FO["regional failover:<br/>detect, fence, promote, scale"]
    FO --> FENCE["fencing, no split brain<br/>→ Distributed — consensus"]
    FO --> DNS["health-checked DNS, short TTL<br/>→ Edge — DNS"]
    FO --> DRILL["DR drills, restore tests<br/>→ Chaos engineering"]

Palette components: sql (standby, replicas, PITR) · objstore (base backups and the WAL archive) · dns (failover records and TTL) · cdn (serves the catalog stale while the origin recovers) · kafka (replays unsent notifications) · app (scaled from 2 to 12 replicas in the standby region). Scenarios: multi-region, db-replicas.
