items.title: Index
items.text:
When a dependency degrades, the naive default — keep sending requests and wait for the answer — reliably produces the cascade of the overview: the caller's threads block, its queue fills, and the failure climbs to users who had nothing to do with the broken dependency. Resilience patterns are design decisions that interrupt this propagation. They do not prevent failures; they limit how far a failure travels1.

Throughout this page we follow one call of BoxOffice: order calls payment, the adapter in front of the external payment provider, to charge a fan's card during the purchase saga (see Messaging — patterns). It is the most dangerous call in the system: it is on the revenue path, it crosses the internet to a third party, and the third party's bad day becomes ours.

Pattern Question it answers Protects against Timeout How long am I willing to wait? Hanging calls holding resources Retry with backoff and jitter Is it worth trying again — when? Transient failures Circuit breaker Should I even try? Hammering a dependency known to be down Fallback What do I answer instead? Losing a whole page for one feature Bulkhead How much of my capacity may one dependency take? Exhaustion spreading between features Load shedding Which work do I refuse when overloaded? Collapse under overload Rate limiting How much does each client get? Abusive clients, bots, spikes Health checks Should traffic reach this instance? Routing to broken instances

items.title: Timeout
items.text:
A timeout is a deadline on an outbound call: if the answer has not arrived in time, the caller abandons it and handles the error. Without a timeout, a hanging dependency holds a thread (and a connection, and memory) indefinitely; with one, the damage a single slow call can do is bounded.

sequenceDiagram
    participant O as order
    participant P as payment adapter
    participant X as payment provider
    O->>+P: POST /charges (deadline 2 s)
    P->>+X: charge card
    Note over X: provider is slow today
    Note over O: 2 s elapsed: give up, free the thread
    O-->>O: handle the error (retry? fallback?)
    X-->>-P: (answer arrives at 4 s)
    P-->>-O: (too late: discarded)

How to choose the value:

  • From the dependency's latency distribution. Set it a little above the p99.9 of normal operation: anything slower is already abnormal. For the provider, with p99.9 ≈ 1.2 s, a 2 s timeout.
  • Two timeouts per HTTP call: the connect timeout (opening the TCP/TLS connection — short, a few hundred milliseconds) and the read timeout (waiting for the response).
  • Per dependency. A cache lookup, a database query and a third-party API have latencies that differ by orders of magnitude. One global timeout is always wrong for most of them.
  • Inside the caller's budget. If the fan's request has 6 s at the gateway, everything below must fit in it, including retries.

items.title: Deadline propagation
items.text:
Timeouts must shrink as a request goes deeper. A deadline set at the edge and propagated with the request (gRPC does this natively with deadlines; over HTTP, a header such as the remaining budget) lets each service know how much time is left, and stop working on a request whose caller has already given up.

Layer Budget Spent on Gateway 6 s everything below + its own work order (purchase handler) 5 s seat-hold check (≤ 300 ms) + payment (≤ 4.5 s) order → payment 2 s per attempt × 2 attempts + backoff ≈ 4.3 s the provider call payment → provider 1.8 s leaves margin for the adapter's own work

Timeouts are only the first step

A timeout converts a hang into a fast error. You still need to decide what to do with the error: retry it (if transient and safe), stop calling for a while (circuit breaker), or answer something else (fallback). And a timeout on a non-idempotent call leaves an unknown outcome — the charge may have succeeded — which is why payment calls carry an idempotency key (see Integrations).

items.title: Retry with backoff and jitter
items.text: A retry repeats a failed call, betting that the failure was transient: a dropped connection, a pod restarting, a leader election. Retries turn many small blips into invisible ones. Done carelessly, they are also the fastest way to turn a small problem into an outage.

items.title: What to retry
items.text: Failure Retry? Why Connection refused / reset, connect timeout Yes Typical transient failure; the request probably never ran Read timeout Only if the operation is idempotent (or has an idempotency key) The request may have run 503 Service Unavailable, 429 Too Many Requests Yes, with backoff; respect Retry-After The server is asking you to come back later 500 Internal Server Error At most once Often a bug that fails again 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422; "card declined" Never The request itself is wrong or the answer is final

items.title: Exponential backoff and jitter
items.text:
Retrying immediately hits a struggling dependency again before it had any chance to recover. Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure:

\[ \text{wait}_n = \min\left(\text{base} \cdot 2^{n},\ \text{cap}\right) \]

With base 200 ms: 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms, … up to the cap. But if many clients failed at the same moment (the provider blipped for everyone), they all retry at the same moments too — synchronized waves. Jitter randomizes the waits; Marc Brooker's analysis at AWS recommends full jitter2:

\[ \text{wait}_n = \text{random}\left(0,\ \min\left(\text{base} \cdot 2^{n},\ \text{cap}\right)\right) \]

items.title: Retries amplify load
items.text:
The simulation below has two experiments with illustrative numbers. On the left, steady purchase traffic (1,000 requests/s) meets a payment provider that degrades for 5 seconds; an overloaded server wastes part of its capacity on requests that time out anyway. On the right, 1,000 clients fail at the same instant (say, a connection reset during a failover) and retry against a server that can take 150 requests per 100 ms.

2026-10-23T08:15:50.727684 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ 0 10 20 30 40 50 60 seconds 0 200 400 600 800 1000 1200 Successful requests/s (shaded: provider slow) no retries 3 retries, backoff + jitter same + retry budget (10%) 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 seconds 0 200 400 600 800 1000 capacity Retries per 100 ms after 1,000 clients fail together backoff + full jitter exponential backoff, no jitter
  • Left — retries can keep a system down. Without retries (grey), successes drop during the degradation and come back the moment it ends. With 3 retries per request (red), each failure becomes up to 4 calls; the extra load keeps the provider overloaded after the trigger is gone, and the system settles in a degraded state — a metastable failure (see the overview). Backoff and jitter do not fix this: they spread retries in time but do not reduce their number. A retry budget (blue) — retries may add at most 10% to the normal traffic — caps the amplification and the system recovers immediately.
  • Right — jitter prevents synchronized waves. Without jitter (orange), all clients that failed together retry together: 1,000 calls in one 100 ms slot, only 150 succeed, the other 850 retry together again… after 15 seconds 250 clients still have not succeeded. With full jitter (blue), the same retries are spread below the capacity line and everyone succeeds in about 1.5 s.

Three rules follow:

  1. Retry at one layer only. If the gateway, order and the payment adapter each retry 3 times, one fan click can become \(3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27\) calls to the provider. Retry close to the failing dependency and let upper layers fail fast.
  2. Cap attempts and total time: few attempts (1–2 retries), all inside the caller's deadline.
  3. Use a retry budget (Envoy, gRPC retry throttling, Finagle): retries are allowed only while they are a small fraction of requests. When the dependency is really down, retries stop by themselves.

Try it in the playground

The retry-storm scenario has clients retrying failed calls with no backoff against a service that suffers a short outage. Press Run and watch the request rate to the service jump to several times the client rate during the outage, and the service stay overloaded after it should have recovered. Then switch the retry policy to exponential backoff with jitter and add a retry budget, and compare the recovery time.

Never retry a non-idempotent call without an idempotency key

Retrying POST /charges after a read timeout can charge the fan twice: the first attempt may have succeeded. The order service sends an Idempotency-Key (the order id) with every charge; the adapter and the provider return the stored result for a key they have already seen. See Messaging — delivery semantics and Integrations.

items.title: Circuit breaker
items.text:
A circuit breaker watches the outcomes of calls to a dependency. When the failure rate crosses a threshold, it opens and rejects calls immediately, without touching the network, for a while; then it lets a few probe calls through to test recovery3.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Closed
    Closed --> Open : failure or slow-call rate ≥ 50% (last 20 calls)
    Open --> HalfOpen : after 30 s
    HalfOpen --> Closed : 3 probe calls succeed
    HalfOpen --> Open : a probe fails

Closed (normal) : Calls pass through; the breaker records successes, failures and slow calls in a sliding window.

Open (failing fast) : Calls fail immediately (CallNotPermittedException in Resilience4j). The caller's threads are free, and the dependency gets breathing room instead of a retry storm.

Half-open (testing) : After the wait duration, a few calls are allowed. If they succeed, the breaker closes; if not, it opens again.

Parameter BoxOffice value for payment Effect Sliding window last 20 calls (count-based) How much history decides Minimum calls 10 Avoids opening on 1 failure out of 2 Failure-rate threshold 50% Sensitivity Slow-call threshold 1.5 s, slow-call rate 50% A slow provider also opens the breaker — essential against gray failures Wait in open state 30 s Time the dependency gets to recover Calls in half-open 3 How carefully recovery is tested

Which errors count matters: a declined card is a correct answer from a healthy provider, not a failure. Configure it as ignored, or a wave of declined cards on a stolen-card attack would open the breaker for every honest fan.

items.title: Fallback and graceful degradation
items.text:
Failing fast is better than hanging, but an error is still an error. A fallback is what the caller does instead. The goal is graceful degradation: lose a feature, not the page.

Dependency down BoxOffice fallback Recommendations ("fans also bought") Hide the widget, or show a static "popular this week" list from the cache Search Serve the last cached results; show "results may be a few minutes old" Seat-map rendering service Show the best-available selector ("2 seats, sector B") instead of the interactive map notification Nothing to do synchronously: the event is already in Kafka and will be delivered later payment No fake success. Keep the seats held, tell the fan "payment temporarily unavailable — your seats are held for 10 minutes, try again", and let the saga retry or release

A fallback must be safe and simple

A fallback that calls another remote service can fail too and needs its own protection. Some operations — charging a card, confirming a seat — must never be faked: failing clearly is the graceful behaviour. And test your fallbacks; a fallback first exercised during an outage usually fails.

items.title: Bulkhead
items.text:
A bulkhead — named after the watertight compartments of a ship — gives each dependency its own limited pool of threads, connections or concurrent calls, so one slow dependency cannot consume the capacity of the others.

flowchart LR
    req["order: 200 request threads"] --> bp["payment bulkhead<br/>max 50 concurrent"]
    req --> bi["inventory bulkhead<br/>max 40 concurrent"]
    req --> bc["catalog bulkhead<br/>max 20 concurrent"]
    bp --> pay["payment<br/>(slow: 4 s)"]
    bi --> inv["inventory<br/>(healthy)"]
    bc --> cat["catalog<br/>(healthy)"]

Sizing comes from Little's Law again. At 100 purchases/s and 200 ms per charge, about 20 calls are in flight. A bulkhead of 50 leaves room for latency to grow 2.5× before calls are rejected; when the provider goes to 4 s, at most 50 threads wait on it (instead of 400), and the other 150 keep serving holds, order pages and everything else. Rejected calls fail in microseconds and go to the fallback.

Resilience4j offers a semaphore bulkhead (limits concurrent calls on the caller's threads; cheap, the default) and a thread-pool bulkhead (runs calls on a dedicated pool). The idea is general: separate connection pools per workload in a database, separate Kafka consumer groups, separate deployments for critical and non-critical traffic, separate queues for confirmations and marketing e-mails.

items.title: Load shedding
items.text:
When demand exceeds capacity, some requests will fail. Load shedding decides which and makes them fail early and cheaply, so the rest succeed. Without it, the server accepts everything, every request gets slow, most time out after consuming resources, and goodput collapses — everyone fails4.

  • Shed at the door. Reject with 503 + Retry-After before doing any work: a rejection costs microseconds, a timed-out request costs its full processing.
  • Shed by priority. During the stadium on-sale, BoxOffice classifies traffic: purchase and seat-hold requests are critical; catalog browsing is important; recommendations, autocomplete and "related events" are sheddable. Under overload, the sheddable go first.
  • Shed stale work. A request that already waited longer than its caller's deadline is useless; drop it from the queue instead of processing it (bounded queues with deadlines, LIFO under overload).
  • Adapt the limit. Instead of a fixed concurrency limit, adaptive limiters (inspired by TCP congestion control, e.g. Netflix's concurrency-limits library) lower the number of concurrent requests when latency rises and raise it when latency is healthy.

BoxOffice: the waiting room is load shedding

The flash-sale waiting room is load shedding done kindly: instead of rejecting fans, it admits them at the rate the system can serve and tells the others their position. Behind it, the gateway still sheds sheddable routes when order latency rises, as a second line of defence.

items.title: Rate limiting
items.text:
Rate limiting caps how many requests a client (an IP, a user, an API key, a partner) may send in a time window. Load shedding protects the server from total overload; rate limiting protects it from individual clients — bots refreshing the seat map hundreds of times per second, a partner's buggy integration, a scraper.

The common algorithm is the token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate (the sustained limit), the bucket's size allows short bursts, and each request takes a token; an empty bucket means 429 Too Many Requests. Limits per user or API key live in the API gateway, backed by a shared store such as Redis, where the authenticated identity is known. Algorithms (token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window) and their implementation are covered in Edge — API gateway; the rate-limiter playground scenario shows a gateway protecting a backend.

items.title: Health checks
items.text:
Health checks let orchestrators and load balancers stop sending traffic to broken instances — automatic failover at the smallest scale.

Liveness : Is the process alive and not stuck? If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container.

Readiness : Can this instance serve traffic now? If it fails, the instance is removed from the load balancer without being restarted (warming up, overloaded, lost its own database connection).

Startup : Has the application finished starting? Liveness and readiness are not checked until it succeeds, so a slow-starting JVM is not killed during boot.

# order Deployment, container spec (Spring Boot Actuator endpoints)
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 30        # up to 150 s to start
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 2

Never put dependencies in the liveness check

If order's liveness checks the payment provider and the provider blips, Kubernetes restarts every order replica at once — turning a third-party hiccup into a full BoxOffice outage while the JVMs boot. Liveness answers only "is this process stuck?". Be careful with readiness too: if every replica depends on the same database, they all become unready together and the service vanishes instead of returning clear errors.

items.title: Putting it together
items.text:
The patterns are layered. For the order → payment call, BoxOffice uses all of them, configured with Resilience4j5:

application.yamlPaymentClient.javaTimeouts (RestClient) 
resilience4j:
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      payment:
        max-concurrent-calls: 50          # Little's Law: 20 in flight normally
        max-wait-duration: 10ms           # do not queue: reject and fall back
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      payment:
        sliding-window-type: COUNT_BASED
        sliding-window-size: 20
        minimum-number-of-calls: 10
        failure-rate-threshold: 50
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 1500ms
        slow-call-rate-threshold: 50      # a slow provider also opens the breaker
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s
        permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 3
        ignore-exceptions:
          - boxoffice.payment.CardDeclinedException   # a correct answer, not a failure
  retry:
    instances:
      payment:
        max-attempts: 2                   # 1 call + 1 retry, at this layer only
        wait-duration: 200ms
        enable-exponential-backoff: true
        exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2
        enable-randomized-wait: true      # jitter
        randomized-wait-factor: 0.5
        retry-exceptions:
          - org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException   # I/O errors, timeouts
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException$ServiceUnavailable
        ignore-exceptions:
          - boxoffice.payment.CardDeclinedException

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentClient {

    private final RestClient payment;

    @Bulkhead(name = "payment")
    @CircuitBreaker(name = "payment", fallbackMethod = "unavailable")
    @Retry(name = "payment")
    public PaymentResult charge(ChargeRequest req) {
        return payment.post().uri("/charges")
            .header("Idempotency-Key", req.orderId())   // a retry never charges twice
            .body(req)
            .retrieve()
            .body(PaymentResult.class);
    }

    // Called when the call fails, the breaker is open or the bulkhead is full.
    private PaymentResult unavailable(ChargeRequest req, Throwable t) {
        return PaymentResult.temporarilyUnavailable(req.orderId());  // seats stay held
    }
}

@Bean
RestClient paymentRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {
    HttpClient http = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))          // connect timeout
        .build();
    JdkClientHttpRequestFactory factory = new JdkClientHttpRequestFactory(http);
    factory.setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));       // read timeout per attempt
    return builder.baseUrl("http://payment:8080").requestFactory(factory).build();
}

How the layers interact — check these before shipping:

  • Order of the decorators. Resilience4j's Spring Boot default is Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter ( Bulkhead ( call ) ) ) ) ): the retry is outermost, so every attempt is counted by the breaker and an open breaker makes the retry fail immediately. Make sure retries never bypass the breaker.
  • Time budget. 2 attempts × 2 s + one backoff of ~200–300 ms ≈ 4.3 s, inside order's 5 s budget and the gateway's 6 s.
  • Metrics. Resilience4j exports breaker state, bulkhead saturation and retry counts through Micrometer; graph them next to the SLO dashboard (Hands-on 8), because a breaker that opens is an incident in progress.
  • Proof. None of this is trustworthy until you have injected the failure and watched it work — chaos engineering and Hands-on 9.

Try it in the playground

Open the cascading-failure scenario in full mode. Run it once as it is (no protection) and note the error rate of the healthy routes. Then add, one at a time, a timeout, a circuit breaker and a bulkhead on the 3rd-party call, running after each change. Which one protects the healthy routes the most? What does each cost the requests that need the 3rd party?

Layer Handles BoxOffice setting Rate limiting (gateway) Abusive clients, bots per-account token bucket Load shedding (gateway) Overload shed recommendations/autocomplete first Bulkhead One slow dependency eating all threads 50 concurrent payment calls Circuit breaker A dependency known to be failing or slow 50% failures or slow calls over 20 calls, open 30 s Timeout Unbounded waiting 300 ms connect, 2 s read Retry + backoff + jitter Transient errors 1 retry, 200 ms ± 50%, idempotency key Fallback What the fan sees "payment temporarily unavailable, seats held"

In the interview

When a design has a call to a third party or a critical dependency, volunteer the protection stack in one breath: "timeout at roughly the p99.9, one retry with jittered backoff and an idempotency key, a circuit breaker that also counts slow calls, a bulkhead sized with Little's Law, and a fallback that tells the user the truth". Then justify one number (the bulkhead or the timeout) with arithmetic. If asked about overload, distinguish rate limiting (per client) from load shedding (whole system, by priority), and mention retry amplification across layers.

Common pitfalls

  • Default timeouts of minutes (or none) in HTTP and database clients.
  • Retries at every layer — 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls per click to a struggling service.
  • Retrying non-idempotent calls without an idempotency key: double charges.
  • Counting business errors as failures: declined cards opening the breaker for everyone.
  • Breakers that only count errors, not slowness: a provider at 4 s per call never trips them.
  • Dependencies in liveness probes: a third-party blip restarts the whole fleet.
  • Untested fallbacks that fail the first time they are needed.

items.text:
flowchart LR
    SLOW["slow dependency<br/>(payment provider)"] --> TO["timeout ≈ p99.9<br/>+ deadline propagation"]
    TO --> RT["retry: backoff, jitter,<br/>retry budget, one layer"]
    RT --> IK["idempotency key<br/>→ Compute — integrations"]
    TO --> CB["circuit breaker<br/>(also counts slow calls)"]
    CB --> FB["fallback: seats held,<br/>tell the truth"]
    SLOW --> BH["bulkhead sized by<br/>Little's Law → Estimation"]
    OVER["overload"] --> LS["load shedding<br/>→ waiting room (Messaging)"]
    OVER --> RL["rate limiting<br/>→ Edge — API gateway"]
    HC["liveness, readiness, startup<br/>→ Cloud-native — Kubernetes"] --> LB["out of the load balancer<br/>→ Edge — load balancing"]
    CB --> CH["prove it under fault<br/>→ Chaos engineering"]

Palette components: thirdparty · payment (the call every pattern on this page protects) · app (the order replicas whose threads the bulkhead guards) · apigw (rate limiting and load shedding at the door) · queue (the waiting room) · healthcheck (liveness, readiness, startup) · lb (drops unready instances). Scenarios: cascading-failure, retry-storm, rate-limiter, payment-system, flash-sale. Continues in: Compute — integrations, Messaging — delivery semantics, Messaging — the waiting room, Edge — API gateway, Edge — load balancing, Cloud-native — Kubernetes, Hands-on 9 — payment and Toxiproxy.

items.title: Index
items.text:
"Is BoxOffice reliable enough?" Nobody can answer that without numbers. The product manager wants to ship a new seat-map feature the week before a stadium on-sale; the on-call engineer says the purchase path had a bad month and wants to freeze deploys. Without a shared definition of "good enough", that discussion is opinion against opinion. Google's Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practice introduced a vocabulary that turns it into arithmetic1, and it is now standard across the industry:

Term Full name Nature BoxOffice example SLI Service Level Indicator A measurement of what users experience % of seat-hold requests that succeed in under 500 ms SLO Service Level Objective An internal target for an SLI, over a window ≥ 99.9% over 28 days Error budget — The failure the SLO allows: 1 − SLO 0.1% of seat-hold requests may fail or be slow SLA Service Level Agreement A contract with customers, with penalties Promised to partner venues: 99.5% monthly, or service credits 
flowchart LR
    tel["Telemetry<br/>(metrics, logs, traces)"] -->|"aggregated into"| sli["SLI<br/>good / valid events"]
    sli -->|"compared with"| slo["SLO<br/>internal target"]
    slo -->|"the gap is"| budget["Error budget<br/>licence to take risk"]
    slo -->|"looser version"| sla["SLA<br/>external contract"]
    budget -->|"drives"| decisions["Ship or freeze?<br/>Page or ticket?"]

items.title: Start from user journeys
items.text:
An SLO is only useful if it measures what users care about. Start by listing BoxOffice's critical user journeys (CUJs) — the few interactions that must work — and then decide how to measure each one.

Critical user journey Why it matters Type of SLI Browse the catalog and event pages Most traffic; first impression Availability + latency Join the waiting room and get admitted The flash sale depends on it Availability + latency of position updates Hold seats Revenue; strongly consistent Availability + latency Pay and get the order confirmed Revenue; external provider involved Availability (end to end, including the saga) Receive tickets by e-mail / in the app Trust; asynchronous Freshness: time from confirmation to delivery Search events Discovery Latency + quality (results not stale)

Not every journey needs the same target. Browsing can tolerate an occasional slow page; a failed payment loses a sale and a fan's trust.

items.title: SLI — measuring what users feel
items.text:
An SLI is best written as a ratio of events, so it always lies between 0% and 100%2:

\[ \text{SLI} = \frac{\text{good events}}{\text{valid events}} \times 100\% \]

Both words matter. Good defines success from the user's point of view — "status is not 5xx and latency is below 500 ms". Valid excludes what should not count — 4xx responses caused by the client, health-check requests, synthetic load tests.

SLI category Good event BoxOffice example Availability Request answered without a server error POST /holds returned non-5xx Latency Request answered faster than a threshold GET /events/{id} in < 300 ms Freshness Data or side effect is recent enough Confirmation e-mail sent < 2 min after OrderConfirmed Correctness Output is right No seat sold twice (checked by a reconciliation job) Durability Stored data can be read back Every confirmed order is readable a day later

Avoid vanity metrics

CPU usage, JVM heap or the number of pods are not SLIs. A service can be at 95% CPU and serve everyone well, or at 5% CPU and be completely down (deadlocked, misrouted). They are useful to diagnose; SLIs must reflect what users experience.

items.title: Where to measure
items.text:
Measurement point Sees Misses Application metrics (OpenTelemetry, Micrometer) Per-route detail, cheap Requests that never reached the app (LB, DNS, network) Load balancer / gateway logs Everything that reached the edge Client-side failures, CDN Synthetic probes A scripted journey from outside, even with no traffic Real users' diversity Client (browser / app) telemetry What users truly experience Noisy; depends on users' networks

A common choice is to compute SLIs at the gateway (close to the user, but under your control) and complement them with synthetic probes of the purchase journey. With OpenTelemetry metrics exported to Prometheus (see Observability), the availability SLI of the seat-hold route over 5 minutes is:

sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="gateway", http_route="/holds", http_response_status_code!~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="gateway", http_route="/holds"}[5m]))

A freshness SLI for asynchronous work

Request SLIs do not see asynchronous failures: POST /orders can be 100% green while the notification consumer is two hours behind (see Messaging). BoxOffice measures the journey "receive tickets" with a freshness SLI: for each OrderConfirmed, the time until the e-mail is accepted by the provider. Good event: under 2 minutes. The SLO: 99% of confirmations over 28 days. Consumer lag in seconds is its early-warning signal.

items.title: SLO — the target
items.text:
An SLO is a target for an SLI over a window:

SLI ≥ target over a window

BoxOffice SLO Meaning Seat holds: 99.9% succeed in < 500 ms, over 28 days At most 1 in 1,000 holds may fail or be slow Catalog pages: 99.5% served in < 300 ms, over 28 days Browsing tolerates more slowness Ticket delivery: 99% within 2 min of confirmation, over 28 days Freshness of the asynchronous path On-sale waiting room: 99.95% of position updates succeed, during each on-sale An event-scoped SLO for the hours that matter most

Use a rolling window (the last 28 days, moving every minute) rather than a calendar month: 28 days always contain four of each weekday, and the budget does not "reset" magically on the 1st.

How to choose the number:

  • Measure first. Look at the SLI over the last 30–90 days, then set the SLO slightly below what you already achieve. A target you already miss every week is noise.
  • Respect the dependency math. order cannot promise more than the product of what it calls synchronously (overview). If the payment provider offers 99.9%, a purchase SLO of 99.99% is fiction.
  • Ask what users notice. Going from 99.9% to 99.99% costs a lot (see the nines table); if fans would not notice, the money is better spent on features.
  • Never 100%. It leaves no room for deploys, maintenance or the unavoidable, and every dependency you have is below it anyway.

items.title: Error budget
items.text:
The error budget is the amount of unreliability the SLO allows — the team's licence to take risk:

\[ \text{Error budget} = 1 - \text{SLO} \] Request-basedTime-based

The purchase path receives about 1,000,000 requests per day. Over 28 days that is 28,000,000 requests, and a 99.9% SLO allows

\[ 0.001 \times 28\,000\,000 = 28\,000 \text{ failed requests} \]

A bad deploy that returns errors for 5% of requests during 3 hours (\(0.05 \times 3 \times 41\,667 \approx 6\,250\) failures) spends about 22% of the month's budget in one afternoon.

For a 99.9% SLO over 28 days:

\[ 0.001 \times 28 \times 24 \times 60 \approx 40.3 \text{ minutes} \]

Time-based budgets are intuitive ("we have 40 minutes of downtime"), but they treat 3 a.m. like 10:00 on an on-sale day. Request-based budgets weight failures by the traffic they hurt.

items.title: Burn rate
items.text:
The burn rate says how fast the budget is being spent relative to the window2:

\[ \text{burn rate} = \frac{\text{observed error rate}}{1 - \text{SLO}} \]

With a 99.9% SLO, an error rate of 0.1% is a burn rate of 1 — the budget lasts exactly the 28 days. An error rate of 1.44% is a burn rate of 14.4, which exhausts the budget in \(28 / 14.4 \approx 1.9\) days.

The simulation below follows the purchase path's budget over one 28-day window with illustrative numbers: a quiet background of 0.01% errors, a bad deploy on day 9 (5% errors for 3 hours) and a slow degradation from day 16 (0.2% errors — a burn rate of only 2).

2026-10-23T08:15:51.097690 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ 1 0 − 1 1 0 0 1 0 1 burn rate page: 14.4x page: 6x budget lasts exactly 28 days 0 5 10 15 20 25 day of the 28-day window −20 0 20 40 60 80 100 error budget left (%) bad deploy: 3 h at 5% errors slow degradation: 0.2% errors (2x)

The two incidents teach different lessons:

  • The bad deploy has a huge burn rate (50×) for a short time. It must page someone within minutes, and the budget shows what it cost: about a fifth of the month.
  • The slow degradation never looks dramatic — 0.2% errors would not alarm anyone on a dashboard — but at 2× it exhausts the budget around day 26. Only a slow-burn alert over a long window catches it.

items.title: Alerting on burn rate
items.text:
Alert on the budget, not on raw error rates or CPU. The SRE Workbook recommends multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts2: a long window to measure significance, a short window to stop the alert quickly once the problem is fixed.

Severity Burn rate Long window Short window Budget consumed when it fires Page 14.4× 1 h 5 min 2% Page 6× 6 h 30 min 5% Ticket 1× 3 days 6 h 10% 
# Prometheus alerting rule: purchase path, SLO 99.9% (budget = 0.001)
- alert: PurchaseErrorBudgetFastBurn
  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="gateway", http_route=~"/holds|/orders", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[1h]))
      / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="gateway", http_route=~"/holds|/orders"}[1h]))
    ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
    and
    (
      sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="gateway", http_route=~"/holds|/orders", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
      / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="gateway", http_route=~"/holds|/orders"}[5m]))
    ) > (14.4 * 0.001)
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "Purchase path burning the 28-day error budget 14.4x faster than allowed"

The details of alert design, routing and on-call are in Observability — alerting.

items.title: The error budget policy
items.text:
An error budget is only a number on a dashboard unless product and engineering agree in advance what happens as it is spent. That agreement is the error budget policy:

BoxOffice error budget policy (purchase path)

  • Budget above 50%: normal operation; deploy any working day; experiments allowed.
  • Budget between 0 and 50%: deploys need a rollback plan and a canary; a reliability item enters every sprint.
  • Budget exhausted: feature deploys to the purchase path are frozen until the 28-day SLI is back above the SLO; only fixes and reliability work ship.
  • On-sale rule: no deploys to the purchase path in the 24 hours before a major on-sale, whatever the budget.
  • Single incident > 20% of the budget: mandatory blameless postmortem with action items (see Incident response).

Signed by the product manager and the engineering lead of the purchase path; reviewed every quarter.

The budget as a negotiation tool

The product manager wants to ship the new seat map; the engineer is nervous. The budget answers objectively: "we have 70% of the budget left and the change goes out behind a feature flag to 5% of fans — ship it." Or: "we have 8% left and the stadium on-sale is on Friday — it waits until next week." Notice it also works the other way: an unspent budget is a signal that the team is being too careful and could move faster.

items.title: SLA — the contract
items.text:
An SLA is a formal agreement with customers that defines the expected service and the remedies (usually service credits) if it is not met. It is a legal document: breaching it costs money.

An SLA typically states: covered services and regions; the commitment (e.g. 99.9% monthly uptime); how it is measured; exclusions (scheduled maintenance, customer-caused problems, force majeure); and the credit schedule.

The commitments below come from the providers' public SLA pages3; conditions change over time, so always read the current page.

Provider Service Monthly commitment Condition AWS Amazon EC2 99.99% (region level) Instances across multiple AZs AWS Amazon RDS 99.95% Multi-AZ deployments AWS Amazon S3 Standard 99.9% — Google Cloud Compute Engine 99.99% Instances in multiple zones Azure Virtual Machines 99.99% Two or more VMs across availability zones

Two lessons hide in that table. First, the highest numbers apply only if you deploy redundantly — redundancy is the price of the extra nine. Second, the remedy is a credit on your bill, not compensation for your lost ticket sales: an SLA transfers a little financial risk; it does not make your system available.

SLO SLA Audience The engineering team Customers, partners, lawyers Nature Internal target Legal contract Strictness Stricter Looser When missed Reliability work, deploy freeze Credits, penalties, reputation

Keep the SLO stricter than the SLA (e.g. SLO 99.95%, SLA 99.9%): the gap is a safety margin that warns you long before the contract is at risk.

In the interview

In the requirements step, turn vague "highly available" into SLOs per journey: "seat holds 99.9% under 500 ms; browsing 99.5%; ticket e-mail within 2 minutes for 99%". Then use them: they justify redundancy (dependency math), asynchrony (removing non-critical dependencies) and alerting (burn rate). Mention that 99.99% means about 4 minutes a month, so it implies automated failover. Interviewers value hearing why a number was chosen more than the number itself.

Common pitfalls

  • Measuring the wrong thing: an SLI from the health-check endpoint says nothing about POST /holds.
  • Averages instead of thresholds or percentiles: a mean of 80 ms can hide 5% of fans waiting 4 s.
  • Too many SLOs: two or three per journey that someone acts on beat thirty nobody reads.
  • Ignoring asynchronous paths: green APIs, three-hour-old e-mails. Add freshness SLIs.
  • SLO without a policy: if nothing changes when the budget is gone, the SLO is decoration.
  • Mixing windows: a budget computed over 30 days compared with an SLO over 28 days gives wrong decisions.

items.text:
flowchart LR
    CUJ["critical user journeys"] --> SLI["SLI = good / valid events"]
    TEL["telemetry at the gateway<br/>→ Observability"] --> SLI
    SLI --> SLO["SLO over a<br/>28-day rolling window"]
    DEP["dependency math<br/>→ composite availability"] --> SLO

Palette components: metrics (the SLI is a ratio of request counters) · alerting (multi-window burn-rate rules) · apigw (where BoxOffice measures the purchase SLI) · kafka (consumer lag, the early warning of the ticket-delivery freshness SLI) · payment (its 99.9% caps the purchase SLO). items.title: Index
items.text:
Lectures and labs show you how things work; the exercises make you do it on your own and prove it with numbers. Each individual exercise trains one skill a system designer uses every week: estimating, composing components, measuring, caching, going asynchronous, autoscaling and writing a design down so that someone else can review it. The team project then puts everything together in one system that you build, load test, break on purpose and defend.

What the exercises are for

By the end of the exercises you will be able to:

  • Estimate load, storage and bandwidth of a system before building it, and use those numbers to pick components.
  • Compose palette components into a design that meets latency, availability and cost goals — and explain why it works.
  • Measure a real service with k6, read percentiles and find its bottleneck.
  • Change an architecture (cache, replica, queue, autoscaler) and prove the effect with a before/after experiment.
  • Communicate a design as a design document with ADRs and defend it orally.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
# Exercise What it trains Related class / lab Due Weight Delivery 1 Estimation Back-of-the-envelope numbers for 5 systems Class 2 · Lab 2 Week 3 10% Page with the estimation sheet 2 Load-test report k6 campaign, percentiles, the knee, bottleneck analysis Class 2 · Labs 2–3 Week 6 15% Page + k6 scripts + raw results 3 Cache & database Cache-aside + read replica, before/after Classes 6–7 · Labs 5–6 Week 8 15% Page + code + measurements 4 Event-driven Transactional outbox + idempotent consumer + DLQ Class 8 · Lab 7 Week 10 15% Page + code + failure demo 5 Kubernetes autoscaling Probes, requests/limits, HPA under k6 load Class 12 · Lab 10 Week 14 10% Page + manifests + video 6 Playground design Composing components to meet SLO + cost goals, under randomness Playground · Classes 4–13 Week 15 15% Exported JSON + rationale + run reports 7 Design doc Written design + ADRs for an interview problem, oral defence Class 16 · Interview Week 17 20% Design doc page + ADRs + oral defence Team project Build, measure, break and defend a whole system All Weeks 3–20 — Repository + docs + presentation

Weeks are relative

"Week n" is the n-th week of the semester. The calendar dates, the quiz days and the exam days are on the planning page. Unless the instructor announces otherwise, an exercise is due on the last class day of its week, at 23:59. The weights are the share of each exercise inside the exercises component of the grade; how that component enters the final grade is on the course page.

items.title: How the exercises are graded
items.text:
Every exercise and every project deliverable receives a concept grade, as in the previous editions (Insper's Notas da Engenharia):

Concept Grade A (+) 9 (10) B (+) 7 (8) C (+) 5 (6) D 4 I 0

Each exercise page has a rubric: one row per criterion and one column per level. The levels always mean the same thing:

Level Meaning I Not delivered, not reproducible, copied, results that were not produced by you — or the oral check failed. D Delivered, but at least one mandatory requirement is missing or wrong. C Every mandatory requirement is met; the analysis is shallow (numbers shown, little explanation). B C, plus a sound analysis: the numbers support the conclusions, trade-offs are named, the page is clear. A B, plus depth: an extra experiment or comparison, a non-obvious insight, polished and fully reproducible.

The final concept of a deliverable is the level that best describes most criteria; a criterion marked (mandatory) caps the grade at D when it is not met. The + is given when the work clearly goes beyond the level's description.

Acceptance criteria first

Every exercise lists its requirements as a checklist. Before submitting, tick every box in your own copy. A checklist with an unticked mandatory item is the most common reason for a D.

items.title: Repository and documentation
items.text:
• One GitHub repository per student for the individual exercises (public, or private with the instructor and the teaching assistant added as collaborators). Suggested name: sysdesign-<your-github-user>.
  • Documentation published on GitHub Pages, built with MkDocs Material or Zensical — you may start from the documentation template. One page per exercise, linked from the home page, with your name and GitHub user on the home page.
  • Everything needed to reproduce your results is in the repository: code, compose.yaml/manifests, k6 scripts, raw results (k6 summary JSON, CSV), screenshots and a short "how to run" section. Do not commit secrets: use .env.example and GitHub secrets.
  • The delivery is a tag: create the tag ex<n> (e.g. ex3) on the commit you want graded and submit the Pages link and the tag on Blackboard. Commits after the tag are ignored for that exercise.
  • Code for the labs and exercises starts from the course repository (repo-classes/pma271); say in your page which parts you changed.

items.title: Use of AI tools
items.text:
AI tools (chat assistants, code assistants, agents) are allowed — they are part of how software is built in 2026, and learning to use them well is part of the course. The rules:

  1. You are responsible for every line and every number. If you submit it, you must be able to explain it, run it and change it on the spot.
  2. Declare the use. Each exercise page ends with an AI usage section: which tools, for what (e.g. "generated the k6 script skeleton", "reviewed my ADR"), and what you checked or changed yourself.
  3. Measurements cannot be generated. Numbers, charts and screenshots must come from runs you did. Invented or "adjusted" results are graded I, and are treated as an academic integrity issue.
  4. Text written by a model still has to be right. Wrong statements written confidently cost more than an honest "we did not test this".

Oral check

Any exercise or project grade may be validated in a short oral check (5–10 minutes): explain a decision, re-run an experiment, change a parameter and predict the result, or walk through a piece of code. If the check shows that you cannot explain your own delivery, that grade becomes I. The design doc always has an oral defence.

items.title: Late policy
items.text:
Late policy — to be defined by the instructor

Placeholder. The rules for late deliveries (grace period, penalty per day, maximum delay, missed oral checks) will be announced by the instructor at the beginning of the semester and published here.

items.title: Collaboration
items.text: Discussing ideas with classmates is encouraged; sharing code, results or text of individual exercises is not. If a classmate helped you, say so in the page (as you do for AI). Team work happens in the project, where the rules for teams are described.

items.title: Index
items.text:
During a BoxOffice on-sale, almost every request is a read of the same few things: the event page, the venue, the price list. Sending each of them to the primary database is like asking the box-office clerk to re-print the poster for every fan in line. In this exercise you put a Redis cache and a PostgreSQL read replica in front of your service, measure what they buy you, and face the price: stale data, replication lag and the cache stampede.

Learning objectives

After this exercise you will be able to:

  • Implement cache-aside with TTL, jitter and invalidation on write, and a read/write split between a primary and a replica.
  • Predict hit ratio and database load from the key distribution, and verify the prediction with measurements.
  • Compare before/after with the same workload: p99, knee, database load.
  • Demonstrate a stale read caused by replication lag (and by the cache) and mitigate it.
  • Reproduce a cache stampede and fix it with request coalescing.

items.title: Context
items.text:
Class 6 covered replication and its consistency anomalies1; Class 7 covered cache patterns, invalidation and failure modes. Lab 5 built cache-aside on catalog and Lab 6 a read replica. Here you combine both, on your service, as an experiment with numbers. Start from the service and the k6 script of the load-test report — that report is your "before".

The read path you will build:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as catalog
    participant R as Redis
    participant P as PostgreSQL replica
    C->>A: GET /events/42
    A->>R: GET event:42
    R-->>A: (miss)
    A->>P: SELECT ... WHERE id = 42
    P-->>A: row
    A->>R: SET event:42 (TTL 60 s + jitter)
    A-->>C: 200 OK
    C->>A: GET /events/42
    A->>R: GET event:42
    R-->>A: (hit)
    A-->>C: 200 OK

items.title: The math you will check
items.text:
With a request rate λ and a hit ratio h, the database receives only the misses:

\[ \lambda_{db} = (1 - h)\,\lambda \qquad \bar{t} \approx h\,t_{cache} + (1 - h)\,(t_{cache} + t_{db}) \]

The hit ratio depends on the key popularity. With a Zipf distribution (exponent 1) over 1,000 events, the 200 most popular events receive about H₂₀₀ / H₁₀₀₀ ≈ 5.88 / 7.49 ≈ 78% of the reads (Hₙ is the harmonic number, ≈ ln n + 0.577). With a 60 s TTL, each key that is read misses about once per TTL, so at most ~1,000 / 60 ≈ 17 misses/s — at 1,000 req/s that is a hit ratio around 98% once the cache is warm. Write your own prediction before measuring.

items.title: Task
items.text:
Starting from your service of the load-test report (the BoxOffice catalog, recommended):

  1. Add cache-aside with Redis on the main read endpoint (GET /events/{id}): TTL with jitter, delete on write after the transaction commits, hit/miss counters.
  2. Add a PostgreSQL streaming replica and route read-only transactions to the replica and writes to the primary.
  3. Run the same k6 workload (with Zipf-distributed keys and a small share of writes) before (ex2 setup) and after, and compare.
  4. Demonstrate a stale read (replica lag and cache) and implement or argue a mitigation.
  5. Reproduce a cache stampede on a hot key and fix it.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• (mandatory) Cache-aside on the read endpoint with TTL and invalidation on write (after commit); a hit and a miss counter exposed as metrics.
  • (mandatory) A streaming replica with a read/write split; evidence that ≥ 90% of read transactions go to the replica (pg_stat_database on both nodes).
  • (mandatory) Before/after with the same k6 script, data and resources; raw results committed.
  • Your prediction of hit ratio and database load, then the measurement: hit ratio ≥ 80% in steady state, and database reads within ±20% of (1 − h) λ (or an explanation of the gap).
  • p99 at the load rate of ex2, and the new knee (stress test), compared with before.
  • Replication lag measured idle and under write load.
  • A stale read demonstrated step by step (pause replay on the replica) and one mitigation implemented or precisely argued (read-your-writes).
  • A stampede reproduced (≈ N database reads for N concurrent misses of the same key) and fixed (≤ 1 database read per instance).
  • A short discussion: what should not be cached in BoxOffice (e.g. seat availability at checkout) and why.
  • AI usage section (see the policy).

items.title: Deliverables
items.text: In your repository (tag ex3): code changes, compose.yaml with Redis and the replica, k6 scripts, raw results (load/results/), and a cache-db page on your documentation site following the template.

items.title: 1. Add Redis and a replica to Compose
items.text:
The replica is created with pg_basebackup from the primary the first time it starts; -R writes the settings that make it a streaming standby.

compose.yaml (excerpt)
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:7
    command: ["redis-server", "--maxmemory", "256mb", "--maxmemory-policy", "allkeys-lru"]
    cpus: "1"
    mem_limit: 512m

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: catalog
      POSTGRES_USER: catalog
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: catalog
    command: ["postgres", "-c", "wal_level=replica", "-c", "max_wal_senders=5", "-c", "hot_standby=on"]
    volumes:
      - ./db/init-replication.sh:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/10-replication.sh:ro
    cpus: "2"
    mem_limit: 1g

  db-replica:
    image: postgres:16
    user: postgres
    environment:
      PGPASSWORD: replicator
    command:
      - bash
      - -c
      - |
        if [ ! -s /var/lib/postgresql/data/PG_VERSION ]; then
          until pg_basebackup -h db -U replicator -D /var/lib/postgresql/data -R -X stream; do sleep 2; done
          chmod 0700 /var/lib/postgresql/data
        fi
        exec postgres -c hot_standby=on
    depends_on:
      - db
    cpus: "2"
    mem_limit: 1g
db/init-replication.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Runs once, when the primary is initialized: a replication user and its pg_hba rule.
set -e
psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
  -c "CREATE ROLE replicator WITH REPLICATION LOGIN PASSWORD 'replicator';"
echo "host replication replicator all scram-sha-256" >> "$PGDATA/pg_hba.conf"

Check that the replica is streaming:

docker compose exec db psql -U catalog -c "select client_addr, state, replay_lag from pg_stat_replication;"
docker compose exec db-replica psql -U catalog -d catalog -c "select pg_is_in_recovery();"

items.title: 2. Cache-aside in the service
items.text:
Write the pattern by hand (instead of @Cacheable) so that you control TTL, invalidation and metrics2.

src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/EventQueryService.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.core.JsonProcessingException;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Counter;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class EventQueryService {

    private static final Duration BASE_TTL = Duration.ofSeconds(60);

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
    private final EventReader reader;   // @Transactional(readOnly = true) -> replica
    private final ObjectMapper json;
    private final Counter hits;
    private final Counter misses;

    public EventQueryService(StringRedisTemplate redis, EventReader reader,
                             ObjectMapper json, MeterRegistry meters) {
        this.redis = redis;
        this.reader = reader;
        this.json = json;
        this.hits = meters.counter("catalog.cache", "result", "hit");
        this.misses = meters.counter("catalog.cache", "result", "miss");
    }

    public Optional<EventDto> findById(long id) {
        String cached = redis.opsForValue().get(key(id));
        if (cached != null) {
            hits.increment();
            return Optional.of(fromJson(cached));
        }
        misses.increment();
        Optional<EventDto> value = reader.findById(id);
        value.ifPresent(e -> redis.opsForValue().set(key(id), toJson(e), ttlWithJitter()));
        return value;
    }

    public void evict(long id) {
        redis.delete(key(id));
    }

    static String key(long id) {
        return "event:" + id;
    }

    // Jitter spreads expirations so that popular keys do not all expire at the same instant.
    private static Duration ttlWithJitter() {
        return BASE_TTL.plusMillis(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(0, 15_000));
    }

    private EventDto fromJson(String s) {
        try {
            return json.readValue(s, EventDto.class);
        } catch (JsonProcessingException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }

    private String toJson(EventDto e) {
        try {
            return json.writeValueAsString(e);
        } catch (JsonProcessingException ex) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(ex);
        }
    }
}

Invalidate after the write commits — deleting before the commit lets a concurrent read put the old value back:

src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/EventCommandService.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class EventCommandService {

    private final EventWriter writer;          // @Transactional -> primary
    private final EventQueryService queries;

    public EventCommandService(EventWriter writer, EventQueryService queries) {
        this.writer = writer;
        this.queries = queries;
    }

    public EventDto update(long id, EventUpdate command) {
        EventDto saved = writer.update(id, command); // the transaction commits when this returns
        queries.evict(id);                          // then the cache entry is deleted
        return saved;
    }
}

items.title: 3. Route reads to the replica
items.text:
A routing DataSource chooses the replica for read-only transactions. LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy delays getting a connection until the transaction's read-only flag is known.

src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/config/DataSourceConfig.java
package boxoffice.catalog.config;

import java.util.Map;
import javax.sql.DataSource;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Primary;
import org.springframework.jdbc.datasource.LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy;
import org.springframework.jdbc.datasource.lookup.AbstractRoutingDataSource;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionSynchronizationManager;

@Configuration
public class DataSourceConfig {

    static class ReadWriteRoutingDataSource extends AbstractRoutingDataSource {
        @Override
        protected Object determineCurrentLookupKey() {
            return TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly() ? "replica" : "primary";
        }
    }

    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties("app.datasource.primary")
    DataSourceProperties primaryProperties() {
        return new DataSourceProperties();
    }

    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties("app.datasource.replica")
    DataSourceProperties replicaProperties() {
        return new DataSourceProperties();
    }

    @Bean
    @Primary
    DataSource dataSource() {
        DataSource primary = primaryProperties().initializeDataSourceBuilder().build();
        DataSource replica = replicaProperties().initializeDataSourceBuilder().build();
        ReadWriteRoutingDataSource routing = new ReadWriteRoutingDataSource();
        routing.setTargetDataSources(Map.of("primary", primary, "replica", replica));
        routing.setDefaultTargetDataSource(primary);
        routing.afterPropertiesSet();
        return new LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy(routing);
    }
}
src/main/resources/application.yaml (excerpt)
app:
  datasource:
    primary:
      url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/catalog
      username: catalog
      password: catalog
    replica:
      url: jdbc:postgresql://db-replica:5432/catalog
      username: catalog
      password: catalog
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: redis
      port: 6379

Annotate the reader's methods with @Transactional(readOnly = true) and the writer's with @Transactional. Check the split by counting committed transactions on each node before and after a test:

for svc in db db-replica; do
  docker compose exec "$svc" psql -U catalog -d catalog -tAc \
    "select '$svc', xact_commit from pg_stat_database where datname = 'catalog';"
done

items.title: 4. The same workload, with popular keys
items.text:
Real traffic is skewed: a few events get most of the views. Replace the uniform ids of the ex2 script with Zipf-distributed ids and add a small share of writes (so that invalidations happen).

load/catalog-zipf.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

const BASE = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:8080';
const RATE = Number(__ENV.RATE || 200);
const N = Number(__ENV.EVENTS || 1000);
const S = Number(__ENV.ZIPF_S || 1.0);
const WRITE_RATIO = Number(__ENV.WRITE_RATIO || 0.02);

// Cumulative distribution of a Zipf(S) popularity over ids 1..N.
const cdf = (() => {
  const acc = [];
  let sum = 0;
  for (let k = 1; k <= N; k++) {
    sum += 1 / Math.pow(k, S);
    acc.push(sum);
  }
  return acc.map((x) => x / sum);
})();

function zipfId() {
  const u = Math.random();
  let lo = 0;
  let hi = N - 1;
  while (lo < hi) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
    if (cdf[mid] < u) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid;
  }
  return lo + 1;
}

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    load: {
      executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: 0, timeUnit: '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 50, maxVUs: 500,
      stages: [
        { target: RATE, duration: '2m' },
        { target: RATE, duration: '10m' },
        { target: 0, duration: '30s' },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<200', 'p(99)<500'],
  },
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'min', 'med', 'p(90)', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
};

export default function () {
  const id = zipfId();
  if (Math.random() < WRITE_RATIO) {
    const body = JSON.stringify({ description: `updated at ${Date.now()}` });
    const res = http.put(`${BASE}/events/${id}`, body, {
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      tags: { name: 'PUT /events/{id}' },
    });
    check(res, { 'write ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  } else {
    const res = http.get(`${BASE}/events/${id}`, { tags: { name: 'GET /events/{id}' } });
    check(res, { 'read ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  }
}

Adapt the PUT to your API (and its authentication). Run the before (cache off, no replica — e.g. a Spring profile) and the after with the same rate, seed data and resources.

items.title: 5. Measure hit ratio, database load and lag
items.text:
Take each counter at the start and at the end of the steady part of the test and use the difference:

docker compose exec redis redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E 'keyspace_(hits|misses)'
curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/catalog.cache | jq '.measurements'
docker compose exec db psql -U catalog -c "select application_name, state, write_lag, replay_lag from pg_stat_replication;"
docker compose exec db-replica psql -U catalog -d catalog -c "select now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() as replica_delay;"

replica_delay grows when the primary is idle (no new transactions to replay), so read it under write load; replay_lag on the primary is the better number.

items.title: 6. Make a stale read happen
items.text:
Replication lag is usually milliseconds — too fast to see. Pause replay on the replica to make it visible and deterministic:

docker compose exec db-replica psql -U postgres -c "select pg_wal_replay_pause();"
curl -s -X PUT localhost:8080/events/1 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"description":"new"}'
curl -s localhost:8080/events/1      # which description do you get, and why?
docker compose exec db-replica psql -U postgres -c "select pg_wal_replay_resume();"

Explain what you observe, including the cache + replica race: the write deletes event:1; the next read misses, reads the old row from the lagging replica, and puts the old value back in the cache — where it stays for a whole TTL. Then mitigate, for example: read from the primary for a few seconds after a write by the same client (read-your-writes), refill the cache from the primary after a write (write-through), or keep the TTL short for data that changes. Justify the choice for BoxOffice.

items.title: 7. Reproduce and fix a stampede
items.text:
When a hot key expires, every concurrent request misses at once and goes to the database — the thundering herd. Reproduce it with 200 simultaneous requests to the same id right after deleting the key:

load/stampede.js
import http from 'k6/http';

const BASE = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:8080';

export const options = {
  scenarios: { herd: { executor: 'per-vu-iterations', vus: 200, iterations: 1 } },
};

export default function () {
  http.get(`${BASE}/events/1`);
}

docker compose exec redis redis-cli DEL event:1
k6 run load/stampede.js
curl -s 'localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/catalog.cache?tag=result:miss' | jq '.measurements'

Count the misses (database reads) for the 200 requests. Then fix it with request coalescing: concurrent misses of the same key in one instance wait for a single load.

EventQueryService.java (coalescing excerpt)
private final ConcurrentHashMap<Long, CompletableFuture<Optional<EventDto>>> inFlight = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

private Optional<EventDto> loadOnce(long id) {
    CompletableFuture<Optional<EventDto>> mine = new CompletableFuture<>();
    CompletableFuture<Optional<EventDto>> existing = inFlight.putIfAbsent(id, mine);
    if (existing != null) {
        return existing.join();                  // another thread is loading this key: wait for it
    }
    try {
        misses.increment();                      // only the loader counts as a database read
        Optional<EventDto> value = reader.findById(id);
        value.ifPresent(e -> redis.opsForValue().set(key(id), toJson(e), ttlWithJitter()));
        mine.complete(value);
        return value;
    } catch (RuntimeException ex) {
        mine.completeExceptionally(ex);
        throw ex;
    } finally {
        inFlight.remove(id);
    }
}

In findById, replace the miss branch (counter, read, SET) by return loadOnce(id);. With k instances you get at most k database reads per expiry. A Redis lock (SET lock:event:1 <token> NX PX 3000) or probabilistic early refresh are alternatives — compare them in your discussion.

items.title: Rubric
items.text:
Levels as defined in How the exercises are graded.

Criterion I D C B A Cache-aside (mandatory) Absent No TTL or no invalidation on write TTL + delete after commit + hit/miss metrics TTL jitter; cache failure does not break reads (fallback to DB) Memory sizing and eviction policy justified with numbers Replica and routing (mandatory) Absent Replica exists but reads not routed ≥ 90% of reads on the replica, shown with counters Writes and read-your-writes paths identified Routing failure handled (replica down → primary) and tested Experiment (mandatory) No before/after Different scripts, data or resources Same workload before/after, raw data committed Prediction stated first and compared with the measurement Sensitivity: hit ratio vs Zipf exponent or TTL, plotted Results — Partial Hit ratio, DB load, p99 and knee reported Gaps between prediction and measurement explained Knee moves explained by the new bottleneck, with evidence Consistency — Not addressed Stale read demonstrated Cache + replica race explained and mitigated Mitigation tested under load, cost discussed Stampede — Not done Reproduced and fixed with numbers Alternatives compared (lock, early refresh) Multi-instance behaviour measured

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Why not just use @Cacheable?

You may in your project. Here, writing cache-aside by hand makes every decision visible: what the key is, when it expires, when it is deleted and what is counted. @Cacheable hides exactly the parts this exercise is about.

Should I delete or update the cache on a write?

Deleting is the default for cache-aside: the next read refills it from the source of truth. Updating (write-through) avoids a miss but can race with concurrent writes and store an older value. Either way, do it after the commit.

My hit ratio is 99.9% — is that suspicious?

Maybe: check that the workload is not reading the same key, that the counters are differences over the steady window (not since start-up) and that writes happen. A very high ratio is plausible for a small, skewed key set and a long TTL — show the arithmetic.

Where does seat availability fit?

Not in this cache. Seat holds need strong consistency (no double booking) and belong to the inventory service and its transactions (Lab 6). A display of availability can be cached for a second or two — at checkout, the database decides.

The replica setup fails with an authentication error.

The init script runs only when the primary's data directory is created. If you started the primary before adding the script, remove its volume (docker compose down -v) and start again.

Do I need two instances of the service for the stampede?

No. One instance is enough to reproduce and fix it. Testing with Nginx and several instances (Lab 3) is an A-level extension: you should see at most one database read per instance.

  1. Martin Kleppmann and Chris Riccomini, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd ed., O'Reilly — chapters on replication (replication lag, read-your-writes). ↩

  2. Redis documentation, "Client-side caching" and "Eviction", redis.io/docs. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
Most architecture decisions in real companies are not made in front of a whiteboard: they are made in a design document that colleagues read, question and approve — and in the ADRs (Architecture Decision Records) that remind everyone, a year later, why things are the way they are. In an interview the same thinking happens out loud in 45 minutes. In this exercise you do both: you write a complete design doc with ADRs for a classic system-design problem, and then you defend it orally, including a change of requirements you did not see coming.

Learning objectives

After this exercise you will be able to:

  • Scope a vague problem into functional and non-functional requirements with numbers.
  • Design a system end to end — estimates, API, data model, high-level architecture with palette components, deep dives.
  • Evaluate alternatives and record decisions as ADRs with their consequences.
  • Identify bottlenecks, failure modes, security and operability concerns, and cost.
  • Defend a design orally and adapt it to a new requirement on the spot.

items.title: Context
items.text: The structure of a good design doc follows the interview framework of Class 1 — clarify → estimate → API & data model → high-level design → deep dives → bottlenecks & trade-offs → wrap-up — and the interview guide. The case studies of Class 16 show complete worked examples; the component catalog gives the vocabulary (use the palette ids in your diagrams). A design doc is not a list of technologies: every component must be justified by a requirement or a number, and every important choice must name the alternative you rejected1.

items.title: Task
items.text:
1. You receive one problem from the list below by draw (at most two students per problem).
  2. Write a design doc following the template, for the scale stated in the problem.
  3. Record at least three ADRs for the decisions that matter most.
  4. Optionally, prototype the design in the playground (start from blank) and attach the exported JSON.
  5. Defend the design in a 15-minute oral defence.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• (mandatory) Design doc with every section of the template (a section may say "not applicable — because …").
  • (mandatory) At least three ADRs, each with context, options considered, decision and consequences (positive and negative).
  • (mandatory) Oral defence done (failing it, or not showing up, grades the exercise I).
  • Requirements: 3–6 functional, non-functional with numbers (latency percentiles, availability, durability, scale), explicit out-of-scope list.
  • Estimates: QPS (average and peak, reads/writes), storage, bandwidth, cache, number of servers — formulas shown (as in the estimation exercise).
  • API (endpoints or messages, with request/response) and data model (entities, keys, chosen store and why, partition key if any).
  • High-level diagram using palette component ids (lb, apigw, app, cache, sql, kafka, …) and a walk-through of the two most important request flows.
  • At least two deep dives on the hardest parts of the problem.
  • Bottlenecks at 10× scale, failure modes with detection and mitigation, security, observability (SLIs/SLOs/alerts) and an order-of-magnitude cost.
  • AI usage section (see the policy).

items.title: Deliverables
items.text: On your documentation site (tag ex7): a page design-doc with the design doc and one page (or section) per ADR, numbered ADR-001, ADR-002, …; diagrams as Mermaid or images with their source; optional playground JSON in playground/design-doc.json. Bring the page open to the oral defence.

items.title: Step by step
items.text:
1. Clarify (≈ 10% of the effort). Write down the questions you would ask an interviewer and answer them yourself as assumptions: who are the users, what are the core use cases, what scale, what matters more — latency, consistency, cost?
  2. Estimate. Turn the scale into QPS, storage, bandwidth and memory. Mark which numbers force a design decision (e.g. "10 TB/day of writes → not a single SQL primary").
  3. API and data model. Define the contract before the boxes. Choose the store per entity from the access pattern, not from habit.
  4. High-level design. Draw the simplest design that meets the functional requirements, then walk the main requests through it.
  5. Deep dives. Pick the two or three parts where the problem is actually hard (ordering, hot keys, fan-out, exactly-once, consistency, real-time, cost of LLM calls…) and go deep: alternatives, numbers, failure behaviour.
  6. Bottlenecks and failures. What breaks first at 10×? What happens when each dependency is slow or down? How do you detect it?
  7. Write the ADRs for the decisions you would want a newcomer to understand in a year.
  8. Wrap-up. Summarise the design in five lines, list the open questions and the risks you accept.
  9. Rehearse the defence. Explain the design in 5 minutes to a classmate and let them change one requirement.

In the interview

The same document, compressed into 45 minutes, is a system-design interview. Practising the written version first makes the spoken version faster: you already know your numbers, your trade-offs and your weak spots.

items.title: Problems
items.text:
# Problem Scope Key challenge 1 Web crawler Crawl 1 B pages per month, politely, and store them for indexing URL frontier, politeness per host, de-duplication 2 Collaborative document editor Real-time co-editing of text documents, up to 50 editors per document Conflict resolution (OT or CRDT), presence, history 3 Distributed job scheduler Run millions of cron-like and one-off jobs per day with at-least-once guarantees Leader election, exactly one execution per schedule, retries 4 Metrics and monitoring platform Ingest metrics from 100 k hosts, query dashboards, fire alerts Write-heavy time series, downsampling, cardinality 5 Game leaderboard Global and friends leaderboards for a game with 50 M daily players Top-K at write speed, sorted sets, sharding a ranking 6 Hotel booking Search availability and book rooms across 1 M hotels Inventory consistency, overbooking, search vs booking paths 7 Food delivery Restaurants, orders, courier assignment and tracking in one country Three-sided marketplace, geo matching, order state machine 8 File sync (Dropbox-like) Sync files across devices for 50 M users Chunking, de-duplication, metadata consistency, conflicts 9 Ad click aggregator Count ad clicks in near real time for billing and dashboards Stream processing, exactly-once counting, late events 10 Webhook delivery platform Deliver events from a SaaS to millions of customer endpoints Retries with backoff, ordering, slow or hostile receivers 11 Proximity service "Restaurants near me" for 200 M users Geospatial index (geohash, quadtree), read-heavy, updates 12 Online code judge Students submit code that is compiled, run and graded Sandboxing, queueing bursts before deadlines, fairness 13 LLM document Q&A for a university Students ask questions about course documents; answers cite sources RAG pipeline, cost per question, guardrails, freshness

The instructor runs the draw in class (or publishes it on Blackboard). Two students with the same problem write independent documents — they will be compared.

items.title: Oral defence
items.text:
The defence takes 15 minutes, with your design doc on the screen:

  1. 5 minutes — walk-through. Requirements and numbers, the diagram, the two main flows, the decision you are most proud of.
  2. 10 minutes — questions. Including one curveball: a change of requirement you must handle live, for example:
    • traffic grows 10× (or one key/user becomes 1,000× hotter);
    • the system must run in a second region with a regional outage tolerated;
    • a new feature (e.g. search, notifications, an AI assistant) must be added;
    • the budget is cut by half;
    • a component you chose is not allowed (e.g. no Kafka, no NoSQL).

Example questions:

  • "Which number in your estimates drives the biggest decision? What if it is wrong by 10×?"
  • "Walk me through what happens when <dependency> takes 5 seconds to answer."
  • "Why this store and not <alternative>? What would make you change your mind?"
  • "Where can data be lost or duplicated? How do you know it did not happen?"
  • "What do you alert on? Who is woken up, and what do they look at first?"
  • "Which ADR would you revisit first, and why?"

Understanding is what is graded: you may say "I did not consider that" and then reason about it. Reading the document aloud is not a defence.

items.title: Rubric
items.text:
Levels as defined in How the exercises are graded. The written document and the oral defence are graded together; the defence weighs as much as all written criteria combined.
