items.title: FAQ
items.text:
How long should the design doc be?

Long enough to cover every section, short enough to be read in 20–30 minutes: typically 6–12 pages with diagrams. Tables and diagrams beat paragraphs.

Can I base my design on a public article or a book chapter?

Yes — cite it. But the doc must show your reasoning for your numbers, and two students with the same problem are compared. Copied structure with different words is easy to spot in the defence.

Do I need to implement anything?

No. A playground prototype is optional and welcome. What matters is a design you can justify and defend.

Which technologies should I name?

Name categories first (palette ids: kafka, nosql, cache) and specific products only when the choice matters (e.g. PostgreSQL vs Cassandra for a write-heavy log). Every named product must have a reason.

What if I cannot answer the curveball?

Think out loud: restate the change, estimate its effect, find what breaks first, propose a fix and name its cost. A structured partial answer is graded much better than silence or a guess.

Can I use AI to write the doc?

You may use AI to review, question or improve your text — and declare it. The defence checks that the decisions are yours: if the document says it and you cannot explain it, the grade is I.

  1. Alex Xu, System Design Interview — An Insider's Guide, vol. 1, ch. 3 "A framework for system design interviews", 2020. ↩

  2. Michael Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions", 2011, cognitect.com; MADR template, adr.github.io/madr. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
At 09:55 the BoxOffice team is staring at a dashboard. In five minutes a stadium show goes on sale: 2 million fans for 60 thousand seats. How many requests per second will hit the catalog? How many seat holds per second will the database take? Does the seat map fit in memory? How many app servers do we need? The answers decide the architecture — and you can get them before writing a single line of code, with a sheet of paper and a few formulas. That is what this exercise trains.

Learning objectives

After this exercise you will be able to:

  • Estimate daily active users, average and peak QPS, read/write ratio, storage, bandwidth and cache size from a short problem statement.
  • Apply Little's Law, peak factors and availability math (series/parallel) to size a system.
  • State assumptions explicitly, keep units straight and round to useful precision.
  • Derive design consequences from the numbers ("this forces a CDN", "one SQL primary is enough").
  • Sanity-check an estimate against a known reference number.

items.title: Context
items.text:
Back-of-the-envelope estimation is the second step of the interview framework and the first thing a reviewer looks for in a design doc1. The goal is the right order of magnitude, not three significant digits: 12 k or 15 k requests per second leads to the same design; 1.2 k or 120 k does not.

The tools come from Class 2 — Estimation: powers of two and ten, the latency and throughput numbers2, Little's Law, utilization, percentiles and availability math. In Lab 2 you will check some of these numbers against a real service.

items.title: Formulas you will use
items.text: Quantity Formula Typical assumption Seconds in a day 86,400 ≈ 10⁵ s round to 10⁵ for mental math Average QPS requests per day ÷ 86,400 — Peak QPS average × peak factor 2–3× for daily peaks; much higher for events Storage items per day × size × retention × replication replication factor 3 for durable stores Bandwidth QPS × payload size separate ingress (writes) and egress (reads) Cache size hot fraction × daily distinct items × item size "80/20": 20% of the items get 80% of the reads Concurrency (Little's Law) L = λ × W λ in req/s, W in seconds Servers peak QPS ÷ (capacity per server × target utilization) target utilization 0.6–0.7 Availability in series A = A₁ × A₂ × … every hop multiplies Availability in parallel A = 1 − (1 − Aᵢ)ⁿ n independent replicas

items.title: Task
items.text:
Fill in an estimation sheet for five systems:

  1. BoxOffice flash sale — mandatory for everybody (facts below).
  2. Four systems chosen from the fact sheets below (at least one read-heavy and one write-heavy).

For each system, estimate the quantities in the template, show the arithmetic, and finish with three design consequences derived from your numbers.

items.title: BoxOffice facts
items.text:
• The on-sale of a stadium show starts at 10:00; 2 M fans arrive in the first 10 minutes; there are 60 k seats, at most 4 per order.
  • A fan who is browsing does, on average, one request every 3 seconds (catalog, seat map, availability polling).
  • A waiting room admits fans to the purchase flow at a rate you must choose so that the sale lasts about 15 minutes.
  • A seat hold lasts 5 minutes; about 30% of holds expire without payment.
  • An order record is about 1 KB; a ticket e-mail about 50 KB; the seat map of the venue is about 200 KB of JSON.
  • Outside on-sales, BoxOffice serves 5 M daily active users browsing ~20 pages each.

items.title: Fact sheets
items.text:
All facts below are illustrative assumptions for the exercise — use them as given and add your own assumptions where needed.

System Facts Real-time chat 50 M DAU; 40 messages sent per user per day; 100 bytes per message; 25% of users online at peak; history kept 5 years Ride-sharing dispatch 2 M active drivers at peak sending a location every 4 s; 10 M rides per day; a location update is 100 bytes; trips kept 3 years Social feed 200 M DAU; 2 posts and 50 timeline reads per user per day; 30% of posts have a 500 KB image; a timeline page has 20 posts Video platform 500 k uploads per day, 5 min average, 4 resolutions totalling 1 GB per video; 1 B views per day of 4 min average at 2 Mbit/s AI support assistant 1 M conversations per day, 6 turns each; 1,500 input tokens (with RAG context) and 300 output tokens per turn; output at 50 tokens/s Notification system 100 M users; 5 notifications per user per day; 30% push, 60% e-mail, 10% SMS; bursts of 10× during campaigns Search autocomplete 100 M DAU; 6 searches per user per day; one request per typed character after the 2nd, average query of 10 characters Metrics platform 50 k hosts; 500 time series per host; one sample every 10 s; 16 bytes per sample; raw data kept 15 days, 1-minute rollups 1 year

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• (mandatory) Five complete sheets: BoxOffice + four fact sheets (at least one read-heavy and one write-heavy).
  • (mandatory) Every number has a unit and every derived number shows its formula (no bare results).
  • (mandatory) Assumptions are listed in a table, separated from the given facts.
  • Average and peak QPS, split into reads and writes.
  • Storage per year (with replication) and bandwidth (ingress and egress).
  • Cache size for the hot set, and whether it fits in one node.
  • Number of servers for the hottest path, using Little's Law for concurrency and a target utilization.
  • Availability of the main request path (series/parallel) compared with a target SLO.
  • One sanity check per system against a reference number (e.g. from the numbers cheat sheet).
  • Three design consequences per system, each pointing to a number in the sheet.
  • AI usage section (see the policy).

items.title: Deliverables
items.text:
• A page estimation in your documentation site with the five sheets (tag ex1).
  • Optional: the spreadsheet or script you used (committed to the repository) — the page must still show the formulas.

items.title: Step by step
items.text:
1. Read the facts and write down the question. "How many seat holds per second at peak?" is a question; "estimate BoxOffice" is not.
  2. List assumptions before computing. Write what you assume and why (e.g. "peak factor 3, from a typical daily curve").
  3. Compute averages, then peaks. Requests per day ÷ 10⁵ gives the average QPS; multiply by the peak factor. For events (on-sales, campaigns) compute the peak directly from the event: users × request rate.
  4. Split reads and writes. They hit different components (cache/CDN vs primary database).
  5. Size the data. Items × size × retention × replication. Then the hot set for the cache.
  6. Size the compute. Little's Law gives the in-flight requests; capacity per server and a target utilization give the number of servers.
  7. Check availability. Multiply the availabilities along the main path; add replicas where the result is below the SLO.
  8. Sanity-check. Compare with something you know (a number from class, a public engineering blog, the cheat sheet).
  9. Write the consequences. Each consequence is a decision justified by a number.

items.title: Worked example: URL shortener
items.text:
Facts (illustrative): 100 M new short URLs per month; read/write ratio 100:1; records kept 5 years; 500 bytes per record.

Quantity Arithmetic Result Writes, average 100 M ÷ (30 × 86,400 s) ≈ 100 M ÷ 2.6 M s ≈ 40 writes/s Writes, peak (×3) 40 × 3 ≈ 120 writes/s Reads, average 40 × 100 ≈ 4,000 reads/s Reads, peak (×3) 4,000 × 3 ≈ 12,000 reads/s Records in 5 years 100 M × 12 × 5 6 B records Storage 6 B × 500 B = 3 TB; × 3 replicas ≈ 9 TB Key length 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 × 10¹² > 6 × 10⁹ 7 base-62 characters Egress bandwidth 4,000 reads/s × 500 B ≈ 2 MB/s Cache (20% of a day's reads) 4,000 × 86,400 ≈ 350 M reads/day; 20% × 500 B ≈ 35 GB → one large node or a small cluster Concurrency at peak L = 12,000 req/s × 0.02 s ≈ 240 requests in flight App servers 12,000 ÷ (1,000 req/s per instance × 0.7) ≈ 18 instances (+2 for N+2) Availability LB 99.99% × app (2 replicas of 99.9%: 1 − 0.001² ≈ 99.9999%) × DB 99.95% ≈ 99.94%

Sanity check: 2 MB/s of egress is tiny — a single 1 Gbit/s NIC moves ~125 MB/s. The bottleneck is not bandwidth.

Design consequences:

  1. 12 k reads/s vs 120 writes/s → read-heavy: a cache in front of the database (hit ratio above 90% removes most database reads).
  2. 9 TB over 5 years → fits one SQL cluster, but a key-value store partitioned by short key keeps growth simple; no join is needed.
  3. 99.94% < 99.99% target → the database is the weakest link: add a standby with automatic failover (or accept the SLO).

BoxOffice — how to start

Start from the event, not from the day: 2 M fans in 10 minutes, one request every 3 s each. How many fans are browsing at the same time (Little's Law again: arrival rate × time spent)? That gives the catalog QPS. Then the waiting room: if the sale must last ~15 minutes for 60 k seats and an order has 2.5 seats on average, how many buyers per minute must be admitted? That number sizes the seat-hold path — and shows why the waiting room exists.

items.title: A tiny helper (optional)
items.text:
Writing the arithmetic as code keeps units honest. You may adapt this script; the page must still show the formulas.

estimate.py
DAY = 86_400  # seconds


def qps(per_day: float, peak_factor: float = 3.0) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Average and peak requests per second."""
    avg = per_day / DAY
    return avg, avg * peak_factor


def servers(peak_qps: float, per_server: float, target_util: float = 0.7, spare: int = 2) -> int:
    """Instances needed at the target utilization, plus spare capacity (N+spare)."""
    from math import ceil
    return ceil(peak_qps / (per_server * target_util)) + spare


def series(*avail: float) -> float:
    """Availability of components in series."""
    out = 1.0
    for a in avail:
        out *= a
    return out


def parallel(a: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Availability of n independent replicas."""
    return 1 - (1 - a) ** n


if __name__ == "__main__":
    writes = 100e6 / 30          # URL shortener: writes per day
    w_avg, w_peak = qps(writes)
    r_avg, r_peak = w_avg * 100, w_peak * 100
    print(f"writes {w_avg:,.0f}/s avg, {w_peak:,.0f}/s peak")
    print(f"reads  {r_avg:,.0f}/s avg, {r_peak:,.0f}/s peak")
    print(f"in flight at peak: {r_peak * 0.020:,.0f}")
    print(f"app servers: {servers(r_peak, 1_000)}")
    print(f"availability: {series(0.9999, parallel(0.999, 2), 0.9995):.4%}")

items.title: Rubric
items.text:
Levels as defined in How the exercises are graded.

Criterion I D C B A Completeness (mandatory) Not delivered Fewer than five sheets or quantities missing Five sheets, every quantity present — — Assumptions None Mixed with facts, unjustified Listed, separated from facts Justified (source or reasoning) Sensitivity noted: which assumption changes the design if wrong Arithmetic and units (mandatory) Bare numbers Unit or order-of-magnitude errors Correct orders of magnitude, units everywhere Formulas shown and consistent rounding Cross-checked two ways (e.g. per user and per second) Use of the formulas — Little's Law or availability missing Peak, Little's Law and availability applied Applied to the right path (hottest, critical) Explains the effect of utilization on latency (the knee) Sanity checks — None One per system Meaningful reference with a source Finds and fixes an own mistake through the check Design consequences — Generic ("use a cache") Three per system Each tied to a number Ranks them and names what would change at 10×

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
How precise must the numbers be?

One significant digit is usually enough. Round aggressively (86,400 ≈ 10⁵) but say that you did. What matters is the order of magnitude and that a reader can follow the arithmetic.

Where do I get the capacity of one server?

Use the numbers from class and the numbers cheat sheet, or — better — what you measured in Lab 2. Always say which one you used.

Can I change the given facts?

No. Facts are the same for everybody so that sheets can be compared. Add assumptions for whatever the facts do not say.

What is a good peak factor?

For daily traffic, 2–3× the average is common. For events (an on-sale, a campaign, a goal in a final) compute the peak from the event itself instead of multiplying the daily average.

The AI gave me a full sheet in seconds. Can I use it?

You may use AI to check your arithmetic or to discuss assumptions, and you must declare it. But the oral check for this exercise is simple: you will be asked to redo one line of a sheet on the board with a changed fact. Practise doing it yourself.

Do I need to include BoxOffice's normal (non-sale) traffic?

Yes, briefly: it shows how different the on-sale peak is from a normal day — which is exactly why BoxOffice needs a waiting room and elastic capacity.

  1. Alex Xu, System Design Interview — An Insider's Guide, vol. 1, ch. 2 "Back-of-the-envelope estimation", 2020. ↩

  2. Jeff Dean, "Numbers Everyone Should Know", in Designs, Lessons and Advice from Building Large Distributed Systems, LADIS 2009. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
A fan pays for two seats, the BoxOffice order service saves the order… and crashes before telling anybody. No ticket e-mail. Or the opposite: the event goes out, the database transaction rolls back, and a fan receives a ticket for an order that does not exist. Or the broker delivers the same event twice and the fan gets two e-mails — and later, two tickets. This is the dual-write problem, and every event-driven system has to solve it. In this exercise you solve it with a transactional outbox, an idempotent consumer and a dead-letter topic, and then you try hard to break it.

Learning objectives

After this exercise you will be able to:

  • Explain why "save to the database, then publish to Kafka" loses or invents events, and how the outbox fixes it.
  • Implement a transactional outbox with a polling relay and an idempotent consumer with retries and a DLQ.
  • Reason about delivery semantics: at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing = effectively-once side effects.
  • Verify correctness under failures with a reconciliation query, and measure end-to-end latency and consumer lag.

items.title: Context
items.text:
Class 8 covered queues, pub/sub and the event log, Kafka's partitions and consumer groups, delivery semantics and the outbox/saga patterns1. Lab 7 set up Kafka (KRaft) with BoxOffice's order and notification services. Here you make that flow correct under failure and prove it.

flowchart LR
    client([k6]) -->|POST /orders| order[order]
    order -->|"1 · one transaction: order + outbox row"| odb[("order_svc<br/>orders · outbox")]
    relay[outbox relay] -->|"2 · poll unpublished rows"| odb
    relay -->|"3 · publish, key = orderId"| kafka{{"Kafka · order-events"}}
    kafka -->|"4 · consume"| notif[notification]
    notif -->|"5 · one transaction: processed_events + ticket_emails"| ndb[("notification_svc<br/>processed_events · ticket_emails")]
    notif -.->|"poison message after retries"| dlt{{"order-events.DLT"}}

Why each piece exists:

Piece Failure it handles Outbox row in the same transaction as the order Crash between "save" and "publish": the event is in the database, it will be published later Relay marks a row as published after the broker ack Broker down or relay crash: the row is retried (→ duplicates are possible: at-least-once) processed_events insert in the same transaction as the side effect Duplicate delivery: the second insert conflicts and the side effect is skipped Retries with backoff, then DLT Transient errors are retried; a poison message does not block the partition forever Kafka key = orderId All events of an order go to the same partition, in order

items.title: Task
items.text:
Implement and verify the flow order confirmed → ticket e-mail for BoxOffice (or the equivalent flow of your own services):

  1. order writes the order and an outbox row (event envelope) in one transaction.
  2. A relay publishes unpublished outbox rows to the order-events topic (key = orderId) and marks them after the broker acknowledges.
  3. notification consumes the events idempotently (deduplication by event id in the same transaction as the side effect), retries transient errors with backoff and sends poison messages to a DLT.
  4. Run a 10-minute load while injecting failures (relay crash, broker outage, consumer crash, duplicate event, poison message) and prove with a reconciliation query that there are zero lost and zero duplicated e-mails.
  5. Measure end-to-end latency and consumer lag, with and without failures.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• (mandatory) Outbox row written in the same transaction as the business change (show the code).
  • (mandatory) Idempotent consumer: deduplication by event id in the same transaction as the side effect.
  • (mandatory) Reconciliation after the 10-minute run with failures: 0 lost and 0 duplicated side effects (query and its output in the report).
  • Event envelope with at least eventId, type, version, occurredAt and the business key.
  • Relay publishes with acks=all and marks rows only after the ack; the outbox returns to 0 unpublished rows after the broker comes back (time measured).
  • Retries with exponential backoff and a DLT; the poison message is in the DLT and the consumer keeps processing the next messages.
  • Failure schedule executed during the load: relay/order crash, broker stopped ≥ 60 s, consumer killed (SIGKILL) mid-processing, one duplicated valid event, one poison message.
  • End-to-end latency (order confirmed → side effect) p50/p95/p99, and consumer lag over time.
  • A discussion of ordering (what the key guarantees and what it does not), and of the real e-mail (an external side effect outside your database).
  • AI usage section (see the policy).

items.title: Deliverables
items.text: In your repository (tag ex4): code of both services, migrations, compose.yaml, k6 script, failure script, the reconciliation and latency queries and their outputs; an event-driven page on your documentation site following the template.

items.title: 1. Kafka (KRaft) and the schemas
items.text:
Reuse the Kafka of Lab 7. For reference, a single-node KRaft broker with the official image:

compose.yaml (excerpt)
services:
  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:3.8.0
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://:9092,CONTROLLER://:9093,EXTERNAL://:29092
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://kafka:9092,EXTERNAL://localhost:29092
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,EXTERNAL:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1
      KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: 0
    ports:
      - "29092:29092"

Each service owns its data. To make the reconciliation a single query, this exercise keeps both services in one PostgreSQL instance with two schemas (Compose service postgres, database boxoffice: order_svc and notification_svc), each service using only its own schema. In production they would be separate databases and the reconciliation a small job.

order/src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__outbox.sql
CREATE TABLE outbox (
    id             UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    aggregate_type VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id   VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
    event_type     VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    payload        JSONB        NOT NULL,
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    published_at   TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON outbox (created_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL;
notification/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__notification.sql
CREATE TABLE processed_events (
    event_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    processed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE ticket_emails (
    id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id   UUID         NOT NULL,
    event_id   UUID         NOT NULL,
    recipient  VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

No unique constraint on ticket_emails.order_id

It is tempting to add one — and in production you might. Here, leave it out: the point is to show that the consumer logic prevents duplicates. A unique constraint would hide a broken consumer.

items.title: 2. Write the order and the event together
3. The relay
items.text:
A polling publisher reads unpublished rows, publishes each one and waits for the broker's acknowledgement before marking it. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets you run a second relay without both publishing the same row at the same time.

order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/OutboxRelay.java
package boxoffice.order;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.JdbcTemplate;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.Scheduled;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Component
public class OutboxRelay {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;

    public OutboxRelay(JdbcTemplate jdbc, KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.kafka = kafka;
    }

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 200)   // requires @EnableScheduling on a configuration class
    @Transactional
    public void publishBatch() {
        List<Map<String, Object>> rows = jdbc.queryForList("""
            SELECT id, aggregate_id, payload::text AS payload
              FROM outbox
             WHERE published_at IS NULL
             ORDER BY created_at
             LIMIT 100
             FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
            """);
        for (Map<String, Object> row : rows) {
            String key = (String) row.get("aggregate_id");
            String payload = (String) row.get("payload");
            kafka.send("order-events", key, payload).join();   // wait for the ack (acks=all)
            jdbc.update("UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = ?", row.get("id"));
        }
    }
}
order/src/main/resources/application.yaml (excerpt)
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka:9092
    producer:
      acks: all
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        delivery.timeout.ms: 30000

If the relay crashes after send and before the transaction commits, the row is published again on the next poll. That is fine — the consumer is idempotent. Change Data Capture with Debezium (reading the outbox from the PostgreSQL WAL) is an alternative relay; it is a good A-level extension.

items.title: 4. The idempotent consumer, retries and the DLT
5. Load and failures
6. Verify and measure
items.text:
verify.sql
-- lost: confirmed orders without exactly one ticket e-mail
SELECT o.id, count(t.id) AS emails
  FROM order_svc.orders o
  LEFT JOIN notification_svc.ticket_emails t ON t.order_id = o.id
 WHERE o.status = 'CONFIRMED'
 GROUP BY o.id
HAVING count(t.id) <> 1;

-- duplicated side effects
SELECT order_id, count(*) FROM notification_svc.ticket_emails GROUP BY order_id HAVING count(*) > 1;

-- outbox backlog (must return to 0)
SELECT count(*) AS unpublished FROM order_svc.outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL;

-- end-to-end latency in seconds: order confirmed -> ticket e-mail recorded
SELECT percentile_cont(ARRAY[0.5, 0.95, 0.99]) WITHIN GROUP (
         ORDER BY extract(epoch FROM t.created_at - o.confirmed_at)) AS p50_p95_p99
  FROM notification_svc.ticket_emails t
  JOIN order_svc.orders o ON o.id = t.order_id;

docker compose exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh \
  --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --group notification
docker compose exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh \
  --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --topic order-events.DLT --from-beginning --timeout-ms 5000

Sample the consumer lag every few seconds during the run (a loop around kafka-consumer-groups.sh, or the Kafka metrics of the observability stack in Lab 8) to plot it over time: you should see it grow while notification is down and drain afterwards.

items.title: Templates
items.text:
EnglishPortuguês 
# Event-driven — outbox and idempotent consumer

## 1. Flow and design
Diagram; event envelope (fields and an example); topic, partitions, key; consumer group.

## 2. Why it is correct

items.title: Rubric
items.text:
Levels as defined in How the exercises are graded.

Criterion I D C B A Transactional outbox (mandatory) Absent Publish outside the transaction (dual write) Outbox in the same transaction, relay marks after ack Envelope versioned; relay safe with two instances CDC (Debezium) relay compared with polling Idempotent consumer (mandatory) Absent Dedup outside the side-effect transaction Dedup by event id in the same transaction Retention/cleanup of processed_events discussed Real e-mail sender idempotent with the provider (key = event id) Retries and DLT — No DLT, or poison blocks the partition Backoff + DLT; consumer keeps going Retryable vs non-retryable errors justified DLT replay procedure documented and tested Verification under failures (mandatory) No proof Some failures not executed All five failures; 0 lost, 0 duplicated Timeline of the run with outbox backlog and lag Additional failure (e.g. network partition) tested Measurements — Only averages p50/p95/p99 end to end + lag With vs without failures compared and explained Lag predicted from rates (backlog ÷ drain rate) and checked Discussion — Missing Ordering and external side effect addressed Trade-offs of exactly-once in Kafka vs idempotency Clear statement of the guarantees of the whole flow

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Kafka has exactly-once semantics. Why do I need all this?

Kafka's transactions give exactly-once inside Kafka (consume → produce → commit offsets). Your side effects — a row in PostgreSQL, an e-mail — live outside Kafka. The robust recipe is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, which makes the effect happen once.

Can I use @TransactionalEventListener instead of an outbox?

It publishes after the commit, but if the process dies between the commit and the publish, the event is lost — the dual-write problem again, only rarer. The outbox survives crashes because the event is in the database.

Will the relay publish events out of order?

With one relay and ORDER BY created_at, events are published in commit order (approximately). Kafka keeps the order per partition, and the key orderId puts all events of an order in the same partition. There is no global order across orders — and BoxOffice does not need one. Explain this in your discussion.

How long do I keep processed_events?

At least as long as a duplicate can arrive (retention of the topic, relay retries). In practice, days; then delete old rows with a scheduled job. Say what you would choose and why.

My consumer lag never goes down after the broker comes back.

Check that the consumer reconnects (logs), that it is not stuck retrying a poison message (is the DLT configured?), and that the topic has as many partitions as you expect. kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe shows the lag per partition.

The duplicate injection did not create a duplicate e-mail. Did it work?

That is the expected result. Prove that the duplicate was delivered: the consumer's log line for a skipped duplicate, or the count of consumed messages vs rows in processed_events.

  1. Chris Richardson, "Pattern: Transactional outbox", microservices.io. ↩

  2. Spring for Apache Kafka reference, "Handling exceptions" and "Publishing dead-letter records", docs.spring.io/spring-kafka. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
At 10:00 the BoxOffice catalog goes from a quiet morning to ten times its normal traffic in under a minute. Nobody can add servers that fast by hand — a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can. But "automatic" is not "instant": metrics are sampled, decisions are periodic, new pods must start, warm up and pass their readiness probe. In this exercise you deploy a service on Kubernetes, put it under a k6 ramp, and measure how fast and how well it scales — and what breaks while it does.

Learning objectives

After this exercise you will be able to:

  • Configure a production-shaped Deployment: requests/limits, startup/readiness/liveness probes, graceful shutdown, Service, Ingress.
  • Configure an HPA (autoscaling/v2) with a CPU target and scaling behavior.
  • Predict the number of replicas with the HPA formula and measure the actual scaling timeline under load.
  • Decompose the scaling lag (metrics window, sync period, pod start-up, JVM warm-up, readiness).
  • Prove a zero-downtime rolling update under load, and find the next bottleneck (connections to the database).

items.title: Context
items.text:
Class 12 covered containers, Kubernetes objects, probes and autoscaling; Class 5 the theory of autoscaling (target tracking, warm-up, predictive). Lab 10 deployed BoxOffice to kind or minikube with an Ingress. This exercise turns that deployment into an experiment.

The HPA controller computes, every sync period (15 s by default)1:

\[ \text{desiredReplicas} = \left\lceil \text{currentReplicas} \times \frac{\text{currentMetricValue}}{\text{targetMetricValue}} \right\rceil \]

For CPU, the metric is the average utilization relative to the pod's CPU request. If 2 pods run at 150% of their request and the target is 60%, the HPA asks for ⌈2 × 150 / 60⌉ = 5 pods.

sequenceDiagram
    participant K as k6 (load ramp)
    participant P as catalog pods
    participant M as metrics-server
    participant H as HPA controller
    participant D as Deployment
    K->>P: requests per second grow
    M->>P: scrape CPU (every ~15 s)
    H->>M: read average utilization
    H->>D: replicas = ceil(current × util / target)
    D->>P: create pods
    P-->>P: start JVM, startup probe, warm-up
    P-->>H: readiness OK: pods receive traffic, utilization drops

items.title: Task
items.text:
1. Deploy the BoxOffice catalog (or your own service) and PostgreSQL on kind or minikube with the manifests below (adapted): requests/limits, three probes, graceful shutdown, Service, Ingress and an HPA (min 2, max 10, CPU target 60%).
  2. E1 — Scale-up timeline: run a k6 ramp from a low rate to a rate that needs ~3× the minimum replicas; record replicas, CPU utilization, p99 and errors over time; then watch it scale down.
  3. E2 — One variable: repeat E1 changing one thing: no readiness probe, a different CPU request, or a different scale-up policy. Compare.
  4. E3 — Rolling update under load: kubectl rollout restart during steady load, with zero failed requests.
  5. Compute the database connection budget at maximum scale and say what breaks first.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• (mandatory) Deployment with CPU/memory requests and limits, startup, readiness and liveness probes and graceful shutdown; Service; Ingress; HPA autoscaling/v2 with behavior.
  • (mandatory) A time series (CSV committed) of desired/current/ready replicas and CPU utilization, every ≤ 5 s, aligned with k6 latency and errors.
  • (mandatory) A chart of replicas and p99 over time for E1, with the load ramp marked.
  • HPA scales from 2 to ≥ 4 replicas during E1 and back down after the stabilization window.
  • The predicted steady-state replicas (formula, with your measured CPU per request) vs the observed ones — within ±1 replica, or the difference explained.
  • The scaling lag decomposed: load step → utilization above target → HPA decision → pod scheduled → pod ready.
  • E2 compared with E1 (same load, one change), with a conclusion.
  • E3: 0 failed requests during a rolling restart at a steady rate (k6 summary).
  • Connection budget: maxReplicas × pool size vs PostgreSQL max_connections, and the fix you would apply.
  • A video of at most 3 minutes showing E1 (k6 running, kubectl get hpa -w, pods appearing).
  • AI usage section (see the policy).

items.title: Deliverables
items.text: In your repository (tag ex5): k8s/ manifests, k6 scripts, the recording script, CSVs and charts in k8s/results/, the video (or a link to it); a kubernetes-autoscaling page on your documentation site following the template.

items.title: 1. Cluster and metrics-server
items.text:
The HPA needs resource metrics, served by metrics-server.

minikubekind 
minikube start --cpus=4 --memory=8g
minikube addons enable metrics-server
minikube addons enable ingress
minikube image load boxoffice/catalog:latest

kind create cluster --config kind.yaml   # with extraPortMappings for the Ingress, as in Lab 10
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml
# kind's kubelets use self-signed certificates
kubectl patch -n kube-system deployment metrics-server --type=json \
  -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]'
kind load docker-image boxoffice/catalog:latest

Check with kubectl top pods -A (it takes about a minute after start-up). PostgreSQL comes from Lab 10 (Secret, PVC, Deployment and Service postgres).

items.title: 2. The Deployment
items.text:
k8s/catalog.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: catalog
data:
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/catalog
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_HIKARI_MAXIMUM_POOL_SIZE: "10"
  SERVER_SHUTDOWN: graceful
  SPRING_LIFECYCLE_TIMEOUT_PER_SHUTDOWN_PHASE: 20s
  MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINT_HEALTH_PROBES_ENABLED: "true"
  JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: catalog
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: catalog
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: catalog
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: catalog
          image: boxoffice/catalog:latest
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: catalog
            - secretRef:
                name: catalog-db   # SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME / SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 512Mi
            limits:
              cpu: "1"
              memory: 768Mi
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health/liveness
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 60   # up to 120 s to start
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health/readiness
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 2
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /actuator/health/liveness
              port: 8080
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              sleep:
                seconds: 5   # let the endpoints update before shutdown (Kubernetes >= 1.30)
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: catalog
spec:
  selector:
    app: catalog
  ports:
    - port: 8080
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: catalog
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: catalog
                port:
                  number: 8080

Why each block matters2:

Block What goes wrong without it requests.cpu The HPA cannot compute utilization (it is relative to the request); the scheduler overcommits nodes limits.memory + MaxRAMPercentage The JVM sizes its heap for the node, not the container, and gets OOM-killed startupProbe A slow JVM start is killed by the liveness probe before it is up (restart loop) readinessProbe New pods receive traffic before they can serve it: errors exactly when you scale up preStop + graceful shutdown + maxUnavailable: 0 In-flight requests fail on every deploy and every scale-down

items.title: 3. The HPA
items.text:
k8s/catalog-hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: catalog
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: catalog
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 100        # at most double the replicas...
          periodSeconds: 30 # ...every 30 s
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 120
      policies:
        - type: Pods
          value: 1
          periodSeconds: 30

kubectl apply -f k8s/catalog.yaml -f k8s/catalog-hpa.yaml
kubectl get hpa catalog -w

items.title: 4. Record the timeline
items.text:
k8s/record.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: ./k8s/record.sh k8s/results/e1-hpa.csv   (stop with Ctrl+C)
OUT=${1:-k8s/results/hpa.csv}
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$OUT")"
echo "ts,desired,current,ready,cpu_util" > "$OUT"
while true; do
  H=$(kubectl get hpa catalog -o jsonpath='{.status.desiredReplicas},{.status.currentReplicas},{.status.currentMetrics[0].resource.current.averageUtilization}')
  R=$(kubectl get deployment catalog -o jsonpath='{.status.readyReplicas}')
  IFS=, read -r DESIRED CURRENT CPU <<< "$H"
  echo "$(date +%s),${DESIRED},${CURRENT},${R:-0},${CPU}" >> "$OUT"
  sleep 5
done

items.title: 5. The load
items.text:
Measure the CPU cost of one request first (a short constant rate with 2 replicas: CPU used ÷ requests per second) so that you can predict the replicas before running E1.

load/hpa-ramp.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

const BASE = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost';
const PEAK = Number(__ENV.PEAK || 600); // req/s at the top of the ramp

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ramp: {
      executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: Math.round(PEAK * 0.1), timeUnit: '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 100, maxVUs: 1000,
      stages: [
        { target: Math.round(PEAK * 0.1), duration: '1m' }, // quiet morning
        { target: PEAK, duration: '1m' },                   // 10:00, the on-sale starts
        { target: PEAK, duration: '6m' },                   // sustained peak
        { target: Math.round(PEAK * 0.1), duration: '1m' },
        { target: Math.round(PEAK * 0.1), duration: '4m' }, // watch the scale-down
      ],
    },
  },
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'med', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
};

export default function () {
  const id = 1 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 1000);
  const res = http.get(`${BASE}/events/${id}`, { tags: { name: 'GET /events/{id}' } });
  check(res, { 'status is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

./k8s/record.sh k8s/results/e1-hpa.csv &
k6 run -e BASE_URL=http://localhost -e PEAK=600 --out csv=k8s/results/e1-k6.csv load/hpa-ramp.js
kill %1

Do not load test through kubectl port-forward

port-forward is a debugging tunnel through the API server; it becomes the bottleneck long before your pods do. Use the Ingress (Lab 10). If your local networking does not allow it, run k6 inside the cluster as a Job (below).

k6 as a Job inside the cluster k8s/k6-job.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: k6-ramp
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: k6
          image: grafana/k6:latest
          args: ["run", "--quiet", "--no-summary", "--out", "csv=/dev/stdout",
                 "-e", "BASE_URL=http://catalog:8080", "-e", "PEAK=600", "/scripts/hpa-ramp.js"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: scripts
              mountPath: /scripts
      volumes:
        - name: scripts
          configMap:
            name: k6-scripts

kubectl create configmap k6-scripts --from-file=load/hpa-ramp.js
kubectl apply -f k8s/k6-job.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/k6-ramp --timeout=20m
kubectl logs job/k6-ramp > k8s/results/e1-k6.csv

k6 then shares the cluster's CPU with your pods — say so in the report.

items.title: 6. Plot replicas and latency together
items.text:
k8s/plot_hpa.py
import csv
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# usage: python k8s/plot_hpa.py k8s/results/e1-hpa.csv k8s/results/e1-k6.csv k8s/results/e1.png
hpa_file, k6_file, out = sys.argv[1:4]

hpa = list(csv.DictReader(open(hpa_file)))
t0 = int(hpa[0]["ts"])
t = [int(r["ts"]) - t0 for r in hpa]

lat, err = defaultdict(list), defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0])
for row in csv.DictReader(open(k6_file)):
    if row.get("metric_name") == "http_req_duration":
        lat[int(float(row["timestamp"])) // 10 * 10].append(float(row["metric_value"]))
    elif row.get("metric_name") == "http_req_failed":
        bucket = err[int(float(row["timestamp"])) // 10 * 10]
        bucket[0] += float(row["metric_value"])
        bucket[1] += 1


def p99(values):
    values = sorted(values)
    return values[int(0.99 * (len(values) - 1))]


windows = sorted(lat)
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
ax1.step(t, [int(r["desired"] or 0) for r in hpa], where="post", label="desired")
ax1.step(t, [int(r["ready"] or 0) for r in hpa], where="post", label="ready")
ax1.set_xlabel("time (s)")
ax1.set_ylabel("replicas")
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.plot([w - t0 for w in windows], [p99(lat[w]) for w in windows], color="tab:red", label="p99 (10 s)")
ax2.set_ylabel("p99 (ms)")
fig.legend(loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(out, dpi=150)
print("error rate per window:", {w - t0: round(e[0] / e[1], 4) for w, e in sorted(err.items()) if e[1]})

items.title: 7. Rolling update under load (E3)
items.text:
Run a constant rate at about half of what the minimum replicas sustain, and restart the Deployment in the middle:

k6 run -e BASE_URL=http://localhost -e PEAK=150 load/hpa-ramp.js &
sleep 120 && kubectl rollout restart deployment/catalog && kubectl rollout status deployment/catalog
wait

The k6 summary must show http_req_failed = 0. If it does not, find which piece is missing: readiness, preStop, graceful shutdown, maxUnavailable: 0.

items.title: 8. The next bottleneck
items.text: Each replica has its own connection pool. At maxReplicas: 10 with a pool of 10, that is 100 connections — exactly PostgreSQL's default max_connections, with nothing left for migrations, admin or a second service. The autoscaler can make things worse by scaling the stateless tier into a database that cannot follow. Compute your budget and propose a fix (smaller pools, PgBouncer, a maxReplicas derived from the database, read replicas, a cache).

items.title: Rubric
items.text:
Levels as defined in How the exercises are graded.

Criterion I D C B A Manifests (mandatory) Do not apply Requests/limits or a probe missing Requests/limits, 3 probes, graceful shutdown, Service, Ingress, HPA v2 with behavior Each setting justified (table) JVM memory, probes and timeouts tuned from measurements Timeline data (mandatory) No data Screenshots only CSV time series + chart of replicas and p99 Lag decomposed into its phases with timestamps Lag reduced by a change and the reduction measured Prediction — None Formula applied Within ±1 replica or difference explained CPU per request measured at several rates (linearity checked) E2 comparison — Not done Done with the same load Clear conclusion with numbers Second variable or a custom metric (e.g. requests per second, KEDA) Zero-downtime update — Errors not investigated 0 failed requests Explains which setting prevents which failure Shows the failure without one setting and with it Next bottleneck and communication — Missing Connection budget computed Fix proposed and argued Fix implemented and tested at max scale; video crisp

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
kubectl get hpa shows <unknown>/60%.

metrics-server is not running or not ready yet (wait a minute after start-up; on kind, check the --kubelet-insecure-tls patch), or the pods have no CPU request — utilization is relative to the request.

The HPA does not scale even with high load.

Check the actual CPU of the pods (kubectl top pods): if the bottleneck is the database or the connection pool, CPU stays low and the HPA has no reason to scale. That is a valid — and important — finding. Say what metric would have scaled correctly.

Pods scale up but errors appear exactly at that moment.

Usually a missing or too permissive readiness probe (traffic before the app is ready) or a cold JVM (the first requests are slow). Compare with E2, and consider a warm-up step before the readiness probe passes.

Scale-down takes forever.

By design: the default scale-down stabilization window is 5 minutes, to avoid flapping. The manifest above shortens it to 2 minutes for the experiment. Discuss the trade-off for BoxOffice (an on-sale may have a second wave).

My laptop cannot generate enough load to need 4 replicas.

Lower the CPU request (e.g. 250m) so that each pod saturates sooner, or make each request more expensive (a heavier endpoint). Explain the choice; the goal is to observe the mechanism, not a big number.

Can I use a cloud cluster instead?

Yes (EKS, GKE, AKS), if you watch the costs and delete it afterwards. The manifests are the same; the Ingress class and the metrics-server setup may differ.

  1. Kubernetes documentation, "Horizontal Pod Autoscaling — Algorithm details", kubernetes.io. ↩

  2. Kubernetes documentation, "Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes", kubernetes.io. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
"How many requests per second does the BoxOffice catalog handle?" is a question with no answer until you add "…with a p99 below 200 ms and less than 1% errors, on this machine". In this exercise you run a small but rigorous k6 campaign against your own service, find the point where latency explodes (the knee), name the resource that causes it, change one thing and prove the change with a new measurement.

Learning objectives

After this exercise you will be able to:

  • Design smoke, load, stress and spike tests with an open workload model and SLO thresholds.
  • Run them reproducibly (fixed resources, repetitions, raw results committed).
  • Read percentiles and throughput-vs-latency curves and locate the knee.
  • Diagnose the bottleneck with resource metrics, the USE method and Little's Law.
  • Verify a hypothesis with a single change and a re-test.

items.title: Context
items.text:
Lab 2 introduced k6 and percentiles on the catalog service; Lab 3 put it behind Nginx with replicas. Class 2 gave you the theory: utilization, queueing, the knee, tail latency and Little's Law. Class 15 goes deeper later in the semester, and the project's load-test campaign reuses everything you build here.

Two ideas make the difference between a load test and a number:

  • Open vs closed model. A closed model (N virtual users in a loop) slows down when the server slows down — it politely stops sending, and hides the problem (coordinated omission). Real users arrive whether or not the server is slow. Use k6's arrival-rate executors (constant-arrival-rate, ramping-arrival-rate): they start iterations at a fixed rate, independent of response times1.
  • Thresholds are SLOs. p(99)<500 and rate<0.01 turn "it seemed fine" into pass/fail.
flowchart LR
    k6["k6 (open model)<br/>arrival rate λ"] --> nginx["nginx (lb)"]
    nginx --> c1["catalog #1"]
    nginx --> c2["catalog #2"]
    c1 --> db[("PostgreSQL")]
    c2 --> db
    stats["docker stats / actuator<br/>CPU, pool, threads"] -.-> c1
    stats -.-> db

items.title: Task
items.text:
Run a load-test campaign against one HTTP endpoint (or a small mix) of your own service — the BoxOffice catalog from the labs (recommended) or another service of yours — and write a report that answers:

  1. What is the maximum sustainable throughput of your setup with p99 below your SLO and errors below 1%?
  2. Where is the knee, and which resource causes it?
  3. What one change moves the knee, and by how much?

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• (mandatory) The service runs with fixed resources (cpus/mem_limit in compose.yaml) and the environment is described (CPU, RAM, OS, versions, where k6 runs).
  • (mandatory) Raw results committed: one k6 summary JSON per run (and CSV if you plot time series).
  • k6 scripts use arrival-rate executors and thresholds for p95/p99 latency and error rate.
  • Smoke test: passes with 0 errors.
  • Load test: at least 10 minutes at a constant rate that meets the SLO, repeated 3 times; report mean and spread (min–max) of p99.
  • Stress test: steps up to at least 2× the load rate (or until failure); a throughput vs p99 chart with the knee marked.
  • Spike test: a sudden jump to ≥ 3× the base rate; report errors during the spike and the recovery time to normal p99.
  • Little's Law check at the load rate: in-flight requests L = λ × W compared with the server threads and the database connection pool.
  • Bottleneck analysis with resource evidence (CPU, memory, threads, pool waits, GC, DB) — not a guess.
  • One change + re-test (e.g. pool size, replicas, an index, virtual threads, a cache) with before/after numbers under the same script and data.
  • A one-sentence capacity statement: "one instance with 2 vCPU sustains X req/s at p99 < Y ms".
  • AI usage section (see the policy).

items.title: Deliverables
items.text: In your repository (tag ex2): the k6 scripts in load/, the raw results in load/results/, the compose.yaml used, any plotting script; on your documentation site a page load-test-report following the template.

items.title: 1. Pin the environment
items.text:
Results are only comparable if the resources do not change. Limit the service and the database in compose.yaml, and seed the database with enough data (e.g. 1,000 events) so that queries are realistic.

compose.yaml (excerpt)
services:
  catalog:
    image: boxoffice/catalog:latest
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/catalog
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_HIKARI_MAXIMUM_POOL_SIZE: "10"
      MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINTS_WEB_EXPOSURE_INCLUDE: health,metrics,prometheus
    cpus: "2"
    mem_limit: 1g
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: catalog
      POSTGRES_USER: catalog
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: catalog
    cpus: "2"
    mem_limit: 1g

k6 also uses CPU

If k6 runs on the same laptop, it competes with the service. Keep the service limited (as above), watch k6's own CPU, and say in the report where k6 ran. If k6 warns about dropped_iterations or insufficient VUs, the load generator — not your service — is the bottleneck.

items.title: 2. Write one script, several test types
items.text:
One script with the test type chosen by an environment variable keeps the request mix identical across tests.

load/catalog.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

const BASE = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:8080';
const TYPE = __ENV.TEST_TYPE || 'smoke';
const RATE = Number(__ENV.RATE || 200);      // load-test rate (req/s)
const EVENTS = Number(__ENV.EVENTS || 1000); // ids seeded in the database

function stressStages() {
  const stages = [];
  for (const f of [0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3]) {
    stages.push({ target: Math.round(RATE * f), duration: '30s' }); // ramp to the step
    stages.push({ target: Math.round(RATE * f), duration: '90s' }); // hold the step
  }
  return stages;
}

const profiles = {
  smoke: {
    executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', rate: 5, timeUnit: '1s',
    duration: '30s', preAllocatedVUs: 5,
  },
  load: {
    executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: 0, timeUnit: '1s',
    preAllocatedVUs: 50, maxVUs: 500,
    stages: [
      { target: RATE, duration: '2m' },  // warm-up ramp
      { target: RATE, duration: '10m' }, // steady state: this is what you report
      { target: 0, duration: '30s' },
    ],
  },
  stress: {
    executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: 0, timeUnit: '1s',
    preAllocatedVUs: 100, maxVUs: 2000, stages: stressStages(),
  },
  spike: {
    executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: Math.round(RATE * 0.3), timeUnit: '1s',
    preAllocatedVUs: 100, maxVUs: 2000,
    stages: [
      { target: Math.round(RATE * 0.3), duration: '1m' },
      { target: RATE * 3, duration: '10s' },               // the spike
      { target: RATE * 3, duration: '1m' },
      { target: Math.round(RATE * 0.3), duration: '10s' },
      { target: Math.round(RATE * 0.3), duration: '2m' },  // recovery
    ],
  },
};

export const options = {
  scenarios: { [TYPE]: profiles[TYPE] },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<200', 'p(99)<500'],
  },
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'min', 'med', 'p(90)', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
};

export default function () {
  const id = 1 + Math.floor(Math.random() * EVENTS);
  const res = http.get(`${BASE}/events/${id}`, { tags: { name: 'GET /events/{id}' } });
  check(res, { 'status is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

Adjust the thresholds to your SLO and the URL to your endpoint. Stress and spike tests are expected to cross the thresholds: what you report is where and how they fail.

items.title: 3. Run and keep everything
items.text:
load/run.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: ./load/run.sh <type> <rate> <run-number>
set -euo pipefail
TYPE=${1:-smoke}; RATE=${2:-200}; RUN=${3:-1}
mkdir -p load/results
# resource usage of every container, every 2 s, in the background
( while true; do
    docker stats --no-stream --format '{{.Name}},{{.CPUPerc}},{{.MemUsage}}' \
      | sed "s/^/$(date +%s),/" >> "load/results/${TYPE}-r${RATE}-run${RUN}-docker.csv"
    sleep 2
  done ) &
STATS=$!
trap 'kill $STATS' EXIT
k6 run -e TEST_TYPE="$TYPE" -e RATE="$RATE" \
  --summary-export "load/results/${TYPE}-r${RATE}-run${RUN}.json" \
  --out csv="load/results/${TYPE}-r${RATE}-run${RUN}.csv" \
  load/catalog.js

Suggested order: smoke → stress (to find the knee) → choose the load rate at about 70% of the knee → load ×3 → spike. Restart the service between runs (or always warm it up) so that runs start from the same state.

items.title: 4. Find the knee
items.text:
Each step of the stress test gives one point (achieved throughput, p99). Plot p99 against throughput: it is flat while utilization is low, then bends sharply as utilization approaches 1 — the knee. The chart below is illustrative (an M/M/1 queue with a 1 ms service time), not a measurement; yours will come from your runs.

2026-10-23T08:15:51.457162 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ 200 400 600 800 1000 throughput (req/s) 0 25 50 75 100 125 150 175 200 p99 latency (ms) SLO: p99 < 50 ms knee Illustrative throughput vs p99 (M/M/1, not measured)

A small script turns your summary files into the same chart:

load/plot_knee.py
import glob
import json
import sys

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# usage: python load/plot_knee.py "load/results/stress-step-*.json"
points = []
for path in sorted(glob.glob(sys.argv[1])):
    m = json.load(open(path))["metrics"]
    points.append((m["http_reqs"]["rate"], m["http_req_duration"]["p(99)"]))
points.sort()
plt.plot([p[0] for p in points], [p[1] for p in points], marker="o")
plt.xlabel("achieved throughput (req/s)")
plt.ylabel("p99 (ms)")
plt.savefig("load/results/knee.png", dpi=150)

One point per step

A single stress run mixes all steps in one summary. Either run one short constant-arrival-rate test per step (e.g. 100, 200, 300… req/s for 2 minutes each, one JSON per step), or compute p99 per step from the CSV output by filtering on the timestamps of each step.

items.title: 5. Find the bottleneck
items.text:
Use the USE method for each resource — Utilization, Saturation, Errors2:

Resource Where to look Saturation sign App CPU docker stats, process.cpu.usage CPU near the cpus limit, throttling Server threads tomcat.threads.busy / executor.active (actuator) busy = max DB connection pool hikaricp.connections.pending, .usage pending > 0 JVM memory / GC jvm.gc.pause, jvm.memory.used long or frequent pauses Database docker stats of db, pg_stat_activity, EXPLAIN ANALYZE CPU at limit, sequential scans, lock waits 
curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.pending | jq '.measurements'
curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/tomcat.threads.busy | jq '.measurements'
docker compose exec db psql -U catalog -c "select state, count(*) from pg_stat_activity group by state;"

Then check with Little's Law. If the load test achieves λ = 400 req/s with a mean latency W = 25 ms, there are L = 400 × 0.025 = 10 requests in flight. If each request holds a database connection for most of its time and the pool has 10 connections, the pool is full: the next request waits — that is the knee. Hikari's default maximum-pool-size is 10, which is why this is the classic first bottleneck of a Spring Boot service.

items.title: 6. Change one thing and re-test
items.text: Form a hypothesis ("the pool is the bottleneck; with 30 connections the knee moves from ~400 to ~1,000 req/s, until the DB CPU saturates"), change only that, and rerun the same stress and load tests. Report before/after side by side. A refuted hypothesis is a valid result if the evidence is clear — say what you learned.

items.title: Rubric
items.text:
Levels as defined in How the exercises are graded.

Criterion I D C B A Reproducibility (mandatory) Numbers without raw data Environment or resources not fixed/described Fixed resources, environment described, raw JSON for every run One command reruns any test A classmate reruns it and gets similar numbers (documented) Test design Closed model only, no thresholds Some test types missing Smoke, load, stress, spike with arrival-rate executors and thresholds Load rate chosen from the knee; warm-up excluded Adds soak or breakpoint and explains what it reveals Rigor Single run Load not repeated 3 load runs with spread reported Discusses variance and outliers Explains a source of noise and controls it Results — Tables only, no curve Throughput vs p99 chart with the knee Percentiles interpreted (tail vs median) Spike recovery analysed over time Bottleneck analysis Guess Resource named without evidence USE evidence for the bottleneck Little's Law check consistent with the evidence Predicts the next bottleneck and checks it Change and re-test — Change without re-test Before/after with the same script Hypothesis stated first, quantified prediction Two iterations, or a refuted hypothesis well explained

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Why not just use vus: 100 and a loop?

That is a closed model: when the service slows down, the virtual users wait and send fewer requests, so the latency you measure is too optimistic (coordinated omission). With arrival-rate executors the request rate is what you ask for, as with real users.

What rate should I use for the load test?

One that your setup sustains within the SLO — about 70% of the knee found in the stress test is a good choice. The load test confirms that this rate is stable for 10 minutes; it is not the place to look for the limit.

My results change a lot between runs.

Check that resources are fixed, that nothing else heavy runs on the machine, that you warm the JVM up (the first minute of a Java service is slower) and that the database starts with the same data. Report the spread; it is part of the result.

k6 says insufficient VUs / dropped_iterations.

The executor could not start iterations at the requested rate because all pre-allocated VUs were busy waiting for responses. Raise maxVUs; if it still happens, the service is saturated (that is a result) or k6 itself is out of CPU.

Can I test through Nginx with several replicas?

Yes — that is Lab 3's setup and makes the bottleneck analysis more interesting (is it the replicas, Nginx, or the shared database?). Describe the topology and give every container fixed resources.

Do I need Grafana?

Not for this exercise: docker stats, actuator metrics and the k6 summaries are enough. If you already have the observability stack of Lab 8, dashboards screenshots are welcome evidence.

  1. Grafana k6 documentation, "Open and closed models" and "Arrival-rate executors", grafana.com/docs/k6. ↩

  2. Brendan Gregg, "The USE Method", brendangregg.com/usemethod.html. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
Knowing what a cache, a queue or a circuit breaker is is not the same as knowing which ones a system needs, where, and how many. In this exercise you get three designs that fail under load in the System Design Playground — a BoxOffice flash sale, a cascade caused by a slow dependency and an AI assistant that is too slow and too expensive — and you must make each one meet its goals within its budget, explain why your design works with the formulas of the course, and show that it still works when the dice are rolled again.

Learning objectives

After this exercise you will be able to:

  • Diagnose a failing design from its metrics and test report (which goal fails, which node is the bottleneck, why).
  • Compose palette components and tune their parameters to meet latency, error, availability and cost goals.
  • Justify replica counts, timeouts and cache sizes with utilization, Little's Law, hit-ratio and cost arithmetic.
  • Evaluate robustness: tell a design that passes by luck from one that passes under random failures.
  • Compare alternatives and defend a trade-off between cost and reliability.

items.title: Context
items.text:
The playground simulates a design under a load profile (the same vocabulary as k6: smoke, load, stress, spike, soak, breakpoint, chaos). What you need for this exercise (the full manual is on the playground page, the lessons of each scenario in the scenario guide):

  • Scenario — a starting design plus a brief, a load profile and goals (e.g. p99 below a threshold, error rate, availability, consumer lag) including a cost goal (US$/month, prices labelled illustrative). The brief and the goals appear in the inspector when nothing is selected.
  • Seed — every random number (arrivals, latencies, failures) comes from one seeded generator. Same seed + same design + same profile ⇒ identical run. The seed is in the toolbar; the 🎲 button draws a new one.
  • Chaos level — off, low, medium, high: how often random events happen (replica crashes, latency degradation of a dependency, traffic spikes, hot keys, cache flushes, zone outages, 3rd-party outages, bad deploys…).
  • Report — when a run ends, the Report tab shows the profile, seed, duration, p50/p95/p99/p999, error rate, availability, cost, the bottleneck (the first node to saturate, with an explanation), the events that happened, and pass/fail for each goal.
  • Export / import JSON — the toolbar saves the current design as a JSON file and loads it back. There is also a share link (the design encoded in the URL after #sdp=).

Design in the full playground (palette + inspector). The embeds on this page are compact: they show the scenario and run it, but you cannot add components there.

items.title: Part A — Three challenges
items.text: For each scenario below, start from the scenario as loaded (do not change its profile, target load, read ratio or goals) and change the design until every goal passes at the scenario's default seed with chaos as defined by the scenario.

items.title: Challenge 1 — flash-sale
items.text:
The BoxOffice on-sale at 10:00: a spike of fans hits the catalog and the seat inventory, and payments go to an external provider.

Try it: press ▶ and watch which node turns red first and when. Look at the report: which goal fails, and what does the bottleneck explanation say? Then ask: how many requests per second can the inventory database really accept, and who decides how many fans get there?

Things to reason about (not a recipe): what can be served without touching the inventory at all (static content, the catalog, seat availability that may be a few seconds old); what admission rate the inventory sustains (utilization below ~0.7); what happens to fans who are not admitted yet (a waiting room is a queue, and a queue has a backlog); where the payment provider's latency ends up.

items.title: Challenge 2 — cascading-failure
items.text:
A 3rd-party dependency becomes slow; with no timeouts, threads pile up and a healthy service fails.

Try it: run it and look at the utilization of the app servers and their threads. CPU is low, yet requests fail — why? Apply Little's Law: what is L = λ × W when W grows from 150 ms to 3 s?

Things to reason about: a timeout value derived from the dependency's normal p99 (not a guess); what a circuit breaker buys you and what it costs; whether a fallback (degraded response) is acceptable for this call; whether retries help or make it worse (see retry-storm).

items.title: Challenge 3 — ai-assistant
items.text:
The BoxOffice support assistant: an orchestrator calls an LLM through a gateway, retrieves context from a memory (RAG) and calls tools. It is slow and expensive.

Try it: run it and open the cost tile. Where does the money go? How many sequential LLM calls does one user request make, and what does that do to latency?

Things to reason about: the number of agent steps (each step is a sequential LLM call); a semantic cache at the LLM gateway (what hit ratio is realistic for support questions?); routing simple questions to a cheaper model; where the safety mesh sits in the path; tokens × price = cost per request.

items.title: Part B — Randomized robustness
items.text:
A design that passes with one seed may pass by luck. Run your final design of each challenge with 5 seeds and chaos level medium, keeping everything else as in Part A:

  • The seeds are published by the instructor on Blackboard. If they are not published, use the last five digits of your enrollment number S and the seeds S, S+1, S+2, S+3, S+4.
  • A challenge is robust when all goals pass in at least 4 of the 5 seeds.
  • For every failing seed, read the event log and explain what happened (which random event, which goal, why your design did not absorb it).

The embed below shows the same scenario with a fixed seed and medium chaos — the settings you will use in the full playground:

items.title: The physics stays fixed
items.text:
You change the architecture, not the laws of nature. Unless you justify it in the rationale (and the justification is accepted), do not edit:

  • capacity per replica, service-time (latencyMs) and variability (sigma) of any component type;
  • prices, and the latency, quota (rateLimit) or outage behaviour of external components (payment, thirdparty, email) and of the LLM;
  • the scenario's goals, profile, target RPS and read ratio.

Cache and CDN hit ratios above 0.95, and semantic-cache hit ratios above 0.4, need a justification based on the workload (key popularity, repetition of questions).

The Show a possible solution button

Each scenario has a reference solution. You may load it and study it. A submission identical (or nearly identical) to the reference solution is capped at C. To reach B or A your design must be your own, and either cheaper than the reference at the same goals or more robust (passes more seeds at medium, or passes at high), and you must explain why.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• (mandatory) For each of the three challenges, the exported JSON imports into the playground and, with the default seed, all goals pass (including the cost goal).
  • (mandatory) The physics rules above are respected (or each exception is justified).
  • (mandatory) Part B: each challenge passes in ≥ 4 of 5 seeds with chaos medium; a table shows seed × goal results.
  • For each challenge, the initial report (failing) and the final report (passing), both showing the seed.
  • A rationale per challenge with: diagnosis, numbered changes with their measured effect (iteration log), the arithmetic that justifies replica counts / timeouts / cache (utilization, Little's Law, hit ratio, cost), and at least one alternative you tried or rejected.
  • For every failing seed in Part B, an explanation from the event log.
  • A comparison with the reference solution (cost, robustness, structure).
  • AI usage section (see the policy).

items.title: Deliverables
items.text:
In your repository (tag ex6):

playground/
├── flash-sale.json
├── cascading-failure.json
├── ai-assistant.json
└── reports/
    ├── flash-sale-initial.png
    ├── flash-sale-final-seed<seed>.png
    ├── flash-sale-medium-seed<seed>.png   # one per seed of Part B
    └── ...                                # same for the other two scenarios

Reports can be screenshots (.png) or the report text copied into a .txt file — what matters is that the seed, profile, chaos level and goal results are visible. On your documentation site, a page playground-design with one section per challenge and the Part B table. Share links (#sdp=…) are a welcome extra next to each design.

items.title: Step by step
items.text:
1. Read the brief and the goals. Write them down in your page: goal, threshold, and the budget.
  2. Run the scenario as it is and save the initial report. Note the first goal that fails and the reported bottleneck.
  3. Make a hypothesis with numbers. Example: "the inventory DB receives 4,000 writes/s and its capacity is 2,500 writes/s, so ρ = 1.6: it cannot work at any latency." Or: "W went from 0.15 s to 3 s, so each replica needs 20× more threads."
  4. Change one thing at a time and run again with the same seed. Keep an iteration log: change → effect on the failing goal → effect on cost. Because the run is deterministic, a difference between two runs is caused by your change.
  5. Stop when every goal passes, then try to remove cost: fewer replicas, smaller components, autoscaling instead of fixed capacity. Each removal must keep all goals passing.
  6. Export the JSON, import it back in a fresh page and run again to check that you get the same report.
  7. Part B: set chaos to medium, run the 5 seeds, fill the table, read the event log of every failure. If fewer than 4 pass, improve the design (redundancy, autoscaling, timeouts, fallbacks) and rerun Part A — the final design must pass both parts.
  8. Compare with the reference solution and write the rationale.

Worked arithmetic — sizing a node

Suppose the report shows that the sql node receives 1,800 req/s and one replica handles 1,000 req/s. With a target utilization of 0.7, replicas = ⌈1,800 ÷ (1,000 × 0.7)⌉ = 3. If a cache in front of it has a hit ratio h = 0.9, the database receives (1 − 0.9) × 1,800 = 180 req/s and one replica is enough (ρ = 0.18) — whether the cache is worth it is then a question of cost and of the consistency you can accept.
