items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Can I change the load profile, the target RPS or the goals?

No. They define the problem. You change only the design: components, connections and their parameters (within the physics rules).

My design passes with seed 42 but fails with seed 43. Is the simulator broken?

Probably not. Different seeds mean different arrivals, latencies and random events. Look at the event log of the failing run: a replica crash with only one replica left, a hot key, a slow dependency without a timeout… That is exactly what Part B is about.

If I run the same seed twice, do I get the same report?

Yes — same seed, same design, same profile and same chaos level give an identical run. That is what makes your iteration log meaningful and lets the instructor reproduce your results. If you see a difference, check that the design really is the same (import your JSON again).

Can I just raise the hit ratio of the cache to 0.99?

Not without a reason. The hit ratio depends on the workload (how skewed the key popularity is, how often data changes). Above 0.95 for caches and CDNs, or above 0.4 for a semantic cache, you must justify it — otherwise it is editing the physics.

Where is my design stored? I closed the tab.

The playground autosaves the current design per scenario in your browser, but browser storage can be cleared. Export JSON often and commit the files.

I think the simulator has a bug.

Send the instructor the JSON, the seed, the profile and the chaos level, and describe what you expected and what you saw. If it is a bug, the exercise will be adjusted for everybody.

Can I use AI to find a design?

You may discuss ideas with an AI and must declare it. But the oral check will ask you to change a parameter and predict the effect before running — only your own understanding of utilization, Little's Law and costs gets you through it.

items.title: Index
items.text:
In the team project you design, build, measure, break and defend one system, from the first estimate to a load-tested deployment on Kubernetes. It is the course in miniature: every class adds a piece, every lab gives you a working example to adapt, and every milestone asks for evidence — a diagram, a passing check, a k6 report, a dashboard — not promises.

Goals

By the end of the project your team will have:

  • Designed a system from requirements to a reviewed design doc with estimates, SLOs and ADRs.
  • Built its core path as services that run with one command (Docker Compose) and on Kubernetes.
  • Scaled it with caching, replication and asynchronous processing, and protected it with resilience patterns.
  • Delivered it continuously (CI/CD with tests, image scan and a performance gate).
  • Proved it meets a target SLO with a load-test campaign, and that it degrades gracefully in a chaos game day.
  • Priced it (cost report with unit economics) and defended it in a final presentation.

items.title: Team rules
items.text:
• 2 to 3 students per team. Teams are registered by week 3 (form on Blackboard) with the chosen system option; changing option after week 5 needs the instructor's approval.
  • One GitHub repository per team (monorepo recommended: services/, deploy/, load/, chaos/, docs/), with every member as a collaborator and the instructor and teaching assistant added.
  • Documentation on GitHub Pages (MkDocs Material or Zensical), one section per milestone; the documentation template is a good start.
  • Ownership table on the home page: each member owns at least one service and at least one cross-cutting area (e.g. observability, CI/CD, load testing, chaos, cost). Owners lead; everybody must understand everything.
  • Every member commits with their own GitHub identity (git config user.name/user.email). Work done in pairs is marked with Co-authored-by: trailers.
  • Milestones are tags: m1 … m9 on the commit to be graded, plus a short entry in the docs ("what we delivered, evidence, what is missing").

Individual grades inside a team

The team grade is, by default, the same for all members. The instructor may adjust an individual grade when the evidence (commit history, ownership table, milestone check-ins, the final oral questions, and a short confidential peer evaluation at the end) shows that a member did not contribute or cannot explain the system. The oral check rule applies to every member.

items.title: System options
items.text:
Pick one option. Each one exercises the whole palette, but stresses a different part of it. Every option has two scales:

  • Design target — the real-world scale, used in the design doc, the estimates and the cost report (you will not run it).
  • Test target — a scaled-down load that your deployment (laptop with Docker Compose or kind/minikube, or a small cloud account) must sustain within the SLOs in the load-test campaign. If your environment cannot reach it, show the bottleneck with numbers and agree a new target with the instructor before week 14.
1. BoxOffice flash sale2. Real-time chat3. Ride-sharing dispatch4. Social feed5. Video platform6. AI support assistant

The course's running example. A stadium show goes on sale at 10:00; 2 M fans arrive for 60 k seats. Fans browse the catalog, enter a waiting room, hold seats for a few minutes, pay through an external provider and receive their tickets by e-mail.

Core requirements: event catalog and search; waiting room with fair admission; seat hold with expiry; order + payment (provider stub with latency and failures); ticket e-mail; no double booking — ever.

SLO / constraint Design target Test target Catalog read latency p99 < 200 ms at 200 k req/s p99 < 200 ms at 1,000 req/s Seat hold latency p99 < 500 ms p99 < 500 ms at 100 holds/s Double bookings 0 0 (checked by a consistency query after every test) Availability during the on-sale 99.9% error rate < 0.1% (excluding 429 from the waiting room) Ticket e-mail p95 < 60 s after payment p95 < 30 s, consumer lag < 10 s

Playground: flash-sale · Case study: ticketing

One-to-one and small-group chat (up to 100 members) with online presence and message history, used on mobile and web.

Core requirements: WebSocket (or SSE) connections behind a load balancer; message fan-out through pub/sub across instances; per-conversation ordering; at-least-once delivery with client-side de-duplication; history pagination; push notification for offline users.

SLO / constraint Design target Test target End-to-end delivery (sender → online receiver) p99 < 300 ms p99 < 500 ms Concurrent connections 10 M 5,000 Messages 1 M msg/s peak 500 msg/s Message loss 0 acknowledged messages lost 0 (checked by sequence numbers) History read p99 < 200 ms p99 < 200 ms at 200 req/s

Playground: chat · Case study: chat

Drivers send their location every few seconds; riders request a ride and get matched with a nearby available driver.

Core requirements: location ingestion (write-heavy); geo index (geohash, H3 or PostGIS) of available drivers; matching with a driver lock (one driver, one ride); trip state machine; pricing stub; notifications to both sides.

SLO / constraint Design target Test target Location update ingestion p99 < 100 ms at 1 M updates/s p99 < 200 ms at 1,250 updates/s (5,000 drivers every 4 s) Nearby-drivers query p99 < 150 ms p99 < 200 ms at 100 req/s Match (request → driver assigned) p95 < 3 s p95 < 3 s at 20 rides/s Double assignment of a driver 0 0 (checked after every test) Location freshness < 10 s < 10 s

Playground: ride-sharing · Case study: ride-sharing

Users post short texts with images and follow other users; the home timeline shows recent posts of the people they follow — including a few celebrities with millions of followers.

Core requirements: posts with media in object storage; follow graph; home timeline with a hybrid fan-out (push for normal users, pull for celebrities); timeline cache; likes counter; notifications.

SLO / constraint Design target Test target Home timeline read p99 < 200 ms at 300 k req/s p99 < 200 ms at 1,000 req/s Post visible to followers p95 < 5 s p95 < 5 s, including one account with 100 k followers Post write p99 < 300 ms p99 < 300 ms at 50 posts/s Availability (reads) 99.95% error rate < 0.1%

Playground: news-feed · Case study: news feed

Creators upload videos; the platform transcodes them into several resolutions; viewers watch them with adaptive streaming (HLS) served from a CDN-like edge.

Core requirements: resumable/multipart upload to object storage (MinIO locally) with pre-signed URLs; transcoding jobs on a queue with workers (FFmpeg); HLS manifests and segments served through a cache (Nginx as the "CDN"); video metadata and search; view counter.

SLO / constraint Design target Test target Upload acknowledged (after the transfer) p99 < 1 s p99 < 1 s Transcoding done p95 < 2× video duration p95 < 2× duration for 20 parallel uploads of 30 s clips Playback start (manifest + first segment) p99 < 300 ms p99 < 300 ms at 500 req/s Edge (cache) hit ratio for segments > 95% > 90%

Playground: video-streaming · Case study: video streaming

A support assistant for BoxOffice (or another domain agreed with the instructor): it answers questions with RAG over the help center and the event catalog, and uses tools to look up or cancel orders — safely.

Core requirements: LLM gateway (LiteLLM) with model routing, fallback and per-user quotas; ingestion pipeline (chunking, embeddings, pgvector); orchestrator with a bounded agent loop and tool calls to existing services; guardrails (prompt injection, PII, output validation); semantic cache; token and cost metrics; an evaluation set.

SLO / constraint Design target Test target Time to first token (TTFT) p95 < 1.5 s p95 < 2 s with a stub LLM (fixed latency distribution) at 20 concurrent chats; measured separately with the real model at 1 req/s Answer quality ≥ 90% on the evaluation set ≥ 80% on a 30-question evaluation set Unsafe tool actions 0 0 on a 20-prompt injection test set Cost per conversation < US$ 0.01 measured and reported (tokens × price)

Playground: ai-assistant · Case study: AI assistant

Other systems

A different system (e.g. food delivery, collaborative editor, payments ledger) is welcome if it has the same breadth. Send a one-page proposal with requirements and target SLOs by week 3; it needs the instructor's approval.

items.title: Mandatory components
items.text:
Whatever the option, the system must have the components below (palette ids in parentheses — see the component catalog). The milestone where each one is first required is in the last column.

Area Requirement Milestone Edge An entry point: API gateway (apigw) or Ingress (ingress) with rate limiting on at least one route M2 Identity Authentication (auth) with JWT or OIDC; at least one protected route M2 Services At least three services of your own (app/worker), each with its own data M2 Data A SQL database (sql) with migrations; a justified second store if needed (nosql, objstore, vectordb) M2 Caching A cache (cache) on a hot read path, with a measured hit ratio M3 Replication A read replica or a connection pool in front of the database, justified by a measurement M3 Messaging A broker (kafka, queue or pubsub) with a transactional outbox or an idempotent consumer, and a DLQ M4 Resilience Timeout + retry with backoff and jitter + circuit breaker on at least one slow/external dependency (payment, thirdparty, email or llmgw) M4 Observability OpenTelemetry → metrics, logs and traces (grafana/otel-lgtm is enough); a RED dashboard; one SLO burn-rate alert M4 Platform Kubernetes (kind/minikube or cloud) with probes, requests/limits and an HPA on at least one service M5 Delivery GitHub Actions: build, tests, image build, image scan, SBOM, and a k6 performance gate M5 Proof k6 load-test campaign against the test target; chaos game day with at least three experiments M6–M7 Cost Cost report for the design target and for the environment you actually used M8

The hands-on labs give you a working version of almost every row: reuse them (and say so).

items.title: Deliverables
items.text:
All deliverables live in the team repository and its GitHub Pages site:

  1. Design doc + ADRs — design doc (M1, kept up to date until the end).
  2. Running system — code, compose.yaml, Kubernetes manifests (or Helm/Kustomize), CI/CD workflows (milestones M2–M5).
  3. Load-test campaign report — plan, k6 scripts, raw results, analysis (load-test campaign, M6).
  4. Game day report — experiment plans, run sheet, findings and action items (game day, M7).
  5. Cost report — design-target and actual costs, unit economics (cost report, M8).
  6. Final presentation — slides, live demo, 3-minute video (presentation, M9).

items.title: Index
items.text:
Every design decision has a price tag. A cache that saves 90% of database reads, a CDN that absorbs the on-sale, three availability zones instead of one, an agent that calls the LLM five times per question — each one shows up on the monthly bill. In the real world, "it scales" is only half an answer; the other half is "and it costs US$ X per month, or US$ Y per ticket sold". Milestone 8 asks your team to price its design honestly, connect the cost to the measurements of the load-test campaign, and say where the money would be better spent.

Goals

With this milestone your team will:

  • Estimate the monthly cost of your design at the design target on one cloud, with an official pricing calculator.
  • Compute unit economics (cost per 1,000 requests and per business unit: ticket, message, ride, view, conversation).
  • Report the cost of the environment you actually used.
  • Analyse sensitivity (×10 traffic, peak vs average, commitments and spot) and compare service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, serverless) for at least one component.
  • Propose saving levers backed by your own measurements.

This milestone builds on the FinOps part of Class 12 — Cloud-native, on your M1 estimates and on the load-test campaign. Due in week 18, weight 10% of the project.

items.title: What to deliver
items.text:
• A cost report page in the docs, following the template.
  • The calculator export (shareable link, PDF or CSV) with the date and the region used — prices change, so the export is the evidence.
  • A small script or spreadsheet with the formulas (committed), so that the numbers can be recomputed.
  • The final update of the design doc (with a changelog of what changed since M1).
  • The tag m8.

items.title: Acceptance criteria
items.text:
• (mandatory) A bill of materials covering every component of your design doc (compute, databases, cache, broker, load balancer, NAT, egress/CDN, storage, observability, and LLM tokens for the AI option), each with quantity, size, hours and the price used.
  • (mandatory) Every price comes from an official pricing calculator or pricing page, with date and region; no price is invented. Assumptions (hours per month, GB transferred, utilization, retention) are listed.
  • Unit economics: cost per 1,000 requests and cost per business unit of your option.
  • Cost of the environment you actually used (laptop, CI minutes, any cloud account — with the bill if a cloud was used).
  • Sensitivity: cost at ×10 traffic, provisioned-for-peak vs autoscaled, and with commitments/spot (reserved instances, savings plans, committed-use discounts).
  • A service-model comparison for at least one component (e.g. Kafka self-managed on Kubernetes vs a managed Kafka service vs a serverless queue): cost, operational effort, limits.
  • ≥ 3 saving levers, each tied to a measurement from M6 (e.g. "hit ratio 95% → database can be one size smaller") with an estimated saving.
  • AI usage section (see the policy).

items.title: 2. Size each component from your numbers
items.text:
Start from the M1 estimates and the M6 measurements, not from guesses: the capacity per replica you measured, the peak of the design target, a target utilization (≈ 0.6–0.7), the hit ratio of the cache, the GB that leave the cloud (egress is often the surprise), retention of logs and metrics, and — for the AI option — tokens per request × requests.

Item Formula Instance-hours per month instances × 730 h (or the autoscaled average × 730 h) Replicas at peak ⌈ peak req/s ÷ (capacity per replica × target utilization) ⌉ Database reads after the cache (1 − hit ratio) × read req/s Egress (GB/month) req/s × response size × 2.6 M s/month (minus what the CDN serves) LLM cost per month requests × (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price) ÷ 10⁶ Cost per 1,000 requests monthly cost ÷ (monthly requests ÷ 1,000) Cost per business unit monthly cost ÷ units per month (tickets, messages, rides, views, conversations)

items.title: 3. Visualize where the money goes
items.text:
A stacked chart of the bill by category makes the dominant costs obvious. The chart below uses illustrative placeholder prices — not real quotes — only to show the shape of the analysis; your report must use the prices of your calculator export.

2026-10-23T08:15:51.607134 image/svg+xml Matplotlib v3.11.2, https://matplotlib.org/ 0 2500 5000 7500 10000 12500 15000 17500 20000 US$ per month (illustrative placeholders, not real prices) provisioned for peak, on demand autoscaled + commitments + cache US$ 16,000/month US$ 9,000/month Compute Database Cache Broker Edge/CDN + egress Observability LLM tokens

items.title: 4. Unit economics
items.text:
Divide by the unit your business cares about. For BoxOffice, cost per ticket sold is the number a product manager understands; for chat, cost per 1,000 messages; for video, cost per hour watched; for the assistant, cost per conversation (with tokens as the main driver). Compare it with what the unit is worth (a ticketing fee, an ad impression) — an architecture that costs more per ticket than the fee is not a business.

BoxOffice — peak versus month

A flash sale lasts minutes, but capacity provisioned for it is paid for all month. Compare: (a) provisioned for the on-sale peak 730 h/month; (b) a baseline plus autoscaling during on-sales; (c) (b) plus a waiting room that caps the inventory path. The waiting room is not only a fairness feature — it is a cost feature: it lets the expensive, strongly consistent path be sized for the admission rate instead of the crowd.

items.title: 5. Service models
items.text:
Pick at least one component and compare how you would run it:

Model Example for the broker You manage Typical trade-off IaaS Kafka on VMs OS, Kafka, upgrades, scaling, backups Lowest unit price, highest effort Containers on your cluster Kafka on Kubernetes (operator) Kafka, storage, upgrades Reuses the cluster; on-call is yours PaaS / managed A managed Kafka service Topics, clients, sizing Higher unit price, much less operations Serverless / SaaS A serverless queue or event service Only the usage Pay per request; limits on throughput, retention or semantics

Put the effort in hours per month next to the bill: an engineer's time is the largest hidden cost of self-managed components.

items.title: 6. Saving levers backed by measurements
items.text: Every lever must point to a measurement: "M6 shows the catalog cache at 95% hit ratio, so the database can drop one instance size (−US$ …)", "CPU of notification averages 8% — move it to serverless or a smaller node pool", "the semantic cache answered 30% of questions — LLM tokens −30%", "logs are 60% of observability cost — sample debug logs and shorten retention". Also consider commitments (1-year reserved capacity or savings plans), spot/preemptible nodes for stateless workers, and the egress saved by the CDN.

items.text:
Levels as defined in How the exercises are graded.

Criterion I D C B A Bill of materials (mandatory) Not delivered Components missing or no quantities Every component with size, quantity, hours, price Sizes derived from M1/M6 numbers Hidden costs found (egress, NAT per GB, log ingestion, cross-AZ traffic) Sources (mandatory) Invented prices Prices without date/region Calculator export with date and region; assumptions listed Formulas committed; numbers recomputable Cross-checked with a second calculator for the largest item Unit economics — Missing Cost per 1,000 requests and per business unit Compared with what the unit is worth Unit cost at ×10 traffic (economies or diseconomies of scale) explained Sensitivity and service models — One scenario only ×10, peak vs autoscaled, commitments; one service-model comparison Effort (h/month) included in the comparison Break-even point between two models computed Saving levers — Generic advice 3 levers with estimated savings Each tied to an M6 measurement One lever implemented and its effect measured Actual environment and design-doc update — Missing Actual cost reported; design doc updated Changelog since M1 linked to ADRs Cost guardrails proposed (budgets, alerts, tagging)

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
We never deployed to a cloud. Do we still need a cloud estimate?

Yes. The estimate is for the design target on one cloud; it does not require a deployment. The "environment actually used" section then says: laptop and CI minutes (and whether you stayed within free tiers).

The calculator does not have exactly our component.

Choose the closest managed service or price it as compute (e.g. a self-hosted search engine on VMs) and say so. What matters is that the assumption is explicit.

How do we price autoscaling?

Use the average number of replicas over the month (from your traffic curve: hours at baseline × baseline replicas + hours at peak × peak replicas) × the instance price. Show the arithmetic.

Do we include engineers' salaries?

Not in the bill, but do include effort in hours per month in the service-model comparison. It is often what decides between self-managed and managed.

Prices changed after we exported the estimate.

That is why the date and region are mandatory. Keep the export; the report is judged against it.

For the AI option, where do token prices come from?

From the model provider's official pricing page (or the cloud's model service in the calculator), with the date. Report tokens per request measured in M6 (input and output separately) and the effect of the semantic cache and model routing.

items.title: Index
items.text:
Before the first line of code, your team agrees on what it is building, how big it must be, how you will know it works and which decisions you are taking. That agreement is the design doc of milestone M1. It is not written once and forgotten: it is the map the whole project follows, it is updated at every milestone, and its final version (M8) is what you defend in the presentation.

Goals

With M1 your team will have:

  • Chosen a system option and turned it into requirements, a design target and a test target.
  • Defined SLOs with their SLIs and how each one will be measured (k6, OpenTelemetry).
  • Estimated the load and sized each service with Little's Law and a per-instance capacity.
  • Drawn the architecture with palette components and assigned data ownership per service.
  • Recorded the first ADRs, a risk register, a test plan sketch and the ownership table.

items.title: What to deliver
items.text:
Due: week 5, tag m1, weight 10%. A Design doc section in the team's documentation site containing the exercise's design doc template — every section filled — plus the project additions below. ADRs use the ADR template, numbered ADR-001, ADR-002, …

The project additions:

items.title: Acceptance criteria
items.text:
• (mandatory) All sections of the design doc template are filled (or marked "not applicable — because …").
  • (mandatory) At least three ADRs; suggested topics: the broker (Kafka vs a queue), the consistency of the critical write (e.g. seat hold with SELECT … FOR UPDATE vs optimistic locking), the cache strategy.
  • (mandatory) SLO table with SLIs, measurement point, tool and window — every SLO of the test target is measurable with the tools of the course.
  • Estimates for the design target and the test target, with formulas.
  • Architecture diagram with palette ids, covering all mandatory components (even if some arrive in later milestones — mark them).
  • Data ownership: no table is written by two services.
  • Capacity model gives a replica count for every service at the test target.
  • Risk register with at least five risks, each with a mitigation and an owner.
  • Ownership table: every member owns a service and a cross-cutting area.
  • AI usage section.

items.title: Step by step
items.text:
1. Pick the option together (week 3) and read its case study and playground scenario.
  2. Write the requirements and targets first. Agree on what is out of scope — it protects your schedule.
  3. Turn every SLO into a measurement. "p99 of POST /holds < 500 ms" becomes "k6 threshold http_req_duration{name:POST /holds} p(99)<500 at 100 holds/s for 10 min". If you cannot say how you will measure it, it is not an SLO yet.
  4. Estimate and size. Use the formulas of the estimation exercise; take per-instance capacities from your ex2 measurements when you have them, and mark assumptions.
  5. Draw the architecture and walk the flows. Then check it against the mandatory components table.
  6. Split ownership of data and services; write the API contracts and event schemas.
  7. Write the ADRs for the decisions that are expensive to change later.
  8. Prototype in the playground (optional but recommended) and attach the exported JSON.
  9. Review as a team, then ask another team to read it for 10 minutes and note their questions — answer them in the doc.

Try it — prototype before you build

Start from the blank scenario in the full playground, build your architecture with the same palette ids as your diagram, set the test-target load and see which node saturates first. Export the JSON and commit it as docs/design/playground.json. The compact view below only runs a design; build yours in the full playground.

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Do we need to implement everything in the diagram?

You must implement the mandatory components. The diagram may show more (e.g. a CDN or a second region) if it is clearly marked as "design target only" and costed in M8.

Can we change the design after M1?

Yes — and you will. Record each change in the changelog with an ADR (new, or superseding an old one). A design doc that never changes after week 5 usually means the team stopped reading it.

We do not know the capacity of one instance yet.

Assume it from the numbers cheat sheet or from the labs, mark it as an assumption, and replace it with your measurement at M3. Showing how the replica count changed is a good sign.

How detailed must the API be?

Enough for another team to call your service: paths, methods, main fields, status codes, idempotency keys. An OpenAPI file generated from stubs is fine at M1.

What is a good risk?

Specific and actionable: "nobody on the team has run Kafka on Kubernetes — mitigation: spike in week 6, fallback to a managed queue, owner: Ana". "The project might be late" is not a risk entry.

items.title: Index
items.text:
Your system passed its load tests on a sunny day. Production is not sunny: the payment provider slows down in the middle of an on-sale, a node dies, the broker restarts, someone ships a bad build. A game day is a planned, supervised exercise in which you break your own system on purpose, under load, to learn whether it degrades the way you designed it to — and whether your team can detect, diagnose and mitigate a failure using only its dashboards and alerts.

Goals

With this milestone your team will:

  • Formulate chaos experiments as hypotheses about steady state, with a bounded blast radius and abort conditions.
  • Inject realistic faults (dependency latency and outage, pod and node loss, broker or database failure, bad deploy) under load.
  • Observe the effect on SLIs with the observability stack, and verify correctness afterwards.
  • Respond to a surprise fault injected by the instructor, measuring time to detect and time to mitigate.
  • Learn from it: a blameless report with action items, owners and follow-up.

This milestone builds on Class 9 — Reliability, Class 10 — Observability and Lab 9 (Resilience4j, Toxiproxy, game day). The game day runs in class in week 17; weight 10% of the project.

items.title: What to deliver
items.text:
• An experiment plan for at least three experiments, committed before the game day, following the template.
  • The run sheet filled during the game day (timeline with timestamps).
  • A game day report: per experiment, hypothesis vs observation, SLO impact, correctness check, time to detect and to mitigate; the surprise fault; action items with owners.
  • Dashboard screenshots and k6 summaries of the runs; the scripts used to inject faults (chaos/).
  • The tag m7.

items.title: Acceptance criteria
items.text:
• (mandatory) Plan committed before the game day with ≥ 3 experiments, each with hypothesis, steady state, blast radius, abort conditions and rollback.
  • (mandatory) Experiments executed under load (k6 at 50–70% of the test target) with a live dashboard; the run sheet records every action with a timestamp.
  • The three experiments cover different failure classes: a slow or failing dependency, loss of compute (pod/node), and loss of a stateful component (broker or database).
  • For each experiment: SLIs during the fault vs steady state, hypothesis confirmed or refuted, correctness check after recovery.
  • The surprise fault is detected through an alert (not by someone staring at a graph by chance); time to detect (TTD) and time to mitigate (TTM) reported.
  • A blameless report with at least three action items, each with an owner and a due milestone.
  • AI usage section (see the policy).

items.title: 1. Principles
items.text:
Chaos engineering is an experiment, not vandalism1:

  1. Define steady state with SLIs you already measure (e.g. hold p99, error rate, consumer lag) at a known load.
  2. Hypothesize that steady state continues (or degrades in a bounded, designed way) during the fault: "When the payment provider adds 3 s of latency, hold p99 stays below 500 ms and order errors stay below 1%, because the payment call has a 1 s timeout and a circuit breaker opens within 10 s."
  3. Inject one fault at a time, with the smallest blast radius that tests the hypothesis.
  4. Observe and compare with steady state; abort if an abort condition is met.
  5. Recover, check correctness, and learn: confirmed hypotheses build confidence, refuted ones are the valuable ones.
flowchart LR
    steady["Steady state<br/>SLIs at known load"] --> hyp["Hypothesis<br/>SLI stays within bounds"]
    hyp --> inject["Inject one fault<br/>small blast radius"]
    inject --> observe["Observe<br/>dashboards, alerts, traces"]
    observe -->|"abort condition met"| rollback["Roll back now"]
    observe --> recover["Remove fault<br/>check correctness"]
    rollback --> recover
    recover --> learn["Learn<br/>confirmed or refuted<br/>action items"]

items.title: 2. Roles
items.text:
Role Responsibility Game master Owns the plan and the clock, announces each step, calls the abort Operator Runs the injection and rollback commands — and nothing else Scribe Writes the run sheet: every action and observation with a timestamp Responders Watch dashboards and alerts, diagnose, propose mitigations

With 2–3 people, combine roles (game master + scribe), but never let the operator also be the only responder. For the surprise fault, the instructor acts as game master and operator; the whole team responds.

items.title: 3. Prepare the tools
items.text:
Toxiproxy sits between a service and a dependency and injects latency, timeouts or outages on demand2. Put it between the payment adapter and the payment provider stub (or between the assistant and the LLM):

compose.yaml (excerpt)
services:
  toxiproxy:
    image: ghcr.io/shopify/toxiproxy:2.9.0
    ports:
      - "8474:8474"   # control API
chaos/payment.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: ./chaos/payment.sh setup|slow|down|heal
# The payment adapter calls http://toxiproxy:9090 instead of the provider.
API=${TOXIPROXY_API:-http://localhost:8474}
case "$1" in
  setup)
    curl -s -X POST "$API/proxies" \
      -d '{"name":"payment","listen":"0.0.0.0:9090","upstream":"payment-provider:8080","enabled":true}' ;;
  slow)   # 3 s +/- 0.5 s on every response
    curl -s -X POST "$API/proxies/payment/toxics" \
      -d '{"name":"slow","type":"latency","stream":"downstream","toxicity":1.0,"attributes":{"latency":3000,"jitter":500}}' ;;
  down)   # connections refused
    curl -s -X POST "$API/proxies/payment" -d '{"enabled":false}' ;;
  heal)
    curl -s -X DELETE "$API/proxies/payment/toxics/slow"
    curl -s -X POST "$API/proxies/payment" -d '{"enabled":true}' ;;
esac

On Kubernetes, run Toxiproxy as a Deployment with a Service and reach its control API with kubectl port-forward svc/toxiproxy 8474 (fine for control commands, not for load).

items.title: 4. Fault library
items.text:
chaos/k8s-faults.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: ./chaos/k8s-faults.sh <fault>
case "$1" in
  kill-one-pod)      # loss of one replica of a stateless service
    kubectl delete "$(kubectl get pod -l app=inventory -o name | head -n 1)" --wait=false ;;
  kill-all-pods)     # loss of the whole service (until the Deployment recreates the pods)
    kubectl delete pod -l app=inventory --wait=false ;;
  stop-kafka)        # broker outage
    kubectl scale statefulset kafka --replicas=0 ;;
  start-kafka)
    kubectl scale statefulset kafka --replicas=1 ;;
  kill-postgres)     # database restart
    kubectl delete pod -l app=postgres --wait=false ;;
  isolate-kafka)     # network partition: nothing can reach the broker
    kubectl apply -f chaos/isolate-kafka.yaml ;;
  heal-kafka)
    kubectl delete -f chaos/isolate-kafka.yaml ;;
  bad-deploy)        # ship an image that fails
    kubectl set image deployment/order order=boxoffice/order:broken ;;
  rollback)
    kubectl rollout undo deployment/order ;;
esac
chaos/isolate-kafka.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: chaos-isolate-kafka
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: kafka
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress: []   # deny all incoming traffic to the broker

NetworkPolicy needs a CNI that enforces it

Recent kind versions enforce NetworkPolicies with their default network plugin; minikube needs a CNI such as Calico (minikube start --cni=calico). Test the policy before the game day: an experiment that silently does nothing teaches nothing. Chaos Mesh or LitmusChaos are optional alternatives with richer faults (CPU stress, clock skew, DNS errors).

items.title: 5. Example experiments
items.text:
# Fault Hypothesis (example) Abort if 1 Payment provider +3 s latency for 3 min (payment.sh slow) Hold p99 < 500 ms; order error rate < 1%; circuit breaker opens in < 10 s; orders queue for retry Error rate on browse > 5% for 1 min 2 Kill one inventory pod under load (kill-one-pod) No failed holds beyond retries; replacement ready in < 60 s; 0 double bookings Availability of holds < 95% for 1 min 3 Stop Kafka for 2 min (stop-kafka) Orders still accepted (outbox grows); lag drains in < 2 min after restart; 0 lost e-mails Outbox write errors appear 4 (optional) Bad deploy of order + rollback Readiness keeps the broken pods out of rotation; rollback in < 2 min Error rate > 10%

Adapt the table to your system option (e.g. LLM gateway outage with model fallback for the AI assistant, Redis loss for the feed timeline cache, WebSocket node loss for chat).

items.title: 6. Run the game day
items.text:
1. T−15 min: environment healthy, data seeded, dashboards open, alerts armed, k6 started at 50–70% of the test target, steady state recorded for 5 minutes.
  2. Per experiment: game master announces; operator injects; scribe logs; responders observe and talk aloud; at the planned end (or abort), operator heals; wait for recovery; run the correctness check; scribe records the end of recovery.
  3. Surprise fault: the instructor injects one fault the team does not know about (chosen from a safe list announced in advance: a Toxiproxy toxic, a deployment scaled to zero, a CPU-hogging pod, a wrong configuration value). The clock starts at injection. Record when the first alert fires (TTD) and when SLIs are back within SLO (TTM), and what the team did in between.
  4. Hot wash (10 min): what surprised you, what worked, what to change.

items.title: 7. Write the report
items.text: Write it blameless: describe what the system and the people did and why it made sense at the time, not who made a mistake3. Every finding becomes an action item with an owner and a milestone (e.g. "add an alert on outbox backlog — Ana — M8").

items.title: Rubric
items.text:
Levels as defined in How the exercises are graded.

Criterion I D C B A Plan (mandatory) None Written after the game day, or < 3 experiments 3 experiments with hypothesis, steady state, blast radius, abort, rollback Hypotheses quantified and tied to designed mechanisms (timeouts, breakers, outbox) Experiments ordered by risk; dry-run of tools documented Execution (mandatory) Not run Not under load, or no run sheet Under load, run sheet with timestamps, correctness checks Abort conditions respected; one variable at a time An extra experiment born from a finding during the day Observation and analysis — Screenshots without interpretation Hypothesis confirmed/refuted per experiment with SLIs Root cause of every refuted hypothesis explained with traces/logs Refuted hypothesis fixed and the experiment rerun before M9 Surprise fault — Not detected, or detected by chance Detected by an alert; TTD and TTM reported Diagnosis path documented (alert → dashboard → trace → cause) TTD and TTM within the team's own targets, with runbook used Learning — No action items ≥ 3 action items with owners Blameless narrative; items prioritized At least one item implemented and verified

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Will the instructor break something permanently?

No. The surprise fault is chosen from a list announced in advance, is reversible, and the instructor heals it if the team cannot within the time box. The goal is to exercise detection and response, not to destroy your data.

Our hypothesis was refuted. Is that bad for the grade?

No — it is the most valuable outcome of a game day, as long as you explain why it failed and what you will change. A team that confirms everything with trivial experiments learns less (and scores less) than one that finds a real weakness.

Can we run the game day on Docker Compose?

Experiments 1 and 3 work on Compose (Toxiproxy, docker compose stop kafka). Loss of compute is more interesting on Kubernetes, where the Deployment and the readiness probes are part of the answer. Prefer the environment you will present.

What if an experiment corrupts data?

That is what the abort conditions and the correctness check are for. Stop, record, restore from the seed (you have a seed script from M6), and treat it as the top action item.

We have no alerts yet.

Alerts are an M4 requirement (one SLO burn-rate alert at least). Without them the surprise fault will be detected late or by luck — which is exactly what the report should then say.

  1. Principles of Chaos Engineering, principlesofchaos.org. ↩

  2. Toxiproxy, github.com/Shopify/toxiproxy. ↩

  3. Betsy Beyer et al. (eds.), Site Reliability Engineering, O'Reilly, 2016 — chapter 15, "Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure". ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
Up to now your system "works". Milestone 6 asks a harder question: does it meet its SLOs at the test target, for long enough, every time — and what breaks first beyond it? A load-test campaign answers it the way a performance team would: a written plan, a realistic workload model, a sequence of test types, repetitions, correctness checks after every run, and a log of hypotheses and fixes until the numbers hold.

Goals

With this milestone your team will:

  • Plan a campaign from the test-target SLOs of your system option: user journeys, mix, arrival rates, data and environment.
  • Model the workload with an open model and per-journey thresholds in k6.
  • Execute smoke, load (×3), stress, spike, soak and breakpoint tests and read them with dashboards.
  • Find the knee and the bottleneck, and improve the system in documented iterations.
  • Guard correctness (no double booking, no lost message) and automate a performance gate in CI.

This milestone builds on the load-test report exercise, Class 15 — Performance and the observability stack of Lab 8. Due in week 16, weight 15% of the project.

items.title: What to deliver
items.text:
• A campaign plan (before running anything) in the docs, following the template.
  • k6 scripts in load/, the data seeding script, raw results (load/results/, one summary JSON per run), dashboard screenshots.
  • A campaign report: results per test, SLO verdict, knee, bottleneck, iteration log, correctness checks.
  • A performance gate job in the CI workflow (Lab 11).
  • The tag m6 on the commit with all of the above.

items.title: Acceptance criteria
items.text:
• (mandatory) Plan written and committed before the first load run (the commit history shows it).
  • (mandatory) At the test target of your option, every SLO holds for ≥ 10 minutes of steady state in 3 repetitions (or, if not reachable, the bottleneck is proven and a new target was agreed with the instructor before week 14).
  • Workload model with at least 3 user journeys, a mix in %, and open-model executors (constant-arrival-rate / ramping-arrival-rate).
  • Per-journey thresholds (tags) that encode the SLOs; k6 exits non-zero when an SLO fails.
  • Smoke, load ×3, stress up to 2× the target, spike, soak ≥ 30 minutes and breakpoint executed; raw results committed.
  • Knee identified (throughput vs p99) and the bottleneck named with evidence (dashboards, USE, Little's Law).
  • ≥ 2 improvement iterations documented with before/after numbers under the same workload.
  • A correctness check after every run (e.g. 0 double bookings) with its output.
  • A performance gate in CI: a k6 smoke run with thresholds that fails the pipeline on regression.
  • AI usage section (see the policy).

items.title: 1. Write the plan first
items.text:
A plan forces the team to agree on what "success" means before the numbers tempt you to move the goalposts. Start from the SLO table of your option; turn each SLO into a k6 threshold; define the journeys and their share of the traffic from your M1 estimates; decide where the tests run (Docker Compose or Kubernetes, which machine, which resources) and what data is seeded.

flowchart LR
    plan["Plan<br/>SLOs → thresholds<br/>journeys, mix, data"] --> smoke["Smoke<br/>script works"]
    smoke --> load["Load ×3<br/>target, ≥ 10 min"]
    load --> stress["Stress<br/>up to 2× target"]
    stress --> spike["Spike"]
    spike --> soak["Soak<br/>≥ 30 min"]
    soak --> bp["Breakpoint"]
    bp --> analyse["Analyse<br/>knee, bottleneck"]
    analyse -->|"hypothesis → change"| load

items.title: 2. Model the workload
items.text:
Real users do not hit one endpoint: a BoxOffice fan browses, joins the waiting room, holds seats and (sometimes) pays. One k6 scenario per journey, each with its own arrival rate, keeps the mix exact and lets you set a threshold per journey1.

load/boxoffice.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

const BASE = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:8080';
const TYPE = __ENV.TEST_TYPE || 'load';
const BROWSE = Number(__ENV.BROWSE_RATE || 1000); // catalog reads/s at the test target
const HOLD = Number(__ENV.HOLD_RATE || 100);      // seat holds/s at the test target
const EVENTS = Number(__ENV.EVENTS || 1000);
const TOKEN = __ENV.TOKEN || '';

const JSON_HEADERS = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', Authorization: `Bearer ${TOKEN}` };
// 409 (seat already taken) and 429 (waiting room full) are business outcomes, not failures
const BUSINESS = http.expectedStatuses({ min: 200, max: 299 }, 409, 429);

function profile(rate) {
  const r = (f) => Math.max(1, Math.round(rate * f));
  const base = { timeUnit: '1s', preAllocatedVUs: Math.max(10, r(0.2)), maxVUs: Math.max(100, r(3)) };
  switch (TYPE) {
    case 'smoke':
      return { ...base, executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', rate: 1, duration: '1m' };
    case 'stress': {
      const stages = [];
      for (const f of [0.5, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2]) {
        stages.push({ target: r(f), duration: '30s' }, { target: r(f), duration: '2m' });
      }
      return { ...base, executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: r(0.1), stages };
    }
    case 'spike':
      return { ...base, executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: r(0.2), stages: [
        { target: r(0.2), duration: '2m' }, { target: r(3), duration: '10s' },
        { target: r(3), duration: '2m' }, { target: r(0.2), duration: '10s' },
        { target: r(0.2), duration: '3m' } ] };
    case 'soak':
      return { ...base, executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: r(0.1), stages: [
        { target: r(1), duration: '2m' }, { target: r(1), duration: '30m' } ] };
    case 'breakpoint':
      return { ...base, executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: r(0.1), stages: [
        { target: r(4), duration: '20m' } ] };
    default: // load
      return { ...base, executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: r(0.1), stages: [
        { target: r(1), duration: '2m' }, { target: r(1), duration: '10m' }, { target: 0, duration: '30s' } ] };
  }
}

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browse: { ...profile(BROWSE), exec: 'browse' },          // 1. browse the catalog
    queue: { ...profile(HOLD * 2), exec: 'joinQueue' },      // 2. join the waiting room
    hold: { ...profile(HOLD * 0.3), exec: 'holdAndLeave' },  // 3. hold and abandon (hold expires)
    purchase: { ...profile(HOLD * 0.7), exec: 'purchase' },  // 4. hold and pay
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{name:catalog}': ['p(99)<200'],
    'http_req_duration{name:hold}': ['p(99)<500'],
    'http_req_failed{scenario:browse}': ['rate<0.001'],
    'http_req_failed{scenario:purchase}': ['rate<0.001'],
    checks: ['rate>0.99'],
  },
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'med', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
};

const eventId = () => 1 + Math.floor(Math.random() * EVENTS);

export function browse() {
  const res = http.get(`${BASE}/events/${eventId()}`, { tags: { name: 'catalog' } });
  check(res, { 'catalog 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

export function joinQueue() {
  const res = http.post(`${BASE}/queue/${eventId()}`, null,
    { headers: JSON_HEADERS, tags: { name: 'queue' }, responseCallback: BUSINESS });
  check(res, { 'queue accepted or full': (r) => r.status === 200 || r.status === 202 || r.status === 429 });
}

function hold() {
  const body = JSON.stringify({ eventId: eventId(), quantity: 1 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 4) });
  return http.post(`${BASE}/holds`, body,
    { headers: JSON_HEADERS, tags: { name: 'hold' }, responseCallback: BUSINESS });
}

export function holdAndLeave() {
  const res = hold();
  check(res, { 'hold created or seat taken': (r) => r.status === 201 || r.status === 409 });
}

export function purchase() {
  const res = hold();
  if (res.status !== 201) {
    return; // seat taken: the fan tries again later
  }
  const pay = http.post(`${BASE}/orders`, JSON.stringify({ holdId: res.json('id') }),
    { headers: JSON_HEADERS, tags: { name: 'pay' } });
  check(pay, { 'order created': (r) => r.status === 201 });
}

Adapt URLs, payloads and authentication to your API (obtain a token in setup() or disable auth for a dedicated test profile — and say so). For other options the journeys change (chat: connect, send, read history; ride-sharing: location updates, nearby query, request ride; feed: read timeline, post, like; video: request manifest/segments, upload; assistant: ask, ask with tool call), but the structure stays the same.

AI support assistant: TTFT with a stub LLM

Load-test the assistant against a stub LLM (a tiny HTTP server that streams tokens with a fixed latency distribution), so that you measure your system and not the model provider. For a streaming endpoint, the time until the first byte arrives is a good proxy for the time to first token:

load/assistant.js (excerpt)
import http from 'k6/http';
import { Trend } from 'k6/metrics';

const ttft = new Trend('ttft', true);

export const options = { thresholds: { ttft: ['p(95)<2000'] } };

export default function () {
  const body = JSON.stringify({ question: 'Can I change the name on my ticket?' });
  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/assistant/chat`, body,
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, tags: { name: 'chat' } });
  ttft.add(res.timings.waiting); // time to first byte of the streamed answer
}

Measure the real model separately at a low rate (e.g. 1 request/s) and report both.

items.title: 3. Seed the data and fix the environment
items.text: Every run starts from the same state: the same events, seats and users, an empty (or known) waiting room, caches flushed or warmed the same way. Write it as a script (load/seed.sh) and run it before each test. Fix the resources (Compose cpus/mem_limit, Kubernetes requests/limits, HPA min/max) and write them in the plan.

items.title: 4. Run the sequence
items.text:
load/campaign.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: ./load/campaign.sh <test-type> <run-number>   e.g. ./load/campaign.sh load 2
set -euo pipefail
TYPE=${1:-smoke}; RUN=${2:-1}
STAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
mkdir -p load/results
./load/seed.sh
k6 run -e TEST_TYPE="$TYPE" -e BASE_URL="${BASE_URL:-http://localhost:8080}" \
  --summary-export "load/results/${TYPE}-run${RUN}-${STAMP}.json" \
  load/boxoffice.js | tee "load/results/${TYPE}-run${RUN}-${STAMP}.txt"
psql "${CHECK_DB_URL:?set CHECK_DB_URL}" -f load/correctness.sql \
  | tee "load/results/${TYPE}-run${RUN}-${STAMP}-correctness.txt"

While each test runs, watch the RED dashboard (rate, errors, duration per service) and the saturation signals (CPU, pool usage, consumer lag, HPA replicas) in Grafana. Take screenshots at the steady state and at the knee; write down timestamps of anything odd.

Test What it answers Pass criterion Smoke Do the script, data and system work? 0 errors Load ×3 Are the SLOs met at the target, repeatably? All thresholds pass in the 3 runs Stress (to 2×) Where is the knee? What saturates first? Knee located; graceful degradation (no crash) Spike Does the system absorb a sudden ×3 (waiting room, autoscaling)? Errors bounded; recovery time measured Soak (≥ 30 min) Leaks, slow growth (memory, connections, lag, disk)? No upward trend in latency or resources Breakpoint What is the maximum before failure? Breaking rate reported

items.title: 5. Check correctness after every run
items.text:
A fast system that sells the same seat twice has failed. After every run, execute a correctness query and keep its output.

load/correctness.sql
-- BoxOffice: a seat may belong to at most one active hold or sold order
SELECT event_id, seat_id, count(*) AS owners
  FROM seat_allocations
 WHERE status IN ('HELD', 'SOLD')
 GROUP BY event_id, seat_id
HAVING count(*) > 1;

-- every paid order has exactly its seats marked SOLD
SELECT o.id
  FROM orders o
  LEFT JOIN seat_allocations s ON s.order_id = o.id AND s.status = 'SOLD'
 WHERE o.status = 'PAID'
 GROUP BY o.id, o.quantity
HAVING count(s.seat_id) <> o.quantity;
Option Correctness check BoxOffice flash sale 0 double bookings; sold seats = seats of paid orders Real-time chat No gaps in per-conversation sequence numbers for acknowledged messages Ride-sharing dispatch No driver assigned to two active trips Social feed Sampled followers see the post within the SLO; counters consistent Video platform Every acknowledged upload has all renditions or a failed job with a reason AI support assistant 0 unsafe tool actions; every tool call logged with the user's identity

items.title: 6. Iterate: hypothesis → change → result
items.text: When a test fails (or to move the knee), write the hypothesis first, with a number: "the inventory pool (10 connections) is exhausted at ~400 holds/s because L = λ × W = 400 × 0.025 = 10". Change one thing, rerun the same test, record the result — confirmed or refuted. Two documented iterations at least; each one is a small story with evidence.

items.title: 7. Gate performance in CI
items.text:
A smoke test with thresholds in the pipeline catches regressions (a missing index, an N+1 query) before they reach the campaign. Add a job to the workflow of Lab 11:

.github/workflows/ci.yaml (excerpt)
  performance-gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: build
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Start the system
        run: docker compose up -d --wait
      - name: Seed test data
        run: ./load/seed.sh
      - uses: grafana/setup-k6-action@v1
      - name: k6 smoke with SLO thresholds (fails the job on regression)
        run: k6 run -e TEST_TYPE=smoke -e BASE_URL=http://localhost:8080 load/boxoffice.js

The runner is small and shared, so the gate uses smoke rates and generous thresholds; it detects regressions, not capacity.

items.title: Rubric
items.text:
Levels as defined in How the exercises are graded.

Criterion I D C B A Plan (mandatory) None Written after the runs, or SLOs missing SLOs, journeys, mix, data, environment, entry/exit criteria Mix and rates derived from the M1 estimates Risks of the test itself (generator limits, data) planned for SLO verdict (mandatory) No load runs Fewer than 3 runs, or < 10 min steady SLOs met at the target in 3 runs (or bottleneck proven and target agreed) Spread across runs reported and explained Margin above the target quantified (e.g. holds at 1.3×) Workload and scripts Single endpoint, closed model Open model but no per-journey thresholds ≥ 3 journeys, open model, per-journey thresholds Business outcomes (409/429) handled correctly Think time, sessions or data skew modelled and justified Test sequence — Some types missing All six types with raw results Each type interpreted (knee, recovery, trends, breaking rate) Soak or spike reveals and fixes a real problem Bottleneck and iterations Guess One iteration or no before/after ≥ 2 iterations with before/after Hypotheses quantified before the change Next bottleneck predicted and confirmed Correctness and CI gate — Correctness not checked Check after every run + CI gate running Gate caught (or would catch) a demonstrated regression Correctness checked under spike and failure, not only at steady state

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Our machine cannot reach the test target. What now?

That is a result, if you prove it: show the bottleneck (often the load generator or the laptop's CPU, not the service), the knee and the evidence. Then agree a new target with the instructor before week 14 — not the night before the deadline.

Should the campaign run on Docker Compose or on Kubernetes?

On the environment you will present, preferably Kubernetes (M5) with the HPA active, since autoscaling is part of how the system meets its SLOs. If you run on Compose, say why and keep the resources fixed.

One of the three load runs failed. Can we drop it?

No. Report all runs. Investigate the failing one (noise, a GC pause, a cold cache, an autoscaling delay); if you fix the cause, rerun all three.

Do 409 and 429 responses count as errors?

Not when they are the designed behaviour (seat taken, waiting room full). Mark them as expected in k6 (responseCallback) and report them separately: a waiting room that rejects 90% of fans is "correct" but deserves a sentence in the report.

How long does the whole campaign take?

Count it: 3 × 13 min of load, ~15 min of stress, ~8 min of spike, 32 min of soak, ~20 min of breakpoint — about two hours of runs, plus analysis and iterations. Start early in the milestone.

Can AI write the k6 script?

It can draft it — declare it. You must be able to explain every scenario, rate and threshold, and why the model is open. Results, as always, must come from your own runs.

  1. Grafana k6 documentation, "Scenarios" and "Thresholds" (tags and per-scenario thresholds), grafana.com/docs/k6. ↩

items.title: Index
items.text:
The project is delivered in nine milestones. Each one adds a layer to the same system, in the order the classes teach it, so that you never build something you have not yet seen in class — and never leave everything to the last two weeks. Every milestone has acceptance criteria you can check yourself before the deadline, and a short check-in in class.

flowchart LR
    m1["M1<br/>design doc<br/>estimates · SLOs"] --> m2["M2<br/>core path<br/>apigw · auth · 3 services · sql"]
    m2 --> m3["M3<br/>scale<br/>cache · replica/pool"]
    m3 --> m4["M4<br/>async & resilience<br/>kafka · outbox · DLQ<br/>timeouts · breaker · OTel"]
    m4 --> m5["M5<br/>platform<br/>K8s · HPA · CI/CD · gate"]
    m5 --> m6["M6<br/>load-test campaign"]
    m6 --> m7["M7<br/>chaos game day"]
    m7 --> m8["M8<br/>cost report"]
    m8 --> m9["M9<br/>presentation"]

Each milestone is graded on the tag m<n> pushed by the deadline (week shown in each section; dates on the planning page) and on the check-in. M1 and M6–M9 have their own pages with details and rubrics; M2–M5 share the rubric at the end of this page.

items.title: M1 — Design doc & estimates
items.text:
Week 5 · 10% · tag m1. Agree on what you are building, how big it is and how you will prove it works.

  • Design doc with every section, project additions, SLO table and capacity model.
  • At least three ADRs, risk register, ownership table.
  • Test target agreed with the instructor.

Details, template and rubric: design doc. Related: estimation and design doc exercises.

Check-in questions: Which SLO is the hardest to meet, and why? Which number in your estimates drives the biggest decision? Who owns what?

items.title: M2 — Core path running
items.text:
Week 7 · 10% · tag m2. The main use case works end to end, locally, with one command.

Acceptance criteria

  • docker compose up from a clean clone brings every container to healthy in under 3 minutes (health checks in compose.yaml).
  • The main use case works end to end through the entry point (e.g. BoxOffice: list events → hold seats → confirm order), shown by a script or a k6 smoke test.
  • Gateway (apigw) routes to at least three services of your own, each with its own schema/database and migrations (Flyway or equivalent).
  • Authentication: login issues a JWT (or OIDC token); at least one route is protected and returns 401 without a token; at least one route is open.
  • Rate limiting on at least one route at the gateway, shown by a burst that receives 429.
  • k6 smoke test (≥ 30 s, low rate) on the main use case passes with 0 errors, committed with its summary.
  • OpenAPI available for every service.

Evidence in the docs: architecture diagram as built, how to run, smoke-test summary, a short screen recording or terminal log of the main use case.

Related: Lab 1 (first service), Lab 2 (k6), Lab 3 (edge), Lab 4 (gateway & identity).

Check-in questions: What happens if the auth service is down — which routes still work? Where is the rate limit enforced and with which algorithm? Show me one service's data: could another service write to it?

items.title: M3 — Scale & cache
items.text:
Week 9 · 10% · tag m3. Make the hot read path cheap and prove it with numbers.

Acceptance criteria

  • A cache (cache, Redis) on the hottest read path, with TTL and invalidation on write; hit/miss metrics exposed.
  • A read replica with read/write routing or a connection pooler (PgBouncer) — chosen and justified by a measurement.
  • At least two replicas of the hottest service behind a load balancer (Nginx or the gateway), with health checks.
  • Before/after k6 test with the same script, data and resources: hit ratio ≥ 80% in steady state (or a justified lower value for your workload), p99 and knee before vs after.
  • The critical write (e.g. seat hold) is consistent under concurrency: a k6 test with concurrent attempts on the same item shows no double booking/assignment (verification query committed).
  • Capacity model of the design doc updated with measured per-instance capacity.

Evidence in the docs: before/after table, hit ratio, knee chart, consistency check output, design-doc changelog entry.

Related: Lab 5 (caching), Lab 6 (data at scale), cache & database and load-test report exercises.

Check-in questions: What would happen to the database if Redis were flushed right now? Show me the query that proves there is no double booking. What is your new bottleneck?

items.title: M4 — Async & resilience
items.text:
Week 12 · 10% · tag m4. Move slow work off the request path, survive slow dependencies, and see what is happening.

Acceptance criteria

  • A broker (kafka, queue or pubsub) carries at least one business event between two services.
  • Transactional outbox on the producer or idempotent consumer (ideally both) — verified by a reconciliation query after a run where the consumer is killed: 0 lost, 0 duplicated side effects.
  • Retries with backoff and a DLQ/DLT; a poison message ends there and processing continues.
  • On the call to the slow/external dependency (payment, thirdparty, email or llmgw): timeout + retry with exponential backoff and jitter + circuit breaker (Resilience4j or equivalent), with a fallback or a clear error.
  • Demonstration with Toxiproxy (or equivalent): with 2 s of injected latency on the dependency, the entry point's p99 stays bounded and threads are not exhausted (numbers before/after).
  • Observability: OpenTelemetry traces across at least three services (one trace screenshot crossing the broker), a RED dashboard (rate, errors, duration) per service, and one SLO burn-rate alert that fires in a test.

Evidence in the docs: event flow diagram, envelope schema, reconciliation output, Toxiproxy experiment table, dashboard and trace screenshots, alert definition.

Related: Lab 7 (async), Lab 8 (observability), Lab 9 (resilience & chaos), event-driven exercise; AI option: Lab 12.

Check-in questions: Kill the consumer now — what happens to the events, and how do you know none is lost? Why this timeout value? Open the dashboard: which service is the slowest and why?

items.title: M5 — Kubernetes + CI/CD
items.text:
Week 14 · 10% · tag m5. Run on a platform and deliver every change automatically and safely.

Acceptance criteria

  • Every service runs on Kubernetes (kind/minikube or a cloud cluster) from manifests in the repository (plain YAML, Kustomize or Helm), with requests/limits, startup/readiness/liveness probes, graceful shutdown and an Ingress (or Gateway API).
  • An HPA on at least one service scales up under a k6 load and back down (replicas-over-time chart).
  • Zero failed requests during a rolling update under steady load.
  • CI (GitHub Actions) on every pull request: build, unit tests, container image, image scan (e.g. Trivy) failing on critical vulnerabilities, SBOM generated and stored as an artifact.
  • Performance gate: a k6 smoke/short-load test with SLO thresholds runs in CI and blocks the merge when a threshold fails (show one red run).
  • CD: merging to main deploys to the cluster (GitOps with Argo CD, or a deploy job), with a documented rollback.
  • Secrets are not in the repository (Kubernetes Secrets from CI secrets, or Sealed Secrets/External Secrets).

Optional A-level extra: add an AI step to the pipeline from Lab 13 — AI in CI/CD (e.g. an AI pull-request reviewer or AI-explained canary analysis), with a short evaluation of what it caught and what it got wrong.

Evidence in the docs: cluster diagram, manifests links, HPA chart, rolling-update k6 summary, links to a green and a red CI run, SBOM artifact, deployment and rollback procedure.

Related: Lab 10 (Kubernetes), Lab 11 (delivery), Kubernetes autoscaling exercise.

Check-in questions: Push a change that breaks a threshold — what happens? How do you roll back, and how long does it take? What limits your maxReplicas?

items.title: M6 — Load-test campaign
items.text:
Week 16 · 15% · tag m6. Prove, with a rigorous k6 campaign, that the system meets the test-target SLOs — and find where it stops meeting them.

  • Campaign plan, scripts, raw results and report.
  • Test-target SLOs met for ≥ 10 minutes in 3 repetitions; knee and bottleneck identified; ≥ 2 improvement iterations.

Details, template and rubric: load-test campaign. Related: Class 15, Lab 2.

Check-in questions: At what load does the first SLO break, and which resource causes it? Which iteration helped most? How do you know the load generator was not the bottleneck?

items.title: M7 — Chaos game day
items.text:
Week 17 · 10% · tag m7. Break the system on purpose, under load, in front of the class — and learn from it.

  • At least three planned experiments plus one surprise fault injected by the instructor.
  • Report with observations, SLO impact, time to detect/mitigate and action items.

Details, templates and rubric: game day. Related: Class 9, Lab 9.

Check-in questions: Which experiment surprised you? How did you detect the surprise fault — alert, dashboard or a user? Which action item matters most?

items.title: M8 — Cost report
items.text:
Week 18 · 10% · tag m8. Put a price on the design target and on what you actually ran, and connect cost to your measurements.

  • Monthly cost of the design target with a bill of materials, unit economics and sensitivity analysis.
  • Final update of the design doc (changelog complete).

Details, template and rubric: cost report. Related: Class 12.

Check-in questions: What is the cost of one ticket sold (or message, ride, view, conversation)? What dominates the bill? What would you change to halve it?

items.title: M9 — Final presentation
items.text:
Weeks 19–20 · 10% · tag final. Show the system working, the evidence that it meets its goals, and what you learned.

  • 15-minute presentation + live demo + 10 minutes of questions; every member presents.
  • 3-minute video and final documentation.

Details, template and rubric: presentation.

items.title: Rubric for M2–M5
items.text:
Levels as defined in How the exercises are graded.

Criterion I D C B A Acceptance criteria (mandatory) Tag missing or system does not run At least one criterion not met All criteria met All met with margin (e.g. better numbers than required) All met plus a relevant extra (e.g. the M5 AI step, CDC relay, multi-instance tests) Evidence and measurements None Claims without evidence Every criterion has evidence in the docs Numbers interpreted, before/after explained Evidence reproducible by the reader with one command Code and configuration quality Broken Fragile, hard-coded secrets or values Clean, configuration externalised, migrations Tests for the critical paths, consistent conventions Code a new member could extend in a day Documentation Missing Outdated or incomplete Milestone section complete, design doc changelog updated Clear diagrams and ADRs for the changes Lessons learned and known limitations stated honestly Check-in Absent Cannot demo or answer Demo works, questions answered by the owners Any member answers any question Team anticipates the follow-up questions

items.title: Check-ins
items.text:
Each milestone has a 10-minute check-in in class during its week:

  1. Demo from a clean clone of the tag (2–3 minutes): git clone, checkout the tag, one command, the use case working. No "it worked on my machine".
  2. Evidence walk-through (2–3 minutes): the docs section of the milestone.
  3. Questions (4–5 minutes): the instructor picks any member for each question (examples are listed in each milestone). Owners may complement, but every member must be able to answer the basics.

A missed check-in without justification caps the milestone at D. Problems discovered during a check-in can be fixed until the deadline of the same week.

items.title: Index
items.text:
Fifteen minutes to show a semester of work. The final presentation is not a tour of every class you used — it is a design review: here is the problem, here is the architecture and why, here it is running under load, here is the evidence that it meets its SLOs, here is what broke on game day, here is what it costs, and here is what we would do next. Then the reviewers ask questions — to each member.

Goals

With this milestone your team will:

  • Tell the story of the system in a structured, time-boxed talk aimed at engineers.
  • Demonstrate the core path live, under load, with dashboards — and have a fallback.
  • Defend decisions and numbers: ADRs, load-test results, game-day findings, cost.
  • Show individual mastery in the Q&A: every member explains and changes any part of the system.
  • Publish the final documentation and a 3-minute video.

Presentations happen in weeks 19–20 (schedule published by the instructor); weight 10% of the project. The documentation quality of the whole site is graded at the same time.

items.title: What to deliver
items.text:
• Slides (PDF or a link in the docs), following the outline.
  • A live demo during the presentation, plus a fallback recording of the same demo.
  • A 3-minute video of the project (link in the docs).
  • The final documentation on GitHub Pages and the final tag final.

items.title: Acceptance criteria
items.text:
• (mandatory) Every member presents a part of the talk and answers individual questions.
  • (mandatory) Talk within 15 minutes (hard stop), followed by 10 minutes of Q&A.
  • The architecture diagram uses palette ids and matches the deployed system (the final design doc).
  • A live demo of the core path under load with the dashboards visible (or the fallback recording, if the live demo fails — say so).
  • Load-test results against the target SLOs (M6), game-day findings (M7) and cost per business unit (M8) presented with numbers.
  • At least two ADRs presented as decisions with alternatives and consequences.
  • 3-minute video published and linked; it stands alone for someone who did not attend.
  • Final docs checklist complete and tag final pushed before the presentation day.
  • AI usage section in the final docs (see the policy).

items.title: 1. Structure the 15 minutes
items.text:
Min Section What the audience must leave with 0–1 Problem and requirements The system option, the users, the design and test targets, the SLOs 1–4 Architecture One diagram with palette ids; the request path of the core use case; data ownership 4–6 Key decisions Two or three ADRs: the decision, the alternatives, the trade-off 6–10 Live demo under load The core path working while k6 runs; RED dashboard; one trace 10–12 Evidence Load-test campaign vs SLOs (knee, bottleneck, iterations); game-day findings 12–14 Cost Monthly cost at the design target, cost per unit, the biggest lever 14–15 Lessons and next steps What you would change, what the system would need at 10×

Split the sections so that every member presents something substantial (not only the title slide). Rehearse with a timer; the stop at 15:00 is real.

items.title: 2. Prepare the demo — and its fallback
items.text:
Live demos fail for boring reasons: Wi-Fi, a cluster that did not start, an expired token. Prepare like an operator:

  • Environment started 30 minutes before, data seeded, caches warmed, dashboards open in a browser tab, terminal font enlarged.
  • A demo script: the exact commands and clicks, in order, with what the audience should notice at each step.
  • A load generator at a known rate (e.g. 50–70% of the test target) started at the beginning of the demo.
  • A fallback recording of the same demo (screen capture with voice), ready to play if anything breaks.
  • One person drives, another narrates.
demo/start.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prepare the live demo: seed, warm up, start the background load.
set -euo pipefail
./load/seed.sh
k6 run -e TEST_TYPE=smoke -e BASE_URL="${BASE_URL:-http://localhost:8080}" load/boxoffice.js > /dev/null
nohup k6 run -e TEST_TYPE=load -e BASE_URL="${BASE_URL:-http://localhost:8080}" \
  -e BROWSE_RATE="${BROWSE_RATE:-600}" -e HOLD_RATE="${HOLD_RATE:-60}" \
  load/boxoffice.js > demo/k6-live.log 2>&1 &
echo "background load started (pid $!) — open the RED dashboard now"

items.title: 3. Record the 3-minute video
items.text: The video is for someone who never saw the course: a recruiter, a future teammate. Suggested cut: problem and SLOs (20 s), architecture (40 s), the system under load with dashboards (60 s), one result from the campaign and one from the game day (40 s), cost and lessons (20 s). Keep it under 3 minutes; subtitles or clear audio; show the team.

items.title: 4. Prepare for the Q&A
items.text:
Questions go to individuals, and any member may be asked about any part of the system. Expect questions such as:

  • "Walk me through what happens, component by component, when a fan holds a seat. Where can it fail?"
  • "Your p99 at the target was 180 ms. What dominates it? How do you know?"
  • "If traffic grows 10×, what breaks first? What would you change, and what would it cost?"
  • "Why Kafka and not a simple queue here? What would make you change your mind?"
  • "Show me the alert that fired on game day. What is its burn-rate window, and why?"
  • "This part was written with AI help. Explain it, and change this parameter: what happens?"

items.title: 5. Finish the documentation
items.text:
• Home page: team, ownership table, system option, one-paragraph summary, architecture diagram, links to every milestone.
  • Final design doc and ADRs (with the changelog since M1).
  • Load-test campaign report, game-day report, cost report.
  • How to run: Compose and Kubernetes, seed data, run a load test — tested from a clean clone.
  • Links: repository, CI runs, slides, video, demo recording.
  • AI usage per deliverable.
  • Tag final pushed; the site built from it.

items.title: Rubric
items.text:
Levels as defined in How the exercises are graded. The individual Q&A can adjust a member's grade (see the team rules).

Criterion I D C B A Participation and time (mandatory) A member absent without justification A member does not present, or > 17 min Every member presents; within 15 min Balanced parts; smooth hand-offs Talk adapted to questions on the fly Story and architecture — List of technologies Problem → SLOs → architecture → decisions Diagram with palette ids matches the deployed system; trade-offs explicit A reviewer could redraw the system after the talk Live demo Nothing shown Fallback recording only, without explanation Core path works under load with dashboards Demo tied to SLIs ("watch p99 here") Failure shown live and the system recovering Evidence — Claims without numbers M6, M7 and M8 numbers presented Numbers interpreted (knee, bottleneck, cost per unit) Clear "what we would do at 10×" with cost Q&A (individual) Cannot explain own work Vague answers Correct answers on own area Correct answers on any area Reasons about changes on the spot with numbers Video and final docs Missing Video > 3 min or docs incomplete Video ≤ 3 min; docs checklist complete Video stands alone; docs reproducible from a clean clone Portfolio quality

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Can we present only a recording instead of a live demo?

The live demo is expected; the recording is the fallback. If the live demo fails, switch to the recording without losing time and say what failed — handling it calmly is itself a good signal.

Do we need slides for every milestone?

No. The talk is a story, not a report: pick the decisions, numbers and findings that best show how the system meets (or misses) its SLOs. Details live in the docs.

Who answers the questions?

The person asked. Others may complement after the answer. Questions are distributed among all members and may cover any part of the system.

Is the video the same as the demo recording?

No. The demo recording is a backup of the live demo; the video is a 3-minute overview of the whole project for people who did not attend.

Can AI make our slides?

It can help with layout and wording — declare it. The content, the numbers and the answers in the Q&A must be yours.

items.title: Index
items.text:
In this lab

  • Install and check the toolchain used in every lab: Docker + Compose, JDK 21, Maven, uv + Python 3.12, k6, kubectl, kind or minikube, Git.
  • Create your BoxOffice repository with the layout that the next twelve labs fill in.
  • Learn the service names, ports, environment variables and conventions that every lab shares.
  • Measure your machine for the first time: how many requests per second can it serve, and with what latency?

During the semester you will build BoxOffice, a ticketing platform for concerts, games and festivals. It starts as one small service on your laptop and grows, lab after lab, into a system with an edge proxy, an API gateway, a cache, a replicated database, an event stream, observability, Kubernetes and an AI assistant. Each lab adds one component of the System Design Playground palette, and each lab ends with a measurement: system design is about trade-offs, and a trade-off is only real when you can put a number on it.

This first lab is short but important: a broken environment costs hours later, in the middle of a load test.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
Time 1–2 hours (most of it is downloads) You need a computer with 8 GB of RAM or more (16 GB is comfortable from lab 4 on), ~20 GB of free disk, administrator rights, internet access Operating system macOS, Linux, or Windows 10/11 with WSL 2 (every command of the course runs in a Linux shell) Start state nothing: this lab creates the boxoffice/ repository from an empty folder

First lab

There is nothing to catch up on: every later lab starts from the state at the end of the previous one, and each lab page offers a ready-made boxoffice-after-lab-<n>.zip if you skip or break a lab.

items.title: Slides
items.text: Click the slides and use ← → to move through them; F goes full screen and P opens the presenter view, with the notes. Open the slides in a new tab

items.title: Where we are going
items.text:
The diagram shows BoxOffice at the end of the semester. Do not worry about the details: every box has its own lab, and the number in each label says which one.
