Theory connection

This lab pairs with class 1, What is system design: the scaling journey of BoxOffice from one server to millions of users is exactly the path the labs follow. The "Measure it" step at the end connects with class 2, Estimation.

items.title: BoxOffice services and ports
items.text:
Every lab — and every team project — uses the names below. Do not rename them: the configuration files, the k6 scripts and the next labs assume them. A service listens on the same port inside its container and on your machine, so http://catalog:8082 (from another container) and http://localhost:8082 (from your terminal) reach the same service.

Application services (one folder each under services/):

Compose service Lab Stack Port Public route prefix DB schema Role edge 3 Nginx 1.30 80 — — reverse proxy, load balancer, rate limiting: the only public entry from lab 3 on gateway 4 Spring Cloud Gateway 8080 all of them — routing, JWT validation, identity headers auth 4 Spring Boot 8081 /auth/** auth users, login, issues JWTs (RS256) and publishes the JWKS catalog 1 Spring Boot 8082 /catalog/** catalog events and venues (read-heavy). Runs as catalog-1, catalog-2, catalog-3 from lab 3 on inventory 6 Spring Boot 8083 /inventory/** inventory seats and holds (strongly consistent) order 7 Spring Boot 8084 /orders/** orders orders, transactional outbox payment 9 Spring Boot 8085 /payments/** payment adapter to the external payment provider notification 7 Spring Boot 8086 /notifications/** notification e-mail/push, idempotent consumer search — (optional) 8087 /search/** — reserved for the project assistant 12 Python 3.12 + FastAPI 8088 /assistant/** assistant AI support assistant (RAG + tools)

Infrastructure (official images, configuration under infra/):

Compose service Lab Image Port(s) on your machine Notes db 1 postgres:17 5432 database boxoffice, user boxoffice, password boxoffice; one schema per service db-replica 6 postgres:17 5433 streaming replica of db, read-only pgbouncer 6 edoburu/pgbouncer:v1.26.0-p0 6432 connection pooler in front of db redis 5 redis:8-alpine 6379 cache (maxmemory + LRU) kafka 7 Apache Kafka (KRaft) 9092 event stream otel-lgtm 8 grafana/otel-lgtm 3000 (Grafana), 4317/4318 (OTLP gRPC/HTTP) metrics, logs, traces toxiproxy 9 ghcr.io/shopify/toxiproxy 8474 (API) latency and fault injection ollama 12 ollama/ollama 11434 local LLM k6 web dashboard 2 — 5665 K6_WEB_DASHBOARD=true k6 run … hello (lab 0 only) 0 nginx:1.30-alpine 8888 target of the baseline measurement

Conventions shared by all services:

Topic Convention Java JDK 21, Spring Boot 4.1.x (Spring Framework 7, Jackson 3), Spring Cloud 2025.1.x, Maven, no Lombok (Java records for DTOs) Python Python 3.12 managed by uv (uv init, uv add <pkg>, uv run <cmd>, uvx <tool>); never pip/venv. Dockerfiles copy uv with COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:latest /uv /uvx /bin/ and run uv sync --frozen Packages boxoffice.<service> (e.g. boxoffice.catalog); Maven groupId boxoffice, artifactId = service name HTTP paths each service serves only under its prefix (catalog → /catalog/...), so the edge and the gateway route without rewriting paths Database one PostgreSQL instance (db), one schema per service, owned by that service's Flyway migrations (src/main/resources/db/migration); no cross-schema joins Health Spring Boot Actuator: /actuator/health, /actuator/health/liveness, /actuator/health/readiness, /actuator/metrics Errors RFC 9457 application/problem+json (spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled: true) Compose file docker-compose.yaml at the repository root, project name boxoffice Load scripts load/*.js (k6), base URL from BASE_URL; results saved under results/

Environment variables (the same name everywhere; defaults in parentheses):

Variable Used by Meaning DB_HOST (db), DB_PORT (5432), DB_NAME (boxoffice), DB_USER (boxoffice), DB_PASSWORD (boxoffice) every service with a database PostgreSQL connection DB_REPLICA_HOST (db-replica), DB_REPLICA_PORT (5432) inventory (lab 6) read replica REDIS_HOST (redis), REDIS_PORT (6379) catalog (lab 5) cache AUTH_JWKS_URI (http://auth:8081/auth/.well-known/jwks.json) gateway public keys used to validate JWTs JWT_ISSUER (boxoffice-auth), JWT_TTL (PT1H) auth, gateway token issuer and lifetime ADMIN_EMAIL (admin@boxoffice.dev), ADMIN_PASSWORD (boxoffice-admin) auth administrator created at startup CATALOG_URL, INVENTORY_URL, ORDER_URL, PAYMENT_URL (http://<service>:<port>) service-to-service calls base URL of another service KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS (kafka:9092) labs 7+ Kafka brokers OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT (http://otel-lgtm:4318) labs 8+ telemetry export BASE_URL k6 scripts http://localhost:8082 in labs 1–2, http://localhost (the edge) from lab 3 on

Headers that cross service boundaries:

Header Set by Meaning Authorization: Bearer <jwt> client identity, validated by the gateway X-User-Id, X-User-Email, X-User-Scope gateway (removed if a client sends them) authenticated user, trusted by the services X-Request-Id edge correlation id, logged by every hop X-Instance catalog which replica answered (lab 3) X-Cache: HIT / MISS catalog cache outcome (lab 5)

Ports already in use?

If something on your machine already uses port 80, 5432 or 6379 (a local PostgreSQL, for instance), stop it, or change only the host side of the mapping in docker-compose.yaml ("15432:5432"). Never change the port inside the container: the other services rely on it.

items.title: 1. Install the tools
items.text:
The table lists what each tool is for; the tabs below show how to install them on each system. k6 is a single binary1; Docker Compose comes with Docker Desktop or as a plugin of Docker Engine2.

Tool Version Used in Why Git any recent all labs version control, delivery of every lab Docker + Compose v2 Docker 27+ all labs every service and database runs in a container JDK 21 (LTS) labs 1–11 Spring Boot services Maven 3.9+ labs 1–11 build and dependencies uv recent labs 2, 12 installs Python 3.12 and runs every Python script and project (no pip, no venv) Python 3.12 (via uv) labs 2, 12 result scripts, the AI assistant k6 1.0+ labs 0–12 load tests (JavaScript scripts) kubectl + kind or minikube recent labs 10–11 local Kubernetes jq, curl any all labs calling and reading the APIs from the terminal Apple macOSLinux Linux (Ubuntu 24.04) Windows

Install Homebrew first, then:

brew install --cask docker          # Docker Desktop (or OrbStack: brew install --cask orbstack)
brew install --cask temurin@21      # Eclipse Temurin JDK 21
brew install maven uv k6 kubectl kind jq git
uv python install 3.12              # Python is managed by uv, not by Homebrew or pip

Open Docker Desktop once so it starts the engine, and give it at least 4 CPUs and 8 GB of memory (Settings → Resources).

# Docker Engine + Compose plugin (official convenience script) and run docker without sudo
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
sudo usermod -aG docker "$USER" && newgrp docker

# JDK 21, Maven, tools
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y openjdk-21-jdk maven git jq curl

# uv (Python package and project manager) and Python 3.12
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
uv python install 3.12

# k6 (official APT repository)
sudo gpg -k
sudo gpg --no-default-keyring --keyring /usr/share/keyrings/k6-archive-keyring.gpg \
  --keyserver hkp://keyserver.ubuntu.com:80 --recv-keys C5AD17C747E3415A3642D57D77C6C491D6AC1D69
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/k6-archive-keyring.gpg] https://dl.k6.io/deb stable main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/k6.list
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y k6

# kubectl and minikube
sudo snap install kubectl --classic
curl -LO https://storage.googleapis.com/minikube/releases/latest/minikube-linux-amd64
sudo install minikube-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/minikube && rm minikube-linux-amd64

Use WSL 2 with Ubuntu: the labs use Bash scripts, and file sharing between Windows and containers is slow and fragile.

wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04
  1. Install Docker Desktop and enable Settings → Resources → WSL integration for Ubuntu.
  2. Open the Ubuntu terminal and follow the Linux tab (skip the Docker Engine lines: Docker Desktop provides it).
  3. Keep your repository inside the WSL file system (~/boxoffice), not under /mnt/c/....

No k6 installed? Run it in a container

k6 is a single binary, but if you cannot install it, the official image works with the same scripts. From the repository root:

docker run --rm -i -v "$PWD":/w -w /w -e BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:8888 grafana/k6 run load/hello.js

Inside a container, localhost is the container itself; host.docker.internal reaches your machine (on Linux add --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway).

items.title: 2. Check your environment
items.text:
Save the script below as scripts/check-env.sh in your repository (next step) and run it. Every line must say ok.

scripts/check-env.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# BoxOffice labs: checks that every tool is installed and prints its version.
# Usage: bash scripts/check-env.sh
set -u
missing=0

check() {            # check <label> <command line>
  local label="$1" cmd="$2" out
  if ! command -v "${cmd%% *}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    printf '  MISS  %-9s not found\n' "$label"; missing=$((missing + 1))
  elif out=$(eval "$cmd" 2>&1); then
    printf '  ok    %-9s %s\n' "$label" "$(echo "$out" | head -n 1)"
  else
    printf '  FAIL  %-9s %s\n' "$label" "$(echo "$out" | head -n 1)"; missing=$((missing + 1))
  fi
}

echo "Tools"
check git      "git --version"
check docker   "docker --version"
check compose  "docker compose version"
check java     "java -version"
check maven    "mvn -v"
check uv       "uv --version"
check k6       "k6 version"
check kubectl  "kubectl version --client"
check jq       "jq --version"
check curl     "curl --version"

echo "Kubernetes (lab 10): kind OR minikube is enough"
if command -v kind >/dev/null 2>&1 || command -v minikube >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  command -v kind >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "  ok    kind      $(kind version 2>&1 | head -n 1)"
  command -v minikube >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "  ok    minikube  $(minikube version --short 2>&1 | head -n 1)"
else
  echo "  MISS  kind / minikube"; missing=$((missing + 1))
fi

echo "Checks"
java_major=$(java -version 2>&1 | head -n 1 | sed -E 's/[^"]*"([0-9]+).*/\1/')
if [ "${java_major:-0}" -ge 21 ] 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "  ok    JDK $java_major (21 or newer)"
else
  echo "  MISS  JDK 21 or newer (found: ${java_major:-none})"; missing=$((missing + 1))
fi
# Python is installed and managed by uv (uv python install 3.12)
if py=$(uv python find '>=3.12' 2>/dev/null); then
  echo "  ok    Python $("$py" -c 'import platform; print(platform.python_version())') (via uv)"
else
  echo "  MISS  Python 3.12 or newer: run  uv python install 3.12"; missing=$((missing + 1))
fi
if docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "  ok    Docker daemon: $(docker info --format '{{.NCPU}} CPUs, {{.MemTotal}} bytes of memory')"
else
  echo "  MISS  Docker daemon is not running"; missing=$((missing + 1))
fi

echo
if [ "$missing" -eq 0 ]; then echo "All set."; else echo "$missing item(s) missing: fix them before lab 1."; fi
bash scripts/check-env.shTools ok git git version 2.47.1 ok docker Docker version 28.4.0, build d8eb465 ok compose Docker Compose version v2.39.2 ok java openjdk version "21.0.8" 2025-07-15 LTS ok maven Apache Maven 3.9.11 ok uv uv 0.9.2 ok k6 k6 v1.3.0 (go1.25.1, linux/amd64) ok kubectl Client Version: v1.34.1 ok jq jq-1.7.1 ok curl curl 8.5.0 (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu)Kubernetes (lab 10): kind OR minikube is enough ok minikube v1.37.0Checks ok JDK 21 (21 or newer) ok Python 3.12.12 (via uv) ok Docker daemon: 8 CPUs, 16651931648 bytes of memoryAll set.

Your version numbers will differ; what matters is that nothing says MISS or FAIL.

Common failures

  • FAIL maven … JAVA_HOME environment variable is not defined correctly: point JAVA_HOME to the JDK 21 folder (export JAVA_HOME=$(/usr/libexec/java_home -v 21) on macOS; /usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk-amd64 on Ubuntu) and add it to your ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc.
  • MISS Docker daemon is not running: start Docker Desktop (macOS/Windows) or sudo systemctl start docker (Linux).
  • permission denied … docker.sock on Linux: you skipped usermod -aG docker; log out and in again.
  • MISS Python 3.12 or newer: run uv python install 3.12. Never pip install into the system Python: every Python step of the course goes through uv (uv run, uv add, uvx).

items.title: 4. Measure it: your machine's baseline
items.text:
Every lab ends with a measurement, and this one sets the reference: how much can your laptop serve when the server does almost nothing? The target is a stock Nginx returning a small static page; any number you get later for BoxOffice will be lower, and the difference is the cost of your code, your database and your network hops.

Save the script as load/hello.js:

load/hello.js
// Lab 0: how fast is *your* machine? The target is a plain Nginx container.
//   docker run -d --rm --name hello -p 8888:80 nginx:1.30-alpine
//   k6 run -e VUS=10 load/hello.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

const BASE_URL = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:8888';

export const options = {
  vus: Number(__ENV.VUS || 10),          // closed model: N users, no think time
  duration: __ENV.DURATION || '20s',
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'med', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],      // fewer than 1% errors
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/`);
  check(res, { 'status is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

Start the target, run k6 with 1, 10 and 50 virtual users (VUs), then stop the target:

docker run -d --rm --name hello -p 8888:80 nginx:1.30-alpine
k6 run -e VUS=1  load/hello.js
k6 run -e VUS=10 load/hello.js
k6 run -e VUS=50 load/hello.js
docker stop hello
k6 run -e VUS=10 load/hello.js █ THRESHOLDS http_req_failed ✓ 'rate<0.01' rate=0.00% █ TOTAL RESULTS checks_succeeded...: 100.00% 249184 out of 249184 HTTP http_req_duration..............: avg=163.61µs med=119.66µs p(95)=405.54µs p(99)=824.01µs max=13.26ms http_req_failed................: 0.00% 0 out of 249184 http_reqs......................: 249184 49808.803836/s EXECUTION vus............................: 10 min=10 max=10

Read the summary like this:

  • http_reqs … /s is the throughput (requests per second, RPS).
  • http_req_duration gives the latency distribution: med is the median (p50), p(95)/p(99) are the 95th/99th percentiles — 1 request in 100 is slower than p99.
  • vus is the concurrency: each virtual user sends a request, waits for the answer, and sends the next one (a closed workload model).

Record the results in results/lab0.md:

results/lab0.md
# Lab 0 — baseline

Machine: <CPU model>, <cores> cores, <RAM> GB; Docker resources: <CPUs> CPUs, <GB> GB

| VUs | Throughput (req/s) | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | Errors |
|----:|-------------------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|-------:|
|   1 |                    |          |          |          |        |
|  10 |                    |          |          |          |        |
|  50 |                    |          |          |          |        |

Little's Law check (VUs ≈ throughput × average latency):
- 10 VUs: ____ req/s × ____ s = ____
Think first: what happens between 10 and 50 VUs?

With 1 VU, the latency is pure service time and the throughput is 1 / latency. Adding VUs raises the throughput while there are idle CPU cores. Once the cores are busy, more VUs only add waiting: throughput stays flat and latency grows in proportion — Little's Law, L = λ × W, with L = VUs, λ = throughput and W = latency. You will see that knee again, with real services, in lab 2.

k6 competes with the server

k6 and the server share the same CPU cores, so above a few tens of thousands of requests per second you measure k6 as much as Nginx. That is fine for a baseline; in lab 2 the target will be much slower than k6, and the problem disappears.

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

Q1. In BoxOffice, catalog listens on port 8082 inside its container and on your machine. From the gateway container, which URL reaches it?

  • A. http://localhost:8082
  • B. http://catalog:8082
  • C. http://127.0.0.1:8082
  • D. http://host.docker.internal:80
Answer

B — http://catalog:8082.

Containers in the same Compose project share a network where each service name is a DNS name. Inside the gateway container, localhost is the gateway itself, so A and C point to the wrong process. host.docker.internal reaches your machine, not a sibling container. From your terminal (outside Docker), http://localhost:8082 works because the port is published.

Q2. Why does every BoxOffice service serve its endpoints only under its own prefix (/catalog/..., /auth/...)?

  • A. Spring Boot requires a prefix for every controller
  • B. So that the edge and the gateway can route by path without rewriting it, and two services never claim the same path
  • C. To make URLs longer and harder to guess
  • D. Because Nginx cannot proxy the root path /
Answer

B — Path-based routing without rewrites.

With unique prefixes, a routing rule is one line (/catalog/** → catalog) at every layer — Nginx, the gateway, a Kubernetes Ingress. Without them, catalog and inventory could both want /events/... and every proxy would need rewrite rules, a classic source of bugs.

Q3. BoxOffice uses one PostgreSQL instance with one schema per service. Which rule keeps the services independent?

  • A. Every service may read every schema, but only catalog writes
  • B. Each schema is created and changed only by the migrations of the service that owns it, and services never join across schemas
  • C. All services share one Flyway history table
  • D. Schemas are created by hand by the instructor before each lab
Answer

B — Ownership: one service, one schema, no cross-schema joins.

The single instance is a laptop-friendly shortcut; the logical separation is what matters. If order joined catalog.events, a change in catalog's table would break order — a hidden coupling. Keeping each schema private means you can later move a service to its own database server without touching the others.

Q4. You ran k6 run -e VUS=10 load/hello.js and got 20,000 req/s with an average latency of 0.5 ms. What does Little's Law (L = λ × W) predict for the concurrency?

  • A. 1
  • B. 10
  • C. 40
  • D. 20,000
Answer

B — 10.

L = λ × W = 20,000 req/s × 0.0005 s = 10. In a closed model without think time, the number of requests in the system equals the number of VUs. When the computed value differs a lot from the VUs you configured, part of the time is being spent outside the measured request (for example in k6 itself).

Q5. With 1 VU, a request takes 2 ms. Ignoring any limit, what is the maximum throughput that single VU can generate?

  • A. 2 req/s
  • B. 50 req/s
  • C. 500 req/s
  • D. 2,000 req/s
Answer

C — 500 req/s.

A closed-model VU sends the next request only after the previous answer arrives: 1 / 0.002 s = 500 req/s. That is why "how many VUs?" and "how many requests per second?" are different questions — the same VUs produce less throughput when the server gets slower.

Q6. Between 10 and 50 VUs your throughput stays at ~20,000 req/s but p99 grows from 1 ms to 5 ms. What happened?

  • A. The network card failed
  • B. k6 has a bug with more than 10 VUs
  • C. The CPU was already saturated at 10 VUs: extra VUs only wait in queues, so latency grows while throughput stays flat
  • D. Nginx started caching responses
Answer

C — Saturation: queueing replaces work.

Once the bottleneck resource is fully busy, throughput cannot grow; extra concurrency turns into waiting time (Little's Law again: 5× the VUs at the same λ → 5× the latency). Recognizing this "flat throughput, rising latency" signature is the core skill of lab 2.

Q7. Why is p99 more useful than the average latency to describe user experience?

  • A. The average is harder to compute
  • B. The average hides the slow tail: 1% of requests (and many more users, who make many requests per page) can be much slower than the mean
  • C. p99 is always lower than the average
  • D. k6 does not report averages
Answer

B — Averages hide the tail.

A page that triggers 20 requests hits the p99 tail in about 1 − 0.99²⁰ ≈ 18% of page loads. Averages mix a few very slow requests with many fast ones and look fine while users suffer. Class 2 (percentiles) explores this in depth.

Q8. Your laptop has 8 cores, but Docker Desktop is configured with 2 CPUs. What happens to your load-test results?

  • A. Nothing, Docker always uses every core
  • B. Every container shares those 2 CPUs: services, databases and (if containerized) k6 compete, and the measured capacity is lower than the machine could give
  • C. Only Java containers are affected
  • D. k6 automatically compensates for the limit
Answer

B — The Docker VM is your real machine.

On macOS and Windows, containers run inside a VM with the resources set in Docker Desktop. Record those numbers in results/lab0.md: without them, nobody (including you, three weeks later) can compare measurements.

Q9. Why should the repository be tagged at the end of each lab (git tag lab4)?

  • A. GitHub requires tags for private repositories
  • B. Tags make the build faster
  • C. To have a named, reproducible state: git diff lab4 lab5 shows what changed when a later lab breaks something, and a measurement can always be tied to the code that produced it
  • D. Tags are needed to run Docker Compose
Answer

C — Reproducibility and diffs.

A measurement without the exact code and configuration that produced it is an anecdote. Tags are the cheapest way to tie results to versions — the same idea behind immutable image tags and GitOps in lab 11.

Q10. Which file should never be committed to your BoxOffice repository?

  • A. docker-compose.yaml
  • B. load/hello.js
  • C. .env with real passwords or API keys
  • D. results/lab0.md
Answer

C — Secrets stay out of Git.

Anything pushed to Git should be considered public forever (history keeps it even after deletion). The lab defaults (boxoffice/boxoffice) are throwaway local values; real secrets go to a secrets manager, a topic of class 11.

items.title: Index
items.text:
In this lab

  • Build catalog, the first BoxOffice service: a REST API for events and venues with Spring Boot 4, PostgreSQL, Flyway and an OpenAPI document.
  • Package it as a container image and run it with its database using Docker Compose.
  • Measure it with a k6 smoke test: the latency of each endpoint when the service is not under load.

Every ticketing site starts with the same page: what is on, where, and when? In BoxOffice that is the job of catalog. It is the most read-heavy service of the system — during a flash sale, millions of fans refresh the event page while only a handful of administrators ever change it — and that is why it will be the guinea pig for load balancing (lab 3), caching (lab 5) and indexing (lab 6). Today you build the simplest version that works, the monolith-first step of the scaling journey.

Catch up

Skipped or broke lab 0? Download boxoffice-after-lab-0.zip, unzip it and cd boxoffice (then git init -b main if you want version control). Every file of this lab is shown in full on the next pages, and the same files are in this lab's code/ folder (for example code/docker-compose.yaml).

items.title: What you will build
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Fan
    participant C as catalog :8082<br/>(Spring Boot)
    participant DB as db :5432<br/>(PostgreSQL, schema catalog)
    Fan->>C: GET /catalog/events?city=Recife
    C->>DB: SELECT events JOIN venues WHERE city = ? ORDER BY starts_at LIMIT 20
    DB-->>C: 20 rows
    C->>DB: SELECT count(*) ... (total for the page links)
    DB-->>C: 20001
    C-->>Fan: 200 {items: [...], page: 0, totalItems: 20001}

The service follows a classic three-layer structure — controller (HTTP, validation, DTOs) → service (business rules, transactions) → repository (SQL through JPA) — with one rule that matters for everything that follows: the API never exposes the database entities, only records (EventOut, VenueOut) that you control.

Method Path Body Answer GET /catalog/events?city=&page=&size= — 200 page of upcoming events, soonest first GET /catalog/events/{id} — 200 event with its venue, or 404 POST /catalog/events EventIn 201 + Location header, or 400 PUT /catalog/events/{id} EventIn 200, 400 or 404 DELETE /catalog/events/{id} — 204 or 404 GET /catalog/venues · /catalog/venues/{id} — 200 venues POST /catalog/venues VenueIn 201 GET /actuator/health · /catalog/openapi · /swagger-ui.html — health, OpenAPI document, interactive docs

The database starts with 50 venues in 10 cities and 200,000 events (one per hour from March 2027), generated by a Flyway migration1. Event 1 is the course's flash-sale show: BoxOffice Fest — Stadium Night, at a 60,000-seat stadium. A realistic volume of data is deliberate: a query that is instant on 10 rows can take tens of milliseconds on 200,000, and that is exactly what you will measure.

Theory connection

  • Class 5, Compute & services: stateless app servers, API styles (REST, resources, status codes, versioning).
  • Class 6, Databases: relational data models, schemas and migrations.

items.title: Measure it: the unloaded baseline
items.text:
Before asking "how much load can it take?" (lab 2), record how fast each endpoint is with a single user. That is the service time: the best latency you will ever see, and the reference for every comparison later.

Save the smoke test as load/smoke.js:

load/smoke.js
// Lab 1: smoke test. One user, 30 seconds: does every endpoint answer, and how fast
// when the service is NOT under load?   k6 run load/smoke.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

const BASE_URL = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:8082';
const CITIES = ['São Paulo', 'Rio de Janeiro', 'Belo Horizonte', 'Porto Alegre', 'Curitiba',
  'Salvador', 'Recife', 'Fortaleza', 'Brasília', 'Manaus'];

export const options = {
  vus: 1,
  duration: '30s',
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'med', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate==0'],
    // one threshold per endpoint makes k6 print one latency line per endpoint
    'http_req_duration{name:GET /catalog/events/{id}}': ['p(95)<200'],
    'http_req_duration{name:GET /catalog/events?city}': ['p(95)<500'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const id = 1 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 200000);
  const detail = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/catalog/events/${id}`,
    { tags: { name: 'GET /catalog/events/{id}' } });
  check(detail, { 'detail is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  const city = CITIES[Math.floor(Math.random() * CITIES.length)];
  const list = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/catalog/events?city=${encodeURIComponent(city)}&page=0&size=20`,
    { tags: { name: 'GET /catalog/events?city' } });
  check(list, {
    'list is 200': (r) => r.status === 200,
    'list has 20 items': (r) => r.json('items').length === 20,
  });

  sleep(0.5);   // think time: a real user does not click non-stop
}

With the stack running (step 3):

k6 run load/smoke.js █ THRESHOLDS http_req_duration{name:GET /catalog/events?city} ✓ 'p(95)<500' p(95)=42.18ms http_req_duration{name:GET /catalog/events/{id}} ✓ 'p(95)<200' p(95)=11.15ms http_req_failed ✓ 'rate==0' rate=0.00% █ TOTAL RESULTS ✓ detail is 200 ✓ list is 200 ✓ list has 20 items http_req_duration.....................: avg=19.33ms med=23.94ms p(95)=37.74ms p(99)=72.02ms max=87.26ms { name:GET /catalog/events?city }...: avg=32.04ms med=30.17ms p(95)=42.18ms p(99)=71.38ms max=87.26ms { name:GET /catalog/events/{id} }...: avg=6.62ms med=4.69ms p(95)=11.15ms p(99)=40.19ms max=73.71ms http_reqs.............................: 112 3.678382/s

The numbers above come from a run on a laptop; yours will differ. Two things should stand out anyway: the listing is several times slower than the detail (it joins two tables, sorts and counts thousands of rows; the detail is a primary-key lookup), and p99 is far from the median even with a single user (JIT compilation, garbage collection, the first connections of the pool).

Record the results in results/lab1.md:

results/lab1.md
# Lab 1 — catalog, unloaded (1 VU, 30 s)

| Endpoint                     | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | max (ms) |
|------------------------------|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|
| GET /catalog/events/{id}     |          |          |          |          |
| GET /catalog/events?city=... |          |          |          |          |

- Startup time ("Started CatalogApplication in ... seconds"): ____ s
- Image size (`docker image ls boxoffice-catalog`): ____ MB
- Seed time (Flyway "Successfully applied 2 migrations ... execution time"): ____ s
- Why is the listing slower than the detail? ____
Think first: run the smoke test twice. Why is the second run faster?

The first requests after a start hit a cold JVM (classes loading, the JIT still interpreting bytecode), an empty connection pool and PostgreSQL pages not yet in its buffer cache. After a few hundred requests everything is warm. Load tests therefore always have a warm-up, and you should never compare a cold run with a warm one.

If your numbers differ

Absolute values depend on your CPU, on the memory given to Docker and on what else is running (close the browser tabs and IDEs you do not need). What must hold everywhere: every check passes, the detail is several times faster than the listing, and the second run is faster than the first. If the detail p95 is above ~100 ms with one user, Docker is probably short of CPU or memory (docker stats).

  • load/smoke.js passes all thresholds; results/lab1.md is filled in.
  • Repository tagged lab1; quiz answered.

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

Q1. Why does catalog return EventOut records instead of the Event JPA entity?

  • A. Records serialize faster than classes
  • B. The API contract stays independent of the table: new columns do not leak, and lazy associations are never serialized outside a transaction
  • C. Spring MVC cannot serialize entities
  • D. Entities cannot have an id field
Answer

B — Decouple the contract from the storage.

An entity is a mapping of a table; a DTO is a promise to clients. If they are the same object, every schema change is an API change, and a lazy venue touched by Jackson after the transaction ends throws LazyInitializationException.

Q2. Listing 20 events without join fetch e.venue runs how many SQL queries (ignoring the count)?

  • A. 1
  • B. 2
  • C. 20
  • D. 21
Answer

D — 21: the N+1 problem.

One query loads the 20 events; then each event.getVenue() triggers one more query. With join fetch it becomes one JOIN. Under load, 21 round trips per request multiply the time each request holds a pooled connection.

Q3. A teammate edits V2__seed_catalog.sql, which already ran on everyone's machine, to fix a typo. What happens at the next startup?

  • A. Flyway applies the new version of V2 automatically
  • B. Flyway detects a checksum mismatch and the service fails to start
  • C. Nothing: Flyway ignores files that already ran
  • D. Hibernate fixes the data with ddl-auto
Answer

B — Checksum mismatch, startup fails.

Flyway stores a checksum of every applied migration. Applied migrations are history and must not change; a fix goes into a new migration (V3__fix_typo.sql). This is what makes every environment converge to the same schema.

Q4. What does spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto: validate do?

  • A. Creates the tables that are missing
  • B. Drops and recreates the schema at every start
  • C. Checks that the entities match the existing tables and fails if they do not, without changing anything
  • D. Validates the JSON of incoming requests
Answer

C — Check, never change.

The schema has a single owner: Flyway. Hibernate only verifies that the mapping is consistent, which catches a missing migration at startup instead of at the first query in production.

Q5. A client calls GET /catalog/events?size=5000. What does the service answer, and why is that a design decision?

  • A. 200 with 5,000 events — the client asked for them
  • B. 400, because size has @Max(50): every collection must be bounded, or one request can load the whole table
  • C. 404, because page 5,000 does not exist
  • D. 500, because Hibernate cannot load more than 50 rows
Answer

B — 400: bounded collections.

An unbounded page size is a denial-of-service vector you ship yourself. The limit belongs to the contract, enforced at the edge of the service, before any query runs.

Q6. In the smoke test, the listing (?city=) is ~5–10× slower than the detail (/{id}). What is the main reason?

  • A. JSON serialization of 20 items
  • B. The listing joins two tables, filters, sorts and counts thousands of rows without an index; the detail is a primary-key lookup
  • C. The listing uses HTTP/1.0
  • D. The city name has an accent
Answer

B — Work done in the database.

The detail touches one row through the primary-key index. The listing scans the events of a whole city twice (page + count(*)) and sorts them. Lab 6 shows the EXPLAIN and fixes it with an index; lab 5 hides it with a cache.

Q7. Why does the catalog container have deploy.resources.limits.cpus: "1.0"?

  • A. Spring Boot cannot use more than one core
  • B. To make each replica a small, fixed-size "server", so measurements are comparable and adding replicas (lab 3) shows a visible effect
  • C. Docker requires a CPU limit for Java images
  • D. To make the build faster
Answer

B — A fixed unit of capacity.

Without a limit, one container can use every core of your laptop, and scaling out would show no gain. Real servers and pods have fixed sizes too; capacity planning is "how many units of this size?".

Q8. Why use a multi-stage Dockerfile?

  • A. It is the only way to build Java images
  • B. The final image has only the JRE and the jar: smaller, faster to pull, and without build tools that enlarge the attack surface
  • C. Multi-stage images start faster because they skip the JIT
  • D. It makes the image run as root
Answer

B — Small runtime image, build tools left behind.

The build stage (JDK + Maven, hundreds of MB) is discarded. Smaller images mean faster deployments and autoscaling (lab 10), and fewer packages to patch.

Q9. catalog starts before PostgreSQL is ready and crashes in Flyway. Which Compose setting fixes it?

  • A. restart: always on db
  • B. depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy with a healthcheck (pg_isready) on db
  • C. links: - db
  • D. Increasing the memory limit of catalog
Answer

B — Wait for health, not for start.

A plain depends_on only waits until the container starts; PostgreSQL needs a few more seconds to accept connections. The healthcheck turns "started" into "ready". In Kubernetes (lab 10) the same idea becomes readiness probes.

Q10. The smoke test shows p50 = 5 ms and p99 = 40 ms for the detail with one user. Which explanation is the most plausible?

  • A. The network between k6 and the container drops packets
  • B. Occasional pauses that do not depend on load: JIT compilation, garbage collection, opening pooled connections, cold database pages
  • C. The database is overloaded
  • D. k6 measures p99 incorrectly
Answer

B — Tail latency exists even without load.

With one user there is no queueing, so the tail comes from the runtime itself. That is why load tests have a warm-up period and why you always look at percentiles, not only at the median.

items.title: Index
items.text: The first step designs the contract of catalog: which resources it exposes, which requests it accepts and what it answers. In an interview this is step 3 of the framework (API and data model); in a real team it is what other teams code against, so it deserves care before any SQL exists.

items.title: 1. Create the project
items.text:
Create the folder services/catalog in your repository with the standard Maven layout:

mkdir -p services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog
mkdir -p services/catalog/src/main/resources/db/migration

Then add the pom.xml:

services/catalog/pom.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>4.1.1</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>

    <groupId>boxoffice</groupId>
    <artifactId>catalog</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    <name>catalog</name>
    <description>BoxOffice catalog: events and venues</description>

    <properties>
        <java.version>21</java.version>
        <springdoc.version>3.1.1</springdoc.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- REST API (Spring MVC on Tomcat) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- Bean Validation (@NotBlank, @Positive, ...) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- JPA + Hibernate -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- health, metrics -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- schema migrations (Boot 4: the starter brings the auto-configuration) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-flyway</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
            <artifactId>flyway-database-postgresql</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
            <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
            <scope>runtime</scope>
        </dependency>
        <!-- OpenAPI document + Swagger UI -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
            <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>
            <version>${springdoc.version}</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <finalName>app</finalName>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
Dependency Why spring-boot-starter-webmvc Spring MVC + embedded Tomcat: one thread per in-flight request (you will count them in lab 2) spring-boot-starter-validation Bean Validation annotations on records and parameters spring-boot-starter-data-jpa JPA/Hibernate, repositories, transactions, the HikariCP connection pool spring-boot-starter-actuator /actuator/health (used by Compose, Nginx and Kubernetes) and /actuator/metrics spring-boot-starter-flyway + flyway-database-postgresql versioned schema migrations (in Spring Boot 4 each technology has its own starter and auto-configuration module; flyway-core alone is no longer picked up) postgresql JDBC driver springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui (3.x) generates the OpenAPI document from the controllers, plus Swagger UI (springdoc 3 is the line for Spring Boot 4)

Prefer a generator?

start.spring.io produces the same skeleton (Maven, Java 21, the dependencies above). Choose Spring Boot 4.1.x, then set the group to boxoffice. The labs are written and tested with Spring Boot 4.1.1 and Spring Cloud 2025.1.3; a newer 4.1.x patch release works the same way.

The entry point is the usual one-liner:

services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/CatalogApplication.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class CatalogApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(CatalogApplication.class, args);
    }
}

items.title: 2. Design the resources
items.text:
Two resources, each a noun with a collection URL and an item URL, all under the service prefix /catalog (see the conventions of lab 0):

classDiagram
    class Venue {
        Long id
        String name
        String city
        int capacity
    }
    class Event {
        Long id
        String title
        Category category
        OffsetDateTime startsAt
        BigDecimal priceFrom
    }
    class Category {
        <<enumeration>>
        CONCERT
        SPORTS
        FESTIVAL
        THEATER
    }
    Event "*" --> "1" Venue : takes place at
    Event --> Category
Decision Choice Why Identifiers BIGINT generated by the database simple, compact, easy to pick at random in k6 (1..200000) Collections paginated (page, size ≤ 50) an unbounded GET /events on 200,000 rows would be a self-inflicted outage Default listing upcoming events, soonest first it is what the home page shows; past events are not for sale Money BigDecimal / NUMERIC(10,2) never double for prices Time OffsetDateTime / TIMESTAMPTZ, ISO-8601 in JSON events happen in different time zones Errors RFC 9457 application/problem+json one machine-readable error shape for every service Create 201 Created + Location: /catalog/events/{id} the client learns where the new resource lives

items.title: 3. Request and response records
items.text:
The API never returns JPA entities. Records are immutable, have no persistence annotations and make the JSON shape explicit — when the table changes, the API does not change by accident.

EventInEventOutVenueInVenueOutPageOutCategory services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/EventIn.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotNull;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.PositiveOrZero;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Size;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.OffsetDateTime;

/** What a client sends to create or update an event. */
public record EventIn(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 200) String title,
        @NotNull Category category,
        @NotNull Long venueId,
        @NotNull OffsetDateTime startsAt,
        @NotNull @PositiveOrZero BigDecimal priceFrom) {
}
services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/EventOut.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.OffsetDateTime;

/** What the API returns: never the JPA entity itself. */
public record EventOut(
        Long id,
        String title,
        Category category,
        OffsetDateTime startsAt,
        BigDecimal priceFrom,
        VenueOut venue) {

    static EventOut of(Event e) {
        return new EventOut(e.getId(), e.getTitle(), e.getCategory(), e.getStartsAt(),
                e.getPriceFrom(), VenueOut.of(e.getVenue()));
    }
}
services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/VenueIn.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Positive;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Size;

public record VenueIn(
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 200) String name,
        @NotBlank @Size(max = 100) String city,
        @Positive int capacity) {
}
services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/VenueOut.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

public record VenueOut(Long id, String name, String city, int capacity) {

    static VenueOut of(Venue v) {
        return new VenueOut(v.getId(), v.getName(), v.getCity(), v.getCapacity());
    }
}
services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/PageOut.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.data.domain.Page;

/** A stable JSON shape for paged results (Spring's Page is not meant to be serialized). */
public record PageOut<T>(List<T> items, int page, int size, long totalItems, int totalPages) {

    static <T> PageOut<T> of(Page<T> p) {
        return new PageOut<>(p.getContent(), p.getNumber(), p.getSize(), p.getTotalElements(), p.getTotalPages());
    }
}
services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/Category.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

public enum Category {
    CONCERT, SPORTS, FESTIVAL, THEATER
}

All of them live in src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/. The static factories EventOut.of(Event) and VenueOut.of(Venue) are the only place where an entity becomes a DTO.

items.title: 4. Controllers
items.text:
Controllers only translate HTTP into method calls: they validate the input, call the service and choose the status code. No SQL, no business rule.

services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/EventController.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Max;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Min;
import java.net.URI;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.DeleteMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PutMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ResponseStatus;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/catalog/events")
public class EventController {

    private final CatalogService service;

    public EventController(CatalogService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }

    @GetMapping
    public PageOut<EventOut> list(
            @RequestParam(required = false) String city,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") @Min(0) int page,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") @Min(1) @Max(50) int size) {
        return service.upcomingEvents(city, page, size);
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public EventOut get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return service.findEvent(id);
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<EventOut> create(@Valid @RequestBody EventIn in) {
        var out = service.createEvent(in);
        return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/catalog/events/" + out.id())).body(out);
    }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public EventOut update(@PathVariable Long id, @Valid @RequestBody EventIn in) {
        return service.updateEvent(id, in);
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
    public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
        service.deleteEvent(id);
    }
}
services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/VenueController.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import java.net.URI;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/catalog/venues")
public class VenueController {

    private final CatalogService service;

    public VenueController(CatalogService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }

    @GetMapping
    public List<VenueOut> list() {
        return service.allVenues();
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public VenueOut get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return service.findVenue(id);
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<VenueOut> create(@Valid @RequestBody VenueIn in) {
        var out = service.createVenue(in);
        return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/catalog/venues/" + out.id())).body(out);
    }
}

How validation works here:

  • @Valid @RequestBody EventIn in checks the annotations of the record (@NotBlank, @NotNull, @PositiveOrZero) and answers 400 before the method runs.
  • @Min(0) / @Max(50) on page and size use Spring's built-in method validation (Spring Framework 6.1+): ?size=5000 is rejected with 400 instead of loading 5,000 rows.
  • With spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled: true (next step), both cases come back as application/problem+json.

What a client sees

GET /catalog/events?size=500 HTTP/1.1

HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"detail":"Validation failure","instance":"/catalog/events",
 "status":400,"title":"Bad Request"}

In the interview

When you sketch the API, say three things out loud: the resources and verbs (GET /events?city=&page=), the pagination strategy (offset now; keyset — WHERE starts_at > :last — when users scroll deep, because OFFSET 100000 still reads 100,000 rows) and the error model. Interviewers listen for whether you bound every collection.

Pitfalls

  • Returning the entity: a lazy venue serialized outside a transaction throws LazyInitializationException, or worse, a new column leaks to clients (a password hash, a cost price).
  • Unbounded lists: every collection endpoint needs a maximum page size.
  • 200 for everything: status codes are part of the contract; proxies, caches and k6 checks rely on them.

The controllers depend on CatalogService, which you write in the next step together with the entities and the database: 2. Persistence.

items.title: Index
items.text:
The last step packages catalog as an image and runs it next to PostgreSQL with Docker Compose. From now on, "running BoxOffice" always means one command: docker compose up.

flowchart LR
    term(["your terminal<br/>curl · k6"]) -->|localhost:8082| catalog
    subgraph compose["docker compose project: boxoffice"]
        catalog["catalog<br/>eclipse-temurin:21-jre<br/>1 CPU · 768 MB"] -->|db:5432| db[("db<br/>postgres:17")]
        db --- vol[("volume db-data")]
    end

items.title: 1. Dockerfile
items.text:
A multi-stage build: the first stage has the JDK and Maven and compiles the jar; the second has only a JRE and the jar. The final image is smaller, has no compiler and does not need Maven on the machine that builds it.

services/catalog/Dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ---- build stage: compile with Maven inside a JDK image -------------------
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY pom.xml .
COPY src ./src
# the cache mount keeps ~/.m2 between builds: dependencies are downloaded once
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q package -DskipTests

# ---- runtime stage: only a JRE and the jar --------------------------------
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
COPY --from=build /src/target/app.jar app.jar
USER app
EXPOSE 8082
# use up to 75% of the container's memory limit for the heap
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75", "-jar", "app.jar"]
services/catalog/.dockerignore
target/
.idea/
.vscode/
*.iml
Line Why --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 BuildKit keeps the Maven repository between builds: the first build downloads the dependencies (a few minutes), the next ones take seconds useradd + USER app the process does not run as root inside the container -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 the JVM sizes its heap from the container memory limit, not from your laptop's RAM .dockerignore a local target/ folder is never sent to the build

items.title: 2. docker-compose.yaml
items.text:
Create it at the root of the repository:

docker-compose.yaml
name: boxoffice

services:

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  catalog:
    build: ./services/catalog
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
      DB_PORT: 5432
      DB_NAME: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
      DB_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
      DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
      DB_POOL_SIZE: ${DB_POOL_SIZE:-10}  # HikariCP pool size (lab 2 experiments with it)
    ports:
      - "8082:8082"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy   # wait until PostgreSQL accepts connections
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"                # one core per replica: makes scaling visible in lab 3
          memory: 768M
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -qO- http://localhost:8082/actuator/health/readiness || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 40s
      retries: 3

volumes:
  db-data:
Setting Why name: boxoffice fixed project name: containers are boxoffice-db-1, boxoffice-catalog-1, … on every machine db.healthcheck + depends_on: condition: service_healthy catalog starts only when PostgreSQL accepts connections; otherwise Flyway fails at startup volumes: db-data the data survives docker compose down; down -v erases it deploy.resources.limits 1 CPU and 768 MB per catalog: a fixed, small "server", so that measurements are comparable and scaling out in lab 3 is visible catalog.healthcheck Compose marks the container healthy only when /actuator/health/readiness answers (the JRE image has wget, not curl)

items.title: 3. Run it
items.text:
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f catalog
docker compose up --build -d Image boxoffice-catalog Built Container boxoffice-db-1 Healthy Container boxoffice-catalog-1 Starteddocker compose logs catalog | grep -E "Migrating|Successfully|Started"Migrating schema "catalog" to version "1 - create catalog"Migrating schema "catalog" to version "2 - seed catalog"Successfully applied 2 migrations to schema "catalog", now at version v2 (execution time 00:01.204s)Started CatalogApplication in 10.4 seconds (process running for 11.178)

Now call the API:

curl -s localhost:8082/catalog/events/1 | jq{ "id": 1, "title": "BoxOffice Fest — Stadium Night", "category": "FESTIVAL", "startsAt": "2027-06-12T23:00:00Z", "priceFrom": 250.00, "venue": { "id": 1, "name": "Stadium São Paulo", "city": "São Paulo", "capacity": 60000 }}curl -s "localhost:8082/catalog/events?city=Recife&size=2" | jq -c '{page, totalItems, first: .items[0].title}'{"page":0,"totalItems":20000,"first":"Concert #12"}curl -s localhost:8082/catalog/events/999999{"detail":"event 999999 not found","instance":"/catalog/events/999999","status":404,"title":"Not Found"}

Create a venue and an event, then break the rules on purpose:

# 201 Created + Location header
curl -i -X POST localhost:8082/catalog/venues -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Arena Insper","city":"São Paulo","capacity":800}'

curl -i -X POST localhost:8082/catalog/events -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Systems Rock","category":"CONCERT","venueId":51,"startsAt":"2027-09-01T21:00:00-03:00","priceFrom":120}'

# 400: missing title and negative price
curl -s -X POST localhost:8082/catalog/events -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"category":"CONCERT","venueId":1,"startsAt":"2027-09-01T21:00:00-03:00","priceFrom":-1}' | jq

# 400: page size above the maximum
curl -s "localhost:8082/catalog/events?size=500" | jq

items.title: 4. Look inside
items.text:
# the tables and the Flyway history, from inside the db container
docker compose exec db psql -U boxoffice -c '\dt catalog.*'
docker compose exec db psql -U boxoffice -c 'SELECT version, description, success FROM catalog.flyway_schema_history'

# how the listing query runs (lab 6 comes back to this)
docker compose exec db psql -U boxoffice -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT e.* FROM catalog.events e JOIN catalog.venues v ON v.id = e.venue_id WHERE v.city = 'Recife' AND e.starts_at >= now() ORDER BY e.starts_at LIMIT 20"

# health, metrics and the OpenAPI document
curl -s localhost:8082/actuator/health | jq
curl -s localhost:8082/actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.max | jq '.measurements[0].value'
curl -s localhost:8082/catalog/openapi | jq '.paths | keys'

Open http://localhost:8082/swagger-ui.html for interactive documentation generated from your controllers — the same OpenAPI document can generate clients in other languages.

items.title: 5. Everyday commands
items.text:
Command Effect docker compose up --build -d rebuild what changed and start everything in the background docker compose logs -f catalog follow one service's logs docker compose restart catalog restart without rebuilding docker compose down stop and remove containers (data kept in db-data) docker compose down -v …and erase the database volume (Flyway seeds again on the next start) docker stats live CPU and memory per container — keep it open during load tests

Pitfalls

  • Port 5432 already allocated: a local PostgreSQL is running; stop it or map "15432:5432".
  • Connection refused from catalog to localhost:5432: inside a container, the database is db, not localhost — check DB_HOST.
  • Changed a migration that already ran → Validate failed: Migrations have failed validation. Restore the file and add a new version, or (on your laptop only) docker compose down -v.
  • Apple Silicon / ARM: all images used in the labs are multi-architecture; do not add platform: linux/amd64.

Back to the lab overview to measure it.

items.title: Index
items.text:
This step connects the API to PostgreSQL: entities map the tables, repositories hold the queries, the service defines the transactions and Flyway creates and seeds the schema. Each service owns one schema — catalog here — and nothing else touches it.

flowchart LR
    ctl["EventController<br/>VenueController"] --> svc["CatalogService<br/>@Transactional"]
    svc --> repo["EventRepository<br/>VenueRepository"]
    repo --> jpa["Hibernate (JPA)"]
    jpa --> pool["HikariCP<br/>10 connections"]
    pool --> db[("PostgreSQL<br/>schema catalog")]
    fly["Flyway<br/>V1, V2"] -->|at startup| db

Keep the connection pool in mind: every request that touches the database borrows one of its 10 connections for the duration of its transaction. In lab 2 that number turns out to be the ceiling of the whole service.

items.title: 1. Entities
items.text:
An entity is a Java class mapped to a table. These two have no public setters: Event changes only through update(...), so every change goes through one method.

Venue.javaEvent.java services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/Venue.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import jakarta.persistence.Column;
import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;

@Entity
@Table(name = "venues", schema = "catalog")
public class Venue {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String city;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private int capacity;

    protected Venue() {
        // required by JPA
    }

    public Venue(String name, String city, int capacity) {
        this.name = name;
        this.city = city;
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public String getCity() { return city; }
    public int getCapacity() { return capacity; }
}
services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/Event.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import jakarta.persistence.Column;
import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.EnumType;
import jakarta.persistence.Enumerated;
import jakarta.persistence.FetchType;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.JoinColumn;
import jakarta.persistence.ManyToOne;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.OffsetDateTime;

@Entity
@Table(name = "events", schema = "catalog")
public class Event {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String title;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private Category category;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "venue_id")
    private Venue venue;

    @Column(name = "starts_at", nullable = false)
    private OffsetDateTime startsAt;

    @Column(name = "price_from", nullable = false)
    private BigDecimal priceFrom;

    protected Event() {
        // required by JPA
    }

    public Event(String title, Category category, Venue venue, OffsetDateTime startsAt, BigDecimal priceFrom) {
        update(title, category, venue, startsAt, priceFrom);
    }

    public void update(String title, Category category, Venue venue, OffsetDateTime startsAt, BigDecimal priceFrom) {
        this.title = title;
        this.category = category;
        this.venue = venue;
        this.startsAt = startsAt;
        this.priceFrom = priceFrom;
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public Category getCategory() { return category; }
    public Venue getVenue() { return venue; }
    public OffsetDateTime getStartsAt() { return startsAt; }
    public BigDecimal getPriceFrom() { return priceFrom; }
}
Annotation Meaning @Table(name = "events", schema = "catalog") explicit schema: the table belongs to this service @GeneratedValue(strategy = IDENTITY) the database generates the id (GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY) @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) stores CONCERT, not 0: reordering the enum cannot corrupt data @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) the venue is loaded only when needed — or eagerly with join fetch in a query

items.title: 2. Repositories
items.text:
Spring Data generates the implementation of these interfaces. The custom queries are written in JPQL (queries over entities, not tables):

services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/EventRepository.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import java.time.OffsetDateTime;
import java.util.Optional;
import org.springframework.data.domain.Page;
import org.springframework.data.domain.Pageable;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.Query;

public interface EventRepository extends JpaRepository<Event, Long> {

    // one query: the event and its venue (no lazy-loading surprise later)
    @Query("select e from Event e join fetch e.venue where e.id = :id")
    Optional<Event> findWithVenue(Long id);

    // upcoming events, soonest first; Page also runs the count query
    @Query(value = """
            select e from Event e join fetch e.venue
            where e.startsAt >= :from
            order by e.startsAt, e.id""",
           countQuery = "select count(e) from Event e where e.startsAt >= :from")
    Page<Event> findUpcoming(OffsetDateTime from, Pageable pageable);

    // the same, filtered by the venue's city
    @Query(value = """
            select e from Event e join fetch e.venue v
            where v.city = :city and e.startsAt >= :from
            order by e.startsAt, e.id""",
           countQuery = """
            select count(e) from Event e join e.venue v
            where v.city = :city and e.startsAt >= :from""")
    Page<Event> findUpcomingInCity(String city, OffsetDateTime from, Pageable pageable);
}
services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/VenueRepository.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface VenueRepository extends JpaRepository<Venue, Long> {
}

The N+1 query problem

Without join fetch, listing 20 events runs 1 query for the events and then 20 more, one per venue, when EventOut.of touches event.getVenue(). With join fetch e.venue, it is a single SQL JOIN. N+1 is invisible with one user and devastating under load: 21 round trips instead of 1, each one holding a pooled connection.

A Page<Event> result costs two queries: the page itself (... ORDER BY starts_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET ?) and a count(*) over every matching row, so the client can show "page 1 of 1,001". On 200,000 events without an index, both are full scans — the listing you will measure in lab 2, cache in lab 5 and index in lab 6.

items.title: 3. The service layer
items.text:
CatalogService is where transactions begin and end. Read methods use @Transactional(readOnly = true): Hibernate skips dirty checking, and in lab 6 the same flag routes reads to a replica.

services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/CatalogService.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import java.time.OffsetDateTime;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.data.domain.PageRequest;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import org.springframework.web.server.ResponseStatusException;

@Service
public class CatalogService {

    private final EventRepository events;
    private final VenueRepository venues;

    public CatalogService(EventRepository events, VenueRepository venues) {
        this.events = events;
        this.venues = venues;
    }

    // ---- events -------------------------------------------------------------

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public EventOut findEvent(Long id) {
        return events.findWithVenue(id)
                .map(EventOut::of)
                .orElseThrow(() -> notFound("event", id));
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public PageOut<EventOut> upcomingEvents(String city, int page, int size) {
        var pageable = PageRequest.of(page, size);
        var now = OffsetDateTime.now();
        var result = (city == null || city.isBlank())
                ? events.findUpcoming(now, pageable)
                : events.findUpcomingInCity(city, now, pageable);
        return PageOut.of(result.map(EventOut::of));
    }

    @Transactional
    public EventOut createEvent(EventIn in) {
        var event = new Event(in.title(), in.category(), venue(in.venueId()), in.startsAt(), in.priceFrom());
        return EventOut.of(events.save(event));
    }

    @Transactional
    public EventOut updateEvent(Long id, EventIn in) {
        var event = events.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> notFound("event", id));
        event.update(in.title(), in.category(), venue(in.venueId()), in.startsAt(), in.priceFrom());
        return EventOut.of(event);   // dirty checking: JPA writes the UPDATE at commit
    }

    @Transactional
    public void deleteEvent(Long id) {
        if (!events.existsById(id)) {
            throw notFound("event", id);
        }
        events.deleteById(id);
    }

    // ---- venues -------------------------------------------------------------

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<VenueOut> allVenues() {
        return venues.findAll().stream().map(VenueOut::of).toList();
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public VenueOut findVenue(Long id) {
        return venues.findById(id).map(VenueOut::of).orElseThrow(() -> notFound("venue", id));
    }

    @Transactional
    public VenueOut createVenue(VenueIn in) {
        return VenueOut.of(venues.save(new Venue(in.name(), in.city(), in.capacity())));
    }

    // ---- helpers ------------------------------------------------------------

    private Venue venue(Long id) {
        return venues.findById(id).orElseThrow(() ->
                new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "venue " + id + " does not exist"));
    }

    private static ResponseStatusException notFound(String what, Long id) {
        return new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, what + " " + id + " not found");
    }
}

Business rules that live here:

  • an unknown event or venue id → 404 Not Found;
  • creating or updating an event with a venue that does not exist → 400 Bad Request;
  • updateEvent does not call save: the entity is managed inside the transaction and Hibernate writes the UPDATE at commit (dirty checking).

items.title: 4. Migrations with Flyway
items.text:
The schema is code: versioned SQL files in src/main/resources/db/migration, applied in order, once, at startup. Flyway records what it ran in catalog.flyway_schema_history, so every environment — your laptop, CI, Kubernetes — converges to the same schema.

V1__create_catalog.sqlV2__seed_catalog.sql services/catalog/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_catalog.sql
-- Flyway runs this once, inside the schema "catalog" (spring.flyway.schemas).
CREATE TABLE catalog.venues (
    id        BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name      VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    city      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    capacity  INTEGER      NOT NULL CHECK (capacity > 0)
);

CREATE TABLE catalog.events (
    id          BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    title       VARCHAR(200)  NOT NULL,
    category    VARCHAR(20)   NOT NULL CHECK (category IN ('CONCERT', 'SPORTS', 'FESTIVAL', 'THEATER')),
    venue_id    BIGINT        NOT NULL REFERENCES catalog.venues (id),
    starts_at   TIMESTAMPTZ   NOT NULL,
    price_from  NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price_from >= 0)
);
-- No secondary indexes on purpose: lab 6 measures the listing query before and after adding them.
services/catalog/src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__seed_catalog.sql
-- Demo data: 10 cities x 5 venues, and 200,000 events (one per hour from March 2027).
-- generate_series makes the seed deterministic and fast (a few seconds).
INSERT INTO catalog.venues (name, city, capacity)
SELECT v.kind || ' ' || c.city,
       c.city,
       CASE v.kind WHEN 'Stadium' THEN 60000 WHEN 'Arena' THEN 15000 WHEN 'Hall' THEN 4000
                   WHEN 'Theater' THEN 1200 ELSE 300 END
FROM (VALUES (1, 'São Paulo'), (2, 'Rio de Janeiro'), (3, 'Belo Horizonte'), (4, 'Porto Alegre'),
             (5, 'Curitiba'), (6, 'Salvador'), (7, 'Recife'), (8, 'Fortaleza'), (9, 'Brasília'),
             (10, 'Manaus')) AS c(n, city)
CROSS JOIN (VALUES (1, 'Stadium'), (2, 'Arena'), (3, 'Hall'), (4, 'Theater'), (5, 'Club')) AS v(n, kind)
ORDER BY c.n, v.n;

-- event 1 is the flash-sale show of the course: 60,000 seats at Stadium São Paulo (venue 1)
INSERT INTO catalog.events (title, category, venue_id, starts_at, price_from)
VALUES ('BoxOffice Fest — Stadium Night', 'FESTIVAL', 1, TIMESTAMPTZ '2027-06-12 20:00:00-03', 250.00);

INSERT INTO catalog.events (title, category, venue_id, starts_at, price_from)
SELECT (ARRAY['Concert', 'Match', 'Festival', 'Play'])[1 + g % 4] || ' #' || g,
       (ARRAY['CONCERT', 'SPORTS', 'FESTIVAL', 'THEATER'])[1 + g % 4],
       1 + (g * 7) % 50,
       TIMESTAMPTZ '2027-03-01 20:00:00-03' + g * INTERVAL '1 hour',
       50 + (g % 20) * 25
FROM generate_series(2, 200000) AS g;

ANALYZE catalog.venues;
ANALYZE catalog.events;

Rules of the game:

  • Name: V<version>__<description>.sql (two underscores). Versions only grow.
  • Never edit a migration that already ran somewhere: Flyway checks a checksum and refuses to start. To change the schema, add V3__....
  • ddl-auto: validate makes Hibernate check that the entities match the tables, but never change them: one owner for the schema.
  • The seed uses generate_series: 200,000 rows in about a second, identical on every machine — so everybody's measurements are comparable.

items.title: 5. Configuration
items.text:
services/catalog/src/main/resources/application.yaml
server:
  port: 8082
  tomcat:
    mbeanregistry:
      enabled: true          # exposes tomcat.threads.* metrics (Little's Law in lab 2)

spring:
  application:
    name: catalog
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://${DB_HOST:localhost}:${DB_PORT:5432}/${DB_NAME:boxoffice}
    username: ${DB_USER:boxoffice}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD:boxoffice}
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: ${DB_POOL_SIZE:10}
  flyway:
    schemas: catalog         # Flyway creates the schema and owns it
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate     # Flyway changes the schema; Hibernate only checks it
  mvc:
    problemdetails:
      enabled: true          # errors as RFC 9457 application/problem+json

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, info, metrics
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true        # /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness

springdoc:
  api-docs:
    path: /catalog/openapi   # OpenAPI document under the service prefix (Swagger UI: /swagger-ui.html)
Property Why ${DB_HOST:localhost} … the connection comes from the environment variables of lab 0; the defaults work from your IDE hikari.maximum-pool-size: ${DB_POOL_SIZE:10} the pool size, configurable without rebuilding — you will change it in lab 2 flyway.schemas: catalog Flyway creates the schema and keeps its history table there open-in-view: false no lazy loading during JSON serialization: the transaction ends in the service tomcat.mbeanregistry.enabled publishes tomcat.threads.busy, used in lab 2 health.probes.enabled /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness, used by Compose now and Kubernetes in lab 10 Think first: why does the count(*) query matter for performance?

It reads every matching row (20,000 per city) just to produce one number, on every page request. Options: cache it (lab 5), estimate it, drop it and return only "has next page" (Spring's Slice), or make it cheap with an index (lab 6). Many large sites show "1,000+ results" for exactly this reason.

In the interview

Name the access patterns before the tables: "the home page lists upcoming events by city, sorted by date, 20 at a time; the event page reads one event by id". The schema and, later, the indexes follow from those queries — not the other way around.

items.title: 6. Checkpoint: does it compile?
items.text:
If you have JDK 21 and Maven installed (lab 0), compile the service now, before Docker enters the picture:

cd services/catalog
mvn -B -DskipTests package
cd ../..

You should see, at the end:

[INFO] Building catalog 1.0.0
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
[INFO] Total time:  4.142 s

and a services/catalog/target/app.jar of about 60 MB (the application plus all its libraries). A COMPILATION ERROR names the file and line: compare that file with the full listing above. The service cannot run yet — it needs PostgreSQL, which the next step provides.

items.title: 10. Kubernetes
items.text:
Goal

Run BoxOffice on a real Kubernetes cluster on your laptop. Create a three-node kind cluster, install an Ingress controller (Traefik) and metrics-server, deploy db, redis and catalog with Kustomize — probes, resource requests and limits, graceful shutdown — and let a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scale catalog under a k6 ramp. Measure how fast capacity follows load, how many requests a rolling update loses, and how long self-healing takes.

In lab 3 you scaled catalog by editing docker-compose.yaml and restarting; in lab 9 you watched a service fall over and had to restart it by hand. At 10:00 on sale day nobody should be editing YAML or restarting containers. Kubernetes turns both into control loops: you declare the desired state — "at least two ready replicas, more when CPU passes 60%" — and controllers keep reality there, every few seconds, forever. This lab is the hands-on side of the cloud-native class.
