items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Objects and controllers
items.text:
Q1. You run kubectl delete pod catalog-8685666c5-5bv8t. A few seconds later a new catalog pod exists. Who created it?

  • A. kubectl, which recreates deleted pods automatically
  • B. The ReplicaSet owned by the catalog Deployment: its controller saw 1 of 2 desired pods and created another
  • C. The HPA
  • D. The kubelet of the node where the pod ran
Answer

B — a controller reconciling desired and actual state.

A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, and a ReplicaSet keeps the number of pods matching its selector equal to replicas. Deleting a pod changes the actual state; the controller's loop notices and acts. This is the core idea of Kubernetes: declare the desired state, let control loops converge to it.

Q2. Why is PostgreSQL a StatefulSet with a volumeClaimTemplates section, while catalog is a Deployment?

  • A. StatefulSets are faster
  • B. The database needs a stable identity (db-0) and its own persistent volume that survives pod restarts and rescheduling; catalog pods are interchangeable and keep no state
  • C. Deployments cannot use environment variables from Secrets
  • D. Only StatefulSets can have readiness probes
Answer

B — stable identity and per-replica storage.

Stateless pods can be killed and recreated anywhere: any replica can serve any request. A database's data must outlive its pod, and each replica (primary, replicas) has its own data and name. For production databases, managed services or operators (CloudNativePG, for instance) add backups, failover and upgrades on top.

Q3. The secretGenerator creates db-credentials-c677754gbf instead of db-credentials. What is the benefit of the hash suffix?

  • A. It encrypts the Secret
  • B. Changing the content produces a new name, and every reference is rewritten: the pods that use it are rolled out with the new values instead of keeping stale ones
  • C. It prevents other namespaces from reading the Secret
  • D. It is required by the Kubernetes API
Answer

B — configuration changes trigger rollouts.

Environment variables from a Secret are read only when a container starts. If the Secret changed in place, running pods would keep the old password until some unrelated restart. A new name changes the pod template, which the Deployment rolls out. (Note: a base64-encoded Secret in Git is not secret; real projects use a secrets manager or sealed/encrypted secrets.)

items.title: Probes and graceful shutdown
items.text:
Q4. A team puts a database check in catalog's liveness probe. During a 20-second database blip, what happens?

  • A. Nothing; liveness only matters at startup
  • B. Every catalog pod fails liveness and Kubernetes restarts all of them, turning a 20-second blip into minutes of outage while JVMs restart
  • C. The pods are removed from the Service until the database returns, then added back
  • D. The HPA adds pods
Answer

B — a dependency in liveness causes mass restarts.

Liveness means "this process is broken beyond repair, restart it". A database blip is not fixed by restarting catalog, and restarting all replicas at once makes things worse. Readiness ("do not send me traffic now") is the right place for conditions that should temporarily remove a pod — and even there, a shared dependency would remove all pods; often it is better to stay ready and fail individual requests fast.

Q5. What does the startupProbe (failure threshold 60, period 5 s) protect against?

  • A. Slow requests
  • B. The liveness probe killing a JVM that is still starting — here the first start also runs Flyway migrations — by disabling the other probes for up to 5 minutes until the app reports it has started
  • C. Pods starting on the wrong node
  • D. Images that are too large
Answer

B — slow starts are not failures.

Without a startup probe, the liveness probe would start checking immediately and restart the container before it finished starting — a crash loop caused by the probe itself. In this lab the first version (30 × 5 s) was too short on a busy laptop: the pod was killed in the middle of the migrations.

Q6. During a rolling update, why do readinessProbe and a preStop sleep of 5 s reduce failed requests?

  • A. They make the JVM start faster
  • B. Readiness keeps a new pod out of the Service until it can serve; the preStop pause keeps an old pod serving while endpoint removal propagates to Traefik and the node proxies, before SIGTERM makes it stop accepting connections
  • C. They disable the HPA during the rollout
  • D. They increase maxSurge
Answer

B — both ends of the pod's life need coordination.

Endpoint removal and the termination signal happen in parallel. Without the pause, the JVM can close its listener while routers still send it requests (connection refused). Without readiness, traffic reaches a container that is not listening yet. With maxUnavailable: 0 as well, capacity never drops during the rollout.

items.title: Autoscaling
items.text:
Q7. catalog requests cpu: 250m. The HPA target is 60%. Two pods use 375m each. How many replicas does the HPA want?

  • A. 2
  • B. 3
  • C. 5
  • D. 8
Answer

C — utilization = 375 / 250 = 150%; desired = ⌈2 × 150 / 60⌉ = 5.

Utilization is relative to the request, not to the limit or the node. The scaleUp policy may cap how fast the HPA gets there (here: at most double, or +2 pods, every 15 s), so 2 → 4 → 5.

Q8. What does scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 120 do?

  • A. Waits 120 s before the first scale-up
  • B. Makes the HPA use the highest replica recommendation of the last 120 s when scaling down, so a short dip in load does not remove pods that will be needed again seconds later
  • C. Deletes pods 120 s after they become ready
  • D. Limits the deployment to 120 pods
Answer

B — damping to avoid flapping.

Load oscillates; without a window, the HPA would scale down at every dip and up again at every peak, paying JVM startup each time. Scale-up has no window here (0 s) because missing capacity costs failed requests, while extra capacity only costs money for two minutes.

Q9. The flash sale starts at 10:00 sharp. Each new catalog pod takes ~40 s to become ready, and the HPA reacts within ~15–30 s. What is the best strategy?

  • A. Rely only on the HPA; it is designed for this
  • B. Pre-scale before 10:00 (raise minReplicas with a scheduled job or by hand), and keep the HPA for the unexpected
  • C. Set maxReplicas to 1 000
  • D. Remove the readiness probe so pods receive traffic sooner
Answer

B — predictable load is scheduled; unpredictable load is reactive.

Reactive autoscaling always lags: detection + decision + startup ≈ a minute or more, during which the existing pods absorb a step change in traffic. For a known event, capacity should be in place before it starts (and the database, which does not autoscale, must be sized for it too).

Q10. The HPA scaled catalog to 8 pods, and now PostgreSQL rejects connections. Why?

  • A. The HPA also scales PostgreSQL down
  • B. Each pod has its own connection pool (e.g. 10 connections): 8 pods open up to 80 connections, exceeding what one database instance allows or handles well — scaling the stateless tier moved the bottleneck to the stateful one
  • C. Traefik limits connections
  • D. The PVC is full
Answer

B — connection fan-in.

Horizontal scaling multiplies connections to shared dependencies. Size max_connections, reduce per-pod pool sizes, or put a pooler (PgBouncer, lab 6) in between. Always ask "what does each new replica cost the dependencies?"

items.title: Ingress
items.text:
Q11. Why did this lab install Traefik instead of ingress-nginx?

  • A. ingress-nginx does not support kind
  • B. The Kubernetes project retired ingress-nginx in March 2026 (archived, no more fixes); Traefik is a maintained controller that supports both the Ingress API and the Gateway API
  • C. Traefik is the only controller that supports pathType: Prefix
  • D. Ingress resources only work with Traefik
Answer

B — choose maintained components.

An Ingress controller is internet-facing: running one that no longer receives security fixes is a liability. Because Ingress is a standard API, switching controllers mostly means changing ingressClassName. The Gateway API is the long-term successor, with role separation (Gateway vs routes) and richer routing.

Q12. curl localhost/catalog/events/1 returns 200. Which chain carried the request?

  • A. localhost:80 → kind node port 30080 (extraPortMappings) → Traefik (NodePort Service) → Ingress rule /catalog → Service catalog → a ready catalog pod
  • B. localhost:80 → the catalog pod directly
  • C. localhost:80 → kube-apiserver → catalog
  • D. localhost:80 → PostgreSQL → catalog
Answer

A — every hop is a component you configured.

kind.yaml maps host port 80 to the node's 30080; the Traefik chart exposes its web entry point on that NodePort; Traefik matches the Ingress rule and sends the request to one of the Service's ready endpoints. The API server is never in the data path — it only stores the desired state the controllers read.

Back to the lab

items.title: 3. Autoscaling
items.text: Lab 3 scaled catalog by hand: three replicas behind Nginx, whatever the load. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) closes the loop — it measures, compares with a target and changes the number of replicas — the autoscaling control loop of the compute class, running every 15 seconds.

items.title: The rule
items.text:
k8s/base/catalog-hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: catalog
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: catalog
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 8
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60     # % of the CPU *request* (250m): scale when pods average > 150m
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0  # react at once to load
      selectPolicy: Max
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 100                 # at most double...
          periodSeconds: 15
        - type: Pods
          value: 2                   # ...or +2 pods, whichever is more, every 15 s
          periodSeconds: 15
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 120  # wait 2 min of lower load before removing pods
      policies:
        - type: Pods
          value: 1
          periodSeconds: 30

The HPA's core formula is simple:

\[ \text{desired replicas} = \left\lceil \text{current replicas} \times \frac{\text{current utilization}}{\text{target utilization}} \right\rceil \]

With 2 pods at 150% of their CPU request and a 60% target: ⌈2 × 150 / 60⌉ = 5 pods. Utilization is a percentage of the request (250m), not of the node: a pod using 150m is at 60%.

behavior field Why it exists scaleUp.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0 scale up as soon as the load is seen — slow scale-up is lost requests scaleUp.policies (100% or +2 pods per 15 s) bounded growth: at most double per period, so one noisy reading cannot explode the deployment scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 120 use the highest recommendation of the last 2 min — no flapping when load oscillates scaleDown.policies (1 pod per 30 s) release capacity slowly; scaling down too fast re-triggers scale-up Why CPU, and when is it the wrong signal?

catalog is CPU-bound when its cache hit ratio is high: more requests → more CPU, almost linearly, so CPU is a good proxy for load. It is the wrong signal when the bottleneck is elsewhere: a service waiting on a database (low CPU, high latency), a Kafka consumer (scale on lag), a WebSocket server (scale on connections). For those, the HPA accepts custom and external metrics (requests per second, queue length) through an adapter such as KEDA or the Prometheus adapter.

items.title: Load it
items.text:
The k6 script ramps the arrival rate (open model) through the Ingress, holds it, and comes back down. The watcher logs what the HPA sees and decides every 5 seconds.

load/catalog-hpa.jsscripts/watch-hpa.sh load/catalog-hpa.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

const BASE_URL = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost'; // the Ingress
const PEAK = Number(__ENV.PEAK || 300);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ramp: {
      executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', // open model: arrivals keep coming even if pods are slow
      startRate: 20,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 100,
      maxVUs: 1000,
      stages: [
        { target: PEAK, duration: '3m' }, // ramp up: watch the HPA react
        { target: PEAK, duration: '4m' }, // hold: does the latency come back down?
        { target: 20, duration: '1m' },   // ramp down
        { target: 20, duration: '3m' },   // quiet: watch the scale-down stabilization
      ],
    },
  },
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'med', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<500'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const id = 1 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 200000);
  const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/catalog/events/${id}`, { tags: { name: 'GET /catalog/events/{id}' } });
  check(res, { 'status 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
scripts/watch-hpa.sh
#!/bin/sh
# Logs time, desired/current replicas, CPU and ready pods every 5 s. Usage: sh scripts/watch-hpa.sh > results/lab10-hpa.csv
echo "time,cpu,desired,current,ready"
while true; do
  HPA=$(kubectl -n boxoffice get hpa catalog -o jsonpath='{.status.currentMetrics[0].resource.current.averageUtilization},{.status.desiredReplicas},{.status.currentReplicas}')
  READY=$(kubectl -n boxoffice get deploy catalog -o jsonpath='{.status.readyReplicas}')
  echo "$(date +%T),$HPA,$READY"
  sleep 5
done

Three terminals:

mkdir -p results && sh scripts/watch-hpa.sh | tee results/lab10-hpa.csv   # 1: the control loop
kubectl -n boxoffice get pods -l app=catalog -w            # 2: pods appearing
k6 run -e PEAK=250 load/catalog-hpa.js                     # 3: the load (≈ 11 min)

Adjust PEAK to your machine: it should be clearly above what two pods can serve (lab 2 gave you that number) but below what the whole laptop can serve.

Expected shape (illustrative)

CPU climbs during the ramp; the HPA adds pods in steps (2 → 4 → 6 …) as fast as the scaleUp policy allows; each new pod needs tens of seconds before it is ready (JVM start + probes), so p95 rises during the ramp and comes back down during the hold. After the load drops, replicas stay up for the 2-minute stabilization window and then leave one by one.

The lag between "load arrives" and "capacity is ready" is the price of reactive autoscaling. For a flash sale at a known time, you would pre-scale (raise minReplicas before 10:00) instead of hoping the HPA is fast enough — reactive scaling handles the unexpected, scheduling handles the expected.

items.title: Pitfalls
items.text:
• No requests, no HPA. Utilization is relative to resources.requests.cpu; without requests the HPA reports <unknown> and does nothing.
  • JVM warm-up looks like load. A starting JVM burns CPU (class loading, JIT): new pods can push the average up and trigger more scale-up. The startup probe keeps unready pods out of traffic but their CPU still counts; the stabilization window and the scale-up policy limit the damage.
  • The database does not autoscale. Eight catalog pods × 10 connections = 80 connections to one PostgreSQL. Scaling the stateless tier moves the bottleneck to the stateful one — check max_connections (or use the PgBouncer of lab 6).
  • Node capacity. If the pods requested do not fit on the nodes, they stay Pending. In the cloud a cluster autoscaler (or Karpenter) adds nodes, which takes minutes, not seconds.

Next: Ingress

items.title: 1. A Local Cluster
items.text: Kubernetes is the same API on a laptop and in a cloud region. This step creates a three-node cluster inside Docker with kind (Kubernetes IN Docker), installs the two add-ons the lab needs — an Ingress controller and metrics-server — and loads your BoxOffice images into it.

items.title: Tools
items.text:
On top of lab 0's kubectl and kind (or minikube), install Helm, the package manager most add-ons are distributed with:

macOSLinux / WSL 
brew install helm kind kubectl

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-4 | bash

Free the ports first

The cluster publishes the Ingress on port 80 of your machine, the same port as the edge of lab 3. Stop Compose before creating the cluster (docker compose down), and give Docker at least 4 CPUs and 8 GB of memory.

items.title: The cluster
items.text:
One control-plane node and two workers, so that you can see pods spread across nodes and survive the loss of one. extraPortMappings publishes port 30080 of the control-plane container — where the Ingress controller will listen — as port 80 of your machine.

k8s/kind.yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
name: boxoffice
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    extraPortMappings:
      - containerPort: 30080   # NodePort of the Ingress controller (Traefik)
        hostPort: 80           # http://localhost
        protocol: TCP
  - role: worker
  - role: worker
kindminikube

kind create cluster --config k8s/kind.yamlCreating cluster "boxoffice" ... ✓ Ensuring node image (kindest/node:v1.37.0) 🖼 ✓ Preparing nodes 📦 📦 📦 ✓ Starting control-plane 🕹️ ✓ Joining worker nodes 🚜Set kubectl context to "kind-boxoffice"kubectl get nodesNAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSIONboxoffice-control-plane Ready control-plane 60s v1.37.0boxoffice-worker Ready <none> 40s v1.37.0boxoffice-worker2 Ready <none> 40s v1.37.0

minikube start --nodes 3 --cpus 2 --memory 4g
kubectl get nodes

With minikube, skip k8s/kind.yaml: after installing Traefik below, reach it with minikube service -n traefik traefik --url (or minikube tunnel with service.type=LoadBalancer), and use that URL wherever this lab says http://localhost.

items.title: The Ingress controller: Traefik
items.text:
An Ingress is only a routing rule ("/catalog → service catalog"); a controller reads those rules and actually proxies the traffic. For years the default choice was ingress-nginx; the Kubernetes project retired it in March 2026 (its repository is archived and receives no more fixes), so this lab uses Traefik, a maintained controller that implements both the Ingress API and its successor, the Gateway API.

helm repo add traefik https://traefik.github.io/charts
helm repo update
helm install traefik traefik/traefik --version 42.0.0 \
  --namespace traefik --create-namespace \
  --set service.type=NodePort \
  --set ports.web.nodePort=30080

ports.web.nodePort=30080 pins the HTTP entry point to the port that kind.yaml maps to your machine's port 80.

items.title: metrics-server
items.text:
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reads CPU usage from the metrics API, served by metrics-server. In kind the kubelets use self-signed certificates, so metrics-server must skip their verification — a lab-only shortcut:

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/download/v0.9.0/components.yaml
kubectl patch -n kube-system deployment metrics-server --type=json \
  -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]'
kubectl top nodes        # works after ~1 minute

items.title: Images
items.text:
The cluster cannot see the images in your Docker; it has its own container runtime. Build with Compose, tag with a fixed tag (never latest: Kubernetes would always try to pull it from a registry) and load the image into every node:

docker compose build catalog-1                     # builds the image "boxoffice-catalog" (lab 3 anchor)
docker tag boxoffice-catalog boxoffice/catalog:dev
kind load docker-image boxoffice/catalog:dev --name boxoffice
# minikube: minikube image load boxoffice/catalog:dev

You should see Image: "boxoffice/catalog:dev" with ID "sha256:…" not yet present on node "boxoffice-worker", loading... once per node.

Repeat for every service you deploy. In lab 11 a CI pipeline will push images to a registry instead, tagged with the commit they were built from.

Next: Deploy BoxOffice

items.title: 2. Deploy BoxOffice
items.text: Compose describes containers to start. Kubernetes manifests describe a desired state — "two ready replicas of catalog, reachable as catalog:8082" — and controllers work continuously to make reality match it: a crashed pod is replaced, a dead node's pods are rescheduled, a new image is rolled out pod by pod. This step writes that desired state for the read path of BoxOffice: db, redis and catalog.

items.title: Layout: base + overlays
items.text:
Manifests live in k8s/ of your repository, organized with Kustomize (built into kubectl): a base with everything that is the same in every environment, and one overlay per environment with only what differs (image tags, secrets, replica counts). Lab 11 adds an overlay for the GitOps deployment without touching the base.

k8s/
├── kind.yaml                      # the cluster (step 1)
├── base/
│   ├── kustomization.yaml
│   ├── namespace.yaml
│   ├── config.yaml                # ConfigMap: DB_HOST, REDIS_HOST, ...
│   ├── db.yaml                    # PostgreSQL StatefulSet + headless Service
│   ├── redis.yaml
│   ├── catalog.yaml               # Deployment + Service
│   ├── catalog-hpa.yaml           # step 3
│   └── ingress.yaml               # step 4
└── overlays/
    └── local/
        └── kustomization.yaml     # image tag "dev" + lab secrets
base/kustomization.yamloverlays/local/kustomization.yamlnamespace.yamlconfig.yaml k8s/base/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: boxoffice
labels:
  - pairs:
      app.kubernetes.io/part-of: boxoffice
resources:
  - namespace.yaml
  - config.yaml
  - db.yaml
  - redis.yaml
  - catalog.yaml
  - catalog-hpa.yaml
  - ingress.yaml
k8s/overlays/local/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - ../../base
images:
  - name: boxoffice/catalog          # the name used in base/catalog.yaml...
    newTag: dev                      # ...and the tag loaded into the local cluster
secretGenerator:
  - name: db-credentials             # lab only: real secrets never live in Git in plain text
    namespace: boxoffice
    literals:
      - DB_USER=boxoffice
      - DB_PASSWORD=boxoffice
k8s/base/namespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: boxoffice
k8s/base/config.yaml
# Non-secret settings shared by the services (the same variables as in docker-compose.yaml)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: boxoffice-config
data:
  DB_HOST: db
  DB_PORT: "5432"
  DB_NAME: boxoffice
  REDIS_HOST: redis
  REDIS_PORT: "6379"

The secretGenerator appends a hash of the content to the Secret's name (db-credentials-c67…) and rewrites every reference to it: changing a password produces a new Secret and therefore a rollout of the pods that use it — a stale credential cannot linger in a running pod.

items.title: Stateful and stateless
items.text:
db.yamlredis.yaml k8s/base/db.yaml
# PostgreSQL as a StatefulSet: a stable name (db-0) and its own persistent volume.
# Fine for a lab; in production use a managed database or an operator (e.g. CloudNativePG).
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  clusterIP: None            # headless: DNS "db" resolves to the pod itself
  selector:
    app: db
  ports:
    - name: postgres
      port: 5432
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  serviceName: db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: db
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:17
          ports:
            - name: postgres
              containerPort: 5432
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_DB
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef: { name: boxoffice-config, key: DB_NAME }
            - name: POSTGRES_USER
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: db-credentials, key: DB_USER }
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: db-credentials, key: DB_PASSWORD }
            - name: PGDATA
              value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
          readinessProbe:
            exec:
              command: ["sh", "-c", "pg_isready -U \"$POSTGRES_USER\" -d \"$POSTGRES_DB\""]
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
            limits: { cpu: "1", memory: 1Gi }
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 2Gi
k8s/base/redis.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: redis
spec:
  selector:
    app: redis
  ports:
    - name: redis
      port: 6379
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: redis
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: redis
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: redis
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: redis
          image: redis:8-alpine
          args: ["--maxmemory", "256mb", "--maxmemory-policy", "allkeys-lru"]
          ports:
            - name: redis
              containerPort: 6379
          readinessProbe:
            exec:
              command: ["redis-cli", "ping"]
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
            limits: { cpu: 500m, memory: 320Mi }

A StatefulSet gives the database what a Deployment does not: a stable identity (db-0) and a PersistentVolumeClaim per replica that survives pod restarts. Deleting the pod keeps the data; deleting the PVC deletes it.

items.title: The catalog Deployment
items.text:
k8s/base/catalog.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: catalog
spec:
  selector:
    app: catalog
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 8082
      targetPort: http
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: catalog
spec:
  replicas: 2                        # the HPA takes over from here
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: catalog
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1                    # one extra pod during a rollout...
      maxUnavailable: 0              # ...and never fewer ready pods than desired
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: catalog
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: catalog
          image: boxoffice/catalog:dev
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8082
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: boxoffice-config
            - secretRef:
                name: db-credentials
          env:
            - name: SERVER_SHUTDOWN
              value: graceful        # finish in-flight requests on SIGTERM
          resources:
            requests:                # what the scheduler reserves; HPA percentages are relative to this
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 512Mi
            limits:
              cpu: "1"
              memory: 768Mi
          startupProbe:              # the JVM needs time: no liveness kills before it has started
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: http }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 60     # up to 5 min: the first start also runs the Flyway migrations
          livenessProbe:             # "restart me": only for a process that is stuck
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: http }
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          readinessProbe:            # "send me traffic": removed from the Service while not ready
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: http }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 2
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              sleep:
                seconds: 5           # let the endpoints update before the JVM stops accepting

The three probes answer three different questions, and confusing them causes outages:

Probe Question On failure Spring Boot endpoint startupProbe has the process finished starting? keeps the other probes off; restart after the budget /actuator/health/liveness livenessProbe is the process stuck beyond repair? restart the container /actuator/health/liveness (internal state only) readinessProbe should this pod receive traffic now? remove from the Service endpoints (no restart) /actuator/health/readiness

Never put a dependency in the liveness probe

If liveness checked the database, a database blip would make Kubernetes restart every catalog pod at once — turning a 10-second blip into minutes of outage while JVMs restart. Spring Boot's liveness group checks only the application's own state; that is why lab 1 enabled management.endpoint.health.probes.

requests are what the scheduler reserves on a node (and the base of HPA percentages); limits are the ceiling — above the memory limit the container is killed (OOMKilled), above the CPU limit it is throttled. Lab 1's Dockerfile sizes the heap with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75, so the JVM respects the 768 Mi limit.

items.title: Apply
items.text:
kubectl apply -k k8s/overlays/localnamespace/boxoffice createdconfigmap/boxoffice-config createdsecret/db-credentials-c677754gbf createdservice/catalog createdservice/db createdservice/redis createddeployment.apps/catalog createddeployment.apps/redis createdstatefulset.apps/db createdhorizontalpodautoscaler.autoscaling/catalog createdingress.networking.k8s.io/boxoffice createdkubectl -n boxoffice get pods -o wideNAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE NODEcatalog-8685666c5-5bv8t 1/1 Running 2 (45s ago) 3m31s boxoffice-workercatalog-8685666c5-9z7n6 1/1 Running 2 (2m ago) 3m31s boxoffice-worker2db-0 1/1 Running 0 3m31s boxoffice-workerredis-6757b9b5ff-9klb4 1/1 Running 0 3m31s boxoffice-workercurl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost/catalog/events/1200 Why did catalog restart twice?

Kubernetes has no depends_on: all pods start at once. catalog started before PostgreSQL accepted connections, Flyway failed, the JVM exited, and Kubernetes restarted it with an exponential back-off until the database was there (kubectl -n boxoffice logs deploy/catalog --previous shows the first failure). This is eventual convergence: instead of ordering the startup, every component retries until its dependencies exist. It also means the first start can be slow — the startup probe allows up to 5 minutes because the first successful start also runs the Flyway migrations of lab 1.

items.title: Watch the controllers work
items.text:
Self-healingLosing a nodeRolling update 
kubectl -n boxoffice delete pod -l app=catalog --wait=false
kubectl -n boxoffice get pods -l app=catalog -w

The Deployment's ReplicaSet sees 0 of 2 pods and creates two new ones immediately. Time how long until both are 1/1 Running again: that is your MTTR (mean time to repair) for a pod crash — dominated by JVM startup.

docker stop boxoffice-worker2
kubectl get nodes -w            # NotReady after about a minute
kubectl -n boxoffice get pods -o wide -w
docker start boxoffice-worker2

Pods on the lost node are replaced on the remaining nodes — but only after the node is declared unhealthy and the pods' tolerations expire (about 5 minutes by default). Detection time dominates recovery, exactly as in the availability math.

kubectl -n boxoffice rollout restart deployment/catalog
kubectl -n boxoffice rollout status deployment/catalog

With maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0, Kubernetes starts one new pod, waits until it is ready, then terminates one old pod, and repeats. In step 5 you will run k6 during a rollout, with and without the readiness probe and the preStop pause, and count the errors.

Graceful shutdown, step by step

When a pod is terminated: (1) it is removed from the Service endpoints and, in parallel, (2) the preStop hook runs (5 s sleep), then (3) SIGTERM reaches the JVM, which with server.shutdown=graceful stops accepting and finishes in-flight requests. Without the preStop pause, step 3 can happen before every node's proxy has stopped sending traffic to the pod — and those requests fail with connection refused.

items.title: 4. Ingress
items.text: A Service gives a set of pods one stable virtual address inside the cluster. The Ingress is the ingress of the palette: the door from the outside world, routing HTTP requests by host and path to Services — the Kubernetes counterpart of the Nginx edge of lab 3.

items.title: The path of a request
items.text:
flowchart LR
    curl["curl localhost/catalog/events/1"] -->|"host :80 → node :30080 (kind.yaml)"| node[control-plane node]
    node -->|NodePort Service| traefik[Traefik pod]
    traefik -->|"rule /catalog → Service catalog:8082"| svc[Service catalog]
    svc -->|"one of the READY endpoints"| p1[catalog pod 1]
    svc --> p2[catalog pod 2]

Traefik watches the Kubernetes API: when an Ingress (or a pod's readiness) changes, its routing table changes within seconds, with no reload. It sends traffic directly to the ready pod endpoints of the Service, so a pod that fails its readiness probe stops receiving requests from the edge too.

items.title: The rule
items.text:
IngressGateway API (HTTPRoute) k8s/base/ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: boxoffice
spec:
  ingressClassName: traefik
  rules:
    - http:
        paths:
          - path: /catalog
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: catalog
                port:
                  name: http

The Gateway API is the successor of Ingress: the same idea, split by role — the platform team owns the Gateway (ports, TLS), each service team owns its HTTPRoute — with features Ingress only had as vendor annotations (header matching, traffic splitting by weight, timeouts). Enable it in Traefik, which then creates a GatewayClass named traefik and a default Gateway named traefik-gateway listening on its web entry point:

# the Gateway API is a set of CRDs: install the version the Traefik chart recommends
kubectl apply --server-side -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.6.2/standard-install.yaml
helm upgrade traefik traefik/traefik --version 42.0.0 --namespace traefik --reuse-values \
  --set providers.kubernetesGateway.enabled=true \
  --set gateway.listeners.web.namespacePolicy.from=All
kubectl get gatewayclass,gateway -A     # ACCEPTED / PROGRAMMED = True
k8s/base/catalog-route.yaml
# Alternative to ingress.yaml with the Gateway API (use one or the other for /catalog)
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: catalog
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: traefik-gateway          # the default Gateway created by the Traefik chart
      namespace: traefik
      sectionName: web
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /catalog
      backendRefs:
        - name: catalog
          port: 8082

To switch, replace ingress.yaml with catalog-route.yaml in k8s/base/kustomization.yaml, apply again and delete the old rule (kubectl apply never deletes what you removed from the files):

kubectl apply -k k8s/overlays/local
kubectl -n boxoffice delete ingress boxoffice
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost/catalog/events/1   # 200, now through the HTTPRoute

Use either the Ingress or the HTTPRoute for /catalog, not both.

Ingress, Service of type LoadBalancer, or API gateway?

A LoadBalancer Service gives one service its own external address (in the cloud, one cloud load balancer each — and one bill each). An Ingress shares one entry point among many services with HTTP routing. An API gateway (Spring Cloud Gateway in lab 4) adds application concerns — authentication, rate limits per user, request transformation. A typical production path is cloud load balancer → Ingress/Gateway → API gateway → services.

items.title: Check the routing
items.text:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost/catalog/events/1        # 200: routed
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost/nothing-here            # 404: no rule matches
for i in $(seq 1 6); do curl -s -D - -o /dev/null localhost/catalog/events/1 | grep -i x-instance; done

If catalog still sets the X-Instance header of lab 3, the last command shows the requests spread over the pods: the pod name is the container hostname.

items.title: 5. Measure It
items.text:
Kubernetes promises elasticity and self-healing. Put numbers on both. As always, run each experiment twice and report the second run; numbers in "expected shape" boxes are illustrative (they come from one run on a laptop, and yours will differ).

# Experiment Knob What you record A fixed replicas vs HPA HPA deleted vs applied p95, p99, errors, max replicas, time to scale B rolling update under load with vs without readiness probe + preStop failed requests during the rollout C self-healing delete a pod / stop a node time until capacity is back (MTTR)

items.title: A. Fixed replicas vs HPA
items.text:
# before: two fixed replicas
kubectl -n boxoffice delete hpa catalog
kubectl -n boxoffice scale deployment catalog --replicas=2
k6 run -e PEAK=250 load/catalog-hpa.js

# after: the HPA
kubectl apply -k k8s/overlays/local
mkdir -p results && sh scripts/watch-hpa.sh > results/lab10-hpa.csv &
k6 run -e PEAK=250 load/catalog-hpa.js
kill %1                                  # stop the watcher

From results/lab10-hpa.csv read: the time the CPU first crossed 60%, the time desired first increased (reaction time), the time ready reached the maximum (time to capacity), and the maximum number of replicas. Plot cpu, desired and ready over time — a spreadsheet is enough — and add the chart to your results.

Expected shape (illustrative)

One run with PEAK=250 on a laptop (kind, 3 nodes sharing 8 CPUs), sampled from the CSV:

t (min:s) CPU (% of request) desired current ready 0:00 8 2 2 2 0:35 105 4 2 2 0:54 153 6 4 2 1:30 137 6 6 4 3:40 197 8 6 4 5:21 115 8 8 8 8:43 6 7 8 7 11:01 5 4 4 4

The HPA asked for more pods 35 s into the ramp, but the eighth pod was ready only after more than five minutes: on a laptop, new JVMs compete for the same CPUs as the pods already overloaded, so starting capacity is slow exactly when it is needed. k6 reported p95 ≈ 7.8 s and dropped iterations during that window, then latency recovered at 8 replicas. After the ramp-down, pods left one at a time after the 2-minute stabilization window. On a real cluster nodes are not shared with the load generator, but the shape — a lag between demand and ready capacity — is the same; that lag is what pre-scaling removes.

items.title: B. Rolling update under load
items.text:
Keep a steady load running (the k6 script of lab 8 works as is) and restart the Deployment in the middle:

k6 run -e RATE=100 -e DURATION=2m load/catalog-otel.js &
sleep 30 && kubectl -n boxoffice rollout restart deployment/catalog
wait                                     # until k6 ends; note http_req_failed

Now remove the readiness probe and the preStop pause, wait for that change to roll out, and repeat:

kubectl -n boxoffice patch deployment catalog --type=json -p '[
  {"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/spec/containers/0/readinessProbe"},
  {"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/spec/containers/0/lifecycle"}]'
kubectl -n boxoffice rollout status deployment/catalog
k6 run -e RATE=100 -e DURATION=2m load/catalog-otel.js &
sleep 30 && kubectl -n boxoffice rollout restart deployment/catalog
wait                                     # until k6 ends; note http_req_failed
kubectl apply -k k8s/overlays/local      # restore the probes and the preStop pause

Without readiness, a new pod receives traffic as soon as its container starts — seconds before Spring Boot listens — and old pods are killed while still in the endpoint lists. Count the failed requests (http_req_failed) in both runs.

items.title: C. Self-healing
items.text:
kubectl -n boxoffice delete pod -l app=catalog --wait=false; date +%T
kubectl -n boxoffice get pods -l app=catalog -w        # note the time both are 1/1 again

Repeat with docker stop boxoffice-worker2 (a node failure) and compare: what dominates each recovery time — detection, scheduling or JVM startup?

items.title: 11. Delivery
items.text:
Goal

Turn git push into a safe, measured deployment. Add an integration test with Testcontainers and a GitHub Actions pipeline (CI) that tests every service, enforces a k6 performance budget, builds the image, scans it (Trivy), produces an SBOM and signed provenance, and publishes it to GHCR. Then deploy by GitOps: a Deploy workflow writes the new image tag to Git, Argo CD applies it to the cluster of lab 10, and Argo Rollouts releases it as a canary that aborts by itself when Prometheus shows errors.

The flash sale is next week and the team ships ten changes a day. Each of them could break checkout: a slow query, a vulnerable library, a version that fails 30% of the requests. Nobody can review every change by hand at that pace — the pipeline must answer "is this change safe to give to 2 million fans?" automatically, and limit the damage when the answer was wrong. This lab is the hands-on side of the delivery page of the cloud-native class.

Start: Tests and CI

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Continuous integration
items.text:
Q1. Why does CatalogApiTest use Testcontainers instead of an in-memory database such as H2?

  • A. Testcontainers is faster than H2
  • B. The test runs the real PostgreSQL 17 (and Redis): Flyway migrations, SQL dialect, constraints and the cache behave exactly as in production, so a passing test means something about production
  • C. H2 cannot be used with Spring Boot 4
  • D. GitHub Actions forbids in-memory databases
Answer

B — test against the real dependency.

An in-memory substitute accepts SQL that PostgreSQL rejects (and the reverse), ignores PostgreSQL-specific features such as ON CONFLICT or partial indexes, and never runs the real migrations. Testcontainers starts the real image in Docker for the duration of the test; the price is a few seconds per test class.

Q2. The workflow has permissions: contents: read at the top, and the image job adds packages: write, id-token: write, attestations: write and security-events: write. Why not give write-all to the whole workflow?

  • A. write-all is not valid YAML
  • B. Least privilege: a compromised step (for example, a malicious dependency in a test) can only do what its job's token allows; the test jobs cannot push images or rewrite the repository
  • C. It makes the workflow faster
  • D. GitHub charges for write permissions
Answer

B — limit the blast radius of every job.

The GITHUB_TOKEN is injected into every job. Jobs that run third-party code (Maven plugins, test dependencies) get read-only access; only the job that must publish gets the permissions to do it, and only for its duration.

Q3. Why is every action pinned to a commit SHA (aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd…, actions/checkout@3d3c42e…) instead of a tag?

  • A. Tags are not supported for third-party actions
  • B. A tag can be moved by whoever controls the action's repository; a full SHA always refers to the same code, so a hijacked tag cannot inject code into your pipeline
  • C. SHAs make the workflow run faster
  • D. Dependabot only works with SHAs
Answer

B — immutable references for code that runs with your token.

Tag hijacking has been used in real supply-chain attacks against CI systems. Pinning to a SHA (with the version in a comment) makes the reference immutable; Dependabot then proposes updates as reviewable pull requests.

items.title: Supply chain
items.text:
Q4. The image job builds with load: true, scans, and only then pushes. What is the advantage over pushing first and scanning the registry image?

  • A. Scanning local images is more accurate
  • B. A vulnerable image is never published: if the gate fails, nothing reaches the registry where a cluster could pull it
  • C. It saves registry storage costs only
  • D. Trivy cannot scan registry images
Answer

B — gate before publish.

Anything in the registry can be deployed by someone (or something, like Argo CD with a moving tag). Failing before the push keeps the registry clean; the push itself is cheap because the layers are already in the build cache.

Q5. Why does the Trivy gate fail only on CRITICAL vulnerabilities with a fix (ignore-unfixed), while the full report lists everything?

  • A. Trivy cannot detect unfixed vulnerabilities
  • B. A gate must be actionable: blocking every change for vulnerabilities nobody can fix today makes the gate permanently red, and teams learn to bypass it; the report keeps the rest visible for prioritization
  • C. HIGH vulnerabilities are never exploitable
  • D. GitHub limits SARIF uploads to critical findings
Answer

B — gates that are always red get ignored.

The gate stops what you can and must fix now (a patched version exists). Everything else goes to the Security tab, where it can be triaged, accepted with an expiry, or fixed when a patch appears.

Q6. What does the build-provenance attestation let you verify with gh attestation verify?

  • A. That the image has no vulnerabilities
  • B. That this exact image digest was built by your repository's workflow, from a specific commit, on GitHub's runners — and has not been modified since
  • C. That the SBOM is complete
  • D. That the image was scanned by Trivy
Answer

B — who built it, from what, and that it was not tampered with.

The attestation is a signed statement (Sigstore, keyless, using the job's OIDC identity) bound to the image digest. A cluster admission policy can refuse images without valid provenance from your repository — the "S" of SLSA.

items.title: Performance gate
items.text:
Q7. The budget test has a 20 s warmup scenario that is not covered by the thresholds. Why?

  • A. To save CI minutes
  • B. A JVM that just started is slower (JIT compilation, empty pools and cache): measuring it would make the gate fail on noise instead of on regressions
  • C. k6 needs time to start its virtual users
  • D. Thresholds cannot apply to the whole test
Answer

B — measure the steady state you promised.

Cold-start latency is real and matters for autoscaling (lab 10), but the budget compares versions of the code: it must measure each one in the same warm state.

Q8. The budget is p95 < 300 ms, and the normal run measures p95 ≈ 7 ms. Isn't such a loose threshold useless?

  • A. Yes, it should be 8 ms
  • B. No: shared CI runners are noisy, so a tight threshold would fail randomly; the gate is there to catch large regressions (the deliberate 400 ms sleep, an N+1 query), while the trend of the numbers over many runs reveals small ones
  • C. Yes, thresholds should always equal the measured value
  • D. No, because k6 rounds latencies
Answer

B — a gate must have a low false-positive rate.

A gate that fails at random trains people to click "re-run" until green — and then it catches nothing. Keep a margin, track the numbers, tighten deliberately.

items.title: GitOps and canary
items.text:
Q9. In this lab, CI never runs kubectl apply against the cluster. How does a new version get deployed?

  • A. Argo CD polls GHCR for new images
  • B. The Deploy workflow commits the new image tag to k8s/overlays/gitops; Argo CD, running inside the cluster, sees the commit and applies the overlay
  • C. Kubernetes pulls the main tag every minute
  • D. The developer runs kubectl apply after CI
Answer

B — pull-based GitOps.

The cluster credentials never leave the cluster; Git holds the complete, audited history of what was deployed; rollback is git revert; and drift is detected and, with selfHeal, undone automatically.

Q10. Someone runs kubectl -n boxoffice scale deployment redis --replicas=0. What happens with selfHeal: true?

  • A. Redis stays at 0 replicas until the next deploy
  • B. Argo CD detects that the cluster differs from Git (OutOfSync) and restores 1 replica within seconds
  • C. Argo CD deletes the Redis Deployment
  • D. The HPA scales Redis back up
Answer

B — Git is the source of truth.

Manual changes are reverted; to change the cluster you change Git. That is also why the HPA's replica count must not be in the Rollout's spec: otherwise Argo CD and the HPA would fight over it.

Q11. The bad release (30% errors) was aborted with the measurements [], 0.068, 0.285 and failureLimit: 1. Why did the first, empty measurement not fail the analysis?

  • A. Argo Rollouts ignores the first measurement
  • B. The success condition len(result) == 0 || isNaN(result[0]) || result[0] < 0.01 treats "no canary traffic yet" as a success; the abort came with the second failure (0.068 and 0.285 > 1%), exceeding failureLimit: 1
  • C. Prometheus was down
  • D. The canary had no pods
Answer

B — handle "no data" explicitly.

Right after a canary starts, the query has no samples. Without the len/isNaN guard, the analysis would fail (or error) immediately on every release. The trade-off: with no traffic, a canary is promoted without evidence — keep load on the service, or lengthen the pauses.

Q12. During a canary, both the old and the new version of catalog run against the same database. Which schema change is safe to ship in the new version?

  • A. Renaming a column the old version reads
  • B. Dropping a column the new version no longer uses
  • C. Adding a new nullable column (expand), with the new code tolerating its absence
  • D. Changing a column's type in place
Answer

C — expand/contract.

Migrations run once, for both versions, and the old version keeps running during the canary — and after an abort. Only backward-compatible changes are safe; the "contract" (drop, rename) happens in a later release, when no running version depends on the old shape.

Back to the lab

items.title: 5. Canary with Argo Rollouts
items.text: A rolling update replaces every pod with the new version as soon as it is ready — but "ready" only means the process started. A version that answers 20% of the requests with 500 is ready too. A canary sends a small share of the traffic to the new version first, measures it against the SLO, and continues only while the numbers are good; otherwise it aborts and the old version keeps serving. With Argo Rollouts the decision is automatic.

items.title: The pieces
items.text:
Object File Role Rollout catalog catalog-rollout.yaml replaces the Deployment's controller; workloadRef reuses the pod template of base/catalog.yaml Service catalog-stable / catalog-canary catalog-services.yaml Argo Rollouts points each at its version's pods (it adds the pod-template hash to the selectors) AnalysisTemplate catalog-slo catalog-analysis.yaml every 30 s, two PromQL queries on the canary: error ratio < 1%, p99 < 500 ms Prometheus k8s/monitoring/prometheus.yaml scrapes the annotated Services and labels every series with service="<Service name>" HPA patched by the overlay now scales the Rollout

The Prometheus of this lab is deliberately minimal (one Deployment, one scrape job):

k8s/monitoring/prometheus.yaml
# A minimal in-cluster Prometheus for the canary analysis (lab 11).
# It discovers the Services of namespace boxoffice annotated with prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
# and labels every series with service="<Service name>" (catalog-stable, catalog-canary, ...).
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: monitoring
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: prometheus
  namespace: monitoring
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: prometheus
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["services", "pods"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: ["discovery.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["endpointslices"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: prometheus
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: prometheus
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: prometheus
    namespace: monitoring
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: prometheus-config
  namespace: monitoring
data:
  prometheus.yml: |
    global:
      scrape_interval: 15s
    scrape_configs:
      - job_name: boxoffice
        metrics_path: /actuator/prometheus
        kubernetes_sd_configs:
          - role: endpointslice
            namespaces:
              names: [boxoffice]
        relabel_configs:
          - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_service_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape]
            regex: "true"
            action: keep
          - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_endpointslice_port_name]
            regex: http
            action: keep
          - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_service_name]
            target_label: service
          - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_name]
            target_label: pod
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: prometheus
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: prometheus
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: prometheus
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: prometheus
      containers:
        - name: prometheus
          image: prom/prometheus:v3.13.4
          args:
            - --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
            - --storage.tsdb.retention.time=2d
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 9090
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /-/ready, port: http }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 256Mi }
            limits: { cpu: "1", memory: 1Gi }
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/prometheus
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: prometheus-config
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: prometheus
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  selector:
    app: prometheus
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 9090
      targetPort: http

The metric is Spring Boot's own (Micrometer) http_server_requests_seconds, exposed at /actuator/prometheus by the dependency added in step 1 and the overlay's MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINTS_WEB_EXPOSURE_INCLUDE patch. Micrometer publishes only _count and _sum by default; the overlay's MANAGEMENT_METRICS_DISTRIBUTION_PERCENTILESHISTOGRAM_HTTP_SERVER_REQUESTS patch adds the _bucket series, without which the p99 query returns nothing and that metric would always pass. With the service label, the same query compares service="catalog-canary" with service="catalog-stable".

The steps of the Rollout (see catalog-rollout.yaml in step 4): 25% → wait 2 min → 50% → wait 2 min → 100%, with the analysis running in the background from the first step. Without a traffic router, Argo Rollouts reaches a weight by replica counts (with 2 replicas, "25%" is 1 canary pod next to the stable ones), so the real share is approximate; the delivery class shows exact weights with the Gateway API plugin.

items.title: Watch a rollout
items.text:
Install the kubectl plugin of Argo Rollouts:

macOSLinux / WSL 
brew install argoproj/tap/kubectl-argo-rollouts

curl -fsSLo kubectl-argo-rollouts https://github.com/argoproj/argo-rollouts/releases/download/v1.10.1/kubectl-argo-rollouts-linux-amd64
chmod +x kubectl-argo-rollouts && sudo mv kubectl-argo-rollouts /usr/local/bin/

Keep load on the service while a new version rolls out — the analysis needs requests to measure — using the k6 script of lab 10 at a modest rate:

k6 run -e PEAK=40 load/catalog-hpa.js &          # about 11 minutes of traffic through the Ingress
kubectl argo rollouts -n boxoffice get rollout catalog --watch

Any commit to services/catalog on main produces a new image and a new rollout; a quick one is a comment in ChaosFilter.java. You should see the steps advance (SetWeight: 25 → 50 → 100), an AnalysisRun with ✔ measurements, and at the end the new ReplicaSet marked stable.

items.title: A bad release
items.text:
Now ship a release that breaks 30% of the requests, through Git. In k8s/overlays/gitops/kustomization.yaml, add one more operation to the Deployment patch (after the MANAGEMENT_METRICS_DISTRIBUTION_PERCENTILESHISTOGRAM_HTTP_SERVER_REQUESTS one):

      - op: add                      # lab 11 experiment: a bad release (remove it afterwards)
        path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/-
        value: { name: CHAOS_ERROR_RATE, value: "0.3" }

CHAOS_ERROR_RATE is read by ChaosFilter, which exists only for this experiment:

services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/ChaosFilter.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.filter.OncePerRequestFilter;

/** Lab 11 only: CHAOS_ERROR_RATE=0.2 makes 20% of the API requests fail, to play a bad release. */
@Component
public class ChaosFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    private final double errorRate;

    public ChaosFilter(@Value("${CHAOS_ERROR_RATE:0}") double errorRate) {
        this.errorRate = errorRate;
    }

    @Override
    protected boolean shouldNotFilter(HttpServletRequest request) {
        return errorRate <= 0 || request.getRequestURI().startsWith("/actuator");
    }

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        if (ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble() < errorRate) {
            response.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "injected failure");
            return;
        }
        chain.doFilter(request, response);
    }
}

Commit, push, and watch (keep the k6 load running):

git commit -am "experiment: bad release" && git pull --rebase && git push
kubectl argo rollouts -n boxoffice get rollout catalog --watch

You should see, about a minute after Argo CD syncs, the rollout aborted and the canary scaled down. From a test run:

Name:            catalog
Namespace:       boxoffice
Status:          ✖ Degraded
Message:         RolloutAborted: Rollout aborted update to revision 2: Background analysis phase error/failed: Metric "error-rate" assessed Failed due to failed (2) > failureLimit (1)
Strategy:        Canary
  Step:          0/4
  SetWeight:     0
  ActualWeight:  0
Images:          boxoffice/catalog:v1 (stable)

(That test run used a locally loaded boxoffice/catalog:v1; yours shows ghcr.io/<you>/boxoffice-catalog:sha-… as the stable image.)

and the measurements of the error-rate metric were [] (no canary traffic yet: counted as a success by len(result) == 0), 0.068 and 0.285 — two failures above failureLimit: 1. The fans who hit the canary saw errors for about a minute; everyone else never noticed.

Degraded is the signal to fix forward in Git: revert the experiment (git revert HEAD && git push), Argo CD syncs, and the next rollout starts from a clean state.

What a canary cannot catch

  • Database migrations run once, for both versions: they must be backward compatible (expand/contract), because the old version keeps running during — and after an aborted — canary.
  • Rare errors need many canary requests to be visible; at low traffic, lengthen the pauses.
  • Side effects (payments, e-mails) of canary requests are real.

Next: Measure it

items.title: 1. Tests and CI
items.text: A pipeline is only as good as the tests it runs. This step adds the first integration test of BoxOffice — the real catalog against a real PostgreSQL and a real Redis, started by Testcontainers — and the GitHub Actions workflow that runs it on every push and pull request. All commands run from the root of your boxoffice repository.

items.title: An integration test with Testcontainers
items.text:
Mocks test what you think the database does. Testcontainers starts the real thing in Docker for the duration of the test: Flyway migrations, JPA mappings, SQL, the Redis cache and the JSON error format are all exercised exactly as in production. Spring Boot's @ServiceConnection points the datasource and the Redis client at the containers — no URLs to configure.

services/catalog/src/test/java/boxoffice/catalog/CatalogApiTest.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.resttestclient.TestRestTemplate;
import org.springframework.boot.resttestclient.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.testcontainers.containers.GenericContainer;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Container;
import org.testcontainers.junit.jupiter.Testcontainers;
import org.testcontainers.postgresql.PostgreSQLContainer;

/**
 * Starts the real service against a real PostgreSQL 17 and a real Redis, in throwaway containers:
 * Flyway migrations, JPA mappings, the cache, JSON and the error format are tested together.
 */
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate
@Testcontainers
class CatalogApiTest {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection // Spring Boot points the datasource at this container
    static PostgreSQLContainer db = new PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:17");

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection(name = "redis") // ... and the Redis client at this one
    static GenericContainer<?> redis = new GenericContainer<>("redis:8-alpine").withExposedPorts(6379);

    @Autowired
    TestRestTemplate http;

    @Test
    void returnsTheFlashSaleEvent() {
        ResponseEntity<EventOut> res = http.getForEntity("/catalog/events/1", EventOut.class);

        assertThat(res.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.OK);
        assertThat(res.getBody()).isNotNull();
        assertThat(res.getBody().title()).isEqualTo("BoxOffice Fest — Stadium Night");
    }

    @Test
    void unknownEventIsAProblem404() {
        ResponseEntity<String> res = http.getForEntity("/catalog/events/999999999", String.class);

        assertThat(res.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
        assertThat(res.getHeaders().getContentType()).isEqualTo(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON);
    }

    @Test
    void invalidEventIsRejected() {
        ResponseEntity<String> res = http.postForEntity("/catalog/events",
                new EventIn("", null, null, null, null), String.class);

        assertThat(res.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
    }
}

The pom.xml of catalog gains the test dependencies (and, for step 5, the Prometheus registry). The complete file:

services/catalog/pom.xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    </parent>

    <groupId>boxoffice</groupId>

    <name>catalog</name>
    <description>BoxOffice catalog: events and venues</description>

    <properties>
        <java.version>21</java.version>
        <springdoc.version>3.1.1</springdoc.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>

        <dependency>

        </dependency>

        <dependency>

        </dependency>
        <!-- JPA + Hibernate -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

        </dependency>

        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

        </dependency>
        <!-- schema migrations (Boot 4: the starter brings the auto-configuration) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>

        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
            <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
            <scope>runtime</scope>
        </dependency>
        <!-- Redis client (Lettuce) + StringRedisTemplate: the cache of lab 5 -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

        </dependency>
        <!-- OpenAPI document + Swagger UI -->

            <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>

            <version>${springdoc.version}</version>
        </dependency>
        <!-- lab 11: /actuator/prometheus, scraped in Kubernetes for the canary analysis -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
            <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- lab 11: tests (JUnit 5, AssertJ, TestRestTemplate) against real containers -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

        </dependency>
        <dependency>

    <build>
        <finalName>app</finalName>
