items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

Q1. Why can catalog be scaled to three replicas without changing its code (except the X-Instance header)?

  • A. Spring Boot replicates memory between instances
  • B. It is stateless: every request carries all it needs, and all shared state lives in PostgreSQL, so any replica can answer any request
  • C. Nginx copies the session to every replica
  • D. Docker Compose synchronizes the replicas
Answer

B — Stateless services scale horizontally.

If a replica kept user data in memory (a session, a shopping cart), requests would have to return to the same replica (sticky sessions) and a crash would lose data. Pushing state into a database or cache is the precondition for easy scale-out.

Q2. With the default Nginx upstream configuration, how are requests distributed?

  • A. Randomly
  • B. Round robin: each replica in turn
  • C. To the replica with the lowest CPU
  • D. By hashing the client IP
Answer

B — Round robin.

That is why 9 requests give 3 per replica. least_conn (fewest active connections), ip_hash/hash (affinity) and random two least_conn (power of two choices) are alternatives, chosen with one directive.

Q3. catalog-3 is paused (frozen) while k6 sends 150 req/s. What do the clients experience?

  • A. Immediate 502 errors
  • B. Nothing at all
  • C. A burst of requests that take about proxy_read_timeout (5 s) before Nginx retries them on another replica, then normal latency once the replica is marked failed
  • D. All requests fail until the replica is unpaused
Answer

C — Slow failures cost a timeout each.

A frozen process accepts the TCP connection but never answers, so Nginx can only detect it by waiting. After max_fails it stops sending traffic for fail_timeout. A crashed replica, by contrast, refuses the connection and the retry is immediate.

Q4. Why is proxy_next_upstream safe for GET /catalog/events/1 but not by default for a POST?

  • A. POST bodies are too large to resend
  • B. GET is idempotent: repeating it has no extra effect; a POST might already have been processed by the first replica, and resending it could, for example, create two orders
  • C. Nginx cannot proxy POST requests
  • D. HTTP forbids retries
Answer

B — Only retry idempotent requests.

A timeout does not tell you whether the server did the work. Retrying non-idempotent operations needs an idempotency key (class 5, lab 9). Nginx retries non-idempotent methods only with non_idempotent explicitly set.

Q5. Why not set proxy_read_timeout 100ms to detect frozen replicas faster?

  • A. Nginx does not accept values below 1 s
  • B. Legitimate slow requests (a listing under load) would be treated as failures and retried, adding load exactly when the system is struggling
  • C. It would disable keep-alive
  • D. It only applies to POST
Answer

B — Timeouts come from measured latency.

Set them slightly above the healthy p99.9 of the endpoint. Too long and a slow replica hurts many requests; too short and you create failures and retry storms out of normal slowness.

Q6. The greedy client sends 50 req/s for 30 s with a limit of 20 r/s and burst=40 nodelay. About how many requests succeed?

  • A. 600
  • B. 640
  • C. 1,500
  • D. 40
Answer

B — ≈ 640.

20 req/s × 30 s = 600 allowed by the rate, plus the burst of 40 served immediately at the start. The other ≈ 860 get 429 Too Many Requests — cheaply, at the edge, without touching the replicas.

Q7. Why does the lab key the rate limit on X-Api-Key and not on the client IP?

  • A. Nginx cannot read IP addresses
  • B. All k6 traffic comes from one IP, so an IP limit would throttle the load tests; in production you limit authenticated identities and also anonymous IPs
  • C. IP limits are illegal
  • D. API keys are encrypted
Answer

B — A lab constraint, explained.

Per-IP limits also misfire behind NATs (a whole university behind one address). And a header chosen by the client can be rotated by an attacker — so real limits use verified identities (API keys you issued, user ids from JWTs).

Q8. You measure capacity 400 req/s with 1 replica and 960 req/s with 3. What is the scaling efficiency, and the most likely cause of the gap?

  • A. 100%; there is no gap
  • B. 80%; the three replicas share one database (and one laptop), which becomes the contended resource
  • C. 33%; Nginx is single-threaded
  • D. 240%; caching kicked in
Answer

B — 960 / (3 × 400) = 80%.

Scaling the stateless tier moves the pressure to the shared stateful tier. The Universal Scalability Law captures this: contention (and coherence) costs make throughput grow sub-linearly with nodes.

Q9. What is the advantage of the resolve flag on the upstream servers?

  • A. It encrypts the traffic to the replicas
  • B. Nginx resolves the names through Docker's DNS at run time: it starts even if a replica is down and notices when a replica comes back with a new IP
  • C. It enables HTTP/2
  • D. It caches responses
Answer

B — Dynamic name resolution.

Without it, Nginx resolves upstream names once at startup and refuses to start if a name does not resolve — a classic outage when a dependency is restarted or rescheduled with a new address.

Q10. Which statement about health checks is correct?

  • A. Open-source Nginx actively probes /actuator/health every few seconds
  • B. Passive checks learn from failures of real requests; active checks probe an endpoint periodically and can remove a replica before users hit it
  • C. Health checks are only needed in Kubernetes
  • D. A passing liveness check means the replica can serve traffic
Answer

B — Passive vs active.

Open-source Nginx is passive (max_fails). Envoy, HAProxy, cloud load balancers, Spring Cloud LoadBalancer (lab 4) and Kubernetes readiness probes (lab 10) do active checks. And readiness (can serve) differs from liveness (process alive).

items.title: Index
items.text:
In this lab

  • Build auth: users, BCrypt passwords, login that returns a JWT signed with RS256, and a public JWKS endpoint.
  • Put Spring Cloud Gateway behind the edge: one place for routing, token validation and authorization (open vs protected vs admin routes).
  • Propagate the user's identity to the services as trusted headers (X-User-Id).
  • Measure what the extra hop and the token check cost, and how many logins per second auth can take.

Until now anyone could create or delete events in the catalog. BoxOffice needs to know who is calling (authentication) and what they may do (authorization) — and it should not ask every service to solve that problem again. The standard answer is an API gateway1: the single front door for the API, where tokens are validated once and requests are routed to the right service. Behind it, services trust the identity the gateway passes along.

Theory connection

items.title: What you will build
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Fan
    participant E as edge :80
    participant G as gateway :8080
    participant A as auth :8081
    participant C as catalog-1..3 :8082
    Fan->>E: POST /auth/login {email, password}
    E->>G: forward
    G->>A: route /auth/** (open)
    A->>A: BCrypt check, sign JWT with private key
    A-->>Fan: 200 {accessToken: "eyJ..."}
    Fan->>E: POST /catalog/events + Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
    E->>G: forward
    G->>A: GET /auth/.well-known/jwks.json (first time only, then cached)
    G->>G: verify signature, exp, iss, aud — scope "admin"?
    G->>C: route lb://catalog + X-User-Id, X-User-Scope
    C-->>Fan: 201 Created

Tokens are JWTs2: signed JSON that any holder of the public key can verify without calling auth.

Route Who may call it Enforced by POST /auth/register, POST /auth/login, GET /auth/.well-known/jwks.json anyone gateway: permitAll GET /catalog/** anyone gateway: permitAll POST/PUT/DELETE /catalog/** tokens with scope admin gateway: hasAuthority("SCOPE_admin") GET /auth/me and every other route (including future ones) any valid token gateway: anyExchange().authenticated()

The topology after this lab: edge (Nginx: TLS termination in production, rate limiting, load balancing over gateway replicas) → gateway (identity, routing, load balancing over service instances) → services.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
• 1. The auth service

    Users table, BCrypt, login, JWT signing with an RSA key pair, the JWKS document.

  • 2. The gateway

    Spring Cloud Gateway routes, client-side load balancing over catalog-1..3, JWT validation, identity headers, the new edge and Compose.

items.title: 3. Try it end to end
items.text:
With both steps done, rebuild and start everything:

docker compose up --build -d
docker compose ps        # db, catalog-1..3, auth, gateway healthy; edge running
curl -s -X POST localhost/auth/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Ana","email":"ana@example.com","password":"secret-123"}'{"id":"0b9d8a6e-…","name":"Ana","email":"ana@example.com","role":"USER"}TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email":"ana@example.com","password":"secret-123"}' | jq -r .accessToken)curl -s localhost/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"{"id":"0b9d8a6e-…","name":"Ana","email":"ana@example.com","role":"USER"}curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" localhost/auth/me401curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X DELETE localhost/catalog/events/2 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"403

Now as the administrator (created at startup from ADMIN_EMAIL/ADMIN_PASSWORD):

ADMIN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"admin@boxoffice.dev","password":"boxoffice-admin"}' | jq -r .accessToken)

curl -s -X PUT localhost/catalog/events/2 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Match #2 (rescheduled)","category":"SPORTS","venueId":15,"startsAt":"2027-03-02T21:00:00-03:00","priceFrom":100}' | jq .title

# look inside the token: header and claims are only Base64URL, NOT encrypted
echo "$ADMIN" | cut -d. -f2 | tr '_-' '/+' | base64 -d 2>/dev/null; echo
Think first: a client sends X-User-Id: <the admin's id> itself. What happens?

Nothing useful for the attacker: the gateway's UserHeadersFilter removes any X-User-* header coming from outside before setting its own from the validated token. Without that line, any client could impersonate any user, because the services trust those headers blindly. That trust is acceptable only because the services are not reachable except through the gateway — zero-trust networks (class 11) go further and authenticate every hop (mTLS, or re-validating the JWT in each service).

Try the other failure cases too: an expired token (start auth with JWT_TTL=PT30S, wait a minute), a token with one character changed (signature check fails), and restarting auth (new key pair: old tokens are rejected because their kid no longer exists in the JWKS — see the warning in step 1).

items.title: Measure it: the price of a front door
items.text:
Every hop and every check costs something. Measure three request types at the same rate — open route through the edge, protected route (JWT validation) through the edge, and the open route straight to the gateway port — plus the throughput of auth itself.

load/gateway.js
// Lab 4: what does the gateway cost? Three request types at the same arrival rate:
//   open       GET /catalog/events/{id}  (no token)
//   protected  GET /auth/me              (JWT validated by the gateway)
//   direct     GET /catalog/events/{id}  straight to the gateway port, skipping the edge
//   k6 run -e RATE=50 load/gateway.js      (3 scenarios: 150 req/s in total)
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

const EDGE = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost';
const GATEWAY = __ENV.GATEWAY_URL || 'http://localhost:8080';
const RATE = Number(__ENV.RATE || 50);

const scenario = (exec) => ({
  executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', exec, rate: RATE, timeUnit: '1s', duration: '1m',
  preAllocatedVUs: 50, maxVUs: 500,
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: { open: scenario('open'), protected: scenario('protectedRoute'), direct: scenario('direct') },
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'med', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{scenario:open}': ['p(99)<500'],
    'http_req_duration{scenario:protected}': ['p(99)<500'],
    'http_req_duration{scenario:direct}': ['p(99)<500'],
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

// runs once: register a fan and log in; every VU reuses the token
export function setup() {
  const email = `fan-${Date.now()}@boxoffice.dev`;
  const json = { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } };
  http.post(`${EDGE}/auth/register`, JSON.stringify({ name: 'Load Fan', email, password: 'secret-123' }), json);
  const login = http.post(`${EDGE}/auth/login`, JSON.stringify({ email, password: 'secret-123' }), json);
  check(login, { 'login is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  return { token: login.json('accessToken') };
}

const randomId = () => 1 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 200000);

export function open() {
  const res = http.get(`${EDGE}/catalog/events/${randomId()}`);
  check(res, { 'open is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

export function protectedRoute(data) {
  const res = http.get(`${EDGE}/auth/me`, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${data.token}` } });
  check(res, { 'protected is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

export function direct() {
  const res = http.get(`${GATEWAY}/catalog/events/${randomId()}`);
  check(res, { 'direct is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
load/login.js
// Lab 4: how many logins per second can auth take? BCrypt is slow on purpose.
//   k6 run -e RATE=20 load/login.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

const BASE_URL = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost';
const RATE = Number(__ENV.RATE || 20);
const json = { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } };

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    logins: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', rate: RATE, timeUnit: '1s', duration: '30s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 20, maxVUs: 300,
    },
  },
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'med', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
  thresholds: { http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'], 'http_req_duration{name:login}': ['p(99)<1000'] },
};

export function setup() {
  const email = `login-${Date.now()}@boxoffice.dev`;
  http.post(`${BASE_URL}/auth/register`, JSON.stringify({ name: 'Login Fan', email, password: 'secret-123' }), json);
  return { email };
}

export default function (data) {
  const res = http.post(`${BASE_URL}/auth/login`,
    JSON.stringify({ email: data.email, password: 'secret-123' }), { ...json, tags: { name: 'login' } });
  check(res, { 'login is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

k6 run -e RATE=50 load/gateway.js        # 3 scenarios × 50 req/s
mkdir -p results/lab4
for r in 5 10 20 40; do k6 run -q -e RATE=$r --summary-export results/lab4/login-$r.json load/login.js; done
uv run scripts/summarize.py results/lab4/login-*.json

results/lab4.md
# Lab 4 — gateway and identity

## Hops (50 req/s each, 1 min)
| Path | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| edge → catalog (lab 3, same rate) | | | |
| gateway → catalog (direct) | | | |
| edge → gateway → catalog (open) | | | |
| edge → gateway → auth, JWT validated (protected) | | | |

Cost of the gateway hop ≈ ____ ms at p50; cost of JWT validation ≈ ____ ms.

## Login capacity
<table from summarize.py: rate, p50, p99, errors>
- Max logins/s with p99 < 1 s: ____ ; CPU of auth at that rate (docker stats): ____ %
- One BCrypt check (cost 10) takes about ____ ms on my machine.

## Questions
- Why does the gateway validate tokens locally instead of calling auth on every request?
- What would happen to the flash sale if every request called /auth/login?

How to read it:

  • The gateway hop adds a fraction of a millisecond to a few milliseconds at p50 (an extra network hop and a non-blocking proxy). Signature checking with RS256 is microseconds of CPU: JWT validation is cheap because it is local — the gateway fetched the public key once and never calls auth per request.
  • Login is expensive on purpose. BCrypt with cost 10 burns tens of milliseconds of CPU per attempt, so auth with 1 CPU tops out at roughly ten to twenty logins per second (in a test run for this lab, 10 logins/s already pushed p99 into seconds). That is exactly what makes password guessing slow — and why clients must reuse tokens instead of logging in per request. During a flash sale, logins should happen before 10:00.

If your numbers differ

On a laptop, the gateway (1 CPU) shares the machine with five other JVMs and PostgreSQL, so the hop can cost more than in production — in a run for this lab on a busy machine, p50 reached hundreds of milliseconds at 150 req/s. Compare relative costs on the same machine and the same run: direct to the gateway vs through the edge vs with JWT. For logins, the ceiling scales with CPU: one core gives roughly 10–20 BCrypt checks per second.

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

Q1. Why does BoxOffice sign tokens with RS256 (asymmetric) instead of HS256 (shared secret)?

  • A. RS256 tokens are smaller
  • B. Only auth holds the private key; the gateway (and any service) verifies with the public key and can never mint a token
  • C. HS256 is not supported by Spring Security
  • D. RS256 encrypts the payload
Answer

B — Separation of signing and verifying.

With HS256 the same secret signs and verifies, so every verifier is also a potential forger, and the secret must be distributed everywhere. With RS256 the public key can be published (JWKS) safely.

Q2. How often does the gateway call auth to validate a token?

  • A. On every request
  • B. Once per user session
  • C. It fetches the JWKS (public keys) once and caches it; each token is verified locally, refetching only for an unknown kid
  • D. Never: the gateway does not validate tokens
Answer

C — Local verification.

That is the whole point of self-contained tokens: no network call per request, so the auth service is not on the hot path. The flip side is revocation — a token stays valid until exp.

Q3. A client sends a request with X-User-Id: <admin id> and no token to /auth/me. What happens?

  • A. auth returns the admin's profile
  • B. The gateway answers 401: /auth/me requires a token, and in any case the gateway strips client-supplied X-User-* headers
  • C. The gateway answers 403
  • D. The edge blocks the header
Answer

B — 401, and the header would be removed anyway.

anyExchange().authenticated() rejects the request; and UserHeadersFilter always deletes incoming X-User-* headers before setting its own from a validated token. Without that removal, header spoofing would be trivial.

Q4. A fan with a valid token (scope user) sends DELETE /catalog/events/2. The answer is:

  • A. 200
  • B. 401 Unauthorized
  • C. 403 Forbidden
  • D. 404 Not Found
Answer

C — 403.

401 means "I do not know who you are" (missing/invalid token); 403 means "I know who you are, and you may not do this" (the rule requires SCOPE_admin).

Q5. Why is anyExchange().authenticated() the last rule?

  • A. Spring requires it
  • B. It is a secure default: any route added later is protected unless someone explicitly opens it
  • C. It makes open routes faster
  • D. It disables CSRF
Answer

B — Deny by default.

Rules are evaluated in order. Listing what is open and protecting everything else means forgetting a rule fails closed (a 401) instead of open (a data leak).

Q6. Your login test shows auth saturating at ~15 logins/s on 1 CPU while /auth/me handles thousands. Why?

  • A. The database is slow for logins
  • B. BCrypt with cost 10 deliberately spends tens of milliseconds of CPU per password check
  • C. JWT signing takes 1 s
  • D. Logins use HTTP/1.0
Answer

B — Password hashing is slow on purpose.

The cost factor makes brute-forcing a leaked hash expensive. Consequences for design: issue tokens and reuse them, protect /auth/login with a strict rate limit, and scale auth for the login peak (before a flash sale opens).

Q7. auth restarts. What happens to tokens issued before the restart, in this lab's implementation?

  • A. They keep working
  • B. They are rejected: the key pair is generated in memory at startup, so the old kid is no longer in the JWKS
  • C. They are refreshed automatically
  • D. Only admin tokens are rejected
Answer

B — Lost key, lost tokens.

Production systems keep the private key in a KMS/secrets manager, publish both the current and previous keys during rotation, and rotate on a schedule. Two auth replicas with in-memory keys would be even worse: each would sign with a different key.

Q8. What does the gateway check in a JWT besides the signature?

  • A. Nothing else
  • B. exp/nbf (time window), iss (the expected issuer) and aud (the token is meant for this API)
  • C. The user's password
  • D. The IP address that requested the token
Answer

B — Time, issuer, audience.

A correctly signed token from another issuer, or one minted for another API (audience), must not be accepted. Skipping aud checks is a classic vulnerability when one identity provider serves several APIs.

Q9. Why is identity propagated to services as headers (X-User-Id) instead of each service validating the JWT again?

  • A. Headers are encrypted
  • B. Simplicity and cost: one validation at the gateway; acceptable only while services are reachable exclusively through the gateway (a trusted network) — zero-trust designs re-validate or use mTLS
  • C. Services cannot parse JSON
  • D. JWTs cannot be forwarded
Answer

B — A trust boundary trade-off.

The pattern is common and cheap, but it rests on network isolation. If an attacker reaches a service directly, they can set any header. Class 11 discusses mTLS, service meshes and forwarding the token itself.

Q10. Why are there two load balancers in the lab 4 topology (Nginx and the gateway's lb://)?

  • A. Redundancy: one is a backup of the other
  • B. They balance different tiers: the edge balances across gateway replicas, the gateway across service instances — like a public cloud load balancer in front of a gateway fleet calling services through internal load balancing
  • C. Spring Cloud Gateway cannot receive traffic directly
  • D. Nginx cannot route by path
Answer

B — One balancer per tier.

Each tier scales independently, so each needs its own distribution and health checking. In Kubernetes (lab 10), the Ingress/Gateway API and Services play these two roles.

items.title: Index
items.text:
auth owns the users of BoxOffice. It does three things: register a user (storing a BCrypt hash, never the password), log in (check the password and issue a signed token) and publish the public key that lets anybody verify those tokens. It is a regular Spring Boot service on port 8081, with its own schema auth.

flowchart LR
    subgraph auth["auth :8081"]
        ctl[AuthController] --> svc[AuthService]
        svc --> repo[UserRepository] --> db[("schema auth<br/>users")]
        svc --> tok["TokenService<br/>RSA key pair"]
    end
    gw[gateway] -->|"GET /auth/.well-known/jwks.json<br/>(public key, cached)"| ctl

items.title: 1. Why a signed token?
items.text:
After login, every request must prove who is calling. Two families of solutions:

Server-side session Self-contained token (JWT) What the client holds a random session id (cookie) the claims themselves, signed: sub, scope, exp… How a request is checked look the id up in a session store (Redis, DB) verify the signature with the public key — no lookup Revocation delete the session: immediate hard: the token is valid until exp (keep it short) Scales with the session store CPU only; every node can verify alone

BoxOffice uses JWTs signed with RS256 (RSA + SHA-256): auth signs with a private key only it knows; the gateway verifies with the public key, published as a JWKS (JSON Web Key Set). The gateway can verify tokens but can never mint one — unlike HS256, where the same shared secret signs and verifies, and every service holding it could forge tokens.

A token looks like header.payload.signature, each part Base64URL-encoded:

decoded payload of a BoxOffice token
{
  "iss": "boxoffice-auth",
  "aud": "boxoffice",
  "sub": "0b9d8a6e-4f3c-4c1e-9d52-1b0f3c2a7e11",
  "email": "ana@example.com",
  "name": "Ana",
  "scope": "user",
  "iat": 1795000000,
  "exp": 1795003600,
  "jti": "7c1f…"
}

Signed is not encrypted

Anybody can decode the payload (try jwt.io or base64 -d). Never put secrets or personal data you would not show the user in a JWT.

Index
items.text:
The gateway is the API's front door: every request that passes the edge goes through it. It is built on Spring Cloud Gateway, which runs on Spring WebFlux and Netty — non-blocking, so a few threads proxy thousands of concurrent requests — on port 8080.

Responsibility How Routing /auth/** → auth; /catalog/** → lb://catalog Load balancing over service instances Spring Cloud LoadBalancer over catalog-1..3, skipping unhealthy ones Authentication validates the JWT: signature (JWKS), exp, iss, aud Authorization (coarse) open / any token / scope admin, per path and method Identity propagation X-User-Id, X-User-Email, X-User-Scope for the services Timeouts and retries connect 1 s, response 5 s; one retry for idempotent GETs

items.title: 1. Project
items.text:
Create services/gateway (same Dockerfile with EXPOSE 8080, same .dockerignore).

services/gateway/pom.xml

package boxoffice.gateway;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class GatewayApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(GatewayApplication.class, args);

items.title: 2. Routes and load balancing
items.text:
services/gateway/src/main/resources/application.yaml
server:
  port: 8080

spring:
  application:
    name: gateway
  cloud:
    gateway:
      server:
        webflux:
          httpclient:
            connect-timeout: 1000          # ms to open a connection to a service
            response-timeout: 5s           # never wait forever for a service
          default-filters:
            # retry idempotent GETs once on another instance when a connection fails
            - name: Retry
              args:
                retries: 1
                methods: GET
                series: SERVER_ERROR
                exceptions: java.io.IOException, java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException
          routes:
            - id: auth
              uri: ${AUTH_URL:http://auth:8081}
              predicates:
                - Path=/auth/**
            - id: catalog
              uri: lb://catalog              # "lb": pick one instance of "catalog" per request
              predicates:
                - Path=/catalog/**
    # the instances behind lb://catalog (a static list; Kubernetes replaces it in lab 10)
    discovery:
      client:
        simple:
          instances:
            catalog:
              - uri: http://catalog-1:8082
              - uri: http://catalog-2:8082
              - uri: http://catalog-3:8082
    loadbalancer:
      configurations: health-check         # skip instances whose /actuator/health is not UP
      health-check:
        interval: 5s
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          jwk-set-uri: ${AUTH_JWKS_URI:http://auth:8081/auth/.well-known/jwks.json}

jwt:
  issuer: ${JWT_ISSUER:boxoffice-auth}
  audience: boxoffice

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, info, metrics, gateway
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
    gateway:
      access: read-only      # GET /actuator/gateway/routes lists the routes
  • A route = id + predicates (when it matches) + URI (where it goes) + filters.
  • uri: lb://catalog asks Spring Cloud LoadBalancer for an instance of catalog on each request (round robin). The instance list here is static (discovery.client.simple); with Kubernetes in lab 10 a Service takes over this job.
  • configurations: health-check makes the balancer poll each instance's /actuator/health every 5 s and skip those that are not UP — an active health check, the thing open-source Nginx could not do in lab 3. It uses a WebClient to probe, which in Spring Boot 4 lives in its own starter: that is why the pom has spring-boot-starter-webclient. Until the first round of probes completes (a few seconds after startup) the balancer knows no healthy instance and the gateway answers 503.
  • Retry re-sends a failed GET once (to another instance); never POSTs, which might not be idempotent.

Two load balancers?

Yes, on purpose: the edge balances across gateway replicas (add gateway-2 to the Nginx upstream when one gateway is not enough), and the gateway balances across service instances. That mirrors the cloud: a public L7 load balancer in front of a fleet of API gateways, which call services through internal load balancing.

items.title: 3. Security: who may call what
4. Identity headers
5. The new edge
items.text:
The edge now forwards everything to the gateway; routing by path moved one hop in. It also hides /actuator/ from the internet.

infra/nginx/nginx.conf
# BoxOffice edge (lab 4): everything goes to the gateway, which routes to the services
user  nginx;
worker_processes  auto;

events {
    worker_connections  4096;
}

http {
    # one line per request: who served it, and how long the upstream took
    log_format  edge  '$remote_addr "$request" $status rt=$request_time '
                      'upstream=$upstream_addr ut=$upstream_response_time id=$request_id';
    access_log  /var/log/nginx/access.log  edge;

    # Docker's embedded DNS: lets nginx start even if a replica is down, and
    # notice replicas that come back (the "resolve" flag below, nginx >= 1.27.3)
    resolver  127.0.0.11  valid=10s  ipv6=off;

    upstream gateway {
        zone gateway 64k;                 # shared memory, required by "resolve"
        server gateway:8080 resolve max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
        # more gateway replicas go here: gateway-2:8080, ...
        keepalive 64;
    }

    # rate limiting per API key: 20 req/s per key, bursts of up to 40.
    # Requests WITHOUT an X-Api-Key header have an empty key and are not limited
    # (in production you would also limit them per client IP).
    limit_req_zone  $http_x_api_key  zone=per_key:10m  rate=20r/s;
    limit_req_status  429;

    server {
        listen  80;

        # the edge's own liveness: does not touch any backend
        location = /healthz {
            access_log  off;
            return  200  "ok\n";
        }

        # internal endpoints are never public
        location /actuator/ {
            return  404;
        }

        location / {
            limit_req  zone=per_key  burst=40  nodelay;

            proxy_pass  http://gateway;
            proxy_http_version  1.1;
            proxy_set_header  Connection         "";      # keep upstream connections alive
            proxy_set_header  Host               $host;
            proxy_set_header  X-Real-IP          $remote_addr;
            proxy_set_header  X-Forwarded-For    $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
            proxy_set_header  X-Forwarded-Proto  $scheme;
            proxy_set_header  X-Request-Id       $request_id;
            add_header        X-Request-Id       $request_id always;

            # passive health checking: a failed attempt is retried on another replica
            proxy_connect_timeout  1s;
            proxy_read_timeout     5s;
            proxy_next_upstream    error timeout http_502 http_503 http_504;
            proxy_next_upstream_tries  2;
        }
    }
}

    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  # three identical replicas; no "ports:" — only the edge is reachable from outside
  catalog-1:
    <<: *catalog
    hostname: catalog-1
  catalog-2:
    <<: *catalog
    hostname: catalog-2
  catalog-3:
    <<: *catalog
    hostname: catalog-3

  auth:
    build: ./services/auth
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
      DB_PORT: 5432
      DB_NAME: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
      DB_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
      DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
      JWT_ISSUER: ${JWT_ISSUER:-boxoffice-auth}
      JWT_TTL: ${JWT_TTL:-PT1H}
      ADMIN_EMAIL: ${ADMIN_EMAIL:-admin@boxoffice.dev}
      ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${ADMIN_PASSWORD:-boxoffice-admin}
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 768M
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -qO- http://localhost:8081/actuator/health/readiness || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 40s
      retries: 3

  gateway:
    build: ./services/gateway
    environment:
      AUTH_URL: http://auth:8081
      AUTH_JWKS_URI: http://auth:8081/auth/.well-known/jwks.json
      JWT_ISSUER: ${JWT_ISSUER:-boxoffice-auth}
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"          # published for experiments; clients use the edge (port 80)
    depends_on:
      - auth
      - catalog-1
      - catalog-2
      - catalog-3
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 768M
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health/readiness || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 40s
      retries: 3

  edge:
    image: nginx:1.30-alpine
    ports:
      - "80:80"
    volumes:
      - ./infra/nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - gateway

volumes:
  db-data:

The gateway publishes port 8080 only so that you can measure it directly; in production only the edge would be exposed.

docker compose up --build -dcurl -s localhost:8080/actuator/gateway/routes | jq -r '.[].route_id'authcatalogcurl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" localhost/catalog/events/1200curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" localhost/actuator/health404

Pitfalls

  • 401 on every protected route right after startup: the gateway fetches the JWKS lazily; if auth was down at that moment, retry — and check AUTH_JWKS_URI.
  • 401 after restarting auth: the old tokens were signed with the old key. Log in again.
  • Clock skew: exp/iat are compared with the gateway's clock; containers share the host clock, but servers in production need NTP (class 3).
  • CORS: a browser front end on another origin needs CORS configured at the gateway (spring.cloud.gateway.server.webflux.globalcors) — not needed for k6 or curl.

Back to the lab overview to try it and measure it.

items.title: Index
items.text:
In this lab

  • Add Redis to BoxOffice and implement cache-aside in catalog: read the cache first, load from PostgreSQL on a miss, store with a TTL.
  • Invalidate on writes, survive a Redis outage, and expose the outcome of every request in an X-Cache header.
  • Measure the hit ratio and its effect on p99 and capacity, with a realistic skewed popularity.
  • Reproduce a cache stampede on a hot key, then fix it with a distributed lock and TTL jitter — and measure the fix.

The catalog is the textbook read-heavy service: during the week of the stadium show, a few thousand popular events receive almost all the traffic, and the listing of "upcoming events in São Paulo" is requested thousands of times per minute while it changes a few times per day. Lab 2 showed that the database (through its connection pool) is what limits catalog. A cache1 answers the repeated questions from memory, so the database only sees the first one.

Caches are also, as every interview guide warns2, the most common source of subtle bugs in system design: stale data, cold starts, hot keys and stampedes. In this lab you will see each of them with your own measurements.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
• 1. Cache-aside with Redis

  • 2. Stampede

items.title: Measure it: hit ratio, p99 and capacity
items.text:
The load script mimics real popularity: 80% of the detail requests go to the 2,000 hottest events (1% of the catalog); listings are spread over 10 cities and the first 3 pages. It reads the X-Cache header of every response, so k6 reports the hit ratio and separate latencies for hits and misses.

load/cache.js
// Lab 5: a realistic read mix with POPULAR events. 80% of the detail requests go to the
// 2,000 hottest events (1% of the catalog), like a real box office the week of a big show.
//   k6 run -e RATE=300 load/cache.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { Rate, Trend } from 'k6/metrics';

const BASE_URL = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost';
const RATE = Number(__ENV.RATE || 300);
const DURATION = __ENV.DURATION || '1m';
const HOT_SHARE = Number(__ENV.HOT_SHARE || 0.8);
const CITIES = ['São Paulo', 'Rio de Janeiro', 'Belo Horizonte', 'Porto Alegre', 'Curitiba',
  'Salvador', 'Recife', 'Fortaleza', 'Brasília', 'Manaus'];

const cacheHit = new Rate('cache_hit');               // share of responses with X-Cache: HIT
const latencyHit = new Trend('latency_hit', true);    // latency of hits only
const latencyMiss = new Trend('latency_miss', true);  // latency of misses (and bypasses)

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    open: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', rate: RATE, timeUnit: '1s', duration: DURATION,
      preAllocatedVUs: Math.max(20, RATE), maxVUs: Math.max(200, RATE * 10),
    },
  },
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'med', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
    'http_req_duration{name:detail}': ['p(99)<500'],
    'http_req_duration{name:list}': ['p(99)<1000'],
    cache_hit: ['rate>=0'],                              // printed in the summary
  },
};

function record(res) {
  const outcome = res.headers['X-Cache'];
  cacheHit.add(outcome === 'HIT');
  (outcome === 'HIT' ? latencyHit : latencyMiss).add(res.timings.duration);
}

export default function () {
  if (Math.random() < 0.2) {
    const city = CITIES[Math.floor(Math.random() * CITIES.length)];
    const page = Math.floor(Math.random() * 3);              // people rarely go past page 3
    const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/catalog/events?city=${encodeURIComponent(city)}&page=${page}`,
      { tags: { name: 'list' } });
    check(res, { 'list is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
    record(res);
  } else {
    const hot = Math.random() < HOT_SHARE;
    const id = 1 + Math.floor(Math.random() * (hot ? 2000 : 200000));
    const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/catalog/events/${id}`, { tags: { name: 'detail' } });
    check(res, { 'detail is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
    record(res);
  }
}

Run the same load without and with the cache — the switch is an environment variable, no rebuild needed:

# 1. no cache (every request goes to PostgreSQL)
CACHE_ENABLED=false docker compose up -d
k6 run -e RATE=300 load/cache.js

# 2. cache on, cold: flush Redis right before the test
CACHE_ENABLED=true docker compose up -d
docker compose exec redis redis-cli FLUSHALL
k6 run -e RATE=300 load/cache.js

# 3. cache on, warm: run it again immediately
k6 run -e RATE=300 load/cache.js

# 4. capacity: repeat the lab 2 sweep, now with the cache, through the edge
BASE_URL=http://localhost OUT=results/lab5-cache bash scripts/sweep.sh 300 600 900 1200 1500

Also look at the cache from Redis's side:

docker compose exec redis redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E "keyspace_(hits|misses)"
docker compose exec redis redis-cli INFO memory | grep used_memory_human
docker compose exec redis redis-cli --scan --pattern 'catalog:event:*' | wc -l
docker compose exec redis redis-cli TTL catalog:event:1

Record in results/lab5.md:

results/lab5.md

## Same load (300 req/s, 80% of details on 1% of events)
| Run | cache_hit | p50 (ms) | p99 (ms) | p99 detail | p99 list | latency_hit p99 | latency_miss p99 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| no cache |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| cold cache |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| warm cache |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

## Capacity (sweep through the edge, 3 replicas)
| Setup | Capacity with p99 < 300 ms (req/s) |
|---|---:|
| lab 3, no cache | |
| lab 5, cache | |

## Redis
- keyspace_hits / keyspace_misses: ____ / ____ → hit ratio ____ %
- keys cached: ____ ; memory used: ____

## Stampede (see step 2)
| CACHE_STAMPEDE_PROTECTION | cache_misses in 1 min | p99 (ms) | max (ms) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| false | | | |
| true  | | | |

## Questions
1. With hit ratio h, the database receives (1 − h) of the reads. Which hit ratio did you need to double the capacity?
2. Change HOT_SHARE to 0.2 (popularity almost uniform). What happens to the hit ratio, and why?
3. An admin changes the price of event 42. For how long can a fan see the old price on the listing page? On the event page?
Think first: why is the warm-cache run much better than the cold one, if both use the same code?

In the cold run, every first request for a key is a miss — and with 2,000 hot events plus thousands of cold ones, the first seconds look exactly like the no-cache run. A cache is only as good as its hit ratio, and the hit ratio depends on the key space, the popularity distribution and the TTL, not on Redis's speed. That is why deploys that flush caches, or new nodes with empty caches, cause latency spikes in production — and why some systems warm caches before taking traffic.

If your numbers differ

The hit ratio after one minute depends on the TTLs and on how many distinct keys k6 touched: a first run with a cold cache stays around 50% (47–53% in runs for this lab at 150–200 req/s), a second run right after is much higher. Hits should be an order of magnitude faster than misses at p50; if they are not, Redis or the network is the bottleneck (docker stats). Your capacity gain depends on how much of the original load was the listing.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix no X-Cache header the catalog image was not rebuilt docker compose up --build -d X-Cache: MISS on every request Redis unreachable (see the catalog logs: cache read failed), or CACHE_TTL_* too short docker compose ps redis; docker compose logs catalog-1 \| grep cache X-Cache: BYPASS CACHE_ENABLED=false is still set in your shell unset CACHE_ENABLED && docker compose up -d env var changes have no effect the containers were not recreated always VAR=value docker compose up -d (not restart) Bind for 0.0.0.0:6379 failed a local Redis is running stop it or map "16379:6379" the stampede run shows the same misses with and without protection the TTL is not short, or the variable did not reach the replicas docker compose exec catalog-1 env \| grep CACHE_ old data after an admin update on the listing page listing keys are not evicted, by design wait CACHE_TTL_LIST (10 s) — it is the bounded staleness of the design

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

Q1. In cache-aside, who writes a value into the cache?

  • A. The database, through a trigger
  • B. The application, after a miss: it loads from the database and stores the result with a TTL
  • C. Redis, automatically, by reading the database
  • D. The client
Answer

B — The application, lazily.

The cache only contains what was requested recently. Read-through moves the loading into the cache layer; write-through writes the cache on every update. Cache-aside is the simplest and most common.

Q2. With a hit ratio of 90%, what fraction of the reads reaches PostgreSQL? And with 99%?

  • A. 90% and 99%
  • B. 10% and 1%
  • C. 9% and 0.9%
  • D. 50% and 5%
Answer

B — 10% and 1%.

Going from 90% to 99% hit ratio divides the database load by ten. Small improvements at high hit ratios are worth a lot — which is why popularity skew (a few very hot keys) makes caches so effective.

Q3. Why does catalog evict the event key on update instead of writing the new value into the cache?

  • A. Redis cannot overwrite keys
  • B. Concurrent updates could write the cache in a different order from the database commits, leaving an old value cached; deleting is idempotent and the next read loads the committed state
  • C. Eviction is faster than writing
  • D. To reduce memory usage
Answer

B — Avoid ordering races.

Even eviction has a narrow race (a slow reader re-caching an old value after the eviction), which is why every key also has a TTL: the TTL bounds how long any inconsistency can last.

Q4. Listing keys are not evicted on updates. What is the consequence?

  • A. Listings are always wrong
  • B. A listing can show old data for up to CACHE_TTL_LIST (10 s + jitter): bounded staleness, accepted to avoid tracking which listing pages contain each event
  • C. Updates fail
  • D. Redis runs out of memory
Answer

B — Bounded staleness by design.

An event appears in many listing pages (city, page, size). Precise invalidation would need an index from event to keys. A short TTL is a simple, explicit trade-off — state it in a design review.

Q5. Redis is stopped. What does catalog do in this lab's implementation?

  • A. Returns 503 Service Unavailable
  • B. Hangs for 60 s per request
  • C. Treats every cache error as a miss and serves from PostgreSQL (with 200 ms Redis timeouts), so it is slower but works
  • D. Switches to an in-memory cache
Answer

C — The cache is an optimization, not a dependency.

But beware: if the cache absorbed 95% of the reads, its failure sends 20× the usual load to the database — which may fall over. Plan database capacity (or load shedding) for a cache outage.

Q6. Why add jitter to the TTL?

  • A. To make keys expire in random order for security
  • B. Keys written at the same time (a cold start, a bulk load) would otherwise expire at the same time and cause a synchronized wave of misses
  • C. Redis requires it
  • D. To save memory
Answer

B — Desynchronize expirations.

Jitter spreads expirations over a window. It does not fix a single hot key expiring — that is the stampede, which needs a lock, early refresh or stale-while-revalidate.

Q7. In the stampede test without protection, cache_misses is 3,000 in a minute with a 3 s TTL. With protection it is ~20. What does each miss represent?

  • A. A failed request
  • B. One execution of the expensive listing query in PostgreSQL
  • C. One Redis eviction
  • D. One k6 iteration that timed out
Answer

B — One heavy query each.

20 expirations per minute should cost 20 queries. Without coordination, every request arriving during the reload runs its own copy; the lock collapses them into one ("single flight").

Q8. Why does the lock have an expiry (PX 2000)?

  • A. Redis requires every key to expire
  • B. If the request holding the lock crashes, the lock frees itself and another request can rebuild the value; without expiry the key could stay locked forever
  • C. To make the lock faster
  • D. To count requests
Answer

B — Liveness of the lock.

And size it above the p99 of the query: if the work takes longer than the lock lives, a second loader gets in. Releasing must check the token so a request never deletes someone else's lock (atomically, with a Lua script, in production).

Q9. The cache is shared in Redis rather than a local HashMap in each replica. Which advantage did you observe?

  • A. Redis is faster than a HashMap
  • B. A value loaded by one replica is a hit for the others, and all replicas see the same version (one eviction invalidates everywhere)
  • C. Local caches cannot have TTLs
  • D. Redis compresses JSON
Answer

B — One cache for all replicas.

Local caches are faster (no network hop) but each replica warms separately and can disagree. Many systems use both: a tiny local cache with a short TTL for the very hottest keys, in front of the shared one.

Q10. HOT_SHARE drops from 0.8 to 0.2 (popularity almost uniform over 200,000 events). What happens to the detail hit ratio, and why?

  • A. It increases, because more keys are cached
  • B. It drops sharply: with a 60 s TTL and uniform access, most events are not requested again before their key expires
  • C. It stays the same; Redis handles it
  • D. It becomes 100% after warm-up
Answer

B — Caches feed on skew.

Hit ratio depends on how often the same key is requested within its TTL. Uniform access over a large key space defeats caching; for such workloads, make the query itself cheap (lab 6) or cache at a coarser grain.

items.title: Index
items.text:
Cache-aside (also called lazy loading) is the most common caching pattern: the application talks to both the cache and the database, and the cache only ever contains what somebody asked for recently.

Pattern Who loads the cache Writes Used here? Cache-aside the application, on a miss go to the database; the app evicts/updates the key yes Read-through the cache itself (a loader plugged into it) — no Write-through — app writes to the cache, which writes to the database synchronously no Write-behind — cache acknowledges, writes to the database later (risk of loss) no

items.title: 1. Redis in Compose
items.text:
Add a redis service and give the catalog replicas the cache settings (the whole file, for reference):

docker-compose.yaml
name: boxoffice

# settings shared by the three catalog replicas (a YAML anchor)
x-catalog: &catalog
  build: ./services/catalog
  image: boxoffice-catalog
  environment:
    DB_HOST: db
    DB_PORT: 5432
    DB_NAME: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
    DB_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
    DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
    DB_POOL_SIZE: ${DB_POOL_SIZE:-10}
    REDIS_HOST: redis
    REDIS_PORT: 6379
    CACHE_ENABLED: ${CACHE_ENABLED:-true}
    CACHE_TTL_EVENT: ${CACHE_TTL_EVENT:-60s}
    CACHE_TTL_LIST: ${CACHE_TTL_LIST:-10s}
    CACHE_STAMPEDE_PROTECTION: ${CACHE_STAMPEDE_PROTECTION:-false}
  depends_on:
    db:
      condition: service_healthy
    redis:
      condition: service_healthy
  deploy:
    resources:
      limits:
        cpus: "1.0"
        memory: 768M
  healthcheck:
    test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -qO- http://localhost:8082/actuator/health/readiness || exit 1"]
    interval: 10s
    timeout: 3s
    start_period: 40s
    retries: 3

services:

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  redis:
    image: redis:8-alpine
    # a pure cache: bounded memory, evict least-recently-used keys, no persistence
    command: ["redis-server", "--maxmemory", "256mb", "--maxmemory-policy", "allkeys-lru",
              "--save", "", "--appendonly", "no"]
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  # three identical replicas; no "ports:" — only the edge is reachable from outside
  catalog-1:
    <<: *catalog
    hostname: catalog-1
  catalog-2:
    <<: *catalog
    hostname: catalog-2
  catalog-3:
    <<: *catalog
    hostname: catalog-3

  auth:
    build: ./services/auth
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
      DB_PORT: 5432
      DB_NAME: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
      DB_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
      DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
      JWT_ISSUER: ${JWT_ISSUER:-boxoffice-auth}
      JWT_TTL: ${JWT_TTL:-PT1H}
      ADMIN_EMAIL: ${ADMIN_EMAIL:-admin@boxoffice.dev}
      ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${ADMIN_PASSWORD:-boxoffice-admin}
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 768M
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -qO- http://localhost:8081/actuator/health/readiness || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 40s
      retries: 3

  gateway:
    build: ./services/gateway
    environment:
      AUTH_URL: http://auth:8081
      AUTH_JWKS_URI: http://auth:8081/auth/.well-known/jwks.json
      JWT_ISSUER: ${JWT_ISSUER:-boxoffice-auth}
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"          # published for experiments; clients use the edge (port 80)
    depends_on:
      - auth
      - catalog-1
      - catalog-2
      - catalog-3
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 768M
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health/readiness || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 40s
      retries: 3

  edge:
    image: nginx:1.30-alpine
    ports:
      - "80:80"
    volumes:
      - ./infra/nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - gateway

volumes:
  db-data:
Setting Why --maxmemory 256mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru a cache must be bounded; when full, Redis evicts the least recently used keys instead of failing writes --save "" --appendonly no no persistence: a cache can always be rebuilt from the database (and a restart is a cold start — measure it!) depends_on: redis: condition: service_healthy start the replicas after Redis answers PING (but they also survive without it, see below) CACHE_* variables turn the cache on/off, change TTLs and stampede protection without rebuilding

items.title: 3. The cache component
4. The controller
items.text:
The GET endpoints now return ResponseEntity<String> — the JSON comes from the cache or is produced on a miss — plus the X-Cache header. Writes evict the event's key after the database commit:

services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/EventController.java
package boxoffice.catalog;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Max;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Min;
import java.net.URI;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.DeleteMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PutMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ResponseStatus;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/catalog/events")
public class EventController {

    private final CatalogService service;
    private final EventCache cache;

    public EventController(CatalogService service, EventCache cache) {
        this.service = service;
        this.cache = cache;
    }

    @GetMapping
    public ResponseEntity<String> list(
            @RequestParam(required = false) String city,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") @Min(0) int page,
            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") @Min(1) @Max(50) int size) {
        var key = "catalog:events:city=" + (city == null ? "" : city) + ":page=" + page + ":size=" + size;
        return json(cache.get(key, cache.listTtl(), () -> service.upcomingEvents(city, page, size)));
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<String> get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return json(cache.get(eventKey(id), cache.eventTtl(), () -> service.findEvent(id)));
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<EventOut> create(@Valid @RequestBody EventIn in) {
        var out = service.createEvent(in);
        return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/catalog/events/" + out.id())).body(out);
    }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public EventOut update(@PathVariable Long id, @Valid @RequestBody EventIn in) {
        var out = service.updateEvent(id, in);
        cache.evict(eventKey(id));       // the next read loads the new version
        return out;
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
    public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
        service.deleteEvent(id);
        cache.evict(eventKey(id));
    }

    private static String eventKey(Long id) {
        return "catalog:event:" + id;
    }

    private static ResponseEntity<String> json(EventCache.Result result) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok()
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .header("X-Cache", result.outcome())
                .body(result.json());
    }
}

Why evict instead of updating the key?

Two concurrent updates can write the cache in the opposite order of the database commits, leaving the older version cached until the TTL. Deleting the key is idempotent: the next read loads whatever the database has. Even eviction has a race (a reader loads the old row just before the update commits and writes it after the eviction), which is why every key also has a TTL: TTL is the safety net of every invalidation scheme.

Listing pages are not evicted: a change to one event can affect thousands of listing keys (every city/page that contains it). They expire after CACHE_TTL_LIST (10 s) instead — a deliberate choice of bounded staleness for the listing in exchange for simplicity.

items.title: 5. Check it
items.text:
docker compose up --build -d
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - localhost/catalog/events/42 | grep -iE "x-cache|x-instance"
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - localhost/catalog/events/42 | grep -iE "x-cache|x-instance"
docker compose exec redis redis-cli GET catalog:event:42
docker compose exec redis redis-cli TTL catalog:event:42
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - localhost/catalog/events/42 | grep -iE "x-cache|x-instance"X-Instance: catalog-2X-Cache: MISScurl -s -o /dev/null -D - localhost/catalog/events/42 | grep -iE "x-cache|x-instance"X-Instance: catalog-3X-Cache: HITdocker compose exec redis redis-cli TTL catalog:event:42(integer) 62

The second request was served by another replica and was still a hit: the cache is shared (distributed), not local to each JVM. With a local cache (Caffeine, a HashMap), each of the three replicas would warm up separately and could hold a different version of the same event.

Now break it on purpose:

# invalidation: update event 42 as admin, then read it
ADMIN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"admin@boxoffice.dev","password":"boxoffice-admin"}' | jq -r .accessToken)
curl -s -X PUT localhost/catalog/events/42 -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Festival #42 (new lineup)","category":"FESTIVAL","venueId":45,"startsAt":"2027-03-03T14:00:00-03:00","priceFrom":175}' > /dev/null
curl -s -D - localhost/catalog/events/42 | grep -iE "x-cache|title"

# resilience: no Redis, still working (slower, all MISS)
docker compose stop redis
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" -D - localhost/catalog/events/42 | grep -iE "x-cache|^200"
docker compose start redis

In the interview

When you add a cache, say four things: what is cached (and the key), the TTL and invalidation strategy (and the staleness you accept), the expected hit ratio (and why — popularity skew), and what happens when the cache fails (fall back to the database, protected against a stampede). Interviewers probe the last two.

Next: 2. Stampede.

items.title: Index
items.text:
A cache stampede (also thundering herd or dog-piling) happens when a hot key expires: every request that arrives before the value is rebuilt misses, and all of them run the same expensive query at the same time. The database, which the cache was protecting, receives a burst of identical work exactly when traffic is highest.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant F1 as Fan 1
    participant F2 as Fan 2..200
    participant C as catalog ×3
    participant R as redis
    participant DB as db
    Note over R: key "São Paulo, page 0" expires
    F1->>C: GET listing
    C->>R: GET → miss
    C->>DB: heavy query (join, sort, count)
    F2->>C: GET listing (same key, same moment)
    C->>R: GET → miss
    C->>DB: the SAME heavy query, ×199
    Note over DB: 200 identical queries, pool of 30 connections: queueing
    DB-->>C: rows (eventually)
    C->>R: SET (200 times, same value)

items.title: 1. Reproduce it
items.text:
Make the problem frequent: a hot listing with a 3 s TTL, hammered by 200 closed-model users without think time.

load/stampede.js
// Lab 5: cache stampede. 200 fans refresh the SAME expensive page non-stop.
// Every time its key expires, how many requests go to the database at once?
//   CACHE_TTL_LIST=3s docker compose up -d      (short TTL: many expirations per minute)
//   k6 run load/stampede.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { Counter } from 'k6/metrics';

const BASE_URL = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost';
const misses = new Counter('cache_misses');          // each MISS = one heavy query in the DB

export const options = {
  vus: Number(__ENV.VUS || 200),
  duration: __ENV.DURATION || '1m',
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'med', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
  thresholds: {
    cache_misses: ['count>=0'],                       // printed in the summary
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

const HOME = `${BASE_URL}/catalog/events?city=${encodeURIComponent('São Paulo')}&page=0`;

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(HOME, { tags: { name: 'home' } });
  check(res, { 'home is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  if (res.headers['X-Cache'] !== 'HIT') {
    misses.add(1);
  }
}

CACHE_TTL_LIST=3s CACHE_STAMPEDE_PROTECTION=false docker compose up -d
k6 run load/stampede.js

In 60 s the key expires about 20 times. Without protection, cache_misses is far above 20 — each expiry lets through every request that arrived during the reload, one heavy query each. Watch docker stats during the test: the CPU of db spikes every ~3 seconds, and so does the latency (look at max and p(99) versus med).

items.title: 2. Fix it: one rebuild per key
items.text:
The fix implemented in EventCache (already in your code, behind a switch) is a distributed lock per key:

  1. Miss → try SET key:lock <token> NX PX 2000. Redis guarantees only one request in the whole cluster (all three replicas) gets it.
  2. The winner double-checks the cache, runs the query, writes the value, releases the lock.
  3. The losers do not query the database: they poll the cache every 25 ms for up to 500 ms and return the value as soon as the winner writes it (a HIT).
  4. If the winner dies, the lock expires after 2 s, so nobody waits forever.
excerpt of services/catalog/src/main/java/boxoffice/catalog/EventCache.java (already in your code)
if (stampedeProtection) {
    var lockKey = key + ":lock";
    var token = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    if (tryLock(lockKey, token)) {
        try {
            cached = read(key);               // someone may have filled it meanwhile
            if (cached != null) {
                return count(new Result(cached, "HIT"));
            }
            return count(load(key, ttl, loader));
        } finally {
            unlock(lockKey, token);
        }
    }
    // another request is already loading this key: wait for it instead of
    // sending one more identical query to the database
    for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
        sleep(Duration.ofMillis(25));
        cached = read(key);
        if (cached != null) {
            return count(new Result(cached, "HIT"));
        }
    }
}

CACHE_TTL_LIST=3s CACHE_STAMPEDE_PROTECTION=true docker compose up -d
k6 run load/stampede.js

Now cache_misses should be close to the number of expirations (~20 per minute). In a test run for this lab (100 VUs, 30 s, TTL 3 s), the misses dropped from 800 to 10 — one database query per expiration instead of eighty. The latency gain on a laptop can be modest (Redis, the edge and the gateway dominate each request), but the database load during each expiration drops by almost two orders of magnitude, and that is what protects it during a real spike. Fill in the stampede table of results/lab5.md.

items.title: 3. Other cures, and their trade-offs
items.text:
Technique Idea Trade-off Lock / single flight (this lab) one loader per key, others wait waiting threads (blocked Tomcat threads; virtual threads — spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true — make the wait cheap) TTL jitter (also in this lab) keys written together expire at different times does not help a single hot key Probabilistic early refresh (XFetch) each request may refresh before expiry, with a probability that grows as expiry approaches no locks; some duplicate work Stale-while-revalidate serve the expired value while one request refreshes in the background clients see slightly stale data Refresh-ahead a background job refreshes hot keys before they expire needs to know which keys are hot Request coalescing at the edge the CDN/proxy collapses identical concurrent misses (proxy_cache_lock in Nginx) only for cacheable HTTP responses

Pitfalls of the lock

  • unlock does get then delete: between the two, the lock could expire and be taken by someone else, and we would delete their lock. The correct version is one atomic Lua script (if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del', KEYS[1]) end). The lab keeps the simple version for readability; the comment in the code says so.
  • A lock that is held longer than its expiry (a 3 s query with a 2 s lock) lets a second loader in. Size the lock TTL above the p99 of the query.
  • The waiters give up after 500 ms and load anyway: under extreme load, a bounded wait is safer than an unbounded queue.
Think first: the hot key is catalog:event:1 (the flash-sale show), read 50,000 times per second. Is the stampede your only problem?

No: even with 100% hits, one key lives on one Redis node. In a Redis Cluster, all 50,000 requests per second hit the same shard — a hot key. Cures: a small local in-process cache in each replica (a few seconds of TTL) in front of Redis, replicating the hot key under several names (event:1#0…event:1#9, picked at random), or pushing the page to the CDN. Class 7 (failure modes) covers these.

Back to the lab overview to record the results.

items.title: Index
items.text:
In this lab

  • Build inventory, the strongly consistent heart of BoxOffice: seats and holds, where one seat can never belong to two fans.
  • Compare three concurrency strategies under a flash sale — naive check-then-act, pessimistic locking (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) and optimistic locking (version column) — and prove which ones double-book2.
  • Add a read replica with streaming replication, route read-only transactions to it, and observe replication lag breaking read-your-writes.
  • Put PgBouncer between the services and PostgreSQL, and use EXPLAIN ANALYZE + indexes to fix the slow catalog listing.
  • Measure each change: conflicts, double bookings, p99, lag, connections, query time.

The flash sale is the moment BoxOffice exists for: at 10:00, 60,000 seats and two million fans. The catalog could be cached because a few seconds of staleness is harmless. Seats are the opposite: selling the same seat twice is the one bug a ticketing company cannot afford. This lab is about the data layer under pressure1 — correctness first (transactions and locks), then scale (replicas, pooling, indexes) — and about the trade-offs between them.

items.text:

items.text:
Try it: the db-replicas scenario has a primary and read replicas, with reads and writes split. Run it, then raise the share of writes: what happens to the primary while the replicas stay idle? Increase the replication lag and watch the "stale reads" indicator. Write down which kind of traffic replicas help with — and which they cannot help with at all.

Then look at the whole sale in flash-sale: the waiting room, inventory in SQL, payment. Lab 7 builds the waiting room; today you build the inventory box.

items.title: Quiz
items.text:
Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

Q1. Under PostgreSQL's default isolation (READ COMMITTED), why does the naive strategy (SELECT, check in Java, UPDATE) double-book seats?

  • A. READ COMMITTED does not use transactions
  • B. Two transactions can both read the seats as AVAILABLE before either writes; the second UPDATE then waits for the first and overwrites it — a lost update
  • C. The UPDATE statement is not atomic
  • D. JdbcClient does not support transactions
Answer

B — Check-then-act race.

Each statement sees committed data, but nothing links the decision made on the SELECT to the state at the time of the UPDATE. The fix must make the check and the write one atomic step: a lock, a version check, or a conditional UPDATE.

Q2. What does SELECT … FOR UPDATE do in the pessimistic strategy?

  • A. Reads the rows faster
  • B. Locks the selected rows until the transaction ends; another transaction trying to lock them waits, then sees the committed (HELD) state and gets a 409
  • C. Prevents anyone from reading the rows
  • D. Updates the rows automatically
Answer

B — Row locks, held until commit.

Plain reads (without FOR UPDATE) are not blocked thanks to MVCC; only other lockers and writers wait. That waiting is the cost of pessimism, visible in the p99 of the hold requests.

Q3. Why do we lock seats ORDER BY id?

  • A. To return them sorted to the client
  • B. To avoid deadlocks: if two holds lock overlapping seats in different orders, each can wait for the other forever
  • C. Because PostgreSQL requires an ORDER BY with FOR UPDATE
  • D. To make the index scan cheaper
Answer

B — A global lock order prevents cycles.

Fan A locks 7 then 8; fan B locks 8 then 7: a cycle. PostgreSQL would detect it and abort one transaction after deadlock_timeout, but ordering acquisition removes the cycle altogether.

Q4. When is optimistic locking (version column) a better choice than pessimistic?

  • A. When contention is high, as in the first rows of a flash sale
  • B. When contention is low: most transactions touch different rows, so they never wait and rarely conflict
  • C. Never: it allows double bookings
  • D. Only with SERIALIZABLE isolation
Answer

B — Low contention.

Optimistic locking is correct (it never double-books) but under high contention most attempts fail and must be retried or rejected. Pessimistic locking serializes contended work more gracefully.

Q5. Which request should not be served by the read replica?

  • A. The seat map of section S07 for a fan browsing
  • B. Availability per section on the event page
  • C. GET /inventory/holds/{id} right after the fan created that hold
  • D. A nightly report of sold seats
Answer

C — Read-your-writes.

Replication is asynchronous; the replica may not have the hold yet, and the fan would see a 404 for something they just created. Reads of one's own recent writes go to the primary.

Q6. With REPLICA_DELAY=1s, most fans do not see their own seat as HELD on the seat map. Which consistency guarantee is violated?

  • A. Linearizability of the primary
  • B. Read-your-writes (a session guarantee)
  • C. Durability
  • D. Atomicity
Answer

B — Read-your-writes.

The system is still eventually consistent: after the lag, the replica catches up. Fixes: read from the primary after a write, sticky routing for a short time, or wait for the replica to reach the write's log position.

Q7. What can read replicas not help with?

  • A. Seat-map traffic during the sale
  • B. Reporting queries that would compete with the sale
  • C. The rate of holds (writes) that the primary must process
  • D. Availability of reads if the primary is busy
Answer

C — Writes.

Every write goes to the primary and is then replayed on every replica. Scaling writes needs less work per write, batching, queues in front (lab 7), or partitioning the data across primaries (sharding).

Q8. Why does Flyway connect to db directly while the application goes through PgBouncer?

  • A. PgBouncer cannot run SQL
  • B. In transaction pooling, session state (such as the session-level advisory lock Flyway uses) does not survive between transactions, because each transaction may get a different server connection
  • C. Flyway is slower through PgBouncer
  • D. PgBouncer blocks DDL
Answer

B — Transaction pooling breaks session state.

SET, session advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY and temporary tables assume one server connection per session. Use session pooling or a direct connection for code that needs them.

Q9. What does PgBouncer change when inventory scales from 1 to 10 replicas with 20 connections each?

  • A. Nothing: PostgreSQL still receives 200 connections
  • B. PostgreSQL receives at most default_pool_size server connections; the 200 client connections are multiplexed, and excess clients queue in PgBouncer instead of failing with "too many clients"
  • C. It makes every query faster
  • D. It caches query results
Answer

B — Many cheap client connections, few expensive server ones.

Each PostgreSQL connection is a process with its own memory; thousands of them degrade the database. A pooler bounds them, which matters most with autoscaling (lab 10).

Q10. Before the index, the plan for the listing showed Seq Scan on events + Sort. After CREATE INDEX … (starts_at, id), what changes?

  • A. Nothing, PostgreSQL ignores indexes on timestamps
  • B. PostgreSQL can walk events already ordered by starts_at through the index and stop after 20 matching rows, avoiding reading and sorting 200,000 rows
  • C. The count query becomes free
  • D. Writes become faster
Answer

B — The index provides both filtering and order.

LIMIT + an index in the right order is one of the most effective optimizations there is. The count still visits all matching rows, and every insert/update now also maintains the indexes — indexes are a write-side cost.

Q11. For the flash sale's seat inventory, which design statement is the strongest in an interview?

  • A. "Put seats in Redis with a TTL; it is faster"
  • B. "Seats need strong consistency: a relational database with row locks or conditional updates and a hold TTL; everything around it (catalog, seat maps, search) can be cached and eventually consistent, and a waiting room limits how many fans reach the inventory at once"
  • C. "Use eventual consistency everywhere and refund double bookings"
  • D. "Shard the seats table by seat number"
Answer

B — Strong where it matters, cheap elsewhere.

It names the invariant, the mechanism that enforces it, the expiry of holds, what can relax, and how to protect the hot rows from overload — the core of the ticketing case study.

items.title: Index
items.text: A hold says "these seats are mine for 10 minutes, while I pay". The invariant: a seat belongs to at most one live hold. Everything in this step is about keeping that invariant true when hundreds of fans click the same seats in the same second.

items.title: 1. Why "check, then update" is not enough
items.text:
The obvious code reads the seats, checks they are AVAILABLE, then updates them. Under concurrency, two transactions can interleave:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Fan A (tx 1)
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant B as Fan B (tx 2)
    A->>DB: SELECT status FROM seats WHERE id IN (7,8)
    DB-->>A: AVAILABLE, AVAILABLE
    B->>DB: SELECT status FROM seats WHERE id IN (7,8)
    DB-->>B: AVAILABLE, AVAILABLE
    A->>DB: UPDATE seats SET status='HELD', hold_id=A ...
    B->>DB: UPDATE seats SET status='HELD', hold_id=B ... (waits for A's row locks)
    A->>DB: COMMIT
    DB-->>B: update proceeds — overwrites A's hold
    B->>DB: COMMIT
    Note over A,B: both fans got a 201 for seats 7 and 8: DOUBLE BOOKING

PostgreSQL's default isolation, READ COMMITTED, does not prevent this lost update: each statement sees committed data, but nothing ties B's decision (made on the SELECT) to the data when B writes. Three fixes:

Strategy How On conflict Good when Pessimistic SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the rows until commit; the second transaction waits, then sees HELD 409 after waiting contention is high (the flash sale: everybody wants the same 100 seats) Optimistic read without locks; UPDATE … WHERE version = :v; 0 rows changed → someone was faster 409 immediately, the transaction rolls back contention is low; no waiting, no lock queues Conditional update UPDATE … WHERE id IN (…) AND status = 'AVAILABLE' and check the row count 409 immediately a single statement can express the check (a variant of optimistic) Serializable isolation SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE the database aborts one transaction (40001), the app retries complex invariants over many rows

items.title: 2. The inventory service
items.text:
Create services/inventory (port 8083, schema inventory, same Dockerfile pattern with EXPOSE 8083). It uses JdbcClient with plain SQL instead of JPA: every lock and every WHERE is visible in the code, which is the point of this lab.

V1__create_inventory.sqlV2__seed_seats.sql services/inventory/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_inventory.sql
-- Seats of every event, and the holds that reserve them for a few minutes.
-- event_id refers to catalog.events, but there is NO foreign key across services.
CREATE TABLE inventory.seats (
    id           BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    event_id     BIGINT        NOT NULL,
    section      VARCHAR(10)   NOT NULL,
    seat_row     INTEGER       NOT NULL,
    seat_number  INTEGER       NOT NULL,
    price        NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
    status       VARCHAR(10)   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'AVAILABLE'
                 CHECK (status IN ('AVAILABLE', 'HELD', 'SOLD')),
    hold_id      UUID,
    version      INTEGER       NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,          -- optimistic locking
    UNIQUE (event_id, section, seat_row, seat_number)       -- also the index for "seats of an event"
);

CREATE TABLE inventory.holds (
    id          UUID         PRIMARY KEY,
    event_id    BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    user_id     VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    status      VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE', 'CONFIRMED', 'RELEASED', 'EXPIRED')),
    expires_at  TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- which seats each hold asked for: lets us AUDIT double bookings afterwards
CREATE TABLE inventory.hold_seats (
    hold_id  UUID   NOT NULL REFERENCES inventory.holds (id),
    seat_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES inventory.seats (id),
    PRIMARY KEY (hold_id, seat_id)
);
services/inventory/src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__seed_seats.sql
-- Event 1 (the flash sale): 30 sections x 40 rows x 50 seats = 60,000 seats.
INSERT INTO inventory.seats (event_id, section, seat_row, seat_number, price)
SELECT 1, 'S' || lpad(s::text, 2, '0'), r, n, 250 + (s % 5) * 100
FROM generate_series(1, 30) AS s, generate_series(1, 40) AS r, generate_series(1, 50) AS n
ORDER BY s, r, n;

-- Events 2..100: 5 sections x 10 rows x 10 seats = 500 seats each.
INSERT INTO inventory.seats (event_id, section, seat_row, seat_number, price)
SELECT e, 'S' || lpad(s::text, 2, '0'), r, n, 80 + s * 20
FROM generate_series(2, 100) AS e, generate_series(1, 5) AS s,
     generate_series(1, 10) AS r, generate_series(1, 10) AS n
ORDER BY e, s, r, n;

ANALYZE inventory.seats;

hold_seats records which seats each hold asked for. The seats.hold_id column can be overwritten by a buggy strategy, but hold_seats keeps the evidence: the audit query counts seats that appear in more than one live hold.
