4. Wire it into the gateway
items.text:
Add the route and open the read endpoints (holds stay protected by the default rule):

services/gateway/src/main/resources/application.yaml
server:
  port: 8080

spring:
  application:
    name: gateway
  cloud:
    gateway:
      server:
        webflux:
          httpclient:
            connect-timeout: 1000          # ms to open a connection to a service
            response-timeout: 5s           # never wait forever for a service
          default-filters:
            # retry idempotent GETs once on another instance when a connection fails
            - name: Retry
              args:
                retries: 1
                methods: GET
                series: SERVER_ERROR
                exceptions: java.io.IOException, java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException
          routes:
            - id: auth
              uri: ${AUTH_URL:http://auth:8081}
              predicates:
                - Path=/auth/**
            - id: catalog
              uri: lb://catalog              # "lb": pick one instance of "catalog" per request
              predicates:
                - Path=/catalog/**
            - id: inventory
              uri: ${INVENTORY_URL:http://inventory:8083}
              predicates:
                - Path=/inventory/**
    # the instances behind lb://catalog (a static list; Kubernetes replaces it in lab 10)
    discovery:
      client:
        simple:
          instances:
            catalog:
              - uri: http://catalog-1:8082
              - uri: http://catalog-2:8082
              - uri: http://catalog-3:8082
    loadbalancer:
      configurations: health-check         # skip instances whose /actuator/health is not UP
      health-check:
        interval: 5s
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          jwk-set-uri: ${AUTH_JWKS_URI:http://auth:8081/auth/.well-known/jwks.json}

jwt:
  issuer: ${JWT_ISSUER:boxoffice-auth}
  audience: boxoffice

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health, info, metrics, gateway
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
    gateway:
      access: read-only      # GET /actuator/gateway/routes lists the routes
services/gateway/src/main/java/boxoffice/gateway/SecurityConfig.java
package boxoffice.gateway;

import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.reactive.EnableWebFluxSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.web.server.ServerHttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.core.DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.JwtClaimValidator;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.JwtValidators;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.NimbusReactiveJwtDecoder;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.ReactiveJwtDecoder;
import org.springframework.security.web.server.SecurityWebFilterChain;

@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    /** Which routes are open, which need a valid token, which need the admin scope. */
    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain security(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
        return http
                .csrf(ServerHttpSecurity.CsrfSpec::disable)        // stateless API, no cookies
                .authorizeExchange(ex -> ex
                        // open: getting a token, and the public keys to check one
                        .pathMatchers("/auth/register", "/auth/login", "/auth/.well-known/**").permitAll()
                        // open: browsing the catalog
                        .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/catalog/**").permitAll()
                        // admin only: changing the catalog (scope claim "user admin")
                        .pathMatchers("/catalog/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_admin")
                        // open: seat maps and availability (lab 6); holds need a token
                        .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/inventory/events/**").permitAll()
                        // health, metrics, routes: the edge never forwards /actuator from outside
                        .pathMatchers("/actuator/**").permitAll()
                        // everything else (and every future route): any valid token
                        .anyExchange().authenticated())
                .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
                .build();
    }

    /** Signature from the JWKS of auth, plus expiry, issuer and audience checks. */
    @Bean
    ReactiveJwtDecoder jwtDecoder(@Value("${spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri}") String jwksUri,
                                  @Value("${jwt.issuer}") String issuer,
                                  @Value("${jwt.audience}") String audience) {
        var decoder = NimbusReactiveJwtDecoder.withJwkSetUri(jwksUri).build();
        decoder.setJwtValidator(new DelegatingOAuth2TokenValidator<>(
                JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(issuer),     // exp, nbf, iss
                new JwtClaimValidator<List<String>>("aud", aud -> aud != null && aud.contains(audience))));
        return decoder;
    }
}

The Compose file with inventory, the replica and PgBouncer is in step 2; bring everything up after that step, or now with the full file.

items.title: 5. Check it by hand
items.text:
With the full stack of step 2 running, log in and walk through a hold. All commands from the repository root:

curl -s -X POST localhost/auth/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ana","email":"ana@example.com","password":"secret-123"}'
export TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ana@example.com","password":"secret-123"}' | jq -r .accessToken)
export ADMIN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"admin@boxoffice.dev","password":"boxoffice-admin"}' | jq -r .accessToken)

curl -s localhost/inventory/events/1/availability | jq -c '.[0]'
HOLD=$(curl -s -X POST localhost/inventory/holds -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"eventId":1,"seatIds":[1,2]}')
echo "$HOLD"
export HOLD_ID=$(echo "$HOLD" | jq -r .id)

# the same seat for somebody else, no token, somebody else's hold
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST localhost/inventory/holds -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"eventId":1,"seatIds":[2,3]}'
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST localhost/inventory/holds \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"eventId":1,"seatIds":[5]}'
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" localhost/inventory/holds/$HOLD_ID -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN"

# pay (lab 7 will do this through order) and look again
curl -s -X POST localhost/inventory/holds/$HOLD_ID/confirm -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq -c '{status, seatIds}'
curl -s localhost/inventory/events/1/availability | jq -c '.[0]'
curl -s localhost/inventory/audit/double-bookings -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

You should see (from a run for this lab; ids and times differ):

{"section":"S01","available":2000,"held":0,"sold":0}
{"id":"c869f791-701d-41dd-b82f-d5a6ba48093e","eventId":1,"status":"ACTIVE","expiresAt":"2026-10-18T17:51:50.567788219Z","seatIds":[1,2]}
409
401
404
{"status":"CONFIRMED","seatIds":[1,2]}
{"section":"S01","available":1998,"held":0,"sold":2}
{"doubleBookedSeats":0}

409: seat 2 is already held. 401: holds need a token. 404: a hold of another user does not exist for you. Run bash scripts/reset-inventory.sh afterwards to put the seats back on sale.

items.title: 6. The flash-sale test
Index
items.text: Since lab 1 the catalog listing — upcoming events in a city, soonest first — has been the slow endpoint. Lab 5 hid it behind a cache. Before reaching for more infrastructure, ask the database how it runs the query. Often the cheapest scaling decision of all is an index.

items.title: 1. Read the plan
items.text:
The query generated by findUpcomingInCity (page + count) is equivalent to:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT e.*, v.*
FROM catalog.events e JOIN catalog.venues v ON v.id = e.venue_id
WHERE v.city = 'Recife' AND e.starts_at >= now()
ORDER BY e.starts_at, e.id
LIMIT 20;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT count(*)
FROM catalog.events e JOIN catalog.venues v ON v.id = e.venue_id
WHERE v.city = 'Recife' AND e.starts_at >= now();

docker compose exec db psql -U boxoffice

Before any index, the plan looks like this (from a test run for this lab, abridged; your numbers will differ):

EXPLAIN ANALYZE — before
Limit  (actual time=35.620..36.762 rows=20)
  ->  Gather Merge
        ->  Sort  (Sort Key: e.starts_at, e.id; Sort Method: top-N heapsort)
              ->  Hash Join  (Hash Cond: (e.venue_id = v.id))
                    ->  Parallel Seq Scan on events e  (rows=100000 loops=2)
                    ->  Hash  ->  Seq Scan on venues v  (Filter: city = 'Recife'; rows=5)
Execution Time: 36.802 ms          -- and 13.9 ms more for the count(*)

How to read a plan:

Node Meaning Seq Scan reads every row of the table Index Scan / Index Only Scan walks a B-tree; Only means it never touches the table Hash Join, Nested Loop, Merge Join three ways to join; nested loop is great when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index Sort sorts in memory (or on disk: external merge) — avoidable when an index already delivers the order actual time=a..b rows=n time to the first and to the last row, and real row count; compare with the estimated rows to spot bad statistics

The problem is visible: 200,000 rows are read and sorted to return 20.

items.title: 2. Add the indexes
items.text:
Add a new migration to catalog — never edit V1/V2:

services/catalog/src/main/resources/db/migration/V3__index_events.sql
-- Lab 6: indexes for the listing "upcoming events in a city, soonest first".
-- Walk events in starts_at order and stop after one page, instead of sorting 20,000 rows:
CREATE INDEX events_starts_at_idx ON catalog.events (starts_at, id);
-- Count/filter the events of a city's venues without reading the whole table:
CREATE INDEX events_venue_starts_at_idx ON catalog.events (venue_id, starts_at);
CREATE INDEX venues_city_idx ON catalog.venues (city);

docker compose up --build -d catalog-1 catalog-2 catalog-3      # Flyway applies V3 on startup
docker compose logs catalog-1 | grep "V3\|version \"3"

Run the two EXPLAIN ANALYZE again:

EXPLAIN ANALYZE — after
Limit  (actual time=0.064..0.442 rows=20)
  ->  Nested Loop
        ->  Index Scan using events_starts_at_idx on events e  (rows=189)
        ->  Index Scan using venues_pkey on venues v  (loops=189)
Execution Time: 0.620 ms

Aggregate  (actual time=4.006..4.006 rows=1)
  ->  Nested Loop
        ->  Seq Scan on venues v  (rows=5)
        ->  Index Only Scan using events_venue_starts_at_idx on events e  (rows=4000 loops=5)
Execution Time: 4.028 ms

With events_starts_at_idx, PostgreSQL walks the events already in date order and stops as soon as it has 20 from Recife (it read 189 index entries instead of 200,000 rows): the page query drops from ~37 ms to well under 1 ms. The count still visits every event of the city, but through the smaller (venue_id, starts_at) index, without touching the table (Index Only Scan): ~14 ms → ~4 ms.

Indexes are not free

Every index is updated on every insert and update of the table, takes disk and memory, and can make the planner choose badly when statistics are stale. On a write-heavy table (seats during the sale!) each extra index slows the critical path. Index for the queries you measured, not for every column. On a large production table, use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (outside a transaction) to avoid blocking writes while it builds.

items.title: 3. Measure it
items.text:
Turn the cache off so that every request reaches PostgreSQL, and repeat the lab 2/3 sweep through the edge:

CACHE_ENABLED=false docker compose up -d catalog-1 catalog-2 catalog-3 && sleep 30
BASE_URL=http://localhost OUT=results/lab6-index bash scripts/sweep.sh 300 600 900 1200 1500
uv run scripts/summarize.py results/lab6-index/rate-*.json

Compare with the no-cache numbers of lab 3. Then turn the cache back on and decide, with numbers, what the listing really needed.

Think first: the count query still reads 20,000 index entries per request. What would you do about it?

Options, from cheapest: cache the count separately with a longer TTL (it changes slowly); return an estimate ("20,000+"); drop it and return only hasNext (a Slice instead of a Page); or maintain a counter per city updated on writes. Each trades exactness for cost — a product decision as much as a technical one.

In the interview

When a query is slow, the order is: measure (which query, how often), explain (what plan), fix the access path (index, rewrite, denormalize), and only then add infrastructure (cache, replica, shard). Interviewers like to hear that you would not cache a query you have not explained.

Back to the lab overview to record the results.

items.title: Index
items.text: During the sale, for every fan who holds a seat, dozens look at the seat map. Those reads do not need the primary: a read replica — a copy of the database kept up to date by streaming the primary's write-ahead log (WAL) — can serve them. Two costs come with it: the copy is slightly behind (replication lag), and you now route queries to two places. This step also adds PgBouncer, because every replica of every service opening its own pool of connections is how PostgreSQL runs out of connections.

items.title: 1. Streaming replication
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant I as inventory
    participant P as db (primary)
    participant R as db-replica (hot standby)
    Note over R: first start: pg_basebackup copies the primary
    I->>P: BEGIN; UPDATE seats ...; COMMIT
    P->>P: write WAL record, flush
    P-->>I: COMMIT ok (asynchronous replication: does not wait for R)
    P->>R: stream WAL
    R->>R: replay (after recovery_min_apply_delay)
    I->>R: SELECT availability (readOnly tx)
    R-->>I: result, possibly a few ms old

The primary needs a user allowed to replicate. This script runs once, when the primary's volume is created:

infra/postgres/10-replication.sh
#!/bin/bash
# Runs once, when the primary's data directory is created (docker-entrypoint-initdb.d).
# Creates the user the replica connects with and allows replication connections.
set -e
psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 --username "$POSTGRES_USER" --dbname "$POSTGRES_DB" <<-SQL
    CREATE ROLE replicator WITH REPLICATION LOGIN PASSWORD '${REPLICATION_PASSWORD:-replicator}';
SQL
echo "host replication replicator all scram-sha-256" >> "$PGDATA/pg_hba.conf"

The replica clones the primary on its first start and then follows it:

infra/postgres/replica-entrypoint.sh
#!/bin/bash
# Starts a streaming replica of "db". The first time, it clones the primary with
# pg_basebackup; -R writes standby.signal + primary_conninfo, so PostgreSQL starts
# as a read-only hot standby that keeps applying the primary's WAL.
set -e
if [ ! -s "$PGDATA/PG_VERSION" ]; then
  echo "cloning the primary..."
  until pg_basebackup -h db -U replicator -D "$PGDATA" -R -X stream -P; do
    echo "primary not ready yet, retrying in 2 s"; sleep 2
  done
  chmod 0700 "$PGDATA"
fi
# REPLICA_DELAY (e.g. 2s) makes the replica apply changes late: replication lag on demand
exec postgres -c hot_standby=on -c recovery_min_apply_delay="${REPLICA_DELAY:-0}"

Recreate the database volume

10-replication.sh only runs on an empty data directory. Your db-data volume exists since lab 1, so recreate it (Flyway seeds everything again on startup): docker compose down -v before the first up of this lab. Remember to chmod +x infra/postgres/*.sh.

items.title: 2. PgBouncer
items.text:
Each PostgreSQL connection is an operating-system process with its own memory; a few hundred are fine, thousands are not. Count the clients: 3 catalog replicas × 10 + auth × 10 + inventory × 20 × 2 pools… and in lab 10 Kubernetes will autoscale replicas. PgBouncer accepts many cheap client connections and multiplexes them onto a small pool of real ones.

infra/pgbouncer/pgbouncer.ini
; PgBouncer: thousands of client connections, a few dozen real PostgreSQL connections.
[databases]
boxoffice = host=db port=5432 dbname=boxoffice

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt
admin_users = boxoffice

; transaction pooling: a server connection is lent for ONE transaction, then returned
pool_mode = transaction
; real connections to PostgreSQL per (database, user) pair
default_pool_size = 20
; client connections PgBouncer accepts (all services and replicas together)
max_client_conn = 1000
; protocol-level prepared statements work in transaction mode (PgBouncer >= 1.21)
max_prepared_statements = 200
ignore_startup_parameters = extra_float_digits,options
infra/pgbouncer/userlist.txt
"boxoffice" "boxoffice"
Pool mode A server connection is lent for… Breaks session the whole client connection nothing, but saves little transaction one transaction session state: SET, session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables statement one statement multi-statement transactions

Transaction pooling is what makes PgBouncer effective — and why Flyway does not go through it: migrations use session-level locks. inventory therefore has two hosts: DB_HOST=pgbouncer for the application, DB_MIGRATION_HOST=db for Flyway.

items.title: 3. Compose
items.text:
docker-compose.yaml
name: boxoffice

# settings shared by the three catalog replicas (a YAML anchor)
x-catalog: &catalog
  build: ./services/catalog
  image: boxoffice-catalog
  environment:
    DB_HOST: db
    DB_PORT: 5432
    DB_NAME: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
    DB_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
    DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
    DB_POOL_SIZE: ${DB_POOL_SIZE:-10}
    REDIS_HOST: redis
    REDIS_PORT: 6379
    CACHE_ENABLED: ${CACHE_ENABLED:-true}
    CACHE_TTL_EVENT: ${CACHE_TTL_EVENT:-60s}
    CACHE_TTL_LIST: ${CACHE_TTL_LIST:-10s}
    CACHE_STAMPEDE_PROTECTION: ${CACHE_STAMPEDE_PROTECTION:-false}
  depends_on:
    db:
      condition: service_healthy
    redis:
      condition: service_healthy
  deploy:

        cpus: "1.0"

  healthcheck:

    interval: 10s

    retries: 3

services:

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    command: ["postgres", "-c", "max_connections=${DB_MAX_CONNECTIONS:-100}"]
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
      REPLICATION_PASSWORD: ${REPLICATION_PASSWORD:-replicator}

      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  # read-only streaming replica of db (hot standby)
  db-replica:
    image: postgres:17
    user: postgres
    entrypoint: ["/usr/local/bin/replica-entrypoint.sh"]
    environment:
      PGPASSWORD: ${REPLICATION_PASSWORD:-replicator}     # used by pg_basebackup
      REPLICA_DELAY: ${REPLICA_DELAY:-0}                   # e.g. 2s: artificial lag
    ports:
      - "5433:5432"
    volumes:
      - replica-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./infra/postgres/replica-entrypoint.sh:/usr/local/bin/replica-entrypoint.sh:ro
    depends_on:

              "--save", "", "--appendonly", "no"]
    ports:

    healthcheck:

chmod +x infra/postgres/*.sh
docker compose down -v
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose exec db psql -U boxoffice -c "SELECT client_addr, state, sent_lsn, replay_lsn FROM pg_stat_replication"
docker compose exec db-replica psql -U boxoffice -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(), now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS lag"

The lag column is the time since the replica replayed the last transaction: while the primary is idle it keeps growing even though the replica is fully up to date. Compare sent_lsn and replay_lsn on the primary for the real distance.

docker compose exec db psql -U boxoffice -c "SELECT client_addr, state FROM pg_stat_replication" client_addr | state-------------+----------- 172.22.0.4 | streamingdocker compose exec db-replica psql -U boxoffice -c "INSERT INTO inventory.holds VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), 1, 'x', 'ACTIVE', now(), now())"ERROR: cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction

items.title: 4. Routing reads to the replica
5. Experiments
items.text:
Replica offload. Run the read load against the replica, then point the "replica" pool at the primary and run it again — no code change:

load/availability.js
// Lab 6: read traffic on the seat map during the sale. These GETs are readOnly
// transactions, so they run on the replica (or on the primary, if you point
// DB_REPLICA_HOST at it to compare).
//   k6 run -e RATE=200 load/availability.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { BASE_URL } from './lib.js';

const RATE = Number(__ENV.RATE || 200);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    readers: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', rate: RATE, timeUnit: '1s', duration: __ENV.DURATION || '1m',
      preAllocatedVUs: Math.max(20, RATE), maxVUs: Math.max(200, RATE * 10),
    },
  },
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'med', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
    'http_req_duration{name:availability}': ['p(99)<1000'],
    'http_req_duration{name:section}': ['p(99)<1000'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  if (Math.random() < 0.5) {
    const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/inventory/events/1/availability`, { tags: { name: 'availability' } });
    check(res, { 'availability is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  } else {
    const section = `S${String(1 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 30)).padStart(2, '0')}`;
    const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/inventory/events/1/seats?section=${section}`, { tags: { name: 'section' } });
    check(res, { 'section is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  }
}

k6 run -e RATE=200 load/availability.js                     # reads on db-replica
DB_REPLICA_HOST=db docker compose up -d inventory && sleep 25
k6 run -e RATE=200 load/availability.js                     # reads on the primary
docker compose up -d inventory                              # back to the replica

Keep docker stats open: the CPU moves from db to db-replica. The seat-map latency barely changes — a replica does not make a query faster, it adds capacity and keeps reads from competing with the writes of the sale.

Read-your-writes. A fan holds a seat and immediately reloads the seat map, served by the replica:

load/read-your-writes.js
// Lab 6: hold a seat, then immediately look at the seat map (served by the replica).
// Does the fan see their own seat as HELD? With replication lag, sometimes not.
//   REPLICA_DELAY=1s docker compose up -d db-replica   (artificial lag)
//   bash scripts/reset-inventory.sh && k6 run load/read-your-writes.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { Rate } from 'k6/metrics';
import { BASE_URL, loginFans, authHeaders } from './lib.js';

http.setResponseCallback(http.expectedStatuses(200, 201, 204, 409));

const stale = new Rate('stale_reads');

export const options = {
  vus: 10,
  iterations: 200,
  thresholds: { stale_reads: ['rate>=0'] },
};

export function setup() {
  const seats = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/inventory/events/2/seats?section=S01`).json();
  return { tokens: loginFans(10), seatIds: seats.map((s) => s.id) };
}

export default function (data) {
  const token = data.tokens[__VU % data.tokens.length];
  const seatId = data.seatIds[Math.floor(Math.random() * data.seatIds.length)];
  const hold = http.post(`${BASE_URL}/inventory/holds`, JSON.stringify({ eventId: 2, seatIds: [seatId] }), authHeaders(token));
  if (hold.status !== 201) {
    return;                                          // seat already taken: try another one
  }
  // read-after-write: the seat map comes from the replica
  const map = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/inventory/events/2/seats?section=S01`).json();
  const seat = map.find((s) => s.id === seatId);
  stale.add(seat.status !== 'HELD');
  check(seat, { 'my seat shows as HELD': (s) => s.status === 'HELD' });
  // and from the primary (GET /holds/{id} is not readOnly): always up to date
  const mine = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/inventory/holds/${hold.json('id')}`, authHeaders(token));
  check(mine, { 'my hold is visible on the primary': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  http.del(`${BASE_URL}/inventory/holds/${hold.json('id')}`, null, authHeaders(token));
}

bash scripts/reset-inventory.sh && k6 run load/read-your-writes.js    # lag ~ milliseconds
REPLICA_DELAY=1s docker compose up -d db-replica && sleep 10
bash scripts/reset-inventory.sh && k6 run load/read-your-writes.js    # lag of 1 second
REPLICA_DELAY=0 docker compose up -d db-replica

Even with no artificial delay, stale_reads is not zero: in a test run for this lab it was about 6% — the replica on the same machine is only milliseconds behind, but the fan's next request arrives within milliseconds too. With REPLICA_DELAY=1s it was 98%: almost no fan saw their own hold on the seat map, although GET /inventory/holds/{id} (primary) shows it. In production, lag grows with write volume, network distance and long queries on the replica — exactly during a flash sale.

Ways out: read your own recent writes from the primary (what find does), route a user to the primary for a few seconds after they write ("sticky" reads), or wait until the replica has replayed the write's LSN (log sequence number).

PgBouncer. Count connections during the flash sale, with and without the pooler:

# during load/flash-sale.js:
docker compose exec db psql -U boxoffice -c "SELECT usename, application_name, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1, 2"
docker compose exec -e PGPASSWORD=boxoffice db psql -h pgbouncer -p 6432 -U boxoffice pgbouncer -c "SHOW POOLS"

# without PgBouncer:
INVENTORY_DB_HOST=db INVENTORY_DB_PORT=5432 docker compose up -d inventory

In a test run for this lab, pg_stat_activity showed about 60 application connections: 30 from the three catalog replicas, 10 from auth, and 20 from PgBouncer — which served all of inventory's client connections. SHOW POOLS showed cl_active 20 against sv_active + sv_idle + sv_used ≤ 20.

Push it: restart with DB_MAX_CONNECTIONS=80 INVENTORY_POOL_SIZE=40 docker compose up -d. Through PgBouncer everything works (PostgreSQL still sees at most 20 connections from it). Directly against db (INVENTORY_DB_HOST=db INVENTORY_DB_PORT=5432), 30 + 10 + 40 connections plus the reserved superuser slots exceed 80, and inventory fails with FATAL: sorry, too many clients already. A pooler turns "too many clients" into queueing (cl_waiting).

In the interview

"Add read replicas" is only an answer for read-heavy load that tolerates staleness. Say which reads go to replicas, how you handle read-your-writes, and what happens to writes — replicas do nothing for them; that needs partitioning (class 6) or less work per write.

Next: 3. Indexes and EXPLAIN.

items.title: 7. Async Messaging
items.text:
Goal

Take the slow, fragile work out of BoxOffice's request path. The order service records each order and an OrderPlaced event in the same database transaction (transactional outbox); a relay publishes the event to Kafka; the notification service consumes it idempotently, sends the e-mail and parks poison messages in a dead-letter topic. Finally, a waiting room queues the flash-sale crowd so that only as many fans enter as the system can serve.

It is 10:00 and the stadium show goes on sale. Every POST /orders that the order service accepts must also produce a confirmation e-mail. If order calls notification over HTTP, the fan waits for the e-mail provider, an e-mail outage becomes an ordering outage, and the 2 million fans who arrive at the same second hit every service at once. This lab replaces that coupling with three ideas from the messaging class: events on a log, at-least-once delivery handled with idempotency, and queues that absorb a spike.

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
Before (synchronous)After (events) 
flowchart LR
    fan[Fan] -->|POST /orders| gw[gateway]
    gw --> order[order]
    order -->|INSERT order| db[(PostgreSQL)]
    order -->|"POST /notifications (waits)"| notification[notification]
    notification -->|SMTP| mail[mailpit]
    notification -->|201 after the e-mail| order
    order -->|201| gw
flowchart LR
    fan[Fan] -->|join| wr[waiting room]
    wr -->|admitted| gw[gateway]
    gw -->|POST /orders| order[order]
    order -->|"INSERT order + outbox (1 tx)"| db[(PostgreSQL)]
    order -->|201 right away| gw
    relay[outbox relay] -->|poll unpublished| db
    relay -->|publish OrderPlaced| kafka[(Kafka: order-events)]
    kafka -->|consumer group notification| notification[notification]
    notification -->|"processed_events (dedupe)"| ndb[(PostgreSQL)]
    notification -->|SMTP| mail[mailpit]
    notification -.->|after 3 failed retries| dlt[(order-events-dlt)]

The fan's request now ends at the database commit. Everything after the commit — publishing, e-mail, retries — happens asynchronously and can be slow, fail or be repeated without the fan noticing.

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Kafka basics
items.text:
Q1. The notification consumer group runs 8 instances on the 6-partition topic order-events. How many instances receive messages?

  • A. 8 — Kafka balances messages round-robin across all members
  • B. 6 — each partition is assigned to one member of the group; 2 instances stay idle
  • C. 1 — a consumer group always has a single active reader
  • D. 48 — every instance reads every partition
Answer

B — 6 active, 2 idle.

Inside a consumer group, a partition is consumed by at most one member at a time; this is how Kafka keeps per-partition order. The number of partitions is therefore the ceiling of the group's parallelism. The idle instances are not useless: they take over partitions when an active member fails.

Q2. The outbox relay publishes each event with key = orderId. What does the key guarantee?

  • A. That each event is delivered exactly once
  • B. That events of the same order go to the same partition and are therefore read in the order they were written
  • C. That the event is encrypted with the key
  • D. That events of different orders never share a partition
Answer

B — same key → same partition → per-key ordering.

The default partitioner hashes the key modulo the number of partitions. Kafka only guarantees order within a partition, so keying by aggregate id gives ordering per order, which is what the consumers need. Different keys can share a partition (D is false), and the key has nothing to do with delivery semantics or encryption.

Q3. A consumer group reads order-events. kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe shows, for partition 2, CURRENT-OFFSET 1200 and LOG-END-OFFSET 1500. What is the lag, and what does it mean?

  • A. 2 700; the broker has 2 700 messages in memory
  • B. 300; the group still has 300 messages of that partition to process
  • C. 1 200; the group processed 1 200 messages since it started
  • D. 300; 300 messages were lost
Answer

B — lag = log-end offset − committed offset = 300 messages still to process.

Lag is the distance between the newest message in the partition and the group's committed position. It is the main health signal of a consumer: growing lag means arrivals exceed the consumer's capacity. Nothing is lost — Kafka keeps the messages for the retention period whether they were read or not.

items.title: Outbox and idempotency
items.text:
Q4. Why can't the order service simply save the order and then call kafkaTemplate.send(...) in the same method?

  • A. Spring does not allow Kafka calls inside a @Transactional method
  • B. Kafka is slower than PostgreSQL
  • C. The two writes go to different systems with no shared transaction: a crash between them stores an order without its event (or publishes an event for an order that was rolled back)
  • D. Kafka requires events to be published from a separate service
Answer

C — the dual-write problem.

PostgreSQL cannot roll back a Kafka publish, and Kafka cannot roll back a database commit. Whatever the order of the two writes, a crash, deploy or timeout between them leaves the systems inconsistent. The transactional outbox writes the event into the same database transaction as the order; a relay publishes it afterwards, retrying until Kafka acknowledges.

Q5. The relay sends a batch, Kafka acknowledges, and the process crashes before UPDATE outbox SET published_at = ... commits. What happens?

  • A. The events are lost
  • B. The events are published again on the next run; consumers see duplicates and must be idempotent
  • C. Kafka detects the duplicate and drops it, because enable.idempotence=true
  • D. The database rolls back the orders too
Answer

B — republished: the outbox is at-least-once.

The rows are still unpublished, so the next run (or another replica) sends them again. Producer idempotence (C) only deduplicates retries within one producer session; after a crash the new producer has a new identity. That is why every event carries an eventId and the consumer deduplicates on it.

Q6. The relay query ends with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. What problem does SKIP LOCKED solve?

  • A. It skips events that failed to serialize
  • B. It lets several order replicas run the relay concurrently: each locks a different set of rows instead of waiting for (or duplicating) the others' rows
  • C. It avoids locking the orders table during inserts
  • D. It makes the query faster by skipping the index
Answer

B — concurrent relays take disjoint batches.

FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows until the transaction ends; SKIP LOCKED makes another transaction skip rows that are already locked instead of blocking on them. Each replica takes a different batch, so the work is shared without double publishing. The same idiom implements job queues in PostgreSQL.

Q7. In NotificationService.handle, the dedupe insert into processed_events and the e-mail send are inside one transaction, in this order. Which failure can still produce a duplicate e-mail?

  • A. The consumer receives the same event twice in a row
  • B. Two consumer instances receive the same event at the same time
  • C. The e-mail is sent, then the database commit fails; the redelivered event is processed again
  • D. The event is malformed JSON
Answer

C — the effect succeeded but the record of it did not.

A and B are handled: the primary key on event_id lets only one transaction claim the event, and later deliveries find it claimed. But the e-mail is an external side effect that the database cannot roll back. If the commit fails after the send, the claim disappears and a retry sends again. The complete fix is an idempotency key accepted by the provider (pass the eventId).

Q8. POST /orders uses INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (hold_id) DO NOTHING. A fan double-clicks "Buy". What happens?

  • A. Two orders are created for the same seats
  • B. The second request fails with a 500 because of the unique violation
  • C. The second request finds the hold already ordered, returns the same order with 200 OK, and writes no second event
  • D. The second request waits until the first e-mail is sent
Answer

C — the unique hold_id makes the request idempotent.

The natural key of the operation (one hold → one order) becomes a unique constraint. PostgreSQL serializes the two inserts: the second one skips, the service reads the existing row and returns it. No duplicate order, no duplicate event — idempotency at the API, not only at the consumer.

items.title: Errors and the DLT
items.text:
Q9. A message on partition 3 makes the listener throw a transient MailSendException every time, and the error handler is configured with 3 retries and exponential backoff (0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s). What happens to the other messages?

  • A. All partitions stop until an operator intervenes
  • B. Messages behind it on partition 3 wait about 3.5 s; other partitions keep flowing; then the record goes to order-events-dlt and partition 3 resumes
  • C. The record is skipped silently after the first failure
  • D. Kafka moves the record to the end of the partition and tries later
Answer

B — blocking retries delay only that partition, then the DLT unblocks it.

DefaultErrorHandler retries in place, so ordering is kept and only the affected partition waits. After the retries, DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer publishes the record (with exception headers) to the DLT and the offset is committed. Kafka never reorders a partition (D).

Q10. Why are JacksonException and IllegalArgumentException registered as not retryable?

  • A. Because Spring Kafka cannot retry checked exceptions
  • B. Because they signal permanent failures: a malformed payload or a rejected address will fail on every attempt, so retrying only delays the partition
  • C. To make the consumer faster in the happy path
  • D. Because the DLT only accepts these exception types
Answer

B — classify errors: transient → retry, permanent → dead-letter now.

Retrying a poison message wastes the backoff time and blocks the partition for nothing. Classifying exceptions is the core design decision of any consumer: timeouts and 5xx from dependencies are transient; validation and parsing errors are permanent.

items.title: Waiting room and capacity
items.text:
Q11. The waiting room admits 500 fans per second. A fan joins and is at position 45 000. What ETA should the page show, and which law justifies it?

  • A. 9 s — position × rate
  • B. 90 s — Little's Law: wait = queue length / throughput
  • C. 45 s — one second per thousand fans
  • D. It cannot be estimated
Answer

B — 45 000 / 500 = 90 s.

Little's Law, L = λ·W, rearranged as W = L / λ: with a constant admission rate the queue drains at λ, so the wait is the position divided by the rate. The k6 experiment E checks this promise against the measured wait (wr_eta_error_seconds).

Q12. With EMAIL_LATENCY=50ms and NOTIFY_CONCURRENCY=1, orders arrive at 100 per second for 60 s. Approximately what is the consumer lag at the end of the burst, and how long does it take to drain?

  • A. 0 messages; Kafka absorbs the burst
  • B. ≈ 4 800 messages; ≈ 240 s
  • C. ≈ 6 000 messages; ≈ 60 s
  • D. ≈ 1 200 messages; ≈ 12 s
Answer

B — capacity 20/s, arrivals 100/s.

One thread at 50 ms per e-mail handles 20 messages/s. The backlog grows at 100 − 20 = 80/s, reaching ≈ 4 800 after 60 s, and drains at 20/s after the burst: 4 800 / 20 = 240 s. With 6 threads (120/s) the lag stays near zero; a seventh thread would be idle, since the topic has 6 partitions.

Q13. The waiting room's admitter is a @Scheduled method in order. You scale order to 3 replicas. What goes wrong, and what is a fix?

  • A. Nothing; Redis serializes the pops
  • B. Each replica admits N fans per second, so the real admission rate triples; run the admitter in a single instance (worker, leader election or a distributed lock)
  • C. Fans lose their position in the queue
  • D. The queue is split into three independent queues
Answer

B — three schedulers, three times the rate.

ZPOPMIN is atomic, so no fan is admitted twice, but every replica pops its own N per second. The admission rate is the capacity knob of the whole on-sale, so it must be enforced once: a dedicated worker, a leader-elected scheduler, or a distributed lock such as ShedLock.

Back to the lab

items.title: 3. Idempotent Consumer and DLT
items.text:
Kafka and the outbox both deliver at least once: a relay that crashes after the ack republishes a batch; a consumer that crashes after sending the e-mail but before committing its offset receives the message again; an operator who rewinds a consumer group replays hours of events. The notification service must therefore make a duplicate harmless, and it must not let one bad message stop the whole partition.

Problem Technique Where in the code the same event arrives twice idempotent consumer: remember processed eventIds, in the same transaction as the effect NotificationService a transient failure (SMTP hiccup) retry with exponential backoff, in place KafkaConfig a message that can never succeed (malformed, invalid address) dead-letter topic (DLT): park it, keep the partition flowing KafkaConfig, DeadLetterListener

items.title: Experiment: replay without duplicates
items.text:
Rewind the whole group and let it consume everything again:

docker compose stop notification
docker compose exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 \
  --group notification --topic order-events --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute
docker compose start notification
docker compose logs notification | grep duplicate
curl -s localhost:8025/api/v1/messages | jq '.total'

The logs show duplicate event ... ignored for each order and Mailpit still has 2 e-mails. Repeat with NOTIFY_IDEMPOTENT=false docker compose up -d notification and count again: every replay sends every e-mail again.

items.title: Experiment: a poison order
items.text:
curl -s -X POST localhost:8084/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"showId":"show-42","holdId":"hold-0003","customerEmail":"poison@example.com","amount":350.00}'
docker compose exec db psql -U boxoffice -d boxoffice \
  -c "SELECT topic, partition, record_offset, reason FROM notification.dead_letters;"

The order succeeds (the fan is not affected), the e-mail fails permanently, and the record lands in order-events-dlt; open it in Kafka UI and look at the kafka_dlt-* headers (original topic, partition, offset, exception).

A DLT nobody reads is a silent data loss

Every dead letter is a customer who did not get an e-mail. In production: alert on DLT growth (lab 8), fix the cause, then replay the records back to order-events (a small tool or kafka-console-consumer | kafka-console-producer with the original keys). Replay is safe precisely because the consumer is idempotent.

items.title: Kafka in KRaft mode
items.text:
Kafka keeps its own metadata (topics, partitions, leaders) in a Raft quorum of controllers — KRaft. ZooKeeper is gone since Kafka 4.0. Here a single node plays both roles, broker,controller. This is the new part of docker-compose.yaml:

docker-compose.yaml (excerpt)
  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:4.3.1
    hostname: kafka
    ports:
      - "9094:9094"
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://:9092,CONTROLLER://:9093,EXTERNAL://:9094
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://kafka:9092,EXTERNAL://localhost:9094
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT,EXTERNAL:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1
      KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: 0
      KAFKA_AUTO_CREATE_TOPICS_ENABLE: "false"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-broker-api-versions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 > /dev/null 2>&1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 10s
      start_period: 60s      # a busy laptop can take a minute to start the broker
      retries: 20

  kafka-init:
    image: apache/kafka:4.3.1
    depends_on:
      kafka:
        condition: service_healthy
    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    command:
      - |
        /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --create --if-not-exists \
          --topic order-events --partitions 6 --replication-factor 1 &&
        /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --create --if-not-exists \
          --topic order-events-dlt --partitions 6 --replication-factor 1
    restart: "no"

  kafka-ui:
    image: kafbat/kafka-ui:v1.5.0
    depends_on:
      kafka:
        condition: service_healthy
    ports:
      - "8089:8080"
    environment:
      KAFKA_CLUSTERS_0_NAME: boxoffice
      KAFKA_CLUSTERS_0_BOOTSTRAPSERVERS: kafka:9092

  mailpit:
    image: axllent/mailpit:v1.31
    ports:
      - "8025:8025"
      - "1025:1025"

Get the complete file

Run from the root of your boxoffice repository (it replaces the lab 6 version; keep a copy if you changed it):

cp docker-compose.yaml docker-compose.lab6.yaml
curl -fsSL -o docker-compose.yaml https://insper.github.io/platform/2027.1/hands-on/7/code/docker-compose.yaml
docker compose config --services

You should see the lab 6 services plus kafka, kafka-init, kafka-ui, mailpit, order and notification. order and notification are built in steps 2 and 3; until then, start only the services named in each command. Delete docker-compose.lab6.yaml before you commit: Git already keeps the lab 6 version (git show lab6:docker-compose.yaml).

    healthcheck:

  auth:

  mailpit:

  order:
    build: ./services/order
    environment:

      DB_PORT: 5432

      DB_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
      DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: kafka:9092
      NOTIFICATION_URL: http://notification:8086
      NOTIFY_MODE: ${NOTIFY_MODE:-outbox}            # outbox (after) | sync (before)
      ADMIT_PER_SECOND: ${ADMIT_PER_SECOND:-20}      # waiting-room admission rate
    ports:
      - "8084:8084"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy

  notification:
    build: ./services/notification
    environment:

      DB_PORT: 5432

      DB_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
      DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
      KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: kafka:9092
      MAIL_HOST: mailpit
      NOTIFY_CONCURRENCY: ${NOTIFY_CONCURRENCY:-3}   # consumer threads (max useful: 6 partitions)
      EMAIL_LATENCY: ${EMAIL_LATENCY:-50ms}          # simulated e-mail provider latency
      NOTIFY_IDEMPOTENT: ${NOTIFY_IDEMPOTENT:-true}  # false = no dedupe (to see duplicates)
    ports:
      - "8086:8086"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      mailpit:
        condition: service_started
      kafka-init:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 768M
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -qO- http://localhost:8086/actuator/health/readiness || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 40s
      retries: 3

volumes:
  db-data:
  replica-data:

Three details matter:

  • Two client listeners. Containers reach the broker as kafka:9092 (PLAINTEXT). A program on your laptop (an IDE run, a CLI) uses localhost:9094 (EXTERNAL). A client first connects to any address, then receives the advertised address of each partition leader and reconnects there — so each listener must advertise a name that its clients can resolve. Mixing them up is the classic "connects, then times out" bug. That is why Kafka is the one exception to the "same port inside and outside" rule of lab 0: services use kafka:9092, your machine uses localhost:9094.
  • Topics are created explicitly (KAFKA_AUTO_CREATE_TOPICS_ENABLE: "false"). Auto-creation uses the broker default of 1 partition, which would silently cap the consumer parallelism at 1.
  • The dead-letter topic has as many partitions as the main topic: Spring's dead-letter publisher writes a failed record to the same partition number in order-events-dlt.

Why 6 partitions?

A partition is consumed by at most one consumer of a group at a time, so the number of partitions is the ceiling of consumer parallelism. Six lets the notification group grow to six consumers. Partitions are cheap to start with and painful to add later: adding partitions changes which partition a key maps to, breaking per-key ordering for keys already in flight.

items.title: A five-minute tour of the log
items.text:
Before Spring hides it, feel how a log differs from a queue. Open two terminals.

In terminal A, start a consumer in group tour:

docker compose exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh \
  --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --topic order-events --group tour \
  --formatter-property print.key=true --formatter-property print.partition=true

In terminal B, produce three keyed messages (key:value):

docker compose exec -T kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh \
  --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --topic order-events \
  --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=: <<'EOF'
order-1:{"hello":"first"}
order-2:{"hello":"second"}
order-1:{"hello":"third"}
EOF

Terminal A prints each message with its partition, for example:

Partition:4 order-1 {"hello":"first"}
Partition:3 order-2 {"hello":"second"}
Partition:4 order-1 {"hello":"third"}

Both order-1 messages land on the same partition — the default partitioner hashes the key (murmur2) modulo the number of partitions — and that is the only ordering Kafka promises: per partition, hence per key.

Now stop the consumer (Ctrl+C) and look at the group:

docker compose exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --group tourConsumer group 'tour' has no active members.GROUP TOPIC PARTITION CURRENT-OFFSET LOG-END-OFFSET LAG CONSUMER-ID HOST CLIENT-IDtour order-events 0 0 0 0 - - -tour order-events 1 0 0 0 - - -tour order-events 2 0 0 0 - - -tour order-events 3 1 1 0 - - -tour order-events 4 2 2 0 - - -tour order-events 5 0 0 0 - - -

The messages are still in the log: consuming does not delete. Each group only stores its offset per partition (CURRENT-OFFSET), and lag = LOG-END-OFFSET − CURRENT-OFFSET is how far behind it is. Rewind the group and read everything again:

docker compose exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 \
  --group tour --topic order-events --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute

That replay ability is what makes Kafka a good backbone for new consumers (analytics can read the whole history) — and also why every consumer must tolerate seeing a message twice.

Keep the tour messages

The three test messages are not valid BoxOffice events. They will be useful later: in step 3 they are exactly the kind of poison message the consumer must survive. Leave them there.

Think first: a consumer group with 8 instances on a 6-partition topic

How many instances receive messages? What do the other ones do?

Six. Each partition is assigned to one member of the group, so two instances stay idle (they take over if another member dies). To use more consumers, the topic needs more partitions.

Next: Transactional outbox

items.title: 5. Measure It
items.text:
Five experiments, one results table. Run each experiment at least twice and report the second run (the first one warms up the JVMs and the connection pools). The numbers in the "expected shape" boxes are illustrative — what matters is that you can explain your numbers.

# Experiment Knob What you record A sync vs outbox NOTIFY_MODE POST /orders p50 / p95 / p99 B notification outage stop the container mid-test error rate, lag peak, time to drain C burst and drain NOTIFY_CONCURRENCY 1 vs 6 lag over time, drain time, e-mail delay p95 D replay NOTIFY_IDEMPOTENT e-mails per order after an offset reset E flash-sale spike waiting room open, ADMIT_PER_SECOND=10 admitted/s, wait p95, ETA error, order p95

items.title: The k6 scripts
A. Sync vs outbox
items.text:
NOTIFY_MODE=sync docker compose up -d order        # "before"
k6 run --summary-trend-stats="avg,p(50),p(95),p(99),max" load/orders-load.js
NOTIFY_MODE=outbox docker compose up -d order      # "after"
k6 run --summary-trend-stats="avg,p(50),p(95),p(99),max" load/orders-load.js

The variables reach the containers because docker-compose.yaml interpolates them (NOTIFY_MODE: ${NOTIFY_MODE:-outbox}), as written in steps 2 and 3.

Expected shape (illustrative)

With EMAIL_LATENCY=50ms on an idle machine, the synchronous p50 sits a little above 50 ms — the fan pays for the e-mail on every order — while the outbox version answers in a few milliseconds (two inserts and a commit). On a busy laptop (the whole lab 7 stack plus other containers, load average above 10 on 8 cores) one test run gave:

50 orders/s for 30 s p50 p95 p99 throughput NOTIFY_MODE=sync 4.12 s 8.14 s 11.51 s 38.7/s (k6 could not keep the rate) NOTIFY_MODE=outbox 47 ms 658 ms 1.29 s 49.5/s

The absolute numbers depend on your machine; the ratio is the lesson: when the e-mail is in the request path, every order waits for it and the service saturates far earlier. If even the outbox version is slow for you, close other containers (docker ps) and run again.

items.title: B. notification outage
items.text:
Run the load for 60 s and, in another terminal, kill notification for 20 s in the middle:

sleep 20; docker compose stop notification; sleep 20; docker compose start notification

Do it once per mode, with sh scripts/kafka-lag.sh running in a third terminal. In sync mode, about a third of the orders fail — an e-mail outage became an ordering outage. In outbox mode no order fails; the lag climbs while notification is down and drains after it comes back.

items.title: C. Burst and drain
items.text:
NOTIFY_CONCURRENCY=1 docker compose up -d notification
RATE=100 k6 run load/orders-load.js           # kafka-lag.sh in another terminal
NOTIFY_CONCURRENCY=6 docker compose up -d notification
RATE=100 k6 run load/orders-load.js

Then measure how late the e-mails were:

-- docker compose exec db psql -U boxoffice -d boxoffice
SELECT count(*) AS emails,
       percentile_cont(0.50) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY extract(epoch FROM sent_at - occurred_at)) AS p50_s,
       percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY extract(epoch FROM sent_at - occurred_at)) AS p95_s
FROM notification.notifications
WHERE sent_at > now() - interval '10 minutes';
Predict before you run: what lag will concurrency 1 reach?

Each consumer thread handles at most 1 / 50 ms = 20 e-mails/s. With one thread and 100 orders/s, the backlog grows at 100 − 20 = 80 messages/s: after 60 s, ≈ 4 800 messages of lag, and it drains at 20/s → ≈ 240 s to empty. With six threads (capacity 120/s > 100/s) the lag stays near zero. More than six threads would not help: the topic has six partitions.

items.title: D. Replay
items.text:
docker compose stop notification
docker compose exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 \
  --group notification --topic order-events --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute
docker compose start notification

Wait until kafka-lag.sh shows 0, then compare e-mails with distinct orders:

SELECT count(*) AS emails, count(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders FROM notification.notifications;

Do it with NOTIFY_IDEMPOTENT=true and with NOTIFY_IDEMPOTENT=false (restart notification with the variable set, as in C).

items.title: E. Flash-sale spike through the waiting room
items.text:
ADMIT_PER_SECOND=10 docker compose up -d order
k6 run --summary-trend-stats="avg,p(50),p(95),p(99),max" load/waiting-room-spike.js

About 700 fans arrive in 40 s, at 20 per second; the room lets 10 per second in. Check in the summary: wr_admitted grows at 10/s, http_req_duration{name:order} stays flat, every bot request gets 403, and wr_eta_error_seconds — the actual wait minus the ETA promised at join — stays within a couple of seconds: Little's Law, wait = position / rate, is an honest promise when the rate is constant.

items.title: Results
items.text:
Copy this table into your repository (results/lab7.md) and fill it in.

Metric Before After A · Throughput (req/s) A · POST /orders p50 (ms) A · POST /orders p95 (ms) A · POST /orders p99 (ms) A · Error rate (%) B · Error rate with notification down 20 s (%) B · Peak lag (messages) / time to drain (s) — C · Peak lag, concurrency 1 vs 6 (messages) C · Drain time, concurrency 1 vs 6 (s) C · E-mail delay p95, concurrency 1 vs 6 (s) D · E-mails / distinct orders after replay (idempotent off vs on) E · Orders per second during the spike — E · Wait p95 (s) / ETA error p95 (s) — E · Order p95 (ms) / bots refused (%) —

Back to the overview Quiz

items.title: 2. Transactional Outbox
items.text: The order service must do two things when a fan places an order: store the order in PostgreSQL and announce it on Kafka. Two different systems, no shared transaction. This step shows why the obvious code is wrong and builds the standard fix, the transactional outbox.

items.title: The dual-write problem
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fan
    participant O as order
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant K as Kafka
    F->>O: POST /orders
    O->>DB: INSERT order + COMMIT
    DB-->>O: ok
    Note over O: crash, deploy or Kafka timeout here
    O--xK: publish OrderPlaced (never happens)
    O-->>F: 500 (but the order exists!)

Any order of the two writes has a failure window:

Write order Crash between the writes Result DB, then Kafka order stored, event lost no e-mail, and no other service ever hears of the order Kafka, then DB event published, DB insert fails a ghost order: e-mail for an order that does not exist Kafka inside a DB transaction Kafka publish succeeds, commit fails same ghost; Kafka cannot be rolled back by PostgreSQL

The outbox removes the second system from the request: the service writes the event as a row in an outbox table in the same local transaction as the order. Either both rows exist or neither. A separate relay reads unpublished rows and publishes them, marking them as published only after Kafka acknowledges.

sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fan
    participant O as order
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant R as outbox relay
    participant K as Kafka
    F->>O: POST /orders
    O->>DB: BEGIN; INSERT orders; INSERT outbox; COMMIT
    O-->>F: 201 Created
    loop every 200 ms
        R->>DB: SELECT ... WHERE published_at IS NULL FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
        R->>K: send (key = orderId), wait for acks=all
        K-->>R: ack
        R->>DB: UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now()
    end

If the relay crashes after Kafka's ack but before the UPDATE, the row is published again on the next run: the outbox gives at-least-once publication. That is fine, because the consumer in step 3 is idempotent and each event carries a unique eventId.

Polling relay or CDC?

The relay here polls the table — simple, no extra infrastructure, a few hundred milliseconds of delay. The alternative is change data capture (CDC): a tool such as Debezium reads the PostgreSQL write-ahead log and publishes each outbox insert, with lower delay and no polling load, at the cost of running and operating Kafka Connect. See the patterns page of the messaging class.

CREATE TABLE outbox (
    id             UUID         PRIMARY KEY,
    aggregate_type VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id   UUID         NOT NULL,

CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON outbox (created_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

hold_id is UNIQUE: one seat hold (from lab 6) can become at most one order. That constraint is what makes POST /orders idempotent — a fan who double-clicks, or a gateway that retries after a timeout, gets the same order back instead of a second one.

items.title: Domain records
The transaction: order + outbox
items.text:
The NOTIFY_MODE switch keeps the "before" version in the code so that you can measure both in step 5: sync calls notification over HTTP inside the request, outbox writes the event row.

OrderService.javaNotificationClient.javaOrderController.java services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/OrderService.java
package boxoffice.order;

import boxoffice.order.OrderProperties.NotifyMode;
import boxoffice.order.outbox.Outbox;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class OrderService {

    public record PlaceResult(OrderView order, boolean created) {
    }

    private static final String SELECT = """
            SELECT id, show_id, hold_id, customer_email, amount, status, created_at
            FROM orders
            """;

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final Outbox outbox;
    private final NotificationClient notifications;
    private final OrderProperties props;

    public OrderService(JdbcClient jdbc, Outbox outbox, NotificationClient notifications,
                        OrderProperties props) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.outbox = outbox;
        this.notifications = notifications;
        this.props = props;
    }

    @Transactional
    public PlaceResult place(OrderRequest req) {
        int inserted = jdbc.sql("""
                INSERT INTO orders (id, show_id, hold_id, customer_email, amount, status)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 'PENDING_PAYMENT')
                ON CONFLICT (hold_id) DO NOTHING
                """)
                .params(UUID.randomUUID(), req.showId(), req.holdId(), req.customerEmail(), req.amount())
                .update();

        OrderView order = jdbc.sql(SELECT + " WHERE hold_id = ?")
                .param(req.holdId())
                .query(OrderView.class)
                .single();

        if (inserted == 0) {
            // same hold already ordered: idempotent replay, no second event
            return new PlaceResult(order, false);
        }

        OrderEvent event = OrderEvent.placed(order);
        if (props.notifyMode() == NotifyMode.SYNC) {
            notifications.send(event); // BEFORE: the fan waits for the e-mail
        } else {
            outbox.append(event.eventId(), "order", order.id(), event.eventType(), event);
        }
        return new PlaceResult(order, true);
    }

    public Optional<OrderView> find(UUID id) {
        return jdbc.sql(SELECT + " WHERE id = ?").param(id).query(OrderView.class).optional();
    }
}
services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/NotificationClient.java
package boxoffice.order;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

/** Only used in NOTIFY_MODE=sync: the "before" architecture. */
@Component
public class NotificationClient {

    private final RestClient http;

    public NotificationClient(RestClient.Builder builder, OrderProperties props) {
        this.http = builder.baseUrl(props.notificationUrl()).build();
    }

    public void send(OrderEvent event) {
        http.post().uri("/notifications").body(event).retrieve().toBodilessEntity();
    }
}
services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/OrderController.java (step 2 version, replaced in step 4)
package boxoffice.order;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import java.net.URI;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
import org.springframework.web.server.ResponseStatusException;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orders;

    public OrderController(OrderService orders) {
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderView> place(@Valid @RequestBody OrderRequest req) {
        OrderService.PlaceResult result = orders.place(req);
        if (!result.created()) {
            return ResponseEntity.ok(result.order());
        }
        return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/orders/" + result.order().id())).body(result.order());
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public OrderView get(@PathVariable UUID id) {
        return orders.find(id).orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND));
    }
}

ON CONFLICT (hold_id) DO NOTHING returns 0 rows when the hold was already ordered; the service then returns the existing order with 200 OK and writes no event. Under concurrency, PostgreSQL makes the second insert wait for the first transaction and then skip — no race, no duplicate.

docker compose up -d --build ordercurl -s -X POST localhost:8084/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"showId":"show-42","holdId":"hold-0001","customerEmail":"ana@example.com","amount":350.00}'{"id":"28cb9305-e1ce-4b49-aba7-665bb1b244b5","showId":"show-42","holdId":"hold-0001","customerEmail":"ana@example.com","amount":350.00,"status":"PENDING_PAYMENT","createdAt":"2026-10-18T17:55:45.063089Z"}docker compose logs order | grep relayedorder-1 | 2026-10-18T17:55:48.594Z INFO 1 --- [order] [ scheduling-1] boxoffice.order.outbox.OutboxRelay : relayed 1 event(s) to order-events

Open Kafka UI (http://localhost:8089) → Topics → order-events → Messages: the event is there, with key = order id and the eventId and eventType headers.

Now prove the two guarantees:

  1. Idempotent request. Send the same curl again: the response is 200 (not 201) with the same id, and no new message appears in the topic.

  2. No lost event. Stop Kafka, place an order, start Kafka again:

    docker compose stop kafka
curl -s -X POST localhost:8084/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"showId":"show-42","holdId":"hold-0002","customerEmail":"bia@example.com","amount":350.00}'
docker compose exec db psql -U boxoffice -d boxoffice \
  -c "SELECT event_type, created_at, published_at FROM orders.outbox ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 2;"
docker compose start kafka

    You should see 201 for the order and, in the first query, the new row with an empty published_at. Wait until docker compose ps kafka says healthy again (about a minute) and run the query once more: published_at is now filled. In a test run:

     event_type  |          created_at           |         published_at
-------------+-------------------------------+-------------------------------
 OrderPlaced | 2026-10-18 18:02:40.865762+00 | 2026-10-18 18:03:51.614915+00
 OrderPlaced | 2026-10-18 17:57:39.391694+00 | 2026-10-18 17:57:39.691802+00

    The order was accepted while Kafka was down and published 71 s later, when Kafka was back; the fan never saw the outage. Meanwhile docker compose logs order shows ERROR … Unexpected error occurred in scheduled task every few seconds: each relay run fails after max.block.ms (5 s) and the next one retries — expected.

Pitfalls

  • Publishing inside the HTTP request "after commit" (e.g. @TransactionalEventListener) still loses the event if the process dies between the commit and the send. Only a durable outbox row survives a crash.
  • Ordering across replicas. With several relays, two events of the same order could be published by different replicas out of order. Here each order has one event at a time; if you emit several per order, relay per aggregate (e.g. ORDER BY aggregate_id, created_at) or use CDC.
  • The outbox is not a queue for the world. It is private to order; other services read the Kafka topic, never the table.

Next: Idempotent consumer and DLT

items.title: 4. Waiting Room
items.text:
At 10:00, 2 million fans press "Buy" for 60 thousand seats. Kafka protects notification from the burst, but the burst first hits the synchronous path: seat holds and orders, backed by a strongly consistent inventory that cannot scale to 2 million requests per second. The usual answer of ticketing and sneaker-drop sites is a virtual waiting room: a queue in front of the system that lets fans in at the rate the system can serve, in arrival order, and tells everyone else their position honestly.

flowchart LR
    fans["2 M fans"] -->|POST join| wr["waiting room (Redis FIFO)"]
    wr -->|"position, ETA"| fans
    adm["admitter (every 1 s)"] -->|"ZPOPMIN N"| wr
    adm -->|"admitted ticket, TTL 5 min"| redis[(Redis)]
    fans -->|"POST /orders + X-Admission-Ticket"| order[order]
    order -->|"ticket admitted?"| redis

This is queue-based load leveling: arrivals are bursty, service is constant, and the queue holds the difference. Little's Law gives the honest ETA a fan sees:

\[ \text{wait} \approx \frac{\text{position in the queue}}{\text{admission rate}} \qquad \text{e.g. } \frac{30\,000}{500\ \text{fans/s}} = 60\ \text{s} \]

items.title: Design
items.text:
Decision Choice here Why Queue store a Redis sorted set per show, score = arrival sequence O(log n) join and rank, atomic pop of the N first (ZPOPMIN) Fairness sequence from INCR, not client timestamps clients' clocks lie; the server decides the order Admission every second, pop admit-per-second tickets and mark them admitted with a TTL the rate is the knob; the TTL frees capacity of fans who give up Gate POST /orders requires an admitted X-Admission-Ticket while the on-sale is open without enforcement, bots skip the queue Position the client polls GET /tickets/{id} simple; at scale, push via SSE/WebSocket or long polling

Where the gate belongs

The gate must cover every expensive step of the on-sale (seat holds in inventory and orders), so in production it lives at the edge: a gateway filter (lab 4) or a CDN waiting-room product. This lab enforces it in order to stay small; moving it to the gateway is a good extension.

8. Observability
items.text:
Goal

Make BoxOffice explain itself. Attach the OpenTelemetry Java agent to every service and send traces, metrics and logs to grafana/otel-lgtm; build a RED dashboard as code; follow one order from the edge through Kafka to the e-mail in a single trace; and turn a promise to users into an SLO with a multiwindow burn-rate alert — then break the database and time how long the alert takes to fire.

The flash sale went live, and the support channel fills up: "checkout is slow", "the page shows an error". Is it every fan or a few? Which of the seven services? The database, the pool, Kafka, the e-mail provider? Until now the only instrument was k6, which measures from the outside. This lab adds the inside view — the three signals of the observability class: metrics say that something is wrong and how much, traces say where in the request the time went, logs say why.
