items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Signals and instrumentation
items.text:
Q1. Support says "checkout is slow". Which signal answers which service and which step made a specific slow request slow?

  • A. A metric: the p99 of http_server_request_duration_seconds
  • B. A trace: the spans of that request, with the time of each hop
  • C. A log line with the word "slow"
  • D. The CPU utilization of each container
Answer

B — a trace.

Metrics aggregate: they say that p99 is high and for which service, but not why one request was slow. A trace records one request as a tree of spans — gateway, order, each SQL statement, the Kafka send — so the slow hop is visible. Logs give the details (why) once you know where to look, ideally reached from the trace through trace_id.

Q2. How does the OpenTelemetry Java agent instrument Spring MVC, JDBC and Kafka without code changes?

  • A. It replaces the Spring Boot starters with instrumented copies at build time
  • B. It is attached with -javaagent and rewrites the bytecode of known libraries as their classes are loaded
  • C. It reads the application logs and converts them into spans
  • D. It proxies all network traffic of the container
Answer

B — bytecode instrumentation at class-loading time.

The JVM calls the agent before main; the agent registers transformers that add span creation, context propagation and metric recording to the methods of supported libraries. That is why JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-javaagent:... is enough, and why startup gets slower.

Q3. The three catalog replicas use the same OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: catalog. Why not catalog-1, catalog-2, catalog-3?

  • A. Because the agent rejects names with digits
  • B. Because they are one service with three instances: dashboards and SLOs aggregate by service, and each instance still gets its own service.instance.id
  • C. Because Prometheus can store only one series per name
  • D. There is no reason; both are equivalent
Answer

B — service vs instance.

Users experience the catalog service, not a replica. With one service name, sum by (service_name) adds the three replicas and the SLO covers the service; when you need the per-replica view, the instance/service_instance_id label is still there. Naming replicas as services would multiply dashboards and break the moment replicas scale.

Q4. Place an order and you find two unrelated traces: one for POST /orders and one starting in the outbox relay. Why does automatic context propagation fail here?

  • A. Kafka does not support headers
  • B. The relay reads a database row later, on a scheduler thread; the request's trace context was never stored in the row, so there is nothing to continue
  • C. The agent does not instrument @Scheduled methods
  • D. Sampling dropped the link
Answer

B — the context did not travel with the data.

The agent propagates context in memory (same thread) and across HTTP and Kafka by injecting the traceparent header. An outbox row is a different carrier that the agent does not know. Storing the request's traceparent in the row and making it current before kafka.send reconnects the trace — the same idea W3C Trace Context uses on HTTP.

items.title: Metrics and dashboards
items.text:
Q5. Three catalog replicas report p95 latencies of 80 ms, 90 ms and 400 ms. What is the p95 of the service?

  • A. 190 ms, the average of the three
  • B. 400 ms, the maximum
  • C. It cannot be computed from the three numbers; it must be computed from the sum of the replicas' histogram buckets
  • D. 90 ms, the median
Answer

C — percentiles do not average.

The p95 of the service depends on how many requests each replica served and how they are distributed. Histograms can be added bucket by bucket, so the correct query is histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(..._bucket[5m]))). Averaging percentiles is one of the most common dashboard mistakes.

Q6. Why does the agent record http_route="/catalog/events/{id}" instead of the real URL /catalog/events/1234?

  • A. To hide the event ids from attackers
  • B. Because each distinct label value creates a new time series; raw URLs would create one series per event id (unbounded cardinality)
  • C. Because Prometheus does not accept digits in label values
  • D. To make the dashboard load faster in the browser
Answer

B — cardinality.

Series count ≈ product of the distinct values of every label. A template has a handful of values; raw URLs have as many as there are events (and attackers can invent more). High cardinality makes Prometheus slow and expensive; identifiers such as user_id or order_id belong in traces and logs, not in metric labels.

Q7. In the RED dashboard, the DB connections panel shows used equal to max and waiting > 0, while CPU is at 35%. What is the bottleneck?

  • A. The CPU
  • B. The connection pool: requests are queuing for a connection, so latency grows even though the CPU is idle
  • C. The garbage collector
  • D. The network between edge and gateway
Answer

B — pool saturation (the S of USE).

When every connection is in use, new requests wait. By Little's Law, the extra concurrency turns into waiting time, so latency rises while CPU stays low. The fix may be a bigger pool, fewer/faster queries, or a pooler such as PgBouncer (lab 6) — but first the evidence: saturation > 0.

items.title: SLOs and alerts
items.text:
Q8. The catalog SLO is 99.5% over 28 days. The current error ratio is 1%. What is the burn rate, and how long would the whole budget last at that pace?

  • A. 1; 28 days
  • B. 2; 14 days
  • C. 0.5; 60 days
  • D. 14.4; about 2 days
Answer

B — burn rate = error ratio / budget ratio = 1% / 0.5% = 2.

A burn rate of 1 spends the budget in exactly the SLO window (28 days); a burn rate of 2 spends it twice as fast, in 14 days. This is the number burn-rate alerts compare against thresholds such as 14.4 (about 2% of the budget in 1 hour) and 6 (about 5% in 6 hours).

Q9. Why does the fast-burn rule require the burn rate to exceed 14.4 over both 1 hour and 5 minutes?

  • A. To double the chance of firing
  • B. The long window proves the problem is significant (not a blip); the short window proves it is still happening, so the alert resolves soon after recovery
  • C. Because Grafana cannot evaluate windows longer than 1 hour alone
  • D. To compare the service with its own past
Answer

B — significance and recency.

A 1-hour window alone would keep paging for up to an hour after the fix (the bad minutes are still inside the window). A 5-minute window alone would page for short blips that cost almost no budget. Requiring both gives high precision and fast reset — the core of the multiwindow, multi-burn-rate method from the Google SRE workbook.

Q10. With steady traffic and an hour of healthy history, db stops and every catalog request fails. Roughly when does the 1-hour burn rate cross 14.4 (SLO 99.5%)?

  • A. After about 5 seconds
  • B. After about 4.3 minutes, when the 1-hour error ratio reaches 7.2%
  • C. After exactly 1 hour
  • D. Never, because the short window resets it
Answer

B — 14.4 × 0.5% = 7.2% of the last hour must be errors: 0.072 × 60 min ≈ 4.3 min.

The short window crosses the threshold within a minute; the long window is the slower condition. Add the for: 1m and the evaluation interval and the page arrives about 5–6 minutes into a total outage — a deliberate trade-off between detection time and false alarms.

Q11. Why is /actuator/health excluded from the availability SLI?

  • A. Because health checks are not HTTP requests
  • B. Because probes are frequent, almost never fail and are not made by users; including them inflates the success ratio and hides user-facing errors
  • C. Because Prometheus cannot store actuator metrics
  • D. Because the health endpoint is slower than the others
Answer

B — the SLI must measure what users experience.

Kubernetes, Docker and the edge call health endpoints every few seconds. Those successful requests dilute real failures: with enough probes, a broken checkout could still show 99.9% "availability". Filter by route (http_route!~"/actuator.*") or measure at the edge.

Q12. You set OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio with argument 0.1 on every service. What happens to the RED dashboard?

  • A. Its rates drop to 10% of the real values
  • B. Nothing: metrics are recorded for every request regardless of trace sampling; only 10% of the traces are stored
  • C. It stops working, because metrics are derived from traces
  • D. Its percentiles become exact
Answer

B — sampling applies to traces, not to the agent's metrics.

The HTTP histograms are recorded for every request, so rates, errors and percentiles stay correct. Traces become examples: 10% of them, complete (the root decides and parentbased makes every downstream service follow), which is enough to explain a pattern at a fraction of the cost.

Back to the lab

items.title: 2. RED Dashboard
items.text:
Data you cannot read in ten seconds during an incident is not observability, it is storage. This step builds one dashboard for every BoxOffice service, provisioned as code, organized around two methods from the signals class:

Method For Signals Question it answers RED (Tom Wilkie) request-driven services Rate, Errors, Duration "Are my users being served well?" USE (Brendan Gregg) resources Utilization, Saturation, Errors "Is a resource the bottleneck?"

RED says that something is wrong for users; USE says where the capacity ran out. The top row of the dashboard is RED per service; the bottom row is USE for the JVMs and their connection pools.

items.title: Dashboards as code
items.text:
Grafana loads dashboards from files listed by a provider. Both files live in your repository, so the dashboard is reviewed, versioned and identical on every laptop:

infra/grafana/dashboards.yaml
apiVersion: 1

providers:
  - name: BoxOffice
    folder: BoxOffice
    type: file
    options:
      path: /otel-lgtm/boxoffice-dashboards

The volumes of step 1 mount this provider into Grafana's provisioning folder and infra/grafana/dashboards/ at the path it points to. Save the dashboard below as infra/grafana/dashboards/boxoffice-red.json and restart: docker compose restart otel-lgtm. It appears under Dashboards → BoxOffice → BoxOffice — RED.

items.title: Reading the panels
items.text:
Every panel is one PromQL query over the histogram the agent exports. Learn the four shapes; every RED dashboard you will ever see is a variation of them.

Panel Query shape Read it as Rate sum by (service_name) (rate(…_count[$__rate_interval])) requests per second, per service Errors rate(…_count{status=~"5.."}) / rate(…_count) the share of requests that fail (not the count) Duration p95 histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (service_name, le) (rate(…_bucket[…]))) 95% of requests were faster than this Slowest routes topk(10, histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (…, http_route, le) …)) where to look first DB connections db_client_connections_usage{state="used"} vs _max, _pending_requests the pool is saturated when waiting > 0

Three habits make the difference:

  • Aggregate before the quantile. histogram_quantile must receive sum by (le) of the bucket rates: you can add buckets across instances, you cannot average percentiles (the average of three p95s is not the p95 of anything).
  • Errors as a ratio. 50 errors per second is a disaster at 60 req/s and noise at 60 000 req/s.
  • Percentiles from buckets are estimates. histogram_quantile interpolates inside a bucket; with the agent's default bucket boundaries (…, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 2.5 s…), a p99 of "0.6 s" means "somewhere between 0.5 and 0.75 s".

Exemplars: from a spike to the trace that caused it

The otel-lgtm Prometheus stores exemplars: a few sample trace ids attached to histogram buckets. In the Duration panel, turn on Exemplars in the query options; the diamonds on the chart are real requests, and clicking one opens its trace in Tempo. This is the shortest path from "p99 went up" to "this SQL statement is slow".

items.title: Exercise: watch a bottleneck appear
items.text:
1. Run the staircase stress test of lab 2 against the edge — it raises the arrival rate in steps up to PEAK and comes back down: k6 run -e BASE_URL=http://localhost -e PEAK=600 load/stress.js.
  2. Watch Duration p95 and DB connections side by side. When waiting leaves zero, the latency curve bends: requests now queue for a connection (Little's Law: with the pool full, extra concurrency becomes waiting time).
  3. Open an exemplar at the top of the curve: the trace shows a long gap before the SQL span — time spent waiting for a connection, not running SQL.

Write in your results which resource saturated first and the request rate at which it happened.

Next: SLO and burn-rate alert

items.title: 1. Instrument Everything
items.text: In this step every Java service starts sending traces, metrics and logs to one container, otel-lgtm, without a single change to business code. Then you fix the one place where automatic instrumentation cannot see the request: the outbox hop of lab 7. All commands run from the root of your boxoffice repository.

items.title: The backend: otel-lgtm
items.text:
grafana/otel-lgtm packs a whole observability backend into one image, for development and teaching: an OpenTelemetry Collector receives OTLP (the OpenTelemetry Protocol) and routes each signal to Prometheus (metrics), Tempo (traces) and Loki (logs), with Grafana on top, already wired so that a metric exemplar opens its trace and a trace opens its logs. In production these are separate, replicated systems (or a managed service); the protocol your services speak — OTLP — stays the same.

docker-compose.yaml (excerpt)
  otel-lgtm:
    image: grafana/otel-lgtm:0.37.0
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"   # Grafana (no login)
      - "4317:4317"   # OTLP gRPC
      - "4318:4318"   # OTLP HTTP
    volumes:
      - ./infra/grafana/dashboards.yaml:/otel-lgtm/grafana/conf/provisioning/dashboards/boxoffice.yaml:ro
      - ./infra/grafana/dashboards:/otel-lgtm/boxoffice-dashboards:ro
      - ./infra/grafana/alerting:/otel-lgtm/grafana/conf/provisioning/alerting:ro

The three volumes load your dashboard and alert rules at startup; their files are created in step 2 and step 3.

items.title: The agent: one jar, no code
items.text:
The OpenTelemetry Java agent is attached to the JVM with -javaagent. At class-loading time it rewrites the bytecode of the libraries it knows — Spring MVC and WebFlux, the HTTP clients, JDBC and HikariCP, Kafka, Redis, logback, the JVM itself — so that each request becomes a span, each library reports metrics with standard names (the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions), and each log line carries the trace id of the request that wrote it.

Download it once into infra/otel/ (it is 26 MB: .gitignore keeps it out of Git, and every clone runs the script):

scripts/get-otel-agent.sh
#!/bin/sh
# Downloads the OpenTelemetry Java agent into infra/otel/ (mounted read-only into every Java service).
# Usage, from the repository root: sh scripts/get-otel-agent.sh
set -e
VERSION=2.32.0
mkdir -p infra/otel
curl -fsSL -o infra/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar \
  "https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java-instrumentation/releases/download/v${VERSION}/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar"
ls -l infra/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar
.gitignore
# build output
target/
*.class
# IDEs and OS
.idea/
.vscode/
*.iml
.DS_Store
# local secrets: never commit them
.env
# k6 HTML reports are big; commit the JSON summaries and the tables in results/*.md
results/*.html
# the OpenTelemetry Java agent is downloaded by scripts/get-otel-agent.sh (lab 8)
infra/otel/*.jar
sh scripts/get-otel-agent.sh-rw-r--r-- 1 you staff 26418479 Oct 18 15:06 infra/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar

The images do not change: Compose mounts infra/otel/ read-only into every Java service and turns the agent on with environment variables shared through a YAML anchor:

docker-compose.yaml (excerpt)
# lab 8: OpenTelemetry settings shared by every Java service (merged into each "environment")
x-otel: &otel
  JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -javaagent:/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar
  OTEL_JAVAAGENT_ENABLED: ${OTEL_ON:-true}          # false = same image, agent off
  OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: http://otel-lgtm:4318
  OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL: "10000"              # 10 s instead of 60 s
  OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES: service.namespace=boxoffice,deployment.environment.name=local
  OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER: ${OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER:-parentbased_always_on}
  OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG: ${OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG:-1.0}
  LOGGING_PATTERN_CORRELATION: "[%X{trace_id:-},%X{span_id:-}] "   # trace id in console logs

# ... and in every Java service, for example:
  order:
    build: ./services/order
    volumes:
      - ./infra/otel:/otel:ro
    environment:
      <<: *otel
      OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: order
Variable Effect JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS the JVM reads it before main: attaches the agent without changing the image or the ENTRYPOINT OTEL_JAVAAGENT_ENABLED false turns the agent off with the same image — used in the Measure it step OTEL_SERVICE_NAME the service.name attribute: the name you filter by everywhere. The replicas catalog-1..3 all use catalog: one service, three instances OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT where to send; the agent uses OTLP over HTTP (4318) by default OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL 10 s instead of the default 60 s, so that dashboards react during a lab OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES extra attributes on every signal; service.namespace groups the BoxOffice services OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER which requests are traced; all of them by default (experiment B of Measure it changes it) LOGGING_PATTERN_CORRELATION Spring Boot's logging.pattern.correlation: prints [trace id,span id] in every console line

Get the complete file of this lab (it is the lab 7 file plus the anchor, the volumes and otel-lgtm):

curl -fsSL -o docker-compose.yaml https://insper.github.io/platform/2027.1/hands-on/8/code/docker-compose.yaml
docker-compose.yaml — the complete file at the end of this lab docker-compose.yaml
name: boxoffice

# lab 8: OpenTelemetry settings shared by every Java service (merged into each "environment")
x-otel: &otel
  JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -javaagent:/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar
  OTEL_JAVAAGENT_ENABLED: ${OTEL_ON:-true}          # false = same image, agent off
  OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: http://otel-lgtm:4318
  OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL: "10000"              # 10 s instead of 60 s
  OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES: service.namespace=boxoffice,deployment.environment.name=local
  OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER: ${OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER:-parentbased_always_on}
  OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG: ${OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG:-1.0}
  LOGGING_PATTERN_CORRELATION: "[%X{trace_id:-},%X{span_id:-}] "   # trace id in console logs

# settings shared by the three catalog replicas (a YAML anchor)
x-catalog: &catalog
  build: ./services/catalog
  image: boxoffice-catalog
  volumes:
    - ./infra/otel:/otel:ro          # lab 8: the Java agent
  environment:
    <<: *otel
    OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: catalog       # three replicas, ONE service
    DB_HOST: db
    DB_PORT: 5432
    DB_NAME: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
    DB_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
    DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
    DB_POOL_SIZE: ${DB_POOL_SIZE:-10}
    REDIS_HOST: redis
    REDIS_PORT: 6379
    CACHE_ENABLED: ${CACHE_ENABLED:-true}
    CACHE_TTL_EVENT: ${CACHE_TTL_EVENT:-60s}
    CACHE_TTL_LIST: ${CACHE_TTL_LIST:-10s}
    CACHE_STAMPEDE_PROTECTION: ${CACHE_STAMPEDE_PROTECTION:-false}
  depends_on:
    db:
      condition: service_healthy
    redis:
      condition: service_healthy
  deploy:
    resources:

Create the provisioning folders (step 2 fills them) and restart everything — the Java services restart to pick up the agent:

mkdir -p infra/grafana/dashboards infra/grafana/alertingdocker compose up -ddocker compose logs catalog-1 | grep -m1 javaagentcatalog-1-1 | [otel.javaagent 2026-10-18 18:08:22:121 +0000] [main] INFO io.opentelemetry.javaagent.tooling.VersionLogger - opentelemetry-javaagent - version: 2.32.0curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost/catalog/events/1200

With the agent, each JVM starts noticeably slower (instrumentation happens at class loading): wait until docker compose ps shows every service healthy.

Open Grafana at http://localhost:3000 (no login in this image) → Explore. You should see:

  • Prometheus: sum by (service_name) (http_server_request_duration_seconds_count) returns one line per service — auth, catalog, gateway, inventory, notification, order. Each series has labels such as http_route="/catalog/events/{id}", http_request_method="GET" and http_response_status_code="200" — the route is the template, never the raw URL, which keeps the number of series bounded.
  • Tempo: search by service gateway. A request through the edge shows spans from gateway and catalog, and inside catalog one span per SQL statement.
  • Loki: {service_name="order"}. Each line has trace_id and span_id, and a button that jumps to the trace. The console has them too: docker compose logs order prints lines like [14263dc50b861be8bcf0bc1f4dbad3c5,a1c96ae57fb41b45] o.s.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet ….

Metric names follow the semantic conventions

The HTTP server duration histogram is called http.server.request.duration in OpenTelemetry; Prometheus receives it as http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket, _count and _sum (dots become underscores, the unit becomes a suffix). Resource attributes such as service.name become labels (service_name) and job becomes boxoffice/catalog (namespace/name). Every dashboard and alert of this lab relies on these names.

items.title: The hop the agent cannot see: the outbox
items.text:
Place an order and look for its trace in Tempo. With the lab 7 code you find two unrelated traces: one for POST /orders (order → INSERTs), and another one that starts in the outbox relay's scheduled job and continues through Kafka to notification. The agent propagates context across HTTP calls and Kafka messages automatically, but the outbox is a database row read later by a different thread: the context of the request is not in the row, so it is lost.

sequenceDiagram
    participant O as order (HTTP thread)
    participant DB as outbox table
    participant R as relay (scheduler thread)
    participant K as Kafka
    participant N as notification
    O->>DB: INSERT outbox row + traceparent of the request
    R->>DB: SELECT row (with its traceparent)
    Note over R: make that context current
    R->>K: send: the agent injects the SAME trace id in the headers
    K->>N: consume: the agent continues the trace

The fix is the same idea W3C Trace Context uses on HTTP: carry the traceparent with the data. Store it in the outbox row, and make it the current context when the relay publishes. Four files of order change:

V2__outbox_traceparent.sqlpom.xmlOutbox.javaOutboxRelay.java services/order/src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__outbox_traceparent.sql
-- W3C trace context of the request that wrote the event: 00-<trace id>-<span id>-<flags>
ALTER TABLE outbox ADD COLUMN traceparent VARCHAR(55);

package boxoffice.order.outbox;

import tools.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import io.opentelemetry.api.trace.propagation.W3CTraceContextPropagator;
import io.opentelemetry.context.Context;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Propagation;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Component
public class Outbox {

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    public Outbox(JdbcClient jdbc, ObjectMapper mapper) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.mapper = mapper;
    }

    /** MANDATORY: fails fast if someone calls it outside the business transaction. */
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.MANDATORY)
    public void append(UUID eventId, String aggregateType, UUID aggregateId, String eventType, Object payload) {
        String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(payload); // Jackson 3: exceptions are unchecked
        // capture the trace context of the current request (null without the agent)
        Map<String, String> carrier = new HashMap<>();
        W3CTraceContextPropagator.getInstance().inject(Context.current(), carrier, (c, k, v) -> c.put(k, v));

        jdbc.sql("""
                INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_type, aggregate_id, event_type, payload, traceparent)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?::jsonb, ?)
                """)
                .params(eventId, aggregateType, aggregateId, eventType, json, carrier.get("traceparent"))
                .update();
    }
}
services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/outbox/OutboxRelay.java
package boxoffice.order.outbox;

import boxoffice.order.OrderProperties;
import io.opentelemetry.api.trace.propagation.W3CTraceContextPropagator;
import io.opentelemetry.context.Context;
import io.opentelemetry.context.Scope;
import io.opentelemetry.context.propagation.TextMapGetter;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.UUID;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.JdbcTemplate;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate;
import org.springframework.kafka.support.SendResult;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.Scheduled;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Component
public class OutboxRelay {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OutboxRelay.class);

    record Pending(UUID id, UUID aggregateId, String eventType, String payload, String traceparent) {
    }

    /** Reads the "traceparent" key from a Pending row. */
    private static final TextMapGetter<Pending> ROW = new TextMapGetter<>() {
        @Override
        public Iterable<String> keys(Pending p) {
            return List.of("traceparent");
        }

        @Override
        public String get(Pending p, String key) {
            return p == null || !"traceparent".equals(key) ? null : p.traceparent();
        }
    };

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;
    private final String topic;

    public OutboxRelay(JdbcClient jdbc, JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate,
                       KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka, OrderProperties props) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.jdbcTemplate = jdbcTemplate;
        this.kafka = kafka;
        this.topic = props.topic();
    }

    @Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${boxoffice.order.relay-interval-ms:200}")
    @Transactional
    public void relay() throws Exception {
        List<Pending> batch = jdbc.sql("""
                SELECT id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload::text AS payload, traceparent
                FROM outbox
                WHERE published_at IS NULL
                ORDER BY created_at
                LIMIT 100
                FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
                """)
                .query(Pending.class)
                .list();
        if (batch.isEmpty()) {
            return;
        }

        List<CompletableFuture<SendResult<String, String>>> acks = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Pending p : batch) {
            ProducerRecord<String, String> record =
                    new ProducerRecord<>(topic, p.aggregateId().toString(), p.payload());
            record.headers().add("eventId", p.id().toString().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            record.headers().add("eventType", p.eventType().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            // continue the trace of the request that created the event
            Context origin = W3CTraceContextPropagator.getInstance().extract(Context.root(), p, ROW);
            try (Scope ignored = origin.makeCurrent()) {
                acks.add(kafka.send(record)); // the agent's producer span is a child of the request
            }
        }
        CompletableFuture.allOf(acks.toArray(new CompletableFuture<?>[0])).get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

        jdbcTemplate.batchUpdate("UPDATE outbox SET published_at = clock_timestamp() WHERE id = ?",
                batch.stream().map(p -> new Object[] {p.id()}).toList());
        log.info("relayed {} event(s) to {}", batch.size(), topic);
    }

    @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 * * * *")
    @Transactional
    public void purge() {
        int n = jdbcTemplate.update(
                "DELETE FROM outbox WHERE published_at < now() - interval '1 day'");
        log.info("purged {} published outbox row(s)", n);
    }
}

The pom.xml adds only io.opentelemetry:opentelemetry-api (the version comes from Spring Boot): without the agent, every call of the API is a no-op, so the service still runs without it.

Rebuild order, place an order and find its trace:

docker compose up -d --build order
curl -s -X POST localhost:8084/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"showId":"show-7","holdId":"trace-1","customerEmail":"t@example.com","amount":10}'

In Grafana → Explore → Tempo, run the TraceQL query {resource.service.name="order" && name="POST /orders"} and open the most recent trace. You should see one trace with spans of both services, like this one from a test run (start offset, service, span, duration):

    0.0 ms  order         POST /orders                         9.0 ms
    5.3 ms  order         INSERT boxoffice.orders              0.4 ms
    5.8 ms  order         SELECT boxoffice.orders              0.2 ms
    6.6 ms  order         INSERT boxoffice.outbox              0.2 ms
   22.3 ms  order         order-events publish                11.2 ms
   36.4 ms  notification  order-events process                67.2 ms
   38.1 ms  notification  INSERT boxoffice.processed_events    0.4 ms
   99.7 ms  notification  INSERT boxoffice.notifications       0.4 ms

The request itself took 9 ms; the relay published 22 ms after it started (its 200 ms polling period puts this anywhere between 0 and 200 ms); notification spent 67 ms, most of it in the simulated 50 ms e-mail provider — the asynchronous latency of lab 7, visible at a glance. The very first order after a restart is much slower (cold JVMs with the agent): look at the second one.

In the interview

"Context propagation breaks at every hop that is not a direct call — queues, outboxes, batch jobs. I carry the W3C traceparent in the message or the row, and the consumer continues the trace; for fan-in (one job processing many messages) I use span links instead of a single parent."

Next: RED dashboard

items.title: 4. Measure It
items.text:
Observability is not free: every span is allocated, every metric point aggregated, every batch sent over the network. This step puts a number on that cost and on the benefit — how long it takes to know that users are hurting. As always, run each experiment twice and report the second run; numbers in "expected shape" boxes are illustrative.

# Experiment Knob What you record A agent overhead OTEL_ON=true vs false p50 / p95 / p99, throughput, CPU %, memory, startup time B trace sampling OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER p95, traces stored per minute C cardinality — number of series per service D time to detect stop db stop → Pending → Firing times

items.title: The k6 script
A. Agent overhead
items.text:
Same image, same load, agent on and off:

OTEL_ON=false docker compose up -d catalog-1 catalog-2 catalog-3k6 run load/catalog-otel.jsdocker stats --no-stream --format '{{.Name}} {{.CPUPerc}} {{.MemUsage}}' | grep catalogOTEL_ON=true docker compose up -d catalog-1 catalog-2 catalog-3k6 run load/catalog-otel.jsdocker stats --no-stream --format '{{.Name}} {{.CPUPerc}} {{.MemUsage}}' | grep catalogdocker compose logs catalog-1 | grep "Started CatalogApplication"

Run docker stats in a second terminal while k6 runs (the numbers after the test are idle numbers). The last command shows the startup time; compare it with the agent on and off.

Expected shape (illustrative)

The agent adds work per request (creating spans, recording histograms) and per process (bytecode instrumentation at startup). Expect a small increase in p50, a few percent more CPU at the same throughput, tens of MB more memory and a noticeably slower startup. If your p99 grows much more than your p50, look at garbage collection: more allocation means more frequent pauses.

items.title: B. Sampling
items.text:
Keeping 100% of the traces is right for a lab and wrong for 2 million fans. Sample 10% at the root and let every downstream service follow the root's decision (parentbased_…), so that a trace is either complete or absent:

The x-otel anchor already reads both settings from the environment (${OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER:-parentbased_always_on}), so no file changes: recreate the services with the two variables set and run the same load.

OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1 docker compose up -d
k6 run load/catalog-otel.js
docker compose up -d        # afterwards: back to 100% (the defaults of the anchor)

Count the traces stored per minute in Tempo (Explore → Tempo → Search, service gateway, last 5 minutes) and compare p95 with experiment A. Note that metrics are not sampled: the RED dashboard still counts every request — that is why rates and percentiles come from metrics, and examples (the why) from traces.

items.title: C. Cardinality
items.text:
Every distinct combination of label values is a separate time series, stored and queried separately. In Grafana Explore (Prometheus), run:

count by (service_name) ({service_namespace="boxoffice"})
count by (__name__) ({service_name="catalog"})

The first gives the series per service; the second shows which metrics are the most expensive. Now imagine adding a label user_id to the HTTP histogram: with 2 million fans and 14 buckets, how many series would catalog create? (Answer it in your results: this is why the agent records http_route, the template, and never the raw URL.)

items.title: D. Time to detect
items.text: Follow "Fire it" in step 3 and record the three times.

Below the table, answer in a paragraph each: is the agent's overhead worth it for BoxOffice? Which sampling rate would you choose for the flash sale, and why? Does your measured time to detect match the prediction of step 3?

items.title: 3. SLO and Burn-Rate Alert
items.text: A dashboard needs someone looking at it. An alert looks for you — and a bad alert wakes you up at 3 a.m. for nothing, until you learn to ignore it. This step turns a user-facing promise into an alert that fires when, and only when, the promise is at risk. The theory is in the alerting class and the SLO class.

items.title: From promise to numbers
items.text:
Term BoxOffice catalog SLI (indicator) share of catalog requests, health checks excluded, not answered with a 5xx SLO (objective) 99.5% over a rolling 28 days (the course standard window: four whole weeks) Error budget 0.5% of the requests may fail: at 100 req/s, 100 × 86 400 × 28 × 0.005 ≈ 1.21 million failed requests, or about 202 minutes of total outage per 28 days Burn rate how fast the budget is being spent, relative to "exactly on budget": error ratio / 0.005

A burn rate of 1 spends the whole budget in exactly 28 days. A burn rate of 14.4 spends about 2.1% of it in one hour (14.4 × 1 h / 672 h ≈ 2.1%) and all of it in less than two days. (The thresholds 14.4 and 6 come from the Google SRE workbook, which derived them for a 30-day window: 2% and 5% of the budget; with 28 days they mean 2.1% and 5.4% — close enough to keep the standard numbers.)

Why exclude /actuator/* from the SLI?

Docker, Kubernetes and the edge call the health endpoints every few seconds, and those calls almost never fail. Counting them inflates the success ratio with requests no user made — the SLI must measure what fans experience. The same reasoning excludes synthetic load you generate yourself from production SLIs, unless it is labeled and filtered.

items.title: Why "error rate > 1%" is a bad alert
items.text:
Alert Problem errors > 1% for 5 min fires on a 5-minute blip that cost about 0.01% of the budget (noise), and stays silent on a 0.8% error rate that burns the whole budget in 17.5 days (missed) errors > 0 pages all the time p99 > 1 s on one instance measures a machine, not users

The Google SRE workbook's answer is the multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alert: page when the budget burns fast over a long window (it is a real problem, not a blip) and over a short window (it is still happening — the alert stops soon after recovery).

Severity Burn rate Long window Short window Budget spent when it fires page 14.4 1 h 5 min ≈ 2.1% page 6 6 h 30 min ≈ 5.4% ticket 1 3 days 6 h ≈ 10.7%

This lab provisions the first rule as a page and the second as a ticket (a slower, cheaper signal for a smaller team); the third is left as an exercise.

items.title: The rules, as code
items.text:
Grafana loads alert rules from YAML files in its provisioning folder (mounted in step 1 from infra/grafana/alerting/). Each rule runs queries A and B — the burn rate over the two windows — and a math expression C that is the condition.

infra/grafana/alerting/slo-catalog.yaml
# Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts for the catalog availability SLO (Google SRE workbook, ch. 5).
# SLI: share of catalog requests (health checks excluded) NOT answered with 5xx. SLO: 99.5% / 28 days.
apiVersion: 1

groups:
  - orgId: 1
    name: catalog-slo
    folder: BoxOffice
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      - uid: catalog-availability-fast-burn
        title: "catalog availability SLO: fast burn"
        condition: C
        data:
          - refId: A          # burn rate over the long window (1 h)
            relativeTimeRange: { from: 3600, to: 0 }
            datasourceUid: prometheus
            model:
              refId: A
              instant: true
              expr: |
                (
                  sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="catalog", http_route!~"/actuator.*", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[1h]))
                  / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="catalog", http_route!~"/actuator.*"}[1h]))
                ) / 0.005
          - refId: B          # burn rate over the short window (5 min): stops paging soon after recovery
            relativeTimeRange: { from: 300, to: 0 }
            datasourceUid: prometheus
            model:
              refId: B
              instant: true
              expr: |
                (
                  sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="catalog", http_route!~"/actuator.*", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
                  / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="catalog", http_route!~"/actuator.*"}[5m]))
                ) / 0.005
          - refId: C
            datasourceUid: __expr__
            model:
              refId: C
              type: math
              expression: "$A > 14.4 && $B > 14.4"
        for: 1m
        noDataState: OK
        execErrState: Error
        labels:
          severity: page
          slo: catalog-availability
        annotations:
          summary: "catalog is burning its 28-day error budget 14.4x too fast"
          description: 'Burn rate {{ printf "%.1f" $values.A.Value }} (1 h) and {{ printf "%.1f" $values.B.Value }} (5 min): at this pace about 2% of the 28-day budget is gone in one hour.'

      - uid: catalog-availability-slow-burn
        title: "catalog availability SLO: slow burn"
        condition: C
        data:
          - refId: A          # 6 h window
            relativeTimeRange: { from: 21600, to: 0 }
            datasourceUid: prometheus
            model:
              refId: A
              instant: true
              expr: |
                (
                  sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="catalog", http_route!~"/actuator.*", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[6h]))
                  / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="catalog", http_route!~"/actuator.*"}[6h]))
                ) / 0.005
          - refId: B          # 30 min window
            relativeTimeRange: { from: 1800, to: 0 }
            datasourceUid: prometheus
            model:
              refId: B
              instant: true
              expr: |
                (
                  sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="catalog", http_route!~"/actuator.*", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[30m]))
                  / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="catalog", http_route!~"/actuator.*"}[30m]))
                ) / 0.005
          - refId: C
            datasourceUid: __expr__
            model:
              refId: C
              type: math
              expression: "$A > 6 && $B > 6"
        for: 5m
        noDataState: OK
        execErrState: Error
        labels:
          severity: ticket
          slo: catalog-availability
        annotations:
          summary: "catalog is burning its error budget 6x too fast"
          description: 'Burn rate {{ printf "%.1f" $values.A.Value }} (6 h) and {{ printf "%.1f" $values.B.Value }} (30 min): about 5% of the 28-day budget in six hours.'

Restart otel-lgtm and open Alerting → Alert rules: both rules are listed in the folder BoxOffice as Normal.

items.title: Fire it
items.text:
Produce steady traffic, then break the database that catalog depends on:

k6 run -e RATE=50 -e DURATION=10m load/catalog-otel.js &sleep 60 && docker compose stop db && date +%T10:12:31# watch Alerting → Alert rules: Normal → Pending → Firingdocker compose start db Predict: how long until the fast-burn rule fires?

During the outage every catalog request fails, so the short (5 min) burn rate jumps to about 1 / 0.005 = 200 within a minute. The long window is the slow one: the 1-hour error ratio must pass 14.4 × 0.5% = 7.2%. With steady traffic and an hour of healthy history, that takes 0.072 × 60 min ≈ 4.3 minutes of outage; add the for: 1m and up to 30 s of evaluation interval: ≈ 5–6 minutes to page. (If the stack has been up for less than an hour, the window holds less healthy history and the alert fires sooner.)

That is the trade-off of burn-rate alerts: a total outage takes minutes to page; a persistent 4% error rate (burn rate 8) is caught by the 6-hour rule once the 6-hour ratio passes 6 × 0.5% = 3%, after about 6 h × 3/4 = 4.5 hours; and a 30-second blip never pages.

In a test run of this lab (with less than an hour of history), the rule became Firing 288 s after db was stopped, with the description "burn rate 18.2 (1 h) and 74.4 (5 min)".

Record in your results the time you stopped db, the time the rule became Pending and Firing, and the burn rates shown in the alert's description.

Pitfalls

  • No traffic, no SLI. Division by zero yields no data; noDataState: OK keeps a quiet night quiet, but a service that receives no traffic because the edge is down looks "healthy". Pair SLO alerts with a synthetic probe or an alert on traffic dropping to zero.
  • Alert on symptoms, investigate causes. CPU, heap and pool panels are for the dashboard; the page is about users. A full disk that does not hurt users yet is a ticket, not a page.
  • Every page needs a runbook link (an annotations.runbook_url) saying what to check first — see the incident response class.

items.title: Exercise: a latency SLO
items.text:
Write a third rule for the promise "95% of GET /catalog/events/{id} complete in under 250 ms". Hint: the SLI is the ratio of the le="0.25" bucket rate to the _count rate for that route; the budget is 5%. Fire it by adding latency (in lab 9 you will use Toxiproxy for exactly this).

Next: Measure it

items.title: 9. Resilience & Chaos
items.text:
Goal

Make the checkout survive a bad day at the payment provider. Build the payment adapter and a fake external provider, put Toxiproxy between the services, watch a slow dependency take down all of order (a cascading failure), and fix it with Resilience4j — timeout, retry with backoff and jitter, circuit breaker, bulkhead — measuring after each pattern. End with a game day: a rehearsed incident with hidden failures and a blameless review.

At 10:00 the flash sale opens and the payment provider, under the load of every ticketing site in the country, starts answering in three seconds instead of three hundred milliseconds. Nothing is "down". Yet within a minute order stops answering everything — even GET /orders/{id}, which never talks to the provider — because every one of its threads is waiting on payment. This lab reproduces that failure on your laptop and applies the patterns of the reliability class, with a number for each.

items.title: Quiz
items.text: Click "Answer" to reveal the correct answer and explanation.

items.title: Cascading failures and timeouts
items.text:
Q1. order has 50 threads. Payments arrive at 20 per second and payment suddenly takes 3 s to answer. GET /orders/{id} does not call payment. What happens to it, and why?

  • A. Nothing: it does not depend on payment
  • B. It slows down and times out too: 20/s × 3 s = 60 threads would be needed just to wait on payment, more than the 50 available, so every request queues
  • C. It becomes faster, because payments are slow and leave the CPU idle
  • D. It fails only if the database is also slow
Answer

B — thread exhaustion: a cascading failure.

By Little's Law, concurrency = arrival rate × time in the system. Calls that wait on a slow dependency hold threads; when the pool is exhausted, requests that never touch the dependency queue behind them. The k6 browse scenario exists to make this collateral damage visible.

Q2. Why is a timeout the first protection to add?

  • A. It makes the dependency faster
  • B. It turns a slow failure into a fast failure: each call holds a thread for at most the timeout, which bounds the concurrency spent on that dependency
  • C. It retries automatically
  • D. It is required by HTTP/1.1
Answer

B — bounded waiting.

With a 1 s read timeout, 20 payments/s hold at most about 20 threads, regardless of how slow payment gets. The price: calls that would have succeeded in 1.5 s now fail. Java HTTP clients wait forever by default, so a missing timeout is the most common root cause of cascades.

Q3. The edge times out after 5 s, the gateway after 10 s, and order waits for payment up to 3 retries × 4 s. What is wrong?

  • A. Nothing; longer inner timeouts are safer
  • B. Inner budgets exceed outer ones: the edge gives up while order and the gateway keep working on requests nobody is waiting for. Budgets must shrink at each hop
  • C. The gateway timeout should be 0
  • D. Retries should be infinite to guarantee success
Answer

B — timeout budgets must decrease from the outside in.

Work done after the caller has given up is pure waste — and it holds threads and connections. A consistent budget is something like edge 10 s > gateway 5 s > order→payment (1 s × 3 attempts + backoff).

items.title: Retries and idempotency
items.text:
Q4. One attempt to call payment fails with probability 0.2, independently. With max-attempts: 3, what is the probability that a payment fails?

  • A. 0.6
  • B. 0.2
  • C. 0.008
  • D. 0.04
Answer

C — 0.2³ = 0.008 (0.8%).

A call fails only if all three attempts fail. Retries are very effective against independent, transient errors — and useless (or harmful) against persistent ones: if payment is down, three attempts just triple the load and the latency.

Q5. Why does PaymentClient send Idempotency-Key: order-<id> on every attempt?

  • A. To authenticate order against payment
  • B. So that a retry of a call whose response was lost (but which succeeded) does not charge the fan twice: payment and the provider return the first result for a known key
  • C. To make the circuit breaker count calls per order
  • D. Because HTTP requires it for POST
Answer

B — retries are only safe on idempotent operations.

A timeout does not mean the call failed — the charge may have succeeded and only the response was lost. Without an idempotency key, the retry creates a second charge. With it, the second request finds the key (UNIQUE in payments, forwarded to the provider) and gets the original result.

Q6. What problem does jitter (randomized wait) solve in retry backoff?

  • A. It reduces the number of retries
  • B. It prevents clients that failed at the same moment from retrying at the same moment, which would create synchronized waves of load on a recovering dependency
  • C. It makes timeouts shorter
  • D. It encrypts the retry requests
Answer

B — desynchronizing retries.

Exponential backoff alone spreads attempts over time, but all clients follow the same schedule: an outage that hits 1 000 clients at once produces waves of 1 000 retries at +200 ms, +400 ms… Adding ±50% randomness turns the waves into a smoother stream. The retry-storm playground scenario shows the amplification.

items.title: Circuit breaker and bulkhead
items.text:
Q7. The circuit breaker has minimum-number-of-calls: 10, failure-rate-threshold: 50 and wait-duration-in-open-state: 10s. payment goes down. What does the breaker do?

  • A. Retries forever until payment returns
  • B. After at least 10 recorded calls with ≥ 50% failures it opens: for 10 s calls fail immediately with CallNotPermittedException; then it goes half-open and lets a few trial calls through to decide whether to close
  • C. Restarts payment
  • D. Sends all calls to a backup payment instance
Answer

B — closed → open → half-open → closed (or open again).

The open state saves the caller's threads and time, and gives the dependency room to recover instead of a flood of doomed calls. Half-open probing detects recovery automatically. A breaker does not repair anything — it limits the damage.

Q8. Why is CallNotPermittedException in the retry's ignore-exceptions?

  • A. Because Resilience4j cannot retry it technically
  • B. Because when the circuit is open, retrying immediately is pointless and only adds latency; the call should fail fast to the fallback
  • C. Because it is a checked exception
  • D. Because the bulkhead handles it
Answer

B — an open circuit is a decision, not a transient error.

With the default aspect order Retry(CircuitBreaker(Bulkhead(call))), the retry sees the breaker's rejection. Retrying it would just collect three rejections and backoff delays. Ignoring it sends the request straight to the fallback — fast and honest.

Q9. Calls to payment succeed but take 700 ms, below both the read timeout and the slow-call threshold. At 70 payments/s, order's 50 threads are nearly all busy and GET /orders/{id} slows down. Which pattern fixes this?

  • A. A shorter timeout
  • B. More retries
  • C. A bulkhead: limit the concurrent calls to payment (e.g. 10), rejecting the excess immediately so the rest of the threads keep serving other endpoints
  • D. A larger circuit breaker window
Answer

C — a bulkhead caps the concurrency one dependency may use.

Nothing is failing, so neither timeout nor breaker reacts. 70/s × 0.7 s ≈ 49 concurrent calls fill the pool. The bulkhead reserves the remaining capacity for everything else; some payments get a fast 503, which is better than the whole service slowing down.

Q10. In PaymentGateway, why is the fallbackMethod on @Retry and not on @CircuitBreaker?

  • A. Because @CircuitBreaker does not support fallbacks
  • B. Because Retry is the outermost aspect: a fallback on the inner circuit breaker would convert every failure into the fallback's exception before the retry could see — and retry — the original transient error
  • C. Because fallbacks must be on the first annotation in the source file
  • D. There is no difference
Answer

B — the fallback belongs on the outermost layer.

Resilience4j's default order is Retry(CircuitBreaker(RateLimiter(TimeLimiter(Bulkhead(call))))). A fallback replaces the exception of the layer it decorates. On the inner breaker, a ResourceAccessException would become PaymentUnavailableException, which is not in retry-exceptions: the retry would silently stop working.

items.title: Chaos and game days
items.text:
Q11. Why does OrderService.pay call payment outside a database transaction?

  • A. Because JDBC does not allow HTTP calls inside transactions
  • B. Because a transaction holds a database connection: waiting 3 s on payment inside it would move the exhaustion from Tomcat threads to the connection pool, affecting every query of order
  • C. To make the payment faster
  • D. Because Resilience4j requires it
Answer

B — never hold scarce resources while waiting on a remote call.

The pool has ~10 connections; a few slow payments inside transactions would starve all other queries. The remote call runs first, then a short transaction updates the status (WHERE status = 'PENDING_PAYMENT' keeps it idempotent) and writes the outbox event.

Q12. What is the purpose of the steady-state hypothesis in a game day?

  • A. To prove the system never fails
  • B. To state, before injecting a failure, the measurable behavior the system should keep (e.g. browse p95 < 200 ms while payment is slow), so that the result is a clear confirmation or refutation
  • C. To schedule the game day when traffic is steady
  • D. To decide who is to blame for failures
Answer

B — no hypothesis, no experiment.

Chaos engineering is an experiment: baseline, hypothesis, injection, observation, conclusion. A refuted hypothesis (the system did not behave as designed) is the most valuable outcome — found on a Tuesday afternoon instead of during the next flash sale. The review is blameless: it fixes systems and processes, not people.

Back to the lab

items.title: 3. Game Day
items.text: The patterns of step 2 were tested one at a time, by the person who wrote them, knowing what would break. Real incidents are not like that. A game day is a rehearsed incident: a team injects failures into a running system, without telling the operators which ones, and checks two hypotheses at once — that the system degrades the way the design says, and that the people notice, diagnose and mitigate in time. It is the practice side of chaos engineering.

items.title: Roles (groups of 3–4)
items.text:
Role Does Must not Game master picks and injects the failures with Toxiproxy, keeps the clock tell the others what was injected Operator(s) watches Grafana (lab 8) and the logs, diagnoses, mitigates look at the game master's terminal Scribe writes the timeline: every observation and decision, with the time fix anything

Rotate roles between rounds, so that everyone operates once.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
1. Steady state. Run load/pay-under-chaos.js with DURATION=30m and write down the normal values from the RED dashboard: order and payment rate, error %, p95. This is the baseline every experiment is compared with.
  2. Hypotheses. For each experiment below, the team writes before injecting what it expects to see (e.g. "with payment +2 s, order p95 for pay stays under 1.5 s and GET /orders/{id} is unaffected").
  3. Blast radius and abort. Only your laptop's BoxOffice. Abort condition: anything outside the experiment breaks (e.g. catalog errors). The abort button is one command: curl -s -X POST localhost:8474/reset (removes every toxic and re-enables every proxy).
  4. Detection. The burn-rate alert from lab 8 watches only catalog. Add the same two rules for order (the lab 8 file with catalog replaced by order, shown below), then docker compose restart otel-lgtm: Alerting → Alert rules now lists four rules in the folder BoxOffice, all Normal, so that the operators can be paged.
infra/grafana/alerting/slo-order.yaml — the complete file infra/grafana/alerting/slo-order.yaml
# Lab 9: slo-catalog.yaml of lab 8 with "catalog" replaced by "order", so the game day can page.
# Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts for the order availability SLO (Google SRE workbook, ch. 5).
# SLI: share of order requests (health checks excluded) NOT answered with 5xx. SLO: 99.5% / 28 days.
apiVersion: 1

groups:
  - orgId: 1
    name: order-slo
    folder: BoxOffice
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      - uid: order-availability-fast-burn
        title: "order availability SLO: fast burn"
        condition: C
        data:
          - refId: A          # burn rate over the long window (1 h)
            relativeTimeRange: { from: 3600, to: 0 }
            datasourceUid: prometheus
            model:
              refId: A
              instant: true
              expr: |
                (
                  sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="order", http_route!~"/actuator.*", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[1h]))
                  / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="order", http_route!~"/actuator.*"}[1h]))
                ) / 0.005
          - refId: B          # burn rate over the short window (5 min): stops paging soon after recovery
            relativeTimeRange: { from: 300, to: 0 }
            datasourceUid: prometheus
            model:
              refId: B
              instant: true
              expr: |
                (
                  sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="order", http_route!~"/actuator.*", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
                  / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="order", http_route!~"/actuator.*"}[5m]))
                ) / 0.005
          - refId: C
            datasourceUid: __expr__
            model:
              refId: C
              type: math
              expression: "$A > 14.4 && $B > 14.4"
        for: 1m
        noDataState: OK
        execErrState: Error
        labels:
          severity: page
          slo: order-availability
        annotations:
          summary: "order is burning its 28-day error budget 14.4x too fast"
          description: 'Burn rate {{ printf "%.1f" $values.A.Value }} (1 h) and {{ printf "%.1f" $values.B.Value }} (5 min): at this pace about 2% of the 28-day budget is gone in one hour.'

      - uid: order-availability-slow-burn
        title: "order availability SLO: slow burn"
        condition: C
        data:
          - refId: A          # 6 h window
            relativeTimeRange: { from: 21600, to: 0 }
            datasourceUid: prometheus
            model:
              refId: A
              instant: true
              expr: |
                (
                  sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="order", http_route!~"/actuator.*", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[6h]))
                  / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="order", http_route!~"/actuator.*"}[6h]))
                ) / 0.005
          - refId: B          # 30 min window
            relativeTimeRange: { from: 1800, to: 0 }
            datasourceUid: prometheus
            model:
              refId: B
              instant: true
              expr: |
                (
                  sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="order", http_route!~"/actuator.*", http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[30m]))
                  / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{service_name="order", http_route!~"/actuator.*"}[30m]))
                ) / 0.005
          - refId: C
            datasourceUid: __expr__
            model:
              refId: C
              type: math
              expression: "$A > 6 && $B > 6"
        for: 5m
        noDataState: OK
        execErrState: Error
        labels:
          severity: ticket
          slo: order-availability
        annotations:
          summary: "order is burning its error budget 6x too fast"
          description: 'Burn rate {{ printf "%.1f" $values.A.Value }} (6 h) and {{ printf "%.1f" $values.B.Value }} (30 min): about 5% of the 28-day budget in six hours.'

items.title: The experiments
items.text:
The game master picks three of these, in any order, 5–8 minutes each with recovery time in between:

# Injection (game master) What a good system does What a good operator does 1 payment +2 s latency timeouts + breaker: fast 503s on pay, browse unaffected finds payment in the trace, sees the breaker open 2 psp black hole (timeout toxic, 0) payment read timeout (2 s) fails calls; order breaker opens follows the trace one hop further, to the provider 3 40% reset_peer on payment retries hide most errors; error rate rises only a little notices retries in the metrics, does not panic 4 payment proxy disabled breaker open, fast 503, orders stay PENDING_PAYMENT communicates "payments down, orders safe" 5 db paused (docker compose pause db) everything slows; the SLO alert fires identifies the shared dependency, not the symptom 6 1 KB/s bandwidth on payment slow responses hit the read timeout distinguishes "slow" from "down"

Injection commands:

scripts/game-day.sh
#!/bin/sh
# Game master helper. Usage: sh scripts/game-day.sh <experiment 1..6 | reset>
API=localhost:8474
toxic() { # proxy, json
  curl -s -X POST "$API/proxies/$1/toxics" -d "$2" > /dev/null
}
echo "$(date +%T) experiment $1"
case "$1" in
  1) toxic payment '{"name":"gd","type":"latency","stream":"downstream","attributes":{"latency":2000,"jitter":300}}' ;;
  2) toxic psp '{"name":"gd","type":"timeout","stream":"downstream","attributes":{"timeout":0}}' ;;
  3) toxic payment '{"name":"gd","type":"reset_peer","toxicity":0.4,"attributes":{"timeout":0}}' ;;
  4) curl -s -X POST "$API/proxies/payment" -d '{"enabled":false}' > /dev/null ;;
  5) docker compose pause db ;;
  6) toxic payment '{"name":"gd","type":"bandwidth","stream":"downstream","attributes":{"rate":1}}' ;;
  reset) curl -s -X POST "$API/reset" > /dev/null; docker compose unpause db 2> /dev/null || true ;;
  *) echo "unknown experiment"; exit 1 ;;
esac

items.title: During the round
items.text:
The operators work as in a real incident (see the incident response class): declare the incident when an alert fires or a symptom is seen, assign an incident commander, diagnose with the dashboard → trace → logs path, mitigate first (e.g. stop sending traffic to a broken path, raise a timeout, scale), investigate later. The scribe records times in this format:

Time Who Observation / decision 10:02:10 GM (hidden) experiment 1 injected 10:04:30 Op order p95 rising on the dashboard; no alert yet 10:05:05 Op trace shows payment span ~2 s; breaker OPEN in actuator …

From the timeline you get the two numbers every incident review asks for: time to detect (injection → first correct observation) and time to mitigate (injection → users no longer affected).

items.title: After: a blameless review
items.text:
Write one review per round in results/lab9-gameday.md. Blameless means the review explains how the system and the process allowed the outcome — never who is to blame.

results/lab9-gameday.md (template)
# Game day — round <n>

**Experiment:** <what was injected, when> · **Duration:** <mm:ss>
**Hypothesis:** <what we expected>
**Result:** <confirmed | refuted> — <one sentence>

## Impact
- Users affected: <which requests, how many, for how long> (from the RED dashboard)
- SLO budget spent: <% of the 28-day budget>

## Timeline
| Time | Event |
|---|---|

## Detection and mitigation
- Time to detect: <min> — how: <alert | dashboard | trace>
- Time to mitigate: <min> — how: <...>

## What went well / what was hard

## Action items
| Action | Type (prevent / detect / mitigate) | Owner |
|---|---|---|

Pitfalls

  • No hypothesis, no experiment. Breaking things to "see what happens" teaches little; a refuted hypothesis is the valuable outcome.
  • Start small. Latency before outages, one dependency before two, a laptop before production.
  • The abort button must work before the first injection. Test reset first.
  • Fix the action items. A game day whose findings stay in a document will be repeated, with the same findings, by a real incident.

Next: Measure it

items.title: 4. Measure It
items.text:
One script drives every experiment of step 2 and the game day. It runs two scenarios at the same time, because a cascading failure is only visible when you also measure what should not be affected:

Scenario Rate Request Touches payment? pay PAY_RATE (default 20/s) place an order, then POST /orders/{id}/pay yes browse 20/s GET /orders/{id} of orders created in setup() no load/pay-under-chaos.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import exec from 'k6/execution';
import { Rate } from 'k6/metrics';

const BASE_URL = __ENV.BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:8084'; // order directly: isolate the service
const RUN = __ENV.RUN || `${Date.now()}`;
const DURATION = __ENV.DURATION || '2m';
const JSON_HEADERS = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' };

const fastFail = new Rate('pay_fast_fail'); // share of payments answered 503 by the fallback

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    pay: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      exec: 'pay',
      rate: Number(__ENV.PAY_RATE || 20),
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: DURATION,
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 600,
    },
    browse: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      exec: 'browse',
      rate: 20,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: DURATION,
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 300,
    },
  },
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'med', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'max'],
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{name:pay}': ['p(95)<1500'],
    'http_req_duration{name:browse}': ['p(95)<200'], // the collateral damage
    'http_req_failed{name:browse}': ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

export function setup() {
  const ids = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
    const res = http.post(`${BASE_URL}/orders`,
      JSON.stringify({ showId: 'show-9', holdId: `browse-${RUN}-${i}`, customerEmail: `b${i}@example.com`, amount: 100.0 }),
      { headers: JSON_HEADERS });
    ids.push(res.json('id'));
  }
  return { ids };
}

export function pay() {
  const n = exec.scenario.iterationInTest;
  const placed = http.post(`${BASE_URL}/orders`,
    JSON.stringify({ showId: 'show-9', holdId: `pay-${RUN}-${n}`, customerEmail: `fan${n}@example.com`, amount: 350.0 }),
    { headers: JSON_HEADERS, tags: { name: 'place' } });
  if (placed.status !== 201) {
    return;
  }
  const res = http.post(`${BASE_URL}/orders/${placed.json('id')}/pay`, null, { tags: { name: 'pay' } });
  fastFail.add(res.status === 503);
  check(res, { 'paid and confirmed': (r) => r.status === 200 && r.json('status') === 'CONFIRMED' });
}

export function browse(data) {
  const id = data.ids[exec.scenario.iterationInTest % data.ids.length];
  const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/orders/${id}`, { tags: { name: 'browse' } });
  check(res, { 'order read': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

Read four lines of the summary after every run: http_req_duration{name:pay} and {name:browse} (p95, p99), the paid and confirmed check (share of confirmed payments; the checks total also counts the order read check of browse), pay_fast_fail, and http_req_failed{name:browse}. Watch the circuit breaker while it runs:

watch -n 1 "curl -s localhost:8084/actuator/circuitbreakers | jq '.circuitBreakers.payment'"

Expected shape (illustrative)

Unprotected with +3 s: pay p95 grows to many seconds and browse p95 grows with it — the cascade. With a timeout: pay fails in about a second, browse is back to milliseconds. With the circuit breaker during an outage: pay answers 503 in milliseconds most of the time (pay_fast_fail close to 1) and calls to payment drop to a trickle of half-open probes. With the bulkhead under slow-but-successful calls: some payments get 503, but browse stays fast.

A test run on a busy laptop (the whole lab 9 stack, 45 s per run, payment + 3 s latency):

Configuration pay p50 / p95 browse p50 / p95 pay_fast_fail unprotected (PAYMENT_RESILIENCE=false, PAYMENT_READ_TIMEOUT=0) 13.8 s / 17.1 s 9.04 s / 13.17 s 0% all patterns (defaults) 5 ms / 1.38 s 6.5 ms / 805 ms 100%

Unprotected, GET /orders/{id} — which never calls payment — waited 9 s at the median: the cascade. With the patterns, the breaker opened within seconds and every payment failed fast with 503, so browse went back to milliseconds (its p95 still shows the first seconds, before the breaker opened). Your absolute numbers will differ; the contrast between the two browse columns is what you must reproduce.

items.title: Results
items.text:
Copy into results/lab9.md. "Before" is the unprotected or disabled configuration of each row; "After" is the one with the pattern.

Experiment (toxic) Metric Before After Baseline (no toxic) pay p95 (ms) / browse p95 (ms) — Timeout (latency 3 s) pay p95 (ms) Timeout (latency 3 s) browse p95 (ms) / browse errors (%) Retry (reset_peer 30%) payments confirmed (%) Retry (reset_peer 30%) pay p95 (ms) Circuit breaker (proxy disabled) pay p95 (ms) / pay_fast_fail (%) Circuit breaker (proxy disabled) time from re-enable to CLOSED (s) — Bulkhead (latency 700 ms, 70 pay/s) browse p95 (ms) Bulkhead (latency 700 ms, 70 pay/s) payments rejected (%) Game day time to detect / time to mitigate (min) —

Below the table, one paragraph per pattern: the mechanism (with Little's Law where it applies), the number that proves it, and the price you paid for it.

Back to the overview Quiz

items.title: 2. Resilience Patterns
items.text: order now calls payment synchronously: POST /orders/{id}/pay charges the fan and, on success, confirms the order. This step first shows what one slow dependency does to an unprotected service, then adds the four patterns of the reliability class one at a time — timeout, retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead — measuring after each.

items.title: The failure we are defending against
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant F as fans (20/s)
    participant O as order (50 threads)
    participant P as payment (+3 s latency)
    F->>O: POST /orders/1/pay
    O->>P: charge (waits 3 s)
    F->>O: POST /orders/2/pay
    O->>P: charge (waits 3 s)
    Note over O: 20 req/s x 3 s = 60 calls in flight > 50 threads
    F->>O: GET /orders/7 (unrelated!)
    Note over O: no free thread: queued, then times out
    O-->>F: 503 / timeout for EVERY endpoint

Little's Law says it all: threads busy = arrival rate × time each call holds a thread. With 20 payments/s and a dependency that takes 3 s, order needs 60 threads just to wait. When the pool (50 here, 200 by default) runs out, every endpoint of order stops — including GET /orders/{id}, which never touches payment. One slow dependency took the whole service down: a cascading failure.

Why order gets only 50 threads in this lab

Tomcat's default pool is 200 threads. A laptop running fourteen containers cannot generate enough load to exhaust 200 threads against a 3-second dependency without k6 itself becoming the bottleneck, so the lab shrinks the pool (server.tomcat.threads.max: 50) — the same trick lab 1 used when it limited catalog to one CPU. The mechanism is identical at any size.
