The new package boxoffice.order.payment holds the client and the protected gateway:

PaymentRequest.java / PaymentResponse.javaPaymentClient.javaPaymentGateway.javaPaymentUnavailableException.java services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/payment/PaymentRequest.java
package boxoffice.order.payment;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.UUID;

public record PaymentRequest(UUID orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
}
services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/payment/PaymentResponse.java
package boxoffice.order.payment;

import java.util.UUID;

/** status: AUTHORIZED or DECLINED */
public record PaymentResponse(UUID id, UUID orderId, String status) {
}
services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/payment/PaymentClient.java
package boxoffice.order.payment;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.http.client.SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

@Component
public class PaymentClient {

    private final RestClient http;

    public PaymentClient(RestClient.Builder builder,
                         @Value("${boxoffice.payment.url}") String url,
                         @Value("${boxoffice.payment.connect-timeout}") Duration connectTimeout,
                         @Value("${boxoffice.payment.read-timeout}") Duration readTimeout) {
        SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory factory = new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory();
        factory.setConnectTimeout(connectTimeout);
        factory.setReadTimeout(readTimeout); // 0 = wait forever (the "before" experiment)
        this.http = builder.baseUrl(url).requestFactory(factory).build();
    }

    public PaymentResponse charge(UUID orderId, java.math.BigDecimal amount) {
        return http.post()
                .uri("/payments")
                .header("Idempotency-Key", "order-" + orderId) // same key on every retry
                .body(new PaymentRequest(orderId, amount))
                .retrieve()
                .body(PaymentResponse.class);
    }
}
services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/payment/PaymentGateway.java
package boxoffice.order.payment;

import io.github.resilience4j.bulkhead.annotation.Bulkhead;
import io.github.resilience4j.circuitbreaker.annotation.CircuitBreaker;
import io.github.resilience4j.retry.annotation.Retry;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

/**
 * Default aspect order: Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( Bulkhead ( call ) ) ).
 * The fallback sits on the OUTERMOST layer, so it runs only after the retries are exhausted,
 * when the circuit is open or when the bulkhead is full.
 */
@Component
public class PaymentGateway {

    private final PaymentClient client;

    public PaymentGateway(PaymentClient client) {
        this.client = client;
    }

    @Retry(name = "payment", fallbackMethod = "unavailable")
    @CircuitBreaker(name = "payment")
    @Bulkhead(name = "payment")
    public PaymentResponse charge(UUID orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        return client.charge(orderId, amount);
    }

    /** The "before" path of the experiments: no Resilience4j at all. */
    public PaymentResponse chargeUnprotected(UUID orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        return client.charge(orderId, amount);
    }

    /** Same parameters + the exception: Resilience4j finds it by name and signature. */
    private PaymentResponse unavailable(UUID orderId, BigDecimal amount, Throwable cause) {
        throw new PaymentUnavailableException(cause);
    }
}
services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/payment/PaymentUnavailableException.java
package boxoffice.order.payment;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ResponseStatus;

/** Fast, explicit failure: the fan sees "try again in a moment", not a 60-second spinner. */
@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE)
public class PaymentUnavailableException extends RuntimeException {

    public PaymentUnavailableException(Throwable cause) {
        super("payment temporarily unavailable: " + cause.getClass().getSimpleName(), cause);
    }
}

OrderService gains pay. Note where the transaction is: the remote call happens with no transaction open, and only the short status update runs in one — holding a database connection while waiting 3 s for a dependency would move the cascade into the connection pool.

OrderService.javaOrderController.java services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/OrderService.java
package boxoffice.order;

import boxoffice.order.OrderProperties.NotifyMode;
import boxoffice.order.outbox.Outbox;
import boxoffice.order.payment.PaymentGateway;
import boxoffice.order.payment.PaymentResponse;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;
import org.springframework.web.server.ResponseStatusException;

@Service
public class OrderService {

    public record PlaceResult(OrderView order, boolean created) {
    }

    private static final String SELECT = """
            SELECT id, show_id, hold_id, customer_email, amount, status, created_at
            FROM orders
            """;

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final Outbox outbox;
    private final NotificationClient notifications;
    private final OrderProperties props;
    private final PaymentGateway payments;
    private final TransactionTemplate tx;
    private final boolean resilience;

    public OrderService(JdbcClient jdbc, Outbox outbox, NotificationClient notifications,
                        OrderProperties props, PaymentGateway payments, TransactionTemplate tx,
                        @Value("${boxoffice.payment.resilience:true}") boolean resilience) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.outbox = outbox;
        this.notifications = notifications;
        this.props = props;
        this.payments = payments;
        this.tx = tx;
        this.resilience = resilience;
    }

    @Transactional
    public PlaceResult place(OrderRequest req) {
        int inserted = jdbc.sql("""
                INSERT INTO orders (id, show_id, hold_id, customer_email, amount, status)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 'PENDING_PAYMENT')
                ON CONFLICT (hold_id) DO NOTHING
                """)
                .params(UUID.randomUUID(), req.showId(), req.holdId(), req.customerEmail(), req.amount())
                .update();

        OrderView order = jdbc.sql(SELECT + " WHERE hold_id = ?")
                .param(req.holdId())
                .query(OrderView.class)
                .single();

        if (inserted == 0) {
            return new PlaceResult(order, false);
        }

        OrderEvent event = OrderEvent.placed(order);
        if (props.notifyMode() == NotifyMode.SYNC) {
            notifications.send(event);
        } else {
            outbox.append(event.eventId(), "order", order.id(), event.eventType(), event);
        }
        return new PlaceResult(order, true);
    }

    /** No @Transactional here: never hold a DB connection during a remote call. */
    public OrderView pay(UUID id) {
        OrderView order = find(id).orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND));
        if (!"PENDING_PAYMENT".equals(order.status())) {
            return order; // already paid or cancelled: paying twice is a no-op
        }
        PaymentResponse payment = resilience
                ? payments.charge(order.id(), order.amount())
                : payments.chargeUnprotected(order.id(), order.amount());
        String next = "AUTHORIZED".equals(payment.status()) ? "CONFIRMED" : "CANCELLED";

        tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
            int changed = jdbc.sql("UPDATE orders SET status = ? WHERE id = ? AND status = 'PENDING_PAYMENT'")
                    .params(next, id)
                    .update();
            if (changed == 1) {
                String type = "CONFIRMED".equals(next) ? "OrderConfirmed" : "OrderCancelled";
                OrderEvent event = new OrderEvent(UUID.randomUUID(), type, order.id(), order.showId(),
                        order.holdId(), order.customerEmail(), order.amount(), Instant.now());
                outbox.append(event.eventId(), "order", order.id(), type, event);
            }
        });
        return find(id).orElseThrow();
    }

    public Optional<OrderView> find(UUID id) {
        return jdbc.sql(SELECT + " WHERE id = ?").param(id).query(OrderView.class).optional();
    }
}
services/order/src/main/java/boxoffice/order/OrderController.java
package boxoffice.order;

import boxoffice.order.waitingroom.WaitingRoom;
import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import java.net.URI;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestHeader;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
import org.springframework.web.server.ResponseStatusException;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orders;
    private final WaitingRoom waitingRoom;

    public OrderController(OrderService orders, WaitingRoom waitingRoom) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.waitingRoom = waitingRoom;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderView> place(
            @Valid @RequestBody OrderRequest req,
            @RequestHeader(name = "X-Admission-Ticket", required = false) String ticket) {
        if (!waitingRoom.mayEnter(req.showId(), ticket)) {
            throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN,
                    "on-sale in progress: join /orders/waiting-room/" + req.showId() + "/join first");
        }
        OrderService.PlaceResult result = orders.place(req);
        if (!result.created()) {
            return ResponseEntity.ok(result.order());
        }
        return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/orders/" + result.order().id())).body(result.order());
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public OrderView get(@PathVariable UUID id) {
        return orders.find(id).orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND));
    }

    @PostMapping("/{id}/pay")
    public OrderView pay(@PathVariable UUID id) {
        return orders.pay(id);
    }
}

Rebuild order and pay an order end to end (from the repository root):

docker compose up -d --build order
ID=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:8084/orders -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"showId":"show-9","holdId":"hold-pay-1","customerEmail":"bia@example.com","amount":350.00}' | jq -r .id)
curl -s -X POST localhost:8084/orders/$ID/pay

You should see the order with "status":"CONFIRMED". The first payment after a restart can answer 503 instead: the cold JVMs of order, payment and WireMock may need more than the 1 s read timeout for the very first call — the fallback at work. Call pay again: payment already stored the charge under the same idempotency key, so the second call answers at once with CONFIRMED (no second charge).

The UPDATE … WHERE status = 'PENDING_PAYMENT' makes the confirmation idempotent too: two concurrent pay calls for the same order may both reach payment (which deduplicates by key), but only one changes the status and writes the OrderConfirmed event.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
All the knobs live in application.yaml (the complete file; the lab 9 parts are server.tomcat, boxoffice.payment, resilience4j and the new actuator endpoints); the environment variables let you switch them off one by one in the experiments without rebuilding.

services/order/src/main/resources/application.yaml
server:
  port: 8084
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 50                        # lab 9: small on purpose, to make thread exhaustion visible

spring:
  application:
    name: order
  mvc:
    problemdetails:
      enabled: true
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://${DB_HOST:db}:${DB_PORT:5432}/${DB_NAME:boxoffice}?currentSchema=orders
    username: ${DB_USER:boxoffice}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD:boxoffice}
  flyway:
    schemas: orders
  data:
    redis:
      host: ${REDIS_HOST:redis}
      port: 6379
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:kafka:9092}
    producer:
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        linger.ms: 5
        max.block.ms: 5000     # Kafka down: fail the relay run in 5 s (default 60 s) and retry

boxoffice:
  order:
    notify-mode: ${NOTIFY_MODE:outbox}
    notification-url: ${NOTIFICATION_URL:http://notification:8086}
    topic: order-events
    relay-interval-ms: 200
  waiting-room:
    admit-per-second: ${ADMIT_PER_SECOND:20}
    admission-ttl: 5m
  payment:                           # lab 9
    url: ${PAYMENT_URL:http://payment:8085}
    resilience: ${PAYMENT_RESILIENCE:true}   # false = call payment with no Resilience4j at all
    connect-timeout: 500ms
    read-timeout: ${PAYMENT_READ_TIMEOUT:1s} # 0 = wait forever

resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      payment:
        max-attempts: ${PAYMENT_RETRY_ATTEMPTS:3}    # 1 = no retry
        wait-duration: 200ms
        enable-exponential-backoff: true
        exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2            # 200 ms, 400 ms ...
        enable-randomized-wait: true
        randomized-wait-factor: 0.5                  # ... each +/- 50% (jitter)
        retry-exceptions:
          - org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException   # timeouts, connection refused/reset
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpServerErrorException  # 5xx
        ignore-exceptions:
          - io.github.resilience4j.circuitbreaker.CallNotPermittedException  # circuit open: fail fast
          - io.github.resilience4j.bulkhead.BulkheadFullException           # bulkhead full: fail fast
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      payment:
        sliding-window-type: COUNT_BASED
        sliding-window-size: 20
        minimum-number-of-calls: 10
        failure-rate-threshold: 50                   # open when >= 50% of the last 20 calls failed...
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 800ms
        slow-call-rate-threshold: 50                 # ... or >= 50% were slower than 800 ms
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 10s
        permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 3
        automatic-transition-from-open-to-half-open-enabled: true
        register-health-indicator: true
        ignore-exceptions:
          - io.github.resilience4j.bulkhead.BulkheadFullException  # our own refusal is not the dependency's fault
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      payment:
        max-concurrent-calls: ${PAYMENT_BULKHEAD:10} # at most 10 of the 50 threads wait on payment
        max-wait-duration: 0                         # full = reject immediately

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,metrics,circuitbreakers,circuitbreakerevents,retries,bulkheads
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true        # /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness
  health:
    circuitbreakers:
      enabled: true          # lab 9: breaker state in /actuator/health

items.title: Pattern by pattern
items.text: Each experiment uses the k6 script of step 4 (load/pay-under-chaos.js): 20 payments per second plus 20 GET /orders/{id} per second, for 2 minutes. Rebuild order once (docker compose up -d --build order), then change only environment variables.

items.title: 0. Unprotected
items.text:
PAYMENT_RESILIENCE=false PAYMENT_READ_TIMEOUT=0 docker compose up -d order
curl -s -X POST localhost:8474/proxies/payment/toxics \
  -d '{"name":"slow","type":"latency","stream":"downstream","attributes":{"latency":3000}}'
k6 run load/pay-under-chaos.js

Watch the browse scenario: GET /orders/{id} — which does not call payment — degrades with pay. That is the cascade.

items.title: 1. Timeout
items.text:
PAYMENT_RESILIENCE=false PAYMENT_READ_TIMEOUT=1s docker compose up -d order
k6 run load/pay-under-chaos.js

Every payment now fails after 1 s instead of hanging for 3 s: a thread is held 1 s, not 3 s, so 20/s × 1 s = 20 threads — inside the pool. GET /orders/{id} recovers. A timeout converts a slow failure into a fast failure, and fast failures do not cascade.

Timeouts must be shorter than the caller's

The edge or the gateway in front of order has its own timeout. If order waits longer for payment than the gateway waits for order, the gateway gives up first and order keeps working for nobody. Budgets shrink at each hop: edge 10 s > gateway 5 s > order→payment 1 s × retries.

items.title: 2. Retry with backoff and jitter
items.text:
Replace the latency with a flaky network — 30% of the connections reset:

curl -s -X DELETE localhost:8474/proxies/payment/toxics/slow
curl -s -X POST localhost:8474/proxies/payment/toxics \
  -d '{"name":"flaky","type":"reset_peer","toxicity":0.3,"attributes":{"timeout":0}}'
PAYMENT_RETRY_ATTEMPTS=1 docker compose up -d order    # resilience on, retry off
k6 run load/pay-under-chaos.js
PAYMENT_RETRY_ATTEMPTS=3 docker compose up -d order
k6 run load/pay-under-chaos.js

With one attempt, a share of the payments fail (not exactly 30%: the toxicity applies per TCP connection, and healthy connections are reused). With three attempts, a payment fails only if all three fail: if one attempt fails with probability p, three fail with p³ — 30% becomes 2.7%. Retries fix transient errors — at the price of extra load on the dependency (up to 3×) and extra latency (the backoff). They are safe only because the request carries an idempotency key.

Why jitter?

Without it, every client that failed at the same instant retries at the same instant (200 ms later, then 400 ms later): synchronized waves that hit a recovering dependency like a hammer. A random ±50% spreads the retries over time. Try the retry-storm scenario in the playground to see the amplification.

items.title: 3. Circuit breaker
items.text:
Now a full outage: disable the proxy, so every connection to payment is refused.

curl -s -X DELETE localhost:8474/proxies/payment/toxics/flaky
curl -s -X POST localhost:8474/proxies/payment -d '{"enabled": false}'
k6 run load/pay-under-chaos.js                                                          # terminal 1
watch -n 1 "curl -s localhost:8084/actuator/circuitbreakers | jq '.circuitBreakers.payment.state'"   # terminal 2

After 10 failed calls (the minimum-number-of-calls) the breaker opens: for the next 10 s, charge fails immediately with CallNotPermittedException — no network call, no retry, no waiting — and the fallback answers 503. Then it goes half-open, lets 3 trial calls through and closes again if they succeed. Re-enable the proxy in the middle of the run (curl -s -X POST localhost:8474/proxies/payment -d '{"enabled": true}') and watch it close. /actuator/circuitbreakerevents lists every transition.

The breaker protects both sides: order stops wasting threads and time on calls that will fail, and payment gets breathing room to recover instead of a flood of retries.

items.title: 4. Bulkhead
items.text:
Back to latency, but this time calls that succeed slowly — 700 ms: under the read timeout (1 s) and under the circuit breaker's slow-call threshold (800 ms), so neither of them reacts — and more of them: 70 payments per second.

curl -s -X POST localhost:8474/proxies/payment -d '{"enabled": true}'
curl -s -X POST localhost:8474/proxies/payment/toxics \
  -d '{"name":"slow","type":"latency","stream":"downstream","attributes":{"latency":700}}'
PAYMENT_BULKHEAD=1000 docker compose up -d order   # effectively no bulkhead
k6 run -e PAY_RATE=70 load/pay-under-chaos.js
PAYMENT_BULKHEAD=10 docker compose up -d order
k6 run -e PAY_RATE=70 load/pay-under-chaos.js
curl -s -X POST localhost:8474/reset                # remove every toxic

Without a bulkhead, 70/s × 0.7 s ≈ 49 threads wait on payment: the pool of 50 is practically full and GET /orders/{id} queues behind the payments. With max-concurrent-calls: 10, at most 10 threads wait on payment; the extra concurrent payments are rejected at once (503), and the other 40 threads keep serving GET /orders/{id} at normal latency. A bulkhead is a budget of concurrency per dependency — named after the watertight compartments of a ship.

Pattern Protects against Cost Timeout waiting forever on a slow dependency some slow-but-successful calls become errors Retry + backoff + jitter transient errors more load on the dependency, more latency; needs idempotency Circuit breaker hammering a dependency that is down rejects calls for wait-duration even if it recovered sooner Bulkhead one dependency consuming all threads rejects calls above the limit even if threads are free elsewhere Fallback showing a raw error must be honest: "try again", not a fake success

In the interview

"Every remote call gets a timeout shorter than its caller's, retries only on transient errors with exponential backoff and jitter, on idempotent operations, behind a circuit breaker; each dependency gets its own bulkhead so one slow dependency cannot exhaust the service."

Next: Game day

items.title: 1. Payment, Provider and Toxiproxy
items.text:
BoxOffice does not move money itself: the payment service is an adapter to an external payment service provider (PSP). That makes it the most dangerous dependency of the checkout — slow on a busy day, outside your control, and the place where a retry can charge a fan twice. This step builds the three pieces the rest of the lab breaks on purpose:

Container Image / build Port Role psp wiremock/wiremock:3.13.2 8080 (internal) a fake external provider: POST /v1/charges answers approved payment services/payment (Spring Boot) 8085 adapter: idempotent POST /payments, calls the PSP with timeouts toxiproxy ghcr.io/shopify/toxiproxy:2.13.0 8474 (API) TCP proxy in front of payment and psp; injects latency, resets, outages 
flowchart LR
    order[order] -->|"PAYMENT_URL = toxiproxy:18085"| tp1["toxiproxy proxy: payment"]
    tp1 --> payment[payment :8085]
    payment -->|"PSP_URL = toxiproxy:18095"| tp2["toxiproxy proxy: psp"]
    tp2 --> psp["psp (WireMock)"]
    payment --> db[(db: schema payment)]
    you[you / game day] -->|"curl :8474 add toxic"| tp1

Every call crosses a Toxiproxy proxy, so you can make any hop slow or broken without touching code: Toxiproxy works at the TCP level, below HTTP, exactly where real networks fail.

items.title: The fake provider
items.text:
WireMock answers HTTP from JSON stub files. One stub is enough: approve every charge and invent a provider reference.

The provider client sets both timeouts explicitly. Without them, a Java HTTP client waits forever for a response — the root cause of most cascading failures.

PspClient.javaPaymentService.javaPaymentController.java services/payment/src/main/java/boxoffice/payment/PspClient.java
package boxoffice.payment;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.Duration;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.http.client.SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

@Component
public class PspClient {

    record ChargeBody(BigDecimal amount, String currency, String reference) {
    }

    record Charge(String id, String status) {
    }

    private final RestClient http;

    public PspClient(RestClient.Builder builder,
                     @Value("${boxoffice.psp.url}") String url,
                     @Value("${boxoffice.psp.connect-timeout}") Duration connectTimeout,
                     @Value("${boxoffice.psp.read-timeout}") Duration readTimeout) {
        SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory factory = new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory();
        factory.setConnectTimeout(connectTimeout); // time to open the TCP connection
        factory.setReadTimeout(readTimeout);       // max silence while waiting for the response
        this.http = builder.baseUrl(url).requestFactory(factory).build();
    }

    /** The provider deduplicates by Idempotency-Key, like real PSPs do. */
    public Charge charge(String idempotencyKey, BigDecimal amount, String reference) {
        return http.post()
                .uri("/v1/charges")
                .header("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
                .body(new ChargeBody(amount, "BRL", reference))
                .retrieve()
                .body(Charge.class);
    }
}

package boxoffice.payment;

import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    public record Result(PaymentOut payment, boolean created) {
    }

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final PspClient psp;

    public PaymentService(JdbcClient jdbc, PspClient psp) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.psp = psp;
    }

    public Result charge(String idempotencyKey, ChargeRequest req) {
        Optional<PaymentOut> done = find(idempotencyKey);
        if (done.isPresent()) {
            return new Result(done.get(), false); // a retry: answer, do not charge again
        }
        // remote call OUTSIDE any database transaction: never hold a connection while waiting
        PspClient.Charge charge = psp.charge(idempotencyKey, req.amount(), "order-" + req.orderId());
        String status = "approved".equals(charge.status()) ? "AUTHORIZED" : "DECLINED";
        jdbc.sql("""
                INSERT INTO payments (id, idempotency_key, order_id, amount, status, provider_ref)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
                ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING
                """)
                .params(UUID.randomUUID(), idempotencyKey, req.orderId(), req.amount(), status, charge.id())
                .update();
        return new Result(find(idempotencyKey).orElseThrow(), true);
    }

    private Optional<PaymentOut> find(String idempotencyKey) {
        return jdbc.sql("""
                SELECT id, order_id, amount, status, provider_ref, created_at
                FROM payments WHERE idempotency_key = ?
                """)
                .param(idempotencyKey)
                .query(PaymentOut.class)
                .optional();
    }
}
services/payment/src/main/java/boxoffice/payment/PaymentController.java
package boxoffice.payment;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import java.net.URI;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestHeader;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/payments")
public class PaymentController {

    private final PaymentService payments;

    public PaymentController(PaymentService payments) {
        this.payments = payments;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<PaymentOut> charge(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String idempotencyKey,
                                             @Valid @RequestBody ChargeRequest req) {
        PaymentService.Result r = payments.charge(idempotencyKey, req);
        return r.created()
                ? ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/payments/" + r.payment().id())).body(r.payment())
                : ResponseEntity.ok(r.payment());
    }
}

Idempotency end to end

The same key travels order → payment → PSP: order sends Idempotency-Key: order-<id>, payment stores it with a UNIQUE constraint and forwards it to the provider. A retry at any layer — Resilience4j in order, a timeout in the gateway, a fan double-clicking — finds the key and gets the first result back. Retries are only safe on top of idempotency; this is the payment-system case study in miniature.

items.title: Toxiproxy
items.text:
Toxiproxy reads its proxies from a JSON file at startup:

infra/toxiproxy/toxiproxy.json
[
  { "name": "payment", "listen": "0.0.0.0:18085", "upstream": "payment:8085", "enabled": true },
  { "name": "psp",     "listen": "0.0.0.0:18095", "upstream": "psp:8080",     "enabled": true }
]

items.title: Compose
items.text:
docker-compose.yaml (excerpt)
  psp:
    image: wiremock/wiremock:3.13.2
    volumes:
      - ./infra/psp:/home/wiremock:ro

  toxiproxy:
    image: ghcr.io/shopify/toxiproxy:2.13.0
    command: ["-host=0.0.0.0", "-config=/config/toxiproxy.json"]
    volumes:
      - ./infra/toxiproxy/toxiproxy.json:/config/toxiproxy.json:ro
    ports:
      - "8474:8474"

  payment:
    build: ./services/payment
    volumes:
      - ./infra/otel:/otel:ro
    environment:
      <<: *otel
      OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: payment
      DB_HOST: db
      DB_PORT: 5432
      DB_NAME: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
      DB_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
      DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}
      PSP_URL: http://toxiproxy:18095                 # the provider, through Toxiproxy
    ports:
      - "8085:8085"
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      toxiproxy:
        condition: service_started
      psp:
        condition: service_started

      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 40s
      retries: 3

and the order service now reaches payment through the proxy (not directly), with the knobs of step 2 as variables:

    DB_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}

services:

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    command: ["postgres", "-c", "max_connections=${DB_MAX_CONNECTIONS:-100}"]
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME:-boxoffice}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USER:-boxoffice}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-boxoffice}

    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}"]

      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

  # read-only streaming replica of db (hot standby)
  db-replica:
    image: postgres:17
    user: postgres
    entrypoint: ["/usr/local/bin/replica-entrypoint.sh"]
    environment:
      PGPASSWORD: ${REPLICATION_PASSWORD:-replicator}     # used by pg_basebackup

    healthcheck:

Start the three new containers and wait until docker compose ps payment shows (healthy) (the first build takes a few minutes, the start about 30 s); then list the proxies and charge once:

docker compose up -d --build psp toxiproxy paymentcurl -s localhost:8474/proxies | jq 'keys'[ "payment", "psp"]curl -s -w '\n%{http_code}\n' -X POST localhost:8085/payments -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Idempotency-Key: test-1' -d '{"orderId":"5b0c2f9e-7d0a-4f43-9a55-1c1c2c8f8e10","amount":350.00}'{"id":"a8744598-4ef4-4d4d-85f2-105e5661233c","orderId":"5b0c2f9e-7d0a-4f43-9a55-1c1c2c8f8e10","amount":350.00,"status":"AUTHORIZED","providerRef":"ch_2zm5esh2yuqd","createdAt":"2026-10-18T18:44:51.939198Z"}201

You should see 201 and a body like {"id":"a8744598-…","orderId":"5b0c2f9e-…","amount":350.00,"status":"AUTHORIZED","providerRef":"ch_2zm5esh2yuqd",…}. Send the same curl again: 200 instead of 201, the same id and the same providerRef.

items.title: Your first toxic
items.text:
Add 3 seconds of latency to every response of the psp proxy, time a payment, remove the toxic:

curl -s -X POST localhost:8474/proxies/psp/toxics \
  -d '{"name":"slow","type":"latency","stream":"downstream","attributes":{"latency":3000}}'
time curl -s -X POST localhost:8085/payments -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Idempotency-Key: test-2' -d '{"orderId":"5b0c2f9e-7d0a-4f43-9a55-1c1c2c8f8e10","amount":350.00}'
curl -s -X DELETE localhost:8474/proxies/psp/toxics/slow

You should see {"…","status":500,"error":"Internal Server Error","path":"/payments"} after real 0m2.2s: the read timeout of PspClient (2 s) fired before the 3 s response arrived. Without it, the thread would have waited the full 3 s — or forever.

Toxic Attributes Simulates latency latency, jitter (ms) a slow dependency, a congested network timeout timeout (ms; 0 = never close) a black hole: packets go in, nothing comes back reset_peer timeout (ms) connection reset by peer (a crash, a load balancer killing connections) bandwidth rate (KB/s) a thin pipe limit_data bytes a connection cut in the middle of a response (proxy disabled) POST /proxies/<name> with {"enabled": false} the dependency is down: connection refused

Each toxic also takes a toxicity between 0 and 1: the probability that it applies to a new connection — perfect for "30% of the calls fail".

items.text:
The reference section is the part of the course you keep open in another tab: while designing in the playground, while doing a lab, while preparing for an interview. Nothing here needs to be read in order. Each page answers one kind of question quickly and links back to the class where the topic is explained in depth.

  • Component catalog

    The 49 components of the palette, one entry each: what it is, when to use it and when not to, key numbers, failure modes, playground parameters, real products on AWS, GCP, Azure and open source, and an interview one-liner.

  • Numbers

    The numbers every estimate starts from: latency ladder, powers of two, requests per second, storage sizes, the nines of availability, throughput of common components and approximate cloud prices.

  • Glossary

  • Tools

About the numbers and prices

Latencies, throughputs and prices in the reference are either well-known published values or orders of magnitude labeled illustrative. items.title: Component catalog
items.text:
Every box you can drop on the canvas of the System Design Playground has an entry in this catalog: what it is, when to use it and when not to, key numbers, failure modes, how it behaves in the playground, real products on AWS, GCP, Azure and in open source, and a one-liner you can say in the interview. The simulator's "learn more" links land on these entries.

The palette has 49 components in 10 categories. They follow a request from left to right: a client reaches the edge, the edge forwards to compute, compute is packaged and scaled in containers (on a Kubernetes cluster), compute reads and writes storage and publishes to messaging, everything is watched by observability, laid out inside a network, and some requests go to AI components or to external providers.

items.title: How to read an entry
items.text:
Use the catalog three ways

  • While designing in the playground: click a node, then "learn more" to see its parameters and failure modes.
  • Before an interview: read only the In the interview box of each component, out loud; then the quick reference.
  • While studying a class: each entry links back to the class pages and to the scenarios where the component matters.

Numbers in the catalog are either well-known published values (with the source named) or clearly marked ≈ illustrative — orders of magnitude to reason with, not benchmarks. Prices are approximate list prices from 2026: always check the providers' calculators. For the full set of numbers, see the numbers cheat sheet; for definitions, the glossary.

items.title: AI & Agents
items.text:
The AI & agents components are the building blocks of applications that use large language models (LLMs). The model itself is an external dependency, slow (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds), expensive (billed per token) and non-deterministic. These components exist to make it usable in a production system: a gateway in front of the providers, an orchestrator that runs the agent loop, a registry of tools the model may call, a memory layer that retrieves your data (RAG), and a safety layer that checks what goes in and what comes out.

In BoxOffice, the assistant service answers fans' questions ("can I get a refund for Saturday's show?", "which gate is closest to section B?"): it retrieves the refund policy and venue information from a vector store, calls catalog and order through registered tools, and never lets the model refund an order the fan does not own.

Component One-liner Playground id LLM Gateway One front door to all model providers: routing, fallbacks, quotas, caching, cost metrics llmgw Orchestrator Runs the agent loop: plan, call tools, call the model again, until done orchestrator Tool Registry The catalog of tools (APIs) the model may call, with schemas and permissions (MCP) toolreg Memory Fabric Retrieval of your data for the prompt (RAG) plus short- and long-term memory memory Safety Mesh Guardrails on inputs, outputs and tool calls: injection, PII, policy, validation safety
