  • Not for inbound traffic: if something must be reachable from the internet, it goes behind a load balancer.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Price ≈ USD 0.045 per hour + ≈ USD 0.045 per GB processed ≈ approximate AWS list price (2026); other clouds are similar in shape Bandwidth scales to tens of Gbps per gateway (AWS documents up to 100 Gbps) Check provider limits Concurrent connections to one destination tens of thousands per public IP (port range) Port exhaustion is a real limit; add IPs Added latency ≈ sub-millisecond Negligible compared with the external call

Failure modes.

  • Port exhaustion — many connections to the same destination IP and port use up the source ports → connection pooling and keep-alive, more NAT IPs.
  • Zonal failure — one NAT gateway for all zones fails or its zone goes down → one NAT per AZ, each zone's private subnets route to their own.
  • Cost surprise — logs, images or backups flowing through NAT → VPC endpoints for provider services, look at the per-GB line of the bill.
  • Missing route — after a network change, private services silently lose outbound access (timeouts to the provider) → synthetic checks of outbound dependencies.

In the playground. nat is a call node placed between private services and external nodes (payment, email, thirdparty). It has a capacity (default 100,000 req/s) and a per-GB cost (payloadKB, default 20 KB per request, at ≈ 0.045 USD/GB) that shows up in the cost panel; when its capacity is exceeded, calls to the outside queue and time out. Scenarios: payment-system, notification-system.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • NAT Gateway — managed, per-AZ NAT with elastic IPs.
  • VPC endpoints (Gateway / Interface, PrivateLink) — reach S3, DynamoDB, SQS and others without NAT.
  • Cloud NAT — managed, software-defined NAT for VMs and GKE nodes without external IPs.
  • Private Google Access / Private Service Connect — reach Google APIs privately.
  • Azure NAT Gateway — managed outbound connectivity for subnets.
  • Private Endpoint / Private Link — private access to Azure services.
  • Linux iptables / nftables masquerading on a VM (a "NAT instance") — cheap, but you own its availability.
  • Kubernetes egress gateways (for example Istio egress gateway) centralize and control outbound traffic.

In the interview

"Services stay in private subnets; outbound calls to the payment provider go through a NAT gateway per zone with fixed IPs the provider can allow-list, and traffic to the cloud's own services uses private endpoints so it doesn't pay NAT per-GB fees."

Learn more: Network & security › Cloud network · Compute › Integrations · Cloud-native › FinOps

items.title: VPN
items.text:
What it is. A Virtual Private Network is an encrypted tunnel that joins two networks over the internet as if they were one. Site-to-site VPNs (usually IPsec) connect a VPC to an office, a data center or another cloud; client VPNs let a person's laptop join the private network. For higher bandwidth and steadier latency, companies use dedicated interconnects (a private fiber link to the cloud) instead of, or in addition to, VPNs.

When to use.

  • Hybrid systems: BoxOffice's legacy box-office system in a stadium data center must reach the inventory service in the cloud privately.
  • Connecting two clouds or two companies' networks for a specific integration.
  • Administrative access to private resources (although modern practice prefers identity-aware proxies and bastion-less access; see zero trust).

When not to (or watch out).

  • Not a security model by itself: "inside the VPN = trusted" is exactly what zero trust rejects. Authenticate and authorize every call anyway.
  • Throughput of a single IPsec tunnel is limited (on the order of 1 Gbps per tunnel on major clouds); heavy data transfer needs several tunnels or a dedicated interconnect.
  • Latency is that of the internet path plus encryption: do not put a VPN hop in a latency-critical synchronous path if you can avoid it.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Throughput per IPsec tunnel ≈ up to 1.25 Gbps (AWS Site-to-Site VPN) ≈ approximate; aggregate several tunnels for more Added latency ≈ 5–20 ms over the internet path Depends on distance; the playground uses a median of 10 ms (≈ 5–20 ms) Dedicated interconnect 1–100 Gbps ports Private, steadier latency, higher fixed cost Availability two tunnels per connection (redundant endpoints) Configure both; one is maintained at a time

Failure modes.

  • Tunnel down — key renegotiation fails or the customer-side device reboots → two tunnels (and ideally two devices), dynamic routing (BGP) for automatic failover, alerting on tunnel status.
  • Bandwidth saturation — a backup job saturates the tunnel and the interactive traffic suffers → quality of service, separate tunnels, or an interconnect.
  • MTU problems — encryption overhead makes large packets fragment or drop, causing mysterious hangs → lower MTU / MSS clamping.
  • Over-trust — a compromised laptop on the VPN reaches everything → least privilege, segmentation, zero-trust access.

In the playground. vpn is a call node that adds latency (median 10 ms, lognormal: roughly 5–20 ms) and can fail as a unit; use it to connect a frame representing an on-premises system to cloud services and see how a synchronous call over a VPN shows up in the p99. Scenarios: multi-region, cascading-failure (add a VPN hop to the slow path and compare).

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • AWS Site-to-Site VPN — IPsec tunnels to a virtual private gateway or transit gateway.
  • AWS Client VPN — managed OpenVPN-based remote access.
  • AWS Direct Connect — dedicated private connection.
  • Cloud VPN (HA VPN) — IPsec with a 99.99% SLA in the high-availability configuration.
  • Cloud Interconnect — dedicated or partner interconnect.
  • Azure VPN Gateway — site-to-site and point-to-site VPN.
  • Azure ExpressRoute — private dedicated connectivity.
  • WireGuard — modern, small and fast VPN protocol built into Linux.
  • OpenVPN — mature TLS-based VPN.
  • strongSwan — IPsec implementation for site-to-site tunnels.

In the interview

"To reach the legacy system in the stadium I'd use a redundant site-to-site VPN (or an interconnect if the volume is high), keep that call off the synchronous purchase path, and still authenticate every request: being on the VPN doesn't make a caller trusted."

Learn more: Network & security › Cloud network · Network & security › Zero trust

items.title: Service Mesh
items.text:
What it is. A service mesh puts a proxy next to every service (a sidecar in each pod, or a per-node proxy in ambient mode) and routes all service-to-service traffic through those proxies. A control plane configures them. Without changing application code you get mutual TLS (mTLS: both sides prove their identity and the traffic is encrypted), retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, traffic splitting for canaries, and uniform metrics and traces for every call.

When to use.

  • Many services (tens or more) owned by different teams, where implementing mTLS, retries and telemetry consistently in every codebase is impractical.
  • Zero-trust requirements inside the cluster: every call authenticated by workload identity, with policies such as "only order may call payment".
  • Progressive delivery: send 5% of catalog traffic to the new version and shift gradually.

When not to (or watch out).

  • A handful of services: a library (Resilience4j, an OpenTelemetry SDK) and the platform's mTLS are simpler. A mesh is a platform to operate, with its own upgrades and failure modes.
  • Every hop through a proxy adds latency (sidecars add two proxies per call) and memory per pod; with deep call chains this adds up.
  • Retries in the mesh and in the application multiply each other (3 × 3 = 9 attempts): decide where retries live.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Added latency per hop ≈ 1 ms or less at p50, more at the tail ≈ illustrative; depends on mode, features and load; the playground adds ~1 ms per hop Sidecar memory tens of MB per pod Ambient / per-node modes reduce it mTLS certificate lifetime hours to a day, rotated automatically Short-lived identities limit the damage of a leak Traffic split granularity 1% steps (or finer) Used for canaries

Failure modes.

  • Control plane outage — proxies keep their last configuration, but new pods may not get certificates or routes → run the control plane highly available, monitor certificate expiry.
  • Retry amplification — retries at several layers turn a blip into a storm → retry budgets, retries in one layer only.
  • Misconfigured policy — a deny-by-default rule blocks a legitimate call after a deploy → policy tests in CI, staged rollout of policies.
  • Proxy resource starvation — sidecars without enough CPU become the bottleneck → set requests and limits for proxies, watch their metrics.

In the playground. mesh is a side node, not a box in the request path: the services attached to it pay about 1 ms of sidecar overhead per outgoing hop and get the mesh defaults on every edge that sets none — timeout meshTimeoutMs (1,000 ms), meshRetries (2) with exponential backoff and jitter, and a circuit breaker. A mesh attached to metrics makes every attached service observed. (mTLS is assumed, not simulated.) Try the cascading-failure scenario with and without a mesh, then compare with setting timeoutMs and circuitBreaker by hand on the edges. Scenarios: cascading-failure, retry-storm, observability-stack.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon VPC Lattice — managed service-to-service networking with auth policies across VPCs and accounts.
  • Istio on Amazon EKS — the common self-managed choice (AWS App Mesh has been discontinued).
  • Cloud Service Mesh — managed, Istio-based mesh for GKE and VMs.
  • Istio-based service mesh add-on for AKS — managed Istio in Azure Kubernetes Service.
  • Istio — the most widely used mesh; sidecar and ambient modes, built on Envoy.
  • Linkerd — lightweight mesh with its own Rust proxy, focused on simplicity.
  • Cilium Service Mesh — eBPF-based networking with mesh features.
  • Envoy — the proxy underneath many meshes and gateways.

In the interview

"With dozens of services I'd use a mesh to get mTLS, timeouts, retries and telemetry on every call without touching code — but it costs latency per hop and a platform to run, so with five services I'd use libraries instead, and I'd keep retries in one layer only."

Learn more: Network & security › Service mesh · Network & security › Zero trust · Reliability › Patterns · Hands-on 9

items.title: Observability
items.text:
Observability is the ability to understand what a system is doing — and why — from the outside, using the signals it emits. It never sits on the request path: these components are side channels that watch the services. But without them you are flying blind: you cannot see which box is saturated, you cannot tell a slow dependency from a slow database, and you find out about outages from angry users. The rule of the course is simple: you can't fix what you don't measure.

The palette has three signals and two actions. Signals: metrics (numbers over time — is something wrong?), logs (detailed events — what exactly happened?) and traces (one request across services — where did the time go?). Actions: alerting (wake a human when users are affected) and health checks (let load balancers and orchestrators route around broken instances automatically). In BoxOffice, a RED dashboard per service, traces from the gateway to the payment provider, and an SLO burn-rate alert on checkout are what tell the on-call engineer, at 10:01 on sale day, that the payment provider is slow — not the database.

Component One-liner Playground id Metrics Numeric time series (rates, errors, latency percentiles, utilization) metrics Logs Timestamped records of discrete events, ideally structured (JSON) logs Tracing The path and timing of one request across services (spans) tracing Alerting Rules on signals that notify a human when users are affected alerting Health Check Endpoint probes that tell LBs/orchestrators if an instance can serve healthcheck 
flowchart LR
    S1[gateway] -.->|OTLP| COL[OpenTelemetry Collector]
    S2[order] -.->|OTLP| COL
    S3[payment] -.->|OTLP| COL
    COL -.-> M[Metrics]
    COL -.-> L[Logs]
    COL -.-> T[Tracing]
    M -.->|SLO burn rate| AL[Alerting]

Question Signal Example Is something wrong? How much? Metrics Checkout error rate jumped from 0.1% to 4% Where is the time going in this slow request? Tracing 3.8 s of 4 s inside payment → provider What exactly happened to order 81234? Logs provider timeout after 2000 ms, retry 2/3 Should someone act now? Alerting SLO burning 14× faster than sustainable Should traffic go to this instance? Health check /health/ready returns 503 during warm-up

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
What it is. Metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time: counters (requests served, errors), gauges (queue depth, memory in use) and histograms (latency distribution, from which you read p50/p95/p99). Each time series is identified by a name and a set of labels (http_requests_total{service="order", route="/orders", status="500"}). They are cheap to store and query because they are pre-aggregated, which makes them the right signal for dashboards, SLOs and alerts. The standard recipes: RED for services (rate, errors, duration), USE for resources (utilization, saturation, errors) and Google's four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation).

When to use.

  • Always, for every service and resource: the RED dashboard of BoxOffice's order, inventory and payment services.
  • SLIs and SLOs: "share of checkout requests under 500 ms" is computed from a latency histogram.
  • Capacity planning and autoscaling: CPU utilization, queue depth and consumer lag drive the autoscaler.
  • Business metrics alongside technical ones: tickets sold per minute, waiting-room size, conversion.

When not to (or watch out).

  • To investigate a single request: metrics are aggregates — use traces and logs.
  • Cardinality: every unique combination of label values is a separate series. Labels like user_id, order_id or full URLs explode the number of series and the cost → keep labels bounded (route templates, status class).
  • Averages hide the tail: record histograms and look at percentiles; never average percentiles across instances.
  • Sampling interval: a 1-minute scrape smooths a 10-second spike away.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Scrape / export interval 15–60 s Prometheus' global default is 1 min; 15 s is common Series count ≈ metrics × label combinations × instances 50 metrics × 200 label combos × 20 pods = 200 k series (≈ illustrative) Cost per sample ≈ 1–2 bytes compressed in modern TSDBs ≈ illustrative; series count matters more than sample count Retention ≈ 15 days raw locally; months to years downsampled Long-term storage in Mimir/Thanos or a managed service Percentiles to watch p50, p95, p99 (p99.9 for high-volume paths) From histograms, per route

Failure modes.

  • Cardinality explosion — someone adds user_id as a label; memory and cost blow up, the metrics backend falls over → label allow-lists, limits per tenant, review metric changes.
  • Missing metric where it mattered — the slow dependency had no client-side latency metric → instrument outbound calls (OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation does).
  • Misleading averages → histograms and percentiles; per-route breakdowns.
  • Monitoring that dies with the system — the metrics stack runs in the same cluster that is down → monitor from outside too (synthetic checks, a separate region or a managed service).
  • Dashboards nobody reads → few dashboards built around SLOs and RED/USE, linked from alerts.

In the playground. metrics is a side channel, not part of the request path. Connect services to it and their utilization becomes visible on the canvas; a service with no metrics node connected shows its utilization as "?" — you can't fix what you don't measure (a "god mode" toggle reveals everything for teaching). It adds a monthly cost. Scenarios: observability-stack, scale-out.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon CloudWatch (metrics, dashboards) — native metrics for AWS services and custom metrics.
  • Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and Amazon Managed Grafana.
  • Cloud Monitoring — metrics, dashboards and SLO monitoring.
  • Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus.
  • Azure Monitor (Metrics) and Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus.
  • Azure Managed Grafana.
  • Prometheus — pull-based metrics collection, PromQL, the de facto standard for Kubernetes.
  • Grafana — dashboards over many data sources.
  • Grafana Mimir, Thanos, VictoriaMetrics — scalable long-term metric storage.
  • OpenTelemetry (SDKs and Collector) — vendor-neutral instrumentation and export (used in Hands-on 8 with grafana/otel-lgtm).

In the interview

"Every service exports RED metrics — rate, errors and a latency histogram per route — and every resource USE metrics. My SLIs and alerts are computed from those histograms, I watch p99, not the average, and I keep labels bounded so cardinality doesn't explode."

Learn more: Observability › Signals · Observability › OpenTelemetry · Estimation › Percentiles · Performance › Methodology · Hands-on 8

items.title: Logs
items.text:
What it is. Logs are timestamped records of discrete events: "order 81234 created", "payment provider timeout after 2000 ms", "user 77 failed login". Modern practice is structured logging — one JSON object per event with fields (level, service, trace_id, order_id, duration_ms) — so logs can be filtered and aggregated, not just grepped. Logs are shipped by an agent or the OpenTelemetry Collector to a central store where they are indexed and searched. Including the trace id in every log line links logs to traces.

When to use.

  • Investigating a specific request or user: "what happened to order 81234?" — search by order_id or trace_id.
  • Errors with context: stack traces, the input that caused them, which retry attempt failed.
  • Audit trails for security and compliance: who refunded what, who changed permissions (kept separately, with longer retention and restricted access).
  • Rare events that are not worth a metric.

When not to (or watch out).

  • As your main way to detect problems: counting log lines to compute error rates is slow and expensive → use metrics, link to logs.
  • Logging every request body at high volume: costs grow linearly with traffic → sample success logs, keep all errors.
  • Sensitive data: passwords, tokens, card numbers and personal data must never be logged (LGPD/GDPR, PCI DSS) → redact at the source.
  • Unstructured text with inconsistent formats makes search nearly impossible.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Log volume estimate requests/s × lines per request × bytes per line 2,000 req/s × 5 lines × 500 B = 5 MB/s ≈ 430 GB/day (≈ illustrative) Typical structured log line ≈ 200 B – 2 KB Grows fast with stack traces and payloads Ingestion-to-searchable delay ≈ seconds Depends on the pipeline Hot retention ≈ 7–30 days Older logs to cheap object storage; audit logs longer Cost driver GB ingested and indexed Index less, sample success logs

Failure modes.

  • Log flood — a failing dependency makes every request log a stack trace; the pipeline backs up and the bill explodes → rate-limit repeated logs, sample, drop debug in production.
  • Missing correlation — logs from 6 services cannot be joined → propagate and log the trace_id.
  • Leaking secrets or personal data → structured fields with redaction, reviews, scanning.
  • Logging blocking the app — synchronous writes to a slow sink add latency → async appenders, local buffering, stdout + agent.
  • Lost logs when a pod dies → write to stdout and let the node agent ship them; buffers with backpressure.

In the playground. logs is a side channel: connecting services to it enables the event log details (what happened to the sampled requests, which errors and retries) in the Events tab. It costs per GB, so it shows up in the cost tile. Scenarios: observability-stack, cascading-failure.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon CloudWatch Logs — log collection, retention and Logs Insights queries.
  • Amazon OpenSearch Service — search and analytics over logs.
  • Cloud Logging — collection, Log Explorer, log-based metrics, sinks to BigQuery or Cloud Storage.
  • Azure Monitor Logs (Log Analytics workspaces) — log storage queried with KQL.
  • Grafana Loki — log aggregation indexed by labels only (cheap); queried with LogQL.
  • OpenSearch / Elasticsearch — full-text indexed log search (the "ELK" stack with Logstash and Kibana).
  • Fluent Bit, Vector, OpenTelemetry Collector — log shippers and processors.

In the interview

"Services write structured JSON logs to stdout with the trace id in every line; an agent ships them to a central store. I use metrics to detect, traces to locate and logs to explain. Errors are always kept, successful requests are sampled, and nothing sensitive is ever logged."

Learn more: Observability › Signals · Observability › OpenTelemetry · Observability › Incident response · Network & security › Zero trust · Hands-on 8

items.title: Tracing
items.text:
What it is. Distributed tracing follows one request across all the services it touches. Each unit of work is a span (name, start, duration, attributes, status) and spans form a tree under one trace id, which is propagated between services in request headers (the W3C traceparent header) and in message metadata. The result is a waterfall: you see that a 4 s checkout spent 3.8 s waiting for the payment provider, or that one page makes 40 sequential database calls (N+1). Because recording every request is expensive, traces are sampled: head sampling (decide at the start, e.g. 5%) or tail sampling (decide at the end, keeping all errors and slow requests).

When to use.

  • Any system with more than a couple of services: finding where latency or errors come from.
  • Diagnosing the critical path: what is sequential that could be parallel, which dependency dominates p99.
  • Understanding fan-out and retries: a trace shows the three retries that tripled the load.
  • LLM applications: a trace per agent run shows each model call, tool call, tokens and latency.

When not to (or watch out).

  • Without context propagation through every hop (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka headers, async jobs), traces break into fragments → use OpenTelemetry instrumentation everywhere.
  • 100% sampling at high volume is expensive; too little sampling misses the rare slow requests → tail-based sampling for errors and slow traces.
  • Traces show one request; for trends use metrics (or metrics derived from spans).
  • Sensitive data in span attributes is as dangerous as in logs.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Spans per trace ≈ tens to hundreds One per service call, query, cache lookup Head sampling rate ≈ 1–10% in high-volume production ≈ illustrative; 100% in development and low-volume services Instrumentation overhead small (≈ microseconds per span) Export is batched and asynchronous Propagation header traceparent (W3C Trace Context) Carries trace id, parent span id, sampled flag Retention ≈ days to a few weeks Traces are for recent investigations

Failure modes.

  • Broken traces — one service or the message broker drops the context → instrument every hop, propagate through Kafka headers and job payloads.
  • Sampling hides the problem — the rare 10-second request was not sampled → tail sampling (keep errors and slow traces), exemplars linking metrics to traces.
  • Collector overload at peak → batching, horizontal Collector scaling, sampling at the edge of the pipeline.
  • Clock skew makes child spans look like they start before the parent → rely on durations within a host, NTP everywhere.

In the playground. tracing is a side channel: when present, the Trace tab shows the waterfall of one sampled slow request, with the time spent queueing and serving in each node — the fastest way to find a slow dependency or a retry storm. It adds cost. Scenarios: observability-stack, cascading-failure, retry-storm, ai-assistant.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • AWS X-Ray — distributed tracing for AWS workloads (accepts OpenTelemetry data).
  • Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals — application performance monitoring built on OpenTelemetry.
  • Cloud Trace — distributed tracing, OpenTelemetry-compatible.
  • Azure Monitor Application Insights — application performance monitoring with distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry distro).
  • OpenTelemetry — the standard APIs, SDKs, auto-instrumentation agents and Collector.
  • Jaeger — tracing back end and UI (CNCF).
  • Grafana Tempo — trace storage on object storage, integrated with Grafana.
  • Zipkin — the original open-source tracing system.

In the interview

"With OpenTelemetry the trace id flows from the gateway through every service and through Kafka headers, so one slow checkout shows up as a waterfall: 3.8 s of 4 s waiting on the payment provider. I keep all error and slow traces with tail sampling and a few percent of the rest."

Learn more: Observability › OpenTelemetry · Observability › Signals · Performance › Bottlenecks · AI systems › Safety & evals · Hands-on 8

items.title: Alerting
items.text:
What it is. Alerting turns signals into notifications for humans: rules evaluated continuously over metrics (or logs) that, when true for long enough, route a message to the right person — a page for urgent problems, a ticket or chat message for the rest. Good alerts are about symptoms users feel (errors, latency, SLO violations), are actionable, and come with a runbook link. The modern standard is SLO-based alerting with burn rates: alert when the error budget is being consumed much faster than sustainable, using two windows (e.g. 1 h and 5 min) so the alert is both fast and not noisy.

When to use.

  • Every user-facing SLO: "checkout availability 99.9% over 28 days" with fast-burn (page) and slow-burn (ticket) alerts.
  • Leading indicators of imminent outages: disk filling up within hours, certificate expiring in 7 days, consumer lag approaching retention.
  • On-call rotations with escalation policies and acknowledgement.

When not to (or watch out).

  • Alerting on causes instead of symptoms ("CPU > 80%") pages people for things that don't affect users → alert fatigue, and real pages get ignored.
  • Alerts without an owner or a runbook.
  • Static thresholds on noisy metrics flap → use windows, burn rates, hysteresis.
  • Alerting depends on the monitoring stack being alive → a "dead man's switch" (an always-firing heartbeat alert that pages when it stops).

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Error budget of a 99.9% SLO over a rolling 28 days ≈ 40 minutes of full downtime 0.1% × 28 days × 24 h × 60 min Fast-burn page (SRE Workbook) burn rate 14.4 over 1 h (with a 5-min check) Consumes 2% of a 28-day budget in one hour Slow-burn ticket burn rate ≈ 1–6 over 6 h – 3 days ≈ illustrative; catches gradual degradation Pages per on-call shift that is sustainable a few at most Google's SRE book suggests ≤ 2 incidents per 12-hour shift Time to acknowledge target ≈ 5–15 min for pages ≈ illustrative; set by the team's policy

Failure modes.

  • Alert fatigue — too many noisy alerts, the real one is missed → delete or demote non-actionable alerts, SLO-based paging only.
  • Silent failure — the metric stopped being reported, so the threshold never fires → alert on absent data, dead man's switch.
  • Alerting stack down with the system → monitor the monitor from outside (synthetic checks, a separate provider).
  • No runbook / wrong owner → each alert links a runbook and routes to the owning team.
  • Flapping → longer evaluation windows, for durations, hysteresis.

In the playground. alerting is a side channel connected to metrics: when present, random failures are detected and fixed faster — the model reduces MTTR by 50%, which shows up as higher availability in the run report. It costs money, like the other observability nodes. Scenarios: observability-stack, multi-region.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon CloudWatch alarms (with composite alarms) routed through Amazon SNS.
  • AWS Incident Manager (Systems Manager) — on-call, escalation and response plans.
  • Cloud Monitoring alerting policies — including SLO burn-rate alerts, with notification channels.
  • Azure Monitor alerts with action groups (e-mail, SMS, webhooks, ITSM).
  • Prometheus Alertmanager — grouping, silencing and routing of Prometheus alerts.
  • Grafana Alerting — alert rules over any Grafana data source.
  • Sloth / Pyrra — generate multi-window burn-rate alerts from SLO definitions.
  • Commercial paging services such as PagerDuty are common for on-call schedules.

In the interview

"I page on symptoms, not causes: multi-window burn-rate alerts on the checkout SLO — 14× burn over an hour pages the on-call, slow burns open a ticket. Every alert has an owner and a runbook, and a heartbeat alert tells us if monitoring itself is down."

Learn more: Observability › Alerting · Reliability › SLOs · Observability › Incident response · Estimation › Availability math · Hands-on 8

items.title: Health Check
items.text:
What it is. A health check is a probe that something outside the instance — a load balancer, Kubernetes, a DNS failover service — sends periodically to decide whether that instance should receive traffic or be restarted. Kubernetes distinguishes three: liveness ("is the process stuck? if it fails, restart it"), readiness ("can it serve traffic right now? if it fails, take it out of the load balancer, don't restart it") and startup ("is it still booting? hold the other probes until it's done"). Load balancers use similar active checks (an HTTP request to /health every few seconds) and sometimes passive checks (outlier detection on real traffic errors).

When to use.

  • Every replica behind a load balancer or a Kubernetes Service: without it, the LB keeps sending traffic to dead or warming-up instances.
  • Readiness during startup and warm-up (JIT, caches, connection pools) and during graceful shutdown (fail readiness first, then drain).
  • Regional failover: DNS health checks decide when to send users to the other region.
  • Load shedding: an overloaded instance can fail readiness temporarily.

When not to (or watch out).

  • Don't check dependencies in liveness: if the database is slow and every pod's liveness checks it, Kubernetes restarts all pods at once — a restart storm that makes the outage worse.
  • Readiness that checks a shared dependency can take every replica out at once → check only what the instance itself needs, and degrade gracefully.
  • Health endpoints must be cheap, fast and unauthenticated-but-not-public (no sensitive details).
  • Too-aggressive thresholds flap; too-lax ones leave dead instances in rotation.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Kubernetes probe defaults periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 1, failureThreshold 3 Documented defaults Detection time ≈ interval × failure threshold K8s defaults: ≈ 30 s; 2 s × 2 ≈ 4 s if tuned AWS ALB target health check defaults interval 30 s, unhealthy threshold 2, healthy threshold 5 Documented defaults; ≈ 60 s to mark unhealthy Probe endpoint latency ≈ milliseconds Must not do heavy work Effect on availability faster detection ⇒ fewer failed requests per incident Failed requests ≈ traffic share × detection time

Failure modes.

  • Restart storm — liveness depends on the database; DB slows; all pods restart → liveness only checks the process itself.
  • Fleet-wide removal — readiness fails everywhere because of a shared dependency; the LB has no healthy targets → degrade instead of failing readiness; LBs that "fail open" when all targets are unhealthy.
  • Zombie instance — health endpoint returns 200 but real requests fail (e.g. a broken thread pool) → passive health checks / outlier detection on real traffic, deeper readiness checks.
  • Slow detection → shorter intervals for critical paths, plus passive checks.
  • Flapping → healthy/unhealthy thresholds with hysteresis.

In the playground. healthcheck is a side channel: connecting it to a service behind a load balancer reduces the LB's failure-detection time from 30 s to 3 s, so after a replica crash far fewer requests are sent to the dead instance. Compare the error spike after a crash with and without it. Scenarios: scale-out, multi-region, observability-stack.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Elastic Load Balancing target health checks (ALB/NLB).
  • Amazon Route 53 health checks — for DNS failover.
  • Cloud Load Balancing health checks.
  • Cloud Monitoring uptime checks — external synthetic probes.
  • Azure Load Balancer health probes and Application Gateway health probes.
  • Application Insights availability tests — external synthetic probes.
  • Kubernetes liveness, readiness and startup probes (used in Hands-on 10).
  • Spring Boot Actuator health groups (/actuator/health/liveness, /actuator/health/readiness).
  • Prometheus Blackbox Exporter — HTTP/TCP/ICMP probes from outside.
  • Envoy outlier detection — passive health checking in proxies and service meshes.

In the interview

"Each replica exposes liveness and readiness separately: liveness only says the process isn't stuck, readiness says it can serve now — it fails during warm-up and shutdown. The load balancer stops routing to a failed replica within seconds, and I never put a database check in liveness, or a slow database restarts the whole fleet."

Learn more: Observability › Signals · Cloud-native › Kubernetes · Reliability › Patterns · Edge › Load balancing · Load Balancer · Hands-on 3 · Hands-on 10

items.title: Storage
items.text:
Storage is where the state of the system lives — and state is what makes systems hard. Compute can be replaced, restarted and multiplied freely; data must survive crashes, be read back correctly and stay consistent when many requests touch it at once. Each storage component in the palette answers a different question: where is the truth? (SQL Database), how does it survive a dead primary, and how much can it lose? (DB Cluster), how do I store huge volumes with simple access? (NoSQL DB), how do I avoid asking the database again? (Cache), where do big files go? (Object Store), how do I analyse history? (Data Warehouse), how do I find things by meaning? (Vector DB).

In BoxOffice, the seat inventory and the orders live in PostgreSQL (the truth, with transactions — no double booking); the catalog of events is read millions of times and sits behind a Redis cache; posters, venue maps and PDF tickets go to an object store; sales history flows into a data warehouse for the "best-selling artists" dashboard; and the support assistant finds the right FAQ answer through a vector index.

Component One-liner Playground id SQL Database Relational tables, SQL, transactions: the default system of record sql DB Cluster Replicated, optionally sharded database with automatic failover dbcluster NoSQL DB Key-value, document or wide-column stores that partition horizontally nosql Cache In-memory copy of hot data: sub-millisecond reads, offloads the database cache Object Store Cheap, durable storage of files (blobs) by key, over HTTP objstore Data Warehouse Columnar analytical store for large scans and aggregations (OLAP) dwh Vector DB Stores embeddings and finds the nearest ones (similarity search) vectordb 
flowchart LR
    APP[App Server] -->|hot reads| CACHE[Cache]
    APP -->|truth: seats, orders| SQL[SQL Database]
    APP -->|huge key-based data| NOSQL[NoSQL DB]
    APP -->|files: posters, tickets| OBJ[Object Store]
    SQL -->|CDC / ETL| DWH[Data Warehouse]
    APP -->|similarity search| VEC[Vector DB]

items.title: SQL Database
items.text:
What it is. A relational database stores data in tables with a fixed schema, related by keys, queried with SQL, and protected by ACID transactions (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability). It is the default system of record: the place where the truth lives. Indexes (usually B-trees) make lookups fast; the query planner chooses how to execute each query. To scale, you add read replicas (copies that serve reads, fed by the primary's log), connection pooling, and — much later — partitioning (sharding) or a distributed SQL engine.

When to use.

  • Data with relations and invariants: BoxOffice seats, holds, orders and payments — "a seat is sold at most once" is enforced by a transaction or a unique constraint.
  • When you need ad-hoc queries, joins, secondary indexes and reporting on current data.
  • As the starting point of almost every system: a single well-indexed PostgreSQL goes much further than most people expect.
  • Read-heavy workloads: add read replicas (scenario db-replicas) and a cache in front.

When not to (or watch out).

  • Write volume beyond one primary (millions of writes per second, e.g. location updates of every driver): partition, or use a store designed for it (NoSQL, event log).
  • Huge blobs (images, videos): store them in an object store and keep only the key in SQL.
  • Replicas scale reads, not writes, and they lag: a read right after a write may not see it (read-your-writes problem).
  • Long transactions and hot rows (every request updating the same counter) serialize the database.
  • Each connection costs memory: hundreds of app replicas × a pool of 20 can exhaust the server → use a pooler (PgBouncer).

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Indexed point query (primary key) ≈ 0.1–1 ms on the server Plus a network round trip in the same zone (≈ 0.5 ms) Throughput of one primary ≈ thousands to tens of thousands of simple queries/s ≈ illustrative; depends on hardware, query mix, indexes Max connections hundreds per server (PostgreSQL default max_connections = 100) Use a connection pooler Replication lag (async, same region) ≈ milliseconds, seconds under heavy write load Grows with write volume Failover to a standby (managed services) ≈ 30 s to a few minutes ≈ approximate; depends on the provider Single-node data size that is comfortable up to a few TB Beyond that, partition or archive

Failure modes.

  • Primary failure → standby with automatic failover (multi-AZ); clients must reconnect and retry idempotently.
  • Connection exhaustion — app replicas scale out and open too many connections → pooler, smaller pools, limit autoscaling.
  • Slow query / missing index — one full scan saturates the CPU and every query slows → EXPLAIN, indexes, query timeouts.
  • Lock contention / hot row — thousands of flash-sale requests updating the same rows → short transactions, SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, a waiting-room queue in front.
  • Replication lag → users don't see their own writes → read from the primary after writes, or wait for the replica position.
  • Disk full / runaway table growth → monitoring, retention policies, archiving to object storage.

In the playground. sql is a storage node with separate read and write capacities. readReplicas multiplies read capacity by (1 + replicas) while write capacity stays the same, and replication lag grows with the write load. Main parameters: capacity (default 3,000 reads/s; a write costs writeCost = 3 reads), latencyMs (median 4 ms), threads (200 connections), queueLimit (400), standby (multi-AZ failover); incoming edges can carry timeoutMs, retries and circuitBreaker. The client's read % decides how much the replicas help. Scenarios: monolith, db-replicas, read-heavy-cache, flash-sale, payment-system.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon RDS — managed PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and Oracle, with multi-AZ standby and read replicas.
  • Amazon Aurora — PostgreSQL/MySQL-compatible engine with a distributed storage layer and up to 15 read replicas.
  • Cloud SQL — managed PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server.
  • AlloyDB for PostgreSQL — PostgreSQL-compatible, tuned for higher throughput and analytics.
  • Spanner — globally distributed SQL database with external consistency (TrueTime).
  • Azure Database for PostgreSQL (Flexible Server) and Azure Database for MySQL — managed open-source engines.
  • Azure SQL Database — managed SQL Server engine.
  • PostgreSQL — the course default: rich SQL, strong transactions, extensions (pgvector, PostGIS).
  • MySQL / MariaDB — widely used relational databases.
  • YugabyteDB — distributed SQL, PostgreSQL-compatible.
  • Vitess — sharding layer for MySQL (born at YouTube).
  • PgBouncer — lightweight connection pooler for PostgreSQL.

In the interview

"The source of truth for seats and orders is a relational database, because I need transactions to guarantee no double booking. I scale reads with replicas and a cache, keep writes on one primary with a standby for failover, and only shard when write volume or data size forces me to."

Learn more: Databases › Data models · Databases › Transactions · Databases › Replication · Case study: ticketing · Hands-on 1 · Hands-on 6

items.title: DB Cluster
items.text:
What it is. A database run as a group of nodes instead of one server: each shard (a slice of the keys) has one primary that accepts the writes and followers that receive a copy of its log, and a cluster manager (or a consensus protocol such as Raft or Paxos) detects a dead primary and promotes a follower automatically. It adds what a single SQL Database node cannot give: read capacity from followers, write capacity from more shards, and survival of a node or zone failure. The two knobs every design must choose are how a write is acknowledged — async (the primary alone, fast, may lose the last writes on failover), sync (the primary plus one follower) or quorum (a majority of the shard's nodes) — and where reads go (primary only: always fresh; followers too: more capacity, possibly stale).

When to use.

  • Any system of record that must survive the loss of a machine or an availability zone without losing confirmed data: BoxOffice orders and payments.
  • Read-heavy workloads that outgrow one node: reads from followers (when a slightly stale answer is acceptable, e.g. the event catalog).
  • Write volume or data size beyond one primary: shard by a key with many distinct, evenly used values (event_id, user_id).
  • When the RPO (data you may lose) and RTO (time you may be down) are explicit requirements: they decide the replication mode and the failover mechanism.

When not to (or watch out).

  • Async replication loses data on failover: the writes still inside the replication lag when the primary dies are gone (RPO > 0). Use sync or quorum for money and seats.
  • Sync and quorum cost latency on every write (a round trip to a follower, often in another AZ); a single synchronous follower that becomes slow slows all writes — quorum tolerates one slow follower.
  • Followers lag: reading from them breaks read-your-writes → read your own writes from the primary, or wait for the follower's position.
  • Sharding is hard to undo: cross-shard joins and transactions become expensive, and a hot key (one popular event) saturates its shard while the others idle.
  • Failover is not instant: detection plus promotion plus clients reconnecting is typically tens of seconds — the RTO.
  • Split brain: two nodes that both believe they are primary corrupt data → consensus-based leader election, fencing.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Replication round trip to a follower in another AZ ≈ 1–2 ms ≈ illustrative; added to every write with sync or quorum Async replication lag (same region) ≈ milliseconds; seconds under heavy write load Lost on failover with async: RPO ≈ the lag at that moment Automatic failover ≈ 30 s (Aurora: typically under 30 s); ≈ 60–120 s (RDS Multi-AZ instance) ≈ approximate; detection + promotion + DNS/client reconnection Patroni (PostgreSQL HA) leader lock ttl 30 s, loop_wait 10 s Documented defaults: a dead primary is replaced after ≈ 30 s Majority of a shard ⌊N/2⌋ + 1 of N nodes 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2 Aurora storage 6 copies in 3 AZs; write quorum 4/6, read quorum 3/6 Survives the loss of an AZ plus one more copy Theoretical availability of a 3-node shard 1 − (1 − 0.999)³ ≈ 99.9999999% Ideal: ignores correlated failures, failover time and bugs

Failure modes.

  • Primary failure — writes to its shard fail until a follower is promoted (RTO); with async replication the last writes are lost (RPO) → sync/quorum for critical data, idempotent client retries.
  • Slow synchronous follower — every write waits for it → quorum instead of a single sync follower, alerts on replication latency.
  • Replication lag → stale reads, users don't see their own writes → read-your-writes routing, lag-aware load balancing, monitoring the lag.
  • Hot shard — skewed keys send most requests to one shard → better shard key, split hot keys, cache in front.
  • Split brain — a network partition leaves two primaries → consensus (Raft/Paxos), fencing tokens, majority-only writes.
  • No followers — a node failure means the shard is down until the node comes back → at least one follower per shard in another AZ.

In the playground. dbcluster is a call node that models a replicated, optionally sharded database. Parameters (defaults in parentheses): shards (1; 1–64), replicasPerShard (2 followers per shard; 0–5), replication (async, or sync / quorum), readsFrom (followers, or primary), failoverS (30 s to detect a dead primary and promote a follower), replRttMs (2 ms replication round trip to a follower, cross-AZ, lognormal), capacity (3,000 reads/s per node), latencyMs (4 ms), threads (200 connections per node), writeCost (3: a write costs 3 reads of capacity) and price (450 USD/month per node, illustrative).

  • Capacity. Writes: shards × capacity ÷ writeCost (only primaries write). Reads: shards × (1 + replicasPerShard) × capacity when reading from followers, shards × capacity when reading from the primary. Keys are spread over the shards with the clients' Zipf skew: the hottest shard receives p₁ + (1 − p₁)/shards of the requests (p₁ = share of the hottest key), so it saturates first; the inspector shows the utilization of the hot shard and of the others.
  • Write latency. async: the primary only. sync: + one round trip to the synchronous follower. quorum: + the round trip of the ⌊(R+1)/2⌋-th fastest follower (a majority of the shard's 1 + R nodes) — so one slow follower hurts sync but not quorum. A latency degradation event on a DB Cluster slows one follower (the synchronous one) ×5–20.
  • Replication lag of the followers that are not part of the acknowledgement (all of them with async, R − 1 with sync, R − ⌊(R+1)/2⌋ with quorum) grows with the primary's write utilization ρw, as for the SQL read replicas: lag ≈ 0.02 s + 0.5 · ρw³ ÷ (1 − ρw) s, without bound above ρw = 1. Stale reads ≈ share of reads served by lagging followers × write share × min(1, lag ÷ 1 s) (the playground assumes a client reads back what it wrote about one second later).
  • Primary failure (random with chaos, injectable with ⚡; an AZ outage also triggers one). The primary of one shard dies: writes to that shard — and reads too with readsFrom = primary — fail for failoverS (the RTO); then a follower is promoted and the shard runs with one node fewer until a replacement joins 120 s later. With async, the writes inside the replication lag at that moment are lost (lost writes ≈ shard write rate × lag; the report counts them — the RPO lesson); with sync or quorum, no writes are lost, at the price of higher write latency. With replicasPerShard = 0 there is no failover: the shard is down (reads and writes) for 120 s until the node comes back — no data lost, just unavailable.
  • Cost = shards × (1 + replicasPerShard) × price. Theoretical availability: per shard 1 − (1 − a)^(1+R) with a = 0.999 per node, all shards in series.

Scenarios: db-failover, db-replicas, sharding.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon Aurora — PostgreSQL/MySQL-compatible; quorum-replicated storage across 3 AZs, up to 15 readers, automatic failover; Aurora Limitless Database for sharding.
  • Amazon RDS Multi-AZ — a synchronous standby (instance) or two readable standbys (Multi-AZ DB cluster).
  • Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon DocumentDB — managed partitioned and replicated stores.
  • Cloud SQL with high availability — a synchronous standby in another zone.
  • AlloyDB for PostgreSQL — HA primary plus read pools.
  • Spanner — sharded (splits), Paxos-replicated SQL with external consistency.
  • Azure SQL Database (Business Critical / zone-redundant) and Azure Database for PostgreSQL with zone-redundant HA.
  • Azure Cosmos DB — partitioned, multi-region, with tunable consistency; Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL (Citus).
  • PostgreSQL with Patroni — streaming replication (async, sync or quorum ANY k) and automatic failover; Citus for sharding.
  • Vitess — sharding and failover for MySQL.
  • CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, TiDB — distributed SQL, Raft per range.
  • MongoDB replica sets + sharding (write concern majority).

In the interview

"The orders database is a cluster: a primary and two followers in different zones. Async replication is cheaper on every write but can lose the last writes on failover, so for orders and seats I use quorum (or sync) replication, which means zero data loss and one cross-zone round trip per write. Failover takes about 30 seconds — that's my RTO — and I shard by event only when one primary can't take the writes."

Learn more: Databases › Replication · Databases › Replication lag · Databases › Partitioning · Databases › Hot partitions · Databases › Transactions · Distributed › Consensus › Majorities · Distributed › CAP & PACELC · Reliability › Disaster recovery

items.title: NoSQL DB
items.text:
What it is. "NoSQL" is a family of databases that give up some relational features (joins, multi-row transactions, a fixed schema) in exchange for horizontal scale and simple, predictable access by key. The main models are key-value (get/put by key), document (JSON documents with flexible fields), wide-column (rows with many columns, grouped by a partition key) and graph. Data is partitioned by a key (usually with consistent hashing) across many nodes and replicated — often with tunable consistency (quorums R + W > N). Many use LSM-trees, which make writes very fast.

When to use.

  • Very high write rates with simple access patterns: driver locations in ride sharing, chat messages, click streams, IoT readings.
  • Data that is naturally accessed by one key: user sessions, shopping carts, a user's timeline, a conversation's messages.
  • Predictable latency at any scale when you know the queries up front (you design the table for the query).
  • Flexible, evolving schemas (document stores) — e.g. event descriptions with different fields per event type.

When not to (or watch out).

  • Ad-hoc queries, joins and reporting: you can only query efficiently by the partition key (and maybe a sort key). New query = new table or index.
  • Multi-item invariants (no double booking across many rows): transactions are limited or absent in many stores.
  • The partition key decides everything: a bad key (e.g. event_id during the flash sale) concentrates the traffic on one partition — a hot partition — and the cluster's total capacity does not help.
  • Eventual consistency by default: a read may return an old value unless you ask for a stronger level.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Single-key read/write latency ≈ 1–10 ms At any table size, if the key is well distributed Throughput scales roughly linearly with nodes/partitions Until a hot key concentrates load DynamoDB item size limit 400 KB Documented limit DynamoDB per-partition limit ≈ 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second Documented; hence the hot-partition problem Replication factor 3 is the usual choice Quorum: W = 2, R = 2

Failure modes.

  • Hot partition / hot key — a celebrity post or the flash-sale event receives most of the requests → spread the key (add a suffix/shard number), cache it, or use a dedicated path.
  • Node failure → replicas serve the data; hinted handoff and anti-entropy repair the missing writes later.
  • Stale reads under eventual consistency → read with quorum or strong consistency when it matters.
  • Write conflicts in multi-leader/leaderless setups → last-write-wins (loses data) or application merge; avoid for money.
  • Rebalancing storms when adding nodes → consistent hashing with virtual nodes; add capacity before the peak.

In the playground. nosql is a storage node whose capacity is capacity × replicas — each replica is a partition (defaults 5,000 ops/s × 4). The client's zipfS (key popularity skew) concentrates a share of the traffic on one partition: with a hot key, the effective capacity drops to that of a single partition even though the others are idle. The chaos event "hot key / celebrity" makes the skew jump. Parameters: replicas, capacity, latencyMs (3 ms), writeCost (1.2). Scenarios: sharding, chat, ride-sharing, news-feed, url-shortener.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon DynamoDB — serverless key-value and document database with on-demand or provisioned capacity.
  • Amazon Keyspaces — managed Cassandra-compatible wide-column service.
  • Amazon DocumentDB — MongoDB-compatible document database.
  • Firestore — serverless document database.
  • Bigtable — wide-column store for very large, low-latency workloads (the system described in the Bigtable paper).
  • Azure Cosmos DB — multi-model, globally distributed database with five selectable consistency levels.
  • Apache Cassandra — leaderless wide-column store with tunable consistency (Dynamo-style).
  • MongoDB (Community Edition, source-available) — document database.
  • Apache HBase — wide-column store on top of HDFS (Bigtable-style).
  • FoundationDB — ordered key-value store with ACID transactions.

In the interview

"For billions of chat messages accessed by conversation, I'd use a wide-column store partitioned by conversation_id and sorted by time: writes scale with nodes and the main query hits one partition. The price is no joins and no ad-hoc queries, and I must watch for hot partitions."

Learn more: Databases › Data models · Databases › Partitioning · Distributed › Consistency · Case study: chat · Case study: URL shortener

items.title: Cache
items.text:
What it is. A cache keeps a copy of frequently read data in memory, close to the code that needs it, so most reads skip the slower source (database, another service). The usual pattern is cache-aside: the app looks in the cache; on a hit it returns; on a miss it reads the database and stores the result with a TTL (time to live). Other patterns: read-through, write-through, write-behind, refresh-ahead. A distributed cache such as Redis is shared by all app replicas, survives app restarts and offers data structures (hashes, sorted sets, counters) that also make it useful for sessions, rate limiting and leaderboards.

When to use.

  • Read-heavy data that changes rarely or can be slightly stale: BoxOffice event catalog, venue details, prices for browsing.
  • Expensive results: rendered pages, aggregated counts, external API responses.
  • Shared ephemeral state: sessions, rate-limiter counters (token buckets), seat-map snapshots refreshed every second.
  • To protect the database from spikes: with a 95% hit ratio the database sees only 1/20 of the reads.

When not to (or watch out).

  • Data that must be exactly current at decision time — seat availability at purchase, account balance: the check must go to the source of truth.
  • Write-heavy data with few re-reads: the cache only adds work.
  • Invalidation is the hard part: decide how stale each item may be, and delete (not update) on writes.
  • A cache is not a database: it can be flushed, evicted or restarted empty. The system must survive a cold cache.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Read from main memory ≈ 100 ns "Latency numbers every programmer should know" Redis GET over the network, same zone ≈ 0.2–1 ms Mostly the network round trip Throughput of one Redis node ≈ 100k+ simple ops/s ≈ illustrative; mostly single-threaded command execution Database load with hit ratio h (1 − h) × reads 90% → 99% hits = 10× fewer DB reads Average latency h × t_cache + (1 − h) × t_db e.g. 0.95 × 1 ms + 0.05 × 20 ms ≈ 2 ms Common TTLs seconds (hot dynamic data) to hours (reference data) Add jitter to avoid synchronized expiry

Failure modes.

  • Cache stampede (thundering herd) — a hot key expires and thousands of misses hit the database at once → request coalescing (single flight), a per-key lock, probabilistic early refresh, stale-while-revalidate, jittered TTLs.
  • Cold cache after a restart or flush → warm up before taking traffic, protect the DB with rate limits, ramp traffic.
  • Hot key — one key (the flash-sale event) saturates one cache node → local in-process cache for that key, replicate the key, split it.
  • Stale or inconsistent data — write races leave an old value → delete on write, versioned keys, short TTLs.
  • Memory pressure / eviction → right-size memory, choose the eviction policy (LRU, LFU), monitor the hit ratio and evictions.
  • Cache unavailable → treat it as optional: fall back to the database with a circuit breaker and load shedding.

In the playground. cache is a cache node: each read hits with probability hitRatio and returns in ≈ 0.5 ms; misses go to the next node (usually sql). Writes pass through to the database and invalidate; the policy parameter switches between cache-aside and write-through. Chaos events "cache flush / cold cache" drop the hit ratio to 0, which then warms back up over cacheWarmS (default 120 s) — watch the database turn red; coalescing stops the stampede. Parameters: hitRatio (0.9), policy, cacheWarmS, coalescing, capacity (80,000 ops/s), replicas. Scenarios: read-heavy-cache, url-shortener, search-autocomplete, news-feed, flash-sale.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon ElastiCache — managed Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached.
  • Amazon MemoryDB — durable, Redis/Valkey-compatible in-memory database.
  • Memorystore — managed Valkey, Redis and Memcached.
  • Azure Cache for Redis / Azure Managed Redis — managed Redis.
  • Redis — the reference in-memory data-structure store (check the license of the version you use).
  • Valkey — Linux Foundation fork of Redis, BSD-licensed.
  • Memcached — simple, multi-threaded key-value cache.
  • Caffeine (Java) — high-performance in-process cache (W-TinyLFU eviction).

In the interview

"I'd put a cache-aside Redis in front of the catalog: with a 95% hit ratio the database sees 20× fewer reads and p99 drops. Entries have a TTL with jitter, writes delete the key, and hot keys are protected against stampedes with request coalescing. Seat availability at purchase time never comes from the cache."

Learn more: Caching › Patterns · Caching › Invalidation · Caching › Failure modes · Caching › Redis · Case study: distributed cache · Hands-on 5

items.title: Object Store
items.text:
What it is. An object store keeps files (objects, blobs) of any size in flat buckets, addressed by a key (posters/2027/coldplay.jpg) and accessed over HTTP (PUT, GET, DELETE, LIST). There are no directories, no in-place edits and no queries: you write a whole object and read it back. In exchange you get practically unlimited capacity, very high durability (data replicated across devices and zones), low price per GB and the ability to serve files directly to clients — usually through a CDN or with pre-signed URLs that grant temporary access.

When to use.

  • Media and documents: BoxOffice event posters, venue maps, generated PDF tickets, user uploads.
  • Video: original uploads and transcoded segments, served through a CDN (scenario video-streaming).
  • Backups, database snapshots, logs archives, data-lake files (Parquet) read by the data warehouse.
  • Static website hosting (the SPA front end) as the CDN's origin.

When not to (or watch out).

  • Small records that change often or need queries: that is a database.
  • Low-latency random access within a file, or appends: objects are written whole.
  • Do not stream large uploads through your app servers: let clients upload directly with a pre-signed URL.
  • Costs hide in requests (per thousand PUT/GET) and egress (per GB leaving the cloud), not only in storage.
  • Bucket permissions: public buckets by mistake are a classic data leak.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Designed durability (Amazon S3 Standard) 99.999999999% ("11 nines") per year Documented design target Time to first byte ≈ 10–100 ms Use a CDN for user-facing reads S3 request rate per prefix 3,500 writes/s and 5,500 reads/s Documented; scale by spreading keys over prefixes Object size from bytes to terabytes Large objects use multipart upload Storage price ≈ USD 0.02 per GB-month (standard class) ≈ approximate (2026); colder classes are cheaper to store, pricier to read

Failure modes.

  • Accidental public exposure → block public access by default, serve through CDN with origin access control, pre-signed URLs.
  • Accidental deletion / overwrite → versioning, object lock, lifecycle policies, cross-region replication for critical data.
  • Request throttling on one prefix → spread keys (hash prefix), cache hot objects in the CDN.
  • Cost surprise — egress or millions of tiny requests → CDN in front, batch small objects, lifecycle to cheaper classes.
  • Regional outage → cross-region replication for the data you cannot lose.

In the playground. objstore is a storage node with high capacity and a higher median latency than a database; it usually sits behind a cdn (the origin) or receives writes from worker nodes (transcoding). Cost is per GB and per request. Parameter: latencyMs (median 30 ms); its capacity (200,000 req/s) is practically unlimited. Scenarios: video-streaming, cdn-static.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon S3 — the reference object store; storage classes from Standard to Glacier Deep Archive.
  • Cloud Storage — object storage with Standard, Nearline, Coldline and Archive classes.
  • Azure Blob Storage — object storage with hot, cool, cold and archive tiers.
  • MinIO — S3-compatible object store (check the license and edition).
  • Ceph (RADOS Gateway) — distributed storage with an S3-compatible interface.
  • SeaweedFS — distributed object/file store for many small files.

In the interview

"Posters and tickets go to an object store, never to the database: it's cheap, practically infinite and extremely durable. Clients upload directly with pre-signed URLs and download through the CDN, so the app servers never carry the bytes; the database keeps only the object key and metadata."

Learn more: Databases › Specialized stores · Edge › DNS & CDN · Case study: video streaming

items.title: Data Warehouse
items.text:
What it is. A data warehouse is an analytical (OLAP) database built for queries that scan and aggregate large amounts of history — "revenue per artist per month in 2026" — rather than for many small transactions (OLTP). It stores data by column (so a query reads only the columns it needs, highly compressed), separates storage from compute, and runs queries in parallel over many machines. Data arrives from the operational databases and event streams through ETL/ELT jobs or change data capture (CDC). A lakehouse keeps the data as open files (Parquet + a table format such as Apache Iceberg) in an object store and queries them with warehouse engines.

When to use.

  • Business analytics and dashboards: sales per event, conversion of the waiting room, fraud patterns, cohort analysis.
  • Questions over months or years of data, joining many sources (orders, payments, marketing, support).
  • Feeding machine-learning features and reports without loading the production database.
  • The analytics service of the palette usually writes here (via a stream or batch jobs).

When not to (or watch out).

  • Serving the product: queries take seconds, not milliseconds, and concurrency is limited — never put the warehouse on the request path of a user.
  • Point updates and small transactions: they are slow and expensive in columnar engines.
  • Freshness: batch ETL makes data hours old; for near-real-time, use CDC/streaming ingestion, at a higher cost.
  • Pay-per-scan pricing: an unfiltered SELECT * on a huge table costs real money — partition and cluster tables, select only needed columns.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Query latency ≈ seconds to minutes Interactive dashboards target a few seconds Scan throughput ≈ GB/s to TB/s across a cluster ≈ illustrative; grows with compute Columnar compression often ≈ 5–10× ≈ illustrative; depends on data Freshness batch: hours; streaming/CDC: seconds to minutes Trade-off: cost vs freshness On-demand pricing (BigQuery) ≈ USD 6 per TiB scanned ≈ approximate list price (2026); flat-rate options exist

Failure modes.

  • Analytics on the production database — a heavy report slows checkout → move analytics to a replica or, better, to the warehouse.
  • Broken or late pipelines — dashboards silently show yesterday's data → data-freshness checks, alerting on pipeline lag.
  • Schema drift — a column renamed in the source breaks the ETL → schema registry / contracts, CDC with schema evolution.
  • Runaway query cost → partitioned tables, cost limits per query/user, materialized aggregates.
  • Duplicates from at-least-once ingestion → idempotent loads (merge by key), deduplication.

In the playground. dwh is a storage node off the critical path: it typically receives an async flow from a stream/kafka node or from analytics, so its latency does not affect the user's p99, but its backlog and cost are visible. Parameters: replicas, capacity (20 queries/s), latencyMs (median 2 s). Scenarios: event-fanout, observability-stack.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon Redshift — columnar data warehouse (provisioned or serverless).
  • Amazon Athena — serverless SQL over files in S3.
  • BigQuery — serverless data warehouse with storage/compute separation.
  • Microsoft Fabric (Data Warehouse, Lakehouse) and Azure Synapse Analytics — analytics platforms.
  • Azure Databricks — Spark-based lakehouse platform.
  • ClickHouse — very fast columnar OLAP database.
  • Apache Spark — distributed batch and streaming processing.
  • Trino — distributed SQL query engine over lakes and databases.
  • Apache Iceberg — open table format for lakehouses.
  • DuckDB — in-process analytical database, great for local analysis.

In the interview

"Analytics never runs on the production database. Order events flow through Kafka (or CDC from the outbox) into a columnar warehouse, where dashboards scan months of history in seconds. The trade-off is freshness — minutes, not milliseconds — which is fine for business reports."

Learn more: Databases › Specialized stores · Messaging › Patterns · Compute › Services · Analytics service

items.title: Vector DB
items.text:
What it is. A vector database stores embeddings — arrays of numbers (typically a few hundred to a few thousand dimensions) produced by a model so that texts or images with similar meaning end up close together — and answers nearest-neighbour queries: "the 5 chunks most similar to this question". Exact search compares against every vector, which is too slow at scale, so vector stores use approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes such as HNSW (a navigable graph) or IVF (clusters), trading a little recall for orders of magnitude of speed. Most also filter by metadata (e.g. only documents of this event) and combine vector with keyword search (hybrid search).

When to use.

  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): the BoxOffice support assistant retrieves the most relevant FAQ and policy chunks and puts them in the LLM prompt.
  • Semantic search ("concerts like this one"), recommendations, deduplication of near-identical content.
  • The semantic cache of an LLM gateway: reuse an answer when a new question is close enough to a previous one.
  • Long-term memory of agents (the palette's memory component uses it).

When not to (or watch out).

  • Exact matches, filters and transactions: a SQL index or a search engine is better and cheaper.
  • Small collections (thousands of vectors): an extension in your existing database (pgvector) is enough — no new system to operate.
  • ANN is approximate: recall below 100% means some relevant chunks are missed; evaluate retrieval quality, not just latency.
  • Changing the embedding model means re-embedding everything: version your embeddings.
  • Memory: HNSW indexes are large and usually kept in RAM.

Key numbers.

Metric Typical value Note Embedding dimensions ≈ 384–3,072 Depends on the model Size of one vector dims × 4 bytes (float32) 1,536 dims ≈ 6 KB; 1 M vectors ≈ 6 GB before index overhead ANN query latency ≈ 1–10 ms for millions of vectors ≈ illustrative; depends on index parameters and hardware Recall@10 with tuned HNSW ≈ 0.9–0.99 Trade-off with latency and memory Quantization savings ≈ 4× (int8) to 32× (binary) less memory At some loss of recall

Failure modes.

  • Poor retrieval — the right chunk is not in the top-k → better chunking, hybrid search, reranking, evaluation sets.
  • Stale index — documents changed but embeddings did not → re-index on change (CDC/events), track versions.
  • Model mismatch — query and documents embedded with different models → store the model version with each vector.
  • Memory exhaustion as the collection grows → quantization, sharding, disk-based indexes.
  • Data leakage across tenants → mandatory metadata filters (tenant, permissions) applied in the query, not in the prompt.

In the playground. vectordb is a storage node usually called by memory (Memory Fabric) or by the orchestrator in the AI scenario; its latency adds to every agent step that retrieves context. Parameters: replicas, capacity (1,500 queries/s), latencyMs (median 12 ms). Scenarios: ai-assistant, search-autocomplete.

Real products.

AWSGCPAzureOpen source
  • Amazon OpenSearch Service — k-NN vector search plus keyword search.
  • Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL / RDS for PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension.
  • Vertex AI Vector Search — managed ANN service.
  • AlloyDB / Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with pgvector.
  • Azure AI Search — vector, keyword and hybrid search.
  • Azure Cosmos DB — integrated vector search.
  • pgvector — vector type and HNSW/IVFFlat indexes inside PostgreSQL (used in Hands-on 12).
  • Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate — dedicated vector databases.
  • FAISS — library for efficient similarity search (Meta).
  • Chroma — lightweight embedding store for prototypes.

In the interview

"For RAG over BoxOffice's policies, I'd chunk the documents, embed them and store the vectors in pgvector next to the data we already have, with an HNSW index and a tenant filter. A dedicated vector database only pays off at tens of millions of vectors; either way, I measure retrieval recall, not just latency."

Learn more: Databases › Specialized stores · AI systems › RAG & memory · Case study: AI assistant · Memory Fabric · Hands-on 12

items.title: Glossary
items.text:
The vocabulary of system design, A to Z: distributed systems, data, caching, messaging, reliability, observability, networking, security, cloud-native platforms and AI systems. Each entry is a one- or two-sentence definition with, when there is one, a link to the class page or the component catalog entry where the idea is taught in depth.

How to use

Use your browser's search (Ctrl/Cmd + F) or the site search to jump to a term. When you read an unfamiliar word in a class, a paper or an interview question, look it up here, then follow the link. Try defining the terms out loud in one sentence before reading the definition: that is exactly what an interviewer will ask you to do. The numbers page has the values behind the formulas mentioned here.

204 terms.

items.title: A
items.text:
• ACID — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the guarantees of a database transaction — all or nothing, invariants kept, concurrent transactions isolated, committed data survives crashes. → Databases › Transactions
  • Active-active / active-passive — Two redundancy styles: in active-active every site serves traffic at the same time; in active-passive a standby takes over only when the primary fails. → Reliability › Disaster recovery
  • Admission control — Limiting how much work enters a system so that what is admitted completes well; a virtual waiting room is admission control for people. → Case study: ticketing
  • Agent (AI) — An LLM running in a loop that decides which tools to call, observes the results and continues until the task is done. → AI systems › Agents
  • Alerting — Rules over signals that notify a human when users are affected; good alerts are about symptoms and are actionable. → Catalog › Alerting
  • Amdahl's Law — The speedup from parallelism is limited by the serial fraction of the work: speedup = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/n). → Estimation
  • ANN (approximate nearest neighbor) — Search that finds vectors close to a query vector quickly by accepting that it may miss a few true nearest neighbors; HNSW is a common index. → Catalog › Vector DB
  • Anycast — Announcing the same IP address from many locations so the network routes each user to the nearest one; used by DNS providers and CDNs. → Edge › DNS & CDN
  • API gateway — The single entry point of an API: routing, authentication, rate limiting, request shaping and observability. → Catalog › API Gateway
  • At-least-once / at-most-once delivery — Messaging guarantees: at-least-once never loses a message but may deliver duplicates; at-most-once never duplicates but may lose messages. → Messaging › Delivery semantics
  • Autoscaling — Adding or removing capacity automatically based on a metric (CPU, queue depth, requests per second) or a schedule. → Compute › Serverless & autoscaling
  • Availability — The fraction of time (or of requests) in which a system works correctly, often expressed in nines: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year. → Estimation › Availability math
  • Availability zone (AZ) — One or more isolated data centers within a cloud region, with independent power and networking; spreading replicas over AZs survives a data-center failure. → Catalog › Subnet

items.title: B
items.text:
• Backoff (exponential) — Waiting longer between successive retries (1 s, 2 s, 4 s…) so that a struggling dependency can recover. → Reliability › Patterns
  • Back-of-the-envelope estimate — A quick calculation of load, storage, bandwidth or cost with rounded numbers, to get the order of magnitude that drives the design. → Estimation › Numbers
  • Backpressure — A signal from a slow consumer that makes producers slow down or reject work instead of letting queues grow without limit. → Messaging › Delivery semantics
  • Bandwidth — The maximum data rate of a link (e.g. 1 Gbps = 125 MB/s); throughput is what you actually achieve. → Estimation › Numbers
  • BFF (backend for frontend) — A gateway or thin service tailored to one client type (web, mobile) that aggregates and shapes backend calls for it. → Edge › API gateway
  • Bloom filter — A compact probabilistic set that answers "definitely not present" or "probably present"; used to skip disk reads and to deduplicate. → Databases › Data models
  • Blue/green deployment — Running the new version in a full second environment and switching all traffic to it at once, with instant rollback by switching back. → Cloud-native › Delivery
  • B-tree — The balanced tree index used by most relational databases: updates pages in place and gives fast point and range reads. → Databases › Data models
  • Bulkhead — Isolating resources (thread pools, connections, instances) per dependency or tenant so one failure cannot consume everything. → Reliability › Patterns
  • Burn rate — How fast an SLO's error budget is being consumed relative to the sustainable rate; a burn rate of 14.4 spends 2% of a 28-day budget in one hour. → Observability › Alerting

items.title: C
items.text:
• Cache — A fast store (usually in memory) holding copies of data that is expensive to fetch or compute. → Catalog › Cache
  • Cache-aside — The application reads the cache first and, on a miss, reads the database and fills the cache; on writes it updates the database and deletes the key. → Caching › Patterns
  • Cache stampede — Many concurrent misses for the same hot key hitting the backend at once, typically when the key expires; also called thundering herd. → Caching › Failure modes
  • Canary release — Sending a small share of traffic to a new version and comparing its metrics with the old one before rolling out further. → Cloud-native › Delivery
  • Capacity planning — Estimating the resources needed to meet expected load with headroom, and when to add more, from measurements and growth forecasts. → Performance › Capacity planning
  • CAP theorem — During a network partition, a replicated system must choose between consistency (refuse or delay) and availability (answer, possibly stale). → Distributed systems › CAP & PACELC
  • Cardinality (metrics) — The number of distinct time series produced by a metric's label combinations; high-cardinality labels such as user ids explode cost. → Catalog › Metrics
  • CDC (change data capture) — Streaming the changes committed to a database (from its log) to other systems such as Kafka, a cache or a data warehouse. → Messaging › Patterns
  • CDN (content delivery network) — A global network of edge caches that serves content from locations close to users. → Catalog › CDN
  • Chaos engineering — Running controlled experiments that inject failures (latency, crashes, zone outages) to find weaknesses before real incidents do. → Reliability › Chaos engineering
  • Circuit breaker — A wrapper around calls to a dependency that stops calling it (fails fast) after too many errors, and probes it again after a pause. → Reliability › Patterns
  • Cold start — The extra latency of the first request to a new instance (function, container, JVM) while it initializes. → Catalog › Serverless
  • Consensus — Getting a group of nodes to agree on a value or an ordered log despite failures, as long as a majority is up (Raft, Paxos). → Distributed systems › Consensus
  • Consistent hashing — Placing nodes and keys on a hash ring so that adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys. → Edge › Load balancing
  • Consumer group — A set of consumers sharing a Kafka topic: each partition is read by exactly one member, so parallelism is at most the partition count. → Catalog › Kafka
  • Container — A process packaged with its dependencies in an image and isolated by the operating system (namespaces, cgroups). → Cloud-native › Containers
  • Coordinated omission — A load-testing error where a slow system makes the client send fewer requests, hiding the latency real users would see. → Performance › Load testing
  • CQRS — Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate models (and often stores) for writes and for reads, kept in sync by events. → Messaging › Patterns
  • Cron — A schedule expression (and the classic Unix tool) for running jobs at fixed times or intervals. → Catalog › Scheduler

items.title: D
items.text:
• Data warehouse — A columnar database for analytics over large history (OLAP), fed from operational systems by ETL/ELT or CDC. → Catalog › Data Warehouse
