items.title: Concept Map: System Design
items.text:
Each class of System Architecture teaches a handful of ideas; the project, the exams and a system-design interview ask you to use them together. This map shows how they connect: 151 concepts from the 16 classes and 252 connections between them, each explained in one sentence.

How it is organized. Each concept sits in the row of the theme of the class where it first appears, in course order: Foundations (C1–C2), Distributed systems (C3), Edge & compute (C4–C5), Storage (C6–C7), Messaging (C8), Operations (C9–C12), AI (C13–C14), Performance & cases (C15–C16). Its column is the stage of a design it belongs to, the same order in which you build and defend a design, at work or in an interview:

Column What it holds Colour Requirements & numbers what must hold and how much: requirements, estimates, Little's Law, percentiles, nines, SLOs, capacity, cost blue Building blocks the components of the palette and how each one works: DNS, CDN, load balancer, gateway, queue, Kafka, cache, Kubernetes, LLM gateway… purple Data & consistency state and correctness: replication, consistency models, quorums, transactions, idempotency, ordering, invalidation, outbox, sagas teal Operate at scale keeping it up and safe in production: failure modes, resilience patterns, observability, alerting, delivery, security, load tests, chaos orange

Reading a row from left to right tells the story of a class: the numbers that motivate it, the components it adds, the correctness questions they raise and how they fail in production. Reading a column from top to bottom shows one skill growing through the course. The code in the corner of each concept is the class page where it first appears (C9.2 = class 9, second page of its roadmap). The colours are the same as in the study cards; blue, purple and orange also mean estimate, design and deep dive in the workbook and the cheat sheet.

Four ways to use it:

  • Tap a concept. Its neighbours light up and the panel shows what it is, the classes where it is taught (linked to the section) and, one sentence each, where it leads and where it comes from. Tap a neighbour to follow the thread.
  • Follow a trail. Each trail walks through one of the course's questions, step by step, such as "why does p99 explode while the CPU is idle?", "a flash sale without double booking" or "why your load test lies". Use ‹ › in the panel or the arrow keys.
  • Pick a class. The buttons are grouped by theme; they light up the concepts the class introduces and the ones it revisits from earlier classes. Each button covers the class's subpages.
  • Search. The search box finds a concept by name or by its definition (Enter opens the first match).

On a phone, the concepts are grouped by theme, the classes sit under one tab per theme and the panel slides up from the bottom of the screen; close it with ×.

To practise the concepts one by one, use the study cards; to see the method, the formulas and the numbers on paper, the cheat sheet; to practise with exercises, the workbook; to rehearse them out loud, the interview preparation.

items.title: Study Cards: System Design
items.text:
One deck for all 16 classes, from C1 (what system design is) to C16 (the case studies), subpages included: 446 cards, each a section of a class, with that class's own numbers and the BoxOffice example. There are two modes.

  • Study. Read the question, answer it in your head and flip the card. Then say how it went: missed, almost or got it. Cards you missed come back first; the ones you got right wait until the end. Your progress is saved in this browser.
  • Challenge. A ten-round game: each round shows a situation from production or from a design interview ("the payment provider is slow and every checkout thread is waiting…") and three concept cards. Pick the card that explains or solves the situation. Right answers in a row multiply your points; each miss costs a life and sends the card to the missed box of the Study mode. There are 272 situations.

The filters build the deck. Pick one or more topics (F foundations, D distributed systems, E edge & compute, S storage, M messaging, O operations, A AI, P performance & cases) and, within them, any classes or class pages you like: study only this week's class or, when reviewing for an exam, only one stage of a design. Each card's colour is its design stage, the same as in the concept map: blue for requirements & numbers, purple for building blocks, teal for data & consistency, orange for operating at scale; the stage's name is also written on the card's band. The dots at the bottom give the level: warm-up, practice or challenge. On the keyboard, space flips the card and 1, 2 and 3 give your grade (or pick a card, in the Challenge).

Every card links to the section of the class where the concept is taught. To see how the concepts connect, use the concept map; to look up formulas and numbers, the cheat sheet; to practise with exercises, the workbook; to rehearse a full design out loud, the interview preparation.

items.title: Index
items.text:
Interview prep System Design 2027.1 System Design Interviews

How to think about, estimate, draw and defend a scalable system out loud, in 45 minutes. A map of what system-design interviews ask, a framework you can rehearse, a quick-diagnosis table, the key concepts with a link to the class where each one is taught, a quiz, a two-week study plan and a checklist to track your progress. Every example uses BoxOffice, the ticketing platform we build in the course.

Contents The 10 a.m. question What a system-design interview looks like How to answer (8 principles) The framework, step by step Quick diagnosis The key concepts Quiz Study plan Checklist Back to 10 a.m. References The 10 a.m. question

A scene that is going to happen to you.

Tuesday, 10 a.m. The last round of the internship process you wanted most, at a company that sells tickets online. No code this time: a shared whiteboard, an engineer from the platform team and 45 minutes. After the introductions, she writes a single line on the board:

"Design a ticketing site for a stadium show. Tickets go on sale Saturday at 10:00."That is all she says. She wants to see how you think.

There is a weak answer: grab the marker and draw, in silence, the usual boxes (a load balancer, three servers, a cache, a database) and say "it scales". And there is a strong one, which starts with questions back: "How many seats, and how many fans do we expect at 10:00? Can we ever sell the same seat twice? How long can a fan hold a seat while paying?" With the answers (say 60,000 seats and 2 million fans) the problem changes shape. Serving 2 million copies of the event page is the easy part: that is what a CDN (content delivery network) is for. The hard part is that 2 million people compete for 60,000 rows in a database in the same minute, and that not one of those rows may be sold twice.

The difference between the two answers is not having memorized more boxes. It is knowing how to connect what you learned: requirements and estimates, where the contention is, what must be strongly consistent and what can be eventually consistent, how a queue turns a spike into a line, and what breaks first. This page lays out that path. At the end, we come back to the 10 a.m. question with the full answer.

What a system-design interview looks like

Four kinds of question, one skill: reasoning about a system out loud, with numbers and trade-offs.

Open design "Design a URL shortener"

The classic 45-minute question. There is no single answer: there are requirements you clarify, numbers you estimate, a design you justify and trade-offs you name. The interviewer steers you into one or two deep dives.

Component deep dive "Make this rate limiter distributed"

One box of a design, in depth: the algorithm (token bucket, sliding window), where the state lives, what happens when that state is unavailable. Tests whether you know the component beyond its name.

Troubleshooting "p99 tripled after the deploy"

A symptom and a request for a diagnosis. Tests whether you read metrics, traces and logs, and whether you know the usual suspects: saturation, a slow dependency, a cold cache, retries, a lock.

Estimation "How many servers do we need?"

Back-of-the-envelope math: users to requests per second, peak factor, storage per year, bandwidth, Little's Law. The order of magnitude is what matters, and saying your assumptions out loud matters more.

What separates candidates

For an internship or a first job, nobody expects you to have run a system with millions of users. What sinks candidates are the basic traps: drawing before asking, designing without a single number, naming technologies without saying why ("I'd use Kafka"), ignoring what happens when something fails, and going silent. Avoid those five and you are already ahead of most.

What the interviewer is assessing Scoping the problem Realistic estimates A sound high-level design Technical depth Trade-offs and bottlenecks Communication and driving DimensionStrong signalRed flag RequirementsSeparates functional from non-functional requirements; asks about scale, consistency and latency before drawingStarts drawing in the first minute EstimationTurns users into requests per second and gigabytes, with the peak, and uses the numbers to decideNumbers that never influence a decision, or no numbers at all High-level designA simple design that covers every requirement, with clear data flowTwenty boxes with no explanation of what flows between them DepthGoes deep where the problem is hard (for BoxOffice: seat contention)Goes deep where it is easy (choosing a frontend framework) Trade-offs"X over Y because… the cost is… I'd revisit if…""X is the best", "it scales" FailureAsks what happens when each box fails; timeouts, retries, idempotencyA design that only works when everything works CommunicationThinks out loud, checks in, drives the next stepLong silences, or waits to be told what to do LevelWhat is expectedWhere to practice Intern / new gradA correct, simple design; clear vocabulary; honest estimates; reacts well to hintsWarm-up problems and the quick reference Mid-levelDrives the whole session; one or two solid deep dives; names failure modes without being askedMedium problems and mock interviews SeniorFinds the hard part fast, quantifies trade-offs, discusses operations, cost and evolutionHard and advanced problems How to answer

8 principles for turning what you know into a design that convinces.

1 Clarify before you draw Who uses it, for what, how many, how fast, and what must never go wrong? Two minutes of questions save twenty of redesign. A well-placed question ("can we ever sell the same seat twice?") shows more maturity than any diagram. Class 1 · Requirements → 2 Say your assumptions, with numbers "I'll assume 10 million daily active users, 20 requests each, a peak of 3× the average: about 7,000 requests per second at peak." The interviewer can correct you; silence they cannot. Round aggressively: one day is about 105 seconds. Class 2 · Estimation → 3 Go broad, then deep First a design that covers every requirement end to end, even if naive; only then the deep dives. Polishing the cache before the write path exists is the most common way to run out of time. 4 Draw and narrate Boxes with names, arrows with what flows on them ("POST /holds", "OrderPlaced event"). Narrate a request as it travels through the diagram. Rehearse with the playground: same palette, same vocabulary. 5 Name the trade-off Every choice costs something. "I'll use a cache-aside Redis for the catalog: reads drop from 20 ms to 1 ms and the database sheds 95% of the load, at the cost of up to 60 s of stale prices, which is fine for a catalog but not for seat availability." 6 Find the bottleneck with numbers Which box hits its limit first? Compare the load you estimated with the capacity of each component (reference numbers). Utilization above about 70–80% is where latency explodes: that is the knee of the queueing curve. Class 2 · Queueing → 7 Design for failure For each arrow, ask: what if it is slow? what if it fails? what if the request arrives twice? Timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, idempotency keys and a dead-letter queue are the standard answers. Class 9 · Resilience patterns → 8 Drive, and check in You lead the session. Propose the next step ("the hard part is seat contention, shall I go deep there?") and check in every few minutes. If the interviewer raises a concern, take it seriously: "good point, let me revisit that".

Practical tip: make the transitions explicit. "That covers the requirements; now a quick estimate." "We have the high-level design; the risky part is the 10:00 spike, let me go deep there." The interviewer always knows where you are, and so do you.

The framework, step by step

Seven steps and a clock for a 45-minute interview. The framework page has templates for each step and BoxOffice worked through end to end.

1 Clarify the requirements · ~5 min Functional requirements (the 3–5 core features, and what is out of scope) and non-functional ones: scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability, cost. End with a short list written on the board. Class 1 → 2 Estimate · ~5 min Requests per second (average and peak), read/write ratio, storage per year, bandwidth, and the one number that decides the design (for BoxOffice: 2 M fans for 60 k seats). Class 2 · Numbers → 3 API and data model · ~5 min The main endpoints or events (with idempotency keys where money or inventory is involved) and the core entities with their keys and access patterns. The access patterns choose the database. Class 5 · API styles → 4 High-level design · ~10 min Clients → edge (DNS, CDN, load balancer, API gateway) → services → storage, with async work behind queues. Walk one read and one write through it. Keep it simple enough to fit on the board. Class 1 · Scaling journey → 5 Deep dives · ~12 min One or two components where the problem is hard: the seat hold (transactions and locks), the feed fan-out, the hot partition, the cache invalidation. This is where depth is assessed. Class 16 · Case studies → 6 Bottlenecks and trade-offs · ~5 min What breaks first at 10× the load? Where are the single points of failure? What did you trade (consistency for latency, cost for availability)? How would you observe and test it? Class 15 · Bottlenecks → 7 Wrap-up · ~3 min Summarize the design in four sentences, restate the key trade-offs, and list what you would do next with more time (multi-region, cost, observability, abuse). Leave the interviewer with a clear picture. The two scoping questions that change everything

Always ask: "Is this read-heavy or write-heavy?" and "What must never be wrong?" A read-heavy system (catalog, feed, URL redirects) is solved with caches, replicas and a CDN. A write-heavy one (location updates, metrics, clicks) is solved with partitioning, queues and append-only storage. And the thing that must never be wrong (a seat, a balance, a payment) is where you pay for strong consistency, transactions and idempotency, while everything else can be eventually consistent.

Quick diagnosis

The symptoms that show up in troubleshooting and deep-dive questions, what they usually point to and what to do next.

In a troubleshooting question, the interviewer describes a symptom and expects a hypothesis, a way to confirm it and a fix. Before proposing a new architecture, rule out the cheap causes: a recent deploy, a saturated resource, a slow dependency, a cold cache, retries.

SymptomLikely causeNext step p99 high but CPU idleThreads or connections exhausted waiting on a slow dependency (Little's Law: concurrency = rate × time)Trace a slow request; add a timeout and a circuit breaker; bulkhead the slow call; size the pool p99 grows sharply as traffic rises, p50 almost flatUtilization past the knee (~70–80%): queueing delayScale out or shed load before the knee; autoscale on utilization; find the saturated resource (USE method) Latency spike right after a deploy or restartCold cache, cold JIT, connection pools refillingWarm up before taking traffic (readiness probe), roll out gradually (canary), pre-warm the cache Database CPU at 100%, mostly readsMissing cache or index; N+1 queriesEXPLAIN the top queries; add an index; cache-aside; read replicas Database melts the moment a popular key expiresCache stampede (thundering herd)Request coalescing / single flight, a lock per key, early probabilistic refresh, staggered TTLs One shard or partition hot, the others idleHot key or a bad partition key (celebrity, flash-sale event)Better key (add a suffix / salt), split the hot key, cache it, or give it a dedicated path An outage gets worse when the dependency recoversRetry storm: retries without backoff multiply the loadExponential backoff with jitter, retry budgets, circuit breaker, idempotent endpoints Consumer lag growing steadilyConsumers slower than producers, or fewer partitions than consumersScale consumers up to the partition count; add partitions; batch; find the slow handler; DLQ for poison messages Users see stale data right after savingRead from a lagging replica or a cache not invalidatedRead-your-writes: read from the leader after a write, or invalidate / version the cache entry Same order charged twiceRetry after a timeout without idempotencyIdempotency key stored with the result; unique constraint; reconcile with the provider Two fans got the same seatCheck-then-act race without a lock or constraintSELECT … FOR UPDATE, a conditional update (WHERE status = 'free'), or a unique constraint on (event, seat) Errors only in one availability zone or regionZonal failure, bad host, network partitionHealth checks and outlier detection; drain the zone; multi-AZ by default Memory slowly grows until the pod restartsLeak; unbounded cache or queueSoak test; heap profile; bound every cache and queue The LLM assistant is slow and expensiveToo many agent steps, no caching, large promptsFewer steps, a semantic cache, a smaller model for routing, streaming for time to first token (TTFT) A complete example "p99 is 4 s, CPU is at 15%"

Ask: since when? after a deploy? all endpoints or one? what does the service call?Hypothesis: a downstream call got slow; every request now holds a thread for seconds, the pool of 200 threads is full and new requests wait in the queue. Little's Law: 100 req/s × 2 s = 200 requests in flight.Confirm: a trace shows 3.8 s inside the call to the payment provider; thread-pool metrics show 200/200 busy.Fix, cheapest first: a 500 ms timeout, a circuit breaker with a fallback ("payment pending"), a separate pool for that dependency (bulkhead); then make payment asynchronous.

Tools by symptom What to use when

RED dashboard (rate, errors, duration): is the service healthy for its users?USE method (utilization, saturation, errors): which resource is the bottleneck?Distributed trace: where does one slow request spend its time?Logs: what exactly happened to this request?Profiler / flame graph: where does the CPU go?EXPLAIN: why is this query slow?Load test (k6) and fault injection (Toxiproxy): reproduce it before you fix it. Class 10 →

The key concepts

The concepts that come up most, in ten themes. Try answering out loud before opening each theme; each answer ends with the class where the topic is taught. For every palette component there is a full entry in the component catalog.

Fundamentals and estimation7 items · classes 1, 2 ▶
  • [1] Functional vs non-functional requirements?Functional: what the system does (buy a ticket, search events). Non-functional: how well (latency, availability, consistency, durability, scale, cost, security). The non-functional ones drive the architecture. Class 1
  • [2] Vertical vs horizontal scaling?Vertical: a bigger machine (simple, has a ceiling, single point of failure). Horizontal: more machines behind a load balancer (needs stateless services, shared state elsewhere). Start vertical, design for horizontal. Class 1
  • [3] How do you go from users to requests per second?Daily active users × requests per user ÷ 86,400 s (≈ 105), times a peak factor (2–10×; for a flash sale, far more). 10 M DAU × 20 ÷ 105 ≈ 2,000 req/s average. Class 2
  • [4] What is Little's Law?L = λ × W: items in the system = arrival rate × time in the system. 1,000 req/s × 0.2 s = 200 requests in flight, so you need about 200 threads or connections. Class 2
  • [5] Why does latency explode near 100% utilization?Queueing: in an M/M/1 queue, the time in system is S / (1 − ρ). At ρ = 0.5 it doubles the service time; at 0.9, ten times. Keep utilization below the knee (~70–80%). Class 2
  • [6] Why look at p99 rather than the average?The average hides the tail, and the tail is what users feel. With fan-out, the tail dominates: a page that calls 100 services, each slow 1% of the time, is slow 1 − 0.99100 ≈ 63% of the time. Class 2
  • [7] How do availabilities combine?In series they multiply (99.9% × 99.9% ≈ 99.8%); in parallel the unavailabilities multiply (1 − 0.01² = 99.99%). 99.9% ≈ 8.8 h of downtime per year; 99.99% ≈ 53 min. Class 2
In class: 1 · What is system design · 2 · Estimation & performance fundamentals Distributed systems7 items · class 3 ▶
  • [8] What does CAP actually say?During a network partition, a replicated system must choose between consistency (refuse or delay) and availability (answer, possibly stale). Without a partition there is no choice to make, which is why PACELC adds: else, latency vs consistency. Class 3
  • [9] Strong vs eventual consistency?Linearizable: every read sees the latest write, as if there were one copy. Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop. In between: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, causal. Pick per data item: seats strong, view counters eventual. Class 3
  • [10] What is a quorum?With N replicas, writing to W and reading from R with R + W > N guarantees the read overlaps the latest write. N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 is the usual choice. Class 3
  • [11] What does consensus (Raft) give you?A group of nodes agreeing on one ordered log despite failures, as long as a majority is up: leader election, replicated configuration, locks. etcd, ZooKeeper and Kafka's KRaft use it. Needs 2f + 1 nodes to tolerate f failures. Class 3
  • [12] Why can't you trust wall clocks?Clocks drift and NTP corrections jump; two machines can disagree by milliseconds or more. Use logical clocks (Lamport, vector) for ordering, or hybrid logical clocks; never "last write wins" on wall time for money. Class 3
  • [13] What is idempotency and why does it matter?Doing an operation twice has the same effect as once. Networks force retries, and retries duplicate requests; an idempotency key (stored with the result) makes "charge" and "hold seat" safe to retry. Class 3
  • [14] Name some fallacies of distributed computing.The network is reliable; latency is zero; bandwidth is infinite; the network is secure; topology doesn't change; there is one administrator; transport cost is zero; the network is homogeneous. Each one is a failure mode to design for. Class 3
In class: 3 · Distributed systems fundamentals Traffic and edge6 items · class 4 ▶
  • [15] What does a CDN do, and what can't it do?Serves cacheable content (images, JS, event pages) from edge locations near users, cutting latency and origin load. It cannot cache personalized or strongly consistent data, like seat availability at 10:00. Class 4
  • [16] L4 vs L7 load balancing?L4 routes TCP/UDP connections by address and port (fast, protocol-agnostic). L7 understands HTTP: routes by path or header, terminates TLS, retries, does canaries. Most web APIs use L7. Class 4
  • [17] Why consistent hashing?With hash(key) mod N, changing N moves almost every key; on a hash ring only about 1/N of the keys move. Virtual nodes even out the load. Used in caches, sharded stores and sticky load balancing. Class 4
  • [18] Token bucket vs sliding window?Token bucket: tokens refill at rate r up to burst b; allows bursts, cheap to store. Sliding window: counts requests in the last T seconds; smoother, a bit more state. Either way the state lives in a shared store (Redis) and the response is 429 with Retry-After. Class 4
  • [19] What does an API gateway do?A single entry point: routing, authentication, rate limiting, request shaping, TLS, observability. Keep business logic out of it; a BFF (backend for frontend) is a gateway tailored to one client. Class 4
  • [20] WebSockets, SSE or polling?WebSockets: bidirectional, long-lived (chat, games). Server-Sent Events: server-to-client stream over HTTP (live scores, LLM tokens). Long polling: the fallback. Each long-lived connection costs memory on a server and complicates load balancing. Class 4
In class: 4 · Traffic & edge · Catalog: edge components Compute and services6 items · class 5 ▶
  • [21] Why stateless app servers?Any replica can serve any request, so you can add, remove and replace replicas freely. Session and state go to a shared store (Redis, database) or into a token. Class 5
  • [22] Monolith or microservices?Start with a (modular) monolith; split a service out when a team, a scaling profile or a failure domain justifies it. Microservices buy independent deploys at the price of network calls, distributed data and operational cost. Class 5
  • [23] REST, gRPC or GraphQL?REST: simple, cacheable, public APIs. gRPC: binary, typed, streaming, service-to-service. GraphQL: clients choose fields, good for varied frontends, harder to cache and rate limit. Class 5
  • [24] When do you move work to a background worker?When the user does not need the result to continue (emails, thumbnails, reports) or when the work is slow or spiky. Respond 202 Accepted, enqueue, and let workers drain the queue at their own pace. Class 5
  • [25] When is serverless a good fit?Spiky or low, event-driven traffic with short tasks: you pay per invocation and scale to zero. Watch cold starts, concurrency limits, time limits and connection storms against the database. Class 5
  • [26] How do you integrate safely with a payment provider?Idempotency keys on every charge, timeouts and retries with backoff, webhooks for the final status (verified and deduplicated), and a daily reconciliation job against the provider's report. Class 5
In class: 5 · Compute & services · Catalog: compute, external Databases and data systems8 items · class 6 ▶
  • [27] SQL or NoSQL?Start from the access patterns. Relations, transactions and ad-hoc queries: SQL. Huge scale with simple key-based access, flexible schema or wide rows: key-value, document or wide-column. "NoSQL scales, SQL doesn't" is a myth worth avoiding. Class 6
  • [28] What does an index cost?Faster reads on the indexed columns; slower writes (every insert updates every index) and more storage. Index for the queries you actually run; check with EXPLAIN. Class 6
  • [29] B-tree vs LSM-tree?B-tree (PostgreSQL, MySQL): in-place updates, fast reads. LSM (Cassandra, RocksDB): append and compact, very fast writes, reads may check several files. Write-heavy workloads favor LSM. Class 6
  • [30] How do you prevent double booking?Make the database enforce it: a transaction with SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the seat, or an atomic conditional update (UPDATE seats SET status='held' WHERE id=? AND status='free'), or a unique constraint. Optimistic locking (a version column) when conflicts are rare. Class 6
  • [31] Isolation levels in one sentence each?Read committed: no dirty reads. Repeatable read / snapshot: a consistent snapshot, but write skew is possible. Serializable: as if transactions ran one at a time, at a cost in throughput and aborts. Class 6
  • [32] What does a read replica buy, and cost?More read capacity and a standby for failover. The cost is replication lag: a read right after a write may not see it. Writes do not scale with replicas. Class 6
  • [33] How do you choose a shard key?High cardinality, even distribution, and aligned with the main query so most queries hit one shard. Hash for even spread, range for range scans. Watch hot keys and resharding. Class 6
  • [34] OLTP vs OLAP?OLTP: many small transactions on current data (orders). OLAP: large scans and aggregates over history (sales per artist per month), in a columnar data warehouse fed by ETL/ELT or change data capture (CDC). Class 6
In class: 6 · Databases & data systems · Catalog: storage components Caching5 items · class 7 ▶
  • [35] Cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind?Cache-aside: the app reads the cache, on a miss reads the database and fills the cache (the default). Read-through: the cache does that for you. Write-through: write to cache and database together. Write-behind: write to cache, flush later (fast, risks loss). Class 7
  • [36] How does hit ratio translate into database load?Database load = requests × (1 − hit ratio). Going from 90% to 99% hits cuts database reads by 10×. Average latency ≈ h × tcache + (1 − h) × tdb. Class 7
  • [37] How do you invalidate?TTL (simple, bounded staleness), delete on write (cache-aside), events / CDC to evict, or versioned keys. "There are only two hard things…": decide how stale each item may be. Class 7
  • [38] What is a cache stampede and how do you stop it?A hot key expires and thousands of requests miss at once and hit the database. Fixes: request coalescing (single flight), a short lock per key, probabilistic early refresh, jittered TTLs, serving stale while revalidating. Class 7
  • [39] LRU, LFU or TTL?LRU evicts the least recently used (good default); LFU the least frequently used (keeps long-term favorites); TTL expires by age regardless of use. Modern caches mix them (e.g. W-TinyLFU). Class 7
In class: 7 · Caching · Catalog: Cache Messaging and events6 items · class 8 ▶
  • [40] Queue, pub/sub or event log?Queue: each message to one consumer (work distribution). Pub/sub: each message to every subscriber (fan-out). Event log (Kafka): an ordered, retained log that many consumer groups read at their own offsets, and can replay. Class 8
  • [41] At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once?At-most-once can lose messages; at-least-once can duplicate them (the common default); "exactly-once" in practice means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing or transactions. Class 8
  • [42] How does Kafka scale consumers?A topic has partitions; within a consumer group each partition goes to one consumer, so parallelism is at most the number of partitions. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition: key by order id or seat id. Class 8
  • [43] What is the transactional outbox?Write the business row and the event in the same database transaction (an outbox table), then a relay publishes the events. Avoids the dual-write problem where the database commits and the publish fails. Class 8
  • [44] Saga: choreography or orchestration?A saga splits a distributed transaction into local steps with compensations (release the seat if payment fails). Choreography: services react to events (loose, harder to follow). Orchestration: a coordinator drives the steps (explicit, one more component). Class 8
  • [45] What is backpressure, and a DLQ?Backpressure: slowing producers or rejecting work when consumers cannot keep up, instead of letting queues grow forever. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) parks messages that keep failing so they don't block the rest. Class 8
In class: 8 · Messaging & event-driven · Catalog: messaging components Reliability and observability7 items · classes 9, 10 ▶
  • [46] SLI, SLO, SLA and error budget?SLI: a measurement (share of requests under 300 ms). SLO: the target (99.9% over 28 days). SLA: a contract with penalties. Error budget: 100% − SLO, the unreliability you may spend on releases and experiments. Class 9
  • [47] Timeout, retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead?Timeout bounds the wait; retry (with backoff and jitter) handles transient errors; a circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that keeps failing; a bulkhead isolates resources so one slow dependency can't take them all. Class 9
  • [48] RPO vs RTO?RPO: how much data you can lose (time since the last good copy). RTO: how long until you are back. Backups give hours; replication gives seconds; multi-region active-active gets close to zero, at a high cost. Class 9
  • [49] Why chaos engineering?To find weaknesses in a controlled experiment rather than in an incident: state a hypothesis about steady state, inject a failure (latency, a crash, a zone outage), observe, fix. Start small, in staging, with a stop button. Class 9
  • [50] Metrics, logs and traces?Metrics: cheap aggregates over time (is something wrong?). Logs: detailed events (what exactly happened?). Traces: one request across services (where is the time going?). OpenTelemetry standardizes all three. Class 10
  • [51] RED, USE and the golden signals?RED for services: rate, errors, duration. USE for resources: utilization, saturation, errors. Google's four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. Class 10
  • [52] What should page someone at 3 a.m.?Symptoms users feel, not causes: an SLO burning its error budget fast (burn-rate alerts over two windows). High CPU alone should not page anyone. Class 10
In class: 9 · Reliability · 10 · Observability · Catalog: observability components Network, security and cloud-native6 items · classes 11, 12, 15 ▶
  • [53] Public vs private subnets, and a NAT gateway?Only the load balancer lives in public subnets; services and databases live in private ones, with no inbound route from the internet. A NAT gateway lets private services call out (to a payment API) without being reachable. Class 11
  • [54] OAuth 2 / OIDC and JWT in one breath?OIDC authenticates the user and the auth server issues a signed token (often a JWT); services verify the signature and claims locally without calling the auth server. Short expiry plus refresh tokens; revocation is the hard part. Class 11
  • [55] What does a service mesh add?A proxy layer (sidecar or ambient) that gives every service mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and telemetry without code changes, at the cost of latency per hop and operational complexity. Class 11
  • [56] Liveness vs readiness probes?Liveness: is the process stuck? (restart it). Readiness: can it take traffic now? (remove it from the load balancer). Checking a dependency in liveness causes restart storms. Class 12
  • [57] Rolling, blue/green or canary?Rolling replaces pods gradually; blue/green switches all traffic between two full environments (fast rollback, double cost); canary sends a small share to the new version and watches the metrics before going further. Class 12
  • [58] Which load test answers which question?Smoke: does it work? Load: does it meet the SLO at expected peak? Stress: where does it break? Spike: does it survive 10:00? Soak: does it degrade over hours? Breakpoint: what is the maximum? Class 15
In class: 11 · Network & security · 12 · Cloud-native · 14 · Performance AI systems and agents5 items · class 13 ▶
  • [59] Why put an LLM gateway in front of model providers?One place for routing between models, fallbacks when a provider fails, quotas and budgets per team, caching (exact and semantic), and token, cost and latency metrics. Class 13
  • [60] What is RAG?Retrieval-augmented generation: chunk your documents, embed them, store the vectors; at question time retrieve the most similar chunks (approximate nearest neighbors, e.g. HNSW), rerank, and put them in the prompt. Grounds the answer in your data. Class 13
  • [61] What is an agent loop, and why is it slow?The model decides on a tool call, the orchestrator runs it, the result goes back to the model, repeat until done. Each step is a full LLM call (often 0.5–2 s), so latency and cost grow with the number of steps; cap the steps. Class 13
  • [62] What is prompt injection and how do you defend?Untrusted text (a web page, an email, a review) carries instructions the model follows. Defenses: least-privilege tools, confirmation for side effects, separating instructions from data, input and output filters, never trusting model output as authorization. Class 13
  • [63] How do you size an LLM endpoint?Think in tokens: requests per second × tokens per request gives tokens per second; time to first token (TTFT) and tokens per second per stream set the latency; cost ≈ input tokens × price + output tokens × price. Class 13
In class: 13 · AI systems & agents · Catalog: AI & agents components Quiz

Twenty-four interview-style questions, three per theme. Filter by theme to review only what you need.

← previous next → ↺ restart quiz Study plan

How to study, and a plan for the two weeks before an interview.

Out loud Practice in pairs

System design is a spoken exam. Reading solutions feels like learning and is not. Do mock interviews with a classmate, with a timer and the rubric, and swap roles: being the interviewer teaches you what a good answer sounds like.

With numbers Know a dozen by heart

Seconds in a day, the latency ladder (memory, SSD, same-datacenter round trip, cross-continent), what one database or one Redis can do, the nines. The quick reference and the numbers page have them.

Under load Break it in the playground

For every design you practice, build it in the playground, run a spike or stress profile, and see which box turns red first. Then fix it and run again. Seeing the knee once is worth reading about it ten times.

Honestly The checklist is your thermometer

Tick an item only when you can explain it to someone without notes, trade-off included. Space your reviews: a day, a week, a month. Whatever you forget between rounds is what needs attention.

DaysWhat to do 1–2Fundamentals and estimation: themes 1–2 above, the quiz for both; estimate five systems from the problem list in ten minutes each 3The framework: read the framework page; solve the URL shortener alone with a 45-minute timer, then compare with the case study 4–5Edge, compute and data: CDN, load balancers, gateway, rate limiting; SQL vs NoSQL, indexes, transactions, replication, sharding; the rate limiter case study 6–7Caching and messaging: patterns, stampede, Kafka, outbox, sagas, idempotency; the news feed and notification case studies 8Reliability and observability: resilience patterns, SLOs, RED/USE; run the cascading-failure and retry-storm scenarios in the playground 9Money and contention: the ticketing and payment case studies; explain double-booking prevention three ways 10Real time and AI: chat, ride sharing, AI assistant 11–12Two mock interviews per day in pairs, timed, with the rubric; the full quiz, going back only to what you got wrong 13Behavioral: write three stories from your project (a trade-off, a failure, a measurement) 14One last pass over the checklist, out loud; rest

To practice in the course's format: the workbook, with exercises at three levels and worked answers. For a quick review: the cheat sheet, the concept map and the study cards.

Checklist

The topics and habits of a good system-design interview. Your progress is saved in this browser.

↺ reset checklist Back to 10 a.m.

The full answer to "design a ticketing site for a stadium show".

Fans per seat ≈ 33 2 M fans for 60 k seats: most fans will not get a ticket, so fairness and a clear "sold out" matter as much as speed. Peak at 10:00 ~10⁵ req/s Illustrative: 2 M fans refreshing every ~10–20 s in the first minutes. Mostly reads of the same event page. Seat writes ~10³/s Illustrative: if the 60 k seats go in the first minute with no waiting room. Small, but all on the same rows: contention, not volume. A waiting room lowers it to the rate you choose. 1Clarify"Core features: browse the event, pick or be assigned seats, hold them for a few minutes, pay, get the ticket by email. Never sell a seat twice; the page must stay up at 10:00; fairness matters; bots are a real threat. Out of scope: resale, venue management." — topics [1], [9]. 2Estimate"2 M fans, 60 k seats, about 33 fans per seat. Reads at the peak are on the order of 105 per second, almost all of the same page; seat writes are a thousand or so per second, all on the same event. The design problem is the spike and the contention, not storage." — topics [3], [4]. 3Absorb the spike at the edge"The event page and assets come from a CDN; seat-map availability is served from a cache refreshed every second or so, which is fine because the authoritative check happens at hold time. A WAF and bot protection, plus a per-user rate limit at the API gateway." — topics [15], [18], [19]. 4Turn the crowd into a line"A virtual waiting room: at 10:00 fans get a random or arrival-ordered position in a queue, and the gateway admits them at the rate the inventory service can sustain, say 2,000 per minute, with a signed admission token. The spike becomes a steady flow." — topics [24], [40], [45]. 5Make the seat the source of truth"Inventory in PostgreSQL, partitioned by event if needed. A hold is one atomic conditional update (status = 'held', hold_until = now() + 10 min WHERE status = 'free'), so two fans can never hold the same seat. An expiry job releases unpaid holds." — topics [30], [31]. 6Pay safely, confirm asynchronously"The order service calls the payment provider with an idempotency key, a timeout and a circuit breaker; the provider's webhook confirms. The order commits and writes an OrderConfirmed event to an outbox; Kafka fans it out to notification, analytics and search." — topics [13], [26], [43], [47]. 7Name the trade-offs and how you'd prove it"Strong consistency only for seats and orders; everything else eventually consistent. The waiting room trades some user patience for a system that does not fall over. I'd load-test with a spike profile and run a game day where the payment provider slows down." — topics [8], [49], [58].

Seven steps, a dozen of the concepts above, and every box justified by a number or a requirement. That is what the interviewer wanted to see: not the boxes you know, but why each one is there. Try it yourself in the playground with the flash-sale scenario, and compare with the ticketing case study.

items.title: Behavioral questions
items.text: Most system-design interview loops include a conversation about what you have done: "tell me about a technical decision you made", "tell me about something that failed". For an internship or a first job, the projects of this course are exactly the material these questions ask for. This page shows how to turn them into short, honest stories that show judgment — the same judgment the design interview is looking for.

items.title: Why they appear in a system-design loop
items.text:
A design interview shows how you reason about a hypothetical system in 45 minutes. A behavioral question checks whether you have reasoned that way for real: chosen between options, lived with the consequences, measured, failed, and learned. Interviewers listen for the same signals in both: trade-offs stated explicitly, numbers, ownership, and the ability to change your mind with evidence.

What they assess What it sounds like Judgment "We chose X over Y because…, it cost us…, we would revisit if…" Ownership "I" for what you did, "we" for the team; no blaming Evidence "p99 went from 900 ms to 180 ms in the k6 load test" Learning "Next time I'd measure before choosing" Collaboration How you handled a disagreement or helped a teammate

items.title: The STAR(L) format
items.text:
Answer in two minutes or less, with this structure:

  • S — Situation: the context in one or two sentences. Which project, which system, what scale.
  • T — Task: what you had to achieve, and what made it hard.
  • A — Action: what you did, with the reasoning and the alternatives you rejected. This is the longest part.
  • R — Result: what happened, with a number if possible.
  • L — Learning: what you would do differently, or what you now do by default.

Talking about trade-offs

Use the same sentence as in the design interview: "We chose X over Y because [requirement or number]. The cost was [what we gave up]. We would revisit it if [condition]." For example: "We chose Redis cache-aside over read replicas for the catalog because 95% of the traffic was reads of the same 200 events. The cost was up to 60 seconds of stale prices. We would revisit it if prices started changing during the sale."

items.title: Turning course work into stories
items.text:
You already have the raw material. Write down one story from each of these before an interview season:

Course activity Story it gives you Typical question Team project A design decision and its trade-off; a disagreement in the team "Tell me about a technical decision you're proud of" Load-test campaign Finding a bottleneck with data, before/after numbers "Tell me about a performance problem you solved" Chaos game day Something that broke, how you diagnosed it, what you changed "Tell me about a failure" Design doc and ADRs Writing down alternatives, defending a choice, accepting feedback "Tell me about a time you changed your mind" Labs (for example Hands-on 9) Adding resilience to a dependency "How do you deal with unreliable dependencies?"

items.title: Ten common questions
items.text:
# Question What is being assessed Outline of a good answer 1 Tell me about a technical decision you made. Judgment, trade-offs Options considered, criteria (numbers, requirements), the choice, its cost, the result 2 Tell me about something that failed. Ownership, learning What broke, your part in it, how you found out, what you fixed, what changed afterwards 3 Tell me about a performance problem you solved. Method, evidence Symptom, measurement, hypothesis, experiment, before/after numbers 4 Tell me about a disagreement with a teammate. Collaboration Both positions fairly, how you decided (data, a spike, a timebox), relationship afterwards 5 Tell me about a time you changed your mind. Openness to evidence The original belief, the evidence, the new decision, what it taught you 6 What's the most complex system you've built? Depth, communication Explain it at two levels: one sentence, then the architecture and the hardest part 7 Tell me about a time you had to learn something fast. Learning ability What, why, how (docs, small experiments, asking), how quickly it became useful 8 Tell me about a deadline you almost missed. Prioritization What you cut and why, how you communicated, the outcome 9 How do you make sure your code works in production? Operability mindset Tests, observability, gradual rollout, alerts — with an example from the course 10 What would you do differently in your project? Reflection One concrete thing with its reason, not "nothing" and not "everything"

A worked answer: question 3, from a BoxOffice project

Situation. "In our System Architecture course, my team of three built a ticketing platform with a catalog, an inventory service for seat holds and an order service, on Kubernetes."

Task. "Our target was to serve 2,000 requests per second on the event page with a p99 under 300 ms. In the first k6 load test, p99 was 1.4 seconds at only 600 requests per second, and I was responsible for the catalog service."

Action. "I didn't want to guess, so I looked at the traces first: 85% of the time was in the database, the same query for the event details, about 40 times per second for the same event. I considered read replicas and a cache. Replicas would add capacity but keep the 20 ms query on every request; a cache-aside Redis would remove most queries, at the cost of stale data. Since event details change rarely, I chose the cache with a 60-second TTL and deleted the key on updates. I also added an index the EXPLAIN showed was missing."

Result. "In the next campaign, p99 was 180 ms at 2,000 requests per second, the hit ratio was 97%, and database CPU went from 90% to 15%."

Learning. "Measuring before choosing saved us from adding replicas we didn't need. Since then I start every performance problem with a trace and a hypothesis written down."

items.title: Pitfalls
items.text:
What makes a good story sound bad

  • "We" all the time. The interviewer is hiring you: say what you did.
  • No numbers. "It got much faster" is weak; "p99 from 1.4 s to 180 ms" is strong.
  • A story with no trade-off or no difficulty. If it was easy, it isn't a good story.
  • Blaming. Teammates, the professor, the cloud provider: describe the situation, own your part.
  • Too long. Two minutes. The interviewer will ask for more detail if they want it.
  • Invented stories. Follow-up questions expose them quickly. A small true story beats a big fake one.

items.title: Your story bank
items.text:
Fill one row per story; aim for six to eight stories that together cover the ten questions.

Story (title) Situation and task Action (and the alternatives) Result (numbers) Learning Answers questions Catalog cache Project; p99 1.4 s at 600 req/s Traces → cache-aside over replicas, plus an index p99 180 ms at 2,000 req/s Measure before choosing 1, 3, 5

Back to the interview page · practice the design side with the problems and mock interviews.

items.title: The interview framework
items.text:
A system-design interview is an open problem with a clock. Without a structure, it is easy to spend twenty minutes on the database schema and never reach the part the interviewer cared about. The framework below is a sequence of seven steps, each with a goal, a time box, phrases to say and a template you can sketch on the board. It is the same framework taught in Class 1 · Interview framework and followed by every case study; here it is written as a checklist you can rehearse.

Throughout the page, the running example is the question from the landing page: "Design a ticketing site for a stadium show. Tickets go on sale Saturday at 10:00." — BoxOffice's flash sale, with 2 million fans for 60,000 seats.

Copy the templates

Each step ends with a template in a text block. Copy it to your notes or to the board and fill it in: after a few practice problems the headings become a habit, and you stop forgetting a whole category (durability, cost, failure) under pressure.

flowchart LR
    A[1. Clarify<br/>~5 min] --> B[2. Estimate<br/>~5 min]
    B --> C[3. API & data model<br/>~5 min]
    C --> D[4. High-level design<br/>~10 min]
    D --> E[5. Deep dives<br/>~12 min]
    E --> F[6. Bottlenecks & trade-offs<br/>~5 min]
    F --> G[7. Wrap-up<br/>~3 min]
    E -.new requirement or concern.-> A

items.title: Timing
items.text:
Step 45-minute interview 60-minute interview Output on the board 1. Clarify the requirements 5 min 6–8 min Short list of functional and non-functional requirements; out of scope 2. Estimate 5 min 5–7 min Peak QPS, read/write ratio, storage, the deciding number 3. API and data model 5 min 6–8 min 3–6 endpoints or events; core entities with keys 4. High-level design 10 min 12–15 min One diagram, one read and one write walked through 5. Deep dives 12 min 15–18 min One or two components in depth 6. Bottlenecks and trade-offs 5 min 5–7 min What breaks first, single points of failure, what you traded 7. Wrap-up 3 min 3–5 min Four-sentence summary and next steps

The clock is yours to manage

Glance at the time at each transition. If you are at minute 20 and still in step 3, say so and compress: "I'll keep the data model short so we have time for the hard part." Interviewers rarely penalize a deliberate shortcut; they do penalize never reaching the deep dive. Five minutes before the end, wrap up even if the interviewer is still asking questions.

items.title: 1. Clarify the requirements
items.text:
Goal. Turn a one-line prompt into a problem with boundaries: who uses it, for what, at what scale, and what must never go wrong. Everything after this step is justified by something written here.

What to say.

  • "Before I draw anything, I'd like to pin down the scope. Can I ask a few questions?"
  • "I'll focus on these three features; I'll leave X and Y out unless you want them."
  • "So the hardest requirement is… — does that match what you had in mind?"

Questions to ask.

  • Users and features: who are the users? What are the 3–5 core actions? What is explicitly out of scope?
  • Scale: how many users (daily active, peak concurrent)? How much data? Growth over the next years?
  • Read/write shape: is it read-heavy or write-heavy? Are there spikes (a sale, a match, a launch)?
  • Consistency: what must never be wrong (money, inventory, permissions)? What can be a few seconds stale?
  • Latency and availability: how fast must the main action be (p99)? What availability is expected?
  • Constraints: regions, regulation (personal data), budget, existing systems, team size.
REQUIREMENTS
Functional (in scope):
  1. ...
  2. ...
  3. ...
Out of scope: ...
Non-functional:
  Scale:        DAU = ..., peak concurrent = ..., data = ...
  Latency:      p99 of <main action> < ... ms
  Availability: ... % (which paths?)
  Consistency:  strong for ..., eventual for ...
  Durability:   never lose ...
  Other:        security / privacy / cost / regions
The hard part (one sentence): ...

Common mistakes

  • Drawing in the first minute, then discovering the system is write-heavy.
  • Asking twenty questions and never committing: after 5 minutes, state assumptions and move on.
  • Forgetting the non-functional requirements — they are what make the design interesting.
  • Not writing the requirements down: you will need them in step 6 to justify the trade-offs.

BoxOffice flash sale — step 1

  • Functional: view the event page and seat map; hold one or more seats for a few minutes; pay; receive the ticket by email and in the app.
  • Out of scope: resale, venue management, recommendations.
  • Non-functional: 2 M fans arrive around 10:00 for 60 k seats; the site must stay up and fair (first come, first served, bots blocked); a seat is never sold twice; holding a seat should feel instant (p99 under ~500 ms after admission); the event page can be a few seconds stale.
  • The hard part: a huge spike of contention on a small, strongly consistent inventory — not the volume of data.

items.title: 2. Estimate
items.text:
Goal. Put orders of magnitude on the requirements so that each later choice has a number behind it. You are not computing a budget; you are finding the one or two numbers that decide the design.

What to say.

  • "Let me do a quick back-of-the-envelope estimate; I'll round aggressively."
  • "One day is about 10⁵ seconds, so 10 million requests a day is about 100 per second on average."
  • "The number that matters here is… because it means we need…"

Questions to ask yourself.

  • Average and peak requests per second (peak factor 2–10× for normal traffic; far more for a flash sale).
  • Read/write ratio; how much each write weighs (bytes).
  • Storage per day/year (and with replication ×3); bandwidth in and out.
  • Concurrency with Little's Law: in-flight requests = rate × time.
  • Which component's limit is closest to these numbers? (See the numbers cheat sheet.)
ESTIMATION (round to powers of 10)
Users:      DAU = ...            peak concurrent = ...
Requests:   per user per day = ...
            avg QPS = DAU x req/user / 1e5 = ...
            peak QPS = avg x peak factor (...) = ...
Read:write  = ... : ...          write QPS = ...
Storage:    item size = ... B    items/day = ...
            per year = ... (x3 replicas = ...)
Bandwidth:  peak QPS x response size = ... MB/s
Concurrency (Little): peak QPS x latency = ... in flight
Deciding number(s): ...  =>  implication: ...

Common mistakes

  • Spending ten minutes on precise arithmetic. One significant digit is enough.
  • Estimating the average and designing for it: always size for the peak.
  • Numbers that never influence a decision. If an estimate doesn't change the design, skip it.
  • Forgetting to say the assumptions out loud, so the interviewer can't correct them.

BoxOffice flash sale — step 2

  • Fans per seat: 2,000,000 ÷ 60,000 ≈ 33. Most fans will not get a ticket: fairness and a clear "sold out" matter.
  • Read peak (≈ illustrative): 2 M fans refreshing every ~10–20 s in the first minutes ⇒ on the order of 10⁵ requests per second, almost all for the same event page and seat map.
  • Write peak (≈ illustrative): 60 k seats held over a few minutes ⇒ on the order of 10³ holds per second — small, but every one of them competes for the same rows.
  • Storage: 60 k orders × ~1 KB ≈ 60 MB per show — irrelevant.
  • Deciding numbers: a 100,000 req/s read spike (⇒ CDN and cache) and ~1,000 contended writes/s on one event (⇒ a waiting room and atomic seat holds).

items.title: 3. API and data model
items.text:
Goal. Make the design concrete: the main operations the clients call (or the events services exchange) and the entities with their keys and access patterns. The access patterns choose the database; the operations that touch money or inventory get idempotency keys.

What to say.

  • "These are the four calls the client needs; the one that matters is…"
  • "This call changes inventory, so it takes an idempotency key — a retry must not hold a second seat."
  • "The main access pattern is 'all seats of an event by section', so I'll key the table by event."

Questions to ask yourself.

  • Which calls are reads and which are writes? Which must be synchronous?
  • What are the keys and the main query of each entity? Which needs transactions?
  • Pagination (cursor-based), versioning, authentication on each call.
API (REST; auth = bearer token)
GET  /events/{id}                       -> event page (cacheable)
GET  /events/{id}/seats?section=...     -> seat map (short TTL cache)
POST /holds         {eventId, seatIds}  Idempotency-Key: ...  -> holdId, expiresAt
POST /orders        {holdId, payment}   Idempotency-Key: ...  -> orderId, status
GET  /orders/{id}                       -> status (PENDING/CONFIRMED/FAILED)
Webhook: POST /payments/webhook (signed by the provider)

DATA MODEL
Entity      Key                 Main access pattern          Store / consistency
event       event_id            read by id                   SQL + cache, eventual OK
seat        (event_id, seat_id) by event + section; hold     SQL, strong (transactions)
order       order_id            by id; by user_id            SQL, strong
...

Common mistakes

  • Designing twenty endpoints. Show the 3–6 that carry the core flows.
  • Choosing the database before writing the access patterns.
  • Forgetting idempotency on writes that may be retried (holds, orders, payments).
  • Offset pagination on large, changing lists (use cursors).

BoxOffice flash sale — step 3

The four calls above are the whole purchase flow. seat rows live in PostgreSQL with a primary key (event_id, seat_id), a status (free, held, sold), hold_until and order_id. POST /holds takes an idempotency key so a double click or a client retry returns the same hold. order stores the payment idempotency key sent to the provider. Event and venue data are read-mostly and will be cached.

items.title: 4. High-level design
items.text:
Goal. One diagram that satisfies every functional requirement end to end, with the data flow labeled. Keep it simple; you will improve it in the deep dives. Walk one read and one write through it out loud.

What to say.

  • "Let me start simple and then evolve it: clients, edge, services, storage, async work."
  • "Here is the path of a hold request…" (trace it through the boxes).
  • "This box is a single point of failure for now; I'll come back to it in step 6."

Questions to ask yourself.

  • Which requests stop at the edge (CDN, cache) and which reach the services?
  • What is synchronous (user waits) and what goes behind a queue?
  • Where is the source of truth of each entity?
HIGH-LEVEL CHECKLIST
[ ] Clients -> DNS -> CDN (static, cacheable pages)
[ ] Edge: WAF / API gateway (auth, rate limit) -> load balancer
[ ] Stateless services (which ones? what does each own?)
[ ] Source of truth per entity (SQL / NoSQL / object store)
[ ] Caches (what, where, TTL)
[ ] Async: queue / event stream, consumers, what is eventual
[ ] External dependencies (payment, email, 3rd party)
[ ] One read and one write traced through the diagram

Common mistakes

  • Twenty boxes with unlabeled arrows. Every arrow says what flows on it.
  • Naming products instead of roles ("Kafka" before you said why you need an event log).
  • Hiding state in "stateless" app servers (sessions in memory).
  • Polishing one box before the whole flow works.

BoxOffice flash sale — step 4

Fans → DNS → CDN for the event page and assets → WAF (bots) → API gateway (JWT auth, per-user rate limit) → load balancer → stateless services: catalog (events, behind a cache), inventory (seats, in PostgreSQL), order, payment (adapter to the external provider), notification (email, behind a queue). The order service publishes OrderConfirmed to Kafka through an outbox; notification, search and analytics consume it. Read path: the seat map comes from a cache refreshed every second. Write path: POST /holds goes to inventory, which updates the seat rows atomically.

items.title: 5. Deep dives
items.text:
Goal. Show depth where the problem is hard. Pick one or two components (or let the interviewer pick), and go into algorithms, data layout, consistency, failure handling and numbers. This is where most of the evaluation happens.

What to say.

  • "The hard part of this problem is…, so I'd like to go deep there. Does that sound good?"
  • "There are three ways to do this: … I'd pick the second because…"
  • "Let me check that with numbers: …"

Questions to ask yourself.

  • Where is the contention, the fan-out, the hot key or the consistency boundary?
  • What happens under the peak load, with a slow dependency, with a retry, with a crash mid-operation?
  • How would you know it works (metrics, a load test)?
DEEP-DIVE CHECKLIST (for the chosen component)
[ ] Why this is the hard part (number from step 2)
[ ] 2-3 options, with the trade-off of each
[ ] Chosen option: algorithm / data layout / keys
[ ] Consistency: what is atomic, what is eventual, how conflicts are prevented
[ ] Capacity: load vs capacity, utilization below the knee
[ ] Failure: slow dependency, crash midway, duplicate request, hot key
[ ] Observability: the metric / trace that proves it works

Common mistakes

  • Going deep on the easy part (the frontend, the login page).
  • Listing options without choosing one.
  • A deep dive with no failure analysis: "what if this node dies?" is always coming.
  • Ignoring the interviewer's hint toward a specific component.

BoxOffice flash sale — step 5

Deep dive 1 — never sell a seat twice. Options: (a) read the status in the app, then write — a race; (b) SELECT … FOR UPDATE in a transaction — correct, but holds row locks while the transaction is open; (c) one atomic conditional update: UPDATE seat SET status='held', hold_until=now()+interval '10 min', order_id=? WHERE event_id=? AND seat_id=? AND status='free' — 1 row updated means the fan got it, 0 means someone else did. Choose (c): short, lock held only for the statement, and the database enforces the invariant. An expiry job releases holds whose hold_until passed. Never keep a transaction open while calling the payment provider.

Deep dive 2 — survive 10:00. A virtual waiting room: fans who arrive get a position (random among those present at 10:00, then arrival order), and the gateway admits them at the rate inventory sustains — say 2,000 per minute — issuing a signed, short-lived admission token required by POST /holds. Little's Law sizes it: 2,000 admitted/min with ~5 min in the purchase flow ⇒ ~10,000 fans inside at once. The queue turns a spike of 10⁵ req/s into a steady flow the database can handle; the cost is waiting time, shown honestly with the position in line.

items.title: 6. Bottlenecks and trade-offs
items.text:
Goal. Step back and stress the design: what breaks first at 10× the load, where the single points of failure are, what you traded and how you would observe and test it. This is where you show judgment.

What to say.

  • "At ten times the load, the first thing to break is…, because…"
  • "I chose X over Y because…; the cost is…; I'd revisit if…"
  • "To be confident, I'd load-test with a spike profile and watch…"

Questions to ask yourself.

  • Which component is closest to its limit (utilization near the knee)? Which is a single point of failure?
  • What happens when each external dependency is slow or down?
  • Which consistency did you relax, and what does the user see because of it?
  • How much does it cost, roughly? What would you monitor (SLIs) and alert on?
TRADE-OFF STATEMENT
We chose <X> over <Y>
because <requirement / number from steps 1-2>.
The cost is <latency / consistency / money / complexity>,
which is acceptable because <...>.
We would revisit it if <condition>.

BOTTLENECK SWEEP
First to break at 10x: ...      fix: ...
Single points of failure: ...   fix: ...
Slow/down dependency: ...       containment: timeout / breaker / queue / fallback
Observability: SLIs = ...       alert on: burn rate of ...
How we'd test it: load profile ... / chaos experiment ...

Common mistakes

  • "It scales" without saying what, to how much, and at what cost.
  • Presenting a design with no weaknesses — every design has some; naming them is the signal.
  • Forgetting operations: deploys, monitoring, on-call, cost.
  • Getting defensive when the interviewer finds a flaw. Say "good point" and adapt.

BoxOffice flash sale — step 6

  • First to break: the payment provider at 10:00 (external quota, latency spikes) → timeout, circuit breaker, a PENDING order state with the seat hold extended; the waiting room admits fewer fans if the provider slows.
  • Single points of failure: the PostgreSQL primary → synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover; Redis → replicated, and the seat map can fall back to a slightly older copy.
  • Trade-offs: strong consistency only for seats and orders, eventual for everything else; the waiting room trades user patience for a system that stays up; the seat map may show a seat as free that is already held (the hold call is the authority).
  • Proof: a k6 spike test to the expected peak and a game day where the payment provider slows down; SLIs: hold success rate and p99, checkout availability; burn-rate alerts on checkout.

items.title: 7. Wrap-up
items.text:
Goal. Leave a clear picture: a short summary, the key trade-offs, and what you would do with more time. End on time.

What to say.

  • "To summarize: …"
  • "The two decisions I'd defend most are… and the main risk is…"
  • "With more time I'd look at…"
WRAP-UP (4 sentences + next steps)
1. The problem in one line and the hard part: ...
2. The design in one line (edge -> services -> storage -> async): ...
3. The key decisions and their trade-offs: ...
4. The main risk and how we contain it: ...
Next with more time: multi-region / cost / abuse & security / analytics / evolution

Common mistakes

  • Running out of time with no summary.
  • Introducing new components in the last two minutes.
  • Repeating the whole walkthrough instead of the decisions.

BoxOffice flash sale — step 7

"We built a ticketing flow for a stadium show where 2 million fans compete for 60,000 seats at 10:00. The CDN and caches absorb the read spike, a waiting room turns the crowd into a steady flow, and seat holds are atomic conditional updates in PostgreSQL, so a seat is never sold twice. Payment goes through an idempotent adapter with timeouts and a circuit breaker, and confirmation flows asynchronously through an outbox and Kafka to email and analytics. The main risk is the payment provider at peak; with more time I'd add a second provider, a second region for the read path and a bot-scoring model in the WAF."

items.text:
flowchart LR

    WAF --> GW[API Gateway: JWT, rate limit, waiting room admission]
