items.title: System Design Playground
items.text:
Draw a system with the components of the course, put it under load, and watch it behave: utilization, queues, latency percentiles, errors, cost — and what happens when things go wrong. Every number on the screen comes from the formulas of the course (utilization, Little's Law, queueing, percentiles, availability), so you can predict it before you press ▶ and explain it afterwards.

Pick a scenario in the toolbar (or Blank canvas), press ▶ and read the panels below the canvas. The scenario guide explains what each scenario teaches. Your design is saved in this browser for each scenario; Reset scenario brings the original back.

What the playground is (and is not)

It is a teaching model: a few dozen lines of math per component, tuned so that the behaviour is realistic and explainable — the knee of the latency curve, a thread pool that runs out, a backlog that drains, a cache stampede. It is not a benchmark: the capacities and prices of the catalog are illustrative, chosen to make the arithmetic easy. Use it to reason about shapes and orders of magnitude, then measure the real system (hands-on labs).

items.title: Quick start
items.text:
1. Choose Scenario → Monolith (already loaded above) and press ▶. The breakpoint profile ramps the load until the system breaks.
  2. When the run ends the Report opens: breaking point, percentiles, the bottleneck with an explanation, and the goals (✓/✗).
  3. Add a Load Balancer from the palette (click + or drag it to the canvas), connect users → Load Balancer → app (drag from the small handle on the right of a node to another node), delete the old edge, and raise the replicas of the app in the inspector.
  4. Press ⟲ (restart the run) and ▶ again. Compare.
  5. Stuck? Open Hints in the right panel, or Show a possible solution.

items.title: Building a design
items.text:
Action How Add a component Click + in the palette (or double-click the item), or drag it onto the canvas. The palette has 49 components in 10 categories: Client, Traffic & edge, Compute, Containers, Storage, Messaging, Observability, Network, AI & agents and External Name it A new component has no label: its block shows only its type. Type a label in the inspector (the type is the placeholder) and the block shows the name and, below it, the type; clearing the label, or typing the type itself, goes back to the type alone Connect A → B (A calls B) Drag from the round handle on the right edge of A and drop on B; or select A, press C, click B Select Click a node, an edge or a frame; click the background to see the scenario brief and goals Edit The inspector (right) shows the description, key numbers, a Learn more link to the component catalog, live values and the parameters (slider + number) Move / pan / zoom Drag a node; drag the background to pan; Ctrl/⌘ + wheel (or pinch) and the ± buttons to zoom; F fits the design to the screen Delete, duplicate, undo Del/⌫, D, Ctrl/⌘+Z and Shift+Ctrl/⌘+Z (also in the toolbar) Frames Add a VPC (region), Subnet (availability zone) or Kubernetes Cluster frame and place nodes inside (a node belongs to a frame when its centre is inside it); drag the frame by its title bar, resize it by the corner. A Kubernetes Cluster runs the services inside it as pods (see below) Side connections Metrics, Logs, Tracing, Alerting, Health Check, Service Registry and Service Mesh are not in the request path: connect them to the services they watch (either direction)

Edges flow one way: a connection that would create a cycle is refused. An edge into a broker (Message Queue, Pub/Sub, Event Stream, Kafka) is asynchronous: the caller only waits for the broker's acknowledgement. Exports (Mermaid, report, events) name a component without a label by its type.

items.title: How the model works
items.text: Time advances in ticks of 0.1 s of simulated time; the speed selector runs 1, 5, 20 or 100 ticks' worth per real tenth of a second. Each tick has two parts: a fluid model that moves rates (requests per second) through the graph, and a sample of synthetic requests (traces) that walk the graph to measure latency percentiles.

items.title: Arrivals and requests
items.text: Each client generates arrivals from the load profile × random noise × traffic events. The number of arrivals in a tick is a Poisson draw with mean \(\lambda \cdot \Delta t\), so even a constant target shows realistic jitter. A request is a read (share set by Read % in the toolbar, or per client) or a write; writes usually cost more downstream (a write on SQL uses 3 reads' worth of capacity). Bots (client parameter bot traffic) are extra load that a WAF or a rate limiter can stop; goals only count real users.

items.title: How a node routes requests
items.text:
Role Components What happens to a request split DNS, Load Balancer, Ingress (API Gateway for 2+ targets of the same type, except Microservice and Container) goes to one healthy target, in proportion to capacity × edge weight; DNS can be failover call App Server, Microservice, Container, Worker, Auth, Search, Serverless, SQL Database, DB Cluster, Orchestrator, … calls every outgoing edge (subject to the edge ratio and read/write filter), one after the other (latencies add) or in parallel (the slowest wins) cache Cache, CDN a read hits with the current hit ratio and returns; misses and writes go to the targets broker Message Queue (competing consumers), Pub/Sub, Event Stream, Kafka (a copy per consumer) the producer gets an ack; messages wait in a backlog that consumers drain at their capacity side Metrics, Logs, Tracing, Alerting, Health Check, Service Registry, Service Mesh not in the path; they change what you can see and how fast failures are detected and repaired source Client, Mobile, Scheduler generate the load (the scheduler: N jobs every T seconds) frame VPC, Subnet, Kubernetes Cluster never receives requests; places the nodes inside it in a region, a zone or a cluster

An API Gateway groups its targets by type: 2+ targets of the same type (say, three App Servers) are load-balanced, as by a split node, and different types are all called (say, Auth and then the service). Microservices and Containers are the exception: each one is a different service, so the gateway treats each as its own route and does not load-balance between them. Choose which requests take which route with the edge ratio and read/write filter (reads → catalog, writes → order). To scale one service, raise its replicas; do not draw copies of it.

items.title: Capacity, utilization and queues
items.text:
For each node, per tick: the offered rate \(\lambda\) is the sum of what its callers send (including retries). Its capacity is \(\mu = \text{healthy replicas} \times \text{capacity per replica}\) (SQL: reads spread over the primary and its read replicas, writes only on the primary; partitioned stores: limited by the busiest partition; DB Cluster: limited by the busiest shard, see below; Container: scaled by the CPU limit, see below). The utilization is

\[\rho = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}\]

When \(\rho < 1\) the mean waiting time in the queue follows Sakasegawa's approximation of the M/M/c queue, where \(S\) is the mean service time and \(c = \mu \cdot S\) the number of requests the node serves in parallel:

\[W_q \approx S \cdot \frac{\rho^{\sqrt{2(c+1)}-1}}{c\,(1-\rho)}\]

(When the thread pool is the limit, \(S\) is the time a request holds a thread and \(c\) the number of threads; \(\rho\) is averaged over 1 s and capped at 0.98 in the formula.) It is small at \(\rho = 0.5\), noticeable at \(0.8\) and explodes near \(1\) — the knee of the latency curve. When \(\lambda > \mu\) the excess accumulates in a bounded queue (queue limit per replica); its wait is \(q / \mu\) and whatever does not fit is rejected (503). The utilization bar of each node is green below 0.7, amber below 0.9 and red above.

items.title: Threads and Little's Law
items.text:
A synchronous service holds a thread (or a DB connection) for the whole time a request spends in it — its own work and the time it waits for its dependencies. By Little's Law the number of threads busy is

\[L = \lambda \cdot W\]

so a node can complete at most \(\text{threads} \times \text{replicas} / W\) requests per second. If a dependency becomes slow, \(W\) grows, the threads run out and the node fails even with its CPU idle — a cascading failure. The inspector shows \(L\) and the Report names the cause (threads exhausted while CPU at 20%). A timeout on the edge caps how long a thread waits.

items.title: Latency and percentiles
items.text: The own work of a node is random: lognormal with the median service time and a spread per type (a cache ≈ 0.5 ms, a database ≈ 4 ms, an app ≈ 10 ms, an LLM ≈ 1.2 s, a third-party API ≈ 150 ms with a long tail), plus rare GC pauses on app servers. Every tick about 40 synthetic requests walk the graph with the current queue waits, cache hits and misses, failures, timeouts and retries. Their latencies fill log-scale histograms: the tiles show p50/p99 over the last 5 s and the Report shows p50, p95, p99 and p99.9 over the steady window. As in k6 thresholds on expected_response:true, latency percentiles count successful requests; failures are counted in the error rate.

items.title: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, fallbacks, bulkheads
items.text:
Edge parameters model the resilience patterns of the course. With a probability \(p\) that one attempt fails (an error or a timeout) and \(r\) retries:

\[\text{load on the target} = \lambda \cdot (1 + p + p^2 + \dots + p^r) \qquad P(\text{call fails}) = p^{\,r+1}\]

When \(p\) is close to 1 the target receives up to \((r+1)\times\) the load — a retry storm. Backoff waits \(100\,\text{ms} \times 2^n\) between attempts (exp+jitter spreads them randomly), which adds latency and smooths the waves but does not reduce the total in a long outage. A circuit breaker opens when more than 50% of the calls fail over 5 s: calls fail at once for 10 s, then a few probe calls (half-open) decide whether to close it. A fallback turns a failed call into a degraded answer (counted as success). A bulkhead limits the share of the caller's threads one call may hold. An idempotency key makes retries to a payment provider safe: without it, a retry after a timeout counts as a possible duplicate charge.

items.title: Caches, CDNs and hot keys
items.text: A cache with hit ratio \(h\) sends only the misses on: database reads \(= \text{reads} \times (1-h)\). With cache-aside frequent writes invalidate entries and lower \(h\); write-through keeps it but makes writes slower. After a flush the hit ratio starts at 0 and climbs back during the warm-up; meanwhile every read misses at once — a stampede. Request coalescing lets concurrent misses for the same key share one query. Key popularity follows a Zipf law: with \(P\) partitions, the busiest one receives \(p_1 + (1-p_1)/P\) of the load, where \(p_1\) is the share of the hottest key — so a hot key saturates a partition no matter how many you add.

items.title: Messaging
items.text: A broker accepts messages up to its capacity and keeps them in a backlog. Consumers pull at their own capacity; with Event Stream and Kafka at most \(\min(\text{partitions}, \text{consumer replicas})\) consumers work in parallel. A message whose processing fails goes back to the backlog (at-least-once). Consumer lag = backlog ÷ successful drain rate. Beyond max backlog (retention) messages are dropped, and those publishes count as errors.

items.title: Autoscaling and serverless
items.text: With autoscaling on, every 15 s a node compares its average CPU utilization with the target and sets \(\lceil \text{replicas} \times \rho / \text{target} \rceil\) replicas (between min and max); new replicas take traffic after the warm-up. The first decision comes at t = 15 s, and a scale-in removes at most half of the replicas at a time. Like a Kubernetes HPA, it watches CPU — a node starved of threads does not scale. A serverless function runs one instance per concurrent request: instances \(= \lambda \cdot W\). Requests beyond the warm instances land on new ones and pay the cold start; beyond the concurrency limit they are throttled (429). Provisioned instances are always warm (and always billed).

items.title: Containers
items.text:
A Container is a compute node with two extra parameters. Its CPU limit \(\ell\) is a multiple of the CPU request its capacity is quoted for: it scales the capacity and, below 1, throttles the container (CFS quota), so its own work takes longer:

\[\mu_{\text{replica}} = \text{capacity} \times \ell \qquad \text{median service time} = \frac{\text{service time p50}}{\min(1, \ell)}\]

A limit of 0.5 halves the req/s and doubles the service time; a limit above 1 adds req/s but does not make a request faster. Its start-up time (default 20 s: image pull + process start + warm-up) replaces the warm-up: it is how long a new replica takes before it gets traffic, whether the autoscaler added it or Kubernetes rescheduled it. A Microservice is a compute node with the defaults of a 2-vCPU pod (400 req/s per replica at 8 ms, 2 replicas, 20 s warm-up); what sets it apart is how an API Gateway routes to it (above) and how a cluster schedules it (below).

items.title: Kubernetes clusters
items.text:
A Kubernetes Cluster frame runs, as pods, the services whose centre is inside it (a node belongs to the first cluster that contains it). Managed services and external providers never run as pods, even when drawn inside: DNS, CDN, Load Balancer, WAF, Serverless, Object Store, Data Warehouse, DB Cluster, Message Queue, Pub/Sub, Event Stream, NAT, VPN, LLM Gateway and the External components. Every replica of a member is a pod, and the cluster has room for

\[C = \text{ready worker nodes} \times \text{pods per node}\]

pods. A pod is ready (serving), starting or Pending (no room). Every tick:

  • Pods beyond \(C\) are Pending: they do not serve. The block of the service shows N pending, the inspector shows them next to the ready and starting replicas, and the frame's title bar shows the live nodes, pods and Pending pods. When the cluster shrinks, the newest pods (starting ones first) are evicted back to Pending.
  • Pending pods take the free slots, one service at a time (round robin). A pod that gets a slot starts and takes traffic after its warm-up (the start-up time of a Container) + 10 s for its endpoints to propagate — 0 s when the service is registered in a Service Registry.
  • The HPA (Autoscaling of a member) works as described above, but counts the pods it asked for, scheduled or not, and the pods it adds first wait for a free slot. The HPA adds pods, never nodes: when the pods do not fit, they stay Pending and the service stays saturated. A scale-in drops Pending pods first.

With the cluster autoscaler on, when the Pending pods are more than the nodes already starting will hold, it starts

\[\text{new nodes} = \left\lceil \frac{\text{Pending} - \text{starting nodes} \times \text{pods per node}}{\text{pods per node}} \right\rceil\]

(up to max nodes), each ready after the node start-up. It removes one node after 120 s during which no node is starting and all the pods asked for (Pending included) fit on one node fewer — demand \(\le (\text{ready} - 1) \times \text{pods per node}\) — and never goes below Worker nodes. The cluster costs \((\text{ready} + \text{starting nodes}) \times \text{node price}\); the pods' own price is not counted (per-request charges still are). Defaults: 3 nodes × 10 pods per node, cluster autoscaler off (max 10 nodes), node start-up 90 s, 140 USD/month per node.

A node failure (an event) kills one ready node. It held \(\min\left(\text{pods per node}, \lceil \text{pods} \div \text{nodes} \rceil\right)\) pods, spread over the services in proportion to their pods (largest remainder). They stop serving at once, but callers keep sending them requests — which hang, as on any dead replica, for 10 s or until the edge timeout — until they notice, after \(\min(\text{detection}, 40\,\text{s})\): 30 s behind a load balancer, 3 s with a Health Check or a Service Registry, 40 s (the node's NotReady timeout) on a direct call. After 40 s Kubernetes recreates the lost pods: they become Pending and start only where there is room. The node comes back when the event ends. A service with no pod at all (and no stale endpoint) answers at once with 503 (no endpoints).

items.title: Service discovery
items.text:
A Service Registry (side node) registers the services connected to it, in either direction. For a registered service:

  • Dead replicas are dropped in 3 s by every caller — a load balancer, an API gateway or another service calling it directly. Without a registry a direct service-to-service call has no one to detect a crash: a crashed replica keeps receiving its share of the calls (which hang) until it is repaired, and pods lost with a Kubernetes node until the 40 s NotReady timeout.
  • New pods take traffic as soon as they are ready: no 10 s wait for the endpoints to propagate.

It costs 30 USD/month + 5 per attached service.

items.title: Replicated databases (DB Cluster)
items.text:
A DB Cluster has \(S\) shards, each with a primary that takes its writes and \(R\) followers per shard that copy them. Defaults: 1 shard, 2 followers, replication async, reads from followers, failover 30 s, replication round trip 2 ms, and per node 3 000 req/s, 4 ms, 200 connections, write cost 3 and 450 USD/month. Its capacity is

\[\mu_{\text{writes}} = \frac{S \times \text{capacity}}{\text{write cost}} \qquad \mu_{\text{reads}} = S \times (1 + R) \times \text{capacity}\]

when reads go to the followers (\(S \times \text{capacity}\) when they go to the primary). Keys follow the Zipf law of the hot key: the hottest shard receives \(h_1 = p_1 + (1-p_1)/S\) of the requests and each of the others \((1-h_1)/(S-1)\). The busiest shard sets the capacity, so a hot key saturates one shard however many you add; the inspector shows the utilization of the hot shard and of the others.

A write is acknowledged after its replication:

Replication Extra latency of a write Followers behind (lagging) Lost on a failover async none all \(R\) the writes inside the lag sync the round trip to the synchronous follower \(R - 1\) none quorum the round trip of the \(\lfloor (R+1)/2 \rfloor\)-th fastest follower \(R - \lfloor (R+1)/2 \rfloor\) none

Each round trip is sampled from a lognormal around the replication round trip. A latency degradation on a DB Cluster slows one follower — the synchronous one: sync waits for it on every write, quorum (with \(R \ge 2\)) answers with the faster ones. The followers behind lag

\[\text{lag} \approx 0.02 + \frac{0.5\,\rho_w^3}{1 - \rho_w}\ \text{s}\]

where \(\rho_w\) is the write utilization of the busiest primary (the lag grows without limit while \(\rho_w \ge 1\)). When reads go to the followers, a share of them is stale (reads a key written within the lag):

\[\text{stale reads} \approx \frac{\text{followers behind}}{1 + R} \times \text{write share} \times \min\left(1, \frac{\text{lag}}{1\,\text{s}}\right)\]

A primary failure (event) hits one shard. Its writes fail for the failover time (the RTO) — its reads too if they go to the primary — then a follower is promoted and the shard runs with one node fewer for 120 s. With async replication the writes not yet replicated are lost: \(\text{lost writes} \approx \text{shard write rate} \times \text{lag}\) (the RPO); sync and quorum lose nothing. With \(R = 0\) there is no failover: the shard is down for 120 s. An AZ outage causes a primary failure on one shard (the cluster spans the zones). The DB Cluster costs \(S \times (1 + R) \times \text{price}\); its theoretical availability is \(1 - (1-a)^{1+R}\) per shard, with the shards in series:

\[A = \left[1 - (1-a)^{1+R}\right]^{S}\]

items.title: External services and AI
items.text: External APIs (3rd Party, Payment, Email) have a quota enforced as a token bucket (2 s of burst): above it they answer 429; they are slower, have a long latency tail and fail more often than your own services. The LLM Gateway includes the model call (≈ 1.2 s), a provider quota, a semantic cache (similar prompts answered in ≈ 20 ms, no tokens) and an optional fallback model. The Orchestrator runs the agent loop: each request makes steps sequential calls to its LLM and tool edges, so latency and cost grow linearly with the steps. A request path that does not go through a Safety Mesh lets prompt-injection attempts (2% of the requests, illustrative) reach the model: the unsafe answers metric.

items.title: Cost and availability
items.text:
The cost tile is USD per month, illustrative, extrapolated from the current rates: replicas × price + per-request and per-GB charges (CDN egress, NAT, LLM tokens, function invocations) + observability. Inside a Kubernetes Cluster you pay for the worker nodes, not the pods; a DB Cluster bills every node of every shard; a Service Registry costs 30 + 5 per attached service. The Report also shows the theoretical availability of the design from per-replica availabilities, with the series/parallel rules of the course:

\[A_{\text{series}} = \prod_i A_i \qquad A_{\text{parallel}} = 1 - \prod_i (1 - A_i)\]

Measured availability is the share of successful requests over the whole run.

items.title: Load profiles
items.text:
The profiles use the vocabulary of k6 and of the performance class. Target RPS (log slider, 1 to 2 000 000) sets the level.

Profile Shape Duration Use it to smoke a few req/s 30 s check that the design works at all load ramp 20 s, hold the target, ramp down 180 s check the goals at the expected load stress +20% of the target every 20 s, up to 3× 300 s see how it degrades beyond the target spike the target, then × N for 30 s (at t = 60 s) 180 s test bursts: queues, autoscaling, cold starts soak the target for 15 minutes 900 s find slow problems (try memory leak on an app) breakpoint linear ramp up to 4× the target, stops when errors > 5% or p99 > 10 × SLO ≤ 300 s find the breaking point and the knee chaos ramp 20 s, then the target, with random failures (chaos ≥ medium) 300 s game day

Goals are evaluated over the steady window of the profile (shaded in the charts), so the ramp-up does not count; availability uses the whole run.

items.title: Randomness: seeds, chaos and events
items.text:
All randomness — arrivals, service times, cache hits, which failures happen and when — comes from one seeded generator, split into independent streams per purpose. Same seed + same design + same profile ⇒ the same run, so you can change one thing and attribute the difference to it. Changing the chaos level does not reshuffle the arrivals. 🎲 draws a new seed; a robust design passes with any seed.

Chaos (off, low, medium, high = ×0, ×1, ×3, ×8) sets the rate of random events. You can also inject any event yourself with the ⚡ button, and scenarios have scripted events at fixed times (e.g. the sale opens). Events appear in the Events tab and as dashed markers on the charts.

Event Effect Replica crash one replica dies; callers keep sending it requests until a load balancer detects it (30 s, or 3 s with a Health Check or when the service is registered in a Service Registry); a direct call detects it only through a Service Registry (3 s) — without one, the dead replica keeps its share of the calls until it is repaired; it comes back after the repair time (halved with Alerting) Latency degradation a node or external dependency becomes 5–20× slower for 20–120 s (on a DB Cluster: one follower, the synchronous one, becomes slower) Viral traffic spike the traffic of the clients × 3–10 for 30–90 s Hot key (celebrity) key popularity skews: one partition / cache shard / DB Cluster shard concentrates the load Cache flush the hit ratio drops to 0 and warms up again AZ outage nodes in that availability zone go down (a node spread over 3 AZs loses a third; a database with standby fails over in ~60 s; a DB Cluster loses the primary of one shard) Region outage every node in that region goes down Network partition one call drops all traffic: callers hang until their timeout 3rd-party outage / throttling an external service fails or its quota drops to 20% Bad deploy a service returns 30% errors until rolled back Noisy neighbour a node loses 30% of its capacity GC pause storm frequent long pauses on an app server Node failure (Kubernetes Cluster) one ready worker node dies with its pods (≈ ⌈pods ÷ nodes⌉, spread over the services); callers keep sending them requests until they notice (min(detection, 40 s)); the lost pods are recreated after 40 s, Pending if there is no room; the node comes back when the event ends (2–5 min) Primary failure (DB Cluster) the primary of one shard dies: its writes fail for the failover time (its reads too if they go to the primary), then a follower is promoted and the shard has one node fewer for 120 s; with async replication the writes inside the lag are lost; with no followers the shard is down for 120 s

Node failure and Primary failure only apply to a Kubernetes Cluster and a DB Cluster: designs without those components never draw them, and their sequence of random events does not change. A DB Cluster never has a Replica crash: its failures are primary failures.

items.title: Goals and the test report
items.text:
Each scenario has 2–4 goals, checked live in the right panel (grey = waiting for the steady window, green = passing, red = failing) and finally in the Report. Metrics you will meet: p99 (ms), error rate (%), availability (%), throughput (req/s), cost (USD/month), consumer lag (s), replication lag (s), breaking point (req/s), duplicate charges, unsafe answers (%), services measured (%), lost writes (writes lost in failovers of a DB Cluster), stale reads (% of the reads of a DB Cluster), p99 (writes) (ms, successful writes only).

The Report lists the profile, seed and duration; p50/p95/p99/p99.9; error rate and availability; mean throughput and the maximum throughput within the SLO; cost; theoretical availability; for breakpoint runs, the breaking point and the knee (where p99 doubles relative to the start); the bottleneck — the first node to pass 85% utilization (or run out of threads, connections or quota, or wait for Pending pods) — with an explanation in the terms of the course; the events of the run; and each goal with the hints when one fails. Copy report (Markdown) puts it, with a Mermaid diagram of your design, in the clipboard — ready for an exercise submission.

items.title: Observability inside the playground
items.text:
The observability components change what you can see, as in real life:

  • Metrics: a service not connected to Metrics shows its utilization as ? — you can't fix what you don't measure. The eye button (god mode) reveals everything; it is on by default except in the observability-stack scenario.
  • Logs: the Events tab shows what happened and where only when a Logs node is connected.
  • Tracing: enables the Trace tab, a waterfall of the slowest sampled request (queue wait hatched).
  • Health Check: failure detection by load balancers and DNS drops from 30 s to 3 s.
  • Alerting (connected to Metrics): halves the time to repair a crashed replica.
  • Service Registry: every caller of a registered service — load balancer or direct call — drops a dead replica in 3 s, and new pods take traffic without the 10 s endpoint delay.
  • Service Mesh: services connected to it get +1 ms per call and default timeouts, retries with backoff and circuit breakers; with Metrics connected to the mesh, every attached service is measured.

items.title: Keyboard shortcuts
items.text:
Shortcuts work when the playground has the focus (click it) and you are not typing in a field; on a focused button, Space and Enter press the button. ? shows them. In compact mode the shortcuts that change the structure (C, D, Del, undo) are off.

Key Action Space run / pause S advance 1 s C connect the selected node to the next node you click D duplicate the selection Del / ⌫ delete the selection Ctrl/⌘ + Z, Shift + Ctrl/⌘ + Z (or Ctrl/⌘ + Y) undo / redo F fit to screen + / - zoom Tab, Enter move to a component, select it Esc cancel / deselect

items.title: Export, import and share
items.text:
• Export (download button) downloads the design and settings as JSON; Import (upload button) loads one back. This is the format to submit in the exercises.
  • Share link (chain button) copies a URL with the design encoded after #sdp=; opening it restores the design in the playground of this page.
  • Mermaid (branch button) copies the design as a flowchart LR, ready to paste in a Markdown page or a design document.
  • Full screen gives the canvas the whole screen.

The JSON of a design is small and readable:

{
  "scenario": "monolith",
  "settings": { "profile": "load", "targetRps": 1500, "readRatio": 0.9, "seed": 7, "chaos": "off" },
  "design": {
    "version": 1,
    "nodes": [
      { "id": "client", "type": "client", "x": 80, "y": 200, "label": "users", "params": {} },
      { "id": "lb", "type": "lb", "x": 280, "y": 200, "label": "", "params": {} },
      { "id": "app", "type": "app", "x": 480, "y": 200, "label": "app", "params": { "replicas": 6 } },
      { "id": "db", "type": "sql", "x": 700, "y": 200, "label": "db", "params": {} }
    ],
    "edges": [
      { "id": "client-lb", "from": "client", "to": "lb", "params": {} },
      { "id": "lb-app", "from": "lb", "to": "app", "params": {} },
      { "id": "app-db", "from": "app", "to": "db", "params": { "timeoutMs": 300 } }
    ],
    "frames": []
  }
}

items.title: Embedding the playground in a page
items.text:
Any page of the site can embed the simulator with a scenario preloaded (this is how the classes use it):

<div class="sdp" data-scenario="read-heavy-cache" data-mode="compact" data-height="480"></div>
  • data-scenario: one of the ids of the scenario guide (blank for an empty canvas).
  • data-mode: full (palette, inspector and all the panels) or compact (canvas, run controls, metrics and one chart; nodes can be inspected and their parameters changed, the structure cannot).
  • Optional: data-height (pixels of the canvas), data-profile, data-seed, data-chaos.

Write a short Try it instruction before each embed: what to change, what to observe.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• It is a fluid model with sampled traces, not a packet-level simulator: queues hold rates, and percentiles come from about 400 sampled requests per simulated second. Very rare events (p99.99) are not resolved.
  • Requests are independent; there are no sessions, transactions or locks (stock reservations are discussed in the classes, not simulated).
  • A Kubernetes cluster is a count of slots (nodes × pods per node): there is no bin packing by CPU and memory, no affinity rules and no pod disruption budgets, and the pods are spread evenly over the nodes.
  • Network latency between users and the system is not added (the latency shown is server-side), except the +70 ms of calls between regions and +1 ms per hop in a service mesh.
  • Capacities and prices are illustrative round numbers. When the playground and a load test disagree, trust the load test — and find out why.

items.title: Scenario guide
items.text: Every scenario of the System Design Playground is a small lab: a realistic situation, an initial design that fails its goals for a reason, and one possible fix. Each section below says what the scenario teaches, what to try, what to watch, the goals, and questions to discuss in class. The embedded simulators are compact (run controls, metrics and parameters); use Open in the playground (↗) to edit the structure.

items.title: How to work on a scenario
items.text:
1. Predict before you run. Estimate utilization (ρ = λ / μ) and the queue behaviour from the numbers in the brief.
  2. Run the initial design and read the Report: which goal fails, and what is the bottleneck?
  3. Change one thing at a time and run again with the same seed — differences are then caused by your change, not by luck.
  4. Change the seed at the end: a good design passes with any seed.
  5. Explain the numbers with the formulas of the manual.

Exercise

The graded exercise playground-design asks you to solve three scenarios and submit the exported JSON plus a short rationale (the Report has a Copy report (Markdown) button).

items.title: All scenarios
items.text: Scenario Lesson Monolith: find the breaking point Every system has a breaking point, and the first component to saturate decides it Scale out behind a load balancer Horizontal scaling needs headroom for failures (N+1), and a load balancer only routes around a dead replica after it detects it Read-heavy catalog: add a cache A cache in front of the database cuts its read load to reads × (1 − hit ratio); a cold cache sends everything back to the database at once (stampede) Offload static content to a CDN Static and cacheable content belongs at the edge Read replicas and replication lag Read replicas multiply read capacity but not write capacity, and they serve slightly old data (replication lag) Partitions and the hot key Partitioning scales with the number of partitions only while keys are spread evenly; a hot key concentrates the load on one partition A queue absorbs the spike A queue decouples the user from slow work Publish an event, let consumers react With an event log each consumer group reads at its own pace Cascading failure: a slow dependency A slow dependency without timeouts exhausts the caller's threads (Little's Law) and takes down requests that never touch it Retry storm: when retries make it worse Immediate retries multiply the load on a struggling service; when answers exceed the timeout, every attempt fails and the system stays down after the trigger is gone (metastable failure) Rate limiting protects the backend Rejecting excess traffic fast (429) protects the backend and the real users; letting it queue degrades everyone Surviving a region outage Surviving a region needs a full second stack and a way to move users Serverless burst: cold starts and limits Functions scale per request Flash sale: a limited-stock launch A flash sale is designed for the peak URL shortener (sho.rt/xyz) A read-heavy key lookup News feed: fan-out on write vs on read Fan-out on write moves work from the read path (frequent) to the write path (rare) Chat for a live event Chat separates storing messages (partitioned, append-heavy) from delivering them (pub/sub to the connected servers) Ride-sharing: a write-heavy geo index Location updates are a write-heavy stream Video streaming: CDN + object store + transcoding Video is bytes at the edge plus heavy batch work in the background Notification system Notifications are asynchronous by nature Payments: retries need idempotency A retry after a timeout may repeat an operation that already happened Search autocomplete Autocomplete is a latency problem AI support assistant (RAG + tools) In an LLM application latency and cost scale with the number of model calls You can't fix what you don't measure Observability changes outcomes Microservices on Kubernetes: pods vs nodes The HPA adds pods, only nodes add room; every synchronous hop adds to the user's wait Kubernetes: losing a node Plan N+1 for nodes too: a lost node takes several pods at once, and they come back only if there is room Database failover: RTO and RPO A failover costs the time without a primary (RTO) and the writes not yet replicated (RPO)

items.title: Monolith: find the breaking point
items.text:
Version 1 of the app: one app server and one PostgreSQL. The breakpoint profile ramps the load until errors pass 5% or p99 explodes. Where does it break, and which component breaks first? Make it survive 2 000 req/s without spending more than 2 000 USD/month.

  • Lesson: Every system has a breaking point, and the first component to saturate decides it. Scaling one tier moves the bottleneck to the next one.
  • Setup: monolith · profile breakpoint · target 600 req/s · 90% reads · seed 7 · chaos off
  • Goals: breaking point ≥ 2,000 req/s · cost/month < US$ 2,000
  • Try: Press ▶ and read the Report: breaking point and bottleneck. Add a Load Balancer in front of the app and raise its replicas; run again.
  • Observe: The knee (p99 doubles) comes well before the break. After scaling the app, the database becomes the bottleneck.
  • Related: What is system design · Estimation
Questions to discuss
  1. Why does latency grow slowly at first and then explode near ρ = 1?
  2. With 6 replicas, which component breaks first, and at what rate? Check it with ρ = λ / μ.
  3. What would you do next if the target were 5 000 req/s?

items.title: Scale out behind a load balancer
items.text:
The catalog gets 1 500 req/s. Two replicas are not enough, and at t = 80 s one replica crashes. The load balancer keeps sending it traffic until it notices (30 s without health checks). Meet the goals with headroom for one failure (N+1).

  • Lesson: Horizontal scaling needs headroom for failures (N+1), and a load balancer only routes around a dead replica after it detects it.
  • Setup: scale-out · profile load · target 1,500 req/s · 90% reads · seed 11 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 80 s — one catalog replica crashes
  • Goals: error rate < 1% · p99 < 250 ms · cost/month < US$ 1,800
  • Try: Raise the app replicas until ρ ≈ 0.6. Then add a Health Check connected to the Load Balancer.
  • Observe: At t = 80 s one replica dies: errors last ~30 s without health checks and ~3 s with them. The survivors must absorb its share.
  • Related: Traffic & edge · Reliability
Questions to discuss
  1. How many replicas do you need so that losing one keeps ρ below 0.85?
  2. Why does a crashed replica keep receiving requests for a while?
  3. What does detection time do to availability (MTTR = detect + repair)?

items.title: Read-heavy catalog: add a cache
items.text:
Users browse the catalog: 3 000 req/s, 95% reads. The app tier is fine; the database is not. At t = 100 s the cache (once you have one) is flushed: will the database survive the stampede of misses?

  • Lesson: A cache in front of the database cuts its read load to reads × (1 − hit ratio); a cold cache sends everything back to the database at once (stampede).
  • Setup: read-heavy-cache · profile load · target 3,000 req/s · 95% reads · seed 3 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 100 s — cache flushed (deploy / restart)
  • Goals: p99 < 100 ms · error rate < 0.5% · cost/month < US$ 3,000
  • Try: Insert a Cache between app and database. Run; then turn request coalescing on and compare what happens at t = 100 s.
  • Observe: The database utilization drops with the hit ratio. At the flush, without coalescing, it saturates for several seconds.
  • Related: Caching
Questions to discuss
  1. With 95% reads and an 88% hit ratio, what is the database load at 3 000 req/s?
  2. Why does cache-aside lower the hit ratio when writes are frequent?
  3. Name two other ways to survive a stampede.

items.title: Offload static content to a CDN
items.text:
Product pages are full of images, styles and scripts: 3 000 req/s, 98% reads, served by the app from object storage. Users far from the region wait, and the app is saturated. Serve them from the edge.

  • Lesson: Static and cacheable content belongs at the edge: the origin only sees misses and writes, and users get a nearby answer.
  • Setup: cdn-static · profile load · target 3,000 req/s · 98% reads · seed 5 · chaos off
  • Goals: p99 < 150 ms · error rate < 0.5%
  • Try: Put a CDN after the DNS (dns → cdn → lb). Lower the app replicas and compare latency and cost.
  • Observe: The app tier falls from saturated to ~35% with fewer replicas. The CDN egress becomes the largest cost line.
  • Related: Traffic & edge
Questions to discuss
  1. What decides the hit ratio of a CDN (TTL, cache key, content)?
  2. Why is egress (USD/GB) often the largest line of a media site?
  3. How would you invalidate an image that changed?

items.title: Read replicas and replication lag
items.text:
4 000 req/s with 10% writes overload the single PostgreSQL primary. Read replicas take reads but never writes, and they lag behind the primary. Keep the lag under 1 s.

  • Lesson: Read replicas multiply read capacity but not write capacity, and they serve slightly old data (replication lag).
  • Setup: db-replicas · profile load · target 4,000 req/s · 90% reads · seed 13 · chaos off
  • Goals: p99 < 150 ms · error rate < 0.5% · replication lag < 1 s
  • Try: Add 2 read replicas to the database. Then raise the write share in the toolbar to 30% and watch the primary.
  • Observe: Reads spread over 1 + replicas; the primary keeps every write and its lag grows with the write load.
  • Related: Databases
Questions to discuss
  1. Which reads can tolerate lag, and which must go to the primary (read-your-writes)?
  2. At what write share do replicas stop helping?
  3. What comes after replicas when writes are the limit?

items.title: Partitions and the hot key
items.text:
Stock lookups and updates (50% writes) at 8 000 req/s on a key-value store with 2 partitions. At t = 60 s a celebrity posts a link to one product: one key gets a huge share of the traffic for a minute. More partitions fix the average — do they fix the hot key?

  • Lesson: Partitioning scales with the number of partitions only while keys are spread evenly; a hot key concentrates the load on one partition.
  • Setup: sharding · profile load · target 8,000 req/s · 50% reads · seed 17 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 60 s — celebrity effect: one hot key
  • Goals: error rate < 0.5% · p99 < 100 ms
  • Try: Raise the partitions to 8 and run. Then add a Cache in front of the NoSQL store for the hot reads.
  • Observe: At t = 60 s the celebrity effect starts: with 8 partitions the busiest one still saturates; the cache absorbs the hot reads.
  • Related: Databases · Caching
Questions to discuss
  1. If the hottest key gets 45% of the traffic, what is the load on its partition with P = 8? With P = 64?
  2. Besides caching, how can you split a hot key (salting, replicas of the key)?
  3. Why is consistent hashing used to place keys?

items.title: A queue absorbs the spike
items.text:
Each order generates a PDF receipt (50 ms of work). Today the order service waits for it. The spike profile multiplies the load by 5 for 30 s: the workers cannot keep up and orders fail. Let the user go and do the work later.

  • Lesson: A queue decouples the user from slow work: the producer waits only for the broker; the backlog absorbs the spike and drains afterwards.
  • Setup: async-queue · profile spike · target 150 req/s · 0% reads · seed 19 · chaos off
  • Goals: error rate < 0.1% · p99 < 100 ms · consumer lag < 60 s
  • Try: Replace the call app → worker by app → Message Queue → worker. Run the spike profile again.
  • Observe: Errors disappear; the backlog grows during the 30 s spike and drains after it. Consumer lag = backlog ÷ drain rate.
  • Related: Messaging · Compute & services
Questions to discuss
  1. How long does the backlog take to drain with 4 workers? Compute it before running.
  2. What happens if the spike never ends (producers > consumers forever)?
  3. Why must the consumer be idempotent with at-least-once delivery?

items.title: Publish an event, let consumers react
items.text:
When an order is placed, the app notifies the buyer, updates analytics and re-indexes availability — today with three synchronous calls in a row. At t = 60 s analytics becomes 20× slower and orders slow down with it. Decouple the order service from its consumers.

  • Lesson: With an event log each consumer group reads at its own pace: a slow consumer lags behind without slowing the producer or the others.
  • Setup: event-fanout · profile load · target 400 req/s · 0% reads · seed 23 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 60 s — analytics is 20× slower
  • Goals: p99 < 120 ms · error rate < 0.1% · consumer lag < 60 s
  • Try: Publish to Kafka (app → kafka) and let notification, analytics and the indexer consume (kafka → each).
  • Observe: When analytics slows down at t = 60 s, only its lag grows; order latency stays flat.
  • Related: Messaging
Questions to discuss
  1. What decides the maximum parallelism of a consumer group?
  2. What guarantees do you lose compared with synchronous calls (ordering, read-your-writes)?
  3. How do you publish the event and write the order atomically (outbox)?

items.title: Cascading failure: a slow dependency
items.text:
Half of the catalog pages call an external recommendations API. At t = 60 s it becomes 20× slower (3 s). Without timeouts every request holds a thread while waiting; the thread pools run out and the whole catalog fails — although the app's CPU is almost idle (Little's Law: threads = λ × W).

  • Lesson: A slow dependency without timeouts exhausts the caller's threads (Little's Law) and takes down requests that never touch it.
  • Setup: cascading-failure · profile load · target 800 req/s · 90% reads · seed 29 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 60 s — recommendations API 20× slower
  • Goals: error rate < 1% · p99 < 500 ms
  • Try: Run as is and read the bottleneck in the Report. Then set a 300 ms timeout on app → recommendations, then add a fallback and a circuit breaker.
  • Observe: Without a timeout the app shows threads exhausted with idle CPU. With the timeout only the recommendation calls fail; with the fallback nobody does.
  • Related: Reliability
Questions to discuss
  1. With 800 req/s, half calling a 3 s dependency, how many threads are busy? (L = λ × W)
  2. Why does a timeout alone not reach zero errors here?
  3. What would a bulkhead change?

items.title: Retry storm: when retries make it worse
items.text:
The inventory service retries every failed query 3 times, immediately, with a 100 ms timeout. At t = 60 s the database restarts (8 s). When it comes back, it receives up to 4× the normal load, its queue fills, answers take longer than the timeout… and it never recovers, although the trigger is long gone (a metastable failure).

  • Lesson: Immediate retries multiply the load on a struggling service; when answers exceed the timeout, every attempt fails and the system stays down after the trigger is gone (metastable failure).
  • Setup: retry-storm · profile load · target 2,000 req/s · 90% reads · seed 31 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 60 s — database restarts
  • Goals: error rate < 15% · p99 < 300 ms
  • Try: Run and watch the edge app → db after the 8 s restart. Then enable the circuit breaker; try also 1 retry with exponential backoff + jitter.
  • Observe: The edge rate jumps to ~4× and errors never recover. With the breaker the database drains its queue and the system recovers.
  • Related: Reliability
Questions to discuss
  1. With p = 0.9 failures per attempt and 3 retries, what is the load multiplier?
  2. Why does a longer timeout or a shorter queue also break the loop?
  3. What is a retry budget?

items.title: Rate limiting protects the backend
items.text:
1 000 req/s of real users — plus scraper bots sending twice that. The catalog melts down for everybody. Reject the excess fast at the gateway (429) instead of letting it queue behind the real users.

  • Lesson: Rejecting excess traffic fast (429) protects the backend and the real users; letting it queue degrades everyone.
  • Setup: rate-limiter · profile load · target 1,000 req/s · 90% reads · seed 37 · chaos off
  • Goals: error rate < 1% · p99 < 200 ms
  • Try: Set a rate limit on the API Gateway below the app capacity (e.g. 1 500 req/s). Alternatively, add a WAF in front.
  • Observe: Bots are cut first (per-client token buckets), real users keep low latency and the app stays below saturation.
  • Related: Traffic & edge
Questions to discuss
  1. Token bucket vs. sliding window: which allows bursts?
  2. Where should the limit live in a system with many gateway replicas?
  3. Why is a 429 better for the client than a timeout?

items.title: Surviving a region outage
items.text:
The app runs in one cloud region. At t = 60 s the whole region goes down. Build a second region and let DNS move users there. Failover time = detection + DNS TTL: check both.

  • Lesson: Surviving a region needs a full second stack and a way to move users: DNS failover takes detection plus TTL.
  • Setup: multi-region · profile load · target 1,000 req/s · 90% reads · seed 41 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 60 s — region sa-east-1 is down
  • Goals: availability ≥ 95% · p99 < 80 ms
  • Try: Draw a second VPC (another region) with LB, app and database; connect DNS to it, attach a Health Check to the DNS and lower its TTL.
  • Observe: At t = 60 s the first region disappears. Errors last about (3 s + TTL) for the users routed there.
  • Related: Reliability · Traffic & edge
Questions to discuss
  1. Active-active or active-passive: which loses fewer requests here?
  2. What happens to data written in the lost region (RPO)?
  3. Why must each app call its own region's database?

items.title: Serverless burst: cold starts and limits
items.text:
A discount-coupon check runs as a function. The spike profile jumps from 200 to 2 000 req/s. New instances start cold (600 ms) and the account has a concurrency limit of 50. Instances needed = λ × W (Little's Law).

  • Lesson: Functions scale per request: instances = λ × W, cold starts hit exactly when traffic jumps, and the concurrency limit throttles the rest.
  • Setup: serverless-burst · profile spike · target 200 req/s · 90% reads · seed 43 · chaos off
  • Goals: error rate < 0.5% · p99 < 300 ms · cost/month < US$ 5,000
  • Try: Raise the concurrency limit, run the spike; then add provisioned instances and compare p99 and cost.
  • Observe: Throttling (429) disappears with a higher limit; cold starts show up in p99 at the start of the spike until warm instances exist.
  • Related: Compute & services
Questions to discuss
  1. How many instances do 2 000 req/s × 40 ms need?
  2. Why do cold starts increase the number of instances needed?
  3. When is a container with autoscaling cheaper than functions?

items.title: Flash sale: a limited-stock launch
items.text:
A limited-stock product goes on sale at t = 60 s: traffic jumps 20× (to ~6 000 req/s) for 90 s. 80% of requests read the product page, 20% try to buy. The database holds the stock (no overselling!) and the payment provider accepts 500 req/s. Today everything collapses. Design for the peak: serve reads from the edge and caches, and put buyers in a waiting room (queue) drained at the speed the inventory and the payment provider can handle.

  • Lesson: A flash sale is designed for the peak: reads are absorbed by the edge and caches, and buyers wait in a queue drained at the pace of the inventory and the payment provider.
  • Setup: flash-sale · profile load · target 300 req/s · 80% reads · seed 2027 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 60 s — the sale opens
  • Goals: p99 < 300 ms · error rate < 1% · consumer lag < 300 s
  • Try: Follow the hints one at a time: CDN, catalog cache, then API Gateway routing writes to a waiting-room queue consumed by order workers.
  • Observe: With the waiting room, errors vanish and p99 stays low; the consumer lag is how long a buyer waits in line.
  • Related: Case studies · Messaging · Caching
Questions to discuss
  1. How many items can be sold per second if payment allows 500 req/s and each order takes one call?
  2. How do you avoid selling more items than are in stock (reservations, SELECT … FOR UPDATE)?
  3. How would you tell users their position in the line?

items.title: URL shortener (sho.rt/xyz)
items.text:
Every order e-mail and shared post carries a short link. 5 000 redirects/s, 99% reads, a few writes (new links). The classic interview problem: what is the read path, and what store fits a key → URL lookup?

  • Lesson: A read-heavy key lookup: cache + key-value store, sized with simple arithmetic.
  • Setup: url-shortener · profile load · target 5,000 req/s · 99% reads · seed 47 · chaos off
  • Goals: p99 < 50 ms · error rate < 0.1% · cost/month < US$ 3,500
  • Try: Replace the SQL database by Cache → NoSQL and size the app tier.
  • Observe: p99 drops to a few tens of ms; most redirects never reach the store.
  • Related: Case studies
Questions to discuss
  1. How many short codes fit in 7 base-62 characters?
  2. How do you generate unique codes without coordination?
  3. 301 or 302 redirect: which one lets you count clicks?

items.title: News feed: fan-out on write vs on read
items.text:
The feed shows posts from the accounts a user follows. Today the feed is assembled when it is read: a heavy query (40 ms) that merges hundreds of sources. 2 000 req/s, 95% reads. Precompute timelines when something is posted instead.

  • Lesson: Fan-out on write moves work from the read path (frequent) to the write path (rare): a feed read becomes one key lookup.
  • Setup: news-feed · profile load · target 2,000 req/s · 95% reads · seed 53 · chaos off
  • Goals: p99 < 100 ms · error rate < 0.5% · consumer lag < 10 s
  • Try: Route reads to a timeline cache over a NoSQL store, and writes to the posts database plus Kafka → fan-out workers → timelines.
  • Observe: Reads become cheap; the fan-out lag shows how long a post takes to reach the timelines.
  • Related: Case studies · Messaging
Questions to discuss
  1. What breaks when an account has 10 million followers?
  2. How does a hybrid approach treat celebrities?
  3. Which consistency does a feed really need?

items.title: Chat for a live event
items.text:
During a live event, users chat in its room: 2 000 req/s, half are new messages. Each message is stored in PostgreSQL and delivered synchronously before the sender gets an answer. Writes overload the database and the sender waits for every delivery.

  • Lesson: Chat separates storing messages (partitioned, append-heavy) from delivering them (pub/sub to the connected servers).
  • Setup: chat · profile load · target 2,000 req/s · 50% reads · seed 59 · chaos off
  • Goals: p99 < 80 ms · error rate < 0.1% · consumer lag < 2 s
  • Try: Store messages in a NoSQL store and publish them to Pub/Sub consumed by the delivery service.
  • Observe: Write load spreads over partitions; senders no longer wait for delivery.
  • Related: Case studies · Traffic & edge
Questions to discuss
  1. How does a message reach a user connected to another websocket server?
  2. How do you order messages in a room?
  3. What happens to messages for users who are offline?

items.title: Ride-sharing: a write-heavy geo index
items.text:
Drivers send their position every 4 s: 20 000 req/s, 90% writes, while riders query nearby drivers. A relational database cannot absorb that write rate. Keep only the latest position per driver in a partitioned store and stream the history.

  • Lesson: Location updates are a write-heavy stream: keep only the latest position in a partitioned store and send the history asynchronously.
  • Setup: ride-sharing · profile load · target 20,000 req/s · 10% reads · seed 61 · chaos off
  • Goals: p99 < 100 ms · error rate < 0.5% · cost/month < US$ 6,000
  • Try: Replace SQL by a partitioned NoSQL geo index; sample positions into Kafka for analytics.
  • Observe: The relational primary was saturated by writes; the partitioned store absorbs them with headroom.
  • Related: Case studies · Databases
Questions to discuss
  1. How many writes/s do 1 million drivers sending every 4 s generate?
  2. How do you find drivers within 2 km (geohash, quadtree, H3)?
  3. What happens to the geo index when a stadium empties?

items.title: Video streaming: CDN + object store + transcoding
items.text:
Creators upload videos; users watch them. 2 000 segment requests/s from viewers go through the app, and each upload is transcoded synchronously (20 s per video) while the uploader waits. Serve segments from the edge and transcode in the background.

  • Lesson: Video is bytes at the edge plus heavy batch work in the background: CDN + object store for viewers, a queue + workers for transcoding.
  • Setup: video-streaming · profile load · target 2,000 req/s · 99% reads · seed 67 · chaos off
  • Goals: p99 < 150 ms · error rate < 0.5% · consumer lag < 120 s
  • Try: Viewers → CDN → Object Store; uploads → API Gateway → app → queue → transcoders.
  • Observe: The app tier almost disappears from the viewing path; the transcoding backlog drains at replicas × 1/20 s.
  • Related: Case studies · Traffic & edge
Questions to discuss
  1. Why are video segments ideal for caching?
  2. How many transcoders do 0.5 uploads/s of 20 s jobs need (Little)?
  3. Why produce several bitrates (adaptive streaming)?

items.title: Notification system
items.text:
Every purchase sends a confirmation e-mail (50 req/s), and a scheduler sends 6 000 digest e-mails every 2 minutes — all at the same instant. The e-mail provider accepts 200 sends/s. Today buyers wait for the provider and fail whenever the digest burst arrives.

  • Lesson: Notifications are asynchronous by nature: queue them, pace them to the provider quota, and never fire scheduled jobs all at once.
  • Setup: notification-system · profile load · target 50 req/s · 0% reads · seed 71 · chaos off
  • Goals: error rate < 0.5% · p99 < 150 ms · consumer lag < 120 s
  • Try: Put a queue in front of the notification service and spread the scheduler's jobs over 60 s.
  • Observe: Buyers no longer feel the digest burst; the provider quota sets the drain rate.
  • Related: Case studies · Compute & services
Questions to discuss
  1. Why is a scheduled burst a self-inflicted spike?
  2. How would you give transactional e-mails priority over digests?
  3. How do you avoid sending the same e-mail twice?

items.title: Payments: retries need idempotency
items.text:
Orders call the payment provider synchronously with a 1 s timeout and 2 immediate retries. At t = 60 s the provider becomes 4× slower: calls time out, and each retry after a timeout may charge the card AGAIN — the provider did receive the first attempt. Make payments safe and keep buyers fast.

  • Lesson: A retry after a timeout may repeat an operation that already happened: payments need idempotency keys, and the buyer should not wait for the provider.
  • Setup: payment-system · profile load · target 300 req/s · 50% reads · seed 73 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 60 s — payment provider 4× slower
  • Goals: duplicate charges < 1 · error rate < 1% · p99 < 1,500 ms
  • Try: Turn on the idempotency key on the payment edge; then move the call behind a queue and a payment worker.
  • Observe: Duplicate charges drop to zero with the key; with the queue, buyer latency no longer depends on the provider.
  • Related: Case studies · Compute & services
Questions to discuss
  1. Why can a timeout not tell "failed" from "succeeded slowly"?
  2. How does the provider use the idempotency key?
  3. How do webhooks and reconciliation close the loop?

items.title: Search autocomplete
items.text:
Every keystroke in the search box asks for suggestions: 10 000 req/s, all reads, and they must feel instant (< 50 ms). The search cluster cannot take it. Most prefixes are popular and repeat a lot.

  • Lesson: Autocomplete is a latency problem: popular prefixes repeat, so a prefix cache answers most keystrokes.
  • Setup: search-autocomplete · profile load · target 10,000 req/s · 100% reads · seed 79 · chaos off
  • Goals: p99 < 50 ms · error rate < 0.1% · cost/month < US$ 5,000
  • Try: Insert a Cache between the app and the search service; size the app tier. Lower the target RPS to simulate client debouncing.
  • Observe: The search cluster load drops by the hit ratio and p99 meets the 50 ms budget.
  • Related: Case studies · Caching
Questions to discuss
  1. How many requests does debouncing at 100 ms save while typing "metallica"?
  2. Trie in memory vs. search engine: trade-offs?
  3. How often must the suggestions be rebuilt?

items.title: AI support assistant (RAG + tools)
items.text:
The support assistant answers questions about products and orders. Its agent loop takes 6 steps (6 LLM calls + tool calls) per question, the provider quota is 10 calls/s, and nothing checks for prompt injection. 2 questions/s already exceed the quota, take seconds, and cost a fortune.

  • Lesson: In an LLM application latency and cost scale with the number of model calls: fewer agent steps, a semantic cache and quota-aware routing matter more than raw capacity; guardrails belong in the path.
  • Setup: ai-assistant · profile load · target 2 req/s · 100% reads · seed 83 · chaos off
  • Goals: error rate < 1% · p99 < 10,000 ms · cost/month < US$ 60,000 · unsafe answers < 0.1%
  • Try: Reduce the agent steps, turn on the semantic cache and a fallback model, and put a Safety Mesh between the gateway and the assistant.
  • Observe: Errors (429) vanish under the quota, cost falls with the calls per question and the unsafe-answer rate drops.
  • Related: AI systems
Questions to discuss
  1. Cost per question = steps × tokens × price: compute it for 6 and for 3 steps.
  2. What does a semantic cache risk (stale or wrong answers)?
  3. Where should the guardrails run: input, output, or both?

items.title: You can't fix what you don't measure
items.text:
Utilization is hidden ("?") until a service is connected to Metrics. At t = 50 s one catalog replica dies; without health checks the load balancer notices only after 30 s, and without alerting nobody repairs it quickly. Wire the observability stack: metrics on every service, health checks, alerting, logs and tracing.

  • Lesson: Observability changes outcomes: health checks shorten detection, alerting shortens repair, and metrics make utilization visible.
  • Setup: observability-stack · profile load · target 600 req/s · 90% reads · seed 89 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 50 s — a catalog replica dies
  • Goals: availability ≥ 99% · p99 < 200 ms · services measured ≥ 100%
  • Try: Connect Metrics to the LB, app and database; add a Health Check on the LB, Alerting on Metrics, plus Logs and Tracing on the app.
  • Observe: The "?" become numbers; the crash at t = 50 s costs seconds instead of half a minute; the Trace tab shows where a slow request spends its time.
  • Related: Observability
Questions to discuss
  1. Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR): which part did each node improve?
  2. Which four golden signals would you put on the dashboard?
  3. Why alert on SLO burn rate instead of CPU?

items.title: Microservices on Kubernetes: pods vs nodes
items.text:
The app was split into catalog, inventory, order and notify microservices, each with its own database, behind an API gateway, on a Kubernetes cluster of 2 nodes × 6 pods. At 2 000 req/s the catalog's HPA asks for more pods than the cluster can schedule: they stay Pending, and the catalog drowns. Buying is a synchronous chain (order → inventory, catalog, notify, its DB): every hop adds its latency to the buyer's wait.

  • Lesson: The HPA adds pods, but only nodes add room: pods beyond nodes × pods per node stay Pending and serve nothing. In a chain of synchronous microservices every hop adds its latency to the user's wait, so work that the user does not need to wait for belongs behind a queue.
  • Setup: microservices · profile load · target 2,000 req/s · 80% reads · seed 2031 · chaos off
  • Goals: error rate < 1% · p99 < 200 ms · cost/month < US$ 8,500
  • Try: Select the cluster frame: pods = nodes × pods per node. Add nodes or turn on the cluster autoscaler (a node takes ~90 s, so keep some headroom), raise the catalog's minimum replicas, and put a queue between order and notify.
  • Observe: As drawn, errors ≈ 25% and p99 ≈ 3.8 s: the catalog's HPA wants ~14 pods, but the 2 × 6 cluster is full (6 catalog + 2 order + 2 inventory + 2 notify), so 9 pods stay Pending; and the buyer also waits for notify (120 ms median, σ 0.6). The possible solution — 3 nodes with the cluster autoscaler (max 6; it adds a 4th node at ~45 s, ready at ~135 s), catalog replicas and minimum 10, and order → queue confirmations → notify — passes with errors ≈ 0%, p99 ≈ 60 ms and ≈ 8 000 USD/month. Read the cost lines: the API gateway's per-request price, not the nodes, dominates the bill.
  • Related: Compute & services · Cloud-native platforms
Questions to discuss
  1. The catalog receives the reads (80% of 2 000 req/s) plus one call per order (400 req/s), at 250 req/s per pod. How many pods does it need at ρ = 0.6, and do they fit in 2 nodes × 6 pods?
  2. Which calls of the buying chain must finish before the buyer gets an answer, and which can become events?
  3. The gateway charges 1 USD per million requests: how much is that per month at 2 000 req/s, and how would you cut it?

items.title: Kubernetes: losing a node
items.text:
Catalog and pricing run 6 pods each on a cluster of 3 nodes × 4 pods: completely full. At t = 60 s a worker node dies and takes a third of the pods with it. Callers keep sending requests to the dead pods until they notice (30 s behind the load balancer, 40 s for the direct catalog → pricing call), and the lost pods have nowhere to be rescheduled. Survive the loss of any one node.

  • Lesson: N+1 applies to nodes, not only to replicas: a lost node takes several pods at once, callers keep calling them until they notice, and Kubernetes can only reschedule them where there is room. A direct service-to-service call needs service discovery and a timeout to stop waiting for dead pods.
  • Setup: k8s-node-failure · profile load · target 1,700 req/s · 90% reads · seed 2033 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 60 s — a worker node dies
  • Goals: error rate < 1% · p99 < 150 ms · cost/month < US$ 2,000
  • Try: Leave room in the cluster (more pods per node or one more node) and size the replicas so the survivors carry the load (ρ after losing a third below ~0.85). Put a timeout with retries on catalog → pricing, and connect a Service Registry to catalog and pricing.
  • Observe: As drawn, the node takes 2 catalog + 2 pricing pods. Catalog → pricing calls keep going to the dead pricing pods for 40 s; each one hangs 10 s, the catalog's threads run out and the failure cascades (~90% errors in that window); after 40 s the lost pods are recreated but stay Pending (no room): ≈ 27% errors and p99 > 4 s over the run. The possible solution — 8 pods per node (3 × 8 = 24 slots: after losing a node, 16 slots for the 16 pods — N+1 for nodes), 8 replicas each, a Service Registry connected to catalog and pricing, and a 300 ms timeout + 2 retries on catalog → pricing — passes with errors ≈ 0.8% and p99 ≈ 43 ms: dead pods are dropped in 3 s, a call that lands on one gives up after 300 ms and is retried on a live pod, the surviving pods carry the load, and the 6 lost pods are all rescheduled after 40 s.
  • Related: Cloud-native platforms · Reliability
Questions to discuss
  1. With 3 nodes × 4 pods and 12 pods, how many pods does one node failure take, and where can Kubernetes put them? And with 8 pods per node and 8 replicas each?
  2. Why does the direct catalog → pricing call hurt more than the load balancer → catalog edge? Use Little's Law with a 10 s hang.
  3. Why should the pods of one service be spread over different nodes and zones (topology spread constraints)?

items.title: Database failover: RTO and RPO
items.text:
Flash-sale checkout: 1 500 req/s, half of them writes (orders), on a DB Cluster with one primary and one follower replicated asynchronously. At t = 90 s the primary dies. Until a follower is promoted (30 s) every write fails, and the writes still inside the replication lag are lost for good: orders paid and forgotten. Make the failover lose nothing and hurt little.

  • Lesson: A failover has two costs: the time without a primary (RTO) and the writes not yet replicated (RPO). Synchronous or quorum replication makes the RPO zero at the price of a round trip per write; a fast failover and more shards shrink the RTO and the share of writes it hits — and every copy is paid.
  • Setup: db-failover · profile load · target 1,500 req/s · 50% reads · seed 2035 · chaos off · scripted events: t = 90 s — the primary of orders-db dies
  • Goals: lost writes < 1 · availability ≥ 99% · p99 (writes) < 100 ms
  • Try: Switch the replication to sync or quorum, shorten the failover time and split the keys into shards. Then inject a latency degradation on the cluster (it slows one follower) and compare sync and quorum on the write p99.
  • Observe: As drawn, ≈ 1 570 writes are lost when the primary dies, writes fail for 30 s (availability ≈ 90.6%), and after the promotion a single node carries reads and writes, so the write p99 reaches ≈ 375 ms. The possible solution — 2 shards, 2 followers each, quorum, failover 5 s — passes with 0 lost writes, availability ≈ 99.2% and a write p99 ≈ 34 ms; but the database bill goes from 900 to 2 700 USD/month (2 shards × 3 nodes × 450).
  • Related: Databases · Reliability
Questions to discuss
  1. Lost writes ≈ write rate × lag: estimate them from the inspector just before t = 90 s.
  2. With one follower slowed down, why does sync suffer and quorum with 2 followers not?
  3. RPO 0 and RTO 5 s triple the database bill: for which data is it worth it (orders, sessions, analytics)?

items.title: Terms and Conditions
items.text:
Agreement

By enrolling in and participating in this course you agree to abide by the terms described on this page. Read them before your first class.

items.title: Participation
items.text:
Lectures follow an active learning format — pre-reading is expected. Each class session assumes you have read the assigned material in advance and are ready to discuss, question, and apply it.

Expectation Details Pre-reading Review assigned sections before each class Engagement Ask questions, participate in discussions, help peers Lab sessions Bring a laptop with the development environment configured (see Prerequisites)

items.title: Academic Integrity
items.text:
Plagiarism

Submitting someone else's work — whether from a peer, a public repository, or an AI tool — as your own is plagiarism and results in a zero for the activity. Repeated violations are referred to the university's academic integrity committee.

What constitutes plagiarism in this course:

  • Copying code, text, or diagrams from another student's submission (even with minor modifications)
  • Submitting output from an AI tool without understanding, editing, and crediting it
  • Reusing your own work from a previous course edition without disclosure
  • Copying from a public GitHub repository without attribution

What is not plagiarism:

  • Using official documentation, Stack Overflow, and tutorials — provided they are cited
  • Using AI tools as a learning aid — provided you follow the AI policy
  • Discussing design approaches with classmates before implementing independently

items.title: Deliverable Format
items.text:
All deliverables must be published on GitHub Pages.

No other format is accepted. A delivery template is provided: documentation template

Requirements for every submission:

Requirement Standard Hosting GitHub Pages — public repository Theme MkDocs Material Repository name Professional and descriptive (e.g., platform, cloud-native-ecommerce) Git authorship Commits must be linked to GitHub accounts (git config user.email) Language English

items.title: Deadlines
items.text:
Deadlines are not extended.

Late submissions receive a grade of zero, with no exceptions. Plan around this: start early, push incremental progress, and do not wait for a "finished" version before your first commit.

If a technical failure on the submission platform occurs (not on your side), contact the instructor immediately with evidence — before the deadline, not after.

items.title: Individual Activities
items.text:
Individual activities include quizzes, microservice exercises, and other tasks assigned to each student personally.

  • Work must be completed independently. Discussion of concepts with peers is permitted; sharing code or answers is not.
  • Quizzes are open-book but not open-peer. You may consult notes and documentation; you may not discuss with classmates during the quiz window.
  • Re-grading requests must be submitted within 5 business days of the grade being posted. Requests must identify the specific item contested and the justification; general "I deserve more points" requests are not considered.

items.title: Team Project
items.text:
Team projects simulate a real engineering team delivering a cloud-native platform over a semester.

Group formation deadline

Groups must be registered by the date specified in the course overview. After that date, unregistered students are assigned to groups by the instructor.

Rules:

  • Teams have 2 to 3 members. Solo submissions are not accepted.
  • All members receive the same grade. There is no individual adjustment within the team unless a member is found not to have contributed (see below).
  • Contribution must be visible in git history. A team member with zero commits to the repository at delivery time may receive a reduced or zero grade, regardless of what teammates report.
  • Code must live in the team's repository. Do not use a personal fork as the delivery repository.

items.title: Code of conduct within the team
items.text: Teams are expected to divide work equitably and communicate proactively. If a team member is not contributing, notify the instructor early — not on delivery week. Late complaints about team dynamics after submission do not change grades retroactively.

items.title: Communication
items.text:
Channel Use Response time Office hours Design questions, architectural doubts, grade disputes During the session GitHub Issues on the course repo Content errors, broken links, unclear instructions Best-effort Email Personal/administrative matters only 2 business days

Do not send solutions or code by email asking for a grade review. Use office hours.

items.title: Code of Conduct
items.text:
This course covers professional-grade engineering practice. The same standards apply to how we treat each other.

  • Critique ideas, not people. Disagreement about technical choices is healthy; personal attacks are not.
  • Do not share another student's work, environment credentials, or AWS account details outside the team.
  • Treat all participants — students, assistants, instructor — with respect in all channels (classroom, GitHub, messaging apps).

Violations of this code of conduct are reported to the institution's student conduct office.

items.title: Changes to These Terms
items.text:
The instructor reserves the right to update these terms during the semester. Changes are announced in class and reflected here with a revision date. Substantial changes affecting grading will not be applied retroactively.

Last updated: 2026.
